en: *Pramāṇavārttikabhāṣya* <2. Chapter on the Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition> <1. First Chapter>

<1. The Definition of the Means of Valid Cognition (Pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa)> <Section 1: The Vārttika on the Nature of Prescriptive Cultivation (vidhibhāvanādi)> (1) A means of valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge (*avisaṃvādi jñānaṃ pramāṇam*).
Homage to the Buddha.

Having prostrated before the Teacher, the Sugata, the Protector, who has become the means of valid cognition and who seeks the welfare of the world, this *Pramāṇasiddhi* is composed according to rule out of compassion for people bewildered by fallacious reasoning. (1)

Generally, those who possess extensive treatises on the subject at hand are not seen at all speaking with great clarity, for they have discarded the trivial sequence of words in their desire to summarize the ultimate truth.

Therefore, in this work, my intellect—with its lofty resolve—is applied toward the consciousness of the fortunate ones of exalted mind, so as to produce an utterly pure understanding by means of the removal of the scattered order [of common discourse]. (2)

[003,iv] Here, at the beginning of the treatise, the expression of praise for the Blessed One is stated by way of his being an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūta*) through the perfection of cause and fruit, because it constitutes the subject matter of the treatise. For it is the Blessed One alone who is established here as the authoritative person.

In this context, the cause consists of the perfection of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*), with reference to conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*). Intention is the desire for the welfare of the world; application is the state of being a Teacher (*śāstṛtva*) through the instruction of the world. The result is the perfection of one’s own and others’ welfare. The perfection of one’s own welfare consists in being a Sugata, based on three aspects: excellence of nature, like a precious gem; the sense of non-return, like a fever completely cured; and the sense of completeness, like a jar filled to the brim. The perfection of others’ welfare consists in being a Protector (*tāyitva*) because of rescuing the world, and because of the continuity [of that activity] due to the quality of not entering final nirvāṇa. Having prostrated to the Blessed One who is thus characterized, it is said: "The establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-siddhi*) is now set forth. For the comprehension of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition, and the Blessed One alone is the means of valid cognition, because he possesses the defining characteristics of a means of valid cognition. A means of valid cognition is that by which something is correctly measured (*pramīyate*).
vi] Therein, he indicates the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general.
Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory knowledge (*jñāna*);

for when there is knowledge, the establishment of a valid ascertainment (*pramiti*) occurs therein. It is non-contradictory, because in the case of contradiction, the opposite is true. Indeed, the conjunction of the sense-faculties with their objects and so forth acquire their status as reality only when characterized by knowledge that is devoid of contradiction. For everyone who is engaged in the search for a means of valid cognition does so seeking non-contradiction.

[003,ix] But surely, non-contradiction is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of that cognition which constitutes the means of proof (*sādhana*). And when that nature is known, it is already known; so what remains to be examined? Alternatively, if there is no self-awareness (*svarūpasamvedana*) of it, then it follows that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all. Nor is this position tenable for you.
That is incorrect. The validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a cognition is neither its own intrinsic nature nor its correspondence (*saṃvāditva*);
rather, it is the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*), which is non-discrepancy (*avisamvādana*).

Indeed, upon the mere apprehension of the nature of cognition itself, it does not occur that "this is a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). What then? It is the accomplishment of an action such as burning or cooking regarding an object; its "stability" (*sthiti*) is its non-deviation (*avisamvādana*) or its establishment (*vyavasthā*). And that causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is future, not present at that time. Therefore, the connection with that [efficacy] is not determined by the mere self-awareness of the cognition's own nature.
[Objection: But surely its being related to that [object] is nothing other than its own nature; so why is there not a determination consisting merely in the self-awareness of that nature? [Response:
This is not so.
The cognition of a relation residing in two things does not arise from the perception of a single form;
rather, the awareness of a relation occurs when there is the grasping of the essential natures of both. (PVA 3)

[004, vi] How, then, does that cognition function at the time of engagement? We shall explain this later. If the preceding means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then is that attainment of purposeful action itself a means of valid cognition or not? Since there can be no attainment of purposeful action by means of what is not a means of valid cognition, it must be a means of valid cognition. If, therefore, the attainment of purposeful action must be sought through yet another [cognition], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
This is not correct:
if the preceding [cognition] possesses the status of a means of valid cognition because of the absence of a subsequent purposeful action, [then...]
"In that very moment, since there is no purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), how could there be such [action] for the subsequent one?
(PVA 4).

That in which the stability of purposeful action is established by another is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to that extent; however, where there is the experience of purposeful action itself at that very moment, that is all the more certainly a means of valid cognition, because "the stability of purposeful action" is defined as non-discrepancy (*avisamvādana*) in general.

[004,x] But surely this purposeful activity, such as burning or cooking, is possible even in dreams, as well as in the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like. However, in the case of a cognition whose object is sound, there is no purposeful activity such as burning or cooking, because such activity is absent both intrinsically and extrinsically. Therefore, it is logical that an uncontradicted cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
That too is incorrect, because:
[004,xii] Even in the case of verbal cognition, [it is valid] because it communicates the speaker's intention.
Non-contradiction;
verbal cognition is that which has sound as its object. By the word "also" (api), it is implied that this applies elsewhere as well. This is the meaning.
Every cognition would be valid simply by virtue of being a cognition of its own nature.
Or, if it were because it is an uncontradicted cognition, why would that not also apply to dreams and the like? (PVA 5)

For the occurrence of a mere cognition—whether it be a dream-cognition or any other—is indeed the same in all cases. That [mere cognition] is not, however, the means for accomplishing the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*). If it is argued that it is the state of being an uncontradicted cognition, that too is equally the same [in both cases]. If it is claimed that there is contradiction by means of a waking cognition, what indeed is this so-called "contradiction"?
If it is maintained that another [cognition] makes known the absence of an object, how could a cognition that is not directed toward its own object make known that absence? (6) (PVA) [004,xvii]

The non-existence of dream-cognition—or indeed any other cognition—is not brought about by another cognition, because at that time it perishes of its own accord. Nor is sublation perceived when a cognition has perished due to the closing of the eyes. For sublation—defined as the negation of an object’s existence through another cognition—does not consist in the removal of its object by that other cognition. A cognition engaged with its own object is not capable of effecting the removal of another object; for it is the nature of cognitions to establish the form of their own objects, whereas the seizure of another’s object is the prerogative of a sovereign.

[005,ii] How, then, can there be the relationship of the sublated and the sublator? Not in any way whatsoever. For this very reason, being unsublated is what constitutes validity (*prāmāṇya*). Therefore, that in which there is no causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is invalid.
Where the arising of an action is not known either by oneself or by another, that is invalid;
for in reality, there is no distinction between dream and non-dream.

This so-called distinction between dream and non-dream is merely a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Likewise, it will be stated that there is a distinction between valid and invalid cognition. Moreover, this [conventional] stability of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is not [ultimately real], because it lacks immutability. In a dream, causal efficacy is determined solely through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); there is no satisfaction therein. If, however, one were to insist on its being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For while the initial lack of contradiction occurs everywhere, if there is a lack of contradiction at a subsequent time, why would there be a lack of contradiction at yet another subsequent time? The appearance of a sublater (*bādhaka*) is possible for every cognition.
"But even there, the absence of sublation might be suspected; so what of it?

(PVA) [005, vi] However, the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all, because there is no attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) accordingly. When the accomplishment of purposeful action consists merely in the shape, then another cognition—namely inference—is the valid means of knowledge. For instance:
[005,vii] A manifestation that is of such a nature is not devoid of configuration; for it is observed otherwise as well, and thus it is an inference.

[005, viii] He who has never observed a deviation is indeed deceived by non-correspondence regarding that which he intends; however, he who is aware of the possibility of deviation proceeds after deliberation. First, the mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is obtained. Regarding the other [object], there is either doubt or error. Therefore, there is inference with respect to the configuration, while there is doubt regarding the other. Thus, these two types of cognition—both valid and invalid—are established. [005, ix]

By this, the cognition of the jewel within the jewel-light has been explained; we shall explain it further as follows. Now, by what means is this duality cognized? To this also we shall reply: the cognition whose object is sound is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it communicates intention. Communication of the actual nature of the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is precisely what constitutes "correspondence" (*saṃvādana*).
[005,xi] In that case, the very establishment of the true nature of the object of knowledge is considered the action;
even in the case of a painting, the result is fully accomplished by the mere act of seeing. (PVA 9)

[005,xii] Indeed, no cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) other than the self-cognition of its own nature (*svarūpasamvedana*) is ever perceived here. For color-form (*rūpa*) and the like are solely intent upon the self-cognition of their own nature; the cognition whose object they are is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to anything else. Since being of that nature and consisting merely of self-cognition is common to all cognition, there is no application of conventional means of valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇa*).
[005,xiii]
Therefore, by means of superimposition, a means of valid cognition whose object is a future thing and which has another object as its domain brings about the understanding of conventional practice.

For the investigation into whether a cognition is valid or invalid has as its purpose the attainment of another object that is yet to be realized (*bhāvyartha*). Just as a distinct object such as touch does not enter into the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of color and so forth, so too, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), the future nature [of an object] does not enter into it. However, through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), there is a unity between that [future nature] and the other object. Therefore, it is said that a cognition is "concordant" (*saṃvādana*) by way of that [future object]. But where that very [future object] itself performs the causal function (*arthakriyā*), there is no dispute at all. In that case, the superimposition of unity upon the future nature is based on its being the cause [of the present cognition]; whereas in the case of touch and so forth, it is based on their dependence on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Thus, there is no difference between them. However, where there is a desired causal function—as when the causal function of a mirage is obtained from a cognition grasping water—that is indeed invalid. For this very reason, he says: "Also in the case of verbal [cognition], because it communicates the intention (*abhiprāya*)."

[006,i] This is also the case elsewhere, such as with a painting and so forth; likewise, there is no status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the case of the cognition of a jar when a cloth is obtained, nor in the succession of cognitions of silver regarding mother-of-pearl, because there is an absence of non-discrepancy with the intended object.
Everything is called a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it does not contradict the intended object, and not merely because of the arising of a cognition similar or dissimilar [to itself].
This same principle applies even to the case of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*). (PVA 11)
In reality, however, it is merely the arising of a cognition of a different kind.
(PVA 12) If the arising of a cognition of a different kind is said to be the sublater, why would the cognition of a cloth not logically be the sublater of the cognition of a jar? (PVA 13)

If it is claimed that there is some subverting factor consisting of the cognition "it is not" by means of the conceptual thought (*pratyaya*), then that very cognition "it is not" has arrived as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (14) [Objection: If it is argued that the definition of non-existence is a means of valid cognition, and therefore it is being examined:
Is it the cognition of another form, or is it the cognition of that non-existence?

(PVA 15) If it were the cognition of another form, it would follow [absurdly] because there is no distinction; for if there were a cognition of its non-existence, the connection "of that" [non-existence] would not hold. (PVA 16)

[006, viii] For non-existence (*abhāva*) is cognized by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). And the nature of non-existence is not cognized as being related to a jar or the like. For when a jar is being perceived, there is no relation of that jar to the non-existence; at that time, the non-existence does not exist. Indeed, there is no death for Devadatta while he is still alive. On the other hand, when the jar is not being perceived, it is impossible to grasp the relation of that jar to the non-existence.

Now, it might be argued that the cognition [of the relation] is like that of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). When the cause exists, the effect subsequently arises; immediately thereafter, through the sequence of its perception, there is the apprehension of the nature [of the effect], and thus the grasping of the connection between cause and effect occurs. In this way, when [the cause] exists, there is non-existence [of the effect], and when [the cause] is absent, there is existence [of the effect]; thus the cognition of the connection comes about.
That too is incorrect, because:
A relation with absolute non-existence is not established for anything whatsoever.
That non-existence does not exist while existence is present, nor is there the reverse in that case. (PVA 17)
Furthermore:
[006,xiii]
The nature of cause and effect is perceived without that [intrinsic nature];
however, non-existence is not perceived without existence.
(18) As for the emptiness of a location, it is equal everywhere.
In that case, the distinction between prior non-existence and the other types [of non-existence] is absolutely impossible.
(PVA 19) Just as the difference of a real entity is perceived by perception, so too is the difference consisting of prior non-existence and the rest perceived without impairment. (PVA 20)
If it is held that its cognition occurs through the means of knowledge known as non-existence (*abhāva*), then [one must ask]:

of which means of knowledge is there non-existence? For if there is no cognition due to the absence of a means of knowledge, why would there not be [non-cognition] of every existing thing, and why would one who is asleep not [perceive] anything at all? (21) (PVA)
If a cognition that apprehends non-existence is itself considered to be a non-existence, then why is this [non-existence] not perceived by anyone even without a cognition of an existent?

If it is argued that the causal complex for that [cognition of non-existence] is precisely this [absence of a cognition of an existent], then there would be no certainty regarding non-existence. (PVA 22–23)
In reality, there is no cognition of an absence that is distinct [from the object];
the cognition "this is not here" cognizes its very distinction [from the presence].
(PVA 24) From what could this arise, if not from the sense faculty, without [the aid of] memory?

If the cognition of non-existence were possible through the conjunction of the sense faculty and mindfulness, then this [cognition] would necessarily be perception itself, following from the operation of the sense faculty. If the sense faculty is engaged with one object, it cannot be the cause of the cognition of another. (PVA 25–26)
How can mental knowledge of non-existence be a means of valid cognition?
It is indeed another means of valid cognition because it is non-discrepant;
for there is no non-discrepancy whatsoever regarding a non-existence that is distinct [from perception].
When there is isolation, the discrepancy is apprehended by that very perception.

(PVA 28) And that apprehension of the "isolated" occurs always without the cognition of an entity [other than itself]. The apprehension of the isolated is the cognition [of it] without the entry of anything else. (PVA 29)
In the case of direct perception where there is the apprehension of a "mere" [absence], the possibility of error exists;
therefore, this non-apprehension is indeed a form of direct perception.
[Objection: But how can the cognition of a "mere" thing be the cognition of an absence?
That [non-existence] also does not exist without pure consciousness; thus there is equality [between existence and non-existence].
Or, just as a solitary non-existence is cognized without an existent thing, so too an existent thing [is cognized without non-existence]; if this were not the case, an infinite regress would result.

If it is argued that there is no cognition of the bare locus (*kevalapratīti*) without the cognition of absence (*abhāvapratīti*), then it is equally true that there is no cognition of absence without the cognition of the bare locus. Or how can absence itself be "bare" without another absence? In that case as well, if one were to postulate further absences, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)—which depends upon the object being remembered—is the very perception (*pratyakṣa*) that establishes absence. As for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding absence, the distinction is that it occurs only in certain instances and not elsewhere, depending on the force of mental impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, just as a waking cognition sublates a dream cognition, so too does a contrary cognition [sublate it] by apprehending the object in its pure form; such is the logical principle. Consequently, the claim that verbal cognition possesses validity because it communicates the speaker's intention is refuted.
Furthermore, auditory perception would not be a valid means of knowledge, as it lacks connection with anything else.

[007,vii] But what is the purpose of the Blessed One, who has become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhūta*), since the accomplishment of all human goals is achieved through conventional means of valid cognition alone?
[007,viii]
This is not so:
perception operates upon the apprehension of its own form, whereas inference operates elsewhere.
Furthermore, it will be stated later that the other [type of cognition] lacks the status of a means of valid cognition.

To begin with, perception does not operate regarding the next world and such, because it will be demonstrated that its nature consists solely in the apprehension of the specific form [of its own object]. As for inference, it does not exist without the apprehension of a relationship (*sambandha*). Furthermore, a relationship cannot be grasped by one who is not omniscient. For the nature of perception, which culminates in the self-cognition of its own form, does not involve the apprehension of a relationship. If the apprehension of a relationship were achieved through inference alone, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). However, perception and inference are valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only insofar as they accord with the proof of an omniscient being through mere conventional usage, and not otherwise. This will be demonstrated later. (1)

[007,xi] Now, even if indeed the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized as perception (*pratyak�sa*) and inference (*anumāna*) do not operate with respect to the next world and so forth—since perception has only its own form as its object, and inference depends upon the apprehension of a relation—scripture (*śāstra*), however, is not like that; therefore, the desired goal is established by it alone. Why, then, is the Blessed One being established as the embodiment of the means of valid cognition?
To this it is replied:
That object which appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker's activity—
In that case, the authority of the word is not based on the actual reality of the object.

[007,xiv] The Chapter on the Refutation of the Self (Ātmapratiṣedhaprakaraṇa) is concluded. The Treatise on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā), composed by the Master Nāgārjuna, is finished. For it will be demonstrated later that words are not non-human (apauruṣeya); rather, they must be human (pauruṣeya). In that case, the speaker’s activity is his intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). The speaker is one who intends to speak. The object which appears in the listener’s cognition is the referent of the intention to speak; it is precisely there that the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it is precisely there that the word’s operation lies. Otherwise, if one were to convey something different from what was intended, one would be acting without foresight. And thus, there would be all the more lack of validity. Furthermore, such an intended speaker is not omniscient regarding everything; otherwise, there would be no mutual contradiction among the scriptures. Nor can mutually contradictory meanings be put into practice. If the purpose were established merely by following whatever is practiced, then the scripture would be useless as a means of valid cognition, because the result would follow even from practicing according to one's own whims.
And thus, let it proceed as desired without dispute;
for no practice whatsoever is ever fruitless for anyone anywhere. (34) (PVA)

[008,i] The Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, just as whatever there is of footprints in the world, the elephant’s footprint is declared their chief by way of size; so too, among all wholesome qualities, the noble eightfold path is declared the chief. And what, monks, is that noble eightfold path? It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the noble eightfold path. “Just as, monks, whatever there is of footprints in the world, the elephant’s footprint is declared their chief by way of size, so too, among all wholesome qualities, the noble eightfold path is declared the chief. “Just as, monks, the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt, so too, this Dhamma and Discipline have but one taste, the taste of liberation. “Just as, monks, the river Ganges slants, slopes, and inclines toward the east, so too, this community of disciples of the Tathāgata slants, slopes, and inclines toward nibbāna. “Just as, monks, a cowherd boy, using a fresh, green, smooth rope, might bind a strong bull to a young palmyra sapling; and as that strong bull, being bound by that fresh, green, smooth rope, would wear it away, gnaw it, and break it, so too, monks, a bhikkhu who dwells diligently wears away the fetters, gnaws them, and breaks them. “Just as, monks, a cowherd boy, using a fresh, green, smooth rope, might bind a strong bull to a young palmyra sapling; Therefore, the authority of a word resides in the object of the speaker’s activity, and is not based on the actual reality of the thing itself. This is the case if the speaker is not omniscient. Even in the case of a non-human (apauruṣeya) scripture, when one understands the meaning for oneself, it is that which appears in the mind; but when it is understood through an interpreter, then the interpreter alone is the "speaker" insofar as he is the object of the speaker’s activity. Furthermore, the meaning that merely appears in the mind is not the [actual] meaning itself. Otherwise, since all desired objects would be established [merely by appearing], no one would ever strive toward their accomplishment. If it is argued that this is not so because the meaning is presented precisely as something to be accomplished (*anuṣṭheya*), then at that time it does not exist in its own form, and thus there can be no cognition of it. If it is cognized as something else, there is doubt due to the absence of a connection [between the cognition and the reality]. Consequently, whatever meaning is cognized is already established, and one does not act out of a desire for it. And that for which one has a desire is not what was cognized. Thus, authority is not based on the reality of the object.

**(2) The Refutation of *Niyoga*:** Now, it may be argued that *niyoga* (an injunction) is not the meaning of a sentence, because there is the cognition "I am enjoined. Therefore, it is precisely because of the *niyoga* that one is unable to desist.

[008,iii] What is meant by *niyoga*? The prefix *ni-* signifies "without remainder," and the root *yoga* signifies "junction" (*yukti*). *Niyoga* is therefore a junction that is without remainder. Its being "without remainder" is due to the absence of even the slightest lack of connection. For *niyoga* is indeed that which must necessarily be performed. Those for whom *niyoga* is the authoritative means of knowledge proceed to act solely on the basis of the comprehension of the *niyoga*.
Here he says: "The operation of the speaker," and so forth. This is the meaning:
injunction (*niyoga*), productive activity (*bhāvanā*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and the mandate (*vidhi*) are declared [to be synonymous].
Those things such as mechanical devices and the like would not accomplish their purposes through their own inherent nature.

Therefore, whatever appears to someone in a particular way, that appearance is the meaning of the sentence; however, this is not the ultimate reality of the object. Furthermore, in whatever manner one explains it, the word does not thereby become defective, nor does the status of the ultimate reality of the object change accordingly.
And what more?
[008, viii]
If cessation were [caused] by that which is appointed [to bring it about], then it would follow that everything [would cease] from that;
for no one could have a non-etherial space, since its very nature is etherial.
Even if its own nature were perceived otherwise due to error, [the same fault would apply].
Who will establish the distinction between error and non-error?

And the thought "I am commanded" does not arise, because there is no engagement with a command that is fruitless. One engages even with a fruitless command from a fierce lord out of fear of misfortune (*apāya*), and that misfortune is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But here, there is no other means of valid cognition. If the command is thus useless, let it be; what is the fault? For indeed, nothing is impossible when it is perceived. However, one who acts with prior reflection is censured on the grounds that he would lack the quality of a reflective person if he engaged in a fruitless command. But in the case of that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*)...

Whose reproach is this? If it is argued that futility is simply not appropriate for that which is non-human (apauruṣeya), we reply: there is no evidence for this, since such [futility] is not observed elsewhere in what is non-human.
And if one were to act merely on the basis of an impersonal injunction, such as "one who desires heaven," then the statement "he should sacrifice" would be fruitless.

For the injunction is understood from the mere statement of the injunction itself. Now, if it is argued that the result is shown for one who desires a result, then the result alone should be shown to him; what is the use of the injunction? He would simply proceed to act out of his own desire for the result.

If it is argued that because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), this objection does not apply even if there is no connection [between the injunction and the result], then the same objection would not apply to an injunction that is fruitless either; thus, it is illogical to claim that the Veda is useless. [009,iv] One must consider whose property this so-called *niyoga* (obligation) is. Indeed, *niyoga* is not perceived as independent, like objects such as cloth; rather, in this case of restriction (*niyama*), it must be the property of one among the factors such as the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), because no other mode is perceived.
For if its status as the property of one who is to be enjoined were its very nature to be performed, how could it be so?
If even that which is already established were to be performed, there would be no cessation of performance.
(PVA 39)

Indeed, it is not possible to bring about the perfection [of what is already perfect]. For "bringing about" (anuṣṭhāna) in that case would mean either a specific action or the production of its own nature (*svarūpa*). First, a specific action is entirely useless; for what purposeful effect could an action have upon that which is already perfected? Furthermore, to say that there is the production of the nature of something already perfected is a contradiction. Nor does there exist another non-perfected state belonging to that which is already perfected, because it is impossible for that which is non-perfected to possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a perfected entity. For whatever is perceived in a certain form possesses that as its intrinsic nature. And it is not possible to perceive that which is unperfected. If you argue that it is perceived later, that is incorrect, because:
Because it possesses that very nature, it cannot be perceived later;
for perception functions by grasping the present form. (PVA 40)
Indeed, perception, which functions by grasping a present form, is not capable of observing prior and posterior forms. Therefore—
There is no occurrence of unity prior to the arising of sensory cognition, nor is there any after it;
because cognition follows upon the senses, it is measured as "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, injunction (*niyoga*) is not the meaning of the word insofar as it is a property of the person to be enjoined. Even if it were a property of the object, since the object is not yet established and lacks its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how could it be understood from the word? For that which does not exist, such as a hare’s horn, is never seen in that way as an object of performance. If it is argued that it exists in one form but not in another, that is incorrect.
That which exists by virtue of a certain state is not performed by that [state];
nor is that which does not exist at all perceived by it. (42) (PVA)

If its state of being established as something to be performed is not [independent], then that alone is its own nature; otherwise, it would not be an injunction (niyoga). (43) (PVA) Being merely perceived is the commonality of all things.

Its status as an injunction (*niyoga*) is due solely to its being something to be performed, and not otherwise. (44) (PVA) If it is the state of being to be performed that appears there, and nothing else, then performance would occur in that case; however, it does not occur upon the mere cognition of a universal. (45) (PVA)
In that case, if there were only a cognition of the general [form], there would be no cognition of the object to be performed;
thus, for those who assert it, the meaning of the sentence would not be the *niyoga* (the mandate).

Because sacrifices and the like are observed in the world, and because the relationship between word and meaning is possible therein, a cognition based on what was previously seen does not establish the actual state of things.
[This is so] for those whose minds are afflicted by the defects of lust, grief, fear, and madness. (PVA 51)
Cognition based on prior [experience] is not a means of establishing what is seen or desired [in scripture].
(PVA 52) In the world, one observes the corruption of the meanings of sentences and words in some cases;

In that case, there is no defect of intention, such as delusion or the like, for anyone.
Yet, why is non-comprehension in that regard not considered a defect for someone?

Nor is it the case that these [Vedic words] lack the status of a means of valid cognition; for why should there not be validity even in the Veda?

Now, if the Veda does not possess a true meaning intrinsically, then since the objects such as sacrifice do not manifest themselves spontaneously in the world, how could there be an observation of the performance of sacrificial acts? Indeed, it is not possible for this [Veda] to teach itself. Therefore, the Veda is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it conveys meanings that are consistent with reality. This is common to all scriptures (*āgama*). For the internal subdivisions of the specific meanings of individual scriptures cannot be established by a mere human being through his own imagination, even if they were observed across all scriptures. Alternatively, just as a cognition does not arise for one who somehow recalls a non-verbal inferential mark (*liṅga*) on his own, so too is the ritual action postulated.
[010,xi] Since the nature of purposeful activity, such as sacrifice and the like, is common to all scriptural traditions,
why is that same capacity for performance not equally present in the Veda as well? (PVA 57)
If being "learned" (śiṣṭa) were not established by those very people, there would be a mutual dependence:
they are learned because they practice the meaning of the Veda, and that [Veda] is authoritative because of their practice.
(PVA 58)
Furthermore:
even those of the twice-born birth are born from the connection with other scriptures.

If it is argued that their minds simply do not delight in evil, from what source does this distinction between the sinful and the non-sinful arise through [mere] authority? [For you,] the state of being sinful follows from not being twice-born, and the state of not being twice-born follows from being sinful. (PVA 59–60)

Furthermore, that which is called "twice-born-ness" can be known through discernment based on birth, lineage, ritual acts, and so forth; but how could the "refinement" (*śiṣṭatā*) of those twice-born be known?

Indeed, the status of being a *dvija* (twice-born) and so forth does not fall within the range of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For that [status] must be characterized either by the connection with a caste (*jāti*), by lineage (*gotra*), or by an excellence in the capacity for ritual action. First of all, no one is able to determine such a caste merely from a specific form (*ākāra*), as is the case with the genus "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like. This is because a confusion of forms is observed; even those who are considered *śūdras* and so forth are perceived to have that very same form. Indeed, unlike the forms of Vāhuleya and others, the individuals of Kauṇḍinya and others are not perceived as distinct from the individuals of classes held to be different. Therefore, because it becomes an object of doubt due to the confusion of individuals, perception accompanied by instruction (*upadeśa*) is the valid means of knowledge.
The authority of another’s instruction is not logical regarding an object that is directly perceived,
for the instruction of people may proceed otherwise than the reality. (62) (PVA)

[010,xix] If, indeed, the caste such as Brahminhood were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then instruction by another would be useless; for instruction from another does not carry greater weight regarding an object already perceived. If that were so, there would be no doubt arising from the instruction of another. Therefore, it is precisely for this reason that one requires the assistance of direct perception.
If the object were established even without the instruction being perceptible,
then it would not be possible otherwise to establish the truth of that instruction.

But when, moreover, perception alone is incapable and instruction is also [incapable], then both are incapable individually as well as together; thus, they would not attain the capacity for the apprehension of a universal (*jāti*). If it is argued that the capacity belongs to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this is not so.
This entire causal complex is recognized only through the observation of its effect.
Just as in the case of a sprout and so forth, here too no effect whatsoever is observed.

Indeed, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for a jar or a cloth does not produce a rice sprout or anything else; for through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is perceived that water and other such factors are the very causes of it. Furthermore, in this case, no such effect characterized by the ascertainment of a genus (*jāti*) is perceived. When there is a doubt regarding the truth of an instruction concerning gold and the like, that doubt is removed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). It is not so with an instruction concerning a genus: when there is a doubt as to its lack of truth, it is not removed by direct perception in the manner of grasping the essential nature of the genus. For in the case of gold and such things, because a specific color exists, the conventional usage "this is indeed gold" reaches its completion, and thus there is no harm to what is seen. But here, however, the claim that "Brahminhood is exactly of this kind" is not a protection consisting merely of stretching out one's feet (i.e., a mere assertion). This is because the ultimate worldly transaction regarding the next world is desired. For gold becomes true by virtue of being a single coherent statement, but Brahminhood does not. Moreover, when there is doubt about that [Brahminhood], one simply investigates the lineage (*gotra*), other instructions, and so forth; there is no other means.
[011,iii] Now, if it is argued that a specific action is known through study and so forth, and not from mere instruction alone— that too is incorrect.

In the state of being twice-born (*dvijātitva*), ritual action is what must be accomplished; however, the status of being twice-born does not arise from ritual action. Furthermore, even the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) would not exist if they were devoid of a determination of caste.

For indeed, the purificatory rites such as the study of the Veda do not bestow the status of the twice-born upon one who is devoid of birth; otherwise, it would follow that everyone is twice-born. Furthermore:
if caste is not perceived through direct perception from the individual alone, [then how can it be established]?
Even from verbal testimony, there can be no cognition of this that is non-contradictory.
(PVA 66) [011.viii]

For perception, when it first arises, is not capable of establishing the discrimination of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) and so forth; therefore, instruction is required thereafter. If one were not to perceive [the caste] through direct perception, one would certainly not perceive it even from verbal testimony. For that verbal testimony merely makes known the very act of apprehension; it does not produce a certainty brought about by the full comprehension of a person’s words. When a person is questioned, "How did you come to know this?", he points only to things such as lineage (*gotra*) and refinement (*saṃskāra*) as the objects of his knowledge; he does not state that there is an apprehension of a [distinct] caste. If it is argued that "that very thing is the caste," the answer has already been given: the ritual action constitutes being twice-born, but that action itself is not the essence of being twice-born.
[011,ix] Now, birth is characterized by lineage (*gotra*). And thus they designate it: "A *brāhmaṇa* is the offspring of Brahmā.
If Brahminhood were to follow merely from being the offspring of a Brahmin, then it would follow that no one could ever be considered non-Brahmin,
for no one is ever found to have been born from a body that is not Brahmanical. (67) [PVA] If there is a distinction of caste in the intermediate stages, how could it exist without a cause?
In the interval [between births], because of the difference in actions, there is no purpose served by lineage for anyone.

(68) Now, if it is maintained that the distinction between lineages such as the twice-born is beginningless, how indeed can it be known, given that no means of valid cognition operates [to establish it]? (69)
Due to the lack of full understanding of that [nature], action results in non-action itself;
furthermore, the continuity of the lineage (*gotra*) cannot be established.
(70) [PVA] The continuity of anyone who is born into a lineage is not certain.
Otherwise, how could the charioteers, bards, and caṇḍālas possibly exist?

If it is argued that they are indeed known by those who know them, there is no restriction [on their existence]. Furthermore, in this beginningless lineage of clans, there has been no lapse regarding women. (PVA 71–72)
Thus it is known: how indeed could women ever be free from the affliction of desire?

Since Brahminhood was established previously, the possibility of belonging to that lineage [could only arise] through its persistence; yet since that [Brahminhood] persists, how can there be this lineage? This is merely a blind tradition.
Now, if Brahminhood is claimed to exist through a specific capacity (*śakti*) in relation to yoga:
[74] (PVA) no such excellence of capacity is observed anywhere at present;
if it is argued that it was heard of in former times, then to say it exists everywhere is a futile statement. [75] (PVA)
The great excellence of the power of those established in all the scriptures—
the ancient perfected ones (*pūrvasiddha*)— is sung by yogins without dispute.
Therefore, it is not logical that being a twice-born consists in possessing a particular capacity;
nor is there any Vedic statement that establishes such things as being a twice-born.
A statement regarding a universal concerning a particular is indeed equivalent to what has not been stated at all.

(PVA 77) For the Veda does not teach the Brāhmaṇahood of Devadatta and others, because they do not exist at all times, whereas the Veda exists at all times. How could the teaching of the Veda be meaningful if its object is non-existent? If it is argued that "it will be so when he comes into existence," [the response follows].
[012,v] How can the Veda be meaningless if it is subsequently connected with a meaning? And how can there be any activity on the part of that which is by nature indifferent? 78. (PVA)

Indeed, no distinction is perceived between the existence and non-existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the Veda. And if it were of such an intrinsic nature, how could it ever be understood as having this division?

Therefore, this [status of] being a Brahmin and so forth is not cognized through perception, nor through instruction, nor from both, nor even from the Veda. Since it is not cognized, how could it be useful? What, then, should be done with it? Consequently, Brahminhood is established merely through conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*). Therefore, even Brahmins do not derive their purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) from the sequence [of injunctions] in the Veda; how then could there be a correspondence with worldly practice based on the Veda? For some, however, practice may even arise from the opposite of the Veda; thus, there is no distinction between the Veda and what is non-Veda. Therefore, it is not logical to engage in activity based solely on an unexamined Veda or mere injunction. Consequently, because it does not incite action, it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
viii] Now, if it is argued that the nature of an injunction (*niyoga*) consists in its enjoiner (*niyoktṛ*), that is incorrect.
Since the enjoiner exists as an established entity, the injunction itself must also be established.
An injunction cannot be something to be accomplished; how could that which is already established be something to be accomplished? (79) (PVA) [012,x]

Indeed, that which is already established and independent of anything else cannot be brought about in any way. If it were so, then the process of accomplishment would never cease, and thus the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be rendered useless. Alternatively, even though an injunction (*niyoga*) possesses the nature of an impeller (*niyojaka*), it acquires its status as such only in dependence upon the person to be impelled (*niyojya*) and the object of the injunction. No injunction whatsoever is perceived that is devoid of a person to be impelled; likewise, there is no quality of being an injunction without an object of the injunction. For instance:
[012,xii] There is the cognition: "I am enjoined here by this [agent]," [which constitutes] the enjoinment (*niyoga*).
[012,xiii]
For an injunction, which consists in the form of an impulsion, never exists anywhere without an object.
Even the person to be enjoined understands his own state of being enjoined. (80) [PVA 012,xvi]

And such an injunction (*niyoga*) is indeed something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). For an injunction is certainly not accomplished without the means for accomplishing its own operation. If this is so, then the injunction consists in the mutual relationship between the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the injunction, and the productive urge (*bhāvanā*). Yet, that [relationship] does not exist at the time of cognition. How then could the sentence-meaning, which is the injunction, not be without a basis (*nirālambana*)? Furthermore, no injunction is perceived as something other than the mutually dependent meanings of the verbal roots and so forth. Moreover, a relationship among things established as cause and effect and occurring in a temporal sequence is not within the range of appearance, because the appearance of an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) has only an existing thing as its object, and the appearance of an extrinsic nature (*pararūpa*) is not an appearance of that [intrinsic nature]. Indeed, one thing does not appear in the form of another. And thus, if it is without a basis, what else could the hearing of words have as its object but the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)? For instance, in the case of "Perform the sacrifice and so forth," the agenthood of the self with respect to the sacrifice is considered to have reached the range of cognition; yet, at the time of cognition, that [agenthood] does not exist. Nor...

[013,i] The Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, just as whatever there is of scent derived from roots, derived from stalks, derived from sapwood, derived from heartwood, or derived from bark—all that scent is encompassed by the elephant’s footprint; so too, the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among them, being the greatest and most extensive—in the same way, bhikkhus, whatever states there are that are wholesome, whether they pertain to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm, all these wholesome states are headed by mindfulness of the body; mindfulness of the body is declared the foremost among them, being the greatest and most excellent. “Bhikkhus, when mindfulness of the body has been developed and cultivated, it fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness. When the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. When the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed and cultivated, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. When true knowledge and liberation have been developed and cultivated, they fulfill final Nibbāna without clinging. “Bhikkhus, how is it that the development and cultivation of mindfulness of the body fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating the body in the body externally... He dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called, bhikkhus, the development and cultivation of mindfulness of the body that fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness. “And how, bhikkhus, do the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. When he dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. When he dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of energy, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. When he dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of rapture, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. When he dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of tranquility, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. When he dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of concentration, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. When he dwells contemplating the body in the body, if there arises in him the enlightenment factor of equanimity, he develops it, and by development it comes to fulfillment. “And how, bhikkhus, do the seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, and results in relinquishment. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena... the enlightenment factor of energy... the enlightenment factor of rapture... the enlightenment factor of tranquility... the enlightenment factor of concentration... the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, and results in relinquishment. “And how, bhikkhus, does true knowledge and liberation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill final Nibbāna without clinging? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. “When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’... ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints,’ then his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. This is called, bhikkhus, the development and cultivation of true knowledge and liberation that fulfills final Nibbāna without clinging. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. The Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint is finished. [013,i]

It is possible to cognize through a word that which was not previously cognized; for only one who has previously perceived another person engaged in an action such as sacrifice understands that state of being—whether it be his own or that of another—and no one else. Furthermore, this cognition, following upon what preceded it, does not transcend having the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object. Nor is agency itself previously apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because direct perception does not function across temporal succession. However, it is called "cognition" with respect to conventional direct perception. In every way, the cognition of the self’s agency results from following a prior cognition.

[013,ii] Furthermore, it may be argued that he is not impelled by way of being an agent (*kartṛ*), but rather solely by way of being an office-holder (*adhikārin*). For one does not become an agent merely by not acting; rather, office-holding consists in fitness (*yogyatā*). This too is incorrect.
In whatever case there is fitness, it does not exist without an object;
and when the object is beyond the senses, how can fitness be perceived?

Indeed, one who does not know his own operation as having fitness as its object cannot cognize that fitness in its essential nature as qualified by that object. Therefore, just as in the case of agency, there is a fault here as well.
How can that which transcends the scope of investigation be described by the activities of words?
The meaning of the sentence is held to be *niyoga* (an injunction) due to the "teacher's fist" [i.e., the secrecy of the tradition].
Indeed, when examined, no such thing as *niyoga* exists, because it cannot withstand logical analysis.
[013, vii] What is proclaimed by others as the application of form to a pure effect? Is it mere impulsion, or is it the connection with the effect, or rather its opposite? (PVA 83)

Is it because of its predominance that the mandate (*niyoga*) is held by others to have the nature of an effect (*kārya*), or is its status as a mandate said to derive from its being the instigator (*prerakatā*)? Furthermore,
when there is a relationship between the effect and the instigation, what constitutes the state of being a mandate?

Is *niyoga* a collection [of the two], or is it something other than those two? (85) (PVA) Is that which is mounted upon a machine (*yantra*) thus desired, or is it the nature of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*)?
Or is the person (*puruṣa*) the *niyoga*? These are the positions formulated by others. (86) (PVA)
(1) This is the view of those who maintain that there is an appointment to a pure effect.
Since the meaning of the suffix and the injunction are perceived as pure,
and since they take the form of what is to be done (*kārya*), this [injunction] is therefore considered here to be a pure *kārya*.
As for whatever other qualification of it is perceived—

It is not tenable that the meaning [of the optative suffix] is the object of the injunction (*pratyayārtha*), for it is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—as in the case of "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*).

However, as for its quality of being an instigator (*prerakatva*) which is accepted here as a qualifier, since that is not denoted by the suffix, the word possesses the nature of enjoining an action (*kāryaniyogatā*). (PVA 88–89)
[013,xv] (2) The doctrine of the application of pure impulsion.
In this context, it is understood that in all cases, the injunction (*niyoga*) consists solely of an instigation (*preraṇā*);
for no one perceives themselves as being enjoined unless they have been instigated.
(PVA 90) [013,xvii]
(3) The position that the commission of action is connected with an instigation:
"When it has previously been known in this way, 'This is my duty to perform'— "
"That [injunction] must be the impeller for its own establishment; otherwise, it would not be established.
(PVA 91) [013,xix] Those who maintain that the impulsion is conjoined with the effect say:
A person is never impelled toward an action here without a task;
therefore, "impulsion" is said to be an injunction conjoined with a task. (92) (PVA)
Those who maintain that it is the effect itself that functions through metaphorical designation say:
[013,xxii]
The object of impulsion is the task to be accomplished, but that task is not itself the impeller;
rather, the operation of the means of valid cognition is metaphorically attributed to the object of cognition.
(PVA 93) [013,xxiii]
(6) Others maintain that the very relationship between the two is the injunction (*niyoga*).
For an instigation (*preraṇā*), in the absence of a task (*kārya*), is not an instigator for anyone at all.
Whether it be the task (*kārya*), the instigation (*preraṇā*), the connection (*yoga*), or the injunction (*niyoga*), it is agreed upon by him [the proponent of the aggregate].
Even in the theory of the aggregate (*samudāyavāda*), this is the intended meaning.

These two are perceived as mutually inseparable, because from this [inseparability] there arises both the injunction (*niyoga*) and the collection (*samudāya*), which consist respectively of the task (*kārya*) and the instigation (*preraṇā*). (PVA 95)
[014,ii] Others, however, say: the meaning of a sentence is that which is free from both natures.
Since Brahman is eternally established as a single entity through sacred tradition, it cannot be something to be produced; how then could it be an impeller? (96) (PVA) [014,iv]
(9) This is the view of those who maintain that [the world] is governed by a mechanical system:
"In whatever place a person has a desire, he will find it there once the [mechanical] arrangement is in place."
"Thinking that the self is mounted upon the object, one engages [in action].
(PVA 97) This is the doctrine of those who maintain that there is a fixed assignment (*niyoga*) of the nature of the object of enjoyment.
[014,vii] "This is mine to be enjoyed"—in this way, the object of enjoyment is perceived.
And the cognition characterized by the sense of "mine" is established solely in the enjoyer. (PVA 98)
For that in which there arises the conceit of ownership toward the enjoyer, that alone should be known as the object of enjoyment; that alone is defined as "one's own" (sva).
By means of which [conceit], in the form of something to be accomplished, it is understood: "This is mine. (PVA 99)
That which is to be enjoyed is designated as "one's own" by means of its form as established [through that injunction].
(PVA 100) For that which is to be enjoyed exists in an already established form; it is not, in that respect, an injunction (*niyoga*).
Here, however, because the object of enjoyment acts as an impeller by virtue of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it possesses the nature of an injunction. (PVA 101)
[014,xi] From those who maintain the doctrine of the appointment by a Supreme Person.
A person always thinks, "This is my task";
thus, for a person, being characterized by a task is the denotation of the *niyoga*.
Once the accomplishment of the task has occurred, the person is then conjoined with it. (PVA 102)
"In this way, the person is established"— thus is the meaning of the sentence expressed.
And in every case regarding the meaning of a sentence, there are eight types of distinctions.
[014,xv] Is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) an application (niyoga), or rather the object of cognition (prameya)? Or is it devoid of both, or perhaps possessing the nature of both? 104. (PVA)
Is the operation of the person one whose nature is the operation of the word, or is it the operation of the person itself?
Or is it of the nature of the operation of both, or indeed the non-operation of both?
To this it is replied: all of this is inconsistent, because:
An effect devoid of instigation is bereft of an agent to be enjoined.
An *niyoga* is not called an *niyoga* for anyone at all [in its primary sense].
(PVA 106) When the word *niyoga* is considered to denote a pure action (*kārya*), by what can its status as an *niyoga* be prevented on the grounds of being a mere name? (PVA 107)
However, when a person is engaged in an action, that [action] is not perceived as such;
how then can that be an *niyoga* (an injunction), like the cognition of something already established or something past?
(PVA 108) This *niyoga* is recognized by the world as a property of the one who enjoins.

If it is argued that this very thing is the effect, then because it is already established, it cannot be something to be accomplished. (PVA 109) If it is maintained that this injunction is designated as such by virtue of its being the object to be accomplished, that is merely a figurative expression applied to the object [of the injunction] by treating it as if it were the [injunction] itself. (PVA 110)

And how can that [object], being unestablished, possess the nature of an instigator? If it is maintained that its status as an instigator consists in its being understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), [we reply:
being an object to be accomplished belongs to what is unestablished, while understanding belongs to that which has an established nature. (PVA 111)
How can that which is mutually contradictory be accepted as one?

(112) (PVA) If it is argued that the cognition [of the injunction] is the motivator because it appears in the form of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then the status of being an injunction would belong to the cognition itself, and not to the injunction in reality. (113) (PVA)
Likewise.
[014,xxvii]

If *niyoga* (the injunction) were the meaning of the sentence, what would constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If the *niyoga* itself is of the nature of a means of cognition, then what would be the object of cognition (*prameya*)? (114) (PVA) If, in reality, *niyoga* is intended to be the activity of the person...
This activity of the person is itself the *bhāvanā*, which expresses something else [i.e., the action].
But in the view that the operation belongs to the sentence, it would be the verbal *bhāvanā* (*śabdabhāvanā*).
Others say that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth express a different kind altogether, namely the *bhāvanā* consisting of the word itself (*śabdātmabhāvanā*). (PVA 115–116)
But if this person has indeed been born from the word itself, why would he engage in activity? If he were not impelled by the word, how could he proceed toward his own function?
(117) [PVA] If he is not enjoined by the word, how can there be such engagement?
When there is an injunction by means of a word, that cognition is without a real objective basis (*nirālambanatā*).
Thus, even things such as those mounted on a machine are defects of the expressed meaning of a sentence; for this reason:
[015,ii] It is said that the relationship between the object of experience and the experiencer exists by virtue of being mounted upon a machine;
yet, there is no such relationship, for at that time the person is not mounted upon the nature of the object of experience. (PVA 119)

At the time of cognition, everything lacks its own intrinsic nature by virtue of being an object to be proven (*sādhya*). If that very [nature] were its form, then the status of being an object to be proven would be lost.
Thus, the injunction (*niyoga*) has been rejected. [Now follows: (3) The rejection of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).
Now, *bhāvanā* (productive activity) is being examined. For *bhāvanā* is twofold: the *bhāvanā* of the word (*śabdabhāvanā*) and the *bhāvanā* of the meaning (*arthabhāvanā*). As it has been said:
"The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth are said to produce one thing alone: the *bhāvanā* whose essence is the word."
But in this case, there exists among them another entirely distinct [efficient force], namely the *bhāvanā* of all meanings, which is designated as "all" (*sarvākhyā*).

(PVA 121) The *śabdabhāvanā* is the operation of the word. For by the word, the operation of the person (*puruṣavyāpāra*) is brought about (*bhāvyate*); by the operation of the person, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); and by the meaning of the verbal root, the result (*phala*).
And this is illogical: for the operation of a word is not denotable by the word itself. With respect to that [operation], the word is not a denoter; it is not a communicator. To explain:
When a word is uttered, it is understood by people that the self is enjoined;
what other injunction could be postulated than this mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
"It is indeed the verbal *bhāvanā* itself that is called 'an injunction' (*niyoga*) by another term.

This is incorrect. If it is an operation of the word, how is it that one who has not grasped the convention does not understand it? For if it were inherently an instigator, the grasping of a convention would be of no use. If you say it is that very same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then surely if that complex operates toward either instigation or *bhāvanā*, this is untenable; for as follows:
When the causal complex for grasping the convention is operative, there is the cognition of the object; once the object is cognized, the person proceeds of his own accord. (PVA 123)

[015,xiv] From the instigation "Do this," there is the cognition of only *preraṇā* (instigation) and *adhyeṣaṇā* (request). In the absence of that cognition, there is no cognition of being "appointed" (*niyuktatva*). And what is called "being appointed" is the state of being engaged in an action. Having perceived the state of one engaged in the action, the appointer appoints [the person]. And that future state of his cannot be directly realized in its own form. For if it were realized in its own form, everything would be accomplished at that very moment, and thus the appointment would not be fruitful. [015,xv]
Just as in that case the instigator has a sublated cognition, so too would the person being instigated; for a word expresses the object of the cognition.

For just as the cognition of the instigator (*prayojaka*)—which is devoid of its own activity—is sublated by the person being instigated (*prayojya*) who perceives himself as lacking that activity, and is thus without a real objective basis (*nirālambana*), so too is the cognition of the person being instigated sublated by him when he perceives himself as engaged in his own activity. If it is argued that "that cognition [of the instigator] arises from the word," this is not the case. That word also merely makes known the object of the intellect (*buddhyartha*). This is because both parties have the same determination (*adhyavasāya*): "It was explained by me in this way" and "It was understood by me in this way. Or rather: "In this way it was understood by me; let the intention of this person be such or not; let the object be so or not; I have simply understood it in this way. For this very reason, he says:
The object that appears in the intellect as the domain of the speaker’s activity—that is where the word possesses authority; it is not based on the actual reality of the object. (3)

[016,i] "The object of the speaker's activity" refers to where a speaker exists. "It appears in the intellect" refers to where such a speaker does not exist. Alternatively, let it be understood that a speaker exists there precisely because of that very utterance, according to the principle that "whatever belongs to a certain class must arise from that [class]. Or else, since there is no distinction [between the two], everything would be non-human (apauruṣeya). If you say this is not so because it is contradicted by human agency, then we ask: since human agency is beyond the senses even in this case, why should it not fail to contradict [the claim of non-human origin]? [016,ii]

Alternatively, that speech is indeed authorless (apauruṣeya), and the notion that "this was composed by me" is merely an illusion on the part of the person. For instance: [016,iii] A text that has been utterly lost appears as if spontaneously to someone's mind.

For one who has developed the conceit "this was composed by me" and whose memory of [the source] has been impaired, even poets imagine that a work which was actually experienced in another life is their own poetic creation. Why is this so? Because, in that case, everything would be non-human (apauruṣeya). Furthermore, since it would likewise be purposeless, the state of being non-human in such a context is useless.
In that case, even with respect to the Veda, its futility is likewise accepted; and if one assumes another meaning, both cases would be identical. (PVA 126)

The futility of both the Vedas and non-Vedas, as well as the postulation of their lack of human authorship, is exactly the same. If it is argued that there is no futility in the case of postulating another meaning,
[the response follows].
In that case, let it be assumed that the conceptualization of a true object is indeed human;
however, the first appearance of an unreal object arises from the Veda.

Therefore, he says: “The object of the speaker’s activity,” and so forth. Having set aside the primary meaning of the Veda, whatever object becomes the domain of the mental activity (*buddhi-vyāpāra*), in that case, the authority belongs to the human intellect alone; it is not based on the reality of the object, nor does it belong to the word. This is the analysis of the syntactical connection of the words. For instance: “Having thus set aside that first meaning of the Veda, man... [016, ix]

The cognition that would construct another object as purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that [cognition] would be a valid knowledge (*pramā*). But since even that is merely the meaning of the Veda, there is no means of valid cognition here for you.
If it is argued that [the latter cognition] arises due to the predominance of the Veda, then why is this not true for the first [cognition] as well?
And if that [Veda] were also for that purpose [of human ends], why would the Veda not be useless?
Such being the case, there is doubt regarding its authority as something of non-human origin.

Because there is no primary [Vedic] statement regarding the truth of the Veda, the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citrayā* [offering]" would be purposeless. If it is argued that this is like a deficiency in ritual action (*karmavaiguṇya*), we say no, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that. Furthermore, any postulation of another purpose, arising from human effort, is simply a human fabrication. As it has been said: "How could that [injunction] not exist for one who somehow remembers it himself, even though it lacks a verbal indicator (*aśabdaliṅgā*)? Moreover, everyone considers themselves enjoined by the Veda according to their prior tradition. And an injunction (*niyoga*) consists in the form of a verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*). If that were the meaning of the sentence, then in the case of "Devadatta should cook," since the agent is not denoted, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply by the rule "the third case is used for the agent and the instrument. However, when the agent is denoted, the third case does not occur because of the governing rule "when [the agent] is not already expressed" (*anabhihitādhikārāt*), as it is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Furthermore, in "he cooks," the agent is also understood. If it is argued that this understanding arises through implication (*ākṣepa*) of the agent by the force of the activity (*vyāpāra*), we say no.
In this way, there would be a cognition of sequence: first, the understanding of the activity; then, by its power, from that [activity], the agent is subsequently cognized. (PVA 131)
Furthermore, no perception of succession is observed; nor would the dual and plural numbers apply, because the operation is unitary.

If it is argued that there will be a difference in activity due to a difference in the agents (*kāraka*), then in the case of the sentence "The mat is being made by Devadatta and Yajñadatta," there would be a great inconsistency. For indeed:
because the object (*karman*) is one, the unity of the action follows; likewise, from its division [into agents], [the plurality of actions would follow].
And if there is thus a difference in the agent, what should be done by the wise? (132) (PVA) [Objection:

But surely, because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is non-different, the singular number is used, as in "Devadatta and Yajñadatta sit down. And that meaning of the verbal root is not the *niyoga* (the injunction), because the *niyoga* is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, that [injunction] is distinct from the meaning of the verbal root. Since it is to be accomplished by the agent, it differs according to the difference in agents; therefore, one says "make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuruta*). However, the pure meaning of the verbal root does not differ due to a difference in the factors of action (*kāraka*). [Reply: That is incorrect.
If that distinction [of the suffix] were due to its connection [with the root], then it would also belong to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
Since that [meaning of the root] is also something to be produced (*nirvartya*), let it be distinguished precisely by that distinction [of the suffix]. (133) (PVA)
But for us:
Since the determination of difference and non-difference is dependent upon the speaker's intention,
all of this is consistent when the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is expressed by its own name.

For action (*kriyā*) is intended to be expressed as distinct from both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*). If that [action] is denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) and not by the agent, then the third case (*tṛtīyā*) occurs for the agent; when it is denoted [by the suffix], then because it is the meaning of the nominative, the first case (*prathamā*) occurs—as in "it is done by the Great Soul" (*kriyate mahātmanā*) and "the Great Soul does" (*karoti mahātme*). This is so when the distinction of this meaning of productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is intended to be known.
The expression by means of the letter *la* [in the verbal suffix] indicates the agent as that which is intended to be reached by the action; this is the sense of the third case (*kartari*).

When there is a desire to express a distinction regarding this agent, it is denoted by the *l*-suffixes; since it has already been expressed by that very [suffix], it should be understood that the third case ending does not apply to the agent. (PVA 135–136)

[017,ix] The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra Entitled “The Questions of Akṣayamati” (Ārya-akṣayamati-paripṛcchā-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra) Chapter One: On the Nature of Phenomena (Dharmatā-lakṣaṇa-parivarta) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—free from outflows, free from taints, having attained mastery over their minds, like great nāgas, accomplished in their task, done with what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, liberated through perfect knowledge, and whose minds were well-freed by right wisdom. Among them were the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the venerable Aśvajit, the venerable Bhadrika, the venerable Mahānāman, the venerable Bāṣpa, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Kaphiṇa, the venerable Kapphiṇa, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Revata, the venerable Svāgata, the venerable Nanda, the venerable Upananda, the venerable Cūḍapanthaka, the venerable Svāgata, the venerable Rāhula, and others such as these, all of whom were arhats. Also present were five hundred bodhisattvas, all of whom had been predicted by the Tathāgatas of the past, who were irreversible from the path to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and who had attained the stage of non-retrogression.
