Among them were the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajramati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Padmamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Siṃhamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Gaganagañja, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta, and others such as these, all of whom were bodhisattva mahāsattvas. At that time, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, bowed toward the Blessed One with palms joined, and addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma discourse entitled ‘The Questions of Akṣayamati,’ which reveals the inexhaustible nature of phenomena, the inexhaustible nature of the mind, the inexhaustible nature of wisdom, the inexhaustible nature of liberation, and the inexhaustible nature of the knowledge and vision of liberation. The Blessed One replied to the venerable Ānanda: “Well said, Ānanda! You have asked this question for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans. Therefore, Ānanda, listen well and attend closely; I shall explain to you. “Even so, Blessed One,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke thus: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of inexhaustibility regarding phenomena. What are the four? They are: the inexhaustibility of the nature of phenomena, the inexhaustibility of the characteristics of phenomena, the inexhaustibility of the manifestation of phenomena, and the inexhaustibility of the cessation of phenomena. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of inexhaustibility regarding phenomena. [017,ix]

But when the agent’s operation (*kartṛvyāpāra*) is conveyed by the suffix *tip*, that very thing is *bhāvanā*. Thus it has been said: “Words denoting action (*karmaśabda*) have the meaning of *bhāva*; *bhāva* is the act of bringing into being (*bhāvana*), which is the suffix of the causative (*ṇyanta*). This being the case, this [suffix] is indeed *bhāvanā*, and *bhāvanā* is the agent’s operation. Being impelled, the agent proceeds toward his own operation. And since the mandate (*niyoga*) is subordinate to that [operation] and is not primary, it does not constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Furthermore, because *bhāvanā* is qualified by the mandate, when it is presented in such a way, one necessarily engages [in the activity]. How could he, having understood his own operation, not engage in it? Otherwise, his own operation would not even be enjoined. This, however, is incorrect.

[017,x] "Why must this activity of mine necessarily exist?"— if one thinks thus, [then] since there would be no fruit at all, from where could there be a sense of accomplishment in its success? (PVA 137)

If you think, "This activity must necessarily be mine," that is incorrect. For no one undertakes something thinking, "I must do this," without seeing a result; one engages in action only when there is a result. It has already been established that no such result is perceived. Furthermore:
In the cases of "he sacrifices" (*yajate*) and "he cooks" (*pacati*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is not perceived.
Since it does not exceed the meaning of the verbal root (*yaj*), how can it be the meaning of the sentence? (138) [Objection:
If one perceives a distinction, such as "he performs cooking" and "he performs sacrifice,"...
If this were so, there would be an infinite regress, which would produce an irrationality.

(PVA 139) [017,xiv] It performs a sacrifice, it accomplishes its own function, it brings about the completion of the sacrifice—these are merely designations that somehow presuppose a distinction. No establishment of the true nature of things arises from these [designations]. Expressions involving a distinction, such as "the body of a stone statue," are seen even in the absence of an actual ontological distinction.
Just as the activity of a twice-born man is also called "sacrifice," so too,
the subsequent perception [of the object] is not itself the act of "doing. (PVA 140)
The act of sacrificing is indeed not something other than the substance due to its particularity;
for it is understood as being co-referential with Devadatta himself.

But surely, from the observation of questions and answers such as "What is Devadatta doing? and "He is cooking" or "He is sacrificing," since it is certain that he "is doing" something while there is doubt regarding the specific acts of sacrificing and so forth, their distinctness is indeed well-established. And thus it has been said: "The body itself is not the intellect, because even when the body is established, there remains doubt regarding the various states of the intellect. This is incorrect.
[018,i] If, in reality, the meaning of "doing" and the meaning of "sacrificing" were distinct, then...
If one thing is doubted while another is being stated, the sequence is difficult to justify.

(PVA 142) For if the act of "doing" (*karoti*) were something other than the specific acts such as sacrifice (*yajati*), then, since "doing" is already certain, how could there be a question regarding something else that is doubtful? A question is only appropriate when the matter is indeed uncertain. If it is argued that the meaning of "doing" is of a general nature, whereas the sacrifice and so forth are of a specific nature—[we reply:]...
Nothing whatsoever is perceived without its particularity;
for that which is implied by the universal cannot truly be said to be unperceived. (PVA 143)
For it has been stated that when there is a cognition of the mere universal, doubt arises regarding the particular aspect.
Now, if it is argued that the particular is implied by the general, then since that too is already perceived, how can there be doubt? For there is no implication other than perception itself.
Alternatively, even if it is indeed perceived, its state of being perceived does not exist in the form of a particular because it is implied only as a generality.

[018,vii] But surely that very universal is the attractor (*ākṣepaka*), and that very thing is what is attracted (*ākṣepya*). How can this be? Nor is there any "universality" (*sāmānyatā*) to be attracted other than the universal itself. If that were the case, there would be another [universal] beyond that, and yet another beyond that, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[018,viii]

[Objection: Is it not the case that doubt is indeed appropriate because of the perception of a general property (*sāmānya*), the non-perception of a particular (*viśeṣa*), and the recollection of a particular? [Reply: No. For one who maintains that non-perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of a general property, non-existence itself is appropriate due to non-apprehension. Otherwise, non-existence results from the non-apprehension of something that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), and not from mere non-apprehension. Even so, since doubt arises from non-apprehension alone, the claim "because of the perception of a general property" is redundant.

If, even when there is perception of a universal (*sāmānya*), the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) does not constitute doubt regarding the universal—because, in the case of the perception of a universal, the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for its own perception simply does not occur—then it follows that this very non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perceptibility is the cause of doubt. Furthermore, the mention of "recollection of particulars" (*viśeṣasmṛti*) would be redundant; for there is no doubt other than that which consists in the recollection of both aspects, since doubt has the nature of a recollection that rests upon two parts [of a contradictory pair]. Indeed, in places such as Kānyakubja, doubt is observed to arise from memory alone, even without the prior perception of a universal. Thus, that very thing—such as a sacrifice (*yajña*) and so forth—which is perceived indistinctly, is the "universal" [known] through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*). And it has been said in this regard: [The verse follows.]
Because it establishes the mere thing as excluded from what does not possess its form,
the logical mark is said to have the universal as its object, since it is not established in particulars. (PVA 144)

The determination of a universal (*sāmānya*) is merely the non-determination of its specific differences. In some cases, cognition itself—being devoid of that specific form—is a cause of doubt because it is common to both existence and non-existence. Likewise, the non-apprehension of such a thing is itself a cause of doubt, whether it takes the form of cognition or the form of the object being apprehended.

But surely, even in the absence of an experience of a common form, doubt is observed, such as "Is this a post or a person? In that case, a commonality consisting of mere height is perceived. If that were the case, then a cognition of two forms would be perceived.
[018,xiii] There is no universal here distinct from the individuals, because the cognitions are distinct.
The distinctness of the object from the form of the cognition [is established].

(PVA 145) [018,xiv] Now, it is indeed perceived that there is a mere verticality at a distance, excluding the essential natures of a man or a post; otherwise, if the experience were included within the forms of a man or a post, no doubt would arise regarding them. Therefore, its appearing as excluded from those [forms] is precisely its difference from them, since difference is characterized by nothing more than this.
That is not tenable.

If there were a distinction based on the mere degree of proximity, why would there not be an appearance at a distance? And why would that which appears at a distance appear so intensely upon being near?

Indeed, that which appears when situated at a distance appears all the more clearly upon the establishment of proximity. And if the universal (*sāmānya*) were a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*), then since it is that very thing which appears, how could there be the conventional usage of "indistinct appearance" [in another case]? For certainly, when a blue object appears, there is no conventional usage of an "indistinct white appearance."

Now, even in your own position, what indeed is this so-called "indistinctness"? It is the state of having an indistinct appearance. For an indistinct appearance may sometimes be a non-appearance, sometimes an appearance of something else, and sometimes an appearance of that very thing itself.
If it is an appearance of that very thing, then it is an indistinct appearance.
How indeed can there be indistinctness when [an object] appears in its own essential nature?
(147) (PVA) Even if it is the appearance of something else, how could that be indistinctness for that very thing?
Without non-appearance, how could there be existence in the act of appearing? (148) (PVA)
If it is the cognition itself that has become thus, appearing indistinctly,
then the object appears indistinctly through the manifestation of the cognition's own nature.
This is incorrect:
when cognition itself arises from that [object] without possessing its form.
Then, the worldly convention of an unclear appearance would be accepted.

(150) (PVA) Now, if that very thing were the universal (*sāmānya*), in that case there would be no appearance of color and shape. Indeed, the universal does not possess color and shape, because those two [color and shape] reside in substances (*dravya*). If, on the other hand, the color and shape belong to the substance, then the universal produced from that [substance] would not appear; rather, it would be only the color and shape that appear. And since those two are common to both a post and a person, it is logical that there is doubt between them.
That too is incorrect, because:
[019,xiii]
If its color is one thing, how could its shape be otherwise?
Since it is perceived in this way, the cognition is understood to be erroneous.

If color and shape appear otherwise, that is merely an error; how, then, could there be perception of a universal (*sāmānya*)? If it is argued that it is the composite whole (*avayavin*) that appears there, and neither the universal nor the color and shape, then [we reply]:
there would be an appearance of something distinct from the forms of color and shape.
Whence could there be a substance? What else appears from that?

(PVA 152) For it is color and so forth—such as blackness—that appear, and not some other substance appearing therein. This is because no substance other than those [qualities] appears apart from them. If it is argued that "that very thing is the substance," we say no; for both shape and color are qualities (*guṇa*).

[019,xvii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his supernatural power, caused them to see the Blessed One Śākyamuni seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. Having seen him, they were filled with joy and faith; their minds became tranquil, and they were freed from fear. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “Avalokiteśvara, these five hundred merchantmen have been terrified by the rākṣasīs. You should go to them and bring them back. Avalokiteśvara replied to the Blessed One: “So be it, Blessed One. Having said this, he took the form of a bhikṣu and went to where the five hundred merchantmen were. Seeing the bhikṣu, they were filled with joy and faith; their minds became tranquil, and they were freed from fear. The bhikṣu then led them out of that place and returned to Jambudvīpa. When they arrived at Jambudvīpa, they told the king, the ministers, and the people of the country: “We have seen the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who possesses the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. He is endowed with all the marks of a Great Man and is adorned with the eighty minor marks. His body is golden in color, radiant and beautiful, like a mountain of pure gold. We have heard the Dharma from him, which is profound, subtle, and difficult to understand. It is beyond the reach of ordinary beings and can only be realized by the wise. We have now returned safely to our own land. Hearing this, the king, the ministers, and the people of the country were all filled with joy and faith; their minds became tranquil, and they were freed from fear. They all went to the place where the Blessed One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One, knowing their thoughts, preached the Dharma to them according to their capacities, causing them to attain various stages of realization. Some attained the fruit of stream-entry, some the fruit of once-returning, some the fruit of non-returning, and some the fruit of arhatship. Some generated the aspiration for the vehicle of the śrāvakas, some for the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and some for the unsurpassed vehicle of the bodhisattvas. All of them, having heard the Dharma, rejoiced and departed. This is called the second chapter, the Chapter on the Five Hundred Merchantmen. [019,xviii] At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara to be able to deliver sentient beings from such great fears? The Blessed One said to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati: “Akṣayamati, if there are sentient beings who hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will be delivered from all fears. If there are women who wish to be free from female form, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, they will not again become female in future lives. If there are those who are bound by fetters, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, the bonds will loosen and they will be released. If there are those who are imprisoned, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, the prison doors will open and they will be released. If there are those who are about to be executed, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, the swords will break and they will be spared. If there are those who are caught in a fire, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, the fire will be extinguished and they will not be burned. If there are those who are caught in water, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, they will not drown and will reach dry land. If there are those who are traveling through dangerous paths, they should call upon the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By virtue of this, they will be protected from robbers and wild beasts, and will reach their destination in safety. For these reasons, Akṣayamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to deliver sentient beings from such great fears. When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati and the entire great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and carried it forth. This is called the third chapter, the Chapter on the Causes and Conditions of Deliverance. [019,xix] At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara to be able to manifest in various forms—such as the form of a Buddha, the form of a śrāvaka, the form of a pratyekabuddha, the form of a deva, the form of a nāga, the form of a yakṣa, the form of a gandharva, the form of an asura, the form of a garuḍa, the form of a kiṃnara, the form of a mahoraga, the form of a human, and the form of a non-human—to teach and transform sentient beings according to their needs? The Blessed One said to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya: “Maitreya, if there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a Buddha, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara manifests in the form of a Buddha to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a śrāvaka, he manifests in the form of a śrāvaka to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a pratyekabuddha, he manifests in the form of a pratyekabuddha to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a deva, he manifests in the form of a deva to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a nāga, he manifests in the form of a nāga to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a yakṣa, he manifests in the form of a yakṣa to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a gandharva, he manifests in the form of a gandharva to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by an asura, he manifests in the form of an asura to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a garuḍa, he manifests in the form of a garuḍa to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a kiṃnara, he manifests in the form of a kiṃnara to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a mahoraga, he manifests in the form of a mahoraga to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a human, he manifests in the form of a human to teach and transform them. If there are sentient beings who are to be taught and transformed by a non-human, he manifests in the form of a non-human to teach and transform them. Maitreya, in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara manifests in various forms to teach and transform sentient beings according to their needs. When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya and the entire great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and carried it forth. This is called the fourth chapter, the Chapter on Manifesting Various Forms. [019,xx] At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mañjuśrī rose

Now, [the opponent claims] that substance (*dravya*) possesses color and shape (*varṇasaṃsthānavat*). This is not so; for there is no appearance of it otherwise apart from those [two]. Indeed, no other substance is perceived apart from clear or unclear color and shape. Furthermore, because an unclear color and shape are sublated by a cognition produced by a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*), such as when a cognition with a clear form arises, one thinks, "This is not of such a nature. And the very non-perception of that [substance], which consists in the perception of its opposite, is the sublater. If it is argued that this is not so because the conceptual cognition "this is not [it]" does not arise, we say: No, for that cognition "this is not [it]" certainly does arise. To explain: a cognition is indeed produced that sublates a shape distinct from that [color], namely, "This color is not this shape. If it is argued that this is not a sublation of something distinct, then precisely because it is a sublation of a shape that is not distinct, a distinct shape must exist.
That is incorrect.
If sublation occurs for that very same thing which was previously perceived, then there is no perception otherwise;
what else remains?

If a certain configuration or substance is apprehended as non-different from color, and if such a thing is sublated, what else remains? Indeed, no distinction of parts exists, by which there could be an established division such that the sublation of one does not entail the sublation of the other.
Or, it might be argued:
At that time, there is no apprehension of that color, nor of the two substances of shape;
therefore, one understands that the substance exists after the apprehension and that it existed previously. (PVA 154)

Furthermore, that which is perceived as having a prior and posterior state and that which is not so perceived— it is not logical for these two to be joined with the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). For every distinction must be established in this very manner, since there is no other means for the opponent to establish a distinction.
That is incorrect.
If that other thing exists in reality, why does it not appear in perception?
In which case is the occurrence of both seen, whether in the prior or in the subsequent?

If that color or shape were ultimately distinct from the substance, or the shape from the color, why would it not appear in perception—either in the former or in the latter? Since it does not appear individually, and since there is no such thing as a "collection" (samudāya) apart from its constituents, to claim it appears therein is the work of great delusion. Furthermore, there is no simultaneous conjunction (*samavadhāna*) of the two; how then can there be a collection? And since synthesis (*anusandhāna*) does not arise from perception, inference is likewise absent due to the lack of that [synthesis]; so from where could there be a cognition of distinction?

Therefore, there is no such thing as a "common" [universal] (*sādhāraṇa*). Since everything is established within its own self, there is only particularity (*viśeṣa*). Consequently, an action such as sacrificing—which is said to be "common" because it is not a "common form"—is not the universal (*sāmānya*) of particulars. Thus, *bhāvanā* cannot consist of the activity of an agent, for it is not perceived apart from that [activity]. Nor does the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) exist apart from substance (*dravya*). Substance itself, appearing in a sequence of prior and posterior states, has a nature whose distinction is conceptually constructed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Even though there is no actual difference, it is metaphorically treated as if different; thus, the claim that "action is distinct from substance and substance is distinct from action" is merely conventional usage. This is not an establishment of the reality of things. Furthermore, the agent's own activity and the meaning of the verbal root are both understood as yet to come at the time of the injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, how can it be said that the cognition which arises based on them—produced by the force of prior latent impressions—is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*)? It has already been explained that it is not without an objective basis.

Furthermore, it might be argued: since perception has only the present as its object, it cannot have the future or the past as its objective support (*ālambana*); however, although verbal testimony (*śabda*) does have those as its objects, it lacks that same [perceptual] nature. To this he says, “Injunction” (*codanā*), and so forth.
That is incorrect.
How can it be determined that even that which is not being perceived exists?

But in inference, there is a relation; such is the established state in that case. (PVA 156) [020,xv] For every cognition whose object is beyond the senses is non-erroneous precisely because of its connection with a real object, just like inferential cognition. Indeed, for that which is not related to something else, there is no necessary rule that it must exist when the other exists. A cognition that is without a basis (*nirālambana*), however, lacks a basis simply because the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that object does not exist; for it has been stated that there can be no apprehension of the intrinsic nature of what is non-existent. Furthermore, there is no rule regarding a relation with a future entity. But in inference, however—

[021,i] An effect is understood from its cause; likewise, it is so from the highest [scriptural] vision. Yet, the status of the *agnihotra* and other rites as causes for a fruit is not perceived, nor is there any certainty regarding the transgression incurred by their non-performance.
Then, perceiving his own capacity and understanding himself to be the instrument of the sacrifice, he will engage in the sacrifice.
[021,iii] This is provided that he does not fail to understand his status as the cause [of the attainment] of heaven.
Even though this [injunction] is taught for the sake of sacrifice, why does one engage in it there?

(PVA 157) For this very reason, it is not tenable to say that "the mutual connection between the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the mandate (*niyoga*), and the meaning of the verbal root, or the connection with the fruit, constitutes the injunction as the sentence-meaning. Since everything is not grasped by a cognition as something to be produced (*bhāvya*), the cognition would indeed be without a basis (*nirālambana*). Therefore, one engages [in action] through the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object; and that [unification] is precisely what is called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). No person acting with foresight would ever engage [in action] based on the Veda alone—enough of this excessive digression.

Therefore: "The object which is the domain of the speaker's activity, which appears in the cognition as something superimposed—that is the validity of the word; it is not based on the actual reality of the object. (2.2)
It is established that there can certainly be no superimposition (adhyāropa) regarding an object that is a real entity without a logical connection (pratibandha).
[021, vii] In the *Prathamavārttikālaṅkāra*, the first section concerning affirmation (*vidhi*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth, is concluded. 2.
<2. Pramāṇasiddhivārttika, the Second> <1. Validity as Conventional—> [021, viii]

If, then, non-contradiction consists in the stability of causal efficacy, then even a cognition such as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)— which functions after one has known "this is that very same thing"— would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as it would partake in non-contradiction. In that case,
a cognition of a previously unknown object (*apūrvārthavijñāna*) must be certain and free from sublation (*bādhavarjita*).
Valid cognition is that which is produced by non-defective causes and is recognized by the world.

[The opponent argues: "A cognition whose object is a composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory. [The author replies: Now, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), arising through the power of a non-conceptualizing awareness (*ālocanājñāna*), is not a valid means of knowledge; nor is [the cognition] of a composite whole [valid] through the power of the cognition of its parts. If that were the case, then even that non-conceptualizing awareness would not be a valid means of knowledge, as it would likewise depend on the power of the contact of the eye (*cakṣuḥ-sannikarṣa*) and so forth. In that regard, if one traces back the succession of causes, it would follow that the eye and other [faculties] are [themselves the primary] means of knowledge. Alternatively, it would follow that the conceptual construction itself is the means of knowledge immediately [following the perception].
To this, it is said:
Because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, conventional cognition is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
for activity regarding things to be avoided or adopted is primarily based upon that [conventional cognition]. (3)

The cognition arising as "this is that very same thing" is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing identity, because an identity that was previously unperceived is not being apprehended; rather, it is merely the recognition of what has already been seen. For identity, when apprehended together with a prior state, enters into the domain of dispute regarding oneness. If oneness were established merely by its present existence, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, since that [present object] was already apprehended by the prior cognition, it is not something else. And by the prior cognition, it was apprehended precisely at the moment it was in a state of passing away, and thus as something new (*apūrva*). Therefore, when it is subsequently reconnected [with the past], it is [re-cognized] exactly as it is.

[022,i] One must either connect what has been apprehended with that which is exactly as it was apprehended; and if it is apprehended as having already been apprehended, this is merely a recollection. Because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, it is not a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇa*), like another instance of recollection. As for its correspondence (*saṃvāda*), however, it arises from the performance of a causal function (*arthakriyā*). And there is no causal function to be accomplished by the object's oneness, because it arises solely from the capacity of the thing itself.

Therefore, this is merely a pair of perceptions, namely "that very same thing is this. If it is argued that identity with the former is perceived [in the latter], that is incorrect; for if the former was not cognized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no means of valid cognition (*pramā*) for their identity.
To claim that identity with what is unperceived is itself perceived is an act of rashness.
(159) Therefore, this unity is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), arising from successive conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
This conventional cognition possesses no validity (*prāmāṇya*) as a means of knowledge. (160)

Even the cognition regarding objects such as a jar that occurs in relation to a collection [of atoms] arises from conceptualizing a composite whole (*samudāya*) upon an object already grasped by those [individual] cognitions.
Indeed, nothing single that exists apart from the composite whole is ever perceived by anyone. (PVA 161)
Due to the firmness of beginningless habitual tendencies, there is the calamity of not apprehending the other [aspect].
(PVA 162) [022, vii] But how, then, can cognition possess validity if there is no comprehension of the preceding, succeeding, and so forth [aspects] as one?
[022, viii] The eight types of persons who have entered the path and attained the fruit.

To this it is replied: A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is defined as that which impels one toward what is to be abandoned or what is to be adopted. In that process of impelling, cognition alone is primary. Even if the object to be realized has not yet been apprehended, it is nonetheless a means of valid cognition because it impels one toward it—just as inference is a means of valid cognition even when its object is not directly grasped. For it will be demonstrated that inference does not involve the direct acceptance of the actual nature of a thing. Furthermore, one does not act solely on the basis of the eyes and other sense organs; rather, even without conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one acts through the intellect due to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, regarding objects to be abandoned or adopted, the preceding cognition alone is the means of valid cognition because it impels one, and not conceptualization and the like. However, where there is no such practice, it is inference itself [that is the means], as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth; thus, there is no over-extension of the definition.

[022,ix] Thus far, the state of being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) has been established on the basis of the desire for a result (*phalārthitā*), insofar as it is conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
[This is because] validity consists in the capacity to effect a distinction between the object of attainment and its result.
[022,x] Now, it is explained by way of distinguishing the objects of the fruits of realization.
And because there is a difference in the forms of the objects, there is a difference in the apprehension of cognitions.

Furthermore, validity belongs to cognition alone and not to anything else. For, due to the distinction in the form of the object, there is a distinction in the apprehension which is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is not a means of valid cognition because it causes one to act, but rather because it is the instrument for comprehension. For once comprehension is known, one may either act or not; nevertheless, it is a means of valid cognition because it establishes the existence of the object as it truly is. Even if one does not act toward the object established by it, this is not a defect of the means of valid cognition. If it is argued that a means of valid cognition is so called because it brings about attainment (*prāpakatva*), we say no; it is a means of valid cognition because of its fitness for bringing about attainment. How is that very fitness known when attainment has not yet occurred? It is known from the perception of a specific characteristic (*rūpaviśeṣa*). But how is that non-deviant characteristic determined?

[022,xiii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. Furthermore, monks, I say that the cessation of craving is the abandonment of these four nutriments, their relinquishment, their rejection, and their non-arising in the future. What is the nutriment for contact? It is feeling. What is the nutriment for feeling? It is contact. What is the nutriment for contact? It is the sixfold sense base. What is the nutriment for the sixfold sense base? It is name-and-form. What is the nutriment for name-and-form? It is consciousness. What is the nutriment for consciousness? It is volitional formations. What is the nutriment for volitional formations? It is ignorance. Thus, monks, through the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; through the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; through the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; through the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the sixfold sense base; through the cessation of the sixfold sense base comes the cessation of contact; through the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; through the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; through the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; through the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering and misery. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Monks, in regard to these four noble truths, there are three turnings and twelve aspects. What are the three turnings and twelve aspects? Here, monks, in regard to this noble truth of suffering, there is the knowledge of what has not yet been known; there is the full understanding of what has not yet been fully understood; there is the final realization of what has not yet been realized. In regard to this noble truth of the origin of suffering, there is the knowledge of what has not yet been known; there is the abandoning of what has not yet been abandoned; there is the final eradication of what has not yet been eradicated. In regard to this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, there is the knowledge of what has not yet been known; there is the realization of what has not yet been realized; there is the final attainment of what has not yet been attained. In regard to this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, there is the knowledge of what has not yet been known; there is the cultivation of what has not yet been cultivated; there is the final perfection of what has not yet been perfected. Monks, for one who possesses these three turnings and twelve aspects regarding these four noble truths, and who dwells having seen them with right wisdom, it is impossible that they should not attain final liberation from all suffering. This, monks, is called the Dharma-eye, pure and stainless. Just as, monks, when rain falls in heavy torrents from the sky, the water flowing down from the mountain crevices, slopes, and valleys converges toward the great ocean; even so, monks, whatever recluses or brahmins possess the Dharma-eye, pure and stainless, all of them converge toward this very Dharma-eye, pure and stainless. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall possess the Dharma-eye, pure and stainless. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. [022,xiv] At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, stood to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well-spoken by the Blessed One were these words: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. ... [as above] ... Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall possess the Dharma-eye, pure and stainless. "Ānanda, it is because I have seen this very Dharma-eye, pure and stainless, that I have proclaimed: 'I have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are two nutriments: nutriment that is gross and nutriment that is subtle. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are three nutriments: nutriment that is internal, nutriment that is external, and nutriment that is both internal and external. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are four nutriments: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are five nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, and the nutriment of body-consciousness. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are six nutriments: the nutriment of form, the nutriment of sound, the nutriment of odor, the nutriment of taste, the nutriment of tangible object, and the nutriment of mental phenomena. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are seven nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, the nutriment of body-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-consciousness, and the nutriment of mind-element. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are eight nutriments: the nutriment of earth, the nutriment of water, the nutriment of fire, the nutriment of air, the nutriment of form, the nutriment of sound, the nutriment of odor, and the nutriment of taste. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are nine nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, the nutriment of body-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-element, and the nutriment of mind-consciousness-contact. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are ten nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, the nutriment of body-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-contact, and the nutriment of mental phenomena. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are eleven nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, the nutriment of body-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-contact, the nutriment of mental phenomena, and the nutriment of ignorance. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are twelve nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, the nutriment of body-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-contact, the nutriment of mental phenomena, the nutriment of ignorance, and the nutriment of volitional formations. "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? "Ānanda, there are thirteen nutriments: the nutriment of eye-consciousness, the nutriment of ear-consciousness, the nutriment of nose-consciousness, the nutriment of tongue-consciousness, the nutriment of body-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-consciousness, the nutriment of mind-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-element, the nutriment of mind-consciousness-contact

In that case, the conventional usage of external objects is finished. For, because it is non-erroneous, in cognition there is only the clear self-awareness of its own nature (*svarūpa-samvedana*). And so, how could there be a perception of external objects, other mental continua (*parasantāna*), and so forth? This we shall explain later. The "object-aspect" (*viṣayākāra*) is the aspect of this [cognition] which is like the form of the object; the "difference of the object-aspect" (*viṣayākārabheda*) is the difference of that [aspect]. Alternatively, the "difference of the object-aspect" is the difference of aspects within the object. An "aspect" (*ākāra*) is the act of forming (*ākaraṇa*); the meaning is "representation" (*ullekha*). It consists of similarity to the object and being directed toward the object. Indeed, from that difference comes the difference in the apprehension of cognitions, such as "the awareness of blue" and "the awareness of its aspect. And this is the apprehension of the object.

The fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is either the apprehension of its own form. Thus it has been said: "For the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition. And that [apprehension], which consists of the form of the object, is the very nature of the cognition; therefore, cognition itself is the means of valid cognition.
But surely, just as the form is of the nature of cognition, so too is the realization; therefore, it follows that cognition alone is the result.
This is true.
The result is not other than the means of valid cognition, nor is the means of valid cognition something beyond the result. Such is the entire relationship between action and its factors. (163) (PVA)
This will be demonstrated later.

Just as the eye and other [senses] are not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too should the form (*ākāra*) not be one. Just as the eye and other [senses], though they are causal factors (*kāraka*) for consciousness, are not a means of valid cognition, so too is the form. He says:
"Because its existence [depends] on the existence of that very thing."

"In its presence" means when the aspect (*ākāra*) is present. This is because of the very existence of this result, which is the realization (*adhigama*). Indeed, the existence of this result does not follow merely from the existence of the eye and other [faculties]; rather, it follows only from the existence of the aspect, because there is no distinction [between them]. Thus, [the aspect] possesses the status of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*). And it is said that "the most effective instrument is the *karaṇa*. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that the status of being the most effective instrument exists when there is no intervention.

How then is it said that "one sees form with the eye"? This is stated by applying the name of the effect to the cause, just as one says, "the village was burned by the thieves. Therefore, cognition alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, how is it to be known that this cognition is a means of attainment (*prāpaka*)? It cannot be known through perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) does not demonstrate the distinction between valid and invalid cognitions, because self-awareness exists in all cognitions whatsoever. Nor is anyone ever deceived while acting at the very moment of the arising of that cognition upon perceiving the distinction between concordant and discordant cognitions; nor would one be subject to doubt. [023,xi]

Now, if validity characterized by non-sublation (*abādhitatva*) is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then how can it be established intrinsically for those who maintain that knowledge is imperceptible (*parokṣajñānavādin*) when it is being established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? Just as the existence of knowledge is established through presumptive testimony, the validity of that knowledge is not known by another means; rather, its status as a valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) is intrinsic. Invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), however, arises from a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), and the validity of that subverting cognition is itself intrinsic.

Furthermore: cognition arises from its causes, but its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). That [intrinsic validity], moreover, is set aside by an exception—that is, by a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) characterized by the absence of sublation.
To this, it is replied:
If validity is intrinsic by virtue of its own cause,
then for that which has arisen in such a manner, there can be no alteration by other subverting factors. (164) (PVA)

Now, if it is argued that the self is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by its very nature because it consists of consciousness, and that even by a thousand subverting factors (*bādhaka*), no modification of it occurs; [we reply:
if invalidity were to arise from the presence of defective causes, [then the objection would hold]. (PVA 165)
Why is validity not accepted as resulting from the connection with a cause possessing qualities?
(PVA 166) If its validity is held to arise solely from the absence of defects, why is its invalidity not understood to arise from the absence of qualities? (PVA 167)
Nor is any other self perceived through means of valid cognition or otherwise,
by virtue of which its status as a means of valid cognition or non-valid cognition could arise from something else.
(168) If that [self] is held to be of the nature of consciousness, then it would exist even during states such as deep sleep.
The state of self-awareness never departs from this [consciousness] at any time.
(PVA 169) If nothing is then experienced, how can it be considered that "the self exists"?
Furthermore, the distinction between cognition and its opposite has gone far, far away. (PVA 170)
Therefore, knowledge arises as either valid or otherwise;
it becomes such solely due to its causes, for its validity does not exist intrinsically. (PVA 171) However, because of the presence of a similar form, there is no ascertainment of its true nature.
Because everything is initially uncontradicted, that [cognition] is not invalid;
however, subsequent contradiction is doubtful, and its ascertainment comes from another source—either through perception or inference—for there is no other means of valid cognition. (PVA 172–173)
If that cognition of correspondence applies to another object,
then how can the validity of the preceding [cognition]— which has already passed— be observed by means of it?
(PVA 174) For even the cognition of the means of proof remains a subject of doubt.

How can it possess the status of a means [of knowledge] when its validity is not recognized? (175) If it is argued that it is a means of knowledge because its nature is cognition, then it would follow that everything is a means of knowledge;
furthermore, even the cognition of an uncontradicted object is not established at the outset. (176)
Now, having recognized the efficacy [of the means] and knowing that its object is valid,
how can there be a cognition of that means of knowledge which was previously unestablished?
(177) (PVA) If the means of knowledge were already established, then it would be the knower of its application to the action.

Cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it leads to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). [Objection: It is held that validity belongs only where there is purposeful action. [Response:
Yet, such things as purposeful action are observed even from a cognition that is not a valid means of knowledge. (PVA 178–179)
If it is argued that there is no purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) [from that], then how can it be considered to come from another?
Since it is observed that at some time it is not obtained even from elsewhere, [it must be so].
If it is held that what is considered a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that from which there is no doubt regarding attainment, [then this applies here too].
For how can there be the cessation of doubt through a common form?
(181) Through repeated practice, a distinct form is subsequently perceived;
therefore, this [claim that] attainment is inseparable from it is a case of mutual dependence. (182)

If it is argued that, when those very things previously seen are now perceived, worldly activity arises from memory produced by the power of consciousness, then in that case, inference would likewise arise from perception, and perception from inference. (PVA 183) And thus,
inference would depend on perception, and perception on inference.
Precisely because of mutual dependence, neither of the two can be established.
(PVA 184) For perception, which discerns intrinsic nature, object, and aspect, is not capable of even bending a blade of grass.
[024,xix] By that [means], no connection between the prior and the posterior is grasped.
A conjunction is said to be a union through the pervasion of different places and times. (PVA 185)
If direct perception were capable of grasping [an object] as pervading other places and times,

it would follow that it must perceive everything in its entirety. Since there is no such pervasion between those two [the object and its cognition], there is therefore no inference [of the object from the cognition].
Since it occurs only occasionally, let there be an inference for its existence everywhere.
(187) Let it be known that "this exists in this form right now" even through the senses;
therefore, there is no apprehension of what resides in another place or time. (188)
And if the location and so forth have not been apprehended, how can their pervasion be apprehended?
Without the apprehension of that [pervasion], there is no inference; this is an extreme rashness.
For, by necessitating another inference, it would lead to an infinite regress.
There would be a failure to understand the subject at hand because of the requirement for each [cognition] to depend on its own [subsequent cognition].
Therefore, validity is established by nature as a general rule;
it is set aside only by the two [conditions]: the occurrence of a subverting cognition and the knowledge of defects in the cause.

If it is argued that it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory and no sublater (*bādhaka*) exists, then it is clearly indeed a valid means of knowledge; for otherwise, it would be a sublater.
To this it is replied:
The certainty of being a means of valid cognition does not arise from the mere absence of a subverting factor.
And how could there be an absence beforehand of that sublation which occurs at the time of attainment?
(193) Let it be known through a means of valid cognition that upon attainment, that capacity for causal efficiency is secured;
and that [attainment] is subsequently discerned from the cognition that is self-aware of its own nature. (194)
But first, inference operates there upon an existent entity;

consequently, that same infinite regress would occur. How, then, could there be any attainment of the status of a means of valid cognition? (195) No means of cognition other than perception and inference is admitted. (196) (PVA)
To this, it is said:
The comprehension of its own nature occurs through itself. 4.
Validity is established by conventional practice.

For the cognition of its own nature (*svarūpa*) occurs by itself, not that of another nature (*pararūpa*). Direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed direct apprehension, and this belongs to the nature of the object itself, not to the future nature characterized by the time of attainment. Furthermore, the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) consists in the non-deviation from the object to be attained; and there can be no apprehension of a relation when the object to be attained has not been apprehended. Nor does something remain determined as a means of valid cognition if it is not so ascertained. Indeed, all cognitions are indistinguishably attached to the form present before them, yet there is no grasping of a relation with a future form, nor is there a grasping of a relation with a previous form through a cognition of future causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). [Therefore, because they consist in the self-cognition of their own nature, there is no grasping of a relation for each individual cognition. Nor is a collective synthesis possible, since the grasping of the means and the causal efficiency occur sequentially. As for the recollection that arises at a later time, it conceptualizes the two as related even though they are unrelated, proceeding according to how they were experienced. However, because it abandons the actual experience, it is merely corrupted by that [experience]; thus, no understanding of the relation arises from it. Consequently, since that relation is not grasped, how could there be an understanding of it later on through inference based on similarity to what was seen? Therefore, the means for the understanding of validity is not [inference]. Thus, "the cognition of its own nature alone occurs by itself, not [that] of validity."
iv] Now, if validity were the very nature [of the cognition] itself, because it is not distinct from that which is expressed by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), then that is incorrect. [025, v]
Validity is of the nature of cognition and is concomitant with the form of the object to be apprehended;
it is said that when there is the grasping of the mere nature [of the cognition], that [validity] is not grasped.

Validity is not the very nature of cognition itself, because it is established as such through its relation to the object to be attained; and it has already been demonstrated that this [validity] is not apprehended. Consequently, there would be nothing but the mere self-awareness of one's own nature, devoid of engagement or withdrawal, and thus there would be no entry into the Buddhist path. Therefore, discerning persons should neither engage in anything nor withdraw from anything at all.

How, then, is validity established as being excluded from invalidity? [The answer is: "Validity is established by means of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). This has been demonstrated to be merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*). And when this worldly convention is subjected to critical analysis, it simply falls apart. In that case, if satisfaction is found with this much, then nothing at all needs to be done; liberation from saṃsāra would follow precisely because of its absolute non-existence. Alternatively, if saṃsāra is accepted as established by worldly convention, then the distinction between valid and invalid cognition also exists. Therefore, no effort need be exerted to establish the nature of validity.

Furthermore, by one who establishes that validity is merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*), it is effectively stated that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), there is only one means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
For it is said: "If validity [were established] through perception or through inference... [025, ix]
Success is attained; doubt regarding the subject matter of legal procedure is in vain.

If the establishment of its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is already perfectly clear through either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), for what purpose is it said to be established by "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*)? Therefore, by relying on an inference established merely through conventional usage, and based on a relationship that is well-known, one engages in the apprehension of the means for touching and so forth—thinking, "This is the accomplishment of purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*)—upon seeing [it]. Subsequently, even without the inference of repeated practice, activity occurs from mere appearance alone; thus, even direct perception is a valid means of cognition because it is instigative (*pravarttaka*). For this reason, it is said: "Validity is established by conventional usage."

Now, it may be objected: by means of vision, only color-form (*rūpa*) is perceived, not the tangible; likewise, only the present is perceived, not the future or the attainable; and likewise, only what is visible to oneself is perceived, not what is visible to another. Therefore, how can perception be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through the attainment of something else? To this it has been said: "The cognition of its own nature occurs by itself. Furthermore:

From the perspective of conventional usage, the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established on account of unity. Because there is no difference in location and so forth, the unity of the substance (*dravya*) is designated. (PVA 199)

This has been stated: “Validity [is established] by means of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, relying upon the unity of the whole (*avayavin*) as established by conventional practice, there occurs the conventional usage of validity based on the determination that “whatever was seen is the very same thing that is attained. And that determination of unity arises from the non-difference of place, time, and so forth. That non-difference, too, results from the production of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) possessing that capacity. Likewise, even in the case of things past and future, there is the conceit of unity due to their belonging to the same continuum and because they perform the same purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Now, [it may be argued that] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is so called because it brings about purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). But is this validity (*prāmāṇya*) a knower of purposeful action, or is it its producer? It cannot be a producer, for in that case the means of cognition would be an instrument (*karaṇa*). If, on the other hand, it is called a means of cognition because it is a knower, that too is incorrect.
[026.vii] It is not a signifier of that object, because there remains doubt regarding its causal efficiency.
Since causal efficiency occurs only occasionally, how could it possess the status of a signifier? (PVA 200)

[026, viii] Even in the absence of the cognition of the means (*sādhanajñāna*), the fulfillment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is observed. How, then, could that [cognition] be the cause of such purposeful action? For even without it, a result might occur by virtue of what is yet to be; nor is it an indicator (*jñāpaka*), since even when the object is seen, purposeful action is sometimes absent. Furthermore, that cognition is not invalid (*apramāṇa*), because it is not devoid of the object. Therefore, in the absence of being either a producer (*kārakatva*) or an indicator (*jñāpakatva*), how can it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that brings about purposeful action?
To this it is replied:
Even if there is doubt regarding the goal (*upeya*), that alone does not mean it is not valid cognition (*pramā*).

Since the means is certain, why is it not a valid cognition (*pramā*) by that much alone? (PVA 201) Indeed, there is no desire to avoid doubt regarding the end (*upeya*), because activity occurs everywhere merely through the certainty of the means. Therefore, once the means is certain, let those who act according to valid cognition proceed like farmers and the like.
That is incorrect, because:
[026,xiii]
Everyone engages in activity or desists from it out of a desire for the goal to be attained;
if there is doubt regarding that [goal], how can [the cognition] be a means of valid knowledge?

Regarding that for which a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought, since there is doubt concerning the goal (*upeya*), what kind of verbal expression is this—that it is a "means of valid cognition"? Now, it may be argued that an object must be made known by a means of valid cognition, but not that the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) must be performed. For how can causal efficacy—which occurs later, arising from some particular collection of conditions (*sāmagrīviśeṣa*)—be made known?
That too is incorrect.
[026,xvii]
If that for whose sake this undertaking was begun remains unaccomplished, then how can the connection with the probandum, being unestablished, be called a means of proof? (203) (PVA) [027,i]

A discerning person is intent on investigating the validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the thought, "May I attain the accomplishment of my desired object through this valid means," and not otherwise; for otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere addiction. Furthermore, if an object is revealed but does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), how is it distinguished from an illusion, such as the hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia? In both cases, there is no difference from what is non-beneficial (*anartha*).

Now, it may happen that at some time there occurs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in that case, but not in the instance of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) and so forth. If this is so, how does one who desires that object proceed? Indeed, one who proceeds out of doubt does not proceed by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For a valid cognition is determinative; it does not produce doubt. If it is argued that there is certainty regarding that which performs purposeful action, then how can there be such certainty when the purposeful action itself has not been ascertained? Or, if it is argued that the object capable of accomplishing the purpose was shown by that valid cognition, but the purposeful action does not occur due to some deficiency, then this is not a fault of the valid cognition.
That too is incorrect:
if it is observed that the non-informativeness of a means of cognition is not a defect, [then what fault is there]?

"There would be no other defect in it, and thus everything would be valid cognition" (PVA). That by which an object is measured—that is, determined—is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And that which does not make known lacks the power of determination; therefore, it is not valid cognition. Consequently, it is understood otherwise.

Cognition is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it brings about the certain realization of the nature of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); this is due to its identity with that [action] and its arising from it. (PVA 205)

Indeed, that cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), because it has the nature of purposeful action itself, leads to the fulfillment of that purposeful action; therefore, with respect to that purposeful action, it alone is the cognition of the means (*sādhanajñāna*). However, as for the preceding cognition of the means: if this object has been determined as stable, then since the prior nature necessarily brings about the future state at the time of attainment, there is the attainment of that [future state]. Consequently, the subsequent nature is in reality nothing but the very nature of the prior one; thus, even in that case, there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*).

Alternatively, that effect which is necessarily bound to arise is indeed the cause, because it is pervaded by it; and whatever is distinct and pervasive is itself the cause, since without it the effect would not exist. [Objection: How can that which has not yet arisen be a cause? [Response: How can that which has already arisen be a cause? The fault is the same in both cases.

Indeed, worldly people understand the causal relationship through such principles as: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises; this exerts an activity here; this is produced by that. Now, for a future entity, there is neither existence, nor arising, nor activity, nor causality, because it is non-existent at that time.
To this, it is replied:
The arising of beings and so forth, because they possess the intrinsic nature of entities, do not belong to another self.
Since it is said "when this exists," there is no possibility of something else that is not part of this very thing. (206) (PVA)

[027, xiii] For arising (*utpāda*) is not something other than the nature (*svabhāva*) of existence (*sattā*). If existence arises from another cause, why does existence arise only immediately after that? If this were so, then the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of one who has been asleep for a long time and has just awakened would not arise from previous habituation, because they would lack the state of being immediate. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that the body and so forth are not the cause. Nor is activity (*vyāpāra*) anything other than the intrinsic nature; thus it follows that it is the essential form itself. And at the time of the effect, the essential form does not exist for the duration of time. [028, i]

The mere state of being invariably concomitant with what precedes it exists even in the case of that which is yet to be; for the effect is necessarily dependent upon its cause, and thus the cause is also that which is yet to be. If it is argued that only that which is observed there as pervading and being the cause is the cause because it precedes, and not that which is yet to be—[we reply: No.
No. It is the perceived object that is understood to have pervasiveness by way of its own nature; this [pervasiveness] could also belong to a future object by way of an imputed form. (PVA 207)

For that which is being perceived is not, by that much alone, the pervader of the pervaded, because the latter is not cognized at that time. And when the pervaded is cognized, then the pervader exists in its future form; otherwise, if the future form were not apprehended, there would be no state of pervasion.
Now, it is not the case that its pervasiveness is perceived by means of that very form in which it was previously seen— that is, by means of its past form— and not by means of its future form.
That is incorrect.
If future form is not perceived, pervasiveness is not perceived;
for pervasion would not be merely partial—it must be such as that. (PVA 208)
