Even though it apprehends what has not yet been apprehended, the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). What is the reason? [It is because] "when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is unknown. That cognition alone is intended to be a valid means of knowledge, and not even that which pertains to a universal. The cognition of a universal that is already known is not a valid means of knowledge; rather, it is the cognition of a particular characteristic that is unknown [which is]. Why is this so? Because of the investigation of the particular characteristic. A person of discernment requires a valid means of knowledge for the purpose of establishing whether something exists or does not exist. And that investigation as to whether it exists or does not exist concerns only the particular characteristic, not the universal, because people have no regard for the latter. Furthermore, wherever there is such an investigation, the valid means of knowledge subsequently attains its own nature [of determining existence or non-existence]; thus, the operation of the valid means of knowledge does not apply to the universal. Therefore, it is not a valid means of knowledge with respect to that [universal].

[031.iv] Now, if the universal (*sāmānya*) is not apprehended, how can one act after knowing "this is that very same thing"? It is not so; for even without the apprehension of a universal, one acts due to extreme habituation (*atyantābhyāsa*). If it is argued that in that case too, the universal alone is the motivator, we reply: no, because there is no knowledge of an unknown entity being a motivator. Even if it were known, if its particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were not known, one would not act. But when the particular characteristic is known, one acts through habituation even without the determination of a universal. Therefore, since it does not motivate action in that regard and lacks the capacity to face toward the object, cognition of the universal is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [031.v]

Or, let it be that [the cognition] is an initiator; even so, because it lacks orientation toward that [object], it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to it. However, if it is apprehended through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then that is simply the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, the means of valid cognition has only the particular characteristic as its object. But when there is non-duality (*advaita*), then there is no universal (*sāmānya*). And in that case, the designation "other" or "not other" occurs only after the realization of the particular characteristic.

*Avit*: that which does not possess *vid* (knowledge) is *avit*. Where? At the time when the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is known; for that knowledge [of the universal] arises. Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a temporal sequence of prior and posterior by which this [universal] could be recognized as occurring at a later time than the knowledge of the particular, or as being of a different nature.
In every case here, it is the particular itself that is perceived in that cognition; and there is no distinction [between them].
[031, viii] The eight types of persons who have entered the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

For what purpose, then, did the Blessed One teach the distinction between perception and inference, as well as the distinction between external objects and consciousness? He replied: "[It was taught] 'with a specific intention' and because of non-contradiction. With the intention regarding the knowledge of those to be trained (*vineya*), and with reference to them, self-awareness alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else. This is out of consideration for disciples who delight in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). There is no contradiction, for the Blessed One's teaching is such that it enables disciples to enter the path to reality (*tattvamārga*) in whatever way possible for them. Why is this so? "Because when analyzed according to its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For when everything is analyzed, it completely falls apart. There is no reality other than non-duality (*advaita*). That very [reality] is analyzed by the Blessed One gradually, because it is impossible to analyze it all at once.
[3] (3) The Authority of the Blessed One:
Now, how can that which revolves externally be self-cognized? This is not so.
The cognition of "external" and "internal" arises from dependence on space, time, and so forth;
for apart from its own intrinsic nature, it is associated with space and time. (PVA 225)
And this will be demonstrated later.

If that is so, how then is the Blessed One an authority? For it is only perception and inference that possess authority by way of mere conventional usage, not the Blessed One; for he is the supreme authority.
To this, it is replied:
In the same way, the Blessed One is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For the Blessed One is a Tathāgata; considering him as such, the Blessed One is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in his very perceptible form, as will be demonstrated later.
From what is this understood? To that he says:

The statement that [the object] "exists" is for the purpose of excluding what has not come to be; since it depends upon a means of proof (*sādhana*), its status as a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is therefore logical. (7)

[032,vii] For the purpose of eliminating error: since that Blessed One’s speech is "true," he alone is omniscient and not anyone else; and thus he is a valid authority (*pramāṇa*). And it has been said: "Therefore, his status as a valid authority is rightly dependent upon the means of proof (*sādhana*). This applies to the Blessed One alone, not to the Veda. For regarding the Veda, there is no means of knowledge whatsoever for its connection with any object. However, for this [Blessed One], his very true speech is the means of knowledge within the domain of valid cognition. As for other matters, we shall explain them later. [032,viii]

Alternatively, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even the Blessed One is an authority only through the realization of non-duality (*advaita*); it is not by virtue of his complete knowledge of all things. Complete knowledge of all things, however, is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) according to worldly usage. Thus it has been said: "The non-dual vehicle is supreme. [Chapter 3: *Īśvaraniṣedha-vārttika* (The Refutation of God).
Section 1: The Lack of Authority of God and Others.]

**(1) The lack of authority for the eternal and the non-eternal:** Now, if it is argued that since perception and inference are not authoritative, only an omniscient being is authoritative—then either an eternal knower such as Īśvara must be the authority, or the eternal Veda is the authority. What is the point of seeking anything else? To this, he says:

[032,x] There is no eternal means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because validity arises from the correspondence with a real entity; since that correspondence is impermanent due to the impermanence of the objects of knowledge, it is non-eternal because it arises sequentially. 8.

[032,xi] Because there is no production from that which is eternal, dependence is impossible. Indeed, there is no eternal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that persists forever, because such a means of valid cognition does not exist. Furthermore, a means of valid cognition is the apprehension of a real entity (*vastusat*), not of anything whatsoever; nor does a real entity exist at all times, such that its apprehension would occur perpetually. Therefore, due to the impermanence of the object of knowledge, that [apprehension] as well is non-eternal.

Now, one might ask: on what basis is it said that cognition is impermanent because its object is impermanent? For there is no possibility of any other alternative: [cognition’s being a means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*)] must consist either in an operation upon the form of the object, or in arising from the form of the object, or in having that [form] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatā*). In this regard, if there is no distinction between that which is operating and that which is not, how can there be a differentiation between "operation" and "other"?

If it is argued that, like a mirror, whatever object is present is precisely what appears [in the cognition], then it follows that the object itself arises in such a way through its own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), and there is no operation on the part of the cognizer.

[033,i] Furthermore, even when the eyes are opened without moving, one perceives objects as they arrive in succession; never is a nature consisting of mutually distinct and successive operations perceived by another, and it is the same for that [consciousness] as well.
To this it is replied:
Even in that case, the activity of the eye is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Positive and negative concomitance do not exist for an eternal post.
Therefore, this is merely an object as it is; since there is no operation of anything whatsoever in its apprehension, how can it be a means of valid cognition?
[033,v] Now, let that object be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, because it is related to it, it is said to be "known" by that [cognition]. This is not tenable, because:
A relationship is established through positive concomitance preceded by negative concomitance;
how can there be the possibility of a relationship for that which is eternal and lacks negative concomitance?
Indeed, it cannot be understood that something eternal and non-distinct is of any utility anywhere.

If it is argued that there is utility because it is seen by that [agent], then this very point has been challenged: "How is it by that? When that [agent] exists, [the object] becomes such; thus it is said to be "by that. But since that [agency] also exists in the case of space and so forth, how could space itself be the seer? Because there is no designation of that purpose for space, it is the agent alone who is the seer, not space and the like.
[033,ix] Explanation is speech; therefore, why is this very thing considered [the cause]?
And if there is no distinction whatsoever, causality is not understood. 228 (PVA)
How does an object that is past or future appear?
If it is a cognition [of it] as being past, how can that [object] be past? (229) Nor is there a transfer into a mirror of what is past and so forth; how could that be?
A reflection of that nature is possible when a mirror exists.
(PVA 230) It has been stated previously that for an eternal entity, there can be no effect;
[if it were so], why would the apprehension of objects not also apply to space and the like? (PVA 231)
In the case of [the claim] that it perceives all objects, what is said to be the meaning of that statement?
If it is not understood that its occurrence is invariably subsequent to that [perception], then the word derived from the perception of all objects would be the designator of everything. (232) (PVA)
A restriction based on the speaker’s intention is not logically possible for that which is eternal.
(233) Those intentions are distinct, and likewise, the perceptions are distinct.
How can there be a unity for you on the part of the perceiver, and how can he be your valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? (234)
If that very same [cognition] were the apprehender of both the intended visible object and something other than it, how could there be a single grasping of them? (235) Why,
then, is the identity of perception and inference not likewise asserted?
If, from the perspective of ultimate reality, even those two are held to be one,
then there is no difference between them, whether they occur successively or simultaneously.
Their single nature is indeed apprehended by means of valid cognition as being successive.

If an object is not cognized as being one by that [cognition] and another, how can it be true that it is one? If it is untrue, such a statement is in vain. (238) Or, even if that [object] is itself understood by the cognizer in every respect as having a self-nature...
"By whom was he created? Let him go thus"—this is merely a matter of words.
It has been established previously that there is nothing other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Therefore, this Lord (*īśvara*) is neither ultimately real nor is he a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

[033,xxii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if cognition is impermanent because its objects are impermanent, that which is the cognizer is permanent. Nor is it logical to say that the impermanence of one thing implies the impermanence of another; for cognition, which arises sequentially, is impermanent due to the impermanence of its objects.
[033,xxiii]

Because there is a dissociation from arising from what is eternal; for arising from what is eternal is impossible. It has been established that what is eternal and all-pervading, like space, is not the cause of anything. If it were to produce [an effect] by means of that very same nature, it would produce it at all times, because there is no distinction [in its nature]. And if there were a distinction, it would be non-eternal.

[034,i] Now, if it is argued that even though there is no difference [in the entity], the effect occurs sequentially due to the presence or absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), [we reply: No. This is because dependence (*apekṣā*) has no utility. If only the auxiliary causes possess positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then they alone are the cause, and not that [entity]. It is not tenable to say that its causality is due to dependence on them; for there is no difference between the state of that [entity] when it is dependent and its other state. Whether this state of being dependent is perceived by itself or by another is merely a matter of words; at best, this is all that can be understood. Therefore, he says: [034,ii]
Because dependence is impossible.

For that which is eternal is always of a single nature; it cannot be assisted by that which is depended upon. Indeed, that which provides no assistance cannot be an object of dependence for it. If that is so, then the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will be non-eternal, yet it does not depend on the practice of giving and so forth. Since its possession of dispassion and sovereignty arises from preceding causes of a similar kind, it never becomes otherwise, nor does it possess an origination that is different [from its prior state].
To this, it is said:
Because it cannot be assisted in any way, non-eternality is indeed not a means of valid cognition.

Even if God were impermanent, there would be no validity [to his authority]; that is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why is this so? "Because he is not benefited in any way. For one who is benefited or harmed by someone in some way—such that, upon experiencing passion and the like, or upon the possibility of realizing the antidotes to passion and so forth, there occurs the teaching of them; and because the teaching is possible through affection for beings and compassion—it becomes a means of valid cognition for the world. It does not arise from the mere existence of his own nature. Nor is this [teaching] his [inherent] proficiency; for one does not become wise simply by being unimpaired.

Now, as for the claim that his complete knowledge is established by its very nature (*svabhāvāsiddhi*), this is incorrect. If he does not experience passion and the like, how can there be an awakening to the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the manifold world (*saṃsāraprapañca*)? If he does experience them, then he is simply a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*); how, then, could he possess the status of a valid authority (*pramāṇatā*)? [The opponent might argue: "It is precisely through the awakening to passion and the like that there is the teaching of the antidotes to the manifold of passion and so forth; indeed, the possession of passion and the like, along with its indestructibility and connection with incomparable power, constitutes omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and thus he alone is the valid authority.
This too is incorrect.
The teaching of the antidote to passion and the like would be purposeless,
if unshakable sovereignty were to exist even while one is joined with passion and the like. (241) (PVA)
[034,x] Now, this is the actual state of things: since the occurrence of sovereignty is not possible for one who possesses passion and the like, there is consequently the teaching of its antidote.
If this is so, then because there is no cultivation, detachment and the like are impossible;
how then could his sovereignty and other qualities be established without a cause?
For it is not known that what arises from the cultivation of the antidotes such as detachment can also arise otherwise.
Furthermore:
He does not possess such power to grant boons by which he might bestow sovereignty upon a petitioner even without the latter performing the required practice. (243) (PVA)
Now, if that capacity does not exist at all, how could there be another [capacity] either?
Since it would be impossible for anything to have the power to assist, the consequence is that [the opponent's position] lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*).

This is also the meaning: even in the case of what is impermanent, there is no lack of authority (*apramāṇatā*). "Authority" (*pramāṇa*) means that which exists in this; the state of not being that is "lack of authority. This amounts to saying that there is no authority in that regard.

[034,xvii] Furthermore, by way of propitiation—that is, by way of the pacification of passion and so forth—there is the performance of beneficial action, because it is impossible to effect such benefit otherwise than through the teaching of the Dharma.
That is incorrect, because:
By what means is it understood that the performance of what was taught by him brings benefit to the world?
If it is understood solely from the scripture he taught, then there is a mutual dependence:
this is a scripture because it was taught by him, and it was taught by him because it is a scripture.
Since they are mutually dependent, how can either one of them be established?
Furthermore:
From what cause has such a capacity of his come? How can it be understood that "this is his very nature"? (247) (PVA)

[035,v] But from what cause has such a power of his—consisting in the favoring of all philosophical systems—come about? If it is argued that the answer must be stated here in terms of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things, as to why they come to be thus, then it is as follows:
To whom can the question "Why is it this way and not otherwise?
be directed? Fire burns, but space does not; what question could there be regarding that?
This is utterly non-existent;
for when intrinsic nature is established through perception, it is questioned by opponents.
To this, the following reply must be stated: "There is no inconsistency with what is observed.

But this is not the case regarding the imperceptible. For here, the meaning of "the answer must be stated by means of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things" is that this is established by means of valid cognitions such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is not a subject for questioning as to how it is so. Just as fire, perceived through direct perception, is not to be questioned as to how it burns the combustible object—lest, by virtue of being an element (*bhūta*), even space should burn—or if [it is argued] that it is due to a specific intrinsic nature, then it is the same for God: though devoid of all causes of qualities, he possesses qualities. [Response: It is not the same, because fire is observed [to do so] while the other is the opposite; therefore, this is no answer. Otherwise, if one were unable to provide an answer in any instance where something is accepted as having a certain nature, then the answer here must be stated by means of the intrinsic natures of things. In this way, the opponent would be victorious in every respect. Therefore, it is well said: "Even in the case of the non-eternal"—by the word "even," it is also meant that there is a lack of validity in the case of the eternal.
(2) Refutation of Īśvara: [035,x] But surely there is a means of valid cognition [for his existence].

[035,xi] Having remained [in its cause], how could the effects— such as activity, specific configuration, and causal efficiency— not establish the existence of the cause through those very effects? (PVA 250)

[035,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. [035,xiii] It was said: “Physical food as gross nutriment. To what extent is it “physical food”? To what extent is it “gross nutriment”? There is physical food that is gross, and there is physical food that is subtle. What is physical food that is gross? It refers to boiled rice, cooked grain, barley-meal, meat, fish, milk, curds, butter, cheese, sesame oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. This is called physical food that is gross. What is physical food that is subtle? It refers to the odors, tastes, and tangibles that are the objects of the tongue’s faculty of gustation. This is called physical food that is subtle. Thus, to this extent it is “physical food,” and to this extent it is “gross nutriment. [035,xiv] It was said: “Contact as the second. To what extent is it “contact”? To what extent is it “nutriment”? There is contact that is not nutriment, and there is contact that is nutriment. What is contact that is not nutriment? It refers to the contact associated with the eye-faculty when it is in a state of non-attention, or the contact associated with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, or mind-faculty when they are in a state of non-attention. This is called contact that is not nutriment. What is contact that is nutriment? It refers to the contact associated with the eye-faculty when it is in a state of attention, or the contact associated with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, or mind-faculty when they are in a state of attention. This is called contact that is nutriment. Thus, to this extent it is “contact,” and to this extent it is “nutriment. [035,xv] It was said: “Mental volition as the third. To what extent is it “mental volition”? To what extent is it “nutriment”? There is mental volition that is not nutriment, and there is mental volition that is nutriment. What is mental volition that is not nutriment? It refers to the mental volition associated with the eye-faculty when it is in a state of non-attention, or the mental volition associated with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, or mind-faculty when they are in a state of non-attention. This is called mental volition that is not nutriment. What is mental volition that is nutriment? It refers to the mental volition associated with the eye-faculty when it is in a state of attention, or the mental volition associated with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, or mind-faculty when they are in a state of attention. This is called mental volition that is nutriment. Thus, to this extent it is “mental volition,” and to this extent it is “nutriment. [035,xvi] It was said: “Consciousness as the fourth. To what extent is it “consciousness”? To what extent is it “nutriment”? There is consciousness that is not nutriment, and there is consciousness that is nutriment. What is consciousness that is not nutriment? It refers to the consciousness associated with the eye-faculty when it is in a state of non-attention, or the consciousness associated with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, or mind-faculty when they are in a state of non-attention. This is called consciousness that is not nutriment. What is consciousness that is nutriment? It refers to the consciousness associated with the eye-faculty when it is in a state of attention, or the consciousness associated with the ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, or mind-faculty when they are in a state of attention. This is called consciousness that is nutriment. Thus, to this extent it is “consciousness,” and to this extent it is “nutriment. [035,xvii] It was said: “For the maintenance of beings who have already come to be. To what extent is it “for the maintenance”? To what extent is it “of beings who have already come to be”? There are beings who have already come to be, and there are beings who have not yet come to be. What are beings who have already come to be? They are those born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by spontaneous generation—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception. These are called beings who have already come to be. What are beings who have not yet come to be? They are those who, having passed away from here, are reborn in the realm of non-perception, or those who, having passed away from here, are reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are called beings who have not yet come to be. Thus, to this extent it is “for the maintenance,” and to this extent it is “of beings who have already come to be. [035,xviii] It was said: “And for the support of those seeking a new existence. To what extent is it “for the support”? To what extent is it “of those seeking a new existence”? There are beings who have not yet come to be, and there are beings who have already come to be. What are beings who have not yet come to be? They are those who, having passed away from here, are reborn in the realm of non-perception, or those who, having passed away from here, are reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are called beings who have not yet come to be. What are beings who have already come to be? They are those born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by spontaneous generation—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception. These are called beings who have already come to be. Thus, to this extent it is “for the support,” and to this extent it is “of those seeking a new existence. [035,xix] It was said: “There are these four nutriments. To what extent is it “four”? To what extent is it “nutriments”? There are nutriments that are internal and there are nutriments that are external. What are the nutriments that are internal? They are the nutriments that are appropriated by one's own continuity. What are the nutriments that are external? They are the nutriments that are not appropriated by one's own continuity. Thus, to this extent it is “four,” and to this extent it is “nutriments. [035,xx] It was said: “For the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. To what extent is it “for the maintenance”? To what extent is it “for the support”? There is maintenance and there is support. What is maintenance? It is the cause for the persistence of those who have already come to be. What is support? It is the cause for the arising of those seeking a new existence. Thus, to this extent it is “for the maintenance,” and to this extent it is “for the support. [035,xxi] It was said: “There are these four nutriments. To what extent is it “four”? To what extent is it “nutriments”? There are nutriments that are past, there are nutriments that are future, and there are nutriments that are present. What are the nutriments that are past? They are the nutriments that have already ceased, already passed away, already vanished, already changed, already become otherwise, already become extinct, already become cool, already become extinguished, and already become ceased. What are the nutriments that are future? They are the nutriments that have not yet been produced, have not yet arisen, have not yet appeared, have not yet manifested, have not yet come to pass, have not yet occurred, have not yet been reached, and have not yet arrived. What are the nutriments that are present? They are the nutriments that have already been produced, have already arisen, have already appeared, have already manifested, have already come to pass, have already occurred, have already been reached, and have already arrived. Thus, to this extent it is “four,” and to this extent it is “nutriments. [035,xxii] It was said: “There are these four nutriments. To what extent is it “four”? To what extent is it “nutriments”? There are nutriments that are internal and there are nutriments that are external. What are the nutriments that are internal? They are the nutriments that are appropriated by one's own continuity. What are

Otherwise, there would be no inference of any other instrument [of action] either. To explain: whatever object, having remained stationary for some time, proceeds toward the accomplishment of its intended purpose, does so because it is presided over by an intelligent cause—just as an axe or similar tool is used for the purpose of splitting wood and the like. Indeed, axes and such do not proceed of their own accord; if they did, they would proceed at all times. Furthermore, since there is proceeding after a period of remaining stationary, there must be some intelligent instigator who sets it in motion. Whatever possesses a specific configuration, dimensionality, and so forth, is produced by an intelligent being, just like a jar or the like. Likewise, whatever performs a causal function is impelled by an intelligent entity, just like jars and other such things. Here, an objection is raised:
[035, xiii] Regarding persistence, activity, specific configuration, purposeful action, and so forth,
there is either the proof of what is already accepted, a lack of proof, or doubt concerning the example. (10)

[035,xiv] These factors, such as "abiding and then proceeding" (*sthitvā pravṛtti*), which are intended to be reasons based on effect (*kāryahetu*), are not valid reasons. For even when these are present, only that which is already desired is established; this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, a [point] already established cannot constitute a thesis (*pakṣa*), because only that which is unestablished is a thesis. Indeed, it is appropriate to present a proof for the sake of establishing that regarding which there is a dispute. Moreover, everything is accepted as being presided over by volition (*cetanā*) characterized as karma. For: [036,i]

"The diversity of the world is born of karma; that [karma] is volition and it is mental. [036, ii] Now, is it not the case that it is not being proven that [the world] is born solely of karma? For it is being proven that [the world] is presided over by the volition of a Lord (īśvara) distinct from karma. And thus he says: "And that [arises] precisely from dharma manifested by the impulse of the Lord. Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the proof that [the world] is preceded by karma presided over by the impulse of the Lord.

[036,iii] The Bodhisattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many kinds of bodhisattvas are there? The Blessed One replied: “Maitreya, there are five kinds of bodhisattvas. “Which five, Blessed One? “They are: the bodhisattva who abides in the lineage; the bodhisattva who has entered the path of practice; the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of certainty; the bodhisattva who has reached the final birth; and the bodhisattva who is in his last existence. “What is the bodhisattva who abides in the lineage? “It is one who possesses the nature of a bodhisattva by virtue of the excellence of their spiritual lineage, but who has not yet entered the path of practice. “What is the bodhisattva who has entered the path of practice? “It is one who, having entered the path of practice through the cultivation of the roots of virtue conducive to penetration, has not yet attained the stage of certainty. “What is the bodhisattva who has attained the stage of certainty? “It is one who has attained the stage of certainty through the cultivation of the roots of virtue conducive to penetration, and who is irreversible from the realization of all-knowledge. “What is the bodhisattva who has reached the final birth? “It is one who, having been born in the Tuṣita heaven, will descend from there and attain supreme perfect enlightenment in this very life. “What is the bodhisattva who is in his last existence? “It is one who, having descended from the Tuṣita heaven, has entered the womb, been born, and has performed all the deeds of a bodhisattva up to the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the bodhisattva who has reached the final birth and the bodhisattva who is in his last existence? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has already descended from the Tuṣita heaven, while the latter has not yet descended. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the bodhisattva who is in his last existence and the Tathāgata? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has not yet abandoned the obscurations of afflictions and cognizable objects, whereas the Tathāgata has abandoned them both. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Tathāgata and the Pratyekabuddha? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has attained the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows through the power of another, whereas the latter has attained it through his own power. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Pratyekabuddha and the Śrāvaka? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has attained the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows through his own power, whereas the latter has attained it through the instruction of another. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Śrāvaka and the bodhisattva? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former seeks only his own benefit, whereas the latter seeks the benefit of both himself and others. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the bodhisattva and the Mahāsattva? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is so called because he has generated the thought of awakening, whereas the latter is so called because he has practiced the great perfections. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Mahāsattva and the Tathāgata? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has not yet fully realized the dharmas of a Buddha, whereas the latter has fully realized them. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Tathāgata and the Arhat? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has abandoned the obscurations of afflictions and cognizable objects, whereas the latter has abandoned only the obscurations of afflictions. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Arhat and the Pratyekabuddha? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has attained the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows through the instruction of another, whereas the latter has attained it through his own power. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Pratyekabuddha and the bodhisattva? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former seeks only his own benefit, whereas the latter seeks the benefit of both himself and others. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the bodhisattva and the Buddha? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former has not yet manifested the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion, whereas the latter has manifested them all. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Buddha and the Dharma? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the one who has realized the Dharma, whereas the latter is the Dharma itself that has been realized. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Dharma and the Saṃgha? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the path to be traversed, whereas the latter is the community of those who have traversed it. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Saṃgha and the Bodhisattva? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former consists of those who have entered the stages of the Śrāvakas, whereas the latter is one who has entered the stages of the Bodhisattvas. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Bodhisattva and the Mahāyāna? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the practitioner, whereas the latter is the vehicle by which he proceeds. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Tathāgata? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the means of attainment, whereas the latter is the one who has attained it. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Tathāgata and the Nirvāṇa? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the one who has entered Nirvāṇa, whereas the latter is the state of peace that has been entered. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between Nirvāṇa and the Dharmadhātu? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the cessation of suffering, whereas the latter is the ultimate reality of all phenomena. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Dharmadhātu and the Tathatā? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the universal nature of all things, whereas the latter is the suchness of that nature. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between Tathatā and the Bodhi? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the object of realization, whereas the latter is the realization itself. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between Bodhi and the Tathāgata? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the wisdom that has awakened, whereas the latter is the person who has awakened. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Tathāgata and the world? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the one who has transcended the world, whereas the latter is the realm of saṃsāra. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the world and the beings therein? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the environment, whereas the latter are the inhabitants. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the inhabitants and the Tathāgata? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former are subject to birth and death, whereas the latter is free from birth and death. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Tathāgata and space? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is conditioned, whereas the latter is unconditioned. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between space and the Dharma? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is non-material, whereas the latter is the essence of all phenomena. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Dharma and emptiness? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the teaching, whereas the latter is its true nature. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between emptiness and the Bodhisattva? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the characteristic of all things, whereas the latter is the one who realizes that characteristic. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Bodhisattva and the Prajñāpāramitā? “Maitreya, the distinction is that the former is the one who practices, whereas the latter is the perfection of wisdom. “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the Prajñāpāramitā and the Tathāgata? “Maitreya

This is not so. If karma were of the nature of volition (*cetanā*), then the means of establishing another's volition would be redundant; for that [karma], being insentient, is incapable of initiating activity on its own, since we observe that activity occurs only after determining "this is it. Therefore, one must either act by determining it oneself—since there is no other alternative—or through the instigation of a determiner. Among these, insentient things lack self-determination. If even determination by another were absent, non-activity would necessarily follow. Thus, the intention is that there must be another, sentient, instigator. In this regard:
If volition alone, being of the nature of action, is the cause of activity,
then even when it is being examined, no further examination of that [volition] is required. (PVA 251)
And thus, the example is unestablished.
Even though they are produced by an intelligent agent, pots and the like were not created by God, because there would be no purpose; otherwise, God himself would be subject to a creator.
If it were to proceed toward its own purposeful activity, an infinite regress would result;
yet, that potter and so forth also proceeds only when set in motion [by another].
The Lord is not ignorant; as one who knows that [reality], he is not impelled by another.
(PVA 253) This living being is ignorant and lacks mastery over its own pleasure and pain.
Impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into hell. (PVA 254)

For one who is ignorant, even if possessed of volition, is incapable of discernment. Because he, like a jar or similar object, is incapable of discernment by himself, he is impelled by another; however, this does not lead to an infinite regress, because the Lord is not incapable of discernment.
That too is incorrect.
For if agency is established, omniscience is established; and from that [omniscience], agency is established once again.
In this state of being the agent, there is a great circularity of dependence (anyonyāśraya).

For if this Supreme Lord is established as the creator of everything, then he would possess omniscience, and not otherwise. And if he possesses omniscience, he must be the impeller; otherwise, there would be another impeller for him as well, resulting in that very same infinite regress.

Furthermore: if he is omniscient, why does he cause ignorant people to engage in improper conduct? For those possessed of discernment are seen to be givers of correct instruction; yet he causes even people who are engaged in error to arise. How, then, can he be a valid authority?

Now, he makes his instruction truly wholesome; therefore, it is authoritative. However, he causes the doer of unrighteousness to experience an undesirable result. Consequently, one who bestows appropriate results is indeed possessed of discernment. [036,xvi] That too is incorrect, because:
[036,xvii] This [creator] indeed causes living beings to engage even in unrighteous acts.
Having caused them to perform what is improper, how could he cause them to engage in what is proper? (PVA) 256

First, he impels one toward evil; then, for the sake of turning away from that, there is dharma. What kind of foresight is this on the part of an Īśvara who acts with deliberation? This has come down to this: "I shall wash it off and then abandon it."

If, on the other hand, he causes one to engage in evil, then he is governed by that very karma; such being the case, there is a loss of his status as a discerning agent (*prekṣākriyā*). Furthermore, the same logical consequence applies as to why he would cause that karma to be performed at all.
If it is argued that he does not cause one to perform unrighteousness (*adharma*), but rather makes one experience its fruit as a doer of unrighteousness, then he is like another god (*īśvara*).
That too is without substance.
Other lords, due to incapacity, do not provide for the prevention of evil;
however, he is held to have a mind that is utterly turned away from those who are incapable.
If, on the other hand, he were indeed incapable,
then it must be declared loudly that "not everything was created by Īśvara."
Since it acts for its own sake like a sinner, what then of dharma and the rest? (258) Furthermore:
[037, viii] Does the world not experience the fruit of unrighteousness without a Lord? If it occurs even without him, who would conceive of his being the cause? (PVA) 259.
Now, since no one experiences the fruit of demerit without [having committed] that [act],
how could a discerning person engage in this which is purposeless?
(260) If his activity were for the sake of sport, how could it be an action preceded by discernment?
One person experiences momentary satisfaction, while another is deprived of life.
Furthermore:
If all other treatises arise from the conceptualization of a creator god,
how can they be a means of valid cognition for teaching what is true or false? (262) (PVA)

That this person is an authority (*pramāṇa*) and possesses great wonderous authority (*prāmāṇikatva*), because he teaches a doctrine that is not contradicted by the mutual oppositions found in the characteristics of all other treatises, and which consists of the adoption of what is true and the rejection of what is false— this is indeed a great marvel.

If, then, it does not perform the purposeful activity (arthakriyā) of the entire scripture, then everything was not created by God, just as in the case of other scriptures. Alternatively, if it is argued that He creates everything only when impelled by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), and that the existence of things cannot occur otherwise; if that were so, then every soul of ordinary people would likewise act solely through the impulsion of merit, demerit, and so forth. Thus, the postulation of a Lord (īśvara) is redundant.
[037,xvii] If it is maintained that the Self is not the agent of everything, then of what "everything" would its status as an agent be of any use? 263 (PVA)
If [it is argued that] by means of all their respective selves, everything is produced by all the instruments [of cognition], then how could anything be abandoned?
Likewise, there would be the action of one by many, and of many by one.
(264) Or, if it is maintained that some single entity alone is the agent of everything—
Otherwise, omniscience would not be possible; thus, no other [being] possesses the status of a creator.

(PVA 265) For those who seek [liberation], this creator is the primary figure for the attainment of the supreme state. Indeed, one is not served by others merely because of being omniscient if he is incapable [of leading them]. (PVA 266)
That too is incorrect.

Even one who is omniscient does not become an object of service if he is incapable of performing actions that bring about benefit or harm, because he provides no assistance— just like molasses or cow’s milk.
And even if omniscience were established, if he were capable of performing all actions [but did not do so], [he would not be served].
Furthermore, his omniscience follows from his being the creator of all things.
(268) If he were a creator who was not omniscient, how could he be an all-knower?
Therefore, if it is argued that this is established by way of an example, then the integrity of the investigation is destroyed. (269) (PVA)
Furthermore, ignorance does not exist in the potter or others regarding their own effects; thus, the Lord is useless.
And once the efficacy of karma is established, what further use is there for an agent?
(270) Even if the potter and others were capable [of acting] when impelled, even though they possess knowledge—
Even the Lord would likewise have to be impelled by another, for there is no distinction [between them].
(271) Now, if he, desiring to establish his own omniscience, has become the impeller of all—by what means is this to be understood? (272)
And furthermore:
The agent who acts after having deliberated for himself is not there an independent creator;
the claim that the intellect of everything originates solely from God is without proof.
The causality of instruction and the like depends upon the instructor, and that [instructor] depends on something other than him.
Because [the teaching] is beginningless, all that was desired is complete.

Therefore, for those who act while remaining [in their own nature], how could there be impulsion by a Lord? Consequently, there is no certainty regarding the agency of primordial matter (pradhāna), the person (puruṣa), and so forth. (PVA 274–275)

The argument that "this is because of the conformity of its configuration" is also not a valid reason. For it is not observed that every configuration whatsoever is preceded by a person; for such a configuration is also seen to arise from mere specific causes such as seeds, just like the configurations of trees and the like. In this regard, as follows: [038,vii] [As in the case of:
For the configuration of trees and the like is accompanied by non-intelligent causes;
likewise, jars and other such things would be so, being unimpelled by Pradhāna or any other [such cause].
Just as a seed produced from a tree is the cause of a tree.
Likewise, even a jar [is produced] from a lump of clay that has not yet been transformed into a jar or the like.
Furthermore, the potter and others are always held to be its witness;
for the body’s color and configuration arise from something else in a similar manner. (PVA 277–278)

A potter and the like are not the producers of that shape and so forth. Indeed, even one who is well-trained is not capable of producing a shape for a tree that is of a different genus from its seed, even if he possesses consciousness.

[Objection: But surely a potter is not observed producing the shape of a lump of clay. [Reply: No, because the lump of clay itself is of such a nature. The lump of clay possesses that very same color and shape [as the jar], just as a banyan seed possesses the color and shape of the banyan tree. If it is asked how that is so, it is said in response:
If the nature of color and shape did not exist in the seed by virtue of its potentiality...
How could that effect arise from it when the cause, the seed, is absent?
(PVA 279) If God is its creator, why does it not arise from something other than the seed? This has already been refuted; how then can God be its cause? (PVA 280)

[038,xiv] The Bodhisattva, having heard this teaching on the Dharma, was filled with joy and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, it is wonderful how well-spoken this teaching on the Dharma is! It is marvelous, Blessed One, how the Tathāgata has so skillfully taught the Dharma by means of the non-arising of all phenomena. Thus he spoke. The Blessed One then said to the Bodhisattva: "Well done, well done, son of good family! It is indeed excellent that you have spoken thus regarding the non-arising of all phenomena. This concludes the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Non-Arising of All Phenomena," from the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*, the Great Vaipulya Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati. Chapter Fourteen. [039,i] At that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the thought of enlightenment? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the arising of the thought of enlightenment is the Tathāgata. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the Tathāgata is the perfection of wisdom. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the perfection of wisdom is the emptiness of all phenomena. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the emptiness of all phenomena? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the emptiness of all phenomena is the absence of conceptualization. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the absence of conceptualization? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the absence of conceptualization is the non-duality of all phenomena. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the non-duality of all phenomena? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the non-duality of all phenomena is the ultimate reality (*tathatā*). The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the ultimate reality? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the ultimate reality is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the mind. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the suchness of the mind? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the suchness of the mind is the non-arising of the mind. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the non-arising of the mind? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the non-arising of the mind is the fact that the mind is originally unborn. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the fact that the mind is originally unborn? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the fact that the mind is originally unborn is the absence of a self, a being, a soul, or a person. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the absence of a self, a being, a soul, or a person? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the absence of a self, a being, a soul, or a person is the emptiness of intrinsic nature. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the emptiness of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the non-apprehension of any phenomenon whatsoever. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the non-apprehension of any phenomenon whatsoever? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the non-apprehension of any phenomenon whatsoever is the cessation of all mental activity. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of all mental activity? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the cessation of all mental activity is the realization of the equality of all phenomena. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the realization of the equality of all phenomena? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the realization of the equality of all phenomena is the liberation from all grasping. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for liberation from all grasping? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for liberation from all grasping is the attainment of the state of non-attachment. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the attainment of the state of non-attachment? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the attainment of the state of non-attachment is the purification of the mind. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the purification of the mind? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the purification of the mind is the cultivation of the perfections. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cultivation of the perfections? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the cultivation of the perfections is the practice of the path. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the practice of the path? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the practice of the path is the accumulation of merit and wisdom. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the accumulation of merit and wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the accumulation of merit and wisdom is the service rendered to the Buddhas. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the service rendered to the Buddhas? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the service rendered to the Buddhas is the generation of the thought of enlightenment. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the generation of the thought of enlightenment? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the generation of the thought of enlightenment is the great compassion for all sentient beings. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for great compassion for all sentient beings? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for great compassion for all sentient beings is the vision of the suffering of saṃsāra. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the vision of the suffering of saṃsāra? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the vision of the suffering of saṃsāra is the hearing of the true Dharma. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the hearing of the true Dharma? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for the hearing of the true Dharma is the meeting with a spiritual friend. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for meeting with a spiritual friend? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the cause and condition for meeting with a spiritual friend is the maturation of past roots of virtue. The venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the maturation of past

For at that time, the seed—the cause of the tree—is not present in the form of its effect; therefore, it is not the cause of the tree’s configuration (*saṃsthāna*), nor is Īśvara. Since a seed of a different species cannot produce a tree, if Īśvara were its cause, why would the configuration of that tree not arise even from a seed of a different species? Therefore, the configuration of the tree exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) within the seed and merely becomes manifest, just as a young child hidden in the darkness [is revealed] by a lamp. Likewise, the configuration also emerges from the lump of clay through the potter. Even in the fashioning of a jar and so forth, the potter’s configuration exists in the form of a potentiality derived precisely from that configuration. Consequently, the person such as the potter is merely a witness and an enjoyer; he has no activity whatsoever. For the *pradhāna*, which exists in the form of a potentiality, proceeds in various ways according to the desire for that enjoyment. Thus it has been said:
The primordial matter (*pradhāna*) proceeds for the sake of accomplishing the experience of the Spirit (*puruṣa*),
just as the performance on a theatrical stage proceeds for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the audience. (281) (PVA)

And from that, there is established the negation of an intelligent cause. Now, since the selves (ātman) are distinct for each individual, there must be another self, free from passion and the like, who is the Lord (īśvara) of all; otherwise, by whom were the specific colors, forms, and so forth of transmigrating beings (saṃsārin-puruṣa) displayed? It is in this regard that the primordial matter (pradhāna) proceeds out of a desire for experience. To this, it has been said:
[038,xvii]

Just as the performance of a drama by an actor is for the sake of removing the spectators' desire to see [the performance] once they have seen it from beginningless instruction, so too is it for transmigrating persons.
How else could milk flow forth for the growth of the calf without knowing [its need]?
In the same way, why is this not accepted: that the Primordial Matter (pradhāna) acts?

(PVA 282) Therefore, since at the final stage one observes a nature characterized by the pursuit of pleasure and so forth, the cause of everything must exist in the form of pleasure and so forth. Since [the argument] is fully established by that much, there is no proof of a Lord (īśvara). Moreover, this is illogical.
The method of those who know reasoning is that insentience is the cause of that [non-perception], because the lack of prior reflection regarding objects is observed in them. (PVA 283)
It is not logical that things lacking foresight should have a cause [such as Pradhāna];
for what is the use of the circular formation of the dung of goats and the like?
(284) [Refutation of Primordial Matter as the Cause]
"In that case, the Sāṃkhyas argue, primordial matter (pradhāna) itself must be the cause.
On this point, the following is said:
If there is a positive concomitance (anvaya) of pleasure and the rest, because they are real entities and because they possess consciousness.
Therefore, why is that [Pradhāna] not accepted as the cause of persons?
(285) (PVA) But color and so forth, as well as configuration, do not exist as real entities in Pradhāna.
How then can it be maintained that color and so forth are the effects produced by Pradhāna? (286) (PVA)
Furthermore, if everything here is accepted as existing in the form of potentiality (*śakti*), then the entity consisting of all these potencies is called *pradhāna*.
Just as there is an inference of causality for that unperceived [entity] based on its being of such a nature, [so too is the case here]. (PVA 287)

For an effect must arise from another effect because it is an effect, like any other effect. (PVA 288) Indeed, a cause that is not a cause is never observed; therefore, the postulation of a cause follows precisely from the observation of its form.

[039,xi] Now, since there is a continuity (*anvaya*) among distinct things, there must be some persisting entity as their cause in that form. But since the cause itself has no continuity with anything else, how can there be another cause for that continuity? For in the case of the difference between jars, bowls, and so forth, they all have a single lump of clay as their antecedent because of the continuity of the nature of clay. However, the lump of clay does not have another lump of clay as its antecedent, because the lump of clay is a single unit. Even for the lump of clay, the staff, and so on, there is ultimately one further [entity] that persists until the very end.

That too is incorrect. It has been stated that another cause for the elements (sattva) and so forth, as well as for the persons (puruṣa), would necessarily follow. Let it be, then, that there is some single cause;
that too is incorrect.
The nature of that *pradhāna* as consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) and so forth is not established.
Since it is associated with the status of being a real entity (*vastu*), let some real entity whatsoever be regarded as the cause. (PVA 289)

[039,xv] Because of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that "the entity is an entity," the effect possesses the nature of an entity by virtue of its cause. And there is no nature of an entity other than the form of clay and so forth. Therefore, it follows that the cause consists precisely of the form of clay and so forth. This being the case, it follows that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) must consist of everything.
This is not so;
an effect conforms to its cause in its essential nature, but not in every respect.
Smoke and so forth are seen to arise differently from fire and other causes that have become otherwise.

(PVA 290) For that which follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something is its cause, but not necessarily its very form (*tadrūpa*). Thus, smoke arises from fire, and water from clouds and the like. In such cases, since there is no similarity of form, there would be no relationship of cause and effect.

[039,xix] Now, if there exists some similar cause even in that case, let it be inferred precisely because the effect is of such a nature. Let it be inferred provided that there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the effect and the cause by way of similarity. But this is not so, because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is argued that "that which involves deviation must also be made the subject (*pakṣa*)," then in that case, there would be nothing at all called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), for one could simply make whatever causes deviation the subject itself. Therefore, because it leads to an infinite regress, this is untenable. <3. Not the causality of karma>
[040,i] Now, it might also be said:
From what is this established—that "this is the transformation of actions"?
For even in the case of action, there is no presence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

Indeed, it is not understood that karma—whether auspicious, inauspicious, or otherwise—is the cause of this diversity of the world. Let this matter rest for now; something else is being stated. As for what was said—that even one possessed of passion and the like might be endowed with all powers, and therefore the creation of the world's diversity for the sake of play and so forth—it is replied to as follows:
The flavor of play belongs to the ignorant who are possessed by passion, not to those of pure nature.
Even with a slight degree of purification, noble beings do not engage in such plays. (PVA 292)

No noble person engages in amusements out of fear of hell and other such states; yet for him, this [fear of hell] does not exist—why then would he desist from them? (293) (PVA) When suffering in hells and other realms arises from passion and the like...
That [distinction] does not exist for him; by what means, then, is this said by your friend?
(PVA 294) The conceptualization of [the axe and sandalwood] as being alike arises from mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*);
thus it is established that the suffering of fear regarding hell and other realms does not afflict [him]. (PVA 295)
In this very way, it is logical that this [world] has arisen from that; however, this is not so.
If it were inherent, then that world would have to be inherent in it.
This manifest world is the work of that one Lord alone;
moreover:
The attainment of lordship by Īśvara and others must likewise come from another; that other’s [attainment] must also come from yet another; thus, Īśvara is not [lordly] by nature. (PVA 297)
If there is an excellence of qualities such that the state of Śakra or Brahmā is possible, then even the status of Īśvara would be attained; thus, there is no eternal existence of an Īśvara.
Or, if this [attainment] also does not exist, then consequently neither the transmigrating being nor the Īśvara exists.
In this case, what possibility is there for the rejection of that which has been rejected elsewhere?

(299) (PVA) For indeed, if one who robs a village is not restrained when in the company of virtuous people, what restraint can there be for him in the forest where protection is impossible? Likewise, if someone denies the possibility of reaching a peak of excellence through the pursuit of a state in which gradation is possible, who would believe that there is no such rejection regarding a thing that lacks such gradation? Therefore:

Entities are established as having an agent because they are produced through the conjunction of shapes; but how could there be any establishment for that which is devoid of causes and qualities? (PVA 300)

<4. The absence of atoms and the like as causes> [040,xvii] It is logical that the capacity [for transformation] arises from a particular application [of effort], based on the observation of degrees of excellence in qualities, even for those things that were previously incapable; this follows from our position. However, it is simply impossible to establish a means of proof for something that is absolutely distinct, whose nature consists of an inherent capacity devoid of any continuity.
Furthermore:
For this so-called "shape" has no established existence in reality;
since it is merely an illusion, those [objects] are indeed nothing but atoms.

Indeed, there exists no substance supported by a substratum that has a body distinct from the atoms; since there are only atoms alone, how can it be said that "atoms" are so called on account of their difference from that?

Now, if it is argued that what is established merely by worldly convention is accepted [as the object], that too is incorrect, because that which is merely constructed by conceptualization lacks probative force (*sādhana*). If, on the other hand, it is said that atoms themselves are spoken of in that form, then in that case atoms would also be effects (*kārya*). Consequently, this very reason—"because they are effects"—is what ought to be put forward. Or, if it is argued that it is the atoms themselves that produce an unreal delusion and are thus spoken of in that way, then in that case:
[041,ii] If atoms appear in their own nature as real entities, then...
"How can there be an intellect belonging to God?

[If it is argued: 'My own arrangement of the instruments [of perception] has been examined,' then if it is said that he lacks such instruments, how can his omniscience exist when the examination of instruments is absent? (PVA 302–303)
Now, the determination of shape occurs through the acceptance by another;
but how can there be acceptance by another of that which one has not apprehended for oneself? (304) Or, if this reply is given on the grounds that the whole (avayavin) exists:
This, which is extremely difficult to establish, will be examined later.

Alternatively, there is doubt regarding the example. Precisely because of that [example], there is doubt and the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). It is the very nature (*svarūpa*) itself that is presented as the cause for performing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). And since that same nature belongs to God (*īśvara*) as well, [the reason] is therefore inconclusive. For that God does not act by acting intermittently, nor is He a performer of purposeful action while being impelled by another. If it is argued that He is himself capable and thus is not impelled by another, then it is equally illogical to say that potters and the like—who are themselves capable—are impelled by another. If it is claimed that they are simply incapable, how can there be incapacity when they are observed to be capable? If you say that even the capability of that observed [potter] exists only through inference, and that the potter has no capability in isolation from the inference of another [cause], then one must infer another God for this God, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore:
[041,viii]
On what basis is it held that there is no spatial configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of atoms?
If you say it is because they are [ultimately] real (*tattvāt*), then from what is this reality to be cognized?

For the atomic nature of atoms is not understood in such a way that their lack of shape would follow. Now, it might be argued as follows: whatever is gross is preceded by an accumulation of parts, just like a mass of water consisting of a collection of many drops. Since everything down to the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is gross, it must therefore consist of a collection of many [parts]; thus, the atom is established.
[041,xi] That too is incorrect.
From what source is there the understanding that form exists beyond the eight-atom [aggregate]?
What is the means of valid cognition (*pramā*) for determining whether this eight-atom form is such or otherwise?
If atoms were perceived, their number would be ascertained. (PVA 307)
If that [duality] were extremely gross, then it would not be a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*).
When a dyad and so forth are not perceived, in relation to what could its "bulkiness" be established?
If it is argued that this bulkiness is inferred in relation to something else, then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results.
The grossness of everything would depend upon that which is being inferred.
Furthermore, if this [grossness] is considered to be the visible form at the limit [of analysis],
why is its circularity or other such configurations not perceived?
If the atom is not established, how can there be the emergence of a composite?
(PVA 311) If atoms were established, how could there be the emergence of a composite?
How could that atom have contact with [another] by means of only one part? (PVA 312)
If conjunction occurred by way of a single part, it would be perceived for the whole as well;
therefore, because of the existence of conjunction, the atom is not [indivisible], just like a gross object.

Furthermore, it might be argued that a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) arises between two atoms as a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*), but not a contact (*saṃsparśa*)— whether by way of their entire being or by way of one part. That too is incorrect.
If conjunction occurs even in the absence of contact, how is it that very same [conjunction]? How could there be cognitions of a single, solid form regarding atoms? (314) (PVA)
If there were another whole [as a distinct entity], then there would be a cognition of a uniform form regarding each respective part;
furthermore, because atoms are eternal, they would be perceived as having intervals between them.
Even if it is granted that atoms are invisible to people like us, [the following consequences would follow].
If God were visible to the senses, it would certainly not be possible for those [beings] [to see Him].
(PVA 316) Furthermore, if He were to perceive duality, how could there be an inherence (*samavāya*)?
In that case, people would merely be under delusion, because they would be seeing things otherwise than they truly are. (PVA 317)

[042,iv] And how is it known that the gross is preceded by the conjunction of parts? Even if this is observed in the case of a lump of clay and the like, it is certainly not observed in the case of a sprout and so forth. For instance:
The seed of the banyan tree is exceedingly small, yet its effect is extremely massive.
How could there be a conjunction of parts therein when they were previously non-existent?

The established tenet is that conjunction belongs only to parts that already exist. However, prior to the gross form of a stalk or the like, there is no perception of its parts; therefore, how can there be conjunction? And from what could a whole (avayavin) arise? Thus, this is entirely a dance in the darkness.
Alternatively, atoms pervading a portion of space are accumulated when aided by visible objects.
That is incorrect.
"Things that exist are accumulated; does something previously non-existent arise from that cause?
Regarding this, we all have a doubt.
(PVA 319) Or, even if it is not seen, it is understood to exist through an example.
By the force of the lamp example, the Sāṃkhya view has been reached;
from that very point, the notion that "God is the creator" has gone far away, and the lamp and other such things have been shown to be manifestors because they are insentient. (PVA 320–321)
If manifestation proceeds from the insentient, how can this be a proof for God? As for the claim that even He is presided over by a sentient being, the answer has already been given previously.
Therefore, let whatever [effect] arise from whatever [cause], let it be so from that very source.
The certainty is that [a cognition] arises from volition in some cases and from something else in others.
(323) Even if it were yellow, it would otherwise be white because it is a real entity, like other white things.
Since there is no sublation by perception, how can there be the thought "it is not" in this case? (324)
The thought "it does not exist for me" is certainly not your non-perception, nor is it a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
If your non-perception were a valid means of knowledge, then it should be understood that God does not exist.

If that perception of yours is invalid, then it should be understood that there is no God. Furthermore, the fact that something is an effect, or has a specific configuration, or is a real entity, does not by itself lead to the inference of a desired cause. Indeed, causes do not function to establish a probandum according to the whim of a person; otherwise, even the opposite of God might be established, which would lead to the absurd consequence of proving anything at all. Therefore, he says: rather, whatever is perceived in a certain manner from a certain source, that very thing leads to the inference of that same source.
It is established that whatever arrangement and so forth follow the presence or absence of a controller is appropriate; therefore, that which is inferred from it is valid. (11)

[042,xix] It is logical that one infers from a specific kind of thing that which is observed to function according to the presence or absence of a controller, or that which is perceived as following the presence or absence of a particular kind of controller; it is from such a thing that that very thing is inferred, not otherwise. This refers to "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*) and so forth—whether it be arrangement, substantiality (*vastutva*), or activity after having remained stationary. It is established that the inference of a particular kind of controller is valid from a particular kind of arrangement that has been observed, and not otherwise. Thus he says:

It is not proper to infer [the presence of] fire from something that is established as distinct in one object but is non-different [from it] merely due to the identity of the word, just as [one would not infer fire] from a white substance and the like. (12)

For if, setting aside the distinction of configuration (*saṃsthāna*), one were to employ as a reason either the mere state of being an entity (*vastutva*)—expressible by the word "configuration" alone—or that which follows from a specific agent, then a valid inference would result, just as fire is inferred from a white substance and so forth. For in that case:
The specific shade of white found in smoke must be identified; if that inference is derived from smoke alone, then what is the use of its whiteness? To this it is replied:
Only a specific kind of whiteness is designated as "smoke.
There is no distinct quality of "smokeness" that serves as a qualifier for that whiteness. (PVA 326)

[043,iv] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? They are: the person who is a seeker of the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), the person who is a seeker of arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka), and the person who is established in the fruit of arhatship (arhat). These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What do you think, monks? Is it fitting for you to say: 'We shall not recognize the Blessed One as the Teacher, nor shall we live in dependence upon him'? "Certainly not, Blessed One.
