What is the meaning of "because of the whiteness found in smoke"? How is it to be understood that [smoke] indeed follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of fire? In this case as well, the inference would have to occur through the apprehension of a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), such that "the nature of smoke is inseparable from fire. And thus, the Lord (*Īśvara*) all the more fails to achieve proof; for one who desires gain ends up losing even the root. Therefore, when there is a difference in entities, the specific entity observed in the example—such as the particularity of being presided over by a person (*puruṣādhiṣṭhānaviśeṣa*) in the case of a jar or similar objects with a specific shape—is not a valid basis for inference if it is taken as non-different due to a mere similarity of words. This is the certain conclusion regarding the Lord as well.

[043,v] Furthermore, it might be argued: "If we were to proceed with an inference based on 'whiteness' as a feature devoid of specific qualifications, then there would be sublation by perception; however, fire-contact does not necessarily accompany all that is white, because the opposite is observed through perception. But in the case of the inference for God, that inference would indeed be sublated.
This is not so;
an inference does not function merely on the grounds that "it is not sublated."
It has been stated that its activity proceeds from the perception of a connection;
otherwise, because a potter produces certain transformations of clay such as jars and the like, it would follow that an anthill is also his work. (327–328)

[043,ix] Indeed, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) in the inference of a potter’s agency regarding an anthill. Nor is mere non-perception itself a sublation; for if a potter were the agent, he would be perceived. But what of the case of God (*īśvara*)? Why is there no perception of Him? Well then, one should not postulate even unseen karma (*adṛṣṭa-karman*). Does this mean that one should now thrust one's knee into a hole? Or, if after postulating karma one further postulates another Lord, then from that another yet again—thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore: [043,x]
Why is a potter not likewise postulated as the unseen agent for that effect?
Is this difficult assumption not equally possible in the case of God as well?

Now, the sequence of the staff, the lump of clay, the wheel, and the hands is not perceived in an anthill. If, then, you possess such great subtle scrutiny, then why does the activity of an intelligent agent not also apply to mountains and the like, which have irregular shapes? Why do you resort to this "half-old-woman" approach (applying the principle of intelligence only partially)? If you say that the purpose of mountains and the like is merely to support the earth, then what is the use of their being formed with specific shapes? It is exactly so.
If the configuration of the earth were produced otherwise than by means of an agent, why would the person not be the cause in that case? Therefore, there is a lack of uniformity. (PVA 329)

[043,xiv] Is it because of a lack of utility that, even if the Puruṣa were the creator, an extremely beautiful structure does not arise, or is it that the Puruṣa is not the creator? This remains a mere doubt.

Surely this fault is the "balancing of the effect" (*kāryasama*). For it is said: "The balancing of the effect occurs because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort. Since sound is an effect because it is invariably concomitant with effort, one might argue that since manifestation is also observed to follow immediately after effort, sound is not necessarily an effect. Likewise, here too, one might say that shape is also observed to be an effect of something other than itself.
That too is incorrect.
When an effect is used as a probans even in a general sense because it is followed by the probandum,
the fault of asserting a difference based on the difference of the related terms is considered to be "balancing the effect" (kāryasama).

[044,iii] The Discourse on the Four Noble Truths. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “What, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering. Union with what is displeasing is suffering; separation from what is pleasing is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of suffering. “What, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is craving, which brings renewal of being, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights in this and that; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. “What, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. “What, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Such, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering; such is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; such is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; such is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Now, bhikkhus, regarding this noble truth of suffering, there has been, in regard to things unheard before, a vision, a knowledge, an understanding, an awakening, and a light. Regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering, there has been, in regard to things unheard before, a vision, a knowledge, an understanding, an awakening, and a light. Regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, there has been, in regard to things unheard before, a vision, a knowledge, an understanding, an awakening, and a light. Regarding this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, there has been, in regard to things unheard before, a vision, a knowledge, an understanding, an awakening, and a light. “Bhikkhus, as long as my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are—through their three rounds and twelve aspects—was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are—through their three rounds and twelve aspects—was thoroughly purified in this way, then I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. “The knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. The Discourse on the Four Noble Truths is concluded. [044,iii]

Indeed, when a proof is offered even by means of a general property such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) which is the probandum, the fault that has been stated regarding the subject of that proof is considered *kāryasama*. It takes the form of the fallacy of *kāryasama*. What kind of fault is it? It is the fault of stating a distinction (*bhedoktidoṣa*). "Stating a distinction" means raising an objection: "Does the so-called 'being an effect' pertain to manifestation (*abhivyakti*), or does it pertain to origination (*utpatti*)? The fault of stating a distinction based on the difference of related entities is *kāryasama*. In that case as well, if one points out that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—that is, that even if [the sound's appearance] is due to the removal of an obstruction following effort, this does not constitute a contradiction—then it is not a *jātyuttara* (a futile rejoinder). Rather, the proof remains valid even as a generality. For even manifestation is indeed contradictory to what is eternal; therefore, it is a *jātyuttara*. Otherwise, the pointing out of an inconclusive reason would truly be a valid [criticism].

Now, the answer to this is as follows: If there were a difference in the nature of the effect, then effort would not be its cause, because the presence of causes for non-perception would be possible. This might be the case if there were a difference between effort and the effect; that is, it might be so regarding the existence of sound. However, since the presence of causes for non-perception—such as obstruction—is possible [in other cases], yet no such cause as obstruction is possible for sound, its manifestation does not occur immediately after effort. Where manifestation occurs immediately after effort, there an obstructing cause of non-perception is applicable; and through the removal of that obstruction, the object is perceived, which constitutes a manifestation distinct from that [non-perception].
To this, it is said:
It would follow that this [sequence] does not belong to sound either; how then, and for what reason, is it perceived?
If the connection with manifestation were possible even for something eternal, [then it could be perceived].
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"Even when a sound is not perceived, there may be causes such as an intervening object."
"Like jars and other such things, it is clearly not seen; therefore, they are not produced by effort.
(PVA 331) [044,x] That too is incorrect.
[044,xi] Let it also be postulated that there exist obstructions and the like for sound;
because sound is recognized through re-cognition, it is not subject to destruction. (PVA) 332.

[044,xii] Even jars and other such objects, which were previously perceived and have not perished during a state of concealment, are recognized upon the removal of that concealment precisely through *pratyabhijñā* (recognition). It is likewise logical for sound to be understood in the same way through recognition. Now, if you claim that such a cognition arises merely from perception by another person and not from *pratyabhijñā*—that is, not from one’s own direct experience—that is a truly profound "vision of reality"!
[044,xiii]
Furthermore:
That [object] is also recognized by another person through recognition or otherwise.
How can its eternality be established even from another?
Therefore, the very same solution mentioned previously applies here: "Even when proving by means of a generality, it must be related," and so forth.
Alternatively:
[044,xvii]

The demonstration that the probandum is not established due to even a slight difference regarding its being an effect is the "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*); this, moreover, is threefold according to the speaker's intention.

Thus, this has been stated by relying on the definition of *kāryasama* (balancing the effect) as formulated by the Teacher [Aksapāda]. However, it has been demonstrated that the definition of *akṣapāda* is incorrect. As for *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative), it is defined as: "Even when there is similarity (*sādharmya*), the statement of a distinction is *vikalpasama*. For example, when impermanence has been established based on the similarity with a pot as before, one says: "Even though this similarity exists, only the pot is impermanent due to its being an effect, its being visible, and so forth, and not anything else."

[Objection: "But surely, even here, the proof is established by means of generalities such as 'being an effect' (kāryatva) or 'having a specific configuration' (saṃsthānatva). For if one were to postulate a connection based on a particular instance, it would result in the fallacy of *kāryasama* (balancing the effect), since one would be postulating configurations such as those of a jar or a mountain.
[Response: That is not true.
There is no universal (sāmānya) in shape and so forth, because it arises from action preceded by cognition;
for this has been observed elsewhere as well, such as in trees and the like, as has been described. (335) (PVA)
Any proof that establishes something by abandoning a specific qualification is utterly irrelevant to the subject's impermanence, like the blackness of a crow.

Here the opponent says: Even if the concomitance with intentional action is not observed, that very [concomitance] may serve as the means of proof for the manifestation of shape (*saṃsthāna*). However, the concomitance with verbal denotability—such as "shape, shape," and so forth—will exist. Therefore, because they possess non-different characteristics, the establishment of their having a single effect follows.
This is incorrect, because:
From a dharma that is fashioned by mere conceptual construction, devoid of proximity to an external object, and from whatever desired object that may arise therefrom— (PVA 337).

Because of the observation of a commonality of words for that which is well-known in another class of beings, it is not logical to establish [the presence of horns] in rabbits and the like on the basis of "cow-ness," just as in the case of [inferring] horns [from the word "cow"]. (15)

For the connection with horns is well-established as belonging to a different genus, being distinct from things such as rabbits; how then could that be inferred merely from the non-difference of the verbal designation "cow"?
It has been stated that even when the object is not different, there is no inference because of its paleness;
how much more so in a case where there is not even an object, but only the word itself which is identical?

To begin with, it is possible for an object to be connected to the desired goal to be accomplished; yet even that is declared by those who possess subtle insight to be non-probative. How much more so, then, is the mere similarity of words, from which even the scent of a connection to the goal has been cast far away? For:
Because they are dependent upon the speaker’s intention, words do not exist anywhere [in reality].
But when the object is established through its existence, everything is established for everyone. (16)

And where do these words not exist? Nowhere, because there is no obstruction to the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). Therefore, if the object is to be proven, it is established; no one would suffer from a failure to establish the object. Consequently, this is a fallacy based on what is non-existent.

By this, the lack of consciousness and other such qualities of the followers of Kapila and others have been examined; likewise, their claim of consciousness for that which is impermanent and so forth has been refuted by the fact of death through the peeling away of the skin. || 17 ||

[046,ii] Since even for the followers of Kapila and others, the absence of consciousness (or its opposite) constitutes the pinnacle of their mansion of proof, it is merely constructed from a similarity of words, as it lacks the actual referent. To explain:
Impermanence is not established for the Sāṃkhya from the perspective of the actual nature of things;
for him, it is the non-manifestation of categories, not their destruction without residue.
Indeed, for the Buddhist, impermanence is not established as the non-manifestation of that which already exists; what then? It is the destruction without residue (*niranvayanāśitā*).

Is it not the case that concealment (*tirobhāva*) is exactly the same as destruction or non-manifestation? What is this concealment? It is the state of being invisible. But then, there would be the consequence of impermanence even for things like a hare’s horn or for primordial matter (*pradhāna*). If you argue that impermanence belongs only to that which exists [but ceases], then primordial matter and the like would also possess impermanence insofar as they exist in the form of being visible. If you say that impermanence consists in the attainment of invisibility by that which was visible, then what is this so-called "visibility"? If it is the very nature of the object, how can there be invisibility of the visible? If its nature were abandoned, the entity itself would no longer exist. If visibility is something other than the entity, then its absence would constitute a total destruction without a trace (*niranvayavināśa*). Furthermore, the concealment of one thing does not occur through the absence of another; otherwise, since that [other] would always be equivalent to primordial matter, there would be no impermanence. Therefore, why is this mere verbal construction accepted as a proof? Likewise, regarding the statement "because of death from the removal of the skin": when all the skin is removed, [the person] dies; thus, this is merely the application of the word "death."

For the Buddhists, death is the cessation of consciousness and so forth; however, for one for whom consciousness is not established in trees, their notion [of death] is likewise unestablished. (PVA 340)

[046,vii] For which Buddhist, then, who has doubts regarding consciousness in trees, would anyone accept that death—which consists of the cessation of consciousness and so forth—is free from doubt? The cessation of consciousness does not exist in the absence of consciousness, nor likewise in the absence of vitality.
[046,viii]

For it is stated: "Life is vitality; it is indeed the support of heat and consciousness. How, then, could one accept death while consciousness is still present? Therefore, he says that death consists in desiccation. And that is not an absolute proof for the absence of consciousness, since it is observed even in mud and such things. If it is argued that this too is established because the term "death" applies [to them], it has been said in response: "[Because it is] dependent upon the speaker's intention. If it is argued that the intention arises here from the observation of the actual object, then this is not a fault.
For once death is established, the word for it becomes fixed [in its application].
And if there is an obstruction of the word, then the establishment of death [from it] follows.

(PVA 341) [046,x] The establishment of death—characterized by the cessation of cognition and so forth—from the word occurs only if it is derived from the observation of such a death. And if the derivation from the observation of such a death is required for the establishment of death, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

[046,xi] Now, if the relationship between word and object were eternal, then it would follow that even horses and the like possess horns. If you argue that the word "cow" applied to horses and so forth is entirely different [from the word "cow" applied to cattle], and thus it is not at all connected to the state of possessing horns, then in that case, the word for "death" (maraṇa) is likewise not distinct from the word for "dying"—what proof do you have for this? Therefore, the proof for [the thesis of] non-eternality and so forth is not established by such arguments as "functioning after having remained stationary" (*sthitvā pravṛtti*). Thus, there is no establishment of the probandum.

If, then, by means of conceptualizing specific qualifications, the probans becomes non-probative—whether it be shape and so forth, or impermanence and so forth, or even other properties such as "being produced"—then everything would be non-probative from the perspective of the opponent, for everything is unestablished through conceptualization. For instance:
[047,i] "Sound is a quality of space" is a property that is unestablished for the opponent.
"The mutual non-establishment of the property in the probandum and the example" (is also incorrect).
ii] That too is false.
Based on scripture, the nature of space is not expressive of anything at all;
however, if one were to postulate specific distinctions, the very reason [for its being non-expressive] would be lost. (PVA 343)
Therefore:

This principle applies when the nature of the entity is unestablished; once it is established, the qualification is not a sublater [of the probandum], even if [the entity] itself is unestablished, just as sound has space as its locus. (18)

For, although sound is unestablished as a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) according to scripture, it is nonetheless established in its own nature (*svarūpa*) as the subject (*dharmin*). Thus, there is no non-establishment of the property (*dharma*). Likewise, even when a qualification (*viśeṣa*) is conceptualized, the reason (*hetu*) is neither unestablished with respect to the subject nor inconclusive due to being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatā*). For the subject is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasiddha*); thus, it is not unestablished simply because a qualification is unestablished. Nor is the conceptualization of a qualification useful in any case; for in such instances, the inclusion of a qualification is not necessary. To illustrate: [047,vii]
The generality of impermanence and being an effect possesses utility; however, the establishment of their specific particulars is not accepted by anyone at all.
[344] (PVA) Being produced immediately after a cause and being destroyed immediately thereafter—
There is no distinction between the word and the jar endowed with a qualifier.

(PVA 345) Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever in that which is devoid of its own prior and posterior natures. Nor does space qualify it, because it is the object of a single conceptual apprehension. That [distinction] is an unreal construction (*vikalpana*). However, the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and so forth, which are tied to that [conceptualization], are simply unestablished. The rest has already been stated. The mere word "configuration" is not at all a proof, because:
Even when the word itself is unestablished, the established entity is proven;
just as for the follower of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣika), the proof of qualities such as gravity was stated by the Buddhist.

[047,xi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having been born in this world, pass away from it and are reborn elsewhere; having been born elsewhere, they pass away from that world and are reborn here. What are these four? They are as follows: one who was formerly of little faith, stingy, and miserly becomes, after passing away from this world, reborn in a state of great wealth, with abundant food and drink, possessing many vehicles, servants, and attendants, and enjoying great power. Having been born there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the first kind of person. Furthermore, Ānanda, there is another person who was formerly of little faith, stingy, and miserly, but who, having cultivated the path of giving, shared his wealth with others, and practiced charity, passes away from this world and is reborn in a state of great wealth, with abundant food and drink, possessing many vehicles, servants, and attendants, and enjoying great power. Having been born there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the second kind of person. Furthermore, Ānanda, there is another person who was formerly of little faith, stingy, and miserly, but who, having cultivated the path of giving, shared his wealth with others, and practiced charity, passes away from this world and is reborn among the gods of the Four Great Kings. Having been born there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the third kind of person. Furthermore, Ānanda, there is another person who was formerly of little faith, stingy, and miserly, but who, having cultivated the path of giving, shared his wealth with others, and practiced charity, passes away from this world and is reborn among the gods of the Thirty-three. Having been born there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the fourth kind of person. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said: “Those who were formerly stingy and miserly, Having practiced the path of giving, Are reborn among humans or gods; Having enjoyed such happiness, They eventually come back again. Therefore, one should always practice giving; One should not be stingy or miserly. By practicing giving, one attains peace; One will never fall into the evil realms. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) The person who has been reborn here from another world; (2) the person who has been reborn in another world from this world; (3) the person who has been reborn here from another world and will be reborn in another world from this world; and (4) the person who has been reborn in another world from this world and will be reborn here from that world. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one of great faith, affectionate, trusting, munificent, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing—such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in another world. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in another world. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in the company of the devas of the Thirty-three. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. [The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one of great faith, affectionate, trusting, munificent, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing—such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in another world. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in another world. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in the company of the devas of the Thirty-three. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. [The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one of great faith, affectionate, trusting, munificent, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing—such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in another world. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in another world. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is reborn here. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, bhikkhus, there is the person who was formerly of little faith, unaffectionate, untrustful, stingy, mean, and miserly, but afterwards has become one who cultivates the path of giving, shares his wealth with others, and practices charity. Such a person, having passed away from this world, is reborn in the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings. Having been reborn there, he passes away from that world and is

The Buddhist has stated a proof against the Vaiśeṣika: "Atoms are impermanent because they possess form (*mūrttatva*). Now, the word used here is not established in the sense mutually accepted by both parties; for the Vaiśeṣikas hold that the word "form" denotes the dimension of a non-pervasive substance, whereas the Buddhists maintain that "form" is the possession of touch. Even though this very word is not established in the sense mutually accepted by both, nevertheless, since the meaning intended by it is established for both, even if the word itself is unestablished, the intended probandum (*sādhya*)—the object desired by the Buddhist—is established for both parties regarding the established entity.

[047,xii] But surely, just as the probandum is established when the real entity is established as being non-deviant, so too it is exactly the same in the case of the word; what then is the difference between these two? No, [047,xiii] it is not so.

Even when that very [reason] is inconclusive and so forth, it should be known as a defective means of proof even in the case of a word, because the establishment of a real entity proceeds from a real entity. (20)

For it is not the case that just as the probandum is established by the force of the real object (*vastu*) even when the word is unestablished, so too is the probandum established by the force of the word even when the real object is unestablished. Rather, one should know that the proof is faulty if there is deviation, non-establishment, or contradiction regarding that very real object, even if the word itself is non-deviant. For as long as there is deviation and so forth regarding the real object, the non-deviance of the word is impossible.
Even granting this, it is said: let the word be non-deviant; nevertheless, the means of proof is defective. Why? Because an entity is established by an entity, not by a word.

Now, if the word is not non-deviant from the probandum (*sādhya*), then how can the probandum be established from that word? Conversely, if the probandum is established from it, how can the word be non-deviant? By this, he demonstrates the following: a word is useful for establishing the probandum only by way of indicating a real entity (*vastu*), but not directly. Therefore, even if one desires the word to be non-deviant, it lacks the capacity to prove the probandum if it abandons its actual referent. Consequently, only an investigation directed toward the object is effective. An examination of whether there is deviation regarding the real entity or not will follow later. Thus, there is no reason (*hetu*) in the form of a [mere] word through which God (*īśvara*) could be established; therefore, it is proven that [the argument] is invalid even with respect to impermanence.
Likewise, even in the case of the eternal.
Furthermore, there can be no distinction between space and so forth and the Lord (*īśvara*) on the grounds of their being causes or non-causes, because they are both eternal. For it is said:
"In the very same way that it is a causal entity, in that very same way it is a non-cause."
When that [world] is held to have a cause, why is it not accepted that it has no cause? (22)

[048, iv] Attributes such as omnipresence and singularity belong to Īśvara just as they do to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth. Therefore, since these qualities are common to both, on what basis is the distinction made that Īśvara is the cause while space and the like are not? If it is argued that this is said because of his connection with cognition characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), that too is incorrect, for that [cognition] is also common to him. Furthermore, [048, v]
It is not observed that the mere desire to act is the cause;
is this a matter of chance, like the "crow and the palm fruit," or is it indeed the cause?
(346) If [the agent] were the instrument, then karma and so forth would be the cause.

Otherwise, why would everything not be accepted as the cause of everything? (347) (PVA) Alternatively, when prior to creation it was without a cause, so too during the state of creation it must remain without a cause, since there is no difference [in its nature]. It is logical that one who is entirely free from passion and the like should maintain equanimity. If it is argued that he does not attain equanimity because of the predominance of the karma of the world, [we reply: No.

[048.viii] Since he is dependent upon other actions, how can this Lord be truly a Lord? If it is argued that there is a distinction due to the sequence of his compassion, then why is he not merciless in fashioning the hells and other such realms? (PVA 348)

"Karma alone is the cause of the world; thus, his powerlessness regarding its creation is not a lack of nobility. For if a noble person has the power to do what is good, why would he perform what is evil? Indifference toward an improper course of action is indeed appropriate for the virtuous. (PVA 349)
It is not a virtuous deed for the righteous to cast salt upon a wound; rather, it is a noble action [to refrain from doing so].

(PVA 350) [048, xiii] Now, if this very nature of things is such that he reveals and acts toward that [object], thinking, "Such indeed is my own nature; it cannot be restrained by me," then people should conduct themselves therein as is appropriate.
[048,xiv] Even with respect to himself, he has no mastery; thus he is clearly not the Lord. Does he have lordship over the world, whose activities are determined by its own karma? (PVA) 351.
If that [world] is impelled by God, then there is a mutual dependence;

in such a case, the existence of even one of them is not logically tenable. (352) (PVA) If God does not exist, then there is no power [to create]; thus, people would simply be the result of their own virtuous karma.
If the world were one that acts independently, then the doctrine of karma would be praised here as exalted.
(PVA 353) Now, it might be argued: "Even for Īśvara, there may at some time be causality, even if it is not known by those like us who do not perceive the truth. If this is so, then:
Only one who perceives reality can know that reality; there can be no other knower of it.
If there were another knower, there would be an infinite regress, resulting in the possibility of multiple lords.
But by us and others, however:
When Caitra’s wound heals due to his connection with a weapon and medicine, why is the causality of an unrelated post not likewise imagined? (23)

[049,ii] Now, if it is argued that the post has no activity and is therefore not the cause due to a lack of connection, [we reply: even the post does indeed have activity at some time; however, it is not perceived by us who do not see reality.
In that case, because it is not perceived, there is no activity of the post. If this is so,
then even activity is not tenable without a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*).
Because that which is eternal is devoid of deviation, its capacity is difficult to establish.

[049,v] Furthermore, how could the activity of a permanent *īśvara*—whether through the permanence of its continuum or otherwise—be tenable without a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of the *īśvara* also" is displaced in order; it means that just as there is a specific distinction produced by a potter and so forth, [so too must there be one for the Lord].
Likewise, even if it were created by Īśvara, there would be the postulation of a capacity;
yet, because that which is eternal is unchanging, its capacity is difficult to establish.
Because it always pervades its locus, there is no absence [of it];
for when certain things exist, that which necessarily arises from them— if one were to imagine something else [as the cause], [it would be redundant].
Because that [consciousness] is the cause, there would be an infinite regress of all causes. (25)

[049,ix] When the potter and others are present and their activity occurs, the desired result indeed comes to be. Nevertheless, to postulate another [agent] in that case would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthiti) among all causes that produce a single effect, such that there would be no finality.

Indeed, there is no other contradiction than the entry into the conceptualization of that which lacks continuity. Alternatively, if that very same eternal being were to remain as the cause for those who are not established [in a continuum], then since that very same cause would suffice, further action would be useless.
Just as the earth is the cause of sprouts and the like while remaining eternally stable, so too would God be; and yet, no beginning of the earth and such things is perceived.
[049,xii] Here is the rebuttal.
[049,xiii]

The cause for the production of a sprout is through the transformation of its own nature; [this applies] to earth and so forth, because a specific quality of that [sprout] is observed when they are refined. (26)

For it is observed that the growth of barley and other crops follows a sequence of transformations produced by specific activities such as plowing; thus, there arises the conceptualization of earth and other elements as their causes.
Furthermore, there are the objection and its refutation:
"Just as the conjunction of object and sense-faculty [occurs] without a particularity (*viśeṣa*)," and so forth.
If it is argued that this [unmanifested] is likewise the cause of cognition, we reply that this is not so, because even in that case there is no specific distinction.
Since those [atoms] are individually incapable and lack any excellence in their continuum, they would likewise be incapable even when combined; therefore, an excellence must be established. (28)

[049,xviii] For the causality of the eye and so forth is determined by the specific nature of the effect. The effect, namely consciousness, is restricted to the apprehension of form, possesses the aspect of form, and has the nature of awareness; since these [factors] function through mutual exclusion, a distinction among them is possible. Thus, the eye and so forth are the causes of the effect, which is consciousness. Because these are individually incapable, there is no awareness-nature in the eye within the aggregate that constitutes the aspect of consciousness; nor is there the restriction to the apprehension of form in the form itself, nor anything other than mental attention (manaskāra). This is because such [causal capacity] is not observed in each one taken individually. [050,i]

Now, it might be argued: "Just as when the eye is opened, although there is the appearance of various successive forms, there is no change in the eye itself; likewise, while the form remains constant, there occurs the arising of successive visual cognitions. Similarly, even though Īśvara is established as eternally uniform, there is the production of successive states. Thus, he is not a non-cause. Regarding this, it has been said: "If space and so forth were also considered causes, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, [the production of effects] occurs due to the specific nature of the eye and also due to the specific nature of the form."
From that [consciousness], there arises the distinctness of consciousness and the causality of form and so forth.
(356) (PVA) From a specific form characterized by a vividly manifest appearance and so on, consciousness accompanied by mental pleasure and other states is produced. (357) (PVA)
<5. Causality in the Assemblage of Causes> Therefore, when a quality is conceived to exist in those things that are individually incapable, [that quality belongs to their assemblage].
Their causality resides in their collection; it does not reside in a creator god (īśvara) or the like, because there is no distinction [between them]. // 29 //

Likewise, due to specific conditions such as the eyes being closed or open, there is a specific difference such as lack of clarity; this [difference] is dependent upon that [condition], and thus it leads one to conceive of that [condition] as the cause by way of its being an effect. However, there is no such reason for postulating God as the cause. Therefore: "If individual [atoms] are individually incapable, and there is no excellence in their continuum (*santānātiśaya*), then even when combined they would lack capacity. Since that very nature is the opposite of a cause, how could it be the cause? What is the answer to this? As for the postulation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth as causes, the reason has already been stated, so there is no fault.
<4. The Fourth Treatise on the Authority of the Blessed One> <1. The Blessed One is an authority because he possesses knowledge> [050, vi]
If, then, there is no cause for the cognition and so forth of God—neither a communicator nor a creator—then such a cause would not exist for anything else either. For:
"Validity consists in the knowledge of an imperceptible object and in the means of achieving that."
Some declare that because of non-existence, there is no practice.

[050, viii] First, as for one who is not omniscient but becomes omniscient: what is the cause for his thorough knowledge of objects beyond the senses (*parokṣārtha*)? Indeed, no such cause whatsoever has been observed from whose practice all-knowledge arises. As for mantras, tantras, and the like, they generally arise only within their respective specific systems (*samaya*). Nor is there a cause for the certain determination of them; for agreement regarding only a single part applies to all words alike. Furthermore, the direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of all supersensible objects is impossible, because sensory cognition is seen to have only proximate objects as its domain.
Even if there were no distinction in the sense-faculties and their objects, if the arising of omniscience were possible,
then everyone would be omniscient precisely because there is no distinction in the sense-faculties and their objects.
Furthermore, the occurrence of non-correspondence regarding impure things and so forth would be unavoidable.
And if the sense-faculties were of the nature of reaching [their objects], how could he be called omniscient?
(359) Even his mental consciousness does not exist independently of the sense-faculties; indeed, no one perceives a mental cognition that is autonomous. (360)
Through practice, its clarity may arise, yet it would not have all things as its object;
even if it were based on scripture, the consequence would be that it is non-erroneous.
But if it were established through inference, no real entity whatsoever could be apprehended.
Therefore, if cultivation does not have all things as its object, how can one be omniscient?

(362) Through the repeated study of treatises and so forth, one may come to understand only those very treatises and such; but from where will the knowledge of everything in its entirety ever come? (363)
It is called "consciousness" because it knows everything; how could there be knowledge of that which is to be known [if consciousness did not exist]?
Indeed, even in the case of knowing that which is to be known, he alone would be the omniscient one.
Furthermore, he who is free from passion and the like, and likewise free from conceptual construction—(PVA 364).
To claim that "the teaching was produced by him" is merely borrowed ornamentation.
(365) Who could possibly understand, even over the course of many eons, each individual thing—past, present, and future, without beginning or end—in its distinct sequence? (366)
Who indeed does not possess some partial knowledge?
For there is not even a single true fact that does not exist within a person of many capacities.
As for one who is seen to possess excellence, that is due to his being established in just that much [knowledge]. (PVA 367)
One might know a mere fraction of what lies between [the senses], but one who knows objects beyond the senses is not so;
(368) (PVA) nor is it logically possible for one who knows the reality of only a single part to be omniscient.
This would be a mere coincidence, like the "crow and the palm fruit," and would only cause further delusion. (369) (PVA)
If all cognitions were simultaneous, how could there be beginningless saṃsāra?
That which one knows to be the final limit is what is called the "beginning" in this context.

To this it is replied: It is not maintained that the Supreme One knows everything as an object of valid cognition; rather, he is one who does not deceive, and let him be capable of accomplishing what is desired. For what reason?
Someone possessing knowledge is sought in order to practice according to what has been taught by him.
By those who fear deception when acting upon the instructions of one who lacks knowledge. || 31 ||

Indeed, one does not seek knowledge from a teacher regarding anything other than what one intends to practice; for even when that [specific point] is ascertained, there remains the possibility of being deceived regarding what was actually intended. Now, if it is argued that in that case one has certainty because he certainly possesses knowledge of that very point, [we reply: this is not so, because knowledge is not possible in all respects. Therefore, he is a valid authority (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to that which is to be known by him and which is known to be known; thus, for the ignorant who suspect deception regarding the cause of the teacher’s instruction, he is an authority only insofar as they know his knowledge of that specific subject. Even in other matters, his knowledge may be presumed. For only he who knows the primary goals of human life and who knows all the principles (*tattva*) as purified by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an authority; by that much alone is he to be venerated. As for everything else, it is the same for all those to be venerated. And whose [knowledge of all things] can be presumed? Only that of the person by whom [the teaching] was imparted. But those who do not speak of the primary goals of human life as seen through the means of valid cognition, and who do not know them—these are not authorities, because even in that regard, the possibility of non-comprehension exists. If it is asked, "How then is the instruction [possible]? [The answer is: It comes from an beginningless tradition, like the instruction of nihilism (*nāstikya*).
[2. Because he is the knower of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, the Blessed One is a means of valid cognition.

Now, if there is no complete knowledge of everything, then because doubt arises regarding all things, it is possible that another person might also lack complete knowledge. Consequently, one who does not conceive of the possibility of universal knowledge—how could such a person conceive of the possibility of complete knowledge even in this case? As for the teaching, however, it is due to a traditional succession of teachings.
[051,xviii] That is incorrect.
In the case of an object that is not authoritative, there is a clear succession of instructions;
however, in the case of an authoritative object, such a succession of instructions is impossible.

For regarding such matters as eternity and so forth, since no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is possible, there is no recourse other than a succession of oral instructions. If an object has been determined by a means of valid cognition, how can there be any suspicion of ignorance regarding it? Or, even if such suspicion were to exist, activity toward that object would necessarily follow, because of the certainty provided by the means of valid cognition. Now, if it is argued that there is no certainty regarding what is seen by a means of valid cognition until its direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), then this consequence follows:
[052,i] This very point has arrived.

Such subtle vision has arisen that even what has been seen by means of valid cognition is scrutinized; since this is suspected even regarding the outsiders, what talk could there be of others? (372) (PVA)

The Blessed Tathāgata speaks of that which is perceived by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even regarding this, for one who harbors doubt, what need is there to mention other religious systems (*tīrtha*) in which there is no conformity with thorough knowledge? Therefore, because he teaches matters established by valid cognition, the Blessed One is indeed valid cognition itself.
A person who knows the Veda is the authority for the path to heaven and liberation;
even if he lacks knowledge of other things, that [authority] regarding them may still exist.
Therefore, let his knowledge concerning what is to be practiced be investigated.
Of what use to us is his complete knowledge of the number of insects? // 32 //
Because:
But here, only the denial of the knowledge of dharma is being negated;
who can prevent another from negating everything else?

Now, if it is argued that the Tathāgata may be considered all-knowing because his knowledge of a single portion is consistent with reality, then by the same logic of consistency—such as in the case of the statement "fire is the antidote to cold"—anyone else could also be so considered; thus, there would be an infinite regress. But this is not the case, because such a practice is impossible due to mutual contradiction.
That too is untrue.

He who makes known the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, as well as the means for their abandonment and adoption, is accepted as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*); however, he is not an authority because he knows everything. (33)

Since he is not the knower of every object that does not constitute a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), it does not follow from that alone that he must be the knower of everything; for it is impossible for anyone not to know at least some portion of what constitutes a human goal. In this context, the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted consists in the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its cessation (*nirodha*). The reality of the means consists in the truths of the origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*), which are the causes of those two [truths]. Therefore, one who knows the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—characterized by the four noble truths—and who is the knower of that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is himself a valid authority (*pramāṇa*). This applies also to the path to heaven, which can be determined through valid cognition. As for anything else, there is nothing in the words of the Sugata that would fail to amaze even women and *śūdras*. Consequently, only the knower of the primary human goals is a valid authority, as no other [kind of knower] is possible.
Therefore.
[052,xiii]
Whether he sees far or not, let him see the truth that is desired;
if one who sees afar were the authority, then let us worship vultures.

For it is not the case that the mere existence of far-sighted vision makes omniscience possible. If it were so, then even vultures and the like would possess it; we would then have to accept vultures and pigs as objects of veneration because of their distant hearing. In this way, the entire path of logic would be abandoned.
[3. The Blessed One is the authority because of his compassion.]
[1] Proof of Other Lives:
Now, is it the case that knowledge of all objects is absolutely impossible and useless, such that only the knowledge of the primary goals of human existence is sought after?
This is not so.
[052,xvii]
It is not denied that one who knows everything might know all;
however, we maintain contentment with the thought that it is impossible for us to know it all.
Indeed, the omniscient one does not know the omniscient one because of the absence of a means [for such knowledge]. For it is thus:
the notion that "he knows everything" arises from knowing the knowledge of those objects to be known.
The knowledge of even a single portion of that [omniscience] arises only for one who already knows it.

(PVA 376) Even regarding trees and such things, which are common objects of knowledge for women and śūdras, the cognition as to whether they are known by another person arises solely from that person's own knowledge. However, when one has not known them oneself, there is no means to determine that "this person has known them. As for those great beings who have attained far-reaching vision, the possibility of their being omniscient is preceded by the thorough knowledge of a single portion; yet even for them, the possibility of their reality is established by another.
[053,iv] But if it is asked: "From where is the proof for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that possesses both characteristics, or what is its reason (*hetu*)? he says:

How is there a means of establishing that validity? It is "from the practice of compassion. And that compassion, "because cognition relies upon the body,"—since that cognition has a body as its support, that compassion, through the cultivation of practice, attains a state of supreme excellence.
[053,vii] Even if there is compassion, how could validity arise from it? There is a possibility, because:
[053,viii]
The desire for another to be separated from suffering and its cause is compassion; one who possesses that [compassion] applies their mind toward acquiring the means for that [separation].
For it will be demonstrated later that one who necessarily desires the separation of others from suffering must seek the means for that end.

Alternatively, compassion is the means; for one possessed of compassion is never devoid of the desire to benefit others. Therefore, through teaching for the sake of others, he is an authority (*pramāṇa*). One possessed of compassion engages in the means; and that means is the proof of his own status as an authority.

From what does that very compassion, characterized by the desire to protect all, arise? He says: "From the practice of compassion. For compassion, through the practice of [contemplating] suffering, extends even toward those who are indifferent or hostile. Since protecting everyone is not possible without omniscience, the practice of its means is undertaken.

But surely, the intellect of the wise rests upon the body, and compassion is nothing other than intellect; therefore, it too must rest upon the body. Consequently, since the body is reduced to ashes, the practice [of compassion] remains unestablished. For if there were the possibility of another birth, then through the accumulation of practice over many lifetimes, the desired goal would be attained. Thus it is said: "The intellect consists of the body, is an effect of the body, and is a quality of the body."
Relying on these three views, the possibility of cultivation does not exist here.
Thus he says: "Because cognition depends upon the body."
If it is argued that practice is unestablished, we say no, because its substratum has been refuted. (35)

Because it is denied that a solitary body, devoid of the preceding continuum of consciousness, can serve as a substratum; indeed, whether it be an effect, a quality, or otherwise, a solitary body cannot function as a substratum.
"Intellect does not depend upon the body and so forth.
[053,xviii]

Is it not the case that consciousness (*buddhi*) is perceived as dependent upon the body and as its effect, since we observe it to rely on the bodies of the mother and father? For instance: the beauty, conduct, mental acuity, and so forth of the offspring are derived from those of the parents and have as their substratum the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the produced body, just as paintings depend upon a wall. These paintings are the effects of the painter, inheriting his form, knowledge, and other qualities; thus, a painting does not remain without a wall, nor does it migrate to another wall, nor does it come from another wall—just like the color produced by the ripening of a mango fruit or the like. Nor does smoke, which is an effect, come from one fire (*dhūmadhvaja*) to another, nor does it travel to another fire. Furthermore, the power of intoxication (*madaśakti*), though residing in wine, arises anew through contact with astringent flavors and the like; when the wine dissolves, this power does not take hold in another wine. So too are the specific cognitions of the sense faculties. Thus it has been said: "Earth, water, fire, and air are the principles (*tattva*). Only earth and the others are the principles, and only the principles are earth and the others; they are not space (*ākāśa*) and the like, nor are they momentariness and the like. Likewise, the principles alone are neither mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*) nor is everything entirely empty, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for either [of those latter positions]. The designation "object," "sense faculty," and "body" applies to the collection of these [elements]. An immeasurable, transformed collection of the great elements themselves constitutes the referent of terms such as "arrow" and the like. From these—the body, the senses, and the objects—consciousness arises, just as the power of intoxication arises from yeast and the like. Therefore, consciousness is like the power of intoxication; it does not possess a point of reconnection (*pratisandhi*) by coming from a previous world. The phrase "like the power of intoxication" is an illustration, as are "like a painting" and "like smoke. Indeed, none of these are observed to be migratory.
That is incorrect.
How can there be the perception of the elements apart from form and the other [sensory objects]? Therefore, the determination of their number as five is illogical. (379) (PVA) [054,iii]

Visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility are the five great elements (*mahābhūta*). The designations "earth" and so forth apply to their collection, because earth and the others cannot be perceived apart from them. Now, if it is argued that taste is merely something tangible, then there would be only four dimensions; even so, it would be incorrect to say "earth and the others," and "visible form and the others" would be the proper designation. As for momentariness and other such qualities, they will be established later as the properties to be proven, and thus they are not rejected here.
Furthermore:
For if everything were simply "the visible, the visible," it would follow that all things are one;
however, if there is a distinction in their modes, it would follow that they are infinite.
Therefore, let that which is apprehended by the five bases be designated as fivefold.
Its internal subdivisions, moreover, do not obstruct its fivefold nature.
(381) (PVA) And as for what was said: "If there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding universal emptiness, then there is no emptiness;
if there is emptiness, then the means of valid cognition does not exist—thus these two [positions] are contradictory. (382) (PVA)
The nature of universal emptiness will be established later;
and as for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that, what haste is there for it to be of any use here?
(383) [This concludes] the refutation of the doctrine that consciousness is an emergent property of the elements (*bhūta-caitanya*).

[054,x] But surely, since the sense faculties and so forth follow the positive and negative concomitance of the bodies of the mother and father, and because they have the great elements of the body as their intrinsic nature, they are observed to be supported by that very body and not otherwise; therefore, how can the doctrine of the existence of a future world be well-founded?
That too is untrue, because:
[054,xii] Life-force, downward breath, the sense faculties, and cognitions do not arise from the body alone.
For those who are independent of their own species, there is birth in the undertaking of a new birth. 36.
Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

For it is not logical that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth arise from specific natures such as fickleness and the like while being independent of their own genus (*svajāti*). Furthermore, fickleness and the rest are associated with the habitual tendencies of the self (*ātman*), not with the habitual tendencies of the mother and father. Otherwise, the nature of the mother and father would not exist due to contact with the wicked and other factors. Therefore, existence does not arise solely from the bodies of the mother and father independently of their own genus. However, if desire and the like already existed within the nature of the mother and father, then it would be logical for the body of the mother, father, and so on, to also be a cause.

Now, if it is admitted that the assumption of birth occurs entirely independently of a future world, then, when such an assumption of birth is accepted, there follows an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Every relation of cause and effect would collapse; and that [relation] is to be ascertained through the determination of inference (*anumāna*).
If all [phenomena], such as inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*), were preceded by practice (*abhyāsa*)...

And how indeed could they be devoid of support if they were lacking their own repeated practice? For this is the nature of an effect: that it does not come into being otherwise than by abandoning its cause; otherwise, it would not be produced by it. The relationship between producer and produced is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, the eyes and other sense organs are preceded solely by the repeated practice of similar types of eyes and so forth.
[055,iv] But is it not so?
Smoke is produced from another instance of smoke, not exclusively from smoke alone.
How then can a lotus-root arise even from śālka-wood, or from cow dung?
Likewise:
"Is the variegation produced from a painter also present in birds? [055, vii]
"That which is a distinction resulting from practice will also occur through another [means]"—
that too is incorrect.
Just as smoke is not known from smoke as it truly is when it comes from another source, so too,
the specific excellence that arises from practice remains established in that same way at the beginning of birth. (PVA 387)

[055,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking birth. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of craving is the cessation of these nutriments, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of these nutriments? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of these nutriments. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of ignorance is the cessation of volitional formations, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of volitional formations is the cessation of consciousness, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of consciousness is the cessation of name-and-form, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of name-and-form? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of name-and-form. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of name-and-form is the cessation of the six sense bases, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of the six sense bases? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of the six sense bases. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of the six sense bases is the cessation of contact, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of contact? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of contact. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of contact is the cessation of feeling, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of feeling is the cessation of craving, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of craving? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of craving. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of craving is the cessation of clinging, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of clinging? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of clinging. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of clinging is the cessation of existence, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of existence? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of existence. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of existence is the cessation of birth, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of birth? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of birth. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of birth is the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and the practice leading to that cessation. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, monks, by the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; by the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness; by the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; by the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; by the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; by the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; by the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; by the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; by the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; by the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; by the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. [055,xiii] Then the Venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and placing his right knee on the ground, bowed toward the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence and said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well has the Blessed One explained the causal relationship and the dependent origination of this entire mass of suffering! [055,xiv] The Blessed One said: “So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda! If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the arising of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the cessation of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the arising of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the cessation of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With the remainderless fading away and cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the arising of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the cessation of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With the remainderless fading away and cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the arising of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the cessation of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With the remainderless fading away and cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the arising of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the cessation of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With the remainderless fading away and cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. If, Ānanda, one were to point out a cause for the arising of this entire mass of suffering, it would be this: ‘With contact as condition,

That very same distinction which arises from the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is seen here to exist even in the absence of practice in this life, provided it is of such a nature. Nor is its connection with practice contradicted, because a past practice cannot be perceived at that time even elsewhere, just like a practice acquired upon arriving from another village. For this very reason, it does not prove that [the distinction] is preceded by practice in a future life, because there is an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) between the cause and the effect; for even an unperceived cause is still its effect. It likewise proves that it is preceded by practice in another place, because there is an invariable concomitance between the cause and the effect; for even an unperceived cause is still its effect, just like the thorough knowledge [of something] preceded by practice in another location. Thus, in this matter, the story of Tauta has been brought forward.
[055,xiii] It is said that once a certain Tautātita was asked by another, "Tell me of the origin: how does the existence of a bull with long horns come about? (PVA) 388.
He replied: "These buffaloes are not born from the mother's womb;
rather, they are merely purchased for their price from those who have come to the market.
(PVA 055, xvi)
This Lokāyata doctrine is indeed exactly like that.

Alternatively, it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): if consciousness as an effect arises from those very primary elements (*mahābhūta*) alone, without any arrival from another birth, why does it not arise in all living beings? If you say, "Because of the existence of a specific transformation (*pariṇativiśeṣa*)," then the same objection applies: why is that specific transformation not present [in all cases]?

[055,xviii] Now, if it is argued that there exists some beginningless transformation (*pariṇati*) or some unperceived specific succession (*paramparāviśeṣa*) by virtue of which some living beings are so and others are not— that too is untenable. [055,xix]
If no specific difference in transformation is perceived, what kind of conceptual construction is this?
That which is capable of being seen but is not seen is not an object for conventional practice. (390) [PVA 055,xxi]

If that specific transformation were [already] present, it would be perceived. If, however, it is postulated solely on the basis of observing the effect, then in that case, only the observed repetition (*abhyāsa*) should be postulated, because of the principle of parsimony regarding the postulation of the unobserved (*adṛṣṭakalpanāgaurava*). Therefore, it has been rightly stated: "Breath and the other [vital functions] are preceded by entities of a similar kind.
Granted that the establishment of causes from effects [is possible] for those occurring in a previous birth, how is there inference for those occurring in a subsequent birth? To this he says:
That which was observed possesses the capacity for reconnection. What was it that it lacked later, by virtue of which it would not possess such reconnection? (37)
For the connection of each preceding [moment] with its successor is established through inference, inference based on inference,
and so forth.

But surely, restlessness and the like arise from the absence of non-restlessness through the practice of that which is characterized by lack of movement, dullness, and so forth; yet that [non-restlessness] arises solely from the great elements themselves. Even if it were to exist from those [elements], just as smoke exists from other smoke, there would be no constant continuity. Therefore, just like smoke, there would also be its cessation, and thus there would be neither the infinity of living beings nor the fault of the appearance of previously non-existent sentient beings. [To this we reply: That is not so.
Through the practice of slow activity, there is also slowness among living beings.
Then, preceded by that [cognition], it [the subsequent cognition] falls into the beginningless wheel of existence.

Indeed, the various states such as dullness and so forth do not belong to living beings by their very nature; rather, they arise from the practice of similar types [of states].
