Just as fickleness and the like result from the habituation to them, so too does dullness and the like result from the habituation to indolence (*kausīdya*). Thus, the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is established. For the sluggishness of the eyes and other faculties arises from the habituation to sleep and the like; consequently, one who has awakened from sleep—possessing fickle eyes and so forth—is joined with fickle eyes and the like through mutual [causality]. Therefore, even at the beginning of a birth, the connection with the eyes and other faculties occurs just like the awakening from sleep, through the arousal of latencies (*vāsanā*) that have become manifest. How can an eye residing in another body be reconnected in a different body? How can a power residing in one substance migrate to another?
Just as the potencies of poison [are removed] from molasses and other substances through the power of mantras, tantras, and so forth,
in that very same way, the potencies of other bodies [are produced] through the power of karma. (PVA 392)
Just as a body in a dream [undergoes] transformations of the waking body through fear, leaping, and running, so too does it do so in other births. (393) Now,
since this [body] is utterly devoid of reality, it is all the more excellent.
If even that which is unreal leads to transformation, what need is there to mention that which is real?
(394) This distinction between reality and unreality is merely a matter of conventional usage;
when the intrinsic nature [of things] is directly realized, such categories as "reality" and so forth are untenable. (395)

Therefore, regarding that which was previously perceived as possessing the capacity for reconnection (*pratisandhāna*), what additional factor did it have that is later absent? Because of the absence of that, it subsequently lacks reconnection. For while the non-arising of an effect occurs when there is a deficiency in its causes, it is a contradiction to claim that an effect does not arise when all its constituent parts are present in the cause.
Is there not indeed a contradiction here? Is it not precisely this: the absence of the causal relation?
For if there were non-production of the effect even when the cause remains identical in all its states—
In that case, the effect would be independent; however, an effect is not such [independent].
(PVA 396) For an effect is dependent upon its cause, and that capable cause produces it by necessity. Even so, in the absence [of the cause], the effect would not come to be.

[056,xv] Now, as for the statement "it does not exist when that is absent," how is it known that the effect does not exist when that is absent? But surely, how is it known that "it necessarily exists when that is present"? Because it is determined to be so, it is likewise determined that "it does not exist when that is absent. As for the question "at all times?", this is the same in both cases. Therefore, one must accept things exactly as they are observed; and both are observed. [057,i]

If it is argued that since it necessarily occurs when that [cause] is present and necessarily does not occur when it is incomplete, both of these must be admitted, and thus there is no relation of cause and effect for what is unobserved;
[we reply: there is no observation of either negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) or positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of universal pervasion (*vyāpti*).
How can there be a perception of this causal relationship?

(PVA 397) If there is no perception by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then the establishment of the causal relationship is not achieved. In that case, it has already been stated that there is no perception of anything else besides the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): "The cognition of its own nature occurs through itself."

There is no world beyond, nor this world, nor the sublation of the world beyond, nor doubt, nor the transformation of the great elements, and so forth; it is merely representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Nevertheless, this is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*); in the same way, the world beyond exists as well.
If you find satisfaction in non-duality, you are liberated in every respect;
if worldly activity persists, then the next world must also be considered.

If a misconception must occur, this kind of misconception is preferable, because it is conducive to tranquility and the attainment of heaven and other such states. For a misconception regarding passion and the like brings about only the loss of all desired qualities, such as being a virtuous person and so forth. To explain: all the various types of passion, such as that for the eye and so on, rely upon the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and do not differ from mere representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Consequently, even for one who is devoid of eyes and other faculties in this life, there is the possession of unimpaired eyes and other faculties again in another birth. Thus, this very same process continues through a succession of births, and the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* is established. As long as the cessation of misconceptions has not occurred, its infinity is likewise established. Even if the eyes and other faculties were real external objects, this nature would still be beginningless; thus, *saṃsāra* is both beginningless and endless.
[057,vii] "Cognition does not arise from the primary elements.
[057,viii]

[Objection: But surely specific qualities of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as solidity and so forth, are indeed perceived. Therefore, even though they arise from the great elements, there is no over-extension of the principle because of those specific qualities. Consequently, it is precisely these specific qualities—solidity and so forth—that constitute the seed-nature, and from that alone the birth of living beings occurs. [Reply: To this it has been said: "In that case, the very relationship of cause and effect would not exist. Moreover:
[057,x] There is not a single part of the earth or other elements where beings born from moisture and so forth do not arise; therefore, everything possesses the nature of a seed. 38.

[057,xi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. “What are the four? Ānanda, here a certain person appears in the world as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One; he teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. This is the first kind of person who appears in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. “Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person appears in the world as a Pratyekabuddha, one who dwells alone like a rhinoceros horn, who has attained the path of awakening by himself, having realized it through his own effort and insight, and who remains in this very life, having personally realized the supreme peace of Nirvāṇa. This is the second kind of person who appears in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. “Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person appears in the world as a disciple of the Tathāgata, a noble hearer who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, who has entered the fixed course toward enlightenment and is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, being assured of reaching full awakening. This is the third kind of person who appears in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. “Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person appears in the world as a disciple of the Tathāgata, a noble hearer who has attained the fruit of once-returning, who, having returned to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering. This is the fourth kind of person who appears in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. “These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.”

Indeed, the differentiation of living beings does not arise from the distinction of qualities such as solidity, because living beings are observed everywhere. For even moisture-born and other types of living beings are certainly not seen to be differentiated by those [qualities]. Therefore, the distinction is not caused by solidity and the like; rather, only action—characterized by volition—remains as the ultimate [differentiator]. Now, if one were to say that a class of living beings is perceived as inherent in wood and so forth, then everything belonging to that same class would consist of living beings of that form. Whatever water is established by its own nature, all of that would consist of living beings of that form. From what, then, would the diversity of color and shape among living beings arise?
For instance, others are seen with red heads, yellow bodies, and so forth, such as aquatic creatures; from where would that form [of a universal] come? (PVA 399)
From seeds of that same nature, the diversity of lotuses and so forth is observed; it is not seen to be indeterminate at any time.
But the diversity of living beings is not [seen to be] indeterminate with respect to their seed; for in this case, there are karmas that act as the determinants.
[This is so] when the eyes and other organs arise without depending on their own genus.
Otherwise, just as there would be transformation for one [entity], it would occur for all without distinction. (39)

Furthermore, the sense faculties (*indriya*) which rely upon the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perform their own respective functions, but the mental consciousness itself does not rely upon them. Therefore, he demonstrates that the arising of the sense faculties occurs from the mental consciousness alone, and not from earth, water, and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with “each individually” (*pratyekam*).

Alternatively, mental consciousness does not arise from that body which is of the nature of an aggregate; rather, inhalation, exhalation, and so forth, are merely transformations of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) derived solely from the seeds of the mother and father. Furthermore, it is the mental consciousness that transmigrates, not the sense faculties and the rest. For:
[058, iv] Severance, reconnection, detachment, decline, death, and rebirth—these belong to the mind.
"Mind-consciousness alone is associated with equanimity during death and rebirth.
(PVA) [058,v] Thus it has been said. Therefore, the mind's state of transmigrating is not due to its dependence on the primary elements (*bhūta*). Why? Because:
Even when each of the sense faculties is impaired, there is no impairment of the mind (manas) for cognition; yet, upon the destruction of this [mind], their destruction is also observed. (40)

[058,vii] For, since changes in the eyes and other sense organs are observed when mental cognition (*manomatī*) undergoes destruction through fear, grief, joy, anger, and so forth, the eyes and other organs are dependent upon mental consciousness. Therefore, at the beginning of birth as well, they must likewise be dependent upon it; thus, the existence of another life is established. Furthermore, mental consciousness is not dependent on the body, because it depends on the effects of the aggregate of the five sense organs, which are themselves modified by mental consciousness.
[058,viii]

Now, if indeed the eye and so forth are transformations of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), how is it that their production arises from those very [organs] themselves? For an object such as a jar, even while undergoing a transformation due to fire, is not produced from the fire alone.
To this, it is replied:
A jar or similar object is perceived differently [at different times]; therefore, it is not that very same thing [as before].
However, the sense faculty is not perceived differently, because of its lack of such modification. (PVA 402)

[058,xi] For every sense organ is perceived as characterized by the features of palaces and the like, but a jar or similar object is not perceived solely through the transformation produced by fire. Therefore, a jar or the like does not serve as a valid example.
Now, even if it is true that mental consciousness is observed to have a basis at this time, why should it be the same at other times as well? This is incorrect.
For although smoke is seen from fire, it arises from that very fire.
"Even at other times, perception is not a means of valid cognition for anyone here.
Therefore:

Just as the understanding that fire preceded smoke occurs through the recognition of it, so too is there the understanding that the mind is subject to transformation, which exists from birth onwards. (PVA 404)

[058,xvi] Since the eyes and other sense organs are recognized at birth and so forth as being subject to modifications corresponding to the mind’s restlessness and other states, it is logical to understand them to be exactly those same organs. This is just as when the production of smoke is observed once to be preceded by fire in a certain place, and it is subsequently recognized in another location as being likewise preceded by fire.
[058,xvii]
Even when there is a deficiency of the sense organs such as the eyes, there is still mental transformation;
since the mind depends on that [body], it follows [therein], and thus there is no restriction for either of the two.
(PVA 405) [058,xviii]

If, because there is no rule that the mind is not modified when there is a modification of the son, the eyes, and so forth, these—such as the son, the eyes, and so on—are not the support [of the mind], then that very absence of a rule is observed for both cases alike. Since the mind of some person is not modified even when there is a modification of the self, the eyes, and so forth, those [latter] are also not the support; thus, the sense-faculties do not possess the status of being the support. If that were so, then mental consciousness would be the support of the sense-faculties, while the sense-faculties would not be the support of the mind, which results in the mind being without a support. Furthermore, there must be some support for all six consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and the rest.

The sense-faculty exists because of the cognition of the mind, and from that, mental consciousness arises; therefore, even in that case, there would be a beginningless and endless persistence of existence. (PVA 406)
If mental cognition (*manomatih*) were likewise not subject to modification through the modification of the sense faculties, then...
When the eyes and other organs are destroyed, mental dejection and the like are observed in various instances.
Since these are dependent upon those [organs], it is inferred that there is nothing unwholesome here [in the mind].
This is not so. There is no rule that everything must necessarily have some substratum. If, however, you insist on this point, it is said in reply:
Therefore, that which is the support for the persistence of cognition is itself dependent upon cognition alone;
it is something that serves as the cause for the sense-faculties. Consequently, the sense-faculties are derived from cognition. (41)

[059,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding the suffering of those beings, through his transcendent power of wisdom, liberated them from that perilous state. Thereupon, the bhikṣus addressed the Blessed One: “O Blessed One, how is it that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by beholding the suffering of those beings, through his transcendent power of wisdom, liberated them from that perilous state? The Blessed One said to the bhikṣus: “If, O bhikṣus, there should be any sons of good family or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, should with single-minded devotion invoke him, then all their perils shall immediately be extinguished; and if they behold the Buddha, they shall attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the World-Honored One further declared in verse: “Should any son of noble family or daughter of noble family, Having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, With single-minded devotion invoke him, Then all their perils shall immediately be extinguished. If one should behold the Buddha, One shall attain supreme, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one should always revere and honor him, And never abandon the thought of the Buddha. At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Blessed One had taught, were filled with joy and put it into practice. Therefore, that which is the support for the persistence of cognition (*buddhi*) is the cause of the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), designated as volition (*cetanā*), characteristic, and action (*karman*). If it is asked, "Does that [volition] then depend upon the sense-faculties such as the eye? he says: "And that depends only upon cognition, not upon the sense-faculties; for the sense-faculties are not its support. This is because of the statement: "Volition is action, or action after having willed (*cetayitvā*). And volition consists of the nature of thinking "this" and "that"; and since it takes the form of a prior connection (*anusandhāna*), it arises depending only upon cognition, not depending upon the body. Furthermore, only a certain [kind of] volition is the support of the sense-faculties, not all of them, because the sense-faculties do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). For the production of the body and the sense-faculties occurs through action accompanied by craving for the body, due to the application of attachment (*abhirati*) toward it. Indeed, attachment arises toward an object once it has been obtained. Therefore, the conclusion is: the sense-faculties arise from cognition, but cognition does not arise from the sense-faculties. Consequently, the mind alone (*manas*) is the cause; thus, by means of the mind, there is the projection (*ākṣepa*) of successive previous births.

If, then, the mental cognition (*manomati*)—which consists of the conceptualization of a self in the form of "I"—belongs to this present life, what is the cause for its continuity in a future life, or how is it that the mind is said to be dependent upon the body? To this he says: [059,xi] The mental cognition, which consists of the conceptualization of a self in the form of "I," belongs to this present life; however, as for its continuity in a future life, what is the cause for its persistence, or how is it that the mind is said to be dependent upon the body?
To this he says:
Whatever kind of projecting [consciousness] it was previously, let it be the same afterwards as well;
because it is assisted by those cognitions, it is said that the mind is dependent on the body. (42)

Whatever kind of grasping at a self the mental cognition (*manobuddhi*) of those transmigrating beings was—which projects the continuity of births beginning from the beginningless past—let that same kind project it even later; it cannot be otherwise. That very same thing constitutes the subsequent appropriation of birth. For whatever possesses a nature not distinct from the nature of performing a certain action, it necessarily performs that action. For example, another fire, though associated with fuel and so forth, possesses a nature not distinct from the nature of producing smoke. Otherwise, there would be no causal relationship and no worldly convention; the world would be devoid of purposeful activity.
(kha) The Proof of Consciousness [059,xiii]

Now, the Blessed One has also established that the mind (*manas*) is dependent upon the body, by stating that body and mind are mutually conforming. To this, the following is the resolution: the Blessed One stated that the mind is dependent on the body because it is assisted by the bodily consciousnesses (*kāyavijñāna*). However, the body is not its direct support (*āśraya*), in the same way that the eyes and other [faculties] are the supports for visual and other consciousnesses. Therefore, the mind, characterized by the notion of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*), is neither dependent on the sense-faculties such as the eye, nor is it dependent on the physical body. It is logical that its support is only a mind of the same class (*samānajātīya-manas*), because it exists even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and its presence there has been demonstrated.
[060,i] Let it be that cognition does not exist without the sense organs; nevertheless, there is no absence of a future world (paraloka), because of their mutual dependence. Thus he says:
Although cognition does not exist without the sense-faculties, nor do they exist without it,
nevertheless, because they are mutual causes, they are therefore mutually dependent.

[060,iii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, are called ‘true sons of the Śākya,’ born from his mouth, born of the Dharma, created by the Dharma, heirs of the Dharma. What are these four? They are: one who is a stream-enterer, one who is a once-returner, one who is a non-returner, and one who is an arhat.”

For just as your own admission is that cognition does not exist without a body because it is observed [to arise] from the sense organs, so too you must admit that those sense organs do not exist without the mind and cognition; for the reason for such an admission—namely, the observation of their co-occurrence—is the same. This being the case, it follows that the two continua are mutually causal, since they provide mutual assistance to one another. And for two things that are mutually causal, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) arises from another causal complex. From that complex as well, the preceding and succeeding body and mind are to be understood as being mutually causal, just as in the intermediate state.

Furthermore, if the body alone were the basis for mental cognition, that cognition would not belong to the body. Therefore, when cognition arises from the body, it must arise either successively or simultaneously, as there is no other possible mode.
In this regard, it cannot first be from non-succession, because:
"There is no arising of successive things from that which is non-successive, nor can there be dependence for that which lacks distinguishing characteristics."
The cognition that arises sequentially from the body also indicates that [the body] is sequential. (44)

For this mental cognition is successive; otherwise, if there were a grasping of its own form as "I," there would follow the consequence of grasping the entire nature of oneself— past, present, and future— which entails the grasping of all one's births.
Furthermore, if the states are not apprehended, there can be no cognition of their pervasion by what precedes and follows.
If the states are not apprehended, how could there be a cognition of the substratum?
Because, when the pervaded is not cognized, the pervader is likewise not cognized.

For if a pervasive state is not perceived, then because the pervaded is not perceived, how could that [pervader] be apprehended as such? Indeed, even if something is not perceived in a certain form, it does not thereby become that [form]. It is perception alone that establishes identity or difference. If its pervasiveness is not perceived, then it follows that it is perceived in another form; consequently, it has no persistence through other times, and thus there is no perception of another time. Therefore, perception is successive; hence, a successive entity cannot arise from what is non-successive.

[060,xii] Now, if indeed the cause is sequential, why must the effect also be of that same nature? For the effect is not necessarily non-different from the cause, since we observe even that which is of a different character.
[060,xiii]
To this it is replied:
If the effect were produced without succession, then the entirety of it would come into being at that very moment.
But at other times, it does not exist at all, because it has reached its completion. (409) (PVA) [061,i]

For it would produce that effect only if it were perceived at the time of the effect; for that which is not being perceived at that time cannot be its cause. If there is perception, then because of its oneness, there must be perception until the point of destruction, and thus it would have to be destroyed at that very moment. For such is its non-momentariness. Consequently, no further effect could arise from what has been destroyed. Or, if an effect were to arise, it would not be the effect of that [cause]. Alternatively, if it is perceived successively, then it is the cause of successive effects. This being the case, it is not non-successive; for what is perceived as blue cannot be non-blue. Or else: [061,ii]
It is not said that the effect arises from the cause as something possessing the same nature;
rather, the relationship of cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). (PVA 410)

Even though the effect is distinct from its cause, it is nonetheless an effect; for the definition of the relationship between cause and effect consists in the conformity to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Where, however, such positive and negative concomitances do not exist, there is neither an effect nor a cause. Furthermore, that which does not arise even when the cause is present in such a manner lacks the quality of conforming to the cause. [Objection: But surely, if it is simply the case that "it arises by means of the existence of that [cause]," then since it necessarily exists whenever that [cause] exists, what is the use of this [conformity]?
If it does not exist even when that [cause] exists, how can it be said to be absent when that is absent?
If you say, "Its absence is necessitated by the absence of that," then from where does that [necessitation] come? 411 (PVA)

If that [effect], despite the cause being capable, does not come into being, then that would not be its cause at all. From what, moreover, is it understood that its non-existence is necessitated by the absence of that [cause]? For just as it does not come into being of its own accord while the cause remains in that same state, so too, even upon the absence of that [cause], it will not come into being of its own accord due to its independence. If it were not independent, then [the effect] would necessarily come into being when the cause possesses its capacity.
For while the non-existence of entities might indeed occur by itself, how could existence— which is dependent on other factors— not arise from a cause? (412) (PVA) [061,ix]

For it is logical that non-existence (*abhāva*) comes about by itself because it is causeless; however, it is not logical that existence (*bhāva*), being dependent upon causes, should not exist when the efficient cause is present. [061,x]

[Objection: Is it not the case that the absence of the effect is logical precisely because [the cause] is independent, such that even when the cause exists, the effect does not necessarily arise? [Response: If that were so, then since the absence [of the effect] would occur in its absence [i.e., the absence of the cause], the absence would not be necessitated by the absence of the cause. How, then, could this be the effect of that [cause]? Consequently, it would simply not exist by itself. And that which does not exist by itself cannot be regulated by anything else. Therefore, just as it does not exist by itself, so too, even if it were to arise, it would not be the effect [of the cause]. However, when the effect necessarily arises while the cause is present, then—even though there is a cessation by its own nature (*svarasanirodha*)—there is the production of successive moments; thus, the interruption of the continuum is due to the very absence of those [subsequent moments], which constitutes dependence upon the cause. Therefore, a sequential entity does not arise from a non-sequential one.

[061,xi] Now, it might be argued that even though [the permanent cause] is non-sequential, it produces a sequential effect by depending on a sequential auxiliary cause. That too is not the case. There is no dependence [on another] for that which lacks distinction and cannot have any excellence added to it; it does not depend on anything for the sake of acquiring excellence, because no excellence exists in it. Or, if there were excellence—if one were to admit an excellence distinct from its permanence—then the effect, arising from that very excellence, would not arise from the permanent entity itself. If it is argued that "this is its excellence," we say no; for "excellence" means the capacity to produce excellence. [062,i]

Or, [it might be argued that it has] the property of producing a cognition of distinction. It does not produce a distinction because it is itself without distinction. If one says "from a distinction comes a distinction," that is simply impermanence; if there were a difference [between them], the previous logical consequence would apply.
Now, suppose it is the cause of the cognition of distinction—that too is incorrect.
If there were no distinction [in the object], there could be no arising of a cognition of distinction;
and if that were so, this [cognition] would be nothing but an error, making all such effort futile. (PVA 413)
For it is understood that "it is eternal" only when there is a cognition of non-distinction.

And if there is no error regarding distinction, how could there be valid cognition of eternity? (414) If it is argued that there is a cognition of non-distinction, how could it occur if [the object] were dependent [on other factors]?
Since it is indifferent, no distinction whatsoever exists for it. (415) If a distinction were possible for it, then dependence upon that [cause] would be logical;
it is for this purpose that the worldly convention of "dependence" exists. (416)
Therefore, it is logical that there is no dependence on a qualifier.
Since cognition arises from the body in a sequence, it makes one aware of the body's sequence.
Otherwise, the very cause of that [cognition]—namely, its own sequence—is clearly established.
(PVA 417) That mental cognition proceeds from each preceding experience.
That too must come from what precedes it; thus, there would be an infinite regress.

(PVA 418) Now, if the body generates cognition sequentially by depending on each preceding cognition, then the body must possess a specific distinction. Consequently, it follows that the cause is the body accompanied by cognition, each preceding instance being of such a nature.
That being so, [062,xv]...
In every moment, for that which is new, each preceding moment must be its cause; therefore, let it be observed that the cause always exists as something directly perceived.

Indeed, that very body which is the auxiliary of cognition and has been previously apprehended as the cause for another [person] is always the cause even at birth and death, just as it is in the intermediate state; thus it is established. Otherwise, because the pervasion (vyāpti) would not be apprehended, no thing whatsoever could be the cause of anything else, due to the absence of any other means [of establishing such a relation].
Therefore, since it is seen once from that [cause], it must be seen from that very same [cause] at other times as well;
in this way alone is the relationship between cause and effect established.
(PVA 419) [062,xviii]

And it has already been established above that the relationship of cause and effect is not denied by those engaged in conventional discourse; therefore, we shall desist from further elaboration. Now, one might argue: "Just as in the intermediate state, the body is perceived to be preceded by a body accompanied by consciousness, so too the body at the beginning of birth must be preceded by a body accompanied by consciousness. Thus, consciousness in this life arises from the consciousness of another birth, and consciousness in a future birth arises from the consciousness of this life; in this way, the existence of the other world is established. Likewise, through another reason, the opposite could also be established, which would constitute the establishment of the opponent's position. For instance:"
Whatever consciousness is that of death does not follow into another birth, because it is a consciousness, just like the perception of death in one who is free from defects. (PVA 420)

That consciousness which is at the moment of death does not link to another mind, just like the dying consciousness of one free from passion (*vītarāga*). Furthermore, since the dying consciousness of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not accepted as having the capacity to link to another birth, there is no linking of rebirth.

Now, this [reason] is not a valid reason at all, because it is connected with the opposite [of what is to be proven]. But then, the opposite [reason] would also not be a valid reason, as it too is connected with this [same conclusion]; thus, the situation is the same. It is not the same. For that which is contradictory to something else would establish the absence of that thing, whereas that which is connected to something else establishes its presence. And there is no contradiction between the mind at death and rebirth.
Why? Because:
What contradiction is there in the final consciousness connecting with another mind? Why, then, is it held that the Arhat’s mind does not so connect? (46)

For when the non-existence [of a subsequent mind] is to be proven regarding the linking of another mind by the final consciousness, what contradiction is there with that [final consciousness], or with its object, by means of which its absence would be established? What contradiction? None at all. It is neither characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) nor characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*). This is because, upon the occurrence of the death-consciousness, the opposite of linking (i.e., non-linking) is not observed. For this very reason, its persistence through the exclusion of that [linking] is not observed; for the linking of another birth is imperceptible. Therefore, the state of being a death-consciousness is not contradictory to linking, since neither form of contradiction is observed. Consequently, it does not prove the absence of linking. However, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is contradictory to the absence of linking; therefore, it is capable of proving its absence. Thus, from the opposite [case], the establishment of linking occurs. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that two things which do not deviate from mutually contradictory objects cannot exist in one place.
[063,vii] But surely, there is indeed here a contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion; how then can there be an absence of contradiction? For:
[063,viii]
For the Arhat, there is no reconnection of consciousness at the moment of death;
like the extinguishing of a lamp, such is the liberation of his mind. (421) (PVA) [063,ix]

For just as the extinction of a lamp is [the case], so it is with the death-consciousness of a person recognized as an Arhat; since it is established that the death-consciousness exists by way of excluding that [extinction], the contradiction is proven through such cognition, and thus the absence of contradiction is not established.

That too is incoherent. By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do you consider that the mind of an Arhat is non-relinking? You have no such means of valid cognition here, because your very effort is directed toward refuting that [position]. If an Arhat is indeed accepted [by you], then his non-relinking is caused by the dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*), and not otherwise. And since that dissociation from the afflictions does not exist for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), how could there be non-relinking even when their minds are at the point of death? For being at the point of death is not opposed to relinking; rather, it is the dissociation from the afflictions that is accepted as being opposed to relinking. And that [opposition] has not been accepted [by you].

But is it not the case that the contradiction is understood from the very established doctrine (siddhānta)? No; for the established doctrine functions solely to demonstrate the contradiction in the very moment of death-consciousness of an Arhat.
Indeed, the established doctrine does not prescribe [a solution] for every contradiction:

where has the reconnection of a mind after it has perished ever been established by means of cognition? (422) (PVA) Now, if the establishment of reconnection is not found through a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [then there is no proof].
"Therefore, because it is not authoritative in that regard, there is the possibility of contradiction.
(PVA 423) This too is incorrect. If a tenet is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is simply not authoritative. How, then, could the desired goal be established on its basis?

If the objective is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is a philosophical tenet (*siddhānta*) followed? If it is because of a deficiency in the reason (*hetu*), then why was that very deficiency not pointed out here? (47)

[064,iv] The Discourse on the Noble Truths of Suffering and its Origin. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!”—“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Monks, what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; sickness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the pleasant is suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering. “Monks, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. “Monks, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of that very craving, its relinquishing, renouncing, liberation, and detachment. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. “Monks, what is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “Monks, this noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood. This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned. This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized. This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed. “Monks, in regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of the origin of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of the origin of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed. “In regard to things previously unheard by me, there arose the vision, the knowledge, the wisdom, the insight, and the light, concerning the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it has come to be: ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed. “Monks, as long as this knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths as they have come to be—consisting of three rounds and twelve aspects—was not fully purified in me, so long, monks, did I not claim in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. “But when, monks, this knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths as they have come to be—consisting of three rounds and twelve aspects—was fully purified in me, then, monks, I claimed in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. And a perception of certainty arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. This is the Discourse on the Noble Truths of Suffering and its Origin. [064,iv]

If the tenet (*siddhānta*) is not itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then no contradiction can be established from it regarding the reconnection of the mind at death. Is this [tenet] followed or adhered to? Certainly not; for even if something is adhered to, it does not thereby become a means of valid cognition. If it were a means of valid cognition, then it would be a means of valid cognition in all cases, and thus the counter-example (*viparyaya*) would be unestablished. If you say it is a means of valid cognition in some cases and not in others, we say no; because such a desire is common to both the proponent and the opponent. Now, if it is argued that the reason (*hetu*)—due to the deficiency of causes—is the establisher of the contradiction rather than the tenet: if that non-reconnection [of the mind] is due to a deficiency of causes, then why was that very deficiency of causes not stated as the reason? Why was the state of being the "mind at death" put forward as an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason? Alternatively, if it is said: "Because of the deficiency of the cause," and if the cause—characterized by the body and so forth—is deficient at the stage of death, then what is further stated here regarding its status as a cause? This too is merely a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); the former was inconclusive, while this one is unestablished (*asiddha*). For that very deficiency of the cause does not exist here. Or rather, why was that very point not stated here? [The word] *no* indicates understanding. According to the rule, "the particles *a*, *mā*, *na*, and *no* express negation," what was "not stated" (*nodita*)? It was "stated" (*dita*). "Stated" (*dita*) means broken (*khaṇḍita*); the meaning is that it was indeed refuted. The deficiency itself is unestablished, because the preceding mind, being unimpaired, is the cause. How this is so has already been demonstrated.

[064,v] Furthermore, it might be argued that this reason—characterized by the deficiency of the probans—is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, the body, whether possessed of sense-faculties or devoid of them, as characterized by the hair, nails, tips of the fingers, and so forth, is the basis (*āśraya*) of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because [mental consciousness] arises from the body itself, specifically from that which is characterized as the heart, or from something else.

That is incorrect. The body has two possible states: either with sense-faculties or without sense-faculties; each of these would be the cause [of mental cognition], or otherwise. First, it cannot be that which possesses sense-faculties.
For, as in the case of those [faculties] themselves, since [objects] would already be apprehended, mental cognition does not arise from that which possesses sense-faculties.
Nor even from all [the causes] together, because of the difference in their capacity to produce knowledge. // 48 //
Because it is insentient, its coexistence with another [the self] does not arise from any other cause, as there is no difference in their causal nature.
Its modification occurs through the medium of objects, like the sense organs, or like color and taste. (49)

[064,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Thereupon, he addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if there be any sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who, during the final five hundred years of this Dharma’s decline, wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should rely upon the skillful means of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. He will show them how to avoid all misfortune and suffering, and cause them to dwell securely in the state of fearlessness. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken these words, the Blessed One further declared to the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if there be any sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who, during the final five hundred years of this Dharma’s decline, wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should rely upon the skillful means of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. He will show them how to avoid all misfortune and suffering, and cause them to dwell securely in the state of fearlessness. This is called the chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the ninth. [065,i] ① The Buddhas of the three times, having attained perfect enlightenment, have all relied upon the Prajñāpāramitā; by relying upon it, they have realized the unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It can remove all suffering and is true and not false. Therefore, one should know that the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is proclaimed as follows: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. ② Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having heard the Buddha’s words, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, including the gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and faithfully practiced what the Buddha had taught.
