To begin with, the body together with the sense-faculties (*sendriya-kāya*) is not the basis for each [mental consciousness] individually. "Together with the sense-faculties" means it exists along with the powers of the sense-faculties; since there is no difference between the power and that which possesses the power, it is simply the form of the sense-faculties themselves. Consequently, the position is that mental consciousness arises from each of the sense-faculties individually. Thus he says: "Mental cognition does not arise from the body together with the sense-faculties, nor from the sense-faculties individually. For, like that [sensory] cognition, it would follow that it apprehends each object separately. Indeed, if the mind necessarily follows the visual faculty, its nature must be such that it follows other faculties as well; otherwise, if the cause of that [mind] did not have that nature, how could it possess that nature? It would thus be without a cause.

[065,i] But surely even a single cause is observed to have the nature of producing both effects that possess its own nature and those that do not. For example, fire has the nature of producing smoke. Furthermore, there exists a distinction in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*): when the causal complex for form is present, the eye produces visual consciousness; in the absence of form, it produces mental consciousness. The same should be stated regarding the ear and the other sense faculties. [065,ii]
That is incorrect.
[065,iii] It is maintained that what arises depending upon the operation of the sense-faculties is "born of the senses" (akṣaja).
Since its operation does not exist there, how could it be produced by the sense organ?

"Because of the attainment of apprehension like that [sensory] cognition. This is its meaning: for sensory cognition (*akṣabuddhi*), following after the operation of the sense organ, is designated as "apprehending the object" because it takes on its form. If the nature of mental cognition (*manobuddhi*) were the same, then it too would be an apprehender by following after the operation of that [sense organ]. Otherwise, how could it be so designated? Furthermore, neither the following after its operation nor the realization of it as being produced from it is perceived; thus, [your position] is contradictory. Moreover, even when the object is not present, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises in the form of determining an object situated in front, like the perception of a mass of hair by one afflicted with ophthalmia (*timira*). Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), however, arises even for one with eyes closed; how then could there be an operation of the sense organ therein? And if there is no modification [in the consciousness] when there is a modification [of the organ], how can it be born from the sense organ? In this regard, the phrase "because of the attainment of apprehension like that cognition" means the attainment of a modified consciousness through the modification of that [organ]. "Apprehension" (*grahaṇa*) is simply consciousness itself. If, moreover, there is no modification [of the consciousness] through the modification of that [organ], then it is not produced from it. The same refutation applies to the view that it is produced from a collection [of causes].

He states another rebuttal: "Because of the difference in the capacity to produce cognition. Regarding the production of cognition, a distinct capacity is indeed observed as something separate and independent of anything else; it is not mutually dependent. Otherwise, if the capacity were dependent on the collection [of causes], then in the absence of even one member, it would not exist—just as a sprout does not arise when there is a deficiency in the earth and other factors. Yet, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) occurs even for those who lack the eyes and other [senses]; therefore, that mind is not bound to the collection. By the word "even" (*api*), the previous reason is conjoined.

Because it is insentient, it does not arise from anything else either, that is, from what lacks sense-faculties. Now, what is the meaning of "because it is insentient"? If it means "due to the absence of sensory consciousness," then that is indeed accepted. But if sensory consciousness does not arise from it, why then does mental consciousness not arise? If, on the other hand, its insentience consists in the absence of mental consciousness, then that very point is what is currently under investigation; thus, the reason would be a mere part of the thesis itself. To this, it is said:
When hair, nails, and so forth are not perceived even while one is intending them, how can it be established that mental cognition arises from them? (425) (PVA)

[065,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not become attached to them. Subhūti, it is in this manner that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom.”

For just as contact and the other [mental factors] are perceived through their respective consciousnesses by virtue of volition (*cetanā*), hair, nails, and so forth are not perceived in that same way by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). If they were bound to it [the body], then in the absence of that [body], the mental consciousness would not exist; and upon its impairment, the mental consciousness would be impaired. If the body were not the support, then how could there be coexistence? To this he says: "Because there is no distinction in the capacity of the cause designated as karma, which effects the rule of coexistence, and because it is established accordingly. "Like the sense organs and like color and taste. Even though the sense organs and the objects—color and taste—are not mutually dependent, there is a rule of coexistence for a certain period of time. Indeed, the relationship of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is not the sole cause for coexistence.

[065,x] But is it not the case that "the eyes and so forth are the supports of visual consciousness and the rest because they undergo change when those [consciousnesses] undergo change"? Likewise, due to changes in the body, there occurs what is called "separation" and so on—a change characterized by becoming motionless and the like—and thus there exists a relationship of support and supported.

That too is incorrect. The transformation of the object—which is the grasped—occurs by way of the door [of the senses]. For one who cannot endure pain, there is a transformation through the cultivation of that [object], that is, through the mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward it. Indeed, weapons, blows, and so forth, when being perceived by the mind, cause pain to the mind; they do not do so by being its physical substratum (*āśraya*). And even though an external object is a cause of transformation, it does not possess the status of a substratum for the mind, because pain arises merely from mental imputation (*āropa*) even in the absence of such an object.
Therefore, both an internal and an external form are experienced as superimposed.

The transformation of the mental faculty (*mānasa*) occurs through the mind (*manas*) and its modifications. (PVA 426) Furthermore, there is no identity between the support (*āśraya*) and the object (*ālambana*); therefore, the body is not the support for that [mental faculty]. Consequently, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) does not depend upon the body. That which is its support will be explained later. The object of the mind is merely the superimposition of the preceding and succeeding [moments]; it is nothing else. Thus, it has no support and no object (*nirālambana-āśraya*).
Moreover:
The mere fact that something is not a benefactor is not the reason for its cessation;
rather, it is a specific kind of causality that brings about the cessation of the effect.
What is that specific reason whose nature is to cause cessation? He states it: "That for which existence is always beneficial due to its constant concomitance."
That cause is expressed by the locative case, and thus it is said, "from that arising. (50)
[066, vii] The seventh section.

For that [cause] is the producer of which existence is beneficial, because it is constantly connected to it. "By its connection to it" means by its following after it. Its existence is beneficial because it follows [the effect] at all times. However, for that whose capacity to assist exists only occasionally, assistance—characterized as a specific quality—may sometimes arise from something else even in the absence of that [primary cause]. Since such a thing does not follow [the effect] constantly, there is no cessation of the effect through the cessation of that [cause]. Furthermore, the existence of the body is not always beneficial, since a modification is sometimes observed even when there is only a prior modification of the mind. Therefore, it is possible that even in the absence of the body, the continuum of consciousness persists due to its support, because it is modified by modifications produced by mental changes. Nor is the body established as a cause by virtue of being always beneficial. For instance:

[066, viii] Whether by itself or through another, the body would be understood as the cause by someone; or else, it would be by means of a cognition that has already arisen—such are the conceptual constructions. (PVA 428)

[066,ix] First of all, a sensation that has not yet arisen does not know, "I shall be," "I am," or "I have been. But when a sensation has arisen, there is the notion "I. For one who apprehends either its own nature or something else, there is simply the cognition of that [object]. How, moreover, could there be a cognition of another [cause], such as "this has arisen from that"? Indeed, by apprehending one thing, one does not cognize another. If that were so, then for the visual consciousness and the others as well, that same conceptual construction would apply; how then could there be the cognition of their causes, such as the eye and so forth? No, because it is possible to understand those through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). To explain: [066,x]
A person, upon merely opening their eyes, perceives directly;
immediately thereafter, it is understood that the vision of form has arisen.
The birth [of cognition] and so forth, directed toward the body, are not perceived as being the cause.
For if there were a prior absence of cognition, what would awaken the state of being a knower?
(430) (PVA) If its perception is by another, how is the prior absence known?
For the non-perception of that which is unobservable does not establish non-existence. (431) (PVA)

Even for one who is asleep, there is awakening prior to the non-perception of cognition; yet in that case, there is no actual apprehension of the prior absence of dream-consciousness. (PVA 432) [066,xiv]
Now, one might think: "If cognition existed previously, there would be self-awareness [of it];
but in the state of deep sleep, it does not exist at all, because of the absence of memory.
For it is observed that one who has awakened possesses a memory of the experience within the dream.
That is incorrect.
Is it that there is no apprehension, or is it that although it exists, it has been forgotten?
For what is done while awake is never remembered by anyone in a dream.
Indeed, no one perceives that the experience of a dream is distinct from waking consciousness; nevertheless, it arises from that very same source.

[067,i] Now, if it is argued that its perception occurs upon awakening, yet it is not perceived even when that [awakening] itself awakens—whence is this known? Therefore, since the body is always providing assistance, there is no logical ground for the claim that consciousness ceases when the body ceases.
<(i) Refutation of the Doctrine of the Elements as the Self>

[067,ii] Now, suppose a lotus-root (*śālūka*) arises from cow dung. Its existence is not assisted by it through a constant connection; nevertheless, in the absence of cow dung, the lotus-root simply does not exist at all.
That too is trivial, because:
iv] The first production from cow dung is of such a nature, and so is the subsequent one.
In the absence of that, no reversal of cognition is ever observed.

For instance, is a lotus root (*śālūka*) which is seen to arise from cow dung found to be exactly like that at other times as well? However, mental consciousness is of the same nature both initially and subsequently; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*ekāntikatā*) on that account.

**(ii) Explanation of the formula “When this exists, that comes to be”:** Now, one might object: Has the Blessed One not stated only this definition of causality—that “when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises”—and has he not investigated any other [definition] that persists at all times? Furthermore, it has been established that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the Blessed One alone is the ultimate authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding the causal relationship, because he has grasped the pervasion through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Moreover, nothing that possesses a possible efficacy is left unspoken by the Blessed One. So how is this [formula] to be understood?

This is not a fault. Precisely because of what we have stated, the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of "always providing assistance" (*sadopakāritva*). For that same reason, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is also employed, expressed as "from arising" (*utpādāt*). The phrase "when this exists, that comes to be" (*asmin satīdaṃ bhavati*) expresses constant concomitance. The word "existing" (*satī*) is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*); otherwise, if it were to occur even in the absence of that [cause], its existence would not be caused by that. Furthermore, the ablative is used in the sense of "source" (*apādāna*), according to the rule: "the source of the agent who is being born. And a source is nothing other than a cause (*nimitta*).

Alternatively, we explain it otherwise: even if [the inference is] from one cognition to a preceding cognition, let it be understood that from the cognition of birth and so forth, there is the cognition of a previous birth, because that [present birth] is its effect. But how is the cognition of a future birth inferred? If you say that the inference of an effect follows from seeing a capable cause, then another definition of a cause would have to be postulated. If, on the other hand, the inference of capacity is made because of doubt regarding the effect, then it is useless, since there is no certainty regarding a future world. For it is only when there is an inference of a future world that the effort of engaging in dharma and so forth becomes fruitful.
To this it is replied: the consciousness of a future birth is itself the cause and also the effect. Why?

That whose existence is always beneficial to another by way of constant concomitance is its cause. For that whose existence is always beneficial to another through such concomitance is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) by virtue of its pervasiveness; and when there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is the cause. When a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) is to be understood, the effect (*kārya*) alone is the reason (*hetu*). That which makes a distinct entity known is only the pervader. Otherwise, due to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*), it would lack probative force. And that which does not exist without another is the cause of that other. If it is asked, "How can a cause be an effect?"—it is not so, because it is the effect of that [cause]. To explain: [067,xi] That whose existence is always beneficial to another by way of constant concomitance is its cause. For that whose existence is always beneficial to another through such concomitance is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) by virtue of its pervasiveness; and when there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is the cause. When a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) is to be understood, the effect (*kārya*) alone is the reason (*hetu*). That which makes a distinct entity known is only the pervader. Otherwise, due to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*), it would lack probative force. And that which does not exist without another is the cause of that other. If it is asked, "How can a cause be an effect?"—it is not so, because it is the effect of that [cause]. To explain:

The transformations of consciousness and the other [mental factors], which establish their arising and so forth, are observed as being modifications of that [consciousness]; and this is what is called "being an effect. (PVA 435)

This would not even be a transformation at all. If it were not to arise through excellence (*abhyudaya*), then how could there be this worldly convention that "this transformation is produced by that"? It is precisely by virtue of this much that causality exists elsewhere as well; for it is solely due to the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) [of the effect from its cause] that something is a cause.
But surely, that which is beneficial is the cause; and how can that which is yet to be (the future) be beneficial? In that case, it follows that the past cannot be a cause.

That too is incorrect. It is not the case that [the cause] does not assist [the effect], because it exists at the time of the effect's arising. What is this "time of arising"? If it is prior to the effect, how can something non-existent be an assistant? For this very reason, the cause is so called because it brings about what was previously non-existent. What is the meaning of "bringing about what was non-existent"? It is the existence of that [effect] occurring immediately after it. This immediate succession is the same from both perspectives; just as it is with respect to what has already occurred (*bhūta*), so it is also with respect to what is yet to be (*bhāvya*). Furthermore, immediate succession alone is not the basis for [causal] reality, since even that which is separated [in time] can be a cause.
For instance:
the consciousness of one who has slept deeply [arises] upon waking from a prior experience.
It is certain that it arises through the intervention of time.

(PVA 436) Indeed, the body is not the cause there in the persistence of previous mental impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), because such a thing is not observed; for even with an identical body, [the mind] arises differently or otherwise in accordance with prior cognition.
Therefore, the conformity to positive and negative concomitance is the basis for the causal relationship; this is found even in that which arises from it. (PVA 437)
Whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance of something is alone its cause; any other distinction is useless.

Now, it might be argued: "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises"—this is the definition of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). And it is not merely positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) that is expressed by this, because:
The locative case indicates prior existence, and the ablative case indicates the demonstration [of the cause].
Furthermore, the state of being another (parabhāva) is indicated by the first [word];
for it is not merely the conformity to its positive and negative concomitance that is demonstrated here, since the demonstration of the relation of priority and posteriority is perfectly clear.

That too is untrue. For it is said that the locative case (*saptamī*) [indicates] "from that" (*tasmāt*) and "due to arising" (*ād utpādāt*). Indeed, neither the locative nor the ablative case (*pañcamī*) indicates a prior existence; rather, they indicate the state of being a mere cause (*nimittatva-mātra*). The meaning is: "this has that as its cause. And the meaning is: when something does not exist, another thing does not arise; that very thing, while existing, is what causes this [other thing]. Thus is the meaning.

But how can that which is yet to be (bhāvī) be designated as "existent" (sat)? Since it is non-existent, such a designation is untenable. Likewise, there is no arising of that which has not yet arisen.

But how can there be existence even for that which has passed away, such that it is designated as "existent"? And how can there be arising for that which has perished? If you say, "It existed," then the same will apply to [the future] as well. What is the difference between antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)? Alternatively, [in the case of the rule] "when this exists, that comes to be," the locative case is used according to the rule "by means of the existence of one thing, another state is characterized. Therefore, by the word "existent" (*satī*), only the status of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) is indicated; it does not mean actual existence at that time. Furthermore, a state is indeed characterized by another state even when it is yet to come (*bhāvinā*), as in the worldly expression: "The omen (*ariṣṭa*) is brought about by death. This is common usage: if death were not to occur, such an omen would certainly not exist. Moreover, the temporal distinction [implied by the ablative] "from arising" (*utpādāt*) is not intended here. Indeed, case endings do not prescribe specific times, because they have the capacity only to indicate the status of a factor of action (*kārakatva*). If it is asked, "How can there be the status of an agent or object for that which is non-existent?"—[we reply: How is it that "the sprout arises" or "he makes a pot"? There is the status of agent and object [even for the non-existent]. Since the status of a factor of action is established by its presence in the intellect, the fact that it is eaten by crows is irrelevant here.
<iii. Explanation of the Cause:> Now,
that whose perception is preceded by the perception of something else is the cause of that thing.
That too is incorrect.
If that which is first perceived were the cause of something,
then a seed located inside a storehouse would not be the cause for the arising of a sprout.

Now, if it is said that [the cause] is so called because it is the first perception of its own kind, how can there be causality for that which has not been perceived? For when one thing is perceived, another thing does not thereby become perceived. There would be, at best, a mere metaphorical designation. Therefore, existence (*sattā*) is indicated by perception. And thus, the meaning remains the same: "when this exists" refers to the state of being a causal condition (*nimittabhāva*) for existence, and that is precisely the state of being an object of non-deviation (*avyabhicāraviṣayatva*). However, if it were the case that "that which is perceived first" [is the cause], then everything preceding [an effect] would result in being a cause. But when there is the state of being an object of non-deviation, that alone constitutes causality.
Furthermore, if it is argued that there was a prior absence while the object was non-deviant, that too is trivial.

If the state of cause and effect arises merely from the fact that [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists, then what contradiction is there? In that case, what is the purpose of the distinction between prior and posterior?
For what utility is there in the state of being prior or posterior? Nor is that which is useless required.
[069,viii] Nevertheless, it might be argued as follows:
If the cause is held to exist in the past, then those who desire it will take up its material cause;
if it exists in the future, there will be an inference based on its capacity to produce that effect. (PVA 441)

For a cause can indeed be grasped by one who seeks its effect; therefore, the existence of the cause is required to precede it. For example, in order to establish a future world hereafter, one must first grasp the present world of this life which precedes it.

That too is not tenable, for it indeed possesses causality; it is simply that the causality of what exists prior [to the effect] is not absent. However, its status as an effect is said to exist in relation to the non-deviation from what is yet to be. And that which is the material cause (upādāna) when there is causality will likewise exist when there is the state of being an effect. For what distinction is there in the material cause? Is it not sufficient merely by the non-deviation [of the cause]? As for what was said—that inference proceeds from a capable cause alone, so what is the use of the state of being an effect therein?
That is incorrect.
For who would cast away wealth already in their hand so that it might fall at their feet?
Or who would endure the need for an axe to cut what can be cut by the fingernails?
For who would cast that which is already in his hand down to his feet? Or who would wait for an axe to cut what can be cut by the fingernail?
[069,xvi] Since it is primarily as an effect (*kārya*) that [the reason] serves as a means of cognition, [it follows] from the sequence of the direct [inference].
If it were a cause that must be established through effort, its status as an indicator would be useless.
Therefore, it is logical that even a future thing can be a cause, provided there is no deviation from the rule.

Thus far, it has been stated by way of its meaning that modification does not proceed from the body by way of being its substratum, as is the case with the eyes and other sense organs. Now, however, this is said while provisionally accepting [that position]:
Or perhaps it may sometimes be a benefactor to the continuum of consciousness, like fire is to jars and the like; yet, by that much alone, there is no cessation [of the continuum]. (51)

Even though the body sometimes acts as a support by being beneficial, the mere fact of its being so does not mean that the mental continuum ceases when the body ceases. Merely being a benefactor does not necessarily entail being a cause of cessation for that which is benefited. For instance, when fire or other such things cease, there is no rule that a jar or similar object—which has received a specific benefit from them—must necessarily cease. Or, even when fire produces a specific characteristic such as fluidity in gold, there is no cessation of the gold upon the cessation of that fire.

Even if that very particularity characterized by fluidity and so forth were to cease, gold would remain in its original state. For one who holds that the mind is the cause of the mental faculty, there is a cessation [of the latter] due to its own deficiency even while the body remains in its original state.
An objection has already been stated against the view that the body alone is the cause; furthermore, another is now being stated.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the mind does not cease while the body remains,
because the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) exist as long as that [body] exists and because they are subject to its control; therefore, the mind is not dependent on the body.

[070,iv] In the absence of a body, as in the state of ashes, there may be cessation due to the absence of causes. But when the body exists, it remains just as it is, and there is no possibility of cessation. Furthermore, this is so because [the nature of the self] persists through all states.
Furthermore, since its function consists of inhalation and exhalation, it ceases upon their deficiency.

That too is incorrect. To say that inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*) arise from the mind alone, but the mind does not arise from them, is no solution. If one asks why this is so, it is because of their presence when [the mind] is present: since those two exist when the mind exists, the reverse is not the case. Furthermore, the mind does not arise from inhalation and exhalation because of its mastery over them. If inhalation and exhalation were the cause of the mind, they would not be subject to its control; yet, their subjection to the mind is observed. Moreover, if they were produced from something else, then the mind’s production would come from that very source, and the mind would be entirely irrelevant. Indeed, that which is dependent on another cannot be controlled by a third party. Since those two are dependent on their own causes, the mind could at most be their delimiting factor. If it is argued that the mind produces them as a cooperative cause for their own causes, then the mind is also a cause of those two, and thus the mind does not arise from them. Alternatively, if inhalation and exhalation—though produced from other primary sources—are regulated by the mind, like a servant by a master, that is also untenable.
The arising of a servant is seen from another source, but not so for those two.
There is no arising of those two from anything other than the mind. (PVA 444)

For inhalation and exhalation are not observed to exist apart from the mind, like servants; therefore, they do not arise from any other cause. Thus, the mind alone is the cause, and it does not [arise] from those two.

Now, it might be argued: because the inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*) exist during the state of sleep, these two cannot have the mind as their cause; for in that state, they do not exist in such a manner. Indeed, he demonstrates that they have no other cause:
"How could there be the impelling and drawing in of the wind without effort (*prayatna*)? [070,x]
There would follow a decrease or increase [of the cognition] due to the decrease or increase of those two. (53)

[070,xi] If consciousness were the effect of inhalation and exhalation, then the impelling and drawing back of the wind would occur without effort; yet this is not the case, because those two consist precisely in impelling and drawing back. Now, if it is argued that for those two, impelling and drawing back alone are dependent on the mind, and not their essential nature—which arises from another cause—then [it follows that] the mind [is the cause], and from that, impelling and drawing back [occur].
That too is incorrect.
If that wind were consciousness even in one who is dead, why would it cease?
If that [cognition] is without a cause, then its body has become the cause.

If the wind (*vāyu*) were permanent and not the cause of consciousness (*cetanā*), then the non-cessation of the mind would necessarily follow. Even if it were the cause, since the wind remains constant even in a dead person, and since inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*) are merely its effects, there would be no cessation of the mind due to their absence; thus, the consequence of non-cessation follows. Furthermore, through the decrease or increase of inhalation and exhalation, a decrease or increase of the mind would result. Since these are its effects, when the cause diminishes or increases excessively, the effect must necessarily undergo diminution or growth; otherwise, that [cause] would not truly be a cause.
The same reductio ad absurdum applies to those two as well; however, it is not the same regarding the cause of the mind, because another cause is accepted as that which impels its persistence. (54)

Or, even if inhalation and exhalation were the cause of the mind, there would still be the undesirable consequence that the mind does not cease as long as it remains in the body. This is because those two—inhaling and exhaling—would also not cease; since they too are effects of the body, they simply do not cease. And because they do not cease, the mind likewise does not cease.
It might be argued: even if the mind were the cause, this same undesirable consequence would follow;
and there would be the consequence of non-cessation as long as the mind remains in the mind.

"And there is no cessation of the previous mind when that [subsequent one] is desired. (PVA 446) To this it is replied: "It is not the same regarding the cause of the mind, because another cause is admitted, namely, that which effects its persistence. Another cause is also admitted for that [mind], designated as the body together with craving and karma.
[071, vii] The seventh section.

A mind does not arise from the mere existence of a preceding mind alone, because there is also the causality of another factor known as the seed of *saṃskāra*, which consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth. When that [seed] is awakened by a preceding mind, the arising of the mind occurs either therein or elsewhere, due to the diversity of the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and their respective awakeners. For example, the vision of dreams in their various forms does not result from the mere presence of an established connection; for even when there is a common meeting with the same [conditions], only at certain times does a particular dream-vision occur, owing to the diversity of the awakening of latent impressions. Indeed, it is because of the diversity of the awakening of latent impressions that [the results] cease, and not because the body alone is the cause, since such a thing is never observed. How could this be so?
Because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind cannot be explained otherwise, everything that awakens these tendencies is a cause, just like the consciousness of a dream. (PVA 447)

If the mere accomplishment of the body were the sole cause, it would follow that everyone would always have identical dream visions; yet, since some person perceives something specific, it is logical that this is produced by the connection with latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), because these predispositions possess manifold forms. Therefore, the entire mind—whether in that body or elsewhere—is characterized by the various activities brought about by the awakening of predispositions; it cannot be conceived otherwise. [Thus,] arising occurs through the power of predispositions.
Alternatively, that which attains its arising through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is indeed unreal, like a dream; yet even that is unreal.
Even in the absence of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), the manifestation of sexual union and the like is not unreal,
because it accomplishes its own purpose through the performance of true causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

For worldly activities such as sexual intercourse, which proceed by relying on the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and are intent upon accomplishing their desired practical effects—how could they be characterized by a nature distracted by the involvement of unreality?
[071,xiii]

Alternatively, even the worldly transactions such as sexual pleasure and the like, though following from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), are not unreal because they are associated with real women and so forth; likewise, the transactions concerning birth and so on are similar. For these too have their basis in the taking up of another real body there; thus, they are not unreal. To explain: birth proceeds by taking up another body produced from semen and blood, even in the absence of the power of latent impressions. How else could the transition to another body be perceived, except as in the case of the transition through the various stages of the body such as childhood, youth, and old age?
Because its unity is established through having a single basis of appropriation,
such a movement into another body simply does not occur. (449) (PVA) [071,xv]

The body is nothing other than the material cause of semen and blood; therefore, there is no transition into another body. However, the bodies of animals and so forth are produced from a different semen and blood, and thus constitute a different body. Since no such transition is observed in such cases, how can it be possible?
Even so, the state of being a different body does not constitute a negative concomitance (vyatirekitā).
The distinctness of the reality is held to be that which brings about cessation.

(PVA 450) For it cannot be said that the body of a child and so forth is one and the same as the body of a youth and so forth; rather, a transition is indeed observed therein. In this context, "transition" is simply the arising [of the subsequent state] concomitantly with that [preceding state]. And since such arising occurs through the force of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is no contradiction.

[072,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive forms as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive eye-contact as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the element of earth as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the truth of suffering as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the truths of origin, cessation, or the path as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of buddhahood as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent while practicing the perfection of wisdom, how then does he train in the perfection of giving, how does he train in the perfection of morality, how does he train in the perfection of patience, how does he train in the perfection of vigor, how does he train in the perfection of meditation, and how does he train in the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a gift, nor does he perceive a giver, nor does he perceive a recipient. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of giving. He does not perceive morality, nor does he perceive one who observes morality, nor does he perceive one who is immoral. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of morality. He does not perceive patience, nor does he perceive one who is patient, nor does he perceive one who is impatient. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of patience. He does not perceive vigor, nor does he perceive one who exerts vigor, nor does he perceive one who is indolent. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of vigor. He does not perceive meditation, nor does he perceive one who meditates, nor does he perceive one who is distracted. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of meditation. He does not perceive wisdom, nor does he perceive one who is wise, nor does he perceive one who is ignorant. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of wisdom. “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the body as a foundation of mindfulness, nor does he perceive feelings, nor does he perceive the mind, nor does he perceive dharmas as a foundation of mindfulness. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the four foundations of mindfulness. He does not perceive right effort, nor does he perceive wrong effort. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the four right efforts. He does not perceive the base of psychic power consisting of concentration due to desire and the formative forces of striving, nor does he perceive the base of psychic power consisting of concentration due to vigor, nor does he perceive the base of psychic power consisting of concentration due to mind, nor does he perceive the base of psychic power consisting of concentration due to investigation and the formative forces of striving. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the four bases of psychic power. He does not perceive the faculty of faith, nor does he perceive the faculties of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the five faculties. He does not perceive the power of faith, nor does he perceive the powers of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the five powers. He does not perceive the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, nor does he perceive the factors of enlightenment that are investigation of dharmas, vigor, joy, tranquility, concentration, or equanimity. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the seven factors of enlightenment. He does not perceive the right view, nor does he perceive right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, or right concentration. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the eightfold noble path. “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of what is possible and impossible, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of the ripening of karma, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of various inclinations, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of the various elements, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of the paths leading everywhere, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of recollecting past abodes, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of death and rebirth, nor does he perceive the power of the Tathāgata that is the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the ten powers of a Tathāgata. He does not perceive the fearlessness of the Tathāgata in claiming perfect enlightenment, nor does he perceive the fearlessness of the Tathāgata in claiming the exhaustion of outflows, nor does he perceive the fearlessness of the Tathāgata in proclaiming the obstacles to the dharma, nor does he perceive the fearlessness of the Tathāgata in proclaiming the path to the cessation of suffering. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the four fearlessnesses. He does not perceive the analytical knowledge of meaning, nor does he perceive the analytical knowledge of dharmas, nor does he perceive the analytical knowledge of language, nor does he perceive the analytical knowledge of eloquence. Now, if it is argued that the transition into another body of a different nature is not observed, that [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the observation of the transition into a dream-body. If it is claimed that this [dream-body] is unreal and thus there is no actual transition at all, we say: no, for what is being perceived cannot be unreal. For just as its unreality [is asserted], so too is the transition therein. What is this so-called "unreality"? If it is defined as being sublated by the waking cognition, then when that [waking] cognition occurs, the [dream] is not sublated; but to say it is sublated at other times is illogical. If it is argued that it is simply not perceived by the waking person at that very time, then the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is the same: that which was perceived by the waking cognition is now not perceived. Furthermore, if it is not perceived upon awakening, how is the distinction between awakening and non-awakening made? Since the cognition "I am awake" arises even in a dream, how can there be a distinction based on that? Therefore, since the perception is equal, it is not logical to claim either non-existence or unreality [of the dream-body].
Alternatively, non-truthfulness is the lack of endurance due to the weakness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), characterized by the weakness of uncommon perception.

In that case, where there is stability due to the firmness of the latent impression (*vāsanā*), there is a reversal; thus, the reality of the transition [of consciousness] is established. And this is so even when there is a common perception.
For indeed, from the firmness of the latent impression, no other [cause for] the arising of unreality follows.

For the wise, the reality of the waking state exists merely through the firmness of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). That cognition which possesses firmness of impression is a waking cognition; it is real and its perception is common to all. In its own nature, however, that [waking state] certainly exists; therefore, the transition [of impressions] is established. But due to the lack of such firmness, there is an immediate dissolution [of the dream]. Furthermore, where a command from a deity appears to both dreamers alike, how could there be unreality in that?
[072,vii] Now, if that were the case, then reality itself would exist; thus, there would be no unreality for the entirety of dream-objects. If that were so, [072,viii]
Because movement is well-established and because a specific distinction is being postulated,
this is clearly a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) known as "balancing the alternative" (*vikalpasama*).
Alternatively, since proficiency— the fruit of mental conditioning— is observed at birth and so forth, it is understood that there is a transition immediately after death.
When the mind, which is characterized by the non-grasping of a body, comes into existence...

[Objection: Why is the transition from one body to another not observed at birth and so forth for embodied beings? [Response: First of all, this nature of the mind—which consists in the non-apprehension of a body at birth and at other times as well—is observed in all living beings as being associated with degrees of intensity and as being the fruit of the degrees of intensity of prior practice. This does not occur without a mind conditioned by the practice of non-apprehension of a body in a previous existence. Therefore, let it be understood that the movement into this body from another body occurs precisely through the power of that [prior practice]; otherwise, there would be no occurrence of inference.
[072,xii] Now, if there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the transition, how can there be comprehension through inference (*anumāna*)? This too is not a fault, because:
[072,xiii]
The object of inference is not perceived; what fault is there in this?
For the object of perception is certainly not the object of inference.
For it is indeed accepted that perception and inference function by mutually excluding each other's domains. How, then, can that very same point be a fault?
Moreover, if one asks how there can be inference without the operation of perception upon that which belongs to its own class, even that is not a fault.
[072,xvi] Since it is observed that [the mind] proceeds from repeated practice,
whether within the body or elsewhere, why is there not an inference from that very fact, rather than from direct perception? (PVA 455)

[072,xvii] The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, have transcended the states of woe, are fixed in destiny, and have attained rightness. What are these four? They are: one who is bound by one fetter, one who is bound by two fetters, one who is bound by three fetters, and one who is bound by four fetters. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, have transcended the states of woe, are fixed in destiny, and have attained rightness. What is the person bound by one fetter? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is endowed with faith, but he has not yet abandoned the five lower fetters. This, Ānanda, is called the person bound by one fetter. What is the person bound by two fetters? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is endowed with faith and endowed with virtue, but he has not yet abandoned the five lower fetters. This, Ānanda, is called the person bound by two fetters. What is the person bound by three fetters? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, and possesses wisdom, but he has not yet abandoned the five lower fetters. This, Ānanda, is called the person bound by three fetters. What is the person bound by four fetters? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue, possesses wisdom, and has abandoned the five lower fetters. This, Ānanda, is called the person bound by four fetters. This is what is being said: how can there be inference regarding that which belongs to such a class without perception, since inference is preceded by perception? To this, the following is the rebuttal: even if the movement itself has not been seen through direct perception, a result consistent with such movement is indeed observed, just like the movement between villages. For example, one who has come from another village or another region is observed taking pleasure in utensils and other objects belonging to the same class as those he previously enjoyed. Even if another person coming from another village is not observed to be exactly like him, nevertheless his arrival from a place of that nature is established through inference. Thus, it is precisely from the inclination toward specific utensils and so forth [that the cause is inferred].

[073,i] Let the arrival from another world also be inferred by means of the operation of inference, based on the mere operation of perception, as in the case of one who has arrived from another village. For when fire is being inferred from smoke, there is no operation of perception regarding that which possesses specific qualities. If it is argued that the operation [of inference] concerns fire in its general form alone, then here too, the operation concerns the movement through places and so forth; thus, the two cases are equal.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "The movement to another place and so forth by means of that very same body is observed without abandoning the body. And just as the movement of the dream-body is unreal, so too here at birth and the like, the non-abandonment and the unreality of the body might occur. This is inconsistent. For it is said:
"The movement to another body and its abandonment are consistent with reality."
If those two were so, then there would truly be proof of a future world.

Just as there is a complete interruption [of continuity] in a dream upon the perception of that dream, if it were likewise [interrupted] before and after death, what would be achieved? (456–457) (PVA)

Indeed, just as movement to another place occurs without a body, if movement to another birth were likewise possible, then a contradictory proof would have been established. Furthermore, since movement in a dream is observed to be associated with a real body, if movement to the next world were also like that, then it would follow that the next world and the previous world are both unreal; this is precisely what the nihilists (nāstika) desire.

Furthermore, just as for one who does not see dreams during the state of sleep, there is either a total cessation of consciousness or a state of unmanifest consciousness, so too, if the next world were like that, what would be the point? The nihilists' view would not be destroyed; what would be gained by those who assert a next world? To this it is said: [073, viii] For movement by means of that very body is contradicted by direct perception.

The abandonment of the previous body and the perception of another [body]—all this is like the experience in a dream, arising from true cognition. And since true cognition arises from a dream, what contradiction could there possibly be? (PVA 458–459)
Every instance of separation is perceived as being accompanied by awakening;
even the separation caused by death is accompanied by the awakening to reality.

This has been stated: consciousness, being perceived in this body as the fruit of the practice of consciousness associated with a previous body, does not occur without the relinquishment of that body; thus, how can there be a relinquishment of the body? If it is argued: "The relinquishment of the previous body is indeed observed; for the very perception of this present body is the perception of the relinquishment of the previous body, so if the previous body is unestablished, how can the relinquishment of the previous body be established?
[073,xii] [We reply: Attachment to a body is not preceded by attachment to a body.
When that previous body is well-known, it is already established for us.

(PVA 461) [073, xiii] The establishment of the previous body follows precisely from the proof of a specific fondness for former [experiences]. Furthermore, that very same body is not perceived at present. Nor does it follow that because it is past and unperceived, it did not exist even then. Therefore, the claim that there is no abandonment of the previous body is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, as it has been said: just as the coming here from a dream and so forth is due to its unreality, so too is it from the next world due to its very unreality. And likewise, just as there is a departure from this world into the unreal body of a dream, so too is there a departure into the next world; thus, the next world is unreal.

This too is untrue; for the unreality of dreams is itself associated with reality, as it is the cause of the cognition of reality. We shall explain that such is the nature of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Alternatively, every cognition does not stand apart from dreams as something distinct.
If we were to speak of it later, that indeed would be the proper occasion for it.
(PVA 462) [073, xviii]

For it will be stated that there is no distinction whatsoever between a dream-cognition and any other [cognition]. Therefore, it is established that just as in the case of a dream-body, there is a transition into a body in the next world; thus, even if for one who has come from elsewhere there is a distinction such as being with or without resistance due to a particular strength of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the destruction of the continuum is certainly not observed. Consequently, since living beings possess an uninterrupted continuum, the next world is established. As for death and so forth, because the latent impressions that characterize the sustaining [continuum] are diverse, there is no consequence of non-cessation; for such a mind simply does not exist when [the continuum] ceases.
In that case, the Cārvāka also has a valid rebuttal, because such a body does not exist. Therefore, he says:
If the body, being defective due to the humors, were the cause [of death] like a wick and other such things,
then there would be a return to life once the humor has been neutralized upon death.

For when the body is rendered dysfunctional by defects such as wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), it becomes exactly like that from which the mind originated; consequently, in the absence of such a body, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the mind's non-cessation.

This is not so. If it were thus, then when the humors (doṣas) of one who has died become balanced, the body would be restored to life through the attainment of health, because of the statement: "The equilibrium of those [humors] is health; their decrease and increase are the opposite.

Now, from what is the equalization of the *doṣas* known? It is known from the observation of disorders such as fever. For *doṣas* that do not produce disorder do not bring about death, because otherwise there would be the consequence of constant death. Otherwise, the body would not be the cause of that consciousness, since [consciousness] does not conform to the presence or absence of its modifications. Indeed, the body is recognized as the cause only if there were a resuscitation;
for if the mind were the cause, there would be no cessation of the mind.
For if there is a defect in the mind, there is no returning even to one's own home;
(463) but if it were the body that is the cause, [the stream] would cease upon a defect in the body.
Yet, how could such a body be the non-cause of the mind? (464)

For if the body were the cause, it would be illogical that the body itself becomes such a cause at one time and not at another; likewise, how could there be this distinction that someone dies when the body has such a defect while another does not? However, if the mind is the cause, then the presence or absence of defects in the mind is the cause of death or its opposite; thus, this distinction is not untenable.
Furthermore, death occurs for some even when the humors have been pacified; conversely, life persists even when the humors are corrupted. Thus, this matter is not fixed. (465) (PVA) [074,x]

Indeed, an effect cannot arise from an improper cause. Therefore, consciousness is not an effect of the body; for if it were an effect of the body, there would follow the absurd consequence of its reviving again.

[Objection: Even when that which produces a defect has ceased, the defect produced by it does not necessarily cease. Indeed, even when fire has been removed, a transformation produced in wood by fire is not seen to have ceased in some cases. Therefore—

If it is argued that [the defect] does not cease because, even when the fire has ceased, the transformation of the wood does not cease—[we reply: no, for [the defect] can be removed through the application of medical treatment. (56)

Just as the transformation of wood does not cease even when the fire is extinguished, so too the transformation caused by the *doṣas* at death will not be reversed. Consequently, there is no possibility of returning to life. Thus it is said: "Because medical treatment is administered. For if the *doṣas* were subject to reversible transformation, then medical treatment applied to reverse them would achieve its intended fruit.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a disorder caused by the *doṣas* is indeed reversible, even if it is slight, prior to the onset of the disorder of death? However, the disorder of death itself will not be reversed. Therefore, because there are disorders caused by *doṣas* that are reversible and those that are irreversible, this is not a fault. [Reply: This is not a valid answer, because:

[074,xvi] Due to the absence of further becoming, one thing produces a certain modification in something else, while another acts by the opposite process, just as fire does with respect to wood and gold. // 57 //

Even for the first [type of defilement], there may be another that cannot be removed; however, whatever transformation has been produced [by it] can be restored, just as the hardness in gold can be eliminated. (58)

[075,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend form as real, nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not apprehend the eye as real, nor does he apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not apprehend forms as real, nor does he apprehend sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not apprehend the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he apprehend the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not apprehend contact as real, nor does he apprehend feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. He does not apprehend the element of earth as real, nor does he apprehend the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not apprehend the truth of suffering as real, nor does he apprehend the truths of origin, cessation, or the path as real. He does not apprehend the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he apprehend the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat as real. He does not apprehend Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he apprehend the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, he is said to practice the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend form as real? How is it that he does not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real? How is it that he does not apprehend the eye as real... [and so on] ...how is it that he does not apprehend the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; it is because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. It is because the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye... [and so on] ...it is because the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty of the intrinsic nature of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Subhūti, since all these dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend them as real.”

This is its meaning: sometimes something initiates a change that is irreversible, such as fire in wood; sometimes it does the opposite, such as that very same [fire] in gold, which does not initiate a change in one place and likewise does not cause a change in another. Here, there is a change in the air, which is the agent of change for something else, or rather, the object of change (*vikārya*). That other [change] is also irreparable. Even the mere blackness produced by fire in wood is irreparable even by one who approaches it; however, in the case of gold, when the fire ceases, it becomes otherwise again. Therefore, since a minor change caused by a defect is reversible, it follows that even a major change characterized by death would be reversible. Consequently, the undesirable consequence of resurrection would follow. For instance, even the change characterized by the cessation of consciousness caused by sleep ceases when the sleep is gone. Now, if it is argued that in that case there is no reversal at all, it is replied: [this is not so].
For that which is of the nature of non-experience is not accepted as experience.
Nevertheless, if its existence were the case, then even for a dead person there would be experience. (466) (PVA)
For in the absence of awareness, there would be no distinction between the dead and the sleeping; as for respiration and so forth, all of that has already been considered as it truly is.

There is no difference between one who is asleep and one who is dead other than the absence of sensation; therefore, just as a sleeper awakens, it would follow that even a dead person could be revived by means such as blows or the application of medicine.

Now, [the opponent might argue that] while for one who is fast asleep there is simply an absence of cognition, for one who is dead there is [an absence] of that [cognition]; this is the distinction. [We reply: No, because the lack of cognition is the same in both cases. If it is said that even in the absence of cognition it exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), then let it be pointed out: what is this potentiality? If the potentiality is indeed cognition, then cognition itself exists; how then can there be an absence of cognition? It is contradictory to say that it both exists and does not exist. If the potentiality is something other than cognition, then it must be the body itself; therefore, since the potentiality that produces consciousness exists in the body, there would be no cessation of that [consciousness]. If it is argued that the body which was the producer has perished and another body that is not a producer has arisen, and thus there is no consciousness—what is this "non-productivity"? If you say it is the state of being devoid of cognition, then since that [absence of cognition] exists even for one who is asleep, there would be no cognition for the sleeper even in the state of waking. If it is argued that in that [sleeping] state there are breaths and so forth, and therefore the body is not non-productive, then its production would have occurred at that very time during the state of sleep, and thus the person would not be asleep at all.

[075,vii] Now, if it is argued that consciousness arises from the body alone, aided by the transformation of sleep and by inhalation (*āśvāsa*) and so forth—what is this thing called "sleep"? If you say it is the absence of cognition, then since that [absence] exists even in a dead person, cognition should arise again upon its transformation. If, on the other hand, one were to say that there is no production from the body alone due to the deficiency of auxiliary factors because of the absence of inhalation, then in states such as fainting where inhalation and so forth are absent, there would likewise be no cognition. Therefore, it has already been demonstrated that inhalation and so forth are not the cause of cognition, nor are inhalation and so forth themselves the cause. Furthermore:
[075,viii]
Upon the cessation of sleep, cognitions of that same kind arise from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior knowledge; therefore, the body is not the cause.

For when the body is produced under identical conditions, cognitions are observed to conform precisely to prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, neither the body nor the vital breaths (*āśvāsa*) and so forth are the cause.
If it is argued that they arise from the body assisted by mental impressions, that is incorrect.
If the formative factor (*saṃskāra*) were to act as a cooperative cause, then it would follow that [the effect] is non-existent; this is difficult to maintain.

For that which does not exist cannot be a cooperative cause for that which exists. Furthermore, in the state of awakening, the previous mind does not exist in the same way that the body does. Nor can that which does not exist be a cooperative cause, because it lacks the capacity to cooperate; indeed, there is no coexistence between what exists and its opposite. Therefore, the previous mind alone is the cause therein, not the body. [Objection: But how is it then that blows and the like act as awakeners? [Reply:
This is not a valid answer, for the state of having attained awakening does not necessarily arise from a blow alone.

Awakening is observed even in the absence of a blow. (PVA 470) For awakening does not arise from the blow alone, since it occurs spontaneously as well. But surely, immediately after awakening, a conceptual construction arises through its connection with objects previously perceived; therefore, how can there be a state of cooperation between the perception and the prior cognition? This too is not correct, because:

Even in this case, no fixed rule is observed regarding the awakening of proximity; for when one has fallen asleep while intent upon something, there is awakening from that very thing which was projected. (PVA 471)

When one has fallen asleep having focused intently upon a certain object, the awakening of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) occurs in accordance with that very object. However, it is not observed that upon awakening, the awakening is restricted solely to what is proximate through the connection of what is perceived. Furthermore, for one who possesses a particular habituation, the awakening is of that same nature and not otherwise. And awakening consists precisely of internal tactile cognitions and so forth. Just as there is a habitual practice regarding a certain thing, the resulting effect is the experience of pleasure in accordance with that; for instance: [076,v] Thus:
The latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of fear, courage, and so forth, as well as the grasping of liquids, weapons, and the like,
arise in the form of awakening for living beings as cognitions of pleasure.

For those who are habituated to the cultivation of the meditation on fear, awakening consists precisely in the experience of the pleasure of flight and so forth; otherwise, however, there is only a state of suffering. For those of a fierce nature, who delight in harming others and inflict injury upon them, [awakening] consists in the experience of the pleasure of grasping weapons and the like. Therefore, neither the body nor [the breaths such as] inhalation (*āśvāsa*) and so forth are the cause of consciousness. Only the preceding consciousness is the cause. If that [preceding consciousness] were produced from the body, then because of the consequence of its non-cessation, that very same fault would persist. Likewise, there would be no continuity with the preceding consciousness. If it is argued that [the body] is not a cause due to being impaired by defects (*doṣa*), then in the absence of defects it would again become a cause. Furthermore, if it were to initiate a change that does not recur, then even a slight change caused by it—such as weakness and so forth, characterized either by the production of dull consciousness or by the interruption of consciousness as in fainting and the like—would be irreversible. For that which initiates a change that does not recur, even a slight [change] is irreversible. However, "that change which is reversible through effort is one whose recurrence is possible, like the hardness in gold. Indeed, the hardness of gold, even if it has occurred, returns once the cause of the change has been removed. Similarly, even the great change consisting of the interruption of consciousness characterized by death would be reversible, and thus one would return to life.

[076,vii] Is it not the case that there is no fault because of this dual nature—namely, that some disorders are reversible due to the application of medical treatment, while others are irreversible due to the occurrence of incurable diseases? He states the rebuttal:
[076,viii]

Because the one who can provide the treatment is difficult to find, something is said to be incurable; or, due to the exhaustion of the lifespan, it is incurable. However, when there is only a [physical] disorder (*doṣa*), there is no such thing as incurability.

[076, ix] For it is said that something is "incurable" due to the absence of a physician and medicine capable of reversing the transformations caused by defects; however, this does not apply to the doctrine that consciousness arises from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because in that case, the impossibility of recovery is simply due to the extreme rarity of a healer.
The rarity of one who possesses meditative concentration is due to the impossibility of reversing transformation;
furthermore, if it were possible to reverse it, there would be no cause for reviving again, and if it did cease, its cessation would be purposeless.
Therefore, upon the cessation of the transformation, there would indeed follow the undesirable consequence of a return to life.

[076,xii] But surely, for the opponent as well, there is indeed the state of being incurable. To this, the reply is: "But for me, it is logical that it is incurable. He says this because the incurability of a disease results from the exhaustion of the lifespan; for it is observed that some die from a disease of such a nature, while another does not.

[077,i] Life is merely an indication; or rather, it is due to the exhaustion of karma. For a disease born of karma, such as leprosy (*śvitra*) and the like, becomes incurable because of the existence of such karma. Therefore, he states that the sovereignty of karma alone is the cause of its persistence. However, when there is only a disturbance of the humors (*doṣa*), there is no incurability of the disease. Therefore, [077,ii]...

If, upon death, poison and the like are removed, or even if the bitten part is cut off, then when the cause of the transformation has vanished, he does not breathe again; how much more so [in the case of one who has attained liberation]? || 60 ||

For when there is the removal of poison and the like from one who has died by means of mantras and so forth; or when there is the spontaneous cessation of the site of the bite through the amputation of that limb; or when the cause of the transformation, such as fever and the like, ceases—then the consequence of their being revived follows. This is established.

Furthermore, there is no cessation of an effect upon the cessation of its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). And the body is not the material cause [of consciousness]. For if it were, then [consciousness] would not undergo modification when that [body] does not undergo modification. Thus:
[077,v] Without a modification of the material cause, there is no modification of the derivative (*upādeya*).
Just as jars and other objects can be fashioned from clay by means of transformation. 61.

For if the body, which is the material cause (*upādāna*), were not subject to modification, it would be impossible for consciousness, which is the effect (*upādeya*), to undergo modification. No modification of a pot or similar object is ever observed without a prior modification of the clay. This is the very nature of a material cause: that its own modification brings about the modification of the effect. Even among many causes, only a specific one is the material cause of something, not merely any cause whatsoever. Furthermore, although the body is a cause, the mind does not necessarily undergo modification solely through a modification of the body; even when the body is unmodified, the mind undergoes modification through mere prior modifications such as fear or grief. And when the body is modified, the mind necessarily undergoes modification.
[077, vii] The seventh section.

But surely, even when there is a change in water, there is a change in the sprout, yet water is not its material cause (*upādāna*). This is because the material cause is that which is the cause of the continuum (*santāna*). The seed is the cause of the continuum, whereas water is not; for water is merely the cause of a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*). The continuum does not arise from water alone, since water is common to barley and other plants as well. Furthermore, the cessation of the rice-continuum does not follow from the cessation of water, because the rice-continuum does not cease even in the absence of water. However, the states such as the sprout do arise from water, and those states cease when water ceases; therefore, water is indeed the material cause of those states. And the subsequent changes in the sprout and so forth occur through the successive transformations of the rice-seed caused by water and other factors. Therefore, although consciousness undergoes transformation even when the body undergoes transformation, the body is not its material cause. Thus he says:
For when one thing is modified without the modification of another entity,
it is not logical for that [unchanged] thing to be the material cause of the former, just as in the case of a cow and a gavaya.

[077,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld the sufferings of those beings and, by his great compassionate heart, resolved to deliver them all from their miseries. Then, while practicing the profound perfection of wisdom, he perceived that the five aggregates are all empty and thereby crossed over the ocean of suffering.
