the venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the venerable Mah

And since consciousness undergoes modification without the body undergoing modification, the body is not its material cause (*upādāna*); therefore, the cessation of the body does not entail the cessation of consciousness. For [consciousness] undergoes modification through the modification of that [body], just as in the case of a cow and a gavaya. One might argue: "Let the gavaya be somehow the cause of a particular state of the cow; yet upon the cessation of that [cow], let only that particular state cease, but let there be no cessation of the continuum (*santāna*) itself. Or: "Let it be that the cow and the gavaya do not stand in a relationship of material cause and effect, and thus one does not cease when the other ceases; but what follows from this for the body and the mind? Indeed, if there were no relationship of material cause and effect, the presence of qualities or defects in one would not entail the presence of qualities or defects in the other, and their coexistence would not be necessary, as in the case of the water in a stream of rice and so forth. To this, it is replied: [The text continues: "It is observed that the body is the material cause of consciousness, because consciousness arises only when the body exists, and because it is modified by the modifications of the body, just like a painting and its canvas, or a fragrance and its flower. Furthermore, the body is the material cause of consciousness because it is the substratum of the sense-faculties, which are themselves the material causes of consciousness; just as the threads are the material cause of a cloth. Moreover, the body is the material cause of consciousness because it is the basis for the manifestation of consciousness, just as the lamp is the basis for the manifestation of light. And since consciousness is a transformation of the body, the cessation of the body entails the cessation of consciousness, just as the cessation of the clay entails the cessation of the jar. Therefore, the body is indeed the material cause of consciousness."
The affliction of the mind and the body arises from that cause, namely the production of an effect;
their coexistence results from mutual assistance, just as fire and the liquefaction of copper. (63)

For no other relationship is established here such that there would be a relation of non-appropriator and appropriated even between the mind and the body, as in the case of a cow and a gavaya, which have only some manner of mutual assistance. It is not necessarily the case that a modification of the mind occurs only through a modification of the body. Therefore, because it is not its material cause (anupādāna-kāraṇa), the mind does not cease even when the body ceases.
An entity that is the cause of a state is not at all the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
For when that which produces the state ceases, let that very state cease.
But that which is the cause of the continuum is the material cause.

Upon the cessation of that [defilement], there would be the cessation of this continuum. (PVA 475) Just as upon the cessation of fire, the fluidity of copper ceases, so too does the mind persist together with the body for that duration. (PVA 476)

Because they function as mutual auxiliaries, like fire and the melting of copper, the effect of those two causes does not remain in the mind, just as gold [remains] after [the melting process]. (PVA 477)

Just as gold, when aided by fire, has fluidity as its material cause, so that fire and the fluidity of copper coexist; likewise, the mind, which is restricted to the body, arises from a mind that has the body as its auxiliary cause. Even for the embryo (*kalala*) and other such stages which are the causes of the body, the body itself becomes an auxiliary cause for the mind. Therefore, there is a coexistence of the two at the moment of the effect's birth. This is what is meant:
because they act as mutual auxiliaries, a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not possible [for them to exist independently].
The coexistence of even these two cooperating factors is not untenable.

(478) [PVA 078, ix] Because the cause of the body—designated as the *kalala* stage and so forth—is a cooperative factor for consciousness, and because consciousness is likewise a cooperative factor for the body, they coexist at the time of the production of their effect, characterized by the body and mind, just like fire and the melting of copper. However, when the body has ceased, the consciousness may be distinguished by another body or become bodiless; thus, there is no cessation of that [consciousness], just like the continuum of gold.

[078,x] Furthermore, it might be argued: just as the specific transformation (*viśeṣa*) of the rice-continuum from water and so forth does not cease when the water ceases, whereas the continuum of fire and so forth—which have their material cause (*upādāna*) impaired—does indeed cease; so too, when the material cause of the mind is impaired by something, it lacks the capacity to serve as a cause for a continuum, yet this does not mean the continuum itself must cease. And just as a lotus root (*śālūka*) arises from cow dung, which is of a different genus, so too its first arising is from the body alone. To this, it is replied:
The material cause of rice and the like is subject to destruction by fire and other factors;
however, consciousness as a material cause is not destroyed by anything. (PVA 479)
The first arising of consciousness from the body is not observed; nor is its cessation possible without the impairment of its material cause. (PVA 480) [078, xiii]

The impairment of the appropriation of consciousness is not like the impairment of the rice-continuum by fire and so forth. Consciousness itself is the appropriation of consciousness; and burning and such [impairments] are not possible for it. If it is argued that there is impairment by sleep and so forth, we say no, because sleep and so forth are causes of only temporary impairment.
Cognition that depends upon prior mental impressions arises even from an object that is obstructed; for it, there is no interruption caused by sleep. (PVA 481)
Indeed, torpor is not capable of obstructing consciousness by means of grasping.
Since arising is observed even from a consciousness that has been interrupted,
there is no established distinction between death, sleep, and such interruption.
Now, if at some time there were indeed a cessation [of the stream], that would be non-existent.
[078,xviii] How could there be no perception of a break without an awakening?
Whence could such a conceptualization of that [break] arise, whether by itself or through another? (PVA 483)

[079,i] First of all, the interruption of cognition is not perceived by itself; for the interruption of a non-cognition is perceived by means of a cognition, but the interruption of a cognition is not perceived by anything at all. If it is argued that it is by means of the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*), then the absence of cognition is unestablished; how could that which is unestablished establish an absence? If it were established, that very establishment would be a cognition; so how could there be an interruption of cognition?
For if a disjunction were never perceived, it would always exist;
thus, that very state would constitute the non-existence of the next world—a position that is difficult to refute. (484) (PVA)
That too is incorrect.
Because it is perceived that awakening depends upon prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*),
the mere cessation of consciousness accompanied by cognition is not observed.

At birth and upon awakening, consciousness is observed to be accompanied precisely by prior latent impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*); thus, no disjunction between the preceding and succeeding limits is perceived. Furthermore, one person does not perceive a disjunction of consciousness in another, because the conditions for perception are absent. Nor can there be a disjunction due to slackening caused by the absence of passion;
for it is generally accepted that "detachment" (*virāga*) consists simply in being free from desire for one's own objects.
One who is indifferent to the welfare of others exists even though free from faults, yet he is not [truly] integrated [with the path].

(486) [PVA] Indeed, faultlessness is not attained merely through indifference to the welfare of others; for that very lack of compassion is itself his fault. Alternatively, there is no fault, as some indeed maintain that a cessation [of activity] occurs when one is free from passion (*vītarāga*). Therefore, consciousness does not cease through the impairment of giving, because the body is not being grasped and because it is impossible to impair the mind.

It might be argued as follows: even if consciousness does not cease through the cessation of its *upādāna*, its cessation through the cessation of its support (*āśraya*) remains unprevented. Since the body is perceived to be that support, then just as there is a cessation of consciousness when a wall or similar object is removed, there would be no proof of a future life.
Even that [movement] does not exist, yet movement is perceived in paintings and the like;
therefore, upon the destruction of the support, there would be the destruction of the object, such as the painting.

For it is understood that patterns and the like do not come from another substratum into a cloth or similar object; consciousness, however, at birth and in the state of awakening, is accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) associated with the bodies of other lives, as well as by those associated with the movement through the body during dreams. Thus, unlike a painting, it does not have a fixed substratum. For if it had a fixed substratum, it would perish upon the destruction of that substratum. Furthermore, since there is no such thing as "substratum-ness" belonging to either the body or anything else anywhere, how could there be destruction upon its destruction?
However, paintings and the like are indeed non-different from the wall and so forth; therefore, they perish only through their own destruction, not through the destruction of their support.
If it is argued that "let there be no relationship of support and supported in case of non-difference, but it will exist between body and mind in case of difference," this is not so.
Because neither the existent nor the non-existent have a basis, there is no basis that acts as a cause for persistence.
If it were the basis of the existent, it would not be distinct from the persisting entity itself.
Even if there is a distinction, what has that cause done for the entity?

[079,xv] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Collection. It should be understood as such. Thus it was said. This concludes the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the chapter on the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, the fifteenth. ② The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his upper robe to bare one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to be able to hear this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices ten things, he will be able to hear this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection. What are the ten? First, he does not abandon the Mahāyāna; second, he does not disparage the Śrāvaka vehicle; third, he does not disparage the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; fourth, he does not disparage other bodhisattvas; fifth, he does not disparage those who practice the precepts; sixth, he does not disparage those who uphold the Dharma; seventh, he does not disparage those who seek the Dharma; eighth, he does not disparage those who preach the Dharma; ninth, he does not disparage those who listen to the Dharma; tenth, he does not disparage those who practice according to the Dharma. Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices these ten things, he will be able to hear this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection. Then the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how many kinds of bodhisattvas are there? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “There are three kinds of bodhisattvas. What are the three? First, the bodhisattva who has newly set out in the vehicle; second, the bodhisattva who has practiced for a long time; third, the bodhisattva who is irreversible. Mañjuśrī, these are the three kinds of bodhisattvas. Then the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition for a bodhisattva to be called a ‘newly set out’ bodhisattva? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “If a bodhisattva, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection, gives rise to a mind of joy, and having given rise to a mind of joy, seeks this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection, and having sought this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection, copies it, recites it, explains it, and practices according to its teaching—Mañjuśrī, this is called a ‘newly set out’ bodhisattva. Then the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition for a bodhisattva to be called a ‘long-practiced’ bodhisattva? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: “If a bodhisattva, having heard this Dharma-discourse of the Great Collection, gives rise to a mind of joy, and having given rise to a mind of joy, seeks this First of all, there is no substratum (*āśraya*) for that which is non-existent; for there is no substratum whatsoever for the horn of a donkey, yet one merely seeks its production from a cause while it remains non-existent. Therefore, for the non-existent, only a cause is possible, not a substratum. Furthermore, a substratum cannot belong to that which is existent, because that which exists is free from all dependence. Nor is it logical to claim that a substratum exists for the sake of the stability of the existent; for stability is not distinct from the thing that stands. If stability were produced, then the thing itself would have been produced. Moreover, there is no production of what already exists, since it is impossible for what has already arisen to arise again. Now, if it is argued that even for that which has arisen, something remains unproduced and the substratum exists for the sake of producing that [unproduced part], we reply: the term "cause" is used when there is production in its entirety, whereas terms such as "support" (*ādhāra*) are used when there is the production of some particular property (*dharma*). Furthermore, stability is not distinct from the thing’s own nature (*svarūpa*); for even in the case of a falling object, its own nature persists despite the absence of stability. If stability were indeed non-distinct [from the nature], then the object would be non-distinct from stability, and thus it would exist at all times. It is therefore logical that stability is distinct [from the nature], because it is excluded when the nature is present due to the imposition of contradictory properties.

[080,i] The Discourse on the Lion’s Roar Spoken by the Buddha. 14th Sūtra. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? They are: the person who is like a śāla tree; the person who is like a lotus flower; the person who is like a nyagrodha tree; and the person who is like a lion. What is the person who is like a śāla tree? Here, a certain person is born into a noble family of high status, possessing great wealth and abundant property. He is handsome, attractive, and pleasing to behold, endowed with supreme physical beauty. He is well-versed in various fields of knowledge, skilled in the arts, and possesses great eloquence. He is learned in the Vedas and their branches, and has mastered the mantras and incantations. Yet, he does not believe in the existence of the results of actions performed in this life or in future lives; he does not believe in the existence of the fruits of good or evil deeds. He does not believe in the existence of this world or the next world. He does not believe in the existence of father or mother, nor does he believe in the existence of spontaneously born beings. He does not believe in the existence of arhats in the world who have attained right conduct and right realization, who have themselves realized through direct knowledge and abide therein, having fully exhausted all taints. He does not believe in the efficacy of giving, sacrifice, or offerings. He does not believe in the existence of the results of good or evil deeds performed in this life or in future lives. He holds such views as these: ‘There is no merit in giving; there is no fruit or result of giving. There is no merit in sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of sacrifice. There is no merit in making offerings; there is no fruit or result of making offerings. There is no this world, nor a next world. There is no mother, nor a father. There are no spontaneously born beings. In the world there are no arhats who have attained right conduct and right realization, who have themselves realized through direct knowledge and abide therein, having fully exhausted all taints. There is no efficacy in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There is no fruit or result of good or evil deeds performed in this life or in future lives. Having held such views, he acts accordingly. Because of these causes and conditions, when his body breaks up after death, he falls into a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell. This is called the person who is like a śāla tree. What is the person who is like a lotus flower? At that time, the Blessed One spoke

That is incorrect. If there is a distinction [between the entity and its stability], then that [stability] is simply its cause; it is the cause of its persistence, not its support (*ādhāra*). If you argue that the support is the support of the entity, we say no, because it performs no function toward the entity itself. If you argue that it is a support because it effects the persistence of the entity, is this persistence something already produced that belongs to the thing to be stabilized, or otherwise? It cannot exist prior to production, because the entity does not yet exist. Therefore, how could a persistence produced from another [cause] belong to the entity, given the absence of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between them? If you argue that it arises as inherent (*samaveta*) in it, what does "inherent" mean? If it means "the persistence exists therein," then there must be another persistence for that persistence, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is distinct [from the entity], why is it not perceived as such? If you say it is due to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), let there be inherence; nevertheless, a thing should be perceived by its own form. How can there be a perception otherwise? If you say it is due to conjunction (*saṃsarga*), what is this so-called "conjunction"? If it is a conjunction in its entirety, there is no distinction [from identity]. If it is a conjunction by way of one part, what is the difference between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence? If you say it is the state of being "joined" (*yuta*) versus "not joined" (*ayuta*) in their establishment, then the parts of a tree and so forth would also entail inherence. If you say it is "being based on the notion 'here' (*iha-buddhi*)," no, because that would result in it being merely conjunction, since we have the perception "the horn is on the head. Alternatively, if "not joined" means "inherence in the parts that are inherent in itself," and the opposite is "joined," even so, inherence is not established because of the perception of difference. Furthermore, there is no conjunction of a partless entity with a part; if there were conjunction with a part, it would follow that there is a perception of difference. It is not correct to say that the difference lies in being "conjoined" or "unconjoined," because such a concomitance (*anvaya*) is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And in the absence of perception, there is no inference; thus, there is no perception of concomitance. Therefore, it is established that a specific object is produced precisely from a specific auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); there is no such thing as "persistence. Thus, the relation of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is nothing but a specific causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Moreover, the body is not the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*); therefore, upon the cessation of the body, there is no cessation [of the self]. If the body were the support because it effects persistence, then as long as the support exists, the persistence of the supported would exist, and there would be no destruction of it.

If it is argued that there would be the consequence of non-destruction because the cause of destruction is not admitted, then the same consequence applies there as well; what then is the use of a cause for stability? (65)
For when a sustainer exists, the occurrence of destruction is impossible.

〈Cessation is without cause〉—Now, it might be argued: "Cessation does not occur while the sustainer exists if there were no cause of cessation; since destruction follows from the presence of a cause of destruction, there is no undesirable consequence of perpetual non-destruction. To this he says: If it is claimed that "that destruction [arises] from a cause of destruction," no; the same undesirable consequence applies there as well. In that case too, regarding destruction, the same undesirable consequence holds: there is no such thing as "destruction" that is something other than the entity itself. And if it were distinct [from the entity], what would that cause of destruction do for the entity? (488) (PVA)

[080, vi] For when destruction is produced by something distinct [from the entity], that [entity] is not truly said to have perished. Consequently, the cause of destruction performs no function whatsoever. Therefore, since there is no destruction, the entity simply remains by itself; what then is the use of a cause of stability? A cause of stability that performs no function is no cause at all. Alternatively, if destruction results from a cause of destruction, then as long as the cause of destruction is absent, the entity remains by itself; what then is the use of a cause of stability? [080, vii]

If it is argued that stability [of the self] follows from the arrival of fasting unto death because it is the nature of things that destruction occurs [only then], then since that destruction is established by truth itself, what is the use of a cause for its continued existence? (66)

[080, viii] Destruction would occur even in the absence of a sustainer, and it could also occur in the absence of a destroyer; however, it perishes only when there is a destroyer who sustains it, and not without a cause of destruction. Therefore, because it exists prior to the destroyer that effects its stability, the sustainer is not purposeless. But if this were so, it would follow that destruction is causeless; thus, the entity itself arises from its own causes as being of such a nature—this is the inherent property (*vastudharmatā*) of destruction. As long as the object exists, this [destruction] remains unimpeded. Since no one can alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing, what is the use of a cause for stability? [081, ii]

Now, [the opponent argues: "An entity perishes even in the absence of a cause for its stability; yet when a cause for stability exists, there is an obstruction to its destruction. But surely that obstruction to destruction is something other than the destruction itself. Consequently, since nothing happens to the destruction, it would simply perish—how then could there be stability? [The proponent replies: "If, at every moment, the perishable entity becomes otherwise due to a stabilizer (*sthāpaka*), then its destruction too is causeless; thus, that very thing is momentary destruction. And since that [change] arises from the stabilizer as something different, the stabilizer is merely a cause [of change], not a stabilizer. "Alternatively, if non-destruction results from the arrival of a non-destructive agent following the stabilizer, then in that case, non-destruction has arisen. Since this is unimpeded, what further need is there for a cause of stability? "If, on the other hand, non-destruction exists only during the time the stabilizer is present, then in that case, a distinct destruction occurs at every moment due to the stabilizer. And by what is the stability of the stabilizer itself produced? If it is produced by its own cause, then the same will apply to the object being stabilized; what then is the use of a stabilizer? "If you argue that there is a distinction such that some things have stability through a stabilizer while others have it by themselves, then why is it not accepted that consciousness (*vijñāna*) also has stability by itself?"

[081,iii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "A region of ground is seen as a receptacle for water, and this perception is not sublated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, because neither the existent nor the non-existent has a basis, the argument is futile due to its contradiction with what is perceived. To this, he replies:
If it is argued that [the self is] the substratum for water and so forth, this is equally applicable here as well. // 67 //
For since entities perish at every moment, the continuum of those entities arises in such a way that it possesses a cause; otherwise, a substratum would be untenable. (68)

A support may exist for things such as water because it prevents their movement; but what need is there for supports for qualities, universals, and actions, which are themselves devoid of motion? (69)

The absence of a substratum even for water and the like in relation to the ground and so forth is indeed logical, whether [the water] exists or does not exist; thus, the example is unobserved (*adṛṣṭa*). But [one might object]: since the state of being a substratum is observed, how can it be said to be unobserved? It is precisely because it is unobserved that you have the conceit that it is observed. According to the principle that "that which is a substratum (*ādhāra*) with respect to an action is so called because of its supporting (*dhāraṇa*) the agent and the object," a substratum is so called because of supporting. And supporting belongs to that which is falling. That which falls cannot be supported, and that which is supported is not perceived as falling, because falling and non-falling are mutually contradictory. If it is argued that there is first falling and subsequently non-falling, then it is not the case that what falls is supported, because oneness is not apprehended through perception. A single persisting entity (*avasthātā*) is not perceived as pervading both the state of falling and its opposite. Furthermore, how can that which is non-pervasive (*avyāpī*) be a persisting entity? For in the apprehension "it persists until now," the persisting entity is grasped in such a way. If it is argued that it is grasped as pervasive through a sequence (*krama*), one must consider what the meaning of "sequence" is. The designation "sequence" applies only to existence and non-existence. And these two, existence and non-existence, belong to things occurring at different times. Whether they belong to the object of cognition (*grāhya*) or the cognizer (*grāhaka*), the oneness [of the object] results from the conjunction of its existence and non-existence. If the cognizer possesses sequence, then the object likewise does; thus, there is no oneness for the persisting entity of the object. Therefore, sequence is merely within the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), where something already past is grasped, something present is being grasped, and something future is yet to be grasped. How, then, could sequence be perceptual? Since it is not perceived, how can the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) be asserted on its basis? Consequently, the statement "neither for the existent nor the non-existent is there a substratum" has this very meaning: the relationship of substratum and superstratum is not actually seen; it is therefore merely a mental construction (*kalpanā*). But how, then, can there be even the construction of a substratum and superstratum without seeing it? It should not exist at all. In that case, it follows that it is a false construction. However, for entities (*bhāva*) that perish moment by moment and arise in successive locations, their arising in a location other than their material cause (*upādāna*) is produced by contact with a substratum. Thus, because it arises in that manner, the ground and so forth are called the "substratum" because they act as a cause. It is only the cause, in a specific state, that is called the "substratum," having superimposed oneness upon the preceding and succeeding moments.

For when there is the superimposition of identity, one does not perceive arising; and by superimposing a cause upon what preceded, a false conceptualization arises through the power of beginningless latencies (*vāsanā*). Precisely because it proceeds from preceding and preceding latencies, its existence as a beginningless continuum establishes the next world—this is the conclusion that follows. To explain further:
All mental conceptualization arises from prior causes;
by virtue of its lack of objective support, it is like the conceptualization of water in a mirage.

The conceptualization of identity between the preceding and succeeding moments does not follow from the existence of a common objective basis (*ālambana*), because such identity is absent. It might be argued that this [conceptualization] arises from a manifold object itself, since its being an effect thereof is not observed. That is incorrect. For the conceptualization of water in a mirage is not based on that alone; rather, it arises from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of having previously seen water. Nor was identity perceived previously; therefore, the conceptualization of identity in another life must be preceded by the grasping of identity in that other life, and that too is likewise [preceded by another], thus establishing an infinite regress of mutual dependence. Consequently, the beginningless continuum of living beings is established. In this way, the cognition associated with the grasping of a self and so forth, existing as an beginningless continuum, is not severed even in the future; thus, *saṃsāra* is without beginning or end. Moreover:
A support may exist for things such as water because it prevents their movement; but what use are supports for qualities, universals, and motions, which are themselves devoid of motion?

[082,v] For it is logical that for water and the like, the substratum (*ādhāra*) is the cause of obstruction to motion; however, what need have qualities (*guṇa*), universals (*sāmānya*), and motions (*karman*)—which are devoid of movement and inactive—of substrata? Furthermore, consciousness (*caitanya*) is either a universal, a quality, or an action; in any case, it is inactive. Thus, it has no requirement for a substratum, and consequently, there is no destruction of the mind (*cetas*) as the supported by the destruction of its substratum. Its co-existence is merely coincidental. How this co-existence occurs has already been explained previously. [082,vi]

[Objection: But surely, just as a quality (*guṇa*) is inherent (*samaveta*) even in the absence of motion, so too is the mind (*cetas*) inherent. And it is not the case that an inherent quality can exist without an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); thus, upon the destruction of that [cause], there is necessarily destruction [of the quality]. [Reply: No. There is no relationship of substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) without the prevention of movement [by the substratum], nor is there inherence without the relationship of substratum and superstratum; for it is stated that "inherence is the basis for the notion of 'here' (*iha-buddhi*) among things that are established separately (*yutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of substratum and superstratum. This very point he states: By this, both inherence (*samavāya*) and the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) [are explained].
The fixed nature of genus and so forth has been refuted, because they lack a substratum. (70)
[082, viii] The eighth chapter.

Even though a universal (*jāti*) is inherent, it does not exist apart from the individual (*vyakti*) that serves as its substratum. If it is argued that because the universal is eternal, it does not cease to exist even in the absence of a substratum, [we reply] that this is the same for consciousness (*cetas*), since it too is dependent upon other causes. Furthermore, there is no relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*). By this very refutation of the relationship between container and contained, inherence (*samavāya*) is refuted, and the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) is also refuted. If that [inherence] were a cause, it would not be a relationship of container and contained; if, on the other hand, it is not a cause, then it lacks the status of an inherent cause. And if it is claimed that the fixed distribution of universals and so forth exists even without causality, that too is refuted.

[082,ix] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a white lotus flower, and the person who is like a supreme lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, in all ways, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. Just as a lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is like a lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains submerged in the water and does not rise above it; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is like a blue lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. Just as a white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is like a white lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a supreme lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. Just as a supreme lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...free from ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is like a supreme lotus flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the four kinds of persons who are like lotus flowers. Come, friends, let us go to the Blessed One and inquire about the meaning of this. "Yes, friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with a number of monks, went to the Blessed One, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Just now, venerable sir, not long after the Blessed One had departed, I addressed the monks: 'Friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the four kinds of persons who are like lotus flowers. Come, friends, let us go to the Blessed One and inquire about the meaning of this. 'Yes, friend,' those monks replied to me. Then, venerable sir, we went to the Blessed One, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, venerable sir, I said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One has spoken of the four kinds of persons who are like lotus flowers. What, venerable sir, is the person who is like a lotus flower? What, venerable sir, is the person who is like a blue lotus flower? What, venerable sir, is the person who is like a white lotus flower? What, venerable sir, is the person who is like a supreme lotus flower? When I had said this, venerable sir, the Blessed One said to me: 'Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a white lotus flower, and the person who is like a supreme lotus flower. [The rest of the discourse follows the same structure as above. "It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: 'There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. And how, venerable sir, is one a person who is like a lotus flower? Alternatively, even if there were inherence (*samavāya*), the very notion of being "restricted to that [substratum] alone" has already been refuted. For a universal (*jāti*), although it depends upon individuals, is not restricted to that one individual alone, because it persists in other individuals as well. Likewise, even though consciousness is dependent [on a body], it will persist in another body even in the absence of the current body; thus, the existence of another world (*paraloka*) is not unestablished. Even in the absence of a single body, there is no contradiction in having such a cognition as its material cause (*upādāna*), just like a cognition that persists across different individuals. Therefore, there is no relation of substrate and superstrate (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) apart from the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
If its destruction occurs due to something else, what is the use of a cause for its duration?
It would perish even without other factors; causes for duration have no power [over it]. (71)
Everything that has stability possesses a substratum, and in the arising of everything, there is likewise a substratum;
therefore, no entity whatsoever ever undergoes destruction. (72)
If its nature is inherently perishable, what other agent could establish it?
If its nature is not inherently perishable, what other agent could establish it? (73)
These are the summary verses.

But surely, even in the absence of the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyatā*), the relation of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is observed between a lamp and its light. For light does not possess the property of falling [downward], yet the lamp serves as its support, and upon the cessation of the lamp, the light ceases. Furthermore, that light does not migrate to another lamp or to anything else. For example, when a lamp is destroyed, its light perishes even if it has reached another location. In the same way, consciousness (*vijñāna*) which depends on the body will cease when the body ceases, even if it has gone toward an object. And even this "going toward an object" is not, in the ultimate sense, anything other than the mere appearance of the object's form within that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
To this, it is said:

Because it undergoes change through the changes of that [other], there is a relationship of substratum and dependent between a lamp and its light; however, this is not the case for the body and the mind, but rather for intellect (*buddhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.
To explain:
Even the decrease and increase of wisdom and other qualities occur through the differentiation of the activity of the intellect, even without the decrease and increase of the body. (74)

This [dependence] does not exist for things such as the light of a lamp that rely [upon it]; therefore, there would be a distinction even from that, since the mind does not provide assistance [to its object]. (75)

[083,ix] Through the power of specific mental formations (*saṃskāra*), the various forms of awakening (*bodhaviśeṣa*)—such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth—evolve as they become increasingly distinguished by the Buddha’s cognition. Even without a specific formation of the body, the preceding cognition itself is the support for the subsequent cognition, not the body. Therefore, the analogy of the light of a lamp does not apply.

But is it not the case that even the light of a lamp is indeed altered by snakes and other such things? No; that alteration characterized by a dim shadow belongs to the lamp itself. Therefore, the light of the lamp becomes different when situated at a distance. However, there is no alteration of the body at the time of the differentiation of mental activity. But is it not observed that a difference [in cognition] arises even from a difference in the body? Therefore, the body must be either the material cause (*upādāna*) or the substratum (*āśraya*).

To this he replies: Even in that case, the body’s state of being modified by modifications occurs solely through the medium of the mind’s assistance. And where there is a specific excellence of wisdom and so forth resulting from elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like for the nourishment of the body—there, because a body characterized by pleasant touch and form has arisen, and because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) corresponding to reality are awakened when the mind is undisturbed, a specific excellence of wisdom arises in a particular person at a particular time. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of everyone everywhere having an identical level of wisdom.
Just as, when hunger is suppressed, there is no arising of distress due to disease.
Upon its cessation, only the commentary as it was practiced proceeds for him.
(PVA 490) Because of the similarity to an elixir and because of his satisfaction, there may even be no [need for] further effort;
the investigation follows exactly what was practiced, since all other commentaries and so forth are non-existent [for him]. (PVA 491)
It is determined that whatever treatise one has practiced in previous lives,
one’s awakening of wisdom occurs specifically in relation to that very treatise.
However, for one who possesses the practice of all [treatises], there arises a distinction in wisdom due to the excellence of that practice.
Otherwise, one would become all-knowing through the application of elixirs (rasāyana).
Apart from perception and memory, there is no other cognition anywhere;
even the distinction between wisdom, intelligence, and so forth, arises solely from the awakening of memory.
Memory as it truly is [occurs] in the context of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth; wisdom is the opposite of that [forgetfulness].
Intelligence (*medhā*) is indeed just memory; the distinction between them is shown therein:
when an object has been utterly forgotten, [its recollection occurs] solely from a previous mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Likewise, he by whom [the truth] is realized through diligent application is celebrated as wise. (496) (PVA) He who understands through the very process of following upon recollection is called intelligent, due to his cultivation of wisdom. (497) (PVA)
Likewise:
The capacity to grasp things that have been apprehended individually is called *medhā* as well as *smṛti* (memory).
However, when these are joined together with one another, that very same capacity becomes specifically *prajñā* (wisdom).
Furthermore, no such thing as "joining" is ever observed to occur without prior practice.
From the fact that it pertains to an object of that same kind, a prior habituation is inferred by means of that [present state].

(PVA 499) Now, one might argue: "Passion (*rāga*) is also merely a particular state of cognition (*buddhi-viśeṣa*). If it were not distinct from cognition, then it would follow that wisdom (*prajñā*) and the like would also not be distinct [from it]. Furthermore, passion and the rest result in the body's nourishment or its decay; therefore, it follows that cognition also arises from the body, otherwise there would be no conformity with it. This is not so.

The increase of passion and so forth arises from nourishment and the like, while pleasure and pain arise occasionally from the proximity of internal objects such as the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu). // 76 //
