The increase of passion and other afflictions does not occur at all times, but only occasionally, when there is the manifestation of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) born of habituation. However, for one who encounters the cultivation of the meditation on the foul (*aśubhabhāvanā*), that very passion is, on the contrary, diminished. As for the increase of passion and so forth arising from pleasure and pain—wherein passion underlies pleasant feeling and hatred underlies painful feeling—that too is simply the awakening of that same aforementioned improper mental attention in one who is happy. But how can there be hatred toward the painful? For one who is suffering, everything is unbearable; therefore, hatred consists precisely in the desire to abandon it. Yet, there is no absolute rule here. Even when the mind is suffering, for one possessed of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), there arises only compassion through the inference of [others'] suffering as one's own. Furthermore, passion certainly occurs toward the cause of its remedy. If it is argued that since pleasure and pain are themselves of the nature of cognition, their production from the body is just like the production of cognition itself, then this contradicts your fundamental position. This is not so. Because of the presence of an internal object characterized by the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātusāmya*), pleasure arises solely through the medium of the sense-object (*viṣaya*), not through the medium of the physical basis (*āśraya*). It is not the body, acting as a basis, that produces pleasure and pain, but rather the object acting as the field. And the body is the basis for those two only insofar as the object is the cause of pleasure and so forth. Since external objects are identical to internal ones in this regard, it would follow that the external is also a basis, which is not accepted. Just as even an internal factor such as the equilibrium of the constituents is not apprehended as an object when one is looking at a beloved person and so on, then at that time the body alone is the basis of pleasure and pain. Nor is the object the basis, nor does the cessation of the object entail the cessation of the feeling. Just as pleasure arises with respect to an internal object, yet one may leave that aside and move toward an external object, so too is it possible in another body, such as in the next world.

By this, cases such as the loss of memory resulting from a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*) and so forth are explained. It is the intellect itself, arising from a particular internal object, that undergoes modification. (77)

In that case as well, when an elixir (*rasāyana*) or similar substance is present internally, a cognition of pleasure and so forth arises; from that, there follows the loss of memory and other such effects. However, this is not like a physical transformation of the body caused by a disorder of the humors (*sannipāta*). Just as visual consciousness arises from the eye and other senses—which serve as its supports—even when they are not being perceived, and changes [in the consciousness] occur through changes in them; it is not the same with a body transformed by an elixir. If [the body] were the cause even when it is not being cognized, it would follow that it is the cause of everything. As for the eyes and other senses, their status as supports is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and because changes in them produce changes in the consciousness. This is not the case for the body, because pleasure and so forth still occur even in its absence, provided external objects are present. Indeed, the loss of memory can occur even upon seeing an external form such as a *rākṣasa* demon.
This very point is demonstrated as follows.
[084, viii]

In certain cases, when there is an excellence in the continuity [of the mind], delusion and other such states arise from the mere hearing or seeing of things such as the blood of a śārdūla, just as [they do] in other instances. (78)

[084,ix] Even from merely hearing the word "tiger," someone may experience delusion or some other state of mind; likewise from seeing blood. Yet, the body is not the substratum [of cognition], nor does cognition cease when that [delusion] ceases. Thus, because an internal object serves as the objective support (*ālambana*), states such as the loss of memory arise during conditions like fainting due to the proximity and production [of that object]; therefore, cognition does not have the body as its substratum. The body is merely the objective support for pleasure and the like; consequently, even those [mental states] do not cease upon the cessation of the body, because they persist when there is another objective support.
Therefore, it invariably follows its own own latent impressions (saṃskāra); since the mind is inseparable from that, it is thus dependent upon the mind. (76)

[085,ii] It is the mental formation alone that necessarily follows the mind; it does not follow the body, because the body is not observed to be its support. For one whose attention is elsewhere, the mind does not arise in another [place]; thus, the mind is supported by the mind itself. To illustrate this:
Due to the greater strength of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), distraction is turned back;
if distraction is more powerful, the mental impression becomes averted.

When the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is exceedingly powerful, then even in the presence of distraction, there is no agitation of the mind; but when the state of agitation is powerful, then even though the formation exists, it does not produce a cognition corresponding to its own effect. Therefore, the mind is necessarily preceded by a prior cognition; thus, it is logical that the cessation of the mind occurs only upon the cessation of the mind itself.

[Objection: Surely, consciousness arises from the sense-faculties, and from that [sense-consciousness], mental consciousness arises. Therefore, since mental consciousness occurs through a succession starting from the body itself, how can the body be without a basis? For even in a succession, fire is not a non-cause for smoke produced from another smoke; nor is that [smoke] not produced from successive fires, being something unprecedented. In the same way, consciousness arising from the body would, like smoke, be subject to cessation. [Reply: No, because it has been established that mental consciousness exists even without sensory cognition, arising from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Just as smoke is of a certain nature and not of that same nature even when derived from smoke, so too the mind, through habituation, possesses exactly the same nature as its primordial origin. (501) (PVA) [085,vii]

For smoke produced from fire and smoke produced from [another] smoke do not possess a single defining characteristic. However, in the case of specific cognitions such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth, their form is identical prior to practice; and since [qualities] such as the grasping of a self are all-pervasive, smoke and the like cannot serve as an example. Furthermore, the continuity of smoke lasts for only a short duration and arises specifically from a particular fire. Wisdom and the rest, however, arise specifically from preceding instances of wisdom and so forth; their persistence is not caused by the body. Moreover: If consciousness were to arise from the sense faculties alone for someone...
The occurrence of the example of smoke is possible only from that which is devoid of prior cognition.

(PVA 502) Even sensory cognition, when arising, does not do so independently of prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). For even when the object and the sense organ are present, [sensory cognition] does not arise if there is a disturbance of the prior cognition. Therefore, it arises from the sense organ only when accompanied by the prior cognition, and not from the sense organ alone. That sensory cognition has indeed arisen; however, due to the absence of ascertainment (*niścaya*), it is conventionally designated as "not arisen."
That is incorrect.
If even a cognition that has arisen is judged to be non-existent because of a lack of certainty, then let it be understood that for such a person, everything is non-existent. (503) (PVA) [085,xii]

If the cognition of absence is not due to the absence of ascertainment but rather due to the absence of cognition, then there is no such thing as the "absence of cognition" anywhere, since in all cases the absence of ascertainment serves as the cause. Now, if in that case there exists a cause for cognition, then cognition is inferred from the presence of its efficient cause. If so, then cognition must also be the cause of ascertainment; therefore, the existence of that [ascertainment] should also be inferred. If it is argued that [ascertainment] is impaired by distraction, why is this not likewise accepted for cognition?

Now, one might ask: why does an unimpaired sense faculty (*indriya*) not produce cognition when its object is unobstructed? It is because the preceding cognition lacks the capacity to act as a producer; rather, it is the sense faculty *together with* the preceding cognition that possesses the power of production. If one asks how this is known, it is because [cognition arises] from sensory cognitions of pleasure and so forth. This will be demonstrated later when the occasion arises. Furthermore, it will be shown subsequently that the cognitions of pleasure, pain, and that which is neither, being sensory in nature, arise through the force of prior habituation (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, the sense faculty produces sensory cognition only in dependence upon a prior mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Consequently, even the very first consciousness does not arise from a sense faculty alone. Thus, it is established that every state of mind (*citta*) is necessarily preceded by another state of mind. Moreover:
[086,i] All sensory cognition arises from the power of cultivation;
because it has the nature of sensory cognition, it is like the nature of dream-consciousness. (PVA 504)

If the sense faculty were the cause, then in the absence of the sense faculty, there would be no cognition possessing the vivid form present before one. Yet such cognition does occur; therefore, since it exists even in its absence, the sense faculty is not its cause. Now, if it is argued that the [cognition in question] is erroneous, whereas non-erroneous cognition arises from the sense faculty itself—this is not so.
Even without complete knowledge, [cognition] arises from the sense faculty;
the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous [perception] is established by the presence or absence of the object.

For every sense organ possesses that form even without consciousness, just like a dream-consciousness. Now, if it is argued that the distinction is that what occurs without a sense organ is erroneous, while the other is otherwise, that is incorrect. For the possession of that form is indeed the very nature of consciousness, and since it is perceived even without a sense organ, the sense organ cannot be its cause. Furthermore, correspondence arises from the existence of the object; thus, it is produced by the object alone and not by the sense organ. Moreover, one thing cannot possess the capacity to produce the effect of another.

Now, if it is argued that the sense faculty exists even in dreams, and therefore the vivid appearance of the object present before one there is also produced by the sense faculty—thus, there is no deviation [from the rule that vividness is caused by the senses]—that too is not logical. Because:
[086, vi] due to habituation, the dream-faculty is a sense faculty, just like the waking sense faculty and others.
The non-difference of causes is established through the non-difference of the nature of their effects.
(PVA 506) By means of the non-distinction of the effect, the non-distinction of the cause is inferred.

Furthermore, there is no difference in the sensory faculty between the state of dreaming and other states. Therefore, since the sensory faculty itself does not arise without the repeated practice of its own kind, it is not the case that the first consciousness arises from the sensory faculty alone; rather, a preceding consciousness is the support for the subsequent consciousness.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let the mind be the support for the mind; even so, our desired conclusion is not established. If the mind is held to be the support for a mind belonging to this life alone, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since we accept that the mind has the minds of the mother and father as its support. If, however, it is held to be the support for a mind belonging to another world (*pāralaukika*), then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*), because it would also follow that the nature of the mother and father is being inherited.

To this it is replied: “Therefore, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) belongs only to that [person],” and so forth. There is no necessary conformity to the nature of the mother and father; for even when there is no change in them, a change is observed [in the offspring], and even when there is a change in them, a lack of change is observed. Moreover, if the offspring’s refinement were derived from theirs, then qualities such as scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) and the like would also [be present]. Just as a tree produced from a banyan tree possesses the nature of a banyan tree due to the nature of the parent tree, so too might the offspring possess the nature of the father or mother through the assistance of those who imparted refinement, such as teachers. But that is not so, because even when such refinement exists, [the offspring] is sometimes lacking in those qualities, and conversely, they exist even in its absence. Since we observe conformity to the refinement of one’s own preceding consciousness existing within one’s own continuum (*svasantāna*), and do not observe conformity to another continuum, if it is argued that the conformity to the teacher’s refinement is nevertheless perceived, we say: no. Because that [conformity] arises from a specific inclination (*abhiruci*) belonging to the preceding consciousness of one’s own continuum, and since it is not seen elsewhere in the absence of that, this [inclination] also arises from one’s own continuum through a causal succession. If it is argued that it arises with inclination as an auxiliary cause, let it be so; nevertheless, without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there can be no conformity to the refinement of another by means of that [inclination].
Without a future world, there would be no continuation of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
The conformity to the nature of the father is not contradictory for one who possesses a future world. (507) (PVA)
This might be so; [087,ii] however—

If it were necessarily only the conformity to the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) residing in one’s own continuum, how could there be conformity to the nature of the father? To this, the rebuttal is: because it would follow that everyone would conform to the nature of their father. [Objection: In that case, even according to the doctrine of the next world (*paraloka*), it would follow that everyone would not conform [to anything]. [Reply: No; because that specific nature was acquired from the previous world by him, just like conforming to the nature of a teacher. Now, just as many trees can arise from a single tree, so too many cognitions (*vijñāna*) can arise from a single cognition. Thus, it follows that the entire world has arisen from a single [source] through a succession of causes. To this, it has been said: because it would follow that [the child] would conform to the nature of the mother and so forth. [Objection: Then for the proponent of the next world, there would be conformity to the entirety of the previous nature. [Reply: No; because some may have fallen away due to confusion, or due to the suffering of remaining in the womb. However, for some, there is indeed conformity to the mental formations, as seen in the case of those who remember their past lives (*jātismara*). As for one who has arisen anew, there is no suffering; that very state is his, and nothing else. If he is the producer by way of being the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), then just as with his own body, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of remembering [events] even in another body related to the son. [Objection: If non-remembrance is due to suffering, that is incorrect.

At that very moment, for one born there, there is no suffering, like that of a poison-insect; however, for one who has passed to another world, that is suffering due to the cultivation of beginningless habituation. (PVA 508)

[087,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the field of giving as real, nor does he perceive the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat as real. He does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of Buddhahood as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive anything as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive anything as real while practicing the perfection of wisdom, how then does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, gives a gift. He does not perceive that gift as real, nor does he perceive the recipient as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Since he does not perceive these three things as real, he does not perceive the accumulation of merit as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of giving of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, having generated the thought of awakening, observes morality. He does not perceive that morality as real, nor does he perceive the person for whom he observes morality as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Since he does not perceive these three things as real, he does not perceive the accumulation of merit as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of morality of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, having generated the thought of awakening, practices patience. He does not perceive that patience as real, nor does he perceive the person toward whom he practices patience as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Since he does not perceive these three things as real, he does not perceive the accumulation of merit as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of patience of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, having generated the thought of awakening, exerts vigor. He does not perceive that vigor as real, nor does he perceive the basis for exerting vigor as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Since he does not perceive these three things as real, he does not perceive the accumulation of merit as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of vigor of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, having generated the thought of awakening, enters into meditative concentration. He does not perceive that meditative concentration as real, nor does he perceive the object of meditative concentration as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Since he does not perceive these three things as real, he does not perceive the accumulation of merit as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of meditation of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, having generated the thought of awakening, cultivates wisdom. He does not perceive that wisdom as real, nor does he perceive the object of wisdom as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Since he does not perceive these three things as real, he does not perceive the accumulation of merit as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real; if he does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; if he does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real; if he does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real; if he does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real; if he does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real; if he does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real; if he does not perceive the field of giving as real, nor does he perceive the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real; if he does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat as real; if he does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of Buddhahood as real—then, Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom train in the six perfections? How does he train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he train in the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom trains in the six perfections by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the knowledge of all modes by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, it is thus: a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom trains in all dharmas by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in all dharmas by way of non-apprehension, what is the distinction, what is the difference, and what is the superiority of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva over a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha perceives form as real, and so on, up to perceiving the knowledge of all modes as real. Subhūti, because they perceive these things as real, they do not transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They do not transcend suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation. Therefore,

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the child] experiencing the suffering of its parents. For example, just as one who has fallen asleep and entered another body experiences suffering in that dream-body; or as when a tree produced from a parent-tree is burned, the parent-tree does not experience it because the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the later tree do not exist in the earlier tree. If this were the case, [we reply: no, for in the present instance, the dream-body is seen within the previous body, and therefore there would simply be a memory of what was previously done. Moreover, in moisture-born beings (*saṃsvedaja*), intelligence would not exist due to the absence of a mother and so forth. Therefore, since the cognition of "I" and so on is observed even in moisture-born creatures in the absence of the cognition of a mother and so on, the cognition of a mother and so on is not the cause of it. Consequently, mental consciousness and the restlessness of the body and other faculties are produced solely by a preceding awareness arising within one's own continuum.

[087,v] But surely one's own continuum is nothing other than the bodies of one's mother and so forth, since a continuity of the body is observed. And consciousness, as well as fickleness and the like, are non-different from that [body]. Therefore, if you seek to prove such a continuity, you are merely proving what is already established.

Now, if the body related to the father and so forth is distinct, then the same would apply to the body in the next world; thus, there would be no continuity between them. Furthermore, since the father and others possess that very same nature of fickleness and so on during the stages of childhood and so forth, there is a continuity within that [same] stream.

That too is incorrect, because one does not observe the conformity to the nature of the mother and so forth by means of either the mind or the body. If it is argued that he is not his father, we say no, because it is observed. Nor is a distinction in that [nature] observed without its own repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, it is precisely his own repeated practice that is inferred. Even though there is non-difference [of the continuum], and even though the mind is a transformation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is still the inference of the great elements of the previous and subsequent worlds. Furthermore, non-difference is not logical; for:
Just as the cultivation (*saṃskāra*) of what was heard and so forth is produced in each successive moment of consciousness.
Because it is manifested in time without distinction, the quality [of the self] may likewise exist even within the body. || 80 ||

[087,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form. He does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. Why is that? Subhūti, form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form. Form itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than consciousness. Consciousness itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is consciousness. [087,x] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form—if form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form—and if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than consciousness—if consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness—then, Blessed One, how can there be the designation of ‘sentient beings,’ ‘beings,’ ‘souls,’ ‘persons,’ ‘individuals,’ ‘human beings,’ or ‘humans’? [087,xi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because of the false conceptualization of dharmas that there is the designation of ‘sentient beings,’ ‘beings,’ ‘souls,’ ‘persons,’ ‘individuals,’ ‘human beings,’ or ‘humans. Subhūti, those dharmas do not exist, nor are they apprehended, by which one could designate them as ‘sentient beings,’ ‘beings,’ ‘souls,’ ‘persons,’ ‘individuals,’ ‘human beings,’ or ‘humans. [087,xii] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; if he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if he does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; if he does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness; if he does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if he does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements; if he does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive aging and death; if he does not perceive the conditioned co-arising of suffering, nor does he perceive the unconditioned co-arising of suffering; if he does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship; if he does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the fruit of a buddha; if he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all modes—then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment? [087,xiii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; because he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; because he does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; because he does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness; because he does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; because he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; because he does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements; because he does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive aging and death; because he does not perceive the conditioned co-arising of suffering, nor does he perceive the unconditioned co-arising of suffering; because he does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship; because he does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the fruit of a buddha; because he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all modes—it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment. [087,xiv] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; if he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if he does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects; if he does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness; if he does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if he does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements; if he does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive aging and death; if he does not perceive the conditioned co-arising of suffering, nor does he perceive the unconditioned co-arising of suffering; if he does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship; if he does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the fruit of a buddha; if he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all modes—then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give gifts? How does he guard morality? How does he cultivate patience? How does he exert vigor? How does he practice meditation? And how does he cultivate wisdom? [087,xv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he gives a gift without perceiving a gift, without perceiving a recipient, and without perceiving a giver. He guards morality without perceiving morality, without perceiving transgression, and without perceiving one who guards morality. He cultivates patience without perceiving patience, without perceiving anger, and without perceiving one who cultivates patience. He exerts vigor without perceiving vigor, without perceiving laziness, and without perceiving one who exerts vigor. He practices meditation without perceiving meditation, without perceiving distraction, and without perceiving one who practices meditation. He cultivates wisdom without perceiving wisdom, without perceiving ignorance, and without perceiving one who cultivates wisdom. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.”

For a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) such as the wholesome (*śubha*) is preceded by practice that is self-cognized; though unmanifest during the state of sleep, it is manifested at the time of the waking state. Likewise, [mental qualities] though unmanifest in the body, are perceived as if they were in the mind due to their non-difference [from it]. Just as qualities of the body, such as leanness and so forth, are perceived by another, why is there not likewise a perception of the qualities of the mind, such as artistic skill and the like? For that which is perceived as being included within [the category of] form (*rūpa*) does not otherwise exist. If it is argued that because [mental qualities] consist of a specific internal tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), they are not perceived by another—[we reply: No, for even external tangibles, such as a wound (*vraṇa*), are not perceived [by another]. For the rough touch of wind associated with a wound is not perceived by another through that [wound]. If it is argued that this is simply the power of the wound itself, then is it perceived differently from how it is perceived by the perceiver [of the wound]? If that were the case, the consequence would be that it is an error (*bhrāntatva*). If it is argued that it is a specific touch belonging to the wound itself, then it follows that the wind would be the perceiver [of the wound’s touch]. And if that were so, the sensation of pain would not belong to the one who has the wound. Or, if it is argued that the touch of the wound being struck by the wind is perceived by that [wind] itself, then the touch of the wound should also be perceived by another. It is not logical to say that what is being touched by another is not perceived, because: [The opponent continues: It is not the case that what is being touched by another is not perceived. Why? Because... [text fragment ends].
If that form which is being seen is not felt when it is touched, then how could that very same thing be known when there is the cognition of another form? (509) (PVA)

[088,ii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. "Monks, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would name-and-form become constituted therein? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "If, after having descended into the mother's womb, consciousness were to depart, would name-and-form come to birth in this world? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "If the consciousness of a young boy or girl, who is growing and developing, were to be cut off, would name-and-form grow and develop? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, monks, it is to be understood by you: 'Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. "What do you think, monks? Is form permanent or impermanent? "Impermanent, Blessed One. "But what is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness? "Suffering, Blessed One. "But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? "Certainly not, Blessed One. [And so on for feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. "Therefore, monks, whatever is form—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that form is to be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever is feeling... perception... formations... consciousness—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all that consciousness is to be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing it thus, as it really is, with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated. One understands: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One in brief is deep and its expression is profound. It is difficult for me to explain it in detail. But if you would allow, friends, let us go to the Venerable Sāriputta and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Venerable Sāriputta explains it to us, so we shall bear it in mind. "Yes, friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda and the group of monks went to the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta: "Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling while speaking in brief on this very matter. Not long after the Blessed One had departed, I addressed the monks... [Ānanda repeats the entire discourse up to the point of entering his dwelling]. "...Therefore, friend Sāriputta, let us go to the Venerable Sāriputta and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Venerable Sāriputta explains it to us, so we shall bear it in mind. "Friend Ānanda, it is well said. Friend Ānanda, it is well said. For the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One in brief is deep and its expression is profound. It is difficult to explain in detail. Yet, friend Ānanda, I shall explain the meaning of this to you as I have heard and mastered it from the Blessed One. Listen, and pay close attention; I shall speak. "Yes, friend," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this: "Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One said: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence,' he said this having in mind the four nutriments. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. When the Blessed One said: 'If consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb... he said this having in mind the nutriment of consciousness. For, friend Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, name-and-form would not become constituted therein. If, after having descended into the mother's womb, consciousness were to depart, name-and-form would not come to birth in this world. If the consciousness of a young boy or girl, who is growing and developing, were to be cut off, name-and-form would not grow and develop. Therefore, friend Ānanda, it is to be understood by you: 'Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form. When the Blessed One said: 'What do you think, monks? Is form permanent or impermanent? and so forth, he said this having in mind the nutriment of contact. For, friend Ānanda, if contact were not to exist, feeling would not arise. Indeed, it is not logical that its form (rūpa) should remain unknown to one whose sense faculties are unimpaired; and thus, it is simply self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). For that which is not self-cognized would be distinct from it [in nature]. Therefore, suffering, pleasure, and the passions (*rāga* etc. must be self-cognition itself; thus, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is other than the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Consequently, it is not logical for self-cognition to have a relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) with the body. If so, how is it that one says, "I have a sensation in my foot" or "I have a sensation in my hand"? It is because at the time when the hand undergoes modification, [the sensation] is absent [from the foot], and thus it occurs in this way, not otherwise. Such designations arise because [the sensation] is concomitant with the modifications of the hands and so forth. To explain:
Due to the mere nature of self-cognition, there is no established relation of container and contained;
for one who is immersed in his own essential nature, there is no conceptualization of a substrate or the like. (PVA 510)

For if there is cognition of the mere intrinsic nature (svarūpa), how could the conceptualization of a locus and its content be possible? Such would occur only upon the apprehension of both. And even in that case, if there were an apprehension of non-duality, then that very thing would simply be non-dual.

Alternatively, such conceptual construction arises due to the restriction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). In that case, that conceptual construction is not distinct from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because it culminates in its own essential nature alone. Even if it consists of great elements produced by the power of latent impressions, there is no fault.
[Furthermore, there is the assumption of rebirth.

Therefore, since the intellect is distinct from the body, it is not born of the mother and father. If it exists as something belonging to its own continuum from the very beginning, then the birth of a living being does not arise from the mere great elements (*mahābhūta*) alone; rather, there is an arrival from another life into the location of the womb and so forth. Consequently, proceeding to an impure place would be illogical, for it is not fitting for one who possesses discernment to act in such a manner. Nor is the impelling by a Creator (*īśvara*) accepted. To this, it is said:
The assumption of a lowly state by one who cannot be led by any other being...
For one who possesses self-attachment, [this occurs] through the desire to abandon suffering and obtain happiness. (81)
In suffering, the distorted mind and craving are the causes of bondage;
he in whom these two do not exist does not undergo rebirth. (82)

This has been stated provided that one is discerning (*prekṣāvān*). If the self-nature (*svarūpa*) were to move by itself, then nothing would ever proceed anywhere toward a village or the like to be reached; consequently, because it would be primordially quiescent (*ādiśāntatvāt*), saṃsāra itself would not exist. Alternatively, if proceeding to a village or the like occurs somehow through a lack of discernment, then proceeding to the location of the womb and so forth would likewise occur. For one who is impelled by self-attachment (*ātmasneha*), even an inferior thing becomes something to be grasped due to cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*). Such is the power of karma (*karmaśakti*) that for one who is led by other beings, as if dependent on others, there is such a movement. Even the occupation of an inferior station occurs through the desire to obtain pleasure and avoid pain, just as a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*) enters the house of a maidservant.

[089,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be learned by you, Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the reason why, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so for the sake of the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has fully awakened to all phenomena as they truly are; he has destroyed the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of the afflictions, and the Māra of death; he has transcended all worldly dharmas; he has attained the supreme state of peace; he has set in motion the wheel of the Dharma that cannot be turned back by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world; and he teaches the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, revealing the holy life that is perfectly complete and pure. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Moreover, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has realized the four bases of psychic power; he has cultivated the five faculties; he has fulfilled the five powers; he has practiced the seven factors of enlightenment; he has realized the noble eightfold path; he has mastered the three knowledges; he has perfected the six superknowledges; and he has attained the great compassion. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma without attachment, free from grasping, unattached to the world, and having abandoned all clinging. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Moreover, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that leads to the cessation of suffering, the destruction of the taints, and the attainment of nirvāṇa. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that is not shared by any ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, and which is not to be overturned. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Moreover, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that is well-expounded, leading to liberation, conducive to calming, and resulting in the realization of nirvāṇa. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Moreover, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that is not dependent on others, that is self-evident, and that is to be realized within oneself. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that is the finality of the holy life, the ultimate goal, and the unsurpassed refuge. Therefore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, the gods of the earth tremble, the gods of the sky rejoice, the gods of the Yāma realm praise it, the gods of the Tuṣita realm are delighted, the gods of the Nirmāṇarati realm are uplifted, the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm are enraptured, and the Brahmā gods are filled with awe. “Moreover, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he does so because he has taught the Dharma that is the cessation of birth, the end of old age, the destruction of death, the overcoming of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
