Now, why does this [being] lack being impelled by a Lord (*īśvara*)? Because it is possible for one who is deluded to act entirely on his own, the postulation of a Lord is not tenable. Furthermore, no such impulsion by a Lord is perceived. And how there is no need to postulate a Lord has already been demonstrated. Indeed, self-attachment (*ātmasneha*) itself is the "Lord," since it is perceived as that which impels him. If it is argued that just as a servant or the like is impelled by another, so too is one impelled in the next world, we say: no, because there is no such rule. Only one who possesses craving for the self is impelled, not everyone. Moreover, even he is impelled only when possessed of craving, and not by someone else who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). If it is argued that he is the impeller because one attains a particular state of rebirth (*gati*) through propitiating him, then it would follow that all founders of religious systems (*tīrthakara*) are Lords. Therefore, it is only one whose mind is perverted who proceeds toward a womb or elsewhere, even though it is suffering, by means of the notion that it is pleasure. Consequently, birth arises from perverted cognition and craving; for one who lacks these two, there is no birth. A Lord is not capable of granting birth to such a person. Nor is this a position accepted even by the proponents of a Lord (*īśvaravādin*).

[089,ii] But surely, for one who lacks the karma that brings about health, a physician is of no use; and for one whose karma is unimpaired and brings about health, the physicians are likewise useless because they are either incapable or unable to act—this being the case, is this not a fault? [089,iii] This is not a fault.
Is the physician’s effort ever in vain, and likewise, is he truly powerless?
If that same [powerlessness] were desired even of God, then he would not be God.

Indeed, it is not the case that the proponents of a creator god (īśvaravādin) accept that some transmigrating being is impelled by God while another is not; rather, they maintain that even the propitiation of Him is useful for attaining a state of rebirth. If that were so, then the propitiation of a donor would also be useful. And since this is true for all founders of religious systems (tīrthakara), what distinction is there between a "God" and a "non-God"? Therefore, ignorance (avidyā) and craving (tṛṣṇā) alone possess the capacity for rebirth, not God.

〈The Body of the Intermediate State〉—If, then, going and coming are with respect to another birth, it follows that those two should be perceived; yet since they are not so perceived, they must simply be non-existent. To this he says:
"If going and coming are not seen, it is because of the lack of proficiency of the sense faculties. [089, vi]
It is like the failure to see thin smoke by one with weak eyesight. 83.

[089,vii] Even though coming and going are not perceived, nevertheless they are not non-existent. Their non-perception is due to the lack of acuity in the sense faculties, not because of their actual absence. For it is not the case that only what is non-existent is unperceived; for example, thin smoke is not an object of perception for one with weak vision, yet it certainly exists.
[089,viii]
For the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not perceived because of its translucence; it is neither non-existent, since it is not seen even when exiting or entering [the womb].

For the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), having arisen through the power of karma by virtue of its translucence, is accessible only to yogins. Like a dream-body, it is not perceived; yet its non-existence does not follow from that alone. If it is argued that it is a false dream-body, we reply: no, because it has been established that it performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*). For this very reason:
"However, due to its subtlety (*tanutva*), even though it possesses form, it is incapable in some respects and in certain places."
Or else, like water in a mirage or gold in dross, it is simply non-existent because it is not perceived. || 84 ||

[089,xi] Just like a dream-body, it is characterized by incapacity because it possesses form; yet even though it possesses form, it is incapable in certain respects, as water is in a jar and the like, or as light is in crystal and the like, or as mercury is in gold. Alternatively, just as water is in mercury, it is not perceived even while existing in gold. Or rather, due to its invisibility, the intermediate state body (*antarābhava-śarīra*) is simply non-existent. For instance:
Because of the similarity between the continuum of rice grains, the arising of an uninterrupted existence is postulated;
that which exists here between the state of death and the state of rebirth is called the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

[090,i] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchants being pursued by the yakṣa Śūraprabha, who was intent on devouring them. Seeing this, he manifested himself as a great mountain and stood before the yakṣa. Then the yakṣa Śūraprabha, seeing that great mountain, became terrified and fled. Having escaped from the presence of the yakṣa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara reassured those five hundred merchants, saying: "Do not fear; I shall protect you all. Having comforted them, he led them out of the perilous place and established them in safety. Thus, O Śāriputra, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is remembered, one is delivered from all fear and calamity. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always remember the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. This is the second chapter, titled "The Deliverance from Fear."

But it is not so in this case, because [the object] arises from a different place and time that are spatially and temporally remote. For instance, someone perceives an uninterrupted journey to Kanyakubja and so forth through traveling to a village and the like; another, while remaining right here, perceives himself at a different location all at once in a dream. It is the same with regard to the destination of motion; thus there is no distinction. Nor can it be argued that the dream is unreal, for if that were so, this [proposed] probandum would also have to be unreal. It is not observed that a corroborative example must possess every similarity. The reality of a future birth may arise from the strength of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), but that is not the case for a dream, because such strength is absent.
If the unreality of a dream is due to the attainment of another appearance, then surely it must be held that the unreality of other births is likewise due to that same reason. (PVA 513)

[090,iii] If it is argued that because there exists another appearance characterized by waking cognition, the unreality of the dream is established while the reality of the waking cognition is its opposite— since the dream-cognition possesses the characteristic of being a different appearance— then there is indeed no distinction regarding their status as erroneous cognitions. If it is further argued that there is a distinction because, in a dream, objects such as jars are perceived quite suddenly, even in the absence of their causes, and therefore there is a difference [between waking and dreaming], [090,iv]
Even for one who is awake, jars and other objects are perceived all of a sudden;
likewise, in dreams, carts and other things are seen when the necessary causal conditions are present.

Even in the waking state, mountains and other objects created by a yogi suddenly come within the range of perception. If it is argued that these objects already existed and were merely perceived earlier, then the specific act of wandering is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in that case; but that is untrue.
For even in a dream, who can deny the prior existence of those things?
If it is argued that [the absence of fire is established] by the non-perception of another [instance], then that [non-perception] is equally present in the case of mountains and so forth.

If mountains and such things already existing are perceived somewhere by one who is awake, why is it not likewise admitted that they are so perceived by one established in the state of dreaming? If it is argued that they do not exist because they are not perceived by another person who is awake, then [we reply] that there is likewise a non-perception of those things perceived while awake by one who has gone into a dream. And just as their perception arises from the causal complex of wandering, so too does the perception of jars and other objects arise suddenly due to the occurrence of another state, namely, the dream. If it is asked how there can be the notion "this is the waking state" or the production of a waking cognition, [the answer follows].
But surely, is there not at times the cognition of being awake even in a dream?
Since all activities such as the opening of the eyes occur there as well, the two cases are equal.

For instance, even in a dream there exists the cognition, "I am awake; I have awakened," as well as [the experience of] going and so forth. Therefore, how can that too be a dream? If you say it is because of its unreality, then it would follow that the state regarded as waking is likewise unreal. For the mutual non-perception of both states is equal.

Now, if it is argued that the unreality of the dream is established because of the cognition "this is unreal," then let the waking cognition also be unreal, since it is similar to that. For reality does not derive from that very cognition; rather, reality exists by virtue of its own defining characteristic. Furthermore, what does even the cognition "it is unreal" take as its objective support? Is it something other than the real, or is it itself real? This is not a negation of that [object].
Because it is perceived as having that form, both [propositions] are utterly untenable.

(PVA 517) Indeed, it is not logical to say that something which is being perceived precisely as having that form is "other than that," nor is it logical to say that it is "not that. For its being other than that consists precisely in its having a form other than that; otherwise, even that [original thing] would become other than itself. Furthermore, it is not the case that what is being perceived simply does not exist, for that would entail the absurd consequence that everything is likewise non-existent. Now, if this cognition arises, let it arise; however, the claim that it has no objective support (*ālambana*) is merely pointless, and one cannot establish the existence of entities based on such a [cognition].
[090,xiii] But surely, since there is no jar or the like at all in the perception of a dream, this cognition is firm and non-contradictory; so how can it be false? To explain:
For one who has just awakened from bathing, there is an instantaneous appearance of not having bathed;
because it corresponds exactly with that [subsequent state], the cognition is non-erroneous.
That is incorrect; for:
[091,ii] The state of passion ceases instantly, just like what is seen in a dream.

And there is no contradiction in that case, because this [experience] is perceived in a dream as well. (519) This distinction between what is a dream and what is other than a dream is not established even now;
for if it were established through the very fact of non-contradiction with the probandum, there would be a circular argument. (520)
Furthermore:
"This does not exist" is not cognized by any other means of cognition;
this is merely a cognition itself, which is its unique characteristic.

These cognitions arise for those engaged in worldly activity due to the existence of such beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). By what specific distinction is this so? It is because there is no perception by one who identifies with the waking self immediately following that [dream state]. Even the identification with the waking state arises solely through the power of latent impressions upon the abandonment of the fallen body; this too is merely conventional and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since even in a dream there is a cognition of "waking. Now, if it is argued that for those in a dream there is no cognition that "there is no waking perception," that itself constitutes bondage.

Their non-existence has been established by those [opponents] through [the failure of] practical application; yet, for them, the occurrence of such things as unimpeded movement and so forth is indeed possible. (522) (PVA) [091,viii]

Since the occurrence of movement and so forth without obstruction is itself possible, non-existence is already understood through action alone; what need is there for another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to establish it? For a conceptual construction establishes even that which is real as being unreal; otherwise, because they would be mutually contradictory, it could not be a conceptual construction. Therefore, the conceit of unreality arises from immediate disappearance, and because of the absence of continuity with the waking state regarding things seen in a dream. Yet, by that much alone, those [dream-objects] are not unreal. Thus, although going and coming are not seen in the case of dream-objects by another [person], they nonetheless exist; therefore, the non-perception [of them by others] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Consequently, it has been established that there is neither an absolute absence nor an absolute presence of going and coming.
(a) Refutation of the Whole (avayavinirāsaḥ):

Moreover, if cognition were non-different from the body, and the body were merely an aggregate of atoms, then it would follow that there must be a cognition of every single atom. Alternatively, if a single gross composite whole (*avayavin*) is perceived as such, even so, because that [whole] resides within the atoms and is in contact with the atoms, there would be a perception of the atoms themselves. If it is argued that cognition arises from those [atoms] but does not reside within them, then how can one understand the meaning of "from them"? Self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is not cognition of another. If it is claimed that there is only cognition of another and no self-cognition, then how is pleasure experienced? Since that [pleasure] would be experienced only as something other [than the cognizer], it is untenable.
If there is a cognition of something that has become other, what else could that cognition be?
That alone is cognition where the determination "this is cognition" resides. (PVA 523)

[091,xi] Since pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, are experienced only as distinct entities, what else is there that acts as the knower? If it is argued that the body itself is the knower, [091,xii] that is not the case.
Without pleasure and so forth, as well as blue and so forth, what is even the body considered to be?
For, by virtue of its being an object of perception, it lacks the status of a perceiver.
(524) (PVA) If it is argued that the eye and other [senses] possess such a nature [of being perceivers], why is a donkey's horn not likewise [considered a perceiver]?
If it is argued that "it is of the nature of a potency (*śakti*)," then how can it be so when there is no perception [of it]?

(PVA 525) Indeed, the eye and other [faculties], being unperceived, are not perceivers, just like a donkey's horn. Since the eye and others exist in the form of potencies, they are therefore not of the nature of non-existence. But from what [source] is it known that even a potency exists when it is unperceived? If it is argued that its perception occurs by way of its effect, then what is their effect? For perception consists in the form of pleasure and so forth.

[091,xv] But surely that [potentiality] also, being a potentiality, is simply not perceived. By the principle of elimination, they must be the forms and so forth themselves. And these are not the effects of the power of consciousness; for if they were the effects of the eye and other [senses], it would follow that they did not exist previously. If you argue that the "effect" is the state of being perceived, then it would follow that every single atom would be perceived. Furthermore, there can be no difference in state when there is no difference in the entity itself. If there were a difference, it would follow that there is self-awareness [of that difference]. If you say that the difference consists precisely in arising together with the potentiality, this is not tenable. Why? [091,xvi]
In the field of literary theory, it is held that the cognition of a word’s power arises from inference;
yet how can this view avoid the fault of mutual dependence?

For the specific characteristic of form and the other [sensory objects] is their state of being perceived. If that perception consists in being accompanied by a capacity for perception, how can there be a proof of accompaniment without a proof of the capacity? If that is not proven, how can there be an inference of the capacity? Therefore, consciousness is simply the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of form and so forth, and of pleasure and so forth; this is because the cognition arises through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "consciousness is pleasure" and so on.
And coreferentiality occurs through the distinction between primary and secondary [application].

"The person is not the staff; likewise, the person is conscious. (PVA 527) If it is argued that this is a non-primary usage, as in "the beds cry out" or "the person is the staff," then that is simply unestablished in this case. This is because, among form and the other [sensory objects], there is no possibility of perceiving a consciousness distinct from form. If it is claimed that this is inferred by means of this very example, we say no, because such an inference is impossible. For the Sāṃkhyas accept a primary grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the sense that "the person is conscious. Therefore, a thing must be accepted exactly as its cognition apprehends it.
Furthermore, through habituation, the stationing of feeling upon form and so forth occurs in such a manner;
it exists by way of transitioning from one form and so forth to another. (528) (PVA)

[092,v] Indeed, consciousness does not mix with anything else apart from its objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, that which is mixed with pleasure and so forth mixes with form and so forth; that which has become mixed with form and so forth mixes with the pleasure and so forth of others. Through practice, by grasping the signs in all their aspects, there arises a cognition of all those aspects. How then could the pleasure, form, and so forth of another be apprehended as remaining in their original state? That is incorrect. [092,vi]
In the case of consciousness regarding its own nature, there is neither "standing on the bank" nor "not standing on the bank.
This distinction is merely a matter of conventional usage, depending solely upon the basis [of the object].

For regarding form, pleasure, and so forth, there is no mode of cognition other than the self-awareness of their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Consequently, how could there be a distinction such as "this is external" or "otherwise"? There is merely a conventional distinction made in relation to the body as a support, such that "this is external" or "otherwise.
[092, viii] But surely, without dependence [on something else], there can be no awareness of that nature.
And for the cognition of that form, there is no dependence on anything else.
(PVA 530) This is true; therefore, this distinction does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
However, this distinction belongs to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); for the conventional cannot withstand critical analysis. (PVA 531)

This indeed is what is called conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*): that which, when analyzed, falls apart; otherwise, it would be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, just as consciousness—which possesses the capacity for transition—exists through identity (*tādātmya*) in the bodies of others with respect to form and so forth, so too does it exist in the body of another’s semen and blood. Consequently, there is no separate "power" (*śakti*) consisting of the nature of consciousness from which the substratum of consciousness could possess activity. It is simply this very consciousness itself, existing in such a state, which is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). [Objection: But how is it that, when consciousness has transitioned through identity, pillars and the like do not move? For if they did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of their own bodies also moving. [Response: That too is incorrect.
Motion is not possible through mere identity or origination;
rather, it arises from the production of a specific nature consisting in the cognition of touch. (PVA 532)

Indeed, when tactile consciousness arises having the nature of volitional consciousness, then movement of the body and so forth arises, and not otherwise. Therefore, consciousness must have the very nature of form and the other [sensory objects]. Consequently, it would follow that there is sensation for every single atom.

Why does it not happen in this way for you as well? Because another consciousness arises having that form. For me too, it is the whole (*avayavin*) that consists of the nature of consciousness, not the atoms (*paramāṇu*). That too is incorrect, because the atoms would also have to attain that same form. If it is argued that "the atoms are indeed distinct entities," no; it follows then that they do not exist at all. For instance:
the body’s existence as atoms is established by its own nature.
The body is established as having the nature of atoms.

(PVA 533) Now, if the atoms of the body do not have consciousness as their nature, then in that case, the atoms do not have the body as their nature. And since they are not perceived, they do not have the object as their nature; thus, atoms do not exist. Therefore, there is only the whole (*avayavin*); and of that—

[093,ii] If the hand and so forth were to move, everything would necessarily move; since a single action is impossible for [all parts], otherwise there would be separate existence [of each part]. (85)
If one [atom] were obstructed, all would be obstructed; if one were unobstructed, all would be unobstructed.
Furthermore, if one were colored, all would appear colored, or else there would be the possibility of the uncolored being perceived. (86)

[093,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is established as a real entity, nor does he perceive any dharma that is not established as a real entity. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are unestablished; they are neither established nor non-established. Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to train in all dharmas as being unestablished should train in this very perfection of wisdom. 124. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva train in this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because form is neither established nor unestablished. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the eye as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the eye is neither established nor unestablished. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive forms as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. He does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because forms are neither established nor unestablished. Sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive eye-consciousness as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because eye-consciousness is neither established nor unestablished. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive eye-contact as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because eye-contact is neither established nor unestablished. Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. Why is that? Because the sensation born of eye-contact is neither established nor unestablished. The sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact is neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the element of earth as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the element of earth is neither established nor unestablished. The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the realm of desire as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the realm of desire is neither established nor unestablished. The realm of form and the formless realm are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive ignorance as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because ignorance is neither established nor unestablished. Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of giving as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the perfection of giving is neither established nor unestablished. The perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the emptiness of the internal is neither established nor unestablished. The emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, and the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the power of recollection as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the power of discernment of phenomena, the power of diligence, the power of joy, the power of tranquility, the power of concentration, or the power of equanimity as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the power of recollection is neither established nor unestablished. The power of discernment of phenomena, the power of diligence, the power of joy, the power of tranquility, the power of concentration, and the power of equanimity are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the foundation of mindfulness on the body as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive the foundations of mindfulness on feelings, mind, or phenomena as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because the foundation of mindfulness on the body is neither established nor unestablished. The foundations of mindfulness on feelings, mind, and phenomena are neither established nor unestablished. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive right effort as established, nor does he perceive it as unestablished. He does not perceive right mindfulness, right concentration, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, or right mindfulness as established, nor does he perceive them as unestablished. Why is that? Because right effort is neither established nor unestablished. Right mindfulness, right concentration,

A substance (*dravya*), by definition, is that which has the form of a whole (*avayavin*), possesses action and qualities, and is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for conjunction and so forth. If it were devoid of action, then because it is the inherent cause of all its parts, it would follow that everything moves. If the whole is variegated, consisting of both moving and non-moving parts, then it follows that a single whole—such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta—would simultaneously possess the forms of both moving and non-moving. Now, if you argue that since unity and the state of being both moving and non-moving are observed, what contradiction is there? What is this so-called "unity"? If it is the non-difference of appearance, that does not exist [in this case]. If it is the performance of a single effect, then even if the effect is one, why must the cause be one? For if the whole is obscured, it follows that everything should be obscured, since there is no distinction in the conjunction [of the whole with the obscuring object]. If the whole is not perceived when a part is obscured, then either everything should be visible or nothing at all should be seen. If you claim that even in the case of unity, everything cannot be seen [simultaneously], how can there be unity between what is seen and what is unseen? This same logical consequence applies even in the case of the experience of color (*rāga*).
[093,v] Therefore, there is no single composite entity; even if there were multiplicity, it would be as before.
If it is argued that motion is not established because there is no distinction [between atoms] and because they are atomic in size, then [the objection] is not proven.
There is no distinction; therefore, because they possess the status of sense-faculties among those that are distinguished, they are not minute.

If the body were manifold, then even in that case of multiplicity, the same fault as before would apply: there would be the consequence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) for every single atom. If it is argued that there is no movement [of the whole] because there is no distinction [between the atoms], this is not so; for the very absence of distinction is not established. Since they are perceived during the state of awareness, there is therefore no non-perceived distinction. For this very reason, even atomicity (*aṇutva*) does not act as an obstacle during the state of self-awareness; thus, although it exists, because it is indistinguishable from what is non-existent, it is not atomic. If it is asked, "How then is a distinction perceived by you?", [the answer is: No; the perception of the object occurs through the nature of self-awareness, but it is actually the perception of the consciousness (*vijñāna*) bearing that form. If it is asked, "Why is the perception of the object not itself the form of the atoms?", this will be explained later.

[Objection: But how can there be such things as obstruction and resistance for that which is merely an atom? For atoms lack the absence of obstruction and so forth. [Response: Indeed. How could there be obstruction, resistance, and the like for a mere atom?
By this, the non-existence of obstructions and so forth is also refuted. (88)

Or how is it that mercury, gold, and other such substances, when mixed with heated stones and the like, become visible? And how is there a perception of things that are individually incapable of being perceived by the senses and so forth? (89)
If it is argued that [the substance] exists because of conjunction, then the same consequence applies here to gold and the thread.
If it is argued that the conjunction is perceptible, then how can there be cognition of it when its substrata are imperceptible? (90)
Furthermore, the connection with taste, form, and so forth would be contradictory if [the word] were used figuratively;
if it is accepted [as primary], then how could there be distinctions in cognition such as "a row" or "long"? (91)
Likewise, the nature of number, conjunction, action, and so forth does not appear in cognition as distinct from its own form and from verbal expression. (92)

[094,ii] It is not tenable to ask how there can be obstruction for atoms due to their lack of contact, for nowhere has an obstruction been observed that is dependent upon a composite whole (*avayavin*). If that were absent, then [obstruction] such as resistance would likewise not exist in the case of atoms. Now, it might be argued as follows:
If cloth and such things were merely an aggregation of atoms held together by their density,
how could there be any obstruction of sunlight or water?

Without a whole (*avayavin*), how could mere atoms—whose mutual interpenetration remains unimpeded—be subject to obscuration? To this it is replied: if they are incapable [of producing a whole], how can even the category of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) be produced? And how do those [atoms] in conjunction produce a whole? For conjunction cannot occur through a single part, since such parts do not exist; nor can it occur through the entire self-nature, for that would entail the consequence of a mass consisting of nothing but atoms. If you say that conjunction produces a distinct category [the whole] itself, then we ask: how do those [atoms] with intervals between them produce that very conjunction? The same logical consequence applies. If you say it is "conjunction" [itself that is produced], then what need is there for another conjunction? The same applies to the whole. Alternatively, if those [atoms] with intervals between them produce both conjunction and the whole, then why do they not likewise produce effects such as obscuration?
Even without the conjunction of atoms, there exists a further aggregation; that which possesses no separate existence even when struck does not exist at all. (535) (PVA)

Just as hairs, mosquitoes, flies, and the like, even when situated at intervals, produce a cognition of a single solid mass, why do they not likewise produce other effects? If it is argued that this is so because a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is perceived there, then here too the cognition of a yogi who perceives the supersensible would be the subverting factor—if such a yogi existed. Furthermore, just as water does not leak from a flawless cup when it is covered on top, so it is with the collection of atoms. Alternatively, how could the union of mercury and gold, in the absence of a composite whole (*avayavin*), possess the capacity for obstruction, resistance, and so forth? Or consider heated stones and the like: "spreading" and so on are indeed other effects produced by a specific cause characterized by a particular configuration (*saṃhati*). The relationship between cause and effect is inconceivable; for instance, although color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities are individually incapable of producing consciousness, they nevertheless produce it when in a state of combination. If it is argued that this is due to "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), then since conjunction itself is an effect, how can [the atoms] produce that very thing? Moreover, conjunction is not perceptible, because there is no movement of that which has an unperceived substratum. If there were movement even of that which has an unperceived substratum, then the established doctrine—that perception arises from the contact of sense-faculty and object—would be undermined. Furthermore, contact is precisely conjunction; thus, because it would be the cause of conjunction, the definition of a quality (*guṇa*)—"that which is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions"—would be lost. If it is argued that [conjunction] is perceived because it inheres in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetatvāt*), then in that case, if the conjunction of atoms exists, there would have to be movement of the atoms; thus, the postulation of a composite whole is useless. Or else, there would have to be movement of all conjunctions, and consequently, there would be no non-perception from a distance. If it is argued that there is simply no conjunction of the sense-faculty with them, then there would likewise be no movement of gross objects either. If it is maintained that there is also a conjunction produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*), then the rule "not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions" is merely a prohibition against its being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). This is not so, because inherence is the basis for the notion of "here" (*iha*) in those cases. When a conjunction is perceived, the cognition "here" necessarily arises; therefore, it follows that it must also be an inherent cause. Moreover: [The text continues with further arguments regarding the nature of conjunction, the necessity of a composite whole, and the critique of atomism.]
If conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) were the cause of perception, then there would be the perception of a substance even when there is only conjunction among atoms. (536) (PVA)

[094, viii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What, monks, is physical food as gross nutriment? It is that which is called ‘food, food’ in the world. This, monks, is what is called physical food as gross nutriment. What, monks, is contact as nutriment? Whatever contact there is, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant; this, monks, is what is called contact as nutriment. What, monks, is mental volition as nutriment? Whatever mental volition there is, whether directed toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; this, monks, is what is called mental volition as nutriment. What, monks, is consciousness as nutriment? Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—this, monks, is what is called consciousness as nutriment. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Furthermore, monks, it is by means of these four nutriments that beings who have already come to be are maintained, and those seeking a new existence are supported. Moreover, monks, when one understands the nutriment, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, one is said to understand suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. What, monks, is the nutriment? It is these four nutriments. What, monks, is the origin of nutriment? It is craving, which gives rise to renewed existence, is bound up with delight and lust, finding delight here and there; this, monks, is the origin of nutriment. What, monks, is the cessation of nutriment? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, the relinquishing of it, the renunciation of it, the liberation from it, and the detachment from it; this, monks, is the cessation of nutriment. What, monks, is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this, monks, is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment. Thus, monks, when one understands nutriment, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, one is said to understand suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. [094, viii]

If conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) were also a cause of perception, then conjunction with an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) would be useless, since the perception of an effect-substance occurs through the conjunction of atoms alone. Alternatively, if one claims that the conjunction of atoms is not postulated when an effect-substance exists, then the perception of jars and the like arises from the conjunction of atoms alone; thus, the postulation of parts (*avayavin*) is useless—this is the very same fault. Or, if there is no whole, the postulation of the conjunction of atoms cannot be otherwise [justified]. The same applies to the reverse case as well. Furthermore, there is no conjunction of atoms in the conjunction of the whole, because there is no spatial or temporal distinction between them. Or else, if there is a conjunction even for the perceived whole, then there must be a conjunction even for that which is visible but lacks conjunction.

Furthermore, if it were argued that visibility [of qualities] occurs through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), then the connection of taste, color, and so forth would not be perceived in a beverage (*pānaka*) and the like when it is being seen. This is because "there is no quality in a quality. For in that case, the color or taste belonging to the constituent parts does not exist [in the whole]. If it is claimed that such a designation is made through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), then a distinction in cognition (*buddhibheda*) would follow. For the very same color or taste that belongs to the constituent parts of curd and so forth is metaphorically attributed [to the whole] due to inherence in a single object; however, there is no perception of a different color or taste [in the whole].
For whatever is the nature of the conjoined things, that would also be the nature of the conjunction itself.
But how could there be a difference in color or taste therein through mere metaphorical designation?

Now, it may be argued that those very color and taste appear as such due to their close association (*saṃsarga*), for extreme proximity is indeed the cause for the cognition of identity between them; thus, there is the apprehension of another taste and another form. If this were so, then there would be no need for a further whole (*avayavin*) other than the atoms themselves, since the mere appearance of the atoms would suffice for such conventional usage as "gross" and so forth. Furthermore, if the grossness of the atoms themselves were not apprehended, then the expression "a long row" would not occur, for there is no such thing as a "row.
To explain: Because they lack conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is no conjunction; for that very reason, it [the row] is not a substance (*dravya*).
Furthermore, length and so forth do not belong to genus and the like, nor is genus and the like accepted [as being long].
Just as cognitions of length and so forth arise due to a particular arrangement [of atoms], so too those [cognitions] have atoms as their object; thus it has been stated. (PVA 538–539)

Length and so forth belong merely to the arrangement [of parts], as in the case of a garland and the like. And since that which is the subject of dispute is intended to be the object of the notion of a "whole," it is not a whole. As for what was said—that the sense organs and other factors produce a cognition of either a conjunction or a distinct whole—regarding that, it is replied: the form of conjunctions and the like is not perceived. It is only the colors and other qualities belonging to the conjoined things themselves that are perceived; there, no further "conjunction" is within the range of perception. If it is asked, "How is it that what is grasped by the cognition 'conjoined' is not such [a distinct entity]?", the answer is: the cognition "conjoined" refers only to the conjoined things themselves, and the word "conjoined" has no other objective referent here.
Those things that have arisen in close proximity are what are joined there; they are the objective basis for the cognition of conjunction, and there is no conjunction other than that. (540) (PVA)
Just as objects situated in front [are perceived], is conjunction likewise situated?
The notion that [perception arises] "from conjunction" is based on the methods of agreement and difference (anvaya-vyatireka).

Indeed, no conjunction distinct from the conjoined things appears as something separate; it is merely that the state of those two being unjoined is not perceived, whereas they themselves are perceived. Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the conclusion is reached that this is a mere mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), however, there is the cognition: "this very thing has become such, it has arisen as such. Consequently, that very state is made known as a distinct entity called "conjunction. For this very reason, in verbal cognition accompanied by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which follows after the differentiation of real entities—
Just as in the case of qualities and so forth, or in the case of objects that are merely conceptualized, or those that have perished or not yet been born. || 93 ||

A distinction between categories (*padārtha*) does not arise merely from a difference in verbal cognition; rather, it arises from a difference in the cognition characterized as perception (*pratyakṣa*). For conceptual cognition (*vikalpikā buddhiḥ*), arising through the power of beginningless predispositions (*anādivāsanā*), fluctuates in various ways. Consequently, it does not find a firm footing in the reality of the object. In that regard, cognitions of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth rely on a distinction imagined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*); thus, the distinction belongs only to the imagined, not to the reality of the object. Furthermore, a distinction between imagined objects arises even from the views of other schools (*tīrthāntara*); therefore, there would be an infinite regress in attempting to establish the reality of the object based on such [views]. By accepting such [views], there would be mutual contradiction. Thus, distinct words and cognitions function with respect to an imagined entity due to the positive and negative concomitance of predispositions. What is this conceptualization like? It follows the distinction of the entity; the non-distinction [of the entity] is its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from what is not as it is. And there is no exclusion other than that which is excluded; therefore, that very thing appears as a distinct internal division in relation to a continuum (*santāna*). Do conceptual constructions proceed as distinct without a distinction of entities? They certainly do proceed; this is observed. For example, among qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth: "one quality," "one inherence" (*samavāya*), "twenty-four qualities. In those cases, number is not [the cause], because number resides in substances (*dravya*), and there is no metaphorical application of the number of the substratum when the substratum is distinct—[for instance,] where universals (*sāmānya*) and the like remain one and the same despite a difference in their substrata. And how could there be oneness and so forth in things that have perished or not yet been born?

If it is held that the metaphorical designation (upacāra) here is based on a certain cause, why is that very same cause not accepted for both [the metaphorical designation and the cognition] in respect of all entities? (94)

[096,iii] If, due to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), there is such a verbal expression and cognition of oneness and so forth regarding things that have perished or not yet arisen, why is that very metaphor not accepted as the basis for all [such cases]? Let the basis simply be the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of beginningless conceptual construction; there is no occasion for the postulation of a real entity (*vastu*).

If it is argued that metaphorical usage does not apply everywhere because there is a distinct qualifier, and if it is asked how there can be a difference in meaning when there is no difference [in the object], provided that [the primary sense] is indeed the primary one— (95)

Even if they have no other object as their cause, words such as "white" and so forth are not synonyms; for if, in those cases as well, there were another object associated with number and the like, [then they would be distinct]. (96)
A quality and a substance may be non-distinct in their essence, yet distinct through the difference in their exclusion (vyāvṛtti);
this would be so even if they do not have different referents, just as in the case of the words "non-action" and "non-substance. (97)

[096, vii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. [096, viii] What, monks, is physical food as gross nutriment? It is that which is called ‘food, food’ in the world; this is what is called physical food as gross nutriment. What, monks, is contact as nutriment? Whatever contact there is—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that is what is called contact as nutriment. What, monks, is mental volition as nutriment? Whatever mental volition there is—whether directed toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena—that is what is called mental volition as nutriment. What, monks, is consciousness as nutriment? Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—that is what is called consciousness as nutriment. [096, ix] Herein, monks, regarding the nutriment physical food as gross nutriment, if one were to say: ‘I will not eat this food at all,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for it and abandon lust for it,’ this is possible. Regarding the nutriment contact, if one were to say: ‘I will not experience any contact at all,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for it and abandon lust for it,’ this is possible. Regarding the nutriment mental volition, if one were to say: ‘I will not have any mental volition at all,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for it and abandon lust for it,’ this is possible. Regarding the nutriment consciousness, if one were to say: ‘I will not have any consciousness at all,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for it and abandon lust for it,’ this is possible. [096, x] Monks, if one were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for these four nutriments and abandon lust for them, yet I shall still undergo birth, grow old, die, pass away, and be reborn,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘Having abandoned desire for these four nutriments and abandoned lust for them, I shall not undergo birth, nor grow old, nor die, nor pass away, nor be reborn,’ this is possible. [096, xi] Monks, when a noble disciple has thus abandoned desire for these four nutriments and abandoned lust for them, he is called a noble disciple who has cut off craving, removed the fetters, and by rightly breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering in this very life. [096, xii] This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks! “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One taught the Dharma with the four nutriments as its theme, and having taught it, he rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Now, friends, if you wish, go to the Blessed One and ask him about the meaning of this. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so you should remember it. “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then those monks approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, exactly as it had been said by the Venerable Ānanda. [096, xiii] “Ānanda, did you not say to those monks: ‘Friends, the Blessed One taught the Dharma with the four nutriments as its theme...’? “Yes, venerable sir. “Ānanda, if anyone were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for these four nutriments and abandon lust for them, yet I shall still undergo birth, grow old, die, pass away, and be reborn,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘Having abandoned desire for these four nutriments and abandoned lust for them, I shall not undergo birth, nor grow old, nor die, nor pass away, nor be reborn,’ this is possible. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, for a long time these four nutriments have been thoroughly understood, well-penetrated, and their origin, cessation, and the way leading to their cessation have been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata. Therefore, Ānanda, if anyone were to say: ‘I will abandon desire for these four nutriments and abandon lust for them, yet I shall still undergo birth, grow old, die, pass away, and be reborn,’ this would be impossible. But if one were to say: ‘Having abandoned desire for these four nutriments and abandoned lust for them, I shall not undergo birth, nor grow old, nor die, nor pass away, nor be reborn,’ this is possible. [Objection: Surely, what is called "metaphorical usage" (*upacāra*) is dependent upon a primary sense (*mukhya*); how could it exist when the primary sense is absent? And the primary sense is that which possesses a distinct qualification (*bhinnaviśeṣaṇa*), like [the word] *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer"). When there is no distinct qualification, there is the status of the secondary (*gauṇī*). But for you, since there is a connection with qualifications produced by successive prior conceptualizations, everything would have the status of being primary due to the absence of distinct qualifications; thus, metaphorical usage is impossible. [Reply: That is incorrect. Why is it that only that which has a distinct qualification is primary? Even that which has no distinct qualification may be primary if it has attained conventional currency (*rūḍhi*) through extreme habituation, even while its qualifications are distinct as produced by conceptualization. For the primary is the object of a cognition whose movement is unerring, while the other is secondary—what is insufficient in this definition? Furthermore, if that which has a distinct qualification is primary and otherwise is metaphorical, then let everything of this kind be non-primary, because of the absence of a distinct qualification. However, the distinction is that in the case of destroyed or unborn things, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) itself is metaphorical. If there were no other qualification at all, then the qualificand alone would be the denotable meaning everywhere; thus, there would be identity of meaning in the form of synonymy, and not grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), for that occurs only when there are distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). That too is not to be said, because: *(The verse follows)* [The verse: "Just as the word 'cow' is applied to a cow, so too is it applied to a horse; therefore, since the word 'cow' applies to both, it is established as synonymous. [Commentary: This is not correct. For the application of the word 'cow' to a cow is based on the universal (*jāti*) "cowness," whereas its application to a horse is based on the universal "horseness"; therefore, they do not have identical meanings. Moreover, the application of the word 'cow' to a horse is metaphorical, not primary. How so? Because it is dependent upon a primary sense. What is the primary sense here? It is the application of the word 'cow' to a cow. Upon what is that based? On the universal "cowness. Thus, the application of the word 'cow' to a horse is metaphorical, being dependent upon that primary sense. Therefore, the claim that the word 'cow' is synonymous with the word 'horse' is not tenable. how can there be the state of being the meaning of words characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? (PVA 542)

[096,ix] This grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) must pertain either to two words or to two objects. First, it cannot pertain to two words, because each word denotes its own specific object. If it is argued that coreferentiality occurs through indirect indication (lakṣitalakṣaṇa), [096,x]
For when there is a connection by means of one [word] alone, that [object] is already indicated;
since there is no employment of a second sound, that [connection] does not exist.
By this very [argument], the co-location (*samānādhāratā*) of objects has been refuted.

Even if a relation exists, how and why could it be cognized? (544) (PVA) If an object is cognized as non-different [from its universal] by the power of inherence (*samavāya*), then another word would become useless, since that [object] is already understood from a single [word]. (545) (PVA)
If it is maintained that by another [word] that very same object is made known, then according to your view as well, would this not result in the same state of synonymy? (546) Or,
if only that which is related to the object "blue" is conveyed by a single sound...
When the inherent cause is perceived, there is no non-perception of the other [effect].
(547) (PVA) Just as when blue is apprehended by direct perception, the lotus is also understood;
likewise, when that very thing is understood from a word, the mention of another sound is redundant. (548) (PVA)
The meaning of a word is indeed fixed; thus, it is not accessible to others [in an arbitrary way].
There is no object whatsoever devoid of its specific qualities; otherwise, speech would be in vain.
(549) (PVA) For instance, the blueness of sapphire, blue lotuses, and so forth, is not merely [the quality of] "blue" alone.
Since it is perceived directly in that way, how could the occurrence of sound be otherwise?

Therefore, it is the cognitions themselves, arising in accordance with their own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), that construct the linguistic conventions of difference, non-difference, and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, there is no consequence of synonymy. For instance:

It has been stated that even when they do not have different referents (*anarthāntara*), non-synonymy is observed in cases such as "white" and so forth. If it is argued that even there [the referents] are distinct entities (*arthāntaratva*), then in that case there would be no distinction between a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*). To explain: "A substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Inherence-causehood would exist because of its connection with qualities. Because of the presence of gravity (*gurutva*), downward motion occurs in things like syrups; thus, there is possession of action. Consequently, since even a quality—such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*)—possesses the characteristics of a substance, it would follow that it is a substance. Therefore, there would be no distinction between quality and substance. Therefore, the word and the cognition are distinct [from their referents], being differentiated by the differentiation of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and by the differentiation of the objects of expression (*abhidheya*). For example, in the cases of "non-action substance" (*akarmadravya*) and "non-substance action" (*adravyaṃ karma*), there is no distinct referent here. Nevertheless, there is non-synonymy for words such as "non-action substance. In that case, the basis is solely the differentiation of exclusion, and not another basis, namely a difference in the occasioning cause of application (*pravṛttinimitta*). How then is the distinction between coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) established? As in: "The cow is white" (*gauḥ śuklaḥ*) versus "The whiteness of the cow" (*goḥ śuklatvam*).

Furthermore, when words denoting an entity express it as if it were distinct— such as words for number and so forth applied to that which possesses them— it serves to differentiate it from other properties.
For one who desires to know only that [specific object], the entire other [portion of] Śruti is not discarded;
it is as if Yoga, in some instances, points out a distinct property with a finger. (99)

The term *yuktāṅgulī* (having joined fingers) denotes the subject (*dharmin*) by implication for all [the fingers], even though it expresses a single well-known object; its established status is likewise prescribed in such cases. (100)

[098,ii] “What is a bodhisattva who has newly entered the vehicle? “It is one who has not yet produced the roots of virtue conducive to penetration. [098,iii] “What is a bodhisattva who has accumulated merit? “It is one who has produced the roots of virtue conducive to penetration. Just as it has been established that synonymy does not arise from the difference between imagined denotata (*vācya*), so too, even when there is no difference in the denotatum, the use of the ablative case (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) occurs due to the existence of an imagined distinction, as in "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*), "the head of Rāhu" (*rāhoḥ śiraḥ*), or "the whiteness of a cow" (*goḥ śuklatvam*). The term "cow" (*gauh*) denotes the entire object associated with the conceptualization of that single form. However, "white" (*śukla*) denotes only one part of it, existing in association with a different conceptualization. This distinction (*vyatireka*) is abstracted through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, in the expression "the quality of white belongs to the cow," the ablative case is used. Furthermore, when there is no apprehension of the cow's form and only "whiteness" is perceived, devoid of any specific related entity, one asks, "Whose is this whiteness? At that time, having determined the nature of the cow based on prior observation, one points it out by saying, "It is a cow. In this case, identity (*tādātmya*) alone is intended as the relation; the distinction is merely due to the initial ascertainment of the isolated [quality]. However, when it is realized that this [quality] cannot exist in isolation—even if there is a dullness in the perception of particulars due to the dim eyesight of observers—[one still asks], "This must be either white or a cow, or something else. Then one asks, "What is this? Is it a white cow or something else? In response, one says, "It is a cow," using grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*). This is because the question itself is framed within that very context. And a response corresponding to that is appropriate, for this is the true meaning of the matter.
When the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
even if there is some cause for the absence of a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). (PVA 552)
This white quality of the horse is to be answered by the wise;
because the question is one of exclusion (*vyatireka*), the determination is that it is "just so" (*tathaiva*).
However, when there is inclusion within a specific [category] through non-exclusion (*avyatireka*)...

Having observed the conduct of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the questioner may pose a question. At that time, one who understands the nature of that [question] will provide a corresponding answer; for there is no occasion here for another course of action. (PVA 554–555)

Because non-difference exists at that time, conventional usage proceeds in exactly that same way. This beginningless worldly convention pervades the entire world; since people do not investigate the ultimate reality of things, their distinction is not sublated. (PVA 557–558)

If, then, the whole does not exist, it would follow that flavor and so forth belong only to themselves and not to the pot—that is, they would be the color and so forth of the pot. For it is not the case that there is a "color of colors," nor is it the case that there is a "pot of the pot. Anticipating this objection from an opponent, he says:
The word "jar" functions without implying the distinct potencies of form and so forth; it serves to exclude those things that do not cause an effect identical to its own. (101)
Therefore, there is no scriptural expression of a single substratum such as "the jar is form.
Consequently, this is the difference between [the words] that denote a genus and those that denote a collection. (102)

"Color and so forth belong to the jar"—in such cases, they are subordinate to that universal [jar]; by this same method, other denotable objects are explained as being specific powers of that [universal]. (103)
[098, viii] The Noble Eightfold Path.

The word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is applied to color and the other [sensory qualities] by implying a common capacity for holding water, while presupposing their distinct, specific capacities. Therefore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "color is the jar. For this very reason, when one intends to express the capacity of the collection, this is a collective term (*samudāya-śabda*). However, a generic term (*jāti-śabda*) applies to each individual when they share a single result, as in "forest" or "tree. How, then, is the designation "the colors, etc., of the jar" used? The meaning is that each [quality] individually possesses the capacity to produce the cognition of color and so forth, which serves as a common effect for the purpose of fetching water. Now, just as "the forest of trees" or "trees are the forest," why does the expression "colors, etc., are the jar" or "the jar of colors, etc. not occur? It certainly does occur if one is not influenced by the linguistic conventions of other systems. But since worldly usage generally follows those conventions, it does not occur in common parlance. However, for one who possesses correct understanding, the realization certainly occurs that certain colors and the like are jars capable of performing a specific function; and fetching water and so forth is that specific function. Or, they are established by a specific configuration (*saṃniveśa*), because from that specific configuration comes the specific capacity for holding water. But the coreferentiality "color is the jar" does not occur, because of the distinction between part and whole, and because there is no mutual pervasion (*vyāpti*) between them.
[098,ix] But surely, since there is no relationship of mutual pervasion between "tree" and "śiṃśapā-ness," how can there be co-referentiality? This is not so, because:
The cognition of a "tree" occurs as distinct even when applied to a single individual;
however, the cognition of a "jar" does not persist with respect to each individual constituent, such as its color and so forth.

Indeed, the cognition of a "jar" does not apply to each individual [quality] such as color and so forth, in the way that the cognition of a "tree" applies to each individual [part] such as the *śiṃśapā* tree. Nor is that distinction of capacities (śaktibheda) implied by the word "jar," because the specific determination of capacity is established through the conventional usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). However, the word "tree" implies even the possession of a distinct capacity; thus there is no fault. In this case as well, the basis is either the establishment of conventional usage or a distinction of capacity; therefore, everything is well-established. Now, one might object: in the cases of "twenty cows" (*viṃśatir gāvaḥ*) and "twenty of cows" (*gavāṃ viṃśatiḥ*), there is no difference whatsoever here.
For by the word "twenty," no other power is expressed here;
only the powers of carrying, milking, and so forth are understood in this context. (PVA 560)
In this case, there is a manifestation of the aggregate as something clearly distinct in its multiplicity.

Therefore, it is said: by this same direction, other designations should also be explained. Here, a specific kind of aggregation (*saṃhati-viśeṣa*) consisting of two groups of ten is intended; and by that [aggregation], the capacity for carrying or milking is not implied, nor is the specific aggregation implied by that [capacity]. Thus, everything is well-established. Alternatively:
[099,iii] For those whose selves are conditioned by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) through beginningless worldly convention...
This linguistic convention is beginningless and arises from conceptual construction and verbal expression. (561) Therefore, no objection whatsoever is raised by anyone;
even if the meaning of words is of such a nature, nothing at all is lost. (562)
What irrationality is observed here that it should be so questioned?

In the case of the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of words in common usage (*prākṛta*), no inconsistency is seen. However, in that regard, a clear distinction between the gender and the number of the word and its referent (*artha*) is observed. (PVA 563)
And there is no irrationality in that, provided this [distinction] pertains to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
For refinement (*saṃskāra*) occurs through a characteristic; thus both the "natural" (*prākṛta*) and the "refined" (*saṃskṛta*) are accepted.
Indeed, the state of being conditioned or unconditioned is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (PVA 564–565)
This is merely a formal convention for the sake of engaging in childish play;

it has been turned into a treatise by foolish practitioners of worldly affairs in whatever way possible, and though it is devoid of meaning, it has been followed by others in the same manner. (PVA 566)

Therefore, we do not know what can be said here by these fools alone. (537) (PVA) Furthermore, talk regarding unseen objects is seen even in the treatises of jesters; yet there is no conviction in them, and thus this is a blind tradition. (568) (PVA)
