[099,xii] If the body arises from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), then either all the parts collectively are the cause for the production of consciousness, as the earth and other elements are for a sprout, or each individually, as combustible grasses are for flames and the like in that context.
And if they were causes as a whole, [the effect] would not arise even when a single factor is missing.
Even if each were individually capable, there would be the simultaneous production of many [effects]. (104)
Nor are inhalation and exhalation the regulators, because multiplicity is equal [in both cases].

Indeed, in a case where many factors operate through mutual cooperation toward a single effect, that effect cannot occur even if one of them is absent; for if it were to occur despite the absence of one, that factor would not truly be a cause. [099,xvi] Now, if the parts produced the cognition independently of one another, then mental consciousness would certainly arise from them even when the ears, nose, and so forth are severed. In that case, it follows that each part possesses individual capacity; consequently, multiple cognitions would arise simultaneously. For it is not the case that when each individual seed is capable, multiple sprouts fail to arise from the state of being many seeds.

[099,xvii] Now, as for the fact that the inhaled and exhaled breaths (*prāṇāpāna*) are the producers [of cognition], any single constituent part of them serves as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). And the effect does not differ because of a difference in the cooperative causes; even in the absence of various different weavers, there is no difference in the cloth and such.
[099,xviii]

To this it is replied: Since the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths are also multiple, that same contingency follows. Even when a single part is deficient, there would either be no [breathing] at all or an occurrence of many [breaths]. For the oneness of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* is not established in the same way as that of the body. Now, if oneness is indeed accepted, we say the following:

If it is argued that even though the cause is a single entity, there is a multiplicity of manifestations because that cause is eternally present, and thus it cannot be the cause of multiple effects— this is not so; for there is no distinction [in the cause], and [manifestation] would also have to occur simultaneously.

[099,xxi] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his supernatural power, transformed himself into a great white ox. He stood before the merchants and said to them: “O merchants, do not fear; I shall carry you all across. Having spoken thus, he lifted up all five hundred merchants upon his back and crossed over to the other shore. When they had reached the opposite bank, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara restored himself to his original form and spoke to the merchants: “O merchants, do not fear; I am Avalokiteśvara, who has come here out of compassion for you. Having spoken thus, he taught them the Dharma. At that time, the five hundred merchants were filled with joy and, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, they became followers of the Buddha. Thus did the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara deliver the five hundred merchants from the peril of the great ocean. This is called the second chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s deliverance of the five hundred merchants.

Even if [the mind] were a single entity, since there are multiple manifestations of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the downward breath (*apāna*), and so forth, it would follow that there are multiple minds characterized by passion and other states, because their cause is eternally present. And it is illogical to say that when a cause is present, that which arises from it has not yet arisen. Now, if one argues that [the vital breaths] cannot be the cause of the manifold [mental states] because the relationship between cause and effect is restricted—indeed, the restriction of the causal relation is not subject to questioning; for smoke arises from fire as a single [effect]—we say no, because there is no distinction [in our case]. For smoke is not perceived as successive instances arising from that very same nature of fire. In this case, however, from that very same nature of the vital breaths and so forth, there occurs the state of various minds such as passion, due to the association with successive awakening conditions (*prabodhakapratyaya*). Nor is there a restriction regarding the awakening condition itself, because the strength or weakness of prior latent impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) is the cause. Therefore, if those vital breaths are not the cause of that consciousness, they would not be the cause even subsequently, as there is no difference [between the two moments]; thus, even in a sequence, there could be no multiplicity of causes, and it would follow that the prior latent impression alone is the cause.
[100,ii] Furthermore, although the oneness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth has been accepted, it is not logically tenable. To explain why:
Since multiple objects are perceived even by a single sense-organ, there is therefore no fixed rule [regarding the number of objects]. // 106 //

Let that [multiplicity] be perceived all at once by a single cognition, since there is no contradiction; nor should it be [perceived] sequentially, for there would be no distinction [between the two cases]. (107)

[100,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.”

Even when there is a single vital breath (*prāṇa*), because multiple cognitions exist during such things as long exhalations, there is no fixed rule regarding the vital breaths and so forth. From what, then, does the rule arise? Precisely from that [cognition] itself, because of its apprehension. Apprehension alone—each preceding one—is the cause for the restriction of each subsequent cognition. Now, it might be argued that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is indeed a single entity that takes the form of apprehending multiple objects in succession; therefore, there are not multiple cognitions. This too is not the case. There is no other "mind" apart from the forms of color and so forth. [The opponent claims: A single, all-pervading mind exists, like a clear mirror, and it is simply joined with the reflections of objects. To this, we reply: if consciousness were indifferent [to the object], and the production of the reflection of the object occurred merely upon reaching it, then because there would be no degree of proximity among objects, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of apprehending all objects simultaneously. If it is argued that this is not so due to the varying degrees of specific mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then that cultivation alone is the cause of the objective form, not the vital breaths, inhalations, and so forth. Furthermore, if consciousness remains stable like a mirror, what contradiction is there such that there is no simultaneous apprehension of objects? If, on the other hand, the capacity [to apprehend] does not exist at that time, then let there be no apprehension of those objects even in succession, since there is no difference [in the lack of capacity].

[100, vi] Furthermore, it might be argued that even there a difference between moments certainly exists; therefore, due to this difference between moments, there is a successive apprehension of multiple objects. This too is not a valid answer, because:
If it is claimed that many momentary vital breaths, which are indeed of a different kind [from the mind],
are postulated as the cause of such [momentary] mental states, 108.
How could they possess succession without a cause that possesses succession?
If their own preceding members were the cause, there would be no possibility for the first one.
[100,ix] Because:

There is no such cause for that [simultaneity]; or, if it did exist, there would certainly be a multiplicity [of cognitions], because the vital breaths occupy different locations. Therefore, cognitions arise simultaneously. (110)

Subhūti, it is for this reason that the Tathāgata calls this 'the perfection of wisdom,' because there

It is already established for us that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are many and momentary; however, this is not established for you. If it is argued that this is established because it is seen through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply: for it is not logical that a single substantial entity (*dravyārtha*) should exist sequentially; therefore, since the effect follows the sequence of its causes, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also sequential. But how could those very vital breaths be sequential, given that they lack sequential causes? If it is argued that it is due to the sequence of causes such as preceding vital breaths, we say no. For if they were caused by their own preceding homogeneous kind, the first [vital breath] would be impossible, because no such preceding [breath] exists. If one accepts the existence of another world (*paraloka*), then birth and so forth would be the cause of the vital breath. If it is argued that the vital breath of the mother and father alone is the cause, we say no; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such [breaths] existing at all times. And if this were so, then intellect (*buddhi*) too would be produced solely from the mother and father, which leads back to the previously mentioned [absurd] consequence.

[100,xii] This is stated while granting the opponent's position: the plurality of breaths follows from their association with different locations. For association with multiple locations is the proof for the existence of multiple things, due to the imposition of contradictory properties. Because of the plurality of breath, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous arising of multiple mental cognitions.

Furthermore, there is the sequential production of minds belonging to the same class. For it is not the case that a difference in effect arises solely from a difference in moment; rather, just as there are multiple causes of the same class, so too is the effect.
[101, ii] Now, one might object: "Only a single [effect] arises from multiple [causes], for it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces. This is no answer.
[101,iii] If multiple [causes] existing at one time were the cause of a single consciousness,
then even when one of them is deficient— as in cases such as shallow breathing— that consciousness would not arise.
Furthermore, if the cause [is the same], there would be no distinction even in the cognition according to the state of the object;
for that [cognition] cannot be the effect of that [object] if it does not differ when the object differs. (112)

[101,v] Regarding the production of a single effect by multiple causes, there is duality either in the form of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) or otherwise. If it were produced in the form of a causal complex, then in cases such as slow breathing or in the absence of breathing, [the effect] would not occur because of the absence of the causal complex. For this is the characteristic of an effect born from a causal complex: that it does not arise when the complete or incomplete [causes] are deficient. Indeed, if it were to arise even in the absence of those [causes], it could not be their effect.

Furthermore, it might be argued that just as a cause is indeed present, it is not necessarily complete. If that were so, then one would have to say that even what is present is not a cause, for it may also be absent. But this is not the case, because the relationship between cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, the rule is this: from a complete [cause], a complete effect arises; from an incomplete [cause], an incomplete [effect]; from what is non-existent, what is non-existent; and from what is otherwise, what is otherwise. For that which does not vary when another varies cannot be its effect. If it is argued that the very fact of an effect's occurrence following the presence of something else is the basis [for their causal relation], we say no. It is precisely by virtue of the effect’s modification following the modification of the other that the fact of its occurrence following that presence is understood.

If the state of being cause and effect were established merely by the fact that one thing exists when another exists, then transformation would be without a cause, and likewise everything would be causeless. (PVA 569)

[101, viii] If one accepts that the mere fact of "occurring when that exists" (*tadbhāvabhāvitvam*) is sufficient, then it follows that the modification based on the causal connection would be entirely causeless. Furthermore, why would that modification not have arisen from that alone at the very first moment? For if it were arising while that [cause] remained unmodified, it would have to exist right from the beginning. Indeed, it has been stated that something which varies even when there is no difference in its cause cannot be its effect. Therefore, just as the variation would be causeless, so too would that entity; how then can its occurrence when that exists be understood? [101, ix]

By this, the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is refuted. As for what is said—that consciousness arises sequentially from the body alone, depending upon specific sequential transformations—that is incorrect.
This sequence of transformation is also impossible based on the body alone.
Since there is no difference in the body, from where could a distinction in that [consciousness] arise?
(PVA 570) Just as there is no distinction in consciousness due to the absence of a specific transformation, so too there is none in the transformation itself due to the absence of a specific body.

[101,xii] But is it not observed that a specific transformation of milk and so forth occurs even when there is no difference in those [conditions], arising merely from the passage of time? The same would apply to the body as well. This is not sound, because:
[101,xiii]
For the transformation of milk and so forth arises from similar milk;
likewise, the bodily transformation is distinguished as being of the same nature.

When there is an equal combination of milk and other ingredients, and an equal presence of heat and other conditions, the resulting transformation into curd and so forth is indeed the same. However, regarding the body, its similarity or dissimilarity is the basis for the distinction or non-distinction between cognitions—such as those arising from corresponding practice, latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it is understood that there is no sequence of cognitions resulting from a sequence of transformations. Consequently, it is established that if something were the effect of a collective whole, a specific distinction would be possible; otherwise, it could not be manifold. Yet, this is not what is observed.
Now, one might object: "Even for one for whom cognition arises solely from cognition, why does not multiple cognition arise? To this, the reply is:
Cognition is the cause of a single [subsequent] cognition because of the restriction of its capacity.
When cognition is defective due to attachment to another object, it apprehends something other than the intended object. // 113 //

[102,ii] Consciousness, in the form of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), is the cause for each [subsequent consciousness]. It is a restriction of capacity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) conforming to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), or a specific attachment. For a consciousness with firm habitual tendencies produces only a certain [specific] consciousness—even if it is separated by an interval—by imparting a particular efficacy to the immediately preceding condition; or it does so solely through awakening in accordance with that immediately preceding condition. To illustrate:
Having attained the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even without an immediately preceding [consciousness],
the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) may occur from a previous consciousness alone.
However, for some [conceptual constructions], it arises from an immediately preceding consciousness due to proximity.
The arising of conceptual construction is observed [to follow immediately] from another [cognition], but not from a distant one.

Indeed, the arising of conceptual constructions—which are latencies (*vāsanā*) of a distant cognition—is never seen to occur through the intervention of something else that falls between them, whether it be another cognition or an object within its scope. Therefore, it is logically established that a single conceptual construction arises from a single cognition.

**(Ṅa) The Accomplishment of Action:** [102, vi] But surely, even when multiple cognitions arise from the body, the restriction [to one at a time] arises from that very cognition itself. Just as, although there is the possibility of cognitions through multiple sense-faculties, at times only a single cognition occurs regarding an object of attachment due to a specific intensity of attachment; to this it is replied:
[102,vii] A cognition produced once from the body is constrained by its own kind.
If it were dependent on something else, why would there be a cessation of the capable body? 114.

[102, viii] If consciousness were to arise from the body, then it would arise again and again from that very same source, because the capacity of the body remains exactly as it was. Even if consciousness, due to the restriction of its own power, produces only a single instance of consciousness, the body nonetheless exists in that same state and thus continues to produce subsequent instances of consciousness. Now, if it is argued that no further consciousness arises from the body because that initial consciousness creates an obstruction to the body’s production of another consciousness—this too is incorrect.
This matter has not been made an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Cognition arises from cognition alone, through the determination of the means of knowledge.

For multiple cognitions do not arise from the body alone when it is devoid of cognition. Furthermore, there is no obstruction to the capacity of one cognition to produce multiple cognitions; for smoke does not impair fire’s power to produce smoke. Therefore, if cognition arises from the body, then even when each individual cognition is produced, the body’s capacity remains unimpaired, and thus it produces a continuous series of further and further cognitions. Indeed, causes possess no such deliberative intelligence by which they might think, "Since a cognition now arises from a preceding cognition, why should the body produce another cognition after this? and thereby fail to produce it.

Now, it might still be argued that there is an obstruction to the cause producing its own effect precisely because of the effect itself. [102,xii] When multiple cognitions arise from the body, immediately thereafter—
When an obstacle to knowledge and vision is perceived, a doubt may nevertheless arise at some point:
"The attachment produced by partiality occurs in this person due to habituation;
thus, the capacity of this [attachment] to govern incorrect cognition arises. (PVA 575–576)

[102,xiv] Therefore, since the causal relationship is established between cognitions of that same kind, a cognition of that kind arises from a cognition of that same kind alone; thus, it arises from cognition itself, not from the body.

But was it not said that since multiple sensory cognitions can arise, there is one cognition from each individual [sensory] cognition? True, this was said; however, a solution does not follow from mere assertion, but rather from reasoned argument. And that [assertion] is not reasonable. For a cognition whose nature is unattached does not exert itself to prevent the arising of another cognition. Nor does attachment occur without prior habituation (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, in whatever type of cognition there has been prior habituation, attachment occurs again toward that very same kind; thus, it is precisely due to prior habituation that other cognitions do not arise. But for one who... [103, ii]
For him, there is no other world, nor is there the possibility of prior practice;
without prior practice, there is no prevention of other cognitions [arising].
Therefore, for the cognitions arising from the body again and again— (PVA 577)
When that body has come into being, the collection [of cognitions] should have been obtained, yet it is not seen.
(578) Now, if the very first moment of this body were the producer of consciousness, then for a subsequent [moment], there would be no causality due to its distinctness. (579) (PVA)

For that which is distinct from the jar—being of a different character—is not the producer of cognitions. Indeed, even if something is distinct from the producer, it is not itself a producer. That too is incorrect.
If the arising of the cognizers were from the very first moment of the body, then the body would be without support; it would be nothing but pure consciousness alone. (580) (PVA) [103, viii]
In the absence of the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, there can be no relationship of support and supported; if that were the case, consciousness would exist in isolation.

Now, if consciousness produces consciousness with the body as its auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*), then it does not exist independently. This being the case, our own position would be established: that consciousness arises from consciousness alone, while the body is merely an auxiliary cause. If, on the other hand, the body is the primary material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)—just as cow dung is for the lotus stalk (*śālūka*), after which the lotus stalk arises from the lotus stalk itself—then even in the absence of cow dung, the lotus stalk would subsequently arise from the lotus stalk alone. Likewise, if consciousness arises from consciousness alone, it follows that it could exist independently. [103,x]
Now, it is observed that the body also functions as a cause. True; however, it is not as an *upādāna*-cause (material cause), but rather as a cooperative (*sahakārin*) cause, as has been stated.
Now, if it were first an *upādāna* and subsequently a cooperative cause, it would not be a cooperative cause after having been an *upādāna*.
[103,xii] If the body is the material cause (*upādāna*), how then can it be the auxiliary condition (*sahakārī*)?
If it is argued that this is so simply because it is observed, we reply: no such observation is accepted here.
And it has been established that a lotus root (*śālūka*) of such a nature does not arise from cow dung or from another lotus root, because there exists a great difference between those two.
In some cases,
that very first perception, having arisen from the clarity of sensory cognition, is observed to be the means for establishing another cognition.
Therefore, consciousness does not arise from the body.

[103,xvi] Now, it might be argued: "If, according to you as well, the body is not the support of consciousness, then it would follow that consciousness could persist even when the body has ceased to exist; for there can be no rule regarding their coexistence if it is without a causal basis. To this, the following objection is raised and then refuted.

[103,xvii] If it is argued that the mind might persist alone even when the body has ceased because it lacks a support, then [we reply]: the cause for the persistence of the mental continuum [is required]. 115.

If it does not attain the status of a factor for the sake of obtaining the activity of its cause, then there would necessarily be the persistence of the [cause] alone; this is the remainder of the sentence. But when...
The cause for the arising of another body is the five sense-bases belonging to this world. (116)

[103,xxi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a ‘Bodhisattva’ as a designation. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation. He does not perceive the levels, nor does he perceive ‘levels’ as a designation. He does not perceive the dharmas of a Buddha, nor does he perceive ‘dharmas of a Buddha’ as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, these dharmas do not exist, and they cannot be apprehended; therefore, they are called ‘Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, when practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘Bodhisattva’ as a designation.”

In that case, how could there be the existence of the solitary [mind]? For the cause of the persistence of the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) is the activity of its own cause—the activity of that which is designated as the "embryo" (*kalala*) and so forth, which consists in being directed toward the production of a body. The acquisition of this [activity] does not exist for the solitary cause of the body; rather, it is the cause of the persistence of the mental continuum. When the preceding mind, designated as "karma," possesses the status of a member—that is, the state of being a cooperative cause—then it possesses that membership when there is craving for a body. If it does not attain that status of membership, then the existence of the solitary [mind] is indeed accepted. Furthermore, in the production of another body, the five sense-bases (*pañcāyatana*) of this life serve as the cause for the production of a body through their nature as formative forces (*saṃskāra*) for those who have passed away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Its status as a member is observed because no production of a body is seen after death [in that realm], whereas the formless realm itself is absolutely unseen. Here, he says:

Non-perception by way of negating its being a constituent part or a cause is said to be non-conclusive; this applies even to the sense faculties and so forth, as they are "possessing a remainder" (śeṣavat).

[104,ii] Even if the status of the five sense-bases (*pañcāyatana*) belonging to this life as a contributing factor in the production of a body in another birth is not perceived, nevertheless, that is not the case for what is designated as "karma," which is the cause of the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*). Thus, the non-existence of that [karma] cannot be determined by mere non-perception alone; since it was already established previously that non-perception does not constitute a definitive proof [of non-existence], what room is there for doubt in this matter?

Furthermore, it is said: here it is not mere non-perception that is being stated, but rather inference preceded by pervasion (*vyāpti*). For example: whatever is a sense faculty does not connect with another sense faculty, just as Devadatta’s eye and so forth do not connect with Yajñadatta’s eye and so forth. And in this case, the sense faculty is connected to the body of this birth; thus, there is the perception of a property pervaded by its contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhiḥ*).

This is not so. Because this [reason] is "by way of remainder" (*śeṣavat*), it is said: "For there is no cognition [of the absence] for one who possesses a remainder. Indeed, the non-reconnection of the sense-faculties in another birth is cognizable only through mere non-perception, and from mere non-perception alone, there is no certainty regarding exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Now, if it is argued that because the reconnection of the sense-faculties occurring in the present body is observed, the same reconnection is inferred for another [life] as well; even in that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since that too belongs to the present life, like the near and far shores of a river. If, on the other hand, it is specified as "the sense-faculty existing between the semen and blood," [the response follows].

That too is incorrect. Here, too, the absence of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not understood except through mere non-perception (*anupalambhamātra*). Nor does the qualification "being within the semen and blood" provide protection, as in the case of a qualification of place or a qualification of the word "pot. For it is thus:
The capacity of the preceding sense organs has been observed within their own respective species; and because transformation is seen, rebirth after rebirth is established. (118)

[104, viii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of giving. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift without perceiving a basis, and he does not perceive that gift as a gift. He does not perceive the recipient of the gift, nor does he perceive himself as the giver. He does not perceive that 'I am giving this gift,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the gift I am giving,' nor does he perceive that 'to this person I am giving. He does not perceive that 'I am giving this gift for the sake of awakening,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the gift I am giving for the sake of awakening,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening I am giving this gift. He does not perceive that 'I am giving this gift for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the gift I am giving for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of the awakening of such-and-such all beings I am giving this gift. He does not perceive that 'I am giving this gift for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the gift I am giving for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such unsurpassed perfect enlightenment I am giving this gift. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of giving. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of morality? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis while undertaking the training in morality. He does not perceive that morality as morality. He does not perceive the one who undertakes the training in morality, nor does he perceive himself as the one undertaking the training in morality. He does not perceive that 'I am undertaking the training in morality,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the training in morality I am undertaking,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening I am undertaking this training in morality. He does not perceive that 'I am undertaking this training in morality for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the training in morality I am undertaking for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening of all beings I am undertaking this training in morality. He does not perceive that 'I am undertaking this training in morality for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the training in morality I am undertaking for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such unsurpassed perfect enlightenment I am undertaking this training in morality. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of morality. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of patience? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis while cultivating patience. He does not perceive that patience as patience. He does not perceive the one who cultivates patience, nor does he perceive himself as the one cultivating patience. He does not perceive that 'I am cultivating patience,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the patience I am cultivating,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening I am cultivating this patience. He does not perceive that 'I am cultivating this patience for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the patience I am cultivating for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening of all beings I am cultivating this patience. He does not perceive that 'I am cultivating this patience for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the patience I am cultivating for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such unsurpassed perfect enlightenment I am cultivating this patience. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of patience. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis while exerting vigor. He does not perceive that vigor as vigor. He does not perceive the one who exerts vigor, nor does he perceive himself as the one exerting vigor. He does not perceive that 'I am exerting vigor,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the vigor I am exerting,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening I am exerting this vigor. He does not perceive that 'I am exerting this vigor for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the vigor I am exerting for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening of all beings I am exerting this vigor. He does not perceive that 'I am exerting this vigor for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the vigor I am exerting for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such unsurpassed perfect enlightenment I am exerting this vigor. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of vigor. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of meditative concentration? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis while entering into meditative concentration. He does not perceive that meditative concentration as meditative concentration. He does not perceive the one who enters into meditative concentration, nor does he perceive himself as the one entering into meditative concentration. He does not perceive that 'I am entering into meditative concentration,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the meditative concentration I am entering into,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening I am entering into this meditative concentration. He does not perceive that 'I am entering into this meditative concentration for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the meditative concentration I am entering into for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening of all beings I am entering into this meditative concentration. He does not perceive that 'I am entering into this meditative concentration for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the meditative concentration I am entering into for the sake of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such unsurpassed perfect enlightenment I am entering into this meditative concentration. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of meditative concentration. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis while practicing the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive that perfection of wisdom as the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the one who practices the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive himself as the one practicing the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive that 'I am practicing the perfection of wisdom,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the perfection of wisdom I am practicing,' nor does he perceive that 'for the sake of such-and-such awakening I am practicing this perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive that 'I am practicing this perfection of wisdom for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'this is the perfection of wisdom I am practicing for the sake of the awakening of all beings,' nor does he perceive that 'for the

For a restriction is not perceived as being limited solely to the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of a specific individual (*vyakti-viśeṣaṇa*); otherwise, no one could engage in any linguistic or practical activity (*vyavahāra*) anywhere, because such activity is preceded by a certainty regarding causal capacity (*śakti*). Furthermore, since practical activity concerns the universal (*sāmānya*), the relationship [of inference] does not have a specific individual as its ultimate object. And so, when an eye or other sense organ, which is associated with fickleness and other qualities, arises in such a state due to the cultivation of habituation (*abhyāsa-bhāvanā*), and when such a thing is observed, then in another instance, that very same kind of thing is inferred. Moreover, at the time of birth, a sense organ of such a nature is not perceived as the cause; therefore, it must be produced by a sense organ from a previous life. Thus, neither "being of this world" (*naihikatva*) nor any other qualification is logical. If, however, that sense organ were one and the same [in successive lives], then the production of a subsequent sense organ by the preceding one would not be established. Even if this were the case, nevertheless:
Since the state of being preceded by repeated practice is observed in cases such as dexterity,
and since such an inference is already established, any other [argument] is useless. (PVA 583)

[104,x] "It is exclusively non-existent"—this is not tenable in every respect, because one infers that the cause is of such a nature from observing effects of that same kind. Furthermore, it has been established that qualities acquired through practice are observed even in another body during a dream.

Furthermore, because successive modifications are observed, the production of successive [entities] is indeed established; thus, one sense organ produces another sense organ during the intermediate state. How then could there not be the production of a different birth’s sense organ? For when a modification constitutes its very nature, there is only difference and no identity, just as in the case of earth and so forth.

Furthermore, it might be argued that there is no absolute difference here because this is merely a designation for a single continuum (*ekasantāna*). This is equally true for other lives as well. Another life is indeed included within the same single continuum, like one who has awakened from sleep; however, due to the intervention of memory, it is perceived as if it were distant.

It might further be argued that cognition does not arise solely from the sense faculties, but rather that first there is production from the body, and subsequently from the sense faculties alone, due to the restriction of their capacity. To this, it is replied:
If that birth were from the body, the same consequence as before would follow.
If it were from the mind, let the birth of another body arise from that very mind. (119)

[105,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive forms, nor the eye-consciousness, nor the contact of the eye, nor the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the ear, nor sounds, nor the ear-consciousness, nor the contact of the ear, nor the feeling born of the contact of the ear as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the nose, nor odors, nor the nose-consciousness, nor the contact of the nose, nor the feeling born of the contact of the nose as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the tongue, nor tastes, nor the tongue-consciousness, nor the contact of the tongue, nor the feeling born of the contact of the tongue as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the body, nor tangibles, nor the body-consciousness, nor the contact of the body, nor the feeling born of the contact of the body as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the mind, nor mental phenomena, nor the mind-consciousness, nor the contact of the mind, nor the feeling born of the contact of the mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the element of earth as a basis for apprehension, nor the element of water, nor the element of fire, nor the element of wind, nor the element of space, nor the element of consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the realm of desire as a basis for apprehension, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the conditioned as a basis for apprehension, nor the unconditioned as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the past as a basis for apprehension, nor the future, nor the present as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the limit of past time as a basis for apprehension, nor the limit of future time, nor the interval between the two as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive all dharmas as a basis for apprehension. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. That which is empty of intrinsic nature is not a dharma, and what is not a dharma cannot be apprehended. Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any dharma whatsoever as a basis for apprehension.”

If [consciousness] arises for the first time from the body, does it arise from a body possessing sense-faculties (*sendriya*) or from one lacking them (*anindriya*)? If it arises from a body possessing sense-faculties, then it must arise from the sense-faculties themselves; thus, even for the very first [instance], since it would arise from sense-faculties, the existence of a previous world (*paraloka*) is established. If it arises from a body lacking sense-faculties, then [consciousness] would have to arise from hair, nails, the tips of the fingers, and so forth, or from a dead body. Furthermore, if there were multiplicity [of consciousnesses], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of multiple sense-faculties arising simultaneously. And if that were so, there would be the consequence of [the body] being of immeasurable size. Likewise, why would there be a cessation of a body that is [otherwise] capable? If, on the other hand, the sense-faculties are merely specific transformations (*pariṇativiśeṣa*) of the body, then the same consequence of non-destruction would follow, namely, that the sense-faculties originate from the body, and so forth. Now, if it is argued that because of the absence of mind (*citta*), sense-faculties do not arise in a dead body, then [consciousness] must arise from the mind itself. From that very mind, there is the birth of another body and the birth of the mind belonging to that other life. What is the point of this insistence on postulating the sense-faculties as the cause? Therefore, the body is not the cause of cognition (*vijñāna*); hence, due to the deficiency of the body—which is not its cause—there is no possibility of another birth, and thus no reconnection (*apratisandhi*). Thus he says: [The opponent objects: "But surely, when a person dies, the sense-faculties are destroyed along with the body, and therefore there is no rebirth. [The author replies: This is not so. For we observe that even when the body is destroyed, the sense-faculties persist in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Just as the seeds of rice and so forth, though destroyed by fire, persist in the form of latent impressions within the soil and give rise to sprouts, so too the sense-faculties, though the body has perished, persist in the form of latent impressions within the mind and produce the sense-faculties of another body. Furthermore, if the sense-faculties were destroyed along with the body, then just as a sprout cannot arise from burnt seeds, consciousness could not arise from a dead body. Moreover, if the sense-faculties were destroyed along with the body, then since the sense-faculties are the cause of the body, the body would never arise again. But we see that bodies do arise. Therefore, the sense-faculties are not destroyed along with the body. Consequently, the sense-faculties persist in the form of latent impressions within the mind, and from those very latent impressions, the sense-faculties of another body are produced. Thus, it is established that the body is not the cause of cognition. Since the body is not the cause, there is no impossibility of another birth due to the body's deficiency; rather, there is indeed reconnection (*pratisandhi*). Thus he says: [The opponent asks: "But how can there be a transformation of the sense-faculties without a cause? [The author replies: There is no fault here. For we observe that even without a direct cause, transformations occur through the power of latent impressions. Just as the transformation of milk into curd occurs without an external agent, so too the transformation of the sense-faculties occurs through the power of latent impressions. Furthermore, if the sense-faculties were destroyed along with the body, then since the body is the cause of the sense-faculties, the sense-faculties would never arise again. But they do arise. Therefore, the sense-faculties are not destroyed along with the body. Consequently, the sense-faculties persist in the form of latent impressions within the mind, and from those very latent impressions, the sense-faculties of another body are produced. Thus, it is established that the body is not the cause of cognition. Since the body is not the cause, there is no impossibility of another birth due to the body's deficiency; rather, there is indeed reconnection. Therefore, it is not due to a deficiency of causes that there is no reconnection for all final moments of consciousness.
For this reason, such a proof is considered to be *śeṣavat* (inference based on what remains).

[105, vi] This is the conclusion. For the cause is the mind conditioned by karma accompanied by craving, which is not connected to another birth; and there is no deficiency in that [cause]. If, however, the body were the cause, then due to its deficiency—namely, a deficiency of the cause—there would be no reconnection [to a new birth]. But this is not the case. Therefore, there is no deficiency of the cause, and thus the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Only "because it is a mind at death" remains. And that is *śeṣavat* (inference from remainder), because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is shown merely through non-perception. [105, vii]

As for what was also stated: "The mind of this life does not link up with another mind, because it resides in a different body, like the mind of Devadatta"—that too is incorrect. This is because the existence of a [mental] state has already been refuted, and because its substratum has been negated.
When functioning as an object, consciousness perceives another moment immediately after [its own].

If the meaning of the proof is that what exists there [in the body] does not produce a consciousness residing elsewhere, then the relationship of support and supported (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is refuted, as is the notion that consciousness is located in a specific place. Furthermore, the body being perceived is not the support of consciousness, because it is an object of perception for cognitions such as pleasure due to its specific internal tactile qualities; indeed, one's own body is merely an object of perception (*ālambana*). Therefore, the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because a cognition perceiving another’s body can arise [without that body being its support]. Nor is "being another body" established merely through the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) of a single continuum (*santāna*); rather, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is a distinction even within the body of a single lifetime due to the differences between stages such as childhood and so forth. Consequently, the benefit to the continuum comes from the body, but the arising of the mind (*manas*) occurs solely from the mental consciousness (*citta*), just like the continuity of a grain of rice. Thus, since the continuum of consciousness is without beginning or end, the establishment of the succession of birth and death is proven, and through the perfection of practice (*abhyāsa*), all qualities—whether omniscience or any other quality—find their scope.

[(c) The Cultivation of Compassion] [105,x] But surely, let there be cultivation; how, however, does it reach the ultimate limit? Because only a slight degree of excellence is observed, as in the case of jumping or the heating of water. To this, the answer is:

[106,i] If it is argued that even though there is excellence through practice, there should be no transgression of one's nature— just as in jumping or heating water— if that [nature] has been infused [with change], then [there is no such restriction]. // 121 //
Furthermore, if it were to depend upon further effort because its basis were unstable, then no excellence would ever increase, nor would its nature be such [as to do so]. (122)
If it is asked, "From what [source] is this known?", he says:

In that regard, because the means of proof lack the capacity to bring about further specificities once their powers have been exhausted, and because there is no abiding in anything other than the eternal, [the result is established]. (123)

[106,v] The mind is not apprehended within the mind; it does not exist externally, nor does it abide internally. It is neither long nor short, neither round nor square. It is neither blue nor yellow, neither red nor white, nor crimson. It is neither fragrant nor foul-smelling, neither bitter nor pungent, neither sour nor sweet, neither salty nor astringent. It is neither smooth nor rough, neither hot nor cold, neither soft nor hard. It is neither male nor female, nor is it neuter. It is not apprehended by the eye, nor by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It is not apprehended by form, nor by sound, odor, taste, tactile objects, or mental phenomena. It is not apprehended by the realm of the eye, nor by the realms of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It is not apprehended by the realm of forms, nor by the realms of sounds, odors, tastes, tactile objects, or mental phenomena. It is not apprehended by the realm of eye-consciousness, nor by the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness. It is not apprehended by the realm of contact, nor by the realms of sensation, perception, volition, or consciousness. It is not apprehended by the realm of ignorance, nor by the realms of formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or aging-and-death. It is not apprehended by the realm of suffering, nor by the realms of origination, cessation, or the path. It is not apprehended by the realm of emptiness, nor by the realms of signlessness, wishlessness, or non-origination. It is not apprehended by the realm of the conditioned, nor by the realm of the unconditioned. It is not apprehended by the realm of the past, nor by the realms of the future or the present. It is not apprehended by the realm of the world of desire, nor by the realms of the world of form or the formless world. It is not apprehended by the realm of the Śrāvakas, nor by the realms of the Pratyekabuddhas or the Bodhisattvas. It is not apprehended by the realm of the Tathāgatas, nor by the realm of the Buddhas. It is not apprehended by the realm of the Buddha-eye, nor by the realms of the Dharma-eye, the wisdom-eye, the divine-eye, or the Samantabhadra-eye. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of all modes, nor by the realm of the knowledge of all aspects. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the paths, nor by the realm of the knowledge of conventionalities. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of others' minds, nor by the realm of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, nor by the realm of the knowledge of death and rebirth, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of outflows, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the extinction of outflows. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all afflictions, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all afflictions. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all views, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all views. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all habitual tendencies, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all habitual tendencies. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all conceptual proliferations, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all conceptual proliferations. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all dharmas, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all dharmas. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all things, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all things. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all phenomena, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all phenomena. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all entities, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all entities. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all natures, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all natures. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all characteristics, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all characteristics. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all signs, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all signs. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all conditions, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all conditions. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all causes, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all causes. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all roots, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all roots. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all seeds, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all seeds. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all elements, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all elements. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all aggregates, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all aggregates. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all constituents, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all constituents. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all bases, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all bases. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all fields, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all fields. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all worlds, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all worlds. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all realms, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all realms. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all times, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all times. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all directions, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all directions. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all moments, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all moments. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all instants, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all instants. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all durations, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all durations. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all continuity, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all continuity. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all succession, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all succession. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all connection, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all connection. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all conjunction, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all conjunction. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all association, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all association. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all accumulation, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all accumulation. It is not apprehended by the realm of the knowledge of the exhaustion of all collection, nor by the realm of the knowledge of the non-arising of all collection.
