Indeed, it is not merely by being a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) that something possesses a fixed excellence. For instance, the distinction between jumping and the heating of water does not result in fixed excellence simply by their own existence; rather, even when a jump has been performed, it requires further effort. A jump obtained through prior exertion is not independent of subsequent effort; on the contrary, it almost invariably requires further effort. However, the heating of water has a stable substrate and does not require further effort, for it does not persist even when the contact with fire has ceased—precisely because its excellence is not fixed. Therefore, fixed excellence is pervaded by both the requirement of further effort and the possession of a stable substrate. Since these two conditions are absent and the opposite is present in the case of mental qualities such as compassion, they do not possess fixed excellence. Furthermore, that which requires further effort is not an inherent nature (*svabhāva*). This is a qualified reason: that which has a stable substrate and is an inherent nature does not have fixed excellence, just as, for example, the lack of disgust (*ghṛṇā*) in a learned *kāpālika*.
But as for that which depends upon effort, its [case is as follows]:

Since a particularity has no inherent nature, when it has been produced even through effort, it would not require further effort; otherwise, that other effort would have to be the producer of the particularity. (124)

Furthermore, that which depends upon effort, even if it attains great increase, nevertheless does not possess the nature of an inherent essence (*svabhāva*). For it is not logical for that which depends on the presence of causes to be an inherent essence; such a designation applies only to that which flows by its own natural force. Therefore, even when there is an increase, there is no ultimate or infinite increase, just as in the cases of jumping or the heating of water.
And it is not the case that mental qualities such as compassion and others, nor any external qualities, are like this; thus he says:
"In the mind, [qualities arise] as fire does in wood, mercury, gold, and so forth. [106,x]
Compassion and the like, born of practice, proceed spontaneously.

For in the case of wood, a specific quality produced by fire—characterized by internal burning and so forth—is self-sustaining once it no longer requires effort; the same applies to mercury, where qualities such as flowing and digesting are produced, and to gold, where qualities are produced by processes such as *puṭapāka* (roasting in a crucible). In exactly the same way, compassion and other virtues in the mind, through the production of specific qualities by repeated cultivation, become non-reverting. When a specific quality of compassion has been produced such that it no longer requires further effort, then another subsequent quality arises which, possessing a power not previously employed, produces further successive distinctions until the ultimate limit of excellence is reached.

[Objection: But surely jumping also depends upon effort, and compassion and the like do as well; so why is one spontaneous while the other is not? [Response: This has been stated here: that which is not spontaneous is not independent of effort, such as the heating of water and the like. Compassion and the like, however, are like the specific qualities produced by fire in wood—they are spontaneous.
Therefore, once they have arisen, their nature becomes a quality.
Therefore, each subsequent effort brings about further excellence. (126)
And since the cognitions of compassion and so forth increase from seeds of a similar kind that preceded them, how could there be stability for them even with the practice of truth? (127)

[107, ii] The state of established excellence consists in the fact that compassion and other such qualities arise solely from preceding cognitions of a similar kind, such as prior compassion, and do not depend upon the presence of an object or other external conditions. For instance:
Even by the mere recollection or hearing [of them], there is the arousal of compassion and the like;
moreover, compassion and the other qualities do not depend upon a return favor or similar considerations.

For those whose mental continuums have been cultivated in that way, even when fresh and constant harms are occurring, compassion and the like do not undergo slackening. Therefore, at the time of the great festival of the meeting with practice, there is no lack of expansion, nor any dullness.

Now, it might be argued: "Even jumping has such practice, which is indeed the cause for its limitless increase; therefore, that [increase] is also attained as a natural property (dharmaprāpta) of it, and thus there is no such reversal. To this he says:
And likewise, jumping does not arise from jumping alone; rather, because the capacity of its causes—strength and effort—is stable, jumping possesses a stable nature. (128)

[107,vii] For it is not the case that from compassion and so forth alone, as from a cause of the same kind, there arises only compassion and so forth; rather, jumping also arises from strength and effort. Even one who has practiced jumping well is no longer capable of jumping when strength and effort have ceased. Both strength and effort possess a stable nature due to the capacity of their own causes. Therefore, jumping too has a stable nature and not otherwise.
[107,viii]

Furthermore, it might be argued: jumping arises solely from practice regarding the object of jumping; otherwise, since strength exists even prior [to practice], there would be the consequence of jumping even then. If it is argued that strength itself did not exist previously and was produced only through practice, then, even though jumping is born from a similar kind [of action], jumping would not be unlimited; thus, the same consequence would apply to compassion and so forth as well. To this it is said: [107,ix] Because of a deficiency in the body at the beginning, there is no jumping later, just as in the case of the [initial] leap.
When defects have been gradually dispelled through effort, one's own strength becomes established.

[107,x] It is not that strength arises from practice; rather, strength is always present, though it may be impaired by phlegm (*śleṣman*) and other factors, rendering one incapable of leaping. Therefore, through the practice of leaping, the deficiency of these two [factors] is removed. Consequently, that very same prior strength remains of its own accord for him. For this reason, leaping occurs later and not earlier. Now, if strength comes from the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*), even that is determined by the specific power of the elixir. Even when the practice of leaping is identical, there is no equality of leaping between a human and the fledgling of a *garuḍa*. To illustrate: [107,xi]
Although the practice of leaping is common to both the Garuḍa and the deer, there is no equality in their leaping despite that commonality. (586) (PVA) [107,xii]

Therefore, even in the case of practice, leaping depends precisely upon the strength born of one's [physical] constitution, and not merely upon practice alone. However, compassion and the like, on the other hand, are indeed independent of anything else.

[Objection: But surely, since strength arises from practice and leaping arises from strength, that very [leaping] is preceded by practice just like compassion and so forth. [Reply: No. Because through excessive practice there is even a loss of strength; thus, there is no fault [in our position].

[107,xiv] If, then, compassion and the like depend solely upon seeds of their own kind, then, due to beginninglessness, they would possess that very nature eternally. And it is not understood that there exists anything which does not arise from its own seed. To this, it is replied:
If compassion, arising from its own seed, is not obstructed by opposing factors arising from their own seeds within the mind, it reaches the state of being its very nature. (130)

[108,i] Although compassion arises from its own seed and has been present for beginningless time, it does not yet constitute a state of naturalization (*sātmībhāva*), because it is obstructed by hatred and other afflictions that likewise arise from their own seeds. If, however, continuity is attained, then even though there is a stable basis, a state of being compassionate in nature occurs through the great effort required to ward off opposing factors such as hatred.
This must necessarily be accepted:
for thus, each preceding practice is the root of each subsequent one.
When there is proficiency in the mental qualities such as compassion, dispassion, and awakening... (131)

For the prior practice of compassion and so forth serves as the cause for the successive arising of each subsequent mental quality with increasing proficiency. Since the arising of a quality already produced occurs through its own seed, it is only the enhancement of that proficiency which must be effected by practice, because the arising itself is already present. Therefore: “For one whose mind is free from obstruction regarding its own welfare and who possesses longing for the welfare of others,” [108,v]
The state of having compassion as one's nature arises from practice, just like aversion, detachment, and passion.

[108, vi] For practice, when performed with no other activity, produces the state of having compassion as one's nature, just as it produces aversion, detachment, and passion. Just as aversion becomes second nature when it is not obstructed by opposing factors—such that, due to its presence, nothing at all appears as something to be grasped—in the same way, detachment and even passion are to be understood.
<4. The Blessed One is an authority because he is the Teacher> <(1) Explanation of being the Teacher> [108,vii]

Thus, one who is compassionate, desiring to dispel the suffering of others, becomes intent upon the means for the removal of that suffering; so it is said: [108, viii] Having perfected the excellence of compassion, he is impelled by an inability to endure the suffering of others. (132)

The compassionate one applies himself to the means for the sake of eliminating suffering. For in one who possesses compassion, effort toward the elimination of one’s own suffering is possible. Without the destruction of one’s own suffering, there is an incapacity to remove the suffering of others. Therefore, he applies himself to the direct realization of the destruction of his own suffering and to the direct realization of all phenomena; because: [108, ix] The compassionate one applies himself to the means for the sake of eliminating suffering. For in one who possesses compassion, effort toward the elimination of one’s own suffering is possible. Without the destruction of one’s own suffering, there is an incapacity to remove the suffering of others. Therefore, he applies himself to the direct realization of the destruction of his own suffering and to the direct realization of all phenomena; because:
[108,x] For it is indeed difficult to explain that which is beyond perception—the goal and its cause. // 133 //

[108,xi] Indeed, for one who lacks the direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) of the causes and fruits of heaven and liberation, it is difficult to explain them to others; for such a person lacks the capacity therein. Even if the teaching of the Four Noble Truths were possible through inference once the Truths have been ascertained, it would still not be possible at all times, because it is impossible during moments when one is striving for one's own welfare. Furthermore, regarding the occurrence of hells and so forth, it is simply impossible to describe the events of world-systems such as the Avīci hell, which are the specific fruits of particular karmas. Therefore, everything must be directly realized.
In that regard, the examination of the cause is the direct means for realization. He states this very point:
[108, xiii] Examining through both reasoning and scripture, one investigates the cause of suffering.
And its nature as impermanent and so forth is [established] by means of the qualifiers of suffering itself. (134)

[109,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. He does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive form as unreal. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive forms as unreal; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the eye-consciousness as unreal; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the earth element as unreal; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive ignorance as unreal; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the conditioned as unreal; he does not perceive the unconditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as unreal. He does not perceive the world as real, nor does he perceive the world as unreal; he does not perceive the transcendence of the world as real, nor does he perceive the transcendence of the world as unreal. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the stream-enterer as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as unreal. He does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the once-returner as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of once-returning as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as unreal. He does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the non-returner as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of non-returning as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as unreal. He does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the arhat as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of arhatship as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as unreal. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the pratyekabuddha as unreal; he does not perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as unreal. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the Tathāgata as unreal; he does not perceive the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, or the Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are unreal, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to all dharmas? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are unreal, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to all dharmas through the power of skillful means. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are ultimately empty that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately empty, what is the distinction between the dharmas of a śrāvaka, the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha, and the dharmas of a Buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are ultimately empty, yet the dharmas of a śrāvaka, the dharmas of a pratyekabuddha, and the dharmas of a Buddha do not become confused. Why is this? Subhūti, it is because the nature of all dharmas is ultimately empty. Subhūti, it is because the nature of all dharmas is ultimately empty that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if the nature of all dharmas is ultimately empty, how can there be the three vehicles—namely, the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the Great Vehicle? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although the nature of all dharmas is ultimately empty, yet sentient beings, through the power of false conceptualization, give rise to various attachments. Because they give rise to various attachments, the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. Subhūti, it is because sentient beings have various inclinations and various dispositions that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are ultimately empty that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings by means of the three vehicles. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately empty, how can there be the distinctions of the ten stages of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are ultimately empty, yet a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gradually fulfills the ten stages. What are the ten? They are: the stage of joy, the stage of purity, the stage of radiance, the stage of brilliance, the stage of difficult victory, the stage of presence, the stage of far-reaching, the stage of immovability, the stage of good intelligence, and the stage of the cloud of dharma. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are ultimately empty that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gradually fulfills these ten stages. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately empty, how can there be the distinctions of the five eyes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are ultimately empty, yet a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, attains the five eyes. What are the five? They are: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are ultimately empty that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, attains the five eyes. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately empty, how can there be the distinctions of the six perfections? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are ultimately empty, yet a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully accomplishes the six perfections. What are the six? They are: the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are ultimately empty that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully accomplishes the six perfections. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately empty, how can there be the distinctions of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all dharmas are ultimately empty, yet a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully accomplishes the thirty-seven

Reasoning (*yukti*) is inference (*anumāna*). And scripture (*āgama*) pertains to that which is beyond the scope of inference; it is the cause for making known objects that transcend the senses. Alternatively, scripture first provides the initial awakening, after which reasoning proceeds with the fruit of making the object known. However, the ascertainment of the object does not arise from scripture alone, because [scripture] functions merely according to the speaker’s intention and lacks an inherent connection to the actual object. All of this applies to one who is oriented toward critical investigation (*vimarśa*), and not otherwise. Therefore, first there is investigation; then, regarding that object, there is its observation within the context of scripture—which consists of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) and is not mere authoritative command. For in a matter established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a discerning speaker, being neither deluded nor acting on mere command, would not speak. Then, having stabilized that object through reasoning, for one who meditates upon it, there is direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*); such is the sequence. In that regard, first one examines the cause of suffering itself, for the purpose of removing suffering by way of removing its cause. Once the cause of suffering has been identified, one further examines its nature—such as its impermanence—in order to determine its suitability for removal through such investigation. For if its suitability for removal were not determined, there would be no enthusiasm whatsoever for its removal. Indeed, if it were causeless or possessed of an eternal cause, any effort toward its removal would be fruitless. As it is said:
That which is causeless possesses permanence; how could there be destruction for that which has a permanent cause?
Without encountering a deficiency of causes, how could an entity cease to exist? (587) (PVA)
That whose existence is produced by a cause would not exist in the absence of that cause.
If it were to exist even in the absence of that [cause], how could there be non-existence for it?
(588) An entity whose cause is impermanent ceases when its cause is absent.

There is no absence of suffering due to the lack of a permanent cause, nor does it cease due to the lack of a cause. Therefore, by means of qualifiers such as impermanence and so forth, one examines the impermanence of that cause of suffering.
Since one perceives that there is no cessation as long as the cause remains in that state,
one examines its opposite in order to abandon that cause of the fruit. (135)
Its opposite is also established through the understanding of the nature of the reason.
[109, viii]

If some eternal cause of suffering, such as Īśvara and so forth, were to exist, then because that [cause] would never be deficient, one might conclude that the cessation of suffering is impossible; consequently, one would not engage in activity for the sake of its removal, for no one engages in what is impossible, nor does one who does so encounter frustration. Furthermore, one examines the opposite of whatever is the cause of a result in order to eliminate that cause; for even for you, there is no cessation without encountering the opposite. Nor can there be an absence of a non-cause simply because its opposite is absent. If it is argued that cessation occurs due to the mere absence of the cause, this refers to the opponent's view that cessation occurs solely from the exhaustion of karma. But this is not so; since karma arises repeatedly from ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no exhaustion of karma. And it will be demonstrated that ignorance is the cause of karma, and thus also of suffering; therefore, there is no fault.

[109,ix] But surely, the cause of suffering does not have a fixed form, because it takes many forms such as separation from the beloved and so forth; therefore, its cessation is impossible. To this it is replied:
Attachment, which has conditioned phenomena as its object, is produced by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. (136)
The vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is the cause that opposes it and its sublater.

[109,xi] Attachment (*sneha*) produced by the clinging to "self" and "mine" (*ātmātmīya*) is the cause of suffering. When attachment ceases, there is no suffering when that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is impaired.

[109,xii] But surely, even if mental suffering does not arise when what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) is being destroyed because of the cessation of affection, how is it that bodily suffering does not arise in the case of the self (*ātman*)? To this it is replied:
[109,xiii]
For one who suffers through the suffering of others, there is no arising of happiness for oneself;
indeed, when there is attachment to "mine," the cessation of self-love occurs.

Indeed, those whose self-love is set aside by love for their children do not experience even physical pain arising from contact with weapons and the like. Furthermore, attachment to what belongs to the self (*ātmīyasneha*) is the cause of the suffering of the view of a real self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); therefore, the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is its sublater because it is its opposite. For a phenomenon that is contrary in aspect to something is its sublater, just as moisture and heat are to wind. Consequently, when selflessness becomes internalized, there is the cessation of the impermanent view of a real self, which possesses the opposite aspect. Then, upon the cessation of the grasping at "self" and "mine," there is the cessation of all physical and mental suffering.
[110,ii] But surely, in cases such as the cutting or burning of the body, how can there be an absence of suffering such as death? This is not so. [110,iii]
There is nothing other than the separation from the body at the end of life; and the arising of another body is what constitutes birth. What sorrow is there in this? (591) (PVA) [110,iv]

When one is separated from one body and joined with another, there occurs for that person both conjunction and recollection regarding the prior and subsequent states. For one whose proficiency in memory has been produced by repeated practice, what pain can there be in that process? It is like the relinquishing and taking up of childhood or old age, or like the taking up and discarding of clothing. Furthermore, apart from the grasping of the continuity of pain, the cause of attachment is precisely where there is habitual practice; however, in the practice of indifference, neither pleasure nor pain exists.
This is because when absolute indifference toward the body and its objects of enjoyment is possible...
There is no suffering even when turning away the view of a sentient being, even if it involves doing harm.
Thus he says:
[110,vii] And for him, over a long period of time, there have been many methods in many ways. || 137 ||
As one practices therein, virtues and faults become manifest. [110,

viii] When all causes of agitation, such as attachment and the like, have been removed through the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), and there is the blossoming of awakening, the virtues and faults of the various successive means practiced for its development become manifest— just as, when studying a treatise, the virtues and faults of that treatise in their many forms become manifest.
For the manifestation of qualities and defects is indeed the proficiency of the intellect.
And through the clarity of the intellect, as well as due to the cause [of practice], latent impressions are abandoned. || 138 ||
This is the distinction of the Great Sage from the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas] and others who act for the sake of others.

And when there is a discernment of virtues and faults brought about by sharp awakening, then one knows the entire collection of faults—even those that are momentary—existing amidst the experienced virtues. Consequently, one strives to eliminate even defects such as verbal lapses, and thus the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) are abandoned. This alone is the distinction of the Blessed Sugata from the Pratyekabuddhas, the Noble Śrāvakas, and the non-Buddhist teachers. Alternatively, even if suffering were indeed abandoned, omniscience would not necessarily follow; otherwise, every person free from passion (*vītarāga*) would be an all-knower. To this it is replied: "By many means, in many ways," and so forth. For the manifold elaboration of means is indeed of many kinds; and through the practice thereof, the manifestation of all worldly virtues and faults occurs over a long period of time.

Just as there is recollection of previous births when there is the presence of proficiency in memory, so too, by following that [memory], there is again the full comprehension of all those [objects]. (PVA 593)

Just as one who has come from another village is recognized by those who know him through the persistence of his habitual impressions, so too is one who has come from another birth recognized. (594) (PVA) [110,xiv]

Just as, for instance, when someone has come from another village, an observer who perceives a specific change produced by contact with that place recognizes him as having come from there; and just as one thereby infers the existence of that other village as a qualifying factor [for the person], in the same way, one infers a previous birth as the cause of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced therein. Even though the object of inference—namely, the occurrence of a previous birth—is beyond direct perception, why should giving and the like not be inferred in this manner?
And from that follows the realization of the necessity of action and its fruit:
"By this action, there was a meeting with this place for one who previously possessed such a form and nature, due to that very meeting. (PVA 595–596)

[111,ii] When one examines the specific nature of the connection between a particular place and so forth and its resulting effect, there occurs the cognition of the relationship between the distinctions among the natures of all causes and their resulting effects; this is the cognition of the totality of specific natures, which constitutes the thorough knowledge of the relationship between all actions, their fruits, and so forth.
When there is a correct understanding of the path to heaven and liberation,
the teaching is considered complete simply by virtue of knowing that which is for the sake of the person's goal.

Nor does the entire world arise independently of the relationship between cause and effect. Therefore, through the continuous cultivation of the various modes of causal relation, the cognition of the entire world becomes faultless; from that, omniscience follows.
[111,v] Now, if it is known through inference, how can this be direct perception? And yet, the Blessed One is held to be a direct seer. That too is merely a trifle.
Inference of all aspects does not differ from direct perception; even the conjunction with a sense faculty does not produce any further distinction beyond that. (PVA 598)

[111, vii] That which is indeed the cognition of the intrinsic nature of an object in all its aspects is precisely what is perception (*pratyakṣa*). For the meaning of "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is "direct realization" (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). Now, if it is argued that "perception" means "that which functions in relation to the sense organ" (*akṣaṃ prati vartate*), this is not the definition of perception; rather, it is the direct cognition of a real object. The sense organ (*akṣa*) is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, if there is an absence of direct vision even when there is a connection with the sense organ, how can that be perception? If it is argued that "it is not even a sense organ because it is impaired," it is said in reply: [111, viii]
If it is held that [the sense organ] is not a sense organ (*anakṣa*) because it is not the cause of direct perception,
then let it be determined that it is a sense organ (*akṣa*) because it is the cause of direct perception.

For it is not logical that the status of being a sense-faculty (*akṣatā*) arises from mere configuration and so forth; for then it would follow that even a damaged [organ] would possess that status. However, if the status of being a sense-faculty consists in being the cause of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), then there is no contradiction in the mind (*manas*) also being such [a faculty]. Furthermore: [111,x] It is precisely through the acuity of the mind that there is a clear perception of the form.
For when the mind is distracted, how can there be clarity in the perception of the senses?

(PVA 111,xi) It is precisely because the mind is concentrated that sensory cognition (*akṣavijñāna*) also becomes direct perception (*sākṣātkārin*). Therefore, being produced by sensory perception is not at all the cause [of its being direct perception]. Consequently, even inference, when it proceeds toward the direct realization of all aspects, is indeed direct perception.
[111,xii] But how can that which operates regarding the past and so forth, which are beyond the senses, be direct perception? This too is not tenable.
[111,xiii]
If there is the actual existence of direct perception, how can this [object] be indirect?
If that which is directly perceived were indirect, then nothing would be non-indirect.

Now, the non-perceptibility of the operation of the sense organ [is asserted]. But how can that very operation of the sense organ be understood without direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*)? If it were understood through direct perception, then even in the inference of all aspects (*sarvākārānumāna*), there would have to be an operation of the sense organ, because the occurrence of the application of inference exists everywhere. Furthermore, the operation of the eye and other senses is also understood through inference. Moreover:
"For when there is an inference of all aspects, it must concern something previously perceived."
In that case, the operation of the self, the eyes, and so forth is also perceived;
sometimes it is yet to be, and sometimes it has already occurred, and it is understood through inference.
Is this not then simply the exclusion of the [actual] sensory organ, designated as "the operation of the sense"? (PVA 602–603)

[111,xvii] When an object that has already arisen or one that is yet to arise (*bhāvin*) is inferred, then the operation of the sense organ (*akṣavyāpāra*) regarding that future object is perceived through inference. When it is past, then it is indeed past. And since that [operation] exists entirely as it is being perceived through inference in its every aspect, how can there be an absence of the operation of the sense organ?
[111,xviii]
Now, one might ask: how can that which is yet to be or that which has already passed exist? This is not so;
for the very act of direct realization is said to be the existence of this entity.
The existence of an entity is understood through its direct perception in all cases.
(PVA 604) Even in the case of an object currently intended as present, such as a pillar, its existence is understood solely from that direct perception and not from anything else.

[112,iii] But surely, even in the case of fire and the like that have not been directly perceived, their existence is accessible through inference? No. Even there, it is only such a thing as has been, is being, or will be directly perceived that is inferred; otherwise, inference would not function. Inference that follows upon perception makes known only that which is perceptible, for otherwise it would be impossible. However, if something has never been seen by anyone, is not being seen, and will not be seen, then it is like the horn of a donkey—it is simply non-existent. The absence of any description of causal capacity is precisely what constitutes "non-description" (anupākhyā). [112,iv]

"Is it not the case," the opponents have argued, "that existence consists in a connection with the present time and not in direct perception? And yet, you maintain that yogins possess direct perception of past and future objects. If they perceive only the present state, however, they would not be perceivers of the past and so forth. Consequently, being no different from ordinary people, how can this person possess the status of a Teacher, a yogin, or anything else? To this, it is replied:
[112,v] There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever by which the passage of time is apprehended.
The apprehension of mere form and so forth occurs through perception and inference;
even when perception has ceased, its operation is still perceived.

[112, vii] By means of perception (*pratyakṣa*), only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth is apprehended, not its connection with time and the like; for perception arises from the mere grasping of that specific form. Indeed, perception does not observe anything except by grasping the form present before it. Otherwise, everyone would be an omniscient seer. Nor is time perceived as something present before one in the manner of a pillar or other objects. Furthermore, there is no inference (*anumāna*) apart from perception. Now, if it is argued that time is either graspable through cognitions such as "quick" or "slow," or is inferable, that too is incorrect. [112, viii]
"‘For a long time,’ and so forth: for cognitions, there is no temporal extension residing in what stands before them.
Without such a form, perception of a cognition is not admitted.
In expressions such as "long done," it is only the jar or the like that appears; no other time-entity exists therein.
[112,x] Now, it might be argued: if it is only jars and the like that appear as possessing the state of being effects, then what is the referent of "long" and so forth? To this it is replied:

The completion of the parts of a jar and so forth occurs through a gradual process of slowness; the sense of "long duration" arises from the absence of time due to the non-proximity of the causes. (PVA 607)
The gradual completion and final accomplishment of the constituent parts of a jar or similar object through a slow process is the meaning of "long duration."

[Objection: But surely, without time (*kāla*), that very slowness and its progression would not be possible. [Reply: No, for that is established merely by the non-presence of the means (*sādhana*). And the non-presence of the means is due to the absence of the causes for its presence. Furthermore, the absence of those causes is itself due to the absence of their own causes; thus, this causal sequence is beginningless (*anādi*). Therefore, there is no such thing as "time.
[112,xiv] Now, if slowness or rapidity were to proceed by the power of time—
In that case, let it be considered what purpose is served by a cause for effects. (PVA 112, xv) 608.

Time is the initiator of effects; what, then, is the result of the operation of causes? If it is argued that time is not capable [of producing effects] without causes, then the production of effects occurs solely through the presence or absence of causes, and time is not capable [of anything]. However, if the incapacity of causes were due to the absence of time, then it would be logical for time to have the status of a cause. Yet there is no such absence of time, because it is all-pervasive and eternal. If it is claimed that production arises from a cause that depends on the conjunction with successive moments of time, then from where does that very conjunction with successive moments of time come? If it is said to come from another cause, then the sequence of effects arises from that alone; what is the use of time? If it is argued that the sequence itself is time, we say no, because "sequence" is simply the state of being conjoined or unconjoined. And since that is nothing other than the nature of things themselves, there is no separate entity called time. Furthermore, if it is claimed that time is simply the movement of the sun and so forth, we say no, because there is no movement apart from the essential nature of the sun and the rest. And that essential nature is accessible only through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The state of having been seen is the past; the state of being seen is the present;
and the state of being about to be seen is the future—such is the determination of time. (PVA 609)
[113,i] How, then, is there this cognition of distinction, namely, "this time belongs to this entity"?
Just as this body of the Son of the Rock (Śiva) possesses a distinct nature,
so too is the distinctness of time consistent with valid cognition.
And thus says the world: "At what time were you born? What have you to do with being well-established and so forth?"
Regarding the question concerning the specific nature of that [object], this statement is appropriate.
(PVA 113,v)

Consequently, the reality of the object—namely, the past and the future—is now invisible. Thus, it follows that the vision of the past and so forth by yogins is a vision of what is not currently visible. In that case, if it is said that they see what is themselves invisible, then it would follow that a woman is both a mother and barren. Therefore, what is the meaning of "seeing the past and so forth"? It means that they see what is not being seen by others; since that [object] exists as something currently visible by virtue of being perceived, there is no fault. Its status as past and so forth is relative to others. Therefore, only that which is directly realized exists; there is no operation of the senses regarding the past, because that which is past does not exist as something currently being directly realized.
Furthermore, when its direct realization occurs through connection with that specific time,
then even though it is non-existent at the present moment, its existence is not difficult to establish. (PVA 612)

[113, vii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. “Monks, I say that the abandonment of these four nutriments is for the sake of the cessation of craving, for the relinquishing of attachment, for the destruction of craving, for the uprooting of desire, for the non-arising of future existence, for the fading away of craving, for cessation, and for Nibbāna. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the abandonment of the four nutriments for the sake of the cessation of craving, for the relinquishing of attachment, for the destruction of craving, for the uprooting of desire, for the non-arising of future existence, for the fading away of craving, for cessation, and for Nibbāna. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the abandonment of the four nutriments? “Friend, the purpose of the abandonment of the four nutriments is the cessation of craving, the relinquishing of attachment, the destruction of craving, the uprooting of desire, the non-arising of future existence, the fading away of craving, cessation, and Nibbāna. When this was said, another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the cessation of craving? “Friend, the purpose of the cessation of craving is the relinquishing of attachment, the destruction of craving, the uprooting of desire, the non-arising of future existence, the fading away of craving, cessation, and Nibbāna. When this was said, yet another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the relinquishing of attachment? “Friend, the purpose of the relinquishing of attachment is the destruction of craving, the uprooting of desire, the non-arising of future existence, the fading away of craving, cessation, and Nibbāna. When this was said, still another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the destruction of craving? “Friend, the purpose of the destruction of craving is the uprooting of desire, the non-arising of future existence, the fading away of craving, cessation, and Nibbāna. When this was said, yet another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the uprooting of desire? “Friend, the purpose of the uprooting of desire is the non-arising of future existence, the fading away of craving, cessation, and Nibbāna. When this was said, still another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the non-arising of future existence? “Friend, the purpose of the non-arising of future existence is the fading away of craving, cessation, and Nibbāna. When this was said, yet another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of the fading away of craving? “Friend, the purpose of the fading away of craving is cessation and Nibbāna. When this was said, still another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of cessation? “Friend, the purpose of cessation is Nibbāna. When this was said, yet another monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the purpose of Nibbāna? “Friend, Nibbāna is itself the purpose; it is the goal, the supreme goal, the ultimate purpose, the ultimate good, the ultimate security from bondage, the ultimate sanctuary, the ultimate refuge, the ultimate peace, the ultimate bliss, the ultimate liberation, the ultimate Nibbāna. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda addressed those monks: “Friends, when one has truly understood the purpose of Nibbāna, one has truly understood the purpose of cessation; when one has truly understood the purpose of cessation, one has truly understood the purpose of the fading away of craving; when one has truly understood the purpose of the fading away of craving, one has truly understood the purpose of the non-arising of future existence; when one has truly understood the purpose of the non-arising of future existence, one has truly understood the purpose of the uprooting of desire; when one has truly understood the purpose of the uprooting of desire, one has truly understood the purpose of the destruction of craving; when one has truly understood the purpose of the destruction of craving, one has truly understood the purpose of the relinquishing of attachment; when one has truly understood the purpose of the relinquishing of attachment, one has truly understood the purpose of the cessation of craving; when one has truly understood the purpose of the cessation of craving, one has truly understood the purpose of the abandonment of the four nutriments. When this was said, those monks addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “It is well said, friend Ānanda!
