Although there is no connection with the present time [for the object], the connection with the presentness of that specific time is indeed directly perceived. Therefore, because it apprehends an object as being present, the cognition of the past and so forth is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*), since it possesses the determination of all aspects. If it is asked, "How then can that [object] be past?", [the answer is: because it is apprehended by the seer as being connected with his own present time, or because it is apprehended by others as being connected with their own time at that moment; and because, after rising from meditative absorption, the yogi engages in conventional discourse regarding it as being past. If it is asked, "How can what was seen by the yogi this very day be considered past?", this is not so, because: [The verse: "Because of the difference in location, the difference in the nature of the perceiver, and the difference in the state of the body, there is no contradiction in the pastness of an object seen by a yogi. (1.26) [The commentary: Just as a single woman is called a mother, a daughter, and a wife according to the difference in her relationship to different persons, so too, due to the difference in location, the difference in the nature of the perceiver, and the difference in the state of the body, there is no contradiction in the pastness of an object seen by a yogi. For example, when a person who has traveled to another continent sees a person born on this continent, he perceives that person as being in the future; yet for those born on this continent, he is already in the past. Furthermore, when a person who has reached the end of his life-span sees someone still living, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those whose lives have not ended, he is already in the past. Moreover, when a person who has attained the power of mastery over his lifespan sees someone who has died, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those whose lives have ended, he is already in the past. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, even though the object is seen by the yogi at the same time, it is designated as "past" based on the conventional usage of other people. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is argued that the designation "past" is merely a matter of linguistic convention, we say no, because it is established through the power of the object itself. For instance, when a person who has traveled to another world-system sees a person born here, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those born here, he is already in the past. Similarly, when a person who has reached the end of his life-span sees someone still living, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those whose lives have not ended, he is already in the past. And when a person who has attained mastery over his lifespan sees someone who has died, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those whose lives have ended, he is already in the past. Thus, the designation "past" is established by the power of the object itself, and not merely by linguistic convention. Therefore, there is no fault. Furthermore, just as the same woman is called a mother, a daughter, and a wife according to the difference in her relationship to different persons, so too, due to the difference in location, the difference in the nature of the perceiver, and the difference in the state of the body, there is no contradiction in the pastness of an object seen by a yogi. For example, when a person who has traveled to another continent sees a person born on this continent, he perceives that person as being in the future; yet for those born on this continent, he is already in the past. Similarly, when a person who has reached the end of his life-span sees someone still living, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those whose lives have not ended, he is already in the past. And when a person who has attained mastery over his lifespan sees someone who has died, he perceives him as being in the future; yet for those whose lives have ended, he is already in the past. Thus, there is no contradiction. Consequently, the cognition of the past and so forth is indeed perception. This concludes the discussion of the section on the proof of the existence of omniscience. Now, the following objection may be raised: "If the Blessed One were omniscient, he would necessarily perceive objects such as the taste of food. But if he were to perceive them, he would experience pleasure or pain arising from them, and thus he would be subject to attachment and aversion. Furthermore, if he were to perceive the suffering of others, he would experience mental suffering himself. Therefore, the Blessed One cannot be omniscient. To refute this, the author says: "If one were to argue that because the Blessed One perceives the taste of food and so forth, he would experience pleasure and pain, and thus attachment and aversion would arise, and because he perceives the suffering of others, mental suffering would arise—this is not so, because he has transcended the afflictions. (1.27) If one were to argue that because the Blessed One perceives the taste of food and so forth, he would experience pleasure and pain, and thus attachment and aversion would arise, and because he perceives the suffering of others, mental suffering would arise—this is not so, because he has transcended the afflictions. For although he perceives the taste of food and so forth, he does not experience pleasure or pain, because he has abandoned the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving and aversion. Likewise, although he perceives the suffering of others, he does not experience mental suffering, because he has abandoned the latent tendency of ignorance. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the latent tendencies? [the answer is: It is known because he has abandoned the afflictions. For one who has abandoned the afflictions has necessarily abandoned the latent tendencies. This is because the latent tendencies are the seeds of the afflictions. Since the Blessed One has abandoned the afflictions, it is established that he has abandoned the latent tendencies. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the afflictions? [the answer is: It is known because he has abandoned the obscurations. For one who has abandoned the obscurations has necessarily abandoned the afflictions. This is because the afflictions are included within the obscurations. Since the Blessed One has abandoned the obscurations, it is established that he has abandoned the afflictions. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the obscurations? [the answer is: It is known because he has abandoned the cognitive obscurations. For one who has abandoned the cognitive obscurations has necessarily abandoned the afflictive obscurations. This is because the afflictive obscurations are included within the cognitive obscurations. Since the Blessed One has abandoned the cognitive obscurations, it is established that he has abandoned the afflictive obscurations. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the cognitive obscurations? [the answer is: It is known because he has abandoned the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). For one who has abandoned the habitual tendencies has necessarily abandoned the cognitive obscurations. This is because the cognitive obscurations are included within the habitual tendencies. Since the Blessed One has abandoned the habitual tendencies, it is established that he has abandoned the cognitive obscurations. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the habitual tendencies? [the answer is: It is known because he has abandoned the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). For one who has abandoned the conceptual proliferations has necessarily abandoned the habitual tendencies. This is because the habitual tendencies are included within the conceptual proliferations. Since the Blessed One has abandoned the conceptual proliferations, it is established that he has abandoned the habitual tendencies. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the conceptual proliferations? [the answer is: It is known because he has abandoned the dualistic grasping. For one who has abandoned the dualistic grasping has necessarily abandoned the conceptual proliferations. This is because the conceptual proliferations are included within the dualistic grasping. Since the Blessed One has abandoned the dualistic grasping, it is established that he has abandoned the conceptual proliferations. Therefore, there is no fault. If it is asked, "How is it known that he has abandoned the dualistic grasping? [the answer is: It is known because he has realized the non-dual reality. For one who has realized the non-dual reality has necessarily abandoned the dualistic grasping. This is because the dualistic grasping is the opposite of realizing the non-dual reality. Since the Blessed One has realized the non-dual reality, it is established that he has abandoned the dualistic grasping. Therefore, there is no fault. Consequently, the Blessed One is indeed omniscient. This concludes the section on the refutation of objections regarding the proof of the existence of omniscience. Now, the following objection may be raised: "If the Blessed One were omniscient, he would necessarily perceive all objects simultaneously. But if he were to perceive them simultaneously, he would be like a sense-cognition, which is limited to its respective object. Therefore, the
It is understood that the state of being at the present time belongs to the seer alone.
How could it be logical for a different time to be a qualifier of something else? (613) (PVA)
For how could that which is the time of the agent belong to another object of cognition? Indeed, the whiteness of a horse is not applicable to a cow.
Now, how can that which is being perceived at that time belong to another time? Because it is perceived as belonging to another time. For instance:
Whatever has the cognition of a certain form, whether at that time or at another time...
That very thing has that same nature; however, it does not have time as its agent.

For time, being perceived as a qualification of another time for the agent’s object, how could it conform to the agent’s state of being at a different time? For the agent subsequently attains a different time, yet he perceives his own [object] as connected to that other time; how then can it be established otherwise? Furthermore, at that moment, even for the agent, only that specific time is perceived. It was stated that the agent’s state of being at a different time is something entirely separate from that time. Therefore, its existence is such that it is perceived as having that time—namely, "I perceived that today. This, however, is merely a conventional usage based on memory, not ultimate reality, because direct perception has ceased. Consequently, that which is perceived in every aspect is indeed direct perception.

[113, xiii] Furthermore, it might be argued: if that [object] were perceptible, how could there be no cognition of it by another? For if one whose son is yet to be has seen him as being currently experienced, how can there be non-erroneousness when he is not perceived [by others]? At present, this realization belongs to the yogin, not to the father of the son.
That too is incorrect;
for just as that [object] was seen as connected with the time of the body and so forth, so too its validity is not sublated.
However, the connection with that specific time was not seen by him; even if it is so perceived, there is no fault.

For he saw him as "his son" in relation to a future body and so forth belonging to that time. Even if it is perceived in that way, it is not sublated. Only if there were no perception at that time would there be sublation.

[114,ii] Now, if that which is seen by him today is seen in the same way by another person, whether a yogi or otherwise, why is there no seeing for him? To claim that it is invalidated because of such non-perception is also without substance.
If it is seen by one person from a distance, is it likewise seen by another?
Even when the existence of a horse or such is present, it is not perceived by everyone. (616) (PVA) Where the capacity of one exists, the capacity of another does not exist there as well.
The established position is that it is "future" because it is not perceived by non-yogins.
(PVA 617) Furthermore, it might be argued: even if it is perceived by this [yogin], since it is cognized in its own nature at that time, how could it be future?
Since non-existence is the non-apprehension of existence,
there is no existence whatsoever for anything even when there is apprehension, provided that non-existence [of the object] is present. (PVA 618)

[114, vii] That which is not being perceived is non-existent—this leads to an over-extension of the principle. Now, if it is argued that whatever is perceived at a particular time is existent at that very time, that too is incorrect.
[114, viii]
Apart from entities (*padārtha*), no such thing as time is observed;
rather, summer and the like are merely certain objects (*viṣaya*).

Indeed, no time whatsoever is perceived apart from specific objects; for coldness and so forth, as well as the particular movements of the sun, constitute the seasons such as summer. And if these are perceived, how can they possess the state of being past or future?
How, then, is the distinction between past and so forth understood in the case of summer and the other seasons?
"If it is not perceived by others, then there is no distinction between the two.

(PVA 620) Even if there is non-perception at that time, nevertheless, there is the state of not being present. Since it is not present now, how is there a distinction as to whether it is past or future? To this, it is said:
Inference should be understood as grasping that "it is just as it has occurred"; likewise, perception also understands that object to be exactly as it is. (PVA 621)

Just as that inference cognizes [an object] by way of its being past, future, and so forth, so too does perception, which is produced by that inference. For perception produced by that inference does not cognize it otherwise. Therefore, let it be understood that an object exists exactly as it is cognized.

[Objection: Surely, for perception that is produced by inference, there must be a gradual realization; and thus, because the realization of the continuum of beginningless and endless entities would never reach completion, how could there be omniscience? [Response: This is not so.
Through extreme habituation, he knows those objects instantaneously.
Just as for embodied beings, there is the cognition of fire from smoke all at once;

for those whose mental continuum is associated with repeated practice, the cognition of fire from smoke does not involve dependence on a sequence. Therefore, since the cognition is not sequential, there is no fault.
[114,xvii] But how can there be a completion of the comprehension of a thing that is beginningless? Or, if there were such completion, how could it be beginningless? This is not so.
[114,xviii]
If the Veda were also beginningless, how could cognitions arise from it? For there is no end to cognitions in that which is beginningless. (PVA 623) [114, xix]

If the Veda is beginningless and endless, how can there be comprehension from it? If, because it is beginningless and endless, there is no completion [of its study], then nothing at all could be performed. For if there was no comprehension from the Veda at another time, or if there will not be, then the Veda is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: Surely there is a cognition today [of this]: "This Veda is my director," because of such a cognition. Let it be otherwise at other times, or let it not exist; nevertheless, because it is that which prompts activity, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it is designated as that which prompts activity. [Reply: This is not so. If this object did not belong to it at other times, from where would it come now? If there is the suspicion that "the Veda was not for this purpose at other times," then it could not be a means of valid cognition even now, just as before. Or if it was exactly like this previously, then it will be so later, and after that even further—there would be no end to it. Therefore, when doubt arises once, there is no confidence in what follows either; thus, it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition. Alternatively, if the universal (*sāmānya*) is cognized all at once previously, then this is simply inference (*anumāna*). Consequently, if everything were inferred in every aspect, then even perception (*pratyakṣa*) would not be functionally distinct. Therefore, there is no perception of that which is beginningless and endless. And therefore...
[115,ii] In the delimitation of one's own continuum, that which is associated with it is perceived; and when that which is associated with it is perceived, there is also the perception of the other.
In this case, the cognition of infinite objects is not difficult to accomplish.

Therefore, through the repeated practice of the distinctions between unlimited causes and effects, there arises the manifestation of all distinct effects; and by the power of that, there also arises the manifestation of the distinction of the causes. This practice of means is the means for the complete comprehension of everything. Consequently, one who possesses compassion must necessarily apply himself to these means. As for the Veda, it has already been established that even when fully understood, it is not a means for the knowledge of heaven and liberation alone.

[115,v] Now, even if it were the case that through the practice of skillful means (*upāya*) both the desired omniscience and the abandonment of passion (*rāga*) are possible, nevertheless, due to the impairment of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), one might still teach otherwise during the state of non-concentration (*asamāhitāvasthā*). Furthermore, the occurrence of hunger and so forth would be an obstacle to the welfare of others; thus, there is no distinction between this [omniscient being] and the Veda. This is not so.
Because the Veda lacks a foundation, it possesses no ultimate authority;
it has no connection with its object, and even its conventional usage is without basis.
(PVA 115.vii)

Indeed, if the Veda were beginningless, there could be no initial apprehension of its connection with meaning; consequently, the ritual practice of the sacrificers would be entirely rootless, resulting in nothing more than a blind tradition. Furthermore, it has been established that even the appearance of conceptualized objects occurs through the power of convention, yet this does not entail the actual attainment of those objects, as is seen elsewhere. In this case, however, the basis is inference; therefore, there is no fault even regarding the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*). Moreover: [115, viii] Due to the cause of the acuity of the intellect, the predisposition is abandoned.
This is the distinction of the Great Sage from the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha] and others who act for the sake of others:

[626] (PVA) [115,ix] For one whose awakening is sharp, the entire collection of qualities and faults, even the most subtle, appears clearly. Although that which causes suffering is desired by one who is devoted to the welfare of sentient beings, he overcomes it through repeated practice. Even hunger and other such afflictions occur only for those possessed of contrary mental cultivation, and not otherwise. To illustrate this:
When, through the recollection of former births, there is a connection with one's previous support,
then, by virtue of being a deity or the like, hunger, wretchedness, and so forth are impossible. (627) (PVA)
Furthermore:
One who eats three times attains the same result through practice as one who eats twice;
even one who eats twice attains it as if eating once. Therefore, hunger is in every respect non-existent.
If, however, this were merely the way things actually exist and not something accomplished through practice, then: [115,xiv] All virtues and faults of embodied beings have their root in practice.

And that practice, which depends upon oneself, is best when directed toward virtues alone. (629) (PVA) [115,xv] For this very reason—namely, through the attainment of proficiency in practice—the Blessed One, the Sugata, is distinguished from the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas. Now, has the Teacher not indicated the teaching as the means for the cessation of suffering? And thus it was said: "He is the Teacher because he instructs the world. Therefore, how can there be practice of the means? This is true; however, the Teacher says that the teaching itself is the means and nothing else.
This very practice of skillful means is considered the teaching, because it has that as its purpose.
Because it exists prior to the accomplishment [of the effect], these two have been stated as the cause.

Indeed, the primary teaching is not what is intended; rather, it is the practice of the means (*upāya*). Why? Because it is for that purpose. For a word can denote something by virtue of being for its sake, just as a pillar intended for Indra is designated by the word "Indra. From where does this state of being for its sake arise? It arises from the presence [of those qualities] therein. Through the practice of the means and the proficiency of the intellect, the teaching (*śāsana*) is accomplished. How is this known? To this he says: "These two are stated to be the cause. Therein, the cause consists of the perfection of intention (*āśaya*) and application (*prayoga*). Intention is the desire for the welfare of the world; application is the state of being a teacher (*śāstṛtva*) through the teaching of the world. Why is it said that "these are stated to be the cause"? Precisely because of the initial liberation; for the primary [liberation] is not the cause of Sugata-hood. Therefore, it should be understood that the practice of the means alone is the teaching, and nothing else. Thus, through the practice of the means, the Blessed One becomes a Sugata.
[5] Because he is a Sugata, the Blessed One is an authority.
To the question, "What is this state of being a Sugata? he says:
The abandonment of the cause possesses three qualities; it is the state of being a Sugata because of its lack of dependence. 140.
The destruction of suffering is taught through the view of selflessness, or else by means of reasoning.

The cause [of suffering] is attachment, which is produced by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*), and which has conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as its object. The abandonment of that cause possesses three qualities because it is excellent, due to being irreversible and due to being an abandonment without remainder. Abandonment is the non-existence of the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. That non-existence is excellent because there is no basis for suffering. However, for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who still grasp at a self and what belongs to a self, their abandonment of suffering is merely a connection with the cause of suffering. For when there is grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, suffering undoubtedly remains. That very [grasping] is what must be abandoned. Why? Precisely from the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*). The abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by vision occurs through vision alone, or else through reasoning (*yukti*). Reasoning is practice, which is cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the mass of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation. Alternatively, "reasoning" (*yukti*) means yoga; it is non-duality (*advaita*) resulting from mutual integration. Or else, it is from the perspective of the vision of non-duality—either once through the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) or through the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). In every way, from the vision of selflessness, there is no reliance upon suffering. Thus, first, excellence is one quality. Second is the quality of irreversibility. To the question, "What is this irreversibility?", he says:
When "return" is mentioned, it refers to the arising of birth and defects. [116, vi] 141.
Through the abandonment of the seed of the view of self, there is no further return.

The arising of birth and the recurrence of defects; the state free from defects due to the absence of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; and non-recurrence, which is the absence of birth—this is the journey to the city of liberation (*mokṣanagara*). It is said that when defects exist, there is a recurrence of birth. Yet those very defects do not arise again because of the absence of the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*), owing to the uprooting of the seed of the view of a self. Furthermore, birth does not occur because of the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*); hence there is no returning. That "birth arises from afflictions and karma" will be demonstrated later. And he asks: since the view of a self is absent, how could there be affliction? He says:
Attachment toward a benefactor arises from the recollection of the benefit received for oneself; hatred arises from the recollection of harm; and delusion is the view of a self and so forth. (630)

Attachment and aversion toward one who benefits or harms the self do not exist because of the non-existence of a self. The view of a self, however, is delusion; it is directly subverted by the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*). In the vision of non-duality (*advaita*), moreover, attachment is even more thoroughly ceased due to the absence of any object.

If it is argued that the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is the result that eliminates the vision of a self (*ātmadarśana*) because it is its opposite, we reply: this mutual opposition is the same for both. Consequently, the vision of a self, once eliminated by the vision of selflessness, would itself become the eliminator; thus, there would be no non-recurrence, and therefore no cessation of everything either. Nor is there any other remainder from which recurrence might arise.
To this, the following is said:
[117,ii] Because its nature is distinct from those elements, it is entirely free from afflictions and devoid of decay. 142.

Deficiency of body, speech, and intellect, or even lack of proficiency in teaching the path—this is because that vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is real, whereas the vision of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is its opposite. Reality is the subverter of unreality by way of opposition; it is merely the opposite and possesses a distinct nature. However, the vision of a self does not possess a distinct nature, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is no self, as the self is unreal. What, then, is the remainder? It is "other" because of the absence of recurrence. To this it is replied: deficiency of body, speech, and intellect.

[117,iv] But surely, if that which was produced by afflictions (*kleśa*) lacks afflictions, how could it possibly arise? Nor does it follow that there is no exhaustion of what is not afflicted, because of the mere persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as in the case of the "outcaste woman" (*vṛṣalī*) example. There is a lack of proficiency in providing various etymological explanations for the Path (*mārga*). Well then, from where comes the abandonment of that remainder? For one who has not fallen away from selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is no other cause for falling away. Furthermore, as long as there is cognition (*buddhi*), there is no abandonment of faults (*doṣa*). Since speech is preceded by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), the Omniscient One (*sarvajñin*) would be proven to be nothing but an error. To this, he says: [117,v]
Through practice, there is the abandonment of everything without exception; by means of speech and so forth, there is the complete destruction of faults.

"No," say some, "because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful and non-deviant. For it has been stated that repetition produces proficiency of the intellect, and from that, latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) are eliminated. However, this is not established by mere assertion, because the proof for passion and so forth—the negative concomitance characterized by the absence of the opposite—remains doubtful. Therefore, because its negative concomitance is doubtful, it lacks probative force. Or, if the thesis (*sādhya*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the statement is deviant, because speech occurs even without discursive thought (*vitarka*) due to extreme habituation; speech indeed proceeds through the force of a mental impulse (*āvedha*). And it has been said: [117, vi] "No," say some, because its negative concomitance is doubtful and non-deviant. For it has been stated that repetition produces proficiency of the intellect, and from that, latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) are eliminated. However, this is not established by mere assertion, because the proof for passion and so forth—the negative concomitance characterized by the absence of the opposite—remains doubtful. Therefore, because its negative concomitance is doubtful, it lacks probative force. Or, if the thesis (*sādhya*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the statement is deviant, because speech occurs even without discursive thought (*vitarka*) due to extreme habituation; speech indeed proceeds through the force of a mental impulse (*āvedha*). And it has been said:
[117, vii] For conceptualization regarding all outflows (*āsrava*), there is no distinction from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor does verbal expression proceed solely because of an indistinct appearance. (PVA 631)

Because words are applied even to pillars and such things that are perceived through direct perception—as in "this is a pillar"—it follows that [the object] is [directly perceived]; otherwise, the word would not be applied.
Furthermore, no lack of clarity in the cognition is observed in this case.
Thus, the application of words elsewhere is not prevented either.
Therefore, it is established that even in the case of verbal expression, one is not at fault.

[117,xi] But surely, since there is no destruction of the defects through any other means, how can there be an absence of defects? For it is not the case that a cause for the destruction of defects has not been observed; nor is it the case that a cause for the destruction of defects does not exist. To this it is replied: How can something unobserved be postulated?
Furthermore, there would be no exhaustion of defects because they are eternal and because there is no means [to remove them]. // 144 //

Or one might imagine that it is due to a lack of thorough knowledge of the means (*upāya*). However, such an imagination does not hold in any way whatsoever; rather, it is possible because there exists a sequence of steps for investigating the underlying cause. If these defects were eternal, they would be inexhaustible even through effort; for it is not possible to bring about the destruction of what is eternal, even by a hundred efforts. Furthermore, if there were no means for their destruction, or if such a means were not perceived, then too they would be inexhaustible. But none of these three cases applies here.
[117,xiv] Because that which is contradictory possesses a cause, it is destroyed through the repeated practice of the [remedial] cause. 145.
By means of the knowledge of the intrinsic nature of causes, that knowledge is also established.

For that which possesses a cause lacks permanence because of its prior non-existence. Since the destruction [of faults] occurs when there is cultivation of the antidote to the cause, it is not the case that there is no means; for the antidote to the cause is the means for the destruction of the defects. Nor is there a lack of thorough knowledge regarding that [antidote]; for through the knowledge of the nature of the cause—which consists in the forms of "self" and "mine"—there arises the knowledge of the antidote, which is the opposite of that. For whatever is the opposite of something is its antidote, just as oil is the antidote to wind because of its being unctuous and hot, whereas cold and dryness are external due to their specific powers and so forth. Even though the external is not the antidote [to the internal], the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is indeed the opposite of the vision of a self (*ātmadarśana*); thus, there is no disagreement at all.
"(6) Because he is a protector (*tāyin*), the Blessed One is an authority (*pramāṇa*).

[118,ii] Even though the Blessed One has attained the state of a Sugata, how can he be an authority for others merely by the fulfillment of his own welfare? For one is an authority by revealing the non-erroneous object; not by revealing what is erroneous, nor by failing to reveal at all. This is not so. The Blessed One is a protector by virtue of compassion and through the application of skillful means (*upāya*). What is this "protection"? He says:
Because teaching the path he has himself realized would be fruitless, he does not speak untruth. (146)
Because of his compassion and because of his application to all undertakings for the sake of others.

For it has never been seen by anyone that such protection (tāya) is impossible; it is rooted solely in manifestation. Furthermore, for one who possesses the state of a Sugata, there is nothing left to be desired. Therefore, because of its fruitlessness, he does not speak untruthfully. Because he is compassionate, his practice of skillful means was performed solely for the sake of others. Consequently, there is no cause for him to speak falsely. Thus, due to the absence of both cause and motive, there is no false speech. Because of the application of compassion, the urging [of others], and the excellence gained through practice, there is no failure to speak [the truth]. Therefore, the Sugata is a *pramāṇa* (valid authority) because it is impossible for him not to reveal the path to liberation that he himself has perceived. [Objection: But merely stating a path one has perceived oneself does not constitute "protection" (*tāya*). Otherwise, all the founders of other sects (*tīrthakara*) would be *pramāṇas*, since they too state a path they have perceived themselves. [Response: That is not so; their teaching is merely a description of a path, yet it does not become [such a path] because it is not the true path. [Objection: In that case, how can there be confidence even in this [Buddhist path]? [Response: It has been stated here: "Because of the perception of selflessness (*nairātmya*), or because of the reasoning associated with it. This path is one perceived through reasoning. However, for those others, there is neither the perception of selflessness nor the reasoning [to support it]; thus, they are not *pramāṇas*. Moreover, their teachings lack the quality of being "perceived by oneself" because they are mutually contradictory.
[118,v] Furthermore, the Blessed One’s illumination of the Four Truths: ⟨...⟩.
Therefore, either the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or the threefold protection (*tāya*) is the illumination of the four truths.

Alternatively, *tāya* is the illumination of the Four Noble Truths and nothing else. Even though the illumination of emptiness exists in the Vedānta, because that [system] maintains the existence of a self (*ātman*), it is not the path at all; thus, the vision of the Four Noble Truths alone is *tāya*. This is the unique definition of the Blessed One’s purpose. Therefore, due to the absence of truth [elsewhere], he alone is the *Tāyin*. Although this path is devoid of [external] reasoning, like the purification of the womb, it is the cause of peace; thus, no other path has been taught. What are those Noble Truths? They are: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Even by these names alone, one may feel revulsion—just as one says "the urinary passage" and not "the vulva. That is not so.
<The Four Noble Truths> (a) The Truth of Suffering: The conditioned aggregates are suffering.
The aggregates of one in saṃsāra are suffering, because we observe the intensification of passion and so forth;
this occurs through habituation, not by chance, nor without a cause, since such birth would be a contradiction. (148)

[119,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchants being pursued by the bandits. Seeing them, he manifested himself in the form of a great elephant and went to the place where the merchants were. There, he caused the bandits to lose their way and dispersed them. Having scattered the bandits, he restored the merchants to safety. Then, having manifested himself in his own form, he spoke these verses: “O merchants, you have escaped from the hands of the bandits; You have reached this place of safety through my power. Do not fear, nor be distressed; I am here to protect you all. I am Avalokiteśvara, the one who hears the cries of the world; I have come here for your sake, out of compassion. Then the merchants, seeing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, bowed down at his feet and said: “O Holy One, we have been saved from the hands of the bandits. We take refuge in you; please grant us your protection. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “O sons of good family, do not fear. You have already escaped from the danger of the bandits. Now, you must practice the Dharma with diligence, for the Dharma is the supreme protection. Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara vanished from that place and returned to Mount Potalaka. The merchants, filled with joy, returned to their homes and recounted this wondrous event to all they met. Thus, the fame of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara spread far and wide. [End of Chapter 119]

[Objection: Is it not the case that passion (*rāga*) is indeed pleasure, because it is a cause of pleasure by virtue of being a limb for embracing a desired woman? Hatred (*dveṣa*) also [is pleasure], as it is the cause for the elimination of an enemy. As for delusion (*moha*), characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is indeed pleasure because it is the cause of the intoxication and pride of the mind through the notion of "I. Likewise, the body and so forth, which serve as the substratum for passion, hatred, and the rest, are also [pleasure]. Therefore, there is no such thing as suffering (*duḥkha*). Even that suffering such as hunger is a cause for the great pleasure of satiety. Consequently, the Truth of Suffering does not exist; thus, the Blessed One’s teaching is useless, and he is not a Protector (*tāyin*). [Reply: This is not correct, because of the following:
Exhausted by contact with the path of saṃsāra, their happiness is destroyed;
the aggregates themselves are great suffering, yet through ignorance one perceives them otherwise. (634) (PVA)
Regarding what was stated— that passion and the other afflictions are causes of pleasure— it is said in response to that:
Attachment and pleasure have practice as their cause immediately following that;
they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature, because they follow the presence or absence of practice.

If indeed passion and the like were to arise by chance, or if they were eternal, or if they were [inherently] pleasant, then that would be improper. However, since they arise solely from habituation—as is evident from their increasing intensity and so forth—they are merely an unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpana*). Therefore, the abandonment of such habituation is superior, just like the abandonment of the practice of childish play. Consequently, there is no pleasure in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*); pleasure is characterized by the mind’s delight. Since even the cessation of the phenomena of cyclic existence occurs through habituation, the practice of reality (*tattvābhyāsa*) alone is better. Why? Because even pleasure is desired only through habituation; neutrality (*audāsīnya*) alone is better. This being the case, all this appears as pleasure only to one who is oppressed by suffering. It is better that the affliction of passion and the like does not arise than the actual presence of passion and the like, such as the embracing of a woman.
Having healed a wound, no person of sound intellect desires it again for the sake of the relief from its pain; such is the case when that [relief] has ceased. (PVA 636)
If the intellect delights in reality and is not subject to modification,
then unafflicted happiness proceeds eternally.
(637) [PVA] If it were to delight in non-reality, how could that happiness exist in cessation?
But as long as one has not transcended reality (*tattva*), even pleasure does not cease [the cycle].
(PVA 638) Therefore, whatever pleasure exists in saṃsāra, all of that is in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) nothing but suffering. To explain:
Just as desire and other such states are observed to be causes of suffering, so too should it be understood that pleasure is likewise a cause of suffering. (639) (PVA)

[119,xii] Just as the suffering of hunger and so forth is the cause for the pleasure of satiety, so too pleasure is the cause for the absolute cessation of suffering upon its departure. Therefore, because it is a cause of suffering, pleasure is not truly pleasure. This being the case, it is established that "the aggregates of those in saṃsāra are suffering," while the intensity of passion and so forth arises from habituation (*abhyāsa*). Since it arises from habituation, it has as its cause a preceding, similar, and such-like cause; thus, the state of being in saṃsāra is also established.
[119,xiii]

[Objection: Is it not the case that the arising of passion does not come from habituation, but rather occurs quite accidentally or from some other cause? Therefore, these [feelings] such as pleasure are ultimate realities. Consequently, the aggregates (*skandhas*) of a transmigrating being are not suffering. Or, just as pleasure and so forth arise from habituation, so too do suffering and so forth; thus, they are not ultimate realities, and the aggregates of a transmigrating being are indeed pleasure. [Response: This is not at all sound when viewed through the lens of logic. Therefore, birth cannot be produced without a cause, any more than [the production of] space and so forth. Nor are pleasure and so forth caused by something else [apart from habituation], because they possess proficiency [only] through habituation. Furthermore, no one habituates themselves to suffering such that suffering would become something derived from habituation. Rather:

When pleasure and the like, through habituation, consist of an active process of accumulation, then in the absence of that [accumulation], there would be suffering; however, the habituation to suffering never occurs in this way. (640) (PVA)

[120,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti said: "As I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata to be seen by virtue of his possession of the marks of a great man? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata is not to be seen by virtue of his possession of the marks of a great man. Why is that? Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the 'Tathāgata' by virtue of his possession of the marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that merit is itself without measure; therefore, it is called 'much merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man. Why is that? Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the 'Tathāgata' by virtue of his possession of the thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that merit is itself without measure; therefore, it is called 'much merit. Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the 'Tathāgata' by virtue of his possession of the thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that merit is itself without measure; therefore, it is called 'much merit. Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man. Why is that? Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the 'Tathāgata' by virtue of his possession of the thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that merit is itself without measure; therefore, it is called 'much merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man. Why is that? Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the 'Tathāgata' by virtue of his possession of the thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that merit is itself without measure; therefore, it is called 'much merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man. Why is that? Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the 'Tathāgata' by virtue of his possession of the thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: "Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that merit is itself without measure; therefore, it is called 'much merit. Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Because what the Blessed One has preached as the 'thirty-two marks of a great man,' that very thing the Blessed One has preached as being 'no marks. Therefore

Indeed, no one practices with the thought, "May suffering not be mine," for everyone engages in every activity solely out of a desire for happiness. Therefore, happiness is achieved through effort, whereas suffering arises by its very nature from the absence of that [effort], and not otherwise. Consequently, even suffering is produced by the habitual practice of happiness; thus, it is happiness itself that must be eliminated. But in ultimate reality, even suffering does not exist at all. That [notion of suffering] also arises only from the cultivation of fear toward it. Thus, suffering comes from the cultivation of fear toward it; and because of the absence of that [fear], there arises the perception of non-suffering in that very suffering, or the perception of happiness in happiness—but this is not in ultimate reality. Therefore, happiness brought about by mental cultivation is actually a cause of suffering. If that [cultivation] were not present, suffering would certainly not occur either. For one who is deeply attached to a son, suffering arises upon the son’s death, while happiness arises for that same person upon the son’s birth; yet neither is [ultimately] real.
[120,iii] There is no eternal separation for anyone from those things that are desirable; all pleasure experienced by those in cyclic existence only results in increased suffering. (PVA 641)
The attainment of happiness by repeatedly binding oneself to suffering does not possess logical justification;
for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
(642) (PVA) Now, if this were the case, no other happiness whatsoever would exist.
How can the avoidance of suffering in states such as hell be considered desirable? (PVA 643) Is there no arising of happiness even from the suffering of the denizens of hell?
For even amidst great suffering, there is a sense of pleasure when there is a cessation of another pain. (PVA 644)

Alternatively, suffering here is characterized by the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), while pleasure is its opposite, characterized by the self (*ātman*) and so forth. That is not so; for even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is through habituation (*abhyāsa*) that the self and so forth are established in such and such a way. And attachment (*rāga*) and the other afflictions have that as their root; they arise precisely from that habituation and not otherwise. If it is argued that since there is no cause for an ultimate reality, habituation itself cannot be a cause—and that what lacks a cause cannot be produced—this is not tenable.
(b) Refutation of the view that attachment and the rest are born from defects such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth.

[120, ix] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Lust and the other afflictions are not born of habituation, but rather are born of wind (*vāta*) and the other humors. For instance, delusion arises from a wind-constitution (*vāta-prakṛti*), hatred from a bile-constitution (*pitta-prakṛti*), and lust from a phlegm-constitution (*kapha-prakṛti*). Just as the root afflictions, so too the derivative afflictions such as envy and the like are born of wind and the others. Since wind and the others exist in an ultimate sense, and since they arise from a cause, lust and the others must also be ultimately real. This too is incorrect. [120, x]

If it is argued that [the property] is not a characteristic of wind and so forth because of deviation due to the mixture of primary elements (*prakṛti*), then why is another property of that [wind] not also observed? (148)

[120,xi] For whatever is the cause of something does not deviate from it, just as smoke [does not deviate] from fire. If great delusion (*mahāmoha*) and the rest were properties of wind and so forth, then they would not deviate from them. But this is not the case; therefore, the opposite is true. Alternatively, one might argue that for one whose nature is wind, there exists another nature that generates passion (*rāga*), and another that generates hatred (*dveṣa*); thus, passion and hatred [arise], and because of this mixture of natures, there is no deviation. That too is incorrect. [120,xii]

If that [effect] is not his property, nor is there any other property belonging to him when the cause is present, how can there be the occurrence of the cause if its effect does not exist? (645) (PVA) [120,
xiii]

If that very thing is its effect, how could there be another effect? If you say it arises from that very same thing, then why is it not identical to it? If it were different, then that difference would not exist; if it were an effect of something else, this would be the same case of deviation [from the cause]. [120, xiv] (PVA) 646.

Therefore, if there were no non-deviation from the properties of wind and so forth, then even if one were to postulate that nature for something else, the effect would also have to be postulated. Since an unobserved effect is not postulated, another nature should likewise not be postulated. Just as the cause is postulated from the effect, so too is the effect [postulated] from the cause due to its unobstructed capacity. Alternatively, if there is no unobstructed general cause, then even an observed effect might exist through the absence of a cause; or rather, let that [absence] not be the cause of it at all. Furthermore: [121, ii]
If, having abandoned a perceived cause, one postulates an unperceived one, then phlegm could not be the cause of passion; rather, something else would have to be postulated. (647) (PVA) [121,iii]

Now, it might be argued: "Whatever is observed is the cause of passion and so forth. But surely passion and the rest are observed everywhere; does that mean everything is a cause? If you say, "This is exactly so, because it is observed to be thus," this is incorrect, because:
"Not every phenomenon is a cause for everyone, for that would entail the consequence of universal passion."
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the self] is like form and so forth, then the same objection applies to that case as well.

If there were no predominance of specific karmas in that regard, then since all phenomena consist of passion and so forth, every living being would necessarily possess them. Consequently, whoever might be subject to phlegm and the like would be the locus of passion and so forth, leading to the absurd consequence that everyone has equal passion. To this, he says:

[121, vii] If it is maintained that passion and the other afflictions have all things as their intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), then there is no such thing as an "incapable" intrinsic nature; how, then, could there be a lack of uniformity in their effects? (PVA 648)

For when desire and the like are held to arise from the entire constitution (*prakṛti*), then the constitution— such as that of phlegm (*kapha*) and so forth— is the cause of desire and the like even when it undergoes increase or decrease; thus, it is impossible to prevent the occurrence of equal degrees of desire and the like.

Now, even if everything is of a common nature (*prakṛti*), because there exists another distinction (*viśeṣa*), there is no equality of passion (*samarāgatā*). If that is so, then since every cause is not possessed of that specific distinction, it would follow that not every phenomenon (*sarvadharma*) is a cause of passion. Alternatively, if it is argued that passion and the like are "all phenomena" because they have as their cause the entire complex of *kapha* and other constitutive humors (*prakṛti*), yet there is no equality of passion due to the specific internal transformation (*pariṇativiśeṣa*) of those very factors—this too is trivial. Why? Because:
[121,x] Just as a particular transformation is observed...
Thus, its lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāritva*) has been correctly demonstrated.

(PVA 649) For when a particular transformation (*pariṇativiśeṣa*) from which a cause of passion (*rāga*) and so forth is observed is itself also the cause of hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, then there is an invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāra*). In that case, even when establishing all properties (*sarvadharma*), the status of being the cause for every specific instance is also established. Since this applies to all specific instances of passion and so forth, the state of having equal passion and so forth is perfectly clear. Therefore, the reason "because of a particular transformation" is untenable, since that [transformation] is also the cause for all specific instances of passion and so forth.

[121,xii] Now, if it is argued that a specific transformation, inferred from a specific effect, is indeed observed as the cause for the non-mixture of passion and so forth— that too is incorrect, because: [121,xiii]
Smoke that has not been seen in the presence of fire would not have fire as its cause;
rather, some specific property of that very location would be the cause of the smoke.
(PVA 650) If smoke exists in a location with fire, it is not a specific property of anything else.
Therefore, smoke cannot possibly occur elsewhere than from that which is devoid of specific qualities.

(PVA 651) [121,xv] If, even though it is never observed, a specific quality is postulated merely on the basis of seeing an effect, then the principle of a fixed causal relationship would collapse everywhere. Alternatively, if one does not postulate a specific quality in that case—because such a postulation is contradicted by the observation of fire—then in this case as well, let the observed repetition be postulated; it is not reasonable to postulate a specific transformation.

[122,i] But surely it is accepted that visible form and the other [sensory objects] have the primary elements (*bhūta*) as their cause. Now, if it is argued that they are distinguished by a particularity of the primary elements, this objection applies only to you, not to us. This is because karma is the specific cause of predominance; otherwise, those [elements] would also be included within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*). Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) on account of them.
Moreover, because there is no distinction among defects even when there is a distinction [in the objects], the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
It is not the case that [the cause] is inferred from a modification by means of a modification, nor are all [modifications] produced by everything. (151)
Furthermore, it is not logical for the effect to be absent while its cause is present;
just as in the case of heat and so forth, there is also a transformation of passion and the like arising from pleasure and so on. (152)

[122,iv] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a mustard seed on the point of a needle; the person who is like a grain of rice, a grain of barley, or a kernel of millet on the point of a needle; the person who is like a banyan fruit on the point of a needle; and the person who is like Mount Sumeru. And how, monks, is a person like a mustard seed on the point of a needle? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, but he does not dwell having made the wholesome root of that faith a basis for his mind. He is endowed with virtuous conduct, but he does not dwell having made the wholesome root of that virtuous conduct a basis for his mind. He is endowed with learning, but he does not dwell having made the wholesome root of that learning a basis for his mind. He is endowed with generosity, but he does not dwell having made the wholesome root of that generosity a basis for his mind. This, monks, is called a person like a mustard seed on the point of a needle. And how, monks, is a person like a grain of rice, a grain of barley, or a kernel of millet on the point of a needle? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith... [as above] ...and is endowed with generosity, but he dwells having made the wholesome root of that generosity a basis for his mind to a small degree. This, monks, is called a person like a grain of rice, a grain of barley, or a kernel of millet on the point of a needle. And how, monks, is a person like a banyan fruit on the point of a needle? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith... [as above] ...and is endowed with generosity, but he dwells having made the wholesome root of that generosity a basis for his mind to a moderate degree. This, monks, is called a person like a banyan fruit on the point of a needle. And how, monks, is a person like Mount Sumeru? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith... [as above] ...and is endowed with generosity, and he dwells having made the wholesome root of that generosity a basis for his mind to a great degree. This, monks, is called a person like Mount Sumeru. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. As it has been said: "Even when other causes are present, the observation of another effect occurs because of the presence of a specific [cause]; thus, one may also postulate a specific unperceived cause. To this, it is replied: Let there indeed be another effect and another specific [cause] therein; however, when there is an excellence of the fruit, how can the excellence of the effect resulting from the excellence of the cause be denied? If it is argued that even in that case there is no other specific [cause], then in that event, that specific [cause] would not be a cause at all—so how could there be a grasp of the causal relationship? Furthermore, it is not logical for a perceptible thing to be an unperceived specific [cause]. Therefore:
[122,v] Through the apprehension of a specific difference based on that [cause], there is the apprehension of its being an effect.
Therefore, if no such specific difference exists, how can there be the apprehension of it being an effect and so forth? || 652 || (PVA)

[122, vi] Is it not the case that the reason “because of a particularity” (*viśeṣāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*)? No, there is no lack of establishment, because when bile (*pitta*) increases, hatred increases for one who is afflicted by the suffering thereof; for hatred arises from the affliction caused by the increase of all [humors], such as phlegm (*kapha*) and the rest. If it is argued that this does not occur for one who is by nature weak in hatred, we reply that this is equally true even when bile is in excess. Furthermore, the claim that it is produced by all [humors] is also incorrect, because it has already been stated that it is not produced by all.

Furthermore, even if there were no other distinct difference, nevertheless, let there be no difference produced by that distinction; why, however, should there be a loss of the effect? For, when the cause increases, an increase of the effect alone is logical, not a decrease. Otherwise, it would not be its cause, as has been stated; for example, heat and so forth increase when bile and so forth increase. [122, viii]

[Objection: But surely, when substances that increase [phlegm] are consumed, an increase in passion (*rāga*) is indeed observed due to the presence of phlegm (*kapha*). [Response: This is not so. For it is hatred (*dveṣa*) alone that arises from the affliction of disease. Indeed, passion and the like arise from pleasure and so forth, not from phlegm and the like. And pleasure is experienced by someone in some way through the awakening of internal latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, it is logical that passion and the other [afflictions] do not arise from the humors (*doṣa*). [122,ix]

Now, although passion does not arise when phlegm (*śleṣman*) is in excess, even so, that [excess] is not the cause [of passion], because its causal power is obstructed by the suffering born of imbalance (*vaiṣamya*). Nor is it the case that something which does not produce an effect due to another obstruction is not a cause; for if that were so, it would follow that everything is non-causal. To this, it is replied:
[122,x] If passion does not arise because of the suffering born of imbalance, [then...]
It must be stated by whom [the intoxication] arises; from that similarity comes the increase of passion. 153.

A man of passion may suffer from the imbalance of the humors, yet another does not; others may suffer from the loss of blood, yet the intoxication of one who is devoted to a single woman does not. (154)
If it is argued that [the cognition] would not be intense for any single [object], nor even for its parts such as form and so forth, we say:
no, because for all [objects] there is no exclusivity, nor would it be indeterminate. (155)

Even for one who does not perceive virtues, that perception of virtue might become a factor [for liberation], provided he were to perceive all virtues as virtues, since there is no distinction in the underlying cause. (156)
In whatever state one is considered to possess attachment, one would likewise not possess aversion;
for those two are of an identical nature, and no fixed rule is observed here. (157)

[123,iii] If, due to the equilibrium of phlegm (*kapha*) and the other humors, there is no occurrence of conflicting diseases and consequently an increase of *mada*—which has semen (*śukra*) as its other name—then that state is designated by the term "passionate love" (*smara-rāga*). This being the case, one whose humors are imbalanced, who is wounded by sexual intercourse, or who is excessively devoted to women would not be passionate, because of the depletion of semen. Furthermore, since semen is common to all women, passion would not be restricted to a single woman. Therefore, in the absence of an equal state of *mada*, there could be no intensity of passion toward one particular woman.

[123,iv] Now, if the object (*viṣaya*) is also a cause, then since there is no distinction between the specific qualities such as its form (*rūpa*) and so forth, form and the rest must also be causes. For instance:
With their minds rendered helpless by the noose of an excellence of form, lovers disregard their own wives and [direct their passion] toward another woman;
sometimes, due to a pretext, they manifest passion toward her. (653) (PVA)
Intoxication alone is not the cause of passion; therefore, there is no such restriction.
Consequently, because the presence of an auxiliary factor of intensity exists in one case but not so in another, there is no fault. This too is not more convincing, since:
viii] Because deviation is observed everywhere, there is no causal status at all for form and so forth, since passion occurs even toward that which is devoid of form. (PVA 655)
If it is argued that [the object] is the cause because of the existence of a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then form (*rūpa*) is not the cause,
since form is possible even in the absence of such a metaphorical designation.
Likewise, passion (*rāga*) and its metaphorical designation cannot logically be the cause of passion.
Since passion is observed even in one who is devoid of both [the object and the subject],
it is not the cause of all [passion]; for otherwise, it would follow that everyone would experience equal passion.

[123,xii] What is the aggregate of formations dissociated from form? It refers to those formations dissociated from form that are included within the aggregate of formations. What are they? They are: acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena, the state of being a common lot (*sabhāgatā*), the life-force (*jīvitendriya*), the two types of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the various unmanifest forms (*avijñaptirūpa*), and the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). What are the characteristics of conditioned phenomena? They are birth, aging, duration, and impermanence. What is acquisition? It is that which causes the possession of the dharmas of sentient beings. What is non-acquisition? It is the opposite of acquisition. What are the characteristics of conditioned phenomena? They are the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena: birth, aging, duration, and impermanence. What is birth? It is that which causes the arising of conditioned phenomena. What is aging? It is that which causes the transformation of conditioned phenomena. What is duration? It is that which causes conditioned phenomena to persist. What is impermanence? It is that which causes the destruction of conditioned phenomena. What is the state of being a common lot? It is the similarity among sentient beings. What is the life-force? It is the continuity of the aggregates of sentient beings. What is the attainment of non-perception? It is the cessation of mind and mental factors in those born in the realm of non-perception. What is the attainment of cessation? It is the cessation of mind and mental factors in those born in the realm of nothingness who have attained the meditative concentration of cessation. What is unmanifest form? It is the restraint or non-restraint of body and speech that follows from a prior manifest action. What are the unconditioned phenomena? They are space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation. What is space? It is that which does not obstruct matter. What is analytical cessation? It is the permanent separation from defilements through wisdom. What is non-analytical cessation? It is the permanent separation from defilements due to the lack of conditions for their arising. These are called the aggregate of formations dissociated from form. What is the aggregate of consciousness? It refers to the aggregate of consciousness that is included within the aggregate of consciousness. What is it? It is the sixfold consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. What is eye-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the eye and forms. What is ear-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the ear and sounds. What is nose-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the nose and odors. What is tongue-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the tongue and tastes. What is body-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the body and tangibles. What is mind-consciousness? It is the cognition that arises depending on the mind and mental objects. This is called the aggregate of consciousness. What is the aggregate of dharmas? It refers to the aggregate of dharmas that is included within the aggregate of dharmas. What is it? It is the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formation aggregate, and all unmanifest form, as well as the unconditioned phenomena. What is the feeling aggregate? It is the aggregate of feeling that is included within the aggregate of feeling. What is it? It is the sixfold feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact. What is the perception aggregate? It is the aggregate of perception that is included within the aggregate of perception. What is it? It is the sixfold perception: perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact. What is the formation aggregate? It is the aggregate of formations that is included within the aggregate of formations. What is it? It is the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the unmanifest form, and the unconditioned phenomena. What are the unmanifest forms? They are the restraint or non-restraint of body and speech that follows from a prior manifest action. What are the unconditioned phenomena? They are space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation. What is space? It is that which does not obstruct matter. What is analytical cessation? It is the permanent separation from defilements through wisdom. What is non-analytical cessation? It is the permanent separation from defilements due to the lack of conditions for their arising.
