Now, if it is maintained that the cause is indeed indeterminate, that too is incorrect. It is not logical to say that something arises from an indeterminate cause. For instance, attachment fixed upon one [object] would not be the motivator for one who is tormented by passion toward a deformed woman who has appeared unexpectedly, even though he is intensely longing to perceive beauty. Furthermore, if intoxication were the cause of attachment, then attachment would arise even in one who does not perceive qualities (*guṇa*). If it is argued that the perception of qualities is also a factor, then it follows that everyone would be attached, because the cause of qualities exists for everyone. If it is argued that the mere presence of qualities does not produce the perception of them, then from what does the perception of qualities arise? If the perception of qualities occurs without an object due to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then it follows that attachment and the like arise solely from habituation. Moreover, in whatever state a person abides when attachment occurs, hatred would not occur in that same state, because attachment and hatred are of a contrary nature due to their inequality. And that which is of a contrary nature does not arise in one established in that very state. If it is argued that it simply does not occur, that too is incorrect; for no such restriction is observed here.

Alternatively: if that nature belongs to both, then it follows that both must be identical. If you say, "It is exactly so," we reply: no, because such a restriction is not observed. For in this case, there is no observation of a restriction regarding simultaneity. If you argue that just as perspiration and the like do not always occur for one whose nature is dominated by bile (*pitta*), but only occasionally, so too it is with passion (*rāga*) and the rest—that is incorrect.
Sweat is produced by contact with heat; in the absence of that, it would not exist.

(658) But for passion and the like, there is no cause other than form and so forth. Since those [causes] are present and their causal conditions are complete, there is no absence of passion and the like. (659)

[123,xvi] Now, if there were a reversal of the restriction due to the convergence of latencies (*vāsanā*) produced by internal assistance, then in that case, the latency alone would be the cause of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, because passion would also arise from the cultivation of the syllable *u*. But it might be argued: "Even for one for whom passion and so forth arise from a distinction in latencies, why is this not a fault? To this he says:
Their activities are bound by the distinctions of the latent impressions of their own respective species. // 158 //
For one who possesses passion and the like, these faults do not necessarily follow.

For when passion and the like arise through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then, wherever a person’s latent impressions from a previous birth are connected, there alone they are awakened—by some means, at some time, and due to some cause. Since there is no requirement for visible forms and so forth in the determination of latent impressions, there is no room for the aforementioned fault.
[124,iii] <The Refutation of Passion and the Like as Being Properties of the Elements>:
Lest it be thought that passion and the like might be properties of the elements rather than properties of the wind and so forth, he says:
By this, the fact that the support is an element (bhūta) and its intrinsic nature (dharmatā) are refuted. 156.
Because of this negation, white and other such qualities do not reside in earth and the other elements.

As for the one who says that these are properties of the primary elements—earth and so forth—namely: "Passion arises when earth and water predominate; hatred arises in fire and air; and delusion arises in water and air"—that too is refuted, because it is inconclusive in all cases. Thus it has been said: "In whatever state one is considered to be passionate," and so on. Furthermore, the relationship between substratum and dependent has been refuted by the passage beginning with, "Because existence and non-existence have no substratum."

[124, vii] But surely, just as whiteness and so forth depend upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), so too do passion and the like. To this he replies: Whiteness and the like do not depend upon earth and the other elements. If they were dependent upon earth and the others, then the admission that form and so forth are distinct from the primary elements would contradict the admission that there are only primary elements; for in the admission of mere primary elements, there can be no relationship of support and supported. If consciousness were dependent on the primary elements, it would follow that there is a multiplicity of ultimate realities (*tattva*). If there were no distinction [between them], then the primary elements themselves would be one, because they are not distinct from consciousness. [124, viii]

But surely, if one accepts that visible forms and so forth arise depending upon the primary elements (*bhūta*), does this not contradict the refutation of a substratum (*āśraya*)? No; for the meaning of "depending upon" (*upādāya*) is not the sense of a substratum, but rather the sense of a cause (*hetu*). As it is said: "And the word 'depending upon' (*upādāya*) has the sense of a cause with respect to its own substratum. (160)

Because they exist inseparably, it is not tenable for them to have a distinct substratum; otherwise, the meaning of "derived" (*upādāya*) would not be that of a substratum (*āśraya*), but rather the meaning of a cause (*hetu*). For it is thus:
The simultaneity of a cause with its effect is not apprehended; for between two things that exist at the same time, there can be no determination of the relationship of cause and effect. (PVA 660)
xiii] From that, there is the relationship of locus and located.

Or, let it be that the relationship of support and supported, or the relationship of cause and effect, exists only between things that are simultaneous. Even so, because they exist inseparably from their own support, it is as follows:
[124,xv] If the restriction of form and so forth were due to the relationship of support and supported...
Let it be understood that these exist in an inseparable state.

(PVA 661) If there were a relationship of container and contained between those two, then in the absence of the contained, the container would either perish or, if it did not perish, it could not function as a container as it did previously. Consequently, it would follow that passion (*rāga*) and the rest also exist inseparably from it. Furthermore, this is stated according to the opponent’s own admission that there is no such thing as the "nature of the great elements" (*mahābhūtarūpa*) apart from form (*rūpa*) and so forth; yet, passion and the rest do not exist in an inseparable state, because they occur in some things at certain times and not others.
[124,xvii] If, like the power of intoxication and so forth, there is no separation from the entity, || 161 ||

If power (*śakti*) were a distinct entity from its substrate, it would perish when the substrate perishes; yet it remains while the substrate remains unimpaired. If it is argued that it departs [from one substrate], that is not so, because there is no difference between them. (162)
Because earth and consciousness are perceived as having distinct appearances:

the power of intoxication resides in a substance such as wine or fermented liquor and exists inseparably from it, because it ceases when the substance remains and because it arises again later. For instance, when a substance that is astringent and sweet comes into being, the previously latent power indeed manifests; and then it disappears once more.

Nor is this [consciousness] of a nature that does not depend on form, because it is perceived as such; likewise, passion and the other [afflictions] would also be dependent solely upon the body. (PVA 662)

That too is incorrect. For power is not a separate entity; indeed, power is not something distinct from the substance, such that the expression "the power of the element" constitutes a designation of difference based on the principle of treating a thing as if it were its own possessor (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), as in the case of expressions like "the body of a stone statue. That this is so will be demonstrated later.

Now, if fire and the like possess no distinct power (*śakti*), then what is it that is obstructed by mantras, tantras, and so forth? It cannot be the person, for he is not burned elsewhere. But if the power itself is negated, then its non-obstruction implies that there would be burning elsewhere. That is incorrect;
for if even the power is negated, how can this distinction be maintained?
For it cannot be said that even this [power] does not exist anywhere and exists somewhere.
(PVA 663) Surely, when there is a multiplicity of powers, is their distinction impossible?
That burning power does not exist [in the water], but another [power] is not prevented [from existing]. (PVA 664)
Alternatively, if something other than the combustible object itself is produced, then that [other thing] is not burned;
for it is by something else that another is burned, since there is no obstruction to its power.
This is not so.
From where have all those capacities of that entity come?
What could be done by those [powers] for this [entity], such that there would be a dependence upon them?

This entity does not depend on them; rather, it is from the cause itself that they are so [ordered]. Furthermore, if those powers did not exist, the effects would not arise in their distinct divisions.
For it is not the case that a multiplicity of effects arises from a multiplicity of potencies,
if [such a distinction] is observed in the case of fire and so forth through the division into burning and other functions.
That would not be possible, or else there could be no occurrence of fire and the like as having a single nature.
If it exists, everything would be combustible; if it does not exist, nothing would be so.
Furthermore, existence and non-existence of a single thing cannot both occur simultaneously anywhere.
That too must not be avoided, because:
[125,xvii]
Just as this [cause] possesses various powers from a single cause alone, why is it not accepted that it also produces various effects? Why is the unseen (adṛṣṭa) postulated?
(PVA 670) Furthermore, because various effects are observed, one postulates various powers.
If it is argued that those very [atoms] exist here, then that is simply their inherent nature (*svabhāvaniyama*).

Such a thing is produced by its own causes in such a way that, when conjoined with mantras and the like, it becomes capable of performing its function through differentiation; thus, [separate] potencies (*śaktayaḥ*) are redundant. (PVA 671–672)
Fire is a deceiver and a universal burner by its very nature even without a mantra;
yet it is only when conjoined with a mantra that it is capable of burning a specific thing.
It is the nature of the combustible substance that it is not burned by that [fire] alone.
"Because it arises from its own cause alone, it is burned by something else.

(PVA 674) Thus, by the negation of [inherent] capacity, the relationship between substratum and that which is supported is impossible. Therefore, that observed example does not prove the point at issue. (PVA 675)
Therefore, it is the entity itself that perishes; however, that which is dependent does not remain, but departs even while the substratum remains entirely intact.

Now, it might be argued that here too, the same would apply to the elements (*bhūta*) and consciousness (*cetanā*). To this, the reply is: because of the difference between the elements and consciousness. Indeed, consciousnesses do not stand as non-different from the elements in the way that capacities do. If one asks why this is so, it is because they are perceived as having distinct appearances.
A difference in appearance is everywhere the proof of a difference in reality.
Indeed, no other means for establishing difference is observed.
(PVA 676) Even if [an object] is apprehended by different sense organs and by different perceivers, if it appears as non-different, [it is not established as distinct].

[126, iii] In that case, how is it that such a cognition (*pratipatti*) is the differentiator, being of the nature of an appearance (*pratibhāsa*), rather than a difference in the cause of cognition? Or, if there is a difference in cognition due to a difference in its causes, then that very difference in cognition is the differentiator; any other factor would be superfluous. Furthermore, in that context, the differentiated appearance consists of the internal experience of consciousness in the form of pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth, and not the object’s state of being grasped in the form of heat (*uṣṇa*) and so forth. Alternatively, pleasure and the like are themselves of the nature of specific internal tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya-viśeṣa*); therefore, they are of the nature of internal experience. [126, iv]
For whatever state exists in a particular way is experienced exactly as such;
just as the perception of trees and other objects varies according to distinctions such as distance and proximity.

For a specific internal tangible object does not appear at a distance. Therefore, because it exists within the body as a part of the self, it is not perceived like an external tree. This is not a valid argument.
If this [tree] were indeed a tangible object, by what means could it be known?
If it were perceived by something else, the consequence would follow that there is a distinct sensation [of that sensation].
(PVA 678) Now, if it is self-perceived, it does not have the nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Why is its self-knowing nature not likewise manifested by another? (PVA 679)
If it is argued that because the reality is contained within the abdomen, there must be internal contact, which is sensation; [then we reply:
For that which touches the internal parts, there would necessarily follow the experience [of pain]; whereas even the touch of an embrace on the exterior is of the nature of pleasure.
When there is mutual contact between the two, let there be experience for both.
If one perceives another's form as "other," how can that which is other not be one's own self-form?

Now, if that very nature of the self becomes happy when touched by another, then it follows that the other must likewise perceive it in that way. If you argue that this is because the other perceives it in all its aspects, then if this object is a single entity, why is there not a perception of all its aspects? If, on the other hand, it is manifold and distinct for every atom, then, given the distinction between atoms of pleasure, there would be a perception of pleasure and so forth by someone [else] even regarding suffering; yet not even a trace of another's pleasure exists [for them]. Furthermore, if only one perceives those things known by oneself, then a man and woman would have identical experiences. If everything were perceived, it would follow that there is a perception of multiple atoms.

[126,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Thus it was said. If that is so, then what is the nutriment for the consciousness that is the seed of rebirth? It is the craving associated with that consciousness. For it is said: “Craving is the cause of the production of renewed existence. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness, being accompanied by craving, comes to be established in a new existence. And it is said: “With craving as the condition, grasping comes to be. Therefore, it is established that craving is the nutriment for the consciousness that is the seed of rebirth. But why is it not said that contact is the nutriment for that very same consciousness? Because contact does not exist at the time when that consciousness is about to arise. For contact exists at the time when the consciousness that has already arisen is present. However, since contact is the cause for the arising of the subsequent consciousness, it is called its nutriment. But if that were so, then the nutriment for the consciousness that is the seed of rebirth would be the contact associated with that consciousness, and not the craving associated with it. This is not a fault, because the nutriment is defined according to its primary function. Since craving is the primary factor in the production of renewed existence, it alone is designated as the nutriment. Furthermore, it is said: “Craving is the root of existence. Now, [it may be argued that] there is mutual conjunction because there is no separation. [We reply: No, because there is no conjunction apart from those [entities]. Or, if such a thing existed, the cognition of their distinction would be unavoidable. If it is argued that the non-cognition of distinction arises from conjunction, then there would be no cognition of their own-nature (svarūpa) at all; for they appear as distinct from other entities through the differentiation of consciousness. If, on the other hand, the whole (avayavin) is one and the same, then the opponent too would perceive it in that way. If it is argued that the opponent is unable to perceive it in its entirety, then its form is not being perceived at all. This is merely an illusion; and even this illusion consists only of a specific internal tangible form. Therefore, it would be perceived by the opponent in that same way. If there were one tangible object and another, such as pleasure and so forth, therein, and if the opponent has a single perception [of them], then [pleasure and so forth] must be other than that [tangible]. Therefore: [The verse follows: ...therefore...
Because the perception of the elements and consciousness appears as distinct,
there is a difference in their intrinsic natures due to the application of contradictory properties. (PVA 681)
If it is maintained that the state of pleasure belongs to that which is being touched by another,
then why does that state belong to the object being touched as a real entity?
If it is argued that beauty is not the cause [of pleasure], then what is this "beauty" considered to be?
For some, [the result] arises from their own inherent fortune (*svabhāgadheya*); for others, it arises from something else that is pleasing to them.
It is karma alone that stands upon the path of worldly convention under the name "fortune" (*bhāgya*).
However, no specific benefit is observed here in this present life.
Thus, even though there is no difference [between the series], the next world is established through consciousness; what is the use of further talk on this matter?
Or rather, if its beauty arises from its production [by causes].

If it were not consciousness itself, then another person might also perceive it. (686) (PVA) Now, if you imagine that it resides within the body of the perceiver, how can that which is perceived as being outside be contained within a body? (687) (PVA)
Since even the manifestation of form is not apprehended by another,
that which consists of self-awareness must be distinct from the primary elements.

Whether it be in a conceptual cognition or otherwise, it is not perceived by another; therefore, that cognition is indeed self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If it were argued that what is contained within another's body is not known, then it would follow as a consequence that another's body itself could never be known.
And if it were contained within the body, how could there be movement for that which is solitary?
For when one conceptualizes another object while situated in darkness, [the mind does not move]. (PVA 689)
One perceives the body without conceptual construction, and consciousness without the body;
therefore, the rule of simultaneous perception does not prove their identity.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let it be that [the mind] is distinct [from the body]. Nevertheless, the body alone is its cause; therefore, pleasure and so forth do not arise dependent upon latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), but are ultimately real. Since the body also arises from semen and other such factors, there is no other world. Because [existence] is exhausted through this very succession of worldly lives, there is no state of cyclic existence (*saṃsāritva*).
To this he says: "And as long as the body undergoes no change, the mind would remain of an identical form. (163)
Like form and so forth, what dependence on an object could conceptual construction possibly have?

For when the body is the cause or the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of passion and the like, then the mind would necessarily be of an identical form prior to any modification of the body, because the cause, the intrinsic nature, and the substratum (*āśraya*) are identical. Otherwise, the relationship of substratum and superstratum, as well as the relationship of cause and effect, would be untenable, since there would be no conformity with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Indeed, the color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities residing in the body do not become dissimilar simply because of the body’s state of similarity [to another]. If it is argued that there is no fault because specific differences are produced by the encounter with successive objects, that too is not tenable. For what dependence on an external object does mental consciousness or pleasure and the like possess? It has already been stated that they arise merely from the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
When, without depending on the body, there is a cause for awakening the latent predispositions (vāsanā), [then it arises]. 164.
Some cognition might arise for someone at some time; by that [cause], some [cognition] would occur.

For if the body were the cause, the aforementioned fault would apply. However, when it is accepted that cognition—specifically mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—arises for someone like birth itself, depending not on the body as its cause but on some cause that awakens the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), then by that cause some cognition would occur even when the body is unaltered, but not because of the body being the cause. Therefore, cognition arises from cognition alone, not from the body; thus, there is the state of cyclic existence (*saṃsāritva*).
[127,xix] He states another reason as well.
And because consciousness does not take up [another] consciousness, it is established. || 165 ||
If it is claimed that every object is connected with the power of consciousness, O Sāṃkhya beast, what other person, possessing a sense of shame, would venture to say such a thing? (166)
"There are a hundred elephants on the tip of a blade of grass, though never seen before"—the form that has now become visible was not seen previously. (167)
Even if the cause were dispersed in a hundred ways, how could that [consciousness] exist?

Because we observe that subsequent consciousnesses are either defective or non-defective depending on whether the preceding consciousness is defective or non-defective, it follows as a rule that they conform to its modifications. Thus, since consciousness does not arise from a body devoid of the appropriation (*upādāna*) of consciousness, the existence of another world is established. Furthermore, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of passion and other afflictions arising simultaneously.

[128,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the mother, the progenitor, and the nourisher of the Tathāgatas. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that this perfection of wisdom is the mother, the progenitor, and the nourisher of the Tathāgatas? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because all the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas arise from this very perfection of wisdom; therefore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the mother, the progenitor, and the nourisher of the Tathāgatas. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are unborn, how can there be the arising of the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas from this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are indeed unborn, yet through the power of skillful means, the dharmas of the Buddhas and the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas do arise from this perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, what is this ‘power of skillful means’? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is the power of skillful means by which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive any dharma as having birth or cessation, nor as being permanent or impermanent, nor as being suffering or happiness, nor as being self or non-self, nor as being empty or non-empty, nor as being with signs or signless, nor as being wishless or wishful, nor as being conditioned or unconditioned, nor as being compounded or uncompounded. This, Subhūti, is called the power of skillful means. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the great compassion for sentient beings; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-existent, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are non-existent, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, perceives the non-existence of all dharmas as they truly are; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like an illusion, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are like an illusion, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the vow to liberate all sentient beings; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like a dream, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are like a dream, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the cultivation of the roots of goodness; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like an echo, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are like an echo, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the teaching of the Dharma; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like a reflection, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are like a reflection, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the practice of the six perfections; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like a mirage, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are like a mirage, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the accumulation of the provisions for enlightenment; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like a magical creation, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are like a magical creation, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the transformation of sentient beings; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately non-arising, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are ultimately non-arising, yet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the path of the Bodhisattva; thus, he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately non-ceasing, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately neither coming nor going, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately without desire, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? For the nature of curd and so forth that was previously perceived cannot be seen again, even if the cause were scattered a hundredfold; how then could it exist there? (PVA 691)
If you cry out that "that very thing exists in another form," do not speak thus:
for if it exists in a form other than consciousness, how can it be [consciousness]?
(692) If it is maintained that it arises from the material cause consisting of the cognition of the atoms and so forth, [then it is not consciousness].

In every way, the excellence of its formative impression (*saṃskāra*) would have to follow [the cause]. (PVA 693) Furthermore, even if it were accepted that the father’s or others’ formative impression exists in the son, there is no universal following of the immediately preceding formative impression. (PVA 694)
Therefore, since consciousness arises from that consciousness existing within its own continuum, the existence of the next world is established.
Furthermore:
[128,xii] It would follow that there is no fixed order for the prior manifestation of passion and the other afflictions. || 168 ||

[128, xiii] If there were no other world, then there would be the manifestation of previously non-existent beings; in that case, there would be no restriction regarding passion and the like, and someone might even be free from passion. However, when there is arrival from another birth, then craving alone is considered the cause of a living being’s birth. Consequently, one who is born cannot be free from passion, because birth does not occur in the absence of passion and the like.

If everyone possesses passion and so forth because they do not transcend their elemental nature (*bhūtātmatā*), then it might be argued as follows: the elemental nature is the cause of passion and so forth, and since that does not depart, there can be no deficiency of passion and so forth due to the absence of a deficiency in its cause. If this is so, then for that very reason—
[128,xvi] Otherwise, everyone would be possessed of equal passion, unless it were due to a specific excellence of the primary elements (*bhūta*). 169.

For it would be so if there were no mutual distinction among beings; that is, if everyone were equally impassioned. But since such a distinction exists, not everyone is equally impassioned. If this is the case:

Even though the vitalizing force of living beings is undifferentiated, that upon which this differentiation depends—possessing decrease and increase—causes those [beings] to diminish or excel according to its own state. (170)

[129,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill this Jambudvīpa with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, that person would produce much merit. Why is that? That merit, Blessed One, is indeed immeasurable and incalculable; therefore, it is called ‘much. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, if someone were to take up even a single four-line verse from this perfection of wisdom and teach it to others, they would on account of that produce much greater merit than the former. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of this very perfection of wisdom. And those dharmas that the Tathāgatas teach—whether they pertain to the level of Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, or to the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha—all these dharmas are taught by the Tathāgatas through this very perfection of wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti, one should know that this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgatas, the giver of birth to the Tathāgatas, and the producer of the Tathāgatas. It is because of her that the Tathāgatas appear in the world. Subhūti, just as all the forms of the great elements are manifested depending upon space, so too, Subhūti, all the dharmas of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are manifested depending upon this perfection of wisdom.”

Regarding what was stated—that there is no fixed rule concerning passion and so forth—the opponent argues: "The aggregate of earth and other elements certainly exists as free from passion. Now, if some living being were to become free from passion, [that would be impossible]. If the objection is that just as a living being cannot be non-living, so too one cannot be free from passion—if this is the case, then just as 'being a living being' is not differentiated [among individuals], so too 'having passion' would not be differentiated; thus, everyone would possess identical passion, just like their status as living beings. Or, if some living beings are different from others, then likewise there could be someone with passion and someone else without it. Furthermore, if 'being a living being' is undifferentiated while passion and the rest are differentiated, then by whatever cause this difference arises—namely, due to the excellence of the primary elements (bhūtas)—so too, in the absence of decrease and excellence, there would also be absolute diminution, and thus one would be free from passion."

[129,ii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even though that cause possesses increase and decrease, nevertheless, the state of equality of the cause of passion and so forth is not diminished. To this, it is replied:

If, despite the difference [between individuals], there were no destruction of the similarity of nature that causes passion and so forth, then passion would be identical everywhere, because its cause possesses a similar nature. (171)

[129,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the power of skillful means, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, perceives that all dharmas are like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage, like a reflection, and like a magical creation. Having perceived them thus, he does not become attached to any dharma. Why is that? Subhūti, because all those dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the six perfections and mature sentient beings, and purify the buddha-field? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, yet because of the great compassion of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, he practices the six perfections, matures sentient beings, and purifies the buddha-field. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, generates the thought: 'I shall establish all sentient beings in the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so forth, up to the state of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Yet, Subhūti, although there is no real dharma whatsoever that attains the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor any that attains the state of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, nevertheless, by means of this non-apprehension of dharmas, a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes sentient beings in the three vehicles. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-apprehensible, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the thought of awakening? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is precisely because all dharmas are non-apprehensible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening. If all dharmas were apprehensible, then a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not generate the thought of awakening. It is because all dharmas are non-apprehensible that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, practices the six perfections and fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-apprehensible, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, or between defiled and pure dharmas, or between conditioned and unconditioned dharmas? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are non-apprehensible, yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the power of conventional designation, distinguishes between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, and so forth, up to conditioned and unconditioned dharmas. However, Subhūti, even that conventional designation is ultimately non-apprehensible. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are ultimately non-apprehensible, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give gifts, guard morality, perfect patience, exert vigor, enter meditative concentration, and cultivate wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives gifts without perceiving a giver, a recipient, or a gift; guards morality without perceiving a transgressor, a precept, or a restraint; perfects patience without perceiving an object of anger or a patient person; exerts vigor without perceiving a body, a mind, or a phenomenon; enters meditative concentration without perceiving a meditator, a state of concentration, or an object of concentration; and cultivates wisdom without perceiving a knower, a known, or a wisdom. Why is that? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty minor characteristics? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics through the power of the perfection of wisdom, yet he does not perceive those marks and characteristics as real. Why is that? Subhūti, because those marks and characteristics are themselves empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities through the power of the perfection of wisdom, yet he does not perceive those powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, or unique qualities as real. Why is that? Subhūti, because those powers, fearlessnesses, analytical knowledges, and unique qualities are themselves empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva turn the wheel of Dharma? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns the wheel of Dharma through the power of the perfection of wisdom, yet he does not perceive a wheel of Dharma, nor a turner, nor a listener. Why is that? Subhūti, because the wheel of Dharma is itself empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva establish sentient beings in the fruit of a stream-enterer, and so forth, up to the state of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva establishes sentient beings in the fruit of a stream-enterer and so forth through the power of the perfection of wisdom, yet he does not perceive any real dharma that attains the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor any that attains the state of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Why is that? Subhūti, because all those fruits and states are themselves empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a śrāvaka vehicle, a pratyekabuddha vehicle, or a Great Vehicle. Why is that? Subhūti, because all those vehicles are themselves empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, mature sentient beings? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, perceives that all sentient beings are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like mirages, like reflections, and like magical creations. Having perceived them thus, he does not conceive of them as real. Why is that? Subhūti, because those sentient beings are themselves empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, purify the buddha-field? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, perceives that all lands are equal to empty space. Having perceived them thus, he purifies the buddha-field. Why is that? Subhūti, because all lands are themselves empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahās

For if that similarity which arises from causes such as passion (*rāga*) is not lost, then similarity alone is the cause of passion. And when the cause is a general property (*sāmānya*), the similarity of the effect must consist of a cause of a similar nature; thus it is logical that the effect also has a similar purpose. However, if the effect were dissimilar despite the similarity of the cause due to the presence of degrees of intensity (*tāratamya*), then it would not be its effect at all, because it would lack the conformity with the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that cause. Therefore, wherever there is a degree of intensity, there must also be absolute non-existence, because of the existence of a degree of diminution—as in the case of qualities such as whiteness—or else it would not deviate from its similarity. What is the reason?
[129,v] For there is nowhere any gradation in the cognition of a cow arising from the same object—
whether in the case of earth and so forth, or here in the case of being a living being and so on.

For the cognition of a "cow" arises from a common nature; yet, with respect to being a living being (*prāṇitva*), there is no distinction among beings, nor even regarding passion and so forth. If there were some distinction... [there would be] that exclusion of its form from something else. Furthermore, it does not possess degrees of intensity—as in the worldly view of "earth" and so on, where one says "cow," "better cow," or "best cow," or "living being," "better living being," or "best living being. Therefore, if there is equality due to a common cause, then in the case of diminution, there would be absolute annihilation.

If it is argued that just as fire is never non-hot despite variations in the degree of its heat, so it is here as well, we say no; for there is no denial of the identity between fire and its heat. (173)

[129, viii] The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called 'The Lion's Roar. It should be learned by you. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. 129.8. The Lion's Roar Sūtra is concluded. 129.9. The Discourse on the Four Noble Truths. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One were to teach me the Dharma-discourse known as 'The Four Noble Truths,' so that I might hear it from the Blessed One. The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, listen attentively and bear it well in mind; I shall speak. "So be it, Blessed One," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then said: "Ānanda, these four noble truths are taught by me. What four? They are: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. What, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the beloved is suffering, not obtaining what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. What, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding pleasure here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. What, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, and detachment. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. What, Ānanda, is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the four noble truths taught by me. And how, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering to be fully understood? How is the noble truth of the origin of suffering to be abandoned? How is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering to be realized? And how is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering to be cultivated? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple, having heard the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, understands as it really is: 'This is the noble truth of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, Ānanda, he understands as it really is: 'This noble truth of suffering must be fully understood. He understands as it really is: 'This noble truth of the origin of suffering must be abandoned. He understands as it really is: 'This noble truth of the cessation of suffering must be realized. He understands as it really is: 'This noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering must be cultivated. As long as, Ānanda, in a noble disciple this vision of the Dharma regarding these four noble truths has not become threefold and twelvefold, and he has not practiced the path in accordance with the Dharma, he is not yet one who has entered the stream, nor is he one who has reached the fruit of stream-entry. But when, Ānanda, in a noble disciple this vision of the Dharma regarding these four noble truths has become threefold and twelvefold, and he has practiced the path in accordance with the Dharma, then he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, firmly established, destined for full enlightenment. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the four noble truths taught by me. And how, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering to be fully understood? By seeing with wisdom as it really is. How is the noble truth of the origin of suffering to be abandoned? By seeing with wisdom as it really is. How is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering to be realized? By seeing with wisdom as it really is. And how is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering to be cultivated? By seeing with wisdom as it really is. When, Ānanda, a noble disciple has seen with wisdom as it really is, then he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, firmly established, destined for full enlightenment. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the four noble truths taught by me. And how, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering to be fully understood? By practicing the path. How is the noble truth of the origin of suffering to be abandoned? By practicing the path. How is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering to be realized? By practicing the path. And how is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering to be cultivated? By practicing the path. When, Ānanda, a noble disciple has practiced the path, then he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, firmly established, destined for full enlightenment. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the four noble truths taught by me. And how, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering to be fully understood? By the destruction of craving. How is the noble truth of the origin of suffering to be abandoned? By the destruction of craving. How is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering to be realized? By the destruction of craving. And how is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering to be cultivated? By the destruction of craving. When, Ānanda, a noble disciple has destroyed craving, then he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, firmly established, destined for full enlightenment. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the four noble truths taught by me. And how, Ānanda, is the noble truth of suffering to be fully understood? By the destruction of ignorance. How is the noble truth of the origin of suffering to be abandoned? By the destruction of ignorance. How is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering to be realized? By the destruction of ignorance. And how is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering to be cultivated? By the destruction of ignorance. When, Ānanda, a noble disciple has destroyed ignorance, then he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, firmly established, destined for full enlightenment. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These,

Indeed, there exists here a gradation (*tāratamya*) of the heat of fire, yet it is not impossible for heat to exist in its entirety [in all fire]. Nevertheless, it is not the case that passion (*rāga*) and the like are entirely impossible in the same way, because passion and the like are not distinct from the body. Here, there is no difference between fire and heat; for "fire" is merely a designation for heat itself. If heat were absent, that which is called fire would simply not exist. However, in the absence of passion and the like, the primary elements (*bhūta*) themselves do not cease to exist. If, however, one imagines that the composite of the primary elements is a separate substratum (*dharmin*) and that heat is its attribute (*dharma*), then heat would indeed be subject to cessation during the state of fever. Or, if one imagines that the flame is the substratum and heat is its attribute—which does not cease even amidst the gradations—this is the opponent’s rebuttal. That too is untenable.
[130,i] Through the power of mantras, tantras, and so forth, it might be that [fire] exists without heat;
however, that a gem is seen to have flames even without heat is not logical. (PVA 695)
The flame does not possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*) with respect to heat, because it is not distinct from it;
for color and shape, such as those of the flame, cannot possibly belong to heat.

It is not logical for that [heat] to be the subject (dharmin); therefore, this is not a valid illustration. A flame does not exist without heat, nor does heat exist without a flame; thus, it is not appropriate for that [heat] to be the subject. Furthermore, the relationship of property and property-possessor (dharmadharmibhāva) does not exist between a flame and its heat if they are not absolutely inseparable. Therefore, the reason (hetu) must be accompanied by a qualification.

The qualities of whatever other existing thing experiences degrees of intensity are obstructed in certain cases when there is a difference in that [substratum], just like white and other colors. // 174 //

[130, viii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, are not subject to falling back. “Which four? “Here, Ānanda, a certain person has abandoned the three fetters and attenuated lust, hatred, and delusion; this one is called a ‘once-returner,’ who, after returning to this world once more, will make an end of suffering. This is the first kind of person who, having entered the stream, is not subject to falling back. Again, Ānanda, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; this is the second kind of person who, having entered the stream, is not subject to falling back. Again, Ānanda, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; this is the third kind of person who, having entered the stream, is not subject to falling back. Again, Ānanda, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained parinirvāṇa with effort while dwelling in this very life; this is the fourth kind of person who, having entered the stream, is not subject to falling back. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, are not subject to falling back.”

The qualities (*guṇa*) of another thing, while existing and undergoing degrees of intensity (*tāratamya*), are nowhere subject to obstruction (*pratighāta*). For example, whiteness and other such qualities in jars and the like. [Objection: But apart from the form of whiteness and so forth, what else is there that constitutes the cloth? By what means could there be the destruction of those [qualities] such as whiteness when the other [the cloth] exists? [Response: This is true; nevertheless, jars and the like have the nature of being tangible (*spṛśyarūpa*), not the nature of being specific colors. Because the cloth exists even in the absence of that [tangibility]. Therefore, the meaning of "of another" is as follows: of that which persists as a continuum (*saṃtāna*), those things which possess the property of arising and the property of ceasing—even if they are of an absolutely ceasing nature—are like whiteness and so forth; this is the sense of the sentence.

Alternatively, even though there is a variation in the degree of the arising and ceasing of heat while non-fireness persists, it is not the case that because of the existence of the destruction of passion and so forth, there is no destruction of their capacity (*śakti*). This is not so, because the capacity is a distinct entity. It is not the case that passion and so forth are themselves the capacity, since the destruction of capacity is observed in some instances. For this very reason, he says:
There is no such restriction for them as there is for form and so forth, because they are inseparable from the primary elements (*bhūta*).
If it is argued that this is the same [for desire and so on], it is not so, because it would entail the consequence that desire and the rest arise simultaneously [with their objects]. (175)

[130,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever as real. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they are not real; because they are not real, they do not arise; because they do not arise, they do not cease; because they do not cease, they are neither defiled nor purified. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Subhūti and those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines is concluded. [130,xi] The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines is completed.
