Indeed, passion and the like are not inseparable from the elements in the same way that color, taste, and so forth are; for the elements exist even in the absence of passion and the like, whereas color and the rest do not exist in the absence of the elements. If it is argued that the same applies there as well [to color and the rest], that too is incorrect. For it would entail the consequence that passion and the like arise simultaneously with the body. There would be no distinction between them and the elements. Furthermore, even the manifestation of color and the rest is not always co-existent with the body. Moreover, for one who maintains that there are only the great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is no otherness of color and the rest from the elements, because that would entail the consequence of a multiplicity of principles (*tattva*). Therefore, their simultaneous arising is characterized by inseparability, since they have the objects as their cause.
If it is argued that there might sometimes be an absence [of cognition] when the object is not present, that is not so.
Furthermore, because they are the objects of conceptual construction, objects are not restrictive [factors].
Nor is there a restriction [of passion and so forth] due to the absence of a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu). // 176 //
Or else, the birth of all cognitions would occur at all times, due to the constant presence of their causes.

Indeed, attachment and the rest do not follow the positive and negative concomitance of their objects, nor do they belong to that same continuum, because they are observed to arise even in the absence of those objects. Furthermore, a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is not admitted for them. Therefore, it is not the case that attachment and the rest never arise due to the absence of those objects. Consequently, the body would either invariably coexist with each individual instance of attachment and so forth, or else all instances of attachment and the rest would coexist with the body at once, since the body—their common cause—is present. If it is argued that there is a specific transformation of the body such that it does not coexist with attachment and the rest, then [it follows as follows]: [131,v]
From what cause could such a transformation of that [cause] arise, by which it would become so?
If you say "from some [unknown] cause," then it might not occur at all times.
If you argue that this is not so because we do not observe it, then nothing whatsoever would be caused.
Smoke might even arise from what is not fire; why should it not be possible for it to arise from anywhere? (698) (PVA) For it could indeed be said that it is a certain transformation of that [fire];
yet even for an entity that lacks a cause, there would have to be a restriction of place and so forth. (699) (PVA)
In that case as well, it can be said that no such restriction is observed.
If one were to embrace everything merely because it has been seen, then non-duality itself would be perceived here, and conventional practice would fall apart. (700) (PVA)

If it is argued that conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) must be postulated because it cannot be abandoned, then how could this same conventional practice regarding the next world and so forth be otherwise?
For all conventional practice is carried out by means of inference (*anumāna*). (PVA 701–702)
In the same way, how could [the existence of] the next world and so forth be established?
There is no distinction in terms of being an object of cognition, nor is there any form such as blue and so on;
it is not established by perception through the relation of preceding and succeeding moments. (703) (PVA)
Therefore, every distinction [between things] exists through inference, just like everyday linguistic practice.
Consequently, no one is able to live by abandoning inference.
To this, the following was replied:
"Those who, having set aside an observed object, postulate another unobserved one... (PVA 705).
Fools, having abandoned the essential mass [of reality], vainly strike at the sense-faculties;

for discrimination regarding what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted does not arise from the functioning of the senses alone. (706) [PVA] Why is it that "this is to be rejected" does not follow merely from perception?
Or, because the state of being acceptable is the negation of the state of being rejectable, there is the establishment of what is to be accepted;
for the opposite of being rejectable is the acceptability of that which possesses causal efficiency for those who seek such efficiency. (707–708) (PVA)
She was not seen by direct perception when one desired to obtain her livelihood;
therefore, there is no cognition of the state of being "to be acquired" through direct perception.
Direct perception does not know a future causal efficacy, nor does it know that which is unperceived.
Even if there were a negation of the state of being avoidable, how could there be the cessation of the desire for what is avoidable?
(710) Therefore, in this case, the cognition that "the object does not exist" is not undermined by the senses;
for when both [objects] are perceived directly, there is no apprehension of anything to be avoided or accepted. (711)
Here too, the previous reasoning recurs:
"If everything is cognized through perception due to extreme habituation, then there can be no habituation regarding what is not cognized; thus, there is a mutual dependence. (PVA 712)
As long as there is no direct perception through repeated practice, there is no cognition of non-existence;
and as long as there is no cognition of non-existence, there is no arising of direct perception through practice.
If, in this case, mere direct perception were the means of valid cognition, there would be no distinction between that which is to be abandoned and its opposite;
for that would be merely the cognition of the thing's own nature, and from that, the consequence of non-duality (advaita) follows. (714) (PVA)

The classification of what is to be abandoned and so forth, based upon inference, pertains to conventional practice; that which is thus established is not further scrutinized for its ultimate reality. (715) Now, if one relies on non-duality to refute the existence of another world...
Let this [objection] also be addressed; it does not stop at this much alone.
(PVA 716) Even in this world, there is no such thing as "it does not exist," and therefore there is no nihilism (*nāstikatā*).
Since the mind withdraws from everything, that being the case, [the objection] is indeed appropriate. (PVA 717)
Now, this very regard for things in this world is itself a delusion.
Who, desiring the destruction of even this, would seek another delusion?
(718) (PVA) From where indeed does this delusion arise, if it is beginningless and endless?
That other world is well-established; what else has been said in vain?
(PVA 719) Or, if this [world] is indeed causeless, then let everything be causeless. That being the case, it follows in vain that you, as a nihilist, have spoken thus. (PVA 720)
If this [inference] that has been stated is not useful anywhere, for what purpose is it sought?
Or, if it has some purpose, let its status as a cause reside in that very [purpose].
Now, if opponents raise such an objection: [721] (PVA) If others proceed with this kind of questioning...
What is the purpose of that which has been done, if it is not the cause of anything? (PVA 722) If this [world] is indeed produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), whose fault is it?
If ignorance is not eradicated, then the discourse of others is in vain. (PVA 723)
Moreover, if ignorance were to be destroyed, the doctrine propounded by the opponent would be rendered meaningless;
or, if it were caused by ignorance, there would have to be a beginningless continuity of ignorance.
This being the case, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is established as a matter of course, beyond dispute.
Ignorance is nothing other than conceptual construction, and that [construction] also arises from prior conceptual constructions; thus,
this beginningless continuity of conceptual construction is established as it appears.

Therefore, pleasure and the like are brought about solely by the maturation of beginningless latencies (*vāsanā*), and do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Consequently, in ultimate reality, everything is indeed suffering.
(d) The Truth of Suffering has four aspects.
[132,xv] Therein, suffering is as follows:

Because it is perceived only occasionally, it is impermanent; because it is the basis of defects, it is suffering; and because it is subject to causes, it is neither a self nor is it governed by one. (177)
A controller cannot exist without a cause, nor can there be a permanent creator;
therefore, that which is manifold does not arise from a single [cause] at a different time. (178)

[132,xviii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is a seeker of the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna); the person who is a seeker of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka), and the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin); the person who is a seeker of non-returning (anāgāmi-pratipannaka), and the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin); the person who is a seeker of arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka), and the person who is an arhat. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the person who is a seeker of the stream? Here, a certain person possesses right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of the stream. What is the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry? Here, a certain person has abandoned the three fetters: namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa). He is not subject to rebirth in the lower realms, is firmly established, and is destined for full awakening. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry. What is the person who is a seeker of once-returning? Here, a certain person has attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill will (vyāpāda). This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of once-returning. What is the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning? Here, a certain person has attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will. Having attained this state, he will return to this world only once more; having returned once more, he will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning. What is the person who is a seeker of non-returning? Here, a certain person has completely abandoned the five lower fetters: namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of non-returning. What is the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning? Here, a certain person has completely abandoned the five lower fetters. By means of this very body, he attains parinirvāṇa; or else, having arisen in a higher realm, he attains parinirvāṇa there. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning. What is the person who is a seeker of arhatship? Here, a certain person dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of arhatship. What is the person who is an arhat? Here, a certain person has abandoned the outflows (āsrava), has lived the holy life, has done what was to be done, has laid down the burden, has attained his own goal, has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge. This, monks, is called the person who is an arhat. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [132,xix] What is the person who is a seeker of the stream? Here, a certain person possesses right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of the stream. What is the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry? Here, a certain person has abandoned the three fetters: namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and adherence to rules and rituals. He is not subject to rebirth in the lower realms, is firmly established, and is destined for full awakening. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry. What is the person who is a seeker of once-returning? Here, a certain person has attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of once-returning. What is the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning? Here, a certain person has attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will. Having attained this state, he will return to this world only once more; having returned once more, he will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning. What is the person who is a seeker of non-returning? Here, a certain person has completely abandoned the five lower fetters: namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of non-returning. What is the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning? Here, a certain person has completely abandoned the five lower fetters. By means of this very body, he attains parinirvāṇa; or else, having arisen in a higher realm, he attains parinirvāṇa there. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning. What is the person who is a seeker of arhatship? Here, a certain person dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of arhatship. What is the person who is an arhat? Here, a certain person has abandoned the outflows, has lived the holy life, has done what was to be done, has laid down the burden, has attained his own goal, has utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge. This, monks, is called the person who is an arhat. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [132,xx] What is the person who is a seeker of the stream? Here, a certain person possesses right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of the stream. What is the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry? Here, a certain person has abandoned the three fetters: namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and adherence to rules and rituals. He is not subject to rebirth in the lower realms, is firmly established, and is destined for full awakening. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of stream-entry. What is the person who is a seeker of once-returning? Here, a certain person has attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of once-returning. What is the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning? Here, a certain person has attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire and ill will. Having attained this state, he will return to this world only once more; having returned once more, he will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of once-returning. What is the person who is a seeker of non-returning? Here, a certain person has completely abandoned the five lower fetters: namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will. This, monks, is called the person who is a seeker of non-returning. What is the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning? Here, a certain person has completely abandoned the five lower fetters. By means of this very body, he attains parinirvāṇa; or else, having arisen in a higher realm, he attains parinirvāṇa there. This, monks, is called the person who is established in the fruit of non-returning. What is the person who is a seeker of arhatship? Here, a certain person dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly

The Truth of Suffering has four aspects: as impermanent (*anitya*), as suffering (*duḥkha*), as empty (*śūnya*), and as non-self (*anātman*). It is impermanent because it is perceived only at certain times. That which is permanent is not impermanent by virtue of being perceived at all times. Indeed, for that which is permanent and always perceived, occasional perception is illogical; for there is a contradiction between the natures of being perceived and not being perceived, as they exist through mutual exclusion. This is because [the opponent] asserts that [the object] is [permanent] precisely by its being perceived. Furthermore, it is impossible to perceive everything at all times, because that which is perceived sequentially must be impermanent. Sequence is not possible in a single entity, because a single thing does not appear as possessing sequence. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not apply here; inference (*anumāna*) is absent in the absence of that [perception], since inference is preceded by direct perception. If [inference] were preceded by inference, it would lead to the fallacy of a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*). Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*) of those in saṃsāra are unstable. They are suffering because they are the basis for defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, and because they are subject to causes. Suffering arises from the obstruction of causes, according to the principle: "Everything dependent on another is suffering. By the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that [they are suffering] because they depend solely on habitual practice (*abhyāsa*). They do not have the nature of a self (*ātman*), nor are they presided over by a non-self. A causeless entity cannot be a presider. There must necessarily be a presider who possesses utility, because a cause is defined by being the source of utility. If the aggregates had the nature of a self, they would be permanent. But a permanent thing cannot be a producer, because the existence of a non-producer is impossible to perceive. Furthermore, a single cognition occurring at different times cannot arise from a single [cause] due to its permanence. Nor is the form of the aggregates perceived as being presided over by a self; rather, that which is perceived is the form of the aggregates.

[133,i] That [world] is impermanent. Now, how do causes that are not presided over by an agent proceed toward their own effects? Therefore, a presiding agent is inferred. No; because [the process] is fully accounted for by mere presiding over by an impermanent consciousness, and that consciousness is beginningless.
When other causes have come together yet the effect does not arise, there may be an inference of another cause; this, however, is not possible in the case of eternal things. (176)

[133,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without characteristics, nor does he perceive that the absence of characteristics is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without characteristics, nor does he perceive that the absence of characteristics is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without aspiration, nor does he perceive that the absence of aspiration is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without aspiration, nor does he perceive that the absence of aspiration is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is unproduced, nor does he perceive that non-production is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unproduced, nor does he perceive that non-production is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is unceasing, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unceasing, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is pure, nor does he perceive that purity is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, nor does he perceive that purity is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without increase, nor does he perceive that non-increase is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without increase, nor does he perceive that non-increase is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without decrease, nor does he perceive that non-decrease is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without decrease, nor does he perceive that non-decrease is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without attainment, nor does he perceive that non-attainment is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attainment, nor does he perceive that non-attainment is consciousness. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, he is said to be practicing the perfection of wisdom. [133,iv] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, become one who has set out correctly? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, a person, a human, a man, a youth, a doer, a feeler, a knower, or a seer. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, the nose-consciousness, the tongue-consciousness, the body-consciousness, or the mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death. He does not perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, he is said to be one who has set out correctly. [134,i] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the reason why a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, a person, a human, a man, a youth, a doer, a feeler, a knower, or a seer? Why does he not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness? Why does he not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind? Why does he not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena? Why does he not perceive eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness? Why does he not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind? Why does he not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind? Why does he not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element? Why does he not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death? Why does he not perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path? Why does he not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship? Why does he not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be perceived. Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a being, nor does he perceive a soul, a person, a human, a man, a youth, a doer, a feeler, a knower, or a seer. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. He does not perceive eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death. He does not perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. [134,ii] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, attain the supreme perfect enlightenment? How can

If other causes, even when combined, are not producers of the effect, then there must exist another cause, whose absence results in the non-arising of the effect. But this is not the case, because the production of the effect is established merely by the specific capacity (*yogyatā-viśeṣa*) of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Furthermore, there can never be an absence of those things that are eternal and omnipresent, such that their absence could be perceived as the cause of the effect's non-existence. If it were argued that the effect arises through mere positive concomitance (*anvaya-mātra*), then everything—including space (*ākāśa*) and so forth—would become a controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), since those [entities] also exist while the causes proceed toward their own effects; for they too are identical in being eternal and omnipresent. If you say that [space etc. are not controllers because they do not possess that very [capacity], then that [capacity] itself is not established by virtue of being eternal and omnipresent.
Even for an eternal entity that is not all-pervading, there would be causality everywhere;
for it is observed that a cause is a cause not only through proximity, but even from afar. (PVA 726)
Even a sound or other object located in a distant place brings about its own effect;
therefore, by mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*), everything would be a cause. (727) (PVA) <(kha) The Truth of Origination>
The fourfold nature of origination: the fact that this suffering has a cause is established by its occasional occurrence. (180)
That which is eternal must be either existent or non-existent, because that which lacks a cause is independent of anything else.

[133, vii] The truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) is likewise fourfold: by way of cause (*hetu*), origination (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), and condition (*pratyaya*). Among these, "cause" is established by the exclusion of non-causality; "origination" by the exclusion of a single [sole] cause; "production" by the exclusion of incapacity—since it is called "production" (*prabhava*) because suffering arises from it; and "condition" by the exclusion of primacy. In this context, it is demonstrated that there is a cause for suffering. [Objection: No.
[133, viii] For it is observed that the connection with a cause belongs to that which occurs only occasionally;
for an entity that is without a cause must either exist eternally or not exist at all. (PVA 728)

For just as the absence of causes constitutes permanence, so too is the case for the cognition of floaters and the like, which occurs without an object. Thus, the dharmadhātu, which is accessible through self-awareness, is without cause. (PVA 729)
An eternal existence, characterized by non-occasionality, is observed [in the case of the son of a barren woman and the like],
because such things are eternally non-existent due to the absence of a causal nature. (PVA 730) [133,xi]
[133,xii] Here, an objection is raised:
[133,xiii]
Just as there is no cause for sharpness and other qualities in thorns and the like, [so it is with the qualities of the self]. (181)
Likewise, some declare that this would be without a cause. [133, xiv]

For those who maintain the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), material form consisting of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is not produced by its own nature (*svabhāva*). Rather, it is the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) alone that are produced through their connection with particularities of place, time, and state. In this regard, the causelessness of these specific qualities is observed. For instance, when a spear, a needle, a trident, a brush, and so forth are fashioned by smiths and others, their nature as iron and the like is not produced; rather, only their sharpness is produced. Furthermore, even for iron and other such materials, their status as earth and so forth is not produced by others, because their nature as iron and so on is already established. Moreover, since sharpness exists in thorns and the like even in the absence of a smith, and since [sharpness] exists even when that [smith] is absent, this very lack of a fixed cause constitutes causelessness. If that were so, then other specific qualities that produce the diversity of the world would likewise be causeless; what contradiction would there be in this? That, however, is incorrect.
When there is birth or even transformation in something, that [birth or transformation] occurs only when that [thing] exists. // 182 //

They say that this is its cause, and that [cause] also exists for them. [134, ii] The intention here is as follows: if only the specific features (*viśeṣa*) are produced, they cannot be without a cause. Indeed, the curvature and sharpness of the jujube tree thorns do not exist apart from the jujube thorn itself. Because they follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that, they are its effects; thus, there is no lack of a cause. If it is argued that they are also produced by a blacksmith, and therefore there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), that too is not correct.
Since we observe actions preceded by intelligence, there must be an intelligent cause;
thus, God may be the agent, and consequently, there is no state of being without a cause. (PVA 731)

Because of that very illustration provided by the jujube thorns and so forth, there is no [need for] postulating a specific distinction; otherwise, let that distinction be based on a cause. (PVA 732) Something arises from the jujube seed, while something else arises from the blacksmith and so forth.
If no distinction is perceived, then no distinction exists at all.
(733) For a distinction is not grasped by mere perception; thus, that very [reality] would result in non-duality, and it would likewise be without cause. (734)
Therefore, those specific qualities arise from that very cause;
for the state of being a specific quality is not established for that which is devoid of a cause.

Therefore, whether there is difference or whether there is external objectivity, everything is necessarily caused; otherwise, the opposite would follow. But surely, if something arises only when another exists, that other must be its cause, which would entail that touch is the cause of vision, since vision does not exist in the absence of touch. That is incorrect, because they are inseparable from one another due to their dependence on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Because of that [dependence], there is no perception of them in the absence of the other;

for in that case, form itself does not exist without touch. If, however, form were to exist, perception would indeed occur. It is not from such a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone that causality is established, but rather by demonstrating the form and then showing that perception is absent when touch is absent. Or alternatively:
Because contact is the cause of form, it possesses the status of a causal condition for vision. 183.

Because there is causality even between two things existing at the same time when they are not mutually dissociated, the primary elements (*bhūta*) are the cause of the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that is contact-form (*sparśarūpa*). Therefore, since contact is indeed a cause for vision through a mediated succession, the reason does not occur in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*); thus, there is no deviation. In this way, the absence of a cause has first been refuted; thus, the single aspect "from a cause" is established.
"Origination" refers to the second aspect:
by the negation of eternal entities, there is no possibility of [origination] from a creator god (īśvara) or the like.

[134,xv] Even though suffering has a cause, by negating that its cause is permanent and unitary, the aspect of the origin (*samudayākāratā*) is determined. For if the cause were to be only one and permanent, it would be independent; and because that which is permanent cannot have any specific quality added to it, such permanent entities as *pradhāna* and so forth have already been refuted. If one asks why this is so: it is because of incapacity, for due to the deficiency of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*)—whether through succession or simultaneity—they lack power. The third aspect is that of craving itself. He says this very thing: [134,xvi]
Therefore, because it lacks the capacity [to produce the effect], the cause is the grasping of the desire for existence. (184)

Because for human beings, the desire to attain a particular place does not derive its power from any other cause, whether it be karma or anything else. Indeed, neither karma nor the body, nor even ignorance, is the source (*prabhava*)—the latter being synonymous with the "efficient cause" (*samarthakāraṇa*). This is because birth is absent when craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is absent; furthermore, the arising of craving is clearly observed. Since grasping (*parigraha*)—which is designated by the synonym "clinging" (*āgraha*)—is produced by the craving to attain that [place], and this grasping constitutes the encounter with birth, therefore birth has craving as its source. The "desire for existence" (*bhavavāñchā*) takes the form of a prayer for future birth.
[134,xviii] But is it not the case that the aspiration for specific locations and so forth is not the truth of origination? For it was said by the Blessed One:

In that regard, what is the noble truth of the origin? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. There is no contradiction here, because: That desire for existence is the engagement in pleasure and pain by one who seeks what has not been attained and wishes to preserve what has been attained.
For even from that [source], sentient beings have their desire for the power of sensual pleasures. || 185 ||

[135,iii] This craving for places, requisites, and so forth, is the craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*); it is the delight in existence (*saṃsāra-tṛṣṇā*), accompanied by joy and passion, finding gratification here and there. All of that is indeed craving for sensual pleasure (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*). That craving for places and so forth is craving for existence; it is the desire for existence. That which takes the form of a longing for heaven is craving for sensual pleasure. That which is the wish for separation from suffering is craving for non-existence. Therefore, the teaching on the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*) is entirely without contradiction; there is no contradiction whatsoever with the scriptures (*āgama*). [135,iv]
Because self-attachment is the cause everywhere, it proceeds forth;
for one who perceives happiness in what is not happiness, craving is therefore the basis of existence. (186)

[135,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a dharma, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a dharma. He does not perceive the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a dharma. He does not perceive forms as dharmas, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as dharmas. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a dharma, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as a dharma. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a dharma. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a dharma. He does not perceive the earth element as a dharma, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as a dharmas. He does not perceive ignorance as a dharma, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as dharmas. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as a dharma, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as a dharma. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one as a dharma. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever.”

Based upon the *ahaṅkāra*, the series of minds (*cittamālā*) is superimposed as a unity. The attachment toward that [series] which operates everywhere—in relation to one's dwelling, requisites, and so forth—is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of the nature of pleasure and the like, since it is actually suffering. Because it causes the engagement of one who is afflicted by the cognitive distortions (*viparyaya*) of the mind, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is therefore the cause and the basis for its arising. For that which is not perceived is never connected to engagement; otherwise, through the application of compassion, it would not be a cause of saṃsāra. Precisely for this reason, because craving acts as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) for engagement, it possesses the status of a mere condition (*pratyayamātratā*) and not that of a substantial material cause (*upādānatva*). In this context, the mind itself is the material cause, while craving is its condition, though at times it may be compassion. By this, the aspect of being "conditioned" (*pratyayataḥ*) has been explained.

[135, vi] But surely, even if it is a condition, craving is not the condition; rather, it is the body. Therefore, one who is attached to the body is not free from passion. He demonstrates this very point:

The Teachers declare that there is no birth for one who is dispassionate, because such a state is never observed; and since passion is never observed in one who is bodiless, passion arises from the body. (187)

[135, viii] For just as birth is not observed in one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), it follows that passion is the cause of birth; for this very reason, it is logical that the body is the cause of passion and so forth, since passion is not observed in one who is bodiless. To this it is replied: birth occurs even without passion. However, its being an object of delight due to the power of compassion is carried away by craving (*tṛṣṇā*); thus, because it is merely a specific cause, it is simply a condition (*pratyaya*) for craving. In this way, he shows that if the body is also merely a condition for passion and so forth, then the improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) alone is the substantial cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), and thus it is precisely what is intended to be included.
However, while the approach toward a causal sign (*nimitta*) is accepted, the [notion of] appropriation (*upādāna*) is rejected;
yet by seeking this argument, one contradicts one's own position. (188)

[135,x] The body, too, following improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), is accepted as being like a cause of passion. At times, it is a cause for the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just like an object. This reasoning establishes that the body is also a cause of passion. Therefore, because they are mutual causes, birth arises from such an beginningless complex of conditions; thus, the existence of other births is established—this has been discussed by the brilliant [author] regarding the arguments of the Cārvākas.
[Objection: Is it not the case that a substance possessing qualities (saguṇa) is what is being denoted? Consequently, these two would lack a mutual causal relationship.
[Response:
If their coexistence were due to simultaneous birth, then passion would be observed even in those who have already been born. (189)

Although it is established that [ignorance] is a cause for the arising of similar types [of states], ignorance was not mentioned [as the primary cause]; rather, it is craving alone that impels the continuum toward existence. (190)

<(b) Craving and karma are the origin of birth—> [136,iii] For if passion and the like were co-existent with birth, then passion and the like would not be the cause of the body; in that case, the body would also not be the cause of passion and the like. Nor, therefore, could there be the consequence of being causeless. Thus it is established as our intended position that passion and the like are produced by causes of a similar kind.

[136,iv] But is it not the case that craving alone is not the sole cause? For ignorance, craving, and karma—these three—are the causes. How then can there be an exposition of the truth of origination as "craving itself which delights here and there"?

This is not so. Even though they are causes, they are not immediate causes. Craving alone is the immediate cause, because it impels the continuum in saṃsāra. For even when delusion and karma exist, there is no impeller in the absence of craving. Indeed, even one who is mistaken does not act without a craving for union. Therefore he said: "[136, vi] Not even karma [is the immediate cause], because even when that exists, [the result] is impossible [without craving]; due to its immediacy."
[136,vii] One who is free from craving abandons even a kingdom and such things acquired through karma.
[136,viii]

[Objection: Is it not the case that cognition follows karma? Therefore, renunciation is itself a specific kind of karma by which one disregards what has been encountered. Or, if it is argued that rebirth is impossible for liberated souls, we reply: even for them, liberation consists precisely in the exhaustion of karma, since otherwise it would be non-existent. To this, it is said:
If there is the complete exhaustion of karma for one who is devoid of craving—
It is only this—that craving is the primary cause—which is logical here.
(737) (PVA) Now, if craving does not exist, there is no exhaustion of this karma;
for one who possesses craving, there will arise further and further karma. (738) (PVA)

[136,xii] Thus, first, the Noble Truth characterized by origination has been explained in its four aspects. Now, he states the Noble Truth of Cessation in its four aspects, namely that this suffering is capable of cessation. <(ga) The Noble Truth of Cessation>
[(a) The establishment of liberation in the absence of cyclic existence:
That [liberation] is not ultimate, because of the possibility of obstacles to the cause and so forth.
Because of being subject to saṃsāra, there would be no liberation; this is not desired [by us], and it is not established [as a fact]. || 191 ||

[136,xiv] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Furthermore, monks, it was said by me: “I shall not recognize an end to suffering so long as these four nutriments are not abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. It is in this sense, monks, that it was said by me: “I shall not recognize an end to suffering so long as these four nutriments are not abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. Why is that? Because, monks, these four nutriments have craving as their source, craving as their origin, craving as their birthplace, and craving as their causal condition. Therefore, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard these four nutriments as suffering, as the origin of suffering, as the cessation of suffering, and as the way leading to the cessation of suffering—they all regard what has been taught by the Tathāgata as suffering, as the origin of suffering, as the cessation of suffering, and as the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata has fully understood these four nutriments, their origin, their cessation, and the path leading to their cessation, and having fully understood them, he teaches the Dhamma to others. Therefore, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard these four nutriments as suffering, as the origin of suffering, as the cessation of suffering, and as the way leading to the cessation of suffering—they all regard what has been taught by the Tathāgata as suffering, as the origin of suffering, as the cessation of suffering, and as the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
