There are four aspects: cessation (*nirodha*), peace (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and liberation (*niḥsaraṇa*). "Cessation" is stated for one who asserts that cessation itself does not exist. "Peace" is stated in refutation of the opponent's admission that even those who are liberated can still experience the arising of passion and other defilements. The aspect of "excellence" follows from the rejection of the claim that there is something superior to liberation. The fourth aspect, "liberation," rejects the notion that even one who is liberated becomes bound again. Regarding the first aspect: [cessation] is neither non-absolute nor absolute; it is that which ceases. Furthermore, the objection that liberation is impossible because of the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāritva*) is not a valid fault, for this is accepted [by us]. Indeed, no one is liberated. For one who is bound, there is no liberation. Since bondage is not the intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāva*) of the liberated, there is no bondage even for the liberated, because they always possess the nature of being liberated. It is simply that, while the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) is impure, a subsequent portion arises as pure through a specific causal complex (*sāmagrīviśeṣa*). Setting that aside, the very state of being a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritā*) is unestablished for that which is completely purified. Moreover, there is no transmigrating being whatsoever in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), because moments (*kṣaṇa*) do not transmigrate, and the continuum (*santāna*) does not exist ultimately. Therefore, the reason "because of being a transmigrating being" is unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor does a liberator exist for whom there could be liberation.

[137,ii] But surely, if one who is bound is not the one who is liberated—if the bondage belongs to one and liberation to another; if hunger belongs to one and satiety to another; if one experiences the suffering of medical treatment while another is free from disease; if one undergoes affliction while another experiences heavenly bliss; if one is exhausted by the study of the treatises while another has mastered them—then for what reason would a discerning person apply themselves to this? Here is the resolution: because [137,iii]...
As long as there is no loss of love for oneself, one suffers.
Having projected suffering upon it, one does not remain at ease;
therefore, effort is made to eliminate false superimposition, even though there is no actual experiencer. (193)
[(b) The abiding of the liberated ones in saṃsāra: [137,v] For those who have abandoned passion while remaining in their state, it is through compassion or even by means of karma.

The intention here is as follows: If this is stated with respect to those who perceive reality (*tattvadarśin*), then it is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For they do not engage in activity anywhere, nor do they exert effort, because of the statement that "phenomena (*dharma*) themselves are to be abandoned. If, on the other hand, it refers to people like us, then because of the conceit of unity (*ekatvābhimāna*), that very same person is bound and that very same person attains liberation; thus, there is indeed a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatā*) for both. It is not the case that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs merely because an entity does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); for conventional usage depends upon cognition (*pratīti*). To illustrate: a snake is not, from the perspective of ultimate truth, the object of avoidance; rather, it is the object of avoidance precisely by way of being perceived as a snake.

[137, vii] Now, even if there were oneness conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), nevertheless, let there be conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). But since oneness does not exist ultimately (*paramārthatas*), how can there be ultimate usage? That is incorrect.
[137, viii]
Conventionally, its being "one" is a conventional usage; that too is merely conventional.
In reality, there is no such thing as "oneness," and thus even the conventional usage is not ultimate.
Indeed, effort (*yatna*) is nowhere other than the very nature of the thing itself.
But the relation of cause and effect does not provide an opening for such an objection:
"Why is this the effect of that?"—what kind of cleverness is this?
For a discerning person, there is never any engagement or withdrawal [from an action] based on such [speculation]. (PVA 740–741)
Because the perception of priority and posteriority is not established by any means of valid cognition,
and because it is impossible for a mere moment to ever initiate activity anywhere.
Consequently, there would be no effort at all for anyone, and thus no delusion. Even granting this, it is said: "The state," and so forth.
For if one does not indeed proceed toward ultimate awakening, there would be no activity for those free from passion that possesses the distinction between prior and subsequent states. (743) (PVA)
Even when there is no cognition of [external] activity, one engages out of compassion, just as a king who seeks the welfare of his subjects exerts effort for the sake of his own lineage;
such is the function of one whose primary focus is the vow, arising from that very vow. (744) (PVA)
Who can be questioned here regarding that which has arisen through the power of karma?
(PVA 745) Therefore, one must exert effort for the sake of abandoning such false superimpositions; otherwise, there is no cessation of the experience of suffering for the deluded person.

[138, ii] If, then, persistence is due to karma, then since there is also karma for another birth, there would be a transition to another birth. Alternatively, if karma were incapable [of causing persistence], there would be no persistence for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). To this it is said:

Because it is desired that what has been projected does not cease [until its completion], [the cause] is sufficient [to produce the effect] through the exhaustion of its auxiliary conditions. // 194 //
For those who have transcended the thirst for existence, no further karma can be projected.

That which has been projected cannot be brought to cessation without effort; yet for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), effort is obstructed. Because of equanimity (*upekṣā*), he has no further investment in anything. Precisely because of this absence of investment, there is no acquisition of another birth, due to the absence of its auxiliary cause, namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Therefore, this present birth alone was produced by prior craving, and there is no other. [Objection: But this so-called compassion (*dayā*) occurs toward a sentient being (*sattva*) who is to be protected from suffering, and not elsewhere. Yet, no such thing as a "sentient being" exists. Nor does the perception of a sentient being exist for those who have abandoned the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*); therefore, it follows that those who possess compassion have not abandoned the view of a self. [Response: To this, the following refutation is offered:

The arising of the properties of things, which carries forward previous formative predispositions and is not in contradiction with the knowledge of suffering, does not conform to the existence of sentient beings. // 195 //

For when all suffering is directly realized as being endowed with the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*), then craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which is characterized as the origin (*samudaya*), departs. For one whose origin has been abandoned, passion and the other afflictions do not remain; this is the non-contradiction with equanimity (*samatā*) toward the entire assembly of sentient beings. Consequently, for the Great Beings (*mahat*), there arises a concern based on the reality [of suffering] from seeing that [beings] are suffering. In that state, it is not out of a grasping for sentient beings that they act, but rather the intention (*āśaya*) to cause those beings who have such grasping to abandon it—that is compassion (*dayā*). And that [compassion] belongs only to one who has abandoned the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*). For how could one who has not abandoned the view of a self strive for the sake of others to bring about its abandonment?
[138,vii] But what is the distinction between passion (*rāga*) and compassion (*dayā*)? This is the distinction:
[138,viii]
Attachment arises toward that which has such a nature through the superimposition of another self;
whereas the emergence of compassion occurs merely through contact with the continuum of suffering. (196)

[138,ix] There is a great difference between compassion (*dayā*) and passion (*rāga*), due to a difference in their causes and a difference in their objects. To explain: passion proceeds from an attribution of a future continuum of existence to the self, thereby becoming subject to an attachment for future pleasure; it also functions toward an object that is not of that nature, yet is perceived as being of that nature. Thus, one who possesses passion is only one whose mind is permeated by the fourfold misconceptions, and no other. Compassion, however, arises solely from the direct perception of the mere continuity of suffering, in order to bring about the removal of false conceit. [138,x]
"How indeed could there be [compassion] without the intention: 'I shall bring about the cessation of this person's suffering'? To this, the response is:
"If one’s activity were for the sake of oneself alone, it would necessarily follow exactly like that."
For those who act solely for the sake of others, there is no perception of a causal agent.
The example of the king has been shown; thus, this [objection] is not inconsistent.
Or rather, activity proceeds from a superior impression (*saṃskāra*) instilled by each preceding moment. (PVA 746–747)
One does not perceive a continuum, nor does anything at all proceed;
it does not remain because of the absence of light—it is merely your delusion.

Thus, this is the distinction between compassion (*dayā*) and attachment (*rāga*); enough with excessive detail. Now, one might object: "Let compassion not be of the nature of attachment, since it arises from those who see reality as it is; however, it must be of the nature of aversion (*dveṣa*), because one perceives impurity and so forth, and thus there is an absence of turning away [from the world]. Furthermore, liberation does not come from the cultivation of the foul (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), but rather from the vision of impermanence (*anitya*) and so on. For when there is a self (*ātman*), that [aversion]..."

[139,i] One might think that anger should arise because [the person] is independent and inflicts suffering upon others; however, when this person instead proceeds as dependent on causes and functions merely by its own nature, it is impossible to inflict harm upon it, since at the very time of the infliction of harm, that [person] no longer exists. Thus, the adoption of anger is futile.
And delusion is the root of all defects, and that [delusion] exists without the grasping of a self. (197)
Therefore, there is no hatred toward the primary cause; hence, the absence of hatred is considered compassion.

[139,iii] If one were to see oneself being harmed, anger would arise. But there is no such thing as a self. Rather, it is merely the apprehension of a sentient being—even in the absence of an actual sentient being—that is the sole cause of anger; and without the apprehension of a sentient being, there is no hatred. As for delusion, it does not exist here, because the very perception of a sentient being is itself an absence of delusion. Therefore, compassion, which is free from all faults, is not a fault. [139,iv]
Now, if one who is free from passion remains while still possessing a body, then he would not be liberated; for there exists a mind that is devoid of defects. Furthermore:
There is no liberation because, upon the exhaustion of prior formative forces, there is no further reconnection with another birth. 198.

Those whose latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) possess undiminished power remain as those free from fault (*anagha*). For how could one who exists with a mind opposed to the reconnection with another birth be unliberated? And because of the exhaustion of the prior latent impressions produced in that birth, there is no reconnection. However, those who lack the desire for the exhaustion of latent impressions in order to prevent reconnection remain indeed as those free from fault, since they persist as long as the latent impressions persist.
And because their compassion is weak, they do not exert great effort in establishing [others]. (199)
Those for whom there is great compassion remain indeed dependent on others.

Because of the diminution of their formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*) and the dullness of their compassion, they lack the effort to remain; thus, they do not remain forever. However, due to the possession of great compassion, they certainly remain, because it is impossible for them not to remain therein.
[And] the departure from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

If the path possessed such power, then non-existence (*abhava*) would occur at the very beginning, on the path of stream-entry itself, because of the departure from the view of a self-identity. For it is by the abandonment of the view of a self-identity, doubt, and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) that one becomes a stream-enterer.

[139,x] "And delusion is the root of the defects, and that [delusion] consists in the grasping of sentient beings. Thus it has been said. Consequently, any other path would be useless. To this, it is replied:
Through the disappearance of the view of a self-identity, there would be non-existence from the very beginning. (200)
If [the self] were on the path, there would be no loss of its innate nature; or, if it were lost, how could existence arise?

Indeed, the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not mean that while the constructed (*ābhisaṃskārika*) [view] is abandoned, there is no abandonment of the innate (*sahaja*) one. For that path consists merely in the vision of the truths. Through such vision, the constructed grasping at a self is abandoned because it is a rootless affliction (*amūlakleśa*). That instructional vision of a self is abandoned by the mere act of seeing its opposite. However, because the innate view of a self-identity has been deeply rooted through beginningless habituation, its abandonment occurs only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as its antidote; thus, the innate is not abandoned by the mere vision of the truths.

But in the view of one for whom there is no loss even of that which is innate (*sahaja*), in that view, how could existence arise even upon the loss [of other qualities]? For, in the case of one possessing sharp wisdom, the very first path itself is endowed with all capacities; thus, for him, that [first path] alone is the nature of the entire path.

[140,i] Is it not the case that the innate perception of a sentient being, if it has the form of a self, would—given the absence of a self—arise from mental construction (*abhisaṃskāra*) alone and not otherwise? If there is an absence of a real entity as a producer, then at most instruction (*upadeśa*) would be the cause. To this, he says:
For one who thirsts, thinking, "May I be happy" or "May I not suffer. (201)
The very cognition that "I am" is itself the innate perception of a self.
For no one feels affection for a self without perceiving it as "I. [140,iii] 202.
And one who desires happiness does not rush toward it without love for the self.

Arising through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), the cognition "I" constitutes this innate perception of a self (*sattvadarśana*), taking such forms as "May I be happy" or "May I not become otherwise. Because that [perception] is not abandoned, there is no cessation of existence (*abhava*). Furthermore, one feels affection for the self while perceiving it as "I," but not while seeing [it as it truly is]. And for one who desires happiness, there is no running toward it without affection for the self. For one whose innate perception of a self has given rise to an association with self-affection, how could there be an absence of rebirth? Therefore, because of this innate perception of a self, there is no end to *saṃsāra* on the very first path. It is certain that [the end of *saṃsāra*] occurs only through the abandonment of the perception of a self. By this, the aspect of "peaceful" (*śānta*) has been explained.

[140,v] But surely, if a self exists, there is bondage and for that very self there is liberation; therefore, liberation is brought about from a particular satisfaction of the self. However, in the absence of a self, whose would be the satisfaction?
[This concludes the section on] the establishment of bondage and liberation.
If it were merely an error, then that would be a state of defect; it would not be liberation. To this, the response is as follows:
Bondage is the state of being a cause for the arising of suffering; how could that belong to something eternal? (203)
Liberation consists in the state of being a cause for the non-arising of suffering; how could that belong to something eternal?
[140, viii]

If the self (*ātman*) were eternal and likewise all-pervading, then, due to the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it would not be capable of producing suffering for itself, just like space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, if it were independent and capable [of acting], why would it produce suffering for itself? Indeed, it is not fitting for a discerning person to undertake an action for their own destruction. If, on the other hand, it were deluded, then, being unaware of itself, how could its non-existence follow from the non-perception of a self? If its nature were such [to suffer], then it would never be otherwise; thus, liberation would never occur. Moreover, even if one knows this, if suffering is not produced by merit (*dharma*), then still, because it is eternal and all-pervading, nothing can be the cause for the production of suffering in it. If it were of the nature of suffering at that time, then it is not logical for suffering to befall suffering. And if it has that nature, there can be no change [into another state]; therefore, there is no liberation. If it were to possess a different nature, it would not be eternal, and thus it would not be the self. If suffering or pleasure were distinct [from the self], then the self would neither be happy nor unhappy; for one thing does not become happy through the happiness of another. If you say it is because of inherence (*samavāya*) therein, then is inherence also something else? If it is not different, the same fault remains. If it has the nature of pleasure, pain, and so forth, then it is impermanent due to having successive natures. If it is argued that it is changeless in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) and that the perception of happiness and so forth is merely an illusion (*bhrānti*), that too is incorrect.
If it is distinct from the self, then the self is not perceived because of that error.
If its own nature is indeed perceived, how can there be error in self-awareness? (749) (PVA)
If there were no excellence in liberation even for one who possesses happiness,
then because delusion exists therein for him, the self does not partake in liberation.
(750) For that person who is satisfied when one moment after another arises...
This liberation of his is established in reality as being free from error and irrationality.
(751) (PVA) If it is argued that bondage and liberation would then result in having different substrates, we reply:
their state of having a single substrate is not denied at the level of conventional truth. (752) (PVA)
What purpose would there be for one who is already liberated in relation to bondage? If you argue that it is because [he thinks], "This was mine previously," even so, what use is that?
One would act with deliberation only after first ascertaining oneness.

If it is argued that this is improper, then indeed that is accepted [by us]. Furthermore, it has been stated again that this formulation is for the sake of others (*parārtha*); its composition is for the sake of liberation, whereas the opposite is the case for others.

[141, viii] Now, it might be argued: "The self is neither eternal, because of the faults previously mentioned, nor is it non-eternal, because that would entail the consequence of acting without foresight; therefore, it is inexpressible in terms of being either eternal or non-eternal. This too is not tenable.
That which is inexpressible in terms of impermanence cannot be the cause of anything. (204)
How could bondage and liberation not exist even for that which is inexpressible?

[141,x] If it is said to be "inexpressible" by virtue of impermanence, then it lacks impermanence; therefore, it cannot be a cause. It has been determined elsewhere that causality is pervaded by impermanence; thus, due to the absence of the pervader, its status as a cause is impossible. Furthermore, for that which lacks even permanence, there is absolute non-existence. [Objection: Impermanence exists because bondage and liberation share a single substratum. [Response: No; the resolution is that it is not permanent because it is a cause. But that is untenable.
An intrinsic nature that is free from both permanence and impermanence is not apprehended,
because everything is apprehended precisely through its aspects of exclusion and inclusion. (756) (PVA)
[141,xii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let there be a dual nature, provided it is not otherwise; even so, there is no fault. Why?
[141,xiii]
The wise call that eternal which is one's own nature that never perishes.
Therefore, having abandoned this shameful view, let that which is eternal be explained.

To say that something is both perishable and eternal is a contradiction; for that which does not perish is eternal. It will be established that "perishing," "non-existence," and "non-apprehension" have the same meaning, and likewise, "non-perishing," "eternality," and "apprehension" have the same meaning. Consequently, the oneness of the eternal and the non-eternal means the oneness of the apprehensible and the non-apprehensible. And how can there be oneness between the apprehensible and the non-apprehensible?
[141,xv] That which is perceived as a unity is established as being one;
if that which was not perceived were to be perceived, that would be an act of extreme audacity. (PVA) 757.

[141,xvi] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is a stream-enterer; the person who is a once-returner; the person who is a non-returner; and the person who is an arhat. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Gone One further spoke these verses: "The stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat—these four kinds of persons are praised by the Buddhas. Among them, the one who has abandoned the five lower fetters is called a 'stream-enterer,' one who will not be subject to rebirth in the states of woe and is fixed for enlightenment. The one who has abandoned three fetters and weakened greed, hatred, and delusion is called a 'once-returner'; having returned once more to this world, he will make an end of suffering. The one who has abandoned the five lower fetters is called a 'non-returner'; having passed away from that world, he will attain parinirvāṇa without returning to this world again. The one who has abandoned all taints (āsava) is called an 'arhat'; having attained mastery over his mind, he dwells having done what was to be done and laid down the burden."

If the permanent and the impermanent were one and the same, then it would follow that the cognized and the uncognized are one; and this is incoherent. That which is perceived as a unity cannot be apprehended otherwise than as such. That which is not perceived at all cannot be determined to be one with something else that is perceived—for instance, a rabbit’s horn, being unperceived by anyone, cannot be ascertained as one with anything perceived. If you argue that in that case there is no cognition of the one [because it is unperceived], here too, when something is unperceived, there must necessarily be non-cognition. For that whose cognition occurs as a unity, its very cognition does not perish, nor does it arise [as something else]. If you claim that the non-cognition of one thing is simply the cognition of another, then there is no cognition consisting of the form of the other; rather, the very absence of cognition in the form of the other is what constitutes the non-cognition of that thing. If this is so, then it follows that the non-existence of that thing arises from that very other form; and this is untenable. Why? Because:
How could one who asserts difference also assert non-difference? If it is said that "there is no difference for that," then impermanence is not established. (758) (PVA)
If there were impermanence, there would be non-apprehension; if there is apprehension, there is no impermanence.
And if there were non-difference, there would be apprehension; and if there is apprehension, there is permanence. By some form it is not apprehended, while by another it is otherwise.
How can it be maintained that its nature is one that has never been cognized?
(760) If it is argued that its cognition occurs as something prior, then it would have existed as such previously;
how then can there be identity between this present form and that [prior] form? (761)
If [the self] is one because it is not separated from the two forms of prior and posterior,
then why is its separation not admitted when separation is actually observed?
If its separation occurs sequentially, then the separation itself would likewise be sequential.

Therefore, it possesses both natures, due to non-separation and separation [respectively]. (PVA 763) Just as its existence is non-sequential, so too must its perception be; for there can be no connection with sequential states for that which exists non-sequentially. (PVA 764)
If its nature as neither prior nor posterior is not perceived, there can be no understanding of its pervasiveness;
and if its pervasiveness occurs sequentially, then that very [nature] cannot possess pervasiveness.
For it is not possible for that single entity to be both seen and unseen.

At that very moment, its being perceived and its not being perceived would be difficult to reconcile. (PVA 766) If there is no difference in time, nothing at all appears inconsistent. Since it is a single entity, how could there be a difference in time for it at one and the same time? (PVA 767)
Furthermore, if there were repeated cognition, the act of grasping would be something already grasped.
For that which is called "grasped" is indeed the object of apprehension being remembered.
Since memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the possibility of grasping [the object] in a sequence is not established.

And that form is not unperceived, by virtue of which it would possess the status of being perceptible. (769) (PVA) If its existence at the present time were not already apprehended by the previous cognition, then since there would be no difference [between the two], how could this division of it be consistent with valid cognition? (770) (PVA)
If it is argued that its state of being seen does not exist [in the past], and thus it always exists in the present,
then by what means could its sequence of prior and posterior be perceived?
If it is claimed to be through the two cognitions of "prior" and "posterior," then from where is the cognition of the distinction between those two [cognitions] derived?
If it is argued that [the cognition of duality] arises from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then the apprehension of duality would not occur from that.
Nor can there be an apprehension of a preceding "other" that does not exist.
If that single self-awareness is intended to possess the state of being a preceding other, [then it is contradictory].
If they were identical, how could there be "priority" [of the object] by virtue of its being directly perceived?
For that which is being directly perceived cannot possess priority, even if it were previously cultivated.
If there were no priority, how could there be a cognition [of it] as prior?
There is no direct perception of this [object], nor is its recollection a cognition of it.
(775) If you claim that this is its recollection, how can it be said to belong to it when this recollection is observed to occur even without it? (776)
If it is argued that [the object] is grasped because of the causal relationship, the grasping would not occur by that much alone.
The state of being the grasped belongs to the object only when it is the direct cause, not otherwise.
Furthermore, memory does not arise directly from the object, as it is mediated by consciousness.
That cognition is not complete; it is incapable of grasping [an object] as being prior.
(PVA 778) Therefore, priority is by no means established through memory alone.
What is called "prior" is the direct perception of what has passed. (PVA 779)
The status of being "existent" is established when an entity is realized as having come into being.

Furthermore, that which is endowed with arising, passing away, and persistence is accepted as being existent. (PVA 780) Otherwise, these very things would lack existence, because they would never be separated from this state of being.
When there is destruction, how can its existence be perceived?
(PVA 781) If its existence was previously perceived, then how can there be destruction of it at that time?
Even if there were permanence, if there is no cognition of this [object], how can existence be perceived? (PVA 781)
Since everything exists only through cognition, how could it otherwise?
Therefore, an entity that is both eternal and non-eternal is never possible anywhere. (PVA 782) [142, xxv]
Is it impermanent or permanent? A real entity must necessarily be one or the other according to reason.
[142,xxvi] Now, in the context of the path, demonstrating the fourth aspect of cessation itself, he says:
[(gha) The Truth of the Path has four aspects:
The path has been explained; through its cultivation, the basis is transformed. 206.

If it is argued that even when [the realization of selflessness] has become habitual (*sātmya*), faults still persist because of a lack of mastery—just as in the case of the path—the answer is that the path was explained previously; through its cultivation, there occurs the complete purification of the basis, whether it be the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) or the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya*). When selflessness—which is the reversal of the grasping at "self" and "mine"—has become habitual, there is a total separation from all faults.
[Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*):

Is it not the case that, just as there is the possession of virtues when there is the possession of faults, so too there is the possession of faults even when there is the possession of virtues? Thus, there would be no escape from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). No.

Because faults are sublated by the emergence of qualities, why does the reverse not occur? It is because qualities are the very nature of reality (*vastu-svabhāva*). If it is asked how this is so, it is explained as follows:
The apprehension of an object is the characteristic of consciousness; it exists exactly as it is. 207.
And he is apprehended as his producer by means of a presently existing self.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the path that impels living beings; its property (*dharma*) is its own nature, which is the apprehension of an object—that by means of which consciousness comes to be. Consciousness does not exist in the absence of perception, because for those things that are not perceived, such [consciousness] is likewise non-existent. And just as it exists, so too, when being apprehended, it is the producer [of the cognition]. For an object is the cause of consciousness insofar as it is capable of imparting its form. Imparting its own form is the property of consciousness; likewise, being perceived in that very way is the property of the object. Therefore, he says that an object characterized by impermanence, selflessness, and so forth, is precisely what is to be grasped by a consciousness of that same nature, and nothing else possesses that intrinsic nature.
Let this be its intrinsic nature; however, it may deviate due to other causes. (208)
In its cessation, it is dependent on conditions and unstable, like the cognition of a snake.

Whatever property has the nature of apprehending such things as selflessness (*anātmatva*) and so forth—that is its *prakṛti* (nature). When that [nature] falters due to the influence of adventitious conditions, it is a groundless lapse. Therefore, upon the cessation of that lapse, because it depends on conditions and is thus groundless, it is unstable, like the cognition of a snake [mistaken for a rope]. [Objection: But surely the causes of the cognition of a snake in a rope are similarity, distance, and so forth. What, however, is the cause of the cognition of permanence? Perception does not operate with respect to permanence, nor does inference. Nor can doubt be said to be without a basis. Furthermore, it will be proven that momentariness is perceived through perception. Thus, from where could there be an apprehension of permanence? To this, he replies: Even while perceiving that impermanence, a person of dull intellect does not ascertain it. This is because they are deceived by the suspicion that the entity exists at all times due to the apprehension of its existence, or they are deceived by the production of successive similar moments; for certainty occurs only for those who perceive the final moment.

This is what is meant: when there is a non-perception of an object that was previously perceived, one indeed perceives its impermanence; for we define impermanence as the state of not remaining in the same condition (*atādavasthya*). However, even when it is no longer perceived, the doubt of a person of dull intellect does not depart. Thus, he suspects its continued existence—that is, he is "one who suspects its existence," wondering: "Does this [object] still exist today, or has it not? Then, through seeing it again or obtaining its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), being no longer deceived, why would he not determine it? Only one who is deceived would determine it to be otherwise due to the failure to obtain it, as in the case of a jar [mistaken for something else]. But when existence is apprehended through the characteristic of causal efficiency, what opportunity is there for a practitioner (*vyavahārī*) to distinguish between error and truth? A thinker of reality (*tattvacintaka*), however, determines it by means of the difference in appearance. The practitioner, moreover, seeks causal efficiency; once satisfied by its attainment, he does not investigate further, because his purpose has been fulfilled. Or, one may be deceived by the production of a similar subsequent moment, for the cognition "this is that very thing" arises toward what is similar. In the first case, the mere absence of the object is intended, as in the case of a magic ball (*māyāgolaka*) and its causal efficiency. For, although fire produced from a series of causes such as successive blades of grass is the object of a single conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), fuel alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) there, not fire itself; for fire certainly does not arise from fire alone, as that would entail the absurdity of its never having failed to arise previously, since there was no prior fire to strike against a stone. Alternatively, if it were produced from that very fire, then all things would likewise be produced from a preceding member of the same class. Or, there is no cause of the same class, since production occurs solely through the sovereign power of karma (*karmādhipatya*). Therefore, the alternative [regarding the cause] is made with respect to this. And that was stated previously according to the view of those who maintain the existence of karma; according to other views, it is the latter—this is the conclusion.

[144,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the name ‘Bodhisattva. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive these three things, he is called a ‘Bodhisattva’ by way of designation. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor the name ‘Bodhisattva,’ how then, Blessed One, can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva train in the perfection of wisdom? How can he go forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. He goes forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this manner, he is training in the perfection of wisdom; he is going forth toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Alternatively, it should be explained as "deceived by the suspicion that it is not that [very same thing]. For when it is that very thing, no suspicion whatsoever exists, because its existence is perceived at all times. Indeed, a suspicion regarding its being that very thing would arise only upon non-perception. But what is the case when there is non-perception in the interval? Even here, one is deceived by the production of another similar [moment], as in the case of hair and nails that have been cut and grown back again. If it is argued that identity is established through recognition of the deceased, we say no; for recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since it cannot be classified as either perception or inference. This will be demonstrated later. Therefore, due to the internal affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*), the impurities are adventitious.
For this very reason, he says:
This mind is luminous by nature; the stains are adventitious.
Because it is grasped as being devoid of permanence, the stains are adventitious.

[144,v] Because the superimposition of what is non-existent lacks any foundation and is merely like the impression of a seal on clay, permanence does not manifest anywhere in the ultimate sense. Therefore, because they are devoid of analytical investigation, the stains are adventitious.
Where could there be a later capacity for those things that were previously incapable, even with respect to that which consists of them?
For they remain just as incapable even at the time of hearing and reflection.
It is not capable of growing indefinitely, like fire upon the earth in a flowing stream. 210.

Even though a thing is capable [of arising], it is [contained] within the womb of the capacity for the arising of an antidote. [144, ix] But surely, even for one who lacks the cause—such as weak faith and so forth—there is indeed the abandonment [of faults] upon attaining arhatship. So how can there be the non-arising of faults? Even if there is the arising of a fault, nevertheless, because the capacity for the arising of an antidote is internalized, the stain, though capable of arising, is not able to grow further; it is like fire produced on moist ground, which does not take root. However, for one established in that which is natural (*sātmya*), there is no arising of faults. For instance:
[144,x] Of that which is by nature free from affliction and is the true reality, [the mind is afflicted] by its opposites. // 211 //
There is no subversion [of the view of self], even with effort, because the intellect has a partiality for that [view].

For an intrinsic nature cannot be turned back by one who lacks effort. And effort proceeds toward virtues in one who perceives faults, and toward faults in one who perceives virtues. But for one whose vision of selflessness has become second nature, there is no perception of virtues in faults, nor perception of faults in virtues, or even non-perception of virtues. This is because the vision of selflessness is free from affliction.
xiii] Therefore, since its nature is that of a real self and is entirely free from affliction, how could it be possible for one possessed of consciousness to abandon it? (PVA) 784
And partiality of the mind does not proceed toward faults;
therefore, no effort whatsoever is exerted by him toward a fault.

Even if a fault should arise for one who is capable of thoroughly investigating the nature of all things, it remains a true matter: like a traveler who has become weary, by encountering a sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*), he abides in a state of neutrality and exerts effort toward the path alone out of partiality for virtue, rather than taking pleasure in faults.

But surely, even though attachment and aversion have contrary forms, there is not the sublation of only one by the other; for we observe that attachment, once sublated by aversion, becomes a sublater again, and likewise aversion. The same would apply to the views of selflessness and the self. This is not so, because:
[144,xvii] Because they have the single source of grasping at a self, and because of their relationship as cause and effect. (212)

Even though there is a distinction between attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*), there is no mutual obstruction between them. This is because both serve as causes for the grasping at a self (*ātma-graha*). As long as the grasping at a self persists, not even one of these two can be utterly eradicated. Furthermore, even if they are mutually contradictory, their non-simultaneous occurrence would still be possible. Moreover:

[145,ii] Furthermore, due to the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*): for whoever is intended [as an object] in relation to a cause of suffering, when that person is afflicted, they necessarily desire the object that is a cause of happiness, whether it be that very object or another. Therefore, there exists a causal relationship between these two: when the cause of happiness is assisted, one is favorably disposed; when it is harmed, one possesses resentment (*pratigha*) because of that harm. Thus, due to this causal relationship, there is no contradiction between attachment (*rāga*) and resentment even though they differ [in their objects]. For this very reason: [145,iii]
Because loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] are not in contradiction with delusion, there is no absolute suppression of the defects. (213)
And all impurities have that as their root; and that is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Although loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to hatred, the foul (*aśubhā*) to passion, compassion (*karuṇā*) is the antidote to cruelty, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the antidote to envy, and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the antidote to everything—even so, there is no absolute suppression of faults, because it does not contradict delusion (*moha*).
vi] But surely, even if delusion persists, there is the abandonment of all defects simply because of the absence of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
This is not correct. That very delusion is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). For afflicted delusion is indeed nothing other than the view of a self-identity.
However, the ignorance of Arhats is not afflicted; therefore, it does not belong to them.
Even in delusion, those whose mental continuums are unrefined possess an inferior view of the transitory collection;
for [delusion] is the opposite of knowledge and is perceived as a mental factor. 214 // 886 // (PVA)
Because it is conjoined with ignorance, false apprehension is something other than that; it is illogical [to say otherwise].

Now, one might object: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) consists in the absence of clear manifestation (*asaṃprakhyāna*), whereas the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of the nature of a positive cognition (*pratipatti*); how then can the view of a self-identity itself be ignorance? There is no fault here, because:

[145,xii] Even if ignorance were established as having the nature of non-apprehension of form and so forth, what indeed would remain when the substrata have perished? For what reality could there be for the substrata once they are destroyed? 787 (PVA)

[145, xiii] For non-apprehension (*asaṃprakhyāna*) exists in the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and in the fundamental attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Now, if that [non-apprehension] does not have the afflictions as its cause, then it is not characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*). It is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that is ignorance because it is the cause of that [non-apprehension], and nothing else. Why?
A dharma other than knowledge (*vidyā*) is non-knowledge (*avidyā*), just as unrighteousness (*adharma*) is the opposite of righteousness; it is like falsehood and so forth.
Knowledge consists in the view of selflessness (*nairātmya-dṛṣṭi*), while its opposite is the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not simply the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*), because that absence exists even in *nirvāṇa*. Nor is it a non-entity (*abhāva*), for a non-entity cannot be a cause. Nor is it something other than that [knowledge], because that would entail the consequence that visible form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates are ignorance. Therefore, ignorance is a factor (*dharma*) opposed to knowledge, just like unrighteousness (*adharma*) or falsehood (*anṛta*). And that is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). To explain: righteousness (*dharma*) is characterized by the benefit of others; unrighteousness is not merely the absence of that, nor is it merely something other than it. Rather, unrighteousness is harm, which is the opposite of benefit. Likewise, falsehood is not merely the absence of communicating the true state of affairs, but rather the communication of what is untrue—untruthful speech. This being the case, if one were to communicate "it exists" while mistakenly thinking it does not exist regarding a real object, there would be no falsity. Conversely, if one were to think it exists regarding a non-existent object, then it would be false. But this is not so.

Words have as their objects those things that are conceptually constructed; in whatever way a thing is determined, a statement corresponding to that is true, while a statement otherwise is false. (PVA 789)

[145,xvii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of suffering? It is this craving which gives rise to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of suffering. What, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very same craving which gives rise to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, the relinquishing of it, its abandonment, its release, and the non-attachment to it. This, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the cessation of suffering. What, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Thus, monks, in regard to things previously unheard by me, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, insight arose, light arose concerning the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering must be developed” – in regard to this, monks, in regard to things previously unheard by me, vision arose, knowledge Monks, as long as my correct knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when my correct knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, had become thoroughly purified in this way, then, monks, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; and I declared to the assembly the attainment of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. The knowledge and vision arose in me: “Unshakable is the liberation of my mind; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. Words have as their object the thing being determined (*adhyavasīyamāna*). It is a logical principle that truth consists precisely in a representation corresponding to such determination; otherwise, it is untruth. For Bodhisattvas, however, deceiving sentient beings even through delusion (*bhrānti*) is the gravest fault. For this very reason, they apply themselves to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) alone is ignorance (*avidyā*), because no other [view] serves as the antidote to knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, because it is a mental factor (*caitta*) and is perceived, false perception itself is ignorance. They are "associated" (*samprayukta*) by way of equality in terms of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance. Thus they are called "associated. And it has been said: "Ignorance is essentially a mode of apprehension contrary to the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*). This is stated in various sūtras: "In that regard, what is the removal of non-knowledge? It is the realization of the non-superimposition of phenomena as they truly are. Likewise, whatever worldly conventions arise, they all arise from attachment to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*); they do not arise from the cessation of attachment to a self. [Objection: But is not attachment to a self a "view" (*dṛṣṭi*)? And that [view] is associated with ignorance. Therefore, one should understand that ignorance is spoken of here by way of the door of "view," but it is not the case that the view of a self-identity is itself ignorance. [Response: This too is not correct.

When explaining through the factors of ignorance (*avidyā*), the manifestation of its own nature is appropriate; however, an explanation by means of something other than that would not demonstrate skill. (790) (PVA)
In this matter, there is no proof whatsoever; thus has ignorance been explained.
However, the proof for its opposite has been demonstrated exactly as it is.

There is no evidence whatsoever here that ignorance alone is defined by way of the views; rather, the evidence presented here is that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) alone is ignorance, which is the root cause of all defects.

Now, is it not the case that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is merely a portion born of delusion (*moha*), while delusion itself—characterized by non-clarity or otherwise—is that which accompanies all afflictions? How then can it be called the "view of a self-identity," given that a term denoting a specific distinction cannot have the meaning of a general category? Likewise, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were simply a view, then the phrase "ignorance associated with views" would lack the sense of association, for a thing cannot be associated with itself. To this objection, the following response is given: "The contradiction here must be explained;
and because of that contradiction, [the term 'view'] is used for those things consisting of it. (215)
The contradiction with all faults is established for one who holds the view of emptiness.

For the object associated [with cognition] is conceptualized as a distinction by way of the relationship between the general and the particular; for example, "a forest possessed of *palāśa* trees. In ultimate reality, it is simply the very nature of the *palāśa* that is expressed. Likewise, by means of the designation of a particular, its nature—which is the primary cause of ignorance—is indicated. Since the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is ignorance, all afflictions (*kleśa*) whatsoever are rooted therein. Through the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), which effects the cutting of the root, they are severed upon the cutting of that root. Because the vision of selflessness is the antidote to all afflictions and does not depart from the yogin, there is no further arising of afflictions. Therefore, cessation (*nirodha*) is described as having the aspect of emergence (*niḥsaraṇākāratā*).
It is not non-perishable because it is a property of a living being, for it is unestablished, like form and so forth. // 216 //

Even when there is a connection with its opposite through the repeated practice of abandonment, there is no recurrence of the fault, because that which opposes it has become like a hardened state. // 217 //
"Because it would not depart due to being of the nature of the self, and because it is inconclusive, like ashes"—
these are the intermediate verses [146,x].

[146,xi] But surely liberation occurs even from the cultivation of the self; so what is the use of the vision of selflessness? To this, the scripture replies: "The self... should be contemplated," and so forth. That too is incorrect, because: [146,xii]
For one who perceives a self, there arises therein a permanent attachment, thinking "I am. (218)
Through affection (*sneha*), one thirsts for pleasures; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) solidifies the defects (*doṣa*).

For one who perceives a self (*ātmadarśin*) is necessarily bound to the self by a permanent affection. And from affection, one possesses craving for its pleasures. Whoever has affection for something, he possesses intense thirst for the pleasure thereof, as in the case of the pleasure of a son and so forth.

[147,ii] But has it not been stated that from the perception of a self arises attachment to the self? Does attachment to wood arise from the perception of wood, or attachment to a woman from the perception of a woman? Therefore, the claim that "attachment occurs toward that which one perceives as a self" is incorrect. This is not so.
How could it be that one who has affection for another lacks affection for oneself?
Affection is indeed observed toward oneself; there is no dispute on this point.
It is extremely difficult to maintain that affection exists elsewhere without self-love.

(PVA 792) [147,v] If affection did not arise merely from the view of a self, then affection would not exist for anyone at all, because no other cause is present. Furthermore, a piece of wood does not perceive itself as being of use to it; therefore, there is no affection for it. And how could one who feels affection for what is useful to the self lack affection for the self itself? If it is argued that, due to a particularity of sentient beings, there is simply no affection for the self, whereas one feels affection for another out of great nobility and compassion—that is incorrect.
If what is called "great majesty" consists merely in benefiting others, then,
given that it would involve acting without prior reflection, such a state would be inconsistent. (PVA 793)
vii] By sacrificing oneself and making it a means for the benefit of others, one would manifest within oneself a great disregard for one's own interest and a state of acting without prior reflection.
[147, viii]
Now, if the performance of the welfare of others alone were happiness, then,
being thus deluded by attachment to that which is happiness, how could he be liberated? And yet, he is so.
Such a person would even perform the physical contact of limbs with courtesans.
If it is argued that this is an unreal transaction, there is no lack of reality in it.

[147,xi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either a bodhisattva or the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive them, he does not apprehend them; since he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell with them. Because he does not dwell with them, he does not become attached to them. Not becoming attached, he does not tremble; being without fear, he has transcended error and attained ultimate nirvāṇa. All those dharmas are unapprehendable because they are devoid of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, is it the case that even all those dharmas are non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is so. All those dharmas are indeed non-existent. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if all those dharmas are non-existent, how can there be the production of the thought of enlightenment? How can there be the practice of the six perfections? How can there be the attainment of the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship? How can there be the attainment of pratyekabuddhahood? How can there be the attainment of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment? Blessed One, if all those dharmas are non-existent, then what dharma is there that is produced, or what dharma is there that attains parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all those dharmas are non-existent, yet through the power of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, the thought of enlightenment is produced; through the power of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, the six perfections are practiced; through the power of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, the fruit of a stream-enterer is attained, up to the fruit of arhatship; through the power of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, pratyekabuddhahood is attained; through the power of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is attained. Subhūti, it is thus: although all those dharmas are non-existent, yet by means of the non-apprehension of all dharmas, one attains parinirvāṇa. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all those dharmas are non-existent, how is it that the Tathāgata, having fully awakened to all those dharmas, knows them as they truly are? Just as one established in their own self desires the bliss of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), so too does one desire the bliss of union with the limbs of a courtesan. Indeed, there is no distinction between that bliss and any other. If it is argued that [the latter] would be unreal, it is not unreal because there is no difference [in its nature]. If it is argued that this is improper because it leads to rebirth in hell and the like, we say no; for it is due to a specific excellence of great spiritual power (*mahānubhāvatā*) that one accepts going to hell for the sake of others. Since such great spiritual power is vast, the practice of what is conventionally regarded as unreal becomes another cause of happiness. Therefore, it is better to accept the conventional reality [of the object]. It is not because there is no difference [between the two states]. Thus, one who is thirsty for the self might, under its influence, equate faults and non-faults; consequently, they proceed to the concealment of faults.
Seeing qualities and becoming intensely thirsty for them, one thinks "this is mine" and takes up the means to achieve them. [147,xii] 219.
Therefore, as long as there is adherence to a self (*ātmābhiniveśa*), so long does one remain in saṃsāra.

If the self were to exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), then whatever benefit (*upakāra*) accrued to it would also be ultimate. Consequently, one would perceive that which provides ultimate benefit as being truly endowed with qualities (*guṇavat*). Thus, seeing qualities, one would appropriate the means of achievement (*sādhana*) thinking "this is mine. Therefore, due to this adherence to a self, there is saṃsāra; one even longs for the touch of a sow in a pit as a means to achieve pleasure.
Therefore, [147,xv]...
When there is a self, there is the notion of "other"; from the division of self and other arise attachment and aversion. (220)
All faults arise bound up with these two.
For the distinction between self and other produces attachment and aversion; from that, faults such as envy and stinginess arise, being bound up with attachment and aversion.

[147,xvii] But it might be argued: "Affection exists only for the self, not for what belongs to the self; therefore, due to the absence of affection for what belongs to the self, there is an absence of the conventional usage of 'non-existent'. To this, it is replied:
Necessarily, one who feels affection for the self does not become dispassionate toward what belongs to it.
Furthermore, there is no cause for the removal of affection toward a faultless self.

For affection directed toward the self does not depart without the presence of some defect; nor can one who possesses affection for the self ever be without affection for what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). Therefore, one who possesses affection for the self and what belongs to the self, by suppressing all defects, remains engaged everywhere; thus, his involvement in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is uninterrupted. Now, since affection for the self and what belongs to the self is the cause of cyclic existence, and because that which is joined with affection is flawed, there should be no affection for what belongs to the self therein.
[(Meditation on the Path)—] Even toward one who is corrupted by other faults, affection is not maintained; how much less so toward one in whom affection itself is corrupted? To this, he says:
If it is argued that affection is accompanied by faults, what follows from that? Its abandonment. (222)
When its object is not defective, it is impossible to abandon that [affection].

For affection does not cease because of a defect in something else; thus, this is logical only if there is a defect in the object itself. However, when the object is not defective, the absence of affection is not logical. There is no defect in the cause of pleasure, because of the presence of its excellence (*guṇa*). If you say, "Affection itself is the defect," let it be so; what will happen? If you argue that affection must be abandoned because it is defective, this is not the case. For there can be no abandonment of affection in the absence of a defect in the object. Therefore:
The abandonment of desire, hatred, and so forth, which are followed by the perception of virtues and faults, [is achieved]. (223)

The non-perception of those two occurs with respect to the object, but not in the same manner as with external objects. For desire and aversion arise from the perception of qualities and defects; the logical principle is that they do not arise in the absence of such perception. A quality is that which is a means to one's own pleasure, and a defect is that which is a means to one's suffering. If that [object] exists, there can be no abandonment of desire and aversion.
[148, viii] Furthermore, it might be argued: even an external object that possesses excellent qualities is abandoned.

That too is incorrect. While an external object, being dependent on external causes, can be abandoned, how can the successive [afflictions] arising through the power of the view of self and attachment (*sneha*) be abandoned? For the object possesses the quality of being the locus of attachment and is the material cause (*upādāna*); since that [quality] is absent [in the case of the affliction itself], there is the abandonment of attachment therein and its non-appropriation. However, attachment does not arise from the possession of qualities as a material cause, but rather from the quality of the object. Therefore, because the causal factor—the quality of the object—exists, how could attachment not arise?
[148,x] Indeed, attachment does not arise from the quality of attachment, but from the perception of the quality of the object. (224)
"When that cause is unimpaired, by what could the effect be prevented?"—
this is the summary.
Moreover:
[148,xiii]
Or what fault has been observed in affection? It is simply the basis of suffering. (225)
Nevertheless, there is no detachment here because of the perception of ownership, just as there is none toward the self.

For the self is first the locus of suffering; when the self exists, attachment subsequently arises, which is the cause of suffering. But in the absence of a self, whose would be the suffering? Therefore, since both are causes of suffering, there is no detachment from either, nor even from one of the two.

[148,xv] Furthermore, it might be argued: "The soul's status as a cause of suffering is due to external adjuncts (*upādhi*); it does not possess an inherent defect (*svagata-doṣa*) itself. The soul, assisted by self-attachment, merit, demerit, and latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*), is the cause of suffering. To this, he says:
If you claim that the self is the cause of suffering only in the absence of those [aggregates], then those aggregates must likewise be such [causes].
In this way, even suffering would be faultless; consequently, there would be no detachment from these two.

Indeed, no one feels detachment toward that which is faultless. Furthermore, the arising of self-attachment does not occur without a self as its basis, and since the causes of suffering are therefore not inherently faulty like the self, detachment is impossible.
If it is argued that through the cultivation of suffering there would be its abandonment, like the removal of a snake's fangs, [it is not so]. (227)
In this case, renunciation occurs through the abandonment of the notion of "mine," but not when there is a misconception;
for the senses and so forth are grasped as the basis for experience. [149.iv] 228.
By what could the cognition of sentient beings be prevented? Whence, then, would there be dispassion toward them?
[149,v] Is it not the case that affection has happiness as its cause? Since the opposite of that cause is possible, there is dispassion; for indeed, there is no affection for one who causes harm.

[149, vi] To this it is replied: It is not observed that the cessation of affection occurs even toward an object of the notion of "mine" (*ātmīya*) when that object is a cause of suffering. Therefore, detachment (*vairāgya*) consists in the abandonment of the notion of "mine. If you argue that it is the abandonment of the notion of "mine" itself [that constitutes detachment], we reply: no one ever abandons the notion of "mine" with respect to the body and so forth, which are apprehended as the basis for experience. For instance, one forms the notion of "mine" toward these things, thinking, "May I be a god," "May I be a serpent," or "May such a distinguished body and so forth be mine. How, then, can one who possesses such a notion be detached? To illustrate: [149, vii]
This is indeed directly perceived by everyone in the case of hair and so forth [falling] from the body. (226)
When things have passed away, that intellect arises as one characterized by aversion; elsewhere, it arises as characterized by longing.

For when hair and so forth are objects of enjoyment, then there arises a sense of "mine" accompanied by longing. But when the reverse occurs, then there is dispassion, which has the nature of the departure of longing and not otherwise; such is the distinction.
Furthermore,
[this applies] to the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
For in that case, the cognition of [the universal] itself arises through relations such as inherence (samavāya). // 230 //

The relationship remains exactly as it was even when [the fault] is perceived. [149,xi] There is the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with pleasure and so forth; conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with the body; the relation of inherence-in-the-conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*) with color-form and other qualities residing in the body; the relation of inherence-in-the-inherent (*samaveta-samavāya*) with the universal "color-ness" and so forth; conjunction with the auditory faculty; and the relation of conjunction-with-the-conjoined (*sāṃyogika-saṃyoga*) with the eye and other organs. Thus, the soul's relationship does not cease. Therefore, even when a fault is observed, affection for those [objects] does not diminish. Now, one might argue that one should not accept relations such as inherence. To that, too, there is a rebuttal.
Even in the absence of inherence and the like, there exists a state of being beneficial in all cases. // 231 //
[149,xiii] For affection is everywhere characterized by the desire to benefit; therefore, how could dispassion and the like arise from it?
Now, another might object:
"If one's own cognition [of the self] were due to the experience of suffering and benefit, as in the case of a finger," [149,xv]
For that is not exclusively suffering; for the most part, it is like food mixed with poison.

[149,xvi] Just as that is suffering, so too is pleasure. It is like poisoned food. For poisoned food is not merely suffering, since the state of being pleasure is also possible therein. Likewise, even the body of a pig in a pit and the like, though characterized by suffering, is indeed pleasure. Therefore, for some reason, the sense faculties and so forth are not objects to be abandoned. [Objection: But surely such a thing, being mixed with suffering, is nothing but suffering. [Response: If that is so, then it follows that what is conjoined with pleasure must be nothing but pleasure. Furthermore: [150,i]
From attachment to a distinguished pleasure, there arises aversion toward that which is contrary to it;
one might renounce some pleasure out of a thirst for a more distinguished pleasure. (233)
But even regarding that which is selfless, one proceeds out of attachment to a self according to what is obtained;
when nothing is obtained, desire for animals is seen in the case of a woman in rut. (234)

[150,iii] If a distinguished happiness were obtainable, there might be detachment (*vairāgya*) otherwise. However, for one lacking discernment (*avivekin*), there is no thirst for distinguished happiness precisely because of the absence of discernment. If it is argued that "discernment will arise," then discernment itself would be the cause of suffering; thus, detachment would consist in discernment alone. If, on the other hand, discernment necessarily arises by the force of causes, then even for one possessing discernment through the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya-avabodha*), [the cessation of suffering] would be unavoidable; therefore, liberation does not result from the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*). Furthermore, the cultivation of a self (*ātmabhāvanā*) is impossible. [150,iv]
In whatever manner this self is indeed the substratum of pleasure and the like,
since there is no cultivation [of a different nature] in that which is of such a kind, how could it otherwise become so?

For this self is the common substratum of cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth; even when cultivated, it would remain exactly as it is. Now, if it were argued that by relying on human effort this self could be made free from defects—that is incorrect.
For charcoal, even when rubbed, never attains whiteness.
The contact with one's own inherent nature cannot be prevented by anyone.
(796) (PVA) And that which is itself defective is not capable of removing its own defect.
How could that which is defective become non-defective? It never becomes something else anywhere. (797) (PVA)
For this very reason, he says:
[The Faults in the Theory of Self].
How can one for whom the self is dear desire its destruction?

The self is not defiled by passion and so forth; therefore, in its conjunction with them, it remains distinct in itself. Just as when one is in contact with a staff, the state of being a staff does not truly belong to the person holding it. (798) (PVA) If passion and so forth were not cognized [by the self], then the occurrence of non-passionate-ness and the like would be impossible.
If passion were due to the cognition [of another], then one would be passionate by virtue of determining that [object];
(799) (PVA) his passion would arise from the connection [with it], and not from the cognition of passion and so forth.
For if it were from the cognition of passion and so forth, the yogi would become passionate through the passion of others. (800) (PVA)
If there is a distinction [between them], what is the difference between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)?
If it is argued that their difference is not perceived, then from where is their difference supposed to be known?
(801) (PVA) If their own essential natures are distinct, how can the self-cognizing self not perceive them?

For it has been established that there is no error regarding the cognition of its own nature. (PVA 802) Now, if this [consciousness], which is not itself cognized, were to be cognized like the form of a jar, then because it would be an object of apprehension, it would become the subject; thus, it would not possess the status of an enjoyer. (PVA 803)
For if taste and the other [objects] were themselves the enjoyer, no state of being an enjoyer would be perceived.
Therefore, the enjoyer must be something distinct from them; and if this were so, there would be an infinite regress.
(PVA 804) If it is argued that enjoyment is inherent in those [objects], and for that reason they are called the enjoyer—
Enjoyment is nothing other than experience, and that [experience] resides in the object of enjoyment as well.
(805) The worldly understanding is such: "I am" and "this is mine.
Therefore, the relationship of the supported and the support exists in both cases. (806) (PVA)
Then, when being inferred, this [self] is designated as the "experiencer.
However, the established rule is that where perception is impossible, there can be no inference.
(PVA 807) Or else, it is taught that this [self] is accessible only to yogis.
Because of its extreme subtlety, it cannot be perceived by people such as us.
(PVA 808) For now, perception of this [subtle object] is not possible for us;
however, we do not know what will happen when those [beings] have reached that state. (PVA 809)
If the determination of things is made by setting aside the state of being a yogi,
then for us, there is neither the non-existence nor the cognition of that [state] by yogis.

Therefore, the self is of the very nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and is quiescent; otherwise, its non-existence would follow as a logical consequence. And if that [self], whose nature is the awareness of pleasure and so forth, were to become otherwise, it would simply be its destruction. How could one who holds the self dear desire its destruction?
Furthermore, if one is not suffering when one is happy, then the self must be desired by him [only] in its state of suffering.

For if the state of suffering were destroyed, the [entity] itself would necessarily be destroyed. (PVA 811) If it is thought that its states are perishable but not the underlying entity (*avasthātṛ*), [we reply:
apart from the nature of that [entity], no "state" is perceived. (PVA 812)
[151,iv] Furthermore, it might be argued: "The nature of consciousness itself does not perish at all; rather, it is only pleasure and the like that perish. This is not so.
It follows that consciousness itself must be diverse due to the diversity of pleasure and so forth,
because no consciousness is perceived apart from pleasure and the like.
That which is distinct as a constituent part of the self is not perceived as non-distinct [from it].
Just as no non-difference is perceived within that very difference;

(814) (PVA) if the difference between "cognition" and "that which is cognized" is distinguished by means of cognition, then for this very reason, even the self of another would become one's own self. (815) (PVA)
The claim that there is no cognition of it at all is also extremely difficult to maintain; for if there were a state of non-cognition, everything else would be devoid of self-nature.
If, on the other hand, that [object] is cognized separately [from the cognition], then unity would never exist anywhere.
Therefore, there is no identity between the prior and subsequent [moments], which constitutes perishability.
And thus: [817] (PVA) [151,x] Furthermore:
How can one who holds the self dear desire its destruction? For, if it were immutable and eternal, one should rather desire its persistence in that very state. (PVA 818)

If it is argued that this does not excessively follow [as a consequence] here due to the power of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), then why is that very recognition not accepted when such a form is possible?
[It would be recognized] as arising solely from beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*) due to the impossibility of an external object. (PVA 819)
Recognition of objects would be the cause of their persistence.
(PVA 820) But surely, if [the self] were immutable and eternal, there could be no successive cognition; nevertheless, let its eternity be established according to your own view. (PVA 821)
Or, if there is a simultaneous perception, this oneness might be accepted;
but if there is a non-simultaneous perception, then since the difference is clear, perishability follows.
Even though there is no successive perception due to its being eternally immutable (*kūṭasthanityatā*), nevertheless, its eternity consists precisely in its being changeless.

Likewise, there is an absence of succession in its perception. Therefore, if its perception were to occur successively, it would follow that its perception is destroyed by its own interruption. And thus, if one desires successive perception, one necessarily desires its destruction. Consequently:
How can one who cherishes the self desire its destruction?

If it is asked, "How can one desire non-perception? [the answer is: weakness is better than death. If he is beloved, let his life be better than a weak vision that obstructs life. [Objection: "But what is to be done with him who is not seen? [Reply: He must be sought again. And this being the case, since they occur in succession, that itself is destruction. This is yet another fault of the proponent of the self (*ātmavādin*).
