Alternatively, because of the perception of an identical form, the identity of the prior and subsequent [moments] is logical; but when there is perception of a different form, their difference is clear. And this being so, there is the destruction of the prior [moment]. Thus, how can one who holds the self dear desire its destruction?

Alternatively, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, the self (*ātman*) is entirely one and the same. It, however, assumes differentiation due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Just as space, though unitary, appears to be divided into "the space within a jar" and "the space within a cloth," so too the differentiation among selves is produced solely by ignorance (*avidyā*). If this is so:

If, due to the absence of delusion in one who is liberated, there were an abiding in the nature of something else, then that [liberated state] would not be the Self; rather, it would be a single [entity], and the state of existence would be its very condition. (823) (PVA) [151,xxii]

If, just as the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) does not exist when the jar is absent, so too the living being (*prāṇin*) would not exist in the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), then it would follow that when the space within a jar is absent, [the universal] space arises as one with another. Consequently, just as there is no division of space, there would be no division of the self (*ātman*); thus, there would be no distinction between self and other, and the self as "I" would simply perish, since its nature as a self consists in its exclusion from others. For one who has attained the state of space, there is no activity, enjoyment, and so forth; thus, there is no difference from space. Therefore, if the self is dear to you, how can you desire its destruction? If you argue that this follows by the force of reality, then the consequence is simply *nairātmya* (selflessness).
[152,i] What is this so-called "pervasion" (*vyāpitā*) attributed to that which consists of nothing but the self-awareness of its own nature?
Pervasion is said, in its primary sense, to be the occupation of multiple locations. (PVA 824)
Permanence is designated when there is an extension over many times.
But since there is neither pervasiveness nor permanence, how is the self established?

If, on the other hand, it were established as having the form of another jar or the like, then it would follow all the more that it is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*), since it is established even in the form of Devadatta and others. Therefore, if it were liberated, its non-existence would be certain, just like space. And there would be no purpose whatsoever for such beings in liberation; oh, what great lack of foresight on the part of the yogins! Now, if it is argued that in ultimate reality the self (*ātman*) is not the substratum of activity, experience, and so forth, and that attachment and the rest belong to it only through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), the following refutation is stated:
It is the substratum of all qualities, wherein the experience and conventional usage of all things have ceased. (235)

How could one desire love? For such is not the nature of love. Since it depends upon the perception of a self that transcends all worldly activity—being like the sky itself which rests upon the mere cotton-wool of self-apprehension—one who possesses love for something does not desire that thing to be otherwise. Such is simply the nature of love. Or, if it were to do so, it would reveal a lack of foresight. In that case, it would be better to desire cyclic existence (saṃsāra) itself, because the pleasures of cyclic existence produce dissatisfaction. If this is argued, it is said in reply:
Even in nirvāṇa there is no pleasure at all capable of producing complete satisfaction; for because it is to be desired absolutely, every [other] pleasure is [merely] pleasure. (826) (PVA)

[152, viii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature."

Indeed, there is no such thing as happiness that does not invite further longing. Therefore, even for one who is currently seated in the midst of all possible wealth of happiness, there certainly exists a desire for a further excellence of bliss beyond that. Thus, because he seeks that very same happiness again and again, his mind is not free from longing. And this so-called "longing" is synonymous with "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*). This is a great suffering for the great; consequently, every form of happiness produces only dissatisfaction. Hence, no one who possesses happiness has attained final nirvana (*parinirvṛta*). Since, in turn, he continues to desire every kind of happiness, he accumulates the karma for happiness and must therefore remain within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Even upon seeing [the faults of existence], he does not practice non-grasping, and thus he remains bound to the cycle of rebirth.

[152,ix] But surely dispassion (*vairāgya*) is indeed observed; it is not as if it is not seen at all. However, that [dispassion] arises because one is weary of the very pursuit of pleasure. Considering the exertion involved in seeking its means to be nothing but suffering, one who is oriented toward pleasure and desirous of another way brings about dispassion; it is not out of a lack of affection for the self. Therefore, he says: [152,x]
In every way, the grasping at a self thoroughly strengthens attachment toward the self. (236)
The seed of attachment to what belongs to a self remains established in its respective state.
This is the ultimate truth in this matter.

As long as there is grasping at a self, so long is one not released from attachment to the self. Consequently, attachment to what belongs to the self also persists, because it relies upon the perceived benefit [of the self]. (827) (PVA)

[152, xiii] But surely, by abandoning the very grasping at a self (*ātmagraha*), he will proceed to eliminate faults; therefore, how can there be attachment to what belongs to the self (*ātmīyasneha*) and so forth? It is said in reply: if he did not have this grasping at a self at all, for what purpose would he seek to dispel faults? For one does not engage in doing anything when there is no desire for it.

If his lot were otherwise than suffering, he would not desire him to be a sufferer; nor is there any grasping toward that [state], for these two [positions] are mutually contradictory. (828) (PVA) If, in his desire to act for the sake of others, he desires him to be happy...
Furthermore, let others indeed maintain their attachment to a self, since even if the self were momentary, a specific moment could still arise;
thus, altruism is indeed possible, and therefore the grasping at a self is futile. (829–830)
If that action were performed by him alone through the power of his great majesty,
then what kind of "great majesty" could there be for one who possesses such false pride?
Therefore, he who does not truly desire himself to be a sufferer [should act accordingly].
That very grasping at a self is what gives rise to his grasping at "mine" in that way.
(PVA 832) Now, if one who desires long-term happiness does not possess grasping at "mine," how could there be a desire for it given that long-term happiness has never been seen? (PVA 833)
If there were no activity [based on the thought] "it might perhaps exist," then it might never have existed;
nor would that "monkey-moonlight" ever have perished.
(834) (PVA) For one who has reached the state of fitness, why should he not become a Brahmin?
In this way, how could there be a functioning based on mutual dependence? Therefore, [it is not possible]. (PVA) [153, viii] Thus:
Even with effort, detachment from one's own self arises by relying on even a mere fragment of virtue. 237.
One who possesses [the notion of] "mine" obstructs detachment and conceals its defects.

He whose very name is the grasping of a self, relying on some slight quality that benefits the self and becoming intent upon it, certainly obstructs detachment regarding what belongs to the self, even while perceiving its defects. If it is argued that this is not so, we say no; for the perception of defects is itself obstructed by that perception of qualities. Therefore, one who is not detached from the self is indeed detached from what belongs to the self.
If there were detachment even toward the self, then there would be no one who is currently becoming detached. (238)

He abandons the self; therefore, the cultivation of suffering is futile. [153, xii] It might be argued: "One is unable to abandon the self. For it is not the case that the self itself is perceived by that [abandonment]. Thus, since there is no abandonment in the way that [the self] exists, and since there is no abandonment in the way that it does not exist, there is no abandonment of the self; it is merely the abandonment of passion. Therefore, through the abandonment of passion, one is always happy. To this, it is replied:
The non-establishment [of the mind] in pleasures is that very attachment, characterized by grasping.
And it has been previously analyzed that "wherever that [non-establishment] exists, there attachment alone exists. (PVA 836)

[153,xiv] And if there is detachment from the self, whose is that detachment? Now there is no one who becomes detached; for it is one thing that becomes detached from another. If that very [self] is by nature non-detached, it does not become detached. To this it is replied:
The self is not [identical] to the self; how could one become detached from it as it exists?
Nor does one become detached from it as it does not exist. (837) For there is no alteration of that [self], nor is there the persistence of another [self] in that way.
Therefore, it is in every way impossible [for a whole] to exist either as a totality or through its parts.
(PVA 838) A single entity has no parts; nor is there non-difference [of the whole] from its parts.
That which possesses parts must be distinct [from them], and if that were so, there would be an infinite regress. (PVA 839)
If it were somehow non-different, even so there would be an infinite regress, because of the lack of termination in those successive conceptualizations. (840) (PVA) [153,
xix]

Therefore, the self itself must be abandoned by him; yet, whether he abandons the self in such a way that it ceases to exist, or whether he does not abandon it in any form whatsoever, the cultivation of suffering is futile because detachment cannot be achieved. Alternatively: [153,xx] If there were detachment even toward the self, then there would be no one who is detached now. (PVA) 841.

Since he abandons that self as if it were non-existent, the cultivation of suffering is useless because there is no abandonment. The cultivation of suffering is not capable of effecting abandonment, for it is certainly not the cause of this dispassion (*virāga*). As it is with the self, so it is with what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*); therefore, one does not become liberated through such dispassion. For this reason also, the cultivation of suffering is useless, since:
[153,xxii]
Even by means of the cultivation of suffering, he would only manifest suffering. (236)
Even though he previously perceived that very same thing directly, nevertheless, he was not free from passion.

If the cultivation of suffering were for the sake of detachment (*virāga*), it would be appropriate; however, when that [cultivation] is practiced, it does not lead to detachment. For the cultivation of suffering is merely a cause for the direct perception of suffering; it does not otherwise lead to detachment. One might think that a continuum of suffering made manifest through cultivation would become detached, but this is not the case. This is because that suffering was already directly perceived previously, since a certainty preceded by direct perception is possible. Otherwise, one would not seek to abandon cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Indeed, suffering that has not been directly perceived does not afflict, nor does detachment arise from such [unperceived] suffering. Therefore, the cultivation of suffering is futile. For the suffering of separation from the beloved and so forth is directly perceived by all people; if one is not detached even then, how could detachment arise through the cultivation of suffering?

[154,ii] Now, if it is argued that the cultivation of suffering—occurring through the recollection and synthesis of all suffering—manifests a vast mass of suffering, and thereby leads to dispassion (*virāga*), then from that agitation (*udvega*) dispassion would indeed arise. But this is not so. Why?
Just as a mass of suffering, when being recollected, causes aversion, so too would a mass of happiness; therefore, this person would become full of passion.
Just as detachment arises from contemplating the continuum of suffering, so too does attachment arise from its opposite; how, then, can there be liberation?
[154,v] Is it not the case that one is not thirsty for the happiness of cyclic existence because of revulsion toward the happiness of tranquility? That also is incorrect, because:
For one who is settled in the view of a self, dwelling in a cemetery is not a cause for either tranquility or agitation. Is it a cause for agitation to a crow? 843 (PVA)
A crow does not find such pleasure in a lotus grove as it finds in association with its dwelling place in an impure location. (844) (PVA) [154,viii]

But surely it is observed: detachment arises from seeing faults in that which is a cause of pleasure. Therefore, why is one not detached even when seeing faults through the cultivation of suffering? This is not so, because:
"Even if, in one case, the mind is momentarily shaken by a fault... (240)
Even there, they are not at all dispassionate, just as a lover is not dispassionate toward another woman.

Although there may be a momentary detachment toward a person who has committed some offense, this is nevertheless not detachment in every respect. Indeed, a man of desire is not detached from one woman, yet he remains undetached from another woman, and even from her in turn by way of succession. For instance, he is detached only from that state which is opposed to passion, but from a state that is not opposed to it, he is indeed undetached. Therefore, he is detached only insofar as he is connected to the power of passion, and not in every respect; for passion is seen to arise toward that very same object once again. For this reason it was said: "O monks, that which is abandoned by noble wisdom is truly abandoned. Therefore, regarding this [detachment]:
Attachment, which arises as a single state through the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, [is that very thing]. (241)
She is the seed of all powers for their successive manifestation.

For one who makes a distinction between what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and what is to be accepted (*upādeya*), there exist desire and aversion. Nothing is to be abandoned at all times, nor is everything to be accepted; rather, desire and aversion arise alternately as seeds for one another. Thus, how could it be logical for one who possesses self-awareness to be free from them? For one who perceives selflessness (*nairātmya*), however, there is equanimity toward everything, because the distinction between the abandonable and the acceptable has ceased. For one who is established in the uprooting of all attachments, how could passion and the like possibly arise? Moreover, detachment (*virāga*) would occur toward an object that possesses a disagreeable form, and not otherwise. Yet, for one who perceives a self, there is never any disagreeability [in its nature]. First of all, this self is not inherently defective. Since affection toward it has a faultless object, it is itself faultless. The means of perception (*upalabdhi-sādhana*) are also faultless. This entire world consists of nothing more than this; so why, then, would such a person become detached?
Affection whose object is faultless is itself faultless, as are its means of accomplishment. 242.
The world is merely this much; where, then, could one become dispassionate toward it?
This is the summary. [154,xiv]
[155,i] Or, it might be argued as follows:
If there is faultiness in that [external object], it is equally present in its own self as well.
In that case, one who is not dispassionate toward it—how could he now become dispassionate toward its defects?

[Objection: But surely defects are also observed in objects, as well as in the body and so forth. [Reply: Indeed, what constitutes the defectiveness of those things that are causes of pleasure? [Objection: Is it not the case that everything is a cause of pleasure at one time and a cause of pain at another? [Reply: But that is exactly the same for the self (*ātman*) as well. If one is not dispassionate toward that very defect within the self, where could one find dispassion? If you say, "The self cannot be abandoned," then there can be no dispassion even toward what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). It is also false to claim that only what belongs to the self can be abandoned because its defects can be abandoned; for when a thing has a defect at a particular time, it is abandoned then, but not at all times. Just as there is the abandonment of defects, so too, due to the impermanence of defects, there is the impermanence of abandonment. If you argue that since great suffering arises later when a cause of pleasure is not abandoned, it is therefore proper to abandon it from the very root—then, by the same logic, since great pleasure follows even when there is pain, pain itself should be accepted. Therefore, for one who perceives a self, there is no dispassion anywhere. Moreover:
The perception of faults should counteract the affection born from the perception of virtues. (244)
And that [is not the case] with respect to the sense faculties and so forth, because it is observed even in the case of children and others;
likewise: [155,v] Thus:
Because it exists even in that which possesses defects, and by its very nature, it also exists in that which possesses qualities. // 245 //
Or else, it is due to the loss of the sense of "mine" regarding things that have passed away and so forth.

Affection for the senses and so forth does not arise from seeing their qualities, but rather from the view of them as "mine. For instance, affection exists toward that which is possessed as "mine" even when it possesses defects; conversely, affection is absent toward others even when they possess qualities. Furthermore, affection occurs in children, cattle, and the like who have not yet discerned qualities or defects, and it ceases when an object is no longer one's own or when it has not yet come to be. Therefore, affection does not cease merely through the perception of defects. If this is the case, then through the perception of defects, the very notion of "mine" will simply not arise, and in the absence of that, affection will not occur; for the perception of "mine" produced by the perception of qualities is dispelled by the perception of defects. This is not at all the case, because: [The original Sanskrit text continues with the argument: Since [affection persists despite the knowledge of defects],... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the full logical argument presented in the preceding portion.)
For that very reason, the perception of qualities is not the cause for the notion of "mine" either; therefore, that notion also does not arise from the failure to see defects. || 246 ||
[155,ix] Because in some cases, even when there is a fault, one's own prosperity occurs; and because it does not occur even when there is a virtue, as in the case of the past and so forth.
Moreover, the attribution of real qualities is indeed observed there due to affection;
therefore, how can a rule that subverts its cause not subvert it? (247)

[155,xi] Indeed, even affection (*sneha*) would be abandoned by the perception of faults if it were merely that; however, to the extent that there is affection, that very perception of faults is warded off by the imposition of the attribution of good qualities. If it is argued that, through a state of mental neutrality, there is both the perception of faults and the non-attribution of qualities, we say: no. Through affection, that very state of neutrality is not attained. At best, this [state of neutrality] is sublated by another affection toward a different object, and not otherwise. And thus: [155,xii]
In that case, the very same injury [caused by the mother] is reversed for him;
just as he was consumed by his mother, so too is he [consumed] by the *ḍākinī*.
Therefore, for one who perceives a self, liberation does not arise from the cultivation of suffering through the renunciation of affection.

[156,i] On this point, the Sāṃkhyas say: "For those who perceive a self, the cultivation of suffering is not possible; rather, liberation comes from the thorough knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. For instance:"
[156,ii] This person is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, of the nature of pure consciousness;
yet, through delusion and without recognizing another nature [of the self], he has resorted to cyclic existence. (PVA 846)

[156,iii] Nature (*prakṛti*) has pleasure and so forth as its intrinsic nature; because it is not grasped through discernment (*viveka*), the self (*ātman*) is not liberated. Therefore, liberation of the self occurs only upon the arising of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). That too is incorrect, because:
Because of the seeking of the higher and the lower, and because of the cognition of destruction and arising. 248.
This person perceives the self as distinct from the sense faculties and so forth;
therefore, even through the view of their identity, one who is attached does not feel affection for the self. (249)
It is by its very nature attached to the internal factors of perception.

The very perception of emergence (*udaya*) is the perception of difference (*bheda*). For difference exists through the state of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): the self (*ātman*) is the concomitant [factor], whereas pleasure and the like are not concomitants. Therefore, there is difference due to the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddha-dharma-adhyāsa*). Now, if one does not even reflect upon this, one is a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). That being so, there is no liberation at all, because the discernment (*viveka*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) [of the self from the non-self] would be impossible. Indeed, one who desires pleasure does not strive for its abandonment. No wise person seeks an *ātman* devoid of pleasure and the like. If it is argued that "transmigration does not exist prior to the contact with the mere seeker, because he perceives identity with the *pradhāna* within himself," that is incorrect.
[156,vii] And for one who is conscious yet sleeping, how can there be the delusion of oneness?
Whence comes the longing for sense-objects, from which follows attachment to cyclic existence? 847 (PVA)
For there is no entry into a primary [substance] therein; how then could there be oneness?
Indeed, it has already been established that there is no error regarding the self.
If it is argued that there is perception by way of being an object, then there would be no apprehension of non-difference.

In the Sāṃkhya system, perception is not tenable because of the absence of cognition (*buddhi*). Furthermore, how could there be desire for perceived objects, the engagement of persons toward them, or the existence of memory prior to the commencement of creation? (849–850) (PVA)
Since desire and memory arise from the very functioning of the nature [of the self],
and since that functioning arises from desire, there is a mutual dependence.
If it is argued that this occurs due to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then its states such as pleasure and so forth would likewise [arise from them].

Furthermore, how could even a latent impression (*vāsanā*) exist prior to a transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*)? (852) Therefore, if that [nature] is held to be the very essence of one's own consciousness, it cannot be made otherwise; thus, this transmigrating being is eternal. (853)
[156,xiv] But surely, since disenchantment is clearly seen to arise from the experience of suffering, how could it be otherwise? To this, he says:
But that which is present as weariness with suffering is such a form of aversion. (250)
There is no dispassion; for even then, he still possesses attachment because he seeks other states.
For:
Because hatred is the source of suffering, it remains established for only that long;
once it has ceased, it returns again to its own original nature. (251)

[156,xviii] Even though agitated by the experience of suffering, one who possesses detachment (*vairāgya*) does not [become hateful], for he perceives both himself and what belongs to himself as disagreeable through that very affection; thus, at that time, he is indeed possessed of aversion. This is merely a conceptualization (*pratyaya*) based on objects such as the foul (*aśubha*). However, for one who perceives a self, there is no liberation from affection even in the case of ultimate detachment, because of the longing for another state; therefore, aversion would always arise therein—yet you claim there is detachment there. This is not so. [156,xix]
As long as that suffering exists, so long does hatred proceed.
But when the cause, which is suffering, has ceased, from where could hatred arise?
(854) If suffering were to persist, then let this liberation bring about auspiciousness.
For one who is constantly overwhelmed by suffering and hatred, the state of downward rebirth is certain.
i] But how can there be liberation without agitation?
For there is no conscious being who, desiring liberation, would not be agitated by cyclic existence;
nor does a person become agitated unless they are overwhelmed by suffering. (856) (PVA)
That is incorrect.
And for that very reason:
[157,v] Indifference toward everything arises from the abandonment of both rejection and acquisition.
For those who are like the axe and the sandalwood, that which is called dispassion is described.

[157, vi] For it is by seeing mere dharmatā that the mind attains freedom from the sense of "mine. Is it not the case, O Noble One, that for yogins in our school, the state of being endowed with dispassion comes about through the abandonment of the antidotes, and not otherwise? If so, why did the Blessed One teach the cultivation of suffering? To this, the reply is as follows:
Having understood the suffering inherent in conditioned formations, the meditation on suffering has been taught. (253)
And that arising of our cognition has its basis in the vision of selflessness;
however, reasoning is for the sake of the vision of emptiness, while the remaining meditations have that as their purpose. (254)
By that very same [reasoning], he taught selflessness from suffering, and likewise from impermanence.

Indeed, the cultivation of suffering was not taught with reference merely to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). For if, for those possessed of passion, there were only the destruction of pleasure through mere [suffering], they would abandon their partiality; thus, it was taught so that they might become fit for the cultivation of the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāraduḥkha*). And that suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) is, in the ultimate sense, nothing but emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, liberation comes only from the vision of emptiness.

The remaining meditations, however, have that [insight] as their sole purpose. For this very reason, the Blessed One’s teaching culminates in the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*). As he said: "O monks, is form permanent or impermanent?—Impermanent, Venerable Sir. What is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?—Suffering, Venerable Sir. That which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—can one rightly regard it as 'this is mine,' 'this am I,' or 'this is my self'?—Certainly not, Venerable Sir. Thus, it is stated that the vision of selflessness alone, through the relationship of cause and effect, is the means to liberation. Furthermore, one who perceives a self is simply not free from attachment.
And one who is not dispassionate, being possessed of craving, relies upon all undertakings. 255.

Such a person, being unliberated from afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, is indeed what is called a "wanderer" (*saṃsārī*). For as long as the seed of the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) remains established, the view of "mine" (*ātmīyadarśana*) remains unimpaired and serves as the cause of *saṃsāra*. Consequently, one who is not dispassionate toward the self and what belongs to the self will necessarily possess craving; from that, one inevitably resorts to the undertaking of all types of karma. Being thus unliberated from afflictions and karma, such a person is nothing but a wanderer in *saṃsāra*. How, then, could there be even a scent of liberation for him?

[157,xiii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "In ultimate reality, that which belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) simply does not exist. Therefore, how could affection arise? For affection, by its very nature, occurs toward an object; it is not without an object. This too is incorrect. [157,xiv]
For one who does not desire even that which belongs to oneself, there exists no enjoyer of it either. // 256 //
Furthermore, at that time, the self would lack both activity and experience, for these two are its defining characteristics.

How could it be possible to establish that what is currently perceived as belonging to the self does not exist? If you argue that this is because everything is bound by ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no; for ignorance does not exist apart from the self. Ignorance is not other than the person (*puruṣa*), according to the scriptural statement: "All this is indeed the Person. Therefore, because its very nature is ignorance, its state of delusion would never depart. For a delusion that is identical with its essence cannot depart from it, lest the self itself be destroyed.

[158,ii] Thus it was said: "The Blessed One has taught that there are three kinds of feeling. How so? It is said: "Monks, whatever is felt is included within suffering. If this is so, how is it that the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling? This is not a fault, for the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with a specific intention (*abhiprāya*). What is that intention? It is as follows: the Blessed One taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering because they are impermanent; he taught that they are suffering because they are subject to change; and he taught that they are suffering because they are associated with the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*). Among these, the suffering of change refers to pleasant feelings. The suffering of conditioning refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings. The suffering of suffering refers to painful feelings. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that all conditioned phenomena are suffering because they are impermanent. Why? Because they are unstable and lack self-mastery. Therefore, since the Blessed One intended to teach that all conditioned phenomena are suffering in the sense that they are impermanent, there is no contradiction in his teaching that there are three kinds of feeling. Moreover, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the desire and form realms; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the desire and formless realms; and painful feelings belong to the desire realm. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three realms of existence (*dhātu*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the desire and form realms; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the desire and formless realms; and painful feelings belong to the desire realm. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three spheres of existence (*bhava*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the desire and form spheres; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the desire and formless spheres; and painful feelings belong to the desire sphere. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three states of existence (*gati*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine states; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless states; and painful feelings belong to the states of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three modes of existence (*yoni*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine modes; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless modes; and painful feelings belong to the modes of birth from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of rebirth (*upapatti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine rebirths; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless rebirths; and painful feelings belong to the rebirths in hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*jāti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*janman*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*utpatti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*prasava*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*prabhava*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*samudaya*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*prādurbhāva*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*nirvṛtti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*abhinirvṛtti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*upapatti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*jāti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*utpatti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*prādurbhāva*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*samudaya*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*nirvṛtti*). Among these, pleasant feelings belong to the human and divine births; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings belong to the human and formless births; and painful feelings belong to the births from eggs, moisture, and womb. Furthermore, the Blessed One taught that there are three kinds of feeling with reference to the three types of sensation experienced by beings in the three types of birth (*abhinirvṛtti*). Among

This [position] has already been refuted. Furthermore, if "one's own" (the self) does not exist, then action and experience do not exist, because the self consists essentially of action and experience. If it is argued that even this is not accepted from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then what grounds are there for the self being for the sake of another? If it is argued that this is because the self is determined by cognition (*saṃvedana*), then it follows that everything would be cognized [by that same self]. If it is argued that [the self] is non-existent due to habituation, like dreams and so forth, that is not tenable; for it would follow that the self is not ultimately real, or else that there is non-duality (*advaita*). In that case, it would be a variegated non-duality (*citrādvaita*). There is no such thing as a "self," because its permanence is not apprehended by perception, which grasps only the present nature [of things], since two perceptions—of the prior and the subsequent—cannot occur simultaneously. Permanence of the self cannot be established by either one of them alone. If it is argued that even this is not accepted from the perspective of ultimate reality, then there is only a mere consciousness (*cit-pratīti*). Nor is there a synthesis [of moments], because memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And since perception is absent, inference is also absent. Therefore, the desired goal is not accomplished through the vision of a self.
Therefore, it has as its seed that which is of a similar nature within a beginningless continuum. (257)
O you who desire liberation, uproot the sprout of the view of a self-entity!
This is the conclusion: liberation arises solely from the vision of selflessness; no other path is authoritative.

< (Liberation is not through scripture alone)—> [158,v] Now, it may be argued that the existence of the self is established through scripture, and its liberation is likewise established; moreover, that liberation consists of absolute bliss and never ceases, whereas worldly pleasure is subject to interruption, and thus one finds no satisfaction therein. Furthermore, since this [liberation] results from rituals such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), the entire previous objection is indeed untenable. And so it has been said:
Those who perceive, through the eye of the sages, entities that are beyond the reach of the senses and inaccessible to ordinary cognition— their word is not sublated by inference. (857) (PVA)
Or, that speech is not of human origin— this too is incorrect.
For those who do not perceive such a basis for the existence of scripture, [the following applies]. // 258 //

One who speaks merely on the grounds of having attained liberation does not produce satisfaction. This is true: the statement of those who do not perceive supersensible objects is sublated by inference. However, that very fact—that the statement is produced by such a person—is not understood, because this [quality of being produced by one who has attained liberation] is common to all scriptures. Furthermore, it is not the case that all scriptures are authoritative, nor is the performance of their contents possible. And it has already been stated that the [scripture's] lack of human authorship (apauruṣeyatva) is not tenable.
[Initiation is ineffective: [158,x] But surely, it is observed that seeds and the like possess the property of not sprouting due to contact with the procedure of initiation. That too is incorrect.
A ritual procedure, even when perfectly accomplished with seeds and other materials, is not capable of preventing the birth of men. (259)
[159,i] Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of liberation resulting even from anointing with oil, exposure to fire, and so forth.
Now, if it is argued that the efficacy of anointing with oil is limited to that alone, then the same applies to initiation (*dīkṣā*). Likewise:
[(a) If the self were formless, there would be no heaviness or lightness of sin: Since the sin was not removed by first making it heavy and subsequently making it light, [260]

Let it not be that for him there is only heaviness (*gaurava*) and no sin, because sin is formless. Even if, for one who has been initiated, there were lightness (*lāghava*) prior to [the teacher], the removal of sin does not follow from that alone. For lightness, when perceived as the opposite of heaviness, leads only to the absence of heaviness, not to the absence of sin; this is because sin is not itself heaviness. If it is argued that "he is heavy precisely because of his sin," from what is this known? If you say "from scripture" (*āgama*), it has already been stated in response to this. Furthermore:
There is no liberation from even that much evil through its destruction;
for, by implication, there is also a capacity for it elsewhere—thus, [the nature of karma] remains undetermined. (PVA 858)
Where indeed is the perception of deities and so forth not found?
If liberation exists everywhere, what then is the distinction? (859) (PVA) [159, vi]

Now, even if the severance of craving in your view indeed results from the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*), it must still be considered how liberation [actually] occurs; for that too is not as it should be. To explain:
[159, vii] "Due to the power of false cognition and the volition of craving arising therefrom... (261)
By that [ignorance], birth occurs as a transition to an inferior state;
for the causal capacity for birth resides in those two alone, because it exists solely in them. (262)
Because:
These volitions themselves are the unbroken karma that is the cause of birth;
indeed, the attainment of place and so forth is observed solely through the power of craving.

[159,xii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. What four? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat not long after the Blessed One had departed, approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta and, having exchanged polite and friendly greetings, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One, having risen from his seat not long after he had spoken these words, entered his dwelling. Then I, friend Sāriputta, having risen from my seat not long after the Blessed One had departed, approached the Venerable Sāriputta... [as above] ...and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, friend Sāriputta, I said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One, having risen from his seat not long after he had spoken these words, entered his dwelling. “In this case, friend Ānanda, you should approach the Blessed One and, having approached, say this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, the Blessed One, having risen from his seat not long after he had spoken these words, entered his dwelling. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of these words; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it. “Friend Sāriputta, I will go to the Blessed One and report this matter to him. “Go, friend Ānanda, and report this matter to the Blessed One as you see fit. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One, having risen from his seat not long after he had spoken these words, entered his dwelling. Then I, venerable sir, having risen from my seat not long after the Blessed One had departed, approached the Venerable Sāriputta... [as above] ...and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, venerable sir, I said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One, having risen from his seat not long after he had spoken these words, entered his dwelling. [The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, if anyone were to practice the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven years, one of two fruits could be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. Let alone seven years, Ānanda—if anyone were to practice the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for six years... five years... four years... three years... two years... one year... seven months... six months... five months... four months... three months... two months... one month... half a month, one of two fruits could be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. Let alone half a month, Ānanda—if anyone were to practice the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. [159,xiii] “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘If anyone were to practice the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. “Indeed, Ānanda, if anyone were to practice the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way for seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. [159,xiv] “How, venerable sir, does one practice the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way? “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one practices the four foundations of mindfulness in such a way. [159,xv] “But how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body? “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long. Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short. He trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out. He trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe in’; he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. Just as a skilled turner or his apprentice, when making a long turn, understands: ‘I make a long turn,’ or when making a short turn, understands: ‘I make a short turn’—even so, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, breathing in long, understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long’... [as above] ...he trains thus: ‘Tranquillizing the bodily formation, I shall breathe out. In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally; or he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally; or he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. Or else, he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of arising; or he dwells contemplating in the body its nature of passing away; or he dwells contemplating in the body both its nature of arising and its nature of passing away. Or else, mindfulness that ‘there is a body’ is simply established in him to the extent necessary for bare knowledge and mindfulness. And he dwells independent, not clinging to anything in the world. It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body. [159,xvi] “And how, venerable sir, does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating feelings in feelings? “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, when experiencing a pleasant feeling, understands: ‘I experience a pleasant feeling’; when experiencing a painful feeling, he understands: ‘I experience a painful feeling’; when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. When experiencing a worldly pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I experience a worldly pleasant feeling’; when experiencing an unworldly pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I experience an unworldly pleasant feeling’; when experiencing a worldly painful feeling, he understands: ‘I experience a worldly painful feeling’; when experiencing an unworldly painful feeling, he understands: ‘I experience an unworldly painful feeling’; when experiencing a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I experience a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling’; when experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘I experience an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally; or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally; or he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally. Or else, he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of arising; or he dwells contemplating in feelings their nature of passing away; or he dwells contemplating in feelings both their nature of arising and their nature of passing away

[Objection: Is it not the case that action (*karman*) is also a cause of birth? Therefore, how can there be the existence [of birth] through that alone? [Reply: That too is incorrect. Those very [mental factors]—the volition characterized by prior [action], such as the actions of giving and so forth, and their latencies (*saṃskāra*)—are themselves the action that results in a subsequent birth. This includes the volitions of false knowledge and the craving arising from it. These alone are the direct action because birth occurs immediately after them. However, the prior [action] is called "action" only figuratively because it is the cause of those; it is not itself the direct cause of a complete birth. Since even one who has been initiated possesses that [prior action], there would be no liberation.
[159,xiii] Or it might be argued:
The causes of motion and cognition are the substratum; these [arise] from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). 263.
Because the unseen (adṛṣṭa) perishes, there is no movement; its latent impression (saṃskāra) is not volition (cetanā).

[159, xv] The tenfold wholesome and likewise the tenfold unwholesome are not characterized by volition. And since that [unseen] is destroyed by means of rituals such as initiation (dīkṣā), [the opponent argues]. That too is incorrect, because the matter is unproven. Moreover:
[159,xvi] Because the production of the instrument occurs through the conformity to presence and absence of causal capacity. 264.
[The sense organs] are perceived in the intellect, yet they do not belong to anything else; do they not exist?

[159,xvii] The instruments, such as the eyes and so forth, which conform to the positive and negative concomitance of the intellect, being directed by the intellect, exist and arise in succession. Therefore, why is there no production? If it is argued that due to the impairment caused by initiation (*dīkṣā*), there is no capacity for production—this being the case:
Retention, propulsion, agitation, and cessation are under the control of volition. [265]

If the qualities of the self, such as cognition (*buddhi*) and the rest, were rendered incapable by initiation (*dīkṣā*), then immediately after that initiation, they would no longer possess the capacity for birth. Consequently, once cognition is incapacitated, these states would not occur: retention, acting according to one's own will, withdrawal from sense objects, impelling toward what is desired, agitation, instability, cessation, and destruction. Alternatively, if it is argued that the incapacity occurs only after death because causes depend upon specific transformations (*pariṇati*), that too is incorrect.
[160,iii] Now, there is no capacity for initiation and the like to produce [a result], if it were to exist only after death; such a distinction does not exist. (PVA 860)

If a capacity were perceived even slightly right now, then, through the attainment of excellence, there might also be something beyond this; however, when no progression at all is observed that partakes in degrees of intensity, then the postulation of liberation is entirely groundless. Furthermore, since passion and the like possess the same nature as the intellect while it exists, the absence of the phenomena of cyclic existence immediately after death follows simply from the absence of the intellect.

That too is incorrect. Why is it that consciousness itself does not exist in another birth? If you say "because of death," then the entire procedure of initiation would be rendered useless, since liberation would occur simply because consciousness is absent at death. Alternatively, if you argue that because consciousness is absent then, there would be no [rebirth], [we reply: one is still bound by impurities. (266)

If those stains were incapable of producing cognition, then even while one is alive, they would be ineffective. For the stains such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, while present, are not the causes for the absence of cognition; thus, there is no lack of cognition [due to their presence]. Now, if it is argued that when passion and the rest are impaired by initiation (*dīkṣā*), they are no longer capable, then they would not be the causes for the reconnection of cognition in one who is living. Consequently, liberation would occur immediately after initiation. If you say, "It [liberation] certainly does occur," that is not so.
[160, viii] Because of the decrease and increase of the opposing side and one's own side during their development, [the former is abandoned and the latter established]. // 267 //
Defects, arising from their own seeds, are not prevented even in one who has been initiated.

For defects are produced from their own seeds—how is this so? Because they diminish when their opposite, the realization of selflessness, flourishes, and because they increase when their own side, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), increases. And since such defects are not prevented even in one who has been initiated, how could he be liberated in this life or in another?
[160,x] Regarding the permanence of the self (*ātman*), there is no rebirth:

But if there is the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*), whose is this liberation? For it is the self, afflicted by the stains of passion and so forth, that becomes pure through some means and is then liberated; for liberation is indeed the cessation of bondage. And in the vision of selflessness, that which is bondage remains precisely bondage. He is not liberated, because the vision of a permanent self persists. That too is incorrect.
[160,xi] For that which is pure, there is neither another, nor nirvāṇa, nor fire, nor a purifier;
nevertheless, this designation "nirvāṇa-fire" remains established. 861 (PVA)

In that regard, in our own position, it is merely a matter of verbal expression that does not hold; and that has been resolved by means of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). But in the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*), the actual meaning itself does not hold, even though it may appear to hold through mere verbal expression. Nor is there any deficiency, because the primary reality is not undermined, and furthermore, there is no illustrative example here for [the opponent's case]. Why?
Because that which is eternal is independent, sequential production is contradicted. // 268 //
In both action and non-action, action belongs to that which is of a similar nature.

For liberation occurs when there is a change of state for the self, provided that it exists in an impure state such that purification is possible. This is because, as determined elsewhere, states cannot be effects produced sequentially by a self that is independent [of external causes], for that would entail the consequence of all states occurring simultaneously. Furthermore, action is contradictory [in this context], because the states of action and non-action are identical in nature.
Furthermore, there would be identity between cause and effect; otherwise, they would be distinct from one another. (266)
There would be the loss of the status of being an agent and an enjoyer, and causal efficacy would not be established.

If there were identity (*tādātmya*), it would follow that the cause and the effect are one, because they would be contained within a single self, just like that self itself. If there is difference between those two—the cause and the effect—then [the self] is neither the agent nor the enjoyer, due to the absence of any connection with the instrument or the enjoyment, as in the case of another self. Even from the perspective of experience, no such connection exists; for just as with another self, the yogi would become both agent and enjoyer simply by directly perceiving the instruments and enjoyments of another self. Now, if it is argued that this is so because of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), that is not the case, precisely because inherence does not exist. Nor is inherence the cause of the cognition of oneness even for yogis. Furthermore, if it is claimed that he becomes the agent and enjoyer through the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) with the cause and the effect, that too is incorrect. Moreover, capacity (*sāmarthya*) is not established; for it has already been demonstrated that a permanent entity possesses no capacity.
[(c) The application of mindfulness to selflessness: But then, even with respect to selflessness, recollection, experience, and so forth would not be established. That is not so.
Furthermore, the undesirable consequences of remembering or experiencing [objects] through another [person] do not constitute a refutation. // 270 //
Because there is no memory; for memory arises from the experience of something by that same [person].

There is no recollection for anyone, because the recollector is absent; nor is there experience, because the experiencer is likewise absent—rather, it is simply recollection. That very [recollection] has the recollector and the object of recollection as its domain; the same should be said regarding experience: pleasure alone is the object of experience, while experience and the experiencer are that [recollection]. And that recollection arises from a cause, namely, from a prior experience. Now, why does it not arise from another experience—one considered to belong to another—or why would there not be an experience of another's karma? This is due to the restrictive rule of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Even in the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*), why does this fault not occur? Because of the distinctness of selves; but from what does that very distinctness arise?

Just as memory does not arise from another source despite the non-distinctness of the self, so too, despite the non-distinctness of the mind, the emergence of recollection does not occur from another source. (862) (PVA)
This distinction among mental states may indeed arise from a difference in their causes; but how could this division of distinction exist for the self, which is without cause? (863) (PVA) [161,x]
Now, if there is no single self (ātman),
how can there be a connection of oneness in such thoughts as "I see" and "I remember"?
This same fault applies equally to the self; there is no cause for rejoicing here.
By what means of valid cognition does the self know both memory and perception as having a single locus? If it is argued that it knows them through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [then...]

It has been established that there is no perception of [an object] as having a prior and posterior state; since direct perception is impossible in that regard, inference does not operate there either. (PVA 865)
If the self were to know itself in its true nature as having a prior form,
then the existence of that prior cognition would be present at this moment.
Consequently, how could there be the occurrence of that cognition as something belonging to the past?

For the prior existence of that which is being experienced is not perceived. (867) (PVA) Priority is derived from memory alone; memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If its reality were established by memory alone, why would it not be accepted in other cases as well? (868) (PVA)
Therefore, even in the theory of a self (*ātman*), unity does not exist in reality;
rather, because those two [the self and the aggregates] occur simultaneously, they are mistakenly conceived as one.
When there is a mere conceit of unity, conventional usage proceeds through differentiation.
And because they have a single effect, this single conventional usage is observed.
This is clearly the power of beginningless habituation to ignorance;
there is no self, yet the Veda alone thus produces the grasping of a self.

[162,iii] How, then, can the process of saṃsāra proceed without a self? Because without a self, the view of a real body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) cannot exist. Furthermore, since memory is incapable of grasping either unity or permanence/impermanence due to the absence of a prior and subsequent form, there would consequently be no saṃsāra at all.

It has been stated here: "In ultimate reality, there is no such thing as saṃsāra, because it is said that the nature of things does not move by itself. Nevertheless, from the perspective of conventional usage, this is so. For instance:
"In the four truths, [there are the notions of] 'stable,' 'pleasurable,' 'mine,' 'I,' and so forth. (271)
Having superimposed sixteen unreal aspects, one becomes intensely thirsty;
(iii) right view is the view of selflessness.
In that very [cognition], there is the apprehension of the form of the reality of its opposite nature. 272.
[(a) Liberation through the exhaustion of craving—
] Right view, when well-cultivated, destroys craving along with its attendants.
[162, viii] The eight types of persons who have entered the path of seeing.

Samsara is indeed merely the superimposition of the unreal; in the ultimate sense, there is no samsara. The sixteen aspects [of the four noble truths] are unreal, and through their superimposition upon one who possesses craving (*paritarṣavat*), there arises the conceit (*abhimāna*) of the transmigration of karma; otherwise, the occurrence of samsara is impossible. Furthermore, this conceit is nothing other than the cognition of "other" and "self"; therefore, even when there is no cognition [of duality], there is the conceit of the self's oneness. Since it is of such a nature, through the possibility of proper mental attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), there is nothing [substantial] here. For one who possesses discernment, through the stability [of practice] and the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is purity; this is the object of direct realization characterized by the complete cessation of all ignorance, which is another name for Nirvana. Therefore, for those who see reality, liberation results from the cessation of craving.
[162,ix] But surely, while karma and the body still persist, how can there be liberation? This is not so, because:
Due to the three causes, there is no arising of karma and the body, even though they both persist.

Just as there is no arising of a sprout without a seed due to the absence of one, so too, in that case, liberation would indeed occur upon the destruction of either karma or the body; as they say: "Liberation results from the exhaustion of karma. This is not correct, because:
Because there is no possibility of an opposing factor, there is no exhaustion of karma and the body. // 274 //

Furthermore, because it is impossible [to eliminate karma] while craving persists—since [karma] arises again—and because effort toward the goal of destroying both [craving and karma] is futile, labor expended for the sake of exhausting karma alone is in vain. (275)
[162, xiii] There is no liberation for one whose karma is not exhausted.

For there is no other counteragent (*vipakṣa*) to karma and the body than the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Subjects such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) have already been explained; [the claim that] scripture (*āgama*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has also been addressed. Furthermore, one who is possessed by craving does not fail to perform actions. Indeed, passion, hatred, and so forth arise from it quite effortlessly. And when both must be destroyed, it is better to simply turn back craving itself. If it is argued that "karma too must certainly be exhausted," we reply: no, because its counteragent is impossible, as has already been stated. For:

[163,i] Furthermore, because a variety of fruits is observed, a diversity of potencies is inferred for actions; therefore, there can be no destruction [of karma] through the affliction of asceticism, since that is not of a single uniform nature. || 276 ||

[163,ii] When an action possesses the capacity to yield manifold fruits and is directed toward the self, how can its exhaustion occur merely through the experience of a single type of fruit? Since the fruit characterized by the affliction of suffering is of a single form, its exhaustion would therefore not be logical. For this reason:

In some way, that fruit produced from it would be small and not of a different kind. For by whatever karma a fruit of that very same kind is to be produced, through the experience of even a fraction of that fruit, it is indeed born of that karma; the fruit is exhausted by the experience of the fruit. There is no depletion of a fruit that is dissimilar to it.
Furthermore, even by the power of asceticism, through the mixing or the destruction of powers, || 277 ||
One would fall away from some affliction entirely through the absence of even a trace of affliction.
[163, vi] If asceticism possesses such power, then the fruit is lost entirely, even by a mere trace—such as the plucking out of a single hair. To this, it is replied:
If that which is desired as distinct from affliction (*kleśa*) is indeed austerity (*tapas*), and if that [austerity] is itself affliction,
then it is the fruit of karma; therefore, there is no confusion of powers (*śakti*) and so forth.

[163, viii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa in the interval. What are these four? They are: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort; and one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa in the interval. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth. What are these four? They are: one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort; one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort; one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who delight in creation. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa with effort. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who delight in creation; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa with effort. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa without effort. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, attain parinirvāṇa without effort. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, go upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who delight in creation. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who delight in creation; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who delight in creation; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who delight in creation; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who delight in creation. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who delight in creation. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who control the creations of others. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others.
