These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. What are these four? They are: one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others; and one who dwells in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having abandoned the five lower fetters, dwell in the realm of the gods who have power over the creations of others.

If austerity were merely affliction (*kleśa*), then the destruction of karma would occur from that alone; what, then, is the use of afflictions such as the "five fires" and so forth? Let all karma be exhausted by that very means. Indeed, there is no understanding of one person's capacity through the action performed by another. Furthermore, affliction itself is not austerity, because it is the fruit of karma. Nor is austerity merely the fruit of karma, for if it were, even animals and others who endure cold and heat would absurdly follow as being ascetics (*tāpasa*). [Objection: This is not the fruit of karma, because it proceeds from desire; whereas the fruit of karma occurs even for one devoid of such desire. [Reply: That too is incorrect. [163, ix]
Could the acquisition of a kingdom and so forth not be the fruit of karma through the power of desire?
There is indeed such karma; the intellect follows after karma.

If that action were not to have a fruit, how then could it be said by you that "the exhaustion of karma occurs through the experience of its fruit"? Therefore, this [experience] is indeed the fruit of the karma. Consequently, there would be the exhaustion of only the evil [karma], but not of actions such as those leading to kingship; thus, even kingship and the like must necessarily be experienced. Now, if it is argued that kingship and so forth are renounced precisely because of a lack of desire for them, yet the suffering of hell and the like, being forced upon one, must necessarily be experienced—and that therefore only torment is desired—then in that case, the suffering of hell must also be experienced. If it is further argued that because both are suffering, they are cleared away as suffering itself, such as by the plucking out of hair in hell and the like, that too is incorrect, because there is valid proof for this as well.
Because it is suffering, it is not the cause for the exhaustion of karmas, like the suffering of cattle.
If it is argued that this [reason] is inconclusive, why is it not so in your own statement as well? (PVA 873)
Moreover:
Just as the absence of the pleasure of sovereignty does not cause affliction for one who is free from desire,
so too, through practice, that hellish suffering does not afflict him.
(PVA 874) By the power of cultivation, all things in the world— such as pain and pleasure— are [transformed].
Therefore, for one established in liberation, there is no such thing as suffering, pleasure, and so forth.

(PVA 875) Now, it might be argued: "There exists karma that leads to the exhaustion of karma; this is precisely your own admission. This would constitute a contradiction of your own tenets. That is incorrect, because:
Even those things which are antagonistic to defects, by destroying the defects that are about to arise, [serve as antidotes]. // 278 //
They would be capable of that very action; how then could there be a loss of what has been done?
Indeed, there is no loss of an action performed, for there is no such thing as the destruction of what has been done. If so, how was the exhaustion of karma taught? To this it is replied:
[164,vii] Such is that karma by which, when another causal complex arises, it yields its fruit; however, this does not occur when there is the presence of something contrary to the karma. (PVA 876)

Furthermore, that which is necessarily capable of yielding a fruit must inevitably yield that fruit; for its sake, ascetics do not exert effort, since it arrives by its own force. However, upon the complete destruction of passion and the like, there is indeed the destruction of future fruits that are the effects of passion, but not of karma already performed that is destined to be experienced. If it is argued that just as there is the renewed emergence of karmas while craving persists, so too there is the arising of craving again while karma persists—this is incorrect, because:
Faults do not arise from action; one does not act because of being corrupted by faults, nor through the reverse.
Without false conceptualization, there is no desire even for pleasure.
When craving exists, one who seeks a result performs karma; otherwise, if craving were absent, one would do nothing at all.

[164,xi] Now, if it were the case that virtuous karma is capable of bestowing happiness, then one who desires happiness would necessarily [pursue it]. But that is not so. For in reality, there is no such thing as happiness even within *saṃsāra*; rather, it is merely a false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*). Without that false conceptual construction, from what could desire arise, or for whom would that happiness belong? Therefore, liberation occurs only through the complete destruction of ignorance characterized by the view of a real self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and not otherwise. Thus, the illumination of the Four Noble Truths alone constitutes "protection" (*tāya*). (c) From this protection, the state of being a Sugata is established.
Therefore, from that which has the characteristic of being the effect— the instruction on the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, it is the means for attaining the stable knowledge of all particulars regarding reality. 281.
Because the root *gam* signifies "attaining awakening," it therefore refers to those beyond the stage of training (*aśaikṣa*) who are superior to the external [practitioners].

For it is by virtue of being a protector (*tāyin*) that the Blessed One is known as the Sugata; and that state of being a Sugata consists in the stable, complete, and specific knowledge of reality. It is the knowledge of reality, the praiseworthy knowledge, the stable knowledge, and the non-returning knowledge. For what is stable does not return again. It is the knowledge of every particularity, the knowledge of all aspects, and the exhaustive knowledge. For here, the root *gam* has the sense of "awakening" (*bodha*). That this exists in the Blessed One is known precisely through his being a protector. Indeed, his status as a protector is not established by inference alone; for such a state of being a protector is not possible for others. If it were established by inference, it would apply to others as well. If the reply is that this [knowledge] has come down to us through tradition regarding inference, then the same would apply to others as well.

[165,i] The Blessed One said: “Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are the four? They are: 1) the self-nature of words as they appear; 2) the self-nature of deluded discrimination; 3) the self-nature of dharma-characteristics; and 4) the perfectly accomplished self-nature. Mahāmati said: “Blessed One, what is meant by the self-nature of words as they appear? The Blessed One replied: “Mahāmati, it refers to the various linguistic expressions arising from the sounds of speech, such as ‘this’ or ‘that,’ which are produced by the conjunction of names and objects. This is called the self-nature of words as they appear. Mahāmati said: “Blessed One, what is meant by the self-nature of deluded discrimination? The Blessed One replied: “Mahāmati, it refers to the false conceptualization that arises from the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance, which manifests as the appearance of objects where there are no external objects. This is called the self-nature of deluded discrimination. Mahāmati said: “Blessed One, what is meant by the self-nature of dharma-characteristics? The Blessed One replied: “Mahāmati, it refers to the characteristics of all dharmas—such as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which are established according to their specific marks. This is called the self-nature of dharma-characteristics. Mahāmati said: “Blessed One, what is meant by the perfectly accomplished self-nature? The Blessed One replied: “Mahāmati, it refers to the realization of the non-existence of external objects, the cessation of the mind and its mental factors, and the attainment of the stage of Tathāgatahood through the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). This is called the perfectly accomplished self-nature. “Furthermore, Mahāmati, these four kinds of self-nature are the realm of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and they are not the realm of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those who follow other teachings. Why is this? Because they have not yet abandoned the views of existence and non-existence, nor have they realized the non-arising of all dharmas. Therefore, Mahāmati, you and other Bodhisattvas should train yourselves in the four kinds of self-nature so as to transcend the realms of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and followers of other paths, and to quickly attain the stage of Tathāgatahood.”

It may be that there is no distinction such that inference occurs in some cases and not in others. Nor does this distinction exist even for a single person, despite the existence of the Blessed One’s teaching. Therefore, it is known that the Blessed One possesses the vision of all aspects of all things; for this [teaching] would not be possible without such a vision of all things in all their aspects. This is because, regarding statements such as "all things are momentary," the possibility of non-conclusiveness (*anekānta*) arises precisely through that which has not been seen. Now, if it is argued that his case will be just like ours, we reply: it is not so for us without his teaching. Consequently, this certainty belongs only to one who is a direct perceiver and to whom another provides instruction, and not to anyone else. Furthermore, there can be no instruction without certainty.
[165,ii] Now, suppose it is argued that this could occur even through error. That is incorrect, because:
If there were permanence, delusion would occur because of the arising of a similar subsequent [moment].
But if there is momentariness, what could be the cause of delusion by which it might arise?

Even with a body, he does not exist [as such], because there is no perception of both [body and non-body] simultaneously, as he relies upon both aspects. Therefore, this instruction is based solely on certainty. And that certainty cannot exist for us through inference without direct realization, nor without our [receiving] the instruction. Furthermore, the Blessed One did not speak this out of doubt, for that would entail the possibility of teaching both [alternatives]. Therefore, due to his possession of stable and complete knowledge of reality, the Blessed One is the Sugata; it is precisely from that [state] that the Blessed One’s superiority over outsiders, learners (*śaikṣa*), and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) follows. This is because of his being the Sugata. [165, vi]
Therefore, the formulation of knowledge for the sake of others is his teaching, which is compassion. (282)
Therefore, because one who has attained his own goal does not cease [his activity], there is the state of being dependent upon the welfare of others.
[165, vii] It is true that the Blessed One possesses the state of a Sugata, but from what cause does that arise? The response is as follows:

The accomplishment of the knowledge of others' welfare, which is designated as "the state of being a Teacher," is inferred as the cause; otherwise, the state of being a Sugata would be impossible. Furthermore, compassion is inferred from that, for without it, there could be no accomplishment of the knowledge of others' welfare.
But surely, what is established by this alone? He is an authority merely by virtue of being a Sugata. This is not so, because:
[165,x] His authority does not arise from mere knowledge, but from his teaching.
"Its validity is always established; otherwise, it would not be a valid cognition for us.
Thus he says:
Therefore, for one whose purpose is already accomplished, there is dependence on the welfare of others because of the non-cessation [of activity].

For, through compassion, when engaged in the accomplishment of knowledge for the sake of others, he always acts solely for the benefit of others. Out of compassion, he does not enter final nirvāṇa, as was stated previously. Furthermore:
"Because he is non-contradictory, the Blessed One is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Out of compassion, he teaches what is beneficial; through knowledge, he explains reality along with its means of attainment. (283)

And because he is one who possesses application (*abhiyoga*) in speaking that [truth], he is therefore an authority (*pramāṇa*). For for one who is compassionate, the teaching of what is beneficial is possible; and due to his knowledge, he speaks what is established and non-erroneous. That knowledge, along with its means, is what he possesses. And because he is one who possesses application in speaking that [knowledge] together with its means—for this reason, consisting of four causes, he is an authority. By this, he says the following:
In these cases— beginning and end, cause and effect, and so forth— the relationship between cause and fruit exists.
Therefore, it is definitively stated that the Blessed One possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge.
[166,i] For this very reason, the Blessed One is praised by means of this very quality, namely, the characteristic of being an authoritative source of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūtatva*). Thus he says:
The praise of the reality of the instruction is based upon that very instruction. // 284 //

Because it is not excluded even from inference for the sake of establishing the reality of the means of valid cognition, or because its application is observed [in the form]: "Whatever has the nature of arising... [285]
"Everything has the nature of cessation," and so forth, in many ways.

Why is there praise for the teaching characterized by its validity as being thus? It is so that the establishment of the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) may occur through that teaching. Among these, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) was taught by the Blessed One himself: "A person endowed with the cognition of blue cognizes blue; but he does not [cognize] 'blue alone'. Inference (*anumāna*) also has not been excluded. Therefore, it is verbal testimony (*śabda*) and the like that are excluded: "All the doctrines of others are empty; I alone am the proponent of reality. Alternatively, there is the demonstration of the formal application (*prayoga*), which is characterized as inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). As he said: "Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the property of cessation."
He says that very thing:
The basis of inference is the logical mark (liṅga), characterized by invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).

That [pervasion] was clearly stated by him through the demonstration of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) with the probandum (*sādhya*). For a reason that is pervaded by the probandum is the means of cognition (*gamaka*). And that pervasion of the reason has been demonstrated in various ways by the Blessed One: "Whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation. Therefore, inference (*anumāna*) too was indeed taught by the Blessed One; thus, the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*) is the very discovery of the Blessed One. And since that belongs to the Blessed One because he is a means of valid cognition, the aforementioned supreme quality of the Blessed One is indeed the means of valid cognition itself.

Because the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, taught the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*) as being endowed with both [aspects], there is nothing beyond that; therefore, the means of valid cognition is the Tathāgata alone, and from him alone all accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises. (879) (PVA)
[166,x] Thus ends the first chapter, "The Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition," in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*. 1.
<3. Chapter on Direct Perception> <2. Pratyakṣaparicchedaḥ> <1. The Number of Means of Valid Cognition>

<1. Disagreement regarding the number [of means of valid cognition]> [169,i] Having thus stated the general definition, he states the specific definition: perception and inference are the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Among these, it is a means of valid cognition because it is non-deceptive (*avisamvāda*). And non-deceptiveness consists in its arising from the object and its non-deviation from the object.
[169,ii] But how is that very non-deviation with respect to the object to be understood?

But surely, words and the like have no connection at all with an object; why? Because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists of two characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises from non-deviation from the object of knowledge. And there can be no non-deviation from an object of knowledge in the absence of an object of knowledge. Furthermore, there is no object of knowledge other than that which is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). As it has been said: "There is indeed no object of knowledge other than the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Perception has the particular as its object; inference has the universal as its object"—this we shall demonstrate. He demonstrates this very point: [169, iv]

Valid cognition is of two kinds because the objects of knowledge are of two kinds, due to their capacity or incapacity for purposeful action; hair and the like are not real objects because they are apprehended as non-objects. (1)

[169,v] It should be understood that there are only two kinds of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), distinguished as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). This will be demonstrated because, otherwise, the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*meyapratipatti*) would be impossible.
The state of being perceptible or inferable depends on the mode of apprehension;
since there is nothing else beyond that, there exists no other supreme means of valid cognition.
(PVA 169.vii)

The realization that an object of cognition is non-erroneous consists precisely in its being either directly perceived or inferable, and nothing else; for there exists no other mode of realization apart from those characterized as universal and particular. Furthermore, the duality of the single object follows from the duality of the modes of realization. And the distinction between modes of realization is the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this very distinction is the distinction of the objects themselves. But how can a distinction in the mode of realization constitute a distinction in the object? For when one thing is distinct, another is not thereby distinguished. This is true. A horse does not possess a distinction simply because it is different from a cow or similar animals.
Because there is no association [between them], it is not accepted that [the relationship] between cognition and the cognizable is thus [direct].
(PVA 2) The establishment of the constant comprehension of objects depends upon cognition;
that very object is inferred from another cognition when it exists as a distinct object. (PVA 3)

When it is perceived as being directly capable of producing cognition, then, because it is characterized by its own form, it is a *svalakṣaṇa* (particular). But when that very same thing is perceived through its capacity for mediation (*pāramparyeṇa*), then, because it is characterized by a general form, it is a *sāmānyalakṣaṇa* (universal).

By way of a traditional succession, incapacity (*aśakti*) is indeed capacity itself through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*), and not merely the absence of capacity. However, in the case of hair and so forth perceived by one with ophthalmia, or perceived through verbal testimony, there is no reality of the object, either directly or through a traditional succession, because they are not cognized as having capacity. This is due to the absence of conviction regarding the object (*arthādhimokṣābhāvāt*), which is brought about by the operation of a means of valid cognition that negates the presence of such conviction. For this reason as well, there is a twofold nature of the objects of cognition (*prameya*):
because of being similar or dissimilar, and because of being an object or a non-object.
Because the presence or absence of cognition occurs when other causes for sound are present [or absent]. (2)
That which is perceived in some way as having a similar form is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); otherwise, it is the particular characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that what stands before one is perceived in a form similar to a cow and so forth? Therefore, is that which is perceived by comparison as "this is a gavaya" the universal-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? [Reply: This is not so.
For that of which the arising of cognition occurs precisely through a similar form—
That would be the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is here the cognition of its own-form (*svarūpa*).

That which is perceived by means of a similar form is a universal; however, in this case, there is the apprehension of a particular (*viśeṣa*). If it is argued that "a similar form is indeed perceived," we say no, because that form is not perceived as distinct [from the particular]. If it is asked, "How then is there the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that 'this is similar'? [the answer follows:]
Indeed, even in the case of determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*), there is no separate perception of similarity;
and since there is no separate apprehension, that itself is the perception of non-duality. (5) (PVA)

[170, vii] The Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the three gates of liberation. What are these three? They are the gate of emptiness, the gate of signlessness, and the gate of wishlessness. Furthermore, what is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the gate of emptiness? Here, the Bodhisattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever as empty, nor does he perceive any phenomenon as non-empty. Why is that? Because all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty. Why is that? Because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature. Why is that? Because all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing. Why is that? Because all phenomena are originally quiescent and by nature in a state of nirvana. Why is that? Because all phenomena are beyond conceptualization and beyond discursive thought. Why is that? Because all phenomena are free from the activity of the mind, intellect, and consciousness. Why is that? Because all phenomena are without self and without what belongs to a self. Why is that? Because all phenomena are without a creator and without an experiencer. Why is that? Because all phenomena are without a knower and without a perceiver. Why is that? Because all phenomena are without a master and without ownership. Why is that? Because all phenomena are without a basis and without support. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like space. Why is that? Because all phenomena are without form, invisible, and non-resistant. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, an echo, a reflection, and a city of the gandharvas. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like the moon reflected in water and like a lightning flash. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a mountain peak, a waterfall, a cloud, and a thunderbolt. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a bubble, a mass of foam, a plantain tree, and a magical creation. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a mirage, a flame of grass, a wheel of fire, and a painting. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a corpse, a skeleton, a withered tree, and a ruined city. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a broken vessel, a scattered heap of sand, a dried-up riverbed, and a discarded garment. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a blind man, a deaf person, a mute, and a person born blind. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person suffering from jaundice, a person with cataracts, a person with a distorted perception, and a person with a confused mind. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who has lost their way, a person who has forgotten the path, a person who has fallen into a pit, and a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who has been bound, a person who has been imprisoned, a person who has been exiled, and a person who has been executed. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is hungry, a person who is thirsty, a person who is cold, and a person who is hot. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is weary, a person who is exhausted, a person who is frightened, and a person who is distressed. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is sick, a person who is old, a person who is dying, and a person who has died. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is angry, a person who is deluded, a person who is proud, and a person who is jealous. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is greedy, a person who is malicious, a person who is deceitful, and a person who is stubborn. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is distracted, a person who is agitated, a person who is depressed, and a person who is elated. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is beaten, a person who is struck, a person who is reviled, and a person who is insulted. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is laughed at, a person who is ridiculed, a person who is mocked, and a person who is derided. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is wept for, a person who is lamented, a person who is mourned, and a person who is grieved for. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is abandoned, a person who is forsaken, a person who is cast out, and a person who is rejected. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is deceived, a person who is betrayed, a person who is cheated, and a person who is defrauded. Why is that? Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is burned by fire, a person who is scorched by the sun, a person who is frozen by the cold, and a person who is parched by thirst. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is thirsty, a person who is hungry, a person who is naked, and a person who is destitute. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is weary, a person who is exhausted, a person who is faint, and a person who is swooning. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is terrified, a person who is agitated, a person who is panicked, and a person who is distraught. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is carried by the wind, a person who is swept away by a river, a person who is tossed about by the waves, and a person who is buffeted by the rain. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is burned by fire, a person who is scorched by the sun, a person who is frozen by the cold, and a person who is parched by thirst. Why is that? Because all phenomena are like a person who is thirsty, a person who is hungry

Indeed, it is not possible to experience a further similarity—distinct from the objects themselves—based on the cognition that "this is similar. For there is no cognition of an object that occurs apart from the representation of the object as it is established. Therefore, since there is no cognition of an actual object here, the cognition of similarity is entirely without an objective basis (*anālambana*). In the case of inferential cognition, however, similarity is the superimposition of a perceived form upon the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). If this is so, then the following answer has been stated regarding the object of words and the like being a universal (*sāmānya*): "The object [of a word] is not [the particular], because of the mental determination (*adhimokṣa*) of what is not the object. This should be understood in other cases as well: the object of a word is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), while the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is its non-object.

[170, viii] But if the object of a word is a general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), then the word itself must also be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because its object is a generality. This is not so.
Inference for the sake of others has as its object that which is universal (*sāmānya*);
it is not said that the object of a word is only the universal.
For it is not stated that the universal is not the object of a word. (PVA 6)
That which is the object of a word is a universal, but it is not the ultimate one.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is the object of the word alone; it is not the case that whatever is the object of a word is necessarily a universal. Nor does it mean that the non-object is exclusively the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, the intended meaning is that the particular is indeed the non-object. Therefore, this fault [of over-extension] does not apply. Consequently, even that which is the object of a word may be a certain non-entity (*anartha*), namely a universal. Likewise, even that which is a non-object may be a certain non-entity, namely a particular. Furthermore, a universal is that in which the cognition exists even when other causes—distinct from the [external] object, such as convention (*samaya*) and mental attention (*ābhoga*)—are present. A particular, however, is that in which the cognition does not exist despite the presence of other causes, such as the eye and so forth. Regarding this point as well, one should speak as previously stated.

Alternatively, that which exists as an object of cognition when other causes are present is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); whereas that which does not exist as an object of cognition when other causes are present is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because it is impossible to characterize what is unperceived by way of its own nature. That universal characteristic is also remote (*parokṣa*). In this context, that which is characterized by way of its own nature is the particular characteristic; otherwise, it is the universal characteristic, which is remote.

Now, by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the distinction between objects characterized as direct (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*) perceived? Is it by perception, by inference, or by another means of valid cognition?
If the duality of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is perceived by another means of valid cognition, [then that other means must itself be established].

The reason would indeed be contradictory, because a third [type] is also possible. (8) (PVA) Or, if it were established by two means of valid cognition, there would be mutual dependence. Even if the object were established by three or more means of valid cognition, (9) (PVA)
The establishment of valid cognition through perception and the other means would not occur; what is intended [by you] is not proven.
For it is the distinction of the object of cognition that establishes the distinction of the means of valid cognition.
How, moreover, could there be the establishment of the imperceptible by means of inference? (PVA 10)
Direct perception does not apply to that which is beyond the senses; nor is inference purposeless when direct perception is functioning.
How could there be "beyond-the-senses" status while direct perception is operating?
It is only through the cessation of direct perception that an object becomes beyond the senses.
In that case, perception does not operate [upon the object]; therefore, that [object] is not cognized by it.
This is an unprecedented verbal construction: to claim "seeing with the eye" while lacking [actual] perception.
Therefore, an object of perception is cognized by means of perception.

But since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding that which is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), how can there be a determination of its twofold nature? (14) [PVA 171,v] Therefore, the twofold nature of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) is unestablished; how then could the proof (*sādhana*) be contradictory? Even if the twofold nature of the objects of cognition were granted, from what [source] would it follow that there must likewise be exactly that many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For when a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established, every logical reason (*hetu*) is uncertain.
Furthermore, the establishment of a necessary connection is not based upon the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (PVA 15)

For how can the universal property of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) be established by perception? If that [universal] is not established, how could the relationship [between the means and its object] be determined by the senses through it? (PVA 16) Thus, there is no establishment of the two types of objects of cognition; however, if it were established by another [means], there would be a contradiction.
Furthermore, because the relationship [of the reason] is unestablished, the reason would indeed be inconclusive.

(PVA 171, ix) To this it is replied: The twofold nature of objects is established by perception itself. For the cognition of similarity and dissimilarity is a property of cognition itself, and that is established by the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Nor is cognition associated with error regarding its own nature. If there were a suspicion of error in that regard, there would be either a total lack of linguistic convention or the failure of the speech of the proponent, the opponent, and the judges to take place. To explain:
[171,x] Without a conscious experience, whose speech could proceed, and where? Speech never occurs anywhere without a coherent basis. (PVA)
If there is a difference in the cognition of things, there is a difference even among other [objects];

how much more so, then, will there not be a difference for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which has that very form? (19) Let there simply be a difference in cognition; how could there be a difference in the means of valid cognition?
[Objection: But surely, the nature of being a means of valid cognition was previously established through the general definition [of perception].
Now, this specific application of its distinctions has become the object of proof. This applies to one who would say that "this is fire" is a conceptualized perception. (PVA 20–21)
The intrinsic nature is established as unimpaired; its status as a cause for an object is due to its similarity with what preceded it.
And if it were not thus apprehended, one who desires an object would not act toward the attainment of that object.
(PVA 171, xv)

The validity [of cognition], characterized by engagement and withdrawal based on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), is already established in the first chapter by means of the general definition alone. What remains to be proven now is merely the conventional distinction [between types of valid cognition]. In this regard, there is only one type of perception, namely the conceptual (*savikalpaka*), such as when one says, "This is fire; it performs the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*. For one who speaks thus, these two [types] are presented. Since there is a difference in cognition due to a difference in the form of the apprehension, external objects too are understood as possessing differentiation. What, then, is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is the very nature of those [objects] in reality? In that case, the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), which has a luminous form, is established through perception itself, because it is a direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) due to having an immediate object. However, the similarity with a previous cause of purposeful action, being perceived as having a common form, is an object of another means of knowledge because it is mediate (*parokṣa*).

[171,xvi] Now, it may be argued that perception alone is the motivator, and not anything else; however, even though another mental state (*manas*) arises subsequently, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For as long as something exists simultaneously with that [perception], it does not thereby become a means of valid cognition, because this would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the body, the ground, and so forth, would also be means of valid cognition. To this, it is replied:
[171,xvii]
Through positive and negative concomitance, the status of something as useful or otherwise is established;
perception alone does not prompt action in the absence of that [concomitance].
(PVA 171, xviii)

Now, it might be argued that perception alone—having been observed to be the motivator through extreme habituation to the absence of that [object]—is not inference, which has the form of grasping similarity.
That too is incorrect. A solitary perception is never seen to be the initial motivator. If you argue, "Let it not be so initially; it will become so later," that is merely a tale of the past.
For if the first entry into that place were to cause disease, then I shall not enter at first; let me enter afterwards. (PVA 24)

[172,i] Since there must first be an initial engagement, how could there be a subsequent activity that is merely habitual? This very fact—that it does not exist without the preceding—is what constitutes the "subsequentness" of the subsequent. Therefore, even a cognition other than perception is necessarily impelling, because otherwise engagement would be impossible. Furthermore:
In some cases, the occurrence of smoke and other signs even with respect to fire and so forth is observed without the object of proof being present; therefore, that [perception] is also fruitless.

Just as, due to extreme habituation, there is engagement based on perception alone even without a mediated cognition (*parokṣapratīti*), so too is there engagement with fire and the like from smoke even without a perceptual cognition; thus, that [inference] is also not a perception that prompts action. [172, iv] Yet, it might be argued:
Without perception, inference cannot establish its own object; however, through repeated practice, perception itself can become the motivator for action even without that [inference]. (PVA 26)

In this case, direct perception alone is the means of valid cognition, and not inference anywhere. Even in the absence of that [inference], its establishment occurs; thus, it possesses the status of direct perception as a means of valid cognition. (PVA 172.vii)
To this it is replied:
It has already been stated in this regard that perception does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without repeated practice.
Therefore, let it be understood that inference alone is the primary means here.
(28) (PVA) If something is useless at one time, it will be useless at other times as well.
Why is it that living beings have a desire for inference even when they have not practiced it? (29) (PVA)
How could there be a desire for anything in that which is devoid of utility?
It is illogical to claim that an object which is not useful can be the domain of desire.
(30) Now, if it is argued that inference is desired for the sake of the operation of perception...
Even perception does not at all function with respect to this [object] when it is indicated by a logical mark (liṅga).
Therefore, it is established that both perception and inference possess validity only within their own respective domains; for such is the common understanding of the world.
[172, xiii] Now, if it were then indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), no; because there is no distinction. For instance:
Even though the process of instigation is the same, if someone is the instigator,
then who now would be the discerning judge between the states of being an instigator and not being one?
And there is no validity other than that of being a producer [of cognition].
Therefore, validity is equal for both perception and its opposite; or rather, it belongs to neither at all.

[172,xvii] Furthermore, it might be argued: even in that case, it is perception (*pratyakṣa*)—having as its object the effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*) and so forth—that is the motivator; whereas non-perception (*anadhyakṣa*), being present merely by its existence, has no functional operation (*vyāpāra*) in motivating it.
[172,xviii]

That too is incorrect. [172,xix] Because it is not perceived in this way; for no one has the conviction that perception alone is the motivator (*pravartaka*) in that case. Nor does perception possess any further status as a motivator than mere existence (*sattāmātra*), since everything is employed toward its effect solely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). According to our tenet (*siddhānta*) that this is merely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no agency (*savyāpāratā*) belonging to anything whatsoever. Agency belongs only to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), not to the ultimate. This will be demonstrated later. Furthermore:
In that case as well, direct perception itself is the means of establishing the next world. Why should we suffer any loss if there is a sublation of an inference by means of a logical mark? (PVA 33)

[172,xxi] If inferential knowledge regarding objects such as fire is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), let it be so; nevertheless, by that very knowledge of the mark (*liṅga*), which functions without overstepping the nature of perception, there is the apprehension of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) and the mark itself, as well as the next world and so forth—thus, there is no loss for us whatsoever.
[172,xxii]
If inference were not a valid means of knowledge, then because the next world and so forth would not be established, one might fall into nihilism; therefore, its lack of validity must be refuted.

Fearing that if inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then its objects—such as the next world (*paraloka*) and so forth—would remain unestablished, leading to the charge of nihilism (*nāstikatā*), we refute the rejection of inference; it is not for any other purpose. If that object of inference, such as the next world, can be apprehended by perception even when it is not currently perceptible, then what need have we for establishing the validity of inference?
For one might as well seek to establish with great effort that which has already been established.
If that object is accomplished without effort, what other person would have a further need for it?

(PVA 173, iii) What discerning person, when an object can be achieved without effort in one way, would resort to another way that becomes a vessel for the occurrence of effort? If the object to be established by inference is already established by perception alone, why is inference offered to us?
Furthermore:

If an object desired to be attained were established even when it is beyond the reach of direct perception, then it would follow that everything is a means of proof for everyone, and everyone would be a knower of all objects.
(36) [PVA] If it is argued that this is not so because there is no connection [between the person and the object], then in that case, it is nothing other than inference.

Indeed, even by proponents of inference, it is not accepted that there can be an inference without a cognition based on a connection [between the reason and the object]. Therefore, that which is cognized through a similar form is precisely the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as established by the perception of the direct experience of reality (*tattvasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). By this, the objective domain of the "effect-reason" (*kāryahetu*) has been demonstrated.

The fact that something is an object of a word is also accessible only through verbal cognition; that very verbal cognition itself establishes the objecthood of what appears within its own manifestation. By this, the demonstration of the object for the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is shown. For instance:
"By means of analogy (*upamāna*), there is the ascertainment of an object that is similar to a cow."
This [object] has been explained by the preceding word "similar" (sadṛśa).
Its own nature (svarūpa) is understood from perceptual cognition alone;
however, its similarity is the domain of verbal cognition.

[173,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One, there is nothing whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One, there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to. The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Subhūti, this is called the 'Perfection of Wisdom'—because there is no perfection whatsoever. Therefore, it is called the 'Perfection of Wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone were to say, 'The Tathāgata has taught a dharma,' they would speak falsely, Subhūti, they would be slandering me with false words. Why is that? There is no dharma whatsoever, Subhūti, which the Tathāgata has taught. Subhūti said: "How wonderful, Blessed One! How wonderful, Sugata! This Perfection of Wisdom is a great perfection, a measureless perfection, an infinite perfection, an unequaled perfection, an incomparable perfection, a perfection without superior, a perfection without end, and a perfection of all dharmas. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom does not apprehend any dharma at all. It does not apprehend form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It does not apprehend the eye, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. It does not apprehend form, nor sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena. It does not apprehend the element of earth, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness. It does not apprehend ignorance, nor the volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death. It does not apprehend suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. It does not apprehend the fruits of the spiritual life, up to and including the fruit of arhatship. It does not apprehend the state of a pratyekabuddha, nor the state of a Buddha. It does not apprehend even the state of omniscience. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is devoid of all dharmas; it is empty of all dharmas. It is neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor purified. Therefore, Blessed One, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to know all dharmas as they truly are should train in this Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, in this Perfection of Wisdom, all the dharmas of a Buddha are contained. Furthermore, Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this Perfection of Wisdom, he trains in the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. He trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. He trains in the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative absorptions, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness concentrations, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, these dharmas of a Buddha are all contained within this Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore, Blessed One, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to train in all the dharmas of a Buddha should train in this Perfection of Wisdom. The Blessed One said: "Well said, well said, Subhūti! It is so, Subhūti, it is so. A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to train in all the dharmas of a Buddha should train in this Perfection of Wisdom. The Blessed One then spoke these verses: "The Buddhas of the past, present, and future, Having relied upon this perfection of wisdom, Have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one who wishes to quickly awaken to Buddhahood Should practice this supreme perfection of wisdom. Just as the great ocean contains all rivers, So too does this perfection of wisdom contain all dharmas. Just as the sun and moon illuminate the world, So too does this perfection of wisdom illuminate all dharmas. Just as the king of mountains is the highest of all peaks, So too is this perfection of wisdom the foremost among perfections. Just as the lion is the king of beasts, So too is this perfection of wisdom the king of perfections. Just as the lotus flower is unstained by mud, So too is this perfection of wisdom unstained by the world. Just as the diamond is the hardest of all things, So too is this perfection of wisdom the most firm and unshakable. Therefore, those who seek the qualities of a Buddha Should always practice this supreme perfection of wisdom. By practicing this perfection of wisdom, One will swiftly attain the state of a Tathāgata. The Blessed One having thus spoken, the Venerable Subhūti and the assembly of monks, as well as the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said. Thus ends the "Chapter on the Proclamation of the Perfection of Wisdom" from the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [173,xi]

For instance: "This is similar to that" and "That is similar to this" have one and the same meaning. Furthermore, the conventional usage of "imitation of that" depends upon two [objects], yet it is not possible to cognize both through perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the nature of similarity is cognized solely as the object of verbal cognition (*śābdapratyaya*), by means of a reason consisting of its own nature (*svabhāvahetu*). This is because "this is similar to that," since the form (*ākāra*) of this is seen there as well; for what is being established is merely the conventional usage of similarity. As for the two forms which serve as the basis for such a cognition, they are apprehended precisely by the preceding and succeeding perceptions. Consequently, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of words. By the mention of "words," conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone is understood; that is to say, it is the object of conceptual construction.

[173,xii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of unarisen suffering, and what is the nutriment that, when abandoned, leads to the cessation of arisen suffering? Physical food as nutriment, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of unarisen suffering, and it is this very nutriment that, when abandoned, leads to the cessation of arisen suffering. Contact as nutriment... Mental volition as nutriment... Consciousness as nutriment, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of unarisen suffering, and it is this very nutriment that, when abandoned, leads to the cessation of arisen suffering. What, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of unarisen suffering, and what is the nutriment that, when abandoned, leads to the cessation of arisen suffering? It is craving, monks, which leads to the origination of unarisen suffering, and it is this very craving, when abandoned, that leads to the cessation of arisen suffering. What, monks, is this craving? It is the craving that gives rise to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of unarisen suffering, and it is this very nutriment that, when abandoned, leads to the cessation of arisen suffering. Thus, monks, the nutriment has been explained, the origin of the nutriment has been explained, the cessation of the nutriment has been explained, and the practice leading to the cessation of the nutriment has been explained. And what, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of the nutriment? It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is the practice leading to the cessation of the nutriment. Thus, monks, the nutriment has been explained, the origin of the nutriment has been explained, the cessation of the nutriment has been explained, and the practice leading to the cessation of the nutriment has been explained. Monks, for one who practices in accordance with this Dharma and Discipline, it is to be expected that he will, before long, realize for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he will abide therein. [173,xii] Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. [173,xiii] At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was seated near the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Lord; it is marvelous, Lord! How well has this exposition of the Dharma been taught by the Blessed One: 'The nutriment has been explained, the origin of the nutriment has been explained, the cessation of the nutriment has been explained, and the practice leading to the cessation of the nutriment has been explained. Lord, how is it that the nutriment has been explained, the origin of the nutriment has been explained, the cessation of the nutriment has been explained, and the practice leading to the cessation of the nutriment has been explained? "Ānanda, it is because of the nutriment that beings who have already come to be are maintained, and those seeking a new existence find support.
