[173,xxii] "Lord, how is it

The introduction of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is as follows: "In the absence of other causes, where there is no existence of cognition, [there is non-existence]. Where there is no existence of cognition, that [object] is non-existent. In this regard, a cognition occurring in one place makes it known—by virtue of its restricted form—that "I have not occurred elsewhere. For it does not apprehend itself as being active everywhere. Therefore, for the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), the understanding of the dual nature [of objects] arises from perception itself, since there is no other way of knowing. Furthermore, all such things as similarity and dissimilarity are the objects of both perceptual and non-perceptual cognitions; and it is understood that these depend upon the capacity or incapacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This will be demonstrated later.
In this regard, as for what is said— that there is no perception regarding that which is beyond the senses— that is incorrect.
That which is not present there is other than that which is directly perceived by me;
it is solely on this basis that the determination of the non-manifestness (*parokṣatva*) of objects is established.
Perception itself knows its own self through the nature of cognition.
The understanding of the non-perceptibility of another [object] occurs precisely through the cognition of its necessity [to be perceived].
(40) Even when [an object] is perceived by direct perception, it is considered "remote" (parokṣa);
in that case, the object itself possesses a mode of existence that is directly perceptible. (41) (PVA)
But surely, if the object is not known through perception, how can there be cognition of an imperceptible object?
For it is only when that [object] is known that its property and its essential nature are cognized.
(PVA 42)

If an imperceptible object were known by means of perception, then its property (*dharma*) would be cognized, because that property has that [object] as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For it is impossible for something that does not have that as its intrinsic nature to be its property, just like any other distinct entity. If it is argued that it is its property due to a relation with it, then the thorough cognition of that [relation] must also occur through perception. Consequently, since the perception cognizing the object connected with imperceptibility would necessarily cognize the imperceptible object as well, it follows that the very object intended to be imperceptible would itself become perceptible. Thus, there would be no scope for inference (*anumāna*), for what is already grasped by perception cannot be the object of inference. To this, it is replied:

Self-awareness functions as direct perception regarding that which is otherwise beyond the senses; however, another cognition, namely sensory perception, functions with respect to its substratum. (PVA 43)

[174, iii] For the cognition of a relation occurs when there is a cognition of two things; and those two cannot be cognized by a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, the property (*dharma*) of the imperceptible object is cognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), whereas the imperceptible subject (*dharmin*) is cognized by another perception, namely sensory consciousness (*indriyajñāna*). From that, the relation is cognized. Consequently, although the imperceptible nature is cognized by perception, the actual thing (*vastu*) is cognized by inference; thus, inference enters the process. Furthermore: [174, iv]
For a positive form of dharma that exists without deviation, cognition is not possible if the object is not apprehended; however, it is not so in the case of the opposite.
(PVA 174,v)

For a positive entity (*vidhirūpa*) that is a property (*dharma*) is inseparable from its substratum (*vastu*), and is apprehended by the same means of valid cognition as that which possesses the property (*sadharmī*). However, "imperceptibility" (*parokṣatva*) is simply the absence of direct perception; it does not depend upon the apprehension of the substratum.
[Objection: But if direct perception does not operate regarding the imperceptible, how can inference function? [Reply: This is of no consequence, because:
The fact that an object is beyond the range of perception is not established by inference;
rather, when there is direct perception, it is the proof of an object whose form has been seen. (PVA 45)

For it is not the case that the fact of being beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*) is established by inference such that the operation of perception would be required therein. Rather, it has already been stated that this state of being beyond the senses is established precisely through the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). When, however, the state of being beyond the senses is established by perception, it is the very form of the object—such as fire—which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*) that is established by inference; and since perception had already operated there previously, there is no contradiction in the subsequent operation of inference. Furthermore:
Because inference lacks the capacity to apprehend that very form [of the object],
its status as a means of cognizing what is beyond the senses is established precisely by that [very fact].
(PVA 46)

For inference possesses the very capacity to function with respect to the nature of that [object], which is not [otherwise] under discussion; and that capacity belongs to it only at that time. Therefore, the operation of perception is not required there beforehand. Nor is there anyone who desires an object as something remote (parokṣa) such that they would require the operation of perception therein. Even when [the object] is undesirable, that [capacity] occurs. By this, the establishment of its validity is also determined;
for its validity is established only upon the proof of the remote object.
Precisely because the object that is beyond the senses is established, its connection [with the cognition] is also established.

(47) (PVA) It is said that validity (*prāmāṇya*) in a cognition consists merely in its being connected with a real object. When the connection with a real object is established, there is no need for an inferential mark (*liṅga*). (48) (PVA)
As for the remainder, since it has already been explained under the section on conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth, it will not be discussed here.

[Objection: But surely the twofold nature of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is just the object itself being divided into two kinds; and the twofold nature of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the effect, while the object of cognition is the cause. How, then, can the effect be established from the cause? To this it is replied:
Since the effect arises from the cause when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present. [174,xvi]
Therefore, how could it be logical for the effect to be established from the cause?

Although it is a logical principle that causes do not necessarily possess their effects, nevertheless, in this context, the establishment of the effect proceeds precisely from the cause. For it is not the case that the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are always established from the two objects of cognition (*prameya*); rather, we maintain that it is through the possibility of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that they are established. We shall demonstrate the possibility of this causal complex later. Furthermore, the establishment of the two objects of cognition necessarily establishes the two means of valid cognition; for that very thing from which its establishment—characterized by certainty—occurs is itself the means of valid cognition. And it has been demonstrated that the establishment of the two does not proceed from a single [cause]. When this [argument] is intended to exclude three or more means of valid cognition, then the exclusion of other means of valid cognition is established due to the absence of their respective objects, because of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition devoid of an object of cognition. If, in the absence of an object of cognition—whether in its own form (*svarūpa*) or another’s form (*pararūpa*)—there is simply no cognition at all, what could then be a means of valid cognition? If one argues that the self (*ātman*) exists, even for that, in the absence of an object of cognition in its own or another’s form, non-existence alone would follow; thus, it cannot be called a "means of valid cognition. Therefore, an entity perceived in its own form is one object; therein, however, the distinction between "self" and "other" is established.
<2. Investigation of the Two Truths> [175,ii] That which is capable of causal efficiency is, in this context, ultimately real.
Anything else is said to be conventionally existent; these two are the particular and universal characteristics. (3)
This is an intermediate verse.
But surely nothing is capable of causal efficiency; how then can the capacity for causal efficiency be the definition of ultimate reality? For instance:
by whom and through what means is the capacity for causal efficiency of anything perceived?
For in that way, the cognition of a means of knowledge (*māna*) and its object (*meyya*) is not possible.

(PVA 175, vi) Neither for the eternal nor for the non-eternal, neither for the knowable nor for the knowledge, is causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) perceived by either perception or inference. To explain:
An eternal entity possesses no causal capacity, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established;
nor does a non-eternal entity possess causal capacity, because its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established. (51) (PVA)
Capacity is observed to be pervaded by positive and negative concomitance.
When both of these are not established, how can capacity be asserted?
(PVA 52)

Indeed, for that which is eternal and all-pervading, there can be no such thing as capacity (*sāmarthya*) with respect to any effect, since it is devoid of activity. If you argue, "Let it not have the capacity of a pervasive entity; rather, it will have the capacity of a non-pervasive one," or "Let it not have the capacity of something eternally abiding; rather, it will have the capacity of something abiding for a limited time"—that is incorrect.
[175,x] Whence could there be non-pervasiveness of space for that [eternal entity], given that it is never perceived? And whence could its eternity be established?
Just as there is no omnipresence for it, so too there is no permanence for this [entity].
(53) Even for an impermanent entity, since it is momentary, how could there be action?
For a momentary entity is established in its mere existence. (54) (PVA)
Now, immediately after this, its capacity for another [effect] is stated:
"Immediately after that, there is also another; therefore, it too has that activity" (55).
For indeed, all precedingness among the moments of all entities consists solely in their dependence on everything [that precedes them].
If it is argued that "even in the absence of that [cause], that [effect] exists," how could this be so in the case of momentary things? (56) (PVA) [175,xvi]

Indeed, it is not possible for a momentary effect to come into being again even in the absence of that [cause], because it exists only at that very time and is non-existent at any other time. Now, if it is argued that the continuum (*santāna*) is both the cause and the effect, and therefore this fault does not apply—[we reply: no, because the continuum does not exist as something distinct from those [moments]. Or, if it did exist, then that causal relationship would belong to the continuum alone, which would entail the non-existence of the moments due to their lack of efficacy. If it is argued that the causal relationship belongs to the moments themselves by virtue of their connection to the continuum—[we reply: no, because there is no relation other than the causal relationship between two distinct entities. Furthermore, since a continuum occurs immediately after every moment, everything would become a continuum. And regarding that [continuum], the same faults already mentioned would apply whether it were permanent or momentary. As it has been said:
If the continuum were something other than those [moments], and if it possessed causal efficacy, then that alone would be real.
Since the moments themselves would lack efficacy, their non-existence would follow, and the conceptualization [of them] would be in vain. (57) (PVA)
If it is argued that capacity is inferred for that which is related to it by virtue of its own capacity—
on the grounds that the ornament lacks primary capacity because it was borrowed—
then the relationship of cause and effect would exist between the continuum and that which is other than it.
For in that case, there would be a continuum of moments for the three worlds.
And since the existence of a continuum depends on its causal efficacy, the capacity to produce effects follows from it;
thus, the very same fault you have pointed out regarding the two positions—eternality and its opposite—would apply to your own view as well.
If there were a transition to another mental continuum, there would indeed be an infinite regress;
for if the continuum itself were an effect, it could not be an effect given its momentariness.
This is because, even in this case, another mental continuum must be the cause of that which possesses the nature of being an effect.
Therefore, that cognition which possesses an effect is not assailed by the tiger of infinite regress.
Moreover:
If the existence of the reason were to depend on an effect other than cognition,
then the effect itself would lack existence without the arising of yet another effect. (63) (PVA)
Therefore, because it is not established, existence does not belong even to the root [cause].

If everything were to have its existence uncontradicted by means of the effect of cognition, then here too, why would there be a cognition of the connection with the object of knowledge through that very effect of cognition? (PVA 64)
The causal relationship between cognition and the objects of cognition is perceived because both appear as existing in front [of the observer].
However, it will not be stated that cognition is an effect in relation to itself or to anything else. (65) (PVA)

It cannot be apprehended by that very same perception, because that perception has not yet occurred previously. But if it were already present, it would lack the nature of an effect; furthermore, it would have occurred before.
Thus, since there would be no finality, how could there be the cognition of its being an effect? (PVA 66–67)
If the relation of cause and effect were to exist only between two things that are simultaneous,
then it would follow— due to the lack of distinction— that this would apply equally to a pillar and a jar existing at the same time.
(68) [In that case,] even in the present context, the proof [of causality] would not be established when two such things are observed to be otherwise.
If even a solitary jar were not seen to be an effect [of a cause], then cognition likewise would not be so;
for without that [cause], there is no occurrence of the perception.
Indeed, that cognition is something else entirely; therefore, there is no deviation [in the logical reason].

"Is this pillar not also something else [than what was perceived before]? For us, there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) arising [in such a case]. And if [the object] were thus eternal, recognition would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
For the form of any single thing is never perceived as both prior and posterior. (PVA 71)

Because each of the preceding and succeeding cognitions lacks apprehension [of the other], memory does not function with respect to both; nor does it possess the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). There is no mutual mixing of the preceding and succeeding cognitions. (PVA 72–73)
Furthermore, the recollection that arises from that [perception] does not know unity.
Even if the self were indeed one, how could there be cognition by means of it?
(PVA 74) It is through means of valid cognition such as direct perception that it understands the object.
Knowledge does not attain the status of a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) merely by virtue of being dependent upon a self.
Even without dependence on a self, there is validity because of non-contradiction;
for the status of a means of valid cognition belongs to that which, after something has been seen, leads to its subsequent attainment.
Without a self, this entity is not apprehended as having the nature of non-existence.
Even if a self were to exist, there would be no means of valid cognition whatsoever for it.
(77) In that case as well, only perception and inference possess the status of valid cognition.
Neither for the self nor for anything else is a nature consisting of prior and posterior states observed.
(78) Whether by itself or by another, that [nature] cannot belong to what is eternal;
therefore, it is not perceived that either cognition or the object is an effect. (79)
The knower of the self knows the self and that which is to be known by it;
the cause and effect exist as being perceived through their sequence of prior and posterior.
Now, if [the cause] is known prior to the effect through inference from the effect...
Therefore, one knows that "this cognition has arisen," thus [knowing] its state as an effect.
(81) (PVA) Furthermore, it has already been established previously that for inference as well, there is no occurrence [of its validity] if the object is not known through perception. (82) (PVA)
If the prior perception were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then inference would not be valid.
If one were to claim that there is an inference even in that case, it would lead to an infinite regress.
(83) [PVA] Let alone the object of cognition such as "being an effect" and so forth; for one who holds such a view, there is no cognition of that [object].
"Because of the absence of a root, it does not proceed further"—this is established. It is not logical for this property (*dharma*) to belong to a subject (*dharmī*) that is itself unestablished.

(PVA 177, ix) When there is an objective support (*sālambanatā*) for cognition, the thing (*vastu*) is established; but when the thing itself is not established, then of what could there be a causal relationship? If it is asked, "How is it that having an objective support is unestablished?", it is replied:

In this world, only that which is a cause is an object of cognition, not merely that which is perceived; however, even for the cognition of one with cataracts, that [object] is attained by means of mere appearance. (85) (PVA)

Whatever object has a specific cause does not exist without that cause; likewise, the existence of cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth is not attained without an objective support (*ālambana*). (86) [PVA 177, xii]

Even without an object, visual and other sensory cognitions are observed to arise bearing the dual forms of the moon and the night. Therefore, since it arises even in the absence of the causal factor that is the object, it is logical that cognition—due to this deviation—is not the effect of the object as its cause. For this relation of cause and effect is simply the relation of pervader and pervaded existing between distinct entities. If an effect were to exist without its cause, it would not be the effect of that cause, nor would it be its cause; thus, because all things would be without objects, nothing at all would be established, and how could there be a relation of cause and effect?
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"The object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not such by virtue of being a cause, but rather by virtue of being the apprehended (*grāhya*). This too is incorrect, because:
[177,xv] There is no other state of being an object of apprehension apart from blue and so forth; and the nature of being blue and so forth appears even in erroneous cognition. (PVA 87)
Or why is it not observed that the state of appearing clearly in front is itself an error?
Therefore, there is no such thing as being an object of apprehension that exceeds what is erroneous. (88) [PVA 177, xvii]
Now, it might be argued that all cognition is indeed erroneous; this is not so, because:
[177,xviii] There is no causal efficacy whatsoever for that which appears to a deluded mind;
therefore, it is an error with respect to a non-existent object, while its opposite is the case elsewhere. (PVA 89)
To this also, it is said:
Is the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of the same nature as that which is cognized, or is it of a different nature?
For if it were [of a different nature], then everything—including that cognition or the action itself—would be non-existent because of the absence of that [nature].
If that action were a different entity, then in its absence, the object would not exist.
For when there is no entity, there is indeed no non-existence of either the effect or the cause.

If the effect, which is intended as purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), does not exist, then its cause would likewise be non-existent; how could this be? For one thing being non-existent does not imply that another thing is non-existent, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Granted, if the effect is absent, the causal capacity itself does not exist; however, it does not mean that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the cause is non-existent. Alternatively, if cognition is what constitutes purposeful activity, there too there are two possibilities: either that very cognition or another [subsequent] cognition. If that same cognition, arising again, is the purposeful activity, then even in the case of an error, erroneous cognition certainly arises repeatedly; for an erroneous cognition does not necessarily occur for only a single moment. If, on the other hand, the cognition of touch and so forth is the purposeful activity, that too is non-existent.
[178,i] Even if it is granted that there is the arising of another [moment], let that very [first moment] be the object while it exists.
But how can the existence of one [subsequent moment] be known through the cognition of another? 92. (PVA)
If there is no confidence even in self-cognition, what can be said of the cognition of another?
Since that [cognition of another] is also unreal, how indeed could doubt not arise? (93) (PVA) How does the cognition of touch differ from the cognition of the eye?
In that case, if there is satisfaction with the object, from what indeed does that satisfaction arise?

(PVA 178, iv) Just as there is indeed a lack of an external support (*nirālambanatā*) in visual consciousness, so it is also in tactile consciousness, because there is no difference between the two in being sensory cognitions (*indriyajñāna*). Furthermore, the possibility of impairment by cataracts and the like is equal in both cases, since perception occurs in both. But suppose it is argued that satisfaction arises from the sensation of heat due to the affliction of fever. Why, then, would there not be satisfaction even during the winter season when there is a sensation of heat due to the affliction of fever? Moreover:
If consciousness is the means of valid cognition, what is the purpose of satisfaction?
If consciousness is not the means of valid cognition, what is the purpose of satisfaction? (95) (PVA)
If cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the establishment of the object follows from that very source; what further dissatisfaction could there be?
That which is not established by direct experience cannot be proven even by hundreds of satisfactions;
for satisfaction is something else entirely and is not a means of proof.

What is the use of satisfaction other than from cognition? If it is argued that it is a means of proof (*sādhana*), how can one thing be established by another? If it is because of a relationship (*sambandha*), by what is that relationship established? If it is by satisfaction, then in that case too the establishment of a relationship must be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is by cognition, then the object is established by that alone; thus, satisfaction is redundant. And in that case, the same fault remains. If the object is established through cognition, why not from a previous cognition? By this, the "conviction regarding the object" (*arthādhimukti*) is also refuted. For instance: [178, ix]
Adherence to an object is not something other than cognition that establishes the object;
if adherence were itself cognition, then cognition would establish all objects.

By this, longing (*abhilāṣa*), memory (*smṛti*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and so forth are also explained. Furthermore, it is a triviality to say that longing and the rest arise from cognition, but cognition does not arise from them.
Now, it might be argued: "Let all cognitions have an object; there is no loss for us. But how is the distinction between valid and invalid cognition established?"

The establishment of what is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and what is not, based on whether it is worldly or transcendent, is a distinction; how can that be known except through the occurrence of sublation (*bādhaka*) or its absence? (98) (PVA)
By what means is the distinction between the sublated and the non-sublated established as worldly or otherwise?
If it were due to the existence of another sublated instance, an infinite regress would result.
If it is claimed that this is unique and non-worldly, while the other is otherwise, then this is trivial. For instance:
there is no cognition of those two, because they are neither perceived nor inferred.
For perception is the cognition of that which is to be perceived; it does not occur elsewhere.
[The thought] "this appears to me" or "to another"—in this regard, perception has no scope. If it is argued that there is cognition through inference:
[178,xviii] How can there be the arising of inference in the absence of the apprehension of a relation?
For an inference does not arise from seeing one's own experience, such as the observation of the action of horripilation and so forth. (PVA) 101.
Through the observation of the effect, smoke, it is that very same fire which is established here;

for inference has a universal as its object and does not perceive particulars. (102) [PVA] In that case, if [the fire] were not one due to the difference in the smoke, then why would there be oneness even in the case of [different] goosebumps?
Even the adherence to oneness is nothing other than cognition itself, like the sun.

If it is argued that there is oneness because the conventional usage "wherever by me the eye was directed, there [the object] was seen by him" occurs, this is equally applicable to the hair and such perceived by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*). In that case too, the two people with ophthalmia have an identical adherence to a single object. Furthermore, if—as in the case of what is perceived by one with ophthalmia—it were held that there is cognition by everyone else in the same way regarding other things like pillars, there would be no proof for this. Nor is there cognition of a pillar by one with ophthalmia. If it is argued that there is no fault even in the absence of cognition because the sense organ is impaired, then from what is this impairment of the sense organ known? If it is argued that it is known from the non-cognition of a real object, this is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): if there is impairment, there is unreality; and if there is unreality, there is impairment. Therefore, nothing at all is perceived by another.

[179,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them to be released from their bonds. Then, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they were freed from all fear. Thus, O Śāriputra, when one invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, one is delivered from all calamities. Therefore, one should always invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be a great mass of fire burning before a person, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, that mass of fire will immediately be extinguished. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Moreover, Śāriputra, if there be a great flood of water, and a person therein should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will not be swept away by the current. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be many hundreds of thousands of yakṣas and rākṣasas who desire to harm a person, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately lose their malicious intent. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Also, Śāriputra, if a person were to fall into a great pit of filth, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they would immediately emerge from that pit of filth. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Likewise, Śāriputra, if a person were to be bound with wooden stocks or manacles, whether by royal decree or otherwise, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those bonds would immediately fall away. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a person were to be led to the place of execution, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the sword of the executioner would immediately shatter into pieces. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Thus, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and such great majestic virtue. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should always invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. If there be a woman who desires a son, and she should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, she will immediately give birth to a son, endowed with handsome features and virtuous conduct, respected by all. If she desires a daughter, she will immediately give birth to a daughter, endowed with beautiful features and virtuous conduct, respected by all. Śāriputra, in this way, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows sons and daughters upon those who invoke his name. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to rob others of their wealth, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to steal. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Also, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to commit adultery with another's wife, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to commit adultery. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Moreover, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to deceive others with false words, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to speak falsely. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to engage in various forms of evil conduct, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to perform evil deeds. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Thus, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and such great majestic virtue. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should always invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. If there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to kill living beings, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to kill. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to engage in various forms of evil speech, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to speak evil. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Also, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to harbor malicious thoughts toward others, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to harbor malice. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Thus, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and such great majestic virtue. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should always invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. If there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to engage in various forms of wrong livelihood, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to engage in wrong livelihood. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to engage in various forms of unwholesome mental states, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to harbor unwholesome thoughts. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Thus, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and such great majestic virtue. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should always invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. If there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to engage in various forms of harmful actions, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to perform harmful acts. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be a person who, for the sake of profit, intends to engage in various forms of worldly distractions, and that person should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will immediately abandon their intention to pursue distractions. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majestic virtue. Thus, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and such great

Now, is it not the case that even the statement "it is not perceived" does not exist at all? For, by means of non-perception itself—in the form of a perception distinct from the nature of what is perceived by another—there is a negation of being perceived by another. Likewise, because that [perception] is an object, there is no negation of the other's direct perception (*parapratyakṣa*). How, then, is the nature of being perceived by another perceived by that [non-perception]? If you say that its nature is indeed perceived, but the state of being perceived by another is not perceived, then what is this "state of being perceived by another" apart from that nature? Is it something other than that nature, or is it that very nature itself? If it is that very nature, how can there be non-perception? If it is a different nature, how can it be perceived by another as a state of being perceived? If the object is not perceived by another, how is it said to be perceived by another? For that whose state of being perceived is itself not perceived is precisely unperceived. And thus, that object would not be perceived by anyone at all. Since each thing is excluded from the others precisely through its own respective state of being perceived, there is perception by both self and other; thus, there is no such thing as a "commonality" (*sādhāraṇatā*) among any perceived objects. Furthermore, since an object does not exist apart from its state of being perceived, it is merely a consciousness consisting only of the apprehension of its own aspect, like the aspect of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); there is no such thing as an external object whose existence is defined by causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*).
[179,iii] Now,
if it is argued that ultimate existence, characterized by causal efficiency, is established because cognitions themselves stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect— that too is incorrect.
If there is only self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), how can there be inference based on perception?
Furthermore, even if a causal relationship exists between two cognitions, how could it be grasped?
For that [cognition] does not grasp itself by means of its own dual nature, since it is aware only of itself.
When there is cognition of the cause, at that time there is no perception of the effect.
How can its status as a cause be apprehended? [Only] upon the perception of the effect.
Even at the time of the effect, that [cause] does not exist; how then can its status as an effect be apprehended? (PVA 105–106)
If it is maintained that the thorough cognition of the cause occurs through inference, then how can that which was not known from inference previously be known now?
[It would follow that] what was previously known through perception is now known through inference. (PVA 107)
Now, how can that knowledge be known through inference?

(108) If it is argued that there is no inference regarding its being "prior," that is not so, because it is cognized by perception. If it is argued that its "priority" is established by inference, then [that priority] does not exist. (109)
The so-called "prior" state does not exist at all, because it is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, there is no cognition whatsoever of a prior form.
That [cognition] is merely memory; it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), because it is self-cognized.
And perception is merely self-awareness, because it is the awareness of itself.
Therefore, there is no cognition of that [object] by means of that [perception], since the latter has another function.
Consequently, the establishment of causal capacity does not exist between the cognition and the object of cognition.
[179,xiii] Moreover.
This relationship of cause and effect does not exist regarding existence or non-existence.
There is no cause whatsoever for that which is non-existent, such as a horse's horn.
Because it is absolutely non-existent, the wise understand that there can be no cause for it. (PVA 113)
But [the claim] that "that which exists prior [to its production] is not the effect" is also a fallacious argument.

(PVA 114) How can there be a prior non-existence if [the effect] exists? And how could it be conceived if it does not exist? There is no prior non-existence for a non-existent thing, such as a donkey’s horn. (PVA 115)
If prior non-existence were defined as being before perception, there would be mutual dependence: as long as there is no state of prior non-existence, so long does its existence not occur.

As long as there is no relation with its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), so long is there no origination; and as long as there is no origination, so long the reality of that prior non-existence does not exist. If it is argued that prior non-existence is simply the cause's being devoid of its effect, that too is incorrect.
[180,iii] Is that emptiness not found in something else that lacks a cause?
Therefore, if it were connected with that [cause], it would become its effect. 117 (PVA)

[180,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of buddhahood as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are neither real nor unreal. Because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any dharma, nor does he perceive any dharma.”

For the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) consists in a relation with antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). And that antecedent non-existence is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) devoid of the effect. Furthermore, that [non-existence], even if it were something other than what is considered the cause, would still possess the nature of antecedent non-existence. Consequently, through a relation with that [non-existence], the status of being an effect would also belong to the positive entity (*bhāva*) which is the actual effect. If you argue that this is not so because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) between them, the answer to this has already been stated. Moreover, what is called "antecedent non-existence" is not graspable by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Only the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of the effect and the cause are perceived. If you claim that the very nature of the cause is antecedent non-existence, then the nature of the effect would likewise be so. If you say that this indeed occurs for the effect in relation to another subsequent effect, then why does it not also occur in relation to what is considered its own cause? If you argue that it is because there is no such cognition (*pratīti*), we ask: what conviction can arise from the mere cognition of a thing that is not actually required?

Therefore, it is not possible for that [cognition] to be grasped by way of the intrinsic nature of the object; nor is there another apprehension therein of its being an effect through [the perception of] blue and so forth. (PVA 118)

[180, vi] Indeed, no one perceives an entity as being "blue" and so forth by way of its being an effect; for an "effect-ness" distinct from blue and the like is not apprehended. Furthermore, since perception does not operate regarding the relation of prior and posterior, how could there be a grasping of prior non-existence and the rest?

Now, it might be argued: "Only that which exists can be an effect, for the activity of causes is possible only when an effect already exists; but if it does not exist, how can there be an activity without an object? To this, it is said:
[180, viii] Having seen, heard, or cognized, does the cause produce the effect?
Because it is insentient, its nature is considered to be dependent upon other causes. (PVA 119)
If God were the cause, He would be the director of causes;
yet there can be no cognition of what is non-existent, because He is the subject of perceptual consciousness.
In that case, is it the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) or is God himself the cause? (PVA 120)
Is it on the basis of the Sāṃkhya doctrine that everything exists everywhere? (PVA) [180,
xiii]

Either the so-called relationship of cause and effect is not perceived at all as something existent, or else the Lord, as the cause of the worlds, having perceived what is non-existent, applies the various causes with their specific determinations. If everything were existent, it would be perceived at all times, and thus the state of the world would be in chaos. To argue that this is not so because of the specific determinations of the perceivers is merely a trifle; for if perceivers also exist everywhere and at all times, what indeed is meant by "specific determination"? Furthermore:
would the effect arise from a non-existent cause, or would the effect itself be non-existent?
"The principle that an effect arises from a non-existent cause is a sound established rule.

(PVA 180, xv) For what indeed is the difference between a negation through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) and an absolute negation (*atyantābhāva*)? If it is argued that "it was a cause because it existed," then it is well said: "When it existed, it was not a cause; at another time, it was a cause. For even this would be the case.
Those things which exist attain the status of causes by virtue of that which does not exist;
for neither in them nor in those [non-existent things] is the presence of an operation observed. (PVA 123)
And if [the cause] exists by virtue of an operation, from what would that operation arise?
If it arises from the entity possessing the operation, then what further purpose does the operation serve there?
(124) If there were an operation even in that case, then that object would be mediated.
If the effect arises solely from the operation [of the cause], then the effect would arise even when [the cause] has died.
And if that were so, why would the effect not arise even when it has long since perished?
This long series of operations—how could anyone have such a lifespan?
If the operation [of the cause] is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then the effect will come into being;
however, if the effect were to exist at the time of the operation, it would follow that they are simultaneous.
(127) (PVA) If the cause does not exist at the time when the effect exists...

If that were the case, what difference would there be between [an object] that has perished after a long interval and one that has perished immediately? (PVA 128) If it is argued that existence occurs at the time of its arising, then for that which follows immediately [after the cause], arising is nothing other than the effect; therefore, it is simultaneous with it. (PVA 129)
After refuting the *syādvāda*, there follows the rejection of the two positions;
since much remains to be said at this point, we desist from it.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "The object is known beforehand by means of inference as being the cause of cognition. That too is incorrect.
[181,x] For that which is cognized through inference and which appeared previously in direct perception—
How can there be a cognition of that causal relation when there is no mutual mixing?

Even if it is granted that the prior non-existence of that which is known through inference is understood, by what means is it apprehended that this [inference] is the cause of the direct perception? For inference does not possess the cognition that "this object perceived by direct perception is the cause of that perception. Indeed, inference does not operate while the object is being directly experienced, because its domain is that which is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). Nor does direct perception operate upon an inferable object, because its domain is that which is present before the senses (*aparokṣa*). Furthermore, that which is being cognized cannot itself be beyond the senses. If it is argued that "that which is being cognized is 'beyond the senses' precisely by virtue of being beyond the senses," this is not so; for: [The verse: "Because there is no cognition whatsoever of the prior non-existence of an object that is currently being perceived. (PV 3.271ab) [The commentary: For there is no cognition at all of the prior non-existence of an object that is being perceived. If it were so, one would perceive the non-existence of the jar even while perceiving the cloth. Therefore, since the prior non-existence of an object is never perceived while that very object is being perceived, it is established that the prior non-existence of an object is not perceived at all. Consequently, it is not the case that the prior non-existence of an object is understood through inference. Thus, the claim that "the prior non-existence of an object is understood through inference" is refuted. Furthermore, the statement "the prior non-existence of an object is understood through inference" is untenable, because inference does not function with respect to an object that is being perceived. This is because inference has as its object that which is beyond the senses, whereas direct perception has as its object that which is present before the senses. Moreover, that which is being cognized cannot be beyond the senses. If it is argued that "that which is being cognized is beyond the senses by virtue of being beyond the senses," this is not so. Why? Because: [The verse: "If that which is being cognized were beyond the senses, then everything would be beyond the senses; therefore, nothing would be perceived. (PV 3.271cd) [The commentary: If that which is being cognized were beyond the senses, then everything would be beyond the senses, and consequently, nothing at all would be perceived. Therefore, it is not the case that that which is being cognized is beyond the senses. This is because inference has as its object
If it is cognized in its own form, what else could this "remoteness" be?
If it is an appearance with an unclear aspect, why is it not considered perception (*pratyakṣa*)? (PVA 181.xii)
For when there is cognition of two forms, both are held to be perceptual;
just as a pillar and so forth are perceived in succession by means of near and distant forms.

If that object consists of both a clear and an unclear aspect, then even when it is known through both perception and inference, it would possess only the nature of being perceived, just as in the case of grasping the near and far parts of a pillar. Alternatively, if clarity and lack of clarity are merely due to adventitious conditions (*upādhi*), then the very nature of the object is simply its blueness. [181,xv] If there were cognition in another form due to a difference in adventitious conditions...
There would never be direct perception [of an object], because its own nature would not be cognized.

(PVA 134) Now, if it is argued that what is called "direct perception" is the cognition of blue and so forth, then inference too would be direct perception, since it involves the cognition of its own nature. (PVA 135)
If direct perception is not considered possible because of the separation from the sense faculty,
why is it that conjunction with the sense faculty is not likewise cognized through inference?

Indeed, the dissociation from the sense faculty (*indriya-viyoga*) itself is not established, because its own nature is known through inference. Since there is no object, there is no contact with the sense faculty. How could that which is being perceived be non-existent when its nature is grasped by an inference? If it were non-existent, how could it be a real entity whose nature is apprehended through inference? Alternatively, if the connection with the sense faculty is not inferred at all, then inference would be useless, and there would be no engagement with it.

It is neither to be seen nor to be touched; engagement with it is in vain. (137) (PVA) [181,xxi] For one who seeks utility engages with an object only after it has been inferred. And since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which prompts such engagement, it would follow that it is not a means of valid cognition at all when it fails to prompt engagement. Now, if it is argued that there is an inference of the sensory contact occurring subsequently, and therefore it is not non-perceptual because the sensory contact was absent at that time—this is incorrect.

For if the relationship were to be established only later, since the form [of the cause] would not have been previously cognized, its status as a cause could not be understood; thus, inference would become useless. (138) (PVA)
At that very moment, while it is being measured, its nature is not yet manifested;
at that very moment, the state of being measured is called "presentness.

Indeed, presentness is not something other [than the object itself], because it appears as its own nature (*svarūpa*). Presentness is simply the appearance of the object's own nature. If it is argued that "non-presentness" consists in appearing in the form of the past and so on—[we reply: how is the state of being past apprehended by inference? For inference operates only upon what has been apprehended by perception, and perception does not operate with respect to the state of being past. When an object is seen by perception, it is not then apprehended as having the state of being past. If you say, "The state of being past belongs to it now," then that [object] has become something entirely different. And since perception does not apply to that [new state], how can there be inference? As for that which will be perceived later, its future state is likewise not apprehended by perception; thus, the application of inference to that case is the same.

[182,ii] But surely this is the same for both parties. For the opponent as well, there is no such cognition through direct perception; so how can there be a manifestation based on the mention of it? No, because his cognition arises in that way through the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and from that [it follows].
Since it arises based on an object and imitates its form,
that [cognition] may possess differentiation from another [object] through some particular aspect.

Thus it will be explained. That cognition does not arise from the object through a direct succession, but rather from the convergence of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*); otherwise, even a cause would be [erroneous], just as the perception of two moons arises from cataracts and the like. Therefore, cognition that has come from a form belonging to a past time is a determination of the past; because it grasps [the object] as being of a past time, it is indeed past and does not exist [in the present]. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being present at this moment.

How, then, is its existence established? Precisely because it exists. How does it exist? Because it is established by means of that visible mark (*liṅga*). Through that [mark], cognition also functions toward that [object]; thus, the conventional process is complete. But surely, if cognition does not apprehend the object, how can it be a motivator for action? Precisely because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). But would not even a mere property (*dharma*) be an establisher? There is no grounds for reproach, for it establishes the object exactly as it is observed to be an establisher, and not otherwise. Furthermore:
Cognition, through its attachment to the form of that [object], brings about [the activity] toward it and nothing else;
and therein, the determination of the object occurs necessarily by the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (PVA 141)

Therefore, it is not cognized by cognition that "that which is being perceived now exists as having its former form. Its form does exist now, yet it is simply not seen; thus, being unseen, it is remote (*parokṣa*). Non-cognition itself is the cognition of remoteness; thus, "this is remote."
If being beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*) were the very nature of the object, then that object would be directly perceived (*adhyakṣa*);
in that case, there could be neither inference nor any possibility of doubt.
Furthermore, such a cognition would not exist once the object has perished. (PVA 142)
Furthermore, there is no identity between the cognition and its object; therefore, that object is not directly perceived.

(PVA 143) Consequently, since inference—which has the nature of grasping an object—also necessarily involves a connection with the eye and other sense organs when it is being inferred, it follows that even an object that is the subject of inference would be [identical to] direct perception itself.

[2. Refutation of the Universal] But this is not so, because a cognition whose object is a remote thing does not have the nature of grasping that object; therefore, there is no causal relationship with what is apprehended by inference. Consequently, there is no relation of cause and effect. For this very reason, he says:
If it is argued that the whole is incapable [of action];
To this, he says: [182,xv] Regarding the seed and so forth in relation to the sprout and so forth.
[182,xvi] Power has been observed;
[182,xvii]
Thus it is said.
For instance: [183,i] To explain:
"I see the arising of the sprout from the seed"—this is worldly cognition.
Let it be accepted as "seeing" in that very context, without further distinction. (PVA 144)

For that in which one has the cognition "I see this" is precisely what is cognized. Furthermore, since the relationship of cause and effect is observed, there exists the conviction "this is mine"; therefore, because such an uncontradicted conviction is possible, one should not suspect that it could be otherwise. To explain:
I remember this object; there is no higher state than resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). Indeed, no connection between the object and the recollection is perceived.

It cannot be established by perception, because remembrance itself is not perceptual. Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), however, directly perceives only the own-nature of the remembrance, not its connection with an external object. Nor does the previous perception operate within the act of remembrance; how, then, could there be a cognition of that connection? Yet, there exists an infallible cognition: "I remember this. Therefore, in all cases, it is simply mental conviction (*adhimukti*) that establishes all conventional arrangements.
To this, it is replied: "If that [conviction] is accepted as being conventional, let it be so, however it may be. (4)

[183, vii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are neither real nor unreal. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, generate the thought of awakening? How can he train in the six perfections? How can he enter the stages of a bodhisattva? How can he purify the buddha-fields? How can he mature sentient beings? How can he turn the wheel of the Dharma? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet by means of skillful means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening. He trains in the six perfections. He enters the stages of a bodhisattva. He purifies the buddha-fields. He matures sentient beings. He turns the wheel of the Dharma. However, Subhūti, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend those dharmas as real, nor does he apprehend them as unreal. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, then what is the distinction between a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva? What is the distinction between their paths and their fruits? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet through the power of their vows and their accumulations of merit and wisdom, there is a distinction between the paths and fruits of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. Subhūti, a śrāvaka realizes emptiness for the sake of his own liberation; a pratyekabuddha realizes emptiness for the sake of both his own liberation and the realization of dependent origination; a bodhisattva mahāsattva realizes emptiness for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings and the attainment of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he avoid falling into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend even the notion of 'I' or 'mine,' and does not dwell in the signs of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, he will not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend the three doors of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as real, he will not fall into those levels. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any dharma, how does he fulfill the six perfections? How does he enter the concentrations? How does he attain the superknowledges? How does he enter the doors of liberation? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any dharma, yet by means of non-apprehension, he fulfills the six perfections. By means of non-apprehension, he enters the concentrations. By means of non-apprehension, he attains the superknowledges. By means of non-apprehension, he enters the doors of liberation. Subhūti, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in the perfection of wisdom."

The intended meaning is as follows: That which is mere conviction (*adhimukti-mātra*), arising from the cultivation of beginningless conventional usage, exists without the establishment of the reality of objects through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti-mātra*). Furthermore, the meaning of "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) is not simply "that which is perceived. For just as in some cases, such as with Devadatta, there may be the conceit of having seen someone even when he has not been seen, and that [conceit] ceases upon further investigation—yet that [person] does not exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*)—so too is all worldly convention exactly like this. Everything is merely conventional; for without valid cognition, convention is merely the conceit of perception. To illustrate:
The understanding of the causal relationship between effect and cause is achieved through positive and negative concomitance;
yet, in that regard, there exists no means of valid cognition, whether it be perception or inference. (PVA 146)
If the understanding of positive and negative concomitance were to come from inference based on perception and non-perception,
there would be a circular dependency.

Because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot be apprehended by perception alone, it is said that the causal relation is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). This is inconsistent, as it entails the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Positive concomitance is not grasped by perception; for perception does not function in such a manner as to think, "When this exists, that comes to be," since its operation consists merely in the apprehension of two [individuals]. Nor is it the case that [one thinks], "This was seen immediately after that, therefore it arises from that. For here only three alternatives can be conceived, as no other possibility exists: (1) "It arises from this alone"; (2) "It arises from this and nothing else"; or (3) "It arises from this and also from something else. If it were the case that "it arises from this alone" and "it does not arise from anything else," then by implication this meaning would follow. Even there, there are two alternatives: "now" or "at another time. If the thought is "if now it arises from this alone," then at another time it must arise from something else. Furthermore, even now, how could it be that it arises from something else in another place? Moreover, the causal relation would not exist in this way due to the lack of necessity (*niyama*). Nor is there the restriction that "it arises only from this," because at another time it might sometimes not arise at all. Therefore, the understanding of positive and negative concomitance does not come from perception. As for the position that "it arises from this and also from something else," the causal relation is not established because one is admitting a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) oneself; thus, this position is also not tenable.

[183,xi] Now, if it is argued that this is understood through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as "it does not exist in the absence of that," then there follows the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). For instance:
Is it perception and so forth that is "other," or is it non-apprehension that is likewise "other"?
For if [the other] were not distinct from perception, it would be a mere name and not a means of proof.
There would indeed be an entry [into the category of inference] if one were to conceive of it as being of the nature of inference.
Since inference occurs when there is a necessary connection established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

(PVA 149) If non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is itself perception (*pratyakṣa*), then that same fault already mentioned regarding perception applies here. If, on the other hand, it is inference, then that [inference] would proceed from a necessary connection based on positive and negative concomitance; thus, in the absence of inference, there can be no grasping of positive and negative concomitance. And in the absence of those two, there is no entry of inference. Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress of inferences.

[184, i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor apprehend any dharma whatsoever as real? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are unapprehendable. Subhūti, since all dharmas are unapprehendable, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever as real. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, what is the reason why a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor apprehend any dharma whatsoever as real? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because form is unapprehendable; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unapprehendable. Subhūti, it is because the eye is unapprehendable; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unapprehendable. Subhūti, it is because forms are unapprehendable; sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are unapprehendable. Subhūti, it is because eye-consciousness is unapprehendable; ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are unapprehendable. Now, [the opponent claims] that the apprehension of an entity's existence in the absence of another is established by the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*abhāva*). That too is incorrect, because from that [non-apprehension] one perceives only the absence [of the object] in those very places and times where it is present. Another says: "The causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is accessible through the means of knowledge called *tarka* (presumption/reasoning). The definition of *tarka* is the cognition of something imperceptible based on a relationship not previously perceived. For instance, while the occurrence of one thing upon the presence of another is observed, the causal relation defined by necessity—as between fire and smoke—is not [directly] perceived. Nor is the causal relation perceived through its connection with that occurrence. Yet worldly people understand: 'Because this exists, therefore that is its effect; because that exists, therefore this is its cause. Thus, the cognition of the effect arises from *tarka*. Alternatively, the cognition of that effect arises through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If this were not the effect of that, its occurrence from that would be impossible; thus, presumptive testimony is the postulation of an unperceived fact. That is also incorrect.
If the cognition of the relation between cause and effect is observed,
let it be seen whether that cognition arises through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or through reasoning (*tarka*). (PVA 150)
Therefore, apart from existence itself, no causal relationship is observed;
for the fault previously mentioned applies there, due to the non-acceptance of a restrictive rule.

For if the relation of cause and effect were to enter the domain of cognition, its cognition would have to arise either through reasoning (*tarka*) or from some other source. Yet, even by one who exerts effort, it is not determined as anything other than the actual existence of the things themselves. Nor is there a cognition [of such a relation] based on the rule that "from this, that necessarily arises," because one perceives only the existence of those things at that specific time. And that is not the relation of cause and effect.

Now, it might be argued that the rule is understood either through inference (*tarka*) or through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): "Since this is perceived immediately after that at present, therefore at other times as well, this must arise from that alone; otherwise, that very thing would not exist. This too is incorrect.

If it is argued that although this [sequence] is perceived here, how can it be known that it is so for other things as well? If you say, "The cognition is exactly like this," then a jar is also perceived immediately after a cloth; in that case too, it would be the same. If you say, "In this case, a deviation is observed," then by that very fact there is no confidence even in that instance. If you say, "Because the cognition lacks confidence, it does not exist at all," [we reply: this is due to the repeated observation of those who do not see far enough. If you say, "The worldly convention is exactly like this," then we have simply returned to the same point: that the understanding of capacity exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*).

For a cognition whose true nature is not determined is considered to be conventional (*saṃvṛti*). (PVA 152) Now, if it is argued that the status of being an effect was already cognized previously because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this very thing at another time is this same effect," otherwise such recognition itself would not occur.
That is incorrect.

As for this recognition—which is associated with a previous perception—is it [produced] by means of perception, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or reasoning (*tarka*)? This has already been refuted previously.
Now, [it is established] through recollection. For instance:
"I remember that this very thing was seen by me"—such is the nature of the cognition [of recollection].
Nor is a connection between recollection and experience admitted.
(PVA 184, xiii) 154.

Furthermore, recollection (*smaraṇa*) is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). That which is established by recollection is established only conventionally (*saṃvṛti-siddha*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "If that [recollection] is accepted as conventional, let it be so, however it may be. In this very way, worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) is not incoherent; for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is employed within worldly transaction, lest there be the consequence of the total collapse of worldly transaction. Its establishment occurs merely through the differentiation of conviction (*adhimukti-vibhāga*), like the transactions determined in a dream. Only the restriction of beginningless latent predispositions (*anādi-vāsanā-niyama*) remains as the source and cause of worldly transaction; otherwise, the very distinction between that which has an object (*sālambana*) and that which is objectless (*nirālambana*) would not be established from the beginningless past. Furthermore, as for one who asks: "Now, what is this convention (*saṃvṛti*)? And what is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?"
If conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is true, what is this [conventional reality]? If it is false, how can there be truth?
For there is no commonality of truth between that which has a deceptive object and the ultimate (*paramārtha*). (PVA 155)

[185,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the past as real, nor does he perceive the future or the present as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive all dharmas as real. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature.”

It is argued that "truth" (*satya*) and "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*) are contradictory. To this it is replied: what is called "conventional reality" is conceptual cognition (*vikalpavijñāna*), which is a mental engagement (*adhimukti*) arising from beginningless habitual tendencies (*anādivāsanā*). Therefore, the meaning is this: there is merely an appearance brought about by the force of beginningless habitual tendencies. For blue and other such objects are unreal, like appearances in a dream; nor is there a consciousness distinct from them. Consequently, they are not ultimate reality (*tattva*). Yet, because they are useful for worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*), they are "truth" (*satya*); thus, there is no contradiction in calling it "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛtisatya*). Therefore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is the exclusion of all intrinsic nature (*sarvātmaviveka*). For neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) can be observed with respect to external objects. However, the causality of habitual tendencies is recognized in the case of dream-appearances; since [dreams] belong to the same class, that [causality] must also apply to other cases. Alternatively, conventional reality is precisely the nature of arising and so forth, because it is not determined by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, "arising conventionally" means that even arising is [designated] precisely as being undetermined by a valid means of knowledge.
[185,iii] Now,
if "conventional reality" (saṃvṛtti) means incapacity because it is devoid of all intrinsic nature, and "arising" (utpāda) means capacity, then these two are contradictory.

That too is incorrect. To say "conventional" (*saṃvṭti*) means that in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) there is no capacity; therefore, production does not exist at all. To say "production exists" is merely a cognition of capacity, as it lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, production certainly exists. Nor is there the fault of "production by means of production. Capacity belongs to that very form in which there is production. In what form is there production? The meaning is: conventionally, not ultimately. Furthermore, "convention" is not a mere matter of naming, because it is designated as such on account of its being unestablished by a means of valid cognition.

As for the refutation regarding the simultaneity of cause and effect—namely, that the effect arises in the second moment after the cause—that too is incorrect.
