For there is no distinction between that which is non-existent long ago and that which is non-existent at the time of arising; since what has long passed is non-existent at the time of the effect’s production. If it is argued that this is not the case for what has just passed, then what is this "time of arising"? If it is the time of coming into being (*bhavana*), then since coming into being is non-different from the entity that comes into being, the cause would indeed be simultaneous with the effect.

[185, vii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. Among these, monks, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is like a man who, having entered a dense forest, sees a great tree with abundant fruit and thick shade, yet climbs it only to pluck its fruit for himself and does not allow others to partake. The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is like a man who, having entered a dense forest, sees a great tree with abundant fruit and thick shade, yet climbs it only to allow others to partake of its fruit and does not partake of it himself. The person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is like a man who, having entered a dense forest, sees a great tree with abundant fruit and thick shade, yet passes by without climbing it, neither partaking of its fruit himself nor allowing others to partake. But the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is like a man who, having entered a dense forest, sees a great tree with abundant fruit and thick shade, and climbs it to partake of its fruit himself and also allows others to partake. Among these, monks, the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, and the supreme among these four persons.”

Now, [if it is argued that] it exists at the time of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); and since this *bhāvanā* is the activity of the producer, then "the time of the *bhāvanā*" would mean existence at the time of the cause. Consequently, even something separated [in time] would possess causality, because it also exists at its own time. And since all moments of the producing entity exist at that [time], there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of causality. If it is argued that this is not so because they belong to different continua (*santāna*), then this is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): if there is no causality, there is a difference of continuum; and if there is a difference of continuum, there is no causality. To say that something is both a cause and belongs to a different continuum is a contradiction.

As for what was also said: "The meaning is that which is cognized without analysis (*avicāra-pratītyartha*). Here, "analysis" refers to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not conceptual consciousness (*vikalpaka-vijñāna*). Therefore, the meaning is "the object of a non-valid cognition. Furthermore, this very same meaning applies to the term "illusory object" (*māyārtha*); it means "the object of worldly cognition" (*loka-pratītyartha*). Since worldly cognition is agreeable only so long as it is not analyzed, there is no fault. However, the cognition of the authors of the treatises is not conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and is therefore not included here. Thus it has been said: "In that regard, what is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti-satya*)? It is whatever constitutes worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*). Even in the distinction between valid and non-valid cognition, it is by way of convention alone. For instance:
Valid cognition is non-deceptive. (2.1)

Attainment (*prāpti*) is the reaching of the object as it was indicated by the non-contradictory [cognition]. Furthermore, attainment is nothing other than the very state of being experienced. If the object has already been cognized, why would one seek its attainment later? Consequently, every cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, if there is a subsequent apprehension of something else that was not indicated [by the first cognition], then let it be a valid means of knowledge through the attainment of that [newly apprehended thing]. In this way, everything would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge.
Or, even if something has been indicated, if there remains something else unindicated, then it would be a valid means of knowledge through the attainment of that [unindicated remainder].
That too is incorrect, because there is no evidence presented; thus, this is merely trivial.

Therefore, let it be as it may that nothing exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); nevertheless, by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), there is no impairment whatsoever to the established distinction between valid and invalid means of cognition (*pramāṇa* and *apramāṇa*). Your position is precisely what we intend; thus, it is impossible to proceed by transgressing the actual nature of things (*vastutattva*). [186, iv] (Investigation of the Universal)

[Objection: "But if, even with respect to the general capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is possible [to attribute existence] by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), then there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition. [The author] replies:
"[186,v] If that [existence] exists everywhere, then it does not [arise] from the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of cognition."
It is not perceived in its general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), just like the cognitions of the eye, visible form, and so forth. // 5 //

Just as the cognitions of the eye, visible forms, and so forth follow upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—having the objective support (*ālambana*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the object (*viṣaya*) as their domain—in that same way it is not with the cognitions of universals (*sāmānya*). This is because the cognition of a universal arises merely from the recollection of a previous perception. Cognitions of visible forms and so forth do not arise solely from internal causes such as the eye; for instance: [186, vi] Just as the cognitions of the eye, visible forms, and so forth follow upon positive and negative concomitance—having the objective support, the dominant condition, and the object as their domain—in that same way it is not with the cognitions of universals. This is because the cognition of a universal arises merely from the recollection of a previous perception. Cognitions of visible forms and so forth do not arise solely from internal causes such as the eye; for instance:
[186,vii] Even if the prior existence of an entity is not seen in reality,
nevertheless, because its absence [in other cases] is observed, there arises the cognition of its existence. (PVA 156)

[186, viii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Monks, here a certain person is one who has entered the stream, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and assured of attaining enlightenment. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a non-returner; having completely transcended the realm of sensual desire, he will attain parinirvāṇa in the form realm itself. This is the third kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is an arhat; with the outflows exhausted, he has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge. This is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said this: "The stream-enterer, the once-returner, The non-returner, and the arhat— These four noble individuals Are the supreme field of merit for the world. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks! "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Monks, here a certain person is one who has entered the stream, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and assured of attaining enlightenment. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a non-returner; having completely transcended the realm of sensual desire, he will attain parinirvāṇa in the form realm itself. This is the third kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is an arhat; with the outflows exhausted, he has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge. This is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. "Monks, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world. Among them, monks, which person is the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the foremost, the best, the choicest, the most distinguished, and the most eminent? When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the arhat is the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the foremost, the best, the choicest, the most distinguished, and the most eminent among these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. "It is so, Ānanda! It is so, Ānanda! The arhat is indeed the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the foremost, the best, the choicest, the most distinguished, and the most eminent among these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the arhat is the one who has reached the ultimate goal, the one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, the one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, the one who has attained the ultimate liberation, and the one who has reached the ultimate perfection of the holy life. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. This is what was said by the Blessed One, and having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said this: "The stream-enterer, the once-returner, The non-returner, and the arhat— Among these four noble individuals, The arhat is declared the best. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks! "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Monks, here a certain person is one who has entered the stream, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and assured of attaining enlightenment. This is the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering. This is the second kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a non-returner; having completely transcended the realm of sensual desire, he will attain parinirvāṇa in the form realm itself. This is the third kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is an arhat; with the outflows exhausted, he has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge. This is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. "Monks, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world. Among them, monks, which person is the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the foremost, the best, the choicest, the most distinguished, and the most eminent? When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the arhat is the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the foremost, the best, the choicest, the most distinguished, and the most eminent among these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. "It is so, Ānanda! It is so, Ānanda! The arhat is indeed the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the foremost, the best, the choicest, the most distinguished, and the most eminent among these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the arhat is the one who has reached the ultimate goal, the one who has attained the ultimate security from bondage, the one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, the one who has attained the ultimate liberation, and the one who has reached the ultimate perfection of the holy life. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. This is what was said by the Blessed One, and having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said this: "The stream-enterer, the once-returner, The non-returner, and the arhat— Among these four noble individuals, The arhat is declared the best."

If the appearance of a mass of pillars, which occurs solely through the eye and is independent of external objects, were to arise wherever the eye is directed—just like the appearance of hair and other such things to one with ophthalmia—it would indeed exist there. But it does not so exist in places devoid of them; therefore, the prior existence of the pillar and so forth [is established]. Thus, because they conform to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the cognitions of jars and the like, as they arise, make known the causal capacity of cloth and other things. Cognitions of universals (*sāmānya*) do not function in this way, because they arise from internal causes alone. Whatever effect arises from a mere collection of conditions makes known within itself the capacity for the existence of factors distinct from those conditions. For example, the visual consciousness arises from the eye and other [conditions] alone.
[186,ix] If it is objected: "But surely the cognition of 'cowness' does not occur with respect to a horse; so how is there no negative concomitance (vyatireka)?
This is not correct. For instance:
because the nature of a cow (gotva) is absent, the cognition of a cow does not arise with respect to a horse.

"Or rather, because there is no awakening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for that [horse], there is no cognition of 'cowness' (*gotva*) therein. This horse does not produce the awakening of the latent impression for cowness; therefore, there is no cognition of cowness in it. This is because the convention that 'this is a cow' was apprehended only with respect to that [cow]; it is not because of an absence of cowness, but rather because such a mental trace (*saṃskāra*) does not exist. Furthermore, apart from the individual instance (*vyakti*), no uniformity of form is perceived therein by which one could establish whether it exists or does not exist. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely a conceptual construction (*pratyaya-mātra*) that is charming only so long as it is not critically examined; it does not exist in ultimate reality."

[187,i] Now, if there is no ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), how is it that "cowness" and "horseness" are mutually excluded? Is this mutual exclusion a property of conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) themselves, or of individual particulars (*vyakti*)? If, even in the absence of particulars, the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) did not occur everywhere through the mere influence of convention (*samaya*), then the universal would not be incapable of being excluded; for a universal is pervasive, and by virtue of that, the cognition of the universal occurs everywhere.

There is the consequence that even things like hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) would likewise [be real]. If it is argued that this is not so because they are not seen by others, then the universal (*sāmānya*) is also not perceived by those lacking its mental application (*ābhoga*) and so forth; thus, the same fault applies there as well. Furthermore, it is not tenable to say that [the universal] is indeed perceived when it exists [in the object]. Are hairs and the like not also perceived by others when ophthalmia is present? If it is argued that because the eye is impaired, ophthalmia causes the perception of what is not real (*atattva*), then what is this "unreality" (*atattva*)? Is it being perceived by an impaired sense organ? What is "impairment"? Is it the state of causing the perception of what is not real? This is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Moreover, even a universal (sāmānya) is perceived within the internal organ only through the arousal of a contrary latent impression (saṃskāra) due to some impairment; thus, this case is the same.
If being a negative concomitant of the universal were due to the absence of its pervader,

then even those things accessible to knowledge produced by cataracts would possess the status of a pervader. (158) If mosquitoes, which are perceived by impaired sense organs, are not real, [then the same logic applies].

If [the object] is unestablished due to its unreality, then no impairment is established. (159) (PVA) If you argue that there is impairment because of unreality due to the non-establishment of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), this applies equally to the universal; thus, there is also impairment for that which apprehends it. (160) (PVA)
Therefore, a universal is not capable of causal efficiency, because it lacks such capacity even with respect to mere cognition.
By this [explanation],
the cognitions regarding the lifting of a jar, universals, numbers, and so forth, are accounted for through the influence of internal factors such as convention and mental application.

[187,ix] A jar is a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of color, taste, smell, and touch. Lifting is an action (*kriyā*). Number is a quality (*guṇa*). The cognition "here" has inherence (*samavāya*) as its object. Inherence is that which is grasped by that [cognition]. Furthermore, those cognitions regarding these [entities] are dependent solely upon internal causes such as the application of conventions (*saṃketābhoga*) and do not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) of the objects. For instance: [187,x]
No substance called "dravya" is perceived apart from form and the other [sensory qualities].
Furthermore, the cognition of a jar does not possess the nature of positive and negative concomitance with respect to the jar itself.

Only form and the other [sensory objects] are perceived by the cognitions of the eye and so forth. Therefore, because perception is limited to just that much, this cognition—which is characterized by an attachment to a single entity such as "this is a jar"—arises and is experienced by people solely from an internal cause consisting of awakened beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*); there exists no other substantial nature (*dravyasvabhāva*) such as a jar when investigated through another means. [Objection: But surely the whole (*avayavin*) is determined by both seeing and touching; for substance is of two kinds: visible and tangible.
That too is incorrect, because:
Whether that substance is apprehended through a difference in form or otherwise,

when there is a cognition of non-difference, it is only the form [that is perceived], not the possessor of form. If it were cognized as distinct, there would be a perception of a cognition possessing two aspects.
The appearance of duality does not arise from the eye or the mind alone.
(PVA 163) Now, if the cognition "this is a jar" is not the same as the cognition "this is color," how then is there no perception of difference? For instance:
The cognition that "the jar or the cloth is red" is non-erroneous;
and there is no cause for the establishment of the existence of objects other than conscious awareness. (PVA 164)
For if there were only the perception of form, the thought would be "this is that" rather than "this is a jar.
That too is incorrect:
the status of being the locus of destruction for an object such as a jar belongs to that which is both colored and uncolored.
The referent of the term "non-pot" is designated by the word "red.

(PVA 165) Therefore, when difference is conceptually constructed through positive and negative concomitance, the designation occurs by way of a difference in meaning, but the real entity does not exist in that manner. (PVA 166)
This has been investigated elsewhere.

Now, if the whole does not exist and only the qualities such as color and so forth exist, how can there be the cognition that "wherever there is color, right there is touch"? That too is merely something trivial.
vii] Because they depend on a single causal complex (*sāmāgrī*), when a collection is conceptualized,
and because they are joined in producing a single effect, there arises the conceptualization "where that is, there [is this]. (PVA 167)

[188, viii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. He does not perceive form as real, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor forms, nor eye-consciousness, nor contact at the eye, nor sensation born of contact at the eye as real. He does not perceive the ear, nor sounds, nor ear-consciousness, nor contact at the ear, nor sensation born of contact at the ear as real. He does not perceive the nose, nor odors, nor nose-consciousness, nor contact at the nose, nor sensation born of contact at the nose as real. He does not perceive the tongue, nor tastes, nor tongue-consciousness, nor contact at the tongue, nor sensation born of contact at the tongue as real. He does not perceive the body, nor tangibles, nor body-consciousness, nor contact at the body, nor sensation born of contact at the body as real. He does not perceive the mind, nor mental phenomena, nor mind-consciousness, nor contact at the mind, nor sensation born of contact at the mind as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor the formative forces, nor consciousness, nor name-and-form, nor the six sense bases, nor contact, nor sensation, nor craving, nor grasping, nor becoming, nor birth, nor aging-and-death as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor the perfection of morality, nor the perfection of patience, nor the perfection of vigor, nor the perfection of meditation, nor the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor the emptiness of the external, nor the emptiness of the internal and external, nor the emptiness of emptiness, nor the great emptiness, nor the emptiness of ultimate reality, nor the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, nor the emptiness of the infinite, nor the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, nor the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor the emptiness of nature, nor the emptiness of all dharmas, nor the emptiness of characteristics, nor the emptiness of non-existence, nor the emptiness of existence, nor the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, nor the emptiness of the ultimate as real. He does not perceive the power of faith as real, nor the power of vigor, nor the power of mindfulness, nor the power of concentration, nor the power of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the faculty of faith as real, nor the faculty of vigor, nor the faculty of mindfulness, nor the faculty of concentration, nor the faculty of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the limb of awakening of mindfulness as real, nor the limb of awakening of discernment of phenomena, nor the limb of awakening of vigor, nor the limb of awakening of joy, nor the limb of awakening of tranquility, nor the limb of awakening of concentration, nor the limb of awakening of equanimity as real. He does not perceive the path of the noble eightfold limbs as real. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor arhatship as real. He does not perceive the state of a Pratyekabuddha as real, nor the state of a Buddha as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real. Subhūti, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that he is called a 'Bodhisattva. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva there is no such thing as a real dharma, nor is there any apprehension of a real dharma. Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom should train himself in this way: 'I shall not abandon any sentient being.'"

Why is it that there is no such designation as "where there is an army, there are men," or likewise, "where there is a forest, there are *khadira* trees and so forth"? For an army is not something distinct from the men, nor is a forest something distinct from the *dhava* trees and so forth. Therefore, because they depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) and produce a single effect, and thus do not exist in separation from one another, people designate them in this way. If that is the case, then the "whole" (*avayavin*) is simply the color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities whose bodies are not mutually distinct; for there is no mutual distinction between color-form and the rest, as there is between a pillar, a jar, and a tree.

Furthermore, the whole (*avayavin*) is not a mere designation, like a forest or similar things. Its parts are established as such through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For instance, there is the cognition of non-distinct location in such statements as, "That very thing which I see, that same thing I touch," and so forth. The quality of being tangible or being tasteable is never perceived apart from the location of the visible form (*rūpa*).
That too is incorrect:
if the form of form and so forth were mutually non-different, [then...]
But from what source could there be a distinction such as "form" and so forth? How could that very same thing be something else?

(PVA 168) For it is not the case that the very same thing becomes something else, because that would entail the consequence of there being no difference in appearance. Now, if it is argued that although it is a single entity, it is perceived as distinct because it is grasped by different sense organs—such that when it is perceived by the visual organ it is "form," by the tactile organ it is "tactile-ness," and by the gustatory organ it is "taste"—[we reply:]
[188,xiii] That is incorrect.

Is that single object perceived as different due to a difference in its apprehension, or is it indeed distinct, established on the path of cognition through a difference in its objective referent? (169) (PVA) [188,xv]

First of all, it is not the case that there is only one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For a single object does not appear as if it were diverse due to a difference in apprehension, because that would entail the consequence of its being erroneous. If it is argued that this very [single object] is called non-erroneous because there is no other way for apprehension to occur and thus no alternative, then why is it not postulated that the object itself is exactly like this?

"But there is no cognition of non-difference; thus, this is not a valid conceptualization. (PVA 170) Now, it might be argued: "If there is difference, how can there be co-location and non-separation? This too is easily explained, because:
Space is not other than that which possesses space, because no distinction between them is perceived.
Furthermore, how could there be an appearance of that which possesses space, since it is itself already broken? (PVA 171)

There is no such thing as "place" distinct from form and the other [sensory objects]. Furthermore, if that [place] were distinct from them, it would be so only because of the appearance of difference; yet, due to the consequence of infinite regress regarding differences in place, it remains entirely unperceived. If there were a difference in their own nature (*svarūpa*), then form and the others would indeed be different. And there is nothing other than the form appearing through the manifestation of its own nature. Moreover, the manifestation itself is what constitutes the difference; for the manifestation of form is not the same as the manifestation of taste, otherwise there would be the absurdity of lacking other sense faculties and the consequence of [all sensations] being non-different. If it is argued that the difference arises from the difference in sense faculties, that is incorrect. For even when the sense faculties differ, a non-different [object] does not appear as different. If it were so, then either the object would be beyond perception (*parokṣa*) or there would be a difference in the [object] itself.

Thus, it follows that the whole (*avayavin*) is nothing more than the mere collection of form and other qualities. Furthermore, if the object were one way and the cognition another due to the capacity of the sense organs, that would be nothing but an error, like the appearance of yellow in a conch shell for one with jaundice. Even so, it might be argued that it is not an error because of its correspondence (*saṃvāda*).

That too is incorrect. Even in the case of correspondence (*saṃvāda*), it is merely a mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*). That appearance, moreover, takes such a form precisely because of the differences in the sense faculties. Therefore, that [correspondence] is also nothing but an error; how then can that which is unestablished be proven by means of what is unestablished? Since both the correspondence and other appearances are produced by the sense faculties, cognition does not follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an external object. Thus, it is well said that "there is no such thing as an object here. For the proof of a whole (*avayavin*) does not serve to prove the non-existence of the object, since that [whole] is intended as a specific kind of object. Therefore, it is not the case that a single entity appears as manifold due to the operation of the senses; rather, it is simply the manifold [elements] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Consequently, the cognition of a "one" is dependent solely on internal causes. Even in the cognition of "lifting," the moments of the hand and so forth, which arise in successive locations, constitute the lifting; thus, this collection is merely conceptual (*kalpanārūpa*) and arises from internal causes alone, not from the power of an external object. If this is so, then the property of being an action (*kriyātva*), manifested by preceding and succeeding moments, would be the object of the cognition of "lifting. This is not the case, because a universal (*sāmānya*) is manifested by its individual instances (*vyakti*). Furthermore, the universal "action-ness" (*kriyātva*) is manifested by an individual instance of action, not by an individual instance of an object-moment. Nor is another individual instance of action perceived as residing in the individual instances of the hand and so forth. Nor does a universal have the property of being manifested by a different individual instance. If it is argued that the generic class of action (*arthajāti*) is manifested by the individual instances of the hand and so forth—[we reply: no.

That too is incorrect, because there is no manifestation by each individual moment. For throwing upward (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other actions are not manifested by a single moment alone, as that would entail their perception at the very first moment. Now, it may be argued that the genus of action (*kriyājāti*) is manifested only by those [moments] occurring at non-simultaneous times. Indeed, we do not necessarily follow the tenets of others; this is precisely our own established philosophical position.

That is incorrect. If a universal (*jāti*) is unmanifest in each individual instance, then it cannot be manifested in their collection either, for no other mode is possible. If you argue that through repetition it is manifested even by a single instance, then repetition itself is the internal cause; thus, that cognition does not depend upon the power of the object. The same should be said regarding the cognitions of conjunction and disjunction. And so it has been stated:
"Number, conjunction, action, and the like are likewise [unmanifest] in their own nature."
Furthermore, a form does not appear in cognition as distinct from its verbal expression.

(PVA 172) [189,v] Now, if it is argued that the definition of a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is "that which is incapable of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā*), then it follows that even things like [illusory] hairs would be universals, since they too are incapable of causal efficiency.
That too is incorrect, because:
Hair and the like are not universals because they lack adherence to [external] objects; since they are apprehended as objects of knowledge, no fault follows regarding non-existents. (7)

[189, viii] For it is the object itself (*artha*) that, when perceived through its universal form (*sāmānyarūpatā*), while being essentially a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), is the universal. If this is a particular because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*), how can it be a universal? And if it does not perform a causal function, how can it be an object (*artha*)? It is an object precisely because it performs a causal function. Furthermore, these two—performing a causal function and [not performing one]—cannot coexist in a single thing. This is not difficult to reconcile. [189, ix]
The universal is directly connected to causal efficiency through its capacity for it in a mediated succession;
it is both that which possesses such efficiency and that which is indeed devoid of it.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is an object by virtue of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object; in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, it is not an object at all. Its status as an object is merely figurative (*upacarita*), because it is indirectly the effect of an object [or: because it has another object as its purpose]. How then can the universal be the object of a word? For there is no such thing as "sugar-cane cart" on the bank of a river, even through a succession of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

This is not so. Let it be that there is no loss for us even if that generality (*sāmānya*) does not exist; rather, it is all the more excellent, as it establishes the non-authoritativeness of verbal testimony (*śabda*). For instance, we accept that a generality is the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If this [generality] were also an object of a means of valid cognition, then verbal testimony would be a means of valid cognition. How then is it said that the generality is the object of verbal testimony? It is not that the generality alone is the object of verbal testimony. What then? The generality is indeed the object of verbal testimony, but it is not [the object] in the sense of being its direct objective domain. Through being the object of verbal testimony, it acquires a continuous form (*anugatākāratā*). Likewise, regarding the statement "the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not an object," it is not that the particular characteristic alone is not an object; rather, it is that which is not an object at all that is the particular characteristic, and not the object. Furthermore, a cognition whose object is hair-tufts and the like is simply not a means of valid cognition. For it has been stated in the general definition: "A means of valid cognition is a non-discrepant cognition" (*pramāṇam avisamvādi jñānam*, *Pramāṇavārttika* 1.1). Having established this general definition, its specific divisions are then justified according to the distinction of their objects.
The distinction, however, is considered to belong to the object itself as that which is to be established;
therefore, how could there be "objecthood" in the case of what is not an object of valid cognition? (PVA 174)

[190,ii] If the object itself is the universal (*sāmānya*), then because non-existence (*abhāva*) lacks the nature of an object, it would not be a universal. Yet, it is not without an objective domain (*aviṣaya*), because it is the domain of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). Furthermore, even in the case of a universal, there is the pervasion of distinctions such as "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*) and "non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*); and there is the pervasion of individual instances (*vyakti*), as in "the non-existence of a jar" or "non-existence at this time.

Here too, there is a rebuttal: because it is apprehended as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). For even non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed an object of knowledge by way of some aspect; for the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is that non-existence is simply the existence of something else (*anyabhāva*), and that is established by the effect of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Alternatively, this too is indeed determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And it is an object because it possesses a purpose; for there is indeed a purpose even through non-existence, since it serves the purpose of moving about without hesitation. Therefore, in that case as well, there is a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the object; thus, non-existence is an object in its own right, and not hair and such, because it is determined as being knowable by a mistaken cognition.

[Objection: But surely, even in the case of hair and so forth, when there arises the cognition that "this hair and so forth is non-existent," or that "it is similar to real hair," then in that case too there certainly exists a basis for its unreality—namely, the purposeful activity of walking unhindered and so on. Consequently, those [objects] would also become objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Reply: If they were determined in such a way, they would possess only a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*); if that were the case, there would be no appearance of vividness (*sphuṭābhatā*). And if, by virtue of appearing vividly, it were considered an object, then it would be nothing other than a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). In that case, the cognition of it would not be purposeless, and thus it would not be an error. To this he says: [190,v]
Since there is no refutation even of their being thus [illusory], there is the appearance of clarity;
because they have the nature of objects by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, the notion [of them] as hair and so forth [is likewise explained]. (8)

It has a universal as its object; the appearance of hair is devoid of reality. [190.vii] If even things such as hair, when perceived by one with an optical disorder (*taimirika*), are determined to be unreal, then what does "unreal" mean? It means that it is not perceived through a cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) or by another person. Since it is determined by the absence of being perceived by those, it is simply a case of being an object of knowledge as a non-existence (*abhāva*). Thus, there is no denial whatsoever of the fact that being an object of knowledge has the nature of a universal (*sāmānyarūpatā*) in its capacity as a non-existence.

[190, viii] Even though this [cognition] is similar to another [object], such as a hair and so forth, the conventional usage of "similarity" occurs within the form of cognition; thus, because it falls within the scope of a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason), the hair and so forth are indeed objects of knowledge (*prameya*). How, then, can there be a clear manifestation (*sphuṭapratibhāsatā*) of the universal (*sāmānya*)? Because it is an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition, that [universal] is in fact a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). In that case, it would be an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, it is; for it is an object of the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If so, how can it have the nature of a universal? It does so because it is made an object by another conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) through its similarity to the previously perceived hair and so forth. For instance: [190, ix]
Previously, hairs and the like were non-existent, yet they were accessible to cognition affected by cataracts;
for they were perceived in exactly that way, being either similar to or identical in form [with real hairs].

For there is no similarity or unreality without following after a prior form; thus, similarity and unreality are determined solely by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that non-conceptual cognition does not operate upon the forms of the preceding and succeeding moments. Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*). If it is asked, "In that case, for which cognition is it 'without an object' (*anartha*)?", [the answer is: sensory cognition appearing as [floating] hairs is without an object. This is the intended meaning: in the case of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it is perception (*pratyakṣa*); regarding the form of [floating] hairs and so forth, conceptual cognition is inference (*anumāna*), while sensory cognition is without an object—such is the distinction.

[Objection: But surely that very sensory cognition is itself self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). For there is no sensory cognition other than self-awareness, since that self-awareness arises by depending upon the sense faculty.
[Response:
Now, this sensory cognition is considered an error in the absence of an object.
Self-awareness, however, does not arise from the sense faculties, because it occurs even without them.
Whatever does not occur in the absence of something else is not the cause of that thing.

[191,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, that which is called 'the perfection of wisdom' is indeed a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, why is it that the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, because form does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because the eye does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because forms do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because eye-consciousness does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because eye-contact does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because feeling born of eye-contact does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because the element of earth does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because ignorance does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because the fruit of a Stream-enterer does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, and an Arhat do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist; because the fruit of Buddhahood does not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Because all dharmas do not exist, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, what is the reason for this? Why is it that the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti, because all dharmas are signless, wishless, unproduced, unarisen, unceasing, non-dual, and non-conceptual, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti, because all dharmas are without self, without being, without soul, without person, without agent, without experiencer, without knower, and without seer, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti, because all dharmas are without beginning, without end, without middle, without coming, without going, without abiding, and without support, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti, because all dharmas are like illusions, dreams, echoes, reflections, and transformations, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti, because all dharmas are like space, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti, because all dharmas are ultimately non-existent, the perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not exist. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are thus non-existent, how can there be the designation of a Bodhisattva? How can there be the designation of a Mahāsattva? How can there be the designation of a Śrāvaka? How can there be the designation of a Pratyekabuddha? How can there be the designation of a Buddha? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is precisely because all dharmas are non-existent that the designation of a Bodhisattva exists, the designation of a Mahāsattva exists, the designation of a Śrāvaka exists, the designation of a Pratyekabuddha exists, and the designation of a Buddha exists. Subhūti, if all dharmas were existent, then the Tathāgata would not have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, because all dharmas are non-existent, the Tathāgata has attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, Subhūti, that dharma would not be a dharma, and therefore it is called a 'dharma. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if that dharma is not a dharma, why is it called a 'dharma'? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, because that dharma is neither real nor unreal, it is therefore called a 'dharma'. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, how can there be the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, between defiled and undefiled dharmas, between worldly and unworldly dharmas, between conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, between the dharmas of a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, or a Buddha? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, although all these dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet through the power of conventional designation, they are established as such. Subhūti, just as an illusionist or the apprentice of an illusionist might, by means of grass, wood, pebbles, or clay, produce the appearance of various forms—such as elephants, horses, cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, men, women, or various garments, food, drink, and vehicles—and though those forms are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to their respective karma, so too, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to their respective karma. Subhūti, just as an echo is neither real nor unreal, yet it is heard according to the conditions of the valley, the mountain, the rock, the cliff, the forest, or the tree, so too, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to the conditions of their own karma. Subhūti, just as a reflection is neither real nor unreal, yet it appears according to the conditions of a mirror, a vessel of oil, a vessel of water, or a vessel of lacquer, so too, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to the conditions of their own karma. Subhūti, just as a transformation is neither real nor unreal, yet it appears according to the conditions of the mind, so too, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to the conditions of their own karma. Subhūti, just as space is neither real nor unreal, yet it pervades everywhere, so too, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to the conditions of their own karma. Subhūti, just as the nature of all dharmas is ultimately non-existent, so too, Subhūti, all dharmas are neither real nor unreal, yet they appear to sentient beings according to the conditions of their own karma. Subhūti, it is in this way that all dharmas, though neither real nor unreal, are established through conventional designation. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are established through conventional designation, then what is the distinction between a Bodhisattva and a Śrāvaka? What is the distinction between a Bodhisattva and a Pratyekabuddha? What is the distinction between a Bodhisattva and a Buddha? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva, having generated the mind of enlightenment, practices the six perfections, matures sentient beings, purifies the Buddha-field, and seeks to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. A Śrāvaka, having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata, practices the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five

[Objection: Surely self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is not at all clear without the sense organ (*akṣa*). [Reply: That too is incorrect. Every self-awareness is indeed clear by its own nature. Whatever appears here in its own form, in the mode of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), that is "clear. And the own-form of every cognition appears directly. For it is impossible for the very own-form to be remote (*parokṣa*), as that would entail the consequence of the non-existence of the own-form itself. Therefore, everything that is remote is indeed indistinct. Furthermore, dream-cognition possesses a clear form even without the sense organs. Consequently, the sense organ operates only toward an object; in the absence of an object, it would be useless. The cognition of [illusory] hair is useless because there is no attainment of hair therein. Thus, the determination is that it is useless only with respect to an object.

[191,v] But surely, if being an object consists in having the nature of cognition, then even a universal would follow as a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and since it would also appear clearly, there would be a contradiction. There is no contradiction, because:
If it were argued that the universal is the object because it has the nature of cognition, then [the following] would follow: 9.
Thus, because it is accepted as such, there is no fault; there is equality by virtue of having the form of the object.

By virtue of being of the nature of cognition, the universal indeed possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇatā*) and a perfectly clear form (*parisphuṭākāratā*). For its clarity is precisely of such a kind. As for the object, it has an indistinct appearance because it appears as something other than that which has a distinct appearance. But in the case of cognition, that very form—relative to what could it be called "indistinct"? Therefore, since its own nature is directly manifested, how could there be any lack of clarity? This alone is clarity: the manifestation of all aspects. Since the nature of the object is different [from that], when it is not manifested, there is no manifestation of clarity.

[191, viii] How, then, is it that this universal has an indistinct appearance? He says: "It is the similarity with the form of the external object. *Rūpaṇa* means "forming" (*rūpa*), which is to say, "determining" (*nirūpaṇa*). Thus, it is similarity through the determination of the object. And there is the indistinctness of the object; for in that regard, because it is beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*), there is both indistinctness and the nature of a universal aspect.
Because it is of a uniform nature everywhere, and because it relies upon the exclusion of that [particular]. // 10 //

[191,x] For in all cases—whether sharp, dull, intense, or mild—the nature of that [perception] is uniform. This is because it is apprehended as equal through a single conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), by way of unifying the perceived object (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized object (*vikalpyārtha*). To explain:
That universal is accepted as the state of being common to those things that are similar;
and the form of cognition is determined as having the nature of that individual manifestation.

The universal form [of cognition] resides in all individuals such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) through its conventional determination (*adhyavasāya*). Thus, the specific form of cognition possesses the nature of a universal. In this regard, the basis for that determination is both its arising from those [individuals] and a specific latent impression (*vāsanā*); hence, there is no fault. For it arises by relying upon their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), since it arises indirectly by depending on excluded objects. Furthermore, because it leads to engagement with excluded objects, and since that state of being excluded is common to all of them, exclusion itself is the universal. Moreover, due to the connection with exclusion, even the form [of the cognition] has the nature of exclusion.

[191, xiii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is bound by all fetters; the person who is freed from the fetters of sensual desire but not yet freed from the fetters pertaining to the higher realms; the person who is freed from the fetters pertaining to both realms; and the person who is neither bound nor freed. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of knowing oneself. Why? Because, monks, when one knows oneself, one does not despise others. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall know ourselves. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is easy to admonish and easy to instruct; the person who is difficult to admonish but easy to instruct; the person who is difficult to admonish and difficult to instruct; and the person who is neither easy to admonish nor easy to instruct. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of knowing others. Why? Because, monks, when one knows others, one does not despise oneself. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall know others. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a well-dug pond; the person who is like a rain-cloud; the person who is like a lotus flower; and the person who is like a great ocean. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of abandoning conceit. Why? Because, monks, when conceit is abandoned, the mind becomes liberated. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall abandon conceit. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a broken pot; the person who is like a leaking jar; the person who is like a vessel with a hole at the bottom; and the person who is like a vessel with a lid. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of guarding the doors of the sense faculties. Why? Because, monks, when the doors of the sense faculties are guarded, the influxes do not arise. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall guard the doors of the sense faculties. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a stone pillar; the person who is like a wooden post; the person who is like a wall; and the person who is like a mountain. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of establishing mindfulness. Why? Because, monks, when mindfulness is established, the mind remains steady. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall establish mindfulness. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a crow; the person who is like a peacock; the person who is like a crane; and the person who is like a swan. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of discerning the nature of beings. Why? Because, monks, when one discerns the nature of beings, one does not become confused regarding their conduct. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall discern the nature of beings. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a blind man; the person who is like a man with cataracts; the person who is like a man with eyes; and the person who is like a man with supernormal vision. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of purifying the eye of wisdom. Why? Because, monks, when the eye of wisdom is purified, one sees things as they truly are. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall purify the eye of wisdom. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a firefly; the person who is like a torch; the person who is like a lightning flash; and the person who is like the sun. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of generating light. Why? Because, monks, when light is generated, darkness is dispelled. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall generate light. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a small stream; the person who is like a large river; the person who is like a lake; and the person who is like the ocean. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of attaining liberation. Why? Because, monks, when liberation is attained, one is no longer subject to rebirth. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall attain liberation. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a debtor; the person who is like a servant; the person who is like a master; and the person who is like a king. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of overcoming suffering. Why? Because, monks, when suffering is overcome, one dwells in peace. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall overcome suffering. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a thief; the person who is like a judge; the person who is like a witness; and the person who is like a judge of judges. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of establishing justice. Why? Because, monks, when justice is established, the world is not disturbed. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall establish justice. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a physician; the person who is like a patient; the person who is like a nurse; and the person who is like a healer. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of curing illness. Why? Because, monks, when illness is cured, one enjoys health. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall cure illness. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a boatman; the person who is like a ferryman; the person who is like a bridge; and the person who is like a ford. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of crossing over the flood. Why? Because, monks, when the flood is crossed, one reaches the further shore. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall cross over the flood. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a merchant; the person who is like a caravan leader; the person who is like a guide; and the person who is like a king of kings. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What is the purpose of this teaching? It is for the sake of attaining sovereignty. Why? Because, monks, when sovereignty is attained, one rules over the world. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall attain sovereignty. It is in this way that you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is like a child; the person who is like a youth; the person who is like an adult; and the person who is like an elder. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.

Now, why is the mental aspect (*ākāra*) the universal? It is simply that form and the other [sensory objects], without distinction, constitute the universal that is the object of inference. For when individual instances are not excluded, those very instances are called the "universal. However, if all individual instances were excluded, it would follow that inference is invalid. Therefore, one who necessarily accepts the validity of inference must admit that its object is the individual instance, by way of a "definition through what is indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*). It does not terminate in the mere mental aspect, for that would entail the consequence that [inference] could not lead to purposeful action. This same fault applies even if only the universal were grasped. Consequently, from that mental aspect of cognition, there is an inference of individual instances; thus, for the proponents of universals among the Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), the inference of the universal has the individual instance as its object.

[192,i] But surely there is no inference of the individual even by means of the universal. Since the universal also appears therein, there would again be no engagement [with the object], and thus inference would be useless. Furthermore, this succession of universals does not end: from one universal there is an inference of another universal, and from that yet another, leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, since the individuals must be understood even at the final limit, the individuals themselves are the universal.
That too is incorrect, because: [192,iii] That [universal] is a non-entity because it is denotable; [furthermore,] the collection of sense faculties is fruitful [only with respect to particulars].
In the utterance of names and so forth, which are connected to the speaker, the hearer, and the object to be expressed. 11.
In the case of a name and so forth that lacks a connection [to its object], there would be no engagement with the referent.

It is not the case that color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] themselves are the universal (*sāmānya*), even when they are perceived by a cognition of a universal. For color-form and the others would have to be perceived by a cognition of a universal either individually or collectively. If they were perceived collectively by a cognition of a universal, then since the cognition of the universal arises from the word, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the sensory apparatus being rendered useless, because the nature of all individual instances (*vyakti*) would be understood through that [cognition]. Indeed, the collection of senses such as the eye is sought for the purpose of perceiving individual instances; yet, if that individual instance is perceived even when the eye and other senses have ceased to function, what is the use of the senses? If it is argued that the sense organs are desired for the sake of pleasure (*sukha*):
For instance, that pleasure which depends upon the sense faculties is otherwise;
that too is untenable, because it is also understood from the word alone. (PVA 178)
If it is argued that cognition alone arises from the word, yet there is no arising of pleasure without the sense organ, [we reply:
even from the sound of the words "arising of pleasure," that arising of pleasure indeed occurs.
(179) If, however, there is no cognition even in that case, then there is no arising of pleasure.
How could that which arises as pleasure not be so when it is apprehended in its own nature?

(PVA 192, ix) If that which arises as pleasure is not such even while being perceived in its own nature, then what confidence can there be in the perception of anything else? For being perceived is itself existence.
[192,xi] Now,
even though the collection of sense-faculties is fruitless, it arises through the power of karma.

Let it be granted that a name is produced; however, it would be perceived as being fruitless, just as there is no perception of form when the eye has perished. But this is not the case; therefore, universals are not perceived through words alone. Consequently, the universal must have a nature distinct from form and the like. If that were so, it would follow that the universal has the nature of a name and so forth. This is not so, because the collection of sense organs would otherwise be rendered useless. That too is incorrect.
For a formation dissociated from mind, when it is connected with the speaker, the listener, and the object—
or even when it is not so connected— there is no engagement with the object even by the speaker. (PVA 181)

For there is no comprehension of this [word] when it is used to convey the name and the sign associated with the speaker and the listener; since there is no such comprehension, how can there be any engagement with an object? If there were engagement even without comprehension, it would follow that engagement could occur everywhere, and it would also follow that comprehension is useless; therefore, this is not tenable. Now, it might be argued: "Because of the similarity between the sign (nimitta) and the object (artha), even though only one is conveyed, there is application to the other—just as when one of a pair of twins is addressed, the reference applies to both Citrāṅgada and Citravīrya. For in that case, it is not that there is no application to the other. This too is incorrect. [193,i]
In this context, error is not error; for if it were error, it would not be a cognition of the real object.
To claim that it is both error and a cognition of the real object is a mutual contradiction.

If that cognition appears as name and sign (*nāmanimitta*), how can it be erroneous? If it is erroneous, it must be without an objective basis (*anālambana*). If that were the case, there would be no apprehension of name and sign, because name and sign do not appear in their own form (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate name and sign even in that [erroneous] state, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, in the case of the non-erroneous apprehension of twins, the appearance of name and sign is precisely what occurs; thus, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*). Even in that case, activity proceeds only from the apprehension of that [name and sign]; therefore, the objection—"How does activity proceed toward the object?"—remains, and since it is included within the side of the thesis (*sādhyapakṣa*), it cannot serve as an example.
Even granting this, it is said:
If it is argued that the operation [of cognition] toward an object occurs due to similarity and error, it would not occur at all times.

And there is a wandering of the country; it is not the case that [the cognition] arises from the same [cause] as the cognition, for such a [cognition] does not arise elsewhere than where that [object] is accepted. (13)
Alternatively, there is a lack of validity regarding the means for the appearance of external objects, because the existence of anything distinct from consciousness is not established. (14)

If this external existence were caused by an illusion produced through similarity even when there is cognition of something else, then it would not occur at all times. For it is not the case that when one of a pair of *yamalaka* fruits is perceived, the other always exists in that very place, since its existence is observed elsewhere as well. Furthermore, there can be no similarity between the corporeal and the incorporeal, because there is an absence of likeness between them; or, if such a likeness did exist, it could not be of the nature of a dissociated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), because it would fall within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) due to having the nature of color and so forth. Moreover, there would be no error regarding location, for it would have been established as being in this very place; indeed, there is no similarity between two things located in different places.

[193,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his miraculous power, transformed himself into a great white ox. He then led them across the great ocean. Having reached the shore, he manifested himself once more as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and spoke these verses: “O merchants, listen well! With one-pointed minds, pay heed to my words. In this world, there is no other refuge; there is no protector other than the Buddha. The Dharma is the supreme refuge; the Saṅgha is the best field of merit. These three jewels are the true refuge; they are the supreme, peerless protection. If you take refuge in the Three Jewels with a sincere heart, you shall never again fall into the evil realms. Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara vanished from that place and appeared before the Tathāgata Śākyamuni in the Sahā world. Arriving, he bowed his head at the feet of the Buddha and withdrew to sit to one side. Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of monks: “Monks, do you see that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara? He has come here from the Sahā world to behold me and to hear the Dharma. The monks replied to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, we see him. The Buddha said: “That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such inconceivable power and virtue. He is able to rescue sentient beings from all sufferings. Therefore, monks, you should single-mindedly take refuge in him. At that time, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: “World-Honored One, for what reason does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bear this name? The Buddha told Ānanda: “If there are sentient beings who are bound by various afflictions and sufferings, and who call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, he will immediately manifest his power and deliver them from their distress. For this reason, he is called ‘Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women who, desiring a son or a daughter, call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, their wish shall be fulfilled according to their desire. For this reason also, he is called ‘Avalokiteśvara. The Buddha then spoke these verses: “If there are those oppressed by various sufferings, Who call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara, He can immediately deliver them from their distress; Therefore, he is named ‘Avalokiteśvara. If there are women who desire a child, And call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara, They shall obtain sons or daughters as they wish; Therefore, he is named ‘Avalokiteśvara. The Buddha further told Ānanda: “If there are sentient beings who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, maintain it in their hearts and recite it, they shall be freed from all calamities and obstacles. They shall attain peace and security, and eventually reach the state of Nirvāṇa. The Buddha having spoken these words, the venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly of monks, as well as the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and all the world, rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught. [193,ix]

Now, even the location (*deśa*) is not presented in its own form; rather, it is presented only as the cause for the name (*nāmanimitta*), since that too is perceived through error. If this is so, then the location is not presented by the name, and thus one would not act toward a specific location. For when the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are presented without reference to a location, no one acts toward a form (*rūpa*) or other objects associated with a specific place or region. If it is argued that one acts because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of identity [between the name-cause and the object], what is this so-called "determination of identity"? If it is said to be the perception of the name-cause as having the form of the object which is the locus of activity, how can one thing be perceived as another? A jar is not perceived in the form of a cloth. If it is argued that its form is superimposed (*adhyasta*) there, then only that which is superimposed is what is perceived. Since the external is superimposed, only the external is perceived, and there is not even a trace of the name-cause. Furthermore, activity would occur only where the superimposition is, and not upon the external object. If it is then argued that the name-cause is superimposed upon that [external object], then since the name-cause is what is thus perceived, how could there be activity toward the external? If it is asked, "In the case of the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl, how does activity occur upon the mother-of-pearl?", [we reply] that the mother-of-pearl also exists there, and its location is grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, there is no grasping of the location of the name-cause. If the location were grasped, there would be no state of being "not located" (*adeśasthatā*). If it is argued that "that is the location of the supporting object (*ādhāra*)," we say no, because there is no distinction [between them]. The location belongs to the mother-of-pearl, not to the silver. If it is argued that the same applies elsewhere, we say no; for silver, due to its non-existence, has no location, whereas for the name-cause, its existence is not a location. Furthermore, the superimposition is of a silver that is seen, but there is no seeing of the name-cause, because it is only at the time of superimposition that it is seen.
