Therefore, this activity toward the object is not due to superimposition. Nor is it the case that it is grasped by a cognition whose movement falters, like the cognition of fire in a boy. If it is argued that this is due to extreme habituation (*atyantābhyāsa*), from what source is this known? There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a cognition. That which is perceived by a means of valid cognition must be accepted as it is, not otherwise. If it is argued that "otherwise, practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would not be possible, and thus it is postulated in this way," we say no; for it will be demonstrated that practical activity occurs even otherwise.

If it is asked: "Even for one for whom cognition arises from a word with only its own form and does not touch the object, how can there be engagement with the object?"—[we reply: No, for this is the same regarding the external object as it is regarding the form within the cognition. Because a mistaken cognition arises, that which is produced by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), taking its own nature—which is based in a specific location—to be the object, prompts the practitioner of worldly discourse; thus, nothing here is contradicted. To explain further: [194,ii]

To the extent that the intrinsic nature [of a cognition] causes [an object] to function through the superimposition of an object, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is completed; what further need is there for another [cognition]?

The conceptual construction that "the name-sign (*nāmanimitta*) is the object" is twofold: either it is apprehended or it is not apprehended. [If one argues] that it is determined as having the form of the object—[we reply: if the name-sign is apprehended in its own nature within verbal cognition, how can it be perceived as the object? For what is apprehended in its own nature cannot be said to be apprehended in another form; indeed, it does not become something else merely by changing its form, since difference consists precisely in a difference of form. Therefore, regarding the claim that the name-sign is perceived as having the form of the object: that form does not belong to the object, because the object is absent there; nor does it belong to the name-sign, because that is impossible for it. That form belongs to the cognition itself. It would be better that this very form of the cognition be perceived as the object; what is the use of this useless internal tumor of a name-sign? It is logical that the cognition has the form of the object because it arises from it through a causal chain; but why is this so? Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the name-sign having the form of the object.

[194,iv] Now, if the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is not distinct even from the name and the sign (*nāmanimitta*), then that very thing is the form of the object; thus, the collection of the sense faculties (*akṣasaṃhati*) is not rendered fruitless. Alternatively, if it does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), then there is no futility in the collection of the sense faculties for the apprehension of that which performs a causal function.

That too is incorrect. Since there would be no apprehension of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it follows that one would simply not act at all. [Objection: One acts due to superimposition (*adhyāropa*). [Response: It has been stated that such superimposition is merely a form of cognition. Otherwise, there would be another name-sign (*nāmanimitta*) for that [superimposition], and yet another for that as well, resulting in an infinite regress; thus, the fault of error remains unaddressed even in that case. There is no proof for the existence of a name-sign. For the determination of an object does not arise from a mistaken cognition. [Objection: That very form [within the cognition] is what determines the object. [Response: No, because there is no distinction [between the form and the object]. Indeed, a distinction cannot be established for a proponent of name-signs like the Sautrāntika, since cognition regarding the object designated as a name-sign arises through mere mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth. Furthermore, if one accepts that the cognition possesses the form of the object, then it is logical that it possesses only the form of the object. [Question: Why is its form not clear? [Response: No, because a mere fragment of a form arises due to differences in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For when something arises with a certain form from a particular cause, it does not do so in its entirety, just as a son resembles his father [only partially].

[194, vi] Is it not the case that all cognition is indeed formless (*anākāra*), and that the form belonging to the object therein—such as the appearance of blue and so forth—is the form of the object, and not the form of the cognition? Therefore, all cognition possesses the object; it does not possess any form of its own. How, then, could there be error? Nor is this form of the cognition external in nature, because it appears as an external form. This is not so. [194, vii]

If it is argued that [the cognition] possesses all objects of knowledge because it appears as such, this is incorrect, since in dreams and other states things are perceived otherwise; nor is it so because of the manifestation of blue and other colors arising from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). (15)

It is not [perceived] because of non-obstruction by blue and so forth; nor is it [perceived] by those whose locations are suitable for it, because it is known by itself even while unknown [to others]; by this, name and so forth have also been described. || 16 ||

[195,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. He does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive the faculty of faith as real, nor does he perceive the faculties of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the power of faith as real, nor does he perceive the powers of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the limb of awakening of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the limbs of awakening of investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, tranquility, concentration, or equanimity as real. He does not perceive the path as real, nor does he perceive the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of awakening, or the noble eightfold path as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat as real. He does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of their own marks; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor purified, neither deficient nor complete. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of their own marks, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gradually ascend the stages and attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all these dharmas are empty of their own marks, yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the cultivation of the roots of goodness. He does not abandon the cultivation of the perfections, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, the meditative concentrations, the attainments, the supernormal knowledges, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, the unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion. He does not abandon the cultivation of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks. He does not abandon the cultivation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata. He does not abandon the cultivation of the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat. He does not abandon the cultivation of the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, nor the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva did not cultivate these roots of goodness, he would not be able to transcend the world of sense-desire, nor the world of form, nor the formless world. He would not be able to enter the emptiness of the internal, nor the emptiness of the external, nor the emptiness of the internal and external, nor the emptiness of emptiness, nor the great emptiness, nor the emptiness of ultimate reality, nor the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, nor the absolute emptiness, nor the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, nor the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor the emptiness of nature, nor the emptiness of all dharmas, nor the emptiness of own-marks, nor the emptiness of non-existence, nor the emptiness of existence, nor the emptiness of non-existence and existence, nor the emptiness of essential nature, nor the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature. He would not be able to fulfill the five supernormal knowledges, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata. He would not be able to manifest the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks. He would not be able to turn the wheel of the Dharma. He would not be able to liberate beings from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Therefore, Subhūti, although all these dharmas are empty of their own marks, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not abandon the cultivation of the roots of goodness, and by means of this, he gradually ascends the stages and attains the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

How is there a pervasion (vyāpti) that all cognition possesses an object? Indeed, it is not from the mere experience of a form that does not reside in front [of one] that [cognition] has an object. If it were so, the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous [cognition] would not exist, because everything would have an objective basis (sālambanatva). If it is argued that even when there is an objective basis, the designation "erroneous" occurs because the causal efficacy (arthakriyā) is not attained, then why is it not accepted that the designation "valid" (prāmāṇya) occurs even when there is no objective basis, provided that causal efficacy is attained? If it is asked, "What is the truth in this matter? [the answer is: It is precisely the lack of an objective basis (anālambanatva). For, since in dreams and the like, the grasping of something residing in front is observed even though there is no objective basis, and since that same grasping is observed elsewhere as well, having an objective basis is untenable. Why is the reverse not the case? This is not a valid answer, because having an objective basis is unestablished (asiddha). Indeed, having an objective basis is not established anywhere. If it is argued that it is established in the waking state, then that state does not exist elsewhere; therefore, cognition in that [other] state is without an objective basis. Thus, [the reason] is inconclusive (anaikāntika) due to the observation otherwise in cases such as dreams. Now, if it is argued that even dream-cognition is not without an objective basis—since dream-cognition has as its objective basis the name and the sign (nimitta)—then it is not established that dream-cognition is without an objective basis.

[195,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld the sufferings of those beings and, by means of his great compassion, looked down upon them from atop Mount Potalaka. Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "O Śāriputra, if any sons or daughters of good family should hear the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, with single-minded devotion, invoke him, he will deliver them from all suffering. O Śāriputra, if there be a multitude of beings—whether women, men, or eunuchs—who fall into a great mass of fire, and if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, that mass of fire will not be able to burn their bodies. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. [196,i] "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings traveling on a perilous path through a wilderness infested with robbers and bandits; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they would escape from the hands of those robbers and bandits and reach safety. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings traveling on a perilous path through a wilderness infested with evil spirits and yakṣas; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those evil spirits and yakṣas would not be able to harm them. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings traveling on a perilous path through a wilderness infested with lions, tigers, wolves, and jackals; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those wild beasts would not be able to harm them. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings traveling on a perilous path through a wilderness infested with snakes and scorpions; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those venomous creatures would not be able to harm them. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. [196,ii] "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were bound in prison; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the shackles and fetters would loosen and fall away. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. [197,i] "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering.
