"O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would shatter into pieces and they would not be killed. Why is that? Because the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is such that he can deliver beings from all suffering. [198,i] "O Śāriputra, suppose there were a multitude of beings who, having committed various evil deeds, were being led to the place of execution; if they should invoke the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords would sh

To this it is replied: Dream-cognition does not have the name and sign (*nāmanimitta*) as its objective support (*ālambana*). Since the name and sign lack that specific form (*tadākāratā*), it is not tenable to say that the objective support there is simply blue and so forth, because the form [of the dream] is distinct from blue and the like. Furthermore, the non-obstructive nature (*apratighatā*) of that [dream-form] does not exist in the case of real blue and so forth; for dream-blue is the opposite of that. Likewise, even in an enclosed space, one sees a herd of elephants. For, in the chamber where he stands and looks, there is no room for a herd of elephants, and it is impossible to go outside since the chamber is closed. Moreover, one observes no effects of a herd of elephants, such as the breaking of branches, nor any effects of fire, such as burning. If it were the case that blue and so forth actually arise in that manner as non-obstructive entities, then why would everyone not see them? [The answer is: It is because for one who is awake there, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for such a perception is absent—specifically, the causal complex of sleep and the dream-objects such as forms that cause the perception. If the causal complex of sleep were the cause of perception for everyone, then all would see the same thing; however, this is not so, because dreams are seen differently by different people in that very same place. This difference in perception arises from the diversity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, for one whose impression belongs to the waking state, the perception does not occur in that [dream-like] way; therefore, it is not the case that everyone perceives everything.

[195,iii] But surely, since there is no *saṃskāra* other than the conditioned continuum of consciousness, consciousness that arises from such [a *saṃskāra*] would grasp whatever object is present; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of grasping everything that is present. Indeed, when consciousness arises from the eye and so forth, it does not grasp anything among even those things that are present and capable of being grasped.

Therefore, something is produced in a dream because it is perceived as distinct. For a distinction would be logical only if there were a perception of a prior form; he whose mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is that of a prior seer is the one who sees that [object], while for another there is no seeing because of the absence of a prior [impression].

[Objection: Let it then be "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*); the object is seen at the very time of its prior existence, yet it is perceived as being at the present time. [Reply: No, because the state of being at that [prior] time does not exist. [Objection: If you say, "It is precisely for this reason that it is called misapprehension," [we reply: ...
To this, it is said:
Or, what is considered the erroneous manifestation of that which is erroneous?
If there is a manifestation of the erroneous, it does not possess error.

If there is no erroneous nature in that which appears erroneously, then its erroneousness does not exist. If, on the other hand, everything possesses erroneousness, it follows that everyone would perceive things in that way. If you argue that even for them there is an erroneous appearance, this is not tenable.
For if the erroneousness of everything depends upon an erroneous cognition, [then the fault remains].
In dependence upon what could there be error? For an error cannot exist by depending on another error.

(PVA 185) Indeed, it is not the case that one person is called "erroneous" simply because they depend upon another who is erroneous; rather, [the latter must be established as such independently]. Furthermore:
[195,xi] Elsewhere, that which is called "misapprehension" has gone to another place;
I would have fallen into mud-free ground, yet my birth has occurred in this mire. (PVA 186)
[196,i] Intending to establish the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) for one who sees a dream, [the author] establishes the theory of misapprehension for those who are awake.

Now, as for the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*): if that "mis-ness" belongs only to the cognition and not to the object, then the object is being perceived in its own form; so what is this "misapprehension"? It is simply that the nature of the cognition itself is one of error. Nor can the form of one cognition belong to another such that the other would also be perceived in that way, because cognitions are distinct from one another. If that is the case, then it is the cognition itself that is perceived in that manner, and thus a dream-vision cannot have an external object as its support (*sālambanatā*). For it is said: "At that time, that object does not exist at all; its arising is due to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)."
That which does not exist is not seen; it is cognition itself that is self-aware.

(PVA 187) It is logical that what is situated in another place might be seen in a different location. However, how can that which is non-existent at a different time be seen? Therefore, it is not an external object that is experienced, because such an object is impossible; rather, it is a cognition arising in that manner from a previous perception that is what is experienced. If even at a different time it were seen as belonging to that [original] time, then there would be a universal misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) even during the waking state in the perception of pillars and other objects. This is not the case here, however, because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*).

[196,v] Is it not the case that the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) is itself a misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*)? If you argue that it is not a misapprehension because the object is attained, we reply: surely the attainment of the object is also nothing but a misapprehension. If you ask, "How can there be a misapprehension when the object exists?", we reply: how can there be non-attainment when the object has been seen? If you say, "Because it does not exist in that manner," then if it does not exist, how can there be its cognition? If you say, "It is something other than the form [of the object]," then why is there no attainment? It is precisely because it was previously existent and is now nonexistent. If so, how then is there the perception of it? [196,vi]

[The opponent] says: Why does the attainment of the form belonging to that time not also belong to that same time? If you say it is because it is impossible, then how can it be seen? If you say it is seen, well then, it is precisely this that is not known: whose seeing is it? [We reply: From recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), there is the certainty that "this is the seeing of the previous [object]. No; for in a dream, there is no recognition of what was seen in another life. If you say that here too there is inference based on similarity with something else that is being recognized, [we reply] no, because this is absent in cases such as a city of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*). Indeed, there is no recognition in those cases. Therefore, everything that is to be recognized is seen only previously; it is not a seeing occurring at the present moment.
By this, the loss of mindfulness is also explained.

The extraordinary (*alaukika*) has also been explained by this very same [author]. To explain: what is this "extraordinary"? It is that which is not perceived by another; it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). [196,ix]

To this it is replied: That [object] is indeed cognition itself; because it is apprehended as an object by another [cognition] situated in a suitable location—just like the form of the apprehender—it is the object, not cognition. There is no apprehension of that [cognition] as an object, for it is apprehended in its own nature (*svarūpa*). Indeed, that object exists in its own nature, not as an object. If the object were [apprehended] as an object, then "object-ness" would be nothing other than its appearance; thus, there would be nothing called an "object" at all. Object-hood is perceived only through the form of the object, yet that is not the object itself. To say that one thing is perceived by another is merely a triviality. [196,x]

If it is argued that the cognition "this is an object, this is an object" arises, we say no. This has already been stated: "An object is not [an object] because of the conviction that it is a non-object" (*Vādanyāya* 2.1). By this, names and so forth are also explained. Furthermore, all cognition here has the appearance of something present before one; it is not the case here that there is "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*). Herein lies the "unworldly nature" (*alaukikārthatā*) of the object. To the question "Why is it not misapprehension here?", he says:
[196,xii] By what reasoning is that very cognition of the eye and so forth considered to possess a desired object?
If it is because the capacity of the object is perceived, then the other [cognition] would result in being purposeless. // 17 //

Furthermore, by whom is this cognition of the eye and so forth—which consists in non-erroneous manifestation, is accompanied by an object, and is produced by the presence of an object—considered to be such? What is the reason for this? For there is no difference in its being perceived. If it is argued that the causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*) of the object is seen through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then it is as follows: first that object is seen by another, and subsequently it is reached by oneself through inference; thus, the efficacy of the object is seen. If this is so, then that other cognition in which this causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is absent would be useless once it has been reached. For instance: [197, ii]
In this case, there is no actual object; the notion that "there is well-being here" is merely conventional. And yet, this notion is non-contradictory. (PVA 188) [197,iii]

For instance: "Only cognition has arisen for me; there is no object here. This was produced by me through the power of previous cultivation (*pūrvabhāvanā*); yet it is not seen by me as such, nor is it my memory, nor is this object extraordinary (*alaukika*). Whatever subverting factor (*bādhaka*) makes its extraordinariness known, by that very [factor] its lack of objective reality is established. Furthermore, that which is perceived as ordinary cannot be extraordinary, because that would entail the fallacy of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*). If you say that it too is extraordinary, no; for that would entail an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if it is only its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*) that is perceived—namely, the thought 'this is not perceived by another'—then in a cognition whose object is a real thing, the fact of being perceived by another is known through inference. If that were so, then there would be no other person possessing a non-erroneous object; one would simply perceive, 'this is my own perception,' and thus conclude, 'this is not an [external] object. Therefore, since there is an appearance of names and so forth, the principle is that there is no objective support (*sālambanatva*) when a connection exists between speaker and listener."
[197,iv] If it is argued that there is no occurrence [of the word] even when there is no connection [with the object], yet it appears as if connected with the object,
then the past and the future could not be denotable, because they have perished [or do not yet exist] in relation to the object. // 18 //

[197,v] If it is admitted that the name-sign (*nāmanimitta*) has a connection with the object, then there would be no engagement [with the object] at all; for it perishes along with the object. If there is no connection, there is even more clearly no engagement. Where there is the consequence of non-engagement due to the perception of the mere connection with the object, there is even more clearly no engagement when there is no connection, because past and future objects do not exist. Even if the name-sign persists, there is still no engagement with the object, because there is no mental impression (*ullekha*) of the object. For engagement does not occur toward one thing when what is perceived is another. The remainder has already been explained.
[2] (2) Faults in the Opponent's View: If it is thought that there is no such undesirable consequence because the word grasps the universal (*sāmānya*), then...
Therefore, it is not [the case] because of the non-apprehension of the universal alone, or even if there were apprehension. (19)
Because it is not distinct from that [unmanifested state], there would be its constant perception;
and if manifestation were the cause of perceptibility, then manifestation itself would have to be eternal. (20)
That which is capable of producing knowledge in the self is indeed always capable;
if it were ever incapable, then it would be forever incapable. (21)

[197,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his supernatural power, transformed himself into a great elephant. He then went to the place where the five hundred merchantmen were, and having arrived there, he said to them: "O merchants, do not be afraid; I shall carry you all across to the other shore. Having spoken thus, he lifted up all five hundred merchantmen with his trunk and crossed over to the other shore. When they had reached the other shore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara restored himself to his original form and said to the five hundred merchantmen: "O merchants, you should now proceed toward the city of Śrāvastī. Having spoken thus, he vanished from that place. The five hundred merchantmen, having reached the city of Śrāvastī, went before the Blessed One and prostrated themselves at his feet. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, behold this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara; he has saved these five hundred merchantmen from the peril of the great ocean. At that time, the monks, having heard what the Blessed One had said, were filled with joy and faith, and they praised the words of the Blessed One. This is called the second chapter, on the crossing of the great ocean.

If the universal (*sāmānya*) is the object of verbal cognition, then that universal must be apprehended either in isolation or otherwise. If it were apprehended in isolation, then even when the individual (*vyakti*) has ceased to exist, the cognition would still occur; however, there could be no cognition of [the universal] as "past" and so forth. For the universal does not possess the nature of being past and so on. Now, if it is argued that the universal is designated or determined as "past" and so forth due to its connection with individuals that are past and so forth, then in that case, it is apprehended only in conjunction with the form of the individual. Yet, past individuals have no existing form. How, then, can there be a cognition of the universal as having a past form by way of the form of a past individual? For that which has not itself been made an object cannot be capable of grasping another thing as possessing that same form.
even if there were the apprehension of a universal alone, how could there be linguistic usage?

Even then, there is another fault: that universal would neither belong to that [individual] nor be manifested by it. For something perceived independently of that [individual] cannot be designated as "belonging to it" or as "manifested by it. A manifestor, such as the light of a lamp, is indeed that which is perceived through its own cognition. If the universal were perceived alone even without the perception of the individual, it would not be manifested by the individual; consequently, it would be perceived eternally. Furthermore, the universal would be perceived even in a location devoid of individuals, just as a word [is heard] in a place where its manifestation (the individual object) is absent. Now, if it is argued that it is not grasped by the sense organ without a manifesting individual, [we reply: a universal being grasped by the sense organ is manifested by the individual, just as jars and the like, when cognized from a word, do not depend on lamps and so forth. However, those [objects] perceived by the sense organ do depend [on such aids]; thus, there is no fault.

That too is incorrect. From a word, it is only the universal (sāmānya) such as "pot" that is cognized; how then can that serve as an example, since the universal is the very subject under debate (pakṣa)? For the subject itself cannot be the example, as that would entail the absence of any defect in the example. Therefore, if the universal is cognized by way of its own form through a word, what is the use of its cognition through perception?

[Objection: But if there is no apprehension through perception, how can there be cognition from a word, given the absence of the apprehension of the relationship [between word and object]? [Response: Now, as for the form that appears from a word, is that the nature of the universal (*sāmānya*), or is it a different form? If it is that very nature, then the individual (*vyakti*) would be manifested; it would be perceived even by perception, since it would produce a cognition in that very same form. If, on the other hand, its nature is not perceived by perception, then how could there be cognition of something else when a convention (*saṅketa*) is made regarding that [unperceived] form? It would have to appear in the verbal cognition with the very same form as was apprehended by perception. Furthermore, an entity of one nature does not appear in another cognition as having the nature of something else. Moreover, the universal is eternal, and thus it must always appear in that very same form. For: [The verse follows: *Na hyanyarūpamanyathā bhāsate...* (For a thing of one nature does not appear otherwise... etc.
Whether it possesses power or lacks power, that which is established by its very nature cannot be remedied because of its permanence; who is capable of exhausting it? (22)
And while conforming to that general cognition, it is manifested;
by whom was that slight trace of the form of blue and so forth produced within it? (23)

[198, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? They are: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. [198, viii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. What is the nutriment of contact? It is that which is contact, having contact as its nature, the state of contact, the aggregate of contact, the sphere of contact, the element of contact, the faculty of contact, and the field of contact. What is the nutriment of mental volition? It is that which is mental volition, having mental volition as its nature, the state of mental volition, the aggregate of mental volition, the sphere of mental volition, the element of mental volition, the faculty of mental volition, and the field of mental volition. What is the nutriment of consciousness? It is that which is consciousness, having consciousness as its nature, the state of consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, the sphere of consciousness, the element of consciousness, the faculty of consciousness, and the field of consciousness. [198, ix] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. For what purpose does one cultivate the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*)? It is for the sake of attaining the cessation of the nutriment of consciousness. Why is it for the sake of attaining the cessation of the nutriment of consciousness? Because the nutriment of consciousness has craving as its root, craving as its source, craving as its origin, and craving as its condition. Why is it that the nutriment of consciousness has craving as its root, craving as its source, craving as its origin, and craving as its condition? Because the nutriment of mental volition has craving as its root... [and so on]. Why is it that the nutriment of mental volition has craving as its root...? Because the nutriment of contact has craving as its root... [and so on]. Why is it that the nutriment of contact has craving as its root...? Because the nutriment of physical food has craving as its root, craving as its source, craving as its origin, and craving as its condition. Why is it that the nutriment of physical food has craving as its root, craving as its source, craving as its origin, and craving as its condition? Because when there is craving, there is seeking; when there is seeking, there is acquisition; when there is acquisition, there is gain; when there is gain, there is decision-making; when there is decision-making, there is desire and lust; when there is desire and lust, there is attachment; when there is attachment, there is possessiveness; when there is possessiveness, there is stinginess; when there is stinginess, there is guarding; because of guarding, various evil and unwholesome states arise, such as the taking up of sticks and weapons, quarrels, disputes, contention, strife, accusations, lying, and other such evil and unwholesome states. Therefore, the nutriment of physical food has craving as its root, craving as its source, craving as its origin, and craving as its condition. [198, x] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three roots? Two nutriments are included within the root of unwholesomeness. How many are included within the root of neither-good-nor-evil? One nutriment is included within the root of neither-good-nor-evil. How many are included within the root of wholesomeness? One nutriment is included within the root of wholesomeness. [198, xi] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three feelings? Three nutriments are included within the feeling of pleasure. How many are included within the feeling of pain? One nutriment is included within the feeling of pain. How many are included within the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure? One nutriment is included within the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. [198, xii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three realms? All four nutriments are included within the realm of desire. How many are included within the realm of form? Three nutriments are included within the realm of form. How many are included within the realm of formlessness? One nutriment is included within the realm of formlessness. [198, xiii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three times? All four nutriments are included within the three times. [198, xiv] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of existence? All four nutriments are included within the three types of existence. [198, xv] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of clinging? All four nutriments are included within the three types of clinging. [198, xvi] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of craving? All four nutriments are included within the three types of craving. [198, xvii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of sensation? All four nutriments are included within the three types of sensation. [198, xviii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of consciousness? All four nutriments are included within the three types of consciousness. [198, xix] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of contact? All four nutriments are included within the three types of contact. [198, xx] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of attention? All four nutriments are included within the three types of attention. [198, xxi] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of feeling? All four nutriments are included within the three types of feeling. [198, xxii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of perception? All four nutriments are included within the three types of perception. [198, xxiii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of thought? All four nutriments are included within the three types of thought. [198, xxiv] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of craving? All four nutriments are included within the three types of craving. [198, xxv] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of view? All four nutriments are included within the three types of view. [198, xxvi] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of existence? All four nutriments are included within the three types of existence. [198, xxvii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of birth? All four nutriments are included within the three types of birth. [198, xxviii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of becoming? All four nutriments are included within the three types of becoming. [198, xxix] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of clinging? All four nutriments are included within the three types of clinging. [198, xxx] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of sensation? All four nutriments are included within the three types of sensation. [198, xxxi] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of consciousness? All four nutriments are included within the three types of consciousness. [198, xxxii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of contact? All four nutriments are included within the three types of contact. [198, xxxiii] It was said: "There are these four nutriments. How many nutriments are included within the three types of attention? All four nutriments are included within the three types of attention. [198, xxxiv] It was said: "There are these four

If there were a cognition of the universal alone from the word, it would have to appear solely in the form of the universal. What room would there be for even a trace of the form of blue and so forth? If you say [it appears] because of the individual (*vyakti*), then since the individual does not appear, how could that be? It is not tenable to say "because it is produced by the individual," for that would entail the non-existence of the universal, since nothing appears apart from it. Furthermore, it has been stated that the nature of the recurring form (*anugatākāratā*) is not something other than the form of blue and so forth. In that case, if objects possess a common form, there would be no such thing as a "universal. If you argue that this is because both are cognized, we say no; then it would follow that the universal is perceivable by the senses (*indriyagrāhyatā*). It is not logical to claim that it is perceivable by the senses simply because the individual is perceived by the senses. Consequently, there would be no cognition of the universal from the word. For there is no cognition that "such a universal exists," due to the absence of any corresponding mental conviction (*sampratyaya*) and because of its appearing as distinct [from the individual]. Therefore, if some entity distinct from the individual were to be conveyed, then when the form of the individual is understood from the word, the coordination with the sense-faculties would either be fruitless or redundant.
If it is argued that the sense organs are not useless because their purpose is to produce direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
then how can there be a cognition appearing as diverse from a sound or other object that is of a single nature? (24)

[198,ix] If the very apprehension of the object’s own nature constitutes perception, then if that [apprehension] exists, the sense organs (*akṣa*) are indeed useless. If it is argued that perception is not the direct apprehension of something as being "present before one" (*purovartitva*), but rather its non-sensory apprehension, we say no; for sound is perceived otherwise. In that case, sound would be grasped only as being present before one, and it would not possess perceptibility (*adhyakṣatā*). If it is argued that it is apprehended in its entirety, then that very same thing is apprehended even from a word, because of the convention (*saṅketa*).

If it is argued that [the term "is"] is used in that very context for the sake of satisfaction, we say no; for satisfaction also exists [in the present]. If it is argued that this is not so because the expression "such was your satisfaction" arises from hearing the word [used] in the past, we say no; for the usage of the word "exists" (bhavati) is possible even with respect to the past. Furthermore, it may be that a word is employed only for the past and the future, and for the present when it is mediated by linguistic convention (*vyavahṛta*), but not for the immediate present when it is being perceived, because in that case such usage would be redundant. Nor is it the case that past forms and so forth do not produce satisfaction, nor that they are not perceived when mediated. Therefore, the sense-faculties are efficacious. If this is argued, it is incorrect.
[199,ii] For how can that which is perceived by way of its own nature be something past and so forth?
Indeed, the past and so forth are not distinguished from form as anything other than being unperceivable. (PVA 189)

[199,iii] Even that which is seen by the eye and other senses produces satisfaction precisely because it reveals its own nature as unmediated. Nor is it the case that the sound of singing, even when mediated, does not produce satisfaction while being perceived in its own nature. If it is argued that, according to the analogy of water waves, it is indeed unmediated because of the manner of its arrival, this too is not sound.
Since it is located in a distant place, how could there be any arrival for its cognition?
If the material cause were distant, there would be the over-extension that everything would be subject to activity.

If even a distant object, though being perceived, were [considered] conjoined with the body’s sense-bases, then visible forms and other such objects would likewise be so. Consequently, when an object is cognized through verbal testimony, inference, or some other conceptual construction, there would follow [the absurdities of] touching a Caṇḍāla, approaching a woman who should not be approached, and so forth. Therefore, if the cognition of the word-meaning occurred by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpeṇa*), pastness and the like would not exist; for even things currently being seen are not non-past and so on precisely because they are cognized by way of their own intrinsic nature. Even in the case of corroboration (*saṃvāda*), it exists indeed by virtue of words such as "corroboration. Now, if it is argued that existence is nothing but perception by means of a sense-faculty, and not mere cognition—since defects of the auditory organ and the like are observed to function even in the absence of actual existence—[we reply: [Note: The provided text contains a complex argument regarding the ontological status of objects and the nature of existence (*astitā*) versus cognition (*pratīti*). The translation above reflects the logical structure of the Sanskrit.]
If existence is established through perception by means of a sense faculty, why do mosquitoes and the like not exist?
If it is because they are impaired, how is that impairment known? (PVA 191)
If there were a cognition otherwise [than through the object], then mosquitoes and the like would not exist;
therefore, the cognition of its own nature is considered to be its existence.

Therefore, since the very apprehension of its own nature constitutes both existence and perceptibility without mediation, there is no distinction between verbal and sensory cognitions; thus, it is not logical for these positions to claim that the purpose of perception lies elsewhere, and they are therefore utterly futile. Furthermore, the universal is a non-entity.
A genus does not have the form of the individual possessing the genus, such that it would depend upon something else.
If it is argued that "dependence" is merely the state of being an effect existing separately [from its cause], [then we reply: 25.

Even though an effect is independent of anything else for its production, it is connected with its own cause through conceptual construction; how could that which is not an effect be so connected in any way? (26)
If it were other, it would be unconnected to that; therefore, its lack of intrinsic nature is established.

A real entity (*vastu*) may be called either "possessing birth" (*jātimat*) or "birth" (*jāti*) itself. In that regard, it is first of all not the case that the universal (*jāti*) is identical in form to the individual (*vyakti*), because individuals are perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being distinct from one another and without dependence on anything else. For what is perceived by a non-erroneous cognition cannot be otherwise than it appears. Thus, brindled cows (*śāvaleyādi*) and the like are perceived individually, independent of anything else. If it is argued that subsequently, when a second or subsequent individual is perceived, it is perceived as dependent upon each preceding one—such that one thinks "this is the same as that"—this too is untenable. Even an effect (*kārya*) is connected with its own cause through the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of the sprout and so forth, since once produced, it is not dependent on anything else. That is to say: as long as [the effect] is unproduced, there is only conceptualization; even at the time of production, because the cause is either simultaneous with it or has already perished, it is not dependent on it. Therefore, the connection of effects with their causes exists only through conceptualization; how much more so in the case of the opposite? Consequently, whether it be an individual or a universal, it is unrelated to other individuals. Hence, the universal lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). For a universal is not something perceived while being unrelated. If that is so, then even a non-entity (*abhāva*) would become a universal if it were perceived as related to existing things, since the lack of intrinsic nature is common to both.
[200,i] There would be the over-extension of non-existence, because there is no dependence between those two due to their being non-existent. // 27 //

[200,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are neither real nor unreal. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in non-apprehension. Why is that? Subhūti, because the perfection of wisdom is itself unapprehendable. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-attachment, non-abiding, and non-apprehension. He should train in the perfection of generosity, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom in the same manner. He should train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path in the same manner. He should train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four truths of the noble ones, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata in the same manner. Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in all these dharmas by way of non-apprehension, non-attachment, and non-abiding. Why is that? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are neither apprehended nor unapprehended. Subhūti, this is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom.”

The universal "rabbit's horn" indeed exists in relation to individual instances, as in the cognition "rabbit's horn, rabbit's horn. If it is asked why this is not so for other individuals, [we reply: even for one who maintains that universals are real entities (*vastu-sāmānya-vādin*), why does "cowness" (*gotva*) not belong to a white horse (*karka*) and the like? Because there is no such dependence. For cowness is not manifested by the individual instance of a white horse. In that case, then, in the case of brindled cows (*śābaleya*) and others, the status of being a universal—such as "donkey's horn"—does not arise precisely because of the absence of such dependence; whereas for "cowness," it does exist because it relies upon those [brindled cows] as its substrata. Furthermore, since it functions with respect to them, there is a relationship characterized by dependence, and thus there is no fault. Nor do those [individuals] possess that form [of the universal], nor is there a relationship of identity (*tādātmya*); nevertheless, it occurs in that way through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*anādi-vāsanā*).
Therefore, although formless, it is conceived as the substratum of forms; it is manifested by words denoting universals for the purpose of introducing its specific distinctions. (28)

[200,iv] Indeed, no form exists at the moment it is produced. Rather, by means of its dependence upon forms, there is a characteristic of production therein through a continuous succession, so that it is perceived as if it possessed form. And for this very reason—because of its production from that and because of the conceptual determination of it—one engages with the particulars when the universal is perceived. Therefore, even by words intended to introduce those particulars, it is that [universal] alone which is manifested, and not something else distinct; such is the conclusion.

Granted that there is the form of the universal (*jāti*), but how can there be a determination of oneness with respect to the individual (*vyakti*)? For while the form is perceived, how can there be a determination of oneness with respect to that which is unperceived? To this it is replied:
"In that [cognition], there is either the appearance of the form, or the grasping of the object as being that [form]."
That is an error, produced by the habitual practice of tendencies from beginningless time. // 26 //

[200, vii] Indeed, the superimposition of that form does not arise merely from seeing reality. Even a succession of errors occurs, such as in the conceptualization of Īśvara and so forth. Even when there is no clear manifestation, because of the perception of something as clear, how is this possible? In this case too, a succession of errors is the only recourse. Therefore, since error arises only from the perception of another error, and that [other error] likewise from yet another, it is best to accept that error is beginningless; thus, there is no purpose for the form [of reality] to be established by perception. Alternatively: [200, viii]
That universal of objects which is characterized by the exclusion of others—that upon which these words are based has no form whatsoever. (30)

Indeed, there is no positive form (*rūpa*) in what is produced, since it is characterized by the exclusion of others. For words effect only an exclusion from that which is dissimilar and undesired. And this exclusion is simply the absence of occurrence therein. It is not the case that one who seeks something desires merely a negation. When one says, "Bring the jar," it is not the non-bringing of cloth and so forth that is being requested. This is not so; rather, by saying "bring," the non-bringing is prohibited. Consequently, bringing occurs of its own accord. Since that [bringing] would also apply to what is not a jar, it is prohibited in that case. Yet, the nature of a prohibition is not a positive form.

[Objection: Will not the meaning of the word of the first injunction be the referent of the word? For in that case, a negation is not possible because the positive state has already been established. [Response: That too is not so;
for it is precisely the non-bringing [of the cow] that is established here, and that which is being negated is that very thing.
Because of indifference, there is nothing beyond that; what other application could there be for it?
(PVA) [200,xii] Here, "non-bringing" is simply a lack of effort; that very thing which is implied is what is negated by the word.
[201,i] But surely, the negation of that very thing is the affirmation of another; how then can it be said that its form does not exist? To this, it is replied:
When that form is negated, the conceptualization of another [form] arises spontaneously;
in that case, there is no operation of words, for the understanding occurs spontaneously through the nature of the object itself.

If it is asked how the very existence of one thing constitutes the non-existence of another, the answer is: because the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of that [non-existence] arises upon the cognition of the other. Or, in the view of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) consisting of conceptual construction, this has already been stated; thus there is no fault. For one who experiences his own cognition as distinct from that [object], there is the realization that "it does not exist.

[Objection: But surely the cognition of a universal (*sāmānya-buddhi*) exists. In that case, whatever is the objective form (*arthākāra*) therein is the universal, and it is indeed existent. Even if it lacks the nature of an external object—since it appears otherwise—it is not logical to say that the universal is not distinct [from the particular]. To this, it is replied: [The author’s response follows: ... [201,iv] ... [the text continues with the refutation of the universal as a real entity].

In the cognition of a universal, even though the universal itself is formless, it is not perceived as such; therefore, that cognition is also accepted as an error regarding the object, because it is superimposed upon the universal. (31)
And because it does not exist as a real entity in the form of an object, it is not possessed of form.

For that which appears in a general cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*) is intended to be the universal (*sāmānya*). If its formlessness—that is, its being devoid of an aspect (*nirākāratā*)—were established, then it would necessarily have to exist as something other than the cognition itself, and thus it would be a universal. However, since it is perceived through a universal form, it is indeed an error regarding the object; for just as that [universal] is not seen in the universal, so too this is recognized as an error. That [error] also is not a universal by way of its own nature, because it is restricted to its own internal aspect (*svākāra*) and is therefore a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); rather, it is so called because it "floats" (*abhiplava*) over objects, appearing as the form of the object, yet it is understood to be non-existent in reality. Indeed, this universal does not exist in objects in the manner that it is perceived as being restricted to them. Therefore, in that form, it is not possessed of a real object (*sālambana*), nor is it endowed with intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*), because it cannot withstand critical examination. Otherwise, even yellow and other colors would truly exist in white conch shells and the like. Consequently, the universal is not a real entity.

[201, viii] Furthermore, because it is inexpressible, the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a real entity (*avastu*). Indeed, even if a universal were inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [the particular], it would still not be a real entity. Why?
Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, it is considered inexpressible; yet, for some reason, it is expressed through speech. (32)
If a thing does not exist, then in no way whatsoever can there be the ineffability of things.

When something is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [another], it lacks intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*). For you must necessarily admit that an entity which is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from another cannot be a real thing. Now, if by the rule that it is indeed expressible as different from another universal (*sāmānya*), there exists a distinction, then the universal must be a real entity (*vastu*) because of its difference from the individual (*vyakti*). If even the individual were inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [the universal], then precisely because of that inexpressibility, it would be a non-entity (*avastu*). If it is argued that the inexpressibility arises solely from the relationship with that [universal], we reply: for distinct things, the only possible relationship is that of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Consequently, all effects would be inexpressible in relation to their causes. Yet, smoke is not inexpressible as being either identical to or different from fire. If it is argued that the universal is inexpressible as distinct from the individual because they occupy the same location (*deśābheda*), we say no; in reality, there is no such thing as "location" apart from the object itself. If no distinction appears, how could there not be an absence of difference? And if a distinction does appear, how can there be non-difference? Therefore, there is no mode of existence for a real entity other than identity or difference; thus, because it is inexpressible in any way whatsoever, it is a non-entity. It is likewise not expressible as different from another universal, since that other universal is also established as a real entity. If it is argued that it is a real entity because it is expressible as different even from an imagined [universal], then even rabbit-horns and the like would follow as real entities due to their mutual differences. If it is argued that their difference is not ultimate because their difference is based on a difference in material cause (*upādāna*), just as the cognition [of them] differs based on the difference in the heads of rabbits and so forth, while the rabbit-horns themselves do not differ—then what contradiction is there in saying this here as well? That is to say: here too, the difference is merely in the cognition based on a difference in the material cause of the individuals, not in the real entity itself. Thus he says:
Nor indeed should it be said that there is a distinction [between them], because the distinction is merely a figurative designation based on the difference in their material causes. // 33 //

[202,ii] Furthermore, if either the universal (*sāmānya*) or the individual (*vyakti*) were the denotable object of words, then the past and the future would not be denotable; yet this is not the case, since—

Even regarding objects past and future, the scriptures apply by means of their connection to general characteristics; how then could there be a distinction between existent and non-existent dharmas? (34)

[202,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as form; he does not perceive feeling as feeling; he does not perceive perception as perception; he does not perceive formations as formations; he does not perceive consciousness as consciousness. He does not perceive the eye as the eye; he does not perceive the ear as the ear; he does not perceive the nose as the nose; he does not perceive the tongue as the tongue; he does not perceive the body as the body; he does not perceive the mind as the mind. He does not perceive forms as forms; he does not perceive sounds as sounds; he does not perceive odors as odors; he does not perceive tastes as tastes; he does not perceive tangibles as tangibles; he does not perceive mental phenomena as mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness as ear-consciousness; he does not perceive the nose-consciousness as nose-consciousness; he does not perceive the tongue-consciousness as tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive the body-consciousness as body-consciousness; he does not perceive the mind-consciousness as mind-consciousness. He does not perceive contact as contact; he does not perceive feeling as feeling; he does not perceive craving as craving; he does not perceive grasping as grasping; he does not perceive existence as existence; he does not perceive birth as birth; he does not perceive aging-and-death as aging-and-death. He does not perceive ignorance as ignorance; he does not perceive formative forces as formative forces; he does not perceive consciousness as consciousness; he does not perceive name-and-form as name-and-form; he does not perceive the six sense bases as the six sense bases; he does not perceive contact as contact; he does not perceive feeling as feeling; he does not perceive craving as craving; he does not perceive grasping as grasping; he does not perceive existence as existence; he does not perceive birth as birth; he does not perceive aging-and-death as aging-and-death. He does not perceive the element of earth as the element of earth; he does not perceive the element of water as the element of water; he does not perceive the element of fire as the element of fire; he does not perceive the element of wind as the element of wind; he does not perceive the element of space as the element of space; he does not perceive the element of consciousness as the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the conditioned as the conditioned; he does not perceive the unconditioned as the unconditioned. He does not perceive the past as the past; he does not perceive the future as the future; he does not perceive the present as the present. He does not perceive the world of desire as the world of desire; he does not perceive the world of form as the world of form; he does not perceive the formless world as the formless world. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as a stream-enterer; he does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as the fruit of stream-entry; he does not perceive the once-returner as a once-returner; he does not perceive the fruit of once-returning as the fruit of once-returning; he does not perceive the non-returner as a non-returner; he does not perceive the fruit of non-returning as the fruit of non-returning; he does not perceive the arhat as an arhat; he does not perceive the fruit of arhatship as the fruit of arhatship. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as a pratyekabuddha; he does not perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as a Tathāgata; he does not perceive the Arhat as an Arhat; he does not perceive the Samyaksaṃbuddha as a Samyaksaṃbuddha; he does not perceive the enlightenment of a Buddha as the enlightenment of a Buddha. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having heard the Blessed One's words, the Venerable Subhūti and those monks were delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [202,iv] End of the second chapter, "The Chapter on Emptiness," in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [203,i] Chapter Three: The Chapter on the Simile of the Illusion. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in this way: just as a magician or a magician’s apprentice might, at a crossroads, conjure up many hundreds of thousands of beings by means of an illusion, and yet he would not perceive those beings as real beings, nor would he perceive that illusion as a real thing. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in this way: 'Just as an illusion is neither real nor unreal, so too should I train. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is like an illusion; feeling is like an illusion; perception is like an illusion; formations are like an illusion; consciousness is like an illusion. The eye is like an illusion; the ear is like an illusion; the nose is like an illusion; the tongue is like an illusion; the body is like an illusion; the mind is like an illusion. Forms are like an illusion; sounds are like an illusion; odors are like an illusion; tastes are like an illusion; tangibles are like an illusion; mental phenomena are like an illusion. Eye-consciousness is like an illusion; ear-consciousness is like an illusion; nose-consciousness is like an illusion; tongue-consciousness is like an illusion; body-consciousness is like an illusion; mind-consciousness is like an illusion. Contact is like an illusion; feeling is like an illusion; craving is like an illusion; grasping is like an illusion; existence is like an illusion; birth is like an illusion; aging-and-death is like an illusion. Ignorance is like an illusion; formative forces are like an illusion; consciousness is like an illusion; name-and-form is like an illusion; the six sense bases are like an illusion; contact is like an illusion; feeling is like an illusion; craving is like an illusion; grasping is like an illusion; existence is like an illusion; birth is like an illusion; aging-and-death is like an illusion. The element of earth is like an illusion; the element of water is like an illusion; the element of fire is like an illusion; the element of wind is like an illusion; the element of space is like an illusion; the element of consciousness is like an illusion. The conditioned is like an illusion; the unconditioned is like an illusion. The past is like an illusion; the future is like an illusion; the present is like an illusion. The world of desire is like an illusion; the world of form is like an illusion; the formless world is like an illusion. The stream-enterer is like an illusion; the fruit of stream-entry is like an illusion; the once-returner is like an illusion; the fruit of once-returning is like an illusion; the non-returner is like an illusion; the fruit of non-returning is like an illusion; the arhat is like an illusion; the fruit of arhatship is like an illusion. The pratyekabuddha is like an illusion; the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha is like an illusion. The Tathāgata is like an illusion; the Arhat is like an illusion; the Samyaksaṃbuddha is like an illusion; the enlightenment of a Buddha is like an illusion. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and they are like an illusion. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having heard the Blessed One's words, the Venerable Subhūti and those monks were delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [203,i] End of the third chapter, "The Chapter on the Simile of the Illusion," in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [204,i] Chapter Four: The Chapter on the Simile of the Reflection. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all these dharmas are like an illusion, then what is the distinction between a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all these dharmas are like an illusion, yet there is a distinction. How so? Subhūti, a śrāvaka trains for the sake of his own parinirvāṇa; a pratyekabuddha trains for the sake of his own parinirvāṇa; but a bodhisattva

If a universal (*sāmānya*) were perceived even with respect to a past or future entity, then how could that universal be a property (*dharma*) of a past or future thing which is non-existent (*asat*), whether it be existent or non-existent? For there can be no property of what is non-existent. If it is argued that [the universal] is a property of another individual (*vyakti*) that is indeed existent, then how can that which is perceived as having that property possess "pastness"? For the pastness of the universal is due to its connection with a past individual, not inherently by itself. Therefore, by the rule that the pastness of the universal arises through its association with the past, the universal is a property of the non-existent—just as the state of being a hare’s horn or the state of being a non-entity (*abhāvatva*). Or, if it is existent, it cannot be a property of the non-existent, such as the capacity to produce an effect found in sprouts and the like. If it is asked, "What is the contradiction [in this]?"—it is simply the absence of a relation (*sambandha*). Indeed, a relation with a non-existent thing cannot be apprehended. If that were so, then the universal would also be perceived as non-existent, just as an individual is [perceived as non-existent] due to the absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*). [Objection: But the individual is also perceived only as existent, because the past and future do exist. [Reply: If it exists, how is it "past"? [Objection: Because the cognition (*pratipatti*) [of it] is past. [Reply: That cognition is also certainly perceived. [Objection: It is a perception in the sense of being non-perceptual (*apratyakṣatayā*). [Reply: No; for it has already been stated that in the case of non-perceptuality, there is an absence of the perception of the very nature [of that cognition]. Therefore, the existent universal is not a property of the non-existent past and so forth.

If it is claimed that this [designation] is accepted through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), then what is the proximity of a present jar to its non-existence, which does not exist in the case of a cloth or other such things? (35)

The reason "because it is non-existent" (*asad*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). It is accepted [as such] only by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*); it is not so in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Thus, the reason "because it has the property of being non-existent" is unestablished. Furthermore, regarding that which is metaphorically designated, it does not exist there in ultimate reality; since the universal (*sāmānya*) lacks existence in ultimate reality with respect to the past and the future, the intention is that the reason "existence" (*sattva*) is unestablished.

Here is the rebuttal: In that case, there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of either a general property (*sāmānya-dharma*), the word itself, or the individual (*vyakti*) with respect to the past and so forth; these are the possible positions. If it is a metaphorical application of the general property, that is incorrect. Regarding a present jar, the metaphorical application of its general property to the past must be based on either a relation or a similarity. Otherwise, if there were metaphorical application in the absence of such proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there can be no relation or similarity with what is non-existent, for that would entail its existence; thus, the claim that the past and so forth exist has already been refuted. If it is a metaphorical application of the word, that too is incorrect, because a word does not function without an object. If it did function [without an object], it would follow that words could function even when the thing is absent. And since that [general property] is not a real entity (*vastu*), it is merely a universal. If it is a metaphorical application of the individual, in that case too there must be a proximity, because metaphorical application is impossible for that which lacks proximity. This same point should be stated regarding the metaphorical application of the word as well. Now, if it is argued that there is metaphorical application because the past and future are identical due to a similarity of form, and that the past is indeed [the same], but causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is absent, and therefore the metaphorical application is based on the absence of causal efficiency—then in that case, the universal alone is being perceived there, and not otherwise. If that is so, then everything exists; how then can there be "pastness"? If you say it is because causal efficiency is absent, then if that [efficiency] is absent, how can it be an existing entity? If you say the entity is also "past" by virtue of its connection to that [efficiency], by what means is that connection apprehended? If it is apprehended, then even a non-entity would be apprehended. Moreover:
Even causal efficiency exists for that [entity] according to the view that "everything exists.
If that [efficiency] were absent, how could the absence of existence be real? (PVA 195)
[203,ii] Now, if it is argued that while the past and so forth exist conventionally, in the ultimate sense everything is simply non-existent;
If this conventional nature of an object consists in its being the objective support of cognition,
then since everything would be nothing but ultimate reality, how could there be any such thing as conventional truth?

For conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) has as its objective support (*ālambana*) entities that do not exist in their true form, because it conceals (*samvaraṇāt*) the ultimate truth (*tattva*). However, when the truth is revealed, there is no such thing as "conventional reality. Furthermore, if the past and so forth were merely conventional and not ultimately real, then since an entity cannot exist apart from its nature as past and so on, it would follow that there is no reality whatsoever. If the present alone is the ultimate reality, then the past and so forth are conventional and not ultimately real; thus, it is established that the universal (*sāmānya*) is a non-entity. For a universal does not exist solely in the present; therefore, all is well [with our position]. Consequently, there is no such thing as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) regarding a real object to be expressed. Indeed, this very thing is a metaphorical designation: the presentation of what is non-existent.

[203,v] Neither the universal (*sāmānya*) nor the individual (*vyakti*) exists [ultimately]. This is the referent of words that denote past entities. For instance, it is precisely that which was previously perceived which is superimposed [upon the present]; yet even that [superimposition] is non-existent.
That form by which it is superimposed is not indeed seen by that very same example;
for that object which is seen is not superimposed by that [example].

Now, a cognition occurring with respect to the past and so forth is perceived as being connected with that place and time. Consequently, even in the case of the past, that very same form previously produced is superimposed [upon it], just as, for example, the superimposition of the previously perceived nature of "cowness" occurs upon a horse. Thus, even when that [object] is not past, it is perceived only as a superimposition of a prior form and not otherwise. Even by means of inference, it is impossible to perceive a universal [as a real entity]. Therefore, in all cases, there is only metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), and no universal exists in an ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because in every instance it is characterized by superimposition.

Now, if it is argued that the universal is apprehended by perception as something actually existing, and therefore it must be ultimately real— then, since it is not cognized by means of inference and so forth, that universal remains a non-entity.

Now, even by means of perception, that form which is common to previous instances and appears indistinctly is perceived; likewise, it is perceived through verbal testimony and through inference. However, it is only the individual (*vyakti*) that is perceived there as distinct. Therefore, even if inference or verbal testimony does not operate upon the specific portion, they certainly do operate upon the general portion (*sāmānyāṃśa*) which appears indistinctly. That too is incorrect. [203,x] There is no such thing as perception here regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), because it is not an object of the senses.
And because this will not be directly realized, it will be explained later [in verse 198].

Indeed, it will be demonstrated that perception does not [grasp] commonality with what is prior. Furthermore, even when the previous particular has perished, how could that which is perceived as common to it be a real entity? It has already been stated: "How could it be a property of both the existent and the non-existent?"

[203,xii] Now, if it were common to both, how could there be non-reality? It would also be reality. That too is untenable; for a present appearance is not perceived as being identical with a past appearance. And when there are multiple appearances, what else can "commonality" mean? Therefore, because it appears in the form of the past and so forth, the object of a word is simply non-existent, and there is no metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) here, because it is the object of an unerring cognition. For: [203,xiii]
The unswerving operation of the intellect always pertains to both the primary and the superimposed meanings;
there is even a worldly proverb to this effect regarding the lion and the boy. (36)

[203,xiv] The unerring operation of cognition alone is the basis for both the primary and the metaphorical; otherwise, a cognition that proceeds erratically would [only] metaphorically attribute "lion-ness" to a boy, whereas in another case it would apply to the lion itself, and thus be primary. But here, in both instances, there is no status as the object of an unerring cognition; therefore, there is no metaphor. If it is argued that metaphor consists in being the object of a cognition whose referent is non-existent: if that were so, then the universal, by its very nature, is established as a non-entity (*avastu*). Furthermore: [204,i]

Where a word has been applied by people through conventional usage even to an unreal object, it is primary (mukhya) there; elsewhere, due to similarity with that [primary sense], it is secondary (gauṇa), its application being faltering (skhaladgati). // 37 //

[204,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all dharmas as being like an illusion. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all dharmas as being like an illusion? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, perceives form as like an illusion. He perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as like an illusion. He perceives the eye as like an illusion... [and so on through the eighteen elements] ...he perceives the mind-consciousness element as like an illusion. He perceives the conditioned as like an illusion, and he perceives the unconditioned as like an illusion. He perceives all dharmas as like an illusion. Thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all dharmas as being like an illusion. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are like an illusion, what is the distinction between an illusion and a bodhisattva? What is the distinction between an illusion and an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, there is no distinction whatsoever between an illusion and a bodhisattva, nor between an illusion and an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is illusion, and illusion is form. Feeling is illusion, and illusion is feeling... [and so on] ...consciousness is illusion, and illusion is consciousness. All dharmas are illusion, and illusion is all dharmas. Therefore, Subhūti, there is no distinction between an illusion and a bodhisattva, nor between an illusion and an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, or a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

For the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is primary when applied to non-existence itself, because its application there is unimpeded. It is a worldly convention that the word "non-existence" is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for something else—such as a son—only when that very thing [the son] is not being utilized; thus it is secondary. Therefore, since the term applies equally to both non-existence and existence, generality (*sāmānya*) is not a real entity (*vastu*) in cases such as the "unperceived"; this is because it is grasped by a cognition that takes on a form identical to one that grasps a non-entity. Now, if you argue that this very [application to a non-entity] is what constitutes its figurative nature—that is, its application to a thing that does not exist—then we ask: how is it established that there is an application to a non-existent thing when there is a similarity of form? If you say, "Because the cognition itself occurs in that way," then surely, even when a cognition has perished, there is no difference in the cognition [between the past and present]. Even the cognition "it has perished" occurs with respect to something that has not [actually] perished. If you say, "There will be doubt," then even doubt would not arise if the object were manifesting [directly]. If you say, "Even while it is manifesting, doubt arises due to similarity," [we reply: ...

[204,iii] But surely, even if there is no difference, it cannot be said that there is similarity between two things that are not perceived as distinct. For if the difference is not perceived, there is only identity, not similarity. Now, if it is argued that the difference arises from a difference in time, that is incorrect.
How can there be a distinction between reality and unreality based on a difference in time?
Even if time possesses real existence, why is there no distinction between the two cognitions?

Just as there is a difference in time between your two cognitions—the earlier and the later—even though their objects are real, so too is there such a difference even when the objects are unreal. Therefore, how can a distinction between that which has a real object and its opposite be made on the basis of a difference in time? If you argue that the object is real because of inference (*anumāna*), surely there is indeed valid cognition (*māna*) regarding both the past and the future. If you say that the distinction between the past and so forth arises from specific logical marks (*liṅga*), then it is as follows: since one thing is known through a mark as being past, another as being present, and yet another as being future, there is no uniformity in the cognition. That is incorrect. For if that cognition, even when arising from a logical mark, were to correspond to the actual entity (*vastu*).
There is no doubt regarding other aspects, because all aspects are fully grasped.

(PVA 200) [204, vii] Therefore, even in that case, it is logical that the aspect is not a real entity (*avastu*), because—like the aspect of a word—it is an object of doubt. For there can be no doubt regarding that which is itself being perceived. If it is argued that "there is doubt regarding another aspect," to this it is replied:
[204, viii] Whether that other form is perceived therein or otherwise;
if it is perceived, there is no doubt, but otherwise that moment remains doubtful. (PVA)

[204,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘Bodhisattva’; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive ‘form’; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive ‘eye’; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he perceive ‘mind. He does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive ‘forms’; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does he perceive ‘mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘eye-consciousness’; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive ‘contact of the eye’; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he perceive ‘contact of the mind. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive ‘feeling born of the contact of the eye’; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he perceive ‘feeling born of the contact of the mind. He does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive ‘earth element’; he does not perceive the water, fire, air, space, or consciousness elements, nor does he perceive ‘consciousness element. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive ‘ignorance’; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor does he perceive ‘aging-and-death. He does not perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path, nor does he perceive ‘the path. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Stream-enterer’; he does not perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of an Arhat. He does not perceive the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the fruit of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Tathāgata. He does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge. It is because he does not perceive anything that he does not become attached to anything. Because he is not attached to anything, he does not tremble. Being without fear, having transcended worldly confusion, he realizes the ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Subhūti, this is the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas. [205,i] 196. The Elder Subhūti then addressed himself to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, is there any dharma whatsoever which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives when he practices the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives when he practices the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if there is no dharma whatsoever which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives when he practices the perfection of wisdom, how then does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, progress toward full awakening? How does he go forth? How does he train? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘Bodhisattva’; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive ‘form’; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive ‘eye’; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he perceive ‘mind. He does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive ‘forms’; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does he perceive ‘mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘eye-consciousness’; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive ‘contact of the eye’; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he perceive ‘contact of the mind. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye, nor does he perceive ‘feeling born of the contact of the eye’; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he perceive ‘feeling born of the contact of the mind. He does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive ‘earth element’; he does not perceive the water, fire, air, space, or consciousness elements, nor does he perceive ‘consciousness element. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive ‘ignorance’; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor does he perceive ‘aging-and-death.
