For if there is cognition of that [object], there is no doubt precisely because of that cognition. If it is not being cognized, it is simply non-manifest; what doubt could there be regarding it? If you claim that the very state of not being cognized constitutes doubt, then everything that is non-manifest would be subject to doubt. If you argue that doubt exists only when something is not being cognized because another wavering conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises, then if there is cognition, how can there be the wavering of a conceptual construction? Furthermore, does this wavering pertain to the nature of the cognition itself, or to the conceptual construction as the object of knowledge (*prameya*)? If it is the wavering of the conceptual construction’s own nature, then how could that cause doubt regarding the object of knowledge? If it is the wavering of the object of knowledge, that is impossible, for there is no wavering of that which is not appearing in consciousness. If you say there is no doubt here, but rather the doubt is "whether I shall see this or not," then that is a doubt regarding the state of being about to be seen. Does that state also appear or not? Thus, the same two-fold alternative (*pakṣadvaya*) recurs without end. If the state of being about to be seen has been perceived, how can there be doubt? If it has not been perceived, what is the basis for the doubt? Now, if you argue that doubt arises from the perception of a generality (*sāmānya*), the non-perception of a particular (*viśeṣa*), and the recollection of the particular—that too is incorrect. Why? If [the term] *paryudāsa* (exclusion) is intended such that "perception" means "cognition other than perception," then since other cognitions are also possessed of an object (*sālambana*), how can there be doubt? If it is not known whether [a cognition] has an object or otherwise, then there is doubt. Even in that case, the question remains whether the state of having an object appears [in the cognition] or not; thus, the same problem recurs. If it is argued that doubt arises because it is possible for that [cognition] to be without an object (*nirālambana*) as well—by way of error—then, since only the appearance itself appears and not the object, how can inference have a real entity (*vastu*) as its domain? Furthermore, the qualification "because the universal is perceived" (*sāmānyapratyakṣāt*) is useless, because doubt persists even regarding what is apprehended by inference. Moreover, regarding the particular (*viśeṣa*) that is not perceived, one must choose between the alternatives: is it that very [particular] or another? If it is that very one, how can its own nature be unperceived? If it is another, how can there be doubt about the former based on seeing the latter? If it is argued that the latter is also seen there, then even if it is seen, let there be a memory of it as "seen"; why the doubt? If it is argued that it was perhaps not seen at all, then let there be a memory that it was not seen at other times; what is the doubt? If it is argued that the doubt arises because both [possibilities] are reasonable, and if it is asked how both could be seen at different times, then let the memory also be just like that; why the doubt? If it is argued that the doubt is precisely because it is not seen here and now, then the claim that "doubt arises from non-perception of the universal" and so forth is incorrect. Therefore, since a cognition without an object is possible, the possibility of doubt exists.

[205,ii] Now, if it is argued that doubt is simply an object appearing in such a manner, this is not so; for there is no conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding it as being an actual object. The conviction in this case is merely toward the cognition itself. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no difference between what is non-worldly and self-cognition. Therefore, doubt does not exist apart from an appearance, nor otherwise. Consequently, if there were doubt regarding a real entity (*vastu*) as the object of inference, it would not be a real entity; yet such doubt exists. Therefore, it is not a real entity. [205,iii]
Now, there is indeed an object there, and that is determined by inference; therefore, how is it that inference does not have a real object as its domain? To this it is replied:
[205,iv] If there were contact with a real object therein, how could there be wavering?
That cognition indeed wavers when one imagines the presence of a fallacious logical mark.
(PVA 205,v)

Even when there is a cognition of fire, if a delusion arises such that one thinks "it is smoke" when it is actually a cloud of gnats, then the cognition of fire wavers and another [cognition] arises. However, such wavering does not occur in the case of perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that this is the same as in that case because of the possibility of an impairment by cataracts (*timira*), we say no; for in that case, the appearance of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) is absent. If it is argued that [the cognition] wavers when the eyes are closed, we say no; for due to the absence of the cause, there is simply no arising [of cognition]. If it is argued that for inference (*anumāna*) as well, there is simply no arising because of the absence of its cause—the logical mark (*liṅga*)—we say no; for even when smoke is present, it is observed that the inference wavers due to the possibility of it being otherwise.

[205, vi] Now, if the possibility of it being otherwise were itself the cause, from what would the occurrence of a cause arise? That is incorrect; for if that [cause] were perceived, there would be no possibility of it being otherwise. Therefore:
When inference is in motion, there is no apprehension of the actual object from it.
To say that one moves by means of a sign while actually seeing [the object] is an extreme audacity.
In direct perception, there is no movement; if there were movement, there would be no seeing.

For that object which has been seen does not possess movement. Indeed, an object does not become something else simply because it is conceptualized otherwise. Even so, when this fire is being seen, it certainly moves.
Fire is not an object of direct perception, for that which is to be touched is not perceived by the eye;
nor is there ever any perception by a sense organ of a future form.

Regarding the statement "fire does not exist here," there are these alternatives: does it mean that this [visible] form does not exist; or that this [form] which is accompanied by the sensation of heat does not exist; or that it refers to an object of cognition yet to be desired? If it means that this very [form] does not exist, then it is impossible, because it is being perceived; for if even what is being perceived were said not to exist, this would apply everywhere. If, on the other hand, fire is conceived as a collection of color and touch, and it is therefore postulated that this color—which is accompanied by touch—does not exist, then that [collection] cannot be grasped by the eye; consequently, it remains unperceived. Therefore, movement belongs only to the unperceived. By this, movement in the state of a future form is explained.

Therefore, it is not logical to claim that conceptual construction is a direct contact with the real object (*vastu*). Consequently, inferential cognition does not involve direct contact with the real object.

If doubt regarding another aspect exists even when something has been perceived, then that doubt pertains to the object of inference; for that which is already perceived cannot be the object of inference. (206) Regarding the non-contradiction of the appearance, perception and its other [inference] are equal.
And the distinction regarding direct perception is made in relation to external objects.
Therefore, even when there is a mental appearance, this distinction between what is a semblance of direct perception and what is inference exists only with respect to external things. (PVA 207–208)
Alternatively, even in the case of inference, if a future object does not appear [to one person], how can it possess reality? It possesses reality because it is perceived by another person.

Now, if one does not perceive that [future object] even by way of its future form, how could it possess reality? Like the appearance of one suffering from ophthalmia, it would simply be unreal. Even when there is a cognition in another person, it is merely inference; how, then, can the reality of that [object] be understood through that very [inference]? That which is unestablished cannot be proven by means of what is unestablished. Furthermore, since the future form exists [only potentially], the inference must be determined as having that [form] as its object. But since that [future form] does not exist at that time, how can inference have a real entity (*vastu*) as its object? If it is argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*) also has its authority only in that same [future state], because reality there too consists precisely in the perception of the future form—otherwise there would be no reality—this is indeed so, and this will be demonstrated later. Therefore, inferential cognition is the same even when [the object] is non-existent. However, perceptual cognition does not occur without a real entity (*vastu*); thus, inference does not have a real entity as its object.

[206, vii] Now, if it is argued that being "non-primary" consists simply in having a non-entity as its object, that too is incorrect. For it has been established that all inference has an entity as its object; moreover, this is not a definition of the non-primary because the opposite is observed. To explain:
[206, viii]

Just as people might apply the designation "non-existence" even to that which exists, or apply it according to their own conceptualization, so too they might apply such designations as "Pradhāna" (the primal matter) to that which is either incapable or capable [of producing effects]. // 38 //

Even when an entity exists, people employ terms such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) based on either its incapacity or its capacity; however, according to your view, these would be primary because they refer to real entities (*vastu*). Yet, in your own system, terms like *sāṅkhya*, *puruṣa*, and so forth, applied to *pradhāna*, *puruṣa*, etc., would be secondary because those things are not real entities (*avastu*)—for both designation and conceptualization [require a real basis]. But this is not the case.

Now, if the terms "primal matter" (pradhāna), "spirit" (puruṣa), and so forth are secondary because they are superimposed upon things such as a son, then the definition of the primary and the secondary is not that they have as their objects an entity and its opposite. For that which is being superimposed elsewhere does not exist there in that form at all. Therefore, this alone is the correct definition. Consequently, it is established that even by means of inference, only a form already perceived in the example is superimposed upon the probandum; thus, inference has as its object something that is not a real entity. Therefore:
From words, whatever kind of cognition is observed—whether [the object] has perished or has not perished.
It is exactly like that; this [error] does not occur for the cognitions of the ear and other senses regarding real objects. (39)
Because both cognitions apprehend only the universal,
the prior apprehension of that universal in its isolation has already been refuted.

For if there were the apprehension of the mere universal, there would be no distinction between the past and so forth; and it has already been established that [the object] is not apprehended in its entirety.

Now, if those very individuals, being apprehended without distinction, constitute the universal, then inference would have a real entity as its object. To this it is replied: if that apprehension of non-distinction pertains only to the form of the cognition itself, it does not pertain to an inference whose object is a real entity. If, on the other hand, it pertains to the entity itself as having the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), that too is incorrect. For instance:
how could there be a non-distinct [nature] for things that are mutually distinct?
Or, if it possesses both form and the absence of form, how could that entity be one? (41)

[206,xvi] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment? It is the edible food that is substantial, whether it be coarse or subtle, whether it be fresh or prepared, whether it be masticated or swallowed, whether it be derived from the earth or from water, whether it be the food of gods or of humans—this is called physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment. What is contact as nutriment? It is the contact associated with the six sense bases—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—this is called contact as nutriment. What is mental volition as nutriment? It is the volition associated with the six sense bases—whether directed toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena—this is called mental volition as nutriment. What is consciousness as nutriment? It is the consciousness associated with the six sense bases—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, distant or near—this is called consciousness as nutriment. Furthermore, monks, if this physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment were not to exist, would the birth, coming-to-be, appearance, and manifestation of sentient beings be discerned? “No, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, because this physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment exists, the birth, coming-to-be, appearance, and manifestation of sentient beings are discerned. Furthermore, monks, if this contact as nutriment were not to exist, would the maintenance, preservation, support, and nourishment of sentient beings who have already come to be be discerned? “No, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, because this contact as nutriment exists, the maintenance, preservation, support, and nourishment of sentient beings who have already come to be are discerned. Furthermore, monks, if this mental volition as nutriment were not to exist, would the seeking of a new existence by sentient beings seeking a new existence be discerned? “No, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, because this mental volition as nutriment exists, the seeking of a new existence by sentient beings seeking a new existence is discerned. Furthermore, monks, if this consciousness as nutriment were not to exist, would the descent of the embryo and the production of name-and-form be discerned? “No, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, because this consciousness as nutriment exists, the descent of the embryo and the production of name-and-form are discerned. Thus, monks, these four nutriments are the cause, condition, origin, and source of this entire mass of suffering. Furthermore, monks, when one fully understands these four nutriments, abandons them, and cultivates the path leading to their cessation, one is said to be practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata, aiming for the complete destruction of suffering. For things that possess distinct forms cannot have an undifferentiated form, because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory entities to be one. If it is argued that "cow" is perceived by direct perception as a single entity consisting of both the inclusive (*anugata*) and the exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*): what is this so-called "inclusion"? Is it that which is cognized as being inclusive in the form "cow, cow"? Does such inclusion exist? If it does, there would be an infinite regress. If it is argued that its very nature is that [inclusion], is it perceived in its own form? If it were perceived, the cognition would have to be of a dual aspect. If it is argued that its form is simply the form of the object, then the inclusion of the form is the oneness of the form; therefore, there would be no difference between individuals, and thus no universal (*sāmānya*). Alternatively, if that form is not one, even then there is no universal. Now, if individuals are indeed perceived and yet there is an inclusive cognition in the form "cow, cow," how else could this be? To this, the following is said:
[207,ii] Let it be explained for what purpose the cognition has a conforming form;
for if it is a cognition, no object whatsoever is seen to be conformed by it. (PVA)

[207,iii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, or between worldly and supramundane dharmas, or between conditioned and unconditioned dharmas? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet for the sake of purifying the minds of sentient beings, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom distinguishes between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, and so forth, up to conditioned and unconditioned dharmas. However, Subhūti, he does not apprehend even a single dharma that is either wholesome or unwholesome, or anything up to conditioned or unconditioned. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and in emptiness there is no distinction between wholesome and unwholesome, or anything up to conditioned and unconditioned. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom generate the thought of awakening? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening by way of non-attachment to all dharmas. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend a thought of awakening apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the six perfections? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections by way of not abandoning any sentient being. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend a sentient being apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva mature sentient beings? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva matures sentient beings by way of teaching them the Dharma according to their capacities, yet without apprehending those sentient beings. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend a sentient being apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva enter into the stages of a bodhisattva? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva enters into the stages of a bodhisattva by way of not falling into the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the stages of a bodhisattva apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the dhāraṇīs and samādhis? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the dhāraṇīs and samādhis by way of retaining all the teachings heard without forgetting them, and by way of entering into the concentration on the signlessness of all dharmas. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the dhāraṇīs and samādhis apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva turn the wheel of Dharma? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva turns the wheel of Dharma by way of turning the wheel of the Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the turning of the wheel of Dharma apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to the fruit of arhatship? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not actually attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, up to the fruit of arhatship, because he has transcended all dharmas. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the attainment of any fruit apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the ten powers of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata by way of knowing the various inclinations and dispositions of all sentient beings. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the four fearlessnesses? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the four fearlessnesses by way of being fearless in the midst of the great assembly. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the four fearlessnesses apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by way of not sharing these qualities with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva purify the buddha-fields? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the buddha-fields by way of purifying the minds of sentient beings. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the purification of a buddha-field apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva manifest the marks and signs of a Great Man? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva manifests the marks and signs of a Great Man by way of accumulating the roots of goodness over three incalculable eons. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and one cannot apprehend the marks and signs of a Great Man apart from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One said:

If the cognition conforms to an object that possesses a recurring form (*anugatākāra*), what follows from this? If you argue that because the cognition itself is recurring, it conforms to that [object], then let that very [cognition] be designated as such; why designate anything else? For blue and so forth are not described as being such by virtue of the designation of the cognition. But blue and so forth are indeed designated in that way. To explain: blue is known through the perception of the form of blue, and not otherwise. This is not the case either. It is not merely the world that designates it thus; rather, one understands the very distinction between blue and yellow, or between pleasure and pain, thinking, "I see blue. If there were a perception of distinction here as well, then one could designate it as "this is recurring here" and "this is otherwise. If you say that this is simply indescribable, then why is the nature of the existent not pointed out? It is because it is impossible to point it out.
For there is nothing that can be designated in its entirety;
that from which this cognition arises is called the universal (sāmānya). (PVA 210)
[207,v] If it is impossible to indicate [the ultimate], how can it be communicated to another? And if it has not been communicated, how can the other person be led to understand it?

But surely, how can pleasure and the like be designated? They too are not worthy of being established by way of their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Since they are directly perceived through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), there is no fault even in not establishing them. If you argue: "What is the point of establishing for you that 'pleasure exists'? But for me, the establishment that 'pleasure arises from seeing' is useful," we say: No. This is merely conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra-mātra*), as is seen in the case of courtesans and the like. If you then say that one understands [the cause] from observing horripilation and so forth, even so, what is the use of establishing it for another? This is trivial, because this entire manifestation of horripilation and so forth culminates merely in the cognition that "this is pleasure" and the like. If you argue: "In this case too, that which is the basis for the mental impression (*ullekha*) 'cloth, cloth' is the universal (*sāmānya*)," we reply: No such universal is established—whether as something distinct with a recurring form (*anugata-ākāra*) or otherwise. This is merely a beginningless conventional usage; thus, it has come down through a succession of conventions regarding an unstable reality. The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of convention itself is its cause, just as in the case of the convention regarding *pradhāna* and so forth. For nothing is experienced as both different and non-different.
The universal is not something other [than the particular], because it is not perceived as being distinct.
Furthermore, how could there even be a position that it is both other and non-other without there being a different mental aspect? (PVA 211)
For instance: "By one [person] it is perceived as reality, by another as its opposite;
that which is reality through its opposite is not known to be anything else.
(PVA 212) Even though there is a difference in terms of being a bracelet, is gold not the same as an earring?
Apart from the bracelet, where else could there be gold?

(PVA 207.x) If you claim that gold is that which possesses the state of being "conjoined" (*anvitatva*), then from where does this state of being conjoined come? This has already been established through the cognition of the conjoined.
[207,xi] Let this matter rest for now. Furthermore, even if the universal were distinct from the individual, it still could not possess a relation [to it].
If the form of those two were entirely different from each other, then the relation expressed as "of those two" would not hold; however, there is no fault in the exclusion [of others]. (42)

[207, xiii] If that [universal] were something entirely different from those two and unconnected to them, then it would not be a universal, because it would be a distinct category of entity (*padārthāntara*). For a jar is not the universal of a cloth. If you argue that it is not a universal because its nature is not that of a universal, that is incorrect.
For if it were of the nature of a universal, it would simply be that universal itself.
But how could there be a relation expressed as "of that" (*tasya*)?
If it is argued that this is because of the nature of its connection [to impermanence], then this is dependent upon that very point:
how can there be impermanence in sound? From impermanence, there is no permanence.
And in this way, there will be no establishment of any entity whatsoever.

Now, since relatedness (*sambaddhatva*) is unestablished, how can that alone be the reason? Otherwise, everything would be established for everyone. Nor is even the so-called "universal nature" established for that which is intended as a universal. If it is argued that the relation is established, even so, there would be the apprehension of all individual instances (*vyakti*), because the universal consists of the nature of all its relata. And there is no other universal apart from the nature of the relata. If it is argued that it is the "identical form" (*samānākāra*), then this "identical form" is merely a designation for the relation itself. For identity of form is relative to the individuals, not relative to their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), since the intrinsic nature of each is fixed within itself. Furthermore, if identity were relative to the individuals, it could not be apprehended without the apprehension of those individuals. This same fault applies to the universal as the "exclusion of others" (*anyavyāvṛtti*). [Reply: No, because exclusion is not faulty. Even for things that are mutually distinct, their exclusion from what is intended by another is not contradictory. The uniform linguistic usage (*samānavyavahāra*) is also not contradictory, because they perform the same purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*). For who can prevent the appearance of an identical form in things whose diversity is not noticed? If it is asked, "How can there be a cognition of identity among non-identical things? [the answer is] no, precisely because they are identical. There is no such thing as "identity" other than being made the object of a cognition of identical form. In that case, the meaning of the objection—"How can there be a cognition of identical form among non-identical things?"—is this: "How can there be a cognition of identity regarding objects of a non-identical cognition? But it is established that they are not objects of such a cognition; for even for the proponent of the universal (*sāmānyavādin*), it is not unestablished that a cognition of a universal does not take them as its object.
Therefore, in this case, the very state of being common is the characteristic of the non-entity in the universal.
If it were an effect, it would be manifold; and that which is manifold is held to be perishable. (43)
Because destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere thing itself, there is no permanence [of things].
Furthermore, universals have no connection [to action] because they are not effects, and they lack form. (44)

[208, vii] Indeed, a state of having a common form cannot be established as anything other than the form of an erroneous cognition. Now, if it is argued that "having a general form" means that wherever two things occur together, they do so accordingly; then, when successive individuals arise, the universal would have an ever-increasing form because it follows the presence and absence of the individuals. In that case, the universal would be merely an effect of the individuals. If this were so, its multiplicity would necessarily follow just as it does for the individuals. If it is argued that its unity is established by the fact of being recognized through re-cognition (pratyabhijñā), then since the universal also possesses a common form, there would be an infinite regress.
[208, viii]

Now, if it is argued that a universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived at all, then the same objection applies to the particular (*vyakti*) as well—it would likewise not be perceived. Furthermore, regarding recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to universals, because recognition is observed even among universals. Moreover, it follows that a universal would be subject to destruction, since it would perish upon the destruction of its particulars; and because it is a real entity (*vastu*), it must be perishable, for it will be proven that destruction is necessarily concomitant with being a mere entity. Furthermore, if a universal were unproduced (*ajanya*), it would follow that it is unrelated and formless. For being a real entity consists in the apprehension of a specific form, and such a form is impossible for a pervasive universal. Indeed, it is impossible to perceive a universal as being pervaded by the entire succession of all moments of time. Since existence (*sattva*) is nothing other than perception, how can there be existence in its absence? If it is argued that its existence arises from its connection with "Being" (*sattā*), then "Being" itself would require a connection with another "Being," leading to an infinite regress. Nor is there a connection with a separate "Being" for the universal, because it possesses existence through its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). And it is not perceived apart from perception itself. Therefore, the universal is non-existent. If it is asked why the horn of a donkey does not possess existence through its own intrinsic nature, [the answer is: why should it not exist for you as well? If you say it is because of the absence of causes, then the universal is also non-existent, for there too the cause is absent. If it is argued that the universal must nevertheless be perceived, it has already been stated in this regard: even things like the horns of a hare are indeed perceived by their respective cognitions; they too would have to be existent. If you say they are not so when examined, then everything is the same.
Furthermore: this universal appears in verbal cognition by the power of convention; thus, it is not a real entity here. For instance:
And that knowledge which arises from the power of the real object is what is required;
it is not dependent on convention, nor is this [dependence] discerned in conceptual cognitions of universals. (45)
[209,iii] For a convention, when being established, is not made by depending on mere proximity; and the cognition that depends upon it is merely superimposed. To explain:
If there were no conventional designation through the superimposition of one thing upon another,
then, due to a lack of pervasion, it would not be the case that [the word] follows from worldly usage. (216) (PVA) [209,v]

If it is argued that cognition occurs at the time of linguistic usage solely through the power of the word itself: if there were no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the prior [upon the posterior], such cognition would not occur. Furthermore, a cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) from a word is never observed without a convention (*saṅketa*). If it is argued that [cognition] certainly arises even without a word upon seeing another individual instance: in that case as well, that very same logical mark (*liṅga*)—the apprehension of a convention—is merely an indicator for the occurrence of a linguistic usage of that form; even the logical mark produces only the superimposition of the prior, nothing more. Thus, the "caste" (*jāti*) of Hūṇas and so forth, as well as the "caste" of Brahmins and so forth, relies solely on the force of convention and does not depend on a real entity (*vastu*). If it is claimed that perception (*pratyakṣa*), when accompanied by convention, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the castes of Brahmins and so forth: no. That which arises by the force of a real entity does not depend on convention; if it depended solely on convention, there would be nothing but a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*). If it is argued that perception also exists as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*): to this it is replied: [The original Sanskrit text follows: *atrocyate |* (Note: The provided text ends with the opening of the response, "To this it is replied," and the subsequent argumentative development is not included in the source.)
If it is apprehended by direct perception, instruction is useless;
if it is not apprehended by direct perception, instruction is useless. (PVA 217)

[209, vii] If it is apprehended by perception, what is the use of instruction, since it is already grasped by that very means? On the other hand, if it is impossible to cognize through perception, can it be made known even by a thousand instructions? For an instruction regarding something perceived would take the form, "I have seen this. But in the case of a supersensible state such as being a twice-born (dvijāti), instruction has no efficacy. He states this very point:
[209, viii]

When two things are perceived, there may be some cognition that follows their difference even without a linguistic convention; that [cognition] is based on the proximity of the objects themselves. (46)

That which originates from the intellect of a person is indeed not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Now, it might be argued: "Even without a convention (*saṅketa*), an intellect with a recurring form (*anugatākārā buddhiḥ*) certainly arises upon the perception of two things; just as the cognition of a 'cow' and so forth arises simply from seeing a *śāvaleyā* (a brindled cow) and the like, and no convention is required therein. If that is the case, then:

Brahminhood would be non-existent as a genus, because it is not perceived as such; nor is the manifestation of a genus like "cow-ness" observed in the case of the birth of a twice-born person or similar categories. (PVA 218) If the external [genus] cow-ness were otherwise [established], who could have any doubt about this?

Regarding the state of being a Brahmin, however, one doubts whether this person is a twice-born because of his voice. In that case, there is no certainty through action, as birth is not known by any other means;
for the birth of Hūṇas and others is not manifested without instruction.
If it is argued that there is no such reality (tattva) in that case, then what is your view regarding [the universal] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth?

Just as a universal is accepted in the case of goats and the like because they are denoted by the single word "animal," why is it not likewise accepted that horses (*karka*) and so forth share the status of being denoted by the single word "horse"? 221 (PVA)
How can there be the state of being denotable by the word "cowness" (*gotva*) when there are infinite individual instances?
For even in that case, is there not infinity due to the difference between individuals?
Indeed, [the argument] would not establish infinity merely through the distinction of high-pitched (*udātta*) and other accents.
[209,xviii] Furthermore, recognition is possible even in cases where there is unity.

For indeed, even in the case of the phoneme *i* and others, there exists a distinction such as high-pitched (*udātta*) or gurgling (*gharghara*), which serves as the basis for their infinite variety. Yet, despite this difference of being gurgling and so forth, identity is established through recognition; this is the same in the case of the *karka* (white horse) and other individuals. Therefore, even in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, there is no "cowness" other than the fact of being denotable by the word "cow. Thus, there is no such thing as a "universal" (*jāti*) anywhere, apart from the proximity to an object, the state of being denotable by a single word, and the production of a single conceptual reflection (*ekaparāmarśa*). If it should be argued that this very state of being denotable by a word and the production of a single conceptual reflection do not exist without a universal, that too is incorrect.

Just as proximity is desired [as the cause] for the eyes and other senses in relation to their effects, which are cognitions, so too is a genus [desired] by which [the cognition] may follow [its objects] through differentiation. (47)

[210,iii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of Non-arising. Ānanda, you should learn this Dharma-discourse as ‘The Exposition of Non-arising. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the non-arising of form? What is the cause and what is the condition for the non-arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, ignorance is the cause and ignorance is the condition for the non-arising of form. Ignorance is the cause and ignorance is the condition for the non-arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of form? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the cessation of ignorance is the cause and the cessation of ignorance is the condition for the cessation of form. The cessation of ignorance is the cause and the cessation of ignorance is the condition for the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of form? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, craving is the cause and craving is the condition for the arising of form. Craving is the cause and craving is the condition for the arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of form? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the cessation of craving is the cause and the cessation of craving is the condition for the cessation of form. The cessation of craving is the cause and the cessation of craving is the condition for the cessation of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of suffering? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of old age and death? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, birth is the cause and birth is the condition for the arising of suffering; birth is the cause and birth is the condition for the arising of old age and death. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of suffering? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of old age and death? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the cessation of birth is the cause and the cessation of birth is the condition for the cessation of suffering; the cessation of birth is the cause and the cessation of birth is the condition for the cessation of old age and death. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of birth? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of existence, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and formations? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, ignorance is the cause and ignorance is the condition for the arising of formations. Consciousness is the cause and consciousness is the condition for the arising of name-and-form. The six sense bases are the cause and the six sense bases are the condition for the arising of contact. Contact is the cause and contact is the condition for the arising of feeling. Craving is the cause and craving is the condition for the arising of grasping. Grasping is the cause and grasping is the condition for the arising of existence. Existence is the cause and existence is the condition for the arising of birth. Birth is the cause and birth is the condition for the arising of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, this entire mass of suffering arises. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of formations? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, and birth? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the cessation of ignorance is the cause and the cessation of ignorance is the condition for the cessation of formations. The cessation of consciousness is the cause and the cessation of consciousness is the condition for the cessation of name-and-form. The cessation of the six sense bases is the cause and the cessation of the six sense bases is the condition for the cessation of contact. The cessation of contact is the cause and the cessation of contact is the condition for the cessation of feeling. The cessation of craving is the cause and the cessation of craving is the condition for the cessation of grasping. The cessation of grasping is the cause and the cessation of grasping is the condition for the cessation of existence. The cessation of existence is the cause and the cessation of existence is the condition for the cessation of birth. The cessation of birth is the cause and the cessation of birth is the condition for the cessation of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, this entire mass of suffering ceases. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the eye? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, name-and-form is the cause and name-and-form is the condition for the arising of the eye. Name-and-form is the cause and name-and-form is the condition for the arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of the eye? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the cessation of name-and-form is the cause and the cessation of name-and-form is the condition for the cessation of the eye. The cessation of name-and-form is the cause and the cessation of name-and-form is the condition for the cessation of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the earth element? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, name-and-form is the cause and name-and-form is the condition for the arising of the earth element. Name-and-form is the cause and name-and-form is the condition for the arising of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of the earth element? What is the cause and what is the condition for the cessation of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the cessation of name-and-form is the cause and the cessation of name-and-form is the condition for the cessation of the earth element. The cessation of name-and-form is the cause and the cessation of name-and-form is the condition for the cessation of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the world? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the path leading to the cessation of the world? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, ignorance is the cause and ignorance is the condition for the arising of the world. Craving is the cause and craving is the condition for the arising of the origin of the world. The cessation of ignorance is the cause and the cessation of ignorance is the condition for the cessation of the world. The cessation of craving is the cause and the cessation of craving is the condition for the cessation of the origin of the world. The Noble Eightfold Path is the cause and the Noble Eightfold Path is the condition for the cessation of the world and for proceeding toward the cessation of the origin of the world. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the self? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the world? What is the cause and what is the condition for the arising of the origin of the world, the cessation of the world,

Indeed, proximity characterized by the production of a single effect is not impossible for the eye, light, and mental attention even without a [real] universal (*jāti*). If it is argued that this is possible for co-operating causes (*sahakārin*), [we reply: even when two distinct things are perceived, there is only co-operation; there is no "single cognition" (*ekabuddhi*) or "identity of form" (*samānākāratā*). If it is argued that this is not so because identity of form in the object of cognition (*prameya*) is never observed apart from the two things themselves—as has been demonstrated—then only the production of a cognition remains. And that is common to the eye and the other factors as well. If it is argued that these too possess the capacity to produce that same single cognition, then the same consequence follows: since the *śābaleya* cow and others also produce a single reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*), nothing else does. If it is argued that only those [specific individuals] are real entities (*vastubhūta*), [we ask: otherwise, how is this distinction made—that only those and not others bring about that cognition? If that is so, then why is this distinction made regarding universals (*jāti*) such that they exist in the *śābaleya* and others but not elsewhere? In that case, there would have to be another universal to effect that distinction, and yet another to serve as the basis for the occurrence of that distinction, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if it is argued that their causal nature is such that only those *śābaleya* individuals etc. are the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) of "cowness" (*gotva*) and its substrates, then, in that case, the production of that reflective awareness occurs through the power of their own causes even without a universal. Why then is it denied? Let go of this stubborn insistence on a universal. Furthermore, there is no universal in the eye and the other [causes].
In no way whatsoever does that form appear within consciousness;
for if the sense organs were the seer, their own form would have appeared [in consciousness]. (48)
Because they possess form; for universals are not perceived in isolation.
And when the individual is grasped, nothing other than the form of that word is seen. (49)

[210, vi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the field of generosity as real, nor does he perceive the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a buddha as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive all dharmas as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of omniscience as real. Subhūti, it is because he does not perceive any dharma as real that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma as real, how does he practice the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How does he train in the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha? How does he train in the great compassion of a tathāgata? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the field of generosity as real, nor does he perceive the fields of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a buddha as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive all dharmas as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of omniscience as real. Subhūti, it is because he does not perceive any dharma as real that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom. “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom gives a gift without perceiving a giver, a recipient, or a gift as real. This is his training in the perfection of giving. He guards morality without perceiving a precept, a transgression, or a moral agent as real. This is his training in the perfection of morality. He is patient without perceiving an object of anger, an offender, or a patient person as real. This is his training in the perfection of patience. He exerts vigor without perceiving a deed, an effort, or a vigorous person as real. This is his training in the perfection of vigor. He enters meditative concentration without perceiving a meditator, an object of concentration, or a state of concentration as real. This is his training in the perfection of meditation. He develops wisdom without perceiving a knower, an object of knowledge, or wisdom itself as real. This is his training in the perfection of wisdom. “In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; he trains in the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha; he trains in the great compassion of a tathāgata; and he trains in the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti, it is because he does not perceive any dharma as real that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the knowledge of all modes.”

Indeed, a universal (*sāmānya*) does not manifest in any way whatsoever within the eyes and other sense organs. Nor is it cognized even by means of its effect (*kārya*). Even when cognized through its effect, it is cognized as that which has a single effect; thus, there would be a relation of those [senses] with a single effect, but not a universal. If it is argued that a universal is simply a single relation existing everywhere, we say no, because a relation also does not manifest in any way. Immediately following that [cognition], there is only the perception of the effect; no further relation is perceived. And it has been stated that even an effect is related only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Now, if it is argued that a single power (*śakti*) belongs to all [the senses], this is not so, because it has already been established that power is not distinct from the possessor of power. Furthermore, even power does not manifest. If it is asked: "Why is power not postulated even if it is unperceived, just as in the case of the sense organs?"—that is incorrect. In that case, we accept their being beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyatva*), and thus our non-perception is like that of the *ajājī* flower and so forth, according to such statements. Moreover, a universal is not something to be understood solely through scripture (*āgama*). Apart from the effect, there is no cause for the manifestation of color-form (*rūpa*) and so on. Is that [cause] something distinct from the state of the eyeball (*golaka*), or otherwise? There is no discernment here [regarding this]. For instance:
[210,vii] There is some distinct entity that is the particularized eyeball;
or else it is a particularity of the latent impression (*vāsanā*). These are the various and diverse opinions. (PVA 224)

For one who does not establish an external object because it is non-distinct from its effect, how could he admit the inference of eyes and other organs as being distinct from their effects? Therefore, since this inference in whatever way it may be formulated has an unstable object of knowledge (*prameya*), there is no apprehension by means of it. As for its having the nature of form (*rūpavattva*), that is simply a matter of scripture (*āgama*). This being the case:
If there were a seer of them, then the eye and the other [senses] would be perceived;
since their status as beyond the reach of the senses is accepted, no other recourse exists.

This [argument] applies only to that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because it is accepted as having a form; however, this does not apply to the universal (*sāmānya*) alone, because the perception of a solitary universal is not admitted. If a yogi were to perceive a universal in its isolation, it would no longer be a universal. If, on the other hand, a cognition with a uniform aspect (*samānākārā buddhi*) arises, and the yogis perceive that "this is the basis for that," such a universal is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For us, the universal is never perceived separately, since the universal is manifested by the particular (*vyakti*); thus, there is no apprehension of it in isolation, just as there is no apprehension of color (*rūpa*) without the apprehension of light.

[211,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of concentration. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of concentration of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of patience. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of patience of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of vigor. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of vigor of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of ethical discipline. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is not included within the perfection of generosity. That too is incorrect. In inference, color (*rūpa*) is apprehended as being non-deviant from touch (*sparśa*) and so forth, even without light. If it were not so apprehended, there would be no exclusion (*vyatireka*) from light at all; nor is it appropriate to accept something as an "exclusion-reason" (*vyatirekin*) whose exclusion is unestablished. Furthermore, a universal (*sāmānya*) is never by itself an object of perception. When it enters into the form of the individual (*vyakti*), it does not exist [as a separate entity] at all; at most, it is merely the name "cow, cow. If it is argued that because they occupy the same location, there is no perception of their distinction—how then can there be a distinction between color, taste, and so on, since they are apprehended by different sense organs? To this we reply: here, however, the lack of discernment arises from extreme conjunction (*atyantasamsarga*).
[211,v] What is this absolute conjunction? Is it the blending of essential natures? For indeed, non-difference itself would result, since that very thing is its nature. (PVA)
Even when the location is not different, why is there no apprehension of difference due to the difference in form?
For a so-called "location" is not perceived as something distinct from form.
Apart from the object itself, what other place could there be? If the object is distinct, then the place is also necessarily distinct; how then can there be non-difference of place?
[211, viii] If difference [of the object] were due to the non-difference of place, from what would that [place's] own difference arise?
For that reason, its non-abiding would likewise result from its being in another location;
moreover, because it does not manifest by way of its own nature, like the horn of a donkey and so forth.
For that very reason, it is incapable even of performing the function of being a mere object of cognition.
Because of that incapacity, it is formless; for that is the defining characteristic of non-entities.

That which, by its own nature, does not manifest as that which is intended to be grasped cannot be an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). If it is argued that it will be a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) because it exists at the time [of cognition] for the purpose of imparting its own form—just like the eye and so forth—we say no; for even in that case, there is an absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
That which is the opposite of what has been stated is held to be the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).

Furthermore, that which appears with its own form (*svākāra*) and whose causal capacity is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is the ultimately real particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is characterized by its own nature (*svarūpa*). [The compound *svalakṣaṇa* means] "that of which the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is its own nature.

But how can there be the relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) when they are identical in their own nature? It is not so, because the relationship between the characterized and the characteristic is conceptual (*kālpānika*).
In this manner, the entire establishment of actions and their factors is of such a nature.

And this will be explained [later]. It is logical that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself and nothing else, because it is impossible in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) for one thing to be defined by another. For a definition by means of another form is merely a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of another form; it is not a definition of its own essential nature. How then is there a "universal definition" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? Because it does not pervade individual instances (*vyakti*). This is true, but in the ultimate sense there is no such thing as a "universal. That too is simply the essential nature of cognition (*jñāna*). It is spoken of in this way only from the standpoint of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), because it occurs through the superimposition of the essential natures of multiple individuals and because it arises from them. If it is a non-entity (*avastu*), how can there be a distinction between the reason of non-perception (*anupalambha*), the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*)? The distinction between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is due to a difference in their objects (*viṣaya*). But for non-perception and the others, there is no difference in object. If you say the distinction is due to a difference in the logical mark (*liṅga*), then surely the same objection was raised and the same answer given—how can this be? For in that case, a difference in the logical mark itself would be illogical. Alternatively, if a sixfold division is observed, then a sixfold division would result. Or rather, it will be stated that two are reasons for establishing a positive entity (*vastu*) and one is a reason for negation (*pratiṣedha*). If they are equally non-entities, how is there a division between "entity" and "non-entity"? To this, he provides the following reply:
And that universal is of three kinds, based on existence, non-existence, and both. // 51 //

[212,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he perceive a recipient of that gift. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he perceive a recipient of that gift? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive the element of space, nor does he perceive the element of consciousness. He does not perceive samsara, nor does he perceive nirvana. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he perceive a recipient of that gift, then how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? How does he turn the wheel of Dharma? And how does he establish sentient beings in the three vehicles? It is because he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; because he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness; because he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness; because he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness; because he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness; because he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness; because he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness; because he does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive the element of space, nor does he perceive the element of consciousness; because he does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm; because he does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he perceive the unconditioned; because he does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive the present; because he does not perceive samsara, nor does he perceive nirvana—for this reason, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom turns the wheel of Dharma.
