In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no distinction [between the three types of reasons], because in all cases they lack substantial reality (*avastutva*). However, due to the distinction in the cognition of the effect—which rests upon existence, non-existence, or both—there is a distinction between the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) and the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) based on their respective causal functions. To explain: a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has existence as its basis arises from the reason of essential nature; one that has non-existence as its basis arises from non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); and a conceptual construction that has both as its basis arises from the reason of effect. Thus, the reason of effect is a means of proof for that which is distinct. For distinction occurs through existence and non-existence, and it is a distinct cause that is the probandum (*sādhya*). Alternatively, even though they lack substantial reality, a distinction in the object (*viṣayabheda*) is established by relying on the distinction in the basis (*upādāna*), namely, the basis of existence and non-existence. Within this, there are three modes of distinction based on the distinction of objects: existence itself is twofold, being either distinct or non-distinct. Among these, the non-perception of the unobservable (*adṛśyānupalabdhi*) pertains to both existent and non-existent objects. The non-perception of the unobservable is the object characterized by the distinction of having both as its basis.

[212,iii] If cognition were dependent upon an existent entity because it follows the existence of that entity, this is not so; for an answer has already been given, and because [cognition] is observed to occur otherwise in the case of past objects and the like. // 52 //

[212,iv] It is not the case that knowledge which has an entity as its basis necessarily arises with respect to that entity. For the status of having an entity as its object follows from the grasping of the entity's own nature (*svarūpa*). And conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, does not grasp the own nature, as it was stated: "Because the collection of sense faculties is fruitless [with respect to the universal]" (2.110).

Now, if it is said that [the cognition] exists when an entity (*bhāva*) exists, that is unproven (*asiddha*), because such a cognition is observed even in the absence of an entity, as in the case of the past and so forth. Whether that cognition refers to a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*), there is no status as an object of the past and so forth for the entity, since an entity being apprehended in its own nature (*svarūpa*) cannot abandon its pastness. The world does not understand the object here to be an entity; rather, the notion that "the entity does not exist" is merely an error, as the cognition is attached to its own form. Furthermore, the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been demonstrated regarding the opposite case. By the phrase "because it is observed," the fallacy of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason is pointed out as intended by the opponent. If, then, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is observed even in the absence of an entity, and also in the presence of one, then the property of being a property of an entity (*bhāvadharmatā*) is lost. If it were thus a property of both, he says:
If it is argued that there would be a loss of its being a property of an entity, we reply: this is not a fault, because that cognition is preceded by the apprehension of the entity.

That very cognition has no object of apprehension therein, because a universal that is beyond perception cannot be an object of knowledge. For a universal is beyond perception; and how could it be an object of knowledge if it is not cognized in its own form?
The object of cognition is the single particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). 53.

[212,ix] That which is called a universal (*sāmānya*) is not an object of cognition (*prameya*), because it cannot be logically applied as it is conceptualized. Only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of cognition from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), because the purpose of its apprehension consists precisely in determining its existence or non-existence.
<ad PV 3.54>
[212,x] From where does this [arise]?
Therefore, because the existence or non-existence [of things] is investigated based on the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*),

For discerning people seek existence and non-existence only in respect to an entity that performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*). It is for the sake of understanding that [function] that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought. Otherwise, the investigation of the means of valid cognition would be nothing but an act lacking foresight. Therefore, a means of valid cognition is purposeful insofar as it is capable of making the presence or absence of an entity that performs a causal function its object. Consequently, both perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) must take only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object; otherwise, they could not be considered means of valid cognition. If the particular characteristic alone is made the object by both, then because they have the same object, it follows that there is only one means of valid cognition. If, on the other hand, even though the object is the same, there is a distinction between the means of valid cognition due to a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then this contradicts the principle that "the means of valid cognition are two because the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are of two kinds," as stated by the Teacher (Dignāga). Furthermore, if the distinction between means of valid cognition were based on a difference in the causal complex, then since the causal complexes for visual consciousness and so forth are distinct, there would be as many means of valid cognition as there are such consciousnesses.

[213,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchants being pursued by the bandits and was moved with great compassion. At that moment, he manifested himself as a merchant leader and went before them. He addressed the bandits, saying: "O you sons of thieves, do not harm these merchants. Why? Because I possess a jewel named 'Giver of All Desires. If you wish to see it, I shall give it to you. The bandit leader replied: "If you truly have such a jewel, we shall not harm these merchants; you may give it to us. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara then spoke to the merchants: "Do not fear; I shall protect you all. Having said this, he took the merchants and went to the place where the bandits were. Upon arriving, he showed the jewel to the bandit leader. The bandit leader saw the jewel and thought: "This jewel is truly marvelous; it can grant all desires. He then said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "I now take refuge in you. Please do not let me commit evil deeds. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara then spoke to the bandits: "O you sons of thieves, do not kill these merchants. If you wish to live, you should abandon your evil ways and instead practice giving, self-restraint, and the precepts. The bandits replied: "We shall follow your instructions. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara then led the bandits to a monastery. There, they met the Arhat Śāntamati. The Arhat Śāntamati addressed the bandits, saying: "O you sons of thieves, do not harbor anger or malice toward others. You should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Why? Because all sentient beings are my children. The bandits heard these words and immediately developed a mind of faith and respect. They prostrated themselves at the feet of the Arhat Śāntamati and requested ordination. The Arhat Śāntamati then granted them the going-forth and full ordination. After they had received the precepts, they diligently practiced meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara then led the merchants back to their own country. Arriving there, he restored their wealth and property to their original state. He then preached the Dharma for them, causing them to attain the stage of Non-Retrogression. The merchants, having seen the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, developed a mind of deep reverence and made this vow: "In the future, when we attain Buddhahood, we shall all be named Avalokiteśvara. The Buddha told Ānanda: "That merchant leader was none other than the present Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Those five hundred merchants were the present five hundred Arhats. And those bandits were the present five hundred Bhikṣus who have attained the fruit of Arhatship. The Buddha further told Ānanda: "If there are sentient beings who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon him, he will immediately manifest his power to deliver them from all suffering and distress. If one constantly calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, one shall never fall into the three evil realms. If one constantly calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, one shall attain the supreme path of the Buddhas. The Buddha then spoke in verse: "If one hears the name of Avalokiteśvara, One shall never again fall into the evil realms. If one constantly calls upon his name, One shall quickly attain the path of the Buddhas. The Buddha told Ānanda: "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such inconceivable power. Therefore, you should always single-mindedly call upon his name. The Buddha then spoke in verse: "The power of Avalokiteśvara is inconceivable; It can deliver all sentient beings from suffering. If one constantly calls upon his name, One shall quickly attain the path of the Buddhas. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, write it down, read it, recite it, or explain it to others, they shall all attain the stage of Non-Retrogression. If there are women who, having heard this chapter, develop a mind of faith and respect, they shall, at the end of their lives, no longer be reborn as women. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard this chapter, copy it, read it, recite it, or explain it to others, I shall protect and shield them, and I shall cause all obstacles and calamities to be forever eliminated. The Buddha then spoke in verse: "If one copies, reads, or recites this chapter, Or explains it to others, I shall protect and shield them, And cause all obstacles to be forever eliminated. [Objection: But surely, if there were a distinction [in means of knowledge] even due to a distinction in the objects of cognition (*prameya*), then because there are infinite objects of cognition such as blue and so forth, it would follow that there are infinite means of knowledge. [Reply: No, because all of them possess the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). There is only one single means of knowledge whose object is that [particular], because its object is one. [Objection: Even though there is a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), since the state of being born from the senses (*akṣajatva*) is present, why is not everything perception (*pratyakṣa*)? [Reply: Because the state of being born from the senses is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This will be demonstrated later. Therefore, the twofoldness [of means of knowledge] follows precisely from the twofoldness of the objects of cognition. Otherwise, there would be an infinity of means of knowledge. [Objection: How is it that the objects of cognition are not infinite? [Reply: Even if they are infinite, insofar as they consist of blue and so forth, the objects of cognition remain only two-fold. For:
Because it is apprehended through both its own form and the form of another, the object of cognition is held to be twofold. (54)

[213,iv] By virtue of appearing in their own form, blue and other such things, despite having infinite distinctions, are indeed *svalakṣaṇas* (particulars), because they are characterized by their own nature.

Is it not the case that the ultimate nature of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is determined by the difference in cognition? For if that cognition is absent and another cognition is present, it would no longer be a particular characteristic. Likewise, at that very same time, one thing is a particular characteristic for one person and otherwise for another. Moreover, there is no difference in the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for each cognizer. Since a difference produced through relative dependence is merely conceptual, it lacks ultimate reality. Furthermore, if a single thing possesses both the nature of being a particular characteristic and its opposite, it would constitute a distinct object of knowledge, and thus a further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would have to arise for it. This is incorrect.
If the ultimate were an object of cognition, there would be an infinity of objects of cognition.
If difference were produced by dependence, then the ultimate could not serve as a defining characteristic.
To this it is replied:
That which is characterized by perception is indeed ultimate reality.
[The existence of] entities is merely the apprehension of their being;
for entities do not appropriate existence for themselves without first attaining the state of being perceived in their own nature.

[213,x] But surely, existence is made known by perception, yet perception itself is not existence. For that which is not perceived—such as a rabbit’s horn—is non-existent; thus, the establishment is that existence is the opposite of non-perception.

Now, even in that case, non-apprehension is the ground for non-existence, but non-apprehension itself is not non-existence. Nor is there any other non-existence apart from non-apprehension. If it is argued that "non-existence is that which is cognized by means of non-apprehension," then what is this non-apprehension? Is it the absence of apprehension, or the apprehension of something else, or is it simply "not-apprehending"? These are the alternatives. If it is the absence of apprehension, how can there be cognition from that? An absence is not a cognition. If that absence too must be cognized through another absence of apprehension, there would be an infinite regress.

Now, it might be argued that there is no further perception of the perception itself; thus, its existence is not cognized through another perception, which would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because cognition is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). If cognition is imperceptible, how can its existence be cognized? Furthermore, just as the non-existence of an object is cognized from its non-perception, so too would it be for cognition; this would be a most grievous error. If, on the other hand, there is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) in that case—since the mirror is perceptible (*aparokṣa*), and therefore the absence of the five means of valid cognition does not apply to it—[then the same must hold for cognition].

But surely presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also nothing but cognition; therefore, one cognition is cognized by another cognition. Consequently, since there is no further presumption in that case, it follows that the cognition of presumption does not exist due to the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, if there is a comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in that case, then presumption would recur, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*) and thus a lack of comprehension.

But surely, a cognition is observed. If one relies on mere observation, what is the use of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? Let it be exactly as it is observed. It is observed directly; let it be so. What is the use of presumptive testimony or the conceptual construction of a "cognition"? [Objection: But presumptive testimony does indeed arise. [Response: If that is the case, then because there would be no finality (*anavasthā*), even the determination of non-cognition would occur. How then could that be undesirable? Furthermore, when the state of being perceived or the state of being direct (*aparokṣatā*) belongs to the cognition, then in the cognition of its absence, there would be an infinite regress.

[214,iv] Now, if the non-perception of objects is itself the non-perception of perception, then it follows that even while perception is not being perceived, perception nonetheless exists. If you argue that this very [non-perception] is non-existence, then it follows that if non-perception is non-existence, perception must be existence. Alternatively, if the non-perception of one thing is simply the perception of another, [214,v]

That too is incorrect. Even if one has merely designated [the cognition] as "perception of another," how does it follow that the other does not exist? If you say, "Because there is no perception of it," the answer to this has already been given: that very perception of one thing is simply not directed toward the other; thus, there is no perception of that other. But even if it is not directed elsewhere, how does that prove its non-existence? If you say, "There is indeed the non-existence of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility," otherwise it would have occurred there as well, since it too would be perceived in the same manner. Yet it is not perceived. By whom, then, is this non-perception—which is the definition of non-existence—established? Thus, the same infinite regress remains. If you say, "Because there is the perception of a specific form," is this not then a *arthāpatti* (presumption)? If you say it is so, the infinite regress has already been stated. If you say, "The perception of a specific form itself is the non-perception of the other," then in that case, there is no such thing as "non-existence" distinct from the existence of something else. Therefore, what is called "non-existence" relative to another is simply the existence of that thing relative to itself. And that nature is restricted precisely to the state of being perceived. Consequently, perception is said to be existence.

[214, vi] But surely, if there is a specific restriction, it is a restriction regarding being perceived, and not that very thing itself which is the restriction. [Objection: But if it is unperceived, how can there be a restriction? [Response: The cognition [of restriction] arises precisely through the grace of being perceived. Therefore, being perceived is itself existence (*sattā*).

Now, if one thinks "I do not perceive," this is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that constitutes non-perception. Yet even that conceptual construction "I do not perceive" follows after non-perception itself, and that non-perception has already been examined. Therefore, perception is existence. Indeed, the very state of being perceived is the reality of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). If, then, that alone were ultimate existence (*paramārtha-sattva*), it could not be otherwise for anyone. But this does not become otherwise; even with respect to another person, it remains exactly as it is, just like blue and so forth. If it is asked: "How can that very thing be cognized as such when it is imperceptible (*parokṣa*)? [The answer is: Even while being imperceptible, it is cognized in that very form. However, if it is not cognized by anyone in that way, nor will it be so cognized, then its inference would be in vain. If it is asked: "How can that which is not being cognized be such? [The reply is: How can it be that very same thing if it exists in a different way? If it is argued that it is "otherwise" because of the absence of perception, then surely, due to the absence of perception, there is simply non-existence. If it is argued: "Even in the case of non-existence, there would be non-perception; how then is there non-existence? [We reply: This should be said only when there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for existence. If it is claimed that inference is the means of valid cognition, even that follows after a form that has already been seen. Since the seeing occurs later, how can there be "present visibility" (*dṛśyamānatā*) of what was previously seen? If there is no present visibility, how can there be existence? If it is argued that it exists because of a subsequent perception, then let its existence be only from that point on; how could it have existed previously?

[215,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-observability, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the state of a bodhisattva or the state of a Tathāgata as real. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not perceive form as real? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and that which is the intrinsic nature of form is not form; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, and that which is the intrinsic nature of consciousness is not consciousness; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive consciousness as real. The eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the eye is not the eye; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the eye as real. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the mind is not the mind; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the mind as real. Forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms, and that which is the intrinsic nature of forms is not forms; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive forms as real. Sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental phenomena, and that which is the intrinsic nature of mental phenomena is not mental phenomena; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive mental phenomena as real. Eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness, and that which is the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness is not eye-consciousness; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive eye-consciousness as real. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-consciousness, and that which is the intrinsic nature of mind-consciousness is not mind-consciousness; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive mind-consciousness as real. Eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-contact, and that which is the intrinsic nature of eye-contact is not eye-contact; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive eye-contact as real. Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-contact, and that which is the intrinsic nature of mind-contact is not mind-contact; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive mind-contact as real. The feeling born of eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of the feeling born of eye-contact, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the feeling born of eye-contact is not the feeling born of eye-contact; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact as real. The feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of the intrinsic nature of the feeling born of mind-contact, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the feeling born of mind-contact is not the feeling born of mind-contact; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the feeling born of mind-contact as real. The earth element is empty of the intrinsic nature of the earth element, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the earth element is not the earth element; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the earth element as real. The water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are empty of the intrinsic nature of the consciousness element, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the consciousness element is not the consciousness element; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the consciousness element as real. The realm of desire is empty of the intrinsic nature of the realm of desire, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the realm of desire is not the realm of desire; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the realm of desire as real. The realm of form and the formless realm are empty of the intrinsic nature of the formless realm, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the formless realm is not the formless realm; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the formless realm as real. Ignorance is empty of the intrinsic nature of ignorance, and that which is the intrinsic nature of ignorance is not ignorance; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive ignorance as real. Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death are empty of the intrinsic nature of aging-and-death, and that which is the intrinsic nature of aging-and-death is not aging-and-death; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive aging-and-death as real. The perfection of giving is empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of giving is not the perfection of giving; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of giving as real. The perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are empty of the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as real. The emptiness of the internal is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the internal, and that which is the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the internal is not the emptiness of the internal; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real. [Objection: But how can that which was previously non-existent be perceived later? [Response: If you say it is because it is perceived as being perceived—meaning that it is perceived as being perceived, and not otherwise—then even at another time it is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) by that very same form; thus, there is no existence in another way (*anyathāsattva*), because it is impossible to apprehend it otherwise. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that inference (*anumāna*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding future existence. [Question: How then is there a different object of cognition (*meyāntara*)? [Answer: Because that very thing is perceived through the form of another. That which is perceived in such a way, by means of a form common to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is a different object of cognition. This is due to the superimposition (*āropa*) of that form through a difference in apprehension, but not in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). [Objection: In that case, since it is produced through dependence (*apekṣā*), it lacks ultimate reality. [Response: True; it has already been established that the universal (*sāmānya*) is not a real entity (*avastu*). This is not being said for the first time. Through correspondence with a real entity (*vastu-saṃvāda*), those engaged in conventional practice (*vyavahārin*), who do not perceive its diversity, employ the term "real entity. Therefore, with reference to that, this twofold nature of the objects of cognition is stated. Those engaged in conventional practice, who do not perceive its diversity, employ the term "real entity"; therefore, with reference to that, this twofold nature of the objects of cognition is stated. [Objection: If the thought is that, because it possesses both forms, there must be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) that grasps both.

That is incorrect, because it is impossible for a single [cognition] to apprehend both forms simultaneously. Or, if it does so apprehend them, then these are simply two distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since a distinction [between cognitions] occurs only when there is a difference in their apprehension. Alternatively, since the definition [of the means of cognition] is not ultimately real due to the difference in apprehension, there is no consequence of it having a dual nature. For the very nature of an object is its being blue and so forth; and that [nature] does not possess differentiation based on a difference in perspective. How then can there be the status of a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) in the absence of an ultimately real object of cognition (*prameya*)?
To this it is replied:
Because difference consists of an imagined nature, it is precisely that which is not ultimately real.
But that which is the form of the object as it is to be attained is not [the object] in the ultimate sense.

[215,v] How, then, can there be a distinction [between perception and inference] on the grounds that [inference] takes the ultimate reality (paramārtha) as its object? For if it were to directly realize the intrinsic nature (svarūpa), it would indeed be perception. If it does not touch upon that [nature], how can it have that as its object? To this, it is said:
The second type of error is held to be that which consists in an adherence that does not correspond to reality.

[215, vii] Just as this object is now distinct here due to a difference in its causes, so too this adherence does not occur; thus it is indeed an error consisting in an adherence that does not correspond to reality. This is because it is produced by the power of the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) generated by previously perceived objects, and because it is a determination that, though lacking contact with a real entity, appears as such. If, then, there is no contact with a real entity, how can it be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that it is indeed a valid means of cognition because it is non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*), then that very contradiction would not exist, since one thing is reached when another is apprehended. To this he says:
If it were to proceed by means of another's form, then there would be no validity for that which is erroneous. (55)

[215,ix] If there is cognition by means of another form, how can that be its cognition? That cognition belongs only to the other form. In that case, if there is error regarding something else, it is merely an error; and error is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Response:
Even though it is erroneous, cognition possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge because it does not contradict one's intended purpose;
furthermore, movement [toward that object] is observed to occur otherwise, and this position has already been answered.

How is it to be understood that there is no adherence (*abhiniveśa*) elsewhere as well? Precisely because the intention (*abhiprāya*) is not contradicted. Since that [non-contradiction] exists here too, there is no adherence to what is unreal. However, people engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahārin*) do not realize that this cognition arises from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and that its differentiation is due to a difference in appearance; this is merely the understanding of the commentator. If it is asked, "How can that very same intention arise from seeing something else?", the answer is: No, because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) lack a fixed correspondence with real objects. This is simply the efficacy of beginningless latent impressions. Therefore, the objection—"How can one proceed toward an object whose true nature is not determined?"—is not valid. Furthermore, when something is actually perceived, there is no possibility of an inconsistency. How does one proceed even in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Even there, there is no determination of the form of the object to be attained, because perception determines only that which is present. On the contrary, it is perception itself that prompts action, since it brings about the attainment of whatever is present. Even in that case, activity toward a future object occurs only through the determination of identity (*ekatvādhyavasāya*) with the present. Therefore, how can the operation of inference be seen as dissimilar, since it functions in exactly the same way? Now, if it is argued that perception is not of the nature of a determination of identity, but is merely a determiner of what is present, whereas the determination of identity occurs at a later time and cannot exist without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that is incorrect.
Because its own nature is grasped even more clearly through inference, it occupies another conceptual construction when there is proximity to the act of apprehension. (PVA 232)

For just as perception— which grasps only the form and other objects present before it— is a motivator for action when there is a superimposition of unity by means of another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), so too inference is even more clearly a grasper of its own nature, which is more immediately present. In that case as well, its status as a motivator arises precisely from the determination of the object to be attained (*bhāvya-adhyavasāya*) by means of another conceptual construction.

Now, if it is argued that inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it impels action by its very nature as a form of determinative ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*), yet does not touch upon the actual object (*avastu-saṃsparśin*), whereas perception (*pratyakṣa*) possesses the status of a valid cognition because it touches upon the actual object— this too is incorrect. For perception is not impelling merely by touching upon the actual object.
However, a single determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) does not exist for perception (233).

For that form by which there is contact with the object, perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the capacity to induce activity. Now, if it is argued that that very form which produces conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is what induces activity;

[216, vi] Now, what kind of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses the capacity to initiate action, by means of which perception (*pratyakṣa*) could be said to have the capacity to initiate action? For that [conceptual construction] is itself not an initiator. What kind of logic is this—to say that it initiates action by generating a conceptual construction that does not initiate action?

If conceptual construction is that which sets [the process] in motion, how can it grasp a non-existent object? Even so, why is it thought that this [conceptualization] functions by means of inference?

If perception functions as an instigator by way of generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then, since it is the conceptual construction that acts as the instigator, it would follow that it possesses the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). This being the case, the validity of inference (*anumāna*) remains entirely unchallenged. If it is argued that inference lacks validity because it does not grasp a real entity and thus does not act as an instigator, then how can this be said of a conceptual construction that arises subsequent to perception? For in that case, it is perception that grasps the real entity; the [conceptual construction] that arises later does not function with respect to that [entity]. If it is argued that there is "functioning" because it functions within the continuum (*santāna*) of that [perception], then how can the first moment possess the nature of a continuum? Furthermore, what has occurred in one place cannot be said to have occurred in another. If it were so, then inference, though occurring in its own form, would also be considered to have occurred in the object itself. This is merely a figurative expression (*upacāra*); it is no answer even from the standpoint of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The claim that "perception occurs in one place and also occurs in another" is not distinct from mere figurative usage. On the contrary, it is contradictory to say that perception occurs in things of that same class (*tajjātīya*) while inference does not occur even there. This is because a conceptual construction arising after perception does not occur in things of that same class. If the defense is that "perception occurs there," then the same applies to inference. Since perception has indeed occurred in the class of objects that are the domain of inference—for instance, perception has already occurred in the fire of the kitchen—[inference] exists in the domain of inference. Thus, everything is equal. To illustrate: *(Note: The provided text ends mid-argument regarding the analogy between the kitchen fire and the mountain-top fire inferred by smoke.)*
Just as perception does not operate within the domain of inference, why should it not likewise be the case for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which arises subsequent to perception? (235) (PVA)
If perception were produced by inference because it occurs with respect to another individual,
then how could that which does not occur with respect to another form be a perception that produces conceptual construction? (236) However, the determination of oneness is equal for both.
In both cases, the universal (*sāmānya*) of the object is apprehended through contact.
(237) (PVA) In that context, the first moment of the fire is the object of the sense-faculty for the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
But has it not been explained that the apprehension of one thing cannot be the apprehension of another? (238) (PVA)
If it is accepted that the apprehension of that [object] occurs upon the apprehension of its correlate,
then in every case of inference as well, the apprehension of the correlate is equally present.
In the case of conceptual construction, the object of perception is seen as causeless; likewise, in inference, the effect is seen.

Just as the perception of an object—which occurs prior to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises subsequent to that perception—bestows validity upon that conceptual construction by functioning with respect to its cause even though it does not function with respect to the construction itself; so too, let the functioning of the effect, even though it does not function with respect to the object of inference, bestow validity upon the inference as well, due to the specific relationship [of causality]. For the causal relationship is the same in both cases. On the contrary, if one were to argue that the cognition of the effect from the cause is non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), then perception alone would be invalid, and not inference.
Now, it may be argued that the pointing out of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] on the grounds of its being perceived is improper.

Now, it might be argued: "In a case where perception (*pratyakṣatā*) occurs regarding that which is merely present, an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) is not raised; however, this is not perception regarding a future thing (*bhāvin*). This objection is also untenable. For even in the case of inference, the object is "belonging to that class" (*tajjātīyatā*), which is itself an object of perception. The distinction is simply this: in that [case of inference], perception has already occurred, whereas here [in the case of the future], it is currently operating. Furthermore, perception does not have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, because it operates upon another individual (*vyaktyantara*) there, while here it operates upon that very [present] one. [Response: No, for there is no identity between the future and the past, and since it is not perceived, the status of having a universal as its object remains the same. Or how could "belonging to that class" be understood in the case of a future object by means of something unperceived? If you say, "Because it is grasped as such elsewhere," then what is understood everywhere as a universal is simply the commonality with other individuals, not a particular (*viśeṣa*). Thus, there is no difference between perception and inference. Alternatively, if it is argued that because the future is necessarily bound to occur (*avaśyambhāvitā*), there is no inconclusiveness—wherever there is a cause, there is necessity, and wherever there is an effect, there is all the more necessity—and it has been established that causality exists only in what is necessary to occur, then there is no difference between perception and inference regarding a future object, whether it be something to be produced (*pravartya*) or something to be attained (*prāpya*).

[217, vii] The Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the three gates of liberation. What are these three? They are: 1) the gate of emptiness, 2) the gate of signlessness, and 3) the gate of wishlessness. Regarding this, what is the gate of emptiness? It is the non-apprehension of all phenomena. What is the gate of signlessness? It is the non-perception of the characteristics of all phenomena. What is the gate of wishlessness? It is the non-arising of desire for any phenomenon whatsoever. Furthermore, what is the gate of emptiness? It is the absence of self and what belongs to a self in all phenomena. What is the gate of signlessness? It is the absence of signs in all conditioned phenomena. What is the gate of wishlessness? It is the absence of delight in all conditioned phenomena. Furthermore, what is the gate of emptiness? It is the non-apprehension of the internal bases. What is the gate of signlessness? It is the non-apprehension of the external bases. What is the gate of wishlessness? It is the non-apprehension of both the internal and external bases. Furthermore, what is the gate of emptiness? It is the non-apprehension of the aggregates. What is the gate of signlessness? It is the non-apprehension of the elements. What is the gate of wishlessness? It is the non-apprehension of the sense-fields. Furthermore, what is the gate of emptiness? It is the non-apprehension of the past. What is the gate of signlessness? It is the non-apprehension of the future. What is the gate of wishlessness? It is the non-apprehension of the present.
