Now, if it is argued that perception alone is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it contacts the actual object (*vastu-saṃsparśa*), whereas inference is not, that too is incorrect. In the absence of contact with the object to be reached, there is no distinction between what is erroneous and what is non-erroneous. If it is argued that the distinction lies in the presence or absence of the object, no; for without corroboration (*saṃvāda*), it is impossible to determine whether that [perception] corresponds to the existence or non-existence of the object. If it is further argued that in perception, even when there is no corroboration by another person, there is still contact with the object because of internal corroboration, that too is merely accessible through inference; thus, there is no distinction. Therefore, since validity arises from non-discrepancy with the intended object, the apprehension of the actual object itself is not the essential factor. Otherwise, even perception would be invalid.

It is explained in that very [text]: "Movement is observed otherwise. Movement is observed even when one is deluded; or, movement is the stepping of the feet, and it is observed "otherwise," even when there is a cognition of another form. How is there attainment? Because of the existence of the object. That which has existence is attained. For instance, there is the observation of attainment even by the touch of the hand when the cause is capable. If it is asked how it is restricted, it is solely by the force of the relationship. Existence too exists only because of the existence of the related entity. How is movement a relation? If it is argued that even in perception, how is there a movement toward a future relation? If it is said, "Because it is seen exactly so," then it is the same in both cases, and thus there is no dispute. If it is argued that therefore only that [initial] perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there because it generates a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then why is that same prior perception not accepted as such because it also generates inference? If it is argued that it is because that [prior perception] is past, then at the time of the arising of the conceptual construction, the perception is indeed already past. For it will be demonstrated that cause and effect are not simultaneous. If it is argued that there is a distinction because perception continues in a stream even at the time of the conceptual construction, [we reply: no, because the subsequent moments of perception would lack validity. If the subsequent ones also have validity, otherwise the future stream could not be ascertained; in that case, the preceding ones would also lack validity, because they do not have the attainable object as their domain. If the preceding ones alone generate the ascertainment, then the subsequent ones would be invalid. For where there is doubt, there is no ascertainment, and where there is ascertainment, there is no doubt; since it is impossible for ascertainment and its opposite to have the same object. If it is argued that the preceding ones are simply invalid, then [the subject] would not act; yet I see the validity of something in this regard: "Is there attainment here or not? This is the same even in the case of inference when one acts. Therefore, even movement, though intended as perceptual, is observed otherwise, namely by way of another form. There is no movement whatsoever in the nature of the object of action in its own form. But elsewhere, in the form of the real thing or its own form, there is movement for both [perception and inference]; so what is the difference regarding future things? How then is there a difference in the objects of perception and inference? The unclear is superimposed upon the clear, and the clear upon the unclear. Or else, otherwise.
Where there is a future state, inference is held to be the means of knowledge;
when there is an occurrence consisting merely of the present, perception is the means of knowledge. (PVA 240)

[218,ii] Where there is an engagement even without conceptualization due to extreme habituation, there perception is the valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, conceptualization would result in being a separate means of cognition, if it were the case that perception is the engaging means of cognition only where conceptualization occurs.

Now, if it is argued that perception alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because the latter apprehends what has already been apprehended—this has already been examined, showing how there is no such thing as apprehending what has already been apprehended. It is stated once more: for instance, "If conceptual construction serves no purpose in the occurrence [of activity], then what is the use of it?"
If the application of conceptual thought toward its operation were a means of cognition, why would it not be a valid source of knowledge?

If conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed useless, how can it be sought as an aid to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? For surely no one has a need for an aid that is useless. If it is argued that without it there would be no engagement [with the object], then direct perception would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*). If it is further argued that without that [conceptualization] one does not engage [at all], then it follows that both are authoritative. Alternatively, if conceptual construction is non-authoritative because it does not touch upon the actual form of the thing (*padārtha*), then it was just stated that direct perception is also non-authoritative because it does not touch upon the form of the object to be attained. Therefore: [218, vi]

If conceptual construction lacks causality in its operation through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then it would follow that it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). [Objection:
The operation of conceptual construction occurs subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If there were such a capacity, then perception would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge due to that intervention.

Now, if even that which is separated [from its object] were not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), then in that case, the eyes and other sense organs would also have to be considered means of valid cognition insofar as they cause one to act. If you say it is not so because they are not cognitions (*ajñānatvāt*), then the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) would be a means of valid cognition. If you say it is not so because its object is different, then it would be a means of valid cognition if the objects were the same. If you say it indeed is [a means of valid cognition], we say no; for in that case, with respect to the object to be acted upon, it is not a cognition. Indeed, the perception (*pratyakṣa*) that grasps the preceding moment does not have the object to be acted upon as its domain. Therefore, due to its immediate succession, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) alone would be the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, even if perception were to cause one to act toward the object of activity by means of mere appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*), conceptualization would still be the means of valid cognition. If you ask how it can be invalid when it grasps what has already been grasped, we say: because it causes one to act, just like an inference based on essential nature (*svabhāva-anumāna*). Perception is not a means of valid cognition by mere appearance alone; otherwise, even though momentariness is grasped by perception, the inference that grasps it as momentary would not be a means of valid cognition, since it would be grasping what has already been grasped. If you argue that conceptualization is a means of valid cognition because it establishes worldly practice (*vyavahāra-sādhana*), then the same would apply equally [to perception]. Therefore, although both cause one to act toward the object of perception, there are two types of means of valid cognition precisely because of the distinction between the clear and the unclear. Even when there is comprehension through another form [than the object itself], it is indeed a means of valid cognition because it is non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*). And it has already been demonstrated how there is no grasping of the actual nature of the thing even when there is non-contradiction. Thus, he shows that even if it is a means of valid cognition due to non-contradiction, it is nonetheless erroneous (*bhrāntatā*).

When two people run toward the light of a jewel and a lamp respectively, thinking it to be a jewel, although there is no difference in their false cognition, there is a difference with respect to purposeful action. (57)
Just so, even though inference and its fallacy lack correspondence with reality,
their status as valid cognition or invalid cognition is established by virtue of their conformity to purposeful action (arthakriyā).
[218,xi] In the case of the luster of a jewel, which possesses a specific form produced by the aperture of the keyhole, yet does not depend upon a specific jewel;

Furthermore, in the light of a lamp, the illusion of a ruby (*sarasiruha-rāga-maṇi*) is not distinguished from [the actual jewel] in one case and another in the other; yet, there is indeed a distinction for someone regarding the attainment of the jewel. Likewise, it is precisely for that reason that inference (*anumāna*) and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) are respectively valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its opposite. Even when the jewel is not seen, one who proceeds with the determination (*adhyavasāya*) that the light of the lamp is the jewel is indeed observed [to reach his goal]. Nor is it a mere error (*bhrānti*); thus, there is no universal identity [between them], because there is a distinction based on the particularity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). For it is not the case that everything is erroneous simply because it is a cognition, nor otherwise. Therefore, even an erroneous cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*), possessing a distinction due to the particularity of the causal complex. Although it is an error consisting of a determined object of illusion, when produced by objects that are [ultimately] connected, it becomes the basis for the arising of valid cognition and the cause for attaining the desired object, just like inferential knowledge which is the basis for the arising of perception. For inference is not a valid means of knowledge without the arising of perception, nor is perception [valid] without the arising of inference; this has already been established. To explain:
Without inference, perception does not function from the outset; likewise, it has been established that without perception, inference does not function. (PVA 244)
The distinction here is simply this: in some cases the sense-faculty (*akṣa*) follows inference, while in others it precedes;
it is held that the sense-faculty does not come after inference, nor is inference preceded by the sense-faculty.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Inference proceeds even without perception, whereas perception does not proceed without inference; therefore, due to this distinction, inference is not equal to perception.
That too is incorrect.
[219, vi] Without inference, perception is not a means of valid cognition regarding self-awareness.
Likewise, there is no such conventional usage; even if it were a means of valid cognition, what would [the consequence] be? (PVA)
And since in a perception consisting of mere self-awareness the object is not established, there would be nothing for the distinction [between subject and object]; thus, non-duality alone remains.
Therefore, there is no proof by means of direct perception for either the object or its distinction.
In the end, its status as a means of valid cognition does not exist without inference.

(PVA 248) Now, it might be argued: perception functions toward a distinct object only by depending on inference, whereas inference functions even without perception; for instance, the inference of fire from smoke occurs at a later time without depending on perception, because the object is attained through that [inference] alone. This is not so.
For the state of being qualified by a location is not perceived by direct perception;
moreover, inference [proceeds] from the cognition of fire without a specific location. (PVA 249)

[219,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the beginningless and endless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, or the emptiness of the unestablished as real. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as real. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as real, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or great compassion as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive anything as real. Because he does not perceive anything as real, he does not become attached to anything. Because he is not attached to anything, he does not tremble. Because he does not tremble, he overcomes fear. Having overcome fear, he attains nirvāṇa. This is the ultimate reality of all dharmas."

Fire concealed by a wall or similar obstruction cannot be apprehended through inference as being located in a specific place. While one might infer in a general sense that "fire exists somewhere beyond the wall," it is through perception that the fire is grasped in its specific location. Furthermore, a fire whose location is not determined cannot come into existence [as a known object]. Even in the case of the cognition of a gem based on its luster, the very failure to grasp the gem in its specific location constitutes a defect. This distinction does not apply to doubt or error; for they differ from valid cognition only in their inability to lead to the attainment of a specific object. Now, it might be argued: "An erroneous cognition (*viparyaya*) is invalid because it causes one to act toward something else, whereas doubt (*saṃśaya*), since it sometimes causes one to act toward the actual object, may be considered valid. That is incorrect.
For doubt, which relies upon both sides, is not a motivator;
it is error that, through its own erroneous nature, impels embodied beings to action. (PVA 250)

[220,i] For doubt is inferior to error. Since it relies upon both sides, how can it impel one whose mind is oscillating? Therefore, that state of oscillation departs from perception. Even error—characterized by the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem—is posterior to inference; thus, there is no distinction between the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem and inference in terms of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued: "But it is indeed a valid means of knowledge," [220,ii]

If that [cognition] is indeed a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it be erroneous? It is precisely such [a cognition] that is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Of what use is consistency (*saṃvāda*) in determining whether it is other than an error?

"Valid cognition is non-erroneous knowledge" (1.1)—this is the general definition. Whether that [non-erroneous nature] exists in the case of error or otherwise, where is this [definition] useful? One might object: "If it were erroneous, there could be no non-discrepancy, and not otherwise. This too is not true;
for non-erroneousness [is established] through non-discrepancy with respect to time, place, and other persons.
There is no non-contradiction of error, because non-error itself is not established.
(PVA 220,v)

The distinction that "this is erroneous" and "this is otherwise" cannot be made without non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*). If it is argued that it is non-erroneous because it is unrefuted (*abādhitatva*), we say no; for that is merely another way of expressing non-contradiction itself. For when contradiction exists, everything is indeed an error. If it is argued that even in the case of being unrefuted, there is still that very same contradiction, then its state of being unrefuted is simply non-contradiction; thus, it is established that non-erroneousness arises precisely from non-contradiction. Furthermore, the view that inference is indeed an error despite its non-contradiction belongs neither to the Mīmāṃsaka nor to the Lokāyata, since both accept that all error is invalid as a means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

[220, vi] If, then, even erroneous perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is the distinction between perception and inference? It will be stated that it is due to a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Even though they are both erroneous, there is a difference in appearance, as in the case of fallacious inference and the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimira*).
Only entirely non-erroneous cognition is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not an error.
What distinction could possibly be observed between that which is erroneous and that which is non-erroneous?

Error (*vibhrama*) is indeed the failure to touch the actual nature (*svarūpa*) [of the object], and this is common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Just as inference fails to touch the nature of the object to be attained (*prāpyarūpa*), so too is it with perception; thus there is no distinction. Therefore, even the cognition of a gem in the luster of a gem is indeed perception. If it is argued that in the case of a future object, it is a future inference that is the means of valid cognition, [we reply: this is the same for the other case, namely perception. If it is argued that in that case (perception) there is no conceit of it being a distinct means of valid cognition, whereas in the case of the cognition of the gem [in the luster] there certainly is, [we reply: through extreme habituation, even in the cognition of the gem there is no conceit of it being a distinct means of valid cognition; thus it is the same. Now, if it is argued that the conceit of error exists in the cognition of the gem in the luster, but not in the cognition of a pillar and so forth, we say: [The opponent says: "But surely, the conceit of error exists in the cognition of the gem in the luster, but not in the cognition of a pillar and so forth. [The author replies: To this it is said: ...

Because there is conceit regarding the equality of the ultimate truth based on what is not a valid means of cognition, the distinction [between them] lacks reality; that [distinction] is merely a matter of two types of valid cognition. (PVA 254)

[220,x] In all cases of perception and inference, there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), yet there is no conceit [of its existence]; however, it is not by this much that there is a difference in the nature of the object. Since a conceit lacking a means of valid cognition may occur in any manner whatsoever, there is no distinction between its existence and non-existence. Therefore:
That cognition is either indeed perception or else inference;
such is the determination of the truth regarding the cognition of a jewel based on the luster of a jewel.

Now, since the actual nature of the jewel is not apprehended, how can it be perceptible? As for pillars and the like, even if their future nature is not apprehended, the apprehension of their nature as it exists at that time certainly does occur. That is incorrect; for:
When the future form is not apprehended, there is the apprehension of another—namely, the cognition and its object—at that time.
It is the same in both cases; however, the attainment [of the object] occurs through a causal connection.

Whether there is the apprehension of a difference in the form of the object to be attained, or whether there is the grasping of its own nature (*svarūpa*) or another's nature (*pararūpa*), there is no distinction [in the result].

[221,i] However, the appearance of a jewel is exactly the same with respect to both the jewel and the luster of the jewel. In that regard, in some cases there is an error regarding location (*deśabhrānti*), in some cases an error regarding essential nature (*svarūpabhrānti*), in some cases both, and in some cases neither. Regarding the cognition of a jewel directed toward the luster of a jewel, there is an error regarding location; regarding the cognition of a jewel directed toward the jewel itself, there is an error regarding the nature of the object to be attained (*prāpyasvarūpabhrānti*). In the case of inference based on a universal (*sāmānyānumāna*), there is an error regarding both. In the case of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), there is neither kind of error; such is the classification. [221,ii]
Therefore, as it was said: "That cognition which exists in the form of equality is just like perceptual cognition.

"That which is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is incorrect. Even the operation of direct perception does not [grasp its object] by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Nor is there any direct perception that is non-erroneous. Just as direct perception is erroneous with respect to its own intrinsic nature, so too is inference and other cognitions considered erroneous; thus, the demonstration of their being erroneous in that manner is of no use anywhere. If this is so, then how is there a distinction in definition between direct perception and inference? It has been stated in this regard: "Because of the difference between clear and otherwise [i.e., unclear] manifestation. From what does that very difference in manifestation arise? That which grasps [its object] independently possesses a clear manifestation. That which is otherwise possesses an unclear manifestation, which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and indirect (*parokṣa*).
How is it that this very thing comes to be such that it is stated thus?
Wherever cognition follows the presence and absence [of an object] through the power of that object, its apprehension is independent; anything other than that is a supersensible entity. (59)

That which has direct manifestation is itself the object that is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), namely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). And there is direct manifestation because the cognition, assuming that form, is produced in accordance with the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) [of the sense organ]. However, that which is determined as having the form of a previously apprehended nature—being an object of appearance due to the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by a prior perception—is other than that [direct object] and is beyond the senses. For in that case, there is no operation of the sense organ; nor is the mode of direct realization possible through it directly perceived. Furthermore, there is no cognition of it other than its own form. Thus, that which is directly [manifested] is not cognized at all. If it is argued that it is "indirect" (*parokṣa*) because of the absence of sequential connection, then it follows that even while being cognized in its own nature, it would be indirect due to the absence of the operation of the sense organ. This is undesirable.
vii] Therefore, if a cognition whose object is beyond the senses does not perceive a real entity,
how can that which is perceived be an object beyond the senses, given that it is not beyond the senses? (PVA 257)

[221, viii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered all beings from suffering and distress. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness; what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they have no characteristics, no birth, no cessation, no defilement, no purity, no decrease, and no increase. Śāriputra, within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touchable object, no mental phenomenon; no realm of the eye up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; likewise, there is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, he has no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It relieves all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of the *prajñāpāramitā* should be proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Chapter 221: The Practice of Avalokiteśvara. Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "If you wish to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, you must cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. This is called cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the four right efforts to attain the fruit of a once-returner? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds his mind, and strives to prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising. He generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds his mind, and strives to abandon arisen evil and unwholesome states. He generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds his mind, and strives to produce unarisen wholesome states. He generates desire, exerts effort, applies energy, upholds his mind, and strives to maintain arisen wholesome states, preventing their decline, increase, cultivation, and fulfillment. This is called cultivating the four right efforts to attain the fruit of a once-returner. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the four bases of psychic power to attain the fruit of a non-returner? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration based on desire and volitional formations. He develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration based on energy and volitional formations. He develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration based on mind and volitional formations. He develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration based on investigation and volitional formations. This is called cultivating the four bases of psychic power to attain the fruit of a non-returner. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the five faculties to attain the fruit of an arhat? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu cultivates the faculty of faith, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the faculty of energy... the faculty of mindfulness... the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. This is called cultivating the five faculties to attain the fruit of an arhat. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the five powers to attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu cultivates the power of faith, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the power of energy... the power of mindfulness... the power of concentration... the power of wisdom, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. This is called cultivating the five powers to attain the fruit of a pratyekabuddha. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment to attain the fruit of an Unsurpassed Enlightened One? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena... the factor of enlightenment of energy... the factor of enlightenment of rapture... the factor of enlightenment of tranquility... the factor of enlightenment of concentration... the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. This is called cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment to attain the fruit of an Unsurpassed Enlightened One. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path to attain the fruit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu cultivates right view, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates right intention... right speech... right action... right livelihood... right effort... right mindfulness... right concentration, which leads to penetration, based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. This is called cultivating the Noble Eightfold Path to attain the fruit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the four applications of mindfulness to attain the fruit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "A bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. This is called cultivating the four applications of mindfulness to attain the fruit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how does one cultivate the four right efforts to attain the fruit of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Buddha

If it is perceived, it is not indirect (*parokṣa*). Nor can there be an object that is a real entity (*vastu*) if there is no contact with the entity. If, however, its object is a universal (*sāmānya*), how can it have an indirect object? For the universal is directly perceived therein, while the real entity itself is not touched; thus, how can the cognition of the universal have an indirect object? If you argue that it is apprehended through "characterization by what is characterized" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇena*), then in what form is the particular (*viśeṣa*) characterized? If it is characterized by the particular itself, let the cognition of sound and so forth arise from that very particular; what is the use of an internal tumor of a universal? If it is characterized by the form of a universal, an infinite regress has been stated. And if it is characterized by the form of a particular, the sense faculty would be rendered useless.

[221, ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. He does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive form as unreal; he does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive forms as unreal; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the eye-consciousness as unreal; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the earth element as unreal; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive ignorance as unreal; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the perfection of generosity as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of generosity as unreal; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the internal as unreal; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of the characteristic of non-nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as unreal; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as real, nor does he perceive the four dhyānas as unreal; he does not perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine serial meditations on the spheres of totality, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as unreal; he does not perceive the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they are not real, nor are they unreal. This, Subhūti, is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. [221,x] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive form as unreal; he does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive forms as unreal; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness as unreal; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the earth element as unreal; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive ignorance as unreal; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the perfection of generosity as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of generosity as unreal; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the internal as unreal; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of the characteristic of non-nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as unreal; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as real, nor does he perceive the four dhyānas as unreal; he does not perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine serial meditations on the spheres of totality, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the superknowledges, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges

Now, it is only the universal (*sāmānya*) that appears; the particular (*viśeṣa*) is beyond perception because it does not appear. Here too, it is only one’s own form, arrived at through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that appears directly. But since the object is beyond perception, how can there be the status of having that as its object? Because [the cognition] causes activity toward it. [Objection: How can there be activity toward what has not been apprehended? [Reply: It has already been established that activity occurs everywhere precisely toward what has not been apprehended; for even when the form of Devadatta is not apprehended, Yajñadatta acts upon him because he perceives something similar. [Objection: If it is argued that there is correspondence (*saṃvāda*) there because activity is observed, [we reply: No, because the cause of non-discrepancy will be explained later. [Objection: Non-discrepancy arises from a connection. [Reply: If this is an error, then since it arises from the force of latent impressions, it is apprehended only within the latent impression itself; so how can there be a determination (*adhyavasāya*) or attainment of the object? [Reply: No, because the awakening of the latent impression is also a cause. Thus, by way of that connection, it belongs to the object—there is no fault. He says the same thing:
Since its own nature is unperceived, another object serves as its locus for that cognition.
If, by means of that locus, it were connected [to the probandum], then it would be a prover. (60)

[222,ii] For an object whose own nature (*svarūpa*) has not been perceived is understood through another thing by virtue of a relationship. If it were understood through anything whatsoever, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it were understood by itself, then everyone would be an all-seeing seer (*sarvadarśin*), because there would be no distinction. And if that other thing is a signifier (*gamaka*) only when it possesses a relationship with that [object] as its basis (*āśraya*), how is this so? It is simply because it is observed to be so.

[Objection: Is it not the case that remembrance occurs there precisely because of a connection? And since that [remembrance] arises from the connection and so forth as well, that same over-extension (atiprasaṅga) remains. [Response: No, because remembrance produced by experience (ābhoga) and so forth does not arise otherwise.
Remembrance of that [object] which is established through instruction and so forth arises from experience and the like.
Because of the meeting with that which is qualified by place and time, and because of its dependence upon that [place and time].

For it is from the perception of an object that is connected to the subject (*dharmin*) and the property to be proven (*sādhya*) that an object which is restricted by place and time and capable of being attained is cognized, and not from mere mental application (*ābhoga*) and so forth. To explain: mental application is a mental activity intent on investigation, such as "What have I seen? In that case, when there is recollection of an object existing at exactly that same place and time, there is no further operation [of the means of knowledge]; therefore, that is not a valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). From the apprehension of similarity, there arises only this much cognition: "This is similar to that. However, similarity does not belong to an object qualified by a specific place and time, because it is always similar [to something]. Furthermore, since the similarity of many things is one thing or another, it does not lead to a specific [conclusion]; thus, it is not a valid cognition. But by means of that which is similar to it, whatever is to be done is done; therefore, in that regard, perception itself is the valid cognition. Otherwise, however, there would be no engagement following from perception at all, and it has already been established that [perception] would not be a valid cognition; thus it is not stated again. In the same way, even a cognition consisting of inference arising from a connection (*sambandha*) is not a valid cognition. To explain:
The mark (*liṅga*) is that which makes known the effect and so forth by virtue of having that as its characteristic;
other than having that as its characteristic, there is no other definition of a mark. (PVA 259)

[222, vii] Thus, this very nature of being a *śiṃśapā*—which performs a causal function—and smoke and so forth, which are produced by fire and so forth, are understood through similarity either as effects or as causes. Furthermore, this existence (*sattva*) is impermanent in nature; because it is devoid of prior and subsequent forms, the nature of impermanence in anything else is not different from this. Therefore, the cognition of inference is of this kind: both that which has a present cause, such as the nature of smoke characterized by some specific feature, and that which lacks a present cause, such as ash and the like, are, according to their respective applications, indicators (*gamaka*). For instance: [222, viii]

Whatever entity is perceived in a certain way at one time, it is exactly so at another; it serves as the awakener of memory and, accordingly, as its instigator. Otherwise, if the memory of what was previously seen were to waver, [the object would not be recognized]. 260 (PVA)
In that case, there would be the occurrence [of the cognition], but not a connection with contradiction.
Direct perception is non-erroneous, whereas memory is based upon it;
if memory were valid, it would be in the form "I remember it exactly as it was. (PVA 261–262)
If it is argued that even when there is deviation in perception, it is not a valid cognition because of that [deviation], then we reply:
even if there is deviation in perception, it is so because memory is otherwise.
For indeed, perception occurs without an object, while memory is otherwise.
Since it possesses an object, it would not be a valid cognition in that way.

(PVA 264) [222, xiii] In the case of recollection, perception is not a valid cognition when it is followed by something else; thus, the defect belongs not to perception itself, but to the recollection. For even that recollection arises otherwise due to similarity, or simply from the intensity of the recollection.

Therefore, memory arises from the effect and the essential nature as that which partakes of the object, being characterized by their true reality; otherwise, there would be an error in memory. (PVA 265)

Therefore, all discrepancy whatsoever is produced solely by an error in memory. Consequently, regarding an object beyond the senses, it is memory itself—being connected to what was previously perceived—that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And that is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). For this very reason, he says:
At that time, there is comprehension only by way of a universal form that follows the indicator;
therefore, no remote object is apprehended in its particularity. (61)

[223,ii] For the cognition of that which is to be understood (*gamya*) is dependent upon the indicator (*gamaka*); and that indicator exists in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), not as a particular (*viśeṣa*), because it is impossible to characterize a particular. If it were an indicator by means of a form that cannot be characterized, there would follow the absurd consequence of cognizing every aspect and the entire succession of causes. Furthermore, that universal, such as smoke, is observed everywhere in relation to fire and so forth; therefore, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), no cognition of a particular arises from it. If it is argued that cognition occurs through the characterization of a particular, we say no, because it is impossible to characterize a specific internal particular. [223,iii]

[Objection: But surely, the indication of a particular (*viśeṣa*) is indeed possible for something. [Response: No; because it is absolutely impossible to perceive a particular. The indication of a particular in that case is produced by relative dependence (*apekṣā*), and only to the extent that there is a measure [of it]. However, for one who has a cognition of all its aspects, because of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), we understand that it is indeed unmanifest (*avyakta*). If it is argued that the cognition of a particular arises from the perception of a particular, [we reply: no; it will be demonstrated that even in that case, the understanding is of the universal (*sāmānya*) alone. He says this very thing:
"And the understanding that occurs regarding a property-bearer (*dharmin*) based on a property (*dharma*) related to it..."
Inference alone is the exclusive means of establishing things that are beyond the reach of the senses.

[223,v] Because there is no other characteristic [of a means of valid cognition] and because the characteristic of inference is possible, there is no means of valid cognition other than inference for objects that are not perceptually evident. Now, one might object: "If one means of valid cognition has another means of valid cognition as its object, then there are not just two means of valid cognition. To this, the response is:
There is no possibility of another object of cognition (prameya) other than the perceptible and the imperceptible;
therefore, because there are two types of objects of cognition, two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are accepted. 63.
[223,vii] Is it not logical that there are two objects of cognition because there are two means of valid cognition? For a means of valid cognition is that which establishes existence.
[223,viii]

This is not so. An object of cognition (*prameya*) is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but the nature of the means of valid cognition itself is established through the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, it has been stated that the very form of cognition, when perceived as both particular and universal, is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). This means that because there are two types of objects, there are two types of forms. For if one were aware of two distinct forms within oneself, it would not be logical for there to be a single [cognition]; nor could there be three or more. Alternatively, the refutation of the numbers three and one follows from the observation of two objects of cognition.
[223,x] Because no object of cognition other than the two [already mentioned] objects of cognition is possible, it has been established that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Now, because a second object of cognition (*prameya*) is possible, he will demonstrate that there is neither one means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor three and so forth. Indeed, when a second object of cognition is possible, there cannot be only one means of cognition, since there exists a means of cognition whose object is that second object of cognition. It is not established by a single means of cognition that there is also a second [object]. [The opponent might argue: "The object of cognition is actually only one, consisting of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*); there is no other. Thus, the two objects of cognition are established. To this, he says:
"If it is your view that there is only one [object], because the non-existent is not an object of cognition, then that is our position as well. (64)

[223, xiii] This very thing is perceived as a cognizable object (*prameya*) other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet it is non-existent. Moreover, that is not a cognizable object; rather, the particular characteristic alone is the cognizable object. It was stated previously that this very [particular characteristic] is characterized as both universal and particular because it is apprehended through its own form and the form of another. Furthermore:
For there is indeed non-uniqueness (anekānta) regarding the state of being unknowable, since even non-existence is ascertained;
or else, the means of knowledge that ascertains it is the second [type].

For even non-existence, characterized as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, is an object of cognition (*prameya*). How, then, can there be a pervasion (*vyāpti*) stating that "the non-existent is not an object of cognition"? And how can a reason (*hetu*) lacking such pervasion be conclusive (*aikāntika*)? To explain: if prior non-existence and the rest were not perceived, everything would be eternal; there would be neither effect nor cause. This will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, if there were mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), substances would become intermingled, and thus the entire world would become a single unity (*advaita*). Its ascertainment is either a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or a second [kind of] cognition. Since it is not a cognition born of the senses (*akṣaja*), [it is said: "Cognition is not born of the senses" (verse 65).

If [cognition] were produced by the force of the object even in the absence [of contact], without depending on the capacity of the object, then sensory cognition would arise even when there is an intervention or other such obstacles. (66)

Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the emptiness of all dharmas? Indeed, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not within the range of the sense faculties (*indriya*), because it is only the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of sound and so forth that appears therein. As for the [judgment] "this is not here," its form as non-existence is not an object of the senses; for even that which is obstructed is established as non-existent [by the senses]. Now, if it is argued that such a determination arises precisely from the perception of a vacant place (*vivikta-pradeśa*), what is this so-called "vacancy"? If it is the form of the place and so forth, then once that has been perceived, how can one know that "the other is not there"? If it is argued that this is because that [place] has the nature of the non-existence of the other, then how can one thing be the non-existence of another? If it is because they do not coexist (*asaṅgama*), then why is there no coexistence? If it is because they are not perceived together (*sahāvedana*), then the establishment of non-existence follows from their being perceived together. But if it is the perception of something else that constitutes the non-perception of that [object], then how is that "otherness" grasped when that [object] is not perceived? If it is argued that it was perceived previously, then since that is not being perceived now, how can there be a cognition of non-existence? Therefore, this determination of non-existence is not born of the senses; hence, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[224,v] Or it might be argued: "It is perception itself, when it ceases, that is the cause for the ascertainment of non-existence. That too is incorrect.
If it is argued that the certainty of perception itself consists in the exclusion [of the object] upon its absence,
then either that very [exclusion] is contradictory, or else it is the probans (liṅga) characterized by both positive and negative concomitance.

[224,vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is edible food? It is that which is called "edible food" by the world, whether it be chewed, swallowed, or licked. This is called edible food. What is contact? It is the contact of the threefold conjunction. This is called contact. What is mental volition? It is the mental volition directed toward the three realms of existence. This is called mental volition. What is consciousness? It is the six classes of consciousness. This is called consciousness. Among these, what is the nutriment edible food? It is the nutriment edible food that is included within the aggregate of form. What is the nutriment contact? It is the nutriment contact that is included within the aggregate of feeling. What is the nutriment mental volition? It is the nutriment mental volition that is included within the aggregate of formations. What is the nutriment consciousness? It is the nutriment consciousness that is included within the aggregate of consciousness. Furthermore, monks, edible food has both a gross aspect and a subtle aspect. What is the gross aspect of edible food? It is that which is called "edible food" by the world, whether it be chewed, swallowed, or licked. This is the gross aspect of edible food. What is the subtle aspect of edible food? It is the odors, tastes, and tangibles that are desired, cherished, delightful, and associated with passion; whatever is experienced through the body and leads to attachment. This is the subtle aspect of edible food. Furthermore, monks, contact has both a gross aspect and a subtle aspect. What is the gross aspect of contact? It is the contact of the five sense-bodies. This is the gross aspect of contact. What is the subtle aspect of contact? It is the contact of the mind-body. This is the subtle aspect of contact. Furthermore, monks, mental volition has both a gross aspect and a subtle aspect. What is the gross aspect of mental volition? It is the volition directed toward the realm of desire. This is the gross aspect of mental volition. What is the subtle aspect of mental volition? It is the volition directed toward the realms of form and the formless. This is the subtle aspect of mental volition. Furthermore, monks, consciousness has both a gross aspect and a subtle aspect. What is the gross aspect of consciousness? It is the consciousness associated with the five sense-bodies. This is the gross aspect of consciousness. What is the subtle aspect of consciousness? It is the consciousness associated with the mind-body. This is the subtle aspect of consciousness. Furthermore, monks, edible food has two aspects: one is the aspect of enjoyment, and the other is the aspect of procreation. Contact, mental volition, and consciousness each have these two aspects.
