If it is argued that the ascertainment of non-existence occurs precisely through the cessation of perception (*pratyakṣa*), this is contradictory: [you claim] that it does not exist, yet there is a cognition of it by means of that [cessation]. For perception, being of the nature of direct experience, produces certainty regarding that object toward which it proceeds; certainty arises from what has been experienced. But how can there be certainty in the absence of experience? Indeed, people say: "I do not know whether something else exists or does not exist," for here there is no equal experience [of both existence and non-existence]. How, then, can there be certainty from a lack of experience, which is itself the cause of uncertainty? If it is argued that the non-perception of something capable of being perceived leads to the ascertainment of its non-existence when the object is present, then there would be no ascertainment of the non-existence of the trans-empirical world (*paraloka*) and so forth. Furthermore, if non-perception is excluded from the presence of an entity, then—being pervaded by its opposite—it becomes a signifier (*gamika*). Thus, because it possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), inference as another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established, since it arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*).
By this, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which are included therein, have been stated as reasons.
He states the reason based on the effect:
"And the two means of valid cognition are established for the sake of apprehending the consciousness of another."
And because of the engagement in speech and so forth, the certainty of its existence is established. 68.

The consciousness of another is not established through direct perception in the same way as one’s own; for indeed, one does not know whether this other person possesses consciousness or not, since such a cognition occurs only through the manifestation of that [other's] form. The determination of specific qualities, such as aversion and so forth, is made through their specific effects.

"Let this be some kind of certainty; however, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is not a fault, because we observe practical activity (*vyavahāra*)—characterized by speech and so forth—that conforms to it. If it is argued that "activity based on some kind of certainty is simply without a valid means of knowledge," we say no, because that would entail the abandonment of inquiry. If it is argued that "one does not abandon it out of necessity, due to the absence of any other means," then even the certainty that "there is an absence of any other means" is itself a valid means of knowledge, and that has been stated to be inference (*anumāna*).

This is stated on the basis of what is accepted by the opponent; therefore, there is no fault. For that which is accepted by the opponent has its application only within the context of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). Indeed, no one establishes [a point] for themselves merely through what is accepted by another. If you say, "I have engaged in this [activity] because I perceive no other way," then let there be such a perception regarding the next world as well. If it is argued that one can live even by abandoning the next world, and thus there is no engagement with it—how do you know that life can be sustained in this manner? Furthermore, does one who seeks life seek past life or present life? In that regard, one does not seek past life simply because it is past. Nor does one seek present life, since that has already been attained. If it is sought as future life, then—since it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that "future life occurs by this means and not otherwise"—this is indeed inference.

[225,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive generosity as real, nor does he perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the power of a Buddha as real, nor does he perceive the power of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the ground of self-confidence as real, nor does he perceive the ground of a Tathāgata’s self-confidence as real. He does not perceive the analytical knowledge as real, nor does he perceive the analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the great friendliness as real, nor does he perceive the great compassion as real. He does not perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as real, nor does he perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of non-nature, or the emptiness of both nature and non-nature as real. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as real, nor does he perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as real. He does not perceive the ten powers as real, nor does he perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four grounds of self-confidence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great friendliness and great compassion as real. He does not perceive the dharma-realm as real, nor does he perceive the expanse of reality as real. He does not perceive the dharma-sphere as real, nor does he perceive the sphere of space as real. He does not perceive the sphere of consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the sphere of nothingness as real. He does not perceive the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as real, nor does he perceive the sphere of cessation as real. He does not perceive the truth of suffering as real, nor does he perceive the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, or the truth of the path as real. He does not perceive the truth of conditioned arising as real, nor does he perceive the truth of dependent origination as real. He does not perceive the truth of the past as real, nor does he perceive the truth of the future or the present as real. He does not perceive the truth of the aggregates as real, nor does he perceive the truth of the elements or the truth of the sense bases as real. He does not perceive the truth of the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the truth of the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the truth of the world as real, nor does he perceive the truth of liberation as real. He does not perceive the truth of nirvāṇa as real, nor does he perceive the truth of the Tathāgata as real. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Because he does not perceive any dharma as real or unreal, he does not apprehend any dharma. Because he does not apprehend any dharma, he does not cling to any dharma. Because he does not cling to any dharma, he does not become attached to any dharma. Because he does not become attached to any dharma, he does not regress from the path of the bodhisattvas. Because he does not regress from the path of the bodhisattvas, he swiftly attains the perfection of wisdom and, having attained the perfection of wisdom, he swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

Furthermore, regarding this linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*)—is it yours alone, or that of another? If it is yours alone, then since it is unestablished for both [parties], how has the other been persuaded? If it belongs to another as well, then there is likewise an absence of any means [of proof]; in that case, the cognition of another's consciousness is necessarily established, so how can this cognition be "just somehow" (*yathākathañcit*)? If you say, "This too occurs just somehow," then, in that case, since there is no conviction on your own part, how can there be a comprehension of another? [If you say,] "I know it thus for myself, but I do not know how it is for another," then silence would be the only result. If you argue, "It will be exactly the same for the other person as well," we say: No, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, this [argument] is trivial. Therefore, there is indeed the cognition of another; consequently, inference must be accepted even by the opponent.

[225,iv] If it is argued that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists because of non-discrepancy, but that there is no confidence in it due to occasional deviation— this is the case with a sign (*liṅga*) that has been poorly perceived. 69.

[225,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of all perfections. Subhūti asked: "For what reason is it so? The Blessed One replied: "Because, Subhūti, within this perfection of wisdom, all the perfections are included; they are not found elsewhere. Subhūti asked: "How is it that all the perfections are included within this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, because the perfection of giving is included in the perfection of wisdom through the absence of conceptualization regarding the gift, the giver, and the recipient. Likewise, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom are included in the perfection of wisdom through the absence of conceptualization regarding the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing. Furthermore, Subhūti, all the perfections are included in this perfection of wisdom by way of the non-apprehension of their own characteristics. Subhūti asked: "Is it only these perfections that are included in this perfection of wisdom, or are other dharmas also included? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, not only are these perfections included in this perfection of wisdom, but all dharmas whatsoever—whether conditioned or unconditioned, worldly or transcendent, with or without outflows—are also included in this perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are empty of their own marks, and this very emptiness of marks is the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "If all dharmas are included in this perfection of wisdom, how then does one train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, one trains in the perfection of wisdom by training in the non-training in all dharmas. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that is trained in or not trained in. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in this manner, trains in the perfection of wisdom and attains the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti asked: "Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva attain the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment after training in this perfection of wisdom for a long time? The Blessed One replied: "No, Subhūti. A bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment even if he has trained in this perfection of wisdom for only a single day. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the producer of the Buddhas, and the guide of the bodhisattvas. Subhūti asked: "How is it that this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the producer of the Buddhas, and the guide of the bodhisattvas? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, just as a mother gives birth to her children, so too does this perfection of wisdom give birth to the bodhisattvas. Just as a mother nourishes her children, so too does this perfection of wisdom nourish the bodhisattvas by means of the dharmas of the Buddhas. Just as a mother protects her children from all dangers, so too does this perfection of wisdom protect the bodhisattvas from all the fears of saṃsāra. Therefore, Subhūti, it is for this reason that this perfection of wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the producer of the Buddhas, and the guide of the bodhisattvas. Subhūti asked: "If this perfection of wisdom is thus the mother of the bodhisattvas, the producer of the Buddhas, and the guide of the bodhisattvas, then why do the bodhisattvas not pay homage to this perfection of wisdom as they would to their mother? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is because the bodhisattvas have already paid homage to this perfection of wisdom in the past when they were under the guidance of former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. Moreover, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this perfection of wisdom being taught and, upon hearing it, feels neither joy nor sorrow, but remains equanimous, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who has practiced this perfection of wisdom for many hundreds of thousands of millions of aeons. Subhūti asked: "What is the cause and condition for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to hear this perfection of wisdom and feel neither joy nor sorrow? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has previously cultivated the roots of goodness under many Buddhas, has planted the seeds of merit, and has been purified by the wisdom of the Buddhas. Furthermore, Subhūti, it is because that bodhisattva mahāsattva has understood that all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, and like a reflection, and thus he does not form any attachment to them. Subhūti asked: "If all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, and like a reflection, then how can there be the distinction between a Buddha and a bodhisattva? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, although all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, and like a reflection, yet the power of past vows and the accumulation of merit and wisdom bring about the manifestation of the Buddha-body and the bodhisattva-body. It is like the case of a skilled magician who creates various illusions; although those illusions are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, they still appear to sentient beings according to their respective karma. In the same way, Subhūti, although all dharmas are ultimately empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, yet through the power of past vows and the accumulation of merit and wisdom, the Buddha-dharmas and the bodhisattva-dharmas manifest for the sake of liberating sentient beings. Subhūti asked: "If all dharmas are ultimately empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, then what is the difference between a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, and a bodhisattva? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, the difference lies in their respective aspirations and practices. The śrāvaka seeks liberation for himself alone and practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The pratyekabuddha seeks liberation for himself and others to some extent, and practices the twelve links of dependent origination. The bodhisattva mahāsattva, however, seeks the great compassion and the benefit of all sentient beings, and practices the six perfections. Although they all realize the emptiness of dharmas, their paths and fruits differ according to their original vows and the objects of their practice. Subhūti asked: "If all three vehicles ultimately reach the same destination of nirvāṇa, why then do the Buddhas distinguish between the three vehicles? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, although the ultimate reality of nirvāṇa is one and the same, yet in accordance with the different capacities and inclinations of sentient beings, the Buddhas provisionally establish the three vehicles. It is like the case of a great physician who prescribes different medicines for different illnesses, though the goal of healing the body is the same. In the same way, Subhūti, the Buddhas, out of great compassion, provisionally establish the three vehicles to lead sentient beings to the one great vehicle, which is the true nature of all dharmas. Subhūti asked: "If the three vehicles are ultimately one great vehicle, then why do the sūtras speak of the five precepts, the ten good deeds, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, although the ultimate reality is one, yet in order to guide sentient beings, the Buddhas teach various dharmas according to their needs. These dharmas are like the rungs of a ladder; by ascending step by step, one eventually reaches the summit. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should not be attached to any dharma, but should practice all the dharmas of the Buddhas with a mind free from conceptualization. Subhūti asked: "If a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices all the dharmas of the Buddhas with a mind free from conceptualization, then how does he avoid falling into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the dharmas of the Buddhas while maintaining the thought of great compassion and never abandoning sentient beings, then he will not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva understands that all dharmas are unborn and unceasing, and that there is no dharma that can be attained or abandoned, then he will not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Non-contradiction (*avisambāda*) is indeed the defining characteristic of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); since this exists for inference (*anumāna*), it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge. Now, if you argue that there is a misconception because non-contradiction is sometimes seen even where it does not exist—for instance, the inference "He is dark-complexioned because he is his son," which is associated with deviation—that is incorrect. This is not actually an inference at all, because it arises from a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). For being his son is not necessarily connected to dark complexion. If you claim that they share the same nature by virtue of depending on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*), that is not so, because there is no dependence on a single causal complex; for there is the possibility of differences in karma, diet, and time. Furthermore, if they depended on a single causal complex, it would follow that they must arise simultaneously. Therefore, the intention to point out a deviation arises from superimposing the status of a reason upon what is not a reason, due to failing to perceive the true nature of the inferential mark.
[225, vi] Now, it might be argued: "All inference is of this very nature and there is no other specific definition; therefore, for what is there non-deviation? That too is incorrect.
Since the cognition of an object is sometimes established in some cases, it must necessarily either be produced from that [object] or have that as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva). (70)

[225, viii] For a logical mark (*liṅga*) is a means of proof only when it is connected by a necessary relation (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), because the other [the probandum] is either identical with it or produced from it. And since the cognition of the probandum is non-deviant, it must arise from that [mark] through a fixed necessity, or it must have that as its restricted essential nature (*tattvasvabhāva*); otherwise, the possibility of a non-deviant understanding would not exist, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, a cognition of everything does not arise from everything, because it is observed to occur only occasionally. Therefore, this cognition is produced by an object that is necessarily related to it. And the necessary relation is... [226, i]

It is indeed of two kinds. Even for that which depends on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), the connection (*pratibandha*) is characterized by its arising from that very source through a succession of steps. It is from this alone that there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). For:
"Without its own cause or its own nature (*svabhāva*), the existence of an object is impossible."
And whatever form is seen in those two, that alone is the characteristic elsewhere.

Furthermore, whatever characteristic is observed for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) or the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) elsewhere is the very same [characteristic] here. It is not the case that this [characteristic] does not exist in the case of "that person's son" and so forth; therefore, there is no lack of confidence in all cases. For if sublation were possible regarding something endowed with its defining characteristic, then that very characteristic would be undermined, and thus there would be a lack of confidence everywhere—this is the logical principle (*nyāya*). Nor is it possible for anything to arise without a cause or a non-existence (*abhāva*); if such a doubt were entertained, there would be no practical activity whatsoever in any matter. This discussion concerns conventional means of valid cognition (*vyāvahārikapramāṇa*), and nothing else. Therefore, one who seeks practical engagement must necessarily seek inference. If it is asked, "How can there be activity toward that which is not a means?"—the answer is no. If it is argued, "Because its status as a means is unestablished, it falls apart when examined," we say no; for examination itself consists of inference. Thus, it is like someone walking along a path who has forgotten that very path.

[226,iv] What, then, is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for non-apprehension? He shows that it is precisely that connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). For instance:

Whether it be in its own nature or its own cause, or in the causes of the seen and the seeing, or in other existing things, or even in that which is not seen—how could there be existence for that which possesses such [a nature]? (72)

Precisely because that [effect or pervaded] is dependent upon that [cause or pervader], for that very reason it does not exist in the absence of the latter. Otherwise, why would it not exist in the absence of something else? Such a consequence would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For this [latter] is indeed dependent insofar as it exists through the absence of the former; otherwise, there would be no dependence. Therefore, wherever there is non-perception of a cause or a pervader that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*), there is the absence of those two. And wherever there is the absence of those two, there is no possibility of the effect or the pervaded. Thus, even non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). In this way, it is established that inference is threefold, characterized by the effect, the essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception.
Because:
[226, viii]

And if the cognition of universals were invalid, its disappearance would follow, just as [the self] does not exist after death; however, if it is perceived by the senses in turn, [there is no such disappearance]. (73)

And that [non-existence] cannot be established through the power of the sense organs, because sensory cognition would be impossible; furthermore, in the apprehension of non-existence, the arising of cognition would be without a cause. (74)

For if conceptual cognition (*sāmānyabuddhi*) were invalid, it would follow that there is no such thing as an imperceptible object of knowledge (*parokṣa-prameya*), just as there is none in the case of the next world (*paraloka*). If one argues that not every imperceptible object is non-existent because it may be perceived by the senses at some point in time, whereas in the case of the next world, the senses do not function even alternately, and thus it is non-existent in that very way—then we ask: when it is perceived, it exists; but how can it be said to exist previously? If you say it existed previously because it was perceived by another [person], then why is it not the case that the next world was also previously perceived by another, or by oneself? Or why is it that everything other than the next world is perceived by another? If you say this is because of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then the validity of inference (*anumāna*) has already been established. Furthermore, there is no alternate functioning of the senses with respect to either the capacity (*yogyatā*) or the object itself, since both are understood solely through inference based on the nature of the effect (*kārya-svabhāva-hetu*). In the absence of that [inference], the arising of cognition would have to be caused solely by the presence of the objects themselves. Therefore, capacity is established through the observation of the effect and through the exclusion of the effect (*kārya-vyatireka*).

[227,i] Furthermore, the eye and so forth, when being inferred, certainly exist. Nor does the operation of the sense organ occur there successively. Therefore, the next world and so forth are exactly like this. Consequently, a universal (*sāmānya*) is not cognized without inference. For:
And perception [operates] upon the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) by way of being free from conceptualization;
there is no grasping of the universal (sāmānya) without conceptualization, and therefore inference [functions] with respect to that.

[227,iii] Even cognitions whose nature consists in the determination of a universal are those that effect conventional usage. And a universal is not apprehended without conceptualization. Nor is perception conceptual, because it is non-discursive. Therefore, inference, which has the universal as its object, is not perception.

If, then, color and so forth are apprehended through aspects such as impermanence and the like, how is this so? This is an apprehension of a general form (sāmānyarūpa). Furthermore, you maintain a restriction regarding the objects of cognition (prameya). Under such a restriction of the objects of cognition, the impermanence of color is not cognized.
That cognition is another means of valid knowledge, because it occurs even without an inferential mark.

[227, vi] The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, coarse or refined; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. 138. It was said: “Physical food, monks, is a nutriment for beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. This has been said by the Blessed One; with reference to what was it said? There are, monks, three kinds of physical food: edible food that is taken by the mouthful, contact as the second, and mental volition as the third. These, monks, are the three kinds of physical food. “Contact as a nutriment” means: there are six classes of contact—the contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Indeed, "restriction" (*niyama*) refers to the fact that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*)—the objects of cognition—are apprehended by their respective restricted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This [cognition], however, is a mixed apprehension, because it consists in the apprehension of both the particular and the universal as being intermingled with one another. Consequently, it follows that this apprehension of two forms must be a distinct means of valid cognition. Since it occurs even without a logical mark (*liṅga*), it is not inference (*anumāna*); and since it grasps a universal, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is it inference regarding a particular characteristic, because it functions without a logical mark and because a universal appears [in its content]. Furthermore, in the case of "inference from the perceived particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), there is no comprehension of the universal, because the connection of the logical mark is not perceived through the universal. As he said:

[227, vii] Because the connection of the mark is not perceived in the case of "inference based on what has been seen specifically" (viśeṣadṛṣṭa), it is a separate means of valid cognition; or else, its multiplicity follows from the multiplicity of the objects to be known. // 77 //
Just as there may be the occurrence of multiple means of valid cognition regarding a single object, so too,
through the "perception of particulars" (viśeṣadṛṣṭa), there would either be the exclusion of the numbers one, two, or three, or it would not.

Because there is no restriction on the object [of inference] and because other objects of knowledge are possible, the claim that "this color and so forth are impermanent" certainly lacks any inferential mark (*liṅga*) here. Nor is it perception, since impermanence is apprehended as a universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, in the case of "perception based on particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), there is the apprehension of only a particular; for there is no apprehension of a connection between that particular mark and a universal. Therefore, according to your own view, this would be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). It is not perception because it is not a direct apprehension, and it is not inference because its object is not a universal.

Furthermore, since there is a multiplicity of objects of cognition (*prameya*) due to the distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and both, there must likewise be a multiplicity of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the restriction to a number of three is not refuted. Nor is the restriction to a single number excluded, because multiple means of valid cognition can operate upon a single object. For instance, just as perception (*pratyakṣa*) operates together with "perception of the particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) upon a single unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), so too does perception operate upon a universal. As for the claim that the exclusion of a single number follows from the observation of two types of objects of cognition—that cannot be, because it is possible for perception itself to operate upon a universal. If the objects were restricted and no other objects of cognition existed, then the exclusion of the numbers three and one might occur; however, by the reasoning already stated, neither of these conditions holds. Therefore, the desired purpose is not achieved. Due to the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) and the multiplicity of objects of cognition, there is a multiplicity of means of valid cognition.

[228,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld the sufferings of those beings and, by means of his compassionate heart, entered into samādhi. At that time, he perceived that all phenomena are empty of self-nature; there is no birth and no cessation, no defilement and no purity, no increase and no decrease. Thus, when one perceives the five aggregates as empty, one is liberated from all suffering and distress. Subhūti, if a good man or a good woman wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should perceive all phenomena in this manner: they should perceive form as empty of form, feeling as empty of feeling, perception as empty of perception, formations as empty of formations, and consciousness as empty of consciousness. Why is this? Because form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Subhūti, therefore, all phenomena are empty of characteristics: they are neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of the eye up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Therefore, Subhūti, since there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted views, they reach ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the unequaled mantra. It is able to remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Subhūti, thus should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā? The Buddha said to Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā by way of non-attachment. Why is this? Subhūti, form is neither attached nor detached; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither attached nor detached. Why is this? Subhūti, because form is empty of the nature of form, it is neither attached nor detached. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty of the nature of consciousness; therefore, they are neither attached nor detached. Furthermore, Subhūti, all phenomena are neither attached nor detached. Why is this? Subhūti, because all phenomena are empty of the nature of all phenomena, they are neither attached nor detached. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, what dharma does he see? The Buddha said to Subhūti: "When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he sees no dharma at all. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not see any dharma, he is called a 'Bodhisattva. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not see any dharma, how does he give rise to the thought of awakening? How does he practice the six perfections? How does he enter the stages, purify the Buddha-lands, mature sentient beings, and attain unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment? The Buddha said to Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives rise to the thought of awakening through the power of the vow of great compassion. He practices the six perfections by way of non-attachment. He enters the stages by way of non-attachment. He purifies the Buddha-lands by way of non-attachment. He matures sentient beings by way of non-attachment. He attains unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment by way of non-attachment. Why is this? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of their own nature, they cannot be grasped. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, Māra and his host will be unable to find an opportunity to harm him. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā in this manner, who will protect and guard him? The Buddha said to Subhūti: "The four heavenly kings, Śakra Devendra, Brahmā Sahāmpati, and the gods of the Pure Abodes will all protect and guard him. Furthermore, Subhūti, the Buddhas of the ten directions will also protect and guard him. Why is this? Subhūti, because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā in this manner has already been empowered by the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva hears this teaching of the profound Prajñāpāramitā and does not feel fear, alarm, or terror, he should be known as a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā for a long time. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. The universal "color-ness" (*varṇṇatva*) is conjoined with impermanence [in the form of the proposition] "color and so forth are impermanent. Therefore, the object of cognition (*prameya*) consists solely of the universal aspect and not both aspects; thus, there is no fault here, because an object of cognition other than that which is restricted to its specific domain is possible. Indeed, this fault would occur if there were a relation of universal and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva*), but not when there is only the state of being a universal. If one conjoins impermanence with color-ness by means of the universal alone, then that [impermanence] would not be a property (*dharma*) of the entity. For whatever property is perceived as conjoined with something belongs to that very thing. And if it is conjoined with the universal, then that form belongs to the universal, not to the entity. Since the universal itself is not a real entity (*avastu*), that property would consequently be a property of a non-entity (*avastu-dharma*).
This is not so; for:
It is not a non-entity, because its very nature is established as such through proof;
if it is argued that one thing cannot be established by another, we say no, because it is established precisely as that very thing. (80)

[228,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of buddhahood as real. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they do not exist, and their essential nature cannot be apprehended.”

If it is not a property of a real entity (*vastu*), because the universal (*sāmānya*) is imagined as being non-substantial, then even [properties] such as its permanence would have to belong to the real entity. If it is argued that both [the universal and its properties] are of the nature of a real entity, we say no; for it is the real entity itself that is established in that way. Whatever appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), such as color-ness or impermanence, exists indeed in the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as well, because the conceptual construction of that form arises precisely from the experience of the particular. If the conceptual construction were not connected with the particular, then the particular would not appear therein; how then could that very [particular] be established in that way? It is not so, because there is an indirect connection (*pāramparya-sambandha*). Even though there is no direct connection, there is an indirect connection; thus, that conceptual construction possesses non-discrepancy (*avisamvāditā*).

[228, vi] But if it is dependent upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can it be dependent upon the thing itself? Because that latent impression is itself dependent upon the thing. He asks: "How so?
For whatever entity is the cause of a cognition possessing a corresponding mark, that cognition of the mark arises from it with respect to that entity as it truly is. (81)

For it has been established that whatever is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must be either the cause or the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the probans (*hetu*). Thus, for one who understands the effect and the pervaded, the cause and the pervader are the probans. If, from that as well, there arises the cognition of the mark (*liṅgadhī*), that cognition is indirectly connected to the real entity (*vastu*). Therefore:
Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real entity,
they are non-deceptive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity].

There is no attainment of the object [merely] from the appearance, because the attainment of the object is possible even through determination (*adhyavasāya*). For one who acts attains [the object]; and acting occurs from the mere appearance. Furthermore, acting is observed to occur even from determination; otherwise, one would not act even from an appearance. One who has first been impelled to act by determination becomes capable of acting subsequently from the appearance due to habituation (*abhyāsa*). Therefore, when there is activity toward what exists, there is attainment. And just as there is existence for that which appears, so too there is existence for the cause and the pervader of that which appears; let there be attainment in both cases alike. Moreover, it was already established previously that there is no attainment of anything that merely appears. And just as it is known that something exists because it appears, so too is it known because its appearance is invariably connected [to the object].

[229,i] Furthermore, if it is held that there is no object of attainment (*prāpti-viṣaya*), then the world would be nothing but mere appearance (*pratibhāsa-mātra*). This is because there would be no determination of the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous; for within mere appearance alone, there can be no discernment of error. Therefore, it is certain that the establishment of the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous occurs only through the cognition of something remote (*parokṣa-gati*), and not otherwise.

Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real entity, they are non-deceptive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity]. (82)

And because there is a determination of those two [cognitions] as having that form, even though they are devoid of that form, the status of being an error is established on the grounds that they do not fail to correspond to that form. (83)

[229,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, there are four kinds of persons who are irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what are those four? If that were so, there would be an infinite regress, for one who knows the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in that case [would require] another inference, and in that case yet another. Even when smoke and the like have already been apprehended by perception, they are then remembered as a logical mark (*liṅga*). This being the case, memory is indeed not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); so what is the point of establishing its non-deceptiveness? For it is not a means of valid cognition in that context; only perception and inference are considered means of valid cognition because they are associated with non-contradiction. If it is argued that memory is also a means of valid cognition through an indirect connection (*pratibandha*), then that very [memory] is the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) and is thus inference itself. Why, then, specify the distinction between the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)? Alternatively, if it is said that memory is not a means of valid cognition because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, then in that case, only the operation of perception would be the means of valid cognition there. And since that [perception] is not devoid of its appearance (*tadābhāsa*), there is a contradiction. Therefore, it is explained otherwise: the cognition of the mark arising from a reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) is itself the cognition of the possessor of the mark, because in the ultimate sense there is no difference between the mark and the possessor of the mark. The cognition of the possessor of the mark arising from a reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) has the cause as its object. Because of that lack of difference, it is not a cognition of the mark. Furthermore, due to extreme familiarity, the cognition of fire does not fail to arise from this smoke, even though it is not a cognition of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) grasped by the cognition of smoke.

[230,i] Furthermore, the very apprehension of smoke in its true nature (*tattva*) constitutes its state of being connected (*pratibaddhatā*). This true nature is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), and recognition arises from the perception of that form; thus, it is nothing other than inference. And the perception of that form is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); due to extreme familiarity (*atyantābhyāsa*), it serves as the cause for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [230,ii]

Therefore, the apprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is simply the grasping of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, the apprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*) of smoke—which is invariably connected with fire—arises from the perception of that form; this is inference itself, which consists in the apprehension of the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*), and thus it is not designated otherwise.
Therefore, when a real entity is to be understood, the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is the object of the mind directed toward the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
That [object] is either the sign (nimitta) or its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and it is the cause for that cognition. // 84 //

And that [pervader] is either the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or the cause (*kāraṇa*) of the mark (*liṅga*), which is the pervaded. Since it is the cause for the cognition of the pervader, a connection (*pratibandha*) is possible through this indirect sequence. Even a contradictory entity leads to the cognition of its absence; this does not occur solely by virtue of the relation of contradiction. For that which is contradictory is not intended to be cognized [as existing]. If it is argued that it is intended [to be cognized] as having the nature of non-existence, then the connection must be considered in terms of non-existence itself, and not a contradiction with that [entity]. If it is argued that "wherever this [contradictory] is present, there non-existence occurs," from what is this known? If it is argued that "it is simply because it was observed to be so previously," then at the time of grasping the contradiction, was there perception of the object or otherwise? If there was perception, how can there be non-existence? If there was no perception, then this results in the negation occurring precisely through non-perception.

Otherwise, by the statement of the existence of one thing, how could the non-existence of another be understood? If it is argued that this is due to contradiction, then that [contradiction] must also be explained. (87)
By what means is it established? If you say "because of coexistence," from what is that understood?
If you say "because of the non-perception of the perceptible," then that is a lack of valid cognition (*apramāṇatā*). || 88 ||
For if, when one thing exists, another were not to exist, then there would be a negation of that other in the case of every existing thing.

Furthermore, even a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is not cognized without non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). If this is so—that contradiction is cognized through non-apprehension—then the cognition of absence proceeds from the mark (*liṅga*) of the contradictory, and not from non-apprehension itself. Alternatively, if there was previously a non-apprehension that established the contradiction, then it is precisely by following that [prior non-apprehension] that the cognition of the absence of the contradictory arises from its mark; thus, that [prior non-apprehension] alone is, in the ultimate sense, the means of proving absence. If this is the case:
[231,iii] That which was observed as being useful for the sake of establishing the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)...
If, therefore, the establishment of the probandum were to occur [from perception], how could inference be a valid means of cognition (*pramā*)?

(269) (PVA) For it is through perception that the relationship upon which inference depends is established; since the establishment of the probandum would thus arise from that [perception] alone, inference would not be a valid means of cognition. (270) (PVA)

No; for since the apprehension of the relationship [between the mark and the object] occurs through perception alone, and it is from that very [perception] that the probandum— fire— is established, how can inference be a separate means of valid cognition?

Now, if it is argued that inference operates there because perception has not occurred with respect to the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), then even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*), which is indeed imperceptible, has non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) operated? Even that which did operate is a non-apprehension of something that met the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). Or is it a non-apprehension of something that met the conditions for apprehension as remembered (*smaryamāṇa*)? That too is poorly reasoned by him, because that which is being remembered does not exist even in inference, just as it does not exist in perception.
In that case as well, the authority belongs solely to direct perception; inference is useless.
Therefore, this is the true nature of the matter here.
For it is through the absence of cold that fire is perceived beforehand;
thus, by the establishment of that [fire], its absence [of cold] is established. (PVA 272)

[231,x] And that non-existence is precisely non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Therefore, it is non-apprehension itself—established through inference—that establishes the conventional usage of non-existence, just as it is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For he will say:
Therefore, this non-apprehension is established by its own direct perception. (Pramāṇavārttika 4.274) [231,xii]

In this case as well, it should be understood that [the absence] is established through inference (*anumāna*). When, however, the absence of horripilation is to be proven, then by means of fire there is the non-perception of cold; through that non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), the absence of horripilation [is established]. Therein, the inference of touch—which is of a hot nature—is based on its dependence upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*) as the fire. And that [touch] has the absence of cold as its essential nature (*svabhāva*). The very perception of that [touch] through inference is itself the non-perception of cold. Therefore, because the reason based on the effect (*kāryahetu*) and the non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) operate in the same instance, there is no other contradictory mark (*virodhi-liṅga*). Consequently, it is non-perception alone, established through inference, which brings about the cognition of absence. Thus, this is an "inference of what has been inferred" (*anumitānumāna*).

[231, xiii] The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called *The Lion’s Roar*. It should be taught to those who have set out for the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. Then the venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called *The Lion’s Roar*? The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, it is because this Dharma-discourse roars like a lion's roar in the midst of the assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; it is because it overcomes all opposing views and false teachers; it is because it establishes the supreme, unsurpassed path of the bodhisattvas. Therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called *The Lion’s Roar*. Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this Dharma-discourse, he should not give rise to fear, nor should he give rise to terror, nor should he give rise to trepidation. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is the treasury of all the buddhas of the past, future, and present; it is the source from which all the perfections arise; it is the foundation upon which the great awakening is established. Thus, Ānanda, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who hears this Dharma-discourse and does not become afraid, does not become terrified, and does not become trepidant, should be known as one who has already been predicted by the Tathāgatas to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. At that time, the venerable Ānanda, having heard these words of the Blessed One, was filled with joy and delight, and paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One. Then, having circumambulated him three times, he withdrew to one side and sat down.
