If it is thus that perception is established by means of inference, and by that [perception] the existence of a real entity (*vastu*) is established, then inference would not have a real entity as its object of validity. That too is trivial; for perception is of the nature of apprehension (*upalambha*), and apprehension is said to be existence (*sattā*). Therefore, inference has a real entity as its object. If it is argued that non-existence (*asattā*) is simply non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), let it be so; what is the fault? There is a great fault in this: that the absence of fire is established by means of non-apprehension, and not by means of fire itself. [Objection: But fire itself is the absence of cold; therefore, that very [fire] is established by that very [inference]. To whatever extent a place is pervaded by heat, to that same extent there is the absence of cold. Thus, the absence of cold is not distinct from the sensation of heat. If you say, "This is a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*)," we certainly accept that non-apprehension functions as a reason based on essential identity. Therefore, in the statement "there is no sensation of cold here because of fire," two types of reasons are indicated: the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the essential-identity reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
Therefore, even though it is expressed by its own term, it is the establisher of non-existence;
that which is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it cannot be expressed in any way by a word of negation. (89)

For when a contradictory thing such as fire is expressed by its own term—even though it is thus stated and demonstrated—it is that very non-apprehension, characterized by the presence of another, which establishes the absence. For one who does not accept that as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), negation cannot be expressed by the existence of the contradictory. Indeed, there is no other way for negation to occur.

By this, the statement of an effect that is contrary to that [probandum] has been explained. The formal argument (*prayoga*) alone is different; in every case, the underlying meaning does not differ. (90)

[232,iii] Regarding the effect of an object such as fire—which is the opposite of that which is to be negated, such as cold—it is precisely non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), established through inference based on an inference (*anumitānumāna*), that brings about the cognition of its absence in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). To explain:
Fire, established from smoke as its effect, proves the absence of cold through the aforementioned reasoning;
for otherwise, the absence of cold could not be established at all, since even in that case, the absence [of fire] would result only through a mediated succession.

From smoke there is fire; from fire, which is the nature of the absence of cold, there is the conventional usage of the absence of cold due to the non-perception [of cold]. Therefore, there exists nothing but the mere arrangement of the words of the formal argument (*prayoga*).

Furthermore, a statement of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) made for the purpose of negation—which neither sets forth nor provides a remedy for what is contradictory—is not in accordance with logic. (91)
This is like the negation of omniscience, sovereign power, and so forth, because a contradiction regarding supersensible objects is unestablished. (92)

[232,ix] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real; if he does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; if he does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real; if he does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real; if he does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; if he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; if he does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real; if he does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real; if he does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real; if he does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; if he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; if he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; if he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; if he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as real; and if he does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, as real—then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real; because he does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; because he does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real; because he does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real; because he does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; because he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; because he does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real; because he does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real; because he does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real; because he does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; because he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; because he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; because he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; because he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as real; and because he does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, as real—it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

Indeed, speech is not necessarily in contradiction with omniscience. Nor is a contradiction established with that which is beyond the senses. Since speech proceeds from cognition itself, how could it prove its absence? If you argue that it is contradicted by omniscience, by what means is that contradiction apprehended? For if a decrease in speech were observed to follow an increase in cognition, then all [your] talk would be consistent; yet in the case of omniscience, there would simply be an absence of all speech. But this is not so. If you say, "We observe speakers who are not omniscient," then why is it that we do not observe the foolishness of everyone? If you say, "The erudition of the speaker is observed," then why would that too not be observed [in an omniscient being]? For instance:
If both reasoning and cognition were real, what relationship of sublated and sublator could there be?
If it is argued that such a relationship exists because one is not perceived, then let that very non-perception be the means of proof. (93)

For just as the speech of a fool is a specific statement even when it lacks actual scholarship, so too, what contradiction is there if such speech occurs even in a state of complete knowledge? Indeed, speech is not inherently opposed to the excellence of all-encompassing knowledge. If you argue that it is indeed opposed when there is absolute excellence, we say no; for no contradiction is perceived. To claim that such a speaker is simply unobserved is no answer, because non-perception is a means of cognition only when it pertains to a perceptible object.
Such non-apprehension has been declared to be non-conclusive;
therefore, regarding things that are absolutely beyond the senses, there can be no certain determination of their existence or non-existence. (94)
For, regarding things that are absolutely beyond perception— such as an omniscient being or existence after death— one cannot determine their non-existence based on mere non-perception.

Now, it might be argued: "If there is knowledge of everything, how could speech arise for one who is non-erroneous? For it is the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), arising from the reflection upon what precedes and follows, that impels words. This too is not correct;
for even when all objects are clearly known, speech proceeds.
In that case, due to the habituation to the desire to speak, how could there be an impossibility of speech?

Indeed, it is not the case that the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) does not arise from repeated practice simultaneous with the perception of objects—whether clearly manifest or otherwise—that are supported by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Even in the absence of an immediate intention to speak, speech occurs due to the momentum of previous impressions (*pūrvāvedha*). For the immediate presence of an intention to speak is not the sole cause of utterances; this is evident from the observation of the distinct recitation of words and sentences even by one whose mind is directed elsewhere, owing to the momentum of previous impressions, and from the observation of the commencement of various actions previously practiced. By this, the objection—"How can there be a response to a present interlocutor without prior reflection on what precedes and follows?"—is answered.
Merely by the presence of an enemy, they proceed without conceptual construction;
and in the morning, the processes for counteracting that [enemy] are produced by the body.

And just as for one who has been suddenly awakened by an enemy through the infliction of a blow and so forth, there arises a corresponding course of action such as drawing a weapon due to prior habituation, so too are all the actions of the Omniscient One; thus, it is not contradictory.
Therefore, the ascertainment of the non-existence of the counter-positive follows only from a contradictory [reason].

Whether a property is distinct or non-distinct from its locus, it follows that it is contradictory; just as "fire" is contradictory when "non-coldness" is to be proven, or "existence" is contradictory when "origination" is to be negated. (95)

[233, vii] Because the sensations of cold and heat are mutually distinct, their opposition is characterized by non-coexistence; whereas the opposition between existence (*sattā*) and birth (*janman*) is characterized by mutual exclusion—thus there is no difference [between the two types of opposition]. Indeed, birth does not exist apart from existence, nor does opposition. For that which already exists is not born. What purpose would birth serve for that which is already existent and free from all doubt? How can there be mutual opposition between two things that are non-distinct? This is stated precisely because the opponent accepts their non-distinction. [233, viii]
Now, what indeed is this so-called contradiction? It is the relationship between that which is to be negated and that which negates. For instance:
when one thing, whose causes are complete, does not occur upon the presence of another, [that other is its contradictory].
A contradiction between these two, whose natures are like cold and fire, is observed.

Now, if it is argued that the non-existence of one thing is produced by another, that is incorrect, because non-existence cannot be an effect. Alternatively, if it is not produced, then what contradiction could there be for something that perishes of its own accord? Furthermore, the destruction of a moment is not produced by another, because the states of being arisen and unarisen are incompatible. What contradiction or destruction could there be for that which is unarisen and non-existent? That which has arisen cannot be destroyed at its own time, because a moment is immutable. At any other time, however, it no longer exists; so whose destruction would it be? If it is argued that it is the "series" (*santati*) that is destroyed, we say no, because apart from those [moments], no series exists.
[233,xii] But surely, the destruction of the continuum itself is just the obstruction of the connection with subsequent moments? That too is incorrect.
[233,xiii]
If the cause is present, how can another [cause] be obstructive? If the cause is present, how can another [cause] be obstructive?

If there is a cause for the production of a subsequent moment, how can there be a contradiction? Or, if there is no cause, then the *kiṃśuka* trees are simply "colored by fate" (*daivarakta*). Or, it might be argued that the deficiency of the cause itself is produced by the opposing factor. That too is incorrect, because:
"If there is a deficiency of what is non-existent, then the *kiṃśuka* tree would be 'colored by fate'."
And what will the deficiency of that which exists by its own nature do?
(278) (PVA) If there is a cause for non-deficiency in that case, how can it be non-existent? Or, if there is no cause for non-deficiency, it is deficient by itself. (279) (PVA)

[233,xvii] For even in the case of a cause, when the non-deficiency of its own cause is present, the deficiency of that [subsequent] cause occurs by its very nature when there is an absence of capacity; what, then, will a contradictory factor do in that regard? Here is the rebuttal:
[233,xviii]

The production of a subsequent cold state from a preceding cold one occurs without fire as a cooperative cause; rather, having encountered a cooperative cause, that which was not cold becomes the cause of it.

For the preceding cold touch—which acts as a cooperative cause for the fire being kindled and which produces a progressively milder and milder cold sensation—ceases to produce further cold sensations once another degree of cold has arisen. Because it ceases of its own accord and because the subsequent [cold] does not arise due to the absence of its cause, fire is designated as the "remover" of cold by way of acting as a cooperative cause that generates a defective cold-cause. Thus, the production of a defective cause by that [fire] results in the non-arising [of cold]; this is designated as its cessation, characterized as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). For causes operate toward production, not toward cessation. Alternatively, cold possesses an inherent nature determined by its own cause, such that in the presence of fire, it does not produce its own subsequent effect (another moment of cold). For the potencies of entities are restricted to specific [effects]. If it is asked how two contradictory things can coexist in one place, the answer is: contradiction is exactly thus, since otherwise it would be impossible. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between two moments, but rather between two continuities (*prabandha*). Indeed, one observes the experience: even while feeling heat, the cold does not yet depart; likewise, dense darkness does not depart. If it is argued that it departs in that very same moment when extremely clear light occurs, we say no. Even in that case, because the light possesses the capacity to generate a different darkness along with its own causes, it is the light itself that arises, not the darkness. If it is argued that "that very [darkness] has perished," we say no, because it had already perished by its own nature [upon arising].
By whatever intrinsic nature it arises, by that very same nature it does not perish; and by whatever nature it does not arise, likewise by that it does not perish. (281) (PVA)
Therefore, it is not that very same thing which has perished.

Is it not the case that non-perception itself is destruction? And yet, since that very destruction is not perceived during its own state, how can there be a cognition of it as "this"? When it is perceived, it is not destroyed; when it is destroyed, it is not perceived. It is destroyed precisely because it is not perceived. Otherwise, if it were being perceived, what would be the meaning of "destruction"? If that which is not being apprehended is destroyed, then a location where a jar is not being apprehended would also have to be considered destroyed. If you say, "That which was previously seen but is no longer apprehended is destroyed," then that too was indeed previously seen. To say that it is destroyed at the very place and time it was seen, yet is not apprehended at that same time—it is being apprehended and yet not apprehended—is a contradiction. If you say it is not apprehended at a subsequent time, then why is it not considered destroyed when it is not apprehended in a subsequent location?
If it is destroyed at another time, why is it not destroyed at another place?
If there is no pervasion by another place, then surely what is the point of another time? (282) (PVA)

[234, vi] If it were impossible for anything at all to pervade another location, then that very thing would not have perished; likewise, it would also be impossible for it to pervade another time, so how could it have perished even then?

But surely, even though it is not perceived in another location, how can that which is perceived in one location be destroyed? In that case, just as with another location, how can that which is perceived at another time be destroyed? If you say it is because it is not perceived at another time, this is the same in both cases. Therefore:
In whatever manner an entity is perceived, it cannot be otherwise than that.
That which is perceived as blue by way of its blueness does not exist as whiteness.

Therefore, it is not that very same thing which has perished, but rather another [thing] that has not arisen due to the absence of a cause. When that [other thing] is not perceived, there is merely the conceit that "it has perished. Consequently, in such a case, the determination of contradiction characterized by non-coexistence is established. In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), contradiction is simply a specific state of the absence of a cause. Contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitalakṣaṇa*) is likewise exactly thus: that which produces a momentary [nature] is incapable of producing a permanent nature; therefore, the non-arising of permanence itself [constitutes the contradiction]. Just as impermanence [is excluded] by permanence, so too are blue-ness and the like mutually [excluded]; thus there is no difference between these two [types of contradiction].

[235,i] “There is no difference between these two contradictions from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, contradiction is simply mutual distinctness (*vilakṣaṇatva*) resulting from the force of causes. And that is nothing other than the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the entities themselves; otherwise, there would be an absence of their own nature. Furthermore, since the perception of those two as distinct from each other’s nature is, in relation to something else, precisely non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), all conventional usage regarding non-existence proceeds solely through non-perception.
"The formal argument (*prayoga*) alone is different; the meaning does not differ in every case" (PV 2.90).

Thus, what has been said is correct. Furthermore, since this contradiction does not apply to supersensible (atīndriya) objects, the perception of a contradictory property (*viruddhopalabdhi*) cannot establish non-existence, nor can mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi-mātra*). The fact that something is not perceived does not mean that it does not exist. Only one whose vision encompasses the existence of all knowable things would be justified in speaking thus. Even then, that very person is the omniscient one; therefore, there is no refutation of the All-Knowing One, nor of the next world and so forth. This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that he is not perceived by an all-seeing being. And the proof for the opposite case has already been stated. Therefore: [235, iv]
Just as a real entity alone is considered the means of proving other entities, so too a real entity alone is the negator of other entities through its own cessation. (96)

[235,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purification is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purification is consciousness. Why is this? Subhūti, because form itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are emptiness, emptiness itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form itself is marklessness, marklessness itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are marklessness, marklessness itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form itself is wishlessness, wishlessness itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are wishlessness, wishlessness itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form itself is non-arising, non-arising itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are non-arising, non-arising itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form itself is non-cessation, non-cessation itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are non-cessation, non-cessation itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form itself is non-defiled, non-defilement itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are non-defiled, non-defilement itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Form itself is non-purified, non-purification itself is form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness themselves are non-purified, non-purification itself is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One further said this to the Venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that the past is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the past; he does not perceive that the future is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the future; he does not perceive that the present is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the present. He does not perceive that the past is without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is the past; he does not perceive that the future is without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is the future; he does not perceive that the present is without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is the present. He does not perceive that the past is wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is the past; he does not perceive that the future is wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is the future; he does not perceive that the present is wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is the present. He does not perceive that the past is non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is the past; he does not perceive that the future is non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is the future; he does not perceive that the present is non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is the present. He does not perceive that the past is non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is the past; he does not perceive that the future is non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is the future; he does not perceive that the present is non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is the present. He does not perceive that the past is non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is the past; he does not perceive that the future is non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is the future; he does not perceive that the present is non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is the present. He does not perceive that the past is non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purification is the past; he does not perceive that the future is non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purification is the future; he does not perceive that the present is non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purification is the present. Why is this? Subhūti, because the past itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is the past; the future itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is the future; the present itself is emptiness, emptiness itself is the present. The past itself is marklessness, marklessness itself is the past; the future itself is marklessness, marklessness itself is the future; the present itself is marklessness, marklessness itself is the present. The past itself is wishlessness, wishlessness itself is the past; the future itself is wishlessness, wishlessness itself is the future; the present itself is wishlessness, wishlessness itself is the present. The past itself is non-arising, non-arising itself is the past; the future itself is non-arising, non-arising itself is the future; the present itself is non-arising, non-arising itself is the present. The past itself is non-cessation, non-cessation itself is the past; the future itself is non-cessation, non-cessation itself is the future; the present itself is non-cessation, non-cessation itself is the present. The past itself is non-defiled, non-defilement itself is the past; the future itself is non-defiled, non-defilement itself is the future; the present itself is non-defiled, non-defilement itself is the present. The past itself is non-purified, non-purification itself is the past; the future itself is non-purified, non-purification itself is the future; the present itself is non-purified, non-purification itself is the present. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One further said this to the Venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that internal form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is internal form; he does not perceive that external form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is external form; he does not perceive that internal and external form is empty, nor does he perceivethat emptiness is internal and external form. Just as a real entity (*vastu*) alone, by virtue of its necessary connection (*pratibandha*), is the means of proving another real entity, so too a real entity alone, upon its own cessation, is the negator of another real entity. For without a necessary connection, one real entity does not negate another real entity when that other ceases. Just as an effect proves its cause and a pervader (*vyāpaka*) proves its pervaded (*vyāpya*), so too the absence of a cause proves the absence of the effect, and the absence of a pervader proves the absence of the pervaded. Otherwise, there would be no such necessary connection at all. Furthermore, this very nature of the necessary connection consists in positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); there is no other necessary connection.

By this, a property such as "being either the subject or one of its similar instances" (pakṣasapakṣānyataratva), which is merely projected by conceptual construction and could occur anywhere, is refuted. 97.

[235, vii] For being either the subject (*pakṣa*) or a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is not tied to either the permanent or the impermanent in any single case. For the subject is established by mere wish; and whatever is a similar instance in accordance with that [subject] is likewise [established by wish]. Therefore, because it is tied to mere wish, it does not lead to the cognition of a real entity (*vastu*). Indeed, that which is tied to something else does not cause another thing to be understood, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it excluded from anything such that it could lead to the cognition of its absence. For even that [absence] has the status of a subject established by mere wish. Consequently, being either the subject or a similar instance is non-probative. The same applies to being a non-dissimilar instance (*avipakṣa*), and so forth. [235, viii]

Therefore, the establishment of affirmation and negation proceeds solely from a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). In that regard as well, it is held that a pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) is the indicator of the absence [of the probandum].
If the exclusion of the pervaded [from a locus] is somehow delimited, [then it would follow that there is a limit to its non-existence]. (98)

[235,x] But is it not the case that the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) is also indeed a means of cognition? This is not so. In that case, there is no relationship of the cognized and the cognizer (*gamyagamakabhāva*) in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). That which is the non-perception of what has met the conditions for perceptibility is simply a non-existence (*abhāva*). Therefore, by means of that established [non-existence], the non-existence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is proven.
To claim that a mark (liṅga) exists only when there is an absence of invalidity is for the sake of those who are utterly deluded; for such a state is not unknown even to cowherds. (99)

This very non-existence is what is called the "non-apprehension of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvānupalambha*). This is well known even to cowherds and their wives. However, the Sāṃkhya, deluded by the perspective of his own treatise, is being awakened [to this truth]. It is solely on account of this [non-apprehension] that the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs elsewhere as well. Otherwise, the distinction between pleasure and so forth, and between selves, could not be established. If it is argued that the distinction is established through the treatise alone, we say no; for the distinction must be grounded in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). Furthermore, there would be no mutual distinction between treatises themselves without the apprehension of them as mutually distinct. And that very apprehension of distinction is itself the non-apprehension of the other. Moreover, the distinction between the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) cannot be established without non-apprehension.

[236,i] This much is the result of certainty regarding non-existence: namely, non-perception. And that [occurs] when the reason (hetu) or the essential nature (svabhāva) is considered to be perceptible, yet is not perceived. || 100 ||

Non-apprehension is indeed threefold: that of the reason (*hetu*), of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and of the essential nature (*svabhāva*). And it is the non-apprehension of such a reason and so forth—provided they have met the conditions for apprehensibility—that serves as the means of cognition, and not that of anything else, nor otherwise. Therefore, the inferential knowledge produced by the effect, the essential nature, and non-apprehension is the communicator of the probandum (*sādhya*) and is non-contradictory. Consequently, by that [knowledge], the real entity itself is established as being thus; hence, it is not a property of a non-entity.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of "the color is impermanent," there is a connection with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of impermanence. So how can it be said that through this connection [one apprehends] the generality of color, and so forth? [Response: This is not so.
The apprehension of impermanence and the like is held to occur through inference.
Validity belongs only [to that], and not elsewhere, because it is considered to be the apprehension of what has already been apprehended. (101)

[236,v] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding those suffering beings, by means of his compassionate power, causes them to transcend all suffering. Therefore, one should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses inconceivable, wondrous, and supreme merit. If there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall single-mindedly take refuge in him, then at the moment of their death, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his spiritual power, will appear before them and they shall not fall into evil realms. If there be any sons or daughters of good family who, with a sincere heart, wish to offer worship to the many hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, they need only take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara; it is as if they had already made offerings to all those Buddhas. If there be any sons or daughters of good family who, for the sake of seeking various treasures, enter the great ocean, and if they can single-mindedly invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then by the spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall not meet with calamities from water monsters, dragons, or fish-eaters; they shall safely reach the shore and obtain whatever treasures they seek. If there be any sons or daughters of good family who travel on land and encounter bandits or robbers, and if they can single-mindedly invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then by the spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those bandits and robbers shall not harm them. If there be any women who, during childbirth, suffer extreme pain and distress, and if they can single-mindedly invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then by the spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately be delivered from suffering. For, having apprehended the color and so forth by means of their specific and general characteristics—namely, as being "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) and "color-ness" (*varṇatva*), respectively—and [having apprehended] impermanence, one synthesizes [them] with the mind, thinking, "The color and so forth are impermanent. As the Teacher has stated: "In that regard, this sequence is described [by the verse beginning] 'From the conjunction with the generality of color' (*pra.vā. 2.79*)," and so on. If impermanence were understood regarding the generality of color-ness through inference, there would be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). By what means would that subject (*dharmin*) possessing that generality be apprehended? If it were apprehended by inference, there would be yet another subject in that case as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And when the knowledge of that which lacks a logical mark (*aliṅga*) occurs subsequent to perception, it is indeed a separate means of valid cognition, because it is a synthesis based on the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). The rebuttal to both cases is the same: there is no validity at all in those instances, because in both cases [the object] is already established by perception alone. Since a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) grasping a generality merely grasps what has already been grasped. [Objection: How is impermanence established by perception? [Response: Because...
There is no other impermanence for this [object], because that [impermanence] is established previously through the senses.
It cannot be said to have multiple forms; rather, it is a property (*dharma*) born of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is expressed.

The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One,

Indeed, impermanence, color-ness, and so forth do not exist apart from the nature of the non-existence [of their opposites]. That very nature of non-existence is of such a kind that, because conceptual thought lacks the capacity to grasp it in its true form, it becomes a "universal" (sāmānya) for that thought. However, it is merely the operation of grasping; it is not a universal in reality. For in the conceptual thought "this is blue," there appears nothing other than the form manifesting in the perception as "this is blue"; rather, that very thing is thus conventionally designated. Now, if it is argued that the universal is grasped by the preceding and succeeding cognitions as "this is just as that blue was," even though it was not grasped by those two cognitions—this too is incorrect. For no universal is perceived apart from the preceding and succeeding forms. That very thing, when being conventionally designated as such, is the universal. And that very particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the basis of that conventional usage.

[236, viii] Is it not the case that there is a mutual difference—that is, a plurality—among universals such as impermanence and so forth, as well as between these and their possessors? To this it is replied: "That which is denoted is not of manifold form. The essence of the particular (svalakṣaṇa) is not manifold; rather, the differentiation belongs solely to conceptual construction (vikalpa), arising from the power of beginningless predispositions (vāsanā). For conceptual construction functions by superimposing difference, due to its operation through the imagination of positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative exclusion (vyatireka) based on the differences of exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
When the substratum of a universal is unestablished, that universal is indeed established [by the inference itself];
for if that were unestablished, it would be precisely through this inference that it is established. (103)

[237,i] For a universal (*sāmānya*) is merely a matter of linguistic convention (*vyavahāramātraka*). And when the object of linguistic convention is established, that convention is established either by way of a common substratum (*sāmānyādhikaraṇya*) or otherwise. However, when the linguistic convention is not established, it is brought into the state of being an object of recollection by demonstrating the cause; that is, for one who has forgotten the cause of the convention, it is led to the status of being an object of memory through the recollection of its causality. Therefore, inference establishes only the mere linguistic convention and nothing else.

[Objection: But surely, by means of an inference based on an effect as the reason (*kāryahetu*), it is the very entity—such as fire—that is established as the probandum (*sādhya*), not the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). [Reply: That too is incorrect.
For even in that case, if the entity itself were being established by means of the inference, [it would be subject to the same critique].
When all aspects are established, there can be no other means of valid cognition regarding that very same object.

If an object such as fire is established through inference, then when there arises a desire to know its specific internal distinctions—such as "What kind of fire is this?"—no other means of valid cognition, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), operates therein. This is because its establishment in all its aspects occurs through that very first inference alone. [The three obstacles are: impossibility (*asambhava*), non-possibility (*asambhava*), and contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*). Possibility (*sambhava*) is the production of an effect from a capable cause. Non-possibility (*asambhava*) is the non-production of an effect in the absence of a cause. Contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) is, for example, that fire is cold. In that regard, the apprehension of all aspects by perception is "possibility"; by inference it is "non-possibility"; and by contradiction with a means of valid cognition it is "contradiction," due to the operation of another means of valid cognition. This is merely the manifestation of darkness (ignorance). For: [The original Sanskrit text follows: *yadyanumānādagnyādivastu prasidhyati tadā tatra kīdṛśo'gnerayamityavāntarabhedajijñāsāyāṃ pramāṇāntaramadhyakṣādikanna pravarttate । tasya prathamānumānata eva sarvākāraprasiddheḥ । prāg<?> sambhavo'sambhavaḥ pramāṇavirodhaśceti । kāraṇāt yogyāt kāryamutpattimaditi sambhavaḥ । kāraṇābhāve kāryānutpattirityasambhavaḥ । pramāṇavirodho 'pi śīto'gneriti । tatrādhyakṣeṇa sarvā'kāragrahaṇamiti sambhavaḥ । anumānenāsambhavaḥ । pramāṇavirodhaśceti । pramāṇāntarapravṛtteḥ । tadetat tamovijṛmbhitaṃ । yataḥ ।* (Note: The bracketed portion *prāg<?>* appears to be a textual corruption or placeholder; the logical flow suggests it refers to the three obstacles mentioned immediately following.)

[237,v] How can there be the apprehension of a real entity when it is either non-existent or contradictory? If a real entity were apprehended, these two [consequences] would follow, which are illogical. ॥ 285 ॥ (PVA)

If, because it is impossible to abandon the aspect that is non-different from that [object], and because there is a contradiction with the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in grasping all aspects, then there is no grasping of the object at all. For how could there be a non-grasping of what is non-different from that which is being grasped? Indeed, it is not logical that the very same thing is both grasped and not grasped; likewise, it is also impossible for cognition to both grasp and not grasp that [object].
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"The apprehension of all aspects has no logical mark (*liṅga*) as its cause, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)."
Because it is non-deviant with respect to the universal and because the particular is not established [as such],
the logical mark (*liṅga*), having been apprehended as common to all individuals, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with regard to any specific individual. (PVA 286) [237,ix]
[237,x] If it is so,
There is no apprehension of a specific distinction that could arise from the capacity of a logical mark (*liṅga*);
since the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), how can there be an apprehension of a real entity?

It is not known which specific fire is here; rather, only "fire" in general is perceived. The cognition that "some fire is here" follows from previous observations of various fires; this is merely a conceptual apprehension (*pratīti*) and does not touch upon the actual reality (*vastu*). If there were contact with the reality through perception, how could doubt regarding its particularity (*bheda*) be possible?

[Objection: But if there is doubt, how can there be attainment (*prāpti*)? [Response: Attainment, too, is precisely in accordance with the doubt, because at some time someone might attain a particular fire. Therefore, even in the case of the reason of effect (*kāryahetu*), there is only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), not the establishment of a real entity.

[237,xiv] But is it not the case that in the case of the essential nature as a reason (*svabhāvahetu*), a real entity is apprehended as being perceived? However, in the case of the effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*), how can there be the apprehension of something unperceived?

The mere fact that an object has not been seen does not entail its non-existence, for it always exists in reality; however, for those seeking that object, there is the cessation of the thing [as perceived] due to error.

Indeed, there is no perception of hair and the like [in the eyes]; nevertheless, the mental function (*vṛtti*) occurs precisely because it has that as its object. The determination is that where [the object] exists, there is attainment, and not elsewhere. Furthermore, in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) or a perceptible reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*), the entity is not grasped [as it actually is], because there would be attainment everywhere of that which is ungrasped. For an entity is to be attained [only] when it is future. And how can its own-nature (*svarūpa*) be grasped? If it is argued that it is grasped by way of its future form, no; for it is not perceived in that way. Even if it is perceived by way of its future form, then being perceived otherwise, it could not arise otherwise [than it is perceived]. If it is argued that it is the perception of the universal (*sāmānya*), then when the universal is perceived, how is there attainment of the particular (*viśeṣa*)? If it is argued that this is because [the particular] is already present, no; for the universal does not exist apart from the particular entity. In that case, smoke and the like as a mark (*liṅga*) also do not exist apart from the other entity; therefore, existence [of the object] follows from that very [mark]. What is the use of a universal? Without the perception of the non-universal [particular], how does one act? One will act upon the perception of the mark itself. But if one perceives one thing, how is there activity toward another? The same fault applies, since the universal is also indeed something else. If it is argued that the universal is not absolutely different [from the particular]... if that is so:
If the object were apprehended through the apprehension of its universal, then that [universal] itself would be the apprehension of the object.
That being the case, how could there be doubt regarding what has already been apprehended? (PVA 289)

[238,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti replied: "As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by virtue of the possession of the marks of a great man? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by virtue of the possession of the marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to say, 'The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man,' would he be speaking correctly? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; he would not be speaking correctly. Why is that? Because those very marks of a great man have been described by the Tathāgata as being 'no-marks. Therefore they are called the 'thirty-two marks of a great man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three-thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that account? Subhūti replied: "Blessed One, that person would generate a vast, immeasurable, and incalculable mass of merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, even greater than that would be the mass of merit generated by a son or daughter of good family who, having taken up this perfection of wisdom and retained it in memory, would read, recite, and master it, and who, relying upon it, would teach, explain, and illuminate it in detail for others, both its meaning and its phrasing. Furthermore, Subhūti, if one were to compare the mass of merit from the former case with the mass of merit from the latter case, the latter would be far more superior, far more excellent, and far more sublime. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma that he has taught? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma that he has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma that has come forth from the Tathāgata? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma that has come forth from the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, or any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught, or any dharma that the Tathāgata has come forth from? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, nor any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught, nor any dharma that the Tathāgata has come forth from. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma by which the Tathāgata perceives that 'I am a Tathāgata'? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma by which the Tathāgata perceives that 'I am a Tathāgata. Why is that? Because that very dharma, Blessed One, which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, or which the Tathāgata has taught, or from which the Tathāgata has come forth—that dharma is ineffable and inexpressible. It is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma. Therefore, the Tathāgata perceives that 'I am a Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If a woman or a man were to take up this perfection of wisdom, retain it in memory, read, recite, and master it, and if, relying upon it, they were to teach, explain, and illuminate it in detail for others, both its meaning and its phrasing, would that woman or man generate much merit on that account? Subhūti replied: "Blessed One, that person would generate a vast, immeasurable, and incalculable mass of merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, even greater than that would be the mass of merit generated by a son or daughter of good family who, having taken up this perfection of wisdom and retained it in memory, would read, recite, and master it, and who, relying upon it, would teach, explain, and illuminate it in detail for others, both its meaning and its phrasing. Furthermore, Subhūti, if one were to compare the mass of merit from the former case with the mass of merit from the latter case, the latter would be far more superior, far more excellent, and far more sublime. Why is that? Because those very marks of a great man have been described by the Tathāgata as being 'no-marks. Therefore they are called the 'thirty-two marks of a great man. Subhūti replied: "Blessed One, that person would generate a vast, immeasurable, and incalculable mass of merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by virtue of the possession of the marks of a great man? If someone were to say, 'The Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man,' would he be speaking correctly? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; he would not be speaking correctly. Why is

If it is argued that there is apprehension in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*) but not in the form of a particular (*viśeṣa*), then how does one act toward the particular? If it is argued that the particular has also indeed been apprehended, for what purpose does one act? If it is for the sake of attainment (*prāpti*), [we reply: surely that attainment is nothing but the cognition of the thing’s own nature (*svarūpa*). If that [cognition] has already occurred, for what purpose does one act? If it is argued that there is cognition in one form but not in another, [we reply: one does not act by means of the form in which there is cognition, because that would be pointless; nor does one act by means of the form in which there is no cognition, because of incapacity. Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding what is cognized, nor regarding what is not cognized, since doubt consists in the contact with both forms simultaneously. If it is argued that because the universal and the particular are of one nature, one acts even when the particular is not cognized, [we reply: no, for it is impossible to act toward that which has not been made an object (*aviṣayīkṛta*). Nor has it been established that what is cognized and what is not cognized can be one. One does not cognize the oneness of what is cognized while not cognizing it; nor does one cognize it at a later time. It has already been established that at a later time there is neither perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor inference (*anumāna*).

[238,iii] Now, if a real entity, due to its impermanence, is grasped entirely in its entirety, how can it be an object of inference? If you say it is so by way of being conventionally designated (*vyavahriyamāṇatayā*), why does that very conventional designation not constitute a definitive certainty (*niścaya*) itself? This is no answer, because:
In some cases, there is a lack of full comprehension of that [object] because another similar thing arises;
this is due to delusion, as one fails to perceive the difference, like [failing to distinguish between] separate illusory balls. (104)

[238,v] Indeed, it is not that the difference between two illusory balls is not perceived; nevertheless, because of their similarity, there arises the cognition "this is that very same one," and thus there is no conventional usage of their difference.

Now, even if the cognition "this is that very same thing" is erroneous, the act of seeing (*darśana*) is nonetheless non-erroneous; why then is there no cognition of difference? If it is argued that the cognition, being suppressed, is effectively as if non-existent, we reply: there is no such thing as suppression between two cognitions that are self-aware of their own nature. For if they exist by mutually excluding one another, it follows that there must be a mutual suppression of the two.
If suppression consists in being established through mutual exclusion, then [the two cognitions would be distinct].
The mutual exclusion of the two is equal for both.

(PVA 290) Just as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), being of the nature of self-cognition, excludes experience by its very nature and thus acts as a subverter of experience, so too would experience act as a subverter of conceptual construction. Now, if the mind is intent upon unity, the cognition of difference does not arise at all. If that were the case, experience itself would not exist; what, then, would be the purpose of subverting it? To this, it is replied:
One does not perceive the object as distinct from its preceding state due to its destruction;
and because of the determination that it is eternal, one thinks, "It is indeed eternal. (PVA 291)

[238,xi] The previous perception of the object has already passed; now, there is merely the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it, and that usage proceeds as if it were permanent. Therefore, how could this past perception negate it? At that time, however, there exists a contrary conceptual determination (*viparītādhyavasāya*). Consequently, [the past perception cannot negate the present].

It is that very [entity] which causes the world to engage in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, its "negation" (*tiraskāra*) consists precisely in the absence of such corresponding conventional practice, because it is not perceived as distinct from one another. Consequently, just as with a ball of illusion, because the second and subsequent moments are not perceived as distinct, there arises the conventional designation "this is that very same thing.
For indeed, even for those as young as children, this [perception] is without a logical mark (*aliṅga*), and it does not involve a connection with a subsequent arising.
Seeing [it], a person indeed determines the destruction of the lamp and so forth. 105.

[239,iii] But surely, in the case of an illusion or a ball of clay and so forth, difference is indeed apprehended through investigation by means of analytical inquiries; however, momentariness is not established in this way. That too is incorrect. For it is defined as follows: non-momentariness, destruction, and impermanence are synonymous. Now, there is no such thing as "remaining in the same state" (*tādavasthya*) for lamps and the like; rather, the successive flames of a lamp are produced from successive fuel in the form of oil, and are themselves distinct. It is only due to similarity or a common causal complex that the conventional usage "this is that very same [lamp]" occurs. [239,iv]
[Objection: Surely, this mass of lamp-flames is produced by the oil all at once; it is a single thing. [Response: This too is not correct, because:
[239,v] If it were produced merely from the first contact [of the wick with the flame], then...
Because it persists for a period of time, oil and the like are useless thereafter.

Indeed, it is not merely from the initial convergence of the causal complex of oil and so forth that a lamp or similar object, once produced, possesses an existence extending through the entire series of temporal moments; for thereafter, the conjunction of the vessel, the ground, the oil, and the flame serves no purpose whatsoever. This is because the nature of what has been produced is independent [of further causes]. If it is argued that even for that which has been produced, its persistence over time occurs only while the oil and other factors continue, and not otherwise—this is not so. For its production itself consists in its enduring through a period of time. As for that which does not endure through a period of time, nothing can be done for it later by the causal complex of oil and so forth; thus, [the continued presence of those factors] would be useless. If something else were produced, that itself would constitute impermanence. And so, if this [lamp] is produced and perceived in its entirety, then since it is perceived in its entirety by the eye and other senses, the continued operation of the eye and so forth would be entirely redundant. If, on the other hand, its persistence over time is grasped through successive perceptions or through a single act of perception, then, because those successive perceptions are discrete, there would be no grasping of persistence over time even by the first one. Furthermore, if the perception itself possessed duration over time, then such grasping would occur all at once; thus, it follows that the continued operation of the eye would be in vain. Therefore, perception does not grasp even the slightest bit of the prior and posterior natures [of an object]; rather, only a single moment appears.
[239,vii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "That very nature of the thing (vastusvabhāva), devoid of prior and posterior, will exist as an extension. That is incorrect.
[239,viii]
If it were the case that everything becomes [manifest] through repeated perception over a long duration of time, then everyone would perceive it so;
rather, it is precisely through the continuity of perception that the long duration of time is cognized.
(PVA 239, ix)

In whatever manner successive perceptions arise in a continuous stream, in that same manner one understands the long duration [of time], and not otherwise. Furthermore, time is not "long" merely because it has been apprehended all at once as being long. Therefore, perception understands only momentariness. If momentariness itself is determined by direct perception as its very nature, how can there be delusion even while it is being determined? To this, it is said:
"Even though a capacity is the very nature of an entity, it is not seen in its effect."
Delusion [arises] from lack of immediacy, due to the lack of proficiency in discernment. 106.
Just as, indeed, a potency, even when delimited, is not ascertained by one who has not perceived its immediate effect.
For the very purpose of removing that [misconception], inference is described;
for those of great intelligence determine all aspects from perception alone. (107)

Even when there is perception, one who is devoid of practice is deluded regarding the entity in all its aspects; therefore, there is no certainty. Consequently, inference proceeds for the sake of turning away that delusion. However, for those who possess causes of certainty—such as proficiency through practice—they are capable of determining [the object] here from the mere observation of a resolute cognition (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, when the substratum is established, the universal is indeed established insofar as there is no delusion. But where delusion exists, there inference [is required].

How then, given the oneness of the object, can a diversity of properties (*nānādharmatā*) be established by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that follow after it? For a conceptual construction following upon the experience of blue does not have the nature of determining yellow. To this, the answer is:
"In that [object], which is excluded from everything else, there are [conceptual exclusions] based upon those very exclusions."
Cognitions operate upon an object that is undivided, as if they were based on distinct substrata. // 108 //
And just as the names correspond to the injunctions, so too, in the absence of any cause for error,
those intuitions naturally reconnect with their respective objects according to their own nature.

[240,iv] Indeed, all things born in the world possess exclusions from both their own class (*sajātīya*) and other classes (*vijātīya*). From whatever [other things] they are excluded, they are perceived as possessing various properties (*nānādharmāṇaḥ*), having taken up each respective basis of differentiation (*upādāna*)—the distinction [of the object] which is conceptually constructed based on the distinction of the limit (*avadhibheda*). If entities are excluded from everything, why is there no certain cognition of all those exclusions at once? We reply: because of the presence of causes for error. This is due to the forgetting of what was previously seen. For there is no certain cognition of the exclusion when the previously seen object is made an object of cognition in exactly that same way. To explain: [240,v]

For certainty is indeed the arising of memory exactly as [the object] was experienced; otherwise, it is error. When there is firmness, there is certainty; when there is wavering of both, there is doubt. (PVA 294)

There is no absence of certainty regarding the recollection of what has been experienced exactly as it was; indeed, this very certainty consists in recollecting it exactly as it was, because of recollecting it exactly so through habituation. Therefore, for those possessing such habituation, certainty occurs immediately after the perception itself. Otherwise, inference would be required to preclude the possibility of recollection; thus it is established. Another says:
"Alternatively, even in this case, destruction is established from the mark of non-perception."

[240, viii] For all entities are connected with arising and passing away. Arising is established by perception and by inference that proves a positive affirmation; passing away is non-existence, and it is established by non-apprehension. Whatever is a negation is entirely established by non-apprehension; there is no other means for establishing negation.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the positive injunction (*vidhi*) which constitutes the very nature of impermanence is apprehended by the very same means of valid cognition as the impermanent entity itself? [Response: This is not so. Impermanence does not consist of the mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone; rather:
"An entity is said to be 'impermanent' because, having existed previously, it no longer exists. (110)
That which, having come into being, no longer exists, is impermanent; it is not so merely by virtue of existing. And that non-existence establishes non-apprehension elsewhere as well.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, according to this proponent, impermanence is indeed existence (*sattā*) which mediates between the two ends, and not characterized by non-existence? And since "the state of having two ends" refers to the prior and posterior limits, and existence cannot be established through non-perception, how can this be so? To this, he says:
"For one for whom the existence mediating between the two ends expresses a relation... [240, xiii]
Therefore, the scriptural mention of impermanence refers to those two; thus they are recorded in the Smṛti.

[241,i] Existence (*sattā*) alone cannot be impermanence, because it would follow that even the self (*ātman*) and other such things are impermanent. Furthermore, impermanence must be described as existence that, without distinction, occupies both ends and the middle of material form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth. And there is no such thing as occupying both ends without the absence of those ends. Moreover, in the transition to non-existence, that [impermanence] is apprehended through the non-perception of existence, and not by any other means.
If there is non-existence both before and after, why is that very thing not impermanence?

[241,iii] If existence, which is delimited by both prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), is impermanence, then why is that very non-existence not accepted as impermanence?
If it is argued that this is because of the impossibility of connecting with the sixth and the first, how could it occur at the two extremes? (112)

[241,v] If this intention is that "impermanence belongs to an entity" (*bhāvasyānityatā*), then there would be no connection expressed by the genitive case and so forth, if impermanence were non-existence (*abhāva*). This is because there is no relation with non-existence; for there is no connection characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the like between an entity and a non-entity, as such a connection is impossible.
By whom can the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified be prevented?
If you say that this too would not exist, then how could it exist in the case of the two extremes?

If, even in the case of the relation between qualifier and qualified, it is not accepted without a relation such as inherence (*samavāya*), then how is that connection by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) or the relation of qualifier and qualified established for the two extremes— whether by existence (*sattā*) or by being (*bhāva*)? For in the formulation of speech, "existence is the intermediary between the two extremes" and "it is qualified by them," there can be no qualification of the two extremes by existence and its relation, because both are eternal (*dhrauvya*).

[241, ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift, Subhūti, what do you think? Would that bodhisattva mahāsattva generate much merit on that basis? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, it would be much. Sugata, it would be much. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, I declare that this son of good family or daughter of good family would generate even more merit than that, if they were to take up, retain, recite, master, and correctly teach to others even just one four-line verse from this perfection of wisdom, and if they were to demonstrate its meaning to others. Why is that? Subhūti, all the dharmas of the Buddhas, the dharmas of the Śrāvakas, and the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas are fully contained within this perfection of wisdom.”

In the statement that "impermanence is existence delimited by both ends, or the relation of existence characterized as inherence (*samavāya*)," it is necessarily accepted that existence and its relation are qualified by the two ends. This, however, is not logical, because both are admitted to be eternal. For how could existence be qualified by the two ends if it were subject to arising and passing away? If, on the other hand, there were no such relation of existence with that entity, then that very entity, being thus qualified, would be impermanent; what then would be the use of existence? If it is argued that the genitive case is not used because there is no distinction [between them], then how can one say "the existence of existence"? Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the impermanence of an entity," the prior non-existence and the non-existence following destruction of the entity are themselves its impermanence. Thus, since there is a distinction, the genitive case of distinction is justified. Alternatively, if the "two ends" refer to cause and effect—the cause being one end and the effect being the second—then the qualification of existence or its relation by those two (cause and effect) has not been stated. Moreover, the relation between cause and effect within an entity is the causal relation itself, which is characterized as inherence. To this, the reply is as follows: [The opponent’s argument continues: If it is said that "existence is delimited by both ends"—meaning that existence is delimited by the prior non-existence and the non-existence following destruction of an entity—then, since these two are the impermanence of the entity, the genitive case expressing distinction is appropriate because of their difference from the entity. Or, if the "two ends" refer to cause and effect, where the cause is one end and the effect is the second, then the qualification of existence or its relation by those two (cause and effect) has not been stated. Furthermore, the relation between cause and effect within an entity is the causal relation itself, which is characterized as inherence. To this, the response is: [The opponent’s argument continues...
