[241,x] If cause and effect were thus at their limits, there would be no distinction whatsoever. 113.
Because there is no connection [between the entity and its prior non-existence], he does not accept that it is the prior non-existence of the entity.
When those [non-existences] are designated by means of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), they too—and the entity itself—are not established [as distinct entities]. || 114 ||

[241,xii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to speak of the measure of the merit of a person who has set their mind on supreme perfect enlightenment, it would not be easy to reach its limit through words. The venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the reason for this? What is the cause? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, suppose there were a man who, having taken up a vessel the size of Mount Sumeru, were to fill it with the finest sandalwood powder and offer it as a gift to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. And suppose another man were to take up even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse and teach it to others. The latter would generate far more merit than the former; it would be incalculable, immeasurable, and beyond reckoning. The venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how much greater would be the merit of that person who, having heard this Dharma-discourse, would understand it, retain it, recite it, master it, and practice according to its teaching? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the merit of that person would be even greater. It would be incalculable, immeasurable, and beyond reckoning. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is the source of all the Buddhas, the source of all the Bodhisattvas, and the source of all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.”

For that whose prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is connected with its own cause, there is no admission of a connection between an entity and its prior non-existence. If such a connection were admitted, then since prior non-existence and posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) would themselves constitute impermanence, there would be an abandonment of the original subject matter and a recourse to a different position. Therefore, there is indeed no connection between an entity and its prior non-existence. Furthermore, this specific designation [of "prior non-existence"] is conditioned by the prior non-existence; in the absence of that [non-existence], there could be no such notion as "this is the effect. Nor is there a cause without an effect. Alternatively, there is no other way in which the relationship of cause and effect would be absent. For: [The verse follows: *na hy abhāvaḥ kāraṇaṃ bhāvasya, nāpi bhāvaḥ kāraṇam abhāvasya.* Indeed, non-existence is not the cause of an entity, nor is an entity the cause of non-existence.
Existence (*sattā*) is the cause because it effects the connection with its own causes; that existence and that relation are eternal. What, then, is the effect here? 115.

[242,ii] For a cause acts by bringing about a connection with existence (*sattā*), and by bringing about a connection with its own cause; for an entity that possesses origination generally inheres in its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Now, there is no status as an effect (*kāryatā*) for either the connection with existence or for existence itself. Even for an entity, it is only through its connection with existence that it becomes an effect, and not otherwise. If it were argued that its status as an effect exists by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*), we say: no. [242,iii]
That whose non-existence would be produced is not an entity possessing prior non-existence;
because no relation is admitted, this entire universe would consequently be eternal. (116)

[242,iv] For there is no connection whatsoever of any entity with its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Even if it were the case that there is no connection because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), nevertheless, this [non-existence] was simply non-existent previously. From that, it will possess the status of being an effect (*kāryatā*).

Now, is it not the case that whatever exists as non-existent is itself non-existent? Otherwise, everything would be non-existent. Consequently, it would follow that there is a relation with prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which is not accepted. Therefore, the entire world would result in being eternal. How, then, can there be a relation with non-existence?
Thus, this [objection] is a source of confusion, even regarding those things intended to be non-different in meaning.
In words, the cognitions that differentiate the denotable objects have exclusion as their basis. (117)

[242, vii] Whether the object is distinct or non-distinct, in every case the relation is merely imagined by the intellect (*buddhiparikalpita*). If a thing were distinct from another thing, what would the relation be? If you say it is simply the state of being distinct (*vyatireka*), then even if they are indeed distinct, what would constitute their relation? Since the state of being distinct is common to all cases, there would be no relation at all. If you say the relation is characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), [242, viii]

If [the cause and effect] are distinct, what kind of relation could there be? Or if they are non-distinct, how could there be a causal relationship? Furthermore, if another entity exists, how could those two [cause and effect] ever be separated or joined?

Indeed, for that which is non-different, there can be no relation because a relation resides in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*); thus, it would not be a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). But why could it not be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*)? No; because in that case, the relation has a conceptualized (*kalpita*) object. For in that case, the two relata are conceptualized; since they are distinct, it is established that there is no relation characterized by identity. If it is argued that it is a cause-and-effect relationship: what is this so-called "causality"? If it is said to be the state of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekitva*), no; because that too is conceptualized, as it is not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, all of this is merely constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanānirmita*) and is not ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Consequently, this use of the ablative case expressing separation (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) proceeds by relying on some kind of conceptualized relation, and there is no other way. Even with respect to antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, the relation of an entity is conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and not ultimate; in the ultimate sense, nothing is related to anything—this is the definitive conclusion. Therefore, [the cognition] based on the conjunction of phonemes and universals is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because there is no separate object of cognition (*prameyāntara*). Furthermore, it does not result in an infinite regress (*aniṣṭhā*) upon repeated recognition, just like memory and so forth; for repeated recognition is indeed nothing but the recollection of what was previously experienced.

[242,xi] But surely, because it conforms to the operation of the sense faculties and because it is non-erroneous, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); how then can it be an invalid means? No; for the operation of the sense faculties has as its object only that which is immediately present. If its object is only that which is immediately present, how is it that one acts on the basis of the thought "this is that very same thing"? This is not so, because a discerning person does not act solely on the basis of the thought "this is that very same thing.

It exists solely as the cause for the attainment of the desired result. Even though it is that very same [entity], it is nevertheless not the object of purposeful activity (*pravartana*). For the actions of discerning persons have as their object the means for accomplishing a purposeful effect (*arthakriyā*). Nor can that [purposeful effect] be accomplished by that [identical entity] alone; for entities possess powers dependent upon their own causes, and they bring about either that [specific] purposeful effect or another, not by virtue of being a locus of identity. Furthermore, the connection with a purposeful effect is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is only the recollection of what was previously seen. And the object of the cognition "this is that very same thing" is its capacity to perform that purposeful effect, not its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). If it were grasped previously as something already seen, then [the present cognition] would be nothing but memory. If, however, there is a synthesis here [of the past and present], then it is inference; for even here, the capacity for that purposeful effect is the basis. The conventional usage of "identity" occurs through the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of non-difference. Non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*) also does not have identity as its object, since the attainment of the purposeful effect occurs even in the absence of identity. As for [the case of] approaching a woman who should not be approached and so forth, this is due solely to being produced from that [cause], and is thus relative to the continuum (*santati*).
Therefore, perception does not have the universal as its object, nor does inference have the particular as its object.
Now, it might be argued that inference based on the perception of particulars (*viśeṣadṛṣṭam anumānam*) recognizes only a particular. That too is incorrect,
because there is no recognition of a particular due to its difference at every moment.
Nor is it an object of particularity, because that [particularity] is grasped through its similarity to what has been perceived. // 118 //

[243,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as being real. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor apprehend any dharma as being real? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real, nor does he apprehend form as being real; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he apprehend the eye as being real; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he apprehend forms as being real; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he apprehend the eye-consciousness as being real; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he apprehend eye-contact as being real; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as real, nor does he apprehend the sensation born of eye-contact as being real; he does not perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he apprehend the earth element as being real; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he apprehend ignorance as being real; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or old age and death as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he apprehend the conditioned as being real; he does not perceive the unconditioned as real, nor does he apprehend the unconditioned as being real. He does not perceive the past as real, nor does he apprehend the past as being real; he does not perceive the future as real, nor does he apprehend the future as being real; he does not perceive the present as real, nor does he apprehend the present as being real. He does not perceive the world of desire as real, nor does he apprehend the world of desire as being real; he does not perceive the world of form as real, nor does he apprehend the world of form as being real; he does not perceive the formless world as real, nor does he apprehend the formless world as being real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he apprehend the stream-enterer as being real; he does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he apprehend the fruit of stream-entry as being real. He does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he apprehend the once-returner as being real; he does not perceive the fruit of once-returning as real, nor does he apprehend the fruit of once-returning as being real. He does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he apprehend the non-returner as being real; he does not perceive the fruit of non-returning as real, nor does he apprehend the fruit of non-returning as being real. He does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he apprehend the arhat as being real; he does not perceive the fruit of arhatship as real, nor does he apprehend the fruit of arhatship as being real. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he apprehend the pratyekabuddha as being real; he does not perceive the path of the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he apprehend the path of the pratyekabuddha as being real. He does not perceive the bodhisattva as real, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva as being real; he does not perceive the path of the bodhisattva as real, nor does he apprehend the path of the bodhisattva as being real. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he apprehend the Tathāgata as being real; he does not perceive the Dharma as real, nor does he apprehend the Dharma as being real; he does not perceive the Saṅgha as real, nor does he apprehend the Saṅgha as being real. He does not perceive the perfection of generosity as real, nor does he apprehend the perfection of generosity as being real; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he apprehend the emptiness of the internal as being real; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainment, or the emptiness of non-repudiation as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he apprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata as being real; he does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he apprehend them as being real. He does not perceive the knowledge of all modes as real, nor does he apprehend the knowledge of all modes as being real. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as being real. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor apprehend any dharma as being real, then how does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of ethical discipline? How does he train in the perfection of patience? How does he train in the perfection of vigor? How does he train in the perfection of meditation? How does he train in the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the emptiness of the internal? How does he train in the emptiness of the external? How does he train in the emptiness of the internal and external? How does he train in the emptiness of emptiness? How does he train in the great emptiness? How does he train in the emptiness of the ultimate? How does he train in the emptiness of the conditioned? How does he train in the emptiness of the unconditioned? How does he train in the absolute emptiness? How does he train in the emptiness of the beginningless and endless? How does he train in the emptiness of dispersion? How does he train in the emptiness of nature? How does he train in the emptiness of all dharmas? How does he train in the emptiness of own-marks? How does he train in the emptiness of non-existence? How does he train in the emptiness of existence? How does he train in the emptiness of non-attainment? How does he train in the emptiness of non-repudiation? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata? How does he train in the four grounds of self-confidence? How does he train in the four analytical knowledges? How does he train in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha? How does he train in the great compassion of a Tathāgata? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of giving, he does not perceive the gift as real, nor does he perceive the recipient as real, nor does he perceive himself as real. Because he does not perceive these three things as real, he gives a gift without apprehending

When fire has indeed been seen and, having subsequently receded and being concealed by an obstruction, it is inferred from smoke, then at that later time, that very same particularity is not recognized due to the possibility of successive differences. And when difference exists, a cognition through the superimposition of oneness takes as its object only the universal (*sāmānya*). But where, in the case of a stable substance, no difference is possible because of the absence of modification, there is the recognition of that very same particularity. How is this to be understood? For there is no certainty that modification is impossible simply because it is not being perceived. If it were seen to be so even elsewhere, then, by analogy with what is seen, the cognition would be of another individual (*vyakti*) and would not have the particular as its object.

If that very same example is what constitutes the non-apprehension of a universal, then since it is already established by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its being an example, what further purpose is served by this? (119)

[243, vii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not the case that the Tathāgata does not know or does not see this; rather, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows this and sees this. However, Ānanda, if he were to teach the Dharma to others concerning this matter, others would not believe him, and that would lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four inconceivable things in the world. What four? The scope of the Buddhas is an inconceivable thing in the world; the scope of the meditative absorption of the Buddhas is an inconceivable thing in the world; the result of karma is an inconceivable thing in the world; and the sphere of the Buddhas is an inconceivable thing in the world. These, Ānanda, are the four inconceivable things in the world. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four unthinkables. What four? The thought of a Buddha is an unthinkable thing; the thought of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is an unthinkable thing; the ripening of karma is an unthinkable thing; and the sphere of a Buddha is an unthinkable thing. These, Ānanda, are the four unthinkables. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four immeasurables. What four? The measure of a Buddha is immeasurable; the measure of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is immeasurable; the measure of the ripening of karma is immeasurable; and the measure of the sphere of a Buddha is immeasurable. These, Ānanda, are the four immeasurables. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four unfathomable things. What four? The fathom of a Buddha is unfathomable; the fathom of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is unfathomable; the fathom of the ripening of karma is unfathomable; and the fathom of the sphere of a Buddha is unfathomable. These, Ānanda, are the four unfathomable things. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be pondered. What four? One who ponders the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who ponders the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who ponders the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who ponders the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be pondered. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be investigated. What four? One who investigates the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who investigates the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who investigates the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who investigates the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be investigated. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be scrutinized. What four? One who scrutinizes the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who scrutinizes the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who scrutinizes the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who scrutinizes the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be scrutinized. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be examined. What four? One who examines the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who examines the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who examines the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who examines the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be examined. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be measured. What four? One who measures the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who measures the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who measures the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who measures the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be measured. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be calculated. What four? One who calculates the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who calculates the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who calculates the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who calculates the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be calculated. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be reckoned. What four? One who reckons the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who reckons the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who reckons the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who reckons the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be reckoned. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be deliberated upon. What four? One who deliberates upon the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who deliberates upon the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who deliberates upon the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who deliberates upon the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be deliberated upon. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be scrutinized. What four? One who scrutinizes the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who scrutinizes the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who scrutinizes the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who scrutinizes the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be scrutinized. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be investigated. What four? One who investigates the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who investigates the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who investigates the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who investigates the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be investigated. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be pondered. What four? One who ponders the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who ponders the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who ponders the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who ponders the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be pondered. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be reckoned. What four? One who reckons the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who reckons the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who reckons the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who reckons the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be reckoned. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be deliberated upon. What four? One who deliberates upon the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who deliberates upon the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who deliberates upon the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who deliberates upon the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined. These, Ānanda, are the four things that are not to be deliberated upon. This is what was said. And it was further said: “Ānanda, there are these four things that are not to be scrutinized. What four? One who scrutinizes the power of a Buddha is ruined; one who scrutinizes the power of the meditative absorption of a Buddha is ruined; one who scrutinizes the power of the ripening of karma is ruined; and one who scrutinizes the power of the sphere of a Buddha is ruined.

If that very same instance is established by a previous perception, then since it has already been grasped by that prior perception, what further need is there for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? There is no role for inference (*anumāna*) here. If it is argued that the previous perception itself is sufficient because it apprehends the existence [of the object] at the time when the inference based on the observation of particulars (*viśeṣadṛṣṭānumāna*) occurs, then what is the use of inference? For it is accepted that inference operates upon what is not the object of perception, and not upon that very [perceived] thing. If it is then claimed that this is precisely why it is called "inference from the observation of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), let it be so; however, it would not be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, if it is held that through perception only an object existing at the same time as the act of seeing is grasped, and not any other, then inference operating toward a future object would indeed be a valid means of cognition. If this is the case, then the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) is one form perceived previously, while the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is another form perceived at a later time by inference. If it is then argued that the object was indeed grasped but merely forgotten, and therefore this fault does not apply, he says:
If it is argued that there is no fault because it has been forgotten, for that very reason it is non-exemplified.

If that [object] which was forgotten is remembered again by means of the logical mark (*liṅga*) in exactly the same way, then inference is not purposeless. But how can there be an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for something that has been forgotten? For the proof proceeds by means of an example; if it has been forgotten, how can it serve as an example? If its memory as an example occurred prior to the logical mark, then what further function would the logical mark have here? If you say that it is that very thing which is being remembered again, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). On the other hand, if it has been forgotten, then it lacks the status of an example. Furthermore, if one apprehends fire from smoke all of a sudden without an example, and another person—having forgotten [the concomitance]—apprehends it from the logical mark, then since that [fire] pervades all moments of time without exception and was already grasped by a previous perception, how can it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for one who does not perceive any new particularity?

If it is argued that [the validity of a reason] exists because there is conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) once recollection has occurred—just as, for instance, when a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is apprehended in its entirety, it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) precisely through such conventional usage—it is not so. For in that case, the fitness for conventional usage is established solely by way of similarity with another observed example (*dṛṣṭānta*). But here it is not so, because [the object] was previously non-existent and because no habituation (*abhyāsa*) has arisen. Even the claim that "this has been seen" is not tenable, since it could have occurred otherwise.

Indeed, it is not established that this is a memory of something already grasped, because there exists the state of being ungrasped; for a form that terminates at its own time is grasped by perception—otherwise, it would be grasped until death, and thus death would occur at that very moment. If it is argued that it is grasped continuously until death, [we reply: with a long [duration of attention] there is grasping for a long time, and with a short [attention] there is grasping for the other.
By means of perception, there is no apprehension of this [object] up until its death at that very moment.

Therefore, that which does not persist cannot encompass a duration of time. Consequently, how can inference proceed based on what has been grasped as a "perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*)? And how can that itself serve as an example? Thus, there is no apprehension of a universal (*sāmānya*).

if it is argued that when something else arises at another time through a connection with a previous time, its identity with that [previous thing] is established, and thus this is merely "inference from the particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), to this it is replied:
If it is argued that the existence [of a thing] is established through a means of valid cognition when that thing is perceived, then [the same must apply] to other objects. || 120 ||
When there is a superimposition of reality, there is error; because that [superimposition] is established, it lacks the status of a valid means of cognition.

Now, if you maintain that even when something else is seen, it is subsequently established as being "this very same thing" at a later time, then that is necessarily a superimposition of its identity upon something other than itself; it is, therefore, an error. For it is not possible for an object actually perceived as one thing to truly exist in its essential nature as another. Furthermore, regarding an object not currently being perceived, one can only superimpose the form of what was previously perceived, and not grasp its true reality. This is because that previously seen object was grasped by the prior cognition precisely as it was associated with a specific, non-different form. If you argue: "Even if it is not grasped [by perception], it is nevertheless grasped as the very same reality through inference, and not as something else," we reply: No, because inference follows the prior apprehension; inference is nothing other than mere recollection. If, on the other hand, inference is of the nature of grasping the actual entity (*vastu*), then:
Because perception and its opposite are one, the establishment of one entails the establishment of both.

[244,ix] If both perception and the other [inference] were one and the same form, then because it would be established by a single means of knowledge—whether perception or the other—the other would become non-authoritative, since no distinction whatsoever would be produced by the other. In that case, the cognition of a clear form would occur in both instances, or else [no clear form at all]. If it is argued that the lack of clarity arises from the non-operation of the eyes and so forth, because clarity is dependent upon them, this is not so.
If this clear manifestation were bound to the eye and other sense organs,
then light would be entirely useless for the apprehension of form.

If clarity is produced by light, then when there is actual light, how can inference have an indistinct appearance? If it is argued that this is because light is only occasional, then even though light exists in reality, it is not perceived; so how can there be a grasping of the object? If it is argued that there is no fault because one grasps the mere object devoid of light, this is audacity—to claim that what was accompanied by light is now grasped as being devoid of it! If that were the case, it would simply be a grasping of a generality (*sāmānya*), and thus this would not be "perception based on a particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, they consider a judgment that is being synthesized with something else to be memory.
If it is argued that it is not memory because it depends on a sign (taccihna), that is not so, because memory does not deviate from its object.

Moreover, this is merely a synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of what was previously seen; it is not an apprehension through a distinct intrinsic nature at that time, but rather memory itself. For when there is identity of form between perception and inference, nothing more is cognized than [was already known]; thus it is simply memory, which does not constitute the grasping of a real entity (*vastu*).

Now, if [the cognition] arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*), how can it be memory? This is not so. For, according to your view, this [cognition] does not possess the nature of a logical mark, because the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are absent due to the identity of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dārṣṭāntika*). In our position, however, it has been established that this is indeed inference, having the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. For that very thing which was previously understood is what is being remembered; it is not an object of direct perception (*grāhya*), since it is not perceived as being currently grasped. Indeed, there is no memory other than the memory arising from an inference. Therefore, that by which the same thing is repeatedly cognized is precisely memory. How, then, is there the cognition "it exists now"? The present existence is understood solely through the power of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). It is understood precisely in this way—through the prior apprehension of the relationship—that the smoke existing in that location is produced by the fire existing in that same location, due to the awakening of beginningless mental impressions (*vāsanā*). This being the case, it is established that all inference is indeed memory. Because the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are of two kinds, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are of two kinds, distinguished as perception and inference. This is because there is no other mode [of cognition] apart from the distinction between direct and indirect cognition.
<4. Investigation of Direct Perception> <(1) Refutation of Misconceptions Regarding the Definition of Direct Perception> [245,ii]
In that regard:
perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.

Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is the non-apprehension of the appearance of a real entity as connected with qualifiers and so forth; otherwise, such an appearance is error. Perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that which is free from both of these.

[Objection: But surely its erroneous nature is understood through perception because it is seen otherwise; however, how can its freedom from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatā*) be known? For inference, which is preceded by perception, does not find an occasion to function in the absence of that [perception]. And every cognition arises precisely from the accompaniment of words; therefore, how could perception—which is itself conceptual—understand its own non-conceptual nature? Even for one who holds that an initial "mere observation" (*ālocanājñāna*) arises free from conceptualization, the arising of a conceptual cognition occurs due to the convergence of the causal complex consisting of memory and so forth. And since that [conceptual cognition] proceeds from the operation of the sense organ, it is indeed perception. How, then, can its non-conceptual nature be established? [Response: To this, the reply is as follows:
Perception, which is free from conceptual construction, is established by perception itself.
Conceptualization, which relies upon names, is personally experienced by everyone. (123)

[245, vii] Perception, being free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is recognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone. For that which is called a conceptual construction produces a name, and that name in turn produces a conceptual construction; such a conceptual construction, based upon names, is experienced as being cognized within oneself, because the conceptual construction is experienced through self-awareness. Consequently, between the cognition of a conceptual construction and other cognitions—such as those of the eye and so forth that perceive visible objects—there is indeed a difference, due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). Even if it were argued that this [perception] is always of the nature of that [conceptual construction], that too is not the case, because:
[245, viii]
Having withdrawn all thought from every side with a tranquil inner self, even while remaining still, one perceives form with the eye; such is cognition born of direct perception.

If the eye does not function at all when it is devoid of the causal complex for conceptualization— such as in the state where conceptualization has been withdrawn or when another conceptualization is manifest— it would not be a grasper of objects. Therefore, in that state, the cognition appearing as free from conceptual construction is understood through perception itself.

[Objection: If it is the case that "there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in this" is precisely what constitutes the cognition [of non-conceptuality], then how can that state be devoid of conceptual construction? Alternatively, if there is no conceptual construction [at all], then how can there be the cognition "this is non-conceptual," given that at that time there is no relationship between a locus and its content (*ādhārādheyabhāva*)? For indeed, there is no linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*) without conceptual construction; nor does one who does not engage in such linguistic practice cause another to understand [the state]. Otherwise, even regarding momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), why would one employ a "reason of essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*) which effects linguistic practice? [Reply: To this it is said: When you subsequently conceptualize something, such a conceptual construction as "it existed" arises for you.
Thus one does not know [the object] when it has gone from the sense organ in the state previously described. || 125 ||

[246,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that the five aggregates were all empty, and he was delivered from all suffering and distress. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or object of mind; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; there is no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death; there is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted views, one reaches ultimate nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. [247,i] At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses: "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that the five aggregates were empty and was delivered from all suffering and distress. 'Form is emptiness, emptiness is form'; 'form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. 'O Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness'; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. 'Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness'; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or object of mind; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; there is no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death; there is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted views, one reaches ultimate nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. [247,ii] When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, along with the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. [248,i] The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume One. Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. [248,ii] The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Volume Two. Chapter on the Profundity of the Dharma. [248,iii] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha told Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should thus contemplate: 'All dharmas are empty in their nature; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates in this way, at that time, form is not form, feeling is not feeling, perception is not perception, mental formations are not mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness. Why is this? Subhūti, form is empty in its own nature; it is neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty in their own nature, they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, at that time, Māra, the King of Demons, will come to that place to create obstacles. Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that Māra, the King of Demons, can seize? Subhūti said to the Buddha: "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? World-Honored One, all dharmas are ungraspable. Why is this? World-Honored One, all dharmas are empty in their own nature; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, World-Honored One, there is no dharma that Māra, the King of Demons, can seize. The Buddha told Subhūti: "It is so, it is so. It is as you say. Subhūti, all dharmas are empty in their own nature; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, at that time, Māra, the King of Demons, cannot find any opportunity to create obstacles. Subhūti, suppose a man were to enter a village or town and see various forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and dharmas. Having seen them, he would not grasp at their characteristics. Why is this? Subhūti, that man has already cultivated the power of mindfulness and concentration in past lives. Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way is also like this. Even if he encounters various forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and dharmas, he does not grasp at their characteristics. Why is this? Subhūti, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already cultivated the power of mindfulness and concentration in past lives. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, at that time, Māra, the King of Demons, cannot find any opportunity to create obstacles. Subhūti, suppose a man were to enter a village or town and see various forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and dharmas. Having seen them, he would not grasp at their characteristics. Why is this? Subhūti, that man has already cultivated the power of mindfulness and concentration in past lives. Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way is also like this. Even if he encounters various forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and dharmas, he does not grasp at their characteristics. Why is this? Subhūti, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already cultivated the power of mindfulness and concentration in past lives. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, at that time, Māra, the King of Demons, cannot find any opportunity to create

Indeed, no such conceptual construction arises for him [the proponent of non-conceptual perception] that "this is non-conceptual. Otherwise, even for one who maintains that perception is conceptual, as long as the certainty that "this is conceptual" has not arisen, how could there be the conventional designation of "conceptuality"? Consequently, even for the conventional designation of conceptuality, another conceptualization would have to be sought, and yet another for that, leading to an infinite regress and thus a lack of comprehension. If it is argued that this [perception] is itself conceptual, what is the need for another? Since even the non-conceptual has the nature of cognition, the question "what is the use of conceptualization? applies equally to both positions.

[246,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form. He does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than consciousness; consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form—if form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form—and if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than consciousness—if consciousness itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is consciousness—then, Blessed One, how can there be the designation of ‘sentient beings,’ ‘individuals,’ ‘beings,’ ‘persons,’ ‘human beings,’ ‘humans,’ ‘those who have a self,’ ‘those who have a soul,’ ‘those who have a life-principle,’ ‘those who have a personhood,’ ‘those who have a human being,’ or ‘those who have a man’? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all these dharmas are empty, they are nevertheless designated by means of names and conventions. Subhūti, those names and conventions do not exist in those dharmas, nor are they found therein. They are merely names and conventions established by the Tathāgata for the sake of teaching the Dharma to sentient beings. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty, how then does the Tathāgata know all dharmas? How does he fully awaken to them? How does he turn the wheel of the Dharma? And how does he teach the Dharma to sentient beings? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: the Tathāgata knows all dharmas as they truly are through the emptiness of intrinsic nature. It is through this emptiness of intrinsic nature that he fully awakens to all dharmas. It is through this emptiness of intrinsic nature that he turns the wheel of the Dharma. And it is through this emptiness of intrinsic nature that he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how does the Tathāgata distinguish between the five classes of persons—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha—and how does he distinguish between the bodhisattva mahāsattva and the tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: although all these dharmas are empty, yet the Tathāgata, through his skill in means, distinguishes between the five classes of persons—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat, and the pratyekabuddha—and distinguishes between the bodhisattva mahāsattva and the tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one. Subhūti, it is because of this emptiness of intrinsic nature that the Tathāgata knows all dharmas as they truly are, and it is because of this emptiness of intrinsic nature that he teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.”

Now, regarding the subsequent conventional usage of "this is conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) with respect to what was previously non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), even here, for one who subsequently reflects, there is the conventional usage that "there was such a succession of conceptualizations," but this does not occur during the state when conceptualization has been withdrawn. For in that state, there is no such conventional usage as "I was in a state of non-conceptuality. If it is asked: "How can there be a conventional usage by means of a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding something that did not exist at that time? [The answer is: How is there the conventional usage "he is dead" regarding one who is dead? If you say, "Because one sees another of that same kind [later]," then here too, repeated observation during the state when conceptualization has been withdrawn is certainly not prevented. Therefore, because of the difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bheda*) and because they are mutually exclusive, there is no identity between the conceptual and the other (the non-conceptual).

if it is argued that because of the presence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), a distinct conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) arises due to the commencement of conceptualization, whereas in its absence a non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpaka*) arises— that is incoherent.
If the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is imagined [to be a single entity], then because blue and yellow are distinct,
this collection must be something entirely different, on the grounds that it has arisen as such.

For in that case, a completely different collection of blue, yellow, and so forth has arisen due to the occurrence of a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Now, if it is argued that because of recognition—through the cognition "this very same blue, and not another collection"—the conceptualization of difference is identical for both of these imagined forms, then perception must indeed be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
[246, viii]

Furthermore, this causal complex consisting of memory and so forth does not constitute the conceptualization of sensory consciousness, because the sense faculty is engaged in the apprehension of the object. Nor can an object apprehended by the senses be conjoined with a word, because the word lacks the capacity to denote that [particular], since linguistic convention does not apply to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). This is because the universal (*sāmānya*) is not apprehended by the senses. If one asks why this is so, he says:
"For a difference observed in one place is not seen elsewhere."
Therefore, there is no other universal distinct from that [particular], because there is no difference in cognition.

[246,x] For difference does not follow from place and time, because what is seen in one place is seen again elsewhere by that same or another perception; since that [entity] does not exist during another time, an entity delimited by its own time is indeed apprehended through perception. Therefore, the former is not perceived in the latter, nor is the latter perceived in the former. If it is argued that one grasps "this is that very same thing" through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), [we reply: no, because recognition is not perception, as there is no operation of the sense faculties therein. For instance: [246,xi]
The functioning of the sense-faculties occurs only with respect to objects situated in a suitable location, not toward those that are past or future;
and the consciousness dependent upon them does not apprehend what exists at another time.

The pervasion [of an object] over time and space is not grasped by sensory cognition; for if that were so, everyone would be a seer of all forms. Now, if the sense organs do not operate upon the past or the future, what contradiction is there for the cognition dependent upon them? If the cognition dependent upon them were to operate upon the past and so forth, then the eye too would have to operate [there]. There is no operation of the eye other than [its own specific function]. Nor is the activity of the eye perceived in the grasping of what precedes and follows, because the grasping of the preceding and succeeding moments occurs through memory and inference. If it is argued that this [grasping] is indeed the operation of the sense organ, we shall demonstrate that this would entail the undesirable consequence that even inference would be perception. Therefore, individual particulars (bhedāḥ) do not possess continuity. If it is argued that the universal (sāmānya), which is continuous, is what is grasped by the senses—that is incorrect, because: [The verse: Since the universal is not distinct from the particular, and since the particular is not established as being without difference, therefore the universal is not perceived by the senses. [247,ii] There is no other universal distinct from that [particular], because there is no difference in cognition.

There is no continuity (*anvaya*) among individuals, nor is there any for the universal (*sāmānya*), precisely because it does not exist. The existence of individuals does not constitute their continuity; nor is there continuity of the universal, for that is not perceived. Because it is non-existent, continuity is impossible within the range of sensory perception. Indeed, the universal does not appear here, since no other form appears; and if there were no distinction [from the individual], the individuals themselves would be [the object]. Yet those individuals are not continuous. For this very reason, the universal is neither different, nor non-different, nor inexpressible.
Therefore, every cognition born of the senses has particulars (*viśeṣa*) as its object.
It is impossible for words to function with respect to particulars. (127)

Because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among particulars, linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) does not apply to them. For when that which possesses positive concomitance appears, it is in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*); nor do words function with respect to a particular (*viśeṣa*), because convention cannot be established due to the lack of positive concomitance. Indeed, convention is desired by those engaged in worldly practice for the sake of functioning across different places and times; otherwise, it would result in nothing but frustration. If it is argued that it is for the sake of dharma and artha, who would accept such a thing? Therefore, convention does not apply to what is restricted to a specific place and time. Consequently, the particular is not the object of words.
Whatever object is the domain of words, that alone can be associated with them. (128)

[247, viii] Therefore, because it involves the apprehension of a connection, it is not devoid of qualification. Consequently, a cognition that apprehends a qualification is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). And whatever is conceptual does not apprehend a particular (*viśeṣa*), because it connects the universal (*sāmānya*) with a word. Why is this so? He says:
In the relation expressed as "this belongs to that," the relation exists only between those two objects that appear [in cognition]; at that time, it is not within the range of the sense faculty.

Even when an object is perceived, the relationship characterized by the signified and the signifier belongs only to those two things—the cognition of which arises in the consciousness that establishes the relationship, namely: "this is the signifier of this," or "this is the signified of this. And at that time, [the relationship] is not within the range of the senses; why? What is the meaning of "this is the signified of this"? It means "this is to be understood from this. By what kind of cognition? Is it by a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) of an imperceptible object, or by a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that realizes [the object]? If it were to be understood by a direct perception that realizes [the object], then the collection of the sense organs would result in futility. If, on the other hand, it is through imperceptibility, then there is no relationship with an object that is within the range of the senses; for at that time, the object is not within the range of the senses. Or, [it might be argued that] even when the object and the word have entered the domain of the signified, the relationship is established as "this is the signifier of this. For instance:
Because at that time the object with its clear manifestation is not perceived as distinct [from consciousness],
for it is the difference in the manifestation within consciousness that distinguishes one thing from another. (130)

[247,xii] For an object that is within the range of the sense faculties possesses a clear manifestation (*viśadapratibhāsa*), whereas an object that is remote possesses an unclear manifestation. And there is no identity despite a difference in manifestation. Now, if cognitions have the very same object even when there is a difference in the degree of clarity due to distance or proximity, how can there be a distinction based on a difference in manifestation? Because there is a distinction based on a difference in causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).

But surely, even when there is a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), there is only a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*), and not a difference in a distinct effect as the defining characteristic of difference. For the difference of a cause is not established by a difference in effects unless it is produced by a difference in appearance; yet, [you might argue,] a difference in appearance certainly exists here as well. If that is so, then let the difference arise from that alone—what is the use of a difference in effects? Furthermore, if the difference of a cause arises from a difference in its effects, then from what does the difference of the effect itself arise? If it is from another difference in effect, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is from a difference in appearance, then let the difference of the cause also arise from that alone—what is the use of a difference in effects? Now, if there is a difference [of the cause] even through a difference in activity, then that very difference in appearance is the differentiator, because only a clear appearance performs causal efficiency. Therefore, an unclear appearance of an object situated at a distance does not have a real entity as its object. If it is argued that they have the same object because of non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*), that is also present in the case of inference; in that case too, the difference [from perception] arises precisely from a difference in appearance. Thus, difference arises solely from a difference in appearance.
[248,ii] But when one, with eyes wide open, establishes a convention for such an object, then the word will have a real entity as its object. To this, the following is the determination:
Even when an object appears before the eye, that which one declares to be "beyond" [the senses] is the very thing associated with words; indeed, it is not the actual range of the sense organ.

[248,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving as a real entity, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a real entity. He does not perceive form as a real entity, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a real entity. He does not perceive the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a real entity. He does not perceive forms as real entities, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real entities. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a real entity, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real entities. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the earth element as a real entity, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real entities. He does not perceive ignorance as a real entity, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real entities. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as a real entity, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, arhatship, or pratyekabuddhahood as real entities. He does not perceive the state of a bodhisattva as a real entity, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata as a real entity. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, these dharmas are all empty; they are not apprehended, they do not exist, and they are not found. Since they are empty, they cannot be apprehended; since they do not exist, they cannot be apprehended; since they are not found, they cannot be apprehended. Therefore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as a real entity.”

Even though there is indeed the appearance of sound, a jar, and so forth, to the eye and the ear, nevertheless, a relation does not exist by virtue of their appearing in their own nature alone. That which one expresses with an ablative case-ending (*vyatireka-vibhakti*) as "this is the designator of that" is precisely what is being abandoned [in direct perception]. Furthermore, the meaning of a case-ending does not appear in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because only the meaning of the nominal stem (*pratipadika*) appears. The meaning of a case-ending, however, is the object of conceptual appearance (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*) alone. For instance, a relation such as "this belongs to that" does not occur without a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva*). Therefore, the case-ending occurs based on a relation characterized by cause and effect between the cognition and the form of the representation—such that sometimes the word arises from the object as the mental domain, and sometimes the object resides in the cognition from the word—but the appearance in direct perception itself is not the cause for establishing a relation, since the relation exists even without it. Moreover, if the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) were applied to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) appearing to the eye and other senses, then only that [particular] would appear; but this is not the case.
Because one whose sense faculties are not engaged does not investigate by means of mere subsequent speech.

Now, it might be argued: "Even if there is no convention regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), what contradiction is there in that very thing being the denotable object? [To this we reply:

"And it is not the case that [the object] would be known by itself without a previously established relation," because that would lead to the absurd consequence [of knowledge arising] spontaneously. (132)

[248, viii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, monks, edible food, whether coarse or subtle, is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Contact is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Mental volition is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Consciousness is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Monks, when a noble disciple has abandoned these four nutriments, he is called one who has cut off craving, removed the fetters, and through the complete destruction of pride, has attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. This, monks, is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks! “Friend,” they replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One taught that there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, friends, edible food, whether coarse or subtle, is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Contact is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Mental volition is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Consciousness is to be abandoned by means of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Friends, when a noble disciple has abandoned these four nutriments, he is called one who has cut off craving, removed the fetters, and through the complete destruction of pride, has attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is called the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. This, friends, is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering. Thus spoke the Venerable Ānanda. Having thus spoken, the Venerable Ānanda sat down on a prepared seat at one side. Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta. Having thus spoken, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
