Alternatively, if the convention pertains to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), how is there a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) in exactly that same way? To this he says: "And not... and so forth. Therefore, sensory cognition cognizes only that which is inexpressible and unrelated; thus it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). How then is the conceptual cognition—"This is a cow," "This is a snake, a snake"—perceived as having a clear manifestation? Nor can it be maintained that the conceptualization exists here as something separate [from the perception], because no other apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is observed. Furthermore, the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) for the conceptualization here cannot be something beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), because that would entail the consequence of two distinct appearances: one clear and the other otherwise. If it is argued that it was manifested even previously, but one does not conceptualize it [then], there is no difference in its status as an object of apprehension at the time of conceptualization. And if one does not produce a distinction regarding the object of apprehension, how can one be an apprehender? That too is incorrect.

Since a distinction is perceived through its being either certain or uncertain, how could it be that there is no distinction here? Nor is there any logical inconsistency in what is observed. (301) (PVA)
[248,x] For that which is being perceived cannot itself be the object of negation. If it is argued that conceptual cognition is non-existent, that is incorrect.
How is the non-existence of the cognizer established? Because it is conceptual.
Let that same non-existence be asserted even in the case of non-conceptual cognition.

It is not the case that something is unreal simply because it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*). For if that were so, it would follow that even non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) cognition is unreal. If you argue that it is not unreal because it is non-conceptual, then this same logic applies equally to conceptual cognition; thus there is no distinction. Furthermore, how could direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) be unreal? Non-conceptual cognition might indeed be unreal due to the absence of ascertainment (*niścaya*); however, when there is a direct perception of an ascertained form, how can there be any suspicion of its unreality?

Now, if it is argued that this ascertainment is inferential, that is incorrect; for since its object is immediate (*aparokṣa*), it cannot be an inference. This is because the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established precisely through the difference in their objects, and because the non-overlapping of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) has already been demonstrated. All of this is untenable, because:
[249, iii] Due to the simultaneous functioning of the mind toward both conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions...
Either through delusion or due to the rapidity of its functioning, one determines the identity of those two.

[249,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, will not be afraid, terrified, or fall into terror—these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have practiced for a long time. Subhūti, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have honored many Buddhas. Subhūti, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have made offerings to many Buddhas.”

This is its meaning: If indeed a non-conceptual [cognition] were to determine the phonemes such as *ga* in the word "cow" (*gauḥ*) and be inclined toward grasping the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then it would be logical to say that this conceptual cognition is one and the same as the perceptual cognition. However, the apprehension of the form of the phonemes is a cognition in which the phonemes appear indistinctly, arising from the awakening of the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) brought about by previous perceptions; it is entirely different from the perceptual cognition in which the pillar standing directly in front appears clearly, because conceptualization is impossible therein. That alone is the perceptual cognition. How then is there a determination of identity? There is none at all. First of all, the cognition "this is a cow" does not determine the identity of the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) with the phonemes *ga*, etc., because their difference is understood precisely through the difference in appearance. Furthermore, the conceptual cognitions of the phonemes *ga*, etc., which arise sequentially, lack unity. Nor is the cognition consisting of the appearance of phonemes itself what has the brindled cow as its object, because the brindled cow appears even in the absence of those [phonemes]. Moreover, that appearance of phonemes persists even when the eyes are closed. If it is argued that "the appearance in its absence is of an uncertain nature, whereas determination (*niścaya*) is a distinct quality," then what is this so-called "determination"? If it is said to be "the clear appearance of a form," no; for it has already appeared previously. If it appears as something prior, it is merely another indistinct form. Therefore, how can there be a determination of one thing while another form is appearing? If it is argued that "it is a determination because of the determination of their identity," how can a determination of identity be real regarding two things appearing as distinct? How then is there the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of identity? It is due to the single effect that prompts action. Because they function as a single effect, there is a determination of their identity. If it is asked, "How then is there not a sequential apprehension? it is simply because the objects are present simultaneously. For at the time of the conceptualization of phonemes, the perceptual object is not absent. And just as you, who maintain rapid functioning, have a determination of sequential apprehension despite the simultaneous presence of the objects, so too is my apprehension; there is no difference.

[249,v] But if conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs only elsewhere, why does its object not appear indistinctly in the form of the denotable (*vācya*)? If it is argued that it has no other object at all, then, being objectless, since it is unestablished even with respect to that [intended] object, there would be an interruption of perception due to the intervention of that [conceptual construction]. No; for there is no intervention. Indeed, an intervention is impossible when they are simultaneous. Furthermore: [249,vi]

If it is argued that "perception would become interrupted by the intervention of conceptual construction," then how could this be the case for a conceptualization of a different class or for anything else? (134)

For one for whom perception is exclusively conceptual, there is no interruption; indeed, it cannot be interrupted by itself. If it is argued that for the proponent of non-conceptual perception, conceptualization is something entirely different and thus constitutes an interruption—[then we reply: this may be so when a conceptualization of a different genus occurs.

How could there not be the perception of another object? For this conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which belongs to a different genus, cannot possess the nature of a perceptual cognition for another person, because it lacks the conceptualization of the form currently being seen. Now, suppose there is indeed an interruption here; however, because it is situated between two acts of seeing, that intermediate non-perception is overpowered by the stronger presence of the two perceptions and does not obtain its own functional status (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, there is an uninterrupted determination (*adhyavasāya*). That is equivalent to direct perception (*akṣasama*). Why?
[250,ii] If the side of existence (*bhāvapakṣa*) is considered powerful, like the vision of a whirling firebrand (*alātadṛṣṭi*).
In other cases as well, there is a simultaneous perception of either the two letters or their phonetic qualities. (135)

If the position that [the cognition] exists is strong, then even in the case of a conceptualization of a similar kind, there is no interruption at all for the proponent of non-conceptuality, because it is the same; thus, there is no fault. This was stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's view]; however, an interruption is not possible. For it is not the case that due to rapidity (*lāghava*), there arises a cognition of non-interruption even when an interruption exists. Because, due to rapidity, there would follow the consequence that two phonemes pronounced quickly would be heard simultaneously, yet this does not occur. Therefore, rapidity is not the cause for the apprehension of non-interruption here, even though there is a sequence. Now, if it is argued that rapidity itself does not exist there, and thus there is no simultaneous hearing, whereas rapidity does exist here—how is that known? If it is argued that it is because of the non-simultaneous operation of two minds, this will be established later. If it is argued that otherwise the very apprehension of simultaneity would not occur, we say no, because simultaneity itself does exist [in some cases]. If it is argued, "In that case, let there be simultaneity even in the piercing of a hundred lotus petals; what is the use of postulating a sequence?", we say no. In that case, the reaching of different locations by means of a sequence is understood through inference. Here, however, there is no such inference; so how can a sequence be postulated? If it is asked, "What is the basis for postulating a lack of sequence?", the answer is: the manifestation itself is the nature of perception. No other proof is observed beyond its direct manifestation. As for what was previously stated—that rapidity alone is not the cause for the simultaneous hearing of phonemes—it is replied to as follows:
[250,iv] Even though all objects are simultaneously in contact with the sense faculties here, that [cognition] which appears as if unobstructed despite being separated by five [layers]— 136.
That cognition appears as if divided because it is mixed with momentary cognitions that are infinite in number; therefore, that variegation is such, and thus let cognitions be simultaneous. (137)

[250, vi] For one who holds that cognitions do not arise simultaneously, there is no other reason for the determination of simultaneity in cases where it occurs than the rapidity of their occurrence; it is due to this swift operation that such a determination arises. To this, it is said: Why does this [determination of simultaneity] not also occur when syllables are pronounced rapidly?

"Is it not the case that such lightness (lāghava) simply does not exist?"—so says the opponent. In that case, there must be an even greater degree of lightness than that, wherein there is the simultaneous convergence of the five sense-objects (*pañcaviṣayī-samavadhāna*) along with the sixfold nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-ṣāḍguṇya*). For example, consider one who hears a sweet song while simultaneously tasting all the flavors from the mouth of a fragrant and beautiful woman. In that situation, the mind is separated from each [object] by five [intervening factors]. Yet, in such a case, there is an extreme absence of lightness, and nevertheless, there is the appearance of simultaneous perception. If, even when there is an intervention by five [factors], the capacity for lightness to establish a single simultaneous determination exists, then why would it not exist here when there is an intervention by momentary cognitions regarding the objects of the phonemes? Therefore, the arising of cognitions at once is logical; otherwise, the contradiction could never be resolved. Thus, this is established: "because of the simultaneous occurrence of equal [cognitions]. Furthermore:
Furthermore, since there is no difference in the appearance [of objects], how could there be [the distinction between] those with intervals and those without?
Moreover, in the case of pure mental conceptualization, there could be no perception of succession. // 138 //

In some cases there is an interval where cognition is separated by a similar [moment], and in other cases there is no interval because it is not separated by a dissimilar conceptualization (*vikalpa*). How do those cognitions with intervals and without intervals come to be if there is no difference in their appearance? Furthermore, in the case of the pure continuum of mental conceptualization, the appearance would not be successive because of its rapid occurrence.
Now, if multiple cognitions were to arise simultaneously, how could there ever be a failure to perceive an object even when it is present? To this, the reply is:
"The non-perception of an object, even though it is present, occurs in some cases because the mind is attached elsewhere."
And this objection applies to both [theories], because of the incapacity [of the cause] and the deficiency in the production of another. // 139 //

[251,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in perfect wisdom should train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in perfect wisdom train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in perfect wisdom does not apprehend form as having the nature of form. He does not apprehend feeling as having the nature of feeling, nor perception as having the nature of perception, nor formations as having the nature of formations, nor consciousness as having the nature of consciousness. He does not apprehend the eye as having the nature of the eye, nor the ear as having the nature of the ear, nor the nose as having the nature of the nose, nor the tongue as having the nature of the tongue, nor the body as having the nature of the body, nor the mind as having the nature of the mind. He does not apprehend eye-consciousness as having the nature of eye-consciousness, nor ear-consciousness as having the nature of ear-consciousness, nor nose-consciousness as having the nature of nose-consciousness, nor tongue-consciousness as having the nature of tongue-consciousness, nor body-consciousness as having the nature of body-consciousness, nor mind-consciousness as having the nature of mind-consciousness. This objection applies equally to both [theories]. It is not equal, however, for the mind (*manas*), because it is attached to one [object] at a time. If it is argued, "Nevertheless, let there be the determination of simultaneous perception; where there is no great attachment, it certainly occurs," we too say this: where there is attachment, there is sequential perception, and elsewhere it is simultaneous. But there is no proof that it is not sequential perception in all cases. Furthermore, no other mind exists apart from the preceding cognition that is an object of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[251,v] But surely, even if sequential apprehension is possible when there is no simultaneous perception, simultaneous appearance is nonetheless possible. This too is not true; for that cognition does not arise from the synthesis of sequentially appearing [elements], but rather, there is indeed simultaneous appearance therein. Because:

The visual perception of a firebrand or similar object, due to its rapid motion, produces the illusion of a circle by obstructing the perception of its successive positions; it does not do so through the synthesis of individual visual perceptions.

[251, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that these four nutriments have a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for these four nutriments? It is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). For when there is craving, monks, physical food as gross nutriment comes to be; when there is craving, contact comes to be; when there is craving, mental volition comes to be; when there is craving, consciousness comes to be. Thus, monks, craving is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for these four nutriments. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that this craving has a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this craving? It is feeling (*vedanā*). For when there is feeling, monks, craving comes to be; when there is feeling, the thirst for existence comes to be; when there is feeling, the thirst for non-existence comes to be; when there is feeling, the thirst for both existence and non-existence comes to be. Thus, monks, feeling is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this craving. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that this feeling has a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this feeling? It is contact (*sparśa*). For when there is contact, monks, feeling comes to be; when there is contact, the experience of pleasure and pain comes to be; when there is contact, the experience of neither-pleasure-nor-pain comes to be. Thus, monks, contact is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this feeling. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that this contact has a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this contact? It is the sixfold sense base (*ṣaḍāyatana*). For when there is the sixfold sense base, monks, contact comes to be; when there is the sixfold sense base, the meeting of the three comes to be; when there is the sixfold sense base, the convergence of the three comes to be. Thus, monks, the sixfold sense base is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this contact. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that this sixfold sense base has a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this sixfold sense base? It is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). For when there is name-and-form, monks, the sixfold sense base comes to be; when there is name-and-form, the manifestation of the faculties comes to be; when there is name-and-form, the differentiation of the faculties comes to be. Thus, monks, name-and-form is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this sixfold sense base. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that this name-and-form has a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this name-and-form? It is consciousness (*vijñāna*). For when there is consciousness, monks, name-and-form comes to be; when there is consciousness, the descent of the embryo comes to be; when there is consciousness, the establishment of name-and-form comes to be. Thus, monks, consciousness is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this name-and-form. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that this consciousness has a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this consciousness? It is karmic formations (*saṃskāra*). For when there are karmic formations, monks, consciousness comes to be; when there are karmic formations, the accumulation of karma comes to be; when there are karmic formations, the projection of rebirth comes to be. Thus, monks, karmic formations are the source, the causal origin, and the condition for this consciousness. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that these karmic formations have a source, a causal origin, and a condition. And what, monks, is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for these karmic formations? It is ignorance (*avidyā*). For when there is ignorance, monks, karmic formations come to be; when there is ignorance, the performance of actions comes to be; when there is ignorance, the undertaking of deeds comes to be. Thus, monks, ignorance is the source, the causal origin, and the condition for these karmic formations. Thus, monks, this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) proceeds in such a way, and it is by means of this dependent origination that one understands the cessation of suffering. When there is no ignorance, karmic formations do not come to be; with the cessation of ignorance, karmic formations cease. When there are no karmic formations, consciousness does not come to be; with the cessation of karmic formations, consciousness ceases. When there is no consciousness, name-and-form does not come to be; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases. When there is no name-and-form, the sixfold sense base does not come to be; with the cessation of name-and-form, the sixfold sense base ceases. When there is no sixfold sense base, contact does not come to be; with the cessation of the sixfold sense base, contact ceases. When there is no contact, feeling does not come to be; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. When there is no feeling, craving does not come to be; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases. When there is no craving, clinging does not come to be; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases. When there is no clinging, becoming does not come to be; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases. When there is no becoming, birth does not come to be; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases. When there is no birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair do not come to be; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus, monks, is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. For it is due to the succession of the moments of a whirling firebrand—which revolve so rapidly—that the eye, being impaired, produces a cognition that appears as a wheel; yet this is not a cognition of the mind [itself], because the side of objective existence is stronger. Now, even in this case, when the five objects are present, the simultaneous appearance is merely an illusion. If you say, "In that case, every simultaneous appearance is indeed illusory," we reply: No, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being an illusion. For simultaneous appearance is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself as non-illusory. If that which is perceived in such a way were illusory despite the absence of any subverting factor (*bādhaka*), then this consequence would apply to all cognitions. Therefore, since there is no subverting factor, the fivefold group of consciousnesses (*vijñāna-pañcaka*) is established as being indeed simultaneous. Consequently, direct perception is exclusively free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).

Some fools assert that because it arises from the sense faculties and so forth, cognition is non-conceptual like the intellect of an infant; and they claim that the cause for conceptualization is the dullness of linguistic convention. (141)

[251,x] Others say that perception is non-conceptual because it is produced by the sense faculties, because it functions in the form of direct experience, because it is not mental, and so forth—just like the sensory cognition of an infant. And the sensory consciousness of an infant is non-conceptual because it is incapable of grasping linguistic conventions.
For those [who lack conceptualization], it would indeed be a matter of direct perception because of their non-conceptuality;
furthermore, due to the absence of the means of linguistic convention, that [perception] would not exist even later. (142)

For those fools who speak in this manner, [the object] would indeed be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*). Let it be so; for a fool, everything is indeed admitted to be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). Yet, even for a fool, there exists no prior and subsequent reflection (*parāmarśa*) regarding purposeful actions (*svārthakriyā*). If such reflection does not exist, then later on, there ought to be no conceptualization either, because of the absence of the means for grasping linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*), since the grasping of conventions occurs through conceptualization, and that [conceptualization] does not exist for the fool. Now, [if one argues]: [252,i]

If it is held that the mind exists as something for which linguistic conventions have not been established, then this would also apply to what is produced by the sense faculties; and such is the remaining argument.

If even for infants there exists a conceptualizing [mind] fallen within the sphere of mental activity (*manovyavahāra*), then because of their subsequent grasping of linguistic conventions (*saṅketa*) by means of that [conceptualizing mind], the mind would possess the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpaka*). If this were so, it would apply to sense-born [cognition] as well; sense-born cognition too would become conceptual, and who could prevent it? Furthermore, since that sense-cognition of an infant is incapable of grasping linguistic conventions, how [could it be conceptual]? If you say "because it is produced by the senses," no; for there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Moreover, even if an infant’s sense-cognition were indeed non-conceptual, from where does one know that it is so in all cases? For a reason is not seen to be a prover without the establishment of a necessary connection through a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) and without an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, if you say that what is sense-born is non-conceptual because it grasps only what is present and is devoid of reflection on the preceding and succeeding [moments], then how is its being devoid of reflection on the preceding and succeeding established? Since direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) lacks [grasping of] the preceding and succeeding, and that which is not direct perception is not perception (*pratyakṣa*). If that is the case, then the argument "because it is sense-born, like the cognition of an infant" is redundant; the non-conceptuality would simply be established by the very fact of its being perceived, since direct perception is experienced as restricted to direct apprehension. Otherwise, if perception were never a means of proving non-conceptuality, how could an inference following upon it proceed?
[252,iii] Now, if the sensory consciousness has the mode of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇākāra*), then other sensory consciousnesses must likewise be of that same nature. If this is so, then:
O child, let that very same proof be stated here as well;
by this, experience and so forth have been explained on the grounds of the equality of the intellects of the senses. (144)

[252,v] The mind, having been previously distracted, becomes concentrated; having been previously concentrated, it becomes distracted. It is neither bound nor liberated. Why? Because it does not exist as a substantial entity. Furthermore, the mind is like an illusion, like a dream, and like the reflection of the moon in water. It is neither bound nor liberated. Why? Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature. Just as space is neither bound nor liberated, so too is the mind. Why? Because it is unconditioned. Just as the dharmadhātu is neither bound nor liberated, so too is the mind. Why? Because it is free from conceptual proliferation. Just as nirvāṇa is neither bound nor liberated, so too is the mind. Why? Because it is beyond all grasping. Therefore, the mind is neither bound nor liberated. Why? Because it is ultimately empty. Since the mind is thus empty, one should know that all phenomena are likewise empty. Why? Because they share the same essential nature. If one realizes this emptiness of the mind, one will not give rise to the view of a self. Why? Because the self is non-existent. If there is no self, how could there be anything belonging to a self? Why? Because both self and what belongs to a self are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of self and what belongs to a self, one will not give rise to the view of a living being. Why? Because a living being is non-existent. If there is no living being, how could there be anything belonging to a living being? Why? Because both living being and what belongs to a living being are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of living being and what belongs to a living being, one will not give rise to the view of a soul. Why? Because a soul is non-existent. If there is no soul, how could there be anything belonging to a soul? Why? Because both soul and what belongs to a soul are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of soul and what belongs to a soul, one will not give rise to the view of a person. Why? Because a person is non-existent. If there is no person, how could there be anything belonging to a person? Why? Because both person and what belongs to a person are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of person and what belongs to a person, one will not give rise to the view of a human. Why? Because a human is non-existent. If there is no human, how could there be anything belonging to a human? Why? Because both human and what belongs to a human are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of human and what belongs to a human, one will not give rise to the view of a man. Why? Because a man is non-existent. If there is no man, how could there be anything belonging to a man? Why? Because both man and what belongs to a man are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of man and what belongs to a man, one will not give rise to the view of a woman. Why? Because a woman is non-existent. If there is no woman, how could there be anything belonging to a woman? Why? Because both woman and what belongs to a woman are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of woman and what belongs to a woman, one will not give rise to the view of a male. Why? Because a male is non-existent. If one realizes this emptiness of female and what belongs to a female, one will not give rise to the view of a self. Why? Because a self is non-existent. If one realizes this emptiness of self and what belongs to a self, one will not give rise to the view of permanence. Why? Because permanence is non-existent. If there is no permanence, how could there be anything permanent? Why? Because both permanence and what is permanent are empty. If one realizes this emptiness of permanence and what is permanent, one will not give rise to the view of annihilation. Why? Because annihilation is non-existent. Since direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is not observed in the case of what is remote (*parokṣa*), whereas it is observed elsewhere, perception (*pratyakṣa*) may be established in a general sense as being non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) because its object is immediate (*aparokṣa*). What, then, is the use of reasons such as "being produced by the sense organs" (*indriyajatva*)? Furthermore, that direct realization is described as being non-conceptual; since conceptualization (*savikalpakatva*) excludes non-conceptuality, whatever is a direct realization is pervaded by non-conceptuality. Thus, this is an "observation of the pervasion of the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Alternatively, direct realization is established by means of non-conceptuality. From that [argument] as well, if perceptuality were established by non-conceptuality through direct realization, then perceptuality would also apply to the cognitions of two moons and the like. Therefore, one must state: "provided it is non-erroneous" (*abhrāntatve sati*).

[252, vi] But surely, let it simply be "erroneous"; what is the use of specifying "non-conceptual"? No, because the qualification is made with respect to the views of others. Thus he says: "The qualification in a definition is dependent on the views of others. In reality, however, all [cognitions] are indeed non-conceptual; all cognitions that are non-erroneous are indeed non-conceptual. And the Master has established their non-erroneousness by way of an exclusion (*apavāda*). [252, vii]

Alternatively, it is *pratyakṣa* (perception) because it occurs in relation to the *akṣa* (the sense organ). By means of that, direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is apprehended. Therefore, all cognitions that function in the form of direct realization are indeed free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*). Alternatively, it is called *akṣa* because it reaches (*aśnute*) or pervades (*vyāpnoti*). And the pervasion of the nature of the object is precisely direct realization; therefore, all [cognitions] born of the senses are indeed free from conceptual construction.

Alternatively, the Master does not include the term "non-erroneous" at all; his definition is simply "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍham*). How, then, is erroneous cognition excluded? Because everything that is a direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Even in the case of the cognition of two moons and the like, there is indeed perception regarding the duality as it appears. Therefore, wherever something is a direct realization, there it is perception. For it is only with respect to the external object that it is erroneous.

And since there is nothing else present apart from the form appearing directly, this is merely a conceptual construction. Thus it has been said: "Because they have as their object the delusions of the mind, they are erroneous.
[253, ii] But is not even non-delusory cognition of an external object merely a conceptual knowledge? This is true. For instance:

[253,iii] This is what comes by the force of the nature of things, as the wise declare: "In whatever way objects are examined, they fall apart in that very way"—so it will be stated (*Pramāṇavārttika* 2.209).
Furthermore: <(2) Refutation of the Universal> [253,iv] Moreover.
Having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, as well as worldly convention, and having synthesized these, one cognizes it in that way and not otherwise.

Just as, for example, because a thing such as a universal (jāti) cannot be determined through its distinction from its locus (dharmin), there is no connection with that [universal]; therefore, even conceptual construction (kalpanā) does not exist here. // 146 //

[253, vii] For conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) consists in the joining together [of attributes], and there can be no joining together without the apprehension of each of the qualifiers and so forth individually. Just as in the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), because the genus and other factors are not determined through their distinction [from one another], there is no joining together of those [attributes] with the possessor; how then could sensory perception be conceptual? To explain:
[253, viii]
For that which has an undifferentiated appearance, what could be joined with what?
As for that which has a differentiated appearance, its joining is not supported by experience.

For if there is a non-differentiated appearance, that is indeed one; what, then, would be the purpose of a synthesis (*yojanā*) therein, since synthesis depends upon two [distinct] things? Alternatively, if there is a dual appearance of distinct entities, then because they appear as mutually separated, there can be no synthesis at all; thus, synthesis is impossible. Therefore, synthesis is not ultimately real.

Or let it be granted that there is a distinct appearance of each [element] such as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth; however, this is not possible for the universal (*jāti*), the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*), and so on. Universals, qualities (*guṇa*), and actions do not appear as distinct from their possessors. If it is argued that "conjunction" (*yojanā*) is simply the appearance of them as combined, we say no. For two things that are distinct cannot logically have an appearance of being combined. If it is argued that this is so because they occupy the same place and time, we say no. Even for things occupying the same place and time, their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) remain distinct. Indeed, even for things occupying different places and times, the appearance of them as such arises solely from the difference in their intrinsic natures, not from the difference in place and time. For if there were no difference in intrinsic nature there, then even when there is a difference in place and so forth, there would be no appearance of difference. Furthermore, even when there is no difference in place, a difference certainly appears between color (*varṇa*) and shape (*saṃsthāna*) according to others, as well as between wind and sunlight; thus, the difference in appearance is not lost due to the non-difference of place and so forth.

[253,xi] Now, if it were the case that things appear as a single unified mass by virtue of the force of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of imagining such a state everywhere. Consequently, every appearance of non-difference would not necessarily be a proof of actual non-difference.

But surely, this cognition consisting of a connection arises precisely from the qualified cognition "cow"; for a qualified cognition is never observed anywhere without the qualified object and the qualifier, just like the cognition "staff-bearer. [Objection: It is not pointed out as "this is that," because it does not appear through distinction. Indeed, even in the cognition "staff-bearer," there is no appearance of the staff through distinction, since only the person appears therein. [Question: Why does it not occur even prior to the connection with the staff? [Answer: No, because in the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the state of being qualified is absent. Furthermore, the state of being qualified is nothing other than the person, since that is not perceived; rather, the staff itself is the state of being qualified. As, for example:

[254,i] Water and so forth are merely the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) for the power of the seed. If, however, there were also the appearance of a staff, then there would be the cognition "the staff and the person. All of this is incorrect. If it were a mere appearance, it could not be a qualifier of that which is not perceived. But if there is an appearance, then there can be [the cognition] "the staff and the person. For just as when there is the appearance of a person alone, there is no perception of a qualified state, so it is also with the case of "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Now, if it is argued that being a qualified state is simply the status of being the object of a qualified cognition, to this it is replied: [254,ii]
A cognition would be distinguished by a distinction inherent in itself, or else by a distinction in the object of cognition; in either case, neither of the two possesses reality.

If the distinction belongs to the cognition itself (*svagata*), then that conceptualization (*kalpanā*)—which consists in the joining [of a qualifier]—does not belong to the object. Indeed, the presence of conceptual content in sensory perception does not arise from a distinction belonging to pleasure and so forth. If it is argued that this very distinction does not belong to the cognition in the absence of an object, we say no; for we shall demonstrate that the distinction is established even through the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). However, if the distinction resides in the object, then both the staff and the man would be perceived. How then could the cognition have the man alone as its object? If it is said that both are perceived in the case of the cognition "staff-bearer," this is stated merely in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), for it is not so in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since conceptualization is devoid of an [external] object. If both were indeed objects, why is there no dual number? This is merely conventional usage, arising from the specific influence of preceding impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, there is no fault. Because the qualifier is subordinate, even though it is being perceived, it is not intended to be expressed; therefore, by the number of the man alone, there is singularity. If, by this reasoning, it is claimed that the object is the man alone, let it be so—but not on account of the absence of appearance.
[254,iv] Or, it might be argued:
The manifestation of isolation (*kaivalya*) belongs to those things distinguished by space, time, and so forth;
yet, in that state, the distinctness of cognition is not unperceived.
In that case as well, there is concentration:
either the association with another category-meaning or a distinct intrinsic nature.
In that case, every opposing position is abandoned.

(PVA 306) [254, viii] If "distinctness" means being distinguished by association with another entity, as in the expression "distinguished by an ornament," then this does not apply to that which appears in the cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth. Indeed, in that case, no other direction appears. If, on the other hand, it means having a different character, then no difference in character is perceived between two jars, one prior and one posterior.

[254,ix] Furthermore, the distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) is simply the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the object; when that [nature] appears, there is indeed non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*). As for being the object of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*), that has already been refuted. Therefore, this is the logical principle: if there is a synthesis (*yojanā*) upon the appearance of two things, then it is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Conceptual construction is not merely the appearance of two things, but rather it is preceded by a synthesis and, prior to that, by the individual perception of each.
But surely universals and the like do indeed appear, because a recurring cognition is perceived. Thus it is said:
[254,xi] "Even though that recurring cognition has the appearance of the word and the individual,..."
For they indeed declare that "cowness" (gotva) is empty of color, shape, letters, and form. // 147 //
Even though it is identical, that very [object] is not perceived when it is within the range of the eye;
because two appearances are absent, a distinction in cognition is difficult to establish. (148)

[254, xiii] The aggregate of form consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements. What are the four great elements? They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. What is the earth element? It is the quality of solidity within the internal body, whether it be long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, smooth, or rough; or whatever else is perceived as internal solidity, this is called the internal earth element. What is the external earth element? It is the quality of solidity found outside the body, such as stones, pebbles, gravel, sand, rock, mountain, iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, gold, crystal, coral, pearl, conch, agate, ruby, emerald, and other such things perceived as external solidity; this is called the external earth element. Just as with the earth element, so too should the water element, the fire element, and the wind element be understood. What is the water element? It is the quality of fluidity within the internal body, whether it be bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else is perceived as internal fluidity; this is called the internal water element. What is the external water element? It is the quality of fluidity found outside the body, such as rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, oceans, wells, springs, rainwater, dew, frost, snow, hail, and other such things perceived as external fluidity; this is called the external water element. What is the fire element? It is the quality of heat within the internal body, whether it be that by which one is warmed, or that by which one digests food and drink, or that which causes fever, or whatever else is perceived as internal heat; this is called the internal fire element. What is the external fire element? It is the quality of heat found outside the body, such as forest fires, lightning, or other such things perceived as external heat; this is called the external fire element. What is the wind element? It is the quality of motion within the internal body, whether it be upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the flanks, winds in the belly, winds in the limbs, winds that cause pain, or whatever else is perceived as internal motion; this is called the internal wind element. What is the external wind element? It is the quality of motion found outside the body, such as east winds, west winds, north winds, south winds, whirlwinds, gentle breezes, or whatever else is perceived as external motion; this is called the external wind element. These are called the four great elements. What is "that which is derived from the four great elements"? It is the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, the tangible objects, the space-element, the light-element, the air-element, the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. This is called "that which is derived from the four great elements. Thus, the aggregate of form consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements. The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are each to be understood in their own respective manner. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of past form, the aggregate of future form, the aggregate of present form, the aggregate of internal form, and the aggregate of external form. The aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also to be understood in the same way. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of inferior form, the aggregate of intermediate form, the aggregate of superior form, the aggregate of internal form, and the aggregate of external form. The aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also to be understood in the same way. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of internal form, the aggregate of external form, the aggregate of internal-external form, the aggregate of internal feeling, the aggregate of external feeling, the aggregate of internal-external feeling, the aggregate of internal perception, the aggregate of external perception, the aggregate of internal-external perception, the aggregate of internal formations, the aggregate of external formations, the aggregate of internal-external formations, the aggregate of internal consciousness, the aggregate of external consciousness, and the aggregate of internal-external consciousness. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of grasping at form, the aggregate of grasping at feeling, the aggregate of grasping at perception, the aggregate of grasping at formations, and the aggregate of grasping at consciousness. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the realm of desire, the aggregate of feeling included in the realm of desire, the aggregate of perception included in the realm of desire, the aggregate of formations included in the realm of desire, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the realm of desire. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the realm of form and the formless realm are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the past, the aggregate of feeling included in the past, the aggregate of perception included in the past, the aggregate of formations included in the past, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the past. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the future and the present are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the internal, the aggregate of feeling included in the internal, the aggregate of perception included in the internal, the aggregate of formations included in the internal, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the internal. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the external are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the inferior, the aggregate of feeling included in the inferior, the aggregate of perception included in the inferior, the aggregate of formations included in the inferior, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the inferior. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the intermediate and the superior are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the conditioned, the aggregate of feeling included in the conditioned, the aggregate of perception included in the conditioned, the aggregate of formations included in the conditioned, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the conditioned. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the unconditioned are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the outflowing, the aggregate of feeling included in the outflowing, the aggregate of perception included in the outflowing, the aggregate of formations included in the outflowing, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the outflowing. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the non-outflowing are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the impure, the aggregate of feeling included in the impure, the aggregate of perception included in the impure, the aggregate of formations included in the impure, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the impure. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the pure are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the tainted, the aggregate of feeling included in the tainted, the aggregate of perception included in the tainted, the aggregate of formations included in the tainted, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the tainted. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the untainted are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the mundane, the aggregate of feeling included in the mundane, the aggregate of perception included in the mundane, the aggregate of formations included in the mundane, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the mundane. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the supramundane are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the learner, the aggregate of feeling included in the learner, the aggregate of perception included in the learner, the aggregate of formations included in the learner, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the learner. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the non-learner and the neither-learner-nor-non-learner are also to be understood in the same way. This is called the five aggregates. Furthermore, the five aggregates are: the aggregate of form included in the wholesome, the aggregate of feeling included in the wholesome, the aggregate of perception included in the wholesome, the aggregate of formations included in the wholesome, and the aggregate of consciousness included in the wholesome. The aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness included in the unwholesome and the ind

That which is indeed a recurring cognition does not appear as a separate universal (*sāmānya*). If it is argued that "an identical form appears," we say no; for nothing other than the individual word and its manifestation appears. If it is argued that "from the word, a cognition of a uniform form appears," we say no; because [the cognition] arises from memory based on the perceived color and configuration (*varṇasaṃsthāna*). Furthermore, no further recurrence (*anugama*) appears here, since only the form of the color and configuration appears. It is merely the association with a name that persists across all [individuals]; both "this is a cow" and "this is also a cow" share the same name and the same causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Alternatively, it is only the reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) itself that is uniform, not any external object.

[255,i] Now, one might argue that the indistinct form arising from a word is the universal (*sāmānya*), because it is common to all [individuals]. This is not so; for even that [form] has the nature of a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). When the word "cow" is uttered, there arises the cognition of a *śābaleya* cow at one time and a *bāhuleya* cow at another, and so forth. There is no cognition of a single identical form, as in the case of recollection following experience. By this word, the connection with all [individuals] has never been previously perceived, just as the word "cow" does not apply to nine different objects simultaneously.

Now, since speech and other [senses] have fixed objects, it is possible for a convention (*saṅketa*) to be established by indicating those objects; however, this applies to the domain of action and perception. But if individuals are not fixed, how can there be a grasping of convention or its application? We shall explain this later. Or, if that [object] itself were identical, then seeing would not have the eye as its object. If it is argued: "For even when there is a clear manifestation in visual consciousness, the cognition 'this is that very same thing'—which has a dim manifestation—does indeed arise," we say no. Because unity is impossible between a clear and a dim manifestation, and because of the difference in their causes, which are the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the eye and so forth. Therefore, in a cognition produced by the eye and other [senses], there is an absence of two manifestations.

[255,iii] Now, if this cognition—which appears both clearly and unclearly—is indeed one and the same, despite the difference between the forms and their causes, then this is said in response: if there were no distinction among cognitions even when there is a difference in the causes of their appearance, then distinction would be difficult to find anywhere else; for in all cases, the perceptual and inferential cognitions occurring at the same time would be one and the same.

But how can there be a non-perception of the relation of inherence? For there is no determination of universals and so forth through their distinction [from their substrates], precisely because of the existence of inherence. This is not sound, because:
[255,v] Due to the perception of inherence by the senses, the non-perception of a [separate] relation is established.

[255, vi] Because inherence (*samavāya*) is beyond the reach of the senses, it is impossible for it to be perceived by the eye or other sense faculties; this has already been established by yourselves. Now, if you argue that inherence exists because of the conventional usage "the cloth is here in these threads," this is not so, because:
These words, such as "the cloth is in the threads," and so forth, are produced by oneself. (149)

[255, viii] Indeed, cognitions such as "the cloth is in the threads" or "the cow is in the horns" do not occur anywhere. Since those [cognitions] are absent, how can there be an apprehension of inherence (*samavāya*)? For:
In common worldly usage, one says "the horn of the cow," whereas "the cow in the horn" would be non-worldly.

Indeed, cognitions proceed in the form "the horn is in the cow," yet the dewlap and other [limbs] are not inherent (*samaveta*) in that [horn]. Furthermore, that which is accepted as being inherent in those [limbs] is not perceived as something to be contained within them. Therefore, this cognition does not arise from inherence (*samavāya*).
[3] Refutation of the Whole (avayavinirāsa):
Furthermore, however...
[255,xii] Because no disintegration of the remaining parts called "cow" is perceived. 150.

[255,xiii] Even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*), the cognition "here" is indeed observed, as in the case of "the sun is on the tree" at the time of sunset. Furthermore, in the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of a cow based on its remaining parts, there arises the notion "the horn is in the cow" because of the conceptualization of the horn as the contained (*ādheya*). For indeed, there exists no cow other than the collection of the horn and so forth, with which it could stand in a relationship of container and contained; this is merely a conceptual construction.
Now, it might be argued: "The cognition 'there is a cloth in these threads' certainly does occur. This is not so;
for by those threads, this garment is called a subsequent effect.
That which is produced from the processing of threads cannot, in any way, exist at one and the same time. || 151 ||

[256,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Then, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Bhagavān, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha said to the venerable Śāriputra: “If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom, he should contemplate in this way: ‘Form is empty; emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Thus spoke the Buddha. Having heard these words, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly rejoiced and faithfully practiced what the Buddha had taught. The Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra in Eight Thousand Lines, Chapter Twenty-Five: The Chapter on Avalokiteśvara. [257,i] At that time, the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: “O Bhagavān, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom train himself? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should train himself thus: He should contemplate all phenomena as empty of self-nature, unproduced, unceased, originally quiescent, and naturally nirvāṇic. Why is this? Because when one contemplates all phenomena as empty of self-nature, there is no attainment and no realization. The venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, is it because of the emptiness of form that there is no attainment and no realization? Is it because of the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that there is no attainment and no realization? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “It is indeed so. It is because of the emptiness of form that there is no attainment and no realization. It is because of the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that there is no attainment and no realization. The venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if all phenomena are empty, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generate the mind of awakening? How can he enter the path of the Bodhisattva? How can he purify the Buddha-lands? How can he mature sentient beings? If there is no attainment and no realization, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, become irreversible? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates the mind of awakening through the emptiness of form, and yet he does not perceive that mind. He generates the mind of awakening through the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and yet he does not perceive that mind. He enters the path of the Bodhisattva through the emptiness of form, and yet he does not perceive that path. He enters the path of the Bodhisattva through the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and yet he does not perceive that path. He purifies the Buddha-lands through the emptiness of form, and yet he does not perceive those lands. He purifies the Buddha-lands through the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and yet he does not perceive those lands. He matures sentient beings through the emptiness of form, and yet he does not perceive those sentient beings. He matures sentient beings through the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and yet he does not perceive those sentient beings. He attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena through the emptiness of form, and yet he does not perceive that patient acceptance. He attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena through the emptiness of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and yet he does not perceive that patient acceptance. For this reason, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva becomes irreversible. The venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if all phenomena are empty, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, or between defiled and pure dharmas? How can he distinguish between the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “Although all phenomena are empty, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on skillful means, distinguishes between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, and between defiled and pure dharmas. Relying on skillful means, he distinguishes between the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas. Furthermore, Subhūti, although all phenomena are empty, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on skillful means, practices the six perfections, matures sentient beings, and purifies the Buddha-lands. Subhūti, it is precisely because of this skillful means that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, but proceeds directly toward supreme perfect enlightenment. The venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, what is this skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “The skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is the perfection of wisdom. By relying on the perfection of wisdom, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the six perfections, matures sentient beings, and purifies the Buddha-lands. Subhūti, it is for this reason that the perfection of wisdom is called the great skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. The venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva relies on the perfection of wisdom, how does he practice the perfection of giving? How does he practice the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives a gift, he does not perceive a giver, nor does he perceive a recipient, nor does he perceive a gift. This is called the perfection of giving of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes the precepts, he does not perceive the precepts, nor does he perceive the breaking of precepts. This is called the perfection of morality of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices patience, he does not perceive anger, nor does he perceive patience. This is called the perfection of patience of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva exerts vigor, he does not perceive laziness, nor does he perceive vigor. This is called the perfection of vigor of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices meditation, he does not perceive distraction, nor does he perceive concentration. This is called the perfection of meditation of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices wisdom, he does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive wisdom. This is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. The venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a giver, a recipient, or a gift while practicing the perfection of giving, how does he dedicate the roots of merit? If he does not perceive the precepts or the breaking of precepts while practicing the perfection of morality, how does he dedicate the roots of merit? If he does not perceive anger or patience while practicing the perfection of patience, how does he dedicate the roots of merit? If he does not perceive laziness or vigor while practicing the perfection of vigor, how does he dedicate the roots of merit? If he does not perceive distraction or concentration while practicing the perfection of meditation, how does he dedicate the roots of merit? If he does not perceive ignorance or wisdom while practicing the perfection of wisdom, how does he dedicate the roots of merit? The Buddha said to the venerable Subhūti: “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates the roots of merit by means of non-dedication. Why is this? Because all phenomena are devoid of a self, a being, a soul, or a person. Therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dedicates the roots of merit by means of non-dedication. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should dedicate the roots of merit in such a way that they do not fall into the level of a śr

For the word "thread" (*tantu*) refers to a specific state that precedes the cloth (*paṭa*). However, the specific state occurring at a time subsequent to that is the "cloth. Therefore, the expression "this garment (*śāṭī*) is made of these threads" designates an effect that occurs at a later time; it does not denote something simultaneous with the threads. Consequently, how could there be a relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*)? Indeed, there is no relationship of container and contained between things existing at different times. There is either merely a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or a total lack of connection. Thus, even the relationship of container and contained is simply a particular kind of causal relationship, because both depend upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatayā*). It is precisely for those two things dependent on the same causal complex—which are designated as the "vessel" and its "contained"—that such conventional usage occurs. Certainly, there is no other mode of existence than this specific nature of theirs. In the case of the threads and the cloth, however, even this conceptualization does not apply. Therefore, there is merely some kind of conceptual construction in whatever way one might imagine it, but there is no actual relationship of container and contained due to the absence of any distinction [between the two]. For the threads do not exist during the state of the cloth.

[256,iii] But surely, if there is no difference [between the two], since the threads do not exist at the stage of the cloth, how can there be the cognition "these are threads" and this [cognition] "this is a cloth"? This is not so. In ultimate reality, those two do not exist there. Why?

By attributing the cause [to the effect], or even by singling out one [part] from the whole, someone might apply the designation "thread" to the effect, thereby demonstrating the basis for the verbal expression. (152)

[256,v] For the cloth is indeed the effect of the threads; at that time, the threads do not exist [as a separate entity]. The cognition of "threads," however, arises from the superimposition of the nature of the cause and is not ultimate. For instance, when there is a memory of what preceded, the cognition occurs: "these are the threads. Or it is by means of the exclusion of the one (*ekāpoha*). For when each individual thread is excluded, there is no other thing called "cloth" remaining. It is those very [threads] in their aggregate that receive the designation "cloth," like an army or a forest. Thus, the cloth exists only as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) is merely imagined. [256,vi]
If, then, that which is called a "cloth" does not exist, how does the word "cloth" function? For words do not function without a basis. To this, the reply is:
[256.vii] "Either the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, or simply the perception [of the parts] as distinct."

[256, viii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how many nutriments are there? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, there are two nutriments: the nutriment that leads to the production of future existence and the nutriment that maintains existing beings. The Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, what is the nutriment that leads to the production of future existence, and what is the nutriment that maintains existing beings? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, the nutriment that leads to the production of future existence is consciousness; the nutriment that maintains existing beings is the three other nutriments. The Venerable Śāriputra asked: "Blessed One, why is it that consciousness is the nutriment that leads to the production of future existence, while the three other nutriments are the nutriment that maintains existing beings? The Blessed One replied: "Śāriputra, consciousness is the seed of future existence, while the three other nutriments are the field for its growth. Therefore, Śāriputra, consciousness is the nutriment that leads to the production of future existence, whereas the three other nutriments are the nutriment that maintains existing beings."

The phrase "the basis for the designation 'cloth'" is the necessary supplement [to the sentence]. Here, this refers to the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakāritva*). Those very threads, when established in a state of mutual reciprocity as beneficiary and benefactor, or by virtue of a particular conjunction (*saṃyoga*), produce purposeful activity such as covering; thus, they come to possess the designation "cloth. It is their state of being beneficiary and benefactor that is designated as "cloth. Furthermore, just as threads are easily led away from one another when separated by the absence of such reciprocal assistance, so it is not the case with things in the state of a cloth. Therefore, since this non-perception of separation is the basis [for the designation], one should not postulate an entity distinct from the [threads] based on the designation alone. For the basis for postulating a category of object is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); designations, however, generally proceed even otherwise.

[256,ix] If, then, there is no basis for the designation that is distinct [from the threads], then in that case the designation "cloth" would not be primary (*mukhya*), just like the designation "cow" applied to *vāhīka* people. For the designation "cow" applied to *vāhīka* people is secondary because, although it is based on their impurity and so forth, there is no universal "cowness" (*gotva*) distinct from them. Likewise, the designation "cloth," though based on the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor and so forth, would likewise be secondary. To this, the following is the refutation:
That which is primary is unerring knowledge, the object of the original linguistic convention.
That which is the object of the primary convention from the very beginning is the primary [referent], because it is a non-erroneous cognition by virtue of being the domain of the initial convention.

That which functions by way of similarity with the object that is the referent of the convention, due to the superimposition of its true nature, is secondary (*amukhya*), because it is the object of a faltering cognition (*skhalat-pratyaya*). This "faltering" occurs when, in the absence of a direct application, one pursues another thing to be conveyed on account of similarity; for that similarity does not exist without such pursuit. Therefore, there is no distinct entity as the cause for words such as "cloth" based on the distinction between primary and secondary meanings. Now, if it is argued that universals (*jāti*) and so forth are established through inference, it is as follows:
A cognition of such a form occurs elsewhere due to a common cause,
just as the perception "one with a staff" arises from a common staff. (PVA 307)

[257,iv] For even among men who possess different characteristics, there arises a uniform cognition—"the man with a staff"—based on the common cause that is the staff. Similarly, in the case of variegated cows and others, the cognition "cow" occurs despite their differences; therein, the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is the cause, just like the staff. That is not a valid answer. (4) The universal is not established through inference.
Because:
Furthermore, there is no inference regarding a thing that is distinct from its genus and so forth.
For indeed, the designation [of a thing] applies everywhere even to such things as a staff, which are merely conventional. (154)
