If the cognitions of "cow" and so forth regarding individual cows such as *śābaleya* function by relying on a common conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) cause, then this is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For even in the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍin*), the staff is not the [real] cause; otherwise, everyone would be "staff-bearers. If it occurs because of a relation (*sambandha*), then the relation itself is understood only from the cognition that "it is related. If one were to postulate another relation for that as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, there is the cognition "it is related" even without a [real] relation, then the relation is likewise merely imagined (*kalpita*); thus, the cognition "staff-bearer" arises from a purely conventional cause. That very relation is common to all. Now, if it is argued that the contact (*saṃśleṣa*) with the staff is real and not conventional—that too is incorrect, because there is no contact apart from those two [entities]. Furthermore, if contact consists merely of the two [entities], then just as a man is "staff-bearer," so too a staff could be "man-bearer. Alternatively, if only the two appear, the cognition would be "these two are mutually conjoined," but there would be no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) between them. If the staff is subordinate because it is a benefactor (*upakāraka*), then that very state of being a benefactor is the conventional cause in that case. And since that does not appear in perception (*pratyakṣa*), the cognition of the qualified object (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*) is not sensory (*aindriyaka*).

[257, viii] Now, it might be argued: "The state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), but the qualifier itself—such as a staff—is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), and the same applies to 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth. No; for the staff is ultimately real because it is apprehended by perception through its distinction [from other things]. If it is argued that "ultimate reality belongs to genus and the like because they are not apprehended through distinction due to inherence (*samavāya*)," then [we ask]: why does inherence not appear through distinction? If it is because of another inherence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore: [257, ix]
The ultimate reality of the object is indeed consistent even in that case;
let its functions, such as carrying or milking, be considered ultimate in that sense.

For just as a real staff, being common [to many], is the cause for the cognition "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*), so too are the dewlap and other [features], or the horns and so forth, the causes for the cognition of "cowness" and the like. If it is argued that there is a difference among the horns and so forth, then since there is likewise a difference among the staffs and the rest, how can the "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) serve as an example? Therefore, it is precisely that which is different but is perceived as non-different.
Or rather, a universal (*jāti*) is observed in some cases as something distinct from the relationship with the dewlap and other such features.
In those cases, when one asks, "What is the *gotva* (cowness) here?", the horns and so forth are pointed out.

For instance, when there is an inquiry regarding the caste of a Brāhmaṇa or others, his lineage (*gotra*), studies, and so on are pointed out; the caste itself is not [directly perceived]. Similarly, in the case of *gotva*, the functions of carrying, milking, and so forth are pointed out. Therefore, no other universal (*jāti*) exists that falls within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, there is no ultimately real cause anywhere that serves as a direct object of designation. Thus, the universal is not an ultimate reality; rather, it is accepted as a cause for designation, and since that [cause] arises only from the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), the universal is useless.
[258,i] Furthermore: if every designation were to proceed by depending upon an ultimate cause, then there would be no independence of the word; yet such independence is observed. For:
Terms such as "building" (*prāsāda*) and "garland" (*mālā*), and so forth, do not depend on anything else.

[258, iii] Regarding the designation among the six categories (*padārtha*) and the designation of "building," "garland," and so forth applied to buildings and the like, these do not depend on any other cause. For within the categories such as substance (*dravya*), there is no further thing called "reality" (*vastutva*). To begin with, substance is not reality; for substance does not inhere in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, nor is it conjoined with them. Nor is a building a substance. It might be argued that it is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but this is not so, because conjunction does not originate from heterogeneous elements. On this point, he says: "Even if a house is indeed a conjunction, what then is a garland? To this he replies:
[258,iv] Even if the house is a conjunction, why would that [conjunction] not be the garland? 155.

[258,v] It is not a substance, nor a quality, nor an action; because a quality does not exist in a substance. For that very reason, it is not a quality. Nor is it an action, because action is dependent upon a substance. It is neither inherence nor particularity, because the effects of those do not exist here. But surely it will be a genus (*jāti*), since a genus exists even in a quality. To this he says: [258,vi]

If it is a genus (*jāti*), then even a single house would have to be called a "row" (*mālā*), just like a tree. Just as even a single tree, such as a *dhava* tree, is called a "tree" due to its connection with the genus "tree," so too a single house would be called a "row" because a genus serves as the basis for designating each individual instance. Alternatively, if a "row" is defined as a specific spatial arrangement (*saṃniveśaviśeṣa*), then things situated facing the same direction and existing simultaneously are what receive the designation "row. Yet even that arrangement is not distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the other categories. If one were to accept it as distinct, it would follow that there is a seventh category of existence; if it is included within the existing categories, the aforementioned fault applies.
And if the garland were a genus (*jāti*), then:
If there is a plurality of garlands, how can that word [denote them], since a universal (jāti) cannot itself be a universal? (156)

[258,x] When there is a plurality of garlands, how can that word [“garland”] apply [to them], as in “these are garlands”? Because a genus does not possess a genus. For a genus is not admitted to exist within a genus; or, if it were admitted, the designation “genus” applied to that [genus] would be without a basis. If it were based on a genus, then yet another genus would be required for that one as well, which is incoherent. To explain: [258,xi]

A universal (*jāti*) is conceptually constructed among individuals for the sake of conventional usage; even here, this usage is based upon another universal. That universal, too, is the object of conventional usage by virtue of yet another universal. (PVA 310)
Thus, because cognition has infinite conditions, it is not tenable;
therefore, the application of words such as "garland" and the like is not based on a real foundation.

Furthermore: how could the conventional usage of terms such as "large garland" (*mālā*) and so forth occur in relation to a garland and the like? This is because the quality of largeness (*mahattva*) inheres in a substance (*dravya*), and a garland and the like are not substances. If it is argued that this is due to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), that is incorrect. Why? [259,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive forms as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the earth element as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive ignorance as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the perfection of generosity as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the emptiness of the infinite, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-observation, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine serial attainments, the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, or the ten powers of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the state of a bodhisattva or the state of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. How is it that there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of "largeness" (*mahattva*) to things such as a garland? For this [largeness] is not perceived as being metaphorical; nor can it be accepted as such when it is not so perceived, since acceptance is based upon perception. If it is argued that this is because largeness, as a distinct entity, does not exist, then from what source is that non-existence established? If non-existence is established, then there is metaphorical application; and if there is metaphorical application, then there is non-existence. This is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If it is argued that because a garland is not a substance (*adravyatva*), largeness—which is a substance—cannot be its property, we say no. For the non-substantiality of the garland itself is unproven. The definition of a substance is: "that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause. If it is argued that it does not possess action, we say no, because the definition consists of the collection [of all three]. It is not the case that space and the like possess action, nor is it the case that the collection of "possessing action" and so forth constitutes a definition for something in every instance. Now, if it is argued that largeness itself does not exist in an ultimate sense when examined, and therefore [the garland] is not a substance, how can one conclude from the existence of the cognition [of largeness] that it does not exist? The claim that the cognition is non-primary (*amukhyatva*) is also not tenable, because it is indistinguishable from a primary cognition. If even that which is indistinguishable from the primary were not primary, then the very distinction between primary and secondary would not exist. Therefore, this is the logical conclusion: due to the absence of any distinction, either everything is primary, or nothing at all is. Consequently, this system of substances and so forth, as formulated by you, does not belong to another [system]. Furthermore, no garland is ever perceived apart from the trees and other components; this is merely a state of cognition and not a specific [real] entity. Therefore, words such as "largeness" applied to a garland are neither metaphorical nor primary. To begin with, it is not primary because it lacks a basis in a distinct object. Nor is it metaphorical because the ground for metaphorical application is absent. For example, in the expression "the forest is in bloom," the metaphorical application of "being in bloom" to the forest occurs through inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*), because the quality of being in bloom is present in the trees that constitute the forest.
That state of having no other cause is equal even in those things considered primary.
What other cause does the word "category" (padārtha) perceive among the six? (158)

As for what was stated—that "the primary cause is one thing, while that which is other than it is the secondary"—that is impossible. For even those things intended as primary referents, such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth, do not have another cause; indeed, it has just been explained that even the staff and the like are merely conventional. Furthermore, when the word "category-entity" (*padārtha*) is applied, what other cause does it require among the six categories, such as substance (*dravya*) and the rest? Moreover, if its application were based on its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then by necessity, that very state of being a non-secondary cause would follow.

Now, it might be argued: "The word *padārtha* functions by means of a different cause; therefore, it is logical that it is primary (*mukhya*) in that case. However, as for the designation of 'the Great One' (*mahat*) and so forth, that is caused by the qualities (*guṇa*). Wherever a term functions without such a cause, it must necessarily be secondary (*gauṇa*) there. Therefore, the meaning 'existent' (*sat*) is primary, while the other is secondary. This too is incorrect, because: Whatever is established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in a certain way, and whatever is expressed in that same way due to its similarity to that [primary object], [is considered secondary].
The primary and the secondary [distinctions] apply even to non-existence with respect to entities, by way of metaphorical designation.

When a term functions otherwise than by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—even in the absence of a primary cause—it is still considered "primary" (*mukhya*) in relation to that which it denotes through such usage. Conversely, where it functions based on an expectation of similarity with that primary sense, it is "secondary" (*amukhya*). This is because we observe the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term "son" and so forth even in the absence of an actual son; thus, conventional usage alone is the basis for primacy when there is a real referent. Otherwise, the reverse is observed. For indeed, the absence of a primary cause would be the basis for the metaphorical application when there is a deviation from the primary sense.

As for what was further stated—that the word "referent" (*padārtha*) is indeed without a basis and is primary precisely as such—then, in that case, being prompted by a cause (*nimitta*) would not constitute primacy, because it exists even in the absence of such a basis. For when something occurs in the absence of another, that other is not its basis; this is because the nature of the relation between cause and effect is defined by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and a cause is precisely what constitutes a basis. Now, how can that very conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) exist without a ground for the application of the word? That too is incorrect, because: [260,i]

Conventional usage follows linguistic convention, and that [usage] follows the speaker's intention; it is established for the sake of practical communication, just as the name of a metre is applied to the body of a verse. (160)

That in which there is the operation of convention (*saṅketa*) is the conventional meaning (*ruḍha-artha*). Convention, moreover, is based upon the speaker’s intention (*vaktṛ-icchā*). For words do not function merely because a basis for their application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) exists; they are observed to function by the speaker’s intention even in the absence of such a basis. This is evident when names such as "lion" are applied to a human being. Therefore, since intention possesses autonomy, it is logical that it alone is the basis for application. Why is a word applied through convention to something even in the absence of a [real] basis? And why [is it applied] to a basis? If you say, "For the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*)," then this same practical usage is equally possible even without a basis for application. For practical usage concerns purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Yet, purposeful action does not necessarily fail to occur in the absence of a [real] basis. If you argue that it does not occur without a basis, we reply: No, for it is not the case that Brahmins lack the capacity for purposeful action in the absence of a [real] caste (*jāti*). There is no proof for this; indeed, there is no proof that any such "caste" exists. It is only reasonable to hold that whatever form is perceived as capable through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is what is effective, for otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, conventions are established for the sake of practical usage even in the absence of a [real] basis, as in the case of the convention that the word *chandas* refers to names such as *gāyatrī*, or the convention regarding *prakṛti* and so forth. There is no real basis there, because *gāyatrī* and the like, as well as *prakṛti* and the like, are imagined according to one's whim. Indeed, there is no real basis in the sequence of phonemes; otherwise, even one who has not grasped the convention would understand them. If something already exists and is perceived, what is the use of a convention there? If you say, "It is manifested (*vyajyate*) by the convention," we say no; for that very thing does not exist without perception. There can be no convention regarding what is unperceived. If you say, "Perception arises from the convention itself," then you fall into the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
As long as the object is not perceived, there is no application of convention; and when convention is not applied, how can perception be possible? (312) (PVA)
But *prakṛti* and the others do not have a fixed nature; for it is as follows:
For some, this verbal root is possible, and subsequently the suffixes *aṭ* and *ām* are applied; for others, it is impossible, as in cases such as *santi*, where elision has occurred.

Therefore, in such cases, convention (*saṅketa*) has as its sole purpose practical usage (*vyavahāra*) and is not prompted by a separate cause. Nor does convention, which follows from mere desire, have a universal (*jāti*) as its cause; for it would be fallacious, since we observe instances of deviation. Consequently, words such as "object" (*vastu*) or "palace" (*prāsāda*) are not based on distinct, real entities. Thus, because there exists a similarity in designation, one need not postulate a universal. If one asks, "How then is there a continuity (*anugama*) of cognitions and words? [the author] replies: The continuity of the cognition does not arise from the continuity of a real entity, but rather from the awakening of the seed of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Just as, even when an object is beautiful, the continuity of "beauty" occurs through the force of habituation, so it is here. For instance:
By the very nature of things, objects are the causes of such a consciousness;
even though there is a difference [between the object and its cognition], wherever that cognition occurs, it apprehends them as being thus.
The cognitions are likewise [diverse] when there is a reflective awareness of non-difference regarding what is distinct;
thus, this continuity of the differentiation of effects does not belong to a single entity. (162)

For it is with respect to an object that consciousness leads one toward such a state, by means of which process the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) results in the arising of a reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of a single form everywhere, just like the experience of pleasure and so forth. Indeed, there is no basis for the "pleasurability" of the cognitions of pleasure and so forth residing in the object itself; for if that were the case, it would follow that suffering could never arise. If, on the other hand, that [pleasurability] were also real, then it would follow that both forms [pleasure and pain] would be perceived simultaneously, just as in the perception of color and shape.

If it is argued that this is not so because of an unseen connection (*adṛṣṭa*), then why is it not accepted that the unseen itself produces such a cognition? If it is argued that the unseen, being a restrictive factor (*niyamaka*), does not act as a producer (*vidhānakārī*), we say no, because there is a lack of evidence. When both a positive injunction (*vidhi*) and a restriction (*niyama*) are possible, the positive injunction is superior, because in the case of a restriction, one must rely on the postulation of many things. For instance:
[261,ii] the fact that an object is associated with pleasure and so forth must be postulated, and likewise another [property].
But when there is a construction of what is not seen, it is merely a construction of the unseen.

Therefore, it is only when there is difference (*bheda*) that there occurs in some cases a unifying reflection (*abhedaparāmarśa*). It is precisely through the persistence of those [individuals] (*tadanvaya*) that the accomplishment of the object occurs by virtue of their functional capacity (*sāmarthya*); what is the use of an internal goiter, namely a "universal" (*sāmānya*)? Furthermore, an internal cause for cognitions must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving two forms—that of the universal and that of its possessor. If it is argued that "through inherence (*samavāya*), there is a state of total fusion (*ekalolībhāva*)," we say no, because there would then follow the perception of a third form, namely that of inherence itself. Therefore, one must admit that the power of cognition in that regard depends solely upon an internal cause. Likewise, cognitions are also "concomitant" (*anvayin*) simply because they produce a single unifying reflection; thus, it is not logical to admit further universals (*jāti*). The remaining consequences have already been stated. Consequently, the conventional usage of "universal" is based on the fact that [the individuals] are the effect of that unifying reflection. If it is argued that "that very status of being an effect is the universal," we say no, because apart from its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is no such thing as "being an effect. Moreover, if that were the case, since earth, water, and so forth also possess the status of being effects of a sprout, there would be a perception of their identity. If it is argued that "the perception of being an effect of that is indeed the perception of a universal," we say no; it would then be exactly like the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*). Therefore, it is established that the perception of a universal occurs only through the non-perception of difference, and not otherwise.

[261,iv] Now, why is it not accepted that it is the universal (*sāmānya*) itself that is perceived there? Nor does there arise here any subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) to the effect that "the universal does not exist. Furthermore, there is no purpose in the exertion of dispute. If it is argued that just as there is the exertion of postulating multiple [entities], so too the exertion of dispute would result in the same contingency, that too is incorrect. Why?
If it is held that the universal is merely a confusion arising from verbal dispute,
then it follows that it is a conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*), being accessible only to an unexamined perspective.

When examined, a universal does not exist; since it is accepted only because it cannot withstand examination, it follows that it is something that can only be appreciated through the very act of examination. However, a single causal function among things does exist;
therefore, verbal usage is grounded in that [function], which resides in the thing itself.

At that very moment, there exists a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by having a single effect, which distinguishes the *śābaleya* cow and others from those things that do not have that effect. Therefore, let the verbal designation (*śruti*) proceed toward the object, being applied precisely to that which serves as its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

How, then, can a cognition of a universal (*sāmānyabuddhi*), which possesses a form (*ākāravatī*), arise from a distinction (*viśleṣa*) that is itself formless? To this, the reply is as follows: The very connection with a cognition possessing a form is necessarily the exclusion (*viśleṣa*) of everything other than it; and that [cognition] possesses a form due to its association with mental impressions (*vāsanā*). For that cognition has come down through a succession of preceding cognitions, each of which was based on what was previously experienced. Furthermore, in the cognition "this is a cow," there is no other object of cognition (*prameya*) apart from the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) and so forth. The determination of an object of cognition occurs through the appearance of the form of that object, and not from a mere cognition devoid of the form of the object. If, then, this cognition is non-discrepant simply because it is bound to that [object] by virtue of the power of beginningless mental impressions, how can there be correspondence with a real entity (*vastu*)? Therefore, one must not conclude [the existence of the external object] merely through the determination of the exclusion of its effects. And that "being its effect" is either the very capacity (*śakti*) of that external thing, or the exclusion [of others], or the very nature of the external thing itself. When there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of that [capacity], that itself is the universal (*jāti*); thus, there is no rejection of the universal. And when that [universal] is determined, it is the external thing itself that is determined, for there is no exclusion of the external form.

[5] Consideration of the Exclusion of Others (Anyāpoha): Even though there is no ultimate reality consisting in the exclusion of external causal capacities, there is nevertheless verbal designation for that [exclusion]. (163)
It is bound to the conceptual reflections that are based upon those [particulars];
therefore, because it is based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to perform the exclusion of others. (164)

[262,iii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. And with reference to this, it was stated: "There are, monks, these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Now, what is the nutriment that is contact? What is the nutriment that is mental volition? What is the nutriment that is consciousness? Herein, what is the nutriment that is contact? It is the sixfold class of contact. What six? Contact associated with the eye, contact associated with the ear, contact associated with the nose, contact associated with the tongue, contact associated with the body, and contact associated with the mind. This is called the nutriment that is contact. And what is the nutriment that is mental volition? It is the threefold class of mental volition. What three? Mental volition associated with the realm of desire, mental volition associated with the realm of form, and mental volition associated with the formless realm. This is called the nutriment that is mental volition. And what is the nutriment that is consciousness? It is the sixfold class of consciousness. What six? Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called the nutriment that is consciousness. Furthermore, monks, whatever kind of contact one experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that contact is the cause, that contact is the condition for the arising of feeling. Whatever kind of feeling one feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that feeling is the cause, that feeling is the condition for the arising of craving. Whatever kind of craving one craves for—whether for sensual pleasures, for existence, or for non-existence—that craving is the cause, that craving is the condition for the arising of grasping. Whatever kind of grasping one grasps at—whether grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, or grasping at a doctrine of self—that grasping is the cause, that grasping is the condition for the arising of existence. Whatever kind of existence comes to be—whether existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, or existence in the formless realm—that existence is the cause, that existence is the condition for the arising of birth. Whatever kind of birth comes to be—whether among gods, among humans, among the host of Yama, among spirits, among the hosts of hungry ghosts, among animals, or in the various hells—that birth is the cause, that birth is the condition for the arising of aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus is the origination of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called dependent origination. Furthermore, monks, whatever kind of contact one experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that contact is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Whatever kind of feeling one feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that feeling is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Whatever kind of craving one craves for—whether for sensual pleasures, for existence, or for non-existence—that craving is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Whatever kind of grasping one grasps at—whether grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, or grasping at a doctrine of self—that grasping is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Whatever kind of existence comes to be—whether existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, or existence in the formless realm—that existence is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Whatever kind of birth comes to be—whether among gods, among humans, among the host of Yama, among spirits, among the hosts of hungry ghosts, among animals, or in the various hells—that birth is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the cessation of dependent origination. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Although a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from a word does not touch the external nature [of its object], nevertheless, because that reflection of the conceptual construction arises by way of the external—arising through a lineage [of causal dependence] upon the external—it is said to be "not touching the object" even though it is "based on the external. Furthermore, that reflection, produced by an entity excluded from others, appears as being itself excluded from others. It is precisely this exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), inseparable from that [entity], which is understood from the word, and not an exclusion distinct from the external. Therefore, because it generates a conceptual construction having the form of exclusion from others, the word is said to perform the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). And because it causes one to engage with things excluded from others, the "exclusion of others" is called the object [of the word]. For, despite the conceptual construction not touching the external, people engaged in worldly practice act toward things excluded from others based on that conceptual construction; thus, the exclusion of others is said to be its object.

[262,iv] But surely, if the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is distinct from cognition, how can it have the nature of cognition? For that which appears as distinct from it cannot be identical to it. Indeed, the appearance of difference is the defining characteristic of difference, since there is no other basis for difference. It is not merely the appearance of non-difference that constitutes this characteristic; rather, it is an *unerroneous* appearance of difference that is the characteristic of difference, and not just any such appearance. This, moreover, is as follows: [262,v]

That reflection of an object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct [from the word], even that is not the essence of the object; it is an illusion consisting of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (165)

[262, vi] Even though it appears as color and shape, it is nevertheless not a real entity (*vastu*), but rather a reflection (*pratibimbaka*). If it is asked, "What is the contradiction [in this]?"—since its production arises from a cause characterized by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), why then is it not a real entity? Because it is dependent solely upon internal causes, like the hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Or, even though it arises through the power of latent predispositions, it is not a real entity in the same way that a real object is; we shall explain this further below.

In that case, it is precisely that entity characterized by cognition which is designated by the word "real thing" (*vastu*). Some maintain that this very thing, as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is the real entity.
When that is expressed by words, what portion of the object is understood?
And if that [object] were not apprehended, the making of a convention for its sake would be useless. (166)

One establishes a convention with the thought that perhaps through a word there might be an apprehension of even a fragment of a real entity (*vastu*), and not merely for the purpose of conveying a mental reflection (*buddhipratibimbaka*). Therefore, the act of establishing a convention would be useless [if it were only for a reflection], because its purpose is the comprehension of a real entity. [Objection: In that case, then, even the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) cannot be the meaning of a word; consequently, the act of establishing a convention would not apply to that either, since that exclusion of others is also a form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*). [Reply: No, because the exclusion of others is precisely the word-meaning of the word itself. For: [262,x] The word-meaning is the exclusion of others, which is the very nature of the word. Since it is the object of the word, it is the exclusion of others. Thus, the convention is established for the sake of that [exclusion]. Furthermore, the exclusion of others is not a separate entity from the word-meaning; rather, it is the word-meaning itself as the negation of what is other. Therefore, the convention is indeed meaningful. Moreover, the exclusion of others is not perceived as something distinct from the word-meaning, just as the universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived as distinct from the individual (*bheda*). Consequently, the convention is established for the sake of that [exclusion]. And since the exclusion of others is the word-meaning, the word-meaning is not non-existent. Thus, the convention is not fruitless. Furthermore, the exclusion of others is not a mere absence (*abhāva*), because it is established by positive determination (*vidhi*). It is not a mere absence, because it is apprehended as having a specific form. Nor is it a mere absence, because it is the basis for the activity of agents. Therefore, the exclusion of others is indeed the word-meaning. And since the convention is established for the sake of that, the objection that the convention would be useless does not hold. Thus, the exclusion of others is the word-meaning. And since the convention is established for the sake of that, the convention is not fruitless. It is said that a word expresses a portion of the object; in that case, it is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha).
Yet, that form does not exist in the object itself; how then can a word expressing it possess the object as its referent? (167)

[262,xi] If that very exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) were the [word-meaning] itself, then in its presentation, the exclusion of others would not constitute a part of the object. For it is precisely a part of the object that is the exclusion of others; thus, when asked "Which part of the object does the word express?", the answer is "the exclusion of others. Yet that form does not exist in the object.

Because it is of the nature of a mental form (*buddhyākāra*). For when there is no external object, the cognition of that [object] is not a cognition of an object, just like the cognition of hairs and so forth by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is held to be the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), because:
"The effect of a recurring word is produced by a recurring object, and that [word]... [263, ii]
The positive concomitance (anvaya) is not [directly perceived] because cognition lacks differentiation; it is constructed through the repeated practice of observation. // 168 //

[263,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “If there be any good sons or good daughters who wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should perceive that all five aggregates are empty and thereby deliver themselves from all suffering. The venerable Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “How should a good son or good daughter perceive that the five aggregates are empty? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said to the venerable Śāriputra: “Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. The same is true for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The venerable Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “Excellent, excellent! What you have said is indeed so. Because all dharmas are marked with emptiness, there is no arising and no ceasing, no defilement and no purity, no increase and no decrease. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the unequaled mantra, which relieves all suffering and is truly not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, having heard what the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara had said, rejoiced and carried it forth. Thus ends the Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā.

For it is observed that the verbal [concept] is concomitant (*anvayin*) with respect to individuals such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*). And that which is concomitant must have a concomitant object as its purpose. However, that form (*ākāra*) is not concomitant, because there is no difference in the cognition; due to being produced by the repeated practice of perception, it is non-concomitant just like the cognition itself. Indeed, it is not logical for an effect to be concomitant, since it differs according to the difference in its causes. Therefore, precisely because it is non-concomitant, the reflection (*pratibimbaka*) is not the exclusion (*apoha*). Consequently, neither the real entity (*vastu*) nor the form of the cognition is the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). How, then, is there a cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*) when an object is understood from a word? For when there is a cognition of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) residing in the real entity, it is the real entity itself that is apprehended, and not a universal.
[263,iv] Now, if the entity (*vastu*) is not cognized, how can there be a comprehension of the exclusion (*anyāpoha*) which has the form of the non-existence of that entity? To this, he says:

Furthermore, because the cognition of the exclusion of others occurs through the superimposition of that form [onto the object], it contradicts the statement that "the meaning of a word is that very [exclusion]. (169)

[263, vi] Through the superimposition that the object is indeed of the very form of cognition, one understands it by determining its identity with that [cognition], but not in an ultimate sense. And since that [form] is excluded from others, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is the meaning of the word. Furthermore, this [exclusion] is everywhere superimposed upon the form of cognition [as if it were the external object]. Consequently, it is perceived as both the universal (*sāmānya*), the exclusion of others, and a constituent part of the real entity (*vastvaṃśa*).
These cognitions produced by words have false appearances;
nevertheless, the word functions through exclusion (apoha) because it follows after this portion of the object.

Because it is a false appearance, it does not have a real entity as its object. Furthermore, because the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is real, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) in that regard; for a sublation does not operate against the form of a real entity, such that one could say, "This is not the exclusion of others. Therefore, the distinction between what is apprehended and what is otherwise is established through conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*) based on the presence or absence of sublation, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, because the demonstration of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is uncontradicted, while the other [positive entity] is contradicted, it is understood that exclusion is the meaning of a word. Consequently, words follow that exclusion as their meaning and function by avoiding what is undesired; thus, verbal cognition (*śruti*) effects this exclusion of others. Alternatively, the "exclusion of others" is simply the reflection (*pratibimbaka*) within conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), which is determined (*adhyavasita*) as if it were external; thus there is no fault, for it does not exist in its own right-form (*svarūpa*). Therefore, nothing exists in its own right-form that could be enjoined by a word; hence, affirmation (*vidhi*) is not the meaning of a word.

[263,xi] But surely, when the intrinsic nature [of the object] appears [in cognition], how does the cognition engage with the external? Through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of it as being external. What is this "determination"? It is the establishment [of the object] as the domain for its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). How can one thing be the domain for the conventional usage of another? Through repeated practice of attachment to it, because of their similarity, just as in the case of a slip of the tongue regarding a name (*gotraskhalana*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that there, *adhyavasāya* (determination) is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of another form? [Response: No, because even superimposition is a distinct cognition (*jñānāntara*). If that [other] cognition has already apprehended that object, what is there to be superimposed? If you say it was apprehended elsewhere, does that [form] exist elsewhere? If you say it exists as such [there], then it is not a superimposition, because it would be real. If, on the other hand, it does not exist [there], then how can there be a superimposition of one thing upon another cognition? For that upon which it is superimposed must also be either of the nature of a cognition or of the nature of an object. In that case, what is the meaning of "superimposition" upon that? If it is apprehended there, or if it is apprehended together with that [object], then it is not a superimposition. If, however, that which is non-existent is perceived as existent, has its non-existence been apprehended by something else? If you say it was apprehended by another [cognition] because its form is not perceived, no; for that [non-existence] is not within the range of perception (*agocara*). How can there be non-existence [of what is not perceived]? For it is the non-perception of an object that has become perceptible (*gocarībhūta*) that indicates [its absence]. If you say this perception occurs due to a defect in the sense faculties (*indriyavaiguṇya*), that is merely a novel perception (*apūrvapratipatti*), not a perception of something non-existent; for that [object] is existent at that very time.

[264,i] Now, if one does not engage in linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) without having reached [the object], because convention is performed only upon reaching it, then it follows that the very performance of convention regarding one thing is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of another; thus, it comes down to this: superimposition is the making of something else the object of linguistic convention.
Therefore, the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For this very reason, he says: "Therefore, even at the time of the convention, it is associated with a perceived object."
In the scripture, the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is connected with the result of one's own cognition.

Even when establishing a convention, the maker of the convention does not establish it by way of affirmation; rather, he does so solely by way of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), because even at the time of the convention, it is only the exclusion of others that is connected to the word, not the actual thing.

[Objection: "In the convention ‘This is Devadatta,’ it is observed that the particular (svalakṣaṇa) itself is being connected [with the name]. [Reply: This is not correct. Even when an object is indicated, it does not characterize a mental reflection (pratibimbaka) in this way.
For instance, the object intended for the sake of cognition is what is meant by both parties in the convention.
The cognition is of the reflection, and not of the unmanifested real entity.

(PVA 316) [264, vii] From the thought "this has this name," another thing must also be understood; therefore, the convention—which necessarily pervades the other time and the state of perception—is intended by both parties, oneself and others. Consequently, it is only the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that is connected with the word, and not the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

[264, viii] Furthermore, it might be argued that there is no comprehension of a pervasion such that "this has this name"; rather, only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the reflection is perceived as the object of the convention, in the sense that "this has this name. No, for such a perception occurs either due to extreme habituation or because of acting with prior deliberation. On the contrary, in the case of the opposite, the perception of the reflection occurs necessarily. Moreover, for one who has understood the convention through linguistic usage, there is necessarily, at the time of the convention, a determination (*adhyavasāya*) in the form of a reflection. For instance: [264, ix]
From this convention consisting of its name, this is understood by a discerning person; otherwise, how could one who is discerning act in such a way?
Now,
when one says, "Bring this," and there is the observation of its being brought;
"By means of the word, this name belongs to this [object], and thus it is to be understood by me as well.

(PVA 318) Alternatively, the object that was previously indicated and established as having the nature of a reflection (*pratibimba*) is conjoined with the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), which consists in differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*). And the result of that reflection is precisely the communication of its differentiation, not the cognition of its own-form (*svarūpa*), because the own-form does not exist in the external object, whereas the differentiation does.

If it is argued that "that exclusion is something else," we say no; for through the conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra-kalpanā*), there is the conventional usage of identity with that [exclusion]. Moreover:

Because its form is not perceived elsewhere, and because it depends on being perceived in some [specific] instance, exclusion (apoha) is connected with the Vedic revelation; this is not tenable in the case of a real entity.

[264,xv] For since a word is observed elsewhere—in that which is of a different class—and yet is also observed in some instances of its own class, it is understood that the convention (*saṅketa*) pertains to exclusion (*apoha*) alone. Why then does the convention not apply to either the universal (*sāmānya*) or the individual (*vyakti*)? It is not so; for if that were the case, it would be by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) alone.

Because it would follow that there must be perception everywhere in relation to a convention, there would have to be a requirement for the mere perception of the universal (*sāmānya*) as well; there would be no requirement for the non-perception [of it] elsewhere. If you say, "It is for the sake of cognizing the universal as being excluded from others," then let that very exclusion from others be what is meant; what is the use of postulating a "universal"? For it is the individual (*vyakti*) itself that should be perceived as possessing that exclusion from others—what is the use of a universal? If you say, "The individual is not perceived," we say no. What is the use of a perceived universal if it exists apart from the individual? If you say, "The individual is also perceived through secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*)," do these two things get perceived here in succession? Is it not the case that one first perceives and takes as an object the mere "cow-ness" (*gotva*), and afterwards the particular such as a *śābaleya*? This is not so, because it is impossible to perceive the internal distinctions among the *śābaleya* and other individuals. Therefore, that too is merely a universal. Consequently, there is no indication of individuals by means of a universal, because it is the universal itself that is indicated. If you say, "There must necessarily be some particularity here, and this is precisely what constitutes the indication," we say no, because the word has no operation (*vyāpāra*) in this regard. There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here to determine whether this has been understood or not. Furthermore, even the universal is not perceived as being the indicator itself. Therefore, that [cognition] is merely a mental construction (*buddhi*), as it is devoid of a real entity (*vastu*). How, then, is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) the meaning of a word? Precisely because the word functions only toward the exclusion of others. If, however, either the universal or the individual were perceived, there would be no discrepancy (*visamvāda*); for there is no discrepancy regarding what has already been perceived. Since there is discrepancy, how can even the exclusion of others be the meaning of a word? Even when something else is seen, one brings something other than that; there is no rule that it brings only that specific thing. For this very reason, because it shares the same form as verbal cognition, inference also establishes only a negation (*vyavaccheda*).

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because it depends on non-observation elsewhere": when the conventional sign (saṅketa) is grasped through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), the grasper of the convention requires what is not observed elsewhere. In some cases, he also requires what is observed among similar instances. Consequently, he understands the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that wherein [the convention] was not observed; however, regarding that wherein the convention was observed, he does not know with discrimination whether it exists or not. For such is the very manner in which the convention is grasped. Why is this? When one says, "Bring this object," the activity pertains to the bringing of an external thing, not to the existence of the thing itself. If it is argued that "what is non-existent cannot be brought," then if this were a royal command, one would certainly bring it. However, by reflecting through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one makes its existence the object of comprehension, or else through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If it is argued that "the word, accompanied by presumptive testimony, is the means of valid cognition for existence," we say no, because presumptive testimony is impossible in this case. This would be like the begging of a child. Therefore, it is brought only when it is possible, and not otherwise; as for anything else, it is simply not brought at all.

Others, however, maintain that because one expects the exclusion from all dissimilar instances (*vijātīya*) while requiring the presence of the term in some locus of affirmation (*vidheya*), the intention lies in the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and not in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*); thus, it is the negative concomitance alone that is primarily conveyed. This is incorrect. Even if one of the two—positive or negative concomitance—is primary, there is still no transgression of the positive injunction as the word-meaning. Furthermore, it is impossible to demonstrate that the positive concomitance is secondary; for even by the perception of a single individual instance, the universal is conveyed in its entirety. Therefore, it is not logical to claim that the positive concomitance is secondary.

[265,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real. He does not perceive form as real, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive contact as real, nor feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, if emptiness were not empty, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not be able to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Because emptiness is empty, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is this emptiness? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is the emptiness of form, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations, and the emptiness of consciousness. It is the emptiness of the eye, the emptiness of the ear, the emptiness of the nose, the emptiness of the tongue, the emptiness of the body, and the emptiness of the mind. It is the emptiness of forms, the emptiness of sounds, the emptiness of odors, the emptiness of tastes, the emptiness of tangibles, and the emptiness of mental objects. It is the emptiness of eye-consciousness, the emptiness of ear-consciousness, the emptiness of nose-consciousness, the emptiness of tongue-consciousness, the emptiness of body-consciousness, and the emptiness of mind-consciousness. It is the emptiness of contact, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of craving, the emptiness of grasping, the emptiness of becoming, the emptiness of birth, and the emptiness of aging-and-death. Subhūti, it is by means of such emptinesses that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

Alternatively, it is because in some cases there is a dependence upon perception (*dṛṣṭi*). One might say, "This has this name," yet it need not always be so designated by that [name]. In the employment of words, however, there is no non-difference [between the object and its name]; rather, it is merely for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that "this is to be designated by this. But in other cases, since there is an absence of such conventional usage, words have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their objective domain. Now, in a case where an object is apprehended through inference (*anumāna*), how can that cognition have the exclusion of others as its objective domain? Even there, the objective domain is indeed admitted to be the exclusion of others. It is not so; for in that case, because there is doubt regarding the specific quality (*viśeṣa*), the cognition is as follows: "This is certainly not a non-fire," but it is not known what kind of fire it is.

[265,v] But if the universal is not determined, how can there be doubt regarding a particular fire? Because doubt arises from mere cognition. This cognition indeed exists: "The particular is not known; is there fire here or not? Or what kind of fire is this? [265,vi]

[Objection: Is it not the case that wherever there is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), fire is necessarily present? [Response: No, because "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) is a specific kind of touch (*sparśaviśeṣa*). And since there is no necessary rule regarding that [specific touch], how can there be a cognition of fire? [For] only heat in general (*uṣṇatāmātra*) is perceived. [Objection: One cognizes the universal (*sāmānya*). [Response: No, because there is only a matter of degree (*tāratamya*). Furthermore, there is no such thing as a universal "heat" apart from the distinctions of degree, such as more or less; and in that case, there is no cognition [of such a universal].

But surely even cognition apprehends only a gradation. Let it so apprehend; however, it is not a single cognition. One might object: "Since different successive cognitions arise—such as 'at one time it was thus' and 'at another time it was thus'—a single thing is apprehended as having multiple forms at once. If this is argued, we reply: there must be some restrictive rule for this non-existent state. Therefore, even in that case, only the mere cognition is real, and nothing else; thus, the meaning of a word is merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and this is not tenable regarding a real entity. It should also be understood that the exclusion (*apoha*) is connected to the logical mark (*liṅga*) as well.

Therefore, because of the connection with that [exclusion], there is no direct denotation (śruti) of universals and the like in their objects; rather, words are applied solely for the purpose of excluding other things. (173)

[266,iii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? They are: one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry, one who has attained the fruit of once-returning, one who has attained the fruit of non-returning, and one who has attained arhatship. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? They are: one who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry, one who has entered the path toward the fruit of once-returning, one who has entered the path toward the fruit of non-returning, and one who has entered the path toward the fruit of arhatship. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? They are: a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; a Tathāgata’s disciple who has attained the fruit of stream-entry; a Tathāgata’s disciple who has attained the fruit of once-returning; and a Tathāgata’s disciple who has attained the fruit of non-returning. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? They are: a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One; a Tathāgata’s disciple who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry; a Tathāgata’s disciple who has entered the path toward the fruit of once-returning; and a Tathāgata’s disciple who has entered the path toward the fruit of non-returning. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [266,iv] The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well-spoken by the Blessed One were these words: ‘There are four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. There are four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [266,v] Just as, Ānanda, whatever seeds and plants that have roots, trunks, joints, buds, or seeds as their cause, all grow, increase, and expand depending upon the earth and resting upon the earth; even so, Ānanda, these four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And how, Ānanda, are these four kinds of persons the unsurpassed field of merit for the world? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dharma thus: ‘The Dharma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of veneration, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [266,vi] The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is as if there were a great reservoir of water, and from that great reservoir of water, four streams of water would flow out in the four directions. Even so, Blessed One, these four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. These four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [266,vii] Just as, Ānanda, whatever seeds and plants that have roots, trunks, joints, buds, or seeds as their cause, all grow, increase, and expand depending upon the earth and resting upon the earth; even so, Ānanda, these four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And how, Ānanda, are these four kinds of persons the unsurpassed field of merit for the world? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four other kinds of persons who are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... This, Ānanda, is how these four kinds of persons are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
