Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the existence of] universals (*jāti*) and so forth, they are non-existent; thus, the postulation of a relation between universals and so on is not possible. Nor is the postulation of a relation with a substance possible, for how could there be such a relation between two things appearing in their own intrinsic forms? If it is argued that this is because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) does appear [to perception], we say: No. For even for one who does not postulate [conjunction], the form of that [conjunction] appears through the perception of one thing by means of the postulation of another. It is impossible for a postulation to arise based on that alone. If it is argued that "that very [appearance] is the postulation," we reply: Since this is accepted, nothing is contradicted. There is no such cognition as "conjunction produced by the action of both," "produced by the action of one," or "produced by conjunction. If it is argued that the cognition is merely of the intrinsic forms [of the two things], we say: No, because the intrinsic form of conjunction itself does not appear. Only the two entities, having arisen in such a state, are the objects of appearance, not a conjunction. As for the cognition "those two very entities are conjoined," even that does not imply a conjunction other than them. [Objection: But there is no cognition of identity with the prior [state]. Indeed, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not operate regarding the relation of prior and posterior. [Response: Even if the prior cognition did not exist, the cognition of being "conjoined" still exists. We say: No.
For that which was previously unconnected becomes connected again;
the cognition "I am the agent" regarding a single effect is what is intended by that [notion]. (PVA 319)
If this cognition did not exist, the postulation of conjunction would be useless;
for in that case, this [object] would be a single entity, and thus non-conjunction would be meaningful.
(320) (PVA) <The Refutation of the Conception of Words in Direct Perception>

There is also no application of words there, because the word is absent at that time. If it is argued that the word existed at the time of the convention, even by that [existence], there is no application. Why?

How can that [conceptual cognition], which consists of the synthesis of what has been seen and employs the recollection of conventions, exist in a visual perception that is devoid of reflection upon the preceding and the succeeding? (174)

The phrase "this is a cow" (*ayaṃ gaur*) does not mean that this very word "cow" (*gośabda*) is the object denoted by the word "cow. Rather, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises from their relationship, just as in the expression "bring in the staff-bearers" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*). Alternatively, a "cow-word" (*gośabda*) is one for which the word "cow" is the signifier; thus, when the term is used for a part of it, as in "this is a cow," this object is understood through the word "cow" as being the denotation of the word "cow. However, in the case of "this is that cow," the word "cow" has been applied here as a convention (*saṅketa*). How, then, can such an entity be grasped by perception (*adhyakṣa*), whose nature is devoid of the reflective awareness of prior and subsequent moments? For this has been stated:
The functioning of the sense organs occurs with respect to objects situated in a suitable location, not toward those that are past or future.
Furthermore, consciousness, which is dependent upon the sense organs, has as its objective domain the activity of the sense organs. (PVA 321)

[267,i] If the activity of the sense organs, such as the eye, were to perceive everything—past and future—even in relation to the prior and subsequent moments, then one might argue: "Indeed, everything that is somehow connected to something else is necessarily perceived as having been previously grasped. This is not so, because there is no perception at all [of such things] at all times. If it is argued that this occurs when there is recollection (*smaraṇa*), then it follows that it is merely recollection itself. If it is argued that identity with the object being recollected is indeed perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), we say no; for recollection is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Since that which is being recollected is non-existent, how could the cognition of its identity with [the present object] be real? [267,ii]

Now, it might be argued: "It is that very same thing because it performs that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). But is it not the case that even the notion "it performs a purposeful action" is merely a memory, and that [memory] is what is denoted by that word? Furthermore, why must the purposeful action be performed by that very same thing? Therefore, this is merely a matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for identity. If it is argued that it is a means of valid cognition precisely because it is non-contradictory in its conventional usage, we say no. Non-contradiction does not reside in identity, but rather in the purposeful action; and that [action] certainly exists. Its status as an object (*arthatā*) is due to its capacity for purposeful action, but its identity with the previous [moment] is not. Now, if this [notion] "this is that very same thing" were to be established as a proof, then if there is no identity between the prior and the posterior, who would be the synthesizer (*anusandhātṛ*)? If the synthesizer is one, then perception, which grasps the prior and the posterior, would be dependent upon that synthesizer. This is not so, because apart from the forms of memory and direct perception (*darśana*), there is no other synthesis. And although perception is dependent upon the self (*ātman*), its status as a means of valid cognition does not derive from that alone. If it is argued that its validity comes from its dependence on the sense organs (*akṣa*), while the grasping of identity comes from its dependence on the self, we say no. Because it functions in accordance with the sense organs, and the sense organ does not function regarding the prior and the posterior. If it is argued that the cognition following that [organ] persists, we say no, because it is impossible for it to follow that [organ]. For in the prior [moment], there is no functioning without following the prior cognition. To say that what follows one thing follows another is sheer audacity. Furthermore, the cognition of identity does not occur without the operation of the sense organs; therefore, the cognition of identity is not born of the senses. If it is argued that whatever [cognition] occurs in perception is indeed [the cognition of identity], we say no, because there is no distinction in the identity itself. If it is argued that there is a distinction due to clarity, we ask: let identity be [known] through clarity, but how can identity be accessible to perception through lack of clarity?

[267,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those sentient beings suffering such miseries and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "If there be any good man or good woman who wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should perceive that all five aggregates are empty and thereby deliver themselves from all suffering. The venerable Śāriputra then said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "How should a good man or good woman who practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā perceive that the five aggregates are empty? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied to the venerable Śāriputra: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: they are all empty. Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked with emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete. Therefore, Śāriputra, within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, accumulation, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies upon Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the heart of non-attachment, free from all hindrances. Because there are no hindrances, there is no fear; transcending all inverted dreams, one attains ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying upon Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra, which relieves all suffering and is truly real, not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Then, the venerable Śāriputra and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara paid homage at the feet of the Buddha and departed. At that time, the Bhagavat having finished preaching this sutra, the venerable Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, and all the assembly, having heard what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly. Now, it may be argued that the oneness of that [object] with this [cognition] is not accessible to perception; however, why should the oneness of this [cognition] with that not be so? It is because they are not equal. If both are not grasped by perception, how can that oneness be an object of perception? If it is argued that oneness is cognized by perception but is not itself a category (padārtha) [of reality], then that oneness would not reside in the category. Since an independent oneness is impossible, that which possesses oneness (*tadvān*) is what is implied. For "implication" (*ākṣepa*) is indeed inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, it is illogical to claim that while there is apprehension of an independent entity through perception, there is apprehension of something otherwise through inference, given that inference is preceded by perception. Consequently, due to the absence of reflection upon the preceding and succeeding moments, the cognition "this is a cow" is not a perceptual realization. Furthermore, even when one has died, such reflection upon the preceding and succeeding moments is possible; how then could this [perception] be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Therefore, the means of valid cognition is the apprehension of only that which is present. And in that case, there is no synthesis; thus, perception is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*). Moreover—

Even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one perceives a visible form with the eye; the non-apprehension of its conventional designation therein is evident, as is the conceptual construction arising from it. (175)

[267,v] Indeed, one does not perceive form and so forth while already conceptualizing, such that memory would serve as an auxiliary cause for the sense faculty. For that which is an auxiliary cause of something cannot perform its own function in its absence—just as a seed lacks the capacity to produce a sprout in the absence of earth and other factors. If it is argued that memory is an auxiliary cause not merely for the production of an effect in general, but specifically for the generation of a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), that too is incorrect.
[Investigation of the Unity of the Variegated] [267,vii] If that [cognition] were conceptual by virtue of a conceptual construction distinct [from its object],...
In another case, it would be a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); otherwise, there would be the possibility of a contradictory superimposition (*viruddhādhyāsa*).

(PVA 322) If [the cognition] functions with a subsequent conceptualization (*vikalpa*) as its companion, then when such conceptualization exists, memory is merely being proven as something already established as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*). However, if it functions by means of a conceptualization that is identical to itself (*ātmabhūta*), then that is not tenable.
Even when that [cause] exists, something may not exist; and even in its absence, that [effect] may be present.
Therefore, given the association with contradictory properties, how can there be oneness between them? (323) (PVA)

[268,i] That conceptual cognition is one thing, and that which was previously non-conceptual is another. If this were so, your recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) would be destroyed, and the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has already been stated. Therefore, it is logical that when something is non-conceptual during a state where the mind is directed elsewhere, whatever else arises is likewise [non-conceptual]. Alternatively, if it were conceptual precisely because of another conceptualization, then auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) would also result in being conceptual, since the ear also functions as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*).

Alternatively, those cognitions are indeed distinct; since the same applies elsewhere as well, there is no distinction. Or, if it is argued that even for one in such a state there is another conceptualization (*vikalpa*), that is incorrect, because it is not perceived. If it is argued that it is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) even though it is not perceived—since conventional usage is never observed in one who is without conceptualization—[then we reply: [it is not so].
The causal relationship between conventional usage and conceptual construction is established;
since inference from effect occurs here, how could there be no apprehension of the convention for it? (PVA 324)

[268,v] Indeed, it is not the case that the application of words is not cognized through inference, for that too possesses validity. If it is argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of this very [inference], we say no; for there is no deviation with respect to the subject (pakṣa). Otherwise, even in the inference of fire from smoke, there would be deviation precisely with respect to the subject. No; because in that case [the fire] is apprehended by inference, and because it is also cognized through tactile experience and linguistic convention.
That the nature of fire is perceived as something imperceptible through the cognition of touch and the conventional usage of "removing cold" is likewise utterly untenable.

If the non-perception of the fire being inferred is the object of doubt— namely, that "perhaps even now smoke might exist without fire"— then the exclusion of such deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is achieved through the cognition of the touch [of heat] or through the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of warming oneself. That too is incorrect,
because if that [fire] is apprehended by means of inference through the touch-cognition and the practical activity, [the reason remains inconclusive].
Furthermore, the non-deviation of that inference would itself depend on another inference;
since the process of inferring is identical in both cases, there would thus be an infinite regress.

If, when there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in an inference, inference itself were the means for establishing non-deviation, then since that [inference] would be identical [to the case at hand], such a suspicion would arise in every definition of inference. Thus, this [argument] proves what is unestablished by means of what is unestablished. Furthermore, color-form (*rūpa*) is not established by touch (*sparśa*), because touch is possible even in the object of the cognition of a yellow conch-shell. And where there is a suspicion of deviation regarding smoke, there it is all the more so regarding the activities preceded by fire, such as heating and so forth. Therefore, if there were deviation by the subject (*pakṣa*) itself in the establishment of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by means of inference, then such a deviation would exist in every inference; thus, this conception is not correct. That is incorrect.
Another person proceeds to infer from smoke by the force of real entities;
and since that inference is seen to be non-contradictory, it is not established as being of such a conceptual nature. (PVA 327)

[268,xii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, monks, what is edible food, coarse or subtle? It is the food that is taken by the mouthful, whether it consists of boiled rice, roasted grain, wheat, barley, meat, fish, salt, sugar-cane juice, molasses, sesame oil, ghee, honey, or sugar. This, monks, is called edible food, coarse or subtle. What, monks, is contact as the second nutriment? It is the contact that arises dependent upon the eye and forms; this, monks, is called the nutriment of contact. What, monks, is mental volition as the third nutriment? It is the volition associated with the three realms of existence; this, monks, is called the nutriment of mental volition. What, monks, is consciousness as the fourth nutriment? It is the sixfold consciousness—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; this, monks, is called the nutriment of consciousness. Furthermore, monks, whatever is felt, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, all that is included within the nutriment of contact. Furthermore, monks, whatever is intended or willed toward the three realms of existence, all that is included within the nutriment of mental volition. Furthermore, monks, whatever is cognized by the sixfold consciousness, whether it be past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, distant or near—all that is included within the nutriment of consciousness. For an inference regarding fire, when it operates upon an object that is beyond the senses, is not sublated by perception, because perception does not have that as its object. However, in the case of establishing a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since the conceptual construction has self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as its perceptual object, [the phrase] "not from afar" implies subtlety only in relation to the perception of another; but with respect to its own nature, just as there is subtlety for the perceived, so too there is for the perceiver. A dog-cooker (*śvapaca*) does not fear a dog-cooker. Furthermore, this very state of being "non-perception" is itself the nature of self-awareness. Nor does inference operate upon a conceptual construction in the same way it does upon fire and the like, because such a cognition does not exist.

[268, xiii] But surely, since conventional usage is impossible without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), how is it that the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not inference? No; for the apprehension of the necessary connection itself occurs in a different manner. To explain:
For one who lacks practice, conventional usage is possible without reflection and so forth; however, with respect to reality, such usage occurs even without them. (328) (PVA) [268,xv]

For conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) does not occur for one who lacks familiarity without prior and subsequent reflection; however, when familiarity exists, it occurs even otherwise, and not otherwise.
Therefore, this conventional practice proceeds even without such familiarity.
In this very context, the perception of living beings is not an inference by way of conventional usage.

(PVA 269, ii) The operation of inference conforms precisely to the apprehension of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*); otherwise, the apprehension of the necessary connection would be useless for inference. And that necessary connection is apprehended only in the state of non-habituation, and nowhere else.
Therefore, there is no [need for] investigation and so forth, because of the conventional usage of inference;
for this very convention is observed even otherwise. (PVA 330)
[269,iv] Otherwise. [269,v]
Since those who possess desire act toward a beautiful woman with a view toward her charms,
one may infer from that very behavior that she possesses beauty even when she appears otherwise.

Therefore, since the non-apprehension of the word perceived at the time of convention is perfectly clear during the conceptualization of another object, the conceptualization arising from that [non-apprehension] does not exist at all.

Now, if the relation with the word is not grasped by perception, how can there be the linguistic usage [of the form] "this is the denotatum of that word"? [Answer: No, because linguistic usage is possible even through error (*bhrānti*). And even error is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) insofar as it is connected to a real entity (*vastu*). For example, the cognitions of people perceiving a "lump" (*piṇḍa*) and so forth in trees: although even there no such thing as "lump-ness" exists, nevertheless the linguistic usage of "tree" is non-discrepant (*avisamvādin*). Likewise, although there is no such thing as "conjunction" (*yojana*), nevertheless the linguistic usage regarding what is to be conjoined is not false. To explain: the cognition whose meaning is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "this is a cow," has the sense that "the word 'cow' is the denoter of this [object]. Therefore, this cognition is of such a nature and is non-discrepant, because one observes the application of this [word] toward such an object. Just as in the case of a tree, the occurrence of the cognition of a "lump" is restricted to that [tree] and not elsewhere; thus, due to this necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there is non-discrepancy. If, then, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not apprehended from the word "cow," how is there the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "this is that" upon seeing it? [The common view is: "That which was previously apprehended by me through naming, this is that"—such is the cognition in the world. [Answer: No, because there is no recognition of what was seen. Recognition takes the form "this is that"; and "that" is a cognition having the form of something remote (*parokṣa*), not the form of direct perception (*darśana*). Therefore, because the two cognitions are mutually distinct in character, they do not have the same object. For a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*) is what differentiates [objects]. If that [object] were of a non-differentiated nature, there would be a difference [in the cognitions]. Or, if the difference [between objects] is due to a difference in causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) and not due to a difference in appearance—[we reply: no, because there is no causal efficacy apart from a difference in appearance. If you say, "It is due to a difference in appearance qualified by causal efficacy," [we reply: if the appearance is devoid of causal efficacy, then that is merely a consciousness without an external support (*nirālambana-vijñāna*), entirely different from a sensory cognition. For the cognition [expressed by] "that" does not grasp a real entity capable of causal efficacy, since it is produced solely by mental impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus, because there is no contact with a real entity, the two cognitions—"that" and "this"—lack coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, the appearance "this" determines a form common to everything present before one in the sense of "this is that. However, in the absence of such commonality, it is strictly non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). And if sensory cognition were of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then another fault would follow.

Conceptual constructions arise only where a word has been applied; therefore, those cognitions born of the senses would proceed according to one's desire and would not perceive the external object. (176)

For a word is applied to an object that is beyond the senses, and since it is not applied there through conceptualization (*kalpanā*), sensory consciousness would not perceive external objects; it would be without an objective basis (*anālambana*), just like verbal cognition. Indeed, that which operates upon what is beyond the senses cannot have an objective basis, because it does not touch upon the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*). If it were operating by touching upon its own nature, it would involve a clear apprehension and would be "this very thing," rather than "that. Alternatively, all memory would become sensory perception, as there would be no distinction between them.

Verbal cognitions do not, indeed, touch upon external forms. Now, if the application of words were directed toward an external object, then, that being the case, just as a verbal cognition proceeds according to one's will, so too would a sense-born cognition. Consequently, even in the absence of an external object, [the cognition] proceeding [in that manner] would be without a basis (*nirālambana*), because there is no distinction [between the two]. If it is argued that where there is no conformity to will, there is conformity to the object, and thus [that cognition] has an external object as its basis—then, if conformity to the object is the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*), sensory consciousness must be exclusively non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). This is because the form of the word is dependent on will; therefore, it does not follow from an external object, since it follows from latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Now, even if the form of the word follows from latent impressions, nevertheless, because that single [cognition] arises from the totality of both latent impressions and the senses, conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) [is established]. For in this way alone is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) possible; otherwise, if it were not made the object of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), there would be no transaction at all. Indeed, we observe that people’s transaction occurs when they ascertain, "This is such-and-such a means to happiness. That too is incorrect. Why? Because:
Just as the arising of conditions from a causal complex is accepted, let conventional usage be exactly like that; for it is precisely here that valid cognition is found. (332) (PVA)

[270,ii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive that which is the coursing in the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive one who trains in the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive that which is the training in the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive one who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does he perceive that which is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He does not perceive one who has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, nor does he perceive that which is unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. He does not perceive one who turns the wheel of Dharma, nor does he perceive that which is the turning of the wheel of Dharma. He does not perceive one who demonstrates the Dharma, nor does he perceive that which is the demonstration of the Dharma. He does not perceive one who teaches the Dharma, nor does he perceive that which is the teaching of the Dharma. He does not perceive one who hears the Dharma, nor does he perceive that which is the hearing of the Dharma. He does not perceive one who understands the Dharma, nor does he perceive that which is the understanding of the Dharma. He does not perceive one who enters parinirvāṇa, nor does he perceive that which is parinirvāṇa. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable."

Since there is non-difference [of the object] despite the difference in causes, and the cause is indeed distinct in the case of the cognition produced by words and that produced by the sense-faculties—regarding the forms of the object—their linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is not as a single unity. This is because the linguistic usage of the two cognitions is established by the mere totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*), and because linguistic usage remains possible even when one constructs a different conceptualization (*vikalpa*). For when another conceptualization is present, there is no making of that [original object] into an objective referent through its reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Nor is linguistic usage based merely on the association with a word; rather, linguistic usage is based on the connection with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and purposeful action consists of what was previously experienced and what will be experienced. It is not the case that the object of sensory cognition is [exclusively] the external, for that would entail the absence of inference. What is the meaning of the statement, "Those born of the senses would not see the external"? It means: those which do not see the external would also follow as being born of the senses, since there is no distinction [between them]. Thus, even when there is an intervention (*vyavadhāna*) and so forth, a cognition born of the senses would arise. That is to say, even when there is an intervention and so forth, whatever cognition occurs would also be born of the senses, just like the "that" (*sa*) portion [of the recognition *sa evāyam*]. And this has already been explained previously. How, then, is there the determination "this is the thing" regarding the thing? It is the determiner of the object situated in front. For in this case, the determination does not have a remote (*parokṣa*) object. And this [determination] is perception (*pratyakṣa*) because its object is proximate; that [claim of yours] is false. We shall demonstrate that this is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*). And if there is no linguistic usage without a subsequent reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), and if what is not reflected upon is not grasped, then: [The opponent asks: If that is so, how is it that the object is determined as "this is a real entity"? [The author replies: It is the determiner of the object standing before one. For in this case, the determination does not have a remote object. And this is perception because its object is present; that [objection] is false. We shall establish that this is mental perception. One might perceive form as "form," but what does one perceive that cognition itself to be?
And since there is an experience of that [cognition], how could it be non-conceptual? 177

[270,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the truth of suffering as real, nor does he perceive the truths of origination, cessation, or the path as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as real. He does not perceive the awakening of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening as real. Subhūti, this is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

For one who maintains that all cognition is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), how could one perceive "this is form" while perceiving the cognition of that form? Indeed, there is no such conceptualization as "there is this cognition of it" in that state. If you argue that even though there is no direct experience (*anubhava*) [of the cognition], there is nonetheless linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), then in your view, linguistic usage regarding a cognition—even when it is not being experienced—could not possibly occur through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or other means; how much less so when it is being experienced with a clear aspect (*spaṣṭākāratā*) due to its non-conceptual nature? Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no experience of that [cognition]. Otherwise, from where would the conceptualization "this is my perception of form" arise? Moreover, pleasure and the like are indeed experienced at that time, yet there is no conceptual experience of them as "this is pleasure" and so forth. Therefore, the experience of cognition is strictly non-conceptual. If linguistic usage regarding form and the like were to occur just as it does for cognition during non-conceptual experience, then let there be linguistic usage regarding form and the like as well. Now, if you say that this conceptualization—"this is my perception of form"—is itself a conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), then there are two possibilities: either that conceptual perception is the very perception of form, or it is something other than the perception of form. Regarding these:
When that very [cognition] experiences [itself], two conceptual constructions are not seen simultaneously.

If that very cognition of form perceives itself by conceptualizing it as such, then there would be the consequence of two simultaneous conceptualizations, because it is impossible for a single [cognition] to occur sequentially. And yet, this is not observed. If it is argued that "it is that same [cognition] which, through a sequence, consists of the experience of the essential natures of form and so forth," then if a single cognition adopts a sequence, it follows that even the sequence is non-sequential. If it is argued that it adopts that [sequence] also sequentially, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Since at the stage of attachment to form there is no attachment to itself, how can there be oneness? For there is no other cognition apart from attachment. If its conceptualization of difference is also distinct, how can there be a sequence for a single [cognition]? If it is argued that "the one who is attached is non-different [from the cognition]," then in that case too, regarding the attachment to its own nature, there must be another subject who is attached; thus, that same infinite regress occurs. Therefore, if it were experienced by that very [cognition], there would be the consequence of two simultaneous conceptualizations.
By this, the experience of other cognitions occurring at the same time is also explained. 178.

[271,ii] Even if there were an experience of a cognition at the same time [as the object], there would be the consequence of two simultaneous conceptualizations. Consequently, there would have to be another conceptualization for that as well, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress of conceptualizations.

Furthermore, it might be argued that it is experienced by another cognition occurring at a later time, whether through perception or through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*). This is not correct, because:
And since memory occurs with respect to what is past, how could it arise for that which was not apprehended?
Furthermore, the cognition of one's own cognition would be non-different in form from the determination of another's cognition. (179)

[271,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does form increase or decrease? Does feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness increase or decrease? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is it because of the non-existence of form that form does not increase or decrease? Is it because of the non-existence of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease? Subhūti said: “It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Sugata. It is because of the non-cessation of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is it because of the non-defilement of form that form does not increase or decrease? It is because of the non-defilement of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is it because of the non-purification of form that form does not increase or decrease? Is it because of the non-purification of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease? Subhūti said: “It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Sugata. It is because of the non-purification of form that form does not increase or decrease. It is because of the non-purification of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is it because of the non-existence of form that form does not increase or decrease? Is it because of the non-existence of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease? Subhūti said: “It is so, Blessed One; it is so, Sugata. It is because of the non-existence of form that form does not increase or decrease. It is because of the non-existence of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness that they do not increase or decrease. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in this way, he trains in all the dharmas of a buddha, and he does not train in anything else.”

If past cognition is not perception with respect to that [past object], because perception has only a present object as its domain, and if it is argued that even then the cognition itself is indeed present, [we reply: in that case, there would be no apprehension of the nature of the grasping of form, nor would there be any other cognition. Therefore, since cognition is of the nature of awareness, whatever object is present within it appears [in it] just like a crystal or a mirror. That is incorrect. In that case, the grasping of form would be merely past; but what use would the nature of awareness be, even if it were present? Consequently, the thought "this is my grasping of form" would not occur. One might think "it was," but such is not the operation of perception. Now, if it is argued that the grasping of form possesses both pastness and presentness, then, since pastness also existed previously, this would be an impossible situation. For instance:
If it were always in a state of having passed away, it would never exist as present. That being the case, it is incorrect to say that the apprehension of form exists at all times. (PVA 333)

[271,vii] The Blessed One said: “O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is edible food, whether coarse or subtle? It is that which is taken by the mouthful, whether it be masticated or not masticated. What is contact as the second? It is the contact associated with the six sense bases. What is mental volition as the third? It is the mental volition associated with the six sense bases. What is consciousness as the fourth? It is the sixfold consciousness. Among these, how many nutriments are included within the aggregate of form? How many are included within the aggregate of feeling? How many are included within the aggregate of perception? How many are included within the aggregate of formations? How many are included within the aggregate of consciousness? Two nutriments are included within the aggregate of form: edible food, coarse or subtle, and the nutriment of contact. One nutriment is included within the aggregate of feeling: the nutriment of mental volition. One nutriment is included within the aggregate of perception: the nutriment of consciousness. Three nutriments are included within the aggregate of formations: the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental volition, and the nutriment of consciousness. Furthermore, among these four nutriments, how many are to be abandoned by seeing? How many are to be abandoned by cultivation? How many are neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation? Two nutriments are to be abandoned by cultivation: the nutriment of contact and the nutriment of consciousness. One nutriment is neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation: the nutriment of mental volition. One nutriment should be considered separately: the nutriment of edible food, coarse or subtle. Why is this so? If [the object] were always past, then since it existed even prior to that [present moment], there would never be a perception of form. Now, if it were first present and subsequently past, in that case, it could not be a single cognition. If, however, there is unity [of the cognition], then there would have to be a simultaneous apprehension of both [states]. If there is apprehension in succession, then it cannot be one at all; for unity and succession are contradictory. The meaning of succession is the abandonment of one and the adoption of the other. Since this has already been established previously, it will not be stated again. Therefore, there is simply no apprehension of the past. Furthermore, since even memory does not occur without apprehension, it follows that there is no apprehension at all of the realization of the perception of form. And if the consciousness is past, then the cognition "this is a consciousness" would not occur. If that were so, it would not be known whose consciousness this is. There would be an equivalence with the apprehension of another's mind, because there is no distinction in the recollection of its pastness. How is this understood? Is it from the "delimitation" (*pariccheda*) of another's mind? What is this "delimitation by another's mind"? Does it mean delimitation *by* another's mind, or the delimitation *of* another's mind? If it is delimitation *by* another's mind, then that is exactly what is accepted by the proponent of non-self-reflexive awareness (*asvasamvedana-vādin*). Otherwise, it is the delimitation *of* another's mind. That is incorrect, because the delimitation of another's mind is impossible. For the delimitation of another's mind occurs through inference. And inference is not a delimiting factor regarding one's own cognitions. Therefore, how can there be an equivalence in the delimitation? To this, it is replied:
This is stated with the intention that the past is beyond perception;
however, when there is direct establishment [of the object], it is impossible for the past to be beyond perception. (PVA 334)

For if that were perceived directly, then, like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it would not be indirect (*parokṣa*), nor would it be past; because that which is being directly experienced is necessarily present, otherwise its very status as present would not exist. Therefore, everything that is indirect must be cognized solely through inference. And since that [inference] takes the form of recollection (*smaraṇa*), there would be a parity between the cognition and the awareness of that cognition.

Now, if the cognition of one's own self is also measured by a means of knowledge other than inference, then that same parity [of the argument] results. If it is argued that the cognition of another is perceived as being related to another, whereas the cognition of oneself is not so perceived because it is perceived only as being related to oneself—and that it is not logical for one thing to be perceived in a manner other than its actual nature—that is incorrect. For this [distinction] would be possible only if apprehension were of the nature of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Because the term "prior" recurs in the case of inference and recollection, he demonstrates that very point:
[335] (PVA) [271,xii] He shows that very thing.

[272,i] An object-cognition that lacks a past instance as a corroborative example and lacks a logical mark—by what means is it established? For in that case, it is neither perceptual nor inferential. || 180 ||

For there is no example for the apprehension of what is past, because of the absence of perception; therefore, inferential knowledge does not cognize a sensation as being related to oneself or another. This is likewise because of the absence of perception. Moreover, it has been stated that if such perception were present, the object would not be "past. Consequently, since a logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot lead to inference without the prior grasping of a relationship, it follows that [inferential cognition] would only be restricted to the determination of a mere mental construct. In the case of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), however, the distinction between "that" and "other" is established solely by its own nature. If it is argued that just as there is inference without a [perceived] relationship, so too is there inference of a distinction [without one], this is also not tenable.
There was previously the apprehension of form here, by which its cognition is observed, just as fire existed previously in this place because of the observation of burning. (PVA 336)

Furthermore, there is no distinction therein as to whether the fire was produced by me or by another. If, however, it is inferred as being connected with another body—that cognition belongs to another—then the distinction is made as "this is one way and that is another. This [distinction] would be appropriate only if the cognition were perceived directly within the self. For instance, when the apprehension of a form is self-cognized, the distinction between "this is so" and "that is otherwise" is logical. Now, suppose it is argued that just as for the Sautrāntika, forms and other objects are apprehended by a consciousness that arises immediately after them and manifests their appearance—even though those objects are already past—and likewise is the apprehension of form. That is incorrect, because:

If that [cognition] were grasped by an immediately succeeding cognition which manifests its own nature— just as form and other objects are grasped— then there would be no apprehension of the preceding cognition. (181)

For forms and so forth do not appear as having their previous form; rather, having been transferred into a present cognition, they appear precisely as being present. And the apprehension of form is nothing other than the apprehension of the cognition of that form. However, this is not the case for [the apprehension of] a cognition, because there is no apprehension of a cognition [by another]. If, on the other hand, at that time the "cognition-of-cognition" (*buddhibuddhi*) is also apprehended, then in that case yet another cognition would have to be apprehended, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This being so, there would be a total non-apprehension of everything. Or, if it is held that the "cognition-of-cognition" is simply not apprehended, then it follows that even the object (*grāhya*) transferred into it would not be apprehended. If it is argued that only that "cognition-of-cognition" which occurs immediately after [the primary cognition] is apprehended, and not the one preceding it, then—assuming a subsequent cognition is admitted to arise immediately after the prior cognition—it will be stated later that there would be no apprehension of the uninterrupted stream of cognitions of form and so forth. If, again, a single cognition arises in a continuous series and immediately thereafter a cognition arises that apprehends all the preceding cognitions, even so, there would be no perception of all those cognitions in their sequential order, because the "cognition-of-cognition" would appear without sequence. If, on the other hand, they appear only in sequence, then there would be no perception of unity through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since they would be apprehended as being interrupted; thus, the fault previously mentioned—that it would be merely a matter of memory (*smṛti*)—remains.

[272,vii] Even if it is granted that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended by a non-conceptual cognition when it is being apprehended by itself, what contradiction is there in the apprehension of a distinct object (*grāhya*) by a conceptual cognition? None at all. However, [272,viii]...

Just as the experience of consciousness regarding its own object is non-conceptual, so too must other things be non-conceptual, for it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention for them. (182)

[272,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these three things, he is called a ‘Bodhisattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom, how then, Blessed One, does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva course in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive its increase or decrease; he does not perceive feeling, nor perception, nor formations, nor consciousness, nor does he perceive their increase or decrease. Subhūti, because he does not perceive form, nor its increase or decrease, and so on up to consciousness, this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva coursing in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive form, nor its increase or decrease, and so on up to consciousness, how then, Blessed One, does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift without perceiving a giver, a recipient, or a gift. This is his training in the perfection of giving. He observes morality without perceiving morality, nor the one who observes it, nor the basis for that morality. This is his training in the perfection of morality. He is patient without perceiving patience, nor the one who is patient, nor the basis for that patience. This is his training in the perfection of patience. He exerts vigor without perceiving vigor, nor the one who exerts it, nor the basis for that vigor. This is his training in the perfection of vigor. He enters meditative concentration without perceiving concentration, nor the one who enters it, nor the basis for that concentration. This is his training in the perfection of meditation. He cultivates wisdom without perceiving wisdom, nor the one who cultivates it, nor the basis for that wisdom. This is his training in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, it is in this way that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the six perfections.”

First of all, why is the apprehension of its own nature (*svarūpa*) graspable by a non-conceptual apprehension? To this, too, the same answer applies: for it is not possible for a nature to be joined with itself, nor with a word, nor with any other property (*dharma*). If this is so, then even form (*rūpa*) and the like cannot be joined by another [cognition], because joining is impossible for that which appears as its own nature. Indeed, that which appears as its own nature is not joined with something else appearing [simultaneously], since no joining is observed apart from the appearance of its own nature. Furthermore, it is not a reality (*paramārtha*) that what does not appear in its own form is joined [with something else]. Now, if it is argued that joining occurs precisely through the appearance in the cognition "this is a cow," this has already been addressed: [the cognition] "this is a cow" is not a cognition that [this object] has the nature of the word "cow"; rather, it is the determination through experience that "this very thing is denotable by the word 'cow'."
Furthermore:

For the Mīmāṃsaka, whose words have only universals as their objects and do not admit conceptual construction as having that same object, how could there be the apprehension of a particular through the absence of non-conceptual [cognition]?
Words have universals as their objects, and conceptual construction has that same single object;
if non-conceptual [perception] were absent, how could there be the apprehension of particulars? (183)

[273,iii] Now, if that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) does not have that same object, then in that case, the particular (*viśeṣa*) would not be joined with the word; thus, the determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*) "this is a cow" would not be a grasper of the particular. For it would follow that the cognition of the joining is one thing and the grasper of the particular is another, because of the difference in their natures—one being clear and the other otherwise—and because of the difference in their causes. To explain:
The cause for the form of the generality of sound is one's own latent predisposition (*vāsanā*);
the manifestation of a clear form and so forth arises from the eye and other sense organs.

For the nature of having the form of a word arises solely through the power of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a word experienced at the time of the convention of linguistic agreement, and not from the eye or other sense organs. The same applies to the nature of having the form of a universal (*sāmānya*). For instance, even in the absence of the eye and other senses, it occurs for one whose mind is conditioned by the latent impressions (*vāsanā-saṃskāra*) of prior experience. Conversely, even when the eye and other senses are present, it is absent for one whose mind lacks the corresponding latent impressions; therefore, it lacks the status of being caused by the eye and other such organs.
Now, if it is thought that there is simply no co-referentiality with objects appearing as bound by causes such as the eye when those causes, like the eye, are absent— that too is trivial.
For an object is indeed seen even in its form as established through inference.
This is because of the co-referentiality with the cognition "this is fire.

Indeed, it is not merely by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that there is the state of being apprehended by a cognition dependent on a single cause that grasps both [referents]. For coreferentiality is possible even when [the referents] are apprehended through other means of cognition, such as inference. Nor is coreferentiality something distinct from the experience of those two forms. What, then, is the distinction between coreferential and non-coreferential [terms]? For the experience of two forms is not impossible even in the case of two objects that have different substrates. This too is easily understood, because: [273,ix] The conventional usage of oneness regarding the performance of a single purpose [arises] from the universal (*jāti*).
The conventional usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also not difficult to establish.

(PVA 339) [273,x] The existence of conventional usage arises from mere causes in whatever way they may be; for the usage of coreferentiality and so forth has come down through a beginningless succession of conventions and is simply incapable of withstanding scrutiny, since when it is being scrutinized, it falls apart. To explain:
The cognition "this is fire" consists here solely of two things;
because it is the manifestation of their own respective forms, there is no relation of co-referentiality (*samānādhāratā*). (PVA 340)
The summary [273,xii]

Why is there a linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even in other cases through the appearance of a pair? Because the restriction of linguistic usage follows from the restriction of latent dispositions (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, the awakening of a latent disposition is itself restricted by the performance of a single causal function. If two cognitions appear, why does a linguistic usage of difference not occur? It has been stated that this is due to the restriction of latent dispositions. Therefore, coreferentiality does not establish the status of a single conceptual cognition. Now, if it is argued that the universal and the particular are not absolutely distinct, then even if they share a single object, the apprehension of the particular would be conceptual; that is incorrect. [273, xiii]
If the cognition of a particular were through non-difference from the universal, then—
whether by way of its entire nature or in some partial manner— the cognizer of all things would become identical with the omniscient one.

If, when there is the appearance of a universal in conceptualization, there is also the appearance of its particular due to the difference from that [universal], then there would also be an appearance of the particular in verbal cognition, because the logic is the same. Indeed, when the logic is the same, it cannot be that the logic is not the same.

Because it would follow that there is an absence of logical propriety (*nyāyyatā*). Now, if it is argued that the particular (*saviśeṣa*) does not appear due to the absence of causes such as the eye, how then is it non-different from that? For it cannot be known to be non-different unless it enters into identity with it. If it is argued that it enters later, then at that time the thing itself no longer exists; for its reality consists precisely in that form, and if it were to appear in that form, how could there be any understanding of its entry [into identity]?
If it does not appear in that form, how can there be an understanding of its entry?

(342) (PVA) If it appears in the very same form in which it was previously seen, then how can there be an understanding of its entry, as in the previous case? If it does not appear in that form, then it lacks that reality; how, then, can there be an understanding of its entry?

Therefore, that which does not appear [to cognition] is neither one nor many. Consequently, the claim that what appeared as distinct earlier subsequently undergoes integration is nonsensical. For that reason, even in the absence of a cause, that which does not appear possesses multiplicity precisely through its unity. Therefore:
In the absence of non-conceptual [knowledge], how could there be the realization of distinctions? (183)
If there exists even a single non-conceptual thing, then all things must have the same cause; for the difference between effects arises from the difference in their causes. (184)

[274, vii] Now, if one were to abandon the form of conceptual construction (*kalpanārūpa*) and claim that there is an apprehension of a particularity (*viśeṣādhigama*) due to the perception of a particularity imparted by causes such as the eye, then that [cognition], being dependent on those causes, would be non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) alone. Indeed, it is not tenable for a difference in entities to be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) without relying on a difference in their causes. Therefore, what is produced from a cause of a certain kind must be of that same kind; and there is no identity of cause between a conceptual and its opposite (non-conceptual) cognition. For instance:
[274, viii]
The application of external objects [to words] occurs through the recollection of convention;
likewise, visual cognition, without depending on convention, arises solely through the power of the object itself. (185)

For when conceptual construction, which has the nature of joining [sensory data], arises through the power of a causal complex whose intrinsic natures are established by mutual exclusion, how could it possibly possess a connection with an intrinsic nature that partakes in the existence of that very causal complex? Joining occurs solely through the force of recollecting a convention that is independent of external objects; whereas sensory cognition is dependent on external objects and independent of conventions. In that case, there is no status as conceptual construction because of the absence of the causes for such construction, for an effect does not arise in the absence of its cause.

Now, it might be argued that sensory cognition, arising through the power of an external relation such as the universal of sound (*śabdasāmānya*), would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*). That too is incorrect, because:
That which has a relation with something else appears together with it.
Because of this necessity, this [ultimate reality] does not fall within the scope of valid cognition.

Thus, does it follow that even in this view there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all related entities? Or [is it argued that] whatever—such as a universal (*sāmānya*)—is established in a particular locus, that very thing appears when it is perceived there? That too is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that the word itself is not apprehended. For a word does not exist in things such as cloth; otherwise, the cognition "cloth" would arise even for one who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*). Furthermore, such is not the case, because doubt is observed regarding the denotable object (*vācyatā*); for even when the object is established, there is no certainty regarding the specific distinctions of the expressive words (*vācaka*). If it is argued that there is indeed certainty because of their identical form, we say no, because that is absent at the first moment of perception. Moreover, this is because it has been demonstrated [in our system] that [the universal] is not distinct from that [particular], and so forth.

[274, xiii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "It is form and so forth alone, depending on the recollection of the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) for the cognition 'cow' and so on, that—acting as a cooperative cause with the sense faculty—produces a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), and not without such dependence, because the effect is accomplished through the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*). When a word, a universal, or some other qualifier was previously apprehended and is now recollected, then the eye and other faculties, aided by that recollection, produce [the cognition]. Therefore, it does not occur for those who lack both the prior apprehension of the convention and the current perception; thus, that [objection] is not well-established. To explain: [275, i]

If form were dependent upon the recollection of a convention in the sensory consciousness, it would not be capable [of producing cognition] without depending on that recollection, just like a logical mark (liṅga). (186)

[275,ii] For there can be no connection with that [word] without a prior experience; nor can there be a connection with specific words and so forth without a specific recollection; nor can there be a specific recollection without the awakening of the seed of that specific recollection; nor can there be the capacity for such specific awakening without perception. Therefore, when there is perception, there is the recollection of its designator, and when there is recollection, there is the connection. Thus, for the perceived object, that which awakens the recollection—namely, the visible form and so forth—is itself the logical mark (*liṅga*). Consequently, the entire cognition of connection is purely inferential (*laiṅgika*).

[275,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding the suffering of those beings, addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if there are any sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should perceive all five aggregates as being like a dream. Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “How should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* perceive the five aggregates as being like a dream? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said: “Śāriputra, form is empty; emptiness is not form. Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form. What is form is emptiness; what is emptiness is form. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are empty, without characteristics, unproduced, undestroyed, stainless, and not stainless, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and even no non-attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all error and inverted views, he attains *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the peerless mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.*” [276,i] Then the venerable Śāriputra and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara rejoiced and departed.
