Now, if the universal (*sāmānya*) is not actually perceived, how can it be cognized through a logical mark (*liṅga*)? For the universal is said to be the similarity of parts (*avayava-samānatā*), and that has indeed been apprehended previously. Therefore, it is remembered, because the possession of such parts is the objective basis for the conventional usage of "similarity. Furthermore, the similarity of the parts themselves arises from the equality of such parts; and this continues up to the similarity of cognitions, which in turn arises from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of such [objects]. This reflective awareness, too, stems from beginningless mental predispositions (*vāsanā*); thus, there is no fault. Consequently, the connection with a word or a universal and so forth, being a memory derived solely from a logical mark, is here considered inference (*anumāna*).

[275,iv] Now, if it is argued that perception is defined as that which is associated with the operation of the sense organs (*akṣavyāpāra*), then it would follow that all inference is indeed perception, since it too is produced by the sense organs. For instance:
In the cognition "there is fire in this place," there is no application of fire to the place;
yet, in the absence of the operation of the senses, why is perceptuality not attained?
[275, vi] Now, if it is argued that perception itself is the application of inference regarding mere fire, that too is ignorance. For it can be said even in this case:
Direct perception extends only to the specific object present before one; the connection, however, is established through inference.
Without the sensory cognition of fire being apprehended, there can be no such connection.

Indeed, connection [of the object] with the fire is possible only through inference, because the operation of the senses is impossible with respect to it. For that which has not been apprehended by perception cannot be connected by it; it is contradictory to say that what is unapprehended is connected with what is apprehended.
[275,ix] But surely there would be no connection even by means of inference, since:
Inference does not apply to a specific location that has not been apprehended; it is sheer audacity to claim that an object perceived through direct perception is apprehended by inference. (PVA 345)

For just as direct perception does not arise regarding a fire that is out of sight, so too there is no inference regarding a place that is directly perceived; the logic is the same. Furthermore, if something were an object of inference, it could not be directly perceived, for the convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-samplava*) is not accepted.
In the ultimate sense, no synthesis of anything is possible;
rather, such a conceptual construction arises immediately following the two [perceptions].

The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that follows upon perception and inference—the cognition that joins [a name] with [an object] as "this is here"—is indeed inference (*anumāna*), specifically inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), because it arises from beginningless conventional usage of such a nature. Therefore, this joining is designated by the term "inference. But how does inference itself arise in the form of a joining? There is no fault here, because it arises from seeing [the object] in that way through perception.
Thus, it is established that perception is not of the nature of a joining; and this has already been demonstrated previously.

[275,xv] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even with respect to an imperceptible object, perception indeed operates when that object is being remembered; therefore, the connection [of the word] occurs through perception itself. This too is untrue, because:
Since that [cognition] arises from contact with that [object], it would be a sensory perception (akṣadhī) rather than a memory;
consequently, it might occur even at a later time, provided there is no distraction. (187)

If it is maintained that the arising of that sensory cognition occurs when there is a connection with memory regarding what is being remembered, then that sensory cognition would arise from memory alone and would not depend upon the presence of the object. Alternatively, if it were to depend upon the presence of the object, then it would not arise from memory at all, because direct perception is distinct from recollection. Or else, it might occur even at a different time, since at that time there could be some distraction characterized by another conceptualization. Consequently, even that sensory consciousness would become a recollection occurring at a later time.
Furthermore: if that object were always the cause of non-conceptual cognition in the same way it was initially, then perception would be exclusively non-conceptual.
If it were the cause of both [conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions] successively, then it would have to exist as such from the very beginning, since there is no difference [in the object].

If that [mind] were the cause of both, then both would have been produced simultaneously from the very beginning. Alternatively, if you argue that the sense faculty, aided by memory, produces conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) and not otherwise—that is incorrect. Indeed, no such assistance of memory to the eye is ever perceived. It is not the case that everything is an aid to everything simply because it is an "aid"; rather, only that which is observed to function as such is an aid. Furthermore, clarity and so forth are certainly not produced in the cognition of the eye and other faculties by means of memory. If you claim that it produces a state of certainty (*niścitarūpatā*), that is untenable; for: [276,iv] [The verse follows: *na hy ālocanavijñāne vyaktībhūto vidhiḥ kvacit / na ca niścayavijñāne vyaktirūpaṃ pratīyate // tasmān na smaraṇād eva niścayo 'yaṃ pravartate / svaviṣayābhimukhena jñānenaiva sa janyate //* For in the sensory perception (*ālocanavijñāna*), no distinct feature (*vidhi*) is ever manifested. Nor is a manifested form perceived in the conceptualizing cognition (*niścayavijñāna*). Therefore, this certainty does not proceed from memory alone; it is produced precisely by a cognition directed toward its own object.
If the ascertainment were already present in that form due to non-difference,
then even when it is not of that form, that [ascertainment] would result from another cognition born of the senses.

If the very form that appeared previously is itself the determination (*niścitatva*) and nothing more, then it is identical to the prior form; thus there is no additional element, because the determination is not distinct from the non-determination. Alternatively, if an additional form appears therein, then that must be a different cognition (*pratyaya*) altogether, as it is connected with a different form. This is because there is no operation of the sense organ (*akṣavyāpāra*) regarding that form or its qualifiers. Now, if it is argued that the mental reference (*ullekha*) "this" operates upon that very same object, and therefore this [determination] possesses the status of perception (*pratyakṣatā*) because it functions as a direct apprehension (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), that too is incorrect. Why? Because:
vii] This conceptual construction of "this" would be non-conceptual,
because it does not construct the sequence of priority and posteriority regarding the connection with causal efficiency and so forth. (PVA 348)

Because it directly perceives only the present form and so forth, and because it lacks the apprehension of relations such as priority and posteriority or causal efficiency, it does not differ from another non-conceptual cognition. For one who is not itself conceptualizing cannot be called "conceptual. Therefore, this [cognition], which has a clear aspect, is indeed distinct from that [non-conceptual cognition] which has an unclear aspect regarding remembered qualifiers and the like. This being the case:
If it is argued that memory is the cause of the cognition of "otherness," then memory is likewise useless in that case as well.

[276,x] Furthermore, it might be argued that the object of sensory cognition is a distinct, vivid form (*ākāra*) entirely different from the form being remembered. If this were so, then memory would be useless in that regard; for memory is not of service in the act of apprehension, since that [vivid form] is perceived in such a way even without memory.

Just as the recollection of a convention (*samayasmṛti*) is desired for the sake of establishing identity, so too must difference be apprehended as non-identical; what, then, would be the purpose of such a recollection in that case? (189)

[276,xii] If that [object] were delineated by the eye and other faculties accompanied by memory as having that form, then in the absence of that [memory], there would be no cognition of it. If you argue that this delineation as "this" simply does not occur, we say no; for even in the absence of the delineation "this," the form of that object still appears. Even if that [memory] were present, since there is no other distinguishing factor [in its absence], what utility would it have? If you claim its utility lies in prompting activity (*pravartana*), we shall demonstrate that activity occurs even without it. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that this is a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*). [276,xiii]

Now, it might be argued: "Since the initial [cognition] of one who has not practiced cannot induce activity without memory, memory is required for that purpose. To this it is replied: If the difference is perceived as disconnected—that is, as entirely unrelated—what else can memory do there? Since memory is sought for the sake of establishing a connection, if that [connection] is not established in such a way, then memory is of no use for its comprehension. As for the induction of activity, that would indeed occur for the initial [cognizer] through another means of valid cognition, namely inference. Therefore, [memory is not required] for conceptual construction.

The operation is directed toward the apprehension of the specific nature (*svarūpa*), not toward the initiation of action; however, through habituation (*abhyāsa*), this very operation proceeds even though it is purposeless. For things do not come into being merely because there is a purpose, since the existence of a thing depends solely upon its cause.

Now, if the apprehension of a specific nature different from the previous one occurs, then this is indeed another cognition, having the form of mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*); this will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, it might be argued: "Only the universal (*sāmānya*) is grasped by that [cognition], not the particular (*bheda*), which was previously unobserved. If that were so, then:
When there is the apprehension of a mere universal, dependence upon particulars is not logical.

If the apprehension of the universal alone were produced by the eye and other sense organs, then, since there would be no possibility of another [cognition] that apprehends difference, there would be no desire to apprehend difference once the universal has been apprehended. Yet such a desire does arise. For instance, when the universal is apprehended through the cognition "this is a cow," people in the world observe, "What kind of cow is this?
Therefore, visual consciousness arises in dependence upon both the eye and the visible form. (190)
Because recollection is of no utility therein, the visual cognition arises from the eye and visible form alone. For it is thus:
The operation of the eye occurs only toward that which is present before it regarding mere form;
otherwise, how could there be an operation for something being apprehended elsewhere?

For it is not possible to conceive of something as being one way when it is perceived in another; indeed, one cannot claim that the eye, while operating upon the mere form present before it, also operates upon sound, generality (*sāmānya*), and so forth, because there is no evidence for such a thing. To assume otherwise would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore: [277,ix] either subsequent to recollection, or prior to the arising of recollection.

Because the object is distinct [from the conceptual content], perception is free from conceptual construction (avikalpaka). (PVA 350) Indeed, a cognition such as "this is fragrant" or "this is foul-smelling," which arises at a time subsequent to recollection, is not perception. This is because the operation of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) pertains only to the visible form (*rūpa*). Therefore, only that which arises based on the eye and other [senses] with respect to an object is perception; nothing else is. Consequently, the forms of words, universals (*sāmānya*), and so forth, are not perceptual. Furthermore, whatever else serves as the cause for a clear manifestation is also accepted as its basis; thus, mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and the like are also perception.
Alternatively, it has been stated that even that [mental perception] is indeed "direct" (*akṣa*), because it reaches—that is, pervades—the form of the object.
<5. Varieties of Direct Perception>
[277,xii] (1) Direct Perception through the Senses (*indriyapratyakṣa*):

Now, why is it called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) when its production is dependent upon the object (*viṣaya*), and not "perception according to each object" (*prativiṣaya*)? For designation by means of the object—such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—is appropriate, but not by means of the sense organ. It is not the case that something is "direct perception" simply because it is produced by a sense organ; rather, everything that functions toward the apprehension of the specific nature of an object is direct perception. However, some direct perception is based on the sense organs (*akṣāśraya*), while another is otherwise. And that designation is appropriate for it which is based on an unerring cause.

[277, xiii] But is not even that which is produced from an object—such as the double moon and so forth—merely an error? Therefore, nothing that arises even from an object is entirely non-erroneous. [Objection: But surely that [double moon] is not even an object, because its cause is incapable of imparting a form [to consciousness]. [Response: In that case, it is not the sense faculty itself that is the cause, because it is impaired; rather, it is the unimpaired sense faculty, while that [double moon] is merely a semblance of the sense faculty (*akṣābhāsa*). If this is so, then: [278, i]
Just as one who produces direct cognition is capable [of perceiving] an object, why then is that [cognition], whose birth depends on two factors, not said to be [dependent] on them? (191)

[278,ii] Since the object and the sense faculty are equal in their status as causes, why is there no designation by means of the object? For those who act with deliberation do not apply or abandon designations merely at random. To this, it is replied:
For a designation is applied only after having observed its indicative power;
and since that [power] exists in the designation "sense-organ" (akṣa), and that property [of being indicative] belongs to it, let it be so designated. (192)

For the adoption and rejection [of a means] are based on its being informative (*gamaka*) or non-informative (*agamaka*). And in the designation of a sense-faculty (*akṣa*), there is informativeness, since perception is dependent upon the sense-faculties. As for the objection regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to a damaged [faculty], that has already been refuted. [Objection: In that case, there is no deviation even with respect to the object (*viṣaya*), because that [perception] does not have the object as its [direct] objective. [Reply: This is not so. [278,v]
If this [external] object did not exist, how could there be perception of another?
Furthermore, the nature of a sense faculty is not qualified by the existence or non-existence of a single [object].

Therefore he says: "Designation by means of a common [property] is observed, as in 'the sound of a drum' or 'a barley sprout. When one says 'barley sprout,' there is no cognition of a non-barley sprout; however, the expression 'earth-sprout' does occur, and the same applies elsewhere.
[278, viii]

Now, if "with respect to each object" (*prativiṣayam*) means the apprehension of the essential nature of the object, then in that case, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone would be perception (*pratyakṣa*), while in other cases there would be a lack of proof [for it being perception]. Alternatively, if it is said to mean the apprehension of the object as it is commonly known in the world (*lokaprasiddha*), then let this very worldly consensus be what constitutes "perception"; what is the use of postulating another designation? Furthermore, according to the systems of the Vaibhāṣikas and others, even mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would result in being perception because it apprehends an object. Therefore, it is more logical that even that [mental consciousness] be designated as "perception. As it has been said: "For an object is common (*sādhāraṇa*) to the various mental consciousnesses belonging to different continua, because it serves as a cause for them. Therefore, the nature of perception—its freedom from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍhatā*)—can be defined by its designation based on the sense faculty (*indriya*), but not by its designation based on the object."

[278,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as existing. Since he does not perceive any dharma, he does not apprehend any dharma; because he does not apprehend any dharma, he does not become attached to any dharma. Not being attached to any dharma, he does not turn back from the path of a bodhisattva. He does not think, ‘I am near to full enlightenment,’ nor does he think, ‘I am far from it. Subhūti, this is the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom.”

But surely it is possible to characterize [the cognition] by means of the object as well? For instance, one might say: "Because it arises through the power (*sāmarthya*) of the object. For that [cognition], being produced by the power of the object, would indeed conform to the form of that [object]. No, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*). There is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the form of a double moon. Or, if you argue that an erroneous [cognition] does not arise through the power of an object, then in that case, its non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpakatva*) would not be established by this reasoning. Therefore, it is the sense faculty itself that is designated here as "[the cause] of the object," because [the cognition] is intent upon the object. Precisely for this reason, since the sense faculty is the indicator (*gamaka*), the designation is made by means of it alone.
Therefore, in this case, the application of the designation based on the nature of the mark is withdrawn, because of the cessation of a nature that is not pervading. (193)
Those who act with prior deliberation state that only a formal injunction (*niyoga*) is indicative; therefore, this alone is the mark (*liṅga*) for being indicative.

[278,xii] But how is it known that the instigator acts with prior deliberation? This is true; the understanding that a statement possesses a real object does not arise from the authority of a person. Rather, it is said thus according to worldly convention. In ultimate reality, however, pervasion is stated by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), whereby one expresses the cessation [of the probandum] through the cessation of the pervading nature.
[278,xiii]

Now, the designation "with respect to each object" (*prativiṣayam*) is an expression that indicates what is commonly known in the world as conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*). Furthermore, that which has a single object existing across prior and subsequent moments is the perception (*pratyakṣa*) that is conceptual. For this is well-known in the world as "perception. Indeed: "This very thing which was seen by me is now cognized through perception."
For all word-meanings are indeed accessible through worldly consensus.

And an uncontradicted cognition is entitled to the designation of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Once something has been cognized by a valid means of knowledge, how could it be otherwise? (352–353)
[279,ii] This, therefore, is simply non-existent.
In this context, the meaning of "direct perception" (pratyakṣa) is simply direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa), which is the very nature of cognition.
For there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apart from inference than direct realization.

Inference alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by non-perceptual apprehension (*asākṣātkaraṇa*). Therefore, if recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) functions through non-perceptual apprehension, it is nothing but inference. Since the quality of being perceptual (*sākṣātkāritā*) pertains only to an object present before one, recognition is not [perception]. Thus, perceptual apprehension is understood only from the designation "sensory" (*indriya*), and not from anything else. By the designation of the "object," there would merely be the state of having an object; it does not constitute a statement of its perceptual nature. Furthermore, what is designated by that [term "sensory"] is not commonly recognized in the world as being perception. And since perception is a means of valid cognition, it is established that perception is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), for there is no awareness other than perceptual apprehension that constitutes perception.
[279,v] How, then, was this said?
In that case, because it is produced by multiple objects, it has a universal as its object with respect to its own referent.
Indeed, non-conceptual [cognition] does not have a universal as its object, because the conceptualization of a universal is in contradiction with it. He says this very thing:
The sense-cognition there arises with respect to a collection that is an aggregate;
and a cognition of a universal is necessarily followed by conceptual construction.

Indeed, when many things existing by mutually excluding one another's essential natures are perceived in that very way, there can be no cognition of a "collection" (samudāya), whether that collection be ultimate (pāramārthika) or conceptual (kalpita). It cannot first be ultimate, because apart from those [individuals], there is no appearance of a universal (sāmānya).
Or, let that other thing which appears as a reflection appear as such;

however, it is not a composite (*samudāya*). Or, if it were a composite in that way, then let those very things become designated as a "composite" through their mutual dependence; what is the use of another?

[279,xii] Now, if another form appears after those forms have been concealed, since that too lacks an existence as such a real entity, how is it not merely a superimposition? And if its object is imagined, its conceptual nature is difficult to avoid. To this, it is replied:
[279,xiii]
Those other atoms which arise due to their connection with different objects are called "aggregated" (sañcita), for they are the cause of the production of cognition. // 195 //
That particularity of atoms cannot exist without other atoms; therefore, because it is not restricted to a single [atom], cognition is said to have the universal as its object. (196)

For atoms, having not yet produced the causal capacity for cognition in others, are incapable of generating consciousness; they are [only] visible to those with subtle vision. Therefore, consciousness must be generated by all [atoms together]. Indeed, it has been stated that a single, fixed object is one whose universal aspect is constructed by cognition. If it is asked, "Why do they not appear as mutually distinct?", [the answer is: surely even hairs and the like, when far away, do not come within the range of perception as being non-conjoined. Thus, if they do not appear because they lack the capacity to impart their own nature—which is restricted by its own causes—then what blame is there here? In that case, since there is no appearance of existence in what is not perceived, there would be error. Furthermore, even in the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), if there is such an appearance, it would possess conceptualization (*savikalpaka*), just like the conceptualization of another universal.
[279,xvi] Now,

if it is argued that there is non-conceptuality because the very nature of cognition appears there as being directly perceived in the form of a single, solid, and gross object— thereby eliminating all conceptualization, since in every instance of conceptual cognition it is only the form of cognition itself that appears— then the following is said: [280,i]

Because there is an absence of subverting cognitions, the non-erroneousness of those born at present is asserted; however, in reality, all [cognitions] are errors with respect to their objective supports.

To those people of the present day, whose power of awakening has not yet dawned, this appears to be non-erroneous. With reference to them, it is said to be "non-erroneous. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), everything is indeed erroneous with respect to its objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore:
"In this way, it is precisely the absence of conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*) that is stated regarding perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
Because it consists of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), it is not combined with grasping.

For that which is conceptual (*savikalpaka*) is not direct perception, because in conceptualization there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a previously apprehended object. Indeed, direct perception itself is not called superimposition; for reality is established through the opposite of that [superimposition]. If this is so, then [the claim that concepts] have the universal as their object is false, because according to worldly consensus they possess the nature of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). And it has been said: "With respect to the particularity of the sense-field (*āyatana-svalakṣaṇa*), these have the particular as their object, but not the particularity of the substance (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*). That too is false.
This distinction was formulated by the former teachers with reference to the ultimate truth;
therefore, there is no contradiction, as it pertains to the same object. (PVA 357)

[280, vi] It is precisely the atoms themselves, when apprehended in such a manner, that constitute the universal. Furthermore, regarding what is said—that everything is indeed free from conceptual construction—we reply to that as follows:
That which has been seen has indeed arrived through the cognition of a means of valid knowledge;
relying on what is established for others, the author of the treatise proclaimed this division.

Relying on the consensus of others, such as the Mīmāṃsakas and so forth, the author of the treatise explains the object through conceptualization by way of recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). Since that [conceptualization] does not exist in direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), he has thus established the distinction between conceptual and non-conceptual [cognition].
[280,ix] Now, even if they belong to a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*), multiple [objects] are not grasped simultaneously.
[280,xi] Therefore, due to the superimposition of an object previously apprehended, it is conceptual.

For if multiple atoms were apprehended simultaneously, there would be no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) upon an object previously apprehended; thus, it would not be conceptual (*savikalpaka*) by virtue of being a recollective construction (*anusmaraṇavikalpa*). However, this is difficult to avoid if they are apprehended sequentially. Furthermore, a single cognition is not capable of apprehending many things at once, because when the mind is occupied with one thing, it cannot simultaneously operate toward another. Or rather, a single composite substance (*avayavidravya*) must be admitted on account of its simultaneous apprehension. [280,xii] "Even though that unity has gone to each individual atom, which is itself manifold and graspable," (PVA 359).
How could there be a simultaneous appearance of grasping in the case of sesame seeds and other such things that are separate? (197)

[280,xiv] If atoms are not perceived simultaneously, then, because of the superimposition of what precedes, we indeed accept that it is conceptual. But if they are seen [simultaneously], then, because of direct perception, its non-conceptual nature is established.

Furthermore: By whom has this been established—that a plurality of objects situated in suitable locations is not perceived simultaneously by a single [cognition]? If it is argued that this is because the mind (*manas*) is unitary, we say no; for the existence of a "mind" as a factor that obstructs the simultaneous arising of cognitions is unproven. This is because what is established is merely *manaskāra* (mental attention), which is the nature of the mind. Moreover, the perception of simultaneous apprehension is indeed observed in the case of sesame seeds and rice grains, or a staff, a water-pot, a vessel, and earrings, even though they are not mutually conjoined. To claim that the appearance of simultaneity is due to the rapidity of apprehension is also incorrect, because: [280,xvi] [The verse follows: ... [the argument continues regarding the impossibility of rapidity accounting for the illusion of simultaneity].

The objection regarding lightness has already been answered in the case of those very cognitions occurring in succession. Why is there no perception of simultaneity? For all cognitions are indeed simultaneous. (198)
Among those [cognitions], some appear to be non-sequential while others appear to be sequential;
therefore, in the apprehension of all objects, this [objection that] it must be non-sequential follows as a consequence. (199)

[281,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, when they pass away from this world, are reborn in the world of the gods. The Venerable Ānanda asked: “What are those four? The Blessed One replied: “In this case, Ānanda, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. When he passes away from this world, he is reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm. This, Ānanda, is the first kind of person who, passing away from this world, is reborn in the world of the gods. Furthermore, Ānanda, another person dwells with a mind full of compassion, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. When he passes away from this world, he is reborn among the gods of the Ābhāsvara realm. This, Ānanda, is the second kind of person who, passing away from this world, is reborn in the world of the gods. Furthermore, Ānanda, another person dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. When he passes away from this world, he is reborn among the gods of the Subhakṛtsna realm. This, Ānanda, is the third kind of person who, passing away from this world, is reborn in the world of the gods. Furthermore, Ānanda, another person dwells with a mind full of equanimity, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. When he passes away from this world, he is reborn among the gods of the Śubha-kiṃśuka realm. This, Ānanda, is the fourth kind of person who, passing away from this world, is reborn in the world of the gods. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, when they pass away from this world, are reborn in the world of the gods. The Venerable Ānanda asked: “Venerable sir, what is the distinction, what is the difference between these four kinds of persons? The Blessed One replied: “In this case, Ānanda, the person who dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, when he passes away from this world, is reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm. There, Ānanda, he dwells for the full lifespan of the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm, and having completed that lifespan, he passes away from there. Having passed away from there, he is reborn in this very Jambudvīpa as a universal monarch, a wheel-turning king, righteous, a king of righteousness, victorious over the four quarters, having established stability in his realm, possessing the seven treasures. What do you think, Ānanda? Is it possible to point out a specific cause for this, such that because of that cause, this person—having dwelt with a mind full of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—is reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm, and having completed the full lifespan there, is reborn here in Jambudvīpa as a universal monarch? “Certainly not, venerable sir. “It is impossible, Ānanda, to point out a specific cause for this, such that because of that cause, this person—having dwelt with a mind full of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—is reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm, and having completed the full lifespan there, is reborn here in Jambudvīpa as a universal monarch. However, Ānanda, it is possible to point out a general cause for this, such that because of that cause, this person—having dwelt with a mind full of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—is reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm, and having completed the full lifespan there, is reborn here in Jambudvīpa as a universal monarch. And what, Ānanda, is that general cause? It is this: that person was previously a human being, and while still a human being, he practiced the practice of a Bodhisattva. Having practiced the practice of a Bodhisattva, he gave gifts, performed meritorious deeds, and undertook vows. Having given gifts, performed meritorious deeds, and undertaken vows, he developed a strong aspiration: ‘May I, through this root of merit, be reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm. Because of that aspiration, Ānanda, this person—having dwelt with a mind full of loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—is reborn among the gods of the Brahmā-kāyika realm. Having completed the full lifespan there, he is reborn here in Jambudvīpa as a universal monarch. This, Ānanda, is the general cause for this; it is not possible to point out a specific cause. It is not the case that simultaneous apprehension is justified on the grounds of rapidity (*lāghava*), because there is no such thing as rapidity [that could account for it], and because [the notion of rapidity] has already been refuted. Why is this so? If it is argued: "It is understood that the impression of simultaneous apprehension arises due to rapidity, just like the piercing of a hundred lotus petals," we say: No. For a matter is not established merely by an example; what is proven in one instance is not necessarily so in another. In the case of piercing a hundred petals, however, the sequence is established through inference, because it is impossible for those connected in a vertical succession to be pierced simultaneously. Furthermore, if such a conceptualization were allowed, an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*) could not be prevented. Therefore, in the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), the claim of error is not established. Moreover, if you maintain that the impression of simultaneous apprehension regarding those very [petals] occurs due to rapidity, then why does this not happen in the same way with things that are previously non-existent [appearing in sequence]? If you argue that it is because of the absence of rapidity [in the latter case], then from where do you derive this [distinction] in the present case as well? If you say it is "because of the impression of simultaneous apprehension," then from where is that derived? This would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): as long as the erroneous nature of the simultaneous apprehension is not established, the establishment of rapidity cannot occur; and as long as that [rapid apprehension] is not established, the erroneous nature [of the simultaneous apprehension] remains unproven. Furthermore:
Since all cognitions are momentary, they are equal in duration. Therefore, why is it that in all cases there is no appearance of a temporal sequence among cognitions? (PVA 360)
For the appearance of the object of cognition occurs for the duration of the measure of the cognition.

Consequently, the entire manifestation of the object of cognition would necessarily be non-sequential. Therefore, even the simultaneous appearance is not caused by rapidity (*lāghava*), because it exists in that very same way [as non-sequential]. However, where there is no simultaneous appearance due to a deficiency in the causes, there is the opposite; such is the established rule.
When there is no apprehension of a single [moment], the possibility of a non-conceptual manifestation arises.
Without the presence of conceptualization, the apprehension of a clear object is impossible.
(361) How could there be a clear manifestation of a superimposition of what was previously seen?
Because there is an absolute absence of cultivation [of that], it is indeed non-conceptual. (362) (PVA)
For in this very way, the cognition of yogins is likewise non-conceptual.
And thus, there is only a simultaneous manifestation, because there is no grasping of a prior form.
Otherwise, how could a single variegated form, such as that of a butterfly and so forth, ever be seen?
If it is argued that this manifold is one, then that is even more extraordinary.

[281,x] If it is argued that because the mind operates on only one object at a time, there is no simultaneous apprehension of multiple things, and therefore one must accept that the variegated color of a butterfly is a single composite whole (*avayavin*), then this acceptance is even more variegated than the variegated butterfly itself. For:
A variegated form does not possess a single nature, just like the appearance of a gem.

The term "variegated" (*citram*) is a designation for an entity whose nature consists of mutually interconnected parts; otherwise, what would be the meaning of "variegated" here? Therefore, just as there is no unity in a collection of gems of various forms, how could there be unity in the nature of a variegated butterfly? If it is argued that the gems are multiple because they are capable of being separated, while the butterfly is not, we say no, because separation is possible in that case as well. Separation is simply the appearance of things as distinct from one another.

[281, xiii] Now, if there were oneness even when there is division, then that would also apply to a collection of jewels. There is another kind of division there called "separation," and therefore, because of that non-separation, even a variegated object would be one. That is not so, because separation is possible in all cases. For instance:
Since separation through cutting, splitting, and so forth is possible everywhere, the destruction of a substance occurs in all such cases; thus, this applies universally. (363) (PVA) [281,xv]

If separation, which is called disjunction, is possible, then there is no single composite whole (*avayavin*) in that collection of jewels. Why then does this not also apply to a variegated butterfly and the like? In that case, since separation arises through effort by means of cutting and so forth, the destruction of the composite whole occurs; therefore, there is no disjunction [of the parts from one another], and thus there is no fault. Let this same reasoning be applied to the collection of jewels as well; the logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) is identical. (The Refutation of the Composite Whole) [282,i]

[Objection: "Even though blue and other colors are perceived as mutually exclusive, since the tactile sensation (*sparśa*) has that same single nature and because the parts are not distinct from one another, the composite whole (*avayavin*) must be one and the same. [Response: That too is incorrect, because:
"The appearance of blue and other colors is the same in variegated cloths and the like. (201)

In artificial variegated paintings and the like, which consist of a collection of threads of different kinds, the same distinction of blue and other colors occurs, accompanied by an inseparable concomitance with the lack of distinction in touch and so forth. In that case, from what source does this distinction arise— namely, that in one instance there is a whole (*avayavin*) and in the other there is not?
If, in that case, only the form of the parts is perceived, then you are seeing a variegated whole that is distinct from the blue and other [colors], having set those aside. (202)

[282,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. He does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive form as unreal. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive forms as unreal; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the eye-consciousness as unreal; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive eye-contact as unreal; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as unreal; he does not perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the earth element as unreal; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive ignorance as unreal; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving as unreal; he does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the internal as unreal; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as unreal; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the four meditative concentrations as real, nor does he perceive the four meditative concentrations as unreal; he does not perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen emptinesses, or the eight liberations as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the nine successive meditative abidings as real, nor does he perceive the nine successive meditative abidings as unreal; he does not perceive the ten totalities as real, nor does he perceive the ten totalities as unreal. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as unreal; he does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or great compassion as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as unreal; he does not perceive the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha as unreal. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditation. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path. He does not perceive the four meditative concentrations, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen emptinesses, the eight liberations, or the nine successive meditative abidings. He does not perceive the ten totalities, nor does he perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or great compassion. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, arhatship, the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, or the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal.
