How does he train in the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen emptinesses, the eight liberations, or the nine successive meditative abidings? How does he train in the ten totalities? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence

If, in the case of artificial objects such as painted cloths, only the form of the constituent parts is perceived as such through an adherence to their unity, then—setting aside blue and other colors which exist in a state of differentiation—there is no other "variegated" (*citra*) quality even in non-artificial objects. In that case, the adherence to unity is the only refuge; yet that adherence exists even in artificial objects without there being a whole (*avayavin*). Therefore, that hope [for a variegated whole] has vanished, and it is not logical for variegation to belong to a whole, because neither perception nor inference establishes it. Furthermore, in the case of magnets, iron balls, and the like, the pulling of one part while another part is pulled is indeed observed. Thus, it is established that multiple things are perceived simultaneously.

vi] Now, if it is argued that there is a distinction such that blue and other colors are perceived sequentially in artificial objects, whereas they are perceived simultaneously elsewhere— that too is incorrect. [282, vii]
When two cognitions are characterized by having identical objects, forms, and times, why is one manifold and successive while the other is unitary and non-successive? (203)

[282, viii] Even though the object, form, and time are identical for both cognitions, one has the appearance of multiple objects and is successive, whereas the other, however, produces only a single object—a whole (*avayavin*)—moving within its own domain and is not successive. What is the basis for this? Indeed, when everything is observed to be identical, difference is not an object of acceptance. This is accepted in the case of what are considered artificial and non-artificial variegated things; yet such an acceptance, being devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), is merely a mere assertion and provides no protection [for your position].
Now, if this distinction between the one and the many arises from the force of some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what fault is there here? This is not tenable, because:
[282,x] For it is through the manifold nature of cognitions themselves that entities possess a manifold nature.
If that [difference] is not a real constituent part, by what means is this established distinction between things accomplished? (204)

[282,xi] Only those cognitions that possess the appearance of unity and multiplicity are authoritative (*pramāṇa*) in establishing such forms; there is no other process of valid cognition (*pramākrama*). Even if these cognitions, whose procedure for establishing things as they are has not been subverted, were to be rejected by another cognition whose authority is merely imagined based on a connection to mere similarity (*sādharmya*), then where indeed could such similarity not be found? Thus, there would be no establishment of entities at all, and everything would become incoherent. Therefore:
For those cognitions, by obstructing the non-establishment of other appearances, declare that the appearance is not purposeless; this is logical.
(PVA 364) If an entity were established merely from similarity alone, [then...]
Where indeed does that not exist? Thus, everything would be established, or perhaps nothing at all.
(PVA 282, xiv)

An inference whose invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been grasped by perception cannot be refuted by another inference that arises in the same manner, nor by another perception that bears the character of its opposite. Indeed, one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not refuted by another means of valid cognition. If they possess equal strength, what constitutes "refutation"? And if it is a means of valid cognition, how can it effect a refutation? On the other hand, if they do not possess equal strength, then that which is sublated by an inference would not be a means of valid cognition at all; and that which is sublated by perception would likewise not be an inference—this is the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). [Objection: "Cognitions of objects may arise in some way due to defects in their causes, but an inference does not. Therefore, only that [inference] is the sublater. [Response: That too is incorrect.
It is logical that, due to a defect in the reason (*hetu*), the cognition regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) might be otherwise;
but how could it be logical regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*), even from a hundred defects in the reason? (PVA 366)

[283,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat as real. He does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real? How is it that he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real? How is it that he does not perceive the eye as real, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real? How is it that he does not perceive forms as real, nor sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real? How is it that he does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real? How is it that he does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real? How is it that he does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real? How is it that he does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real? How is it that he does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor the realm of form or the formless realm as real? How is it that he does not perceive ignorance as real, nor volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real? How is it that he does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat as real? How is it that he does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. The eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the eye as real. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. Forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. Sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental phenomena; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. Eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-consciousness; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. Eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-contact; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-contact; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. That which arises from eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from eye-contact; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. That which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from mind-contact; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. The element of earth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of earth; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of consciousness; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. The realm of desire is empty of the intrinsic nature of the realm of desire; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. The realm of form and the formless realm are empty of the intrinsic nature of the formless realm; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. Ignorance is empty of the intrinsic nature of ignorance; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. Volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are empty of the intrinsic nature of old age and death; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. The fruit of a Stream-enterer is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of a Stream-enterer; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. The fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, and an Arhat are empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of an Arhat; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive them as real. The fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. The state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is empty of the intrinsic nature of the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; therefore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive it as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, then what is this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom? What is this perfection of wisdom that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices? What is this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of form, and what is this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness? What is this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the eye, and what is this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind? What is this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of forms, and what is this emptiness of the intrinsic nature of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles,

It is not tenable to claim that a nature which appears sequentially becomes non-sequential due to a defect in the cause; for it would follow that the nature of a single entity is manifold, which leads to the absurdity of its being perceived as such. If you argue that there is no appearance of the single entity [in its sequential form], we say no; for this would entail the absence of its very own-being (*svabhāva*). Indeed, when there is no appearance, there is no such thing as "appearance. To say that non-appearance has appearance as its own-being is a contradiction. If you then maintain that only sequential appearance is real and that anything else is merely an illusion, we ask: what is this illusion? Is it non-appearance, or is it appearance in another form? And what follows from this?
If error were non-appearance, it would be unrestrained everywhere. Since that very thing appears in this way, how can it be called "error"? (367) (PVA)

[283,v] If every appearance were an error, then it would follow that deep sleep and even stones are erroneous. Furthermore, if there is no appearance of succession, then succession itself appears unimpaired; how, then, could there be error? For the mere appearance of a pillar or the like is not itself an error.
If error is the appearance of something else, how can there be an appearance of its own nature?
And if there is no appearance of its own nature, how can there be the delusion that "that exists"?

If the appearance of that [object] other than what is intended to be expressed is erroneous, then in that case, there is no appearance of its own nature at all; how then can that cognition exist? If a cognition exists even while not appearing, then it must be said that all cognitions of everyone exist at all times, as well as their error. Or, if that cognition does not exist at all, then how is it an error for a non-existent sequential cognition to appear as non-sequential and as having arisen from another? Or, if it is an error because its object of cognition (*prameya*) does not exist. [283, viii]

But surely, in the case of sesame seeds and the like which lack succession, there exists an object of cognition (*prameya*) for a cognition that itself lacks succession; on the contrary, for a cognition possessing succession, there is an impossibility of an object of cognition because it appears otherwise. If it is argued that the object of cognition itself is not non-successive, and therefore this is so, then even with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), there would be no appearance of succession; consequently, there could be no connection with error (*bhrānti*). Or else:
[283, ix] If another cognition were to grasp the cognition as having grasped [the object], regarding its own nature...
How can there be an appearance of simultaneity for that which has the nature of being grasped sequentially?

(PVA 369) [283,x] If a cognition possessing sequence were to be grasped by another cognition, then there would be no appearance of simultaneity for objects of cognition such as jewels, pearls, and so forth, because the cognition grasping them would proceed sequentially. Furthermore, the cognition grasping [the first] cognition does not operate upon the object of cognition; nor does a sequential process appear as non-sequential.
If it is argued that its appearance occurs through error, then that very [cognition] would follow as being non-erroneous.
Why, then, should its apprehension of the object of cognition not be accepted as such? (PVA 370)

[283,xii] The Blessed One said: "The eye, monks, is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. And so on, up to: "The mind, monks, is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self; what is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus, by means of the eye and the other [faculties], one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, this body would not be subject to sickness, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore this body is subject to sickness, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, this consciousness would not be subject to sickness, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore this consciousness is subject to sickness, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the five aggregates, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, the eye were the self, the eye would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my eye be thus, let my eye not be thus. But because the eye, monks, is non-self, therefore the eye is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my eye be thus, let my eye not be thus. And so on, up to: "If the mind were the self, the mind would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my mind be thus, let my mind not be thus. But because the mind, monks, is non-self, therefore the mind is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my mind be thus, let my mind not be thus. Thus, by means of the twelve bases, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not lead to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore consciousness leads to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the eighteen elements, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore consciousness is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the four truths, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, this body would not be subject to sickness, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore this body is subject to sickness, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, this consciousness would not be subject to sickness, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore this consciousness is subject to sickness, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the twelve links of dependent origination, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore consciousness is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the six internal and external bases, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore consciousness is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the four nutriments, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore consciousness is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the three feelings, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is non-self, therefore consciousness is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. Thus, by means of the three realms, one should understand that there is no self. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: "If, monks, form were the self, form would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. But because form, monks, is non-self, therefore form is subject to affliction, and one cannot obtain it at will: ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus. And so on, up to: "If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to affliction, and one could obtain it at will: ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus. But because consciousness, monks, is

If cognition arises as appearing in succession, then it must likewise be so for the cognition of that cognition. If you argue that there is simultaneous apprehension due to error, then it would follow that a single [cognition] could apprehend many things simultaneously. For there is no perception of oneness among the preceding and succeeding acts of apprehension, because such a perception does not exist. If you say that the subsequent cognition perceives them as one, how can that [subsequent cognition], which itself possesses succession, perceive oneness? Indeed, the time of the apprehended object does not transcend the time of the apprehending subject. Alternatively, if that [cognition] were non-successive, then by means of that single [cognition] there would be the apprehension of many things. If you then argue that this is precisely why it is an error, even so, the appearance of multiple forms remains unrefuted. If you claim that a variegated cognition is indeed a single entity, then why are gems, pearls, and so forth—not to mention blue and other colors—not also considered the nature of cognition, even though they appear in diverse forms? If they were, it would follow that every object of knowledge (*prameya*) is likewise [of the nature of cognition]. Therefore, even in the case of error, the simultaneous appearance of many things is not logical. Consequently, whatever is experienced—whether simultaneously or otherwise—must be accepted exactly as it is, because that is the very sequence of investigation. Otherwise, there would be no stable status for objects of knowledge.

[284,i] But surely, a variegated cognition (*citrabuddhi*) is observed in relation to paintings and the like; how then is unity not tenable? However, in the case of jewels, pearls, and so forth, there is no single variegated cognition; therefore, this distinction arises from the very differentiation of the appearance within cognition itself. No, that is not so, because it contradicts your own established tenets (*svasamaya*). For: [284,ii]
Because heterogeneous atoms do not initiate [a new effect], there can be no perception of variety in paintings and the like;
nor is conjunction itself variegated, because it lacks form, and it cannot serve as the locus for such a figurative attribution. (206)

[284,iii] If the intellect is followed, then one's own tenet—that there is no production of heterogeneous things—is abandoned; for a cloth or similar object produced from the conjunction of threads of heterogeneous types does not possess a variegated nature as its constituent parts.
Now, even if this cognition is erroneous, there is nevertheless simultaneous apprehension.
If it apprehends an unreal form, why does it not apprehend a real form?

For even a mistaken cognition, when it arises, indeed functions toward the apprehension of many things simultaneously. What distinction is there between the real and the unreal when it comes to the appearance of being present before one? If you say that this form belongs to the cognition itself, that is incorrect.
How could that which is the very nature of a real cognition not be real?
If there were a single essence, this distinction would be unreal, or else there would be no unity.
(372) (PVA) Or rather, it might be argued as follows:
Because there is no cognition of a self, that which consists of yellow and so forth is real in that form, whereas the external form is unreal.
This is not the essence; if that [external form] were not its form, then this conceptual construction regarding it would not be logically consistent. (373) (PVA)

[284,x] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even a single cognition can operate upon multiple objects within its own form (*ātmarūpa*), because there is no effort required therein. However, with respect to the form of another (*pararūpa*), there is great effort on the part of the mind, characterized by movement and so forth; therefore, simultaneous apprehension by a single [cognition] is impossible, because apprehension cannot occur at once in contradictory locations. If, then, the mind is not the cause of apprehension when it moves, [284,xi]

It is impossible for the branch and the moon to be perceived simultaneously. If it is argued that there is the appearance of simultaneous perception because of the rapid movement [of the eye], we say no; for such rapidity is impossible at an extreme distance. Furthermore, what is the proof here that the eye and other senses function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārin*)? The opponent replies: Because perception and non-perception depend respectively on the presence or absence of an obstruction, and because they depend on proximity or distance. If the eye and other senses were not *prāpyakārin*, as it has been said: "The eye, the ear, and the mind have objects that are not reached," then there would be no case where non-perception occurs due to the existence of an obstruction and perception occurs otherwise. For in that case, an obstruction would not be capable of causing interference. However, if they function by reaching the object, interference is possible due to the resistance (*pratighāta*) of material substances. And in the case of extreme distance, there is simply no reaching. That is incorrect. Even if they function without reaching the object, they still depend on a suitable location, just like a magnet. Indeed, a magnet, while operating by attracting without reaching its object, is not capable of attracting every piece of iron. Now, if you argue that in that case too there is indeed contact with the iron—though it is unobserved due to its subtlety, just as the contact of the ocular rays is unobserved—we reply: [this is not so].
[284,xii] But surely this very point is established by another [means]; how then can that itself be the means of proof? Therefore:
[284,xiii]
This fabrication of painful hypotheses regarding that which is being made absolutely non-existent serves only for the ridicule of the wise, and not for true understanding.

Now, it might be argued: "It is observed that what is conjoined is attracted; therefore, this [attraction] must also apply to that which is being pulled by a magnet. No; for in that case, the mantra would also be seen as an attractor, and since that which is attracted would also possess touch, there would be an over-extension of the principle. If you say, "Let it be so even in that case," we reply: no, because sound is a quality (*guṇa*). Or else, if that very same property is attributed even to a subject where the concomitance has been shown to be non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), then nothing could ever be non-conclusive. For instance, upon seeing the deviation in the argument "He is dark-skinned because he is his son," one might face the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the fair-skinned son must also be dark-skinned. Why is he not seen to be so? Let the cause of his not being seen be investigated.

[285,i] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti said: "No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti said: "As I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has known or seen, saying: 'By this dharma have I fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'? Furthermore: if the visual rays (*cakṣūraśmi*) go out and come into contact [with the object], why is there no perception even at a great distance, as there is with the rays of a lamp when unobstructed? This is not a fault. For if that were the case, it would follow that one could perceive what is extremely close; for the rays of a lamp do not fail to function in extreme proximity. Therefore, some other property of the eyes and so forth must be admitted, distinct from that of a lamp; that alone is the cause of apprehension, not the contact of rays. Moreover, if there were rays of the eyes and so forth, there would be the consequence of apprehension even when they are not directed toward an object. If it is argued that this speed belongs to the mind (*manas*), then let it produce simultaneous apprehension (*sakṛdgrahaṇa*) itself; what is the use of this cumbersome hypothesis? Furthermore, such a mind is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is simply mental attention (*manaskāra*), consisting of a preceding cognition, which performs that causal function. Since cognition does not arise elsewhere when there is a deficiency in the mind's application to another object, the non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is thus accounted for. Consequently, because it is established otherwise, the mind is not understood from that inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, cognition is designated as the grasper of that [object’s] form;
it is like a pair of tongs, not because of a visual perception of the grasping of the object itself. (PVA 375)

Therefore, the simultaneous apprehension of multiple forms in a painting is indeed non-erroneous. Now, if it is argued that in this case it is the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is variegated, and not the form of a composite whole (*avayavin*), that is incorrect. Because conjunction is a quality (*guṇa*), there can be no inherence (*samavāya*) of color-form (*rūpa*) therein. If that were the case, it would follow that it is a substance (*dravya*) because it possesses qualities. And thus, the established tenet—that "like kinds do not originate unlike kinds"—would be violated.

Now, [the opponent claims] that the variety of the conjunction is due to metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). That too is incorrect. For if this were the case, then just as there is the cognition "forest of blossoming flowers" (*vanaṅkusuma*) through inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), so too would this [cognition of a variegated cloth] be. But there is no equality between these two cases. For in the case of a "forest," it has been stated that the plurality (*bahutva-saṅkhyā*) inherent in the trees is where the state of being in bloom (*kusumitatva*) resides; thus, there is inherence in a single object. However, in this case [of the variegated cloth], variegation (*citratva*) does not inhere in the parts (*avayava*) where the conjunction resides. As it has been said: "[285,v] Because each [part] individually is not variegated."

Indeed, there is no variegatedness (*citrātā*) in the individual elements such as the threads and so forth, by virtue of which the conjunction inhering in them would also be likewise variegated. Now, it might be argued that just as when "fire-ness" is perceived in a fire, the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire—brought about by the perception of common properties such as sharpness—causes one to remember and superimpose (*adhyāropayati*) the nature of fire upon a young boy; similarly, at the time of perceiving any one of the blue and other colors perceived in succession, one superimposes them upon that which is being perceived, and thus there is the cognition of variegation. This is untenable, because:
And when [objects] are apprehended sequentially, there is no synthesis by a single [cognition] of multiple [objects], because many [objects] cannot be grasped by one [cognition]. (207)

[285, viii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, stood to one side, and said to him: "Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard it, the bhikkhus might dwell with diligence. "Ānanda, what do you think? Is physical food as gross nutriment permanent or impermanent? "Impermanent, venerable sir. "But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? "Suffering, venerable sir. "But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'? "No, venerable sir. [And so on for contact, mental volition, and consciousness. "Therefore, Ānanda, whatever kind of form there is—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever kind of feeling... perception... formations... consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus with right wisdom exactly as it is, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: 'It is liberated. One understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the Venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus! "Venerable sir," they replied. The Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. If, bhikkhus, these four nutriments were not found, would any being come to be or be maintained? "No, venerable sir. "Since, bhikkhus, these four nutriments are found, beings come to be and are maintained. [The Buddha then explains how each nutriment leads to the arising of further suffering. "Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: 'We will not allow any craving for the nutriment of physical food to arise within us, nor any delight in it, nor any infatuation with it, nor any attachment to it, nor any grasping at it, nor any inclination toward it, nor any underlying tendency toward it. Thus should you train yourselves. [And so on for the other three nutriments. When, bhikkhus, you have abandoned craving for these four nutriments, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising, then, bhikkhus, you will be those who have reached the end of the journey, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and become emancipated through final knowledge. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: "Friends, bhikkhus! "Friend," they replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling after saying this, he did so thinking: 'Now, bhikkhus, being alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, you should reflect upon this discourse on the nutriments in such a way that, by doing so, you may achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life. It is in this way, friends, that I understand the meaning of this discourse on the nutriments spoken by the Blessed One. Then the bhikkhus, having understood the meaning of the Venerable Ānanda's words, reflected upon this discourse on the nutriments in such a way that, by doing so, they achieved the destruction of the taints in this very life. And some of them, having seen with wisdom, attained final Nibbāna in that very life; others, having become non-returners, will attain final Nibbāna without ever returning to this world; others, having become once-returners, will return to this world once more and then make an end of suffering; and others, having become stream-enterers, are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds and are firmly established, destined for full enlightenment.

For in that case [of a single color], there is a similarity of sharpness which serves as the basis for superimposition (*adhyāropa*); but here, how can there be a superimposition of the blue and other colors being perceived? If you say it is due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), that is only tenable when there is simultaneous perception. However, in the case of sequential perception, there is no apprehension of proximity. If you argue that this is because they are perceived in the same location, even when they are perceived in the same location, there is no apprehension of variegation (*citrata*) between the preceding and succeeding moments. To say it occurs through superimposition is not logical, since that very point is what remains to be examined. If you argue that what is being remembered appears as if it were being perceived because their difference is not apprehended—how can one thing be perceived as another? If it appears by abandoning its nature as something remembered, then it is simply a case of perception; therefore, there is no "synthesis" (*saṅkalana*). If you claim that synthesis is indeed of the nature of perception, then it would follow that multiple things are perceived as one, which is not accepted, since we observe the cognition of the whole through the operation of the eye. Therefore, he says: "Thus, these [theories] are useless, devised by dull-witted people stained by the stains of incoherent conceptualization."
Therefore, it would involve multiple objects; consequently, it is established that [the cognition] is indeed free from conceptual construction (*avikalpika*).
Even while conceptualizing a single object, one perceives something else as well. // 208 //

[286,i] For when there is a variegated appearance consisting of various forms such as blue and so forth, even while one conceptualizes "this is blue," one certainly perceives the yellow and other colors situated at the periphery; yet, multiple simultaneous conceptualizations are not possible. If it is argued that "it is precisely the variegated [object] that is conceptualized," we say no, because there is no necessity. For it is not necessarily the case that one must conceptualize it as "variegated," since conceptualization is observed even regarding a single [color]. And thus, the cognition that simultaneously possesses all forms such as blue and so forth is itself a single cognition with a variegated form. To this, the following objection is raised: [286,ii]
If unity is not tenable regarding objects that appear as variegated, then how can that very cognition—which manifests as variegated—be a single [entity]? (209)
This demonstrates the following.
Just as you maintain that cognition possesses variegated forms,
if an external object likewise possesses such divisions, what is the cause of this?
For it is due to the manifold nature of cognitions that things possess a variegated form.
What then will not belong to the intellect that has mounted upon it?
Therefore, in the case of the intellect as an example, this [argument] that "it is manifold precisely because of its variegated nature" is not inconclusive. To this, the following is said:
[286, vii] This is what has come by the force of reality, as the wise declare:
"In whatever way objects are analyzed, in that very way they fall apart. (210)
Because:
How could there be such variety in a single [cognition]? It would not exist even in that cognition itself.
If it is these objects themselves that appear so to one's own mind, then what part do we have in it? (211)

This is the meaning: indeed, even cognition (*buddhi*), though being one, is not manifold. For even there, because it possesses multiple forms (*ākāra*), it is as if multiple; since a real entity (*vastu*) is characterized by its forms, and by the multiplicity of forms, the entity itself is necessarily manifold. Therefore, if there are just that many cognitions, what harm is there for the proponent of the latter position? If, however, cognitions were distinct, then there would be as many cognitions as there are atoms, which would entail the consequence of perceiving individual atoms and the consequence of having multiple simultaneous perceptions, because there is no mutual perception [of those atoms] due to their lack of contact. Indeed, there is no perception of multiplicity among things that are self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*). For if there were, it would entail the consequence of the appearance of other mental continua (*santāna*) as well. This is not so, because it is actually observed. For there is no such thing as "impossibility" regarding what is observed. [Objection: In that case, there is no self-cognition, because there is also the cognition of others. [Reply: No, because cognition is impossible without self-cognition. And this will be demonstrated later. As for the cognition of another, there is simply no purpose in it. Then who could perceive the plurality? No one at all, because there is no perceiver apart from that [plurality]. Therefore:
Neither unity nor plurality is logically possible for cognitions.
If they were one, there would be an absence of variety; if they were many, it would be even more impossible. (PVA 376)

Therefore, in whatever way a thing is analyzed, it simply falls apart; what can we do about this? Thus he says: "Since consciousness is empty of the nature of consciousness, it is logical that all phenomena are indeed empty."

Now, how is it that what appears does not arise merely from the conceptual construction of unity or multiplicity? Even as a conceptual construction, it certainly appears. There is no fault in its being non-existent, just like the appearances of illusions, mirages, and so forth. [Objection: If those things are non-existent, how can there be an appearance? [Response: If there is an appearance, how can they be non-existent? [It is because] they lack causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*). Since existence is defined by causal efficacy, the conventional usage of "existence" is not based on mere appearance; for even in the case of the appearance of hair-nets and the like, their non-existence is certain. (Causal efficacy...)

[286,xiv] Now, what is this "purposeful activity" (*arthakriyā*)? Is it something other than that which appears, or is it that very thing itself? If it is something other, then of that [other thing] as well...

If it is admitted that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) belongs to something other than the appearing form, there would be an infinite regress and thus no cognition [of the object]. If, on the other hand, that [efficiency] is identical [to the appearance], then it follows that all appearances must be real; thus, illusions (*māyā*) and the like would not be unreal. To this it is replied:
for some [appearances], [the efficiency] is indeed distinct [from the appearance], while for others, it is the opposite.
This is the intrinsic nature of entities: their establishment through differentiation.

For not everything that appears necessarily possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Only that which appears as having causal efficiency possesses the nature of causal efficiency. And since the establishment of existence (*sattva*) occurs through the presence of causal efficiency and the exclusion of it through its absence, it follows that not all appearances are non-existent, because some are connected with causal efficiency. [Response: No, for this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) made from the perspective of the opponent's own admission. Proponents of existence (*sattvavādins*) admit that existence is defined by causal efficiency. Yet, apart from the appearance [of the object], no causal efficiency is perceived; for nothing other than the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth appears as "causal efficiency. Whatever one desires is itself the causal efficiency. But this is entirely unstable, as something or other is desired by someone. If it is argued that causal efficiency consists in the removal of suffering and the production of pleasure, we say no, because suffering and pleasure themselves are not fixed. Furthermore, since everything arises through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and since [the object] is absent when that cultivation is absent, its non-existence is established in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). If this is so, then by the power of cultivation, it is simply cognition that becomes such, but not non-existence. Non-existence is precisely the state of being produced under the influence of ignorance (*avidyā*), because that which exists in such a way lacks a stable nature. Since it exists merely as an appearance—delightful only so long as it is not investigated—it is indeed conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

[287,v] Therefore, the appearance of grossness exists neither in objects nor in cognition, because it is denied in the case of a single [atom]; since it is impossible in one, it is not possible even in many.

For among objects—whether they be atoms or composite wholes—there is no appearance of grossness (*sthūla*). Indeed, grossness consists in being differentiated by spatial directions (*digbhāga*); and since spatial directions exclude one another, there is no single location. Alternatively, if grossness is the appearance of many [atoms], then indeed many atoms of the same kind appearing without interruption are designated as "gross. This too is not tenable; for these many [atoms] individually lack grossness. If it is argued that it belongs to the collection (*samudāya*), what other collection is there besides them? Furthermore, the appearance of a single solid mass is what receives the designation "gross. But where there is an appearance of mutually distinct [parts], there can be no single solid mass, because the intervening spaces also appear. If [those spaces] do not appear, then those [atoms] would not be appearing at all. Now, if it is argued that upon the dissolution of the atoms, a different composite whole (*avayavin*) arises from their conjunction, wherein neither atoms nor any parts exist, then if a different composite has arisen, the atoms would perish and the composite would be newly produced, like a sprout from a seed. Consequently, the principle that atoms aided by conjunction initiate a composite inherent in themselves would fail; for a relation must reside in two things. Moreover, the cognition "here" (*iha*) would be without a basis, because the referent of the locative case would be non-existent. Or, if that partless [whole] were perceived, there would be the consequence of perceiving its "other side" (*parabhāga*) and so forth. When the "other side" is seen, the "further side" (*apara*) would also be seen, since that too is a part of the whole; thus, seeing the "other side," everyone would become an all-seeing seer. If the "other side" is not seen, then since the "other side" itself does not exist, how can it be seen by another? If it is argued that this [further side] is something entirely different, then it is not the whole, nor is it gross. If it is argued that it is seen successively, no; for succession is impossible in a single entity. Nor can it be established that it is the very same thing, given that it is perceived as both tangible and visible. If it is argued that it is the "whole" because it is perceived through touch and sight, no; for there is a lack of proof. If it is perceived by excluding each other's nature, how can there be oneness? This mutual distinction is created by the act of grasping; yet the object grasped is one and the same. In that case, every distinction would dissolve, and there would be only a duality. Since nothing appears apart from those two, all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty. Nor is there any proof that whatever is seen is the very same thing that is touched. Therefore, neither the whole nor the parts are within the range of appearance. Let it simply be "appearance. If, then, this is merely appearance, it follows that it is either consciousness (*vijñāna*) or non-cognition (*avijñāna*). How, then, can there be the emptiness of all phenomena? To this, it is said: [The following passage continues the argument regarding the nature of appearance and the refutation of external objects.]
This internal portion of cognition appears as if it were external; for the appearance of differentiation within non-differentiated cognition is indeed a cognitive distortion.

[288, ii] If this cognition is also self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), then because it terminates in its own nature, the appearance of difference is not tenable. For in self-cognition there is no cognition of another; therefore, there is no manifestation of difference. If, on the other hand, there is cognition by means of one another, then there is difference. In that case as well:
If there were a cognition of each [object] individually, there would be valid cognition [of it] as in the case of another mental continuum;
however, [the thought] "it was thus determined by me" does not exist in the absence of self-awareness.

If you maintain that there is both self-awareness and awareness of another within the two cognitions of self and other, then it follows that there must be two distinct self-cognitions; for the cognition of one's own nature does not enter into the cognition of another. Alternatively, if there is no self-cognition, then the cognition of the other would occur through the two [cognizers] themselves. In that case, the two would not be perceived as such, just as Devadatta and Yajñadatta do not perceive each other’s objects. Furthermore, the thought "this has been known by me" would not occur, because the agent would not appear as self-cognizing. Consequently, those two [objects] would have to be self-cognized [by separate subjects], and thus, like the perceptions of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*), there would be no cognition of the two. For this very reason, the opponent maintains that a single self is postulated as the perceiver of the two, otherwise this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow. To this, we reply:
Whether it be self-awareness or something else, because one does not transcend the previous reasoning,
that too is not liberated from this same critical inquiry. (PVA 379)

[288, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four modes of practice. What four? There is a mode of practice that leads to the repulsive; there is a mode of practice that leads to the pleasant; there is a mode of practice that leads neither to the repulsive nor to the pleasant; and there is a mode of practice that leads to the destruction of craving. "What, monks, is the mode of practice that leads to the repulsive? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the mode of practice that leads to the repulsive. "And what, monks, is the mode of practice that leads to the pleasant? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind imbued with loving-kindness, radiating it toward one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. He dwells with his mind imbued with compassion... with sympathetic joy... with equanimity, radiating it toward one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. This, monks, is called the mode of practice that leads to the pleasant. "And what, monks, is the mode of practice that leads neither to the repulsive nor to the pleasant? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving 'space is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. With the complete transcending of the base of infinite space, perceiving 'consciousness is infinite,' he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. With the complete transcending of the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving 'there is nothing,' he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. This, monks, is called the mode of practice that leads neither to the repulsive nor to the pleasant. "And what, monks, is the mode of practice that leads to the destruction of craving? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating arising and vanishing in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating arising and vanishing in feelings... in the mind... in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the mode of practice that leads to the destruction of craving."

If the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of cognition (*samvedana*), then because each [cognition] is submerged within its own self, there is no cognition of another. If it is argued, "What contradiction is there in the cognition of another?", one must choose between these two alternatives: does it know the other by means of that [other's] form, or does it know it by means of its own [distinct] form? It is not logical that it knows by means of its own form, because its own form is established within itself. How can a form that is fixed in its own nature and directed only toward itself know another? If it is directed toward another, then by that [form] its own self is not perceived. Consequently, as in the case of perceiving another continuum (*santānāntara*), there would be no perception of both. If it is argued, "He who possesses those two faces is one," then who is the one who perceives "these two"? If it is he himself, then there is again the requirement for two faces, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the three [the self, the object, and the cognition] would have to be cognitions of their own selves. From that, another self would have to be admitted to perceive that [set of three], and yet another to perceive that—resulting in a great succession of calamities. Therefore, since there is only a single cognition from the act of knowing, the appearance of difference in non-dual knowledge is an illusion (*upaplava*). Thus, knowledge, not being perceived by way of its own nature, is simply non-existent; only emptiness (*śūnyatā*) remains. For: *(The original Sanskrit verse follows here)* ...therefore, [emptiness remains].
[288, viii] In that regard, through the absence of even one, both are likewise discarded.
Therefore, the very reality of that [subject] is also the emptiness of duality. 214.

It might be argued: "If one [of the two] is abandoned, there will be mere cognition (*jñānamātra*). If that which appears is abandoned, then both are likewise [non-existent], or else nothing at all—this is the certain conclusion. If it is said, "Let both exist," we reply: No, because this has already been answered. This is because it has been established that there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) apart from the cognition of another. Therefore, it is logical that emptiness alone is superior.

Now he establishes the meaning of emptiness according to the systems of the Mādhyamika, the Yogācāra, and the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*). [The conceptual] determination of entities such as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is that [determination].
And this establishment of the differentiation of entities is based upon their differentiation.
And when there is the state of being a distortion of that [reality], their difference is also a distortion. (215)
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) because it cognizes.
There exists no characteristic external [to consciousness] consisting of the forms of the grasped and the grasper;
therefore, because they are empty of characteristics, they are revealed as being without intrinsic nature. (216)

The definition of all things, such as the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth, is specifically conditioned by their functional activity; and since that activity is not the ultimate reality, these things are not distinct from it in their true nature. // 217 //
These are the intermediate verses.
One might ask: "How is it to be explained that the Blessed One’s teaching on the forms and other qualities of external objects is one thing, while his [other] teaching is different?
To this he says:
"Just as for those whose minds are overwhelmed by ignorance, [the appearance arises] in dependence upon their own respective cognitions..."
Representation arises with a false aspect, like [the appearance of] water and so forth. // 218 //
And that [reality] is not understood in its true nature by all other philosophical systems, because for them it is impossible without the distortions of the grasped and the grasper. (219)
Having neglected the true meaning of reality and closing their eyes like elephants, they merely extend external investigations based solely on worldly intellect. (220)

Now, if everything is indeed empty from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and the Blessed One is a seer of reality (*tattvadarśin*), then how can there be a teaching by the Blessed One regarding external objects? For one who sees reality does not teach that which is not reality. Or, if he were to teach it, how could he be understood as a seer of reality? To this it is replied: The Blessed One’s teaching of external things is not for the purpose of establishing external objects, but rather for the sake of restatement (*anuvāda*). This is because his intention is to negate the self by means of that restatement. But how can there be a restatement for one who perceives emptiness, since [external objects] do not appear to him? No; for restatement is possible precisely through the cognition of worldly people (*loka-buddhi*). And such a cognition exists in the world due to the practice of beginningless ignorance (*anādi-avidyā*).

[289,x] But if the Blessed One possesses the worldly intellect, how can he be a seer of reality? No; for teaching is possible through the momentum of previous [realization], like the spinning of a wheel. Therefore, it is not contradictory that he introduces the world to teachings of manifold forms.

Thus far, the refutation of the charge of inconclusiveness has been made by accepting the emptiness of cognition. Now, he refutes it by accepting its variegated nature (*citra*). Even though cognition appears as variegated, it is indeed one, because it is distinct from an external variegated object. A variegated object is capable of being analyzed into many parts, whereas the blue and other elements of cognition cannot be so analyzed. For: "In the cognition of a variegated [object], the blue and so forth are attributes of the cognition itself and do not exist apart from it. [289,xii]
It is impossible to perceive [the whole], for one who discriminates it with respect to its constituent parts falls [into error]. // 221 //

This, Ānanda, is the first kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, another person dwells having made others an island, having made others a refuge, not making himself a refuge; he has transcended both merit and demerit and stands upon the ground of the noble ones. This, Ānanda, is the second kind of person found existing in the world. Furthermore, Ānanda, another person dwells having made himself an island and having made others an island, having made himself a refuge and having made others a refuge; he has transcended both merit and demerit and stands upon the ground of the noble ones. This, Ānanda, is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. That which consists of variegated cognition—such as blue and so forth—is by itself impossible to perceive, because it is impossible to separate [the parts] from it; therefore, even in a variegated cognition, there is only oneness. If, then, even a variegated thing is one, then that which appears as sound and so forth would also be one. Let it be so, if it cannot be separated. But if, even when the ears are covered, color and so forth are still perceived, then there is multiplicity due to the perception of [those elements] individually. That too is incorrect. For there is no separation within the cognition itself, because at that time the previous appearance has ceased to exist. Since it does not appear, if you argue that the sound remains unperceived and therefore exists as distinct [from the color], that is not the case, because at that time the cognition is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). For if one were to distinguish [them] in this way, one would fall into the position that the object itself is what falls away, since the object is not being cognized.

[289,xiv] Now, if it is argued that there is a discrimination such that "this which appears alone now is different from the form of the preceding cognition which appeared together with it," that too is incorrect. For perception does not operate with respect to "prior-ness"; rather, [290,i]

It might be said that "in whatever way a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way. However, it does not follow that "it was experienced as appearing. For the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*) does not operate upon what is hidden (*parokṣa*), because what is hidden is not self-aware.

[290,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, perceives form as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as form. He perceives feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as consciousness. He perceives the eye as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the eye; he perceives the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the mind. He perceives forms as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as forms; he perceives sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as mental phenomena. He perceives eye-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as eye-consciousness; he perceives ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as mind-consciousness. He perceives eye-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as eye-contact; he perceives ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as mind-contact. He perceives feeling born of eye-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as feeling born of eye-contact; he perceives feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as feeling born of mind-contact. He perceives the element of earth as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the element of earth; he perceives the elements of water, fire, air, space, and consciousness as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the element of consciousness. He perceives the realm of desire as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the realm of desire; he perceives the realm of form and the formless realm as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the formless realm. He perceives conditioned phenomena as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as conditioned phenomena; he perceives unconditioned phenomena as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as unconditioned phenomena. He perceives the limit of past time as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the limit of past time; he perceives the limit of future time and the present time as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the present time. He perceives the beginning of saṃsāra as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the beginning of saṃsāra; he perceives the end of saṃsāra and the middle of saṃsāra as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the middle of saṃsāra. He perceives the knowledge of the path as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the knowledge of the path; he perceives the knowledge of all modes as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the knowledge of all modes. He perceives the fruit of a stream-enterer as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the fruit of a stream-enterer; he perceives the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the fruit of arhatship. He perceives the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood; he perceives the fruit of buddhahood as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the fruit of buddhahood. He perceives the dharma-body as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the dharma-body; he perceives the enjoyment-body and the emanation-body as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the emanation-body. He perceives the ten powers as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the ten powers; he perceives the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, great compassion, and the thirty-two marks and eighty minor marks of a great man as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the eighty minor marks. He perceives the dharma-realm as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the dharma-realm; he perceives the expanse of reality, the limit of reality, the suchness, the unaltered suchness, and the unvarying suchness as empty of intrinsic nature, and he does not perceive that emptiness of intrinsic nature as the unvarying suchness. Now, if it is argued that [the object] is known through recollection (*smṛti*), this is not correct, because recollection is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). If it is argued that recollection is indeed a valid means of knowledge because it arises from direct experience (*anubhava*), [we reply: it is not the case that recollection arises from experience; for there is no evidence here that recollection exists at the time of experience, since it is absent then. Furthermore, the recollection does not know, "I have arisen from this experience," because the experience is not perceived by that recollection. Or, if the experience were perceived by the recollection, it would not be recollection; it would simply be experience itself. Therefore, there is no fault in the view that a single, variegated entity is impossible to distinguish [into separate parts]. If it is argued that external objects are also one because they are impossible to distinguish, we say: no, because at that very moment another person perceives it as one.

[290.iv] Now, if that which is seen by another is indeed something else, then the distinction is all the more clear. If it is argued that "only what is seen by oneself [is real]," [we reply: no, because due to its appearance in self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), that is simply cognition itself.
Thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind that possesses variegated forms. (222)

For there is no discernment that exists apart from the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*). Nor is it the case that this variegation is not [non-dual], because it is impossible to establish it as distinct from the non-variegated. Consequently, it is established that consciousness alone is non-dual, due to the absence of anything else. If there is a grasping of the relation between the object to be established (*bhāvyartha*) and the cause of firmness, then inference (*anumāna*) is logical. For proponents of inference maintain that "inference is the cognition of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*) based on a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Now, if it is argued that inference occurs even without the grasping of such a connection because it has been observed [to happen], then an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) follows. Precisely because it has not been observed, it should not occur. Indeed, it is impossible to unify what has been observed with what is otherwise. If one were to offer a defense based on its having been observed, one must consider whether this observation was by means of inference or by perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it was by means of inference, then that very inference is what is being considered; how, then, could it be established by itself? If it was by perception, that is incorrect. For inference cannot be observed by perception, since the latter has only perceptible objects as its domain. Since perception does not operate upon the imperceptible, how can inference—which is defined by having an imperceptible object—be accepted? Indeed, one cannot understand inference as qualified by that [imperceptible object] without first making the imperceptible an object of cognition.

And how, monks, is a person like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family—whether a kṣatriya family, a brahmin family, or a householder family—and is handsome, attractive, and pleasing to behold, possessing supreme beauty of form. He is well-versed in the Vedas, having mastered the three Vedas with their vocabularies, ritual manuals, phonology, and etymology, as well as the histories as the fifth; he is skilled in philology and grammar, and is a debater and a logician.
