[291,xi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of all perfections. Subhūti asked: “How is it, Blessed One, that this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of all perfections? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, because within this perfection of wisdom, all the perfections—beginning with the perfection of generosity and ending with the perfection of wisdom—are fully contained and subsumed. Furthermore, Subhūti, within this perfection of wisdom, all the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the dharmas of the bodhisattvas and the dharmas of the Buddhas, are fully contained and subsumed. Therefore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is called the perfection of all perfections. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that within this perfection of wisdom, the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas are fully contained and subsumed? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are fully contained and subsumed within this perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. The dharmas of the bodhisattvas are fully contained and subsumed within this perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. The dharmas of the Buddhas are fully contained and subsumed within this perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, it is in this manner that the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas are fully contained and subsumed within this perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are fully contained and subsumed within this perfection of wisdom, then what is the distinction, what is the difference, and what is the specific characteristic between this perfection of wisdom and those other dharmas? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, there is no distinction, no difference, and no specific characteristic whatsoever between this perfection of wisdom and those other dharmas, except for the distinction, the difference, and the specific characteristic of the skillful means of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is by means of this skillful means that the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully contained and subsumed all the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas within this perfection of wisdom, does not realize the reality-limit midway, but rather, having matured sentient beings and purified the buddha-field, proceeds directly to the seat of awakening and, having sat upon the seat of awakening, conquers Māra and his hosts, and having realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, turns the wheel of the Dharma. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does the bodhisattva mahāsattva, having fully contained and subsumed all the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas within this perfection of wisdom, not realize the reality-limit midway, but rather, having matured sentient beings and purified the buddha-field, proceed directly to the seat of awakening, conquer Māra and his hosts, realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and turn the wheel of the Dharma? He does not apprehend the eye, nor does he apprehend the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. (395) (PVA)
Because it lacks the capacity for self-differentiation, whether by itself or through another,
that which cannot be led away by being separated, nor seen, nor otherwise, [is not a substance].
For even when broken, gold retains its status as the material cause of the object [it constitutes].

[292,xi] Now, if memory were also born at the same time as a perceptual cognition, it would have to be considered one with it. Consequently, perception itself would result in being conceptual (*savikalpaka*), and thus the established position that "perception is free from conceptual construction" (*vikalpaka*) would be lost. This is like falling into the mud while intending to land on dry ground. That is not correct.
[292,xii] Starting from the proponent of difference, the distinctness of memory is stated:
"The entire [world] is differentiated by the difference in causes and intrinsic natures. (PVA 397)

For those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādin*), every distinction arises from a difference in causes due to a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). In that regard, memory arises from mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), whereas sensory cognition does not; memory has an imperceptible object, while sensory perception does not. Therefore, the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) is awakened by his own admission that there is a distinction between these two, just as there is between a pillar and other things. But for the proponent of non-difference (*abhedavādin*), from where does this division arise?
For cognition does not possess a cause in the same way [as other things], because such a cause is not apprehended by perception;
nor does inference operate without perception.

Indeed, there is no apprehension of two things—the prior and the posterior—through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). At the time of apprehending that which is considered the effect, there is only remembrance (*smaraṇa*) of that which is considered the cause. When that [cause] is apprehended, it is apprehended only in its own essential form (*svarūpa*), not as a cause, because the effect has not yet been apprehended. And at the time of apprehending the effect, that [cause] is past and is thus within the range of remembrance alone. Now, there can be no remembrance of what was never experienced, and there is no experience of "causality" [itself]; how then could there be remembrance? If the view is that it is also experienced at the time of the effect, then, since there is no experience of its prior nature and because they are inseparable due to their simultaneity, they would be non-different; how then could there be a relation of cause and effect? Alternatively, if it is established by means of remembrance that "this was previously experienced in its own right," then, through this discrimination (*vivecana*), there is indeed a distinction.

[292,xvi] Now, what is this recollection? Is it inference, or is it mere memory? If it were inference, how could it occur without perception? For there is no prior apprehension of "pastness" by means of perception; indeed, every perception grasps only the present.
[292,xvii]

Now, as for the claim that whatever is apprehended by direct perception with a fixed limit and unmixed with anything else is designated as "prior" in relation to a subsequent apprehension— that too is incorrect. For the operation of a prior perception does not occur in dependence upon something posterior.
Therefore, by that [subsequent cognition], the state of being "prior" is not apprehended, because it rests within itself.

For a prior perception, while grasping its own time, how could it know itself as dependent on another? The same applies to the subsequent perception. Consequently, this sequence of prior and subsequent perceptions cannot be grasped by those prior and subsequent perceptions; therefore, how can even memory function with respect to it?
Therefore, dependence is perceived neither through direct perception nor through memory. Consequently, why would inference proceed with respect to what has already been cognized? (PVA 400)
Now, if that [cognition] were merely recollection, how could it be a valid means of knowledge?
Let it be understood that there must be a dependence on what precedes and follows, by which one becomes a knower of the effect.

Now, if it is argued that by the power of causal totality (*sāmagrī*), the very cognition "this is that same" grasps identity, and from that [identity] follows discrimination—[we reply: even the cognition "this is that same" consists of two cognitions, namely recollection and direct experience. Therefore, by what means is identity grasped? If you say, "It is seen being grasped," we reply: it is not seen through grasping alone, but rather through both recollection and grasping. If so, why is there no perception of the remembered and the perceived as distinct, like a cart and its driver? If such a perception were examined, it would be found that there is no perception of identity between the forms of recollection and direct perception. Were that the case, those two [forms] would not exist at all. And thus, there is no perception of identity between the prior and the posterior. For it is impossible for something to be "prior" while it is not being perceived in the form of recollection; the logical rule is that when there is direct perception, there is only presentness, not priority. If it is argued that identity is established because of observed worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), this is merely dancing in the dark.
[293,ii] Whether it be the distinction between things that have already been established and those that do not, or otherwise,
how can there be an understanding of what is not established through cognition, given that linguistic usage proceeds from such cognition? (PVA 402)

[293,iii] What indeed is the status of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*): is it a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is a valid means of knowledge, it has been established that because it would be included within either perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), it lacks the capacity to establish [its object]. Alternatively, if it is not a valid means of knowledge, how can the establishment of difference [be possible]? Therefore, let this be investigated. But if there is no difference, how then does conventional usage proceed? Is it not the case that this is the same even when there is difference? It is not the same; for one who seeks an object proceeds toward it because there exists something to be attained that is distinct from cognition. However, in the case of [the absence of] difference, it is simply inconsistent. To this, it is said: [293,iv]
If that [difference] is known even when there is a distinction, for what purpose would one act?
Or, if it is unknown, how could one act on account of the son of a barren woman?
(403) [PVA] From the non-existence of that [distinction] and the existence of this [identity], why is only this much considered [as the basis for action]?
Since contact and so forth have been perceived previously, one should have acted at that very time.
Now, how can there be activity when such perception is impossible? If it is argued that there is cognition through inference, for whose sake then does one act? (PVA 404–405)
If there is cognition of that universal, how could it apply to the particular?
If the universal were non-different [from the particular], its application would be fruitless.
If it is both different and non-different, then how can one who possesses [cognition] apply toward it as something differentiated?
Since there is no difference [between the object and its cognition] due to the attainment of that [object], for what purpose would there be an engagement with it?
(407) (PVA) If engagement is observed, is it through perception or otherwise?
For engagement is not observed through perception, because [perception] consists in the awareness of its own object. (408) (PVA)
For in that case, the cognizer of the sense organ does not possess a mental state (*vṛtti*) whose nature consists of a prior and a subsequent [moment];
nor is there inference, for what is not perceived cannot be inferred; therefore, neither is there a cognition of the mental state.
Thus, the objection—“How can there be a mental state even in the absence of duality?”—is refuted.
As is Bali, so is the Yakṣa; what connection is there between them?

By this, the following objection is also refuted: "How can one engage in activity for the sake of awakening another in a state of non-duality (advaita)? This is because the distinction between self and other is not established here. This "other," while not being truly other, arises as something that is self-cognized. In ultimate reality, there is no division here. I am the questioner and the other is the speaker; for both, it is simply the cognition colored by their own respective forms, and there is no actual division, just as in the case of a dream-cognition or the prattle of a madman. [If it is argued: "In that case, the proponent is like a madman; how then can there even be a realization of non-duality from that? [293,xiii]

Is this not merely a proliferation of all manner of fallacious arguments, wherein no actual cognition arises? What, then, is to be done by the opponent or anyone else? Is anything at all seen being accomplished? And it has already been demonstrated that nothing is so seen. How, then, can there be the existence of a thing without a cause?
In this case, what is it whose existence you perceive as resulting from a cause?
It has been established that there is no perception of a causal relationship.
[411] (PVA) [293,xv] In that case, existence would be accidental; thus, it would never cease for anything at any time. It is so.
"An entity must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because it does not depend on anything else" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.34).
This too is not a fault; for:
[293, xviii] Have you ever observed anywhere that this existence ceases?
Furthermore, this is merely the babbling of one who is dull-witted, arising from occasionalism.

This path has been shown for the sake of those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādin*). In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), however, it will turn out that there is no division even by means of cognition. Therefore, it is established that cognition is a single entity appearing as variegated.
[294,ii] Now,
if it is argued that there is no contradiction in the form of a jar and so forth being variegated yet single, just like cognition itself, [294,iii] then:
If the form of the cloth and so forth were a single unity, it would likewise be non-discriminative.

[294, iv] If the form of the cloth and so forth is non-discriminative, then it must be of the very nature of cognition (*buddhi*), because it possesses properties identical to those of cognition. For just as cognition is not seen by another, nor at a later time, nor when covered up piece by piece—likewise, if the external object were also such, then that object would be nothing but cognition. It would be merely "me" (*mātra*) as the external. Now, if upon being covered up something else arises in that manner, which is seen through its partiality and so forth, then from that [it follows]:
Whatever exists in a certain way, that is exactly how it is perceived.
Thus, why should there not be a single entity even in a mind possessing variegated forms? (PVA 413)
In this regard, there is concentration.
If it were the case that an object arises exactly as it is perceived,
then it would not arise by way of being imperceptible or perceptible by another;
[therefore] let it be understood that it does not arise from other causes.
That which is born from the causes of consciousness is indeed consciousness itself.

(415) (PVA) Indeed, an object is not perceived as something remote, nor is it perceived through the perception of another. Nor does it arise from other causes; rather, since its production proceeds precisely from the same causes—such as the eye—as the apprehending subject, how could it not be consciousness?
[294,x] Now, whatever is perceived is all merely an object. Even pleasure and the like do not have the nature of cognition.
The opponent claims that the interval itself is a real entity. This too is incorrect, because:
If the status of being a real entity were postulated for everything that is perceived, [then...]
The existence of a cognition that is not perceived would be without any means of valid cognition (apramāṇika).
If it is argued that the object is perceived by that which perceives it, then that [perceiving] cognition is also non-existent.
If that were the case, there would be a cognition of what is perceived by itself. (PVA 416–417)
If there is no perception of the apprehender, how can it be said that "it exists"? It is from the perception of the perceived object that the apprehender is inferred. (418) (PVA) [294,xv]

Or it is apprehension. Otherwise, if there were no presumption (*arthāpatti*), the objection—"By what has this been apprehended?"—would remain unanswered, and thus there would be no resolution at all. Therefore, the claim that the existence of consciousness is known through presumption is false, because the very nature of being apprehended is itself subject to investigation. As for the phrase "by another" and "by oneself":
if the cause of being apprehended by another is apprehended by someone, [then the same question arises].
If it is argued that "that [cognition] too is perceived by another," then an infinite regress would follow.
(PVA 419) If the object were to be perceived by itself, then the same consequence would apply to it as well;
therefore, let every entity be grasped as having the nature of its own cognition, just like the self. (PVA 420)

[294,xviii] Now, the self is perceived as having the nature of its own cognition, whereas form and so forth are perceived through dependence on another; for there is the certain designation: "this was perceived by me" and "this was perceived by another.
If dependence on another is known, how is there no cognition of the other?
Without the other, how can there be dependence on another;
and how could that which is doubtful be determined by means of things that are themselves doubtful? (PVA 421)
For that which is uncertain, there exists no capacity to function as a logical reason for the sake of certainty.
(422) [PVA 294,xxi] Now, if it is argued that knowability is established through self-awareness by depending upon a self;
All cognition would be self-cognizing like the self, and not cognized by another;
for there is no other intellect, since it is complete in that much alone. (PVA 423)

[294,xxiii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Just as there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expressions 'I am the self,' 'I am the agent,' and 'I am the knower,' so too there would be such coreferentiality in 'I am a wall,' 'I am a jar,' 'I am a cloth,' and 'I am a cart. Likewise, just as there is 'my cognition,' so too there would be 'my color,' 'my touch,' and 'my smell. But that is quite trivial.
If oneness results from the favor of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
why is there not likewise a common substratum in such expressions as "I am white" (*ahaṃ gauraḥ*)?
Where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*),
if there were necessarily oneness in that case, then due to the absence of that [oneness], there would be manifoldness.
In that case, if there were multiplicity, neither the probandum nor its opposite would exist.
Likewise, in the expression "Rāhu’s head," even though there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*amānādhikaraṇya*), there is no actual difference.
If it is argued that [the error] is sublated by the perception of difference— just as Rāhu’s head [is distinguished from his body]—
then here too, self-awareness exists as the sublater of the superimposition of difference. (PVA 426)

Just as the superimposition of a distinction, such as "Rāhu’s head," is sublated by the perception of its opposite, so too should the [superimposition] "my cognition" or "my seeing of form" be sublated by mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). For the awareness of one's own nature is established as being without distinction, unlike the awareness of a blue body, a face, or other such objects.
An object that has arisen and is cognized is perceived through its co-referentiality;
what is there that is not so cognized, such that one could imagine a distinction between the cognition and the object of cognition?
How, then, can there be a superimposition of difference when ultimate difference is not perceived? Indeed, nothing arises without a basis.
This conceptualization of difference is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
One who understands positive and negative concomitance through the influence of beginningless predispositions perceives even form and other objects by means of another, even in the absence of me.

[295,xii] Let it remain unexamined; or rather, let it exist elsewhere. From that, through the connection of place, time, and intrinsic nature, there arises the conceptualization of difference. Furthermore, it has been established that there is no ultimate perception of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For:
[295,xiii]
Through perception, there is the cognition of the positive concomitance itself and of its essential nature;
yet, regarding the distinction between existence and non-existence, it is a mere pretense of cognition in the absence of actual cognition.

Even in the absence of sensation, some have the conceit (*abhimāna*) of sensation, such as thinking, "This was done by me," or "This was seen by me. If it is argued that in those cases, because the sensation has passed away, there is a conceit arising from forgetfulness (*vismaraṇa*), then what is this so-called "forgetfulness"? If it is argued that it is the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the contrary, then the same applies here as well. If it is argued that it is the exhaustion (*kṣaya*) of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), no; for there is no such thing as a mental impression [in this context]. Indeed, there can be no exhaustion of a mental impression except through its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). It has already been established that it is impossible to bring about the exhaustion of what has already come into being. Furthermore, if the absence of a mental impression were the cause of the superimposition of the contrary, then the superimposition of difference and the superimposition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) would also have to be so; what contradiction is there in this? Moreover, in reality, there is no cognition of positive and negative concomitance other than mere conceit. Thus, everything is merely conceit. Therefore, even if there is a perception through discrimination (*viveka*), one must admit the identity of the preceding and succeeding moments; otherwise, it would be nothing but mere cognition. And that identity cannot be admitted, because: [The verse follows: *ekapratyavamarśasya hetutvād ekatā matā / jñānasyārthāntarābheṣe sā tadekātmikā kutaḥ //* "Unity is considered to belong to cognition because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). If that [awareness] appears as something distinct from the object, how could it possess that [object's] singular nature?"* [The commentary continues: If the unity of the object is not admitted, then the unity of the cognition itself cannot be maintained. Since the cognition is momentary, it cannot persist to produce a single, unified reflective awareness spanning before and after. Therefore, the identity of the preceding and succeeding moments must be accepted; otherwise, the world would be reduced to a mere flux of discrete cognitions. But such an identity cannot be accepted, because: [The verse follows: *arthāntarābhaśaktīnāṃ niyamo na ca yuktimān / tāsāṃ tadvyatirekeṇa vyatirekānavagrahāt //* "And a restriction on the powers of cognitions to appear as distinct objects is not logical, because their distinction is not perceived apart from [the appearance of] those objects. [The commentary continues: A restriction on the capacities of successive cognitions to manifest as different objects is untenable, since we do not perceive any distinction between those capacities themselves apart from the objects they manifest. If the capacity were distinct from the cognition, it would be unperceivable; if it were not distinct, then the cognition itself would be manifold. Thus, the notion of a single, enduring entity is merely a conceptual construction (*abhimāna*). Consequently, even when things are grasped through their differentiation, one must accept the identity of the prior and subsequent states; otherwise, there would be nothing but isolated moments of consciousness. Yet, such an identity cannot be logically maintained. Why? Because: [The verse follows: *na cānekārthajanyatvāt svāmarśo 'rtheṣu bhedinām / jñānāntarair avicchedād ekatvenāvasāyitā //* "And the reflective awareness regarding distinct objects does not arise from their being produced by multiple causes, because [those objects] are not interrupted by other cognitions, leading to the determination of them as one. [The commentary continues: It is not the case that the reflective awareness of distinct objects arises simply because they are produced by multiple causes. Since there is no interruption by other intervening cognitions, they are determined as a single unit. However, this is merely a conceptual construction. Therefore, even when there is a grasp of distinctions, the identity of the preceding and succeeding moments must be admitted; otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere stream of cognitions. But that identity cannot be admitted, because: [The verse follows: *avicchinnā na bhāseta tatsamvittir mṛṣāsthitau / vicchinneti ca jānīyād antareṇānyasaṃvidaḥ //* "If that [reflective] awareness were falsely established, it would not appear as uninterrupted; and one would not perceive it as interrupted without another intervening cognition. [The commentary continues: If the status of that awareness were false, it would not manifest as continuous. Furthermore, one could not recognize it as being interrupted unless there were another intervening cognition. Thus, the very notion of continuity or interruption is based on the superimposition of a conceptual framework onto a flow of discrete moments. Therefore, even when things are apprehended through their differentiation, one must accept the identity of the prior and subsequent states; otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere succession of cognitions. And that identity cannot be accepted, because: [The verse follows: *ekatvenāvasāyaśca jñānasyaivāvikalpataḥ / na tv arthasya tathābhāvaḥ kṣaṇikatvād bhedinām api //* "And the determination of cognition as a unity occurs through its own non-conceptual nature; but the object does not exist in that way, because even distinct things are momentary. [The commentary continues: The determination of cognition as a single entity arises from the cognition’s own non-conceptual character. However, the object does not possess such a nature, because even distinct entities are momentary and thus lack persistence. Therefore, the unity of the preceding and succeeding moments must be admitted; otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere flash of knowledge. Yet, that unity cannot be admitted, because: [The verse follows: *na cāpy anugataḥ kaścid dharmo bhedānugāmiṣu / dṛśyate rūpam evātra kevalaṃ tu vivicyate //* "Nor is any recurring property (*anugata-dharma*) observed among distinct things; only their form (*rūpa*) is seen here, though it is distinguished [as different]. [The commentary continues: No common property is perceived that persists through various distinct things. What is actually perceived is only the specific form of each, which is differentiated. Thus, the idea of a single, underlying essence is a mental fabrication. Consequently, even when there is a grasp of distinctions, the identity of the prior and subsequent moments must be accepted; otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere series of cognitions. But that identity cannot be accepted, because: [The verse follows: *na caikayā dvayajñānaṃ niyamād akṣacetasaḥ / ekārthābhiniṣṭhatvād anyonyākṣaviṣayāvadhiḥ //* "And there is no simultaneous cognition of two [objects] by a single sensory consciousness, because the sense-cognition is restricted to one object, limited by the respective spheres of the senses. [The commentary continues: A single sensory cognition cannot simultaneously cognize two objects, because it is restricted to a single object and delimited by the specific range of each sense organ. Therefore, the notion of a single, enduring subject is merely a conceptual construct. Consequently, even when there is a grasp of distinctions, the identity of the prior and subsequent moments must be admitted; otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere stream of cognitions. But that identity cannot be admitted, because: [The verse follows: *na caikayā dvayajñānaṃ niyamād akṣacetasaḥ / ekārthābhiniṣṭhatvād anyonyākṣaviṣayāvadhiḥ //* "And there is no simultaneous cognition of two [objects] by a single sensory consciousness, because the sense-cognition is restricted to one object, limited by the respective spheres of the senses. [The commentary continues: A single sensory cognition cannot simultaneously cognize two objects, because it is restricted to a single object and delimited by the specific range of each sense organ. Therefore, the notion of a single, enduring subject is merely a conceptual construct. Consequently, even when there is a grasp of distinctions, the identity of the prior and subsequent moments must be admitted; otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere stream of cognitions. But that identity cannot be admitted, because: [The verse follows: *na caikayā dvayajñānaṃ niyamād akṣacetasaḥ / ekārthābhiniṣṭhatvād anyonyākṣavi
[295,xv] When distinct entities are excluded, the distinct entity itself is not perceived at another time. ॥ 223 ॥

For it is not possible to maintain that something exists when it is not being perceived. And in the absence of such a thing, it is impossible to establish the existence of a "whole" (avayavin) that is indistinguishable from its parts and lacks any distinction [from them]. Therefore, by one who accepts an external object, its simultaneous apprehension must be accepted.

Now, how can that which is manifold be seen by a single [cognition] all at once? For a cognition that has engaged with one object is not capable of engaging with another at that very same time. If it has been established that the perception of the manifold is exactly thus and not otherwise, then in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is indeed only one; it is impossible for one thing to be apprehended by another. Furthermore, what is called "apprehension" does not belong to anything else, but rather is the arising of the intellect (*buddhi*) in the form of that [object]. And that which is manifold cannot be the producer of a single [cognition], because: [296,i] ... [text continues] ... because:

[296,ii] Or what contradiction is there if many [causes], having produced an excellence, were to exist as the cause of a single cognition simultaneously, provided it is not like the self, the sense organs, and so forth? (224)

For just as the sense-faculties, objects, and mental attention— or the contact between the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the objects— simultaneously produce a single sensory consciousness, so too, if atoms were to do the same, what contradiction would there be?

But surely, even if atoms are impermanent, what excellence do they possess? For atoms do not become large even when their auxiliary causes are present. And if they do not abandon their subtlety, how can they be perceived? That too is incorrect;
for in this case, there is no excellence of magnitude, but rather an excellence of capacity.
Because it lacks efficacy, it is not a cause; furthermore, because it is not great, it is not accepted as such.

If visibility consists in the production of a cognition that conforms to the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the atom, then this is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for such [conformity] does not exist at all. If, however, it consists merely in the production of consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), then that indeed exists and is not contradictory, as is seen in the case of [the appearance of] hair and the like. Just as hairs, even when not in contact with one another at a great distance, appear as a dense mass, so too are atoms; thus there is no contradiction. If it is argued that those [atoms] are somehow conveyed as subtle just like the isolated hairs, we reply: because the isolated ones lack the capacity [to produce such an effect]. It is precisely the lack of capacity that is incompatible with being a cause, not their subtlety. Furthermore, no specific quality such as grossness arises in the sense organs and so forth during the state of causal totality (*sāmagrī*), yet they possess productivity solely due to a specific capacity. But if that is so, why is that capacity not perceived when another [atom] is present? And if it is not perceived, how can it be said to exist? Moreover, since they are equal [in respect to their nature], how is the distinction made that the effect is produced by one and not by the other? [The answer is: because of the distinction in auxiliary conditions (*sahakāritā*), such as being at a distance.

[296, vii] But surely, since those very hairs are at a distance, why is there no perception of them? This has already been examined: it is because they have entered into a different causal complex (*sāmagryantara*). If perception were due to being a cause, then the eyes and other sense organs would also follow as objects of perception, because they too are causes. To this he says:
[296, viii]
Apart from being a causal state, there is no other such thing as "being an object of cognition.
In that regard, when a cognition has a certain appearance, that [cause] is said to be its object of cognition. (225)

The conformity to that form by way of the generality of the sense-field of visible forms (*rūpāyatana-sāmānya*) does not exist in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). For instance, the cognition’s conformity to the form of blue arises from an accumulation of blue atoms; let there be no conformity to the form of the atoms themselves.

Now, if the form of atoms does not appear, from what source is it known that "this much blue-form belongs to the atoms"? There is no fault here, for otherwise it would be impossible. Furthermore, if multiple things are not apprehended simultaneously, then there is this other fault, as it has been said:
"How indeed could a whole (avayavin) be perceived simultaneously with its own parts?"
If it is argued that it is indeed apprehended, we say: no.
For the cognition of a cow is not observed when the dewlap and other [characteristic features] are not perceived. (226)

If it is held that the apprehension of the subordinate and the principal occurs simultaneously, then neither would the whole with its constituent parts be grasped at once, nor would the possessor of qualities be so grasped. (227)

[296,xv] Because one grasps only that specific part which is intended to be taken as a qualifier, there is no grasping of the whole entity with all its parts. If it is argued that "all of them are indeed qualifiers," we say: No.
Because the status of qualifier and qualified is dependent upon the speaker's intention, that which is employed as a subordinate member is indeed apprehended by that very [intention]. (228)

[297,ii] Indeed, the relationship between qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*) is not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). This is because that which is a qualifier at one time or by another person may be perceived as the qualified by that same person at another time. For instance, we perceive various modes of cognition such as: "the horn of a cow," "the horned cow," "the cow is white," or "the cow is not round or circular. There is no simultaneous grasping of all qualifiers, because it is impossible to grasp many things as qualifiers all at once. Furthermore, the apprehension of the relationship between qualifier and qualified does not occur without conceptual construction (*avikalpita*). [297,iii]
Moreover:
Because a quality and so forth, which would serve as a differentiator, are not distinct from the entity itself, nor from other entities.
Due to non-apprehension [of the difference], there would be a cognition of difference even for one who perceives another [instance]. 229.

[297,v] For indeed, a cow is neither a cow by itself nor a non-cow; it is a cow through its connection with "cowness" (*gotva*). Likewise, white is neither white nor non-white; it is white through its connection with "whiteness," and so forth. Consequently, because the distinction between qualities and so on is perceived simultaneously, even when perceiving the higher and lower [categories], there would be only a single cognition. It would follow that the quality is apprehended only subsequently in isolation. [297,vi]
Now, it might be argued that the cognition of difference will arise later due to the perception of qualities (*guṇa*). To this it is replied:
[297, vii] If the apprehension of multiplicity results from the perception of the difference between qualities and so forth...
Let it be so; nevertheless, there would still be a confusion of their relations.

[297, viii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream of the Dharma, have crossed over the mire of saṃsāra, reached the dry land of nirvāṇa, and attained security. What are these four? They are: the person who is a stream-enterer, the person who is a once-returner, the person who is a non-returner, and the person who is an arhat. Thus it was said. What is the meaning of this? Here, “stream” (srotas) refers to the Noble Eightfold Path. Because they have entered this stream, they are called “stream-enterers” (srotāpanna). Because they will return to this world only one more time, they are called “once-returners” (sakṛdāgāmin). Because they will not return to this world again, they are called “non-returners” (anāgāmin). Because they have killed the enemy of the afflictions (kleśa), they are called “arhats” (arhan). Among these, the stream-enterer is further divided into two types: one who is bound by seven births (saptakṛdbhavaparama) and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin). The once-returner is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born (upapadyaparinirvāyin) and one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin). The non-returner is of five types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon being born, one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort, one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort (anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin), and one who goes upstream (ūrdhvasrotas). The arhat is of six types: one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), one who falls away (parihāṇadharman), one who maintains what has been attained (anurakṣaṇādharman), one who transforms his destiny (cetovimuktidharman), and one who is immovable (akopyadharman). These are the four kinds of persons. Furthermore, among these, the stream-enterer is of two types: one who is fixed in destiny (niyata) and one who is not yet fixed in destiny (aniyata). The once-returner is also of two types: one who is fixed in destiny and one who is not yet fixed in destiny. The non-returner is also of two types: one who is fixed in destiny and one who is not yet fixed in destiny. The arhat is also of two types: one who is fixed in destiny and one who is not yet fixed in destiny. Among these, the stream-enterer who is fixed in destiny is further divided into two: one who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births and one who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment. The once-returner who is fixed in destiny is also of two types: one who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births and one who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment. The non-returner who is fixed in destiny is also of two types: one who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births and one who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment. The arhat who is fixed in destiny is also of two types: one who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births and one who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment. Among these, the stream-enterer who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births is further divided into two: one who is bound by seven births and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. The once-returner who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born and one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort. The non-returner who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births is also of five types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon being born, one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort, one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort, and one who goes upstream. The arhat who is fixed in destiny regarding the number of births is also of six types: one liberated by wisdom, one liberated both ways, one who falls away, one who maintains what has been attained, one who transforms his destiny, and one who is immovable. The stream-enterer who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment is further divided into two: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (dr̥ṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin) and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life (upapadyaparinirvāyin). The once-returner who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life. The non-returner who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life. The arhat who is fixed in destiny regarding the time of attainment is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life and one who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life. Among these, the stream-enterer who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life is further divided into two: one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion and one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion. The once-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion and one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion. The non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion and one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion. The arhat who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion and one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion. Among these, the stream-enterer who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life is further divided into two: one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort and one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. The once-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort and one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. The non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort and one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. The arhat who attains parinirvāṇa in the next life is also of two types: one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort and one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. Among these, the stream-enterer who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life through exertion is further divided into two: one who is liberated by wisdom and one who is liberated both ways. The stream-enterer who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life without exertion is also of two types: one who is liberated by wisdom and one who is liberated both ways. The once-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life through exertion is also of two types: one who is liberated by wisdom and one who is liberated both ways. The once-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life without exertion is also of two types: one who is liberated by wisdom and one who is liberated both ways. The non-returner who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life through exertion is also of two types: one who

If a substance is first apprehended as a unity and subsequently a qualifier is apprehended, there can be no distinct connection [between them]; thus, the consequence of confusion (saṅkara) follows. For instance, if a substance is apprehended as one and then multiple qualifiers—even though they are distinct—are joined to that very same [substance], it would follow that multiple qualifiers belong to a single [thing]. If it is argued that [the substance] is not one because the qualifiers are joined to different locations, we say no; for since location-difference itself is a qualifier, that location-difference too would belong to the single [substance] alone. Therefore, multiple [qualifiers] are not apprehended at once, and if the qualifier is apprehended later, it would not be known to which [subject] it belongs. Furthermore, on the view that the qualifier is both distinct and non-distinct [from the qualified], nothing whatsoever possesses distinction; thus, the confusion of related entities is even more extreme.
But in the Sāṃkhya system:

Since sound and the other [objects] are manifold, their simultaneous apprehension as many is established; for it is impossible to apprehend a configuration without apprehending the things that possess that configuration. (231)

[297,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive 'Bodhisattva' as a designation. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive 'perfection of wisdom' as a designation. He does not perceive the six perfections, nor does he perceive 'six perfections' as a designation. He does not perceive the three doors of liberation, nor does he perceive 'three doors of liberation' as a designation. He does not perceive the ten stages, nor does he perceive 'ten stages' as a designation. He does not perceive the five eyes, nor does he perceive 'five eyes' as a designation. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive 'ten powers of a Tathāgata' as a designation. He does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, nor does he perceive 'four grounds of self-confidence' as a designation. He does not perceive the four analytical knowledges, nor does he perceive 'four analytical knowledges' as a designation. He does not perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he perceive 'eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha' as a designation. He does not perceive omniscience, nor does he perceive 'omniscience' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. [298,i] Subhūti said: "Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive 'Bodhisattva' as a designation? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form, nor does he perceive 'form' as a designation; he does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive 'feeling' as a designation; he does not perceive perception, nor does he perceive 'perception' as a designation; he does not perceive formations, nor does he perceive 'formations' as a designation; he does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive 'consciousness' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is non-existent and unapprehendable. Feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive 'eye' as a designation; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive 'ear' as a designation; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive 'nose' as a designation; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive 'tongue' as a designation; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive 'body' as a designation; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive 'mind' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the eye is non-existent and unapprehendable. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive 'forms' as a designation; he does not perceive sounds, nor does he perceive 'sounds' as a designation; he does not perceive odors, nor does he perceive 'odors' as a designation; he does not perceive tastes, nor does he perceive 'tastes' as a designation; he does not perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive 'tangibles' as a designation; he does not perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive 'mental phenomena' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, forms are non-existent and unapprehendable. Sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive 'eye-consciousness' as a designation; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nor does he perceive 'ear-consciousness' as a designation; he does not perceive the nose-consciousness, nor does he perceive 'nose-consciousness' as a designation; he does not perceive the tongue-consciousness, nor does he perceive 'tongue-consciousness' as a designation; he does not perceive the body-consciousness, nor does he perceive 'body-consciousness' as a designation; he does not perceive the mind-consciousness, nor does he perceive 'mind-consciousness' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, eye-consciousness is non-existent and unapprehendable. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive eye-contact, nor does he perceive 'eye-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive ear-contact, nor does he perceive 'ear-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive nose-contact, nor does he perceive 'nose-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive tongue-contact, nor does he perceive 'tongue-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive body-contact, nor does he perceive 'body-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive mind-contact, nor does he perceive 'mind-contact' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, eye-contact is non-existent and unapprehendable. Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact, nor does he perceive 'feeling born of eye-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nor does he perceive 'feeling born of ear-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive the feeling born of nose-contact, nor does he perceive 'feeling born of nose-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive the feeling born of tongue-contact, nor does he perceive 'feeling born of tongue-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive the feeling born of body-contact, nor does he perceive 'feeling born of body-contact' as a designation; he does not perceive the feeling born of mind-contact, nor does he perceive 'feeling born of mind-contact' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the feeling born of eye-contact is non-existent and unapprehendable. The feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the earth element, nor does he perceive 'earth element' as a designation; he does not perceive the water element, nor does he perceive 'water element' as a designation; he does not perceive the fire element, nor does he perceive 'fire element' as a designation; he does not perceive the wind element, nor does he perceive 'wind element' as a designation; he does not perceive the space element, nor does he perceive 'space element' as a designation; he does not perceive the consciousness element, nor does he perceive 'consciousness element' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the earth element is non-existent and unapprehendable. The water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are non-existent and unapprehendable. Since they are non-existent and unapprehendable, they cannot be perceived. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive 'ignorance' as a designation; he does not perceive formative forces, nor does he perceive 'formative forces' as a designation; he does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive 'consciousness' as a designation; he does not perceive name-and-form, nor does he perceive 'name-and-form' as a designation; he does not perceive the six sense bases, nor does he perceive 'six sense bases' as a designation; he does not perceive contact, nor does he perceive 'contact' as a designation; he does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive 'feeling' as a designation; he does not perceive craving, nor does he perceive 'craving' as a designation; he does not perceive grasping, nor does he perceive 'grasping' as a designation; he does not perceive existence, nor does he perceive 'existence' as a designation

A specific arrangement of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) constitutes a complete object such as a jar, which consists of the three *guṇas*. Therefore, upon the perception of sound and so forth, there is the perception of the three *guṇas* or the perception of the subtle elements. It is not possible to perceive the arrangement of those [elements] without perceiving them; one does not perceive a fist when the fingers are not perceived. Furthermore, it is not the case that the ear itself is something produced [from a cause]. This is because every effect is held to be non-different from its cause. Moreover, they accept the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and not the theory of [new] production (*kāryapakṣa*). Transformation is the relinquishing of one property and the arising of another by that which has not deviated from its essential nature (*tattva*). In this regard, space (*ākāśa*) is the transformation of sound; air (*vāyu*) is the transformation of sound and touch; fire (*tejas*) is the transformation of sound, touch, and form; water (*udaka*) is the transformation of sound, touch, form, and taste; and earth (*pṛthivī*) is the transformation of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus, jars and other objects possess multiplicity. Through the perception of that [multiplicity], the perception of the one [whole] is established. The remaining refutation is exactly as before.
Therefore, even when multiple things are apprehended simultaneously, there is no conceptualization; it is established that perception is exclusively non-conceptual.

If perception is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), how then can there be a grasping of the subject (*dharmin*), its properties (*dharma*), and so forth, through perception? If the subject is not grasped by perception, there would be no entry of inference (*anumāna*) regarding that subject. If the subject were grasped by inference, then since that too would require a subject, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. Furthermore, if the subject is grasped, it is grasped as having a nature variegated by manifold properties; how, then, could it be non-conceptual? To this, it is replied:
[298,ii] There is no complete comprehension of a subject (*dharmin*) that possesses multiple forms through the sense-faculty.
The object-sphere of the sense-faculty is a form that is self-cognizable and inexpressible. (PVA 431)

For no substratum (*dharmin*) endowed with multiple properties such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth is ever apprehended. Rather, even by sensory cognition, it is apprehended only in its own specific form; and that very form is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To explain:
The apprehension of form and so forth from the eye and so forth occurs through their mutual dissociation,
because it is not understood that they possess a single substratum.

Indeed, it is not perceived by the sensory consciousnesses of form and so forth. For it has already been established that since only form and the other [sensory objects] are grasped as mutually distinct, there is no further substratum nor anything residing therein that falls within the scope of perception.

[298, vi] But surely, from the cognition "that very thing which I saw, I now touch," one understands a common substratum or identity. No; for it has been established that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Rather, such a cognition arises from the awakening of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) triggered by the cognitions of color-form and touch, resulting in the emergence of a corresponding conceptualization. To explain:

It is observed that visual consciousness arises with regard to mere form, and another [type of consciousness] arises with regard to the mere tangible, while feeling arises with regard to sensation. (433) (PVA)

Nor is a mutual conjunction of those two perceived by another [sense]. If it is argued that "this [eye] sees while touching," no; because there is no presence of touch within visible form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, their identity would be established only if there were a cognition of them being situated in a single object.

[Objection: But surely it is observed that a white object, when soiled by touch, is perceived as being attached to the hand. How then can there not be an adherence to a single object? [Response: This is merely grasping at a hollow space in the sky. For when that object is touched, and when one is within the range of that touch—

If there is no cognition of that [object] by him at that time, then inference is not a means of proof. (PVA 434) When two perceptions—those of the apprehended and the apprehender—are not mutually adhered to, and when the difference between them is determined by perception, then even a thousand inferences cannot enter the path of efficacy. Now, if it is argued that "I am touching that very thing" constitutes a mental cognition (*mānasa-pratyaya*) which is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), we reply: it is not the case that only that which is produced by the sense organs (*indriya-ja*) is a valid means of knowledge; for the status of being a *pramāṇa* enters [the domain of logic] through non-deviation from the object, not because of being produced by the sense organs. For it is also possible [for a cognition] to be produced by the mind (*mānasa-ja*). This is not so, because:
"The reliability of the cognition 'I saw exactly that which I saw,' and so forth, no person of limited vision can understand without inference. (PVA 435)

[298, xiii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, monks, physical food as gross nutriment is for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth; it is not, however, for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage that is the goal of the holy life. Contact as nutriment, mental volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment are for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth; they are also, however, for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage that is the goal of the holy life. Why is that? Because, monks, when consciousness is present, name-and-form comes to be; when consciousness arises, name-and-form arises. Monks, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb, would name-and-form coagulate there? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “If, after having descended into the mother’s womb, consciousness were to depart, would name-and-form come to be manifested in this world? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “If the consciousness of one who has already grown up and attained maturity were to be cut off, would name-and-form come to grow up and reach maturity? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the origin, this is the source, this is the condition for name-and-form, namely, consciousness. [299] “What do you think, monks? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Blessed One. “Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, Blessed One. “Is what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, indeed, Blessed One. “Is feeling permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Blessed One. “Is perception permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Blessed One. “Are formations permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Blessed One. “Is consciousness permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, Blessed One. “Therefore, monks, whatever form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling... whatever perception... whatever formations... whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing it thus with right wisdom exactly as it is, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One knows: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. [300] “Monks, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean, and a blind turtle were to surface once every hundred years. What do you think, monks? Would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, eventually insert its neck into that yoke with a single hole? “Certainly, Blessed One; after a long time, perhaps, it might happen. “Even slower than that, monks, is the acquisition of human birth. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall guard the door of our sense faculties; we shall be moderate in eating; we shall be devoted to wakefulness; we shall cultivate wholesome states; we shall take delight in the higher mind. [301] “And how, monks, does one guard the door of one’s sense faculties? Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil and unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might arise, he practices for its restraint, guards the eye faculty, and achieves the restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having smelled an odor with the nose... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having touched a tangible object with the body... Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil and unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might arise, he practices for its restraint, guards the mind faculty, and achieves the restraint of the mind faculty. It is in this way, monks, that one guards the door of one’s sense faculties. And how, monks, is one moderate in eating? Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, takes his food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for the sake of physical beauty and attractiveness, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for the ending of discomfort, and for supporting the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling. It is in this way, monks, that one is moderate in eating. And how, monks, is one devoted to wakefulness? Here, monks, a monk during the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the thought of rising. After the last watch of the night, having risen, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. It is in this way, monks, that one is devoted to wakefulness. And how, monks, does one cultivate wholesome states? Here, monks, a monk cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he cultivates the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. It is in this way, monks, that one cultivates wholesome states. And how, monks, does one take delight in the higher mind? Here, monks, a monk, detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of detachment. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and mental unification, without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. It is in this way, monks, that one takes delight in the higher mind. [302] “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who goes upstream against the stream; the person who stands firm; the person who crosses over and goes beyond; and the person who has reached the far shore. And how, monks, is one a person who goes upstream against the stream? Here, monks, a monk dwells with his mind bent toward seclusion, withdrawn, secluded, aloof from society, and delighting in solitude. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who goes upstream against the stream. And how, monks, is one a person who stands firm? Here, monks, a monk is one who has attained the fruit of non-returning. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who stands firm. And how, monks, is one a person who crosses over and goes beyond? Here, monks, a monk is one who has attained the fruit of once-returning. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who crosses over and goes beyond. And how, monks, is one a person who has reached the far shore? For in that case, if someone were to question: "How do you have the cognition that what was previously seen is now being touched?"—if one were to say, "The cognition is exactly like this," that is not so. For that which was seen is not seen at the time of touching; therefore, how can there be the cognition, "That very same thing is being touched"? To this, the answer is precisely this: "By that [touch], it has been made dirty. From this, it is known; thus he teaches an inference. [Objection: But then, how is non-tangibility made dirty? Or rather, why is tangibility not cognized as "this is white," given that tangibility and whiteness (and its opposite) have the same form? [Reply: This is not a valid answer.
[298,xiv] That a single entity is both identical and non-identical is a rash assertion.

Since touch possesses both similarity and dissimilarity to form, it is not logical for the two to be one, because of the imposition of contradictory properties. Therefore, this is investigated: is it apprehended by a cognition of a single form, or by a cognition of multiple forms? If it is being apprehended by a cognition of multiple forms, how can it be one? Or if it is by a cognition of a single form, that is false; for while touch is being apprehended, how can form—which is not being apprehended—be grasped as having a single form? Indeed, that which is being apprehended and that which is not being apprehended cannot be the object of cognition, because it is impossible for there to be non-apprehension [of one part] while there is apprehension [of another]. Therefore, there is no such thing as a "whole" (avayavin) distinct from form and the other qualities. Consequently, they are cognized only by their own respective forms.

[299,i] Form and the other [sensory objects] do not exist by way of each other's form. Likewise, form is only self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*) and not cognizable by another; therefore, because it cannot be indicated to another by means of words, sensory consciousness has an inexpressible object (*avācyagocara*). If, then, the object of the senses is not indicated by words, how is there the understanding: "I see that very thing which I heard"? For how can there be such a cognition of something that has not been indicated? Therefore, it is concluded that it must indeed be expressible. This is incorrect, because: [299,ii]

It has been established that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, how can this object be considered cognized on the basis of that [recognition]? (436) (PVA) [299,iii]

At the time of comprehension from a word, that object does not appear [directly]. There is indeed doubt regarding the object derived from a word; otherwise, as in the case of what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be no possibility of doubt.

Now, since the appearance [of an object] from a word is the same whether the object exists or does not exist, there is doubt regarding its reality. Why does this [doubt] not occur even in the case of perception? In that case (perception), it does not occur precisely because one perceives a specific distinction in the appearance. Here too (in verbal cognition), by what means could the apprehension of a specific distinction be removed? It is simply because no such distinction exists. Therefore, the conceptual cognition arising from words does not grasp the actual nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing, because it is distinct in character from perception. If, however, it were to convey the thing's own-form (*svarūpa*), then direct observation would be non-valid, as it would be grasping what has already been grasped; furthermore, there would be an absence of the object, since the form and nature of the thing would be understood through the word alone. If, on the other hand, it is cognized in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), then even one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice would perceive white as yellow; and since that too is generally consistent, it would follow that it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If you say, "Let that also be a valid means of knowledge," we say no, because it is sublated (*bādhana*). The cognition produced by the word "Bring the cow" is indeed a valid means of knowledge because it is not sublated—[you might argue]. But no, for even here there is sublation. If, in the command "Bring the cow," existence is implied, then it may sometimes not exist. If it is not implied, then since bringing is impossible, it is all the more clearly non-valid. If you say the speaker’s intention is "bring it if it exists," then because the instruction to bring is uncertain, it is certainly non-valid. If you say, "The very thing that is uncertain was what was instructed," then every doubtful cognition would be a valid means of knowledge. Yet, a real entity is not grasped by a non-valid means of knowledge. How then is there non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) regarding the act of bringing and so forth? There is no possibility of non-deviation, because someone may fail to act. For one does not necessarily do what they have been instructed to do.
Furthermore:
If it is held that a word is either a causal factor (*kāraka*) in an action or a communicator (*jñāpaka*),
then if it were a causal factor, it would lack the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of the absence of non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*).

For there is no conventional usage such as "the agent is non-contradictory. Reliability (*āpti*), however, occurs only when the action has been performed, based on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for being an indicator (*jñāpaka*), this is impossible for an essential nature (*svarūpa*) because of the existence of a future action. For an action that does not exist cannot be apprehended by way of its own nature. If it were apprehended by way of its own nature, it would not be something "future. If it is argued that "it is the universal (*sāmānya*) that is apprehended," then since that universal exists even in the absence of the action, one would not engage in the action upon the cognition of the universal. Therefore, a word is not an indicator of a sense-object. Consequently, the domain of the senses is indeed inexpressible.
How, then, is there the cognition of the multiplicity of the subject (dharmin) and its properties (dharma)? To this it is said:
"For that which is excluded from everything, there is an exclusion from this or that [particular thing]."
The multiplicity of the subject (dharmin) is that which has its distinctions inferred from the distinctions among those [attributes]. (232)

[299,xi] For the conventional usage of the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth is constructed based on the distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). To explain: does a golden vase, appearing at the very first moment, manifest as distinct from its color, shape, and so forth? Or do those [qualities] manifest as distinct from it?

However, it is only a single entity consisting of color and so forth that is the direct object of manifestation. In this regard, those who have fallen into the river of saṃsāra and abide within the path of conventional usage construct distinctions through the conceptualization of analytical abstraction (*apoddhāra*), based on the exclusion of other objects possessing various successive forms.
[300, ii] If there were no difference between the color and the particular arrangement, then...
How can a blue pot be distinguished from a non-blue pot?

If there were indeed no difference between color, shape, and so forth, then the exclusion of blue from a non-blue jar would not occur; for even that which is non-blue would have to be blue by virtue of having that same shape, since shape is non-different from the color blue. Yet, a non-blue object is also perceived as distinct from its shape. Therefore, the world’s conceptualization of a difference between the two is merely a manifestation of mental construction (*kalpanā*). If it is argued that the difference is then ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), we reply: it is not logical for something to be ultimately real when it is merely metaphorically attributed through mental construction alone. If that very whiteness and so forth were to appear as not being of the nature of shape, then the difference would be ultimately real. If it is argued that because inherence (*samavāya*) in a single substrate is the cause for the appearance of non-difference, there is thus an appearance of non-difference even where a difference exists—we respond: surely, even in the case of inherence in a single substrate, there is an appearance of difference between color and taste. If you say that this is because they are apprehended by different sense organs, then if inherence possesses a power that causes them to appear as non-different, their being apprehended by different sense organs would be impossible. Furthermore, the claim that they appear as non-different because they occupy the same location is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the example of color, taste, and so forth. Thus, it is established that through the conceptual construction of difference, properties such as "being a Śābaleya" are established as distinct from "cowness," and "being a Khaṇḍa" or "Muṇḍa" are established as distinct from "being a Śābaleya."

[300, iv] In this regard, in some cases a substratum (*dharmin*) is postulated as distinct from [its qualities], such as a jar. If the jar were not a single composite whole (*avayavin*), then upon the successive perception of its color and taste, there would be no cognition of the "jar. This is an instance of a property (*dharma*). If "cowness" (*gotva*) were neither non-distinct nor both distinct and non-distinct, then there would be no distinction among the various cows—such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others—which are non-distinct from it. Other cases should be applied in the same way. Therefore, difference is to be inferred by taking recourse to the difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). [300, v]

Surely, even a difference known through inference is indeed a difference. True, provided that the inference is not preceded by perception. Just as fire, having been manifested in perception, remains exactly the same when cognized through inference. If it is argued, "In that case, the distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-possessor (*dharmin*) would never appear; if it does appear, what is the use of inference?", this is equally true for fire. If it is argued that inference occurs at a later time and so forth, let it be the same here as well.
If, on the other hand, it is claimed that here there is only constant inferability (*nityānumeyatā*), that too is incorrect.

[300,vii] By what means can an example be established in reality for that which is to be inferred eternally? If it is not established by another inference, this is merely a blind succession. (PVA 439)
