For a single unifying cognition (*ekaparāmarśa*) is indeed possible because it is directly perceived; likewise, it must be possible through a non-difference that is not being perceived. Those imagined distinctions of form are not the object of a non-conceptual mind; they are the occasional domain of a variegated [mind] appearing as variegated. (233)

For perception (*pratyakṣa*) functions by way of direct manifestation; it is therefore not logical that it should possess the form of an object that has been mentally constructed (*utprekṣita*). Furthermore, the appearance of an object in perception occurs only occasionally, as it depends upon the existence of the thing itself; however, the appearances of conceptualized forms are non-occasional. Moreover, perception has a single form, whereas conceptualization possesses multiple forms. Thus, there is a distinction between conceptualization and perception both because of the difference in their forms and because of the difference in their causes; such is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

[Objection: But surely there exist distinctions among properties such as whiteness and so forth that are not conceptualized; these will be the objects of the senses. [Response: This objection is not valid, because:
Even if whiteness and the like do exist, they are of such a nature that they are the objects of the senses.
It is not denoted by words because of the difference in the forms of the two cognitions. // 234 //

[301, vii] White is not grasped by the sense-faculty as a *dharmatā* (essential nature) or as a *dharmin* (possessor of properties) belonging to anything, nor is it grasped through its differentiation from its configuration (*saṃsthāna*). But by means of the word, there is a grasp of it as differentiated—namely, as being a *dharmin* and so forth, or as being indistinct and so forth. Thus, the cognitions of the sense-faculties do not apprehend a form that is truly indefinable. Therefore, because of the difference in the aspects of cognition, verbal cognition does not operate upon those things grasped by the sense-faculties. Consequently, a difference in the form of the object is not tenable if there is identity of referent.
[301, viii]

Now, it might be argued: "The difference in form will arise from the difference in the basis (*āśraya*). For instance, one whose visual power is impaired by the affliction of jaundice sees even a white object as yellow due to the difference in the basis; a person with cataracts sees things unclearly. Thus, there is no fault for one who accepts a difference in form despite the objects being the same. This is not so.
If that were the case, even when cognitions have the same object, [the difference in form would arise] through their having different bases.
Now, how is it that the [senses] such as the ear, though distinct from one another, have distinct objects? // 235 //

[301,x] For if a difference in form were possible due to a difference in substratum, then the determination of multiplicity would be lost, since a single object can also possess a difference in form. In the case of sound and so forth as well, the difference in form arises precisely from the difference in their substrata, such as the ear. Furthermore, the erroneous nature of appearances such as yellow would then apply to sound and other objects as well. By this, the distinction of capacities (*śakti*) is also refuted.

As for the one who says: "The power of the word itself is such that it brings about a cognition of difference and also otherwise; if it were otherwise, the state of being erroneous in the case of a different cognition would not need to be investigated.

But surely, even when an object is presented otherwise by a word, it is seen to perform its causal function (*arthakriyā*). How, then, is it logical to say that this [word] is erroneous? For instance, that very same [thing], such as wine and so forth, is presented by words like "wine" (*vakra*) and the like, and it performs that very causal function. This causal function is not dependent upon the external object, but rather upon mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); just as the pacification of poison and so forth depends upon the mental cultivation of [the deity] Garuḍa and others. Therefore, there is no difference in form despite the difference in their bases, provided they have the same referent. Furthermore: "A thing that has arisen is indeed different from the basis of another's mind."
How can that which is a single entity appear as having various forms? (236)

[302,iii] For while a difference in the cognition might produce an appearance of non-difference, it cannot do so for the object itself. The object, such as blue and so forth, is indeed one; it would have to appear in that cognition in a single form. There can be no appearance of what does not exist. If there is an appearance, then it is not that [non-existent thing] which appears. Nor is there a logical connection whereby one thing appears through another thing appearing. If it is argued that the object appears because it is the cause of the cognition, then its status as an object would consist merely in being a cause; consequently, it would follow that the eyes and other sense organs are also objects. [302,iv]

If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—the answer is: there is a contradiction with the principle of having a single object (*ekārthatā*). For even that which is visual [is an object] because it is an object (*viṣayatva*). Indeed, if there were objecthood while maintaining a single object, the established doctrine regarding cognitions would be subverted. For when there is objecthood, there can be no status as a substratum (*āśrayabhāva*). Therefore, this is an external object. If it is argued that even if there is a single object, it is due to the multiplicity of the objects of the cognitions, then there is a mutual contradiction. Consequently, objecthood consists solely in appearing in its own form; there is no other way. Now, if the rebuttal is that [it is an object] because it is the substratum of the word, then from the perceived word there is a perception of the object in its own form. Yet that [word] is not the object of the perception of the object, because it is itself already perceived. In that case, the object also would not be the object [of the cognition], since it is perceived in its own form.

Thus, they are empty of intrinsic nature. This is the meaning of the statement that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. Now, [the opponent claims] that the object is "the attainment of that mirror-image from that [external object]. This is incorrect. What kind of relationship exists such that "its attainment is from that"? For it is attained in its own form (*svarūpa*). How can it be said to be attained from something else? If it is argued that this is because of activity (*pravṛtti*) [toward it], then one must consider how this activity arises from cognition. If it is argued that the attainment of that [object] is seen from that mental image (*ākāra*), then that very image is what is cognized from it; thus, activity toward it is inferential, and the attainment would not be verbal (*śābdī*). Consequently, it follows that this [object] is the domain of inference alone, not of the word. Therefore, the form of sensory cognition (*indriyabuddhi*) is indeed inexpressible (*anirdeśya*). In that case, it would follow that it is the domain of inference. But even in inference, that intrinsic form does not appear. How then is there activity toward what does not appear? It has already been established that activity occurs only toward what has appeared in every respect.

[302, vi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of contact with the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, air, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects as real. Subhūti, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any of these things as real that he is called a 'Bodhisattva'."

[Objection: But surely one proceeds [in action] with the thought, "This has been perceived by me. [Response: True; nevertheless, this is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For all activity whatsoever proceeds from the conceit of perception regarding what is actually unperceived. This alone is the ultimate reality: that which is the object of such conceit is indeed the object. If it is argued that while the ultimate status of an object as a domain of words is denied for the object of sensory cognition, its conventional status is not, then there is no fault. If the opponent accepts that very point, then what we desire is established. However, if that [object] were perceived in its own form, then its ultimate status as an object would be demonstrated. Therefore, even if it rests upon various bases, that which is not perceived in its own form is not an object. If it is argued that it is indeed an object because some aspect of its nature enters into it, then if that part has ultimately entered into the perception by the word, it should also be perceived by another [cognition] that grasps a clear form. For it is impossible to perceive something otherwise when it has already entered [into the cognition].
[302,vii] But surely, because of recognition, unity is not contradicted even when there is a difference in form? That too is not true, because:
[302,viii]

Because mental activity does not involve the conceptualization of the perceptible object, the recognition of cows and other such things—which arises from the observation [of them]—is excluded from both verbal expression and conceptual construction. (237)

[303,i] Just now, even that visible object which is not touched by verbal expression or conceptual construction is recognized as having been previously grasped. Yet, there is no grasping by means of words or conceptual constructions; so how can there be recognition? How, then, does the cognition arise that "this is that very same thing which was demonstrated to me by him at that time"?

But surely, even when there is no actual realization, one may have the conceit of having realized it. How then is this not sublated? It is indeed sublated for one who reflects upon it. For it is the difference in cognition that constitutes sublation, and that exists precisely between verbal designation and conceptual construction, because their objects are merely remembered. That memory pertains to what was previously grasped, while [the object] being seen is present. If, however, the conceptual construction of verbal designations were itself a direct reflection of the perceived object, then it has already been established that what would be the use of perception? Therefore, even recognition is merely a matter of conceit and is not a realization in the ultimate sense. Rather, based on prior experience, it is only a conceptual construction that establishes the conventional usage of identity, and it does not involve the apprehension of ultimate reality.

Furthermore, that inference based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*) which [is said to occur] between verbal designation and conceptual construction regarding perceptible objects such as cows and the like— that too has been refuted by this very [argument]. (238)

[303,iv] For there is no contact with a real entity through either verbal designation or conceptual construction. Indeed, no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is apprehended of anything in the ultimate sense; this has been established by showing that such [apprehension] is merely a conceit (*abhimāna*). This is because one remembers only what was previously perceived. And when the object of perception (*dṛśya*) is not being touched [by cognition], a form that is a positive concomitant related to that perceived object is not apprehended. Therefore, there is no cognition that "the universal exists as a perceived object. If so, how then does the single conceptual construction arise, such as "this is that very same cow"? To this, he says: [303,v]
It has been described that even distinct perceptions, by their very nature, produce a single conceptual construction designated as "recognition. (239)

Indeed, perceptions arise by grasping objects that are distinguished as superior or inferior; they do not stand within the range of a capacity to grasp what is either distinct from or non-distinct from a single form. Rather, having entered into the turbulence of the proficiency and power of awakening the seeds of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) corresponding to their own nature, and because there is no other alternative, they produce the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of recognition. It is in accordance with that [recognition] that the path toward the useless conceptualization of universals (*jāti*) and so forth is set forth. Therefore, it is established that perception has an inexpressible object.
<2. Mental Perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*)>
The self-awareness of mental factors such as desire for objects is non-conceptual. (Pramāṇasamuccaya) [303,
viii]

Mental cognition (*mānasa*) as well is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is free from conceptual construction (*akalpaka*) and consists of the self-awareness of the nature of objects, such as attachment. This is because it functions in the form of immediate experience (*anubhava*).

[Objection: But it is only visual consciousness and the like that are observed to function in the form of immediate experience; that is, only sensory consciousness produced by the eye and other faculties. [Response: If mental consciousness arises from that [sensory consciousness], then it must grasp what was previously experienced by it.
[303,x] If it apprehends what was previously experienced, mental perception would lack the status of a valid means of cognition (apramāṇatā).

For it is not possible to cognize what was previously experienced in a manner that is not being remembered. If it were directly perceived while not being remembered, how could it be said to have been "experienced"? If you argue that it is indeed a prior experience in reality, how is this to be understood? Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) has already been refuted. Now, suppose it apprehends what has not been seen. If that were the case: [303, xii] If there were apprehension of the unseen, then even the blind and others would perceive objects. (240)

The mind also possesses the capacity for objects; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of it grasping all objects, as well as others. From this, the distinction between the blind and the deaf would cease to exist.
Because the past perception is momentary, its existence is impossible;
even if it were non-momentary, its definition would have to be stated with specific qualifications. (241)

[304,iii] For all entities are momentary; therefore, how could there be a grasping of what is past, by which one would grasp that which has already been grasped? Alternatively, if non-momentariness is admitted, then because it has already been grasped by a previous perception, the grasping of what is already grasped is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like memory. Or, even if it were to grasp what has already been grasped, if the mental [perception] is to be considered a valid means of knowledge, then its definition must be stated with a qualification.
Furthermore:
[304,v] When the action has already been accomplished, [a cause] does not produce any further distinction.
Why is another means, whether it be an organ of sense or something else, sought for the sake of action? || 242 ||

For one whose own nature is determined by sensory consciousness alone, what further function could another [consciousness] perform? If it is argued that "that very same nature is being determined," then once it has been determined, what is the purpose of determination? It would be exactly the same as before. If it is argued that even when undetermined there is a purpose for determination—namely, the manifestation of its own nature—then what fault is there in this being the case elsewhere as well?

[Objection: In that case, the eternal [entity] remains eternally delimited. What, then, will another do there? [Response: Now it is delimited by another. [Objection: No, because of its eternity; even now it is delimited by that very same [delimitor], so another has no capacity. [Response: It is not logical to say "because of the absence of that delimitor," for if there is an absence of a delimitor, the eternal entity would not be apprehended. [Objection: It will be apprehended by another. [Response: No, because it would lack a basis for cognition (*apratyayatvāt*). How could another, while cognizing only its own time, cognize eternity? Therefore, it must exist by means of that very same delimitor; thus, another apprehending subject is useless, as the comprehension occurs through that form alone.
[304, viii] Furthermore, all cognitions produced by that same entity would arise simultaneously;
for it is contradictory for a thing that possesses no difference in its causal efficacy to depend on other factors. (243)

[304, ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and their caravan being pursued by the yakṣa Vajraśṛṅga; seeing them terrified and seized with fear, he resolved to rescue them from that peril. Then, having transformed himself into a great garuḍa king, he descended upon the head of the yakṣa Vajraśṛṅga. At that moment, the yakṣa Vajraśṛṅga, terrified by the sight of the garuḍa, released the merchantmen and fled. When the yakṣa had departed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara restored the merchantmen to their former state and led them safely out of the great ocean. Having delivered them from that danger, he established them in the bliss of the Dharma. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a protector for those who have fallen into the great ocean. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any woman who desires a son, and she calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, she shall obtain a son, handsome, virtuous, and endowed with wisdom. If she desires a daughter, she shall obtain a daughter, beautiful, virtuous, and endowed with wisdom. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara fulfills the wishes of all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having bound themselves with ropes or shackles, calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those bonds shall immediately break asunder. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara delivers sentient beings from all calamities. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having committed various evil deeds, calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall be freed from all suffering and attain rebirth in the realm of Sukhāvatī. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great compassionate savior for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, maintains it in their heart with single-minded devotion, they shall be freed from all fears and attain peace and happiness. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great refuge for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, recites it even once, they shall be freed from all sins and attain rebirth in the presence of the Buddha Amitābha. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great guide for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, recites it with a pure mind, they shall be freed from all obstacles and attain the stage of non-retrogression. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great teacher for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, recites it with unwavering faith, they shall be freed from all afflictions and attain the realization of the true nature of reality. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great liberator for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, recites it with deep reverence, they shall be freed from all worldly attachments and attain the state of liberation. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great benefactor for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, recites it with a focused mind, they shall be freed from all delusions and attain the wisdom of omniscience. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great light for all sentient beings. Therefore, O Śāriputra, one should always revere and honor the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great power and majesty. If there be any man or woman who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, recites it with a joyful heart, they shall be freed from all sorrows and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa. For if all cognition were to operate at the same time toward an eternal object by entering into its form, then what contradiction would there be in its having eternity and unity as its object? [It would be none,] because of the difference in forms. Or, if it arises at a later time from another cause, even then it must necessarily involve an adherence to that [same] time, otherwise its apprehension of that [object] would be impossible, as in the case of a true dream-vision. Indeed, a true dream-vision is observed to be a grasper precisely by following along with that [past] time. Furthermore, no other form of experience consisting of sensory cognition is perceived. And it is not logical to say that there is perception of something not perceived, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But others, however, [say]:
If there were no apprehension by means of the mental consciousness, then there would likewise be no recollection by means of the mental consciousness.
For that which has not been known by oneself here cannot ever be recollected by another.

If that which was apprehended by sensory consciousness is not remembered by the mind because they are distinct, then it would likewise not be remembered even if it were apprehended by conceptual cognition, since those two are also distinct. If you argue that this is because the latter is mental (*mānasatvāt*), then one could equally say it is because it is a consciousness (*vijñānatvāt*).
Therefore, [the subsequent cognition] arises from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) of sensory consciousness.
Therefore, one whose vision is blinded by passion perceives only another as the object of desire.

Mental perception (*mānasa*) is also a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), produced by sensory consciousness acting in conjunction with an object that is immediately subsequent to its own object. Now, if it occurs at the same time as the sensory consciousness, then since it would be apprehended by that very sensory consciousness, mental perception would be redundant. Alternatively, if it occurs after the sensory consciousness has ceased, it would not be perceived at all; so of what would this be the definition? To this, it is said:

That cognition which, through repeated practice, apprehends an object situated before one as "this" and so forth by means of direct perception— that indeed is accepted as mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*).

"This" refers to mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) which functions by way of direct apprehension toward that which is present before one. Alternatively, it is indeed visual (*cākṣuṣa*) because it arises from the operation of the eye. It is not the case that the eye is employed merely for the appearance of form; rather, the insistence [on its identity] is due to prior habituation (*pūrvābhyāsa*). Therefore, since there is no operation of the eye here, and because it arises from the characteristic of prior habituation, this is mental perception.

Now, it might be argued: "Since the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [object] is apprehended by visual consciousness and so forth alone, mental [consciousness] is redundant. It is not redundant, because there is the possibility of a superior resolve (*adhimukti*). Acting on the thought "this is indeed [it]," it proceeds; therefore, because it prompts action, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, sensory perception would not be a prompter [of action]. This is not so, because even when another conceptualization occurs due to extreme habituation, sensory perception still functions as a means of valid cognition. Therefore, such a mental [consciousness] does not perceive what was previously apprehended, but rather arises at a subsequent time. Furthermore, it is not the case that it apprehends what has already been apprehended, because the prior apprehension does not recur while the object is present. [Objection: In that case, two aspects would be obtained simultaneously.

[305,v] But surely this consists of two distinct forms; how then can there be a determination of oneness? There is no fault here, for it is according to the analogy of two moons seen by two people with ophthalmia (*taimirika*). In that case, even pleasure and the like—which arise from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) and grasp an object-form present before one—would result in being mental perceptions (*mānasapratyakṣa*); consequently, the claim that "pleasure is sensory" would be undermined.

True. This has indeed been omitted; nothing is lost by this omission. If it is argued that this contradicts the statement that pleasure and pain arise solely from the sense faculties (*aindriya*), here too the words of the Fundamental Master (*Mūlācārya*) are contradicted: "In the case of attachment, aversion, delusion, pleasure, pain, and so forth, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) because it does not depend on the sense faculties. Thus, Dharmakīrti’s reputation for consistency is undermined by the claim that pleasure and pain are *aindriya* alone. By the word "pleasure" (*sukha*) and so forth, it is not only the causes of pleasure, such as taste, that are meant. Rather, it means that even for one who is non-conceptualizing (*avikalpayat*), something bitter appears as sweet through sensory cognition (*indriya-jñāna*). Alternatively, it is called "mental" (*mānasa*) precisely because of its common property of being non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*); thus, there is no contradiction. If it is then argued that mental [perception] would grasp one thing while sensory cognition grasps another, resulting in a manifold form (*anekākāra*), we say: No. That same consequence applies to sensory cognition as well. Even sensory consciousness, proceeding with various forms according to habituation (*yathābhyāsa*), cannot be prevented.

If that is so, then even the cognition "this is such-and-such" should arise from the sense faculty alone due to habituation. No; for it is perceived as having a mental nature because of its distinct operation. This operation of the mind is precisely "this is such-and-such," since it is perceived in exactly this way.
How then is it that this mental cognition does not even function with respect to what is imperceptible, such as "that"? This is not tenable;
for that which functions with respect to the imperceptible possesses the mode of direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
"Is it not so? Let it be determined how its status as perception [is established].

(PVA 444) [305,x] The meaning of "perception" (*pratyakṣatā*) is precisely "immediacy" (*sākṣātkāritva*). Why is it that this very [immediacy] exists in some cases as a mental form of immediate apprehension and does not exist in others? [Objection: But why is sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) also sometimes erroneous and sometimes not? [Reply: If you say it is because of the presence of another causal complex (*sāmagryantara*), such as the condition of cataracts (*timira*), then here too there certainly is another causal complex. For:
A cognition born of the sense faculties is a cause that possesses only the object’s own nature and its internal concomitance;
therefore, even when it apprehends something else, it is considered to have a restricted range of objects to be grasped.

The "own object" (*svārtha*) of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) is either its first moment or its continuous stream (*prabandha*). A subsequent moment of the object that follows it produces both sensory and mental cognition (*mānasa*) only in dependence upon that object. However, whatever arises from this causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not non-perceptual (*apratyakṣa*). For this very reason, because its apprehension is restricted, there is no cognition of another object; for it is not produced by another object. If you ask, "Why is it produced by that [specific object] alone and not by another?"—this is the same even regarding sensory cognition. Why is visual cognition (*cakṣurvijñāna*) not produced by sound? If you say, "Because the relationship between cause and effect is restricted," then here too there is no "curse of Brahmā" (i.e., no logical flaw); it is the same elsewhere as well.

[306,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the name ‘Bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive the designation ‘Bodhisattva. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive the designation ‘form. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive the designations ‘feeling,’ ‘perception,’ ‘mental formations,’ or ‘consciousness. He does not perceive the designation ‘perfection of wisdom,’ nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom itself. He does not perceive the designation ‘all-knowledge,’ nor does he perceive all-knowledge itself. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Because he is not attached, he does not tremble; being without fear, he passes beyond all error and attains the ultimate *nirvāṇa*. This is the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of the perfection of wisdom, train in the six perfections? How does he train in the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How does he train in the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of both internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-own-being, and the emptiness of own-being? How does he train in the eighteen emptinesses? How does he train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive the name ‘Bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive the designation ‘Bodhisattva. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive the designation ‘form. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive the designations ‘feeling,’ ‘perception,’ ‘mental formations,’ or ‘consciousness. He does not perceive the designation ‘perfection of wisdom,’ nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom itself. He does not perceive the designation ‘all-knowledge,’ nor does he perceive all-knowledge itself. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Because he is not attached, he does not tremble; being without fear, he passes beyond all error and attains the ultimate *nirvāṇa*. This is the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. “Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he trains in the six perfections by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of both internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-own-being, and the emptiness of own-being by way of non-apprehension. He trains in the eighteen emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, this is how a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through the perfection of wisdom, trains in the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion.”

For an object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not simultaneous with the sensory consciousness (*indriyavijñāna*), because it [the object] precedes that mental consciousness. An object is a cause, and there is no simultaneity between a cause and its effect. For if there were simultaneity with the effect, there would be non-existence prior [to the effect]; and what is non-existent lacks causal capacity (*asāmarthya*) beforehand. If it is argued that "there is causal capacity at the time of the effect," then since the effect already exists at the time of the action [of the cause], such capacity is redundant. Indeed, if that [time of the effect] were the time of the effect, then the effect would already exist; therefore, all causes must exist prior [to the effect]. Consequently, an object is a cause and does not exist simultaneously with the cognition that apprehends it as an effect.

If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be apprehended, those who know the truth and are skilled in reasoning understand its apprehensibility to consist solely in its being a cause capable of imparting its form to the cognition. (248)

[306, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, monks, what is edible food, gross or subtle? It is that which is called "edible food" by the wise in the world. This is what is called edible food, gross or subtle. And what, monks, is contact as the second nutriment? It is the contact associated with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is what is called contact as the second nutriment. And what, monks, is mental volition as the third nutriment? It is the volition associated with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is what is called mental volition as the third nutriment. And what, monks, is consciousness as the fourth nutriment? It is the consciousness associated with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is what is called consciousness as the fourth nutriment. Monks, if there were no edible food, gross or subtle, would bodily form be produced here or would it increase? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for bodily form, namely, edible food. If there were no contact, would feeling be produced here or would it increase? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for feeling, namely, contact. If there were no mental volition, would volitional formations be produced here or would they increase? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for volitional formations, namely, mental volition. If there were no consciousness, would name-and-form be produced here or would it increase? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for name-and-form, namely, consciousness. Furthermore, monks, if there were no edible food, gross or subtle, would craving for the sake of further existence arise in one who seeks a new existence? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for craving for the sake of further existence, namely, edible food. If there were no contact, would craving for the sake of further existence arise in one who seeks a new existence? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for craving for the sake of further existence, namely, contact. If there were no mental volition, would craving for the sake of further existence arise in one who seeks a new existence? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for craving for the sake of further existence, namely, mental volition. If there were no consciousness, would craving for the sake of further existence arise in one who seeks a new existence? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for craving for the sake of further existence, namely, consciousness. Furthermore, monks, if there were no edible food, gross or subtle, would the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, edible food. If there were no contact, would the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, contact. If there were no mental volition, would the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, mental volition. If there were no consciousness, would the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the arising of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, consciousness. Furthermore, monks, if there were no edible food, gross or subtle, would the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, edible food. If there were no contact, would the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, contact. If there were no mental volition, would the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, mental volition. If there were no consciousness, would the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair occur? No, Blessed One. Therefore, monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely, consciousness. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, monks! "Friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friends, the Blessed One taught the Dharma in brief: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Friends, you should train yourselves in this Dharma taught in brief by the Blessed One, and you should dwell reflecting upon it. Is it not the case that being manifest in its own form is what constitutes "graspability" (*grāhyatā*), rather than the production of a cognition possessing that form? And since manifestation occurs simultaneously with the cognition, how can graspability consist solely in causality? What is this so-called "manifestation"? Is it the very nature of the object, or something else entirely? If it were the nature of the object, like blue and so forth, then because that nature never departs from the object, it would follow that the object is always manifest. If you argue that there is no manifestation because of the absence of cognition, we reply: surely that same [nature] must be produced by the cognition, yet since it already exists prior [to the cognition], why was it not manifest before? If you say the cognition is useless, this is another fault of yours alone; it is not the case that the nature of the thing itself was not manifest previously. It is contradictory to say that "it exists" and "it does not exist. If you say that it is seen when cognition is present and not otherwise, then does the cognition have a productive function (*kārakatva*) regarding the manifestation? But it cannot have a productive function because of their simultaneity, as has been established in the discussion beginning with "of that which is non-existent. If it is seen simultaneously [with the cognition] and yet not without the cognition—what can we do about that? In that case, the eye itself would have arisen at that very moment. Therefore, it is not the nature of the object, since it arises now while the object existed previously.
When something has arisen while another thing remains, it perishes while that very thing still persists.
Therefore, let it be considered as something else entirely, since the defining characteristic of difference is present. (445) (PVA)
For the reflection of the face arises within the face;
therefore, let it appear to us as distinct from the face.
(446) [PVA] If the reflection were distinct because of its being in a different location, then...
And that distinction between the face and its reflection is established by means of valid cognition.
(447) No proof for the distinction of the appearance is seen to come from the object itself;
therefore, on account of having the same object, the unity of the appearances of blue and so forth is established. (448)
[307,i] In that case, then:
Just as the appearance [of objects] now arises from the eyes and other sense organs,
so too would it arise from blue and other [objects], because they are equal in their capacity for yoga (i.e., causal efficacy).
Just as the object exists prior to the eyes and other [senses], [so too would it exist prior to the cognition].
"In that case, it would be like the appearance [of an object]; however, this is not observed at all.
For if it were accepted that blue and so forth appear as distinct from the appearance..."
[307,v] Let it be accepted that there is first the appearance of an object such as blue, which possesses existence;
immediately after that, there arises the appearance of the blue and so forth.

Consciousness is the grasper of that [object], just as a father is the grasper of his son’s form. (PVA 452) For when an effect arises imitating [its causes] despite having multiple causes, it is said that the effect is "grasped" because it has been imparted with that very form by those [causes]. (249)

<3. Self-awareness as direct perception> [307,ix] Even pleasure and the like have self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as mental direct perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*). [Objection: If this were so, it would follow that the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not directly perceived; and thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a doctrine in which consciousness is always indirect (*parokṣa*). [Response: No, because the self-awareness of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is direct perception. The mention of pleasure and the like, however, is for the purpose of demonstrating that self-awareness is clearly experienced.

[307,x] But surely, since conceptual cognition lacks non-conceptuality, how can it be perception? For the nature of conceptual cognition is not itself non-conceptual. If it is argued that its status as conceptual pertains only to the object, that is incorrect; for:
If it is argued that [cognition] is conceptual with respect to its object, then it must also be conceptual with respect to its own nature;
for it is not logically possible for it to have any other nature than its own.
To this, he says:
"For the nature of passion and the like cannot be conventionally designated, as it does not belong to anything else."
Therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression.

[307,xiv] The section on the four types of persons. What are the four? They are: the person who has entered the stream (srotāpanna), the person who returns once more (sakṛdāgāmin), the person who does not return (anāgāmin), and the person who has attained parinirvāṇa in this very life (arhat). What is the person who has entered the stream? It refers to one who, having abandoned the three fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa)—has become one who will not fall back and is destined for full enlightenment, with seven births at most remaining. This is called the person who has entered the stream. What is the person who returns once more? It refers to one who, having further attenuated the two fetters of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill-will (vyāpāda), returns to this world only once more to put an end to suffering. This is called the person who returns once more. What is the person who does not return? It refers to one who, having completely abandoned the five lower fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, adherence to rules and rituals, sensual desire, and ill-will—is reborn spontaneously (upapāduka) and attains parinirvāṇa there without returning from that world. This is called the person who does not return. What is the person who has attained parinirvāṇa in this very life? It refers to one who, having abandoned the five higher fetters—namely, craving for form (rūparāga), craving for the formless (ārūpyarāga), restlessness (auddhatya), pride (māna), and ignorance (avidyā)—attains parinirvāṇa in this very life. This is called the person who has attained parinirvāṇa in this very life. These are called the four types of persons. Furthermore, what is the person who has entered the stream?
