At the very moment it arises, pleasure and the like assume the state of being objects for cognitions, because those cognitions do not exist apart from them. And at that time, what occasion is there for the application of designations such as "prior" or "subsequent"? If it is argued that the application occurs later, we say no; because at that [later] time, they are non-existent. For if pleasure and the like were perceived by another [cognition] while still possessing their prior form, then at that time there would be no perception of them at all. Indeed, pleasure and the like do not become known when they are being perceived through a prior form or otherwise, just as one does not perceive the pleasure of another. Therefore, when pleasure and the like are grasped in their present state or with clarity, the apprehension is strictly non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Now, if the view is held that mental pleasure is to be grasped by conceptual apprehension, that too is incorrect, because: [The verse follows: If pleasure and so forth, having attained their own nature, bear the status of objects for cognitions at the very moment of their arising—since there is no cognition of them apart from that [nature]—then what opportunity is there for the application of designations regarding priority and posteriority? If it is claimed that the application occurs subsequently, it is not so, because at that time they are absent. For if they were perceived by another [cognition] while retaining their prior form, then at that time there would be no perception of them at all. Indeed, pleasure and the like do not become known when they are being perceived in a prior form or otherwise, just like the perception of another's pleasure. Therefore, when pleasure and the like are grasped as being present or with clarity, the apprehension is exclusively non-conceptual. Now, if the thought is that mental pleasure is to be grasped by conceptual apprehension, that too is false, because:
[307,xv] If it is argued that because it is not perceived by mindfulness, it must be mental, [we reply:
there is no perception of pleasure therein, because it was already perceived previously. (PVA 454)
At that very moment, when it is directly cognized, there is no conceptual construction [of it];

if you argue that this is because of the association with verbal expression (*abhilāpa*), we say no, for there is no such verbalization. (455) If pleasure were distinct from that [cognition], how could its association be possible?
This is not called a "conjunction" merely because of simultaneity.
(456) (PVA) Even a mental form of color and so forth does not abide within itself;
since it exists only at the very moment of its arising, how could it be the object of a conceptual construction? (457) (PVA)
But how is it reasonable for this [cognition] to possess the nature of conceptualization even with respect to an object?
Because the object is not apprehended by it, its own form is likewise not conceptualized.
What you have said is indeed true:
"If the apprehension of an object is conceptual construction, how can that [construction] exist in this case?"
Now, if there is no apprehension of an object, how can there be conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in this case?

(459) (PVA) Or, if it is defined as being conceptual because of the superimposition of an object upon that [mental image], even there, apart from apprehension and non-apprehension, there is no other object. (460) (PVA)
If it is thought that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) exists when there is both apprehension (*grahaṇa*) and superimposition (*āropa*), [we reply:
since apprehension and superimposition are identical, the occurrence of both is impossible. (461) In that regard, the fault inherent in the single position has already been described previously.
If there were a distinction between the two, it would follow that there are indeed two [cognitions]:
a conceptual cognition and at that very same time, a non-conceptual one.
Therefore:
[308, viii]
Where there is the conceit of grasping, that is called the apprehension of destruction;
for it is precisely this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is observed in our position.
What else could "conceit" (*abhimāna*) be there, other than the grasping or non-grasping [of an object]? (463) (PVA)

If it is argued that [the cognition] possesses the status of an agent with respect to the activity toward the apprehended object, then why is that same capacity to incite activity not present everywhere even when the object is not apprehended? And if the capacity to incite activity exists even when the object is apprehended, then for what reason does one engage in activity at all? (PVA 464–465)
In that case, all cognition would now be conceptual,
since one acts based on every cognition even when its object has not been apprehended.
To this we reply:
xiii] Where there is a form that is not a direct perception, it would involve other conceptual constructions.

In this context, that very conventional usage is what is accepted by the world as conceptual construction. (467) (PVA) Where there is the inclination toward seeing [the object], that cognition is non-conceptual; because it is a resolute conviction through direct perception, it is called "perception. (468) (PVA)
From the ultimate standpoint, however, all cognition is indeed non-conceptual,
because for everyone, its operation regarding its own apprehended object is free from conceptualization. (469) (PVA) [308,xvi]
Furthermore: [308,xvii] By the power of latent impressions (vāsanā) and in accordance with the distinctions of prior cognitions.
Whatever cognition arises anywhere is called *savikalpaka* (conceptual).
It proceeds by assuming dependence upon the reality of the object;
it is called *nirvikalpaka* (non-conceptual) only by way of conventional usage regarding that cognition. (PVA 470–471)
Since pleasure and the like, as well as form, are non-conceptual due to self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*),
their non-conceptual nature is accepted by everyone.
Therefore, their self-awareness is not accompanied by a generic character (*abhijāti*).
In this context, it is not appropriate to speak of it as having the nature of an action.

(PVA 473) Furthermore, when a cognition in the form of an ascertainment (*adhimukti*) arises—such as "this is pleasure" and so forth—with respect to pleasure and the like, appearing in a continuous stream, why is it not conceptual? In this regard, mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) has been described as being like [the perception of] an object. For instance:
When the cognition "this" occurs with respect to an object, a form, pleasure, and so forth,
and when there is direct apprehension of its own nature, all that is accepted as mental [perception]. (PVA 474)
For even in that case, there is no possibility for conceptual construction in any way. Therefore, because it is free from conceptualization, it is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[Objection: Surely, when both [cognitions]—self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and mental [perception] (*mānasa*)—are present together, since they do not touch one another, why is there no cognition of two forms? [Reply: It certainly occurs. However, due to the adherence to a single object, as in the analogy of two people with ophthalmia seeing two moons, such [dual] linguistic usage does not take place. [Objection: Even in that case, why does such linguistic usage not occur if it is self-cognized? [Reply: Because inference functions in that way. For in that case, upon seeing an effect in the form of a universal, there is a linguistic usage of their identity based on the inference of the second [instance] through its oneness with the first. But here, since both are seen, how can there be a linguistic usage of identity? Moreover, there is no inference here. And if it is self-cognized, what is the use of inference? [Objection: Since there is mutual non-cognition, how is the pair cognized? If you say, "There is one person, and for him that pair is cognized," [we reply: No, because there is no person apart from cognition. Nor is there a cognition of the pair by means of those two [individual cognitions]. [Objection: Perhaps the cognition of the two is like the cognition of color and taste. [Reply: Even in that case, how is it so while being self-cognized?
It has been demonstrated through a reductio ad absurdum that this applies even to the cognition of another; therefore, it has been established that self-cognition alone is of a manifold form.

Furthermore, this is stated by relying upon external objects and by accepting the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), everything is merely self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) alone, and there is no distinction between cognitions such as those produced by the sense organs. This is because even the operation of the sense organs is cognized simultaneously, just like visible form (*rūpa*) and other objects. Alternatively, if it is argued that the eyes and so forth possess causality only in terms of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then the same applies to the distinction between mental cognition (*mānasavijñāna*) and sensory cognition (*indriyavijñāna*), which are both equally [self-]cognized.

[Objection: But surely, in this case, there is no conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*). [Response: Even inferential usage is indeed conventional; thus, there is no fault. [Objection: In that case, since even the usage regarding the self (*ātman*) and so forth is merely inferential, it would follow that these too must exist. [Response: No, because in those cases there exists a subverting conventional usage (*bādhaka-vyavahāra*). Therefore, it is established that for pleasure and the like, the self as a specific entity cannot be the object of linguistic convention (*samaya*).
Furthermore, since they do not cognize another, how could they know their own nature in any way?
Some maintain that it is to be known by consciousness which rests upon a single object. (251)
[309,v] Furthermore, even for consciousness, which is supposedly the knower of another, there is no self-awareness; how much less so for pleasure and the like, which are known by others?

[Objection: Surely pleasure and so forth must be self-cognized because they are objects of cognition; otherwise, there would be no cognition at all. [Response: No, because self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is unestablished. If it were cognized by another [cognition], then like a jar and so forth, it would not be self-cognized. [Objection: In that case, it follows that it would be perceived as being in an external location, just like a jar. [Response: No, because it is cognized by a consciousness that is inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*). For jars and the like do not have inherence in the same object as consciousness; therefore, they are cognized as being external and in the form of objects (*grāhya*). Pleasure and so forth, however, are perceived non-differently from consciousness; having attained a form similar to consciousness, they are cognized as being situated within as the aspect of the subject (*grāhakākāra*). Thus, the consequence of being like a jar does not apply, according to some. Regarding them:
Entities that possess a certain nature or its opposite are produced from causes that possess that nature or its opposite.
Therefore, why is pleasure and so forth not cognition, since they are produced from causes non-different from those of cognition? (252)
This [object] is certainly not established for you by perception alone;
its cognition through inference is not admitted without a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Indeed, pleasure and the like are not perceived as distinct from consciousness, because it is impossible for them to coexist in the same substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) while being contradictory [to its nature]. Furthermore, inference does not operate without a logical mark (*liṅga*). There might be a logical mark here if a difference in causes could be demonstrated; for that which is imperceptible cannot be understood without inference. You must understand the distinction through a difference in causes, since a difference in effects necessarily follows from a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). However, a difference in effects does not prove a difference [in the cause], because we observe a difference in effects even from a single cause, as in the case of ash and smoke. Moreover, no difference in effects is perceived that would establish a difference between pleasure and the like and consciousness. Therefore, only a difference in causes should be pointed out, and yet that does not exist. Why? Because when something is perceived as having an identical cause and an identical form, what proof is there that it is designated as "distinct"? This is the point.

Alternatively, if consciousness (*vijñāna*) were distinct from pleasure and the other [feelings], what would be the cause of pleasure and the rest for that consciousness? [If you say] "the eye, visible form, and mental attention," then pleasure and the rest would indeed arise from those causes of consciousness, such as the eye and so forth. And in that case, why is that [feeling] not experienced by the consciousness, just as [consciousness itself is]? If you argue that it does not exist at all, we say no; since it arises with consciousness as its cause, how can it be unperceivable? If you ask, "Why is this not the case in your own position as well? we say no; because in our view, the specific awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) is the cause. By the power of the distinction in the awakening of these predispositions, consciousness sometimes takes the form of pleasure, sometimes the form of pain, or otherwise; thus, there is no logical inconsistency. [The author] demonstrates that the causes are indeed the same:

When the object is present, the sense faculty is suitable, and the respective mind is also present, the arising of pleasure and so forth is observed; that is likewise the case for mental cognitions as well. (253)

[310,ii] There is no occasion for the seeing of form without the eye, nor without a form that captivates the mind, nor when the mind is impaired by grief and the like. This very same causal complex (sāmagrī) is also required for the arising of consciousness; therefore, a difference in the cause is not what makes the difference known. Nor is it logical that pleasure produced from the causal complex of form and so forth, in the conjunction of the self and the mind, should be devoid of consciousness. If, on the other hand, pleasure had not arisen at all at that time, then being necessarily non-existent, it would be unconscious. For that which is non-existent cannot be apprehended. To this, it is replied: [310,iii]

Whether these [causes] exist or do not exist, neither birth nor non-birth is ever observed anywhere for pleasure and the like, or for cognition; therefore, those [pleasures and cognitions] are not distinct from that [mind]. (254)

Furthermore, it is certainly not the case that pleasure and so forth arise only when the eye, visible forms, light, and attention are present, such that one would have to postulate a cause for pleasure and so forth other than consciousness. Therefore, the very cause of consciousness is itself the cause of pleasure and so forth. If it were argued that there is both that [consciousness] and something else which is the cause of pleasure and so forth—namely, merit (*dharma*) and so on, or demerit (*adharma*) and so on—that too is not the case. Why? Because even when the eye and other factors are present, the non-arising [of pleasure] is not observed; thus, there is no room for the postulation of another cause based on the exclusion of the effect.

Now, even in the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), merit (*dharma*) and so forth are indeed causes; for what is desired is pleasure and what is undesired is pain, and in that regard, the causality of merit and demerit (*adharma*) is necessary. This is established as being well-known to all proponents of philosophical systems, with the sole exception of the Cārvākas. That too is incorrect:
The efficacy of merit and the other factors is not established through the absence of negative concomitance (*avyatirekataḥ*).
The capacity of *dharma* and so forth is restricted to pleasure and the like; it does not establish what is desired [in itself].

(PVA 476) For *dharma* and the rest depend equally upon the means for achieving pleasure and so forth, and not upon pleasure and the like themselves. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of pleasure arising even without its means. Now, it might be argued: "Even when forms and other objects—which are the means for pleasure or pain—are present, pleasure arises through the power of internal causes when one is afflicted by grief and the like. Therefore, it is understood that *dharma* alone is the cause, and not form and the rest. This is illogical, because:
When the collection of conditions such as grief is presented by unrighteousness (*adharma*) itself, the suffering that arises from it does not have unrighteousness as its cause. (477) (PVA)
[310,ix] Let the very collection of grief and so forth, brought about by unrighteousness (*adharma*), be the cause of that suffering; let its suffering arise by itself.

Alternatively, let it be that pleasure arises from dharma and pain from something else; even so, why must a distinct cognition be produced by that [pleasure]? For even if pleasure is produced as non-different from the cognition, nothing has been assisted by your dharma. Indeed, you have a need for pleasure and the like, yet even though it is non-different from cognition, it does not become unpleasant. If it is argued that there is a distinction due to a difference in causes, that too is incorrect;
because: [310,xi] There is indeed a distinction between the cognition of pleasure and pure consciousness.
But that absolute difference which is asserted is not established by this much alone.

(PVA 478) For it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) together with its properties (*dharma*) that produces that very same specific effect, and not something entirely distinct. This is because the distinction belongs to that very complex through an additional contribution. Indeed, when there is moist fuel, smoke is not over and above the ash; for smoke is not absolutely distinct from the ash, since the darkening and soiling inherent in smoke is possible there as well. Therefore, one cannot determine a capacity for producing an absolute separation from the properties and so forth. For this very reason, he says:
[310, xiii] Furthermore, the distinctions among those very [cognitions], such as pleasure and pain, arise specifically from the particularities of that same [consciousness],
just as dullness and acuity belong to cognition itself. || 255 ||

[310,xiv] If consciousness, pleasure, and so forth have the same causes, let it be simply that "consciousness" is "consciousness"; how then can there be a distinction between pleasure and the rest? Because there is no difference in that very causal complex (*sāmagrī*). It is like the causal complex of a seed and so forth when watered with milk and such. For indeed, [311,i]...

Even when there is an abundance of irrigation with milk and other substances, the *dhātrī* plant produces an effect that is indeed distinct from the seed; however, it does so without overstepping its own nature, being instead governed by other specific conditions. Now, why does it not produce something entirely different? It is not the case that it does not; rather, one must say that it produces only what is distinct [from the seed]. In this way, the distinction [of the effect] is established through the distinction of the cause, provided that it is proven that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces a distinct effect.

Furthermore, qualities such as wisdom (*prajñā*) also possess origination from the very beginning; therefore, it follows that they too must be distinct from cognition (*buddhi*). If it is argued that wisdom and so forth arise from practice and the like, rather than from merit (*dharma*) and so forth, then pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest would likewise arise from the practice of what is desirable or undesirable, and thus merit would not be their cause. If it is claimed that the proximity of the desirable and so forth is due to merit, then pleasure and the rest do not originate from merit at all, but rather from unimpaired mental attention (*manaskāra*) and the like. And since that unimpaired state of mental attention and so forth is also a cause for cognition, pleasure and the rest are not produced by a causal complex distinct from that of cognition.

[311,iii] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Wisdom and the other faculties do not have pleasure and so forth as their causes, nor do they have dharma and so forth as their causes, because wisdom exists [independently]. Therefore, that which is pleasure is itself caused by dharma and so forth; thus, the fact that pleasure and the others are of the same nature is unestablished. This too is not well-said, because:
"Discrimination and the rest do not arise from objects such as dharmas, but rather these arise from pleasure and the like"—
how can this be established by means of valid cognition for those such as yourself?

For that which is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—merely the illumination of one's own system and its intended purpose—is not sufficient to satisfy others. Nor do wisdom and the other [faculties] arise from anything other than *dharma*. If it is argued that they are seen even without *dharma* through practice (*abhyāsa*), we say no; for without *dharma*, that very practice cannot be complete. If it is argued that its incompleteness is due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), then the same must apply to pleasure and so forth, as their occurrence also arises solely from a particularity of the mental continuum (*santāna-viśeṣa*). To illustrate: pleasure exists naturally when there is freedom from distress, which is the cause of all calamities.
[It arises] precisely from an excellence of the mental continuum, due to the activation of prior practice.

(PVA 480) [311, vii] Pleasure [arises] precisely from an excellence of its own nature, because it is activated by prior practice; for even those of bad conduct who lack [virtue] are seen [to experience it], and because there is an absence of one who perceives equanimity even when dharma exists. If it is argued that it arises from dharma and so forth alone, with the assistance of the opposite of the practice of cultivating equanimity—then in that case, dharma has no efficacy, because [pleasure] is preceded by practice, just like wisdom (*prajñā*) and the rest. Furthermore, pleasure and the other [feelings] are essentially of the nature of cognition (*bodharūpa*).

[311, viii] But is it not the case that pleasure and so forth arise from objects and other such causes, whereas cognitions arise from a formation called "cultivation" which has cognition as its cause? Thus, there is a difference in their causes. For instance:
"This is that which I saw previously, arising from past impressions"—
is such a cognition of that form present in pleasure and the like?

That is incorrect. For this [cultivation] is also the cause of pleasure and so forth; for it has already been established that even pleasure and the like arise solely by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Now, it might be argued: "Pleasure and the like are purely mental (*mānasa*) and arise from latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*), not from the sense organs. If that were so, then mental consciousness itself would likewise arise from latent dispositions, and thus the case would be the same. Furthermore, even for sense-produced consciousness, specific qualities such as acuity arise precisely from specific instances of cultivation. Therefore, even for pleasure and the like produced by the senses, their acuity and so forth derive from that very source; thus, the situation is identical.
Furthermore, it has been established that all pleasure and so forth are exclusively mental.

Is it not the case that when some object has been apprehended, proficiency is logical because of the repeated arising of cognition regarding that very same object through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? If pleasure and the like are also apprehended by this cognition, then it is logical that their apprehension becomes proficient. But in the view of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what kind of mental cultivation could there be? For instance: If self-awareness has already arisen, what kind of mental cultivation could there be therein?

If self-awareness has not arisen, what kind of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) could there be in that case? (PVA 482) [312, i] Since one distinct experience of pleasure arises after another, there is no connection of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). However, if that very same thing is perceived again and again, then the designation "practice" applies. But in the case of an object, since it is a single entity, cultivation would consist in its being experienced by successive cognitions.

[312,ii] But surely, why could even pleasure not be one? And what, moreover, is the meaning of "repeatedly" (*punaḥ-punaḥ*) for a single thing? Even if the object is a single entity, repetition is produced by the recurrence of experience. That too is incorrect.
If there is a distinction between cognition and its objects, from what source does it arise?
If it is due to the grace of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), why is this not the case for pleasure and so forth as well?

But surely pleasure is not one; how then can there be recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) therein? In the case of an object, however, recognition is appropriate because of its oneness, even though the cognitions are distinct. But is it not the case that recognition pertains to the object, whereas [the term] "perception" (*upalambha*) pertains to the cognition? And since there is no single perception when the cognitions are distinct, how could there be recognition in respect to the cognition? In reality, there is no recognition there.

Now, having superimposed that unity upon it by means of its oneness, it is conventionally designated as "one cognition. Here, this is investigated: Is this position stated as being self-cognizing knowledge (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*), or is it cognizable by another cognition, or cognizable through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*)? What follows from this? If one relies on self-cognition, how could there be recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)?

For there can be no delusion of unity at that very time through the distinction of what is being perceived. (PVA 484) Indeed, on the view of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), when the perception of difference is perfectly clear, how could there be a delusion of superimposition caused by that [difference] at that same time, even though the objects are not distinct? This is the same even in the case of cognition by another cognition. However, in the case of cognition through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*), the conceptualization of the cognition conforms to the object; therefore, the cognition itself must be conceived as non-different. If one argues that presumptive proof consists in the fact that "otherwise it would not be possible," [the reply is: [The text continues: ...[the opponent might say: "If it were otherwise, it would not be established. The object consists of nothing but sensation, and it is produced by the mere construction of sensation.
Since a single object cannot be grasped by multiple [cognitions], let it be postulated as one. (PVA 485)

[312,x] For it is not possible to conceive that a single object exists across preceding and succeeding times by means of multiple cognitions occurring at different times, each determining its own temporal object; this is because a single [cognition] lacks such pervasive activity, and a collection [of cognitions] does not exist.
The self alone is the synthesizer, because remembrance is possible for it;
for its capacity exists both in remembrance and in synthesis.
This is incorrect:
under the view that the self has the nature of consciousness, this is not seen to be logical.
How can the recurrence of this [object], which is of a single form, be endowed with validity?

(PVA 487) If it is argued that there is no fault in the position that its nature is both different and non-different: [we reply that] there is no recognition in the form by which it is non-different, because it is differentiated by the differentiation of cognitions. If cognition were non-different, then for that which is non-different from it, differentiation would not exist. However, in the form by which it is different from cognition, there is unity; therefore, there is no recurrence.

[312,xv] Now, if the self were of a non-cognitive nature, then it would not be cognized by cognition; and since that [self] is distinct [from cognition], how could there be a grasping of their non-difference? Therefore, the apprehension of unity through the distinction of cognitions is logical only if one cognition is postulated as a single entity by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Now, if the distinction between cognitions is apprehended through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), even so, unity is not perceived within consciousness; therefore, how can there be recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? If it is argued that recognition occurs for that whose diversity is unobserved, then this would apply to pleasure and the like as well. Since their unity is possible conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), there is repeated experience of those very things; thus, through habituation (*abhyāsa*), there arises the specific intensity and other qualities of pleasure and the like. Furthermore, the arising of pleasure and the like from habituation consists precisely of their nature as cognitions (*bodharūpa*).

[312,xviii] But surely, through practice, even walking and other such actions take on forms such as those of a leaping tiger (*vikaṭa*), and yet they are not of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*). To this it is replied:
From the practice of that which is of the nature of non-awareness, only non-awareness arises.
Likewise, from the practice of that which is of the nature of awareness, why should the arising of the nature of awareness not occur?

It is just like [the case of] wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth. [313,i] Now, it might be argued: "What is this 'practice of the nature of cognition' (*bodharūpābhyāsa*)? Is it the practice of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), or is it the practice of the object grasped by the nature of cognition? If it is the practice of self-cognition, that self-cognition is unestablished. If it is the second position, it is indeed untenable because of the possibility of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). For even when there is the practice of movement grasped by the nature of cognition, the nature of cognition is not perceived in the movement and so forth. To this, it is said:
Whatever is practiced as it truly is, that very thing is intensified accordingly;
thus, the practice of internal awareness of pleasure and so forth has a corresponding result. (PVA 489)

[313,iii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. [313,iv] It was said: “There are these four nutriments. In what sense were they said? They were said in the sense of cause. For nutriment is the cause of beings who have already come to be, and it is the cause of those seeking a new existence. How so? Edible food is the cause for the maintenance of this body, and it is the cause for the production of future aggregates. Contact is the cause for the maintenance of the faculties, and it is the cause for the production of future feeling. Mental volition is the cause for the production of future existence. Consciousness is the cause for the production of future name-and-form. Therefore, it was said: “There are these four nutriments. [313,v] It was said: “Edible food, coarse or subtle. What is edible food? It is of three kinds: physical food taken by the mouthful, contact, and mental volition. Among these, physical food taken by the mouthful is the nutriment for beings in the desire realm. Contact is the nutriment for beings in the form realm. Mental volition is the nutriment for beings in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Furthermore, all three are nutriments for beings in the desire realm. However, physical food taken by the mouthful is the primary one. Why? Because it is the most gross and because it is the basis for the other two. [313,vi] It was said: “Contact. What is contact? It is the conjunction of the three—sense faculty, object, and consciousness. It is the cause for the arising of feeling. [313,vii] It was said: “Mental volition. What is mental volition? It is the volitional activity of the mind. It is the cause for the production of future existence. [313,viii] It was said: “Consciousness. What is consciousness? It is the sixfold consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. It is the cause for the production of future name-and-form. Thus, these four nutriments sustain beings who have already come to be and support those seeking a new existence. [313,ix] Furthermore, these four nutriments are to be abandoned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Among them, edible food is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation. Contact and mental volition are to be abandoned by both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation. Consciousness is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation. Thus, through the abandonment of these nutriments, one attains the cessation of suffering. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,x] Furthermore, these four nutriments are included within the twelve links of dependent origination. Edible food is included within the link of existence. Contact is included within the links of ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling. Mental volition is included within the link of formations. Consciousness is included within the link of consciousness. Thus, by understanding the nature of these nutriments, one understands dependent origination. By understanding dependent origination, one understands the Dharma. By understanding the Dharma, one attains liberation. This is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. [313,xi] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the basis for the arising of craving. When there is craving, there is grasping. When there is grasping, there is becoming. When there is becoming, there is birth. When there is birth, there is old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. Therefore, the wise practitioner, understanding the danger in these nutriments, should cultivate detachment, should cultivate dispassion, and should attain liberation. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xii] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the field for the growth of the seeds of karma. Karma is the seed. Ignorance is the moisture. Craving is the fertilizer. From these conditions, the sprout of future existence arises. Therefore, the wise practitioner should uproot the seeds of karma, dry up the moisture of ignorance, and destroy the fertilizer of craving. Having done so, one cuts off the continuity of future existence and attains the state of peace. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xiii] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the support for the five aggregates. The aggregate of form is supported by edible food. The aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are supported by contact, mental volition, and consciousness respectively. Since these aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, the wise practitioner should not delight in them, should not take pleasure in them, and should not dwell in attachment to them. Rather, they should cultivate the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception of renunciation. Through such practice, they will transcend birth, old age, sickness, and death, and will realize the unsurpassed bliss of Nirvana. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xiv] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the basis for the arising of the three types of sensation. Edible food gives rise to the sensation of pleasure. Contact gives rise to the sensation of pain. Mental volition gives rise to the sensation of equanimity. Consciousness gives rise to all three sensations. Therefore, the wise practitioner, observing the arising and passing away of these sensations, should not be led astray by them. They should understand that all sensations are empty, signless, and wishless. Having understood this, they should abide in the concentration on emptiness, the concentration on signlessness, and the concentration on wishlessness. Abiding thus, they will attain the fruit of Arhatship and enter Parinirvana. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xv] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the basis for the arising of the three poisons. Edible food nourishes the poison of greed. Contact nourishes the poison of hatred. Mental volition nourishes the poison of delusion. Consciousness nourishes all three poisons. Therefore, the wise practitioner should apply the antidote of the three trainings: the training in higher morality to counteract the poison of greed, the training in higher concentration to counteract the poison of hatred, and the training in higher wisdom to counteract the poison of delusion. By applying these antidotes, they will extinguish the three poisons and attain the state of purity. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xvi] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the basis for the arising of the four perversions. Edible food is perceived as pure; this is the perversion of purity. Contact is perceived as pleasant; this is the perversion of happiness. Mental volition is perceived as self; this is the perversion of self. Consciousness is perceived as eternal; this is the perversion of permanence. Therefore, the wise practitioner should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness to abandon these perversions: mindfulness of the body to abandon the perversion of purity, mindfulness of feelings to abandon the perversion of happiness, mindfulness of the mind to abandon the perversion of self, and mindfulness of phenomena to abandon the perversion of permanence. Having abandoned these perversions, they will realize the true nature of reality. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xvii] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the basis for the arising of the five hindrances. Edible food increases the hindrance of sensual desire. Contact increases the hindrance of ill-will. Mental volition increases the hindrance of restlessness and remorse. Consciousness increases the hindrances of sloth and torpor and doubt. Therefore, the wise practitioner should cultivate the five spiritual faculties to overcome these hindrances: the faculty of faith to overcome doubt, the faculty of energy to overcome sloth and torpor, the faculty of mindfulness to overcome ill-will, the faculty of concentration to overcome restlessness and remorse, and the faculty of wisdom to overcome sensual desire. Having overcome these hindrances, they will attain the first dhyāna and progress through the stages of meditation until they reach the cessation of perception and feeling. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. [313,xviii] Furthermore, these four nutriments are the basis for the arising of the six internal and external sense bases. Edible food is the basis for the eye-base and the form-base. Contact is the basis for the ear-base and the sound-base, the nose-base and the odor-base, the tongue-base and the taste-base, the body-base and the tangible-base, and the mind-base and the mental-object-base. Therefore, the wise practitioner should observe the six sense bases as empty and devoid of self. Observing them thus, they will not be bound by the fetters of attachment. Being unbound, they will cross over the ocean of sa

For pleasure and the like are perceived as having the nature of internal awareness (*saṃvedana*). That they, being insentient in nature, are nevertheless perceived through inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) is merely a satisfaction derived from the attainment of awareness. Therefore, one practices that very nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Consequently, through the practice of the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it would manifest in exactly that form. [Objection: In that case, there would initially be an absence of self-awareness. [Reply: No; because by the words "of whatever kind," etc., even that [initial state] is of such a nature. Therefore, it is established that those things arising through the power of cultivation, like wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth, have awareness as their very essence.
By this, the following point as well is refuted.
Entities possessing that or another form are produced from causes possessing that or another form;
how then can that which has such a form be ignorance, given that it arises from causes non-different from those of consciousness? (252)

This is its meaning: by virtue of mutual cooperation, the eye, mental attention, and objects such as a cart standing before one—arising from a common causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—would all either be of the nature of cognition (*bodha-rūpa*) or not of the nature of cognition. For in that case, there is no distinction between what is primary and what is secondary. Indeed, that causal complex of form and so forth has been observed to have the power to produce multiple effects, both cognitive and non-cognitive; it cannot be established otherwise. If it is argued that for this very reason the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), we say no, because the intended meaning of the reason is different.
Just as wisdom and other such qualities arise from cultivation, so too do pleasure and the like; why then, for what reason, are they not self-cognizing?

The meaning of the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that whatever is practiced in a certain way becomes exactly so. However, it is impossible for form (*rūpa*) and other such qualities to be practiced as having an internal nature (*āntarasvabhāva*). As for one who holds that specific excellences of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth are to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), how can he understand that they are inherent in the self (*ātmasamavāyin*)? Presumptive testimony merely allows one to infer that which, without something else, would otherwise be inexplicable. Yet, there is nothing that is inexplicable except insofar as it lacks the nature of cognition (*abodharūpatā*) and lacks inherence in a self. There must simply be some other [factor] by virtue of which the object becomes imperceptible (*parokṣatā*). Therefore, how can there be an understanding of inherence in a self and so forth? Consequently, the resolution is this: people have practiced the very internality of cognition—thinking "this has been understood by me"—by which the perception of internality arises.

[313,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend that form is permanent or impermanent; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is permanent or impermanent. He does not apprehend that form is ease or suffering; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is ease or suffering. He does not apprehend that form is self or non-self; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is self or non-self. He does not apprehend that form is peaceful or unpeaceful; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is peaceful or unpeaceful. He does not apprehend that form is empty or non-empty; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is empty or non-empty. He does not apprehend that form is with signs or signless; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is with signs or signless. He does not apprehend that form is wishful or wishless; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is wishful or wishless. He does not apprehend that form is conditioned or unconditioned; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is conditioned or unconditioned. He does not apprehend that form is defiled or undefiled; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is defiled or undefiled. He does not apprehend that form is with outflows or without outflows; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is with outflows or without outflows. He does not apprehend that form is mundane or supramundane; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is mundane or supramundane. He does not apprehend that form is common or uncommon; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is common or uncommon. He does not apprehend that form is cognizable by the eye or not cognizable by the eye; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is cognizable by the eye or not cognizable by the eye. He does not apprehend that form is cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, or not cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, or not cognizable by the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. He does not apprehend that form is past, future, or present; he does not apprehend that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is past, future, or present. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend anything whatsoever.”

Even for those who describe another cognition as being perceptible within [the first] cognition, it must necessarily be admitted that this [perceptibility] appears as something inherent in the self (*ātman*) and consisting of the nature of awareness (*bodharūpa*). Otherwise, it would simply be a distinct entity. However, its status as a grasper (*grāhaka*) is well-established. Therefore, in another perception, it appears as having the grasper-nature superimposed upon it. And this being the case, that object also appears therein. But how can there be an appearance of what has perished? How could a solitary cognition, while appearing, appear as either a grasper or as the grasped? If one objects that the same applies to the self (*ātman*) and so forth, the resolution would be that the superimposition of inherence in the self arises from beginningless time. And this being so, wisdom (*prajñā*) and the like, or even pleasure (*sukha*) and the like, which arise through the force of such cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are indeed of the nature of awareness itself.

[314,i] But even so, do not others maintain that cognition and the like do not possess the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)? Indeed, it has been established that even if they were not self-aware, they would lack both perceptibility and internality. However, if they are self-aware, then it is logical that this very [cognition] illuminates itself in such a manner and also illuminates the object.

Furthermore, even by the force of cultivation, pleasure and the like, though arising and perishing, exist as inherent in the self and are apprehended by a cognition that is inherent in the same object.
Through contact with that cognition, they appear in the form of consciousness.
But why is it not imagined that [the self exists] by way of its nature as consciousness?
To this, it is said: [491] (PVA) [314,iv] [Response: It is said here:
Because this state of affairs— namely, "it is thus"— is established through beginningless cultivation and so forth,
a conceptual construction of a different process is not introduced by the world. (PVA 492)

It is established that this arises through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); no further process is perceived therein, such as "it arises in this way" or "in that way. Rather, the conventional usage is simply that "this is exactly as it is seen" due to the power of cultivation. Furthermore, what is the purpose of postulating a "conjunction with a single substance" (*ekārthasamavāya*)? If conjunction with a self (*ātman*) is not accepted, then to whom does that pleasure belong? Likewise, if its conjunction elsewhere is not admitted, then to whom does that self belong?
If the self were independent because of its eternity, how could it possibly be dependent on another?
However, since pleasure and the like are impermanent, the assumption of their dependence on another is logical.

It is indeed logical that the self (*ātman*), by virtue of its permanence, ought to be independent and unconditioned; however, pleasure and the like are qualities (*guṇa*) and are impermanent, and therefore they must necessarily exist as dependent. This is incorrect, because:
If there were dependence, there would be the state of being a quality; or if there were the state of being a quality, there would be dependence upon a substratum.
Thus, due to mutual dependence, there would be no establishment of either one.

(PVA 314, xi) If the quality-ness were first established, then the conceptualization that it must be supported by a substance would arise. But that is not established, because its establishment depends on something else. It has already been demonstrated that there is no relationship of support and supported for anything whatsoever.
[314,xii] Although it has been stated that the self is independent because of its permanence, whereas pleasure and so forth are not, for the opposite is the case; yet—
Even that which is impermanent, because it arises from causes, is independent; since it has no "thing-to-be-done" (*kartavyatā*), how could there be dependence on another? (495) (PVA)

[314,xiv] If that [entity] has not arisen at all, how can it have dependence on another? If, on the other hand, it has arisen from some cause, then what kind of dependence on another does it possess? If you say that its dependence on another consists in its production of its own effect, we reply: since the production of the effect belongs to it solely by virtue of its own cause, there is no possibility of dependence on something else. Enough of this digression. [314,xv]
Therefore, let pleasure and the rest be independent; what is the use of postulating a substratum in the form of a self?

Furthermore, if pleasure and the rest were not self-cognized (*asvasamvedana*), how could they possess the capacity to apprehend objects? If it is argued that this will occur through a cognition that is a co-inherent cause (*ekārthasamavāyin*) with them, we reply: are they cognized by a sense-produced cognition that is co-inherent with them, or by another? First of all, they are not cognized by a sense-cognition. Why? Because:

[314,xvii] Since those cognitions, such as pleasure and so forth, arise through the occurrence of a certain object, how could that cognition apprehend pleasure and so forth alone, while excluding that object? 256.

[315,i] How can that very sensory cognition, which is directed toward form and so forth, apprehend pleasure and the like—given that it is engaged with form and the rest by means of the eye and other faculties? For there is no such cognition as "the eye is mine" when it is active toward pleasure. If it is argued that the consciousness which apprehends pleasure will operate while already engaged with form itself, then, if that were the case, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would follow, as has already been demonstrated; furthermore, it would entail the consequence that even inference would be visual.

Now, since no other form of a grasper (*grāhakākāra*) is perceived apart from the sensory cognition itself, it is said that [the object] is grasped by that very [cognition]. In that case, it follows that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), occurring at the same time as the sensory consciousness, would also be grasped by that very [sensory consciousness]. This has already been pointed out as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding the object of inference (*anumeya*), for no other form of a grasper is perceived there either. If you argue that the form of the grasper is thus postulated [only] because of the form of the graspable (*grāhyākāra*), this applies equally to the word that is to be conceptualized. If it is asked: "Why is the form of a grasper not postulated even in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth?"—[we reply: No, because they are experienced as being graspable objects. For it cannot be said that something lacks the status of a graspable object simply because it is not grasped by another act of grasping, even when it is inherent in the same substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*). If it is argued that [pleasure and its cognition] are apprehended as a single fused mass (*ekalolībhāva*), then that [fused mass] must be either the nature of the pleasure or the nature of the cognition. Since even a single entity is not grasped in its own distinct form [in that state], there is only the experience of the form of pleasure. If it is argued that for the other [the cognition], which is not itself experienced, there is an absence of pleasure, [we reply: No, because it is not perceived that [the pleasure] is conditioned by something else, just like the perception of the form of a cluster of trees. If it is argued that the fact of being conditioned by something else is established through inference—that whatever is perceived is conditioned by something else, like the cluster—[we reply: No, because this would entail the non-existence of external objects, since it is possible for [the appearance] to be conditioned by mental impressions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, whatever is perceived in a certain way must be accepted exactly as it is; it should not be established otherwise by means of inference. Consequently, an external object, being perceived as a graspable object in its own form, is established as such, because establishing [something] is necessarily bound to its perception. Pleasure and the like, however, are not experienced as graspable objects; therefore, they are self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*).

[315,iii] Now, if cognition produced merely from the conjunction of the self and the mind is the grasper of pleasure and so forth, and not sensory cognition—then, since cognitions do not arise simultaneously, there must be a sequential apprehension. And therefore:
If there were a grasping of succession, that cognition would not appear as uninterrupted.

For if the grasping of succession is admitted, the cognition of pleasure and so forth would not manifest as an unbroken stream. Indeed, this very succession is what is called "non-simultaneity. Yet, the apprehension of pleasure and so forth is observed to occur simultaneously with the apprehension of form and other objects. In that case, "simultaneous apprehension" is a contradiction; for two contradictory things cannot exist in the same place.
If it is argued that this is due to its extreme rapidity, then why is there no awareness of it being equal to that? (257)

[315,vii] If the perception of pleasure is understood as an uninterrupted cognition due to its rapid occurrence, then that very rapidity applies equally to the non-perception of pleasure and so forth; thus, it follows that the non-perception of the two forms of pleasure would itself appear as uninterrupted. Or, perhaps even the non-perception appears as uninterrupted. For:
[315,viii]
For there is no apprehension of pleasure other than the apprehension of form;
nor is there any apprehension of form other than the apprehension of pleasure.

And thus, the meaning of "there would be an uninterrupted non-apprehension of the pleasant face" is that there is an uninterrupted apprehension of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. This being the case, it must likewise be stated regarding the opposite [case]. Therefore, this [argument] is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for why would there not be non-apprehension? To this it is replied:
The existence of one thing is defined as the non-existence of another.
Because that non-existence is conceived through its being distinct from that [object].

(PVA 497) For this non-existence does not belong to anything by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), but rather by way of its being distinct from that [object]. Consequently, if one accepts that the apprehension of form is perceived as distinct from the apprehension of pleasure, then the apprehension of what is distinct from it occurs with ease; thus, since the non-interruption of that [apprehension] is possible, how could there be the cognition of pleasure? Since the same sequence applies to the cognition of pleasure as well, there would be no apprehension of either.

[316,i] It has been well said: "Why is it not simply non-apprehension? For even when one thing is perceived, there is no apprehension of another as distinct from it. If it is argued that this is because the apprehension of it as distinct [from the other] is itself the nature of that [other], since its own essence does not enter into it—[we reply: No. Because even if there is an apprehension in which the essences of two things do not enter into each other, a simultaneous apprehension is possible; for it is accepted that the parts and the whole are apprehended at the same time. [316,ii]

[Objection: But surely, when one perceives several hairs at a distance with intervals between them, even though the intervals are not perceived, the form of the hair itself is indeed not perceived. In that case, just as the perception of the continuous form of the hair sublates the non-perception of the intervals, so too the non-perception of the intervals does not sublate the perception of the hair. Likewise here, non-perception cannot be a sublater of the perception of the interval. [Reply: To this it is said: How could the perception of the interval therein be real, such that it would act as a sublater? *antaragrahaṇantatra naiva sadbādhakaṃ katham //*316,iii//*]
The world does not desire even a proximate object that causes suffering; it desires only what is desired.
[498] (PVA) [316, iv] If it is asked: why is there no apprehension of an intermediate state?
This very capacity belongs to entities; why should it be questioned?
Therefore, the non-apprehension of internal objects when they have not yet arisen does not constitute a refutation. (PVA 499)

Nor is it sublated; rather, it is merely that a certain designation has become established in common worldly usage in some way or another. However, in this case, it is not logical to say that while there is the grasping of the form of pleasure and so forth, the grasping [of the sequence] has not arisen. For if that were so, the possibility of grasping a sequence would not exist. If you argue that there certainly is non-grasping there, but that another grasping has simply not arisen, this is not the case.
In the act of grasping, there is no grasper; in the grasper, there is no further grasper. Others also accept this very point; otherwise, it would be incoherent. (PVA 500) [316, viii]

For apprehension must be self-luminous by nature; however, for the apprehender—which is either a causal entity or an agent—one would have to postulate another apprehender. If apprehension were non-luminous, it would follow that no objects whatsoever could be apprehended. If it is argued: "But apprehension is self-luminous, whether it arises from the sense organs or from something else; so what need is there for another apprehender?"—this is yet another fault of that very position. For there is no such thing as an apprehension that is itself non-luminous. If it is claimed that it is made luminous by another, then surely the illumination by that other is also imperceptible (*parokṣa*), and that too would require another, leading to the consequence that the entire world would be reduced to mere potentiality (*arthatā*). This will be demonstrated later. Furthermore, how can that which appears as distinct in terms of mutual temporal sequence, having arisen [simultaneously], not be a sublater of the other? This is quite trivial. Now, if it is argued that the apprehension of pleasure is indeed sublated at times because only color and so forth are apprehended—just as when seeing a captivating form, there is sometimes no experience of pleasure, and thus the apprehension of pleasure is established as being sublated because the apprehension of other objects has arisen—this is not correct either. Why? Because: [The following verse follows: "Because even when the apprehension of color and so forth is present, pleasure is experienced; therefore, the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects. (PV 3.246) Even when the apprehension of color and so forth is occurring, pleasure is experienced. Therefore, the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects. It is not the case that pleasure is never experienced when one sees a beautiful form; rather, it is simply that it is not perceived at that time due to the influence of other conditions. Thus, the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects. Nor is it the case that the apprehension of color and so forth is always sublated by the apprehension of pleasure. For even when pleasure is being experienced, color and so forth are clearly perceived. Therefore, since both are perceived simultaneously, they cannot be mutually sublaters. Furthermore, if it were the case that the apprehension of color and so forth were sublated by the apprehension of pleasure, then one would never perceive color and so forth while experiencing pleasure. But this is not observed. Consequently, the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects. And since the apprehension of color and so forth is not sublated by the apprehension of pleasure, the two are not mutually sublaters. Thus, it is established that the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects.
