And since the apprehension of color and so forth is not sublated by the apprehension of pleasure, the two are not mutually sublaters. Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects. And since the apprehension of color and so forth is not sublated by the apprehension of pleasure, the two are not mutually sublaters. Thus, it is established that the apprehension of pleasure is not sublated by the apprehension of other objects. And since the apprehension of color and so forth is not sublated by the apprehension of pleasure, the two are not mutually sublaters. Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of pleasure

[316,ix] Or rather, why is there no contradiction at all? Just as in the case of one who perceives other hairs, at that time the arising of pleasure and so forth is not accepted by the world. (PVA) 501

Just as the perception of [illusory] hair always subverts the perception of what lies between them, so too would the perception of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth subvert the perception of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. Yet, in ultimate reality, that perception of hair does not exist, because the true nature of the hair is not apprehended. When there is no apprehension of pleasure during the mere perception of color-form and so on, it follows that pleasure itself has not arisen; it is not established that something has arisen but is merely unapprehended. If you argue that the conventional designation "unproduced" is due to non-perception, then the conventional designations of "production" and so forth are now likewise undermined, since they too are based on non-perception. Therefore, at the very moment that the production of pleasure and so forth is perceived, that is precisely when pleasure and so forth arise. Even then, there is no suppression by the perception of color-form and so forth; otherwise, according to your view, it would follow that [pleasure] is suppressed just as the hair is not perceived amidst the intervals. Now, suppose one argues: "A single sensory cognition will then proceed toward the apprehension of pleasure and so forth, and thus this fault of sequential apprehension would not occur. This is incorrect, as he says: *naikendriyabalena syād buddhirakṣāntare 'pi hi | viṣayāntarasañcāras tasmād asti svabhāvataḥ ||* "For a cognition regarding another sense-object could not occur through the power of a single sense-organ alone; therefore, the transition to another object occurs by its own nature. If it were the case that a single cognition of the eye, for instance, could simultaneously apprehend both color-form and pleasure, then the objection regarding sequential apprehension would indeed be invalid. However, this is not the case. Since the mind (*manas*) is dependent upon the senses, it cannot function independently of them. Thus, the simultaneous apprehension of multiple objects by a single sense-cognition is impossible. Consequently, the sequence of apprehension remains a valid refutation of the opponent's position.

Nor can there be knowledge of two things by means of a single [cognition], because of the restriction on the sensory consciousness; for even in the absence of pleasure and so forth, that [consciousness] arises from the object, since its capacity [to produce pleasure, etc. is not established. (258)

[317,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of form as a dharma. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of consciousness as a dharma. He does not perceive the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the eye as a dharma. He does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the mind as a dharma. He does not perceive forms as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of forms as dharmas. He does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of mental phenomena as dharmas. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of eye-consciousness as a dharma. He does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of mind-consciousness as a dharma. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the contact of the eye as a dharma. He does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the contact of the mind as a dharma. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a dharma. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the feeling born of the contact of the mind as a dharma. He does not perceive the earth element as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the earth element as a dharma. He does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the consciousness element as a dharma. He does not perceive the realm of desire as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the realm of desire as a dharma. He does not perceive the realm of form as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the realm of form as a dharma. He does not perceive the formless realm as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the formless realm as a dharma. He does not perceive ignorance as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of ignorance as a dharma. He does not perceive aging and death as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of aging and death as a dharma. He does not perceive the conditioned co-arising of all dharmas as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the conditioned co-arising of all dharmas as a dharma. He does not perceive the perfection of generosity as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the perfection of generosity as a dharma. He does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the perfection of wisdom as a dharma. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the emptiness of the internal as a dharma. He does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the beginningless emptiness, the nature-emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the emptiness of the essential nature of non-entities as a dharma. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as a dharma. He does not perceive the four applications of mindfulness as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the four applications of mindfulness as a dharma. He does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the eightfold noble path as a dharma. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the ten powers of a Tathāgata as a dharma. He does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the great compassion of a Tathāgata as a dharma. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the fruit of a stream-enterer as a dharma. He does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as dharmas, nor does he perceive the non-existence of arhatship as a dharma. He does not perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the state of a pratyekabuddha as a dharma. He does not perceive the state of a buddha as a dharma, nor does he perceive the non-existence of the state of a buddha as a dharma. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he perceive the non-existence of any dharma whatsoever. This is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he perceive the non-existence of any dharma whatsoever, then how does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of ethical discipline? How does he train in the perfection of patience? How does he train in the perfection of diligence? How does he train in the perfection of concentration? And how does he train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he gives a gift without perceiving a giver, a recipient, or a gift. This is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of giving. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he observes the precepts without perceiving the precepts, the transgression of the precepts, or the one who observes the precepts. This is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of ethical discipline. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he is patient toward all beings without perceiving the one who harms, the one who is harmed, or the act of harming. This is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of patience. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he exerts vigor without perceiving the one who exerts vigor, the act of exerting vigor, or that which is to be accomplished through vigor. This is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of diligence. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he enters into meditative absorption without perceiving the one who enters, the act of entering, or the object of absorption. This is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of concentration. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he discerns all dharmas without perceiving the one who discerns, the act of discerning, or the dharmas to be discerned. This is called the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a giver, a recipient, or a gift; if he does not

If it is argued that sensory cognition itself is what grasps objects, pleasure, and so forth, this is not tenable, as has already been established. This is because [the opponent] accepts that pleasure and the like are grasped by a non-sensory cognition produced solely from the conjunction of the self and the mind. Now, even if someone were to accept this, it would still be untenable; for since sensory cognition arises from the object alone even in the absence of pleasure and the like, one cannot determine that pleasure and the like are its causes. For when something does not arise in the absence of another, while other capable conditions are present, only the latter is determined to be its cause. And sensory consciousness does not fail to arise even in the absence of the causal complex of form and so forth, provided that pleasure and the like are absent.

[317,ii] Furthermore, it might be argued: when blue appears in sensory cognition together with yellow, it would then lack causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*), because [the cognition] arises from the yellow even in the absence of the blue. Yet, in that case as well, it possesses causal efficacy. If it is then said that the consciousness manifesting blue and yellow does not arise from the yellow alone, then by the same logic, the manifestation of the form of pleasure also does not arise from form alone; thus the principle is identical. This is not the same. [317,iii]
Since the capacity for blue is observed separately in the sensory consciousness, its power is established even in the aggregate; however, pleasure is not perceived in this manner.
Or, if it were admitted [that they have distinct capacities],
then if each had its own capacity separately, pleasure [and so forth] would be like blue and other such [distinct objects].
It would be apprehended as something isolated; for that [isolated thing] is not apprehended as having that [other] as its cause. // 259 //
For it is neither logical nor observed that anyone experiences [consciousness itself].

That sensory consciousness arises from form and so forth alone, which are devoid of pleasure and the like. Indeed, there is no pleasure or the like prior to the consciousness, as there is with form; for that [pleasure] arises from those very same [forms] simultaneously with the consciousness. Now, if it is claimed that even things existing at the same time can have the status of a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), that is incorrect. Let two things be mutually dependent by way of being co-existent causes—just as the primary elements are—but there is no relationship of the experienced and the experiencer (*vedya-vedaka-bhāva*) between them.
There is no mutual apprehension of that which is of the nature of non-apprehension; there is no mutual apprehension of that which is of the nature of self-awareness. (503) (PVA)
If it is claimed that there is apprehension because [the cognition] is oriented toward its own cause,
then even for this [cognition] which is simultaneous [with the object], since it consists in the awareness of another,
how could that which is oriented toward that [object] be considered born of the sense-faculties in the case of pleasure? (PVA 504)
The activity of the sense organs is not perceived therein; this has already been explained previously.

Moreover, if they possessed separate causal capacities, pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth would be apprehended in isolation. If it is argued that they are indeed apprehended just like blue, we say no; for it is not logical to apprehend pleasure and so forth without the apprehension of the form (*rūpa*) and other qualities that cause that pleasure. Even if it were being experienced, such an experience would be untenable. Indeed, no one seeks pleasure without the perception of a woman’s gracefulness; at that very moment, every lustful person desires that pleasure. Yet, such an [independent] perception does not occur. If, on the other hand, that [pleasure] alone possesses the capacity [to appear], then by the same logic, there would also be a second moon. For this very reason, he says: "When apprehended together with the object itself... (*arthenaiva saha-grahe*).
What capacity do pleasure and the other [feelings] possess, such that cognition is not admitted to arise from them? (260)

For the establishment of causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) does not occur without positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Nor is it accepted; indeed, for our opponents, cognition arising from the eyes and so forth is not even admitted. Furthermore:
If there were no object, then pleasure and the like would never be perceived by the eyes and other senses;
nor could form and so forth ever be grasped through the verbal designation of distinctions such as "woman" and the like. (261)

[317,xv] Because they are the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and because they are either agreeable or disagreeable, form (*rūpa*) and the rest would not be perceived as being accompanied by [pleasure and pain]. If there were some cause for their perception alone, then such a cognition would arise. If you argue that the cause is the perception of them together [with pleasure], then there would likewise be a perception of blue and the other [colors] as being mutual causes; yet this does not occur. Therefore, this is untenable. Furthermore, if pleasure could be perceived by the eye and the other senses in isolation, then the perception of form and the rest would never arise at all. For: [318,ii]
For when an object is present internally, the cognition of the capacity [of that object] does not appear as something external.

[318,iii] If the experience of pleasure itself could not occur without the perception of external distinctions such as women and so forth, then that perception of the external would be inseparable from the experience of pleasure. However, if it is held that the apprehension of the object is indeed admitted [to occur], then this is another fault.
[318,iv] If there were apprehension of an external object, there would be no experience of pleasure and so forth that arise from it. (262)

[318,v] For although pleasure arises at the time of apprehending an object, nevertheless, there is no causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for its apprehension. The apprehension of objects such as form occurs by means of the mind (*manas*) which arises from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and the mind; and there is no other mind, because the simultaneous arising of cognitions is not admitted. Therefore, pleasure and so forth produced by that [mind] would not be apprehended. If, on the other hand, the simultaneous arising of cognitions is accepted, then there is yet another fault; thus he says: [318,vi]

If cognitions were to arise simultaneously, because their respective objects would be present together, there would be the experience of pleasure and pain at once when the object is encountered. (263)
[318,vii] When there is the possibility of an object being either desired or undesired, it is impossible to prevent the simultaneous experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
[318,viii]

[Objection: But surely this is indeed observed. For instance, during the cold season, pleasure and pain are experienced as arising from the sensations of cold and heat respectively. [Response: That too is incorrect, because the intention [of the objection] is that they would have to exist at all times. Furthermore, for one whose mind is intent on the passion for battle, who is devoted to demonstrating honor and service to his master, and who desires to make himself successful, there is no experience of the pain caused by contact with the treatise. Moreover, when the cause of suffering is present, its production is inevitable; consequently, there would follow the absurd consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain simultaneously.

Now, [the opponent claims] that there is no cognition of another [object] because it is overwhelmed by another. That is incorrect, because such overwhelming is impossible. It is not right to say that overwhelming occurs through [the presence of] largeness and so forth; for this would entail the absurd consequence that an elephant and a mosquito could never be perceived simultaneously. Nor is it correct to say it is due to [one being] desired [to be seen]; for both are seen together, since it has already been established that pleasure and pain are experienced simultaneously. If you argue that there is experience [of one] in some cases due to a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), we say no; for no impression other than mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is observed. And if their arising is indeed by the power of mental cultivation, then it has been demonstrated that, for you, pleasure and the rest are of the very nature of consciousness.
[318,x] Or it might be argued:
Through the power of cultivation, cognition arises with respect to pleasure and so forth;
however, pleasure and the like arise solely from causes such as visible form.
This too is a false conceptualization; for:
[318, xiii] Regarding that cognition which arises from the power of the object itself, there is no need for cultivation.
The learned do not accept this; for if they did, it would be inconsistent.

If pleasure and so forth were already present [in the object], they would indeed be perceived even without the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) [of them]. For it is not the case that objects never before thought of or experienced could suddenly become objects of perception. If you argue that in those cases there is a cultivation [of the object] even though it is spatially or temporally remote (*vyavahita*), what is the proof for this? Furthermore, the cultivation of a cognition does not occur without the cultivation of the form of the object, because it is impossible to cultivate a cognition in isolation. If cognition arises by the power of cultivation, why would it depend on an object and so forth? Alternatively, if [you say] it is due to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) with the object, then in that case the form of the object also arises solely from the power of cultivation. This being so, just like dream-cognition and the like, cognition is entirely devoid of an object; thus, by one who wishes to prove that pleasure and so forth have no external form based on the cognition of external forms, the very lack of externality of the object itself is proven. What great skill in refuting others this opponent possesses!
Furthermore, there is the thought: because pleasure and pain simply cannot arise simultaneously.

If it is your view that even when there is a different entity as the material cause, suffering and so forth arise in cognition, yet that [cognition] is not the material cause of what is contradictory [to itself], and that [cognition] is one; || 264 ||
By what means does consciousness serve as the material cause for non-consciousness?
However, it is observed that [consciousness] exercises sovereignty even over that which is its opposite. (265)
Just as a single light for the eyes simultaneously produces both the impairment and the non-impairment of the perception of form in one who moves at night and in others. // 266 //

[319,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive them as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive form as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive form as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive them as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive the eye as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the eye as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive them as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive forms as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive forms as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive them as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the eye-consciousness as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive them as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive contact as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive contact as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive them as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive the conditioned phenomena as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the conditioned phenomena as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive the unconditioned phenomena as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the unconditioned phenomena as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive the past as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the past as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive the future as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the future as something other than a substantial entity; he does not perceive the present as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the present as something other than a substantial entity. He does not perceive all dharmas as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive all dharmas as something other than a substantial entity. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, and they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature. Since they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they are not perceived. Because they are not perceived, they are not grasped. Because they are not grasped, they are not clung to. Because they are not clung to, there is no production. Because there is no production, there is no cessation. Because there is no cessation, there is no affliction. Because there is no affliction, there is no purification. Because there is no purification, there is no attainment. Because there is no attainment, there is no non-attainment. Because there is no attainment and no non-attainment, there is no conceit. Because there is no conceit, there is no pride. Because there is no pride, there is no arrogance. Because there is no arrogance, there is no haughtiness. Because there is no haughtiness, there is no agitation. Because there is no agitation, there is no distraction. Because there is no distraction, there is no conceptual proliferation. Because there is no conceptual proliferation, there is no duality. Because there is no duality, there is no discrimination. Because there is no discrimination, there is no grasping. Because there is no grasping, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, there is no bondage. Because there is no bondage, there is liberation. Because there is liberation, there is no further rebirth. Because there is no further rebirth, there is no suffering. Because there is no suffering, there is the end of suffering. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Subhūti and the assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken. Thus ends the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.

If pleasure and so forth arise in dependence upon a cognition that has a specific material cause (*upādāna*), then it is not logical for a single material cause to produce two contradictory [states]. However, that [single cause] is indeed untenable, for we observe the cognition of even contradictory things, such as pleasure and so forth. Alternatively, if there is no material cause for what is contradictory, then how could cognition be the material cause of another cognition? Furthermore, the state of being a material cause is merely a form of predominance (*ādhipatya*) among causes with respect to their effect; and this [predominance] exists even in the case of what is contradictory. For example, from a single light source, both eyes may experience either impairment or non-impairment.

Therefore, pleasure and the other [feelings], which appear as having transferred into themselves the objects, are the perceivers of their own selves; their arising from those objects is merely [their appearance]. (267)

[319, vii] If pleasure and the like, though non-cognitive in nature, arise simultaneously with consciousness from the same causal complex as form and so forth, then there would always be a simultaneous experience of both pleasure and pain whenever desirable and undesirable objects are present before one. If you ask, "Why does this not happen for you as well?"—it is not so, because there is no such awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) as there is in the case of the conceptualization of form and so forth. Only at certain times, for a certain person, does a specific cause for the awakening of a latent predisposition occur. If you say, "The same applies to me," it is not so; for:
[319, viii]
If it were produced by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it would necessarily follow that it is simply cognition itself;
for latent impression is defined as the cause of memory and recognition.

[Objection: But surely recollection and the like are not of the nature of self-awareness (*svarūpasamvedana*), because in those cases too it is only the object that appears. It is only the form of the object—consisting of color and shape—that appears therein; the nature of the cognition itself is not another entity present there as an object of awareness. Therefore, every cognition is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*). [319,x] If only the object exists there as the domain of appearance...
The apprehension of that object would be as consistent as perception itself.

(PVA 509) For an object appearing in its own form cannot be considered perceptual, because only the manifestation of its own nature constitutes perception, and there is no other defining characteristic of perception. If this were the case, there would be no distinction between perception and memory. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the object appears as "prior" and as "non-evident" (*parokṣa*), then what is this so-called non-evidence? Indeed, it has not been apprehended by perception.
And memory functions only with respect to what has been perceived through direct perception;
otherwise, if the previous form were not grasped, how could there be memory? (PVA 510)

[319, xiii] For recollection does not have as its object a thing previously apprehended. If it is thought that recollection is such because it grasps the very thing already apprehended as being beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*), that too is incorrect.
Is this hiddenness the nature of the object, or is it the nature of the cognition?
If it were the nature of the object, it should appear in direct perception.

For that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an object appears in perception, just as blueness and so forth do. If it is argued that [the nature of the object] appears only in memory due to a restriction of causal capacity (*śaktiniyama*), [we reply: just as in an entity consisting of both existence and non-existence, its aspect of existence is grasped by perception while its aspect of non-existence is the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as "existence" (*bhāva*) through the form of another [positive entity]. That too is a partiality for one's own position. To explain:
if non-existence were indeed an existence, how could it not be grasped by perception?
If there were a distinction between them, how could that entity possess both existence and non-existence?

(512) For the distinction between entities is characterized by a difference in form (*ākāra*). If there were no difference despite the difference in form, then everything would be of a single nature. Now, two entities do not share identity because of a difference in form and so forth; however, this is not the case for existence and non-existence, because non-existence is distinct from existence. Furthermore, there is no further entity beyond existence and non-existence; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.
If non-existence were non-different from existence, how could there be a perception of difference?
If it is argued that this is due to a difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then from what source would the perception of non-difference arise? (PVA 513)

[320,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either a bodhisattva or the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive them, he does not apprehend them. Because he does not apprehend them, he does not think, 'I am a bodhisattva,' nor does he think, 'This is the perfection of wisdom. He does not even think, 'I am practicing the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he does not become attached to anything. Because he is unattached, he is not afraid. Being unafraid, he passes beyond all suffering to nirvāṇa. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. 169. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of this perfection of wisdom, surpasses the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having generated the thought of awakening, does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as real. He does not perceive form, nor does he apprehend form; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he apprehend the eye; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive forms, nor does he apprehend forms; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he apprehend the eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive contact, nor does he apprehend contact; he does not perceive feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he apprehend the conditioned; he does not perceive the unconditioned, nor does he apprehend the unconditioned. He does not perceive the world of desire, nor does he apprehend the world of desire; he does not perceive the world of form, nor does he apprehend the world of form; he does not perceive the formless world, nor does he apprehend the formless world. He does not perceive the level of the śrāvakas, nor does he apprehend the level of the śrāvakas; he does not perceive the level of the pratyekabuddhas, nor does he apprehend the level of the pratyekabuddhas. He does not perceive the level of a Buddha, nor does he apprehend the level of a Buddha. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom and proceeds toward all-knowledge. 170. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is it because of the non-apprehension of form that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom? Is it because of the non-apprehension of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness... [and so on through the rest of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and so forth] ...is it because of the non-apprehension of the level of a Buddha that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is indeed so. It is because of the non-apprehension of form that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom. It is because of the non-apprehension of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness... [and so on through the rest of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and so forth] ...it is because of the non-apprehension of the level of a Buddha that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom and proceeds toward all-knowledge. 171. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is it because of the non-apprehension of the perfection of giving that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom? Is it because of the non-apprehension of the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is indeed so. It is because of the non-apprehension of the perfection of giving that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom. It is because of the non-apprehension of the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom and proceeds toward all-knowledge. 172. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is it because of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of form that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom? Is it because of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness... [and so on through the rest of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and so forth] ...is it because of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the level of a Buddha that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is indeed so. It is because of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of form that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom. It is because of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness... [and so on through the rest of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, dependent origination, and so forth] ...it is because of the non-apprehension of the emptiness of the level of a Buddha that the bodhisattva mahāsattva transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he transcends the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas by means of this perfection of wisdom and proceeds toward all-knowledge. 173. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is it because of the non-apprehension of the signlessness of form that

If the positive aspect of an entity is apprehended by perception and the negative aspect by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then since they are understood as mutually unmixed, how can there be a cognition that a single thing consists of both existence and non-existence? If the cognition of form occurs through visual consciousness and that of sound and so forth through another, how is there a cognition of the unity of the agent, such that one thinks, "I have perceived both"? [The opponent replies: "This cognition arises from beginningless mental impressions (*vāsanā*) and not from reality; who can be blamed for this? [The author says: If it is so here as well, then if the cognition of the exclusion of non-existence also occurs solely by the power of beginningless mental impressions, what is the use of postulating a separate object? That which is called the means of knowledge known as "non-existence" is likewise produced by the power of mental impressions and is not ultimate. Therefore, since it is distinct from that [positive entity], what is the use of a "non-existence" that is excluded from it? Furthermore, this distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) appears through perception itself. Thus, the subsequent cognition that "this is not here," which arises through the force of that [perception] and grasps what has already been grasped, is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); there is no such thing as a separate means of knowledge called "non-existence. This individual conventional usage—"I have apprehended non-existence by the means of knowledge called non-existence"—is merely a personal convention. For the world, however, the conventional usage is identical in meaning: "That which was fit to be seen and was not perceived by me does not exist here, and its non-existence is established here. We shall explain later that this non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is indeed just perception. In ultimate reality, there is no such thing as a separate means of knowledge called "non-existence," nor is there an object of knowledge (*prameya*) corresponding to it; thus, the example is unestablished even regarding the restriction of capacity within that very nature.

Furthermore, just as non-existence (*abhāva*) would be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too would memory (*smṛti*). If it is argued that memory is indeed a means of valid cognition when its object is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), we say no; for it lacks the defining characteristics of a means of valid cognition.
Even if the imperceptible nature [of the object] is apprehended, what purpose is accomplished?
For the operation of inference depends upon the cognition of the connection with the subject (*dharmin*).

It might be argued: "When there is knowledge of something being beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), since there is no occasion for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) at that time, discerning people employ inference (*anumāna*); therefore, this is the purpose of knowing its being beyond the senses—namely, the validity of memory. This is not so, because inference proceeds solely from the grasping of the relation (*sambandha*) and the reliance upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). Indeed, no one, immediately after perceiving an effect such as smoke, first determines the "being-beyond-the-senses" nature of the fire grasped by the subsequent inference; nor is there any purpose in such a determination. If it is argued that someone might determine it at some point, that too is trivial. For instance:
Is any factor observed as being occasional by virtue of its being an occasioning cause? Or does some object, as an occasioning cause, cease from being a cause? (PVA 515)

For an instigator (*prayojaka*) is indeed a cause (*kāraṇa*). And causality does not exist when there is a deviation from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because that is the defining characteristic of it. Furthermore:
By means of recollection, the state of being beyond the senses is made known of what object?
That which is reached through inference is the object within the scope of recollection.

For an object that exists at the time of inference is not within the scope of memory; otherwise, inference would result in being rendered useless, since it would already have been apprehended by memory due to its being remote (*parokṣatā*). If it is argued that memory perceives only its remoteness and not its existence at that [present] time, then of what is that remoteness perceived? If it is argued that it is of the object previously apprehended, then it is only of the entity as delimited by that [past] time. In that case, memory knows the remoteness of one thing and not another; thus, such memory is indeed useless. If it is argued that one acts after having remembered the remoteness, and therefore memory is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it initiates inference, this must be examined: does one act toward its existence at that [past] time, or toward its existence at the present time?
If it were to exist at that time, it would be impossible to attain;
and one who desires attainment would act only as a discerning person, and not otherwise. (517) (PVA)

[321,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who had been practicing the religious life for fifty years and were observing the dhūta ascetic practices; seeing them, he addressed the Bhagavat: “Bhagavat, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs have been practicing the religious life for fifty years and are observing the dhūta ascetic practices. May the Bhagavat grant them the prediction of their future enlightenment. Then the Bhagavat said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “Avalokiteśvara, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Padmottara. They shall each have a retinue of one thousand bhikṣus, and they shall live for twenty intermediate kalpas. When the Bhagavat had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs rejoiced and praised what the Bhagavat had said. Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled “The Prediction for the Five Hundred Bhikṣuṇīs. [321,iv] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Bhagavat, and addressed him: “Bhagavat, by what causes and conditions does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara come to this Sahā world? The Bhagavat said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati: “Akṣayamati, there is a world-system called Abhirati. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Akṣobhya. That Tathāgata has a son named Avalokiteśvara, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. He possesses great supernatural power and great majesty. He travels through the worlds of the ten directions, bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings, and he comes to this Sahā world to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati asked the Bhagavat: “Bhagavat, what are the names of the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones in the worlds of the ten directions where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara preaches the Dharma? The Bhagavat said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati: “In the eastern direction, there is a world-system called Ratnavatī. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnārcis. In the southern direction, there is a world-system called Gandhavatī. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Gandhottama. In the western direction, there is a world-system called Padmavati. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmottara. In the northern direction, there is a world-system called Vidyutvatī. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vidyuddeva. In the nadir, there is a world-system called Sumeruvati. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sumerukalpa. In the zenith, there is a world-system called Sarvaratnavicitrā. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvaratnavicitrasaṃkusumitābhijña. In the southeast, there is a world-system called Ratnavyūhā. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ratnavyūharāja. In the southwest, there is a world-system called Gandhapradhānā. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Gandhapradhānarāja. In the northwest, there is a world-system called Padmavyūhā. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmavyūharāja. In the northeast, there is a world-system called Vajravatī. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vajradhvaja. In the region between the nadir and the zenith, there is a world-system called Sarvabuddhakṣetraguṇavyūhālaṃkārā. There dwells a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvabuddhakṣetraguṇavyūhālaṃkāraśrī. When the Bhagavat had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati and the entire assembly rejoiced and praised what the Bhagavat had said. Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled “The Names of the Buddhas. [322,i] At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Bhagavat, and addressed him: “Bhagavat, how many kinds of bodhicitta are there? The Bhagavat said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: “Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of aspiration; second, the bodhicitta of practice. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the śrāvakas; second, the bodhicitta of the bodhisattvas. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the pratyekabuddhas; second, the bodhicitta of the bodhisattvas. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the provisional vehicle; second, the bodhicitta of the ultimate vehicle. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the inferior vehicle; second, the bodhicitta of the superior vehicle. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the mundane; second, the bodhicitta of the supramundane. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the conditioned; second, the bodhicitta of the unconditioned. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of birth and death; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of saṃsāra; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of nirvāṇa. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of affliction; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of purification. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of defilement; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of purity. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of bondage; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of liberation. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of samsāric existence; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of non-existence. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of grasping; second, the bodhicitta of the dharma of non-grasping. Furthermore, Maitreya, there are two kinds of bodhicitta. What are the two? First, the bodhicitta of the dharma of attachment; second, the bodhicitta

The existence at the present time is not known through memory; therefore, how can it have the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? At the previous time, the object was perceived as remote (*parokṣa*), and that [existence] cannot be attained [now]. Alternatively, the apprehension of remoteness occurs through perception itself: that which is apprehended by perception as limited to that specific time is precisely what constitutes "remoteness" in relation to a subsequent time. However, its having that form (*tadākāratā*) is essentially inherent to the memory due to the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). If it is argued that this [memory] is indeed an object of such a nature, we say no, because there is no conviction (*adhimukti*) regarding its being an object. It is solely by virtue of conviction that the determination of reality is established. For a thing's own nature, when being cognized through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), does not attain the status of being determined as either "an object" or "not an object. That determination occurs through a subsequent conviction. And such [conviction] does not exist in the form of memory. For instance, discerning people understand: "That is the object which was seen previously; but this form, moreover, now participates in arising solely through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)."

Therefore, pleasure and the like are the perceivers of objects that appear as having been transferred into their own [nature]; and for these [pleasures], their arising from objects is merely [a matter of] their own self. (267)

Just as memory, arising from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), is a single cognition together with the form of the object transferred into itself, so too are pleasure and the like. For these also are the perceivers of that very specific tangible which has become their own nature, having been brought forth by the mental impression of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). How then is there a dependence on objects such as visible form? It is because, through those [objects], the corresponding latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) are awakened.
From the perception of a form of pleasure arising from contact with a tangible object, a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced; its awakening occurs through the sight of that same object.

For the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the pleasure of an embrace becomes deeply rooted; when it is awakened again by the sight of such a form, it generates an internal experience of the pleasure of touch exactly as it was before. This very point he demonstrates:
[321, viii] "The object-nature, having become one's own self, is experienced by them through those [sensations]."
Therefore, the manifestation of the experience of an object is the objective support, while its appearance as that [object] is the apprehended aspect.

[321,ix] It is precisely an internal particularity of the tangible, which has become one's own self, that is experienced through pleasure and so forth; it is in this very sense that there is the manifestation of the experience of the object. Otherwise, if there were cognition of something else, the relation expressed by "by that" would not be possible. For instance:
The experience of its own nature is logical, since its own nature arises from its cause.
How could there be an experience of another's form when that [other] is distinct? (519) For the form of one thing does not belong to another; how then could it be manifested by that? (PVA)

Just as from a lamp there arises in a jar a luminosity of such a nature, so it is not the case that an object is produced as a manifestation from cognition, which is itself a manifestation. For if [the object] were an effect [of cognition], how could its apprehension arise from that cognition? (PVA 520–521)

For it is a logical principle that an effect does not reveal its cause by means of that very cause. Otherwise, a physical activity arising from a cognition of something else would have to be known by that [cause]. Therefore, it is logical that only its own nature (*ātmarūpa*) should be experienced. If it is argued that experience occurs because [the object] is oriented toward [it], rather than through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), that is incorrect.
If the manifestation of its own nature arises from its own cause, what does that have to do with the object here, by virtue of which it could be known as such? (522) (PVA) Or,
if it is argued that the manifestation of that [consciousness] is directed toward the object...
Is the eye’s state of being directed toward [an object] not itself the cognition of that [object]?

(523) (PVA) If it is argued that the eye is directed toward the object, how can there be cognition [of that direction]? For the perception of the object’s being directed toward [the eye] would only occur when there is a perception of the object. (524) (PVA)

[321,xvii] For if the object is not perceived in its own form (*svarūpa*), the perception of its being directed toward that [object] cannot be perceived. If the object is indeed perceived by itself, what then is the use of cognition? It certainly does not serve as a useful assistant once it has already been established. If it is argued that without that [cognition], the appearance of the object is not perceived, then let there be an appearance *together with* that [cognition]; however, it is not something further than that. To say "therefore, there is the grasping of that" is merely a borrowed ornament (*yācitakamaṇḍana*). Another [says]: [322,i]
Someone claims that pleasure and so forth, which are external, insentient, and objects of apprehension, are perceived [by the mind];
yet even for him, the simultaneous apprehension of both [the object and its cognition] is not logical. (269)

[322,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchants being pursued by the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi. Having seen them, he addressed the merchant leader Sudhana: “Do not fear, O merchant leader; do not fear. I shall protect you all from this yakṣa Śūlapāṇi. Then the merchant leader Sudhana and his five hundred merchants, having heard these words of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, were filled with joy and their hair stood on end. They paid homage at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and proceeded along the path. Meanwhile, the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi, seeing the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara approaching from afar, became terrified, his hair stood on end, and his body trembled. He thought to himself: “This must be some great being, a powerful deity, or a powerful nāga, or a powerful yakṣa, or a powerful gandharva, or a powerful asura, or a powerful garuḍa, or a powerful kiṃnara, or a powerful mahoraga, or a powerful human, or a powerful non-human, who has come here to destroy me. Having thought this, he fled far away. At that time, the merchant leader Sudhana and his five hundred merchants reached the place where the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara was. Upon arriving, they paid homage at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the merchant leader Sudhana said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “O son of noble family, we have been pursued by the yakṣa Śūlapāṇi. How did you cause him to flee far away? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “O merchant leader, when those beings hear my name, they will immediately be freed from all fear of fire, water, poison, weapons, and enemies. O merchant leader, if those beings who are bound in prison should hear my name, they will be released from their bonds. O merchant leader, if those beings who are afflicted by various diseases should hear my name, they will be freed from all their ailments. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling on the road should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of robbers, lions, tigers, wolves, wild dogs, elephants, snakes, and scorpions. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling by sea should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of waves, whirlpools, and sea monsters. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the wilderness should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of hunger, thirst, and exhaustion. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the mountains should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of precipices and thorns. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the forests should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of wild beasts. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the deserts should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of heat and thirst. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the borderlands should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of hostile kings and bandits. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the realms of the asuras should hear my name, they will be freed from all dangers of the asuras’ weapons and conflicts. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the realms of the pretas should hear my name, they will be freed from all their sufferings of hunger and thirst. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the realms of the animals should hear my name, they will be freed from all their sufferings of mutual devouring. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the realms of the hells should hear my name, they will be freed from all their sufferings of heat and cold. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the realms of the gods should hear my name, they will be freed from all their sufferings of pride and negligence. O merchant leader, if those beings who are traveling through the realm of saṃsāra should hear my name, they will be freed from all the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair. The merchant leader Sudhana said: “O son of noble family, how should a bodhisattva practice so that he may attain such a power? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “O merchant leader, a bodhisattva should practice the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. He should practice the four bases of psychic power, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the eight liberations, the nine successive absorptions, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion. He should practice the skillful means, the vows, the superknowledges, and the dhāraṇīs. O merchant leader, a bodhisattva should practice in this way so that he may attain such a power. The merchant leader Sudhana said: “O son of noble family, what is the name of this samādhi? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “O merchant leader, this samādhi is named ‘The King of Samādhis that Pervades All Directions. The merchant leader Sudhana said: “O son of noble family, I wish to hear the names of the other bodhisattvas who dwell in the world-system of the Buddha Akṣobhya. The phrase "necessarily" (*niyamena*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. For there is no reason why pleasure and so forth should necessarily be perceived together with something else, such as blue and so forth, as if they were independent objects of perception like blue itself. Now, it may be argued that these [pleasures] are transformations of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) in the form of pleasure, pain, and so on. Indeed, such is the process: from *pradhāna* comes the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the I-principle (*ahaṃkāra*); from the I-principle, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the five sense organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the mind; and from the five subtle elements, the five gross elements. This entire collection of modifications is nothing more than this. Furthermore, a modification conforms to the nature of its material cause (*prakṛti*), just as a jar and other such things are modifications of clay. To this, it is replied:

If it is argued that because the stalk and so forth possess a nature non-different from pleasure and the like, they are not perceived simultaneously, then what is this non-difference between the two cognitions which appear as distinct? [322,iv] How is it known that pleasure and the like are indeed of the nature of the primary form of pleasure and so forth? If it is argued that this is because their conformity to that nature is observed— namely, for instance, that modifications of clay are seen to conform to it—

But this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Sound is produced from the conjunction of a drum and a stick, yet it does not possess the form of the drum or the stick. Even if it is maintained that air, atoms, and sound attain the state of being "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), nevertheless, this is not established. Now, if one postulates a cause of the same genus (*samānajātīya*) here as well, as in the case of a modification of clay, then [the following follows]: whatever is an effect possesses that [material] form, and all such things arise from a heterogeneous cause (*vijātīya*), such as sound and so forth; and since effects like jars and the like also arise only from a heterogeneous cause—namely, the potter and so forth—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "everything that arises exists only from a homogeneous cause" is not established. On the contrary, the opposite is proven: that things arise from both homogeneous and heterogeneous causes. Nowhere is a homogeneous cause ever seen to exist without assistance.

[322, vi] Now, if it is observed that everything is indeed accompanied by pleasure and so forth, then the cause of the transformations of clay must have the nature of pleasure and so forth, just as a lump of clay is the cause of its own products. To this it has been said: because another factor acts as a concomitant cause, it follows that the cause must be of both similar and dissimilar kinds; thus, the existence of *pradhāna* (the primal matter) is not established.

Moreover, because pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest also possess the property of being objects of cognition (*grāhyatā*), another object of cognition, namely *pradhāna*, is established. Consequently, ultimately, the cause would be "objectivity" (*grāhyatā*), "substantiality" (*vastutva*), and so forth. Now, if that [cause] is also of the nature of pleasure and the rest—because the persisting category of "thingness" (*padārthatva*) and so on consists of pleasure and the rest—then it follows that since pleasure and the rest consist of pots and the like, *pradhāna* must consist of pots and the like. If you accept that it indeed consists of the nature of all things, then if the entire collection of transformations is perceived within the self of *pradhāna* by that very same self-form which is mutually distinct, what kind of relationship between material cause (*prakṛti*) and transformation (*vikāra*) could there be? If you say it is merely appearance (*āvirbhāva*) and disappearance (*tirobhāva*), where appearance is the transformation and disappearance is the material cause, then what is this so-called "appearance," and what is "disappearance"? If you say that appearance is manifestation (*vyakti*) and disappearance is its absence, then what is this manifestation? It is the state of being perceptible (*dṛśyātmatā*). Its absence is non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), which is disappearance. If that is so, then when something is not perceived, it is not perceived; when it is perceived, it is perceived. What else could there be? Therefore, the distinction between material cause and transformation is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Thus, the proof of *pradhāna* is refuted. Furthermore, if the existence of *pradhāna* were established through inference, then since it is not perceived, it would follow that it does not exist. If it is argued that it exists because it is inferred, then since it is not perceived, it is not established. Therefore, the existence of *pradhāna* is not established. Nor is it established by means of verbal testimony (*āgama*), for no such scripture is found. Even if one were to assume a scripture, it would be contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, the existence of *pradhāna* is not proven. [322, viii] Is it not the case that if the nature [of things] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its non-perception cannot be maintained? But if it is unestablished, then its very non-existence constitutes its production; thus, there is no establishment of *pradhāna*. Furthermore, if jars and other such things remain exactly as they were previously even when unperceived, what is the purpose of postulating *pradhāna* as their cause? If it is argued that their very nature as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is *pradhāna*, we say no, because they are perceived as distinct from the nature of pleasure and so on. How can that which appears as diverse and is apprehended by the mind be non-different? Moreover: [323, ii]
If that [external object] were without distinction, then due to the gradation of cultivation, there would be a gradation in the intellect, but not in pleasure and pain. (271)

[323,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred women and addressed them thus: “Sisters, do not fear. I shall deliver you from this great mass of suffering. Then, by his miraculous power, he caused the five hundred women to see him standing before them. Having seen him, they were filled with joy and delight, and their minds became tranquil. They prostrated themselves at his feet and said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “O Noble One, we have committed many evil deeds; we have been born into a lowly family, and we have fallen into the state of female rebirth. We are now afflicted by old age, sickness, and death. O Noble One, how may we escape from this female form? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: “Sisters, if you wish to escape from this female form, you should all take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. You should cultivate the roots of goodness, practice the ten wholesome paths of action, and constantly recollect the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. By so doing, you will surely escape from this female form. Hearing these words, the five hundred women took refuge in the Triple Gem, cultivated the roots of goodness, practiced the ten wholesome paths of action, and constantly recollected the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Because of this, their female forms disappeared and they were all reborn as men. Then, having attained the male body, they approached the Buddha and paid homage at his feet. The Buddha then granted them the prediction of enlightenment. Having received the prediction, they rejoiced and departed. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, through his great compassion, delivers sentient beings from the three evil realms and leads them to the path of liberation. This is called the second chapter, on the Deliverance from the Female Form.

If pleasure and the like were indeed external forms such as blue and so forth, then—just as with blue and the like—it would not be possible for specific variations such as joy or torment to arise from specific variations in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Indeed, no manifestation of the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth is ever observed to be differentiated by specific variations in mental cultivation. If that were the case, then everything internal and external would follow as being merely a consequence of mental cultivation; thus, the entire world would result in being entirely unreal, produced solely by the power of cultivation. Furthermore, if pleasure and the like were external, there would be the undesirable consequence of their appearing as external forms. If it is argued that this is an illusion (*bhrānti*), we say no, because no cause for such an illusion is perceived and because there is no sublation (*bādhana*) of it.
If even cognition, by virtue of having pleasure and so forth as its nature, is not in contradiction [with external objects],
then how is it understood that this [external object] possesses pleasure and so forth as its nature? (272)

He does not perceive that the eye is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the eye; he does not perceive that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the mind. He does not perceive that forms are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is forms; he does not perceive that sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty, nor does he perceve that emptiness is mental phenomena. He does not perceive that eye-consciousness is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is eye-consciousness; he does not perceive that ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is mind-consciousness. He does not perceive that eye-contact is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is eye-contact; he does not perceive that ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is mind-contact. He does not perceive that feeling born of eye-contact is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is feeling born of eye-contact; he does not perceive that feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is feeling born of mind-contact. He does not perceive that ignorance is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is ignorance; he does not perceive that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is old age and death. He does not perceive that suffering is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is suffering; he does not perceive that origination, cessation, and the path are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the path.
