This might be the intended argument: Just as sound and the other [objects] have the nature of being transformations of *pradhāna*, so too does the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, when the self experiences pleasure and so forth in the form of the intellect, there is necessarily an experience of that which is not external in form. Through the gradation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is a gradation in the intellect; and through that gradation in the intellect, there is also a gradation in pleasure and so forth in their own nature. For what is called "mental cultivation" is set in motion by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the mind (*manas*). And since that ego-sense consists of the notion "I am," it resides in the intellect. Furthermore, because the mind consists of volition (*saṅkalpa*), mental cultivation is simply the repeated volitional activity. Consequently, the intellect—being dependent on the *sāttvika* ego-sense and having attained the nature of pleasure—manifests in that way. If this is so, how is it understood that pleasure and so forth are external in form? To argue that even external things like sound and the rest are of the nature of transformations of *pradhāna* is not a coherent resolution [to the problem].

[323, vi] From what has this very [doctrine] arisen? [It is said: "These [qualities], such as sound and the rest, arise from the transformation of the Pradhāna; there is no observation of their being followed by its nature. (PVA 525)

[323, vii] If the presence of pleasure and so forth in sound and other phenomena were established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—just as it is in the case of cognition—then the inhabitants of the world would know that the effect follows its cause, and thus understand that they are produced from such a cause. If you argue that this determination arises precisely from the transformation of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) in the form of pleasure and so forth, this is nothing but a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). For instance:
[323, viii]
If its transformation from *pradhāna* is known, it would possess the nature of pleasure and so forth;
through the thorough knowledge of this nature of pleasure and so forth, there arises the ascertainment of the true reality of sound and the other objects.

If sound and the other objects were transformations of *pradhāna*, they would possess the concomitance of pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest. And if that concomitance with pleasure and so forth is established, then their nature as transformations of *pradhāna* follows; thus, if one of the two is not established, neither is established.

Furthermore, even if smoke were indeed a transformation of fire, how could its luminosity be proven? If you argue that it is not so because it is contradicted by perception, the same applies to sound and the others.

[323,xi] This might be so: if sound and the other objects were not of the nature of pleasure, there would be no cognition that apprehends them, because it is impossible for two things of different classes to stand in the relation of apprehender and apprehended. To this, it is replied:

If, because they belong to different classes, the person were not the grasper of that which is not grasped [by it], then he would be a non-grasper of everything, and consequently his status as an enjoyer would be lost. (273)

For the person (*puruṣa*) is not of the same genus as sound and so forth, because he does not consist of the primary nature (*apradhānātmaka*); whereas the case is the opposite for pleasure and the rest. If it is argued that he may be a non-apprehender, we say no; for it would follow that he lacks the status of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), and the person is indeed accepted as an enjoyer. Furthermore, there is no state of being an enjoyer other than direct experience (*anubhava*).
By this, the relationship of cause and effect is refuted; why? [324,ii] Because:
[324,iii] Regarding cause and effect: because the state of being the grasped and the grasper is absent, that [state] would exist elsewhere as well, even in the case of existence. // 254 //

In the case of pleasure derived from cognition, words, and so forth, the relationship of apprehended object (*grāhya*) and apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) exists precisely because of their presence. For a blue object or the like is "apprehended" because it generates a cognition by imparting its own form; otherwise, there would be no status as an apprehended object, since that status consists in the relation of cause and effect. Therefore, the relation of cause and effect is established solely through the status of being an apprehended object. And since this status of being an apprehended object—which bestows the quality of being an effect—exists in the person (*pums*) with respect to sounds and so forth as well, that person too would be an effect of them. Since it is not so, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Alternatively, he states that the relation of cause and effect is refuted by this very argument because it is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*): because in the case of cognition (*buddhi*) and pleasure (*sukha*), there exists the state of being the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakatā*). For where there is the state of being the apprehended and the apprehender, there is no relation of cause and effect, as in the case of the self (*puruṣa*) and sound (*śabda*) and so forth, or pleasure. If it is argued that for cognition, pleasure, and the like, the relation of cause and effect follows precisely from their state of being the apprehended and the apprehender, then that relation of cause and effect would indeed be based on that very [state]. This being the case, it would follow that the self (*puṃs*) is also an effect, which is undesirable; or else, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*) for that very same reason.

Alternatively, cognition and pleasure are not cause and effect, because the relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject does not exist between them; or, if it did exist, that same relationship would have to occur elsewhere as well.
Therefore, they are indeed internal; and because they are objects of experience, they are sentient.
Why? [324,ix]
That which is not of a certain nature cannot indeed be the cognition of that [nature]. (275)
Because there is no means of valid cognition for its externality, and because it is experienced precisely as internal.
In whatever manner an object is cognized, it is accepted as being exactly so.
Without cognition, there is no determination of the existence of entities.

For that which is not the experience of a form cannot be its cognition. Furthermore, the experience of pleasure and so forth does not conform to an external form; otherwise, it would be illogical for the experience to be one thing and the object another. Indeed, it is not tenable to say, "this is the experience of blue" and "that is the experience of yellow. Thus, when cognition proceeds by way of being self-cognizing (*svavidrūpatā*), it cognizes only its own self-cognizing nature. For pleasure and so forth, when perceived by another [consciousness], are not experienced [as they truly are]. Whereas forms and the like are experienced through the mediation of the eye and other faculties, and thus are of a non-self-cognizing nature. Alternatively, pleasure and so forth are not apprehended without an aspect (*nirākāra*); therefore, they are experienced precisely through the aspect of pleasure, and thus the fact that consciousness possesses the aspect of pleasure is established. It is thereby established that the pleasure contained within that [consciousness] is of the very nature of awareness (*bodharūpa*). If it is argued that, like jars and the like, pleasure and so forth must also be external, this is not correct. It is not logical [to claim they are external] because, although the aspect of a jar and so forth belongs to the very essence of consciousness, it arises through the influence of something else (*paropadhāna*), and no operation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is perceived therein. By contrast, because the aspect of pleasure and so forth is intensified through the power of mental cultivation, it does not depend on the influence of something else.

[324,xiv] But even if they depend upon cultivation (*bhāvanā*), pleasure and the like do not possess the nature of cognition (*saṃvedana*), because they are experienced through an experience that does not have that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For pleasure and the like, even when intensified through cultivation, do not become of the nature of cognition. To this it is replied:

If experience, which does not have that [pleasure, etc. as its intrinsic nature (*atatsvabhāva*), were to inhere in those mental states (*bauddha*), then—given that pleasure and the like possess the nature of awareness (*bodharūpatā*) by virtue of being self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*)—they could not be known by another self (*ātman*) that lacks their form. Consequently, the person (*pums*) cannot be the effect [of those mental states] either. Its status as an effect would arise from its having the form of that [mental state] and being produced from it; however, this is not the case, because the self lacks that form. Indeed, experience—or what inheres within the intellect (*buddhi*)—is precisely that which does not have that [pleasure, etc. as its intrinsic nature. Therefore, the notion of identity between cognition and the intellect arises only from the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
Apart from the forms of direct perception and recollection, what other cognition could there be in this case? (276)
[325,iii] What is this cognition? It is determination. What is this awareness? It is experience.

[Objection: Is this not said only when there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a difference [between them]? Furthermore, "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*) and "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) are mere synonyms. If it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of the form of the object and is not itself of the nature of cognition, whereas the cognition of the formless is the nature of consciousness (*bodha*), [we reply: there is no proof here that cognition is formless. [Objection: If it is argued that there is no proof because cognition is imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*), [we reply: No, because an admission (*abhyupagama*) is not a reason. For even inference does not arise from the absence of perception; therefore, such an admission is simply not logical. [Objection: If there were no other cognition, it would follow that pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth could not be experienced. [Reply: What contradiction is there in their being experienced through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? Since all practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is accomplished by that alone, another [cognition] is useless.
[325,v] Furthermore, it might be argued: "If consciousness is not admitted to exist at all, then what would happen in the state of liberation?
How can one who is devoid of both pleasure and pain be liberated?
For if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were abandoned, it would follow that the substratum (*dharmin*) itself is destroyed.

For it is not possible to abandon one’s own nature. However, pleasure and the like, which are distinct [from the self] and have been made objects of conceptual superimposition (*vivekādhyāropa*), are merely words that can be abandoned, even if they are currently perceived as non-different from the self in the present state. Even if this were desired, it would still not be established, because it is not proven by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). An object does not become established simply because "I desire it" or because it lacks a means of valid cognition. Furthermore, causes do not conform to one's desires; nor is there any evidence that such a thing has a cause. For at the very moment of attaining cultivation (*bhāvanā*), a slight diminution is observed. It is simply another consciousness that arises in that way at present, but there is no realization of a difference between that consciousness and the experience of pleasure and so forth. The same applies to the state of liberation; thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore:
Depending upon various objects, the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth appears as a single [unit]; however, that which exists in the interval is not seen. 277.

[325, ix] But surely, is there not a difference [between these states] simply because of the difference in designations such as "cognition," "pleasure," and "pain"? Otherwise, how could there be a difference in designation without a difference in the object? No; we perceive this very same [entity] as a transformation (*vivarta*) appearing in various forms such as joy, despondency, and so forth. Let names be applied to it as one pleases. The use of different designations is solely for the purpose of indicating the difference in its states, just like the designations "seed," "sprout," "leaf," and "stalk.
If non-distinction [between things] were due to contact, like a firebrand and fire, then the established distinction between difference and non-difference would be destroyed for all entities. (278)

[325,xi] If it is assumed that these two are conjoined merely because there is an example—even without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—then, in the case of pillars and the like, which are perceived as having a single form, the establishment of their oneness would not occur. And if oneness is not established, then multiplicity, which consists of an aggregate of those [units], would likewise not be established; thus, the entire system of entities would collapse, for an entity cannot exist apart from being either one or many. To explain:
If that which has undivided sensation were a unity, then that which possesses such differentiation would not be established;
since this [unity] lacks a means of proof, the proof for differentiation is not established. (276)

Therefore, when one is unestablished, both are unestablished. Consequently, it is logical that there is only a non-differentiated cognition, whereas from its opposite, there is multiplicity. But for the Sāṃkhya:

If suffering and so forth appear as distinct, while cognition and feeling are non-distinct, then if these two [cognition and feeling] were distinct despite appearing non-distinct, upon what would difference and non-difference depend? (280)
[326,iii] Thus is an intermediate verse.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Just as no mutual distinction is perceived among mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and volition (*cetanā*), which belong to the category of universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), or even if a distinction is admitted despite not being perceived, why is that same distinction not also admitted between cognition (*buddhi*) and sensation (*samvedana*)? If you claim that a single, undivided sensation is the mind, this is inconclusive because of the mental factors that constitute its retinue. To this, it is said:
"Because even those [mental factors] that are obscured by a sharp [primary factor] are at times seen to have distinctions."
Within the stream of consciousness and its mental factors, the establishment of their distinction is proven. (281)

[326, vi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. It should be understood as such. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great vehicle of the Tathāgatas, and because it is the supreme vehicle among all vehicles, it is therefore called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it carries across the great mass of suffering of sentient beings, because it leads to the attainment of the great fruit of omniscience, and because it is the unsurpassed path to liberation, it is therefore called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Moreover, Ānanda, because it contains within it the vast collection of perfections, the vast collection of meditative concentrations, the vast collection of dhāraṇīs, and the vast collection of analytical knowledges, it is therefore called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Also, Ānanda, because it reveals the vast realm of phenomena, the vast realm of consciousness, the vast realm of space, and the vast realm of the Dharma, it is therefore called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Finally, Ānanda, because it is the source from which all Buddhas of the past, present, and future arise, and because it is the foundation upon which the wheel of the Dharma is turned, it is therefore called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, was filled with joy and practiced accordingly. This is not accepted [by us], because of the statement: "Mental factors (*caitasāḥ*) are not other than the mind (*citta*). This is a refutation made while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. Even if, at one time, [mental factors] such as volition (*cetanā*) are eclipsed by another mental factor with a more intense activity and thus do not become objects of intense perception, they nevertheless become objects of perception at other times; therefore, volition and the rest are indeed distinct from feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors], because they are perceived in their own nature at other times. Just as a cluster of stars, whose power of self-illumination has been suppressed by the mass of the sun’s rays, does not cease to exist [at that time], yet there is never a clear apprehension of the distinction between cognition (*buddhi*) and its awareness (*samvedana*) even at one time, whereas among the mental factors, some are occasionally perceived when they have become manifest.

[326, vii] Is it not the case that the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) and so forth are perceived only in conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*) and not in non-conceptual cognition? No; for even there, mental factors (*caitasāḥ*) certainly exist. To explain: sometimes immediately following experience there arises a conceptualization of a sign, and sometimes a conceptualization such as "I shall do this" and so forth. Therefore, from the fact that conceptualizations follow upon experience, it is established that non-conceptual mental factors also exist. Consequently, there is not even a trace of logical reasoning for a distinction between these [mental factors] on the one hand and cognition (*buddhi*) and self-awareness (*samvedana*) on the other; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). || 0 ||
< (4) Yogic Perception > [326,
viii] That cognition of yogins mentioned previously is produced from their meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
With the web of conceptual construction shaken off, it appears with perfect clarity. // 282 //

The knowledge of yogins regarding the domain of the four noble truths was previously mentioned. From what cause does it arise? He says: It consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), has cultivation as its cause, and through the power of cultivation, it appears clearly. Precisely because it appears clearly, it is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*); therefore, it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But surely, since it arises through the power of an object, it is logical that non-conceptual cognition has a present object as its domain. How, then, can there be non-conceptuality for that which has past or future objects, or for that which has non-existent objects, based on mere cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? He shows that even in the case of non-existent objects, cultivation is capable of producing an effect just like the present:
"For instance, those who are afflicted by desire, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and so forth... [326,xi]
They see even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them.

[326,xii] For a cognition whose object is non-existent does not arise through the causal efficiency (*arthasāmarthya*) of an object. Nor is that [cognition] conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because it is seen as being present before one. Thus, by virtue of its nature as direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) and is perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that even though it is conceptual, it is non-conceptual because it appears clearly (*spaṣṭābha*), that is not so.
For one who is bound by conceptual construction, there is no appearance of a clear object;
even in a dream, that which is remembered is a memory-cognition and does not possess such an object.

[327, ii] It has been established that the very nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that its object is hidden (*parokṣa*). If this were not the case, it would not be conceptual at all. Even in dreams, conceptual constructions are experienced as having the form of hidden objects; yet they do not appear clearly. If clarity were due to the power of some distortion (*viplava*), then nothing in dreams and the like would ever be unclear. However, conceptual constructions are seen in dreams to have the form of memories of what was previously experienced; therefore, the clarity of a conceptual construction does not arise from distortion. Consequently, only a non-conceptual cognition possesses a perfectly clear form.

[327,iii] Here the Vaibhāṣikas say: "Is it not logical that when a thing is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there occurs a clear appearance through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? For when the turbidity of ignorance (*avidyā*) has been removed by cultivation, the object appears in its own form (*svarūpa*). But if it does not exist, there is no own-form; so what could there be that appears? However, for yogins, there is knowledge of past and future objects because the past and future do exist. To this he replies: [327,iv]

Even that which is unreal, such as the meditation on impurity or the totality of earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsna*), is seen clearly and without conceptual construction when produced by the power of meditative cultivation. (285)

[327,v] Because they involve mental attention that is not directed toward reality (*atattvamanaskāra*), earth and the other elements do not exist in space within the context of the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) and so forth. Now, it might be argued that earth and the others do indeed exist because they are seen through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogis. A yogi does not become such merely through cultivation (*bhāvanā*); rather, having grasped objects by means of knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*) and having established them through reasoning consisting of reflection (*yukticintāmayajñāna*), one cultivates them. Upon the completion of that cultivation, that which has an unerring object is itself the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the yogis are endowed with that. Thus, there is the statement: "Yoga is the path that proceeds by the union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). [327,vi]

In that regard, although these [objects] appear to yogins, nevertheless, because this cultivation is for the sake of a specific purpose, it is of a non-real nature; therefore, they appear to them precisely as having a non-real nature. Consequently, if they appear to yogins by way of a non-real nature, how could they possess existence on that account? Therefore, even for those things appearing in the cognition of yogins, their nature is indeed non-real. For reality does not follow from mere appearance, but rather from critical investigation (*parīkṣā*). Furthermore, cultivation that arises from mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not a cause for the realization of reality; rather, it is only that which has come through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is so—this is the definitive conclusion. To illustrate:
That which is produced merely through mental cultivation is said to be unreal;
however, because there is a cognition that extracts the actual object, a determination of the real object is intended. (PVA 529)
But it is merely through cultivation.
Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon, at the completion of that meditation, results in a cognition that is vivid and free from conceptual construction. (286)

[327,x] For it is not only that which already exists that is cultivated, since even other things can be the object of cultivation. Therefore, if whatever is intensely cultivated results in a clear and non-conceptual cognition, that is indeed "intense cultivation" (abhibhāvana) when the cultivation has reached its perfection. Indeed, cultivation is never seen to result otherwise.

In this regard, that [cognition] which accords with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like an object previously determined, and which arises from the cultivation [of that object], is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); all others are distortions (*upaplava*). (287)

Indeed, that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has as its object only those things previously determined—such as the next world, the four noble truths, and so forth—which, even when cultivated through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are capable of being non-deceptive; it does not have desire and the like as its objects. Because these appear with such vivid clarity, they are merely a cognitive distortion (*upaplava*), even though they are free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). By this, it is established that dream-cognitions and the like, which are deceptive, are certainly not direct perceptions.

But surely, if perceptual knowledge arises from the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it would follow that the consciousness shared by all non-Buddhist sectarians (*tīrthika*) is also perceptual. For it cannot be said that they lack such meditative cultivation. To explain:
Whatever object is common to the world may possibly exist for someone.
Thus, what restriction exists that operates without overstepping logic?

(PVA 530) [328, iii] Consequently, why is it that for those other teachers as well, the masses of categories included within their own elaborate systems—which are established by perception arising from cultivation—do not exist? And therefore, why should one not act according to their instructions? If it is argued that this is not so because they are sublated by inference and other means of knowledge, we say: no.
Those who perceive with the eye of the ṛṣis those things that are beyond the senses and not accessible to ordinary cognition—
their words regarding these entities are not sublated by inference. (PVA 531)

[328,v] Now, it might be argued that it is not known by them whether "this was seen by him. If they do see it, then this statement is not contradicted. If it is asked, "How is it known that even the Blessed One realized the Truths and so forth?"—that is incorrect.
For in the word of the Tathāgata, a correspondence with valid cognition is observed;
whereas in the case of others, there is sublation by valid cognition. Therefore, the Tathāgata is the seer.
But surely, human cognition is non-authoritative regarding supersensible objects; how then can there be proof or refutation of a supersensible object by means of it?
For the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is established only when they have the same object.
And regarding that which is beyond the senses, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates for those wandering in *saṃsāra*.
Even by the knowledge of a yogi, there is only the sublation of those [opposing views]. For it is thus:
Since the word of the Tathāgata is established in contradiction to those [other doctrines],
it should be demonstrated that their words are sublated by the cognition of the reasons [contained therein]. (PVA 534)
This same [argument] applies equally to the contrary case as well. That is incorrect, because:
If a knower were to speak only of supersensuous objects, no wise person whatsoever would act based on his words.
For indeed, everyone possesses speech concerning supersensuous matters. (PVA 535)
Furthermore, because they are mutually contradictory, there can be no application [of both] therein.

Therefore, one who intends to demonstrate something to another must demonstrate only that which is capable of being determined by others. If it is argued that this is not so because of impossibility, then one must consider from where even the knowledge of a yogin could possibly arise in that regard.

[328,xv] If it is argued that "the Veda is established by its own nature, or the yogi is its proponent," then if such a determination exists, how can there be valid cognition regarding this entity? (PVA) 537.
Now, it is incorrect to say that the section on sound is not to be adopted by those seeking it; for the cessation of suffering is not secondary. (538) (PVA) [328,xvii]
Indeed, the complete removal of all suffering is certainly not something that should not be adopted. For it is said:
[328,xviii] Through the obsession with grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, sentient beings encounter suffering.

Upon its disappearance, there arises the dissolution of all sufferings. (PVA 539) If this [cessation] were likewise [the case] for pleasures, then the mere absence of suffering would be the supreme pleasure; provided that one remains experiencing the reversal of suffering at all times. (PVA 540)
Beyond that, what other [state] consistent with reason could be attainable?
If it is argued that it is like the extinction of a lamp, we say no, for that lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
This is because:
[328,xxii] "Indeed, cognition cannot be severed by means of burning, cutting, and so forth."

Then, due to the uninterrupted continuity [of that state], one remains indeed undisturbed. (PVA 542) For one who has entered that state, there would be aversion through discernment; if there is aversion toward what is loathsome, then what contradiction is there? (PVA 543)
For one who perceives equanimity, what cause could there be for aversion?
Since he possesses the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), no afflictions whatsoever can trouble him.
(544) Because he has mastered hunger, pain, and the like, everything is brought under his control.
Consequently, even all the afflictions caused by weapons and the like are perceived by him [through meditation].
(PVA 545) Through the power of cultivation, everything such as valor and fortitude becomes possible;
for without steadfastness, food does not lead to the nourishment of anyone. (PVA 546)
However, for anyone who, through the practice of mental fortitude (*dhṛti*), [seeks] the nourishment of food even without such [external] means, the attainment of this goal is possible;
likewise, the awareness of other births and so forth arises solely from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). (PVA 547)
From that arises knowledge of the fruits of karma, and from that, the perception of everything.
When the causal relationship is specifically and definitively ascertained,
his knowledge of the past and future will become clearly manifest.
If it is argued that knowledge [arising] from the power of cultivation occurs even for outsiders, we accept this;
however, for the Protectors, it possesses all aspects—stable, immediate, momentary, and the realization of selflessness and so forth. (PVA 550)
Because they are distracted by passion and other afflictions, the knowledge of the non-Buddhists is not such [as described].
(PVA 551) The comprehension of the author of such words regarding these matters is like his knowledge;
there is no perfectly pure speech without one who possesses perfectly pure knowledge. (PVA 552)

If this proliferation of various [doctrines] arises from the recollection of one's own reasoning, then even the knowledge resulting from meditative cultivation exists; for there is no disregard for that which has a real object. Therefore, when he is free from passion (*vītarāga*), the possibility of knowing all objects arises.
"It is certain that everything shines forth for one who is concentrated.
(PVA 554) "Why does this not exist for all those who are free from passion?
For they apply effort solely toward the destruction of passion and the like. (PVA 555)
When that [state] has ceased, for those who still harbor the conceit of a self and have not yet achieved their goal,
there is no further effort at that time, as they desire the pleasure of rest. However, later on, for those who possess a longing for the qualities of an omniscient one, [effort arises again].
The attainment of omniscience through slight effort is thus unimpeded.
(557) (PVA) If it is argued that this is like the extinguishing of a lamp, that is not possible;
for how could dispassion arise in a self that is free from afflictions? (558) (PVA)

If even for one who acts with foresight that [pleasure] is desired as something superior, why would he not desire it when it is available? (559) (PVA) There is no pleasure born from the embrace of a woman for one who is free from passion.
But for one free from hatred, how could there be the suffering born from the crushing of an enemy army?
For one free from delusion, there is no pleasure born from attachment to a self.
Therefore, what use would such liberation be for living beings?
Therefore, consider this: drinking liquor and such like acts are likewise unreal.
O twice-born ones, there is no lasting pleasure here in drinking liquor and the like;
it is like the pleasure of city-dwelling pigs in eating excrement. (PVA 562)

Without protection, there is no happiness whatsoever in the accomplishment of non-human goals. (563) (PVA) Does the happiness derived from a master’s favor and the like exist for one who is not a servant? It is not; it would be like the pleasure of having one's head struck by a slave. (564) (PVA)
Thus, all this that has been sought is found among those possessed of resolute faith;
even the union with the hips of one’s mother and so forth does not exist in the land of Aparasīka.
And for one who has not reached the Avīci hell, there is never any happiness derived from separation from those [objects]. (PVA 565)
Then, falling into hell and so forth would be experienced by all living beings.

(PVA 329,xxi) Now, if a distinguished pleasure is intended, then that very thing we desire has arrived. But how is the knowledge of everything possible, or how could there be correspondence with it? Furthermore, if everything were known, how could faults such as passion and the like arise through the direct perception of the passions and minds of others? To this he says:
Because it possesses manifold means and is joined with the vastness of time,
it is logical that he attains omniscience through practice. (567) (PVA)

[329,xxiii] Indeed, what is there that cannot be attained through practice over incalculable eons? Furthermore, we maintain that there is no correspondence regarding the cognition of everything; this is precisely what is intended here. And so it has been said:
[329,xxiv]
Who, not being all-knowing, could possibly describe you, the All-Knowing One? Homage be to you, whose vast majesty is known by yourself!

One who is not omniscient does not know the omniscient one. Likewise: "O monks, let no person judge another person; neither may I judge, nor anyone else who is not of such a kind. However, the claim that an omniscient being knows the passion and so forth of other mental continua in their entirety implies that he possesses passion and so forth himself, which is not the case. For it is as follows:
[329,xxvii] When there is cognition of another's mental continuum, if one perceives that person to be free from passion,
it is utterly impossible to claim that they also possess passion. (PVA 569)

If it is argued that at the very moment this person is possessed of passion when perceiving another’s passion, he is likewise free from passion when perceiving another who is free from passion— and thus both states exist simultaneously— that is not so.
If there is an absence of even a single experience, how can attachment be considered possible?
For one who is a mere bystander, there is no occurrence of being attached or the like.

For instance, when a jar is perceived, it does not become the perceiver. Likewise, even passions (*rāga*) and so forth, when belonging to another's mental continuum and being apprehended from a distance, do not establish the state of being a passionate person.

[330, ii] Now, if it is argued that when there is perception in its entirety, just as he himself knows, so too does the other, and thus there is no loss of the state of being passionate—that is incorrect.
If it were cognizable in that very same form, then since passion would exist in itself,
the cognition of another's passion and so forth could not be established in any way whatsoever. (PVA 571)

For if it does not enter into the nature of that [other person], there can be no cognition of another's passion and so forth; [if one were to argue] that "this very [passion] is one's own," this too is another fault. To explain:
If it were cognized as being external, there would be no cognition of it as such;
but if it were cognized as being of that very nature, the consequence would be nothing other than passion.
That is incorrect; for instance:
by means of passion and so forth residing in another, there occurs a transformation of one's own speech and body.
The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of passion and so forth does not belong to another at all.

For it is passion, arising from the power of its own latent impression, that brings about the state of being impassioned; it is not brought about by the force of another’s latent impression, since it is experienced as something that presents itself as established.
[330,ix] But surely, if there is self-awareness of its own nature, why does this person not experience bodily changes such as horripilation, as well as changes in speech? This is not correct.
This transformation of body and speech arises from the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
for one whose predispositions have been abandoned, neither of these two is possible.

Is it not the case that the cognition of another's mind arises solely from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that cultivation is a formative impression (*saṃskāra*) which is itself a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*)? If such a formative impression of cultivation exists, how could there not be a latent predisposition? For there is no distinction whatsoever between the latent predisposition of cultivation and [cultivation] itself. This is not correct. To explain:
When the specific characteristic of the indicator is perceived with focused intent... [330,xii]
There is a manifestation of a specific quality when there is cognition of another's mind.

(PVA 330, xiii) For in that case, the operation of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists in the discernment of a specific logical mark (*liṅga*). And in that instance, there is no cultivation of the object to be known; or even if there were, it would not be as something related to oneself. Therefore, because there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding that [object], there is no passion (*rāgitā*) even though there is a manifestation.
By this, the objection regarding the perception of impure tastes and so forth has also been answered.
There would be a connection with impurity for this person upon the perception [of an object] by means of a sense faculty produced by karma,
but not by any other [faculty] arising from the power of meditative cultivation.

If it is argued that there is no fault in producing a sensation by generating a relish through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then there would likewise be no fault in sexual intercourse with an unapproachable woman (*agamyā*) in a dream. If you say that there is no fault because that [dream-act] is unreal (*asatya*), how can it be unreal when it corresponds to reality (*saṃvāda*)?
In that case, even a mother’s dream could be of such a nature.
In that case, why would the fault of approaching what is unapproachable not accrue to you?
Therefore, the opponent's position is untenable.
If it is asked, "How can there be the perception of an object that has no beginning if perception occurs sequentially?"— it is not so, because all objects are perceived simultaneously. (PVA 578)
Just as the meaning of an entire treatise, when well-practiced,
appears in the mind in a single moment, so too does the cognition of the infinite and so forth.

For just as the meaning of a treatise, through thorough practice, appears to the mind in a single moment, so too does the beginningless and endless Veda. If it is argued that this is because the treatise possesses a finite measure (*parimāṇavat*), we say no; it is not that the appearance itself has a finite measure, but rather that it arises from practice. If it is further argued that all the subject matter of the treatise has appeared [to him] and thus appears in his memory, we say no; for even previously unknown meanings of the treatise appear [to him].

[Objection: But surely the meaning of the treatises is mutually connected; in that case, by some cause of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), another [meaning] also appears there, yet this is not so for things that are beginningless and endless. How, then, can there be an appearance of the *apūrva*? [Response: This is the same for all [cases]. For it is said:
[331,i] There exists nothing that is not inseparable from the relationship of cause and effect.
Is this proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of things not also present in everyday linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)?

(580) [PVA 331, ii] For in the treatises, the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between things is what constitutes proximity; from that, there is the appearance of the preceding [cause]. And thus it is the same in everyday usage as well. To explain: "This is indeed its transformation; such must be its cause. And that cause is the indirect producer of so many effects.
One who knows the minds of others perceives whether such prior conditions exist for this person, by which his auxiliary causes either do or do not exist. (581) (PVA)
And through the knowledge of previous births and so forth, being connected to one another by way of a continuous succession, he knows them in every respect; thus, he also knows other eons.
(PVA 582) Through the knowledge of the causal relationship [between one eon and the next], there is the arising of one eon from another eon.
"He knows the reality of the entire world and its intermediate state" (PVA 583).

Thus, the knowledge of all objects has been demonstrated by setting aside all [partial] viewpoints (*naya*). Now, let others easily examine even that which follows the [correct] viewpoint here. (PVA 584)
[5] An Investigation of Fallacious Perception (pratyakṣābhāsa-cintā) [331,
viii]

If a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses a clear aspect (*spaṣṭākāra*) through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanābalataḥ*), then it would not be a valid means of knowledge, since a clear aspect is absent [in conceptual cognition]. If, on the other hand, it is held that there is no lack of a clear aspect regarding the object (*artha*), otherwise it would not be a valid means of knowledge, then let it be accepted as such regarding its own nature (*svarūpa*) as well. [Objection: No; its own nature is indeed of a clear aspect, but the object is not so. Therefore, with respect to its own nature, that [cognition] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), whereas with respect to the object, it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); thus, there is recollection (*smaraṇa*) [of the object]. Recollection of the object is perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding its own nature. Why is this? Because it is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*) regarding its own nature, but erroneous regarding the object. This is because one’s own nature is not cognizable by anything else, whereas the form of another is cognized by a different cognition. Consequently, because it cognizes that [object] in a manner other than it is, there is sublation (*bādhā*), and from that, error (*bhrānti*). For recollection is impossible regarding its own nature, since that [nature] arises at that very time and is already experienced. Moreover, if the own nature existed previously but does not exist now, then recollection could not occur now. If, however, recollection occurs now by means of that very [nature], then it follows that even a dead cock must crow. For this very reason, he said: [The verse: "Because of the absence of a clear aspect, conceptual cognition is not a valid means of knowledge. If it is held that there is no lack of a clear aspect regarding the object, then let it be accepted as such regarding its own nature as well. [Commentary: If it is argued that the clear aspect belongs to the object and not to the cognition itself, then the cognition would be conceptual with respect to the object and non-conceptual with respect to its own nature. However, since the own nature is self-cognizing and the object is cognized by another cognition, the cognition is erroneous regarding the object due to the discrepancy between how it is perceived and how it actually exists. Recollection cannot arise regarding the own nature at the time of the original experience, for that nature has already perished. If one claims that the same nature is being recollected now, then one would have to admit that a dead cock can still crow. Thus, the point stands.
Even conceptual construction is admitted [as valid] in regard to self-awareness, but not in regard to the object, because it involves conceptualization;
for its own nature is non-conceptual, and [if it were otherwise], its being beyond perception could not be established. (PVA 585)
Because, by means of that very [cognition], its apprehension is possible through direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
For this very reason, cognition is said to be direct perception (pratyakṣa). Because:
Whatever cognition apprehends the meaning of a word with respect to a certain object, that cognition is conceptual (kalpanā) with respect to that object.
And the intrinsic nature [of a thing] is not the meaning of a word; in that regard, everything is perceived through direct perception. (288)

[331,xiv] Neither the nature of the conceptual nor that of the other is the referent of words, nor is it a universal, nor is it an object of ultimate reality. This being so, because there is an absence of association with words and an absence of connection with universals, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Furthermore, cognition that apprehends the referent of a word is conceptualization (*kalpanā*); therefore, it is indistinct. Why does it not have a clear appearance? It is indeed clear; why then is it said that it is not? [331,xv]
Because of the abandonment of that form, it is described as "unclear.
Let it be understood how there can be an abandonment of its own nature.

It is not possible to abandon one's own nature (*svarūpa*); it has been stated that if that were abandoned, there would be no cognition at all. And thus, there would be neither self-cognition nor cognition of another; indeed, everything would be non-existent. If it is argued that there is cognition through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*), then there is no cognition of one's own nature. No; even for presumptive proof, the nature must be understood precisely through cognition. If there is presumptive proof even here, then that too would require another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the cognition of the object is already established, what is the use of presumptive proof regarding the cognition of the object? If you say, "The object is established, but the cognition of the object is not," then what is this "establishment" of the object? If it is its arising, then there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of cognizing all objects. If it is the knowledge of the object, then this is the meaning: "From the knowledge of the object, there is the cognition of the knowledge of the object"—this is a fine way of speaking! If it is argued that the cognition of the knowledge of the object arises from the object itself making itself known, then what is this "knowability" of the object? If it is appearing within the knowledge, how is the appearance of knowledge known when [the object] is unknown, or when it is known? If you say, "An object that appears is precisely perceptible (*pratyakṣa*)," then let it be so established as perceptible; why postulate something else? This very thing would be perceptible otherwise if knowledge were not perceptible. If this occurs when the eye is active and not otherwise, what is the use of knowledge? If you say, "Perception is the functioning of the ear and other senses," then what is this "functioning of the ear and others"? If it is knowledge, then how is that knowledge known if it is beyond perception (*parokṣa*)? If you say, "The functioning of the ear and others is itself knowledge," then the functioning of the ear and others is perceptible, but by what is the knowledge known? If you ask, "Otherwise, what is the point of the manifestation of the ear and others?"—do entities come into being depending on your purpose?
The existence of entities arises solely from their causes, not from a purpose. Otherwise, according to your view, existence would not occur even when a purpose is absent. (PVA 587)

[332,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld the sufferings of those beings and, by means of his great compassionate heart, manifested himself in various forms to deliver them from their distress. If there were those bound in fetters, he would manifest as a monk to liberate them from their bonds. If there were those suffering from various diseases, he would manifest as a physician to cure them of their ailments. If there were those who had lost their way, he would manifest as a guide to lead them back to the right path. If there were those who were impoverished and lacked the necessities of life, he would manifest as a wealthy man to provide them with all that they required. If there were those who were terrified by robbers and bandits, he would manifest as a powerful hero to protect them from fear. If there were those who were about to fall into the evil realms, he would manifest as a spiritual friend to encourage them to cultivate wholesome deeds. If there were those who were about to commit the five heinous crimes or the ten unwholesome paths of action, he would manifest as a king to restrain them from such evil. If there were those who were about to engage in sexual misconduct, he would manifest as a father or mother to prevent them from such transgression. If there were those who were about to steal the property of others, he would manifest as a watchman to stop them from taking what was not given. If there were those who were about to kill living beings, he would manifest as a compassionate being to dissuade them from taking life. If there were those who were about to speak falsehoods, he would manifest as a witness to cause them to speak the truth. If there were those who were about to engage in divisive speech, he would manifest as a mediator to reconcile their differences. If there were those who were about to speak harsh words, he would manifest as a gentle person to cause them to speak kindly. If there were those who were about to engage in idle chatter, he would manifest as a teacher of the Dharma to cause them to speak meaningfully. If there were those who were about to harbor covetousness, he would manifest as a contented person to cause them to abandon greed. If there were those who were about to harbor ill will, he would manifest as a benevolent person to cause them to abandon malice. If there were those who held wrong views, he would manifest as a wise person to cause them to abandon delusion. In this manner, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, through his great compassionate heart, manifests in various forms to deliver sentient beings from suffering. Those who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara shall be liberated from all fears. Those who keep his name in mind shall be freed from all calamities. Those who offer him worship and praise shall attain supreme enlightenment. Therefore, you should all single-mindedly take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. He is able to grant protection to all who call upon him. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa at Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. Among them were many great śrāvakas, such as the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bāṣpa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Kapphiṇa, the Venerable Ānanda, and so forth—great śrāvakas of such kind, numbering twelve thousand. Also present were many bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, such as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, and so forth—bodhisattvas mahāsattvas of such kind, numbering eight thousand. Furthermore, there were many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other human and non-human beings, all gathered around the Buddha. At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, if there are good sons or good daughters who wish to cultivate the practice of Avalokiteśvara, they should always recite his name. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great power and great compassion; he can deliver sentient beings from all sufferings. [End of Fascicle 332] Fascicle 333. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "Bhagavān, for what reason does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bear this name? The Buddha told Ānanda: "If there are sentient beings who are bound in fetters, whether they be kings, ministers, or commoners, and they are imprisoned in jail, if they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately be released from their bonds. If there are those who are about to be executed, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, their swords shall break and their weapons shall shatter, and they shall not suffer death. If there are those who are about to be burned in fire, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the fire shall be extinguished and they shall not suffer the heat. If there are those who are about to be drowned in water, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the water shall part and they shall not suffer drowning. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter fierce winds and waves, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately reach the shore of safety. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter sea monsters, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the sea monsters shall not harm them. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter demons, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the demons shall not harm them. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter thieves, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the thieves shall not harm them. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter dragons, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the dragons shall not harm them. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter fish, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the fish shall not harm them. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter crocodiles, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the crocodiles shall not harm them. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter whirlpools, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately escape the whirlpool. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter storms, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the storm shall immediately subside. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter rain, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the rain shall immediately cease. If there are those who are traveling on the great ocean and encounter lightning, and they can single-mindedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the lightning shall immediately vanish. If there are those who are traveling on the great

Even if [the object] does not come face-to-face with the auditory organ, what has happened to the cognition? If cognition had not arisen, the object would remain merely beyond perception (*parokṣa*). If cognition has arisen, what has happened to the object? Even so, it would still be merely beyond perception. For the arising of cognition is not the perceptibility of the object; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the object remains beyond perception, since [the arising of cognition] itself is beyond perception. But if it is observed [to be perceived], then let it be exactly as it is observed. If you ask, "How is that so for you as well?", [the answer is: it is the "knownness" (*jñātatva*) of the object, which consists in the cognition having the form of that [object]. And that [knownness] is accessible through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), not through another cognition possessing that same form, by which an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would ensue. Therefore, it is logical that self-awareness alone is the means of establishing the nature of cognition.

[332,iii] If, then, perception that has attained clarity through the power of cultivation is indeed obtained as perception, and non-contradiction also exists therein—since there too one attains the destination of one's journey—this is not so. Why?

Erroneous cognition, conventional cognition, inference and its result, memory, and desire— these, along with that which is accompanied by visual impairment, are pseudo-perceptions. (588) (PVA) [332,v]
Conceptual cognition that appears as direct perception is of two kinds: erroneous and non-erroneous. Furthermore, it is fourfold. As it is said:
"The three types of conceptual cognition arise from the affliction of the basis."
And non-conceptual [perception] is of one kind; thus, there are four types that resemble direct perception.

[332, vii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “What are the four? “Here, Ānanda, one person is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. Another person is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. Another person is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And another person is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. “Among these, Ānanda, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is one who practices for his own benefit but does not practice for the benefit of others. The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is one who practices for the benefit of others but does not practice for his own benefit. The person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others. And the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. “Among these, Ānanda, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is inferior; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is middling; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is the lowest of all; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is the best of all. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking these words: ‘Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world…’” When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement made by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is one who practices for his own benefit but does not practice for the benefit of others’? “Friend, it is in reference to the Pratyekabuddha that this was said by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is one who practices for his own benefit but does not practice for the benefit of others. “But friend, how is it that the Pratyekabuddha practices for his own benefit but does not practice for the benefit of others? “Friend, the Pratyekabuddha, having realized the Dharma for himself alone, does not teach the Dharma to others. It is in this way, friend, that the Pratyekabuddha practices for his own benefit but does not practice for the benefit of others. “Friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement made by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is one who practices for the benefit of others but does not practice for his own benefit’? “Friend, it is in reference to the Bodhisattva that this was said by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is one who practices for the benefit of others but does not practice for his own benefit. “But friend, how is it that the Bodhisattva practices for the benefit of others but does not practice for his own benefit? “Friend, the Bodhisattva, while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, does not seek the attainment of parinirvāṇa for himself. It is in this way, friend, that the Bodhisattva practices for the benefit of others but does not practice for his own benefit. “Friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement made by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others’? “Friend, it is in reference to the icchantika that this was said by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others. “But friend, how is it that the icchantika practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others? “Friend, the icchantika has severed all roots of goodness and lacks the seed of enlightenment. It is in this way, friend, that the icchantika practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others. “Friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement made by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others’? “Friend, it is in reference to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, that this was said by the Blessed One: ‘The person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. “But friend, how is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others? “Friend, the Tathāgata, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, teaches the Dharma to others. It is in this way, friend, that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. “Friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement made by the Blessed One: ‘Among these, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is inferior; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is middling; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is the lowest of all; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is the best of all’? “Friend, it is in reference to the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata, respectively, that this was said by the Blessed One. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, it is wonderful, it is marvelous, how well this teaching of the Dharma has been spoken by the Blessed One! For indeed, friend, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the best of all. “Indeed, friend Kāśyapa, it is so. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the best of all. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Those monks were satisfied and delighted in the Venerable Ānanda’s words. [332, viii] At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was seated not far from the Blessed One. Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful, it is marvelous, how well this teaching of the Dharma has been spoken by the Blessed One! For indeed, Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the best of all. “Kāśyapa, it is so. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the best of all. “Blessed One, what is the reason, what is the cause, why the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the best of all? “Kāśyapa, because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and because he teaches the Dharma to others, he is the best of all. “Blessed One, what is the reason, what is the cause, why the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has fully awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? “Kāśyapa, because the Tathāgata has fully understood, as they really are, the nature of all phenomena—whether they be conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, tainted or untainted, with outflows or without outflows, with taints or without taints, with grasping or without grasping, with attachment or without attachment, with clinging or without clinging, with obstruction or without obstruction, with darkness or without darkness, with light or without light, with darkness and light or without darkness and light, with form or without form, with perception or without perception, with neither perception nor non-perception, conditioned or unconditioned, past, future, or present

That very [perception] is of two kinds; through a threefold division, it becomes fourfold. Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpodha*); therefore, all three types of conceptual construction are pseudo-perceptions (*pratyakṣābhāsa*). Among these, erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*)—such as that regarding a mirage—is a pseudo-perception because it functions through the conceptualization of water and so forth. This is because, with respect to things existing only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), it functions through the conceptualization of their form by superimposing something else upon them. Cognition of inference, its result, and so on, is not perception because it involves the conceptualization of what was previously experienced. However, the appearance of a shimmering mass of rays of light is indeed perception; the conceptualization of water and such is pseudo-perception, because it lacks the mode of direct apprehension (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) regarding water. Even in the case of conventionally existent things, perception consists merely in the grasping of color-form (*rūpa*) and the like. As for the "whole" (*avayavin*), however, there is no direct apprehension of it, because one superimposes another object—such as touch—which was previously seen, onto that which is intended to be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of it; or rather, it is a substance imagined through a series of preceding cognitions. A "whole" never appears in perception apart from color-form and the rest. Inferential cognition is the cognition of a mark (*liṅga*); its result is the cognition of the mark, which does not exist without a prior experience. And this inferential cognition is sometimes non-perceptual, but sometimes it is indeed perception, as in the sudden realization of fire from smoke. For in that case, there is no conceptualization of a prior experience. If it is asked, "How can there be a cognition of the mark without conceptualization?", [the answer is: "Because it is seen exactly so. Indeed, it is not logical for what has been seen to be otherwise.

[333,i] But why is there an exposition of the different types of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)? If it is argued that this is for the sake of elaborating examples, we say no, because there is no difference in their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, if one were to provide a mere enumeration of elaborations, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is not the case; there is another purpose. To explain: [333,ii]
The two [types of perception] were stated for the purpose of establishing that [perception] is not produced by words, because of the observation of error;
the mention of inference and so forth is established only for the sake of proving those two preceding ones. (290)

[333,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either real or unreal, nor does he perceive a dharma that is wholesome or unwholesome, nor does he perceive a dharma that is worldly or supramundane, nor does he perceive a dharma that is with outflows or without outflows, nor does he perceive a dharma that is conditioned or unconditioned, nor does he perceive a dharma that is common or uncommon, nor does he perceive a dharma that is a śrāvaka-dharma or a pratyekabuddha-dharma, nor does he perceive a dharma that is a bodhisattva-dharma or a buddha-dharma. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of the non-apprehension of all dharmas. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; he does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive the element of space, nor does he perceive the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive volitional formations, nor does he perceive consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or old age and death. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, nor does he perceive the fruit of a non-returner, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship, nor does he perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, nor does he perceive the fruit of buddhahood. Why is that? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out on the path? For what purpose does he train in the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? For what purpose does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? For what purpose does he train in the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the scattered, the emptiness of the unscattered, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of other-nature? For what purpose does he train in the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion? For what purpose does he train in the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks? For what purpose does he train in the dhāraṇī-doors and the samādhi-doors? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is for the sake of the benefit and happiness of the world, including its gods, humans, and asuras, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out on the path. It is for the sake of the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, happiness, and welfare of gods and humans, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. It is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. It is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the scattered, the emptiness of the unscattered, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of other-nature. It is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion. It is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks. It is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the dhāraṇī-doors and the samādhi-doors. Subhūti, it is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out on the path, and it is for the sake of the purification of the field of merit that he trains in the six perfections, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, the great compassion, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty minor marks. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the purification of the field of merit, how does he purify the field of merit? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the field of merit by means of the non-purification of all dharmas. Why is that? Subhūti, all these dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, he purifies the field of merit. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the field of merit by means of the non-perception of the giver, the receiver, and the gift. Why is that? Subhūti, because the three spheres are non-existent and unapprehendable. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the three spheres are non-existent and unapprehendable, he purifies the field of merit. Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva purifies the field of merit by means of the non-perception of the field of merit itself. Why is that? Subhūti, because the field of merit is non-existent and unapprehendable.
