The opponents’ delusion that this [cognition] is indeed produced by the senses is like the cognition of water in a mirage. For instance, in the definition: “Perception is cognition produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbalizable and non-erroneous,” the term “non-erroneous” (*avyabhicāri*) was included in order to exclude the cognition of water in a mirage. If, however, that [mirage-cognition] were not produced by the senses at all, it would have been excluded by the very first word [“produced by a sense-organ”]; what then would be the purpose of including the term “non-erroneous”? If it is argued that it is for the sake of excluding cognitions such as that of two moons, which lack a real object (*anarthasaṃbhūta*), we say no. Such cases are already excluded by the inclusion of the phrase “contact with an object” (*arthasannikarṣa*). The inclusion of the word “sense-organ” (*indriya*) excludes what is not produced by the senses. As for the opponents’ conceit that [cognitions] having conventionally real objects (*saṃvṛtisat*) are produced by the senses, that is indeed a matter of dispute. In that case, the mention of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth would be redundant; for inference and the rest do not establish that [the object] is not produced by the senses, since the fact that inference and so forth are not produced by the senses is already established. To this, it is replied:
Even though inference and the like are already established, they are included because they serve as means of proof;
for in every case, there is a need for an established example. (PVA 589)
For that which is unestablished is not proven by means of what is unestablished. If it is asked, "What is the cause of error here, such that the two preceding [reasons] are to be proven? he says:

In the conceptualization that superimposes another object based on linguistic convention, there may occasionally be a cause for error because [the concept] does not exclude what is present to direct perception. (291)

[333, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is a victim of both past and future actions; the person who is a victim of past actions but not of future actions; the person who is a victim of future actions but not of past actions; and the person who is a victim of neither past nor future actions. And how, monks, is one a person who is a victim of both past and future actions? Here, monks, a certain person has previously committed an unwholesome deed and later performs an unwholesome deed again. This person, monks, is called one who is a victim of both past and future actions. And how, monks, is one a person who is a victim of past actions but not of future actions? Here, monks, a certain person has previously committed an unwholesome deed but later performs a wholesome deed. This person, monks, is called one who is a victim of past actions but not of future actions. And how, monks, is one a person who is a victim of future actions but not of past actions? Here, monks, a certain person has not previously committed an unwholesome deed but later performs an unwholesome deed. This person, monks, is called one who is a victim of future actions but not of past actions. And how, monks, is one a person who is a victim of neither past nor future actions? Here, monks, a certain person has not previously committed an unwholesome deed and does not later perform an unwholesome deed. This person, monks, is called one who is a victim of neither past nor future actions. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One further said this: "One who has done evil in the past and continues to do so now, That person is called 'a victim of both past and future. But one who has done evil in the past and now does what is good, That person is called 'a victim of past actions, but not of the future. One who has not done evil in the past but now does what is evil, That person is called 'a victim of future actions, but not of the past. But one who has not done evil in the past and does not do what is evil now, That person is called 'a victim of neither past nor future. Thus have I heard. [as above] ...that person is called 'a victim of neither past nor future actions. Thus spoke the Blessed One. The whole (*avayavin*) is dependent upon convention (*saṅketa*), because it is convention alone that serves as the basis for its establishment. "Water" refers to another object. "Superimposition" (*samāropa*) is an excessive attribution (*adhikādhyāropa*). "Conceptualization" (*vikalpana*) is recollection (*smaraṇa*); for water is remembered because it was previously perceived. It is not merely the superimposition [of the word] upon that [object], since perception exists equally [with respect to both]. Alternatively, "superimposition" is the error [regarding] water, while "conceptualization" is [the cognition of] the whole. Or, in both cases, both [apply]. And those two—superimposition and conceptualization—do not at any time fail to occur when perception arising from the sense faculties is not present; thus, this non-exclusion of the absent, or that very [non-exclusion], is the cause of error therein. When this cause of error exists, there is inference by way of an example.
Just as this conceptualization of an imperceptible object, such as memory and the like, depends upon convention and does not determine the object through direct perception. (292)

Likewise, without the recollection of what was previously experienced, there would be no continuous cognition regarding jars and other objects; and that [recollection] is lost through direct perception. (293)

[333,x] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. This, Subhūti, is the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift without perceiving a donor, a recipient, or a thing given. This, Subhūti, is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of giving while practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of morality? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, observes morality without perceiving a transgression or a non-transgression. This, Subhūti, is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of morality while practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of patience? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, generates patience without perceiving an object of anger or a person who is angry. This, Subhūti, is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of patience while practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, exerts vigor without perceiving a body or a mind. This, Subhūti, is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of vigor while practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of concentration? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, enters into meditative concentration without perceiving a state of concentration or one who is concentrated. This, Subhūti, is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of concentration while practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. This, Subhūti, is the training of a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom while practicing the perfection of wisdom.”

For conceptualization such as inference depends upon the apprehension of a relation, and the apprehension of that relation itself is the convention (*samaya*). Therefore, the cognition of an imperceptible object arises from that relation, not through direct perception (*adhyakṣa*); for that [cognition] would have to occur through immediate intuition (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). In this way, even regarding jars and the like, once color and so forth have been perceived by some sense organ, there subsequently follows a recollection of taste and so forth based on the remainder, in accordance with previous experience. If it is argued that there is recollection only of taste and so forth, and not of the whole (*avayavin*), we say no; for that [whole] is not observed apart from taste and the other qualities. If it is argued that the whole is the object of the cognition of identity—such as "that which is white is the same as that which is rough"—[we reply: it is not the case that there is identity between color and touch.

[334,i] Consequently, there would either be no cognition of unity at all if the whole (*avayavin*) did not exist; or, even if the whole exists, how could there be grammatical co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between color, touch, and so forth? For these two [qualities] do not possess identity. If it is argued that they are one because they have a single substratum, this is merely a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Moreover, there is no apprehension of such a metaphor here; for if there were an apprehension of the metaphor, the whole would not be established, since co-referentiality can occur through metaphor even otherwise. [334,ii]
Because they do not occupy the same location, because they are employed for a single purpose,
and because one undergoes modification when the other does, their identity is designated.

The very same location that is perceived for touch is also perceived for color; therefore, there is a determination of their identity. That which is the effect of touch—namely, the supporting of water and so forth—is precisely where the operation of color also occurs. When the tangible object is rendered smooth, the color also possesses qualities such as glossiness. Consequently, from the linguistic convention and the determination [of experience], there arises the notion: "This is indeed one. If, however, the substratum were something else entirely, then that substratum would have to be perceived separately from color and the other [qualities], through a distinct cognition. But what is not perceived, even though it meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), is non-existent. Now, why is it that these [qualities] do not fall apart from one another in the absence of a whole (*avayavin*)?
[334,iv] Even if there were a whole (*avayavin*), why would this [dissociation] not occur among the triad?
By virtue of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), let that [relation] also be subject to separation. (591) (PVA)
If this very nature is [already present], then why is it said at the outset:
"This is the nature of form and the other [sensory objects], which arises from its own cause"?
Consider this: how can there be such a thing as an eternal inherence?

Even if the whole (*avayavin*) is something distinct, why does this triad [of parts, qualities, and the whole] not disintegrate, since all three are equally [distinct]? If you say that *inherence* (*samavāya*) is the cause of their non-disintegration, then why does that [inherence] itself not disintegrate? To say "its very nature is such" is no answer; let that nature belong to color and the rest themselves—what is the point of postulating a separate entity? It is logical to hold that the nature of color and the rest arises from their own causes. But how can there be a nature for inherence, which is itself causeless? If you argue that the nature of the substratum of inherence arises from its own cause, such that inherence is thus [non-disintegrating], then what is the use of this succession? Those [parts] must possess such a nature by virtue of their own causes so that inherence may effect their non-disintegration. Since the cause of those [parts] is itself the cause of their non-disintegration, what is lacking here for which a succession is sought? If you say, "This is seen to be so," then let it be so, provided it is actually seen, for it is impossible to conceptualize what is being perceived otherwise. However, only color and the rest are seen as mutually inseparable, and nothing additional to them; therefore, let it be imagined that this nature belongs to these alone. Consequently, the superimposition of a "whole" is not perceptual.

[334, viii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as coarse or subtle nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, O monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking birth. Furthermore, O monks, what is physical food as nutriment? It is that which is called "food," whether it be boiled rice, roasted grain, wheat, barley, beans, lentils, sesame, millet, wild rice, or whatever else is considered edible by being chewed, swallowed, or consumed. This, O monks, is called physical food as nutriment. What, O monks, is contact as nutriment? Whatever contact there is—whether of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind—this, O monks, is called contact as nutriment. What, O monks, is mental volition as nutriment? Whatever volition there is—whether directed toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena—this, O monks, is called mental volition as nutriment. What, O monks, is consciousness as nutriment? Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—this, O monks, is called consciousness as nutriment. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this consciousness were not to exist, would name-and-form be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for name-and-form, namely consciousness. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this name-and-form were not to exist, would contact be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for contact, namely name-and-form. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this contact were not to exist, would feeling be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for feeling, namely contact. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this feeling were not to exist, would craving be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for craving, namely feeling. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this craving were not to exist, would clinging be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for clinging, namely craving. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this clinging were not to exist, would becoming be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for becoming, namely clinging. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this becoming were not to exist, would birth be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for birth, namely becoming. Then, O monks, one should reflect thus: "If this birth were not to exist, would aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair be manifest? "No, indeed, Blessed One. "Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, this is the causal basis for aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, namely birth. Thus, O monks, from the cessation of this very nutriment comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of contact; from the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; from the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; from the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; from the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming; from the cessation of becoming comes the cessation of birth; from the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, O monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. This, O monks, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This, O monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The presentation of the example and the illustrated case is for the purpose of demonstrating this detailed exposition of the system. For what purpose is the mention of "one with cataracts" (*sataimirika*)? Someone might argue that even a vision affected by cataracts is conceptual (*savikalpaka*); it is mentioned for the sake of excluding that view. Otherwise, since such a perception would already be included under the category of "recollection" (*smārta*) and so forth, its separate inclusion would be redundant. If [it were argued that] non-conceptual [perception] is established as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), [we reply: not everything that is free from conceptual construction is direct perception; rather, it must also be non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). Thus, "direct perception is non-erroneous and free from conceptual construction," not everything [that is free from conceptual construction]. Why? Because the general rule (*utsarga*) operates only after the scope of exceptions (*apavāda*) has been conceptually set aside. If it is asked, "What is the exception? [the answer follows].
[334,ix] Here, the fourth [type of error] is denial (apavāda); therefore, it is said to be born from impairment.
In that context, however, "timira" (darkness/blindness) is merely an indicative mark for impairment.

[334,x] From among the three types of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the inclusion of the fourth—namely, the apprehension by one with cataracts—is the exception (*apavāda*). "Free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is the general prescription for perception; "by one free from cataracts" (*ataimira*) is the prescription for the state of being a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsatā*) in the specific case. And that which is prescribed specifically sublates what is prescribed generally. What is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for this? The cognition of the general is sublated by the cognition of the specific. For: [334,xi]
When an inference *śeṣavat* proceeds against the opponent based merely on the absence of prior observation and the mere quality of being free from conceptual construction,
there is a clear sublation of that [inference] which has become excessively overextended with respect to its specific [subject]. (593) (PVA)
Therefore, its occurrence as that former [entity] is in that very same other [entity].

For an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) is not sublated by another perception or inference merely because the [probandum] is not seen in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, it is established by perception. The relationship of sublation and being sublated (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) exists between the particular and the universal; that same relationship of sublation and being sublated also exists between the two statements that indicate those respective objects. If this is so, why did the Teacher state the definition [of perception] based on inference from general observation? It is not that the Teacher intended only inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣato dṳṣṭam*); rather, because its meaning cannot be indicated by a single statement, he did not state it without including an exception (*apavāda*). Why, then, was the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) not stated together with the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), instead of adopting the "bathing of an elephant" approach? There is no difference [in result]: the purpose of the term "non-erroneous" is obtained either through the exception consisting of the term "accompanied by darkness" (*sataimira*) or otherwise. If you argue that the term "free from conceptual construction" should have been obtained immediately [after the definition], we say no, because there is no difference [in the outcome].
For in reality, there is no immediate succession between things that are dissimilar; it is not a cause.

And the reason for doing so is that the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*)— which is the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— is indicated; for it is not necessarily the case that the sublator occurs immediately after.

If it is asked, "Why not simply employ the term 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*) alone?"—this is true. For perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed direct apprehension (*sākṣātkārin*), and that can be demonstrated by the term "non-erroneous. For that which does not have the form of direct apprehension cannot be non-erroneous, because conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is erroneous. However, others maintain that even conceptual cognition, when it has the form of direct apprehension, is non-erroneous. It is with respect to this view that these two [terms] are stated. Thus he says: "In the definition of the qualifier, however, all [cognitions] are indeed non-conceptual, with reference to the views of others. Alternatively, [335,v]
The entire system of the sublated and the sublator depends upon the cognizer.
One who has not previously perceived a sublation first understands [the object] in a general way.

One does not understand the teacher’s intention, thinking that "this specific point is intended here. However, even he later understands the specific point upon seeing a sublater (*bādhaka*). But in the case of a non-human (Vedic) word, because it lacks a foundation in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no relationship of the sublated and the sublater. In the case of a human [word], however, the falsity of the prior cognition is made known by a subsequent cognition rooted in a means of valid cognition. But from the Veda, the arising of a false cognition does not occur; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything would be true simply because the Veda is authoritative. If it is argued that [the Veda] is indeed a means of valid cognition as long as it is not sublated, we say: No, because a sublater may still occur later on. If it is argued that when one reflects further, a different meaning arises, and thus the same applies to the means of valid cognition, we say: No, because a means of valid cognition is stable. Consequently, the proponents of the Veda must abandon the scriptural meaning that contradicts the means of valid cognition. Otherwise, the explanation of [certain passages as] mere explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) would be groundless. Therefore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublater exists only in the case of human speech. If it is argued that only "timira" (a visual disorder) is the sublater, and not "kāmalā" (jaundice) and so forth, he says: Everything has been stated by him to be produced by an impairment. Furthermore, "timira" is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of impairment; it does not exclude other types of impairment. For: *(The verse follows)*
Because it is devoid of an object and because it is not a direct realization,
the status of being a semblance of perception is assigned, thereby negating its status as true perception. (PVA 596)

Furthermore, that emptiness of objects is not diminished by even a fraction for those whose power of vision is impaired by the thick veil of passion; therefore, it should be understood by proponents of right reasoning that this perception is a grasping accompanied by a visual disorder (*taimira*). Here, "visual disorder" is an indicator of every kind of impairment.

Others, however, hold that the mention of "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is merely a counter-example and not an exception. Thus he says: "[335,x] Some say that even that is mental; for them, the text is contradicted."
This [argument] that even the sense organs are the cause of cognitions such as the blue or the double moon— 295.

This cognition of two moons and so forth is purely mental, like the cognition of water in a mirage. For instance, in the case of mirages, first there arises a non-erroneous sensory cognition; subsequently, however, due to the awakening of the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for the experience of water, there arises a conceptual cognition of water. And that—

Awakening occurs from the very sight of the mirage; the rays of light, possessing similarity, have such a nature. Likewise here too, there is first a non-erroneous cognition regarding the moon, followed by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form of two moons.

Regarding this, some say: "The single moon situated between the eyes of one with steady vision is perceived as if simultaneously on both sides due to the subtlety of time; and thus the superimposition of duality upon the two sides occurs. Their view contradicts the scriptural texts.
"Even though atoms are the cause of sensory cognition, because they do not appear as such, those atoms are not its object, just as the sense organs are not. (PVA 597)

For it is those very atoms of the eye and so forth, existing both in that state and otherwise, which are the causes for the appearance of two moons, blue, and so on. Indeed, if the manifestation of two moons were purely mental, the statement that it has the sense organ as its cause would not be tenable.

Now, if it is mental in nature, the fact that the sense organ is an indirect cause is not contradicted. However, the fact that the sense organ is a direct cause is contradicted by its being mental, as in the case of the cognition of two moons. To this it is replied:
"If it is an indirect cause with respect to the object-domain of sensory cognition..."
When this is being investigated, what kind of scope for mental activity is there here? (296)

[336, vii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking birth. What are these four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is edible food, coarse or subtle? It is that which is taken by mouthfuls, whether it be masticated or swallowed. What is contact as the second? It is the contact of the six sense bases. What is mental volition as the third? It is the mental volition directed toward the three realms of existence. What is consciousness as the fourth? It is the sixfold consciousness. Furthermore, O monks, if there were no edible food, coarse or subtle, would the embryo enter the mother's womb? No, indeed, Blessed One. If there were no contact, would the craving for existence arise? No, indeed, Blessed One. If there were no mental volition, would karma leading to rebirth be performed and accumulated? No, indeed, Blessed One. If there were no consciousness, would name-and-form descend into the mother's womb? No, indeed, Blessed One. Therefore, O monks, this is the cause, this is the condition, this is the origin, and this is the causal basis for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking birth. Thus, O monks, when one sees with right wisdom according to reality, as it truly is, the arising of the world, the cessation of the world, the gratification of the world, the danger of the world, and the escape from the world, then, O monks, one becomes disenchanted with the world, dispassionate toward the world, and through dispassion, one is liberated. Upon liberation, there is the knowledge: "I am liberated. One understands: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Thus, O monks, these four noble truths have been fully realized by me through direct knowledge. And having fully realized them, I claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, its generation of ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; and I teach the Dharma to others. And this, O monks, is the first wheel of Dharma set in motion by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, its generation of ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—a wheel that cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. Furthermore, O monks, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perceives that a certain person possesses the faculties capable of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, he teaches the Dharma to that person concerning the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. When that person hears the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, they understand the noble truth of suffering as it really is, they understand the noble truth of the origin of suffering as it really is, they understand the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as it really is, and they understand the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. Having understood these, their vision regarding the Four Noble Truths becomes clear and purified. Just as, O monks, a cloth that is clean, bright, and free from stains, when placed in a dye-vat, would take on the dye perfectly, even so, O monks, when a person possesses the faculties capable of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, and the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to them concerning the Four Noble Truths, they understand the Four Noble Truths as they really are. Having understood them, their vision regarding the Four Noble Truths becomes clear and purified. This, O monks, is the second wheel of Dharma set in motion by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One... [and so on, repeating the process for the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship]. And this, O monks, is the fourth wheel of Dharma set in motion by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, its generation of ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—a wheel that cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. Furthermore, O monks, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, perceives that a certain person possesses the faculties capable of attaining the fruit of stream-entry, he teaches the Dharma to that person concerning the Four Noble Truths. When that person hears the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, they understand the Four Noble Truths as they really are. Having understood them, their vision regarding the Four Noble Truths becomes clear and purified. At that time, O monks, the Tathāgata knows: "This person will attain parinirvāṇa in this very life. And at that time, O monks, the Tathāgata does not know: "After passing away, this person will be reborn in such and such a place. This, O monks, is the fifth wheel of Dharma set in motion by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One... [and so on]. When it is asked, "What is the object (*gocara*) of sensory cognition? the opponent must state whether [the object] is that from which sensory cognition arises directly, by way of assuming its form (*tadākāratayā*), or otherwise. First, it cannot be the object by way of assuming its form, because that is impossible; for atoms lack the grossness (*sthūlatva*) of a single, unified form. Now, if it is argued that even that which does not assume its form is the object insofar as it is the cause [of the cognition], that too is incorrect. Just like the sense organ itself, there would be no status as an object even if it were a cause of a cognition with a different form. In this regard, if the Master’s statement beginning with "for those very [atoms]" intends a causal relationship through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*), then he should not have implied the status of the sense organ as an object toward the opponent. This is because the opponent has already asserted that atoms are the object when they are the direct cause. If that is so, one should say that the reductio (*prasaṅga*) itself is not logical. Why, then, is it said: "What kind of occasion is there here for mental [cognition]? The intention is as follows: [The opponent argues: If the atoms are the direct cause of the visual cognition, then they should be its object, since the opponent has stated that being an object consists in being the direct cause. If, however, the atoms are the cause of the mental cognition only indirectly, then they are not its object, just as the sense organ is not. Therefore, the Master’s statement—"For those very [atoms]..."—is intended to show that the atoms are the cause of the mental cognition only through a mediated succession, and thus they are not its object. If this is the case, then the Master’s words do not imply that the sense organ is the object of the visual cognition. Consequently, the objection regarding the status of the sense organ as an object is not applicable. Thus, the question "What kind of occasion is there here for mental [cognition]? is raised to clarify the context. This is the underlying intention.
[336, viii] The initial appearance consists of atoms mutually distinct;
however, from conceptual cognition, there arises the manifestation of a dense form. (PVA 598)

[336,ix] An opponent says: "The appearance as a single, solid mass belongs to conceptual cognition; because atoms are its cause through a continuous succession, they are its object, just as an external object is the object of memory. The Master says:
Because it does not appear as that [object], its atoms are not its object, unlike the sense-faculties.

Just as the sense organs (*akṣa*), despite being causes through a succession of steps, are not the object [of cognition], so too are atoms. For otherwise, the sense organs would be the indirect cause of the cognition of two moons. Regarding this, it has been said: "When the domain of sensory cognition is being investigated, what occasion is there here for mental [cognition]? Furthermore, if it were mental, the determination of its object would not be valid, because it would be objectless. Thus, the Master’s correct response is that "there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever in this case," rather than the objection regarding an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). That very point was stated by the words "what occasion is there here for mental [cognition]," and so forth.

Others, however, say: "When one states that the sense faculties are the cause for a mental cognition such as the perception of two moons, then the consideration of 'having an object' (prativiṣayatva) would apply only to the mental [cognition]. Therefore, what kind of context is this? This response has been shown to be incorrect. Or rather: "If that which conforms to the presence or absence of the senses is sensory..."
If it is argued that [the self] is similar to that [body] and possesses transformation, then why is this very [transformation] not denied? (297)

If, first of all, this cognition of two moons and so forth were mental (*mānasa*), it would not conform to the presence or absence of the sense faculty. Alternatively, even if it conforms to the presence or absence of the sense faculty, if it were nonetheless purely mental, then it would follow that cognitions of pillars and the like would also be mental. If [you argue] that the cognition first possesses its own form and only subsequently acquires the form of the object within the mind, then it follows that the mind itself is the sense faculty. If you claim that even for the sensory [cognition] there is a modification [of the mind], then it follows that both [types of cognition] are produced by the sense faculty. If you say "because it is direct," no; for no other modification is observed. If you say that the [sensory cognition] must be known as modified in accordance with this [mental cognition], then since that too is purely mental because it is modified in the same way as this one, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, this [cognition of two moons] alone is produced by the sense faculty.
And like the error regarding a snake and so forth, there would be a cessation of this [error] even when there is no defect in the sense organs;
it would not cease even when the impairment of the sense organs has been removed. (298)

If it is argued that mental cognition of two moons and the like ceases even when there is no impairment of the sense organ—since the delusion of a snake ceases upon investigation despite the presence of a sensory defect, whereas the delusion of two moons does not—then [we reply]: even the delusion of a snake, characterized by its dark color and so forth, does not cease. For in a dark place, the delusion of a snake arises because the rope and such objects possess a dark form even without ophthalmia (*timira*); yet, when ophthalmia is removed, even though the eyes have returned to their normal state, the dark form remains. How then could that [darkness] cease even when the sensory defect is gone? Therefore, since the cessation [of the delusion] is unproven, how can it serve as a valid proof?

As for what might be said—that [the error] would not cease even when the sensory defect has ceased—that too is incorrect. For a delusion of water in the mind is never observed in one whose sensory defect has ceased; this is because such a delusion occurs only when the awakening condition—the state of being heated by the sun—is absent. Nor is the transmission of a delusion of water observed in another mental continuum. Furthermore, this [delusion] does not arise from the words of another who is not himself tormented [by heat]. Moreover, the appearance of the form of a snake does not depend upon the recollection of what was previously seen, since qualities such as blackness and so forth exist even prior to that. Indeed, a vivid manifestation belongs to a mental delusion as well, as in dreams and the like. Therefore, the claim that it would not appear vividly is entirely untenable. As for the fact that an effect arises through the presence of its cause and the modification of the cause producing a modification in the effect, this certainly occurs even through a mediated succession. To this, it is replied:
The appearance of blueness and so forth that occurs therein is indeed sensory in nature.
To claim that properties such as non-cessation reside therein is not a valid response. (PVA 599)

[337, vii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, O monks, edible food, whether coarse or subtle, has its origin in craving; craving has its origin in feeling; feeling has its origin in contact; contact has its origin in the six sense bases; the six sense bases have their origin in name-and-form; name-and-form has its origin in consciousness; consciousness has its origin in formations; and formations have their origin in ignorance. Thus, O monks, this entire mass of suffering originates. This, O monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. Furthermore, O monks, that which is the complete cessation of this very craving—accompanied by dispassion, relinquishment, and cessation—that is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, O monks, the path leading to the cessation of suffering is the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, O monks, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, O monks, that noble truth of the origin of suffering, which was previously unheard by me, I have now fully understood; that noble truth of the origin of suffering, which was previously unheard by me, I have now abandoned; that noble truth of the cessation of suffering, which was previously unheard by me, I have now realized; and that noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering, which was previously unheard by me, I have now cultivated. Monks, as long as this knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was not purified, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, its generation of ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when this knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was purified, then, monks, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, its generation of ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; and I established the wheel of dharma, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. This, monks, is the third turning of the wheel of dharma, and it is wonderful and marvelous. And again, monks, at the moment when the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was completely purified, at that moment, monks, the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, was conquered by the Tathāgata through the conquest of the four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects. Therefore, monks, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. For the appearance of blackness and so forth in that case necessarily arises from the sense faculty; as long as that [sensory] modification does not cease, it does not cease. Clarity (*parisphuṭatā*) also occurs only when there is production by the sense faculty, not when there is mental cognition (*mānasatva*). If it is argued that, due to the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), this clarity belongs to mental cognition even for one scorched by the heat of the sun, we reply: in its state of clarity, this [cognition] is indeed non-conceptual (*avikalpika*); thus, it does not differ from what is produced by the sense faculty. And in this way, the status of the apprehension of a visual disorder (*timira*) as an exception (*apavāda*) is not contradicted. For the opponents intend "conceptuality" (*savikalpakatva*) to follow from being mental, not merely "mental-ness" (*mānasatvamātra*). Thus, the point to be proven here is simply that [the cognition] is non-conceptual and unitary. There are two kinds of fallacies of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*): conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and the distortion of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpakaviplava*). It is only then that all such erroneous cognitions involving conceptualization are refuted, and not otherwise. If it is argued, "In that case, let the error of the double moon and so forth, though clear, be mental," we say no. Because such [errors] do not occur in the absence of mental states. Indeed, through the power of cultivation, a mental state may attain clarity; but in the absence of that [cultivation], the fact that it is produced by the sense faculty cannot be denied. There are only two causes for the form of clarity: the sense faculty and cultivation. If it is argued that even here, cultivation exists albeit mediated [by other factors], then the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*) is abandoned. Enough of this digression.

[337, viii] What, then, is the mental illusion of a snake and so forth, for which the illusions of water and so forth serve as examples? It is the appearance of being harmful or beneficial; for even when there is a defect in the sense organ, the appearance of being harmful or beneficial ceases, yet it does not cease at all for one who reflects on it even when the impairment of the sense organ has ceased. Other cases should be applied in the same way. And thus:
Whether one is asleep or awake, whatever cognition appears clearly is non-conceptual in both cases; otherwise, it is conceptual. (300)
Whether it be by way of being mental, or otherwise, or even both ways, its non-conceptual nature has been established here on the grounds of its clarity; thus it is demonstrated.
Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, its status as a valid means of cognition is denied because it is deceptive; and for that reason, pseudo-perception is said to be of two kinds. (301)

The Teacher has shown that the appearance of what is not perception (pratyakṣābhāsa) is of only two kinds, by way of conceptual construction (vikalpa) and error (bhrāntatā). This is because, through the use of the instrumental case (iti-karaṇa), the perversion characterized by "floaters" (taimira) is specified separately from that which arises by the power of conceptual construction; otherwise, if it were not specified separately, it would imply a lack of skill on the part of the author, as there would be no purpose for such a separate mention.

How then was that stated? [It was said]: "Because it is an object of mental error, it is deviant. This was stated from the perspective of another's [opinion]. For one who holds the definition that "perception is that which arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object," for him, the status of being an object of mental error and being deviant is established for [cognition] that is additional [to the sensory contact]. Indeed, deviation is not possible for that which arises solely from the contact of a sense faculty with its object. By process of elimination, deviation occurs in that conceptualization which is additional [to the sensory input] by means of the mind (*manas*).

But surely, that which arises from the sense-faculty alone even in the absence of an object is also erroneous; why then is it said to be "within the scope of mental delusion"? No, because such [cognition] is excluded by the very definition of grasping an object. Even though it exists, it is as if non-existent. And thus it has been said:
"In that which arises from the sense-faculty and its object, there is no possibility of [the object being] designated and so forth."
It should be understood that [the objects] such as the "designatable" (vyapadeśya) and so forth are exclusively mental.

[Objection: But surely words such as "non-designatable" (*avyapadeśya*) and so forth do not serve to exclude [perception from other means of knowledge]; rather, they are intended to describe its essential nature (*svarūpa*). That [perception] arises from the contact of a sense-organ with an object; it is of such a kind and not otherwise. [Reply: No, because [if that were the case], the term "determinate in nature" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) would not function as an exclusion.

For it is not only that which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with an object that is determinate in nature, since inference (*anumāna*) is also determinate in nature. Therefore, since only that which is determinate in nature is perception, and anything else is not, it is logical that these terms serve precisely as exclusions.

[338,xi] Now, if one part [of the definition] serves as an exclusionary qualifier (*vyāvartaka*) and another part serves as a description of its own nature (*svarūpa-kathana*), then by that [definition], if [cognition] is produced from the contact of a sense-organ with an object and is of a determinate nature (*vyavasāyātmaka*), it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) and also non-verbalizable (*avyapadeśya*).

Therefore, it is improper to claim that non-deviation is the defining characteristic; for validity consists precisely in this. What, then, is the point of specifying "having an object that cannot be designated"? For validity is not established by that alone, since validity exists even otherwise. Thus, this argument is trivial. Furthermore, if one were merely describing the essential nature [of perception], there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the contact of the self (*ātman*) and so forth with existing objects would also [erroneously] be included. If you argue that only that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*) to the state of being perception is described, and not the self and so forth which are not unique, then in that case, the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) serves to differentiate [perception from other means of knowledge] rather than being intended as a description of its essential nature.

By this, the mention of "contact with the existent" (*satsannikarṣa*) and so forth is refuted. For instance, this would have to be either a definition or a description of its own nature intended for the sake of establishing another point. In that regard, if it were a definition, one should simply say "contact with the existent. Or, if it is perception that apprehends an existent object, it is perception produced by the sense faculties, or perception that is non-sublated. Alternatively, if the essential nature is restated for the purpose of demonstrating that it is not a cause with respect to *dharma*, even then one should simply say "produced by the sense faculties"; what is the use of further useless chatter?
Furthermore, a mere restatement is improper. For it is said:
"An effort must be made by the proponents of the Veda to establish the existence of external objects."
Therefore, the Mīmāṃsakas refute others by means of their defining characteristics.

For the definition of perception accepted by the Buddhists and others is otherwise and does not conform to our own system; therefore, in order to exclude that, a definition must necessarily be formulated differently. Since the definition of the Sāṃkhyas conforms to the doctrines of Vijñānavāda and Śūnyatāvāda, it is certainly fitting to formulate a different definition in order to refute them; one cannot carry off a camel with the horns of a goat. Or rather, what fault is there in formulating a definition? If you say it is because it is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is as follows: [339, iii]
The definition must be established by means of valid cognition, and from that, certainty arises;
yet because they are mutually dependent causes, not even one of these two is established here.

Because they are mutually dependent, not even one of them is established; thus, there can be no formulation of a definition. If this is so, then even a restatement (anuvāda) is not appropriate for that which is not established by valid cognition. If you say that its establishment comes from worldly consensus, then dharma likewise will be established merely through worldly consensus, rendering Mīmāṃsā useless. If you argue that because we observe the subversion of dharma, it is simply unestablished in the ultimate sense, then why has Mīmāṃsā itself not been prevented by force from causing such subversion of dharma?
Otherwise, over such a long period of time, this name would not exist according to other doctrines.
Therefore, even a restatement must be made based on what is established by valid cognition; likewise, the definition must also be faultless.

Nor is this a definition even by implication, because it is a restatement of a well-known fact. For just as the restatement is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the senses] are not causes with respect to *dharma*, so too it is for the purpose of demonstrating that they are causes; thus, it is the same in both cases. And how this is so has already been demonstrated previously. Therefore, "perception is the cognition of an object from that" is indeed the definition. By the word "from that" (*tataḥ*), since there is no other subject under discussion, it is understood as "only from that which is seen by perception. By this, the cognition of a double moon and the like is excluded; for that does not arise from that very [object], but rather from something else. How then was it stated by the Teacher?
That which appears is not that [object]; therefore, the fivefold [sensory group] has the mind as its objective support.

Visual and other sensory cognitions do not arise with the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*). If even a cognition that possesses a different form were to have an object simply by virtue of being its cause, it would follow that the atoms of the eye and so forth would also be objects. For those atoms, whether existing in that manner or otherwise, would be the cause of a cognition appearing as two moons, blue, and so on. This has been stated with reference to ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); however, the analysis of the debate is conducted according to worldly convention (*lokaprasiddhi*). For the world does not entertain conceptual constructions such as atoms; what is established in the world as perception (*pratyakṣa*) is only this much, but when subjected to critical investigation, it is not tenable.
Therefore, the lack of established status regarding being "other than the object" and so forth is clearly inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*).
This would be inconclusive with respect to atoms (*paramāṇu*).

If you claim that atoms alone are the producers [of cognition], then they cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*), because this would lead to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the eyes and other sense organs. If, on the other hand, it is said that "those" refers to what appears [in consciousness], then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For there can be no production of something that exists simultaneously [with its cause]; furthermore, the reason would be inconclusive due to the case of the double moon and similar illusions. If you argue that even a simultaneous thing can be a producer, that too is incorrect, because a composite whole (*samudāya*) is not a real entity. Moreover, the reason is inconclusive with respect to erroneous cognitions. If, finally, you claim that it is a producer existing at a prior time, then the reason remains unestablished.

For that which exists prior to the cognition is not grasped by that very cognition; if it were grasped by another [cognition], then that [second cognition] would likewise be subject to the same inquiry. (PVA 604)
If [the cognition] were known through inference, that [inference] would arise from perception itself;
yet, if these two were mutually dependent causes, which one could possibly exist first?
There is never a simultaneity between perception and the subsequent cognition.
Therefore, this definition is indeed unestablished from the perspective of ultimate reality;
however, it is not contradicted when considered in relation to worldly convention.
[339,xvii] As for what is also said— that perception is the operation of the auditory and other sense faculties— that too is incorrect.
The functioning of the auditory organ and the rest does indeed exist even in one who is deluded;
moreover, the functioning of the auditory organ and the rest is not possible without cognition.

For one who desires to act must seek a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception. And how can the activity of the ears and other senses be defined if it is unknown? How could this person act based on something that has not been characterized? If it is argued that the activity of the ears and so forth is perceived through perception itself, then the definition of that very perception must be stated. To this, the rebuttal is: perception is that which has the form of direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), and that is perceived by itself. This being the case, that very direct realization—being non-erroneous—is the definition. Furthermore, even in the case of an erroneous cognition, how could the activity of the ears and so forth constitute the definition? [The opponent replies: There is no fault, for it is "activity with respect to objects. Activity with respect to objects means being directed toward objects; and that is indeed present even in an erroneous cognition. [The author replies: If it is the self-awareness (*svarūpasamvedana*) of that [cognition], then that very self-awareness is the definition. And that is nothing other than direct realization, which is synonymous with being non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). Therefore, there is no other definition at all.

What, then, is the fruit (*phala*) of this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It is the comprehension of the object of cognition (*prameyādhigati*). And it has been said: "For the comprehension of the object of cognition is dependent upon the means of valid cognition.

[340, iv] Now, if that very cognition is both the means and the fruit, what then is the means of valid cognition? Some say: "The contact between the sense faculty and the object, the initial perception (*ālocana*), and the cognition of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*). That is incorrect; for that alone is rightly considered the instrument of comprehension from which that comprehension arises.

[340,v] But surely, the arising of cognition is indeed observed from the sense faculties and so forth; therefore, the apprehension [of the object] must likewise arise from those very same causes—so what is the use of this conceptual construction?
Indeed, an assumption other than what is perceived cannot be supported by reason;
for if that were the case, an infinite regress regarding the object of cognition would be unavoidable.
This is not so;
for everything that is a means of accomplishing an action is [the instrument] of every action.
For that action by which something is accomplished is indeed the means of accomplishing it. (302)

[340,x] If it were the case that whatever capacity is observed in one instance could be employed as a means for another instance as well—such that by employing any arbitrary means, all desired ends would be accomplished—the entire world would be well-situated with minimal effort. But this is not so. Therefore, only that action from which a result is observed is the means for that specific end, and nothing else.

In that case, since cognition is of a uniform nature consisting merely of experience, it must possess that specific character by which its variation with respect to each object is accounted for. (303)

For that experience is common to blue, yellow, and so forth, merely by its existence. Therefore, it would establish everything, just like the object established as intended; or else, it would not be fit to establish anything, even that which is not established, because there is no distinction in its nature. To explain:
[340, xiii]
Just as that object is a cognizer of something, so too it is a non-cognizer of that same thing.
When it is a cognizer, by what means is it not accepted as a non-cognizer according to your view?

For, while taking possession of the specific state of being unoccupied, one might understand that "this is occupied here"; nevertheless, does it deviate from its own nature? If the self were the knower, then even though it has become the very essence of that [object], if it does not know it, then that object would simply not have been known by it; consequently, there would be no status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This world understands the object of enjoyment as being of the very nature of the person (*puruṣa*).
And that self does not recognize that the arrangement of enjoyments is excellent.

If it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) establishes itself as having the nature of the determination (*avasāya*) of pleasure, blue, and so forth, then that very [intellect] must be the enjoyer; what need is there for another consciousness (*saṃvedana*)? Since the intellect has the form of the determination of pleasure and so on, its very form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that the person (*puruṣa*) perceives the object determined by the intellect, then it must be stated: what is this intellect? What is this determination? And who is this person? If it is said that the intellect is the instrument (*karaṇa*), determination is the action (*karman*), and the person is the agent (*kartṛ*), then the person understands the object, and therefore the agent of the determination is the person—what then is the use of the intellect? If it is argued that the intellect is the means for determination, whereas the person is the means for understanding (*avagama*), we see no difference between understanding and determination. Understanding is the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of the form of that [object]; that is precisely what determination is. If it is argued that determination is merely having that form and not the direct realization, [we reply: [This argument is untenable. If the intellect were to determine an object without being of that [object's] form, then it would be determining everything, since it is not restricted by any specific form. Furthermore, if the intellect were to assume the form of the object, then it would follow that the intellect itself is the enjoyer, because it is the direct realization of that form. If you say that the intellect does not take on the form of the object, then how could it ever determine it? For one cannot determine something without first perceiving it. If it is claimed that the intellect determines an object even without perceiving it, then it would follow that the blind man could determine colors. Therefore, the intellect is indeed the enjoyer, and there is no separate enjoyer other than the intellect. Thus, the person is nothing more than a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Consequently, the self (*ātman*) is not established as a distinct entity. ||| 102 || ||| 103 || ||| 104 || ||| 105 || ||| 106 || ||| 107 || ||| 108 || ||| 109 || ||| 110 || ||| 111 || ||| 112 || ||| Even if that cognition possesses the form of that object,
why is it not the case that the object itself is likewise [directly perceived], since its nature is being directly realized? (PVA 611)

When a cognition possessing that form is directly perceived, it is [erroneously concluded] that "the object itself is thus"; therefore, a cognition with the form of an object is useless. The form of the object is presented to the cognition; consequently, there is the apprehension of it as being at a non-distant location. Since the self is all-pervading, everything is indeed at a non-distant location from it. Thus, there would be no apprehension of it as being at a distant location, nor would there be an object distinct from the cognition possessing that form.

If it is asked, "From what does the cognition have that form in the absence of an object?"—surely it is from the cognition itself that objects are held to possess that form; so why this reversal? One's own face cannot be perceived unless it has been transferred [to a mirror]. It is not because the face lacks the capacity for transfer that its transfer to a mirror or similar surface is denied. Rather, it is because the face occupies an unsuitable location.

It is not so for others; and how can there be a cognition of a mirror that has not itself been transferred [into another]? If it is argued that this [mirror] also is transferred into the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*), then one must likewise accept that the intellect is an intellect and is not transferred into another mirror. If it is argued that the intellect may remain unperceived, then the world would be useless, as the Self would not be directly perceived. If the Self were not an object of perception, then let the object itself be known by it—what is the use of the intellect here? If it is asked, "How does it see without an instrument?", the eyes and so forth are the instruments. If it is argued that there is a need for an internal instrument (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then there would be an infinite regress, as there would also be a need for an internal instrument for that internal instrument. Furthermore, an instrument cannot be something that provides no assistance. It is manifested by them [the senses]. If it is the Person (*puruṣa*) who is manifested, then, like one who is indifferent, he would lack the capacity for apprehension due to such manifestation. Therefore, there must exist a Self that is distinct from the objects.

If it is argued that, as in the case of a mirror, there is the appearance of that form [of the object] therein without causing any modification [in the consciousness], we say: no. It is in dependence upon the mirror that a cognition arises having that form; therefore, there is indeed a modification. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of "transference" if there were no modification? In the case of a mirror, it is the form facing [the object] that appears.

The arising cognition is erroneous. In this case as well, the cognition bearing the form of an object is indeed erroneous; there is no manifold world of objects in ultimate reality, because the world consists merely of *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and *puruṣa* (the self). If it is argued that even the nature of being *pradhāna* is then erroneous for the world—just like the nature of jars and so forth—and likewise the nature of being *puruṣa*, we shall establish this later; otherwise, it would not be according to the Sāṃkhya system.
Therefore, this pure experience must be realized by that Self, by which the distinction between action and object—such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow"—is established.

Even though a distinction exists within the causes, it does not belong to the entity itself;
for that which is undifferentiated cannot be the regulator of differentiation when the action is differentiated. (304)

For this single person, there is no distinct determining factor for each individual object such as blue and so forth, in the form of a difference between the sense organs and other faculties. For that [difference] would have to be a determining factor either as a producer (*kāraka*) or as a communicator (*jñāpaka*). If it were a determining factor as a producer, it would not be logical because [the self] is eternal; furthermore, it would entail the consequence that [the self] possesses a mental aspect (*sākāratā*). If it lacks a mental aspect, the same fault applies, because it would follow that [the self] experiences itself alone. Now, suppose it is a determining factor by way of being a communicator. How can something be a communicator regarding an object that is not yet known? If the knowledge of the restriction [of the object] comes from the communicator, and the communicator is known through the knowledge of the restriction, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If you say, "It is a communicator like light in the world," we say no. Even for those [objects], if they are to be made known, there would be a need for another communicator, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, light is not a communicator in all cases. Furthermore, once something is made known by light, what further use would there be for the eyes and other senses? If you argue that in this case, sound and other objects are themselves like light, even so, how does that [self], which consists of the nature of its own cognition, know [them]? We shall explain later that it cannot abide in its own nature [if it knows external objects].

Therefore, since this [cognition] has a distinction of its own nature and its apprehension [occurs], this restriction of the object for an action is established; that [action] is proven by that [restriction]. (305)

Because, in the case of a self-nature reason (*svarūpahetu*), there is this restriction regarding that cognition: "this is the apprehension of blue, and this is the apprehension of yellow. That apprehension, moreover, is established by its own means of proof, since this restriction exists solely on account of that [cognition] itself. And so it has been said:
[342, viii]
Since this [cognition] exists only when that [object] exists,
this connection of the object does not arise from similarity to it, but rather from the cognition itself; for:

[342,x] For nothing other than the form of the object can connect this [cognition] with that object; for there is no other way whatsoever for something distinct from itself to differentiate cognition. (306)
Therefore, the means of cognizing the object of knowledge is the conformity of the cognition to the form of that object;
for if the means were something else, the true nature of its action upon that object would not be established. (307)

For it is the cognition possessing that form which establishes the object as "blue" or "yellow. We shall demonstrate later how cognition is endowed with such a form. However, in other proofs, one's own purpose is not accomplished by that action because of its conventional nature (*saṃvṛtti*). If the possession of that form is abandoned, how can there be a rule that "this is the cognition of that"? If it is argued that the rule will arise from direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) itself, [we ask]: what is this direct perception? Is it the intrinsic nature of the object, or is it the cognition, or is it something else entirely?
If the direct realization of the object is held to be its form,
how could cognition— which is itself direct realization— possibly belong to the object?
Now, if it is held that the very nature of cognition is direct perception (*sākṣātkriyā*),
then how can that object be directly perceived? For one thing cannot possess the nature of another.
Even if there were otherness, this fault would certainly remain unavoidable.

For instance, if the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) of an object were its own nature (*svabhāva*), such as blue and so forth, then that object would be commonly perceived by everyone. Furthermore, it is not logical for direct realization to belong to the object, because it is a property of cognition (*jñāna*). If it is argued that this [realization] is a property of cognition whose object is the thing, and therefore the object is said to be "perceived," then what is the meaning of "having the object as its domain" (*arthaviṣaya*)? If you say it is because it has the nature of perceiving the object, then what is "the perception of the object"? If you say it is because the perception has the form of the object (*artharūpatva*), then that is simply the fact that the perception possesses the aspect (*ākāra*) of the object. Alternatively, if the perception of the object is due to the object being known, then in that case, since the eye is also known, it would follow that there is a "perception of the eye. If you argue that one sees the object and not the eye, then what is the meaning of "seeing the object"? If you say that while seeing the object, it is seen by means of that [cognition], and thus it is called "seeing," then by what does it see? It sees by its own nature (*svarūpa*). In that case, just as it sees its own nature through the nature of perception, so too it sees the object through the nature of the object; thus, the object has the nature of the object, and the perception has the nature of perception. Therefore, only the possession of that aspect (*tadākāratā*) establishes everything. No other intrinsic nature distinguishes consciousness and connects it with the object.
And since that [cognition] is indeed its very self, the result is not a separate entity from it.

For those who maintain that the result [of cognition] is a distinct entity, everything becomes difficult to establish. Indeed, the very fact that the form of the object is identical with the cognition itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and the cognition, being identical with that [form], is the result of the means of valid cognition. Apart from the experience of the form of the object, there is no other apprehension of the object. For the experience of the object does not consist in the form of pleasure and so forth; otherwise, it would follow that one would experience the specific object simply by virtue of the particularity of that [pleasure]. If it is argued that the experience of the object occurs because the object serves as its cause, then if the form of the object were absent, only pleasure alone would be experienced. If it is argued that there is an experience of pleasure *with respect to* the object, why then is there not an experience of yellow with respect to blue? If you say this is because they differ from one another, this merely undermines your own position. The same could be said for pleasure and blue; enough of this grinding of what is already ground. If it is argued that the nature of the object itself is such, and that it is not an operation of cognition [that produces the form], then...
To this, it is said:
[343, viii]
And he maintains that [knowledge] within himself by means of the nature of the apprehension of objects. // 308 //
Though it is itself devoid of causal agency, it appears as if active in its own function by virtue of that [agent], because its own establishment depends upon him. (309)

[343,x] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving as a sign. He does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a sign. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as a sign, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainment, or the emptiness of phenomena as phenomena as signs. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as signs, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as signs. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as a sign, nor does he perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship as a sign. He does not perceive Pratyekabuddhahood as a sign, nor does he perceive unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as a sign.”

In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no activity whatsoever belonging to anything. For the wise who know the truth, it is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of things that, appearing in such a way, is called "activity," though it is not so in ultimate reality. Furthermore, cognition (*jñāna*) is for the person (*puruṣa*) his own end (*svārtha*), just like the cognition of pleasure. Therefore, when the cognition of pleasure arises, it is his own end; yet nothing at all is produced by that cognition of pleasure. Likewise, the cognition of form and so forth is its own end by its very nature, but it is not "cognized" [by something else]. Since the conventional usage is exhausted by the fact that it arises from the object, what is the use of postulating an "activity"? If that is so, then the apprehension of the object is not the result (*phala*). There is no contradiction in saying that the result is the apprehension which bears the form of the object—that is, the apprehension of the object. How then is the conventional usage of distinction expressed as "he cognizes the object"? It is designated thus because it cognizes by bearing that very form of the object. For instance, when visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) operates upon blue after abandoning yellow, it appears as if it has an activity characterized by abandonment and acquisition. If the cognition of blue were merely the form of blue itself, then yellow would not pass away, for the nature of one thing cannot become another. Therefore, that [blue] is established by reasoning as being distinct [from the cognition], and that [apparent] activity is simply a presumption (*arthāpatti*). In ultimate reality, however, there is only successive cognition bearing this or that form; therein, neither activity nor distinction exists.

The conceptualization of distinct operations based on positive and negative concomitance does not presuppose the manifestation of real entities, due to the attachment to beginningless latent predispositions. (PVA 614)

That [notion of self], which is produced by the impressions deposited through the experience of cognitions from previous births, is the seed for the conceptualization of difference; it is merely a blind tradition.
— Two intermediate verses:

[344,v] Now, if that cognition which possesses the form of the object is produced by it, then that very object would be excluded (*vyāvṛta*) therein, but not the cognition with respect to the object; how then can there be the certainty that "cognition grasps"?
vi] Herein is the meditative concentration (samādhi).
Just as in the world, because an effect arises with a nature similar to its causes, it is said that the cause "grasps" the form [of the effect], even though it possesses activity. (311)
