For example, in the world, it is said that a son who resembles his father takes on the father’s form, even though there is no actual act of grasping [the form]; likewise, what contradiction is there in applying such a designation to cognition? In that case, having observed the assumption of that form [in the world], how can it be so here [in the case of cognition]? Even here, it is indeed observed; for instance, in cases of desire, grief, and so forth, the cognition itself possesses that form. The objection is: "That assumption of the form belongs to the cognition alone, not to the object. To this, the meaning of the statement is as follows: First, the assumption of that form is perceived as occurring. If there is the capacity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then the assumption of that form arises from experience as the cause of perception. However, if one engages with something never before seen or heard, then, due to the absence of the capacity of latent impressions, the assumption of that form must come from something else—namely, the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is the form itself. For it is thus: (0) [The verse follows]...
That which arises from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) belongs to that one person alone; however, if an object were to exist [externally], its appearance would be common to all. (616) (PVA)
Therefore, the very fact of having the form of the object is the means of proof.

Therefore, the validity of these—namely, visual perception, the connection with the sense organ, and the cognition of qualifiers—is not accepted [as direct] with respect to the action, because of their mediation. (310)

[344,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. What is the nutriment that is contact? It is the contact associated with the six groups of consciousness. What is the nutriment that is mental volition? It is the volitional impulse associated with the six groups of consciousness. What is the nutriment that is consciousness? It is the consciousness associated with the six groups of consciousness. Among these, what is the nutriment that is edible food, coarse or subtle? It is the nutriment that is edible food, whether coarse or subtle, belonging to this world or to another world, whether manifest or unmanifest, whether past, future, or present. This is called the nutriment that is edible food, coarse or subtle. What is the nutriment that is contact? It is the nutriment that is contact, whether it belongs to the sphere of form, the sphere of formlessness, or the sphere of cessation, whether it is associated with the six groups of consciousness, whether it is past, future, or present. This is called the nutriment that is contact. What is the nutriment that is mental volition? It is the nutriment that is mental volition, whether it belongs to the sphere of desire, the sphere of form, or the sphere of formlessness, whether it is associated with the six groups of consciousness, whether it is past, future, or present. This is called the nutriment that is mental volition. What is the nutriment that is consciousness? It is the nutriment that is consciousness, whether it belongs to the sphere of desire, the sphere of form, or the sphere of formlessness, whether it is associated with the six groups of consciousness, whether it is past, future, or present. This is called the nutriment that is consciousness. Furthermore, monks, the nutriment that is edible food, coarse or subtle, leads to the continuation of beings who have already come to be and to their support; it also leads to the production of new existence and to the arising of craving for renewed existence. The nutriment that is contact leads to the continuation of beings who have already come to be and to their support; it also leads to the production of new existence and to the arising of craving for renewed existence. The nutriment that is mental volition leads to the continuation of beings who have already come to be and to their support; it also leads to the production of new existence and to the arising of craving for renewed existence. The nutriment that is consciousness leads to the continuation of beings who have already come to be and to their support; it also leads to the production of new existence and to the arising of craving for renewed existence. Furthermore, monks, the nutriment that is edible food, coarse or subtle, should be abandoned; the nutriment that is contact should be abandoned; the nutriment that is mental volition should be abandoned; the nutriment that is consciousness should be abandoned. Some say that the cognition of mere observation (*ālocanājñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and following that, the result (*phala*) consists of the ascertainment of an object qualified by its genus and other attributes. From that comes activity, from that attainment, and from that pleasure; such is the sequence where each preceding stage is the means and each succeeding stage is the result. For it is solely by the power of the form (*ākāra*) that there is the determination of specific objects, and not otherwise. If the cognition of observation did not assume a specific form, how could it be said, "This is the observation of this [object]"? Now, even subsequent cognitions such as ascertainment and so forth acquire their status as "real" in exactly this same way. However, while the preceding stages are causes for the production of each succeeding one, they are not the cause for the determination of specific objects; rather, it is the very possession of that form which is the proof (*sādhana*) in that regard.
Although all the factors of action (kārakas) are employed with respect to an action, that which is the final differentiator of it is considered its most effective instrument (sādhakatama). [344,xiii]

[344,xiv] That which is the cause (*kāraṇa*) is designated by the suffix *kṛt* (according to Pāṇini 1.4.42). And although all factors of action (*kāraka*) are employed toward that [action], how is there a pre-eminence (*prakarṣa*) regarding the action? For it is not merely the accomplishment of the action [that constitutes pre-eminence]. Even in the case of a state of being (*bhāva*), that which has immediate succession (*ānantarya*) with respect to the action is precisely the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). For instance, even when the sense faculties and so forth are present, if a specific form were not apprehended due to proximity and other such factors, [the result would not be achieved].

The determination of the object as having that form is the action; since it appears immediately after that [contact], that very [contact] is the instrument (*karaṇa*). But surely, proximity alone is the means of accomplishment, for even when there is proximity, if the sense organ is impaired, there is no determination of the object with certainty. Then, let the non-impairment [of the sense organ] be the means of accomplishment. This also is not so, because:
"The non-impairment of the sense organ [is established] through the particularity of its form."
Therefore, the object of cognition is thereby obstructed.

(PVA 617) [345, iii] Now, it might be argued that it is that very form which is obstructed; for by means of that form, what is ascertained is unimpaired and serves as the cause for the establishment of a specific object. This is not correct, because:
If the restriction of form is established by the existence of an object, then why is the arrow maintained as a cause when it has already been established as causeless? (PVA 618)

[345,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal.”

A non-established determination of form does not prove that which is followed by the sense-faculties (*akṣa*). If that [determination] were established, then that itself would be the establishment of the object; the non-deficiency of the sense-faculties would be entirely redundant. Indeed, nothing can establish what has already been established, because it is impossible to prove what is already proven. Therefore, what is required by that which brings about the presence of what is already established? If it is argued that even regarding the possession of that form, another certainty is required for a restricted determination, we say no. This is because the present context concerns the validity of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For when there is the possibility of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), direct perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it functions and brings about certainty even without [explicit] certainty, based solely on the mere form [of the object]. But when there is a dependence upon certainty, then inference (*anumāna*) is the means of valid cognition, since its activity also proceeds from the mere form alone. There is no dependence on anything else. Therefore, there is no instrument other than the form, and thus it is the unique [cause]. In this regard:
Because all [objects] are the common cause of the senses, there is no such thing as this [specificity].
For even when those [objects] differ, how could there be the notion "this belongs to that" regarding something that is undifferentiated? (313)

[345, vii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence, and for the assistance of those seeking existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is edible food, coarse or subtle? It is that which is taken by mouthfuls, whether it be masticated or swallowed. What is contact as the second? It is the contact of the six sense bases. What is mental volition as the third? It is the mental volition associated with the three realms of existence. What is consciousness as the fourth? It is the sixfold consciousness. Furthermore, O monks, edible food, coarse or subtle, should be seen as having its origin in craving; contact has its origin in feeling; mental volition has its origin in perception; and consciousness has its origin in name-and-form. Moreover, O monks, craving has its origin in feeling; feeling has its origin in contact; contact has its origin in the six sense bases; the six sense bases have their origin in name-and-form; name-and-form has its origin in consciousness; consciousness has its origin in formations; and formations have their origin in ignorance. Thus, O monks, this entire mass of suffering originates. Furthermore, O monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: "This is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—then, O monks, for one who thus sees with right wisdom as it really is, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases; with the cessation of grasping, becoming ceases; with the cessation of becoming, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, O monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, O monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: "This is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering"—then, O monks, for one who thus sees with right wisdom as it really is, the mind becomes dispassionate toward the world, and through dispassion, it is liberated; through liberation, there is the knowledge: "It is liberated. One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. For the sense organ (*akṣa*) is not a differentiator, because it serves as a cause in a general sense for every object, such as blue, yellow, and so forth. [Objection: But surely there will be distinct sense organs for each respective object—blue, yellow, both, and so on; for in those cases, the "orientation" (*ābhimukhyatā*) toward them is indeed different. Thus, since there is a difference in the properties of the sense organs, the cognition of difference arises precisely from that difference in the organs. Why, then, do you say "because it is a cause in a general sense for everything"? [Response: That is incorrect. Because it is impossible to apprehend orientation without a distinction in the form of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇākāra*). Even if that [orientation] were different, how could one establish that "this belongs to this [organ]" or "this is the orientation toward objects such as blue and yellow" for an [organ] devoid of form? For there is no apprehension of a specific orientation without the apprehension of the specific [objects] such as blue. If that [apprehension of the object] exists, what is the use now of postulating "orientation"? Alternatively, regarding the phrase "even if there is a difference in that [object], [the organ] remains undifferentiated": even if there is a difference in that cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth, how can one establish that "this is the instrument for this [cognition]" for an undifferentiated sense organ? If you argue that the distinction [in the organ] comes from the distinction in orientation, we have already stated that it is impossible to apprehend a distinction in "orientation-ness" without apprehending a distinction in the causal form. Therefore, one must seek the distinction in the form itself. If that [form] exists, what is the use of anything else?

[345, viii] But surely the form (*ākāra*) belongs to the object alone and not to the cognition, since it is apprehended as being the object itself. For that form is perceived as having an insentient nature (*jaḍarūpatā*), consisting of color and shape; whereas cognition is perceived as the opposite of that, by virtue of its nature as awareness (*bodharūpatā*). This is because it is impossible to perceive the nature of awareness apart from the form, for no other form of cognition is observed apart from blue and so forth, or pleasure and so forth. [If this were so,] it would follow that cognition is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) and that it does not exist at all.
That is incorrect. For it is said:
[345,x] If that cognition is imperceptible, how can it be known simply as "cognition"?
Who is capable of characterizing the nature of that which is imperceptible?

(619) (PVA) If it is thought that cognition is the very fact of an object’s perceptibility, then let there be the cognition of an object’s perceptibility; what further role does another [cognition] have therein? (620) (PVA)
But in the case of persistence, this [cognition] does not arise for one who is not persisting;
therefore, the statement "it arises by means of the object" is established without effort.
By this, non-existence as well has been refuted.

Furthermore, at the time of experiencing blue and so forth, nothing is experienced apart from its immediacy (*aparokṣatā*). Therefore, that [experience] possesses the form of blue and so on; however, the blue itself is merely another thing serving as its substrate (*upadhāna*). Just as the reflection of a face in a mirror and the like is merely the form "face" and is not the object itself, so too is this case. Now, one might object: "In the case of both the mirror and the reflected face, there is a perception of two things; but here, there is no perception of an object apart from its form. We shall demonstrate this later, so let us leave it for now. Moreover, how can an insentient nature (*jaḍarūpatā*) be established for something that shines forth by itself? If there were some other factor distinct from the immediacy of the object from which this [insentience] is proven, then it would be a latent impression (*vāsanā*). This form of consciousness would arise through the power of the latent impression. But an object cannot exist by the power of a latent impression, because that would entail the non-existence of the object.
But surely, that which arises through the power of latent impressions is devoid of an external object, like the forms in a dream?
In that case, there is the possibility of some specific latent impression (*vāsanā*) by which the form perceived during the waking state does not become devoid of an object.

For it is observed that mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are indeed the producers of forms in dreams and similar states; therefore, this [object] which has become an object of waking perception is likewise produced from that very source, because it belongs to the same class.

[Objection: But surely its being an aspect (*ākāratva*) is unestablished, because it is understood that this is simply the object itself. [Response: No, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For the aspect of a dream-cognition is indeed understood to be an object. [Objection: If you say that through further investigation (*paryālocana*) there is a different understanding, [Response: Here too, investigation is not devoured by crows. It is better to postulate that it is a specific latent impression (*vāsanāviśeṣa*)—the form of the waking state—that is the object. [Objection: Even a cognition such as a dream is not with-aspect (*sākāra*), for even there an object is possible. [Response: We shall demonstrate that later. Now, if the state of having the object's aspect is not immediate, then the object itself, such as blue and so on, is the "aspect of the object"; however, that [aspect] is perceived due to proximity to the thing, like a reflection in a mirror. For, due to the proximity of the face, the mirror, though itself without aspect, appears as if it were possessed of an aspect. Or it is like the light of a lamp and so forth. For the light of a lamp, though itself without aspect, when reflected in a jar or similar object, appears as if it were possessed of the aspect of the jar.
That is untrue.
Even though it is distinct from the face and other such things, the mirror and so forth are perceived; however, that which is not distinct from the form is not perceived as something immediate.

For directness (*aparokṣatā*) is always observed as being essentially identical with the form of blue itself, and not otherwise. Therefore, for what purpose does it appear through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) in such a way that it appears as if by those very [forms]? What is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for this? If you ask, "What is the proof for you [the opponent]?"—it is simply the perception of non-difference (*abhedopalabdhi*). If you say, "This is merely an illusion (*bhrānti*)," we say no, because there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka*). If you say, "It is the attainment of the object (*arthaprāpti*)," [we reply: No; for even attainment is characterized by the form [of the object]. We shall demonstrate later that there is no attainment apart from having that form. If that form were not of such a nature, no one could establish a specific object.
By this, the rest is explained: furthermore, for cognitions of qualifiers, there is no difference even when they lack that nature, or likewise for other cognitions as well. (314)

They are: one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry; one who has attained the fruit of once-returning; one who has attained the fruit of non-returning; and one who has attained arhatship. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having been born here, will not be reborn here again. The remaining factors, such as the contact [of the sense organ] with the object for the sake of perception, are also not established as the most effective means (*asādhakatama*) toward the action, because they are intervened by [the cognition of the qualifier]. Furthermore, if there were no assumption of that form [of the object], the cognition of the qualifier itself would not be established; thus, there is the status of being a cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and so forth. If even those [factors] are not instruments, then how is it to be known at that time that "this is the qualifier" when the cognition of the qualifier has not yet occurred? For there is no such thing as "qualifier-ness" apart from a form mounted upon the qualified, nor is there a grasping of qualifier-ness without the grasping of its being mounted upon that [qualified]. And if its form is grasped, the qualified is already grasped; so how could a further cognition of the qualified be something to be accomplished based on that? If it is argued: "At that very moment, what is being grasped is not the object of a grasper produced by a grasper-cognition that grasps it, because the qualifier does not appear at that time," then the prior grasping of it is useless. It is also not tenable to say that the qualified appears even earlier, precisely because that would entail the absence of its status as a means (*sādhana*). Moreover, since the cognition of the qualifier has the qualifier as its object and the cognition of the qualified has the qualified as its object, a difference in the objects of the action and the means is incurred. If it is asked: "Let it be so; what is the fault? [the answer follows].
[347,ii] Nor is the division of the object desired for both the action and the instrument;
if they were one and the same thing, the two would be redundant, and there could be no occurrence in succession. || 315 ||

[347,iii] The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: the self-nature of words (*nāma-svabhāva*), the self-nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*), the self-nature of attachment to names (*nāma-abhiniveśa-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the establishment of reality (*vastu-siddhi-svabhāva*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of self-nature. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of self-nature, there are four kinds of logical reasoning (*yukti*). What are these four? They are: the reasoning of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), the reasoning of causal efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*), the reasoning of establishment (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*), and the reasoning of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of logical reasoning. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of logical reasoning, there are four kinds of knowledge (*jñāna*). What are these four? They are: the knowledge of dependence (*apekṣā-jñāna*), the knowledge of causal efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-jñāna*), the knowledge of establishment (*upapatti-sādhana-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the nature of things (*dharmatā-jñāna*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of knowledge. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of knowledge, there are four kinds of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). What are these four? They are: the meditative concentration of the light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka-samādhi*), the meditative concentration of the manifestation of the body (*kāya-vibhāga-samādhi*), the meditative concentration of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma-samādhi*), and the meditative concentration of the lion’s sport (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of meditative concentration. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of meditative concentration, there are four kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*). What are these four? They are: mastery over the mind (*citta-vaśitā*), mastery over the meditative concentrations (*samādhi-vaśitā*), mastery over the dharmas (*dharma-vaśitā*), and mastery over the buddha-fields (*kṣetra-vaśitā*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of mastery. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of mastery, there are four kinds of birth. What are these four? They are: miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), birth from an egg (*aṇḍaja*), birth from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), and birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of birth. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of birth, there are four kinds of lineage (*gotra*). What are these four? They are: the lineage of the śrāvakas (*śrāvaka-gotra*), the lineage of the pratyekabuddhas (*pratyekabuddha-gotra*), the lineage of the tathāgatas (*tathāgata-gotra*), and the indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of lineage. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of lineage, there are four kinds of nirvana. What are these four? They are: the nirvana of the extinction of the aggregates (*skandha-nirodha-nirvāṇa*), the nirvana of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti-nirvāṇa*), the nirvana of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-nirvāṇa*), and the nirvana of the non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anutpāda-nirvāṇa*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of nirvana. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of nirvana, there are four kinds of dharma-teaching. What are these four? They are: the teaching of the existence of external objects (*bāhya-artha-astitva-deśanā*), the teaching of the non-existence of external objects (*bāhya-artha-nāstitva-deśanā*), the teaching of the non-duality of existence and non-existence (*astitva-nāstitva-advaya-deśanā*), and the teaching of the ineffable nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-anabhilāpya-svabhāva-deśanā*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of dharma-teaching. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of dharma-teaching, there are four kinds of realization. What are these four? They are: the realization of the meaning of words (*nāmartha-prativedha*), the realization of the meaning of characteristics (*lakṣaṇārtha-prativedha*), the realization of the meaning of the establishment of reality (*vastusiddhyartha-prativedha*), and the realization of the meaning of the nature of things (*dharmatārtha-prativedha*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of realization. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of realization, there are four kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*). What are these four? They are: the eloquence of the meaning of words (*nāmartha-pratibhāna*), the eloquence of the meaning of characteristics (*lakṣaṇārtha-pratibhāna*), the eloquence of the meaning of the establishment of reality (*vastusiddhyartha-pratibhāna*), and the eloquence of the meaning of the nature of things (*dharmatārtha-pratibhāna*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of eloquence. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of eloquence, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). What are these four? They are: the skillful means of the gate of letters (*akṣara-mukha-upāya*), the skillful means of the gate of meanings (*arthamukha-upāya*), the skillful means of the gate of non-duality (*advayamukha-upāya*), and the skillful means of the gate of the ineffable (*anabhilāpyamukha-upāya*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of skillful means. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of skillful means, there are four kinds of dhāraṇī. What are these four? They are: the dhāraṇī of retaining what has been heard (*śruta-dhāraṇī*), the dhāraṇī of retaining the meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*), the dhāraṇī of retaining the spells (*mantra-dhāraṇī*), and the dhāraṇī of retaining the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-dharma-dhāraṇī*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of dhāraṇī. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of dhāraṇī, there are four kinds of sameness. What are these four? They are: the sameness of the letters (*akṣara-samatā*), the sameness of the meanings (*artha-samatā*), the sameness of the dharmas (*dharma-samatā*), and the sameness of the nature of things (*dharmatā-samatā*). These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of sameness. The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on the four kinds of sameness, there are four kinds of liberation (*vimukti*). What are these four? They are: liberation through the cessation of the grasping of names (*nāmagrahaṇa-nirodha-vimukti*), liberation through the cessation of the grasping of characteristics (*lakṣaṇagrahaṇa-nirodha-vimukti*), liberation through the cessation of the grasping of the establishment of reality (*vastusiddhigrahaṇa-nirodha-vimukti*), and liberation through the cessation of the grasping of the nature of things (*dh

Indeed, the application of instruments such as an axe toward a *palāśa* tree does not result in cutting a *nyagrodha* tree; for if they were a single object, the same consequence as previously mentioned would follow, and both [the axe and the tree] would be rendered useless. Furthermore, the sequential occurrence of all those cognitions which are the causes of that [single] object is contradictory, because succession is impossible in the case of identity. If it is argued that "succession exists due to a difference in repetition (*āvṛtti*)," we say no, because a difference in repetition cannot be apprehended by perception. If that very same cognition were to repeat itself, there would always be the cognition of repetition. Moreover, among those [cognitions] which grasp an identical nature, there can be no mutual relationship of action and instrument, even if there is succession; for even in succession, the preceding [cognition] performs only the act of producing the subsequent one, not the act of cognizing it, since it is no different from the preceding. It has been established elsewhere that even the act of production is nothing other than the nature of that [object] itself.
If two parts of a cognition were to exist simultaneously, there would be no relationship of the proven and the prover between them.
It is by relying upon the determination of those [parts] that the establishment of the proven and the prover occurs. (316)
this is an intermediate verse.
Nor is sense-contact the means of valid cognition,
because even when connected with an object in its entirety, it is apprehended only by some [cognitions].
That restriction would not exist by means of [specific] properties, because there is no distinction in the relationship.

[347, viii] The Blessed One said: “O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are these four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, O monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What is the nutriment that leads to the origination of future existence? It is this craving which leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—that is, the craving for sensual pleasure, the craving for existence, and the craving for non-existence. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the origination of future existence. What is the nutriment that leads to the cessation of future existence? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving which leads to rebirth, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—that is, the craving for sensual pleasure, the craving for existence, and the craving for non-existence. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the cessation of future existence. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen suffering and to the increase of arisen suffering? It is ignorance. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen suffering and to the increase of arisen suffering. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen suffering and to the cessation of arisen suffering? It is wisdom. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen suffering and to the cessation of arisen suffering. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen defilements and to the increase of arisen defilements? It is improper attention. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen defilements and to the increase of arisen defilements. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen defilements and to the cessation of arisen defilements? It is proper attention. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen defilements and to the cessation of arisen defilements. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen fetters and to the increase of arisen fetters? It is association with persons of wrong view. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen fetters and to the increase of arisen fetters. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen fetters and to the cessation of arisen fetters? It is association with persons of right view. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen fetters and to the cessation of arisen fetters. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen enmity and to the increase of arisen enmity? It is anger and resentment. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen enmity and to the increase of arisen enmity. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen enmity and to the cessation of arisen enmity? It is patience and gentleness. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen enmity and to the cessation of arisen enmity. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen harm and to the increase of arisen harm? It is lack of restraint. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen harm and to the increase of arisen harm. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen harm and to the cessation of arisen harm? It is restraint. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen harm and to the cessation of arisen harm. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen fear and to the increase of arisen fear? It is unwholesome conduct. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen fear and to the increase of arisen fear. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen fear and to the cessation of arisen fear? It is wholesome conduct. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen fear and to the cessation of arisen fear. What is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen sorrow and to the increase of arisen sorrow? It is improper reflection. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the arising of unarisen sorrow and to the increase of arisen sorrow. What is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen sorrow and to the cessation of arisen sorrow? It is proper reflection. This, O monks, is the nutriment that leads to the non-arising of unarisen sorrow and to the cessation of arisen sorrow. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and departed. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta and, having approached, he said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, it was wonderful, it was marvelous how the Blessed One, in this very assembly, taught the Dhamma in such a way that it was clear, well-proclaimed, and free from ambiguity. “Indeed, friend Ānanda, it was wonderful, it was marvelous how the Blessed One, in this very assembly, taught the Dhamma in such a way that it was clear, well-proclaimed, and free from ambiguity. For what reason? Because, friend Ānanda, when one has properly understood the nutriment, the origin of the nutriment, the cessation of the nutriment, and the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment, then one has properly understood suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. And why? Because, friend Ānanda, nutriment is the root of suffering, its origin is its source, its cessation is its end, and the way leading to its cessation is the path. If the contact between the sense organ and its object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the apprehension of the object is its result. That contact is: conjunction (*saṃyoga*); inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*); inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*); inherence (*samavāya*); inherence in what inheres (*samavetasamavāya*); and the relation of qualifier and qualified in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Conjunction is the contact of the sense organ with a jar or the like. Inherence in what is conjoined is [the contact] with a quality that inheres in the jar. Inherence in what inheres in what is conjoined is [the contact] with whiteness or the like, which inheres in a quality that is conjoined [with the jar]. Inherence is [the contact] of the auditory organ, whose nature is space, with sound. Inherence in what inheres is [the contact] with "soundness," which inheres in sound. The relation of qualifier and qualified in what is conjoined is [the contact] of the sense organ with the absence of a jar in a particular location. In that regard, even if there is indeed a connection with what is conjoined, why is there the apprehension of that [absence]? Otherwise, there would be the cognition of fire and the like merely through their connection with smoke. If it is argued that there is apprehension because of the relation of inherence, then in that case, there would also be apprehension by the eye of touch and so forth, which inhere in the same object. If you say this is refuted by the fact of being in the same location, then just as there is apprehension of those things that inhere in the same object within a continuum, so too would there be [apprehension] of touch and the like. If you say there is no apprehension because they are not objects of the eye, then this is precisely the point under discussion.
[347,ix] It is considered how it is not so, because of their inherence in a single object.

Therefore, it is not logical to claim that [an object] is perceived through some properties alone, even though it is connected [to the sense organ] in its entirety. For if the atoms of the eye and other senses were to go out and move to another location for the sake of grasping an object, such that there is contact with it, then—because of this connection in its entirety—the entire form would be apprehended; consequently, properties such as the pot's [color] and so forth would also appear clearly, as would its color, and not merely its shape. Likewise, there would be the manifestation of all remaining universals (*jāti*) and so on. If it is argued that the instrument lacks the capacity at a distance and the like, then if it lacks capacity, let there simply be no apprehension at any time. If it is argued that such is the nature of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that the apprehension occurs in such a way, we say: no, because there is no difference [in the object].
[348,i] Of shape, by way of color.

For shape is not determined as distinct from color. If it is argued that [shape] is determined even apart from color—as in the case of [perceiving] "this is a jar"—that too is incorrect, because there too a dark color is perceived upon perception. If it is argued that there is no perception of color because darkness is not a real entity (*avastu*), that too is untenable, because it is impossible for that which is being perceived to be a non-entity. If it is argued that this occurs even in light for one whose eyes are closed, no; for that [cognition] is erroneous. And it does not follow that because one thing is erroneous, everything is erroneous, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting in the non-existence of external objects. Therefore, it must be stated once more: some cognition is erroneous and some is not. Consequently, the apprehension of shape occurs only in light, not in darkness; only when nearby, not at a distance.
Even though there is no difference in that [cognition], this distinction exists because it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, it is logical that there should be either the apprehension or the non-apprehension of that [object] by its entire nature. And even though that object is without differentiation, the differentiation of the cognition arises precisely from the form of blue and so forth, not from an external form. Therefore, the form alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might argue that even a cognition devoid of form could establish a specific object through its configuration (*saṃsthāna*). To this, he says: [348,v] "If [it is argued that it is] due to a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), [we reply: no, because even that [impression] is not established in the absence of that [form]. (318)

For a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), being itself restricted, would produce for cognition a restricted object-domain only if preceded by a restricted determination. For example, a memory arises exactly as the object was experienced; yet, the experience is not restricted to a specific object [without a cause]. Without a form (*ākāra*), how could there be such a restriction? How, then, could there be a restriction of the impression from which a restriction of the specific object follows? This would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): if the experience is restricted, the impression is restricted; and if the impression is restricted, the inference is restricted. Thus, not even one of them would exist. If cognition with a form (*sākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that very thing is the result (*phala*), which entails the identity of the action and the instrument, because the form is not distinct from the apprehension. To this, it is replied:
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between the action and the instrument being one and the same, this is incorrect;
for while we admit a distinction in their properties (*dharma*), the underlying entity (*vastu*) is held to be non-different. (319)
In this manner, the entire configuration of action and its factors exists through the superimposition [of distinctions] upon entities that are conceived as being non-different. (320)

If it is argued that it is illogical for action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kāraka*) to be identical from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), that is incorrect. For action, which consists of the causal factor, does not contradict the nature of the causal factors themselves. Indeed, activity (*vyāpāra*) is not distinct from the entity (*padārtha*). Rising and falling are not separate from the axe; rather, it is the very same [axe] whose production in successive points of space is designated in such a way. And this [activity] is not other than its own nature (*svarūpa*). Nor does it, by virtue of its own nature, contradict its identity with that [entity]. Now, if it is the conventional (*vyāvahārika*) action that is contradictory to the unity of the causal factor, then that is precisely what we accept. Since we admit a distinction of properties (*dharma-bheda*), the distinction of properties established through conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pariniṣṭhita*) is indeed accepted. It is precisely in this manner that the distinction between action and causal factors is established as possessing an imagined difference. To explain:
Based on positive and negative concomitance, one may conceive of identity or difference;
yet, conventional usage is established through the distinction between action and its factors.

[348,xi] Devadatta is first established as being one and the same by the force of recognition. His movement from one place to another consists in his occupying different locations. Consequently, a difference between the two actions is postulated; for that which differs while its substrate remains non-different must be distinct from it. However, in ultimate reality, it is Devadatta alone who appears as distinct due to the difference in states. Therefore, even among entities that are considered different by the world, [349,i]...

It functions by means of the superimposition of identity. Consequently, the distinction between action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka) is established in accordance with that [superimposition], but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha). Likewise, the mental aspect (ākāra) is not all-pervasive with respect to the attainment of the result; rather, the attainment itself pervades all aspects. Therefore, the distinction between the cognition (pramiti) and the means of cognition (pramāṇa) is based on differentiation. However, in ultimate reality, the cognition is simply the aspect itself as it manifests. Thus, the aspect is the means of cognition, and the awareness of the object is the result; the result is indeed non-different from the means of cognition, or conversely, the means of cognition is non-different from the result. As it has been said: [349,ii]
Because it is perceived as possessing an operation, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is itself the result (phala), namely,
self-cognition (svasaṃvedana).

Alternatively, self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the fruit here. For consciousness, which manifests as both [the object and itself], self-awareness alone is the fruit. [Objection: But surely the awareness of the object is the fruit, for one seeks the object. To this it is replied:
[349, iv] It is illogical that people seek the object when there is no awareness of the object.
The desire of people for an object that has never been seen is never possible;
for what is heard through tradition is indeed just like what has been seen.

[349, vi] But surely objects such as blue are indeed cognized; how then can there be an object that is not cognized? To this, the following objection is raised:
The agreement regarding the object is simply this: that which is the direct perception of each individual cognition.
Why is that cognition of the object not considered erroneous, given its conformity [to the object]? (321)

[349, viii] If the specific feeling or the cognition is what is perceived, then the claim that "cognition with a form (*sākārajñāna*) is itself the perception of the object" is merely a verbal designation; the actual perception of the object is not established.

Now, if it is argued that there is a cognition of an object precisely because of its conformity (*tādrūpya*)—since such conformity cannot exist without an object of that nature—we say: no, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as in the case of [the perception of] hair, flies, and so forth.
If it is asked, "Where then does this experience reside?", that very point is what is being investigated here.

[349,xi] If there is no connection with an object, then what is this experience? For experience must reside in that which is being experienced. How, then, can there be an experience of hair-threads and the like for one suffering from ophthalmia?

Is it not the case that something is indeed observed as being grounded in an external object? That very point is what is being investigated here. As for the claim that "the object is seen," it is not so seen; for the object itself is not perceived. If the cognition of an object were to arise from the mere act of impingement, then it would follow that the eye is also cognized, since [the cognition] arises from it. Likewise, just as an object is inferred from the observation of its effect through inference, the eye should also be inferred. Therefore, let it be postulated that the cognition itself possesses that form. If you argue that it is postulated as being external because it appears with the form of an external location, then why is there no postulation of a face existing in that location based on the form of the face in a mirror? Consequently, one must postulate that everything situated within the self appears in the form of a reflection, just like a face.
By what means do those atoms assume a similar form, and how is it that they appear as something gross?

[350,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld the sufferings of those beings and, by means of his compassionate heart, caused them all to transcend suffering. Thereupon, the Bhagavat addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “If there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall with single-minded devotion invoke him, then that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara will immediately perceive their voices and deliver them from all suffering. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there be any who, during a time of great conflagration, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, that great fire will be extinguished before it can reach them. Likewise, Ānanda, if there be any who, when adrift upon the great ocean, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then they shall not be harmed by waves, sea-monsters, or evil winds; by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, they shall safely reach the shore. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there be any kings, ministers, or their retinues who harbor malicious intent toward others, or if there be robbers who intend to plunder and harm others, and if those people should invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority, those malicious intentions shall be transformed into thoughts of benevolence and compassion. Thus spoke the Bhagavat. Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One further addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should observe that all phenomena are marked by emptiness and should thus give rise to the mind of non-attachment. They should observe that within form there is no self, no sentient being, no life-span, and no person; and so on for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—within each of these there is no self, no sentient being, no life-span, and no person. By observing in this way, one transcends the five aggregates of grasping. One should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to deliver those who invoke his name. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha: “Bhagavat, how should sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* observe it? The Buddha told Ānanda: “Sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should observe that all phenomena are empty, and they should not give rise to attachment toward form, nor toward feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Why is this? Because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. Furthermore, Ānanda, form is neither eternal nor impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither eternal nor impermanent. Form is neither painful nor pleasant; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither painful nor pleasant. Form is neither self nor non-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither self nor non-self. Form is neither pure nor impure; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither pure nor impure. Therefore, Ānanda, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should observe that all phenomena are empty and should give rise to the mind of non-attachment. This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, Māra and the Māra-hosts cannot find an opportunity to harm them. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the emptiness of all phenomena, they have transcended the realm of Māra. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha: “Bhagavat, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how should they dwell in the emptiness of all phenomena? The Buddha told Subhūti: “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should dwell in the emptiness of form, the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Why is this? Because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti, because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, it is neither increasing nor decreasing; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, being empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, are likewise neither increasing nor decreasing. Why is this? Because in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; there is no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon; there is no realm of the eye up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; there is no ignorance, no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death; there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should give rise to the mind of non-attachment, and yet they should not perceive that mind as an object of perception. Why is this? Because that mind is itself empty of the intrinsic nature of mind. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, then Māra and the Māra-hosts cannot find an opportunity to harm them. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has practiced the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the emptiness of all phenomena, they have transcended the realm of Māra. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha: “Bhagavat, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should not perceive the perfection of giving, nor the perfection of morality, patience, diligence, meditation, or wisdom. Why is this? Because these perfections are themselves empty of the intrinsic nature of perfection. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor the four noble truths, nor the four bases of psychic power, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, the eight liberations, the nine successive absorptions, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four grounds of self-confidence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Buddha. Why is this? Because these dharmas are themselves empty of the intrinsic nature of dharma. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor the fruit of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat; nor should they perceive the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha, nor the fruit of a Buddha. Why is this? Because these fruits are themselves empty of the intrinsic nature of fruit. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should not perceive the stage of Dry Wisdom, nor the stage of Heat, the stage of Peak, the stage of Patience, the stage of Supreme Mundane Dharma, the stage of the Path of Seeing, the stage of the Path of Cultivation, the stage of No-More-Learning, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha, or the stage of the Buddha. Why is this? Because these stages are themselves empty of the intrinsic nature of stage. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should not perceive the mark of permanence, nor the mark of suffering, the mark of emptiness, the mark of non-self, the mark of tranquility, the mark of detachment, the mark of cessation, or the mark of the unborn. Why is this? Because these marks are themselves empty of the intrinsic nature of mark. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā

If the object consists of atoms alone, then since there is no similarity between the object and the cognition that appears as something gross (*sthūla*), how can it be the object of that cognition? It would be merely an error, like the perception of a single mass such as a tree. If it is argued that [atoms] produce similarity by having the form of color (*varṇa*), we say no; for there is no shape (*saṃsthāna*) apart from color. If shape were possessed of the nature of color, then grossness itself would result. Now, if grossness is a property of the apprehension (*grahaṇadharma*), whereas color is a property of the object to be apprehended (*grāhyadharma*), and the designation "gross" occurs when many [atoms] are being apprehended, but not in each individual atom—whereas blueness and so forth exist in each one, and thus that is a property of the object to be apprehended—if this is the case, then because atoms with intervals are apprehended as being without intervals, it is indeed an error. If it is argued that it is not an error because the interval also appears [in the cognition], albeit not as an object (*aviṣayatayā*), then since the interval lacks any description of causal capacity and is thus non-existent (*nirupākhyam*), the interval would have no reality at all. Therefore, the entity must be conceived as being entirely without intervals. If it is argued that this is impossible because there can be no such thing as a truly interval-less [entity], we reply: a composite entity with parts is not tenable. An entity must be partless, just like cognition; thus, the atom is established. This is not so, because there is no logical connection (*pratibandha*) [between the premises and the conclusion]. Furthermore, this proposition is untenable because it is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*). And since there is no inference without direct perception, [your position fails]. If it is argued that the gross is merely a collection of subtle [atoms], [we respond as follows: *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly here. The translation reflects the full argument up to this point.)*
The answer to this has already been given previously; therefore, it is not stated again.
Therefore, its nature as an object is not capable of establishing the existence of the cognition of that [object], because it does not invariably deviate from a real object. (323)

[350, vi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not even the slightest dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti said: “As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata’s body a body made of real flesh? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata’s body is not a body made of real flesh; it is a Dharma-body. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of physical marks? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the possession of physical marks. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If a woman or a man were to fill as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, would that woman or man on account of this generate a great mass of merit? Subhūti said: “A great mass of merit, Blessed One; a great mass of merit, Sugata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, I declare to you, I proclaim to you: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up, retain, recite, and master even so much as a four-line verse from this perfection of wisdom and teach it to others, they would on account of this generate a greater mass of merit, immeasurable and incalculable. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma whatsoever by which he perceives that ‘I am a Tathāgata’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma whatsoever by which he perceives that ‘I am a Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Even though the nature of having the form of an object (*artharūpatā*) exists, it is subject to deviation; therefore, it is established that there is no cognition of an object through such cultivation (*bhāvanā*). For that which deviates cannot establish [its object], because the meaning of "proof" (*sādhana*) consists in non-deviation. If even that which deviates were a proof, then everything would be a proof for everything. Proof is the establishment of existence; however, deviation implies that at some time this [object] may not exist, thereby suggesting the possibility of non-existence. Thus, existence and its opposite are contradictory in one and the same place. Therefore, it is not the case that the status of consciousness as a proof of an object follows solely from its having the form of blue and so forth; this is not an absolute rule. Furthermore, although there is a similarity (*sārūpya*) between cognitions and objects, there is no mutual state of being a cognizer and a cognized between them. For indeed, even that which is similar to the cognition of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) is neither a cognizer nor a cognized object.

[350,vii] If the characteristics of being cognized consist in similarity to that [object] and arising from that [object], then the immediately preceding consciousness (*samanantaravijñāna*) which shares the same object would also be cognized. 324.

[350, viii] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: (1) the self-nature of attachment to words, (2) the self-nature of attachment to multiplicity of objects, (3) the self-nature of attachment to false discrimination, and (4) the perfectly accomplished self-nature. These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of self-nature. Among them, Mahāmati, the self-nature of attachment to words arises from the habit-energy of clinging to various names and expressions since beginningless time. The self-nature of attachment to multiplicity of objects arises from the habit-energy of clinging to the external world as having a manifold character. The self-nature of attachment to false discrimination arises from the habit-energy of clinging to the duality of grasped and grasper within the realm of one's own mind. And the perfectly accomplished self-nature, Mahāmati, is that which is free from the habit-energy of all false discriminations, is beyond the reach of the intellect, and is realized by noble wisdom. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the habit-energy of false discrimination and to enter the stage of the Tathāgata through the realization of the perfectly accomplished self-nature. Thus it is said: The self-nature of attachment to words, The self-nature of attachment to objects, The self-nature of false discrimination, And the perfectly accomplished nature— These are the four kinds of self-nature.

If that which is produced from something is perceived as having a form similar to it, then the immediately preceding consciousness (*samanantara-vijñāna*) would be the object, since it possesses an identical objective field (*viṣaya*). For instance, when both the preceding and the subsequent [moments] possess a blue aspect and arise from that same immediate predecessor, then because the preceding one possesses a similar form and is the cause of its arising, it follows that it must be an object. Alternatively, if the blue aspect that arises from something is the object of that [consciousness] by virtue of possessing that aspect, then in the case of a consciousness with an identical object, the aspect [of the first moment] would not be the immediate predecessor; otherwise, a yellow cognition would not arise immediately after a blue-aspected [cognition]. Therefore, it is established that the blue aspect and so forth are produced by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and thus that [preceding cognition] does not have the status of an object. Others explain: When a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) with a blue aspect arises immediately after a [non-conceptual] blue [cognition], the former [blue cognition] would be its object because it is what provides the aspect. This too is not incorrect, for it is indeed accepted that memory has the experienced object as its domain, and this is well known. Indeed, the entire world perceives the experience of an object through memory. Following upon this, one directly observes the object itself. All memory is observed to function toward the experience of the object, provided there is no lapse of memory. Consequently, its status as an object of experience is certainly accepted. And an admission [of this] is not a fault. Furthermore: Why consider the object of this memory at all? Here is the sequence: when a [conceptual] cognition arises due to the force of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) based on a previous experience of blue, that previous [experience] becomes its object. If it is asked, "How can that be its immediate predecessor?"—it is because there is no intervening experience of a similar kind of the same class. If it is asked, "How can it be its producer?"—the answer has already been given: it has been demonstrated that even a remote [cause] can be a producer. Alternatively, the very aspect of the conceptualization, being a clear aspect produced by cultivation, would be the object that produces the clear aspect. Therefore, the object cannot be established from that aspect [alone]. According to the principle that "this aspect of the object belongs to the same class as that which arose from the force of cultivation," there is no logical necessity for postulating an external object. Thus, the immediately preceding consciousness alone is the object. If this is so:
[(kha) An Examination of Proximity regarding the Seen and the Seer: [351,ii] That wherein there arises a determinative cognition such as, "This has been seen," or "This has been heard."
That experience of it, and that very proximity, is what is being investigated. (325)
That by which the seen and the seeing are established is considered the means for them; relying upon the relationship between these two, this determination of the observer arises. (326)

[351,iv] If the determination of an object depends upon certainty, and it is claimed that this certainty does not arise from anything other than the object itself—for indeed, there is no certainty that "this is the immediately preceding condition" (samanantarapratyaya)—but rather, "this experience of mine has no object; its object is not the immediately preceding condition"—for it is not logical to have the certainty that "this is an object" without an experience of the object, since certainty follows the experience.

To this it is replied: the determination of an object does not arise from experience alone, but rather from the certainty that follows it. Thus, it comes to this: one object does not itself follow the path; rather, being drawn along by it, a second [cognition] follows—this is truly a great marvel! For instance:
a cognition that arises directly from an object does not perceive [the object as it is].

To claim that another person, even one inferior to him, understands that same object is sheer audacity. (PVA 626) [351,vii] Since the ascertainment follows from experience, it is through that very ascertainment that the experience of the object is understood, and not merely the intrinsic nature [of the cognition]. If it were otherwise, the ascertainment would occur in exactly that same way [as the object itself].

This is incorrect. For indeed, it is not even known whose experience it is; how then can its conformity to experience be established? If it is asked, "From what, then, does certainty arise?", we have already demonstrated that it arises from habituation (*abhyāsa*) alone. And since that habituation also arises from experience, how could there be a contrary certainty? This too is no solution, because if this were the case, no one would ever have a contrary certainty, yet such is observed. Therefore, this is untenable.

Is it not the case that mere observation does not effect discrimination, and that discrimination between what is beneficial and what is harmful arises only from ascertainment? If this were so, then even ascertainment would not effect discrimination; for the cognition of two moons does not effect the ascertainment of one moon. If it is argued that ascertainment becomes a means of discrimination through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), we say no; for practice is without a fixed cause. Indeed, practice could only be established as real if it were restricted to a specific, determinate experience. Furthermore, even the ascertainment that "this is an object" is intended only in the sense of being capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). And that causal efficiency is nothing other than another appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Nor is there a non-arising of one appearance from another appearance. Therefore, the determination of an object does not result from ascertainment.
As for what was also said: "Now, where does that experience belong? To that also it is replied:
That [self] is its experience, and it belongs to no one else;
even its being known through direct perception is its very nature as that [self]. (327)

[352,iii] For since the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of entities does not arise without a cause, an inquiry into the cause is logical. Therefore, [the question] "from what" is appropriate. But what is the meaning of the question "where is this"? To explain:

When it is asked, "Where is this experience? and an answer is given, then there would again be a question regarding that object: "Where is that object? Thus, there is an infinite regress. (627) (PVA) [352,v]

If it is argued that such a question is merely a playful inquiry, we reply: no, because an ultimate limit is observed. For instance, when one asks "Where is that object? the answer is "On the ground. Then one asks "Where is that [ground]? and the answer is "It is seen exactly in this way," at which point there is no further questioning. If this is so, since the object is not perceived [beyond its own locus], let experience itself be seen as abiding in its own nature; what is the use of postulating a substratum? By this, the questioning regarding the meaning of the genitive case is also refuted.
Thus he says: "And that [experience] does not belong to anything else."

[352, vii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is edible food? It is that which is called "edible food" in the world, whether it be masticated or consumed by drinking. Furthermore, whatever other form exists that is similar to this, all such things are collectively termed "edible food. What is contact as nutriment? It is that which is called "contact" in the world. Furthermore, whatever other feeling exists that arises from contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, all such things are collectively termed "contact as nutriment. What is mental volition as nutriment? It is that which is called "mental volition" in the world. Furthermore, whatever other volition exists that is directed toward the realm of form, the realm of formlessness, or toward liberation, all such things are collectively termed "mental volition as nutriment. What is consciousness as nutriment? It is that which is called "consciousness" in the world. Furthermore, whatever other consciousness exists that is associated with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, all such things are collectively termed "consciousness as nutriment. These four nutriments sustain beings who have already come to be and support those seeking birth. Regarding this, what is the nutriment that sustains beings who have already come to be? It is the aforementioned three nutriments, excluding edible food. What is the nutriment that supports those seeking birth? It is edible food. Why is this so? Because when a being is conceived in a mother's womb, it first takes hold of the kalala through edible food. Having taken hold of the kalala, it subsequently develops through the remaining three nutriments. Therefore, it is established that edible food is the nutriment that supports those seeking birth. As for the three nutriments—contact, mental volition, and consciousness—they sustain beings who have already come to be, but they do not support those seeking birth. Why is this so? Because at the time of conception in the mother's womb, the kalala does not yet possess contact, mental volition, or consciousness. Since these three nutriments do not exist at that stage, they cannot support those seeking birth. However, once the kalala has developed, these three nutriments do sustain beings who have already come to be. How, then, can an object known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) be refuted? To explain: those who possess [the cognition] see blue through direct perception. It has been stated that this is not because of seeing an external object; rather, it is only the form of that [cognition] which is known through direct perception, and not a separate object. It is precisely this form that is conventionally designated as "blue," and nothing else. Therefore, the experience whose nature is blue is called "the experience of blue," just as one says "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputraka*). For a distinction is not established merely by the existence of a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*), since such a relation exists in some way or another. Alternatively, how could that experience be "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) if there were no other experience of it? Its status as direct perception is all the more established by the experience residing within its own nature (*svarūpa*), for direct perception is impossible in the case of another's form. Indeed, that form does not belong to another. If it did, it would be something entirely different. Or, if the object were that of which the non-obscured (*aparokṣa*) consciousness is the experience, then that [consciousness] would be the self (*ātman*) of that [object], because it is not known elsewhere. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the fault? [we reply: "And that [self] does not belong to another. If the self of an object were [shared], it would exist exactly the same for another person as well, and thus everyone would be a perceiver of it. Yet it is not so for another.

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended; since they cannot be apprehended, they are neither real nor unreal.
