Is it not the case that [the object] is not known by itself through perception? No; having established that very form as distinct [from the cognition], there is such a designation through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Therefore, experience is simply the nature of blue and so forth, which is not cognizable by anything other than itself. Alternatively, if the object is not experienced, why is it that this [object] appears within the range of experience as being connected to an external location? It is the self (*ātman*) alone that is experienced; it is the mind (*citta*) alone that is experienced. How can there be an "external location"? And that [experience] does not belong to another. Therefore, how could it be external? Alternatively, it is the self, for you yourself accept that "this is the object" is indeed the self. And its experience belongs to that [self] alone, and not to another, because there exists no entity distinct from it. Or, if you say it belongs to "that" (the self), no; because it is to be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For its being known through direct perception occurs only by means of the self itself, and not otherwise.

[352,ix] But surely this entails the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*). No; because there is the cognition of variegated forms. That which arises through the power of ignorance is merely cognition; it does not serve the purpose of a doctrine of a self. On the contrary, the absence of a self (*nirātmakatva*) is conducive to the pacification of passion and the like, and thus there is no fault. This very point he demonstrates with the following: [352,x]
There is nothing else to be experienced by it, nor is there any other experience of it;
since the same objection applies to that as well, it shines forth by itself. (328)

[352,xi] That which is experienced by cognition does not exist as something other [than itself]. Just as there is no other object to be experienced, so it has been explained. Well then, let there be for that cognition an experience of something other than itself. No; even in that case, there is an absence of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper. For how can that which is established in its own nature as pure self-awareness (*samvedana*) be an experience of another? Direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) and the like have already been refuted. And if it were to enter into that awareness, the two would become one and the same. Thus, it is established that it is that very [cognition] which shines forth by itself, and nothing other than that. [353,i]

How, then, is there the cognition of another’s mind for yogins? This will be addressed later. Therefore, because it illuminates its own nature by itself, it exists in that manner. If this is so, let it be the experience of its own nature; how then does the manifestation "experience of blue" occur? To this, he says:
[353,ii] "The establishment of the experience of blue and so forth..."
This [cognition] has blue and other forms as its intrinsic nature, and it is an experience;
because it experiences blue and so forth, it is known as such, even though it is an experience of its own nature. (329)

Because it has the nature of blue, there is the experience of blue, but not a separate experience of the blue; for there is no such thing as a pure experience [independent of its object]. For whatever is non-different from something else is the object of conventional usage precisely in that form.
For if it were pure, it would be determined as such;
however, even in its own nature, a distinction is observed, and therefore it is not so.
(PVA 353,v)

It is logical that what is called "the experience of blue" exists precisely as it appears—that is, as having both the nature of blue and the nature of experience. Furthermore, a difference [between two things] does not arise merely from the use of distinct designations; for it has already been established that such distinct designations are observed to occur even through the power of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), regardless of how they may be applied.

Now, one might ask: how can blue manifest its own nature? For objects such as jars, which are to be illuminated, do not become their own illuminators by means of a lamp or the like. An action upon itself is a contradiction; indeed, a sword-blade cannot cut itself with that very same blade.
[353,vii] Here is the rebuttal.
[353,viii]
Being manifest, it illuminates its own nature through identity; just as light is held to be so, so too is cognition the illuminator of the self. (330)
[353,ix] It has the form of the cognized and the cognizer;

From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it understood that there is a contradiction in an action operating upon itself? For the establishment of a matter does not proceed from a mere example (*dṛṣṭānta*), since an example—such as a lamp—is possible even in the case of the opposite of what is intended. If a jar is illuminated by a lamp through its external nature, and the lamp likewise by another such [lamp], there is no objection. Nor is it the case that even the jar is illuminated by the lamp; rather, it is produced as something already of such a nature. If it is argued that the lamp too is illuminated by another, such as the eye, we say no. For although the eye and so forth are common to all jars and other objects, even when the eye is present, the jar requires the lamp as its illuminator; thus the lamp would be in the same position. If it is then argued that the jar is indeed produced, and its illumination is performed by the eye and so forth, then in that case:
Just as there is illumination by a lamp even when the external object is not itself luminous,
let it be accepted that the eye and other [senses] are also the objects of designation. (629) (PVA)

Just as, even though a jar of such a nature arises from that [lamp], there is the designation "the jar is manifested by the lamp," so too there is a designation based on its arising in that very way from the eye and other [causes]. Now, if both are illuminators of the jar and so forth, while for the lamp and so forth only one is, then in that case:
[353, xiii]
One [cause] may manifest for someone else, while two alone manifest for another;
as the case may be, let it be that even one does not manifest for yet another—what loss is there?

For one who is absolutely incapable, there are two [results]; for another, one; and for yet another, not even one. This is simply the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*); what harm is there in this? Now, if it is argued that there is a contradiction of an action upon itself:
when that very nature is its own, how can there be any contradiction?
For if there were contradiction by way of their own intrinsic nature, everything would simply perish.

For there is no contradiction with something by its own very nature; if that were the case, nothing would exist by its own nature, and everything would vanish. Furthermore, "cutting" is the production of something distinct, and a thing cannot be produced by itself. This is precisely what is meant by the "contradiction of an action upon itself. However, its nature as self-luminous is not contradicted by that very nature. If one asks why this is so, it must be said: because its own cause is of such a kind. The logical principle is that if that cause does not exist, then [the effect] could not exist, and not otherwise. Therefore, the opponent must state that self-luminosity is simply not observed. To that, the answer has already been given: because everything is manifested by its own nature. Again, it is said:
And if that [consciousness] were to perceive an object distinct from itself, then the relationship between the perceived and the perceiver would be difficult to establish.

Cognition must be either distinct from its object or self-luminous. If it were self-luminous, it would manifest by its own nature; if that were so, then the object would be manifested by it as something other than itself. If cognition were not luminous, such a designation [of the object as "manifested"] could not occur. If, however, cognition does manifest, then the object must likewise manifest at that very same time; how then could there be a manifestation of the object by another [the cognition]? For at that moment, there is no distinction between the manifested and the manifestor. If it is argued that a distinction in apprehension arises because the operation of that [cognition] occurs sequentially, then it is as follows: [354, iv]
When a lamp or similar object is brought near, its specific quality is perceived;
therefore, why is it not accepted that the reality of both of them arises in that same way?

"A particularity manifests. Its manifestation occurs by means of its own very form; therefore, it is the manifestation of its own nature that takes place in such a way. Consequently, even at the end, there is only self-manifestation. Now, if it is argued that "it manifests itself" is not perceived, and that no such linguistic usage occurs, for that very reason it is said:

Indeed, it is only practice that conforms to experience that ought to be validated as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not every practice. If, however, every practice were a means of knowledge, then nothing at all would need to be said to inform an opponent. Therefore, one’s acceptance [of a doctrine] must accord with how it is perceived.

Now, it is not logical for what is called "consciousness" (*saṃvedana*) to be imperceptible; likewise, it is a rule that the object of consciousness is not always so [imperceptible]. It is also logical for the object of consciousness to be imperceptible. But if it were always known [simultaneously with its cognition], then no distinction between the cognition and the object could be apprehended.
That is incorrect.
Blue and other such objects are not perceived apart from their state of being experienced.
If it is argued that there is perception even of what is not experienced, how could that be possible in the absence of experience?

To say that something is apprehended while remaining unexperienced is contradictory; thus, the meaning would be that what is unapprehended is apprehended. Now, if it is argued that what is not being experienced is nevertheless apprehended by perception or inference, that too is incorrect. For the position is that an object is nothing other than its state of being experienced, and not that it is merely experienced by perception. Even inferential apprehension, regarding its own nature, is indeed an apprehension by perception with respect to the object to be grasped.

[Objection: But surely there is also an object beyond that, whether it is seen by another or otherwise. [Response: No. Since there is no cognition [of it], how can it be said to exist when it is not being cognized? [Objection: It is cognized precisely by means of inference (*anumāna*). [Response: In that case, it would not be an inference at all, because the object is being directly perceived (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). [Objection: [It is cognized] by way of non-direct perception. [Response: What does this mean? To say "that [object] does not exist" and yet "that exists" is illogical. What is the meaning of "non-direct perception" being "cognition"? If its own nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended, that itself is direct perception; if it is not, then it is simply not cognized—this is the principle.
If it is cognized in its own nature, that is indeed direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
If it is not cognized in its own nature, then it is entirely uncognized. (634) Even if it is cognized in its own nature, if it were not directly perceived, [it would be as if uncognized].
In that case, how could there be a difference in the cognition of the blue form?

For the difference between blue and other [objects] arises from a difference in their apprehension; since they possess a single nature, how can the difference of one thing be supported by valid cognition when it resides in something else? (PVA 635–636)
If its suchness [non-duality] were due to association with that [the object], how could it be immediate?
And for one who has attained identity with that, how could it be considered so from that [association]?
(637) Through positive and negative concomitance, there is no real extraction of difference.

For direct perception does not [itself] possess positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). (638) (PVA) If it is argued that the cognition [of concomitance] comes from inference, then inference would not be preceded by perception.
In the absence of that [perception], there would be an absence of inference, resulting in an infinite regress of dependence. (639) (PVA)
For how could even the pervaded exist without the pervader?
And if it is not perceived, how indeed can it then be called a "pervader"?

For if that which is to be perceived is perceived at that time as being restricted to that very [object], how can it have the status of being the object? Or, if it is not perceived, how can there be a perception of its pervasiveness? If you say, "It was previously perceived as pervasive," then what is the use of inference now? If you say, "Its existence at this present time was not apprehended, therefore inference is not redundant," then how is there a perception of pervasiveness? [355, viii] If it was perceived previously, why is it not perceived now; and if it is not perceived now, how is there a comprehension of pervasiveness?
If that [inference] is merely a cognition, how is its pervasion stated?
(641) For if the cognition in the form of smoke does not exist without fire, then this very cognition of fire must also be admitted to exist without fire. (642)
How can smoke, which is the effect of fire, be a mere cognition?
That is incorrect. For instance: if smoke and the like were effects of fire, they would possess an external form.

And if its externality were established, then it could be the effect of fire. This [argument], being established through mutual dependence, is a matter whose reality is not properly set forth and is therefore not to be presented at all. By this, the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has been refuted. As for the one who says that the state of "consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātratā*) is rejected by the very force of recognition—for instance:
[355,xiv] If the object of recognition resides within cognition, what is the purpose of recognition?
On the other hand, if the nature of the object is not cognized, how can there be "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*)? (PVA 644)

[355, xv] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his supernatural power, transformed himself into a great white ox. With his horns he lifted up the ship, and with his hooves he struck the water. Thereupon, the ship was raised high above the waves and carried away from the sea. At that time, the five hundred merchants were filled with fear and cried out in unison: "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Dharma! Homage to the Saṅgha! Having uttered these words, they immediately saw the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara standing upon the ship, his body golden in color, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Seeing him, their minds were filled with joy, and they all bowed down to him. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara spoke to the five hundred merchants, saying: "Do not be afraid. I shall now lead you all to the shore of safety. Having said this, he took them across the great ocean until they reached the shore. Thereupon, the five hundred merchants, having escaped from the peril of the great ocean, offered various kinds of incense and flowers to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. They then returned to their own country and reported the matter to the King, saying: "Great King, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Avalokiteśvara who has come to our land. He possesses great spiritual power and can deliver sentient beings from all perils. Hearing this, the King was overjoyed and went forth to meet the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Upon seeing him, he bowed down at his feet and circumambulated him three times. He then invited the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara into the palace and provided him with every kind of offering. After the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara had accepted the offerings, he preached the Dharma for the King and his retinue, causing them to give rise to the aspiration for supreme perfect enlightenment. Thus did the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara rescue the five hundred merchants from the peril of the great ocean and cause them to attain the fruit of supreme perfect enlightenment. This is called the second chapter on the rescue from the peril of the great ocean. [356,i] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should fall into a great fire, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, that great fire will be extinguished and they will not suffer harm. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,ii] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should fall into a great river, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will not be swept away by the current and will safely reach the other shore. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,iii] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should encounter robbers or enemies, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those robbers and enemies will not be able to harm them. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,iv] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be imprisoned or bound in shackles, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, their bonds will loosen and they will be released. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,v] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be afflicted by various diseases, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those diseases will be cured and they will regain their health. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,vi] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be pursued by a wicked king or an enemy king, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will find protection and escape from danger. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,vii] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be threatened by the calamity of fire, water, wind, or thunderbolts, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will be spared from such disasters. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,viii] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be afflicted by various evil spirits, demons, or ghosts, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those spirits and demons will depart and no longer cause harm. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,ix] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be in a place of great darkness or deep gloom, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, light will appear and they will see clearly. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,x] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be in a state of extreme poverty or lacking in the necessities of life, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will obtain wealth and provisions. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears. [356,xi] Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, having heard it, keep it in mind, then if they should be in a state of mental distress or suffering from sorrow, by virtue of calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, their minds will become peaceful and their sorrows will be dispelled. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassion and great spiritual power, and is able to deliver sentient beings from all fears

It is not the case that the middle existence (*madhyasattā*) is perceived through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), because it is perceived as being present within consciousness by way of its own immediacy (*aparokṣatā*). This is incorrect. For instance: if you argue that even perception through mediacy (*parokṣatā*) is simply the object’s being included within cognition—since there is no perception of what is not included within cognition—this has already been established. If you ask, "How can one recognize [the middle] without perceiving the middle existence? [we reply: It is observed that recognition occurs merely from the perception of the similarity between the prior and posterior states; it will be exactly like that, so what is the need for anything else? It is like the recognition of hair or nails that have been cut off and grown back again. Now, if you say that in those cases the recognition-cognition has the genus (*jāti*) and so forth as its object, let it be recognized as such; however, the oneness of the individual (*vyakti*) is not thereby established. Furthermore, the genus itself does not exist in the middle, due to a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). If you claim that recognition is the valid evidence, no; for the mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the prior and posterior is the basis of recognition, and that alone is the objective support (*ālambana*) of recognition. Nor does that very recognition-cognition have the middle form as its support, because the middle form is not experienced. Indeed, what is mediately perceived and unseen cannot be taken as an objective support. And if it were seen, then because it is immediate, it would be nothing other than consciousness itself. If you object: "But if it is mediate, how can it be consciousness? At whatever stage it exists, it is indeed immediate. [We reply: Even if it is mediate now due to having passed away, there is no loss of its status as consciousness. If that were the case, then the object (*artha*) would also lose its status as an object. If you say, "The object also certainly loses its status as an object when it has passed away," [we reply: then the middle existence would not have the status of an object, since that too has passed away. If you say, "Even if it has passed away, and even if it is mediate, its status as an object does not depart, because there is no contradiction," [we reply: But how can there be the status of consciousness (*samvedanatva*) for that which is not experienced? Then how can there be the status of an object for that which does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*)? For that which is not experienced is not capable of performing a causal function. Perception of it through inference has been rejected. If it were experienced by another [cognition] in the middle, then that [middle state] would be the very nature of consciousness, and its being known by another would not be recognized through recognition. Therefore, there is no oneness with that [middle state], because oneness is not established through recognition. Furthermore, the form of inference arises from the force of mental impressions (*vāsanā*); thus, it is one in the nature of consciousness. Consequently, the entire form—even that which appears with vivid clarity—is [produced] from that very impression.

[356,i] But surely, since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is of a single nature, how can there be a difference in the forms of the cognitions? If it is argued that the difference arises from a difference in the latent impressions: if the latent impressions, which possess infinite distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth, are the producers of cognition, then what is the difference between this external form and the form belonging to the cognition? For "latent impression" is merely a name.
That is incorrect.
Or rather, that capacity which is produced by the preceding cognition is what is called [the cause].
Since that [mental impression] lacks the nature of being formless, how can there be an identity of object?

(PVA 645) For those who know the true nature of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) maintain that it is a capacity produced by a preceding cognition. An object (*artha*), however, possesses a formal nature and is always a source of affliction.

[356,v] But surely even an object is a cause of affliction only when it is in a state of being cognized, not at all times. Therefore, whether the appearance that arises by the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the cause of affliction or the object itself, what is the difference between these two?
That is incorrect;
for even though there is no distinction in the external object, there is a distinction in its clarity and so forth.
Through the excellence of cultivation, the object does not appear [as it is].

(PVA 646) For when, by the power of cultivation, the unreal is reached and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of error cease, at the moment of encountering the desired latent impressions, there is the cessation of the undesired and the attainment of the desired; this is a great distinction. Therefore, the entire appearance of differentiation is produced solely by the latent impressions that constitute the nature of cognition.

[356,ix] But surely, since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is of the same nature as the single consciousness, when an awakening factor is present, all latent impressions would be awakened, resulting in the arising of a consciousness containing infinite appearances; this is a great inconsistency. However, there is no such fault if external objects are admitted, for only that object which is proximate is perceived. No, for it is admitted that even what is not proximate is perceived. To explain:

Some maintain that it is a loss of memory; others, a perverted cognition; while still others hold it to be the apprehension of the non-existent. According to yet another view, everything exists everywhere.

For those for whom everything exists everywhere, the fault is exactly the same. Even in the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the manifestation of all things that are non-existent. As for one who maintains that it is a lapse of memory (*smṛtivipramoṣa*), why was there not previously a perception of the manifold? This [question] is the same even in the Idealist doctrine (*vijñānavāda*); thus, he is not at fault. Whether it is consciousness that is remembered as having occurred previously, or the object—what is the difference? Even in the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), whether it proceeds toward what was previously seen or otherwise, why does it not occur everywhere? The same objection applies; furthermore, in that case, that very same restriction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) must be explained, so it is the same. Nor is the mental impression (*vāsanā*) held to be of the nature of the immediately preceding consciousness (*samanantaravijñāna*). For a mental impression is a clear manifestation of a previous state of self-awareness.
How could it be so, since it produces a self-awareness of that very nature, without [an object]?
[356,xiii]
It is observed that when there is the presence of an awakener, the birth of cognitions occurs according to their respective natures,
as they are associated with the appearances of blue, yellow, and so forth. (648) (PVA) [356,xiv]

In this case, it is observed that a prior cognition—characterized by the appearance of either a desired or an undesired object and governed by modes such as intensity—gives rise subsequently, either immediately or after an interval of time, to a similar cognition. Just as a perception during the waking state produces a dream-appearance. If it is asked how there can be an arising from something separated [in time], the answer is: memory, dream-cognitions, and the like are seen to arise even from what is separated; thus, there is no objection to what is observed.

[Objection: But surely that [past object] does not produce [the cognition]; rather, it is that very [object] which appears due to the power of a vow (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth. [Reply: No, because there is no appearance of what is past. [Objection: It is observed that even the past appears. [Reply: What does it mean for "what is non-existent" to appear? It means nothing other than a cognition having that [past object's] form. Therefore, memory, arising from that experience, makes known a specific capacity belonging to that very [experience]. That... [357,i]

Nor can that be designated as a specific power (*śaktiviśeṭha*). Furthermore, this very nature of cause and effect is indeed observed to be such. Therefore, there is no lack of evidence for the existence of latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) and the distinction between preceding cognitions; for the beginninglessness of objects is established precisely by the beginninglessness of the latent dispositions.
As it has been stated: "The external continuum of cause and effect is without beginning."
In the same way, why is it not accepted that the continuum of consciousness is beginningless?
If it is asked, "What is the cause for the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?", that is incorrect.
The distinction between latencies (*vāsanā*) certainly exists, because its cause is possible.
For the distinction between cognitions is its cause, and from that, in turn, arises the distinction [between the latencies]. (PVA 650)

[357,v] Or rather, the very distinction between preceding cognitions is the basis for the distinction between latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the distinction between cognitions likewise arises from that very same distinction between latent impressions; what fault is there in this? [One might object: "In this case, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). That is not so, because:
That very same latent impression cannot be both produced by it and its cause for that [cognition],
because otherwise there would be this fault of mutual dependence.

However, one latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the cause of a particular consciousness, while another condition (*pratyaya*) is the cause of that other latent impression; it is produced by the differentiation of a prior latent impression. Therefore, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). This is equally the case even when there is the perception of an external object (*arthadarśana*). For instance:
"If the differentiation of the object is the cause, then how, in turn, is its differentiation [established]?"

For if the difference [in objects] were due to the difference in cognitions, there would indeed be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Indeed, a difference in objects cannot be without a cause, for it is impossible for that [difference] to be based solely on the difference in cognitions; thus, if the difference in cognitions were the cause, there would be the fault of mutual dependence. To say that the difference in objects itself is the cause of the difference in objects is even more inconsistent. If one argues that a different difference in objects is the basis for another difference in objects, and that too for yet another, this same logic applies equally to mental impressions (*vāsanā*).

[357,x] But surely, it is logical that consciousness is differentiated because the differentiation of objects appears; however, what is the solution regarding the latent impression (*vāsanā*)? If the latent impression also appears, then like the object, it is the object itself, and only the name differs. In that case, being active in grasping only the latent impression, it would produce only a difference in the grasper, not in the grasped. For instance, a latent impression produced from experience is seen to generate only memory. Here is the solution: [357,xi]
It was stated previously that here, the preceding consciousness itself is the "impression" (*vāsanā*).
Does that consciousness, which produces subsequent cognitions with various forms, not possess a non-differentiating nature?
(PVA 653) For just as a chain-binding brings about a steady movement, [so too does the preceding consciousness produce the subsequent].
Even in the absence of a self, the cause for the transition to that form is observed.

(PVA 654) A distinction is seen even in the form of the apprehended object due to the distinction of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), as in cases such as desire, grief, and fear, even though external objects are absent. (PVA 655)

[357,xiv] Now, even in that case, the external object itself—characterized by difference in place and time—is the objective support (*ālambana*) for all cognitions, because they possess an objective support. Even if it is not apprehended there at that very moment, let it not exist then and there; however, what proof is there that it does not exist elsewhere at another time? For instance, when a jar is not perceived in a certain place at a certain time, it is absent then and there, but not everywhere. To this, it is replied:
How can there be difference by way of location and so forth for that which is perceived here?
For you, does that which is seen as blue and so on possess any other form? (656) (PVA) [357,xvi]

If even that which is in another location is perceived as being in another location, then the same applies to the blue form; this is equal [in both cases]. Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a different form, it is not otherwise; thus, the rebuttal that "it is in another location" is met by the same rebuttal that "it is otherwise. There is no sublation regarding the form, but there is sublation regarding the location; therefore, it is that very [object] associated with a location that does not exist, but not the form. In that case, then, [the cognition] would be without an objective support (*nirālambana*); consequently, the claim that "everything has an objective support" (*sālambana*) is unestablished. But surely it does have an objective support even there, because:
No connection whatsoever is observed apart from the location and the object contained therein. And if those two were the objective support, how could cognition lack an objective support? (657) (PVA)

[357,xix] In that case, it is precisely the form of the location and what is contained therein that appears; and if those two exist, why would form be without an object? For there is no other relation between them; thus, every consciousness has an object.
If [cognition] has an object-support even during [mental] union (*yoga*), why is it not the same in the case of attainment (*prāpti*)?
Even in the absence of attainment, to claim that it possesses an object-support would be inconsistent.

If there is no such thing as "attainment" (*prāpti*), then even so-called "misapprehension with an object" (*sālambana-viparītakhyāti*) would likewise not exist; thus, there is a contradiction with your own tenet. Furthermore, let everything simply be misapprehension in that manner—what is the point of imagining it otherwise? This has already been demonstrated, so it will not be stated again. If it is argued that this is not the case because there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), [we reply: even the absence of a subverting cognition is itself a form of misapprehension; therefore, it lacks the capacity to be a true subverter. Moreover, in cases where there is a difference in time, it is perceived that the operation belongs to the mental impression (*vāsanā*) alone, and not to the object. The specific form [of the cognition] arises from a prior experience itself; it is not the manifestation of the form of an object that does not currently exist. Now, if consciousness is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), how can there be the relationship of the "perfumed" and the "perfumer" (*vāsya-vāsaka-bhāva*) therein?
That which has not yet arisen cannot be perfumed, nor is that which is past a perfumer.

Even if they occur together, there can be no relationship of "perfumer and perfumed" (*vāsyavāsakabhāva*) between them due to their mutual lack of connection. That is incorrect; for it has been established that the relationship of "perfumer and perfumed" is nothing other than a specific kind of cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Furthermore, since this [relationship] exists only for momentary things and not for eternal ones, the argument "because of momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatvāt*) is actually a proof of the opposite. And therefore:
In memory, the perceiving subject (*grāhaka*) is distinct and is not devoid of the form of the perceived object (*grāhyākāra*).
In that case, the object does not exist as a presence before [the mind] by way of its own being.
Furthermore, since cognitions are momentary and destruction is without residue, the relationship between the perfumed and the perfumer is impossible;
it could only be postulated if there were permanence.
A moment arises as something distinct while still being produced from the preceding moment;
subsequently, at another time, an effect other than that [preceding moment] is born from it.
This relationship of the perfumer and the perfumed is nothing other than that of cause and effect.
For that which is perishing might be impressed by the preceding as the succeeding arises;
however, entities that remain stable are not impressed by other stable entities, because they are already established. (PVA 662)

For since that which is eternal is unchanging, how could there be the relation of cause and effect? Being established as it is, it cannot undergo contact with a latent impression (*vāsanā*) different from its prior state.
Or rather, due to its lack of distinction [from the previous state], no new latent impression would ever arise for it, just as before. (PVA 663)
Even though [the mind] is fragile, there is a latent impression (*vāsanā*) because of its similarity to what preceded it and because it is distinct [from it].
And that conformity certainly exists even if cognitions are momentary;
why should the subsequent [cognition] not arise from the preceding cognition produced at that time? (PVA 664–665)
It is not accepted that this very moment produces another effect;
therefore, even though it perishes immediately after arising, there is an "undertaking" because it persists for a moment.
What loss is there to the correspondence [of cause and effect] if destruction occurs without leaving a trace?

If there were no dharma whatsoever belonging to that [previous cognition] in subsequent cognitions, then there would be no uniformity based on a cognition of similar reflection. Furthermore, if the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the cognition of a cow were to exist only when it corresponds [to its object], [there would be no recollection]. (PVA 667–668)
In that case, there would be no latent impression (*vāsanā*) because of the difference in cognition, such as [the cognition] of an elephant;
otherwise, even when there is an interruption, the latent impression persists due to its prior firmness. A firmly induced cognition produces its effect even when there is an interruption. (PVA 669)
From the cognition of an elephant, the cognition of an elephant proceeds from a preceding [moment] (670).
In the interim, a cognition with a different characteristic arises from a different latent impression (vāsanā).
Nor are all latent impressions destroyed by the destruction of a single cognition (671).
For when the flower has perished, from what could color arise?
How could the seed, sprout, stalk, and so forth [be the cause], given that they are of a different nature?
Even those [subsequent stages] are produced by that [seed] alone, acting as the causes of the effect through a sequence.
Why is it that this [cognition] does not likewise exist for cognitions such as that of a buffalo?
Therefore, a cognition arising in all its aspects from all these [causes] ought not to undergo destruction in a single moment alone. (PVA 673–674)
Even when that substratum is destroyed, there may be another substratum for the capacity;
nor is there a loss of momentariness, because the capacity is not distinct [from the entity itself].
However, the stream of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is not at all like the stream of cognitions.

For those who understand latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is accepted that a latent impression is indeed of the nature of a potentiality (*śakti*). (676) From a latent impression that cognition arises, and from those [cognitions] a latent impression [arises];
these two would indeed act equally upon one another at some time. (677) (PVA)
Even though the cause is dissimilar, it exists as having the nature of a specific capacity;
therefore, from that dissimilar cause, a dissimilar effect arises.
Thus, this [causal relation] is conceptually constructed within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) without being distinct [from it].
If it were not a real entity, what other effect could possibly arise from it?

(679) (PVA) But for one who maintains that there is a stable cognizer and that the cultivation of knowledge is accepted, for him there is no substratum for the latent impression (*vāsanā*), nor is that [cognizer] considered to be the latent impression itself. (680) (PVA)

When lac-dye or similar substances are poured over the flower of a citron tree (*bījapūra*) and so forth, it is the very form of that [dye] which is transferred to its fruit; this is "impregnation" (*vāsanā*).
For this refutation of external objects is based on the postulation of such an impregnation, which is established by logical reasoning. (PVA 681)

Nevertheless, this attachment to external objects has caused this entire world to be seized by a demonic possession. (682) (PVA) Therefore, every distinct form [appearing to cognition] arises through the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
since it is devoid of being an external object, cognition is without an objective support (*anālambana*). (683) (PVA)

For this very reason, the purification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in the proof that all cognitions are without an external object (*anālambana*), because they are cognitions, just like the cognition of a dream. For it is precisely this state of being without an external object which consists in the experience of the form of the self (*ātma-ākāra-vedanatva*).

[Objection: But if all cognitions are made the subject of the inference, there is no corroborative instance; how then can there be an inference? [Reply: No, because of a misunderstanding of the meaning.
For this is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) when the proof depends upon that very means of valid cognition.
For, because the example is established from this, the argument beginning with "all" and so forth is logical.

Only those waking cognitions that have become the subject of dispute are made the *pakṣa* (the subject of the thesis). As for dream-cognitions, their lack of an external object (*nirālambanatva*) is already established by the fact that they follow the presence and absence of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is used as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). How is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established? By the principle: "Whatever kind of thing is established from whatever source [that kind of thing arises from that]. Otherwise, there would be an absence of the causal relation for all things, due to a lack of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Those who know the truth declare that the very nature of cause and effect consists in following the presence and absence [of one with respect to the other].
For what is seen in the waking state is observed to be associated with repeated practice and intense interest.
"Therefore, let it be understood that knowledge in a dream is likewise [without an external object].
(PVA 685) [Objection: But surely, dreams are not without an objective basis (*anālambana*) because they are cognitions; rather, it is because of the existence of a sublater (*bādhaka*). For instance:
Furthermore, what is seen in a dream is not seen by one who has awakened; therefore,
at that time it is not perceived by others, and for that reason, it is without an objective basis.
The subverting cognition, by negating its object,
produces a well-ascertained knowledge that there is no plurality of objects in this case.
And yet, in the case of waking cognition, there is no sublater in the same way as there is in dream-cognition. Therefore, how can that serve as an example?

This is not so. For how could a subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) be capable of removing the object of another [cognition]? Indeed, the function of a cognition is not the removal of an object, as is the case with sprouts and the like. What then? Its function is precisely that of making known. And thus, it must be made known by another that "this [first cognition] has no object. Furthermore, it is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone that makes known absence, according to the statement: "Non-apprehension is the sole cause for negation. Since even contradiction (*virodha*) is established through non-apprehension alone, the subverting cognition must therefore effect only the realization of the emptiness of its [the first cognition's] object. And since the absence of that [object] is simply the existence of something else, the nature of being a subverter consists precisely in having that other thing as its objective support (*ālambana*). And all of this is possible even in the case of a waking cognition.
[359,xiv] But surely, by means of a waking cognition itself, one thinks, "This is not so"; how then can that [waking cognition] be sublated?

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not the case that this is thus, and that is thus"? The result [is determined] by non-cognition or otherwise; therefore, how can there be a determination based on the result rather than on cognition? For if determination were by means of a result, it would be merely conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*) due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is asked, "How can there be a result without cognition?", [the answer is: because there is cognition within non-cognition. In this way, that [cognition] would indeed be a means of cognition for its result, but not otherwise.
Therefore, it is precisely this—its grasping of another form—that constitutes its sublation; and this applies with respect to all cognitions, as well as to other cognitions.

[360, vi] Now, is the knowledge that establishes the distinction between dream-cognition and non-dream cognition a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? There are these two possibilities. If it is a valid means of knowledge, then it must have an objective basis (*sālambana*); thus, your argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If, on the other hand, it is not a valid means of knowledge, then there is no established subject (*pakṣa*) or example (*dṛṣṭānta*), so how can inference (*anumāna*) proceed? And how, then, could the lack of an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*) be established? [360, vii]

That is incorrect. There is no fault, for that [dream-cognition] is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor is every valid means of knowledge possessed of an objective referent (*sālambana*), because inference lacks an objective referent. Even though it lacks an objective referent, it is considered a valid means of knowledge here with respect to its non-contradiction in worldly practice (*vyavahārāvisamvāda*). Furthermore, although the distinction between those two—dream-consciousness and other consciousnesses—is established, the proof of that [distinction] does not consist of a valid means of knowledge that possesses an objective referent; thus, there is no undesirable consequence of everything being possessed of an objective referent.
Once the difference from that [dream-state] has been established by means of ordinary worldly cognition itself...
This consideration regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is based upon appearances.

When one is questioned as to how the Veda is established as *dharma* through its distinction from worldly speech, what should be said? If it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it resembles worldly speech, how can it possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of that distinction? If, on the other hand, one were to establish its validity and then explain the distinction, what would be the point of presenting such a proof? How then is that objection to be resolved? Nor is the distinction between the composition of the Veda established merely by a specific sequence of vowels and consonants, for such a distinction is equally established among other texts. Suppose one argues: "Let this composition exist; we shall investigate whether it is the Veda or not. If it proves to be a means of valid cognition, it is indeed the Veda; otherwise, we shall discard it as being useless. If that is so, then this [objection] applies equally here as well: we shall discard it if no conviction is observed. Thus, in this case too, conviction is indeed observed.

[360,xi] In the conceptualization of whether the established nature of dreams is different from this [waking state] or not, or even in the thought "that which will come to be, we shall perceive it as such," [the same applies]. (PVA) 693.

[361,i] The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, the Tathāgata has taught that there are four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings. What are these four? They are: the person who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the person who is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), the person who is a non-returner (anāgāmin), and the person who is an arhat (arhan). These, Ānanda, are the four persons who are worthy of offerings. The venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One would explain in detail the distinction between these four persons who are worthy of offerings. The Blessed One said: "In this case, Ānanda, a certain person, having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata, applies his mind correctly and develops the thought of renunciation. Having developed the thought of renunciation, he attains the fruit of stream-entry. This, Ānanda, is called the first person who is worthy of offerings. Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person, having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata, applies his mind correctly and develops the thought of renunciation. Having developed the thought of renunciation, he attains the fruit of once-returning. This, Ānanda, is called the second person who is worthy of offerings. Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person, having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata, applies his mind correctly and develops the thought of renunciation. Having developed the thought of renunciation, he attains the fruit of non-returning. This, Ānanda, is called the third person who is worthy of offerings. Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person, having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata, applies his mind correctly and develops the thought of renunciation. Having developed the thought of renunciation, he attains the fruit of arhatship. This, Ānanda, is called the fourth person who is worthy of offerings. These, Ānanda, are the four persons who are worthy of offerings."

If, upon subsequent investigation, dream-cognition or any other cognition should be found—either mutually distinct or non-distinct from the perspective of ultimate reality—we shall accept it as such. In that case, if there exists some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their distinction when being examined, we shall establish their non-difference. What contradiction could there be in this? If you argue that the prior cognition apprehending difference was invalid (*apramāṇa*), let it be so; what is the fault? If you say that the distinction between the thesis and other members of the syllogism would not occur, let it not occur now; what have we lost? This very fact—that the means of proving non-difference is invalid—is precisely what we require. Thus, then:

If there were such a realization of a common subject, then no other means of valid cognition would exist; likewise, another [means of cognition] would be merely a gateway [to that same realization]. (694) (PVA)
