Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not grasp at them; because he does not grasp at them, he does not become attached to them. Because he is not attached, he is not terrified, nor is he frightened, nor is he terrified by fear. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the dharma of the past, nor does he perceive the dharma of the future, nor does he perceive the dharma of the present? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the dharma of the past, nor does he perceive 'dharma of the past'; he does not perceive the dharma of the future, nor does he perceive 'dharma of the future'; he does not perceive the dharma of the present, nor does he perceive 'dharma of the present. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not grasp at them; because he does not grasp at them, he does not become attached to them. Because he is not attached, he is not terrified, nor is he frightened, nor is he terrified by fear. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the dharma of the conditioned, nor does he perceive the dharma of the unconditioned? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the dharma of the conditioned, nor does he perceive 'dharma of the conditioned'; he does not perceive the dharma of the unconditioned, nor does he perceive 'dharma of the unconditioned. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not grasp at them; because he does not grasp at them, he does not become attached to them. Because he is not attached, he is not terrified, nor is he frightened, nor is he terrified by fear. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the dharma of existence, nor does he perceive the dharma of non-existence? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the dharma of existence, nor does he perceive 'dharma of existence'; he does not perceive the d

The cognition of the subject (*dharmin*)—which is common to both that which possesses the characteristics of the Veda as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and that which does not—would itself be invalid, because it is subsequently sublated by the proof of its being a means of valid knowledge. Consequently, since the proof of the subject is invalid, the proof of validity through that [subject] would also be invalid; thus, the establishment of the validity of the Veda would not occur. As a result, the entire practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) regarding what is to be proven (*sādhya*) and the means of proof (*sādhana*) would collapse. Alternatively, even if the subject is apprehended as something common [to both], the cognition grasping it is not invalid, because the additional property of validity is established in that very [subject]. If the measurement of that object of cognition were performed by another [means of knowledge], then there might be invalidity.
That too is incorrect, because:
For when validity is the very nature of that subject itself,
how can there be valid cognition even if it is apprehended while excluding that [nature]?

For the very nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the Vedic word; when its opposite is apprehended and that which is to be measured by it (the object) is subverted by another, how could it not become invalid? Indeed, there is no superiority in something by its own nature alone. If it is argued that the designation "superiority" applies only when it is apprehended, then if it is not apprehended, how can there be validity? If it is argued that this is because some aspect of its form is apprehended, we say no, because there is no difference [between the nature and the aspect]. If it is argued that this is not so because one accepts distinct properties (*dharma*), we say no, because that would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

When a property (*dharma*) is distinct [from its substratum], there must be a further connection with it; and if there were yet another connection with that [connection], there would be an infinite regress and a collapse of the nature of properties.
(696) (PVA) If it is accepted that "being connected to that" is simply the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of those two [the property and the substratum].
In that case, validity is established for us; what contradiction could there be?
(697) Even when a superimposition is apprehended as distinct from reality, why would the cognition of its non-difference through subsequent reflective awareness not be valid? (698)
[361,x] Furthermore, it might be argued: "For you who perceive non-difference, how can there be the application of a proof through the distinction of isolating a subject (*pakṣīkaraṇa*) and so forth?

That is incorrect. With respect to the cognition of another, this is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), and since one employs the means of proof (*sādhana*) oneself as well through prior habituation, there is nothing faulty in it. Another person is made to understand by means of the thought, "It was so for me too.
[361,xii] If it is argued that all cognition is like the subverting cognition of dreams and the like, why is that not the case?
It may be established that [cognitions] possess an object, because they are cognitions, even by others.

Just as it is argued that "all cognitions are without an object, because they are cognitions, like a dream-cognition," so too it could be argued that "all cognitions possess an object, just like a cognition that sublates a dream. To this, it is replied:

[361,xiv] Since there is no difference in their being cognitions, what proof is there for the claim that another cognition— distinct from the cognition of a dream— is without an objective basis? (PVA) 700.

Just as the proof for the absence of an objective support (*anālambanatva*) proceeds from the connection with the certainty established by a subverting means of cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), based on the lack of distinction between dream-cognition and waking cognition, so too would it be if there were an objective support (*sālambanatva*). In that case, it would be a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) reason, and thus neither [of the two positions] would be established; that very state is what constitutes the absence of an objective support. Furthermore, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) when "having an objective support" is the probandum. However, both are shown to be without an objective support through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). For instance: [361,xvi] Thus: *tathā hi* (for instance).
Just as there is no cognition of anything other than the mere consciousness of its own nature,
so it is held to be in the case of dream-cognitions and likewise in waking cognitions.

For even that which is known through the appearance in the waking state is not perceived by another; this has already been stated, because it is perceived only by a subsequent cognition. If it is argued that even in that case there is indeed an objective support (*ālambana*), [we reply: therefore, it does not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Even if it does not perform causal efficiency, that which is being perceived certainly exists. For the absence of one thing does not entail the absence of another; fire does not cease to exist simply because smoke is absent. If it is argued that because everything is absent, it does not exist at all—like a heap of *kiṃśuka* flowers—we reply: in that case, it does not perform that particular causal efficiency like a heap of *kiṃśuka* flowers. Let it exist in its own form. Let the heap of *kiṃśuka* flowers perform causal efficiency in its own form, but not that which is perceived in a dream. For food eaten in a dream does not produce nourishment. If it is argued that the form itself is of such a nature, and therefore [the dream object] is not [an external thing], we say: no. Because it is experienced as having its own specific form, it is rightly said to be nothing but consciousness (*vijñāna*). Now, what contradiction is there in its being of the nature of consciousness? Its being produced by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and its being perceived by itself. If it is argued that the object itself will be of such a nature, this is merely a matter of naming. If you ask why it is not so for you [the opponent] as well, we say: no, because it has been demonstrated that [the object] is dependent upon infinite causes. Therefore, it is nothing but consciousness. And thus:
And if that [consciousness] were to perceive an object distinct from itself, the relationship between the perceived and the perceiver would be difficult to establish.

[362,ii] For that which is a different object cannot be the very form of that [cognition]. Therefore, if there is no entry [of the object into cognition], there is no perception; if there is entry, it is not a different object. But if the nature of the cognition itself is that [object], then it must exist as blue and so forth through its own self-awareness. How, then, can there be perception by another? No; this is an illusion, like the vision of two moons by two people with ophthalmia. If it is argued that even in that case, it is simply the object, then it is as follows: [362,iii]
Just as a non-erroneous cognition is considered the cognizer of objects,
so too even an erroneous cognition is the cognizer of the object itself, provided it is common to others.
Just as the object of a cognition considered erroneous is perceived as being common [to all], so too is the other [object]. This is incorrect;
for the commonality of an object is not observed through direct perception.
Because direct perception is impossible here, there is neither inference nor verbal testimony.

First of all, commonality with the cognition of another is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the cognitions of all others even without an inferential mark (*liṅga*). If it is argued that what is being perceived by another is of exactly the same nature [as one's own], and therefore that very thing constitutes its commonality—namely, the worldly consensus that "just as this is perceived by me, so too is it perceived by another situated in a suitable place"—we say no. For such a consensus does not exist in the case of hair-flies seen by those with ophthalmia (*taimirika*) or things seen in dreams. If it is argued that even in those cases, [the object] indeed exists, [we reply: then this very form must exist even in the state of dreaming; consequently, because of that similarity, that [dream-object] would also be external. This is not so, for the worldly consensus is that in the case of intense meditation (*bhāvanā*) and the like, there is only the appearance of the self (*ātmapratibhāsa*) in that manner, but no other [external object] exists there. It is the same in this present state as well. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), in both cases there is merely the appearance of one's own form (*svarūpapratibhāsamātra*); thus, there is no objective support (*sālambanatā*).
[362,vii] But surely, since everything in a dream is disordered and accomplished without effort, how can there be a similarity between cognitions? That is incorrect.
[362,viii]
Apart from the appearances of blue and so forth, what other confusion is perceived?
That [confusion] also arises through the power of habituation; therefore, how can this state [of confusion] exist?

If it is argued that there is merely the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth, and why else would there be confusion therein or its occurrence without effort? [The opponent replies: "In a dream, things such as trees appear instantly in their place without effort, as do attachment and the like. [The author asks: But by whom is it accepted that there is existence without effort? A cognition occurring at the time of the effect perceives only the effect; one occurring at the time of the cause perceives only the cause. The sequence is: "This arises from that. The determination is also a sequence: "Without this, that [does not arise]. Here, there is neither perception nor inference. Nor is it known by anyone that "this is confused. Furthermore, even in a dream, the state of being unconfused and so forth arises from a particular kind of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The same applies to the waking state. As for the observation of confusion in portents (*ariṣṭa*) and the like—if you say it is due to the defect of the portent itself, we say no; for there is no distinction between a portent and a non-portent. In that case too, there must be another factor that performs the discrimination. If you say there is yet another [factor] for that, there is no such thing from which discrimination could arise. If you say the discrimination is self-evident, we say no; because it consists merely in abiding in its own nature. For that which abides in its own nature has no awareness of another. Awareness of mere nature is the same whether one is confused or unconfused. If you say that "unconfused" means that which persists over a long period and is free from deviation, we say no; because persistence over a long period is not grasped by perception. Therefore, nothing remains but conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And through that, there is no comprehension of the object. Even from that, there is no established certainty, because that too is perceptual in its own nature. If it is argued that the conceptual construction produced by the experience of a real object is consistent (*saṃvādī*), we say no; because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not grasped. When there is the experience of the object, there is no conceptual construction; when there is the conceptual construction, there is no experience. How, then, can there be the apprehension of a true object here? If you say it is by means of the conceptual construction, this too is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since that too depends on a connection, there would be another conceptual construction, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If this is so, how then is the connection grasped even by mental impressions (*vāsanā*)? No; it has been demonstrated that, from the ultimate standpoint (*paramārthataḥ*), this is precisely our position.

The causal relationship known as the "relation between effect and cause" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is accepted as a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) by the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), but not by the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*). (PVA 705)

[363,iii] There is no fault, for it has already been established that this is "consciousness-only" even apart from being produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Now, one might object: "The state of being conditioned by latent impressions is not perceived in waking consciousness. To this we reply: "In the dream state, there is no manifestation of a dream"—this point is the same [for both]. If you argue, "For one who has awakened, such [conditioning] exists in the waking state, but not so [in the dream]," that too is trivial. For instance: [363,iv]
This has already been stated: for even in a dream, awakening is experienced;
therefore, the state of waking does not have a characteristic different from that of a dream.
(PVA 363,v)

Even in a dream, the thought "I am awake" certainly occurs. Therefore, how can there be a determination based on the appearance of being awake? If it is argued that this [dream] state is reduced to the condition of dreaming by another awakening, [we reply: this [awakening] is not so reduced by anything at all. For this very reason, although the determination of objects is not exactly as it appears, nevertheless, because of its similarity [to waking], it does not constitute a valid basis for cognition. For smoke existing at the time of inference is not an inference simply because its status as preceded by fire is established; rather, it is an inference by virtue of possessing the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) thereof. In the same way, this waking state also possesses that nature precisely because it possesses the defining characteristic thereof.
[363, vi] But surely, no activity of cultivation (bhāvanā) is perceived there during the waking state; how, then, can there be equality with a dream? To this he says:
Even when there is an interruption in cultivation, the manifestation certainly occurs, just as that which was seen by a child is perceived again in old age;
so too, that which was seen in another birth and so forth is perceived upon the occurrence of death-sleep. (PVA 707)
Why is it not understood that a dream is the arising of another birth?
Just as it is during sleep at night, so too it is during the night of death. (PVA 363, ix) 708.
[363,x] Is it not strange that seeing occurs here day after day, unlike the transition from sleep to waking?
This is because the seeing of the previous moment is the cause for the perception of objects; thus, there is indeed equality between the two cases. (PVA) 709 ||

Just as what was seen on a previous day is the cause for seeing a dream during the night, so too what was seen on each preceding day is the very cause for seeing a dream on a subsequent day, even when separated by another night; thus, this succession of dreams is vast. If it is argued that there is also the perception of something entirely new, then the same applies to what is considered a dream, and everything is identical.
Just as going and coming in a dream produces the perception of various things, why is it not accepted that going and coming also occur in the waking state, even within a dream? (710) (PVA) [363,xiii]

If it is argued that there is no conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), why is this very inference not sufficient for the usage of the wise? Just as the usage of cause and effect is based on inference, so too is this; thus, they are the same. Furthermore, if there is no conventional usage regarding momentariness, why should that [momentariness] not exist? If you say it does not exist, we shall demonstrate that point later. [363,xiv]

Is it not the case that because sleep is impaired, the perception of dreams has unreal objects? But how can that which is vividly manifest be a dream? For at the onset of sleep, the state of dreaming is not yet applicable. If you argue that the very beginning of sleep is the cause of that appearance, we say no; for we observe specific appearances resulting from specific types of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Even when the onset of sleep is identical, one person may somehow become a dreamer while another does not. If you claim this is because the dream would be absent in the absence of that [onset], let it be so as a mere instrumental condition (*nimitta*); nevertheless, it is not the cause of the specific nature of the appearance.

If it is argued that this appearance also occurs immediately after sleep, and therefore its similarity to a dream persists even upon waking—no, for there is no "waking" apart from the appearance itself. If it is argued that "waking" is the cognition "I am awake"—no, for it has been stated that such a cognition exists even in a dream. Therefore, there is no distinction between the dream state and its opposite. Consequently, the refutation of one who claims a distinction between having an object (*sālambana*) and lacking an object (*nirālambana*) based on the observation of a difference is invalid, as that distinction is unestablished. Nor does it follow that the existence of an object is now established because waking cognitions are indistinguishable [from dreams], which would result in the establishment of the opposite. No, for that would entail the absurd consequence that erroneous cognitions (*viparītakhyāti*) and so forth do not exist; thus, like waking cognitions, they would have to be accepted as such, which contradicts your own tenets. Furthermore:

The sublating cognition is manifest by means of reasons such as "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*); otherwise, it could not be established. By this [reason], the sublation of the manifest [cognition] is not [precluded]. (PVA 711)

For a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), characterized by non-perception and consisting in the perception of the opposite, which is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), cannot be subverted by inference through such qualities as being a cognition. If, in the inference of fire from smoke, there subsequently occurs the operation of direct perception regarding the opposite, how can inference be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?

[Objection: But even in the case of the occurrence of perception, if inference is the sublater regarding the object of two moons, then what is that perception? The logic is the same. [Response: No. Even there, it is perception itself that is the sublater, because one [moon] was previously seen. Otherwise, inference itself would not be possible.

But perception is not preceded by inference. If it were so, then in that case too, inference alone would be the sublater; thus, in the face of sublation by inference, perception would be non-authoritative. And in that way, due to mutual contradiction, nothing at all would be established. Therefore, inference has perception as its basis, but perception does not have inference as its basis.
[364, vi] But is it not established that perception itself has inference as its basis? Thus:
Without inference, perception does not first initiate activity;
there would be initiation only when the relation has been grasped through inference. (PVA 712)

[364, viii] The Blessed One said: "If, Mahāmati, there were no such thing as the non-existence of all dharmas, then the teaching of the non-existence of all dharmas would not be proclaimed by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. However, Mahāmati, because all dharmas are devoid of self-nature, they are said to be non-existent. Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is because of the absence of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones teach the non-existence of all dharmas. Thus it was said. What is meant here by the "non-existence of all dharmas"? It means that all dharmas are devoid of the intrinsic nature of arising; it does not mean that all dharmas are utterly non-existent like the horns of a hare. Why? Because, Mahāmati, if all dharmas were utterly non-existent like the horns of a hare, then the teaching of the non-existence of all dharmas would be impossible. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is because of the absence of the intrinsic nature of arising that all dharmas are said to be non-existent. Moreover, Mahāmati, even though all dharmas are non-existent, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not abandon the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Why? Because, Mahāmati, if the conventional truth were abandoned, then the teaching of the non-existence of all dharmas would also be abandoned. Therefore, Mahāmati, although all dharmas are non-existent, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not abandon the conventional truth. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the ultimate truth is not the conventional truth. Why? Because, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is characterized by the manifestation of false appearances, while the ultimate truth is characterized by the cessation of all mental fabrications. Therefore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is not the ultimate truth, and the ultimate truth is not the conventional truth. Nevertheless, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is the gateway to the ultimate truth. Why? Because, Mahāmati, by relying upon the conventional truth, one enters into the realization of the ultimate truth. Therefore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is the gateway to the ultimate truth. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is established by means of words and letters, while the ultimate truth is established by means of the non-duality of words and letters. Why? Because, Mahāmati, words and letters are the realm of the ignorant, whereas the ultimate truth is the realm of the wise. Therefore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is established by means of words and letters, while the ultimate truth is established by means of the non-duality of words and letters. Thus it was said. What is meant here by the "conventional truth"? It means that all dharmas are established by means of worldly conventions, such as names, signs, and designations. It does not mean that there is a real entity corresponding to those names, signs, and designations. Why? Because, Mahāmati, if there were a real entity corresponding to names, signs, and designations, then the teaching of the non-existence of all dharmas would be contradicted. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is because all dharmas are devoid of the intrinsic nature of names, signs, and designations that the conventional truth is established by means of worldly conventions. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is not the ultimate truth, and the ultimate truth is not the conventional truth. Why? Because, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is characterized by the proliferation of conceptualization, while the ultimate truth is characterized by the cessation of all conceptual proliferation. Therefore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is not the ultimate truth, and the ultimate truth is not the conventional truth. Nevertheless, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is the support for the ultimate truth. Why? Because, Mahāmati, by relying upon the conventional truth, one attains mastery over the ultimate truth. Therefore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is the support for the ultimate truth. Moreover, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is the domain of the two vehicles, while the ultimate truth is the domain of the Tathāgatas. Why? Because, Mahāmati, the two vehicles abide in the view of the non-existence of all dharmas, whereas the Tathāgatas abide in the non-dual nature of all dharmas. Therefore, Mahāmati, the conventional truth is the domain of the two vehicles, while the ultimate truth is the domain of the Tathāgatas. Thus it was said. What is meant here by the "domain of the two vehicles"? It means that the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having realized the non-existence of the self and the aggregates, abide in the state of tranquility. It does not mean that they have realized the non-dual nature of all dharmas. Why? Because, Mahāmati, if the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas had realized the non-dual nature of all dharmas, then they would be Tathāgatas. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is because they have not yet realized the non-dual nature of all dharmas that the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are called the "two vehicles. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the two vehicles do not perceive the ultimate truth; the Tathāgatas alone perceive the ultimate truth. Why? Because, Mahāmati, the two vehicles perceive only the non-existence of the self and the aggregates, whereas the Tathāgatas perceive the non-arising and non-ceasing of all dharmas. Therefore, Mahāmati, the two vehicles do not perceive the ultimate truth; the Tathāgatas alone perceive the ultimate truth. Thus it was said. What is meant here by the "ultimate truth"? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty, signless, wishless, and beyond conceptualization. It does not mean that there is a separate dharma called the "ultimate truth" apart from all dharmas. Why? Because, Mahāmati, if there were a separate dharma called the "ultimate truth" apart from all dharmas, then the ultimate truth would be a conditioned phenomenon. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is because all dharmas are themselves the ultimate truth that the ultimate truth is said to be empty, signless, wishless, and beyond conceptualization. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the ultimate truth is not something to be attained through effort; the ultimate truth is the very nature of all dharmas. Why? Because, Mahāmati, all dharmas are originally quiescent and naturally extinguished. Therefore, Mahāmati, the ultimate truth is not something to be attained through effort; the ultimate truth is the very nature of all dharmas. Thus it was said. What is meant here by the "very nature of all dharmas"? It means that all dharmas are devoid of the intrinsic nature of arising, devoid of the intrinsic nature of abiding, and devoid of the intrinsic nature of ceasing. It does not mean that all dharmas are like the horns of a hare. Why? Because, Mahāmati, if all dharmas were like the horns of a hare, then the teaching of the non-existence of all dharmas would be impossible. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is because all dharmas are devoid of the intrinsic nature of arising, abiding, and ceasing that the very nature of all dharmas is called the ultimate truth. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the ultimate truth is not a dharma that can be expressed by words; the ultimate truth is a dharma that transcends all verbal expression. Why? Because, Mahāmati, words are the realm of the ignorant, whereas the ultimate truth is the realm of the wise. Therefore, Mahāmati, the ultimate truth is not a dharma that can be expressed by words; the ultimate truth is a dharma that transcends all verbal expression. Thus it was said. What is meant here by the "realm of the ignorant"? It means that the ignorant, relying on false conceptualization, give rise to various attachments. It does not mean that they perceive the true nature of dharmas. Why? Because, Mahāmati, if the ignorant perceived the true nature of dharmas, they would not give rise to various attachments. Therefore, Mahāmati, it is because they give rise to various attachments based on false conceptualization that the ignorant are called "ignorant. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the realm of the ignorant is not the realm of the wise; the realm of the wise is not the realm of the ignorant. Why? Because, Mahāmati, the ignorant are attached to the characteristics of existence and non-existence, whereas the wise are detached from the characteristics of existence and non-existence. Therefore, Mahāmati, the realm of the ignorant is not the realm of the wise; the realm of the wise is not the realm of the ignorant. Nevertheless, Mahāmati, the realm of the ignorant is the gateway to the realm of the wise. Why? Because, Mahāmati, by observing the realm of the ignorant, one enters into the realization of the realm of the wise. Therefore, Mah

For if the apprehension of the relationship [between means and end] occurs through inference, then perception is the initiator by means of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); thus, from that inference, perception is the authority, and from perception, inference—thereby, there is a mutual sublation of equal force. If this were so, there would indeed be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), and not the authority of even one of them. This has been stated: the cognition of the intrinsic nature [of a cognition] is self-evident (*svataḥ*); its authority, however, regarding the object-self distinct [from itself] which is the locus of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), is established through practice. And that [practice] proceeds from a beginningless succession of the blind. Furthermore, that [authority] is established as valid through correspondence (*saṃvāda*), and correspondence exists in the future. In the future, there is only the experience [of the result]. Therefore, how can authority have the external object as its domain? If it is argued that inference, too, [establishes its own] intrinsic nature without perception, we say no; for in that case, it is precisely perception [that functions] therein. Thus, by means of inference, perception is sublated regarding the distinct [object], because that [distinct object] is the domain of inference, since it is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). If it is asked, "How can perception be an authority regarding what is beyond the senses? [we reply: It is by way of being the initiator (*pravarttaka*), not by way of grasping (*grahaṇa*). If it were by way of grasping, it would simply not be an initiator. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues here.]
If this very [cognition] were to proceed toward that which appeared in the previous perception,
for what purpose would it do so, since [the object] has already been attained in its own nature? (PVA 713)

The activity of one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is not directed toward that [object] when it has already been revealed; for if it were already manifest, there would be no further engagement. (714) Even when the purposeful action has been revealed, one proceeds toward it for the sake of its attainment.
Because it does not appear at the time of attainment, its occurrence must be within that which does not appear.

In that case, if it is not sublated by inference, then our desired conclusion is all the more established. To explain: perception is directed toward an object distinct [from itself] by means of inference; and since that [object] is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), it is the domain of inference. Therefore, it is only there that perception could be sublated by inference. And if inference were sublated therein, it would mean that inference itself has been sublated by inference. But such an inference is one that has come down through a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*). There can never be any harm to it, whether it is sublated by another inference or by perception. This is the logical principle: that neither inference nor perception is sublated by inference, nor is either sublated by perception.

[365,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, he is called one who has reached the ‘fruit of the path. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, what is meant by the ‘fruit of the path’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is the state of being established in the fruit of non-returning after having abandoned the five lower fetters; this is called the ‘fruit of the path. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, what is the distinction between the ‘fruit of the path’ and the ‘attainment of the fruit’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, the ‘fruit of the path’ refers to the realization of the fruit itself, while the ‘attainment of the fruit’ refers to the stability and maintenance of that realization. Furthermore, Ānanda, the ‘fruit of the path’ is the actualization of the cessation of suffering, whereas the ‘attainment of the fruit’ is the non-retrogression from that state. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, does he still possess the latent tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the higher realms? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, although he has abandoned the five lower fetters, he still possesses the latent tendencies associated with the form and formless realms. However, because he has realized the fruit of non-returning, he will never again be reborn in the desire realm. This is why he is called one who has reached the ‘fruit of the path. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of non-returners are there? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are five kinds of non-returners: 1) the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin); 2) the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin); 3) the one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin); 4) the one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort (anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin); and 5) the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven (ūrdhvasrotas). These are the five types of non-returners. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, among these, which one is most excellent? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort is the most excellent, as he realizes the fruit through the power of his own cultivation without further exertion. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, can he fall back from that state? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, no. Once a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, he cannot fall back from that state. He is irreversible from the attainment of the fruit of non-returning. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, what is the cause and condition for a bhikṣu to attain the fruit of non-returning? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is through the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. By practicing these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, a bhikṣu abandons the five lower fetters and attains the fruit of non-returning. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how should a bhikṣu dwell in order to abandon the five lower fetters? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, a bhikṣu should dwell contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. He should dwell contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. By dwelling thus, a bhikṣu abandons the five lower fetters and attains the fruit of non-returning. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, what is the difference between a bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters and one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, the difference is that the stream-enterer has not yet abandoned the five lower fetters, whereas the non-returner has completely abandoned them. Furthermore, the stream-enterer may still be reborn seven times at most in the human and celestial realms, whereas the non-returner will never again be reborn in the desire realm. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, is he still subject to birth and death? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, although he is still subject to birth and death within the form and formless realms, he is no longer subject to birth and death in the desire realm. Because he has severed the continuity of existence in the lower realms, he is called one who has reached the ‘fruit of the path. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how long does it take for a bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters to attain parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it depends on the individual. Some may attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, some upon rebirth, some with effort, some without effort, and some by proceeding upward to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Thus, the time varies according to their respective capacities and practices. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, what is his destiny? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, his destiny is to attain parinirvāṇa. Having exhausted the outflows of the form and formless realms, he will enter final nirvāṇa. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, can he teach others the Dharma? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, he can indeed teach the Dharma. However, his teaching is primarily for the sake of encouraging others to strive for the same fruit of non-returning or even the higher fruits of arhatship. His discourse is focused on the cessation of suffering and the realization of the path. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, how should he conduct himself? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, he should conduct himself with mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding all unwholesome states, cultivating the wholesome, and remaining detached from worldly concerns. He should live in accordance with the Dharma, honoring the precepts and training in the higher training of morality, concentration, and wisdom. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, is he still subject to the influence of Māra? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, he is no longer subject to the influence of Māra in the sense of being bound by the fetters of the desire realm. However, because he still dwells in the form and formless realms, he remains within the sphere of conditioned existence and is thus still subject to the subtle influence of Māra until he attains final parinirvāṇa. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, what is his final destination? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, his final destination is the realm of Akaniṣṭha, where he will attain parinirvāṇa. Having transcended the realms of form and formlessness, he will reach the end of suffering. Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, if a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the fruit of non-returning, can he be led astray by false teachers? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, no. Having realized the truth of the Dharma,

[Objection: But surely even the perception whose object is two moons is indeed sublated by another [perception] occurring subsequently that manifests a single moon, or by some other [means], because it is not a valid perception (*apratyakṣatvāt*). [Reply: Why? Because it is being sublated. How can there be a relationship of the sublated and the sublator between two things that exist through mutual exclusion? If you say, "It is so," then there would be a relationship of the sublated and the sublator between both. No; for one is the sublator precisely because it is a means of attainment (*prāpakatva*). For in one case there is the attainment of the intended object, while in the other there is not. If that is so, then it follows indirectly that inference itself is what is sublated. Therefore, what is the meaning of the claim that "all cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like dream-cognitions"? It means they have their own form as their objective basis (*svarūpālambana*). And in that regard, perception and the inference produced from it—which is of the nature of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)—cannot be sublated by inference or anything else. However, a proof for an objective basis distinct [from the cognition's own form] is neither perception nor the inference produced from it, because they are handed down blindly from one to the other. In this context, the rule is absolute: only inference or perception can be the sublator. Therefore, the claim that "all [cognitions] have an objective basis, like waking cognitions," is not established by a counter-means of knowledge (*pratipramāṇa*), because the cognition that sublates the objective basis of dreams and the like is itself without an objective basis. If that is the case, how can the existence of an objective basis be proven by using that as an example?

[365,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is either conditioned or unconditioned. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor perceive a dharma that is either conditioned or unconditioned? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive forms as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive eye-contact as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive feeling born of eye-contact as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the element of earth as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the realm of desire as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive ignorance as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the scattered, the emptiness of the unscattered, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-arising, the emptiness of non-cessation, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of other-nature as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, or an arhat as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of an omniscient one as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the conditioned as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the unconditioned as existent or non-existent. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is either conditioned or unconditioned. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the reason why a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor perceive a dharma that is either conditioned or unconditioned? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of wisdom itself as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned, he does not perceive form as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive form as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—he does not perceive the eye as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive the eye as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—he does not perceive forms as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive forms as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—he does not perceive eye-consciousness as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive eye-consciousness as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—he does not perceive eye-contact as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive eye-contact as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—he does not perceive feeling born of eye-contact as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive feeling born of eye-contact as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—he does not perceive the element of earth as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive the element of earth as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—he does not perceive the realm of desire as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive the realm of desire as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for the realm of form and the formless realm—he does not perceive ignorance as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive ignorance as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—he does not perceive the perfection of giving as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does not perceive the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned. Because he does not perceive the perfection of giving as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned—and likewise for the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom—he does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as existent or non-existent, nor as conditioned or unconditioned; he does

But surely, objectlessness (*nirālambanatva*) residing in another cognition is established by this [present] cognition; and that [objectlessness] is distinct. Therefore, since every other cognition also has a distinct object as its proven content because it is a cognition, how can it be considered a counter-proof (*pratipramāṇa*)? Even if this [present cognition] has a non-distinct object because it is preceded by perception, what follows from that for the contrary cognition which is seized by error, such that it too must be accepted as being thus [non-distinct]? Moreover, this [contrary cognition] does not establish a distinction, because it establishes mere worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). Another [cognition] confirms the object as either distinct or non-distinct, and that confirmation occurs at that very time through an attachment to that experience. Consequently, the thought "this does not appear to me here now" arises; rather, one thinks, "I am limited to my own internal form. Thus, it demonstrates itself to be indeed without an external object. Therefore, by means of this [cognition], which is itself without an object, another [cognition] is not established as having an object.

[(gha) Determination of the appearance in the form of the apprehended and the apprehender—] [365,iii] But if it does not take that form as its object, how is it established by this [cognition]? To this it was said: "Because of the contradiction. It is known that it has been taken as an object because of the contradiction. Therefore, he says:
It possesses neither the form of the cognized object nor that of the cognizer; it is perceived by those who are deluded. (331)

This [cognition] has its conventional status established in such a way that it is a distortion consisting of the forms of the grasped and the grasper with distinct characteristics, just like the difference in cognitions of [illusory] hair and so forth. (332)
At that time, it is not characterized by the subject, the object, or the act of apprehension.

Even with respect to an object that is not actually known (*avedya*), there arises the form of a knower (*vedakākāra*) regarding things such as [illusory] hair; for in that case, with respect to the hair being reached, the cognition is not a knower of it because of its non-existence. Yet, by those who are deluded, it is perceived as "it is known upon reaching it. And from this perception, they proceed to act. Now, for those who have thus proceeded, there is no actual attainment (*prāpti*) of that object; therefore, its lack of a supporting object (*anālambanatva*) is perfectly clear. By this, another instance of the lack of a supporting object is established. Because the perception of a similar form does not entail the perception of what is distinct from it. Furthermore, a state of having a supporting object (*sālambanatva*) has never been perceived anywhere; how then can the universal establishment of all cognitions having a supporting object follow from similarity to that? For it is not perceived that the form appearing at the time of reaching [the object] is the same as that which appeared previously; otherwise, since it would have appeared differently, there would be no impulse to act, as has already been stated. If it is argued that one acts again for the sake of perceiving what was already perceived, then that which is being perceived now has not been perceived before. If one proceeds toward that too because it is being perceived, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Again...

And for what purpose does this appearing [of an object] exist? If it is said to be for the sake of pleasure or for the sake of grasping, then one acts for that purpose; yet that [object] remains unmanifested. Therefore, since everything is an object only while remaining unmanifested, all cognition is without an objective support (*anālambana*). How, then, can error be established on that basis? Furthermore, how does one act toward that which has not been made an object?
That is incorrect.
For it has been asked: "Even when an object has been made the focus of cognition, how does activity [toward it] occur?"
This very relationship of cause and effect is established in this manner alone.

The cognition [of an object] occurs immediately after its own self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), either through the power of its own cause or without a cause. Therefore, one should accept it exactly as it is observed. For this very reason it has been said: "All phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*). Alternatively, since there was no prior cognition of anything distinct [from consciousness], and since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a difference between the object to be attained and [the cognition] afterwards, how could there be a cognition of something distinct? By this, the causal relationship (*sahakāryakāraṇabhāva*) [between cognition and an external object] based on purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is also refuted. Because no difference is perceived between the preceding and succeeding moments, and because that which is simultaneous [with the cognition] cannot be produced, purposeful action is merely the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*). And since that [nature] exists even in a dream, the case is the same. Therefore, cognition possesses only the forms of the non-objectifiable (*avedya*) and the non-apprehending (*avedaka*). The distinct characteristics of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) are merely a cognitive distortion (*viplava*). Consequently, from the recollection of a previous experience, only a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises, which is nothing other than the self-cognition of its own nature. Thus, the established status [of subject and object] is not a reality in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*); therein, suchness does not exist. For instance, when the cognition of [illusory] hairs occurs, it is only through the recollection of a previous [experience] that there is an attainment following such an appearance. Therefore, the conceptual construction arises with the mental representation (*ullekha*) of apprehended and apprehender. Even that [construction], though devoid of the forms of apprehended and apprehender in its own nature, is established by another in that way. It is not established by itself.
By means of cognition, the externality of the object is not established;
yet, if it were to exist outside of cognition, that very [object] would not be established. (PVA 717)
If blue is perceived, how can it be called external?
If blue is not perceived, how can it be called external?
(718) [PVA] If it were perceived by another, how could it be called external?
If it were perceived by another [consciousness], there would be an infinite regress of "by this" and "by that.
(719) Furthermore, how is this perception by another established by itself?
It cannot be established through the observation of its effect, because the state of being such an effect is unproven. (720)
[366,ix] It has already been explained that the relationship of cause and effect is not established, because it has been described that inference has only the universal as its object. [366,x]
The very claim that "it is seen by another" is not established.
Just as the oneness of that [single cause] is established from the observation of effects such as the bristling of body hair,
so too the oneness of pleasure and the rest is established for that very reason.
Its pleasure is one thing, and its object of apprehension may be another.

(722) (PVA) If it is thought that pleasure and the like are distinct because of their difference in location, how can a difference in location be established in reality if there is oneness? (723) (PVA)
Why then do other [phenomena] such as horripilation not arise from that very same pleasure?
If you argue that there is a difference between pleasure and horripilation because they are distinct, [we reply:
if they are distinct, why is it that the object of perception (*grāhya*) is not also perceived as something distinct? (PVA 724)
If even [phenomena] such as horripilation were contained within our own consciousness,
how could there be a clear appearance of mutual pleasure and so forth? If his horripilation and the like occurred even without our pleasure, [how could they be caused by it]?
Even without our perception of it, why would its horripilation and so forth not occur?
If a difference is admitted there even due to a difference in time, what will a difference in time do for that which is non-different by its own nature? (727) (PVA)
"Let there also be non-difference; even so, that [non-difference] would not be imperceptible.
How could that one thing exist apart from the cognition? (PVA 366, xviii)

[366,xix] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. Furthermore, monks, I say that the cessation of craving is the relinquishing of these four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. And what, monks, is the cessation of craving? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. This, monks, is called the relinquishing of the four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. Moreover, monks, I say that the cessation of ignorance is the relinquishing of these four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. And what, monks, is the cessation of ignorance? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. This, monks, is called the relinquishing of the four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. Furthermore, monks, I say that the cessation of the conceit "I am" is the relinquishing of these four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. And what, monks, is the cessation of the conceit "I am"? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very conceit "I am," its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. This, monks, is called the relinquishing of the four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. Moreover, monks, I say that the cessation of the underlying tendency toward grasping at a self is the relinquishing of these four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. And what, monks, is the cessation of the underlying tendency toward grasping at a self? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very underlying tendency toward grasping at a self, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. This, monks, is called the relinquishing of the four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. Furthermore, monks, I say that the cessation of the underlying tendency toward lust for existence is the relinquishing of these four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. And what, monks, is the cessation of the underlying tendency toward lust for existence? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very underlying tendency toward lust for existence, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. This, monks, is called the relinquishing of the four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. Moreover, monks, I say that the cessation of the underlying tendency toward ignorance is the relinquishing of these four nutriments, their fading away, their cessation, their abandonment, and their non-arising. And what, monks, is the cessation of the underlying tendency toward ignorance? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very underlying tendency toward ignorance, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. If that [object] remains as one and the same even now, how can it be "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*)? Furthermore, since it is established through the mutual exclusion of their respective cognitions, the thought "how can it be one? is indeed something to be reflected upon. And if its commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) appears [to you], then why the question, "Was it seen by you or not? [Is it] for the sake of corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If one does not believe it on the basis of perception, one will certainly not believe it on the basis of speech either. That [speech] too merely indicates one's own appearance, namely, "What appeared to you appears to me. Therefore, even by that, it should be known to be in vain; thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Moreover, how can that which was not apprehended by perception be believed on the basis of speech? For in the case of an object of perception, the instruction of another is not more authoritative. Furthermore:
If perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition;
if verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition, then perception is so—this [mutual dependence] is incorrect. (PVA 729)
There is no mutual assistance between two people suffering from ophthalmia;
for if each individual lacks the capacity, the collective as a whole cannot possess it either.

Therefore, because it is self-cognized in dependence upon instruments such as the eye, cognition itself is the blue object and so forth; thus, cognition is of the nature of cognition whose forms are neither the cognized nor the cognizer. This cognition is established in that very way, for it is experienced in that very way—this is the ultimate truth. Consequently, self-cognition alone is the result, and the certainty that "the object" exists is also located therein; there is no such thing as the "cognition of an external object. As for what was said—that there is no example for the case where the cognizer grasps its own form—since the absence of the opposite [i.e., the existence of an external object] has been established through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), how can it be claimed that there is no example? An unperceived thing like a rabbit’s horn serves as an example. Or, if [the object] were established by perception, what would be the need for an example? Therefore, if we are able to clearly refute the status of our own part as the object of cognition, then your position, being pure and devoid of qualifications, would simply be a refutation of the object. And that position is sublated by perception, since for the entire class of cognitions beginning with perception, only the external remains as the objective support once the status of one's own part as the object is refuted. Thus, what was stated by the opponent—that these waking cognitions possess an objective support precisely because they are not sublated by their own certainty—is incorrect. For we have demonstrated that perception lacks an external object. If you argue that those waking cognitions possess an objective support because they are not sublated by their own certainty, we say: No.
The state of being ascertained by oneself is observed only in respect to their own constituent parts;
however, there is no ascertainment regarding an external object that has not appeared [to consciousness]. (PVA 731)

[367, vi] There is no such thing as "ascertainment" (niścaya) apart from appearance and recollection. First of all, there is no appearance of an object; and in the absence of appearance, there is no recollection. Therefore, since there is no other ascertainment, the statement that "ascertainment is an external object" is merely words and is thus futile.
Indeed, a negation is appropriate regarding an object apprehended by a defective cognition;

why would a negation of that which apprehends what was not previously apprehended not be logical? (732) (PVA) But if there were a sublation of everything merely apprehended, one's own position would suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*).

How can you speak of that which has not been apprehended? (733) (PVA) Furthermore, because the qualifier and the qualified are distinct and ungraspable, it must be stated that either both are unestablished or one of the two is unestablished. (734) (PVA)
Because difference is apprehended first and the nature of reality is determined afterwards, there is no difference in the ultimate sense; therefore, how could this be contradictory?
The relationship between qualifier and qualified is merely constructed through conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
In the Buddhist tenet that effects are produced, [the object] has not come within the range of hearing.
(PVA 736) The cognition of the qualifier and the qualified by means of the eye and the ear—since that is without an objective basis, there is no contradiction of one's own words for anyone. (PVA 737)
The possibility of a distinction between the qualifier and the qualified exists; therefore, why is the investigation of the meaning of the thesis not excellent? (738) (PVA) [367,xv]

that which is called "objectlessness" (nirālambanatā) is not understood as any kind of real entity whatsoever.

Therefore, a question regarding its exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth is simply not tenable. Or perhaps it is established by means of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). (740) (PVA)
What kind of conceptualization can there be of a non-existent thing? In that case, the object would be attached to the afflictions.

This has already been stated: the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is constructed by means of forms imagined through distinct exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). The state of being without an objective support (*nirālambanatva*) is established as if it were distinct from the imagined difference of external objects. Such a distinction is not propounded in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) for the purpose of making known the nature of things as they truly are, because the reality consists in non-difference (*abheda*). If it is asked, "How can there be conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) regarding a non-entity (*avastu*)?", the answer is: precisely for that reason. Otherwise, what kind of conceptual construction would there be of a real entity? In that case, it would follow that the entity itself is a non-entity.

In the absence [of an object], there is the occurrence of conceptual construction, yet that real entity does not exist. (742) (PVA) Now, this term "cognition" (*pratyaya*) might refer to an action (*karman*), a state of being (*bhāva*), and so forth. If it refers to a state of being and so on, there would be a contradiction; if it is an action, it is a case of proving what is already established. (743) (PVA)

It is not said that "action" (*karman*) is the "condition" (*pratyaya*). This [term *pratyaya*] would be of a different nature as a substratum (*dharmin*), or it might be derived from the verbal root *kṛ* (to act), such that it is "that by which something is made known," hence a "condition. Alternatively, a "condition" (*pratyaya*) is "cognition" (*pratīti*). Or, it is a "condition" because it causes cognition or that by which cognition is caused. Whether it takes the form of an abstract state (*bhāva*), an agent (*kartṛ*), or an instrument (*karaṇa*), all of this is untenable. If cognition is the condition, it does not exist without that which is to be cognized. The same applies to the agent and so forth. Consequently, the term "condition" is dependent upon an external object. To say it is "without support" (*nirālambana*) while asserting its existence is a mutual contradiction.

[368, vi] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his supernormal power, transformed himself into a great fish. Having assumed this form, he entered the great ocean and carried all those merchants upon his back. He then brought them safely to the shore of the great ocean. Having reached the shore, he abandoned his form as a great fish and resumed his own original form as a bodhisattva. Then, having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, he withdrew to one side and sat down. The Blessed One then addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and say to him: ‘Householder, the Blessed One has arrived at the great ocean with five hundred merchants; he is now staying on the shore of the great ocean. “Very well, Blessed One,” replied the venerable Ānanda to the Blessed One. Having received these instructions, he went to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and said to him: “Householder, the Blessed One has arrived at the great ocean with five hundred merchants; he is now staying on the shore of the great ocean. Upon hearing this, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was filled with joy and satisfaction. He then prepared a great ship, equipped it with a mast, a rudder, and a sail, and set out for the shore of the great ocean. Having reached the shore, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and stood to one side. Standing there, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, I have prepared a great ship, equipped it with a mast, a rudder, and a sail, and have come here. May the Blessed One board this ship together with the community of monks. The Blessed One then boarded the ship together with the community of monks. At that time, the Blessed One, seated upon the ship, spoke these verses: “Just as a great ship, laden with many treasures, Safely carries its cargo across the vast ocean; So too does the Dharma-ship of the Sugata, Carrying the multitude of beings, cross over saṃsāra. Just as a great ship, driven by the wind, Swiftly reaches the desired destination; So too does the Dharma-ship of the Sugata, Carried by the wind of wisdom, reach nirvāṇa. Just as a great ship, free from all defects, Is not destroyed by the waves of the ocean; So too does the Dharma-ship of the Sugata, Not destroyed by the waves of the afflictions, reach the further shore. Having spoken these verses, the Blessed One proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī. When the Blessed One had reached the vicinity of Śrāvastī, he stayed at the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the Blessed One smiled? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is because of the great benefit of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada that I smiled. For it is through the householder Anāthapiṇḍada that the Dharma-eye of many hundreds of thousands of beings has been purified. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
