That is incorrect. If cognition (*pratīti*) is the act of cognizing (*pratyaya*), how can it be said that it is restricted to itself and does not exist without another [object]? Because no other [object] is perceived therein. Indeed, its own nature (*svarūpa*) alone will be what is cognized there; what need is there for another? And this has been established: "The self alone is that which causes one to cognize and that by which one is cognized"—what contradiction is there in this? If it is argued that "objectness" (*karmatva*) is not understood, [we reply]: for blue and so forth appear in their own nature, but there is no further thing called "objectness" belonging to them. If such a thing were perceived as being sought by another agent through its own operation, then that would indeed be the objective support (*ālambana*) for another; but that is precisely what is being refuted. If [you say], "How then is [the object] established?"—[we reply]: it is not established even as something being sought. Therefore, how can it have the status of an objective support by way of being an object (*karman*)? If it is apprehended in its own nature, then this is now a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
[368,vii] But surely, when it is being apprehended by itself, it is cognized as "I perceive blue. That is incorrect.
[368,viii]
Even that cognition which is "I" is a knower of the body, the sense-faculties, and the self,
because it is experienced as having a common locus with such [attributes] as "I am one-eyed," "I am happy," or "I am fair-skinned.
For we do not perceive the self as something other than the senses and so forth as the objective support of the notion of "I";
for if that self were the one who impels these [senses], it would not be known by anything else.
The proof for these [entities] arises from their own respective natures; there is no other proof anywhere.
(745) And if that from which their arising is observed is itself the impeller, then they are mutually impellers by virtue of being reciprocal conditions. (746)
When another aggregate is possible from that [initial] aggregate,
worldly transaction proceeds by way of the relation of cause and effect. Apart from the distinction of the nature of cognition, no other impelling agent is observed.
Alternatively, in some cases, the preceding repetition of such a state may be the impeller.

(748) (PVA) If another cognition arises from a cognition that has the form of the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*), how could that [subsequent cognition] have attained the form of blue and so forth? [Otherwise], how could there be the status of it being both the object and the agent? (749) (PVA)
Alternatively, if they occur at the same time, there is no reciprocal operation;
therefore, the existence of factors such as the object (*karman*) and so forth is not logically tenable.
As for what was said:
"For it is maintained that the cognition of form and so forth is without an objective support (nirālambana)."
For, by virtue of its nature as self-cognition, it does not apprehend anything at all;
indeed, that [object] is absolutely non-existent, because:
[368, xix] It is not maintained that the cognition of form and so forth is without an object;
for this [cognition], being excluded from what is non-cognitive in nature, takes its own constituent part as its object. (PVA 752)

[369,i] However, it has been demonstrated that the state of being without an object (*nirālambanatā*) follows even more strongly from the fact that consciousness is of the nature of cognition itself, rather than from having a distinct external object as its objective support. Furthermore, as for what was further asserted:
Whether in the capacity of an agent (*kartṛ*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*), the two words would also possess the status of being a subject (*pakṣa*).
Consequently, because they would lack a referent (*nirālambanatva*), the fallacy of the absence of a subject (*pakṣābhāva*) would follow. (PVA 753)

That is very well said; for it is by those two terms, "unsupported" (*nirālambana*) and "cognition" (*pratyaya*), that [the object] is indeed made known. Therefore, even those two possess the nature of being cognitions (*pratyayatva*). Thus, by virtue of their lack of an objective support (*anālambanatva*), something is directly perceived; it is merely the word itself as it exists in the sound.

In that case, the object of interest is not the objective support (*ālambana*); rather, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the domain of the word. Because it merely accords with reality, its status as the subject of the thesis (*pakṣatva*) is not contradicted.

The subject (*pakṣa*) is not merely the object of a word, because it is the domain of the means of proof (*sādhana*). And the means of proof is non-apprehension characterized by perception. Therefore, that which is to be proven—namely, the state of having its own form as an objective support—is the subject. How, then, can there be an absence of a subject? Furthermore, in this context, "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is understood from the context to mean knowledge; so how could there be an occasion for a refutation based on the door of words? For it is not the case that everything which is made an object through etymological derivation is necessarily what is conveyed by a word; rather, it is only that which arrives through the context [that is meant]. Otherwise, there would be no comprehension of meaning from words. Even general terms are observed to function with reference to a particular based on context, as in the command "bring the *saindhava*"; at the time of a meal, only salt is understood. This point has already been settled by a single puff of breath, as he said: [The opponent objects: But if the cognition is the subject, then since it is not an object of the senses, it cannot be apprehended by perception. And if it is not apprehended by perception, it cannot be negated by non-apprehension either, because non-apprehension is dependent upon perception. Thus, since the subject is unestablished, the reason is one whose locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddha*). [The author replies: This is not so. For we do not say that the cognition is the subject in the sense that it is the object of the word "cognition. Rather, the cognition is the subject insofar as it is the object of the means of proof. And the means of proof here is non-apprehension. Therefore, the state of having its own form as an objective support is what is to be proven, and that is the subject. Without a sentence that causes cognition, there is no possibility of an agent or other factors;
or, if the cause of that [cognition] is itself a cognition, your own statement contradicts you. (755) (PVA)

If it does not cause anything to be cognized, or if nothing is cognized by it, how can it be such [a means of cognition]? Or, in the absence of an object of cognition, what would the cognition have as its object? For: [369,x] Since:
For without a distinct object to be made known, there could be no possibility of an agent and so forth;

and if that [object] is the cause of the suffix, how can there be a contradiction with one's own words? (756) (PVA) The agent, the object, and so forth are merely conceptualized; they do not exist in the ultimate sense.
"It is defined as the self destroying itself by means of itself.
xii] Furthermore, since the referent of the word "cognition" does not have an external cause, there is no contradiction with one's own statement.
Even if it were a cognition by way of conventional usage, nevertheless,
for us, the object as a grasper is established as being a cognition of another entity. (758) (PVA)

Even in its conventional sense, the word *pratyaya* (cognition) is established as referring to a distinct entity independent of mere common understanding; thus, it is already established by worldly consensus that its object is an external thing. For what is well-established in the world cannot be otherwise ordained.
That is incorrect.
The establishment of things does not occur by mere worldly consensus.
The world of the investigator serves as the cause for the establishment of an object.

(PVA 759) What world, other than cognition itself, exists for the sake of establishing an object? If the world is nothing but cognition, then that [object] has not been made into an objective support. (PVA 760)
If the world could discern reality without conscious experience,
then all these beings, such as stones and the like, would discern it.
As for what is also said:
"If, having accepted that [position], one then asserts a thesis, what has been accepted is contradicted."
And for you, there is the non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in such a case, whereas for us, it is not so.
In such a case—namely, in a cognition that makes another object known, which is unestablished for you—the qualificand is for us a cognition of a different nature. Likewise:
Even if one were to conceive of the self and phenomena as being independent, it would be the same.
And there is no such thing as "mere conditionality," because it cannot be defined. 763.

For instance: if the cognition (*pratyaya*) were made the subject (*pakṣa*) by accepting that its means of proof (*sādhana*) is distinct [from the self], then such a subject would not be established for you. For the Buddhist does not accept this. If, on the other hand, the acceptance of the opposite—that the means of proof is non-distinct—were the case, then it would be unestablished for us, the opponents. For we do not accept that cognition has means of proof that are non-distinct; likewise, being a property of the self (*ātma-dharmatva*) is unestablished for the Buddhists, and independence (*svatantratva*) is unestablished for the Mīmāṃsakas. Nor does there exist a mere cognition (*pratyayamātra*) whose status as a subject could be defined independently of both positions. Thus, it has been stated in some way or another that "there is a face," because this has already been said.
That which constitutes the subject of dispute must necessarily be unestablished. If its establishment were already known, for whom would the proof be a proof? (764) (PVA)

For that very probative property (*sādhanadharma*) which is distinct [from the subject] and is unestablished as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*), by means of its own non-establishment, serves your purpose in pointing out the non-establishment of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). That very thing which has become the locus of dispute is what you intend to prove; and by that qualification, the non-establishment of the subject is indeed admitted. If, however, at the time of the proof that [qualification] were already established, what would be the use of a proof for things already established? Yet, a thesis whose qualification is unestablished is indeed defective, such as the statement "sound is perishable" when addressed to a Sāṃkhya.
That is incorrect; for:
[370,x] Even with respect to the Sāṃkhya, the defectiveness of the thesis has been refuted.

For when the object of the example is established, the subject (pakṣa) does not have an unestablished qualification. (765) (PVA) Alternatively, if destruction is unestablished in the example, there would be a defect in the reason (hetu), namely that it is either inconclusive (anaikāntika) or contradictory (viruddha). (766) (PVA)

[370,xii] If it is argued that there is a fault because "destruction" (*nirāma*, i.e., self-destruction) is not established in the subject (*pakṣa*), that is incorrect. It is precisely from that [subject] that it is being proved. Therefore, the fact that the qualification is unestablished is not a fault of the subject; how could this be a fault? For the essential nature [of the subject] itself is not a fault. If, on the other hand, it is unestablished in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then that is a fault of the example or a fault of the reason (*hetu*), but not a fault of the subject.
[370,xiii]
And if the nature of the self (*ātman*) were not established, then phenomena (*dharma*) could not have it as their objective support (*pratyaya*).
For sound does not fail to be established as a subject (*dharmin*) simply because the qualities of space (*ākāśa*) are not established.

Its status as a subject (*dharmin*) is established by the mere act of being apprehended through hearing; otherwise, nothing could function as a subject, because a property (*dharma*) proposed by an opponent would be unestablished in every case. Therefore, this objection is entirely without merit. For that very reason, another point stated by the opponent is also incorrect:
"Just as for others, there is a determination [of the subject] in the form of the mere meaning of the word... [370,xvi]
Nevertheless, for you who do not accept a distinction between the proponent and the opponent, this would not be possible.

Because he does not admit any distinction between the designator and other things designated, and because for that proponent it is impossible even to define [the object] as being merely the form of the word’s meaning—given the non-admission of a universal (sāmānya)—that opponent is unable to raise an objection against him when such conceptual constructions as "dharma" and so forth are made.

That is incorrect. For the term "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is used without qualification to mean the mere object of a word, which is synonymous with "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) or "manifestation" (*pratibhāsana*); since this is already established, [your objection] is invalid. [We reply: This is not so. That which constitutes "cognitiveness" (*pratyayatva*) in the case of the cognition of a double moon and other such instances is indeed established as being the object of a reflective awareness (*parāmarṣa*) of a single form. However, as for its ultimate nature (*tattva*), everything else remains to be investigated; thus, because it occupies the middle ground of what is yet to be proven (*sādhya*), how could it be improper to say it is unestablished (*asiddha*)? The charge of unestablishedness will be raised and refuted later. For now, another point is stated: [371, iii]
If here, "lack of objective support" is being proven in every respect, there would be an unestablished qualification and no illustrative example exists. (769) (PVA) [371,iv]

If it is argued that every cognition whatsoever is to be proven as being without an object (*nirālambana*), what is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for that? If the waking cognition is cited, even so the example remains unestablished; for even a dream-cognition has an object in some sense, since it has as its object things belonging either to that time or to another time. If, on the other hand, the absence of an object at that specific time is intended, then if it is said to be "without an object" in that particular manner:
Because the cognition of taste is devoid of form and so forth, this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

(PVA 770) Just as that which has a particular object of cognition—whether at that same time or at another time—must be accepted as having that as its object, even so, if it were without an object, it would follow that the cognition of taste is also without an object in terms of form; and since that is precisely what is desired, it is a case of proving the already established.
vii] Now, if it is argued that the exclusion of an object occurs because cognition possesses a certain form,
then since the possession of its own form is admitted, the non-existence of that [object] is contradicted. (PVA 771)

For you maintain that the subjective aspect of cognition does not consist in having the form of an object, but rather consists solely in having the form of cognition itself. Consequently, it follows that cognition would now lack an object of apprehension, which is undesirable. In that case, there must be something to be apprehended as the objective support; yet, if it is not an external thing, what could it be?
That is incorrect.
[371,x] If, even though there is no external object as a support, there is nevertheless the apprehension that "it is external,"...
"In a pillar and the like, there is no such cognition at all"—thus [the argument] proves what is already established.

(PVA 772) Even here, in the cognition "the jar is outside," the jar itself is not the objective support; rather, it is the external object alone. However, due to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [external object], there arises a corresponding notion regarding the jar.
[371,xii] Now,
if it is argued that cognition is without an object in the form of a pillar and so forth,
then a contradiction with what is perceived follows. (PVA 773)
If it is argued that [the case of] the double moon and so forth is similar because it arises from the non-attainment of the sense faculty,
then in those cases there would be a statement of "lack of an objective basis" (*anālambana*) due to the absence of cognition of an object, and not otherwise.

The intellect (*buddhi*) grasps what has been reached by the sense-faculties, such as the eye; thus it is said to be "without an objective support" (*nirālambana*), as in the case of the cognition of two moons and so forth. However, that [cognition] does not have that [double moon] as its objective support at all. Previously, this person had a perception of a single moon; therefore, through contact with that sense-faculty, there is no objective support for the pair [of moons]. But it is not the case that the object simply never exists. When there is the vision of a single moon, in its absence [as a double moon], the lack of objective support occurs; this is the reason for the realization of the lack of objective support. He demonstrates this very point:
"In all cases, it is not by virtue of the existence or non-existence of the contact between the object and the sense-faculties [that the cognition is without an objective support]."

While consciousness exists, there is the establishment of the apprehension of both the existent and the non-existent. For you, however, since the sense organs and so forth are absent apart from the act of grasping, there can be no reason for [an object] to be an objective support; therefore, your negation is untenable.

[372,i] "Conditions are without an objective basis. This is a great manifestation of delusion, for it is a mind stained by the impurity of false conceptualization that has been made public by another as a form of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). To explain:
If it is well-established by means of valid cognition that the word *nirālambana* has as its denotation something that takes its own part (*svāṃśa*) as its objective support,
how can there be a refutation?

Through the negation of an object of apprehension perceivable by the senses as imagined by others, it is understood from the context and so forth that this word is employed with reference only to its own part (*svāṃśa*). Otherwise, there would be no cognition of an object from a word. In that case, since this object is cognized from the word in common worldly usage, how could it be impossible to define?

[Objection: But surely, even for that [word], there is no difference from other denoters or from other denotable objects; so how can it be said that the mere word-meaning serves as the locus (*dharmin*)?

[The opponent says: "It is true that [your statement] was stated incorrectly; what of it? This does not immediately result in non-duality (advaita), because there would not be a lack of distinction, but rather [the cognition] is indeed distinct from other cognitions and from one another. In this regard, the cognition [arising] from the word ‘pot’ is one thing, and the pot itself is another, and so forth. Furthermore, words bring the very object previously apprehended within the scope of memory. In that context, what is incorrect about [our position] when we inform you that those cognitions which appear as objects of experience by having blue and so forth as their objective supports (*ālambana*) are actually without such objective supports? If someone were to perceive smoke that is devoid of fire, should he not be told: ‘The smoke that you perceive as being without fire is not so’? Or why would there be any suspicion of fault in the speaker? [The opponent replies: ‘In that case, he can be informed by means of fire as previously perceived; but how can this be done here? [We reply: Here too, a cognition of a visual disorder (*taimirika-jñāna*) is established as being without an objective support due to the impossibility of an external object. If [the opponent argues] that even there, space (*gagana*) is the objective support, [we say] no; for just as space is the objective support for the perception of hair-tufts, so too in the perception of space, something else entirely is the support. This is because that which is appearing lacks the status of being an objective support. If [the opponent argues] that in the cognition of space, that which is appearing is itself the objective support, then let it be so here as well. In every case, there is the loss of memory regarding erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*). Whether one assumes a beginning in worldly perceptions or not, the conclusion remains the same: [all cognitions are without external objects].”

Now, it is logical that for one who has perceived a cognition of a single moon as having an object (*sālambana*), the cognition of two moons is without an object (*nirālambana*). But how is it with the cognition of a single moon? That too has been established as being of the same nature [as the former]. If it is argued that it is because it is sublated (*bādhitatvāt*), it has been demonstrated that in that case as well there is sublation. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that what does not appear [in consciousness] cannot be the object. And we shall demonstrate that blue and so forth are themselves cognitions. Just as the cognition of hair and the like is without an object in the form of [actual] hair, so too it follows that the cognition of a blue form would have yellow, sweet, and so forth as its objects. How then can the proof of the cognition of form (*rūpajñāna*) being without an object in the form of taste and so forth be considered a "proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*)? If you say: "The cognition of water does not occur without parched ground heated by rays [of the sun], but does the cognition of form occur without taste and so forth? [We reply: It does occur; for the cognition of water occurs even in real water without parched ground heated by rays. If you say there is a distinction in that case, then since there is a mutual distinction between the two, it follows that both are either without an object or else [both] have an object. If you say: "Let both have an object," then if it appears as "parched ground heated by rays" and so on, this should not be said [of the cognition]. If you say the non-appearing is the object by way of being the cause (*kāraṇatvena*), then mental impressions (*vāsanā*) will be that [cause], and our desired point is established. If you say: "Then let it be only that which appears; what is the use of anything else? [We reply: Because it would follow that there is no difference between perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); if only that which appears were [the object], everything would be nothing but perception.
Furthermore, the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous would not possess worldly consensus;
for everything is non-erroneous with respect to its own nature, while there is error with respect to the nature of another. (PVA 778)
If it is argued that attainment possesses an objective support, it has already been established that there is no such thing as attainment;
yet, even so, there would still be an attainment of the illusion of water in a mirage.
"It does not exist at all times, nor is it seen as 'not so' at all places; because of its momentariness, it would indeed be non-perishing—how then could it be perishable? (780) (PVA)
Recognition is thereby refuted; consequently, everything is consistent.
Therefore, since everything is perceived through perception and inference, it is entirely without an objective basis (*anālambana*). The remainder has been stated.
Thus, if one refutes a qualification imagined by another after having restated it, what fault could there be in this? By this, the following is also refuted, as he said:
For it is thus:
Since external existence is not established, cognition is therefore without an object. How can this be proven when this very subject (*pakṣa*) is not even known?
Just as [a reason] cannot bring about the understanding of something else when the qualification is unestablished.
In the same way, there would be the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣasiddhi*) regarding the qualification of a qualification.
For the meaning of a sentence is not understood when the referent of a word is unestablished;
and since it is preceded by that [word-meaning], the thesis will be established as the meaning of a sentence. (PVA 782–783)
It will be established that the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is the probandum (*sādhya*).

This is simply non-existent. Since an external object of apprehension is not established from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is merely accepted by the opponent and for that very reason is negated. We shall demonstrate later that the application of a proof (*sādhana*) is for the purpose of dispelling error; however, how could the non-existence of something established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be proven? If you argue that it is by way of subverting the valid cognition itself, we say no. For if one valid cognition were subverted by another valid cognition, there would be a lack of confidence, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the status of valid cognition altogether. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that what is called a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is impossible. If you argue that what is observed in a certain place and time can be negated elsewhere, we say no, because of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
[373,xii] For that which is observed in one place is not postulated for another location and so forth;
since there is no error in that case, the proof of its non-existence there is futile. (PVA) 784.

[373, xiii] Now, if there is a conceptual construction elsewhere due to some treatise or other because of the absence of means of valid cognition [to the contrary], for indeed errors are not unobserved. In that case, then:

When there is an error regarding a certain place or other object that has been perceived by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that error is sublated by the *pramāṇa*; but what lack of tolerance is there toward an error itself?

For that which is an occasional error is what is to be removed. But as for that which is perpetual, why should it not be removed? Great human effort is required for its removal. [373, xvi] [Objection: Surely that [occasional error] is removed by demonstrating a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) elsewhere; but how can that which is always an error itself be removed? And since there is no subverting proof, how can it be called an "error"? [Response: That too is incorrect, because there is no such thing as a "subverting proof" at all. To explain:
[373,xvii] Is it a sublater, or is it that which cuts off [the object], or is it that which causes the loss of the apprehended?
Or is it an indicator in the absence of the apprehended? There are these three positions; whence could there be another? (PVA) 786.
[373,xix] If the sublater produces the absence of the sublated cognition, or the absence of its object, then is that [absence] produced or unproduced?
How can the non-existence of that which is unarisen be established by him?
Never has the destruction of a donkey’s horn been brought about by anyone.
(787) (PVA) Likewise, the non-existence of an entity that has already arisen is not established [in that manner].
To say "it exists because of that cause" and "it does not exist because of a sublater" is mere audacity.
(PVA 788) If this entity has already arisen, by what could its non-existence be produced? The *kiṃśuka* trees are naturally red; who now colors them?

[374, ii] Now, if it exists in the same manner as it was produced from its cause, then since it exists exactly as it was born, how can there be an onset of destruction? If that were the case, it would be a great contradiction for that very thing to be destroyed and yet that very same thing to be existent. Alternatively, if it is destroyed in the same manner as it was not born, then in that case:
If that which is born in one form were to be destroyed by another,
then blue and other such things would be destroyed by yellow and other such forms.
And that form does not belong to it; thus, they alone are "colored by destiny. And by that very nature, it is either destroyed later or else [it remains] forever.
If it were to perish later, it would have possessed that nature previously.
How could there be a subsequent destruction of that which was born with that very nature?
That which was born with that nature at that very time is what is subsequently destroyed. (PVA 790–791)
If that *kiṃśuka* tree was previously colored by fate, then its absence of that form later must also be due to fate;
for if its destruction occurred earlier, it was precisely because of that very cause.
Let it be examined what further function the destroyer has for this [object].
This is the same even in the case of the destruction of its objective support (*ālambana*). For instance:
Just as that which has arisen is not destroyed by that form, so too that which has not arisen is not destroyed by that form either. (793) (PVA)

Because it is purposeless, because it is impossible, and because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition, how could even the conceptualization of this object occur to those possessed of intelligence? (PVA 794) [374,xii]
Now, it is argued that the subverting proof (bādhaka) makes known the non-existence of the object;
that too is incorrect.
When that entity is perceived, then its non-existence does not exist;
when the entity is not perceived, that non-perception is the sublater of it. (PVA 795)
Furthermore, when an entity is not established, a negation with a qualifier cannot exist;
and if the qualifier is unestablished, how can there be any power of cognition for you?
Or, if the qualifier is established elsewhere, it would here function as a mere reference (*anuvāda*).
For that which has the nature of a positive entity cannot be a qualifier of non-existence.
(797) (PVA) If it is thus established that "that very thing does not exist elsewhere," then what is the purpose of negating that which has already been so understood? (798) (PVA)
Even for one who has understood otherwise, there is still no negation;
since this very point has been stated previously, it is not repeated again and again. (799) (PVA) When an entity is not perceived, then there can be no negation.
If its negation were performed there by means of a memory that is unqualified [by the object], (800) (PVA) then, when there is apprehension in accordance with memory, there is no negation whatsoever.
If the memory apprehends its own form, it cannot be a qualifier of non-existence. (801) (PVA)
Now, whether in memory or in conceptual construction, whatever appears is only that much which exists; an external form does not exist. (802) (PVA) [374,xxii]
In that case,
then, regarding what is commonly recognized in the world as appearing elsewhere as "external":
There exists only that much, yet that reality is not perceived.
(803) (PVA) It is mere cognition that is the objective support, but no external object corresponding to it is perceived;
for there is indeed no apprehension of any distinction between this [waking state] and cognitions such as those in dreams. (804) (PVA)

Since this [cognition] arises from mere appearance, produced by the force of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is no discernment of specific distinctions; thus, cognition is without an objective support (*anālambana*).
How, then, is the cognition of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator [possible]?
[374,xxvii] It is because the unity of that which is being cognized persists even when there is a future contradiction.
When a subverting cognition occurs, the subverting [cognition] would have to exist in the interval between them.
(PVA 806) If this were not a subverting cognition, then this [previous cognition] would remain exactly as it was;
therefore, if it is uninterrupted, the subverting cognition is considered to be without cause. (PVA 807)

[374,xxix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound prajñāpāramitā, clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, and he delivers those beings from the perilous perils of birth, old age, sickness, and death. At that time, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, he should perceive all phenomena as empty and devoid of characteristics. Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, therefore, all phenomena are emptiness; they are without characteristics, without birth, without cessation, without defilement, without purity, and without decrease or increase. Śāriputra, within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; no realm of the eye up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and also no non-attainment. Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a bodhisattva relies on prajñāpāramitā and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, one ultimately rests in nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, by relying on prajñāpāramitā, have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, know that prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra, which is able to remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Śāriputra, the profound prajñāpāramitā is thus the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra. All you bhikṣus should study and uphold it. [375,i] At that time, having heard from the Buddha’s mouth this profound prajñāpāramitā, the hearts of the five thousand arrogant śrāvakas were filled with remorse, and they rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, placed their palms together before the Buddha, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, we now confess our transgressions before the Buddha. We have long held ourselves in high esteem, thinking ourselves to be arhats. World-Honored One, if we had truly been arhats, we would not have come to this assembly. World-Honored One, from today onward, we shall diligently seek the bodhi of the Buddhas. Then the Buddha told the five thousand śrāvakas: "Well done, well done! Sons of good family, if you can now seek the bodhi of the Buddhas, you will surely attain it. At that time, the eight thousand gods of the desire realm, the gods of the form realm, and the gods of the formless realm, hearing the Buddha praise the profound prajñāpāramitā, rejoiced at heart and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, we too shall seek the bodhi of the Buddhas. Then the Buddha told the gods of the desire, form, and formless realms: "Sons of good family, if you can seek the bodhi of the Buddhas, you will surely attain it. At that time, the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his palms together before the Buddha, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell? The Buddha told the venerable Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should dwell with a mind like empty space, without grasping at any phenomenon. Why? Subhūti, form is neither bound nor liberated. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, the nature of form is neither bound nor liberated. The natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, the ultimate limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. The ultimate limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, the past limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. The past limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, the future limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. The future limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, the present limit of form is neither bound nor liberated. The present limits of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, the self-nature of form is neither bound nor liberated. The self-natures of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why? Subhūti, all dharmas are ultimately empty and have no characteristics. They cannot be apprehended, and they cannot be grasped. Why? Subhūti, because all dharmas are originally quiescent and ultimately empty. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā in this way, Māra and his host will be unable to find an opportunity to harm them. At that time, the venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, what is called a 'bodhisattva'? What is called 'mahāsattva'? The Buddha told the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva is so called because they awaken to all dharmas. Subhūti, a mahāsattva is so called because they are superior to all sentient beings. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva is so called because they awaken to all dharmas, then are all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas also called bodhisattvas? The Buddha told the venerable Subhūti: "They are also called bodhisattvas, but they are not called mahāsattvas. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, why is it that while they are called bodhisattvas, they are not called mahāsattvas? The Buddha told the venerable Subhūti: "Because they do not seek the supreme, perfect enlightenment of all dharmas. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate all dharmas as empty in nature. Why? Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any dharma, they are called a mahāsattva. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate all dharmas as having no characteristics. Why? Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any dharma, they are called a mahāsattva. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate all dharmas as wishless. Why? Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any dharma, they are called a mahāsattva. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate all dharmas as signless. Why? Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any dharma, they are called a mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate all dharmas as empty in nature, as having no characteristics, as wishless, and as signless. World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas in this way, they will not fall into the stage of śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Why? World-Honored One, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not grasp at any dharma, they

For indeed, every entity persists for a period of time. During that interval, when another cognition arises that determines a different nature [for the object], then the previous objective support (*ālambana*) or cognition is interrupted by it; thus, that [subsequent cognition] is established as the sublater (*bādhaka*). For if this [subsequent cognition] were not present, the objective support of the previous cognition would remain uninterrupted, just as at other times. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that [the previous cognition] has been interrupted by the sublater. This applies likewise to the relationship between the destroyer and the destroyed, as well as the relationship between the objective support and the supported. To explain:
[375,ii] When an object such as a jar has been determined to be present even though it is out of sight,
the cognition that arises with its form is established as having that very thing as its objective support. 808 (PVA)
[375,iii] Likewise [375,iv]
Knowledge is as clear as crystal; whatever object is presented to it, having assumed that particular form, it shines forth in exactly that way.

First of all, it is established through some scripture or through inference that there exists a direct perception (*aparokṣa*) and that consciousness is clear. If this object did not exist, the mind would merely fluctuate, wondering "does this exist? or "does it not exist here? But when the nature of the object has been perceived, the mind—like one who was floating—reaches the shore and becomes stable; therefore, it is determined that the object is its support (*ālambana*). For instance:
"One whose mind is occupied with reflection, with a mind that was previously floating... [375, vi]
"This was seen at that time"—thus it becomes stabilized upon what was previously seen.

(PVA 810) For when one conceptualizes something previously seen or heard that has been forgotten—searching amidst the proliferation of discourse as to "what was seen there? or "what was heard?"—and when one brings to mind what was heard and so forth, then that which is brought to mind appears with stability. It is established as an objective support (*ālambana*) for the purpose of abandoning the state of floating [in uncertainty]; such is worldly convention.
[375, viii] If it is argued that "the reality itself is thus," then this entity would not exist;
for it is a non-entity because it is not apprehended through either perception or inference. (PVA 811)

[375,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern regions, beheld five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were being tormented by Māra. Seeing them, he felt great compassion for those bhikṣuṇīs and addressed them as follows: “Sisters, do not fear; I shall protect you from the afflictions caused by Māra. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recited this dhāraṇī-mantra for the sake of those bhikṣuṇīs: Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Namaḥ avalokiteśvarasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya | Tadyathā | oṃ maṇi-padme hūṃ | svāhā || By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra, the afflictions caused by Māra were immediately dispelled, and those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara departed from that place and proceeded toward the western region. Upon arriving there, he saw five hundred śrāmaṇeras who were being tormented by Yakṣas. Seeing them, he felt great compassion for those śrāmaṇeras and addressed them as follows: “Young men, do not fear; I shall protect you from the afflictions caused by the Yakṣas. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recited this dhāraṇī-mantra for the sake of those śrāmaṇeras: Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Namaḥ avalokiteśvarasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya | Tadyathā | oṃ padma-śānti-vijaye hūṃ phaṭ | svāhā || By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra, the afflictions caused by the Yakṣas were immediately dispelled, and those five hundred śrāmaṇeras attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara departed from that place and proceeded toward the northern region. Upon arriving there, he saw five hundred upāsakas who were being tormented by Rākṣasīs. Seeing them, he felt great compassion for those upāsakas and addressed them as follows: “Lay brothers, do not fear; I shall protect you from the afflictions caused by the Rākṣasīs. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recited this dhāraṇī-mantra for the sake of those upāsakas: Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Namaḥ avalokiteśvarasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya | Tadyathā | oṃ vajra-dharma-samaya hūṃ | svāhā || By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra, the afflictions caused by the Rākṣasīs were immediately dispelled, and those five hundred upāsakas attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara departed from that place and proceeded toward the eastern region. Upon arriving there, he saw five hundred upāsikās who were being tormented by Piśācas. Seeing them, he felt great compassion for those upāsikās and addressed them as follows: “Sisters, do not fear; I shall protect you from the afflictions caused by the Piśācas. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recited this dhāraṇī-mantra for the sake of those upāsikās: Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Namaḥ avalokiteśvarasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya | Tadyathā | oṃ padma-krodha-hūṃ phaṭ | svāhā || By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra, the afflictions caused by the Piśācas were immediately dispelled, and those five hundred upāsikās attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara departed from that place and proceeded toward the nadir. Upon arriving there, he saw five hundred pretas who were being tormented by hunger and thirst. Seeing them, he felt great compassion for those pretas and addressed them as follows: “Hungry ghosts, do not fear; I shall protect you from the afflictions of hunger and thirst. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recited this dhāraṇī-mantra for the sake of those pretas: Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Namaḥ avalokiteśvarasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya | Tadyathā | oṃ amṛta-tejo-jvala hūṃ | svāhā || By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra, their hunger and thirst were immediately appeased, and those five hundred pretas attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara departed from that place and proceeded toward the zenith. Upon arriving there, he saw five hundred devaputras who were being tormented by the afflictions of pride and arrogance. Seeing them, he felt great compassion for those devaputras and addressed them as follows: “Sons of gods, do not fear; I shall protect you from the afflictions of pride and arrogance. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recited this dhāraṇī-mantra for the sake of those devaputras: Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām | Namaḥ avalokiteśvarasya bodhisattvasya mahāsattvasya | Tadyathā | oṃ jñāna-mudrā-samaya hūṃ | svāhā || By the power of this dhāraṇī-mantra, their pride and arrogance were immediately subdued, and those five hundred devaputras attained the stage of non-retrogression. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having liberated beings throughout the ten directions, returned to the Sahā world-system. Arriving at the Jetavana Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park in Śrāvastī, he approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side. Seated there, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara recounted to the Blessed One all the deeds he had performed for the sake of liberating sentient beings throughout the ten directions. Having heard this, the Blessed One praised him, saying: “Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You have indeed performed a great work of benefit for the world. Because you have recited these dhāraṇī-mantras, all those beings have been liberated from suffering and established in the stage of non-retrogression. Thus spoke the Blessed One, and with this, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and the entire assembly rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught.

First of all, the existence of that which is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since that [perception] is absent, inference (*anumāna*) is also impossible; how then could it occur? If there were a cognition of the beyond-the-senses, then, upon its existence, the fact that direct perception has that as its objective support (*ālambana*) would be established. And if direct perception had such an objective support, it would be established as being connected to a real entity (*vastu*). From that, inference—arising from a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with that entity—would make the entity known. Then, because direct perception would have as its object an entity established through inference, it would possess an objective support. From that, there would be a connection of inference with the real entity, and from that, the comprehension of the entity; thus, there would be a circularity (*cakraka*) and a lack of finality, and consequently, the apprehension of a real entity would be impossible.

For when an object has not been thus apprehended, assent is merely [subjective], because it is possible for there to have been a prior cognition even without the recognition of the form of a means of valid cognition. (812) (PVA)

Following that [conventional] understanding, I previously established this relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatā*), out of a desire to avoid disregarding its conventional form. But if you, on the other hand, do not accept such a consideration, how can there be any cognition of this?
If, upon such investigation, that [object] does not exist in reality, then it simply does not exist;
what fault is there in that, such that one should be questioned?
If [you argue] that there is a relationship of sublated and sublator between two cognitions, where the latter is preceded by the former...

In one's own cognition, whose fault is it that one should be questioned? Does anyone ever perceive themselves as being subject to questioning? (816) [PVA] Whence does his error arise? The self is not the object of such questioning.

If it is indeed an error, what is the point of searching for its cause? (817) (PVA) When the opponent has been made to understand this very clearly in such a manner, then he too will certainly not say: "Why do I have such an error? (818) (PVA)

For when, upon the occurrence of an error, one who possesses self-reflection subsequently turns away from it, thinking "this is not silver," does anyone then direct a challenge to oneself? [One might ask: "How could I, while silver has not been apprehended, establish its qualification as non-existence? And if that qualification is unestablished, how could I know that remote qualification by which my position would be free from fault? This is exactly the same even in the case of instructing another.

[Objection: "Surely, an error is possible there where a real silver is perceived; but here, since nothing at all is seen, how can there be an error? We shall explain this later. Furthermore, if an error is somehow understood to exist in an ultimate sense, what is the point now of the exertion in searching for its cause? If there were no cause, the error itself would not occur. This is not so.
[376,ii] When a cause exists, there is no error even with respect to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it too has a cause.
If it is argued that error exists because it has a cause, then even in that case, what is desired [by the opponent] is undermined. (819) (PVA)

The very notion that "there is no cause" is itself an error; otherwise, every cognition of yours would be an error. Even regarding what is not an error, one must certainly inquire: "Whence does this error arise? If you say, "Because it is perceived as such," then this is equally applicable to error. If error is preceded by non-error, then if there is no such thing as non-error at all due to the absence of a cause, how could error possibly exist? Let it be so; but how is it to be understood? For error is established as being the opposite of non-error. This is the same in the other case as well: non-error is established as being the opposite of error. Now, if you argue that error exists as a positive entity (*vidhi-rūpa*) and not as the mere opposite of non-error, and that error occurs only when there is a sublater (*bādhaka*), and therefore error arises from the very opposite of non-error—[we reply: [This argument is untenable. If error were a positive entity, it would have to be perceived even when the sublater is absent. Furthermore, if error were merely the absence of non-error, then since non-error is defined as the absence of error, the two would be mutually dependent, leading to a logical circularity. Moreover, if error were a positive entity, it would never cease, for a positive entity cannot be destroyed by its opposite. Therefore, error is not a positive reality, but rather the mistaken apprehension of an object as something it is not. Thus, the distinction between error and non-error is established through their mutual opposition. Consequently, the claim that error exists independently of non-error is refuted. It follows that the absence of a cause for error is untenable, and thus the existence of external objects is established.
That too is incorrect.
Whatever is perceived in a positive form is understood as being exactly that;
the certainty is that there is no external positive entity there, for that is an illusion.
Now, it is not said that wherever there is a cause, that is delusion; rather, whatever is delusion does not exist without a cause. In that case, the reason is qualified:
delusion occurs because of the existence of the causes of delusion, and not otherwise.
And once the nature of the error has been known, there is the ascertainment of its cause.

For if the reason (*hetu*) is accompanied by a qualification, the error must first be known, and that error too must arise from a cause; thus there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, let that which is the form of the error be the cause for its establishment simply through the cognition of that form, or let it not be so. For an entity exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), not by way of the nature of its cause. If it is asked, "From where does that own-nature come?", what does this matter? Why should this apprehension of the nature of the error not itself be an error? If it is apprehended in such a way, let it be so—what is the fault? If it is argued that the preceding [cognition] is not an error, that too is incorrect.

In the cognition of silver, there would be the cessation of the cognition of mother-of-pearl; and if there were another cause for the cessation of that cognition of mother-of-pearl as well, [then it would be a case of error]. (PVA 822)
Then, how could that cognition of silver be true? Or rather, why is it not seen that both [the silver and its negation] do not exist?
(823) Furthermore, if its truth were perceived somewhere else, then it might be so.
In that case, because of the existence of a firm basis, there is the opposite in the other instance.
(PVA 824) For it is when there is a subverting cognition that the opposite occurs in the other case;
if there were no subverting cognition at all, that would establish the truth of the opposite. (PVA 825)
Who could then establish the non-existence of error?
To this it is replied:
[376,xvi] If there is a cognition of the opposite, or otherwise, how indeed could there be a determination of non-existence?

Furthermore, if certainty is produced by non-apprehension, what need is there for another factor that produces certainty? (826) (PVA) If it is argued that the apprehension of the opposite constitutes the proof of its non-existence, then let there be merely self-awareness; consequently, there is no awareness of an external object. (827) (PVA)

Therefore, it is the principle that non-apprehension alone is the subverting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and nothing else. Since that [non-apprehension] exists here as well, how could consciousness have an objective support? Consequently, the cognition whose nature consists of neither the cognized nor the cognizer [is established].
Furthermore, as for the claim that the negation of the possessive sense (*matvartha*) is what is being proven, that too is utterly untenable;
for it is precisely the absence of the possessive sense that is being proven here from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
Otherwise, the proof of its being without an objective support would not be possible.

"Consciousness is without an object. Since the absence of object-status (*ālambanatva*) is what is set forth to be proven, that very thing is what is to be proven; how could it be cast aside? For that which is made the subject (*pakṣa*) by one's own intention—how could it be treated otherwise? Whatever is intended to be proven is precisely the subject. Now, if such a thing is impossible to prove, then this is simply a fault of the reason (*hetu*), not a fault of the subject. When proving [the absence] by way of its being "possessing non-existence," the suffix denoting possession (*matvartha*) is indeed present.

But there is no ultimate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the state of being that which is to be proven (*sādhya*) through a possessive suffix (*matvartha*). This is because one relies upon an imagined relationship between a subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*). A property that is in fact identical with the essence (*svabhāva*) of the thing is established as if distinct by way of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), and is thus conceptually constructed (*kalpyate*) for the sake of meaningfulness. Although this is indeed a conventional linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) from the perspective of the relative truth (*saṃvṛti*), there is no harm in that. Let this linguistic usage proceed for now like the closing of an elephant's eyes; yet, when further investigated, it too will surely fall apart.

Now, what is this "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*)? If it is a real entity, then that very thing should be stated; what is the point of another name for it? On the other hand, if nothing exists there, then what is the point of the name "conventional reality"? It is merely an appearance of truth, but it is not reality from the perspective of the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

When its emptiness is being investigated, it is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). (PVA 829) Because it conceals reality, it is a convention. For it is not logical that a form which is appearing should be non-existent merely by virtue of that appearance. However, when it is subjected to investigation, because it is non-existent, there is the ascertainment of its absence. Therefore, with respect to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is called "conventional. It exists conventionally means it exists from the perspective of deluded people. And since no sublation arises for the deluded person, they have the conceit of its reality; thus it is called "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛtisatya*). Consequently, this too can indeed be stated:
[377, viii] If it is non-existent, what is this delusion? If it is existent, how can it be delusion?
If delusion is the appearance of what is not real, why is that which is not real not simply the conventional? (PVA) 830.
If there were no reality in what is unreal, would it not be a semblance of reality?
Therefore, the claim that "conventional reality" is merely a "semblance of reality" is a deceptive statement,
like saying that a crow is a crane.
For one whose illumination is real, it would be inconsistent even if it were directed toward the unreal.
(832) (PVA) If one speaks of its appearing as unreal, what deception could there possibly be?
Therefore, when one does not know the intentions of others, out of a desire to express self-exaltation, (833) (PVA) [one acts in this way].
[377,xiii] Therefore, there is no deception other than mere idle chatter.
Let this matter rest for now; something else is stated. Regarding this very point, it has been said by another:
"Whether it be a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) or an absolute negation (*niṣedha*), [it refers to] a distinct entity (*vyatirikta-vastu*)."

If [the world] is not distinct from being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). (PVA 834) Since everything in the world is consciousness, there is no distinctness whatsoever in terms of being an object of cognition; because there is no external objective support (*ālambana*) that is separate [from consciousness], the proof is indeed already established.

[377,xvii] And if it is argued that [the cognition] is objectless because it is absolutely distinct [from its object], then if [you mean] in some way [it is not objectless], your previous thesis is contradicted by what you have postulated. (PVA 835)
Cognition is held to be without an objective basis due to the distinction between the forms of objects and so forth;

however, if it were non-different from the apprehending subject, a diversity of capacities would be contradicted. Furthermore, if the arising of a cognition that is without an objective basis is what is being established, [then...]

Because it is observed, we accept that [cognition] is devoid of both external objects and a grasper; yet you do not admit its correctness in any way, for this [cognition] terminates within its own part, like the cognition of water in a mirage. (837–838) (PVA)
If the objectlessness of the conditions such as the shrine (*caitya*) and so forth—
which constitutes their true nature (*dharmabhūta*)— were not apprehended by the cognition arising from the proof,
then, because of the diversity of objects, there would be no negation of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). (839) (PVA)

If [it is argued that] the attainment of an object from a form is already established, by what could it be prevented? (840) (PVA) If even the word "condition" (*pratyaya*) is taken as being a condition, and its status as an object of cognition (*ālambana*) is denied, then this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). (841) (PVA)
If the capacity to produce cognition is what is to be excluded, then the probandum is not established;
for, according to you, there can be no employment of a means of proof without its being indicative [of the object].
(842) Furthermore, there is no denotation without a connection, and such a connection does not exist because of [the opponent's claim of] difference.
And this [inference] does not occur without a cognition that makes known the distinction residing therein.

Furthermore, when the sentence—composed of its various parts—is not grasped by the judges, nor are the thesis, the reason, the example, the proponent, and the opponent [individually grasped], [the inference cannot take place]. (843–844) (PVA)
If it is maintained that the application of a means of proof is intended for the sake of producing that [cognition],
then the thesis is contradicted by one's own prior admission.
Thus, all this is merely something of that nature;
for it is said to be "without an objective support" (nirālambana) because it is not distinct from consciousness.
And blue and so forth do not exist apart from cognition; therefore, as its properties, they are not distinct from it.

Even though it possesses that property [of being an object] by virtue of such attributes as "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) and so forth, it is nonetheless distinct because of the absence of "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). For a *caṇḍāla*, despite possessing humanity (*manuṣyatva*), is not non-distinct from a Brahmin. Therefore, cognition is not "possessed of an object" (*sālambana*) by means of an object that is distinct from itself; the sense is that it is [not so] by means of that which is devoid of cognition-ness, as understood from the context. Furthermore, since "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is non-distinct from the object of knowledge, how could there be a difference between this [object] and cognition? Thus, how can this be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)?
If it is argued that there is no difference between cognition and that which is other than it because both are objects of knowledge (*prameyatvāt*), then [we reply]:
its being other than cognition does not exist at all; it is simply cognition itself.
(847) [This holds] when establishing the absence of an object-support (*anālambana*) with respect to something that is absolutely distinct.
Why is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*)?

Because if there were a difference in every respect, there would be absolute difference; for it is impossible to perceive that which is both different and non-different. Therefore, if that which is different has absolute difference, then when it serves as an object, it is merely an object of its own part (*svāṅga*). Consequently, how can there be the fallacy of proving the already established? Even if there is no difference in terms of being a form of cognition (*jñānākāratā*), let there be a subordinate difference in the object of apprehension (*grāhya*); nevertheless, the object remains non-distinct from that [cognition].
If there were the existence of two things having the nature of cognition, how could both have an object?
Even if both were of the nature of cognition, that [object] does not exist in the case of pleasure and pain.

If there is a distinction between the grasped and the grasper, how can there be a distinction between white, blue, and so forth for those two which are non-different from cognition? For whom does the absence of non-difference not exist?
Just as this distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth exists even though they are of the nature of cognition. (PVA 850)
Even though there is a distinction between white, pleasure, and so forth, it is not the case that there is a cognition of a self distinct from the apprehended and the other [the apprehender].

Just as there is a difference in reality between pleasure and pain despite their non-difference in being cognitions, so too, what contradiction is there in their being distinct by virtue of having the nature of white, pleasure, and so on? However, the state of having the form of the apprehended and the apprehender does not appear at all; for apart from white, pleasure, and so forth, no such thing as "apprehending-ness" is perceived as appearing.
Therefore, the designation of "grasper" and so forth has been propounded by evil-minded people who have been led astray by their own fanciful imaginings.
If it is being established that even a Buddha is without an object of cognition (*nirālambana*), why is this very same position presented as distinct from the previous position?
[For] every cognition is without an object, and likewise, everything that arises is so. (PVA 852)

There is no difference between the two proofs; how then could the property (*dharma*) not be proven? (853) This very property must be proven by the cognition arising from the means of proof (*sādhana*); for if there were an absence of an object (*nirālambanatā*), the state of having an object (*sālambanatva*) in cognition would be destroyed. (854)

For when it is established that all cognition arises as being without an objective support (*nirālambana*), then, by implication, it is precisely the state of being without an objective support that is established as the property (*dharma*) of the subject. This being so, the state of having an objective support (*sālambanatā*), which is accepted only through the power of error, is indeed refuted. How so?

The presentation of the proof is redundant. For it has already been established that the word "pratyaya" does not itself function as a "pratyaya" within this context due to the specific topic at hand. Therefore, how could there be the fallacy of proving what is already established by the argument that "the word is not of the nature of cognition"? Furthermore, the intended aim is not the negation of the capacity to produce a cognition—by which the proof would become redundant—for it is not the case that cognition itself is devoid of origination. This is the meaning of the doctrine of "lack of objective support" (*nirālambanavāda*). [379,ii]

Now, if cognition, even when it arises, is without an objective basis (nirālambanā), what is the use of its arising? If, on the other hand, it has an objective basis (sālambanā), then there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) due to that very fact.
That too is incorrect.

Since it is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that is to be proven, and since the differentiation from others is accomplished by the means of proof (*sādhana*), how could that means of proof be useless? (PVA 855)
