The point that "all cognition is without an objective basis" (*nirālambana*) must be understood through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, how could there be the presentation of a proof (*sādhana*)? Consequently, by means of that proof, the very lack of an objective basis is established even for the cognition of the lack of an objective basis itself. If that [proof-cognition] lacks an objective basis, how can the establishment of the lack of an objective basis occur? [Objection: It is not because the validity of inference comes from correspondence (*saṃvāda*), but rather from its having an objective basis (*sālambanatva*). [Reply: Since there is no objective basis, how can there be correspondence? [Objection: Because the objective basis is not perceived. [Reply: How can there be correspondence for a cognition that thinks "it does not exist," unless that object is subsequently not perceived due to the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*)? If this is so, then even a cognition without an objective basis is the cause for the determination of reality. Therefore, the employment of a proof is indeed a communicator of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), not a non-communicator. Thus, even when the word-meaning is the exclusion of others, a relation between things certainly exists. Even difference (*bheda*) is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). Furthermore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) possesses parts and, by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtti*), truly becomes the object of the apprehension of difference. Why should the apprehension of difference by the proponent and the opponent crumble right at the outset? Moreover, since even that [apprehension] is later without an objective basis—just like a dream—once the task has been accomplished, what will the objection regarding "unestablishedness" (*asiddhatā*) and so forth achieve now? Furthermore, since this was already explained previously, what is the use of raising this objection again?
[379,vii] It was merely for the purpose of astonishing women and śūdras that this was spoken by those wretched, wicked people who are ignorant of reality.
[379,viii]
Furthermore, for one who lacks the realization of reality, that which is joined with illogicality does not come to an end.

Therefore, even if one provisionally accepts the position of the manifoldness of difference and so forth— closing one's eyes like an elephant— one incurs no fault by subsequently establishing its non-existence through the process of critical investigation.

[379,x] But surely, by asserting that "I perceive only my own manifestation," one who seeks to understand another is contradicted by that other person, for that [other's cognition] is indeed perceived as well. Therefore, how can it be established that cognition has its own constituent part as its objective support?

That is incorrect. It has already been established that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "it is perceived by another. Even for the members of the assembly (*prāśnika*), there is no perception of anything other than their own respective parts. Thus, from the statement that [cognition] is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), perception certainly exists. Therefore, from what source of valid cognition does this perception of yours arise, such that for the members of the assembly the operation of the proof (*sādhana*) does not occur without the apprehension of difference? If you argue that those who do not possess the perception of difference are not members of the assembly, that too is incorrect.
If those who understand reality in this matter do not possess the status of judges, then those who do not know reality certainly have no qualification for being judges. (857) (PVA)
Furthermore, by being partial to one side, the status of an arbiter does not exist;
for how could one who is free from partiality [ever arise]?
(PVA 858) For it is improper to understand two things that are mutually contradictory.
From the cognition of each individual [position], there arises a partiality toward one side.
Consequently, when two arbiters themselves hold mutually contradictory views, other arbiters would be required to settle their dispute; thus, there is an infinite regress.
If the disputant were to become the arbiter, there would be a mutual dependence;
for surely, even they would have a partiality toward their own side.
Therefore, when it comes to the application of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there must be an acceptance that is free from bias.

Whatever was previously accepted, that is contradicted by you in this state. (PVA 862) When the judges have the perception of a distinction among the proponent, the opponent, and the thesis, even so, if the [proponent] reverses [his position] due to the words of the disputant—provided it is arrived at through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—they should not contradict him therein. If, as they investigate with their own intellects, that [position] becomes purified for them, what reason is there for them not to accept it? Therefore, by his word, he is somehow bound by his prior acceptance.
[380,iii] But surely, even by this force of valid cognition, [the existence] of the preceding one is established; why then is this being said so loudly, as if it were not already evident?
"In that case where there is the conceit of reality, that cognition is without an objective basis"—
if this is the thesis, there is a contradiction for one who does not accept that [conceit's] reality.
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"And when dharma, adharma, and so forth are not unestablished in the ultimate sense, regarding their cognition..."
Furthermore, the instruction regarding the qualities (*dharma*) and so forth for both the disciple and oneself is rendered possible [only by such a distinction].
Through the practice of that [instruction], the Buddhas clearly intend a distinction [between themselves and others].
Since this would be accepted in other sūtras, there would be a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*). (PVA 864–865)

Furthermore, by contradicting what is established for all the world, there would be a subversion of one's own position. And if the cognition of the entire means of proof is held to be false, then either a total non-existence [of the proof] or a deficiency [in the argument] would be asserted at will. (PVA 866)

If those [cognitions] were to have an object, the reason would be inconclusive due to the winds. (867) (PVA) If it is argued that the thesis refers to something other than those, then the cognition of that "other" is false; for since it is not included within the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth, it cannot possess the status of being part of the subject or the like. (868) (PVA)
By the consequence of that falsity, nothing whatsoever established previously would be proven;
for at that time, there would be no distinction between the probandum and the cognition of the means of proof.
To whatever extent the very thesis itself is stated as being distinct from that [probandum], [it remains unestablished].
To that same extent, there would be no sublation of the falsity and other [defects] of others.
There is neither the state of being a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*) nor sublation by means of inference.
In this manner, a counter-proof (*pratisādhana*) should be stated for all such positions.
"The cognition that has external objects as its objective support is a correct cognition,
because it is a cognition free from sublation, just like the cognition that sublates dreams and the like.
(872) If one were to say that this [cognition] is also false, provided that dreams and the like are not sublated;
In that case, you would have no example based on similarity for your proof at this point.
(PVA 873) Likewise, if the cognition of the existence, difference, momentariness, and so forth [of consciousness] were accepted as being real, then [your reason] would be inconclusive. (PVA 874)
Or, if there were a wrong practice regarding that [self], it would follow that the thesis is contradicted;
and thus the established distinction between the bound and the liberated could not be conceived.
Consequently, it follows for you that the effort toward liberation would be fruitless. (PVA 875–876)
This is incorrect, because:
If the notion of a transmigrating being were established with reference to something else [than the aggregates],

then this consideration of dharma, adharma, and so forth would be entirely inconsistent. Even if it were not a reality, the state of desiring [certain things] and so on would be spoken of as if it were a child’s play.
Therefore, dharma is not taught for the sake of accomplishing what is desired.

(PVA 878) [380,xxiii] This transmigrating being certainly determines the distinction that "dharma is the means of accomplishing what is desired" and "that which is other than this is non-dharma," because his latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for differentiation has not been removed. And when he attains liberation, he has no purpose whatsoever. For one who knows the ultimate truth does not engage in activities for the sake of accomplishing what is desired within the objects of childish play; because:
All people proceed toward that which they perceive as reality;
for what reason, out of passion and the notion of beauty, would one not act toward that which is ugly? (PVA 879)
Therefore, why not— closing one's eyes like an elephant— teach each person that which leads them to act with the notion of reality even toward what is unreal?
By this, it is established that the practice therein is not contradictory.

What contradiction could there be with the statements in the Sūtras intended for that purpose? (881) (PVA) Furthermore, if there were a sublation by the cognition of one who does not know reality, it would be a case of proving what is already established;
for [the teaching] was not directed toward him regarding the lack of objective support in all cases. (882) (PVA)
And when the cognition of the complete means of accomplishment lacks an object of support (*anālambana*),
if one is awakened to reality, there is no fault even in the absence of everything.
At that time, the absence of everything whose nature is an object of support is accepted.
If that means of proof lacks a real objective basis, then it cannot establish its conclusion. Therefore, by that [means], what is to be proven is the existence of a non-objective basis;
since this is observed to share the same nature as that [lack of a basis], how can there be any inconclusiveness?
If it is accepted that there is a proposition regarding something other than that, then the falsity of the cognition of that other thing is also not admitted.
How then can the fault based on its falsity be maintained, given that what is desired is not established? (PVA 886)

In the case of a proposition concerning something other than that, there is no infinite regress. (887) (PVA) Where there is the conceit of existence, that is considered to be without an objective basis; even when there is correspondence with something else, the state of being without an objective basis has been established. (888) (PVA)
And in this way, how can a counter-argument be demonstrated? It has been established that [the reason] "having a cognition devoid of sublation" is unproven (*asiddha*).
The cognition of sublation in dreams and the like has been established through the non-perception of reality.

Because the inference arising from that [perception] is subverting, there is a lack of proof [for the reason]. (PVA 890) Furthermore, when proving that cognition is endowed with an object, the objection that the reason is inconclusive because of cognitions such as [the cognition of] momentariness and so forth [is invalid]. (PVA 891)
That is incorrect, because cognition is momentary and devoid of external objects.
Since the momentariness of consciousness and form has been established, this cognition of momentariness possesses an object;
therefore, the position [of the opponent] that there is no external object is not proven, for it is precisely with the sense of "having an object" that the thesis is maintained.

"Cognitive conditions do not have external objects as their objective supports, just like dream-cognition"—thus has the specific thesis been formulated. If it is argued that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the cognition of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and so forth, we say no. For in the system of the Yogācāras, what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is that momentariness is of the very nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore, by means of the example of consciousness, the possession of an objective support is established as being of such a nature, despite the difference [in the case of momentariness]. Alternatively, an external object is already established [as non-existent]; the cognition of momentariness does not have an external object. To explain: [381,xviii]
The cognition of momentariness and so forth is neither perception nor inference;
for it is established that inference does not have as its object anything other than what is apprehended by another [cognition].
For the wise, the state of having an object does not follow merely from non-contradiction.

For that non-contradiction which belongs to inference is mediated by another cognition; therefore, inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it produces such another cognition, and not merely from the grasping of its own form. And this other cognition is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*), for it is only in direct realization that there is the conceit of grasping the object. Now, that direct realization—which is the very nature of the momentary cognition—is apprehended through self-awareness (*samvedana*) alone; it cannot be grasped by a cognition other than that which constitutes its own essence. Furthermore, if there were another means of valid cognition, that very position of self-awareness would not be established.
For when that very form is being experienced and nothing else is experienced, who then can prevent the self-awareness of its own nature? (894) (PVA)
If it is argued that there is cognition through non-cognition, why is there not cognition through everything?
If it is replied that this is not seen to be so, then what else is observed to be otherwise?
[895] (PVA) Since this follows from the exhaustion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), one should accept things exactly as they are observed.
If the self is perceived as an experiencer, from what source is that perception held to arise?
(896) (PVA) If it is argued that this is due to self-awareness (*svavedana*), then this is no more [required] for blue and other objects.
If the substantiality of the self is not established by being measured [by cognition], (897) (PVA)
Why is it that the occurrence of blueness in blue and so forth does not likewise arise from cognition?

Just as the substantial nature (*dravyarūpatā*) of the self is perceived through another conventional cognition (*saṃvṛti*), why is it not likewise admitted for blue and other such objects? For blue, too, there will be its own nature as consciousness (*svabodharūpatā*) and a distinct substantial nature; thus, like the self, blue and the rest are also of the nature of self-consciousness. If it is argued that this dual nature is unestablished for the Buddhist, then that lack of establishment is equally applicable to anyone else. Indeed, it is impossible for a single thing to possess two natures merely by way of a name. The means of valid cognition (*māna*) functions on the principle that "that which is of a single nature must be one."

If that which has multiple forms were one, it would follow that everything is one. (898) (PVA) If the object of cognition and the cognizer were one, why is blue and so forth not accepted as such? For in that case, the self and the blue would both be the single object and the single cognizer. (899) (PVA)
If [the difference between things] is not due to their being in different locations, why is it not due to their having different forms?
For a difference based on a difference in form is well-established and recognized by everyone in the world.
(900) Indeed, how could there be a difference through a difference in location if there is no difference in form?
And this being the case, there would either be a distinction of place and so forth, or else a distinction based on pervasiveness.
Therefore, without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cognition itself is not established; thus, every cognition is indeed without an external object (*anālambana*).
Even the distinction between the bound and the liberated does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for indeed, no distinction appears at all to those who perceive with equanimity everywhere. (PVA 902)
Even the effort toward liberation and the like does not maintain any ultimate state anywhere in the world.
If the consideration of its futility is logical in that case, why should it not also be applied to the horn of a rabbit?
Just as that effort is not ultimate, so too is the distinction between those who are bound and those who are liberated; this is the same for both. Furthermore:
the cognition of external existence and so forth, which arises through conceptual construction, is false.
However, the discrimination between external and internal objects is not established by non-conceptual cognition.

(PVA 904) Only by means of conceptualization does one establish what is external, internal, common, or caused by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and so forth. But it has already been demonstrated above that non-conceptual cognition, being of the nature of direct perception, cognizes only its own form and not the form of another; therefore, this [objection] is refuted.
If the cognition of the existence of knowledge and so forth, arising as a conceptual construction,
is held to be false, then no apprehension of it through another means of valid cognition is observed here. (PVA 905)
Because of the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the existence of knowledge and so forth is difficult to establish by that [means].

It is said that non-conceptual [perception] has the form of the external object itself. Negation is to be understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). And since that presumptive testimony is conceptual in nature, and for the Buddhist there is no such thing as conceptual valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the existence of knowledge and so forth would necessarily collapse due to the absence of any means of valid cognition.
This is incorrect, because:
[382,xvii] If it is argued that the validity of conceptual construction is logical only when other [means of knowledge] are absent,
then it is logical to say that the validity of conceptual construction is not tenable.

When neither conceptual construction nor anything else possesses the status of a valid means of cognition, then even as it falls apart, who can find fault with this [position]? If worldly convention were not thus, by whom could it be prevented from existing conventionally?

[382,xx] But is it not the case that conceptual construction itself is the conventional? If that [conventional] is the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), then that very thing is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), because it is non-contradictory with worldly transaction.
That too is incorrect,
because it is possible for an appearance whose form has not been discerned to occur.
If, due to the presence of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of non-contradictory misapprehension (*avisamvādy-akhyāti*),

there is mutual non-contradiction between two people suffering from jaundice by means of their respective perceptions of silver and so forth, what therein constitutes ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*)? (909–910) (PVA)
[382,xxiv] But this we shall explain:
Furthermore, all the false cognitions of those such as ourselves arise from conceptual construction;
and it is not difficult to find [the distinction between] proximity and distance, nor [the presence of] existence and so forth.

This is the presence of the Blessed One; from that arises the teaching of the Dharma and its opposite. Whether "this exists" or "this does not exist" is indeed difficult to establish, because the means of proving it—consisting of conceptual construction—is unreal. Nevertheless, by the necessity of the force of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), even that which is non-existent in the ultimate sense appears as existent.
Thus, even partiality toward the Buddhist view is justified.
Even if cognitions were false, no sublation is ever perceived. (912) Because the latent impression (*vāsanā*) exists in that manner, that very impression is the cause of the sublation.
How can there be awareness of error in the absence of a respondent? (913)
This has already been established previously; it is not stated again and again.

If, for you, the appearances of the real and the unreal belong to a living being who is under the power of others solely due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and if those two cannot be sublated, then what is the use of this dispute or of instructing opponents? If his latent impression is oriented toward awakening, he will understand by himself; otherwise, he will not, even through hundreds of words.
[383, viii] That is untrue.

"Having understood that 'just as this awakening of latent predispositions occurred for me by means of this [statement], so it has occurred for him too,' the other person should employ speech. (PVA 914)
[383,x] Therefore, as for what was said [in 383,xi]:
If the falsity of cognition were [independent], why is sublation not perceived?
If that [falsity] were to exist even without sublation, no systematic order could be established.
Furthermore, when the counter-correlative—the waking cognition—is seen, [the dream cognition] would be false.

For us, the cognition of dreams and so forth is [of the same nature]; what, then, causes the difference therein? (916) (PVA) Furthermore, there exists no other suitable counter-correlate for waking cognition by the perception of which the cognition of pillars and the like would be recognized as false. (917) (PVA)
The status of being a counter-correlate to dreams and so forth is well-established by common consensus among all people;
this is because of the difference in properties between those [dream objects] and the subverting cognition, just as in the case of [the negation of] that [dream].

That too has been refuted. Even though the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone constitutes everyone’s experience—whether it be correct cognition or delusion—nevertheless, speech must indeed be employed for the sake of communicating to others. For instance, one engages in speech with the understanding that "this very awakening of latent impressions which occurred to me in this manner will likewise occur to another," so as to awaken specific latent impressions in them. Having ascertained the desire to awaken such latent impressions, it is therefore not futile. Consequently, if cognition is false, why is no sublation perceived? Because there is an absence of the awakening of latent impressions corresponding to that [sublating] state. How, then, is falsity fully understood? Precisely from the knowledge that [cognition] is bound by latent impressions. For falsity is twofold: being non-existent in fact (*asadarthatva*) and being non-concordant (*visamvāditva*). Non-concordance arises from the awakening of contrary latent impressions, while concordance arises from the awakening of non-erroneous latent impressions.

[383,xviii] But if there is correspondence, how can there be a lack of real objects? For even the form of non-contradiction is dependent upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Indeed, even in the case of a corresponding appearance, there is no conformity with the presence or absence of an external object. This very fact constitutes its lack of real objects; therefore, because it is similar to cognitions such as those in dreams, it lacks real objects. It is not the case that the lack of real objects for dream-cognitions and the like is due to a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), such that—by the absence of such a subversion—the truth of waking cognitions would be established.
If [cognition] were bound by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how could this be distinguished? "This one is consistent, while the other is not; there is no contradiction in a single case.
That is incorrect.
For even when there is a restriction by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is still differentiation according to blue and other colors.
And why is it that there is no such correspondence regarding the destruction of dreams and the like?
(920) (PVA) If something is similar in some respect, is it similar in every respect?
How is it that, while humanity is common, there is still the distinction between being a Brahmin and otherwise? (921) (PVA)
If [cognition] were tied to the object as it truly is, then no cognition would ever be subject to non-correspondence;
likewise, even in the case of error, why should this [non-correspondence] be impossible?
(922) For those who know the object, there is no such thing as being tied to a mental impression (*vāsanā*) in any way whatsoever.
"For the penetration of the object is indeed observed in all [cognitions].
This is incorrect.
If that object exists exactly as it is perceived by one seeking it, then let there be the attainment of real objects; how could there be a subverting cognition? (PVA 924)
Because it is supramundane, because of its connection with both natures, because of the loss of memory, and because of erroneous cognition, it possesses sublativeness;
however, there is no such existence of the object, and therefore that [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge by way of correspondence.

Because it is not an object that can be verified by correspondence with an extra-worldly (alaukika) object. Alternatively, there is both the existence and non-existence of that entity; therefore, even while being perceived, it is also sublated. Or else, an unreal object being remembered—located in another place—appears as if it were present before the eyes, rather than being located right there. Consequently, there is no attainment (*aprāpti*) of it in that very place. This should be applied in the same way to the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*). Thus, this is the operation of invalid cognition (*apramāṇavṛtta*):
"Nowhere does the notion of a snake arise in a rope for one who has never previously seen a snake."
Since it follows from what was previously seen, how can latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) not be the cause?

For without a prior perception, the cognition of a snake does not arise in relation to a rope. It is the consensus of the entire world that, due to a prior perception, there is the realization that "this object does not exist here. Otherwise, the relationship between cause and effect would be utterly destroyed, because it is impossible to apprehend anything through mere appearance alone; for in mere appearance, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone exists, being devoid of any external cause—this has already been established. Therefore, the causal relationship exists precisely through that ascertainment. There is no perception here of a connection with an erroneous appearance or the like. Now, it might be argued: "This too is merely an erroneous appearance; no object exists here at all."

If that which is cognized erroneously and so forth were to have the status of a cause for a prior cognition, then let it be admitted that other cognitions as well are likewise produced from that very same source. (PVA 927)
The attainment of an object occurs elsewhere; therefore, there is no such thing as "extraordinary" [perception] and so forth.
It has been established previously that there is no attainment of an object in all cases.
If it is argued that this is not so because there is certainty regarding the object, that is not tenable.

Why is there not a certainty that "the object is external" even in the case of the non-worldly [cognition] and so forth? (929) (PVA) However, because the certainty "this is an object" does not occur regarding what is actually no object, this certainty of it being no object lacks inconclusiveness. (930) (PVA)
The knowledge that [the dream state] is rooted in latent impressions (*vāsanā*) constitutes its reality; it is not sublated by that [waking cognition].
Therefore, there is no possibility of the waking cognitions being counter-correlatives [to the dream ones].
Let that [dream] cognition also arise from a previous perception, and let that too [arise] from something else.
All cognition is produced by limbs [of the mind] born from beginningless latent predispositions;
for this very reason, this doctrine of the absence of external objects shines forth.
For this very reason, the following point is also refuted:
[384,xxii]
The cognition of yogis arises as a sublater of its opposite;
therefore, cognitions of pillars and so forth during the waking state are equal to those in dreams and the like.
This state is attained by all living beings as well. (PVA 933)
Therefore, this sublation will occur, and by it, the state of having a counter-positive is established.

For, indeed, through the power of the cultivation of objects purified by valid cognition, there necessarily arises in yogins a direct perception that functions as a valid means of knowledge and which sublates error. By that—
"In this life, it is not perceived by some; yet we do not know what will happen to those who have entered that state. (PVA 935)

[385,iii] Thus it is refuted; for since the capacity of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is indeed known, why should we not know that this cognition will necessarily arise? Therefore, what has been said is entirely consistent. [385,iv] What is stated [is as follows]:
Furthermore, for us yogins, there will arise a subverting cognition that is either the opposite of what you have stated or contrary to what you have asserted.
Thus. For:
[385, vii] It arises from the power of cultivation attained through the power of the immeasurables.
Why then are the cognitions of those yogins not overwhelmed by sorrow and the like?
(937) (PVA) It has been established that such a case exists as an example for the cognitions of yogins;
however, for you, not a single example is available. (938) (PVA)
Therefore, cognitions of pillars and the like would possess a counter-correlate,
or else they would be sublatable, because they are cognitions, just like the cognition of a mirage and so forth.
(PVA 939) It is accepted that the cognitions of mirages and the like possess a counter-correlate.

If it is argued that sublation occurs both by way of its own nature and by being another object of apprehension, this is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*); for in this way, the status of being a sublater is not established. Indeed, the mere intention to speak of something as a "sublater" does not effect a root destruction [of the object].
To say this in any way whatsoever is merely a manifestation of dullness.

For it is not mere counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) that is intended, but rather counter-correlativity with respect to a sublater (*bādhaka*). Therefore, to establish mere counter-correlativity as the proof is irrelevant.
Furthermore, there is sublation and the fallacy of inconclusiveness; and its being other than that is as before.
(942) (PVA) The cognition that establishes the difference from the cognitions of Buddha and others is false;
regarding this as well, our response has already been set forth previously. (943) (PVA)
Every cognition of a Buddha and so forth has as its object only one's own internal states;
however, the establishment of conventional usage will be explained accordingly.
[944] (PVA) For you, there would be the status of being the counter-correlate of false cognition, just as in the case of dreams and the like.
Thus, what was previously established is not stated again as a subsequent point. For instance:

If all cognitions were false, this relationship of the sublated and the sublator would exist due to the presence of degrees of intensity and so forth, arising from the varying degrees of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (946) (PVA)
Just as, even though falsity exists, this relationship of the sublated and the sublator occurs for you without dispute due to conformity with external entities. (947) (PVA) [385,xxiii]

In that case, because it is a cognition of a distorted nature (*viparītādikhyāti*), there is no fault here either, as the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) depends on the presence or absence of the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanādārḍhyabhāvābhāva*). Now, an objection: the cognition of the Blessed Buddha possesses the causes for being a yogi, such as the destruction of passion and so forth; therefore, [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it sublates the specific property (*viśeṣya*) of that [subject]. To explain: [386, i] ... For instance:

Likewise, whatever specific distinction may be intended— such as being the source for the destruction of passion and so forth, or being characterized by signs and the like— it would be contradictory because it is subject to all refutation. (PVA 948)

[386,iii] Regarding the cognition of the Buddha and others, which subverts cognitions such as those of a pillar, there are as many specific qualities as there are—such as being caused by the destruction of passion and so forth—and because these would subvert [the opponent's position], the reason (*hetu*) would also be contradictory (*viruddha*). For instance, at the very moment that the status of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of false cognition is established for cognitions such as dreams, then the cognition of the Tathāgata would also follow as being false due to its being a counter-correlate, just like the cognition of a pillar that subverts a dream. To this, it is said:
If it is argued that the reason here is not refuted because there is no damage due to the contradiction of a specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*), then indeed that contradiction—
which obstructs the entire power of all reasons— is not absent in its entirety.

Just as dream-cognition is established as being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the cognition of pillars and the like which are false, so too the state of being a counter-correlate to a cognition is established simply because it is a cognition, just like dream-cognition. Likewise, just as smoke establishes fire, it also establishes the non-existence of fire at this particular place and time; thus, no reason whatsoever would be a prover of its intended object (*sādhya*). Furthermore, because it is a cognition, it establishes merely the state of being a counter-correlate, not a specific counter-correlate. For example, just as the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) proves the impermanence of sound, it would also follow that it proves the opposite of its being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*). Nor is the state of being a quality of space a *sādhya* by virtue of being accepted in a treatise (*śāstra*), for it will be stated that "only what is intended [by the proponent] is the *sādhya*. Therefore, "contradiction with a specific [property]" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) is not a flaw of the reason.
[386,vii] Is it not so?
[386,viii]
And for the sake of the great multitude, as for those possessing the intellect of the present day,
one must state either a sublation by inference or a counter-argument.

The cognition of pillars and the like is true, just like the present subverting cognition, because there is an absence of a subverting cognition by the majority of people; the cognition of pillars that is the subject of dispute is unsublated, because no subverting cognition arises for the majority of people regarding its object, as in the case of a subverting cognition for dreams and the like.
This is incorrect. For instance:

If the establishment of the probandum were intended to consist merely in the demonstration of a perception that is invariably concomitant with the connection [between the reason and the probandum], then such a response would indeed be appropriate. (PVA 951)

Furthermore, the cognition of a dream-illusion is not uncontradicted from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because a contradicting cognition is indeed observed to be perceptual. However, since it is uncontradicted from the standpoint of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), there is no loss for us even if the cognition of pillars and the like were likewise uncontradicted.
If it is unreal, how then can there be sublation by cognition, as in the case of dreams and so forth?
It has already been explained previously that this is because of the existence of a gradation [in its intensity].
Furthermore:
waking cognition does not sublate the vision of a dream because of its own reality.

Because that object of knowledge is not perceived, what could there be for that which is unreal? (953) [PVA 386, xvii] This has been established: a sublater is not a sublater by virtue of the reality of its own objective support, but rather because of the non-perception of that [object]. And that non-perception consists precisely in the perception of its opposite. And this is not lost even when there is self-awareness of its own part. For instance:
Whether it be another object of cognition or its own nature, all of this is the opposite of that [dream state].
Therefore, the other [waking cognition], even while abiding in its own part, is sublated by the waking consciousness. (PVA 954)
[387,iv] But if this [awakened cognition] is also an error, then on what basis is that dream-cognition sublated?
That too is incorrect:
once the purpose of the means has ceased, there would be a similarity to a dream-cognition.
What purpose would there be for us then in terms of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator?
vii] But surely something else is being said.
[387, viii] Furthermore, the defects of the previous proof must now be considered for this [new reason]:
because it is non-different from the probandum and because it is inexpressible, the reason is not established for both parties. (PVA 956)

[387,ix] Regarding the term *bodhana*, there are the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that it is "awakening" or "that by which one awakens. In this regard, as before, the faults apply: because it is not distinct from the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*)—is a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*) and thus cannot be uncontradicted; consequently, it is not established for both parties (*nobhayasiddhatā*).

[Objection: But surely, since the particular cognition is the subject (*dharmin*) and the universal is the probans (*sādhana*), there is no fallacy of the probans being a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
To this, he says:
Neither a universal nor the state of being a condition exists as either distinct or non-distinct;
nor does anything exist that is absolutely distinct, even in the case of direct perception. (PVA 957)
That there is neither similarity nor exclusion from others will be demonstrated later.
Therefore, a universal as a logical reason is not established for either of the two parties.
This is not tenable because:
[387,xvi] For us, both the universal and the nature of being a cause are held to be both distinct and non-distinct.
"But by means of that [exclusion], the state of equality is turned away from [other things] as 'not this'—this will be stated [in verse 959].

For that very reason, because of its connection with reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), a cognition is called a 'cognition' due to its indirect connection with the real object through a causal chain. What is the meaning of 'cognition'? It is mere experience, which is simply the awareness of its own nature. Therefore, this [objection] is unproven."
Furthermore, the two specific properties residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) and its similar instance (*sapakṣa*) could not function as a logical reason,
because they would lack the property of being present in all similar instances and because they would not be properties of that [subject]. (PVA 960)
[387,xix] Thus it is.
Nor can that cognition, being devoid of an object, serve as a logical reason (*hetu*).
Furthermore, the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) has been stated because the subject (*viśeṣya*) is not established.
Likewise, there is the contradiction of the reason (*viruddhatva*) and the absence of the probandum (*sādhyahīnatā*) in the example.

This has already been thoroughly refuted previously through the very same analysis of the impossibility of the qualification and its meaning; therefore, this [objection] is invalid. Consequently, this remains faultless: "All cognitions are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), because they are cognitions, like dream-cognitions."
[(Ṅa) Refutation of External Objects:
Therefore, all cognitions are without an objective support.
Then, because there is no cognition of another, self-cognition is held to be the fruit. // 333 //

Self-awareness alone is the fruit. Consciousness, arising by itself, illuminates its own nature and not an external object, because it lacks the capacity to establish an object and because such establishment is never observed. To this, it is replied:
If an external object were experienced, what fault would there be? None at all. Why then was this said: "That external object is not experienced"? (334)

[388,v] What is the use of this subtle scrutiny? External objects are indeed experienced. What is the fruit of this effort? Let things remain as they are according to worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*). Nor does the demonstration that [cognition] is without an objective support (*anālambanatva*) result in a different mode of convention; and there is no fruit here other than convention. [388,vi]
That too is indeed non-existent.
vii] If conventional usage is what is to be established, then conventional usage is just as it is.
What is the fruit of your effort regarding the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Veda?

(963) [PVA 388, viii] Indeed, that which is established by beginningless usage is not proven to be either human-made or otherwise, such that its absence would entail [the Veda’s] being so. If it is argued that this very point is being examined for the sake of establishing its true meaning, then other matters as well should be examined. If it is argued that if it were human-made, there would be no validity at all, this is equally true for the other case as well; for even if it were non-human, there would be an absence of validity. Furthermore:
When there is an absence of external grasping, then passion and the like are abandoned; for they function by the power of mental cultivation, and in its absence, the opposite occurs. (964) (PVA)

[388,x] For it has been established that the destruction of defects such as passion occurs through the investigation of reality (*tattva*), and that this is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, reality is now investigated. There is no perception of an external object. To explain: what is the meaning of the statement "an external object is perceived"? Is it designated as "perceived" because of the existence of its entry into the perception, or simply because of its non-entry? Regarding this, he says: [388,xi]
If cognition possesses that form, then it exists as something that assumes a form;
it is this which deserves investigation: whether that form comes from an external object or from something else. (335)

What is the meaning of "cognition has that form"? [It means] it has the form of blue and so forth. But is this not precisely what is being investigated now? From where does it have that form? [If you say] "therefore cognition has that form," then for the sake of such thorough knowledge, that [form] must be seen again; and in that seeing as well, there would be only the state of having that form, leading to an infinite regress. Alternatively, if it is seen by a formless [cognition], then why postulate a form for that very act of seeing? Or, if "having that form" means "having the form of determining that," then it is simply said to be that [determination]; what is the meaning of "that determination is that seeing"? Or, if both are seen, then in their own nature both are seen; consequently, there would be no mutual apprehension, or rather, no apprehension of either, and thus it is established that both are self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*). Now, if it is argued that this [self-cognition] cannot exist without an external object, then it follows that immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) cannot exist without cognition. If it is held that immediacy is indeed perceived, then an external [object] must be postulated; yet cognition having that form is also indeed perceived—so why postulate something else? For: [The verse: "The form of the object is not distinct from the cognition; Therefore, how can there be an external object? (PV III.428) [The commentary: Since the form of the object is not distinct from the cognition, how can there be an external object? It is not logical that the form of the object exists elsewhere [than in the cognition]. Nor is it logical that the cognition lacks a form, because [the cognition] is perceived as having a form. Since the form of the object is not distinct from the cognition, and since the cognition is perceived as having a form, therefore the form of the object is nothing other than the cognition itself. Thus, the existence of an external object is not proven. Furthermore, if the cognition were formless, then even when one says "I see blue," the cognition would be formless; and since the cognition is not perceived as formless, it is established that the cognition possesses a form. And since the form of the object is not distinct from the cognition, the existence of an external object is not proven. Therefore, the existence of an external object is not established. Consequently, the position of those who maintain that the object is external is untenable. Thus, the proof of the non-existence of an external object is established. Because that which is devoid of the adjunct of perception is not apprehended, whereas it is apprehended when perception is apprehended, perception itself appears as blue; there is no external object existing in isolation. (336)

[389,i] Only that which is perceived is accepted. For indeed, by virtue of its appearance, it is precisely that [cognition] itself which appears as blue, and nothing else. Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apart from the appearance; consequently, there is no acceptance [of an external object]. If it is argued that what belongs to the appearance does not appear as such because the appearance is internal while the blue and so forth manifest externally—[we reply: there is no appearance of something distinct [from the appearance], because it appears in its own nature as something immediate (aparokṣa). For instance: [389,ii]
If there were the existence of something distinct [from the cognition], blue would not possess immediacy.
Since it possesses immediacy by its own nature, it has no other [external] immediacy.

For in this very way, the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*) is immediate (*aparokṣa*) by its own nature, not because of the existence of another apprehender; likewise, blue and so forth, though simultaneous with it, [are not so]. And just as the form of the apprehender arises from the eyes and other [senses], so too does that which has a form similar to it, because the relation of cause and effect is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The existence of an object prior to or posterior to [the cognition] is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not operate regarding what is prior or posterior. Now, if it is asked: "How is it known that this [object] did not exist previously? Or why is the form of the apprehender, or even the intellect (*buddhi*) or pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, not postulated to have existed previously? If it is argued that it is exactly so because the self (*ātman*) is eternal, then why is it not postulated that immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) also existed previously? If it is argued that there is a contradiction, we reply: no, for it is not logical that there be immediacy without being perceived. It is logical that the object, being distinct from that [cognition], may exist even while unperceived. By whom is it understood that it is "distinct"? Precisely for this reason, there is the prompting of doubt: "It might exist at some time. If it is asked why immediacy is not likewise [subject to doubt], [we say] because of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [everything] being immediate. On account of the immediacy of one thing, there could be no conception that "this is remote (*parokṣa*) to me," just as in the case of whiteness and so forth. Although whiteness does not belong to a single pot, it certainly belongs to another substance. Therefore, apart from immediacy, there is no other [entity] such as blue.

[389,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has taught as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer conceive the notion: ‘I am a stream-enterer’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a once-returner conceive the notion: ‘I am a once-returner’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a non-returner conceive the notion: ‘I am a non-returner’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does an arhat conceive the notion: ‘I am an arhat’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a pratyekabuddha conceive the notion: ‘I am a pratyekabuddha’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva mahāsattva conceive the notion: ‘I am a bodhisattva’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva is called a ‘bodhisattva. Because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma whatsoever, therefore he is called a ‘bodhisattva. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to perceive a dharma, he would not be called a ‘bodhisattva. Why is that? It is because all dharmas are without self-nature, and because they are devoid of any intrinsic nature.”

Now, when the whiteness of an object departs, does it go elsewhere? No. Nor does perceptibility (*aparokṣatā*) go elsewhere when it ceases. If that is so, then because [perceptibility] is not distinct from it, the object itself would also cease to exist upon its absence. If you say that the non-distinction is not certain, then in the case of fire as well, the absence of the nature of fire would not be established upon the absence [of fire]. If you say that this is because fire is absent apart from that [nature], no; for the non-distinction is unestablished. Everything is the same insofar as [the object] is not observed apart from that [nature]. Therefore, perceptibility is indeed non-existent apart from the object. Inference (*anumāna*) also does not establish a distinction from perceptibility. How does it not establish it? When it establishes it even in the state of being remote (*parokṣa*), then blue certainly exists, such that one will later cognize it. For there is no cognition there based on following a previous form. Memory follows that experience, and that experience belongs only to that which has a perceptible form. And memory does not have as its object blue and so forth by setting aside a separate perceptible form. If you ask, "How is there cognition here [in inference]?"—here too, exactly that [previous form] is superimposed (*adhyāropita*). If it abandons the previous perceptible form, it must necessarily abandon the blue form as well, because they are not distinct; for there is no memory of them separately. If you say that memory is not inference because it lacks the apprehension of something additional, no; for there is no cause for the apprehension of something additional. If you ask, "How is there the apprehension of that additional thing?"—it is not because of its absence. How then is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established at the very first moment. When one sees smoke arising from fire in connection with various fires in different places, then one’s cognition is as follows: "Wherever this [smoke] is brought, there it produces smoke. One place does not produce what is connected to another place. Therefore, if fire exists elsewhere, it certainly produces [smoke] there too. Thus, the location of the smoke is already known to belong to fire. And that future smoke or fire is superimposed as having that very form, for it cannot be otherwise. Therefore, from the sight of additional smoke, there is the cognition of additional fire. But for one who has an immediate cognition of fire without any prior superimposition upon seeing smoke, how is that possible? Even for him, there is no cognition without a general connection (*sāmānya-pratibandha*). For instance, even if there is an immediate cognition, when he is questioned, "If there is smoke here, why is there fire?", he says, "Because it was seen exactly like this. He must then say: "And that seeing is not in the ultimate sense, but rather due to the determination (*vyavasāya*) of the identity between seeing and superimposition. Otherwise, if one were to conceptualize [the object] as distinct from what is being seen, the seeker of the object would not act; one seeking to see would not be instructed. For one who does not perceive the state of being seen is not a seeker of seeing. If you say, "That which exists is perceived," if the connection with seeing is not grasped, how can the mere apprehension of existence be a motivator for action? Therefore, the seeker acts only by perceiving the state of being seen, and not otherwise. Indeed, one seeking blue is never seen not understanding its blueness. Therefore, inferential or other conceptual cognition does not understand blueness and so forth as distinct from the state of being seen. If so, how is inference a cognition of a remote object? It is through the superimposition of a previous perceptibility. How then is there the cognition "there is fire there"? Because the superimposition occurs in that way, like water in a mirage previously seen. If you say, "That upon which it is superimposed is the other [remote] fire," no; for that is not perceived in its own form (*svarūpa*). If you say, "That very [mirage] is its form," then it is precisely perceptible; how then is it remote? If you say, "The state of being remote is simply the perception of it by another," this is no solution, for that is the same as perceptibility. Furthermore, "perception by another" is merely a superimposition by the force of a connection. Therefore, the claim of "perception by another" is false. Even if the perception of a remote external object were logical, since one sees it oneself later, there is a superimposition of identity, thinking "this was remote before. If you say this is the "perception by another," namely, "it was remote before," then that too does not exist. This "perception by another" is merely the thought, "It was remote before. Therefore, the so-called "remote" is non-existent. Consequently, there is simply no grasping of an object devoid of the condition of being seen. How then is there the comprehension of the object's distinction? If there is no object distinct from consciousness, from where comes the difference in the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth? It arises from the eye and other [faculties] alone, like the appearance of hair [to those with ophthalmia]. If you say the appearance of hair is due to the power of a defect (*upaghāta*), from where does the defect come? If you say from the appearance of hair, then let it be postulated from the appearance of blue and so forth. But if it were so, there would be a single form, just as with hair, even in different locations; there would not be a multiplicity of blues and so forth. Is blue and so forth not like the hair that moves when the eye moves? And if the external is accepted as the cause of visual consciousness, why is blue and so forth not external? Just as the eye is the cause for the grasping of color, so is that which is beyond it the cause for the grasping of what is further within. Thus, the external object is established. [This is so] because of the specific restriction of consciousness (*samvit-pratiniyama*).
To this, it is said:
For someone, a particular [object] alone serves as the awakener of an internal latent impression (*vāsanā*);
therefore, the restriction of cognitions is not dependent upon external objects. (337)

[390,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen who had been seized by the yakṣas and was moved with compassion for them. Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara manifested himself as a yakṣa king and went to where those five hundred merchantmen were being held captive by the yakṣas. Having arrived there, he addressed those yakṣas with these words: "O friends, release these five hundred merchantmen; do not cause them to suffer. When the yakṣas heard these words of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they released the five hundred merchantmen. Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having manifested himself as a yakṣa king, vanished from that place and returned to Mount Potalaka. Thereupon, the five hundred merchantmen, having escaped from the hands of the yakṣas, rejoiced and were filled with great joy. They then proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī, where they arrived safely and without hindrance. Having reached Śrāvastī, they informed the Licchavi Vimalakīrti of their arrival. Upon hearing this, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti went out to meet them and welcomed them with these words: "Welcome, noble sons! Welcome, noble sons! You have come from afar. Have you escaped from the hands of the yakṣas? They replied, "We have indeed escaped, O noble son! Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed those five hundred merchantmen with these verses: "O merchants, you have come from afar, Having escaped from the hands of the yakṣas. You have seen the power of the Great Being, The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. He is the protector of all beings, The refuge and the island for the world. He is the light for those in darkness, The guide for those lost on the path. He is the physician for the sick, The father and mother to the destitute. He is the boat for those crossing the ocean, The bridge for those seeking the shore. He is the rain for those scorched by heat, The wind for those oppressed by dust. He is the sun for those in the gloom, The moon for those in the darkness. He is the fire for those in the cold, The water for those in the heat. He is the friend to the solitary, The kinsman to the stranger. He is the teacher to the ignorant, The preceptor to the disciples. He is the leader to the wanderers, The caravan leader for the travelers. He is the king to the lawless, The minister to the ruler. He is the jewel to the poor, The treasure to the seeker. He is the medicine to the afflicted, The healer of all diseases. He is the liberation for the bound, The peace for the agitated. He is the strength for the weak, The courage for the timid. He is the wisdom for the deluded, The clarity for the confused. Thus, O merchants, you have seen him, The one who brings benefit to all. Go now and pay homage to him, For he is the source of all blessings. Having spoken these verses, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti led the five hundred merchantmen to the presence of the Buddha. Upon seeing the Buddha, they prostrated themselves at his feet and sat down to one side. Then the Buddha, knowing their thoughts, spoke to them with these verses: "Excellent, O merchants, that you have come, Having seen the power of the Compassionate One. Now listen well to my teaching, Which leads to the cessation of suffering. All conditioned things are impermanent, Subject to arising and passing away. By realizing their nature of change, One attains the peace of Nirvāṇa. All phenomena are devoid of self, Empty and lacking inherent existence. By understanding this non-self, One is liberated from all bonds. All dharmas are quiescent by nature, Beyond conceptual construction and expression. By realizing this ultimate truth, One transcends the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, cultivate the mind of awakening, And practice the six perfections. Dedicate all roots of virtue To the attainment of supreme enlightenment. When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, the five hundred merchantmen, having heard the Dharma, attained the stage of irreversibility on the path to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. All the gods and humans present also rejoiced and praised the Buddha’s teaching. Thus ends the chapter on the "Manifestation of the Yakṣa King," the thirty-ninth in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

This has already been stated: an external object is not established through direct perception; it is postulated on the basis of the absence [of its cognition] when the effect [is absent]. And rather than postulating a distinct entity as the cause, it is better to postulate that the very perceived eye and so forth are qualified [by a specific state]. That too is said only out of deference to others. It is better to postulate a specific modification of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) itself. If the body is also considered a cause, we say no. This is because the body does not exist apart from its own appearance (*pratibhāsa*). If it is argued that it exists when that appearance occurs, even so, cognition arises from cognition alone, and the simultaneity with the appearance of the body belongs to the appearance itself; thus, the body lacks causal efficacy. For instance:
Just as the restriction of time and so forth regarding the conceptualization of passion and the like is evident—
whether through the restriction of an awakener or even without those awakeners— [966] (PVA).
In the same way, there is the convergence of determinate appearances such as blue and so forth.

For desire and the other afflictions arise in specific places, times, and states by virtue of awakening conditions; however, there is no restriction regarding their objects (*ālambana*), because such restriction is subject to deviation. Furthermore, there is a restriction regarding the appearance of thoughts of women, hunchbacks, and so forth, depending on whether an awakening condition is present or otherwise. Nor is it the case that only external things serve as awakening conditions, since the appearance of a thought awakens the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of another thought through its own capacity. This occurs when enjoyment (*ābhoga*) is possible by means of its own power; for enjoyment itself has no partiality toward any particular object. Even when enjoyment is equal, a certain form may appear with clarity.

What is the cause for the specific restriction of cognitions such as dreams, whether it arises from a mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*), from past habituation (*abhyāsa*), or otherwise? If it is argued that the external object perceived in another life and so forth is the cause of this restriction, we say no; because everything has already been seen, and since that [external object] is absent at the time [of the dream], what is the cause for its restriction to that particular time?
[391,ii] Only an external object restricted by place and other factors can be the determiner of the appearance.
If that object is absent from that location, from where does that restriction arise?

(967) (PVA) [391,iii] If no external object existed there, then how could there be an appearance restricted to that particular time and place? Or, if the restriction [of time and place] occurs even without such a time and so forth, on account of having previously seen the object—then what is the point now? For the restriction would be possible from the previous appearance alone. To explain:
The conceptualization of an object is intended so that there might not be an appearance empty of an object.
If the restriction [of the appearance] arises from the previous object itself, what has been accomplished by the manifestation? (PVA 968)

[391,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘Bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive ‘form,’ nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive ‘eye,’ nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive ‘forms,’ nor does he perceive eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive ‘ear,’ nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ‘sounds,’ nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive ‘nose,’ nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive ‘odors,’ nor does he perceive nose-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive ‘tongue,’ nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive ‘tastes,’ nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive ‘body,’ nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive ‘tangibles,’ nor does he perceive body-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive ‘mind,’ nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive ‘mental phenomena,’ nor does he perceive mind-consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive ‘element of earth,’ nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive ‘element of water,’ nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive ‘element of fire,’ nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive ‘element of wind. He does not perceive the sphere of infinite space, nor does he perceive ‘sphere of infinite space,’ nor does he perceive the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor does he perceive ‘sphere of infinite consciousness,’ nor does he perceive the sphere of nothingness, nor does he perceive ‘sphere of nothingness,’ nor does he perceive the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor does he perceive ‘sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he perceive ‘conditioned,’ nor does he perceive the unconditioned, nor does he perceive ‘unconditioned. He does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive ‘past,’ nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive ‘future,’ nor does he perceive the present, nor does he perceive ‘present. He does not perceive the level of a Stream-enterer, nor does he perceive ‘level of a Stream-enterer,’ nor does he perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Stream-enterer. He does not perceive the level of a Once-returner, nor does he perceive ‘level of a Once-returner,’ nor does he perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Once-returner. He does not perceive the level of a Non-returner, nor does he perceive ‘level of a Non-returner,’ nor does he perceive the fruit of a Non-returner, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Non-returner. He does not perceive the level of an Arhat, nor does he perceive ‘level of an Arhat,’ nor does he perceive the fruit of an Arhat, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of an Arhat. He does not perceive the level of a Pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive ‘level of a Pratyekabuddha,’ nor does he perceive the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Pratyekabuddha. He does not perceive the level of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive ‘level of a Tathāgata,’ nor does he perceive the fruit of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive ‘fruit of a Tathāgata. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive anything at all. Because he perceives nothing, he is not afraid; having transcended all error, he reaches the ultimate end of Nirvāṇa. All the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot surpass him. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha told Subhūti: “A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom by means of non-apprehension. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty of their own nature. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without marks. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are wishless. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are signless. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are undifferentiated. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are unarisen. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are unceasing. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are originally quiescent. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are naturally extinguished. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are beyond conceptualization. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are beyond discursive thought. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without speech. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are ineffable. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without words. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without letters. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without sound. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without hearing. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without seeing. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without form. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without characteristics. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without boundaries. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without limits. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without center. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without periphery. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without beginning. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without end. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without middle. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without birth. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without death. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without abiding. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without duration. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without change. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without transformation. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without coming. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without going. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without arrival. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without departure. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without increase. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without decrease. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without attainment. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without realization. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without knowledge. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without ignorance. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without light. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without darkness. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without duality. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without non-duality. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without distinction. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without confusion. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without obstruction. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without hindrance. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without grasping. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without attachment. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without clinging. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without desire. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without craving. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without thirst. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without fever. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are without burning. Subhūti

Now, it is not logical that there be an appearance here without an object; for since the appearance has already ceased previously, there is no appearance of that [object]. Indeed, an external object is not postulated on the grounds that something non-existent appears here now. If, however, an object that is non-existent but was seen at a previous time and place appears here, then let that very appearance from the previous time and so forth appear; what is the use of postulating an object? For even by the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), the appearance itself is admitted. If it is argued that in that case the external object itself appears, whereas here it does not appear because of a lack of connection (*ayoga*), then from where does this "connection" arise? If you say it arises from correspondence (*saṃvāda*), then surely is it not also logical that correspondence arises from another correspondence? Therefore, rather than a correspondence [to an object], a succession of appearances of correspondence is the only logical conclusion.

[391, vi] But surely, that which, having arisen, is subsequently destroyed is a false cognition, such as "this is not silver. However, since this pillar and so forth are firmly determined by themselves, how can they be erroneous?
That is incorrect;
because the latent impression (vāsanā) is firm, there is no destruction immediately following it.

Just as conceptual constructions such as attachment, which arise through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), depend solely upon the force of those impressions—being devoid of any external object—even so, this construction does not suddenly dissolve even when one's eyes have failed. Likewise, the continuous narrative of a dream does not dissolve by any means, due to the firmness of the latent impressions. For instance, that very same person who was the reciter before continues to be explained again and again in the dream upon waking up. Therefore, the rule is not dependent upon an external object. To illustrate:
This dream-example does not in any way correspond to the waking state;
such a condition is like the urination of a child. (PVA 970)

The state of urination seen by a child in a dream persists even in the waking state, but not in states such as youth and so forth. Furthermore, since the non-deviation from causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has already been established previously, it will not be elaborated upon again.
(c) The dual nature of cognition (*vijñānadvairūpya*):
Therefore, there is a single [cognition] possessing two forms, which is thus experienced and remembered; the awareness of this [cognition] as having both aspects is the result. (338)

[391, xiii] It is said to be "of two forms" because it possesses the form of cognition and the form of blue; yet it is one, since no distinction between them is perceived. It is of two forms only through conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra-parikalpanā*). Why is this so? Because it is thus experienced and remembered. Therefore, since there is no cognition other than that which possesses both forms, the conclusion is that the cognition of the object is not the result of [a separate act of] cognizing that which has both forms. [Objection: But it is perceived as the cognition of an object; how then can it be self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? [392, i]
To this it is replied:
When another person— whether desired or undesired— is established as having that very nature, [then the result follows].
The object is the cause of its representation, and likewise, there is the experience of it.

[392,iii] At that time, because the cause—the established existence of that [object]—is absent, there is only the cognition of the experience itself as having the nature of blue and so forth; therefore, the experience occurs precisely as blue and so on. Thus, this is self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) in the ultimate sense, not the cognition of an object. This is so even if there is an experience [of something] as an object, just like the cognition in a dream. Or rather, the cognition of the object itself is the result. For: [392,iv]
When cognition, together with its object, is established as having the nature of cognition itself, then that very self-experience is the determination of the object. (340)

[392,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as form; he does not perceive feeling as feeling; he does not perceive perception as perception; he does not perceive formations as formations; he does not perceive consciousness as consciousness. He does not perceive the eye as the eye; he does not perceive the ear as the ear; he does not perceive the nose as the nose; he does not perceive the tongue as the tongue; he does not perceive the body as the body; he does not perceive the mind as the mind. He does not perceive forms as forms; he does not perceive sounds as sounds; he does not perceive odors as odors; he does not perceive tastes as tastes; he does not perceive tangibles as tangibles; he does not perceive mental phenomena as mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness as ear-consciousness; he does not perceive the nose-consciousness as nose-consciousness; he does not perceive the tongue-consciousness as tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive the body-consciousness as body-consciousness; he does not perceive the mind-consciousness as mind-consciousness. For it is not possible to say that when consciousness is otherwise, the object is otherwise. Therefore, since the determination of the object follows precisely the consciousness, and because [the object] shares the same fate as that [consciousness] (*tadabhinnayogakṣematvāt*), the cognition of the external is indeed self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). It is for this reason that, by way of metaphor (*upacāra*), it is called "cognition of the external. For: If the nature of this cognition is the desired form, yet the object is experienced otherwise—as either desired or undesired—then, even if it is desired, it is experienced through a form that is either desired or undesired; in that case, the object is known in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛttyā*) by means of that [form], but otherwise it is merely metaphorical. Therefore, he demonstrates that self-cognition alone is the result, even with respect to an external object.
