[392,xi] Even in the Vijñānavāda, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not accepted as a matter of necessity, but rather because it is that very cognition itself. If it is accepted only out of necessity, why is the external object not likewise accepted? For:
If the external does not exist, of what could there be cognition? If, out of necessity, it is the cognition of its own nature, why is it not considered to be that of the external itself? (343)

[392, xiii] It is the cognition of similarity. Therefore, it must be said that only the self-awareness (*svarūpasamvedana*) of the cognition is observed, not its non-cognition. In that case, if even with respect to an external object only self-awareness is observed, let that be so. However, the awareness of an object is not tenable and is therefore abandoned. For since cognitions are distinct by their own nature, it is logical that there be the experience of various forms for each individual; but it is not logical that there be the experience of various forms belonging to an object. [393, i]

Because it would follow that a single entity possesses a manifold nature by its very essence. It is the view of the externalist (bāhyadarśin) that even when not perceived as having multiple forms, an object is indeed one; therefore, it is illogical for a single thing to be experienced as having multiple forms. If it is argued that the object itself consists of multiple forms, we say no:
even if such a position were accepted, there could be no distinct experience of two [different] things.

[393,iii] There would not be the experience of two [cognitions] regarding one and the same object, because each is complete within its own form. If another form were also to appear by entering into that very same [object], then there might be the apprehension of unity. Alternatively, the meaning of the term *vastu* (the real thing) is that there would not be the experience of two [forms]. Or else, there would not be an experience through distinctness—that is, through each terminating in itself—because it would follow that everyone would experience multiple forms simultaneously.
If it is argued that [the cognition] is not [unreal] because it is unobstructed by the unseen (adṛṣṭa), then there would be no comprehension of the meaning by virtue of the name. 344.

[393,v] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivered all suffering. Thus, O Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. O Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, O Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no sphere of the eye and so forth up to no sphere of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and also no non-attainment. Therefore, O Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all error and delusion, he reaches ultimate *nirvāṇa*. All the Buddhas of the three times, relying on this *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It removes all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* should be proclaimed: *Tadyathā—gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.* Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, including the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught. Thus ends the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom.

If it is argued that the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is an obscuration, then the non-perception of duality is already precluded by the perception [of oneness] itself; so how could there be any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for oneness? For the unseen might exist like a visual impairment (*timira*). In that case, the perception of one moon would be the very perception of two moons, since this [perception] too would be a conceptual construction resulting from the prevention of the perception of the second [moon] by the unseen. Therefore, because the unseen is equivalent to a visual impairment, there is no movement toward the object based on its own power. Why is it not accepted that consciousness devoid of external objects is produced by the unseen alone? Alternatively, it must be explained how the unseen is capable of preventing the apprehension of an object situated in a location suitable for it.
How indeed could that unseen [cognition], which presents an entity consisting of multiple natures as having a single nature, be the knower of an object? (345)
Thus is the summary verse.
[393,viii]
Moreover:
[393,ix] The cognition of desired and undesired objects is produced through the power of habituation.

The fact that [an object] is seen is established through perception; how then is it understood here [that it is not real]? If you say that "that very thing" is what is unperceived, then our desired conclusion is already proven, because it is established that everything arises from the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

[393,xi] But surely the object does not appear as desirable or undesirable; rather, it is only the mental construction (*kalpanā*) that takes on such forms according to the aspect of the object. To this, it is replied:

If conceptual constructions, which manifest as desirable and undesirable, were not sensory cognitions, then there would be no lack of connection [between them] even in cases such as a fatal omen; for in that case too, there is a sequence of mental cognitions.
[393,xiii] Even the cognition of the sense faculties is seen to be otherwise in those seized by fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*); therefore, this is correct.
Therefore, even when the object of cognition is external, it is logical that self-awareness is the result;
for the determination of the object occurs exactly according to its own nature.

Therefore, even with respect to an external object, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the result; it is not the awareness of the object, because that [awareness of the object] is subsumed within self-awareness. In this case as well, regarding the result, the very form of the object (*viṣayākāratā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As the Teacher said:

But when the external object itself is the object of cognition (*prameya*), then the very fact of its appearing in the form of that object is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, although cognition is self-cognizable, it does not depend upon its own nature; rather, its appearing as the object is its means of valid cognition, because that object is measured by it. Just as the form of the object appears and enters [into the cognition] as something pleasant and so forth, that object is cognized in that form. Thus, the status of the means of valid cognition and the object of cognition is metaphorically attributed according to the distinction between forms. [394,i] But surely, since it is not distinct [from the cognition], why is the subjective form (*grāhakākāra*) also not the means of valid cognition? To this it is said:

[394,ii] At that time, the appearance of the object itself is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not the apprehending nature even though it exists; for the latter is not for the sake of another, whereas the former is considered in relation to external objects. // 348 //

For there is no external object existing in accordance with that [cognition], because it is not for the sake of another. Indeed, self-cognition does not establish anything for the sake of another, since it is identical in all cases apart from its own form (*ākāra*).

Because, just as that object-nature is deposited in the cognition, it is determined as "it is deposited thus"; for, by virtue of its form, the cognition [thinks]: "The object itself, such as blue and so forth, is deposited in this way with its own form. Therefore, the very form of the object is the cause for the conceptualization of the object; hence, that alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If that is the case, then the experience of the object itself is the result; what, then, is the use of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)?
This is not so, because that conceptualization of the object is precisely in accordance with self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*). He says this very thing:
Of self-awareness. 349.

Thus, the cognition of the object is itself what is intended, because the nature of the object is not perceived. Since that which is unperceived is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could there be an operation of perception regarding an object that is beyond the senses? Furthermore, the determination of the fruit of perception is the topic at hand; therefore, because the object is not cognized through the perception of its own form, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the fruit.
The object to be established by that [cognition] is its means of accomplishment; that [cognition] is its action.

Therefore, it is produced by that [cognition], and thus it is its fruit, because it manifests through its sequence. If this is so, then the form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the external object, while the self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) is the fruit with respect to its own nature; thus, there is a difference in their respective objects.
That is incorrect; for:
[394, xiii] For in whatever manner that object is apprehended, in that very manner it appears.
Because the stability of objects consists in that very nature [of consciousness], self-awareness is also considered to be awareness of objects. (350)

[394,xiv] From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), this is self-cognition alone; from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahārataḥ*), it is the cognition of an object. Therefore, with respect to conventional usage, the object itself is the result (*phala*), and the object itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How, then, could there be a difference in their objects? Even from the perspective of ultimate reality, both are [identical] in their own nature (*svarūpa*). Why is that? He says this very thing: [394,xv]
Therefore, there is no difference in the object either;
[this is the section on] the result, which is the cognition of the object.

If it is asked, "In that case, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the result with respect to the external object; why was it not stated as such regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*? he says: "[Self-awareness is the result].
[395,i] Self-awareness is the result.
It has been stated in the investigation of intrinsic nature [that there is no cognition of an object] because of the identity between the cognition and the object. (351)

[395,ii] From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is also the cognition of that object. Even if it is indeed the cognition of that object, when one seeks to determine the nature of cognition itself—which has not yet been determined—it is simply self-cognition.

Now, if the object does not appear by way of its own form (*svarūpa*), but rather it is cognition alone that manifests by way of its own form, how can the object be the object of cognition (*prameya*)? If you say, "Because the mirror is of such a nature," we ask: how is it known that it is "of such a nature"? For it has been stated that cognitions possess manifold forms (*nānākārā vijñaptayaḥ*).
To this, it is replied:

Even if an object appears in such a way to a cognition— whether it be similar or dissimilar to that appearance— the object is still accepted as the object of cognition (*prameya*), because it is the cause of that cognition. (352)

vi] Although a cognition appearing as water arises even in the absence of water, nevertheless, because it arises in dependence upon shimmering heat-mirages (marīcikā) and possesses, in some sense, the status of being a cause for an object, it is said to have an object as its support (sālambana). [395, vii]

Now, if being an object (*ālambanatā*) follows solely from being a cause, then it is logical that [the cognition] has *vāsanā* as its cause; for it is not the case that *vāsanā* is not a cause. Moreover, the capacity of *vāsanā* to produce that [specific] form has been observed, and this has been established by you yourself. If, however, that possession of the form [of the object] could not exist without an object existing in such a way, then the perception of the object would be logical. Otherwise, however: In whatever way the form of that object appears through reasoning, [it is so]. [395, viii]
How can there be the apprehension of an object? Truly, I do not know even this much.

[395,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those sentient beings suffering such various miseries. Seeing them, he addressed the Buddha Śākyamuni: “World-Honored One, by what means can these sentient beings be delivered from their sufferings? The Buddha Śākyamuni replied to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “Good son, if there are sentient beings who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall all be delivered from their sufferings. If there are those bound in fetters and shackles, whether they have committed crimes or not, if they call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the fetters and shackles shall all break apart. If there are those who travel on the great ocean, beset by perilous winds and waves, and if they call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately find safety. If there are those who encounter robbers and bandits, and if they call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the robbers and bandits shall lose their murderous intent. Thus spoke the Buddha. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if there are good men or good women who wish to cultivate the practice of the Perfection of Wisdom, they should observe that all phenomena are empty in nature; this is called the Perfection of Wisdom. Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, together with the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, returned to the Sahā world. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. The above is the "Universal Gateway" chapter of the Lotus Sūtra. It is said that if one recites the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one will be liberated from all sufferings. This is the origin of the practice of "Namu Kannon. The above is the "Universal Gateway" chapter of the Lotus Sūtra. It is said that if one recites the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one will be liberated from all sufferings. When there is the appearance of that form even in the absence of a proximate object, then at that time, that object is not being apprehended. If it is argued that what is being apprehended is something seen in another location, [we ask]: if it does not exist even in another location, how can there be an appearance? If it is argued that the appearance occurs where it exists, [we reply]: if it does not exist anywhere at all, what means is there to know this? It is known from the appearance itself. Since an appearance has never been observed without an object, such an understanding arises through logical necessity (*pratibandha*). If that is so, then since it has not been seen, how does it appear? If it is argued that it too was indeed seen in another life and so forth, we say no; because there is no such restriction, an appearance is admitted even for what has not been seen. If that is the case, then:
For even though not seen in a particular place or time, an object appears elsewhere;
if everything were [simultaneously present], then it would follow that everyone is an all-seeing seer. (PVA 974)

[395,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as existing. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, not apprehend any dharma as real, nor perceive any dharma as existing? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend form as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the eye as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend forms as real, nor does he perceive them as existing; he does not apprehend sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend feeling born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the faculty of faith as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the faculties of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the power of faith as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the powers of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the limb of awakening of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the limbs of awakening of investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, tranquility, concentration, or equanimity as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the path as real, nor does he perceive it as existing. He does not apprehend the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, or the emptiness of the essential nature as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive them as existing; he does not apprehend the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship as real, nor does he perceive them as existing. He does not apprehend the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the state of a bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive it as existing; he does not apprehend the state of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive it as existing. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as existing. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend any dharma as real, nor perceive any dharma as existing, how then does he train in the six perfections? How does he train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata? How does he train in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship? How does he train in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood? How does he train in the state of a bodhisattva? How does he train in the state of a Tathāgata? How does he fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of giving by means of the non-apprehension of a gift, a giver, and a recipient. He trains in the perfection of morality by means of the non-apprehension of transgression and non-transgression. He trains in the perfection of patience by means of the non-apprehension of an object of anger and the absence of resentment. He trains in the perfection of vigor by means of the non-apprehension of laziness and diligence. He trains in the perfection of concentration by means of the non-apprehension of distraction and one-pointedness. He trains in the perfection of wisdom by means of the non-apprehension of ignorance and knowledge. He trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment by means of the non-apprehension of those factors. He trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata by means of the non-apprehension of them. He trains in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship by means of the non-apprehension of them. He trains in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood by means of the non-apprehension of it. He trains in the state of a bodhisattva by means of the non-apprehension of it. He trains in the state of a Tathāgata by means of the non-apprehension of it. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

If even that which is unseen were to appear while situated in another place or the like, it would follow that everyone would be an all-seeing seer. [Objection: It does not appear except under specific conditions. [Response: If you say it appears due to cataracts (*timira*) and so forth, no; since cataracts are common to all, it would follow that everything would appear to everyone. Furthermore, cataracts cause the impairment of vision; how then could they themselves be the cause of vision? If they were the cause of vision, it would follow that everything would be seen. [Objection: It produces vision only of that which is actually being seen. [Response: In that case, what is being seen is precisely that which does not exist. [Objection: Let that very thing produce the vision of the non-existent; however, vision has never been observed to occur without an object. [Response: Vision has likewise never been observed to occur without the object being situated in a location suitable for perception. [Objection: If you say there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from this rule, it is the same for both cases. [Objection: That very thing is the object. [Response: No, because it lacks the nature of being an object (*arthatva*). [Objection: Such a thing is indeed the object. [Response: Then everything would be such an object. If it is extraordinary (*alaukika*), then everything is extraordinary. For it has already been established that there is no other distinction apart from the vision itself. [Objection: There is "attainment" (*prāpti*). [Response: That too is simply vision. By this, vision and the rest have been explained.
Just as the first cognition depends upon its own attainment, so too that attainment must depend upon another attainment; thus, there is an infinite regress. (PVA 975)

If it were maintained that for some [cognition] there is the nature of being a valid apprehension (*prāpti*) by its very own nature, then since that same state would also apply to the first [cognition], all [subsequent cognitions] would be identical.
Or, if the reality of the [first cognition] is due to its being a valid apprehension preceded by another [valid apprehension], [then an infinite regress follows].
[The opponent claims] it is a case of mutual dependence; [we reply] that this is not so for both [cognitions] when the object is real.
(977) However, the extreme reality of a cognition arises from the purity of its causal object;
likewise, the reality of that subsequent cognition arises from the purity of its own cause. (978)
Thus, due to this mutual dependence, an infinite regress results.

The state of being produced by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is established even in the case of the water of a mirage. Therefore, all of this should be conceived in such a way that it remains free from confusion.

For one for whom blue and other objects [are external], no fault whatsoever is observed, since their manifestations are bound by the attachment of beginningless latent predispositions (*anādivāsanā*). (PVA 980) [396.vii]
But how can even the obstruction by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exist within the nature of self-cognizing awareness (*svasaṃvedana-jñāna*)?
If the other [cognition] is obstructed from its own nature, by what is it apprehended?
If it were indeed its own nature, then the name would be the only thing established.

If the relation (*pratibandha*) has a nature distinct from its own essence, then self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) occurs through the apprehension of that which is separate. If, however, there is no state of being separate, then the relation and the relata do not exist at all; thus, the apprehension of a relation would be impossible.
This too is incorrect, because:
This obstruction by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is perceived quite easily;
remembrance is perceived as being dependent upon prior cognition. (PVA 982)

[396,xiii] Memory, as it arises, demonstrates its own connection to a prior experience; it is for this reason, by virtue of that very determination, that it is so described. But then, how can there be a cognition of being bound by a latent impression (*vāsanā*) through memory? For instance:
The recollection, "This was seen by me," occurs only when there has been a prior cognition;
however, non-recollection does not communicate its own existence to anyone.

While recollecting, one determines "this was seen," because otherwise it would be impossible to determine that something was seen. However, in the case of a cognition that lacks recollection, there is no perception of its following upon a prior vision; therefore, how could there be a cognition that it is "bound by a latent impression" (*vāsanā*)? For even in that case, there is the cognition "this was seen. This is because, by unifying the remembered with the being-seen, there is a cognition of that [object] as well, and otherwise practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible. Thus, there is a cognition of the identity between the remembered and the being-seen. Consequently, everything is indeed bound by latent impressions. Now, if it is argued that the cognition of the identity between the remembered and the being-seen is an error, we say no, because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
"I remember this very thing"—this prior perception of mine exists here, and there is no sublation present; thus, there is identity between that [past perception] and the memory. (PVA 984)

[396,xvii] Now, if the prior form is not grasped by way of the mode of recollection, then how could there be a cognition of difference between the prior and the subsequent? Therefore, there is indeed non-duality (advaita). This being so, it is all the more so from the perspective of the nature of consciousness itself. Furthermore, because it is impossible to establish a rule of the causal relationship regarding external objects; for instance:
[396,xviii]
Since the external object was not previously perceived, how could it be the effect of consciousness?
But since consciousness is indeed perceived, its being the effect of consciousness is logical.
Likewise:
[396,xx] Because that effect arises differently depending on the conditions of place, time, and so forth.

The necessity of the causal relationship is not logically tenable. (PVA 986) But in the case of the theory of cognition (*samvedanapakṣa*), a preceding cognition arises from cognition itself. Even though smoke may occur without fire, it nonetheless arises from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of smoke; thus, it is neither causeless nor a mere mental appearance, as in the case of the light of a gnat, a mirage, or smoke and water [seen in a dream]. If it is argued that the external object itself arises through the power of latent impressions, we certainly accept this. Since it is dependent on the power of external latent impressions, it would be nothing more than a mere name; and since that is already accepted by the world itself, what is your specific contribution in this matter?

[397,i] But surely, it does not appear as an effect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); how then can it have the nature of being an effect of latent impressions? When one perceives fire from smoke without [prior] deliberation, does the fact that it is an effect [of latent impressions] appear to him? If you say it occurs for one who reflects upon it, then this is the same even regarding the nature of being an effect of latent impressions, because the awakening of latent impressions from another life and so forth is also possible—just as, for example, the occurrence of dreams involving children’s play is possible for a Buddha. And therefore:
It is said that there is an appearance of what was seen in previous births and so forth;
the determination is that this appearance exists due to the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Consequently, there is the manifestation of each preceding consciousness.
In all cases, that which is external has been established as being indeed external to consciousness.

For those whose minds are brought under the sway of the attachment to beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), this manifold appearance occurs within a single [consciousness], just as for those who see dreams. (PVA 988–989)
Because it is an effect, every effect arises from the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*),
just like the work of a potter or other craftsmen, or like the effects seen in dreams. [Whatever else may be postulated, such as] primordial matter (*pradhāna*), God (*īśvara*), or karma— (PVA 990)
That very movement is the mind deluded by attachment to latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Among all primary causes, that is the primary one; likewise, among all lords, it is the lord.
The supreme deity is the latent impression, the creator of the entire world. (PVA 991–992)
How could one who acts with foresight be the creator of a world that functions in such a discordant manner, proceeding with such agitation?
[993] (PVA) For one who exists in independence, who is capable, and who possesses full knowledge—

If one’s conduct is inconsistent [with one's own teaching], who could be instructed by whom? (994) (PVA) If he is the giver of instruction, yet he himself is the author of such deformity in his own subsequent births, what consistency with logic can there be for him? (995) (PVA)
If the Creator intended to bring about what is improper,
then it would be better to avoid touching impurity from afar than to wash it away.
(996) (PVA) Since it is impossible to act otherwise in this matter, how can his power be considered real?
"By the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that too proceeds from that very source.
(PVA 397, xiv) Thus, the rivers of doctrines asserting Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), God (*īśvara*), or a Creator have been flowing swiftly and continuously since time immemorial.
Entering indeed, they proceed toward inexhaustibility— that very ocean of immeasurable latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
O deluded ones, it is better that these very latent impressions be purified by means of a virtuous method.
From that alone comes the accomplishment of all that is desired.

(PVA 397, xvii) Therefore, as for the question "How is there the apprehension of an object?", you should not ask me; however, I am by no means able to justify this position of yours, which aims at following its intended meaning to its ultimate conclusion.
[397,xviii] But who is capable of justifying that which is extremely ill-conceived? What can a farmer do with a seed that is utterly rotten? (PVA) 1000.
[397, xix] The Establishment of the Means of Cognition and its Result within the State of Representation-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*):

Now, if there is no form of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), how can there be such conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)? This too is merely your own delusion; for even the conventional usage of "the grasped" and so forth is not perceived as something distinct, because it is submerged within the very nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*). The meaning is that conventional usage is of the same essence as that [consciousness]. To explain:
Although it is without division, the nature of cognition— due to the distorted vision of those whose perception is inverted—
is perceived as if it possessed the distinction between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and the act of awareness. (354)
Just as for those whose senses are impaired by spells and the like, objects such as lumps of clay appear in a completely different way, even though they lack that [erroneous] form. (355)

[397,xxii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as existing. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature."

That the nature of cognition (*buddhyātman*) is undivided is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and this has already been demonstrated. However, it is apprehended as having the form of an object (*grāhya*) and so forth by those whose vision is distorted. This is not the case; rather, it is merely characterized as such. Even though it does not exist for another, it appears [to them] as if it were; thus, having superimposed this distortion, they engage in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). They think: "This is my perception now, but the external object was indeed seen by another. Yet, this person does not reflect upon this: "How is it that what was seen by another was seen by me? For even another person does not know it in this way. For him too, that [perception] is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), just like our own self-awareness. If it is argued that he also knows "it was seen by me" through inference alone, then there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If it is argued that this is because of the existence of the observation of an effect, we say no, because it would follow that there is no realization of identity. For fire arising from smoke is not known to be located specifically in a kitchen simply because the smoke is different [from other fires]. If it is argued that the smoke is different, then because the effects such as horripilation are different, the perceived form of another must be different for the other. Furthermore, horripilation and so forth arise from self-awareness, not from the object. Moreover, there is no realization of a mixing of two perceptions with one another; otherwise, inference would not be required. For inference does not operate where there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[398,i] The Blessed One said: "Ananda, this Dharma-discourse is called 'The Lion’s Roar of the Tathāgata. You should learn it thus. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having heard the Buddha's teaching, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

If it is argued that only the visible form (*rūpa*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas its being seen by another is not directly perceived therein and is therefore known through inference (*anumāna*), we reply: there is certainly no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "being seen by another exists therein. If you say, "In this very case, there is doubt," then why would the state of being yellow not also be a subject of doubt when what is being seen is the state of being blue? As for fire in a place where it will be perceived later, how do you know that the nature of fire exists there? [We know it] precisely because of the later perception. But in the present case, regarding the state of being seen by another, there is no perception even later on. If it is argued that "if the state of being seen by another is not cognized, then linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) itself cannot exist," we say no; for linguistic convention is established through mere similarity alone. As for the claim that "linguistic convention does not exist without identity (*ekatva*)," from what source is this known?

[398, ii] But surely, if inference operates with respect to that which is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), it must also operate with respect to unity; if not, how could it operate even with respect to similarity? True, this is so. From where does inference arise even with respect to similarity? It is merely a conventional transaction (*vyavahāra*) based solely on the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object. In ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, inference has as its objective support only the specific intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) itself. If it is asked, "How then can it have an imperceptible object as its domain?"—it is not so. [398, iii]

How can it be logical for knowledge to have an imperceptible object? For if that object appears [in consciousness], how can there be any imperceptibility at all? On the other hand, if imperceptibility means the object exists apart from its appearing, then the statement "there is cognition of it" is a mere verbal convention devoid of reality.
If it is argued that the cognition of that object arises from its subsequent correspondence [with reality]...

If it is argued that "attainment exists," then let it be stated that it exists at the time of attainment. But by what means of knowledge can its prior existence be known? If it were apprehended even without that [prior] state, then [the argument would fail]. (PVA 1002–1003)
If there is no inference of a future object, how can there be cognition of it?
It is certain that in all cases there is cognition of a future form. If both—the present and the future—are cognized, [then what is the distinction?]
How could there be the cognition of a single form for two things that are yet to come into being?
Therefore, there is no cognition through inference in an ultimate sense.
If a jar is imperceptible and does not exist, how can it be cognized later?
If the conjunction with sunrise occurs at that very time, how could it be so without a cause?
Since this is indeed observed, who here is subject to further questioning?
Because it is observed, why is its prior existence not postulated?

It is not seen in that way, nor is it conceptualized in that way. (1008) Nevertheless, there is no inference for that which is being perceived exactly as it appears. By what other means could it be known to exist? This is a poor reply. (1009)
Because:
Even another person does not understand that "it is known by another";

for even in the case of that [other], there would be a reliance on yet another knower through inference. When it is said that "it exists" because it is known by someone, that [existence] is common to others as well.
The validity of the inference regarding its existence is due to an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*).
Therefore, when existence is known through perception, there may be an inference with respect to it;
and when existence is known through inference, there is the apprehension of that [existence] by perception. (PVA 1011–1012)
Thus, due to mutual dependence, even a single one of them cannot possibly exist;
indeed, no instance of mutual dependence is observed anywhere else either.

Therefore, by relying on inference—which functions through a beginningless succession of such inferences—and in the conceptualization of external objects, the conceptualization of the apprehended and the apprehender proceeds; thus it is established that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the conceptualization of the apprehended and so forth is nothing but undivided cognition itself. If it is asked: "From what source does this realization of yours arise? [The answer is: Because things such as fragments of clay, when aided by spells (*mantra*) and the like, appear in the form of snakes and so forth even though they lack that nature. For those people, even while others do not see them, they behave as if they were visible, as long as their [correct] understanding has not developed. If, however, an object were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) exactly as its own nature is, they would not depend upon such understanding. If it is argued that even direct perception depends upon understanding to be [validly] such, no; for the capacity [to establish the object] is seen in inference. If it is argued that the capacity belongs to direct perception alone, no; for it would follow that inference lacks validity (*prāmāṇya*). If it is argued: "Let it be that direct perception is indeed that [the ultimate]," then the fact that even direct perception is derived from the power of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) means it is not ultimately real. Moreover, even in the case of the opposite [view], inference certainly exists; so how could there be two types of inference? If it is argued: "Let it be both," no; for it would follow that the status of entities is fixed for each individual person. If it is asked: "What is the fault in that? [The answer is: That very thing arrives at self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), because [each cognition] is unique due to the non-mixture of one with another. Therefore, although another person does not perceive it in that way, there is still a perception of it as something common. Now, why is it that another person does not possess such a perception? If it is argued: "By means of inference," then inference should proceed even in the case of the opposite. If it is argued: "In the case of the opposite, inference is non-existent," how so? Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not grasped as identity. Even in the case of similarity, inference has already fulfilled its purpose. But here, furthermore, an action observed in accordance with non-perception necessarily infers that non-perception. And this is precisely what the opponent must accept.
Likewise, because they are not perceived by those whose minds are undisturbed; or just as even a very small thing appears large from afar in deserts. (356)

[399,iii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is a seeker of the stream (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), the person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), the person who is a seeker of arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka), and the person who has attained the fruit of arhatship (arhat). These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, do not fall away? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are seven kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, do not fall away. What seven? They are: the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the interval (antarā-parinirvāyin), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin), the one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin), the one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin), the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven (ūrdhvasrota akaniṣṭhaga), the one who passes from realm to realm (pluta), and the one who passes from one peak to another (sarvasthānacyuta). These, Ānanda, are the seven kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, do not fall away. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, do fall away? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are two kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, do fall away. What two? They are: the one who falls away from the wholesome roots (kuśalamūla-vyavakīrṇa) and the one who falls away from the meditative attainments (samāpatti-vyavakīrṇa). These, Ānanda, are the two kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, do fall away. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, neither fall away nor attain parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are three kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, neither fall away nor attain parinirvāṇa. What three? They are: the one who is bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana), the one who is bound by five fetters (pañcabandhana), and the one who is bound by nine fetters (navabandhana). These, Ānanda, are the three kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, neither fall away nor attain parinirvāṇa. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, attain parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, attain parinirvāṇa. What four? They are: the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the interval, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort, and the one who attains parinirvāṇa without effort. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, attain parinirvāṇa. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, go upstream? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are two kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, go upstream. What two? They are: the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and the one who passes from one peak to another. These, Ānanda, are the two kinds of persons who, having entered the stream, go upstream. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, pass from realm to realm? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there is only one kind of person who, having entered the stream, passes from realm to realm. What one? It is the one who passes from one peak to another. This, Ānanda, is the one kind of person who, having entered the stream, passes from realm to realm. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how many kinds of persons are there who, having entered the stream, pass from one peak to another? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there is only one kind of person who, having entered the stream, passes from one peak to another. What one? It is the one who passes from one peak to another. This, Ānanda, is the one kind of person who, having entered the stream, passes from one peak to another.
