If it is argued that "this object is seen by another as well," such an admission applies equally to the other party. Likewise, since approaching [an object] with the desire for it occurs through the common recognition that "this is indeed great," one must abandon inference in its alternative form on the grounds that it is common to all. Thus, the entire inference known to all people would be discarded. However, for those who perceive reality, [inference is valid] only by virtue of the opponent's own admission. Alternatively, when something is perceived exactly as it is, what occasion is there to postulate an external object? Even inference, when it culminates in nothing more than its own internal form, is nothing but perception itself.

[399, iv] But surely, for those engaged in worldly discourse (*vyavahārin*), there is indeed the cognition that "the external object exists here, whether it is being perceived or not being perceived. Let it be so; yet even that [cognition] is submerged within its own self (*svātman*) as long as it is regarded as perception. By "submerged within its own self," the understanding is that there is no object existing outside of the cognition itself. Furthermore, even common consensus (*sādhāraṇapratīti*) arises solely through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), just as in a dream. How then can the status of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the result (*phala*) be established?
To this it is replied:
This establishment of the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and the result exists according to how things appear.
Even though it does not exist, [the distinction between] the grasped, the grasper, and consciousness is constructed. // 357 //

That very object which is being perceived exists there; as the object of perception, it is the apprehended (*grāhya*). It is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and independent of anything else. Because it exists in that very way by itself, the apprehender (*grāhaka*) is the form of perception, which is consciousness (*samvit*). It is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from experience. "Subsequent observation" (*anudarśana*) is a conceptual construction corresponding to the direct perception. Even though it does not exist [as a separate entity], [it is so designated].
In an object that lacks a real external basis, there is the apprehension of the grasped, the grasper, and consciousness;

or rather, by the term "apprehension of what is non-existent," it refers to the grasped and so forth in cases such as common objects. The rest has already been stated by others: therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is only consciousness, not a triad.

[399,x] But surely, since everything is merely a transformation of the self (*ātman*), why is there non-existence? Even if those various transformations of difference belong to that [self] which has not fallen away from its true nature (*tattva*).
Thus he says: [399,xii] Otherwise, for a single entity appearing in various forms...
How could there be aspects [of cognition] if truth were to result from the abandonment of that unity? (358)
[400,i] — If it is one, how can it appear as manifold? If it appears as manifold, then its oneness is lost. For:
And because the otherness of one thing [from another] would be lost; there is no non-difference, because their forms are not seen to be identical.
For the cognition, perceiving the identity of form, determines non-difference. (356)

[400,iii] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great community of bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are these four supports for the mind. What four? The support of food, the support of contact, the support of mental volition, and the support of consciousness. These, bhikṣus, are the four supports for the mind. [401,i] Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said to him: “It would be well, Blessed One, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma discourse entitled ‘The Four Supports. Having heard it from the Blessed One, I shall remember it. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, Blessed One,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke: “Ānanda, what are the four supports? They are the support of food, the support of contact, the support of mental volition, and the support of consciousness. Now, Ānanda, regarding the support of food: what is the support of food? It is the four kinds of nutriment. Which four? Edible food, coarse or fine; secondly, contact; thirdly, mental volition; and fourthly, consciousness. These, Ānanda, are called the four supports. Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding the support of contact: what is the support of contact? It is the six classes of contact. Which six? Contact of the eye, contact of the ear, contact of the nose, contact of the tongue, contact of the body, and contact of the mind. These, Ānanda, are called the support of contact. Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding the support of mental volition: what is the support of mental volition? It is the six classes of mental volition. Which six? Mental volition regarding forms, mental volition regarding sounds, mental volition regarding odors, mental volition regarding tastes, mental volition regarding tangibles, and mental volition regarding dharmas. These, Ānanda, are called the support of mental volition. Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding the support of consciousness: what is the support of consciousness? It is the six classes of consciousness. Which six? Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These, Ānanda, are called the support of consciousness. Moreover, Ānanda, when a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, he understands as it really is the arising and passing away of the support of food. He understands as it really is its attraction, its danger, and the escape from it. When he understands this as it really is, his mind becomes dispassionate toward the support of food, and he attains liberation. By means of the liberation of the mind, he realizes through direct knowledge: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This, Ānanda, is called a bhikṣu who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Just as, Ānanda, a mountain peak, high, towering, and reaching to the sky, when struck by the wind, falls to the ground; even so, Ānanda, when a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body... [the same applies to the other supports]. [402,i] Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said: “Just as a mountain peak, high and vast, / Reaching to the sky, / When struck by the wind, falls to the ground; / So too, for one who dwells contemplating the body, / Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, / With a mind concentrated and one-pointed, / The mind becomes dispassionate from the support of food. / Having seen the danger in the support of food, / And having known the escape from it, / The wise one, having abandoned craving, / Is liberated from all suffering. [403,i] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, together with a great community of bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number. At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “It would be well, Blessed One, if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma discourse entitled ‘The Four Supports,’ as taught to Ānanda. The Blessed One said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: “Kāśyapa, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, Blessed One,” the Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke: “Kāśyapa, what are the four supports? They are the support of food, the support of contact, the support of mental volition, and the support of consciousness. Now, Kāśyapa, regarding the support of food: what is the support of food? It is the four kinds of nutriment. Which four? Edible food, coarse or fine; secondly, contact; thirdly, mental volition; and fourthly, consciousness. These, Kāśyapa, are called the four supports. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, regarding the support of contact: what is the support of contact? It is the six classes of contact. Which six? Contact of the eye, contact of the ear, contact of the nose, contact of the tongue, contact of the body, and contact of the mind. These, Kāśyapa, are called the support of contact. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, regarding the support of mental volition: what is the support of mental volition? It is the six classes of mental volition. Which six? Mental volition regarding forms, mental volition regarding sounds, mental volition regarding odors, mental volition regarding tastes, mental volition regarding tangibles, and mental volition regarding dharmas. These, Kāśyapa, are called the support of mental volition. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, regarding the support of consciousness: what is the support of consciousness? It is the six classes of consciousness. Which six? Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These, Kāśyapa, are called the support of consciousness. Moreover, Kāśyapa, when a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world, he understands as it really is the arising and passing away of the support of food. He understands as it really is its attraction, its danger, and the escape from it. When he understands this as it really is, his mind becomes dispassionate toward the support of food, and he attains liberation. By means of the liberation of the mind, he realizes through direct knowledge: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. This, Kāśyapa, is called a bhikṣu who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. Just as, Kāśyapa, a mountain peak, high, towering, and reaching to the sky, when struck by the wind, falls to the ground; even so, Kāśyapa, when a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body... [the same applies to the other supports]. [404,i] Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One, the Teacher, further said: “Just as a mountain peak, high and vast, / Reaching to the sky, / When struck by the wind, falls to the ground; / So too, for one who dwells contemplating the body, / Ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, / With a mind concentrated and one-pointed, / The mind becomes dispassionate from the support of food. / Having seen the danger in the support of food, / And having known the escape from it, / The wise one, having abandoned craving,

For anything else as well, this very reality is what is called the appearance of non-difference (*abhedapratibhāsana*). For anything else, there is simply no "otherness" (*anyathātva*) at all. If you say, "It is simply not accepted [as real]," then how can there be an admission of non-difference when there is an appearance of a difference in form? Even if you do not accept difference, how can it be admitted when it does not even appear? For an admission is valid only when a non-difference in form is perceived. If all those differences are of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśarūpa*), then all of them must be real. But if they are not of the nature of manifestation, how can things that are unmanifest be non-different from manifestation? If they were manifest, then like the Self (*ātman*), all of them would have to be real—just like the Self. Indeed, the very nature of the Self is its being of the nature of manifestation; therefore, all things would be Selves. Consequently, the position of transformation (*pariṇāmapakṣa*) would collapse. Now, if you claim that the multiplicity is an illusion (*bhrānti*), then it follows that nothing exists at all, and everything would become a void. Furthermore, even so-called "illusion" does not exist apart from the Self. What is the point of applying the name "illusion"? Since illusion is non-existent, none of this would occur; thus, difference is not a reality. Therefore, because it is caused by the appearance of what is unreal, it is established as "non-illusion" (*abhrānti*).
[400,iv] As long as its status as something to be revoked is not established, it possesses no erroneous nature.
And once it is understood that [the object] is to be turned away from, it is recognized as being merely an illusion.
(1014) Having attained the certainty that it is an illusion, one would act for the sake of desisting;
thus, since desistance follows from that, by what means can this circularity be resolved? (1015)
Therefore.
[400, viii]
That form by which entities are determined does not exist in reality, because neither a single nor a manifold form is found in them. (360)

[400,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the Tathāgata to manifest such a great supernatural power? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, it is because the Tathāgata wishes to reveal the profound and subtle Dharma that he manifests such a great supernatural power. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the profound and subtle Dharma that the Tathāgata reveals? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, it is the Dharma-gate called ‘the non-arising of all phenomena. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does one enter this Dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are originally unborn, then they have entered this Dharma-gate of the non-arising of all phenomena. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are originally unborn? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that the nature of all phenomena is like empty space, then they perceive that all phenomena are originally unborn. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that the nature of all phenomena is like empty space? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are devoid of self and belong to no one, then they perceive that the nature of all phenomena is like empty space. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are devoid of self and belong to no one? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, then they perceive that all phenomena are devoid of self and belong to no one. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are beyond conceptualization and free from discursive thought, then they perceive that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are beyond conceptualization and free from discursive thought? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa, then they perceive that all phenomena are beyond conceptualization and free from discursive thought. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, then they perceive that all phenomena are equal to nirvāṇa. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and unceasing, then they perceive that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and unceasing? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, shadows, mirages, and magical transformations, then they perceive that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen and unceasing. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, shadows, mirages, and magical transformations? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are merely designations, then they perceive that all phenomena are like illusions, dreams, echoes, shadows, mirages, and magical transformations. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are merely designations? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are like the reflection of the moon in water, then they perceive that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and are merely designations. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are like the reflection of the moon in water? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are ungraspable and cannot be apprehended, then they perceive that all phenomena are like the reflection of the moon in water. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are ungraspable and cannot be apprehended? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are beyond the reach of the eye and the scope of cognition, then they perceive that all phenomena are ungraspable and cannot be apprehended. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are beyond the reach of the eye and the scope of cognition? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are ultimately ineffable and inexpressible, then they perceive that all phenomena are beyond the reach of the eye and the scope of cognition. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are ultimately ineffable and inexpressible? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are like the sound of an echo, then they perceive that all phenomena are ultimately ineffable and inexpressible. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are like the sound of an echo? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are produced by conditions and lack a real essence, then they perceive that all phenomena are like the sound of an echo. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are produced by conditions and lack a real essence? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and do not exist independently, then they perceive that all phenomena are produced by conditions and lack a real essence. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and do not exist independently? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are like a dream within a dream, then they perceive that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and do not exist independently. Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceive that all phenomena are like a dream within a dream? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva perceives that all phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent, then they perceive that all phenomena are like a dream within a dream. Maitreya addressed

The one does not exist as a plurality because it appears as such. Furthermore, that which is not experienced does not appear; therefore, since it does appear, it must have the nature of experience (*samvedana*). Moreover, in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), plurality is not perceived. If it is argued that [the parts] are perceived because they are included within that [unity], we reply that it cannot be said that their being included within it is not perceived—this has already been stated. Alternatively, since a single variegated form does not actually exist as a plurality, how then is there the appearance of difference? It has been established, and will be further demonstrated, that difference does not appear. Or rather, the entire form of difference and its opposite appears through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); thus, it is unreal, for those who cultivate [it] can turn it away by means of contrary cultivation. Therefore, because there is no certainty regarding its impossibility of being turned away, it is unreal.
[400,x] But surely!
In the world, an error arises from the perception of similarity through the determination of identity in that which lacks it; this is not the case here.
"Because not even a single being of that nature is seen in this world.
To this it is replied: "Error does not arise from the mere observation of similarity alone."
[400,xiv] Let this [cognition] also exist, which arises from an internal disturbance. 362.

By its very nature, that [cognition] arises from a defect and appears as something expanded, without depending on the perception of similarity and so forth, just like the visual impairment known as *timira*. (363)

Indeed, for those whose vision is obscured by cataracts, mosquitoes, flies, and the like do not arise through the power of another perception; rather, they arise solely from the cause of the cataract itself.

[Objection: But surely that which arises even from a visual disorder (*timira*) does so by the power of the object itself, not by the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*). [Response: We intend only to specify that it has an internal cause; for in all cases, the internal cause is indeed nothing but latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), as in the case of cognitions such as dreams. That predisposition, when awakened in some way or another, is the cause for the production of a cognition corresponding to itself. In this context, each preceding perception is the perception of similarity (*sādharmyadarśana*). What was seen at the beginning, by virtue of which this error occurs? It must be explained how there can be a perception of that [similarity] within the perception itself. If that were the case, then because of their identity, the entire series would be non-erroneous. Or, if the perception were otherwise, how could the whole be erroneous? [If you say] "because of the perception of similarity," [we reply: No. This is merely a succession of errors; it has been established that there is no non-erroneous state. Therefore, this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of the conceptual construction of unreal predispositions, is beginningless. [Objection: How then is the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth possible within its own nature?
[401,iii] To this it is replied:
In that regard, the determination of cognition is considered to be its apprehending form;
because of their identity, the self-knowing of that [cognition] is held to be the means of establishing it. (364)
That very thing is the probandum, that very thing is the proof, and that very thing is the establishment.

In that regard, just as there is the experience of passion and so forth when the self is the object of cognition, this same framework for the object, the means of knowledge, and the result should be applied everywhere. (365)

For it has been established that objects and so forth, arising through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that consists in the awareness of pleasure and so forth is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); in that case, the distinction between the means of cognition, the object of cognition, and the act of cognizing is indeed non-distinct. As it is said:
[401, viii]
And thus, reality is fully encompassed within these four: the knower (*pramātṛ*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the result of knowledge (*pramiti*).

This is incorrect, because everything is fully encompassed within a single one. If it is argued that while there is indeed non-distinction in the case of pleasure and so forth, there is distinction in the case of yellow and so forth, we say no; this very same establishment of the object, the means, and the result is to be applied everywhere.

Just as it is in the case of the cognition of an object (*artha*) and so forth, so it is also in the case of the cognition of blue and so forth. Whether it be called "the form of blue" or "the form of the object," what difference is there between these two? For both are cognized by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the cognition of blue, pleasure, or the body is entirely by way of its own nature alone, not by way of another's nature. If it is by way of its own nature, then everything is indeed self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). [Objection: But surely, through the cognition of blue and so forth, the subjective aspect (*grāhakākāra*), being identical with [that cognition], is like pleasure and so forth; how then can that serve as an example [for external objects]? [Reply: How is it that pleasure and so forth are like the Self (*ātman*)? Because they consist of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśātmakatva*). What is this so-called "nature of luminosity"? It is the state of being immediate (*aparokṣarūpatā*), just as [you describe] the Self.
In that case as well, because they consist of the nature of experience, they are capable of self-awareness;
thus, that capacity is the means of cognition (*māna*), the self is the object of cognition (*meyam*), and self-awareness is the result (*phalam*). // 366 //

The nature of self-determination, which is reckoned as the form of the grasper within itself, is called "capacity"; and this is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) consisting in the self-awareness [of consciousness]. (367)

Those [objects], such as blue and so forth, are also of the nature of experience because they possess a non-mediated (aparokṣa) form. Therefore, just like pleasure and the like, they are capable of being self-cognized. For even those objects, such as blue and so forth, are not non-mediated by way of another's form.

[Objection: Is it not the case that blue and other objects are directly perceived through the power of the eye and so forth? [Response: No, because they are directly perceived by their very own nature (*svarūpa*). For it is not the case that whatever direction the eye extends toward, the object in that direction becomes directly perceived; even when the eye extends toward a seed, it does not necessarily perceive it as directly present. This is because direct perception is possible even when the sense organ does not extend [toward the object]. To illustrate: when passion and the like arise, a visible form appears in one way [but is otherwise].
"Even though the eye is extended [toward the object], its own nature is not manifested.

(PVA 1016) [402, iv] If, even when the eye and other [senses] are directed toward [an object], the object is not manifested in its own form, how can it be said to be "immediate" (aparokṣa)? Manifestation of its own form is precisely what constitutes immediacy. Now, if this defect of the eye is due to the force of mental cultivation (bhāvanā), then he says:

[402,v] If, through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is a transformation of the eye and other faculties, then by the power of that cultivation, everything— including blue and so forth— would appear [as such]. (PVA 1017)

For cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which has another name, "predisposition" (*vāsanā*), is the cause of the appearance of the eye and so forth. At that time, the appearances of blue and other such objects arise solely through the power of predisposition.

Surely, appearing otherwise is caused by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), whereas appearing as its own nature occurs without latent predispositions; thus, it is dependent on the eyes and other sense organs, not upon mutual dependence, because all things are distinct from one another. Therefore, through the appearance of many [aspects], how can one know what the true nature (*svarūpa*) is? If appearance is not non-deviant, how can there be confidence? Consequently:
Every appearance whatsoever is produced by the presence or absence of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Like that which possesses a nature appearing as something other than what is intended to be its own nature,

(PVA 1018) [402,ix] the relationship of sublated and sublator has already been refuted. Therefore, even with respect to an external object, self-awareness alone is the result, while its form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[402,x] But is it not the case that the claim "consciousness possesses an aspect" (sākāra) is untenable? For instance:
If [the eye] were as clear as a mirror, then it would follow that it perceives objects through the influence of external adjuncts;
yet the eye and other [senses] are not observed to do so.
Whatever is present [within its range], all that appears in a mirror. (PVA 1019)

Consequently, it would follow that there is an appearance of everything, such as visible form and so forth. (PVA 1020) Now, if the eye were the cause of the appearance just like a mirror, then there would be a perception of what has been transferred [into it], as in the case of a mirror and the like, even though [the object] is not coarse. (PVA 1021)
Consequently, it is not known what the form [of the cognition] is like, nor what its magnitude is;
there is even a distortion of color, as in the case of glass or a film of clouds.
Or, having emerged from the eyeball, [the rays] do not fall upon the objects such as visible forms. (PVA 1022)
Apprehenders are known in their own forms within [the categories] beginning with the Great One (*mahat*).
(1023) A specific form arises from the contact with the light of a lamp;
if there were self-awareness [of cognition], it would be like the contact with the light of a lamp. (1024)
Furthermore, in that case as well, there would be an infinite regress due to the operation of yet another [consciousness].
If, on the other hand, it is self-awareness [that occurs], then how could those rays [of light] [be perceived]?
Therefore, when the object is present, cognition proceeds bearing its form.
Therefore, if it were to follow that [the cognition] possesses all forms merely from its arising,
then if it were to possess the form of that [object] precisely because it arises from it,
it would also possess the form of the eye, since it also arises from the visual consciousness. (PVA 1026–1027)
To this, it is said:
[402,xxiii]
All consciousness indeed arises from objects; even though its cause is that object, it somehow bears the form of the object. (368)
[403,i] For it is not the case that whatever arises must necessarily possess the very form of that [cause]. To illustrate:
Just as in the birth of an offspring, although factors such as food and time are causes, it assumes the form of one of the parents and not that of any other whatsoever. (369)

[403,iii] For that which arises from two parents does not possess the identical form of both; rather, it arises from one or the other. Therefore, the form of the object [in cognition] comes from the object itself. To explain:

For consciousness arises in the form of a tree situated in a distant place; it is always observed that [consciousness] does not take the form of the sense organ. Even though [the sense organ] is equal to other objects in being a cause of that [consciousness], it is held [to be distinct].
The state of being an object [occurs] through that part; in its absence, it would not exist.

The object is not such by virtue of being a cause, but rather by virtue of being the cause of a cognition that possesses its form. If being an object were simply being a cause, then the eyes and other sense organs would also be objects. Furthermore, if it were merely by possessing its form, then even water located in another place could be the object of a cognition of water in a mirage. Indeed, it has been demonstrated that a cognition whose nature is awareness—whether it is being experienced or otherwise—is incapable of establishing the status of an object as having that form without [the object itself] possessing that form, because the states of being perceived and not being perceived are incompatible. If that [object] is perceived, what is the use of anything else? For it would be redundant. If, on the other hand, it is not perceived, then [the cognition] lacks the capacity [to establish it]. For that which is not being perceived cannot be the object of perception. And if it is being perceived, that very perception is its being perceived as having that form. Moreover, it has been demonstrated hundreds of times that an action distinct [from the agent or the subject] is not tenable.

[403,vii] But surely, in the proof of the existence of mental aspects (sākārasiddhi), it would be the case that the aspect is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) is the result (phala). How, then, is that very point established? It has been stated regarding this; moreover:
[403,viii]
The nature of cognition consists in the distinction between the knowledge of an object and the knowledge of that [knowledge].

The cognition of an object such as form (*rūpa*) has the appearance of that object and its own appearance. However, the cognition of the cognition of an object has the appearance of the cognition conforming to the object and its own appearance. Otherwise, if the cognition of an object were to have only the form of the object, or if the cognition of the cognition of an object were to have only its own form, it would be indistinguishable from that [object]. The proposition to be proven is: "The cognition of an object has the appearance of that object and its own appearance. The subsequent [statement] is the logical reason (*hetu*). "Otherwise," etc., constitutes the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). When one reflects, "What was my cognition like?", one then engages with the memory precisely as the appearance of the object, and not otherwise. Furthermore, whatever is made an object through a particular conceptual determination (*adhimokṣa*) becomes exactly so; for example, a brindled cow (*śāvaleya*) when made an object through the conceptual determination "cow. To illustrate:
[403,x] Since such an appearance does not exist within cognition, what then is the nature of the object?
Thus, by abandoning the object, there is no determination of the object for cognition. (PVA 1029)

[403,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is permanent or impermanent; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is permanent or impermanent. He does not perceive that form is suffering or happiness; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is suffering or happiness. He does not perceive that form is self or non-self; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is self or non-self. He does not perceive that form is beautiful or ugly; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is beautiful or ugly. He does not perceive that form is empty or non-empty; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is empty or non-empty. He does not perceive that form is with signs or signless; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is with signs or signless. He does not perceive that form is wishful or wishless; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is wishful or wishless. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of wisdom itself as permanent or impermanent, nor does he perceive it as suffering or happiness, self or non-self, beautiful or ugly, empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, or wishful or wishless. For what reason? Because the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving as permanent or impermanent, nor does he perceive it as suffering or happiness, self or non-self, beautiful or ugly, empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, or wishful or wishless. Why is this? Because the perfection of giving is free from conceptual proliferation. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, or the perfection of meditation as permanent or impermanent, nor does he perceive them as suffering or happiness, self or non-self, beautiful or ugly, empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, or wishful or wishless. Why is this? Because those perfections are free from conceptual proliferation. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as permanent or impermanent, nor does he perceive it as suffering or happiness, self or non-self, beautiful or ugly, empty or non-empty, with signs or signless, or wishful or wishless. Why is this? Because the perfection of wisdom is free from conceptual proliferation. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the venerable Subhūti and the monks, as well as the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said. Thus ends the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, the Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom. This concludes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, in eight thousand lines. If someone challenges [this view], asking, "How is that object known by you?", then one replies: "There is no certainty as to whether the appearance of the object is such-and-such, or whether such an object exists there or not; nor is there certainty as to whether it is of such a nature or otherwise. Therefore, cognition is merely the appearance itself, which may abandon the external object. But if the object were a single unity, how could there be certainty in that very same thing and uncertainty in that very same thing? This is because certainty and uncertainty are contradictory. Furthermore, the object is not the certainty within the appearance. Nor is there a distinction between them; thus, what appears there is simply "an appearance of such a kind," while the rest is "not so. Consequently, that very object is both certain and uncertain, because of the existence of these two parts. This will be explained further below. Moreover:

[403,xii] Even if the mind possesses an object, there might still be a suspicion that it lacks a form; however, this is not the case once the apprehension of a past object is established, because self-awareness consists of a dual nature.
[403,xiii] Someone says: "Cognition does not appear because there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*); nor is it remembered, for in all cases it is only the object that is remembered.

Because of recollection. In that regard, just as the existence of cognition is postulated for an object through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), so too, because of the impossibility of recollection, there can be no cognition that is not cognized, nor can it have a form; therefore, the claim that "cognition is twofold" is contradicted by perception.
Since the statement of a reason is made when there is doubt, a reason that is refuted lacks a basis.
And when the necessary connection is apprehended in the example, it occurs through the operation of the logical reason.

If it is argued that this is not the case because the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is a subject of dispute in all instances, this is incorrect. For while a doubt might indeed arise in cases where an external object exists—namely, that the [perceived] form is not the form of the cognition—in a mind devoid of an object, such as in the case of [illusory] hair-tufts or the appearance of yellow and so forth, the possession of two forms (the form of the object and the form of the cognition) and the self-awareness (*samvedana*) are established. In those cases, the claim that consciousness is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) is directly contradicted by perception. Therefore, through the observation of those examples, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is grasped. Consequently, how could the certainty that "its manifestation is of such a nature" pertain to an external object? Since such a certainty occurs in every instance of cognition, the existence of the form [within the cognition] is proven. This very nature of the certainty regarding the manifestation is the nature of the cognition of the object within that [subsequent] cognition. Now, if one were to say that even there an object must exist, yet its individuality (*vyakti*) does not, then it would simply be the universal (*jāti*).
[(Jha) Refutation of the permanence and impermanence of the universal—
iv] To this it is replied:
Because it is differentiated by the appearance of blue and so forth, the object is not a universal (*jāti*), for that [universal] does not possess those [qualities].
Moreover, if it were impermanent, it would not be a universal; if it were permanent, how could it be a producer? (372)

A universal (*jāti*) such as "blue" and so forth does not exist, because it is devoid of the forms of color and other qualities. Furthermore, it cannot be a universal because it would be impermanent by virtue of being a cause; and it has already been established that what is eternal cannot be a producer, since an eternal entity lacks the capacity for production.
Names and so forth were refuted previously; this is not the sequence for those things that possess real meaning.
Because they are dependent upon mere whim, the power of a real object is not established. (373)
All of this has already been established previously, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
(2) *Smṛticintā* (Investigation of Memory).
[KA] What is memory that has the form of an object?
Memory is a cognition of this kind, and its arising occurs from experience.
And since that [cognition] is devoid of the form of the object, how can it now possess that [object]? (374)

[404,x] Since memory arises from experience, how can it possess the form of blue and so forth if it exists without an object? Or, if memory possesses that form precisely because of the object itself, then he says:
The existence [of memory] does not arise from the object, because that [object] is absent at that time; it would be the same even if there were such an experience.

If memory arose directly from the object, then the object would have to exist in exactly that same way [as it was experienced]. But that is not the case. If, on the other hand, memory bearing that form arises even from an object that is no longer present, then the experience itself must likewise be of that nature; and how this is so has already been demonstrated. Here too, it is now being demonstrated.
And that aspect does not belong to the object, because it is distinct from a clear aspect. (375)

[405,i] And the object, possessing a distinct form, is apprehended through its experience. If that [form] is the form of the object, then it must exist as such [i.e., as something experienced]. Alternatively, if it appears as such because it is cognized by memory, then, since it is cognized by experience, its clarity belongs to that [experience] and not to the object.
Another person likewise would perceive that form as distinct [from the cognition].

If that object were perceived even by another, then it would not be exclusively connected to oneself; rather, it would appear to the other as well. What is the meaning of "connected to oneself"? Does it mean it is an effect of the self, or that it is identical with the self? If it were an effect, then it would certainly appear to the other; for its status as an effect does not preclude its being common to both. If, on the other hand, it were identical with the self, then it would necessarily consist of consciousness itself. And if there were identity, it would be eternally connected to the self and could not be otherwise. In that case, even if it were explained, it would not be perceived [by another]. If, however, it is perceived [by another], then it must be perceived in some other way. For instance, external objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) are perceived by another even when they have not been explained. If you argue that what is perceived when explained is something entirely different [from the unexplained object], then in that case:
And if there were an eternal connection with the self, one would not fail to perceive what has been stated. [376]
Even with each individual connection, reconnection is not tenable.
To the question, "What kind of reconnection is it? he says:
[405,vii] Its nature is the adherence to a single object;
[405,viii]
There would be no cognition that "this is one," because it is distinct. To which two does this connection belong? He says: between the minds of the speaker and the listener. (377)
Because those two cognitions are engaged in apprehending distinct objects.

If the single conventional usage [of "pot"] regarding two things that do not appear as such [i.e., as non-pots] is due to similarity, then how could an object of a distinct nature be grasped? In that case, cognition would be devoid of its object. (378)

[405,xii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, what is physical food as gross nutriment? It is that which is edible, chewed, tasted, and swallowed, whether it consists of rice, barley, wheat, millet, beans, sesame, meat, fish, salt, sugar, molasses, honey, oil, butter, curd, milk, or ghee. This is called physical food as gross nutriment. What is contact as nutriment? It is the contact associated with the six sense bases. What is mental volition as nutriment? It is the volition associated with the six sense bases. What is consciousness as nutriment? It is the sixfold consciousness. Among these, what is physical food as gross nutriment? For that linguistic convention of "oneness" which occurs on the basis of similarity applies only to things that are perceived, and not otherwise. And the perception of what is seen by another never occurs in such a way [as direct experience]; how then could there be a convention of oneness? For here, there is only the appearance of objects as mutually distinct. If, however, similarity were a real entity (*vastubhūta*), then one might, in accordance with it, cognize this [other's state] as one with one's own. In that case, even when nothing has been said, one would cognize what resides in another in accordance with one's own cognition. Even when another does not say, "I have also cognized it thus," if one says, "It is true," then how can there be such a cognition without the object itself? If you say, "It is perceived exactly in this way," then in that case, cognition would be devoid of an object. Just as a cognition that determines the appearance of another [person] would exist without the appearance of another, so too would it possess a form (*sākāra*) without the appearance of an object; thus, the fact that knowledge possesses a form is established. Granted that for some—such as memory and the like—knowledge possesses a form due to analytical reflection or the force of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), from where does this arise for *all* [cognitions]? To this, he says:
And that consciousness of experience is followed by a cognition which, while apprehending both parts, possesses a single specific form. (379)

The experience-consciousness, which has the form of non-recollection and takes blue and other objects as its domain, is followed by, inferred from, and reflected upon by a second consciousness in the form of recollection having that same object. By what kind of [second consciousness]? By one that relies on both parts [of the cognition], thinking: "I had a cognition in which blue appeared."

But it is not ascertained by others through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as it truly is; rather, someone merely follows that which has become such [as established by the object]. Furthermore, presumptive testimony does not arise for any worldly person. For no one in the world understands in this way: "Since the object was seen by him, I possess another cognition [of it].
Indeed, presumptive testimony is not established regarding the intrinsic nature of a cognition.
For that form is difficult to determine; it is not possible to determine it.

(PVA 406, iii) No one is able to ascertain through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) or by any other means that cognition possesses a form other than the manifestation of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. If it is argued that it is ascertained by way of its nature as consciousness (*bodharūpatā*), then indeed that very nature of consciousness is not known. For there is no difference in the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) merely because of a difference in the suffix (*pratyaya*), nor is there a difference in the meaning of the suffix itself.
[406,iv] By whom was the distinction of names for an object first conceived? If there is no difference in the object, how could an explanation of it proceed by means of that [distinction]? (PVA 1032)

Therefore, cognition is not defined as "awakening" (bodha) or "intellection" (buddhi) distinct from blue and so forth; rather, it is simply a differentiation of attributes inherent in the very nature of that blue and so forth—such as "the cognition of blue" or "the cognition having blue as its object. Thus, when one reflects, "I had a cognition having blue as its object," it is precisely the conformity to that form which is being reflected upon. For it is thus:
No cognition as a subject is observed apart from the blue object;
the distinction [between them] following upon the cognition is constructed by the artisan of conceptual construction.

If, then, it is maintained that the cognition of blue and so forth is designated as distinct from their very nature, then blue and so forth alone would not be what is called "cognition. Just as whiteness and the like do not exist apart from a cloth, it follows that cognition itself is not ultimately real. Yet, you maintain that the external object is ultimately real. This is incorrect; for instance:
In some cases, the negation of something occurs by relying upon something else;
that which is established by a means of valid cognition serves as the gateway for the negation of another. (PVA 1034)
