If the object is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since there is no other cognition apart from it, cognition is abandoned. Alternatively, if cognition is established by means of valid cognition, then so is the object. In that case, since the object is established by means of cognition, cognition cannot be abandoned by one who possesses the object. However, for one who possesses cognition, because [cognition] is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cognition is not something to be accomplished by means of the object; therefore, it can be accepted even in the absence of an object. Thus, having accepted cognition, one abandons the object distinct from it. Alternatively, if the object were also established by self-awareness, then in that case, cognition itself would be the object distinct from it. Since the object exists even when unperceived, it is abandoned due to its non-apprehension. But cognition is not like that, and thus it is not to be abandoned. Furthermore:
Just as a substance is not admitted to exist apart from qualities such as whiteness,
so too let it be understood that an object is not perceived apart from cognition. (PVA 1035)
For example:
Momentariness is in no way distinct from blue and other such things;
nevertheless, it is not shown that momentariness is non-existent.

Therefore, because cognition is determined as having the very form of blue and so forth by another cognition, and because both parts [of that cognition] are abandoned [by that other], cognition is not apprehended at all; how then is it not of two forms? Alternatively, cognition is apprehended by a second knowledge as being qualified by a single form; the meaning is that it is apprehended by one form. To the question "By what kind of single form?", he says:
"by that which apprehends both parts."

[406,xvii] By that which pervades both parts; for that very reason, there is the conceptualization of both parts. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), those two forms have indeed entered into that single form. Therefore, they exist as a pervasion. Those two forms, moreover, are the nature of cognition (*bodharūpatā*) and the form of blue (*nīlākāratā*).

In the previous explanation, it should be understood that "by means of a specific single form" means "by means of an additional single form. Even if it is established as having two forms, how can it be said to have two forms? To this it is replied:
otherwise, how could that which does not possess those forms ascend into cognition?

If one did not experience that cognition as possessing that form through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), how could the cognition, by virtue of having that form, ascend into memory? For its "ascending" consists in the production of that form; from what source, then, does it ascend? It is because it is apprehended in exactly that way.
Knowledge increases by one aspect at each stage, for thus it becomes higher and higher.

[407,v] This must necessarily be accepted; for indeed, each subsequent [cognition] becomes increasingly superior by means of each successive aspect, and not otherwise. To illustrate: by the first [cognition], blue is apprehended; by the next, the cognition of blue; by the next, the cognition of the cognition of blue; and by the one following that, it ascertains that this too is superior to the former. This would not be possible otherwise. He demonstrates this very point through an example: [407,vi]
Its form as an object, or some other form whatsoever, is indeed discerned by a second cognition through a third cognition. (381)

[407, vii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard this teaching on the perfection of wisdom, does not become afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror, then he should be known as a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, how should one know that a bodhisattva mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when this perfection of wisdom is being taught, does not tremble, is not frightened, and does not become terrified, then he courses in the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when this perfection of wisdom is being taught, does not think, 'I am coursing in the perfection of wisdom,' then he courses in the perfection of wisdom. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva there is no such dharma as 'a bodhisattva. It is thus, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who courses in the perfection of wisdom."

The second cognition is perceived as having the form of the two preceding cognitions as well as its own form. By the third and fourth [moments], that same pair is perceived with one additional form, to the extent that one is able to count or remember it. Now, the cognition itself is not known in the second moment alone; rather, because that cognition is engaged with the object, it is connected to it. Therefore, when there is a memory of that [cognition], since the object is invariably concomitant with it, there is also a memory of the object. Thus, it is impossible to remember the cognition otherwise, and so it is remembered in that way. Consequently, because of its engagement with that [object], it possesses its form; this synthesis is the perception of its having that form through error. To this, it is replied:
If it is argued that the recollection of the object occurs within the recollection of the cognition because the cognition has the object as its causal effect,
and that this is a synthesis due to error, then that same synthesis would also occur in the case of the mental attention directed toward light.

[407,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he does not become attached to them. Because he is not attached, he does not tremble; being unafraid, he passes beyond all error and dwells having attained the ultimate *parinirvāṇa*. Subhūti, this is the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great beings. Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the reason, what is the cause, for which the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation? And why, Blessed One, does he not become attached to them? Why, Blessed One, is he not attached? Why, Blessed One, does he not tremble? Why, Blessed One, is he unafraid? Why, Blessed One, does he pass beyond all error and dwell having attained the ultimate *parinirvāṇa*? The Blessed One said: “Śāriputra, it is because form is empty that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is not form, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is not consciousness, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither conjoined with nor separated from form, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither conjoined with nor separated from consciousness, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither past, nor future, nor present, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither past, nor future, nor present, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither produced nor ceased, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither produced nor ceased, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither defiled nor purified, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither defiled nor purified, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither diminished nor increased, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither diminished nor increased, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither coming nor going, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither coming nor going, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither apprehended nor non-apprehended, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither apprehended nor non-apprehended, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither bound nor liberated, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither bound nor liberated, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither past, nor future, nor present, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither past, nor future, nor present, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither produced nor ceased, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither produced nor ceased, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither defiled nor purified, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither defiled nor purified, that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation; he does not perceive all-knowledge, nor does he perceive ‘all-knowledge’ as a designation. Śāriputra, it is because the emptiness of form is neither diminished nor increased, and the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither diminished nor increased,

The connection is with the word "error. Whether cognition is the effect of the object, or whether it has an operation directed toward the object, there is necessarily a recollection of the object in the recollection of the cognition; therefore, for one whose mental continuum possesses such a hidden [latent] disposition (*vāsanā*), the apprehension occurs in that manner. If this were so, then even in the case of attention (*manaskāra*)—which is light—one would have a similar apprehension. Just as cognition is the effect of the object, it is also the effect of light and the effect of attention; thus, it should be apprehended through the synthesis of both. For there is no difference in their status as effects. Now, if you argue that the synthesis occurs because [cognition] is operative (*vyāpṛta*) toward the object, whereas it is not operative toward attention, then the same applies to light: its operation is identical. For it does not operate toward form while abandoning light.

This is incorrect. Therefore, just as it is not the case that there is "appearance as light," so too there should not be "appearance as form" (*rūpa*). If it is argued that light itself is included within the object, and thus it is apprehended precisely through the determination of the appearance of form—no; since light functions as an illuminator, it lacks the status of being an object (*viṣaya*), so how could there be an operation [of cognition] upon it? If it is further argued that although light is an illuminator, it becomes an object because it falls upon form and thus becomes form itself—then, in that case, cognition (*jñāna*) is also an illuminator, and because it falls upon form, it too becomes form itself. Consequently, just like light with its form, consciousness (*vijñāna*) would also possess a form. Just as light cannot be perceived without form, so too is consciousness. Indeed, no one knows "consciousness exists for me" apart from the illuminated objects such as form. Therefore, consciousness possesses the very forms of form and so forth; it is only by way of being an effect that it is apprehended in such a manner.
If all effects were apprehended in that same way as their causes,
then a jar would not be remembered separately from the potter and other such factors. (383)

[408,ii] Even an effect such as a jar produced by a potter and others would not be remembered apart from its own causes. Now, if it is argued that there exists some excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by the object within the cognition, by virtue of which the object is also remembered when the cognition is remembered, and the object is apprehended when the cognition is apprehended—whereas cognition alone is neither apprehended nor remembered—that too serves to undermine your own position. For instance:

Since cognition, by virtue of its excellence, is the receptacle for the connection with an object, what else could that [excellence] be than similarity (sārūpya), given the observation of twins and the like? (384)

[408,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of giving. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift, and he does not perceive that gift as a gift, nor does he perceive a recipient, nor does he perceive himself as a giver. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of giving. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of morality? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, having undertaken the training rules, does not perceive that training rule as a training rule, nor does he perceive transgression, nor does he perceive himself as one who has undertaken the training. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of morality. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of patience? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, even if his body were to be cut to pieces with a sharp sword, he would not give rise to a thought of malice toward anyone. He thinks thus: 'This is the nature of dharmas; it is the very nature of dharmas that they are empty. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of patience. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, generates the thought: 'I shall purify a buddha-field, I shall mature sentient beings, I shall realize full enlightenment. And he exerts vigor that is unshakable by any world, including the gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and by any ascetics or brahmins, or by any being whatsoever. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of vigor. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of meditation? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, enters into the concentrations, yet he does not perceive those concentrations as concentrations, nor does he perceive himself as one who has entered them. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of meditation. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the emptiness of form, and so on, up to the emptiness of all dharmas? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, perceives form as empty of form, and so on, up to consciousness as empty of consciousness. He perceives the eye as empty of the eye, and so on, up to the mind as empty of the mind. He perceives form as empty of form, and so on, up to mental phenomena as empty of mental phenomena. He perceives eye-consciousness as empty of eye-consciousness, and so on, up to mind-consciousness as empty of mind-consciousness. He perceives contact as empty of contact, and so on, up to feeling as empty of feeling. He perceives the conditioned co-arising of this whole mass of suffering as empty of conditioned co-arising. He perceives the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as empty of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. He perceives the four noble truths as empty of the four noble truths. He perceives the powers of a Tathāgata as empty of the powers of a Tathāgata, and so on, up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as empty of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the emptiness of form, and so on, up to the emptiness of all dharmas. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the signless, the wishless, and the non-origination of all dharmas? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive any sign in any dharma, nor does he perceive any wish for any dharma, nor does he perceive the origination of any dharma. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the signless, the wishless, and the non-origination of all dharmas. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the non-apprehension of all dharmas? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend form, nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not apprehend the eye, nor does he apprehend forms, nor does he apprehend eye-consciousness. He does not apprehend the ear, nor does he apprehend sounds, nor does he apprehend ear-consciousness. He does not apprehend the nose, nor does he apprehend odors, nor does he apprehend nose-consciousness. He does not apprehend the tongue, nor does he apprehend tastes, nor does he apprehend tongue-consciousness. He does not apprehend the body, nor does he apprehend tangibles, nor does he apprehend body-consciousness. He does not apprehend the mind, nor does he apprehend mental phenomena, nor does he apprehend mind-consciousness. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the non-apprehension of all dharmas. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the non-duality of all dharmas? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the duality of any dharma, nor does he perceive its non-duality. This is how, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the non-duality of all dharmas. Subhūti asked: "How, Blessed One, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the fact that all dharmas are like an illusion? The Blessed One replied: "Here, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection

If that consciousness does not possess the form of the object, then what is this restriction that consciousness is grasped and remembered only simultaneously with the grasping of the object? However, because it is included within that object, it is necessarily grasped by the very act of grasping it; thus, there is a restriction. Therefore, consciousness is indeed the very nature of the object, such that its grasping is inseparable from the grasping of the object, and its remembrance is inseparable from the remembrance of it. Furthermore, it is observed that when one of a pair of twins is grasped, there is the appearance of the other, as well as the remembrance "this is he. And there is the conceit of grasping a tree through its dark form. But if, having experienced the first consciousness, one perceives only the form of the grasper, and likewise the second [consciousness], then he says:
For if the first were of neither nature, then the second would not be distinguished by the reflective consciousness as being established in a single form. (385)

For by a subsequent reflective cognition (*parāmarśacetas*), a second [moment] could not be established as distinct from the first, because that second reflective cognition—given that it lacks both the nature of the first and its opposite—would likewise be established as having only a single form, namely, the very form of the apprehending subject (*grāhakākāra*). Consequently, how could there be a determination of distinction? Therefore, consciousness possesses only the form of the object; for this very reason.

The second type of intellect, characterized by the synthesis and cohesion of objects, subsequently takes as its support that very cognition which appears before it in the form of blue and other such [sensory data]. (386)

[408, viii] Therefore, because it possesses the form of the object, the second cognition takes as its support the preceding first cognition; it "clings to" (*āśliṣyati*) the synthesis of the object, and thus it is called "clinging to the synthesis of the object" (*arthasaṃkalanāśleṣā*). "Clinging" (*āśleṣa*) means "it clings" (*āśliṣyati*). The meaning is that this second cognition, which has a clinging through the synthesis of the object, takes that [first cognition] as its support. For if it did not possess that form [of the object], it would take only the [first cognition] itself as its support.
[Objection: But surely one does indeed apprehend the mere [form] alone; for instance, they remember only the subject, thinking, "I do not know what was seen by me at that time.
[Response: That too is incorrect.
Because there is doubt regarding the apprehended object (*grāhya*), there is likewise doubt regarding the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).
When there is apprehension by way of a generality (*sāmānya*), this same principle applies equally to the apprehended object as well. (PVA 1037)

[408, xiii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not easy for you to understand the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding the past. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the past limit of beings as follows: “There were such-and-such beings in the past; they were thus named, thus born, thus descended, thus of sustenance, thus long-lived, thus long-enduring, thus short-lived, thus experienced much pleasure, thus experienced much suffering, thus experienced much of both pleasure and suffering. There were those who passed away from there and were reborn here; and there were those who passed away from here and were reborn there. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the past limit of beings in its manifold aspects, with its various characteristics, its various descriptions, and its various conditions. This, Ānanda, is the first inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata, which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and beyond the sphere of logic, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only by the wise. Regarding this, the Tathāgata dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge. And because he dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge, the Tathāgata is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the first inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the future limit of beings as follows: “There will be such-and-such beings in the future; they will be thus named, thus born, thus descended, thus of sustenance, thus long-lived, thus long-enduring, thus short-lived, thus experienced much pleasure, thus experienced much suffering, thus experienced much of both pleasure and suffering. There will be those who pass away from there and are reborn here; and there will be those who pass away from here and are reborn there. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the future limit of beings in its manifold aspects, with its various characteristics, its various descriptions, and its various conditions. This, Ānanda, is the second inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata, which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and beyond the sphere of logic, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only by the wise. Regarding this, the Tathāgata dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge. And because he dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge, the Tathāgata is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the second inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the present middle period of beings as follows: “These beings exist in the present middle period; they are thus named, thus born, thus descended, thus of sustenance, thus long-lived, thus long-enduring, thus short-lived, thus experienced much pleasure, thus experienced much suffering, thus experienced much of both pleasure and suffering. There are those who pass away from there and are reborn here; and there are those who pass away from here and are reborn there. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the present middle period of beings in its manifold aspects, with its various characteristics, its various descriptions, and its various conditions. This, Ānanda, is the third inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata, which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and beyond the sphere of logic, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only by the wise. Regarding this, the Tathāgata dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge. And because he dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge, the Tathāgata is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the third inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the realm of sentient beings as it truly is, encompassing all realms of sentient beings: the realm of beings with form and the realm of beings without form; the realm of beings with perception and the realm of beings without perception; the realm of beings with neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the realm of beings in the state of non-ideation; the realm of beings in the attainment of cessation; the realm of beings who have gone to a good destination and the realm of beings who have gone to a bad destination; the realm of beings who are inferior and the realm of beings who are superior; and the realm of beings who are liberated in both ways and the realm of beings who are liberated by wisdom. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the realm of sentient beings as it truly is, encompassing all realms of sentient beings. This, Ānanda, is the fourth inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata, which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and beyond the sphere of logic, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only by the wise. Regarding this, the Tathāgata dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge. And because he dwells having fully realized it through direct knowledge, the Tathāgata is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the fourth inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the faculties of sentient beings as they truly are: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; the dull faculty and the sharp faculty; the well-purified faculty and the poorly-purified faculty; the faculty that has been cultivated and the faculty that has not been cultivated; the noble faculty and the ignoble faculty; the faculty that leads to penetration and the faculty that does not lead to penetration. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the faculties of sentient beings as they truly are. This, Ānanda, is the fifth inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata, which is difficult to see, difficult to understand, and beyond the sphere of logic, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only by the wise. This is the fifth inconceivable quality of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of sentient beings as they truly are. In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of sentient beings as they truly are. By the same logic that applies to the recollection of the subject (*grāhaka*) in a general sense, it applies equally to the object (*grāhya*). To explain: the recollection occurs precisely in the form of a general appearance of what was seen, such as "someone was seen by me. If, however, the very nature of the subject were recollected while devoid of its engagement with the object, then that would be its true nature, and it would not have been otherwise during the presence of the object. Consequently, how could that which is recollected later—possessing a different, non-subject nature—be the subject of that very [prior] state? Alternatively, if it is recollected in its actual reality (*tattvena*) as being situated within the object, then how can there be a recollection of it alone? Therefore, its nature as mounted upon that [object] cannot be separated [from it]. Thus, it is a single entity in the form of both [subject and object]; for if cognition did not possess a dual nature, then only the first [moment of] cognition would have the form of blue, and the subsequent ones would not. As the Ācārya said: "Furthermore, subsequent cognitions would not have the appearance of the objects of preceding cognitions, because those [preceding objects] are not their objects. For:

Otherwise, only the very first cognition would be connected [to the object], because the object exists [only then]; for a subsequent cognition is not connected with a preceding object whose relationship has not been perceived. (387)

[409,iii] For a subsequent cognition of the nature of consciousness does not have the object of a preceding cognition as its own object. And how can that which is not an object be apprehended? When the first [cognition] possesses the form of the object, then the second [cognition] also [possesses it]; for that which arises from it has the form of the awareness of that object-form. To explain:
When knowledge or ignorance arises regarding the cognition of that object’s form,
there is a connection by virtue of having that form, just as in the case of a distant tree and so forth.
(PVA 409,v)

Now, it might be argued that knowledge cannot be remembered otherwise; it is remembered only together with its object. Its very nature is defined by being mounted upon that [object], which is characterized by its engagement with it. Therefore, there is a memory of it as accompanied by the object. However, in the case of jars and the like, their nature can exist even alone and is not necessarily accompanied by a potter or other factors. An object, on the other hand, is perceived only in association with consciousness; therefore, it is remembered precisely as it was when it existed in that state. But this is not the case for jars and the like. That too is incorrect, because: [409, vi] [The verse follows:]... [text missing in source] ...because:
[409,vii] It is logical that there is a conjunction when two things are perceived as distinct; however, there is no determination of cognition apart from its blue form. (PVA 1039)
That this very thing exists as having the nature of pleasure and so forth is not established for you.

For it is not established for you that consciousness has the nature of pleasure and so forth, because pleasure and so forth are objects. And just as there is no consciousness other than pleasure and so forth, so too there is none other than blue and so forth. If it is argued that blue and so forth are merely objects of cognition because they exist in external space, [we reply: no, for even though they are not external, pleasure and so forth are admitted to be objects of cognition. Furthermore, in their being experienced, it is not ultimately logical to speak of "external" or "internal. Pleasure and so forth do not possess the status of a grasper with respect to blue and so forth, because even in the absence of [blue], pleasure and so forth appear in that very same way. And whatever occurs even without something else cannot be produced by that thing; yet pleasure and so forth occur even without the grasping of blue and so forth. Therefore, it has been demonstrated that the grasping of blue and so forth is produced solely by a specific intrinsic nature, since it exists even in the absence of [the object]. Consequently, it is established that there are two aspects: the aspect of the direct manifestation of blue and so forth, and the aspect of the experience [of that manifestation]. Moreover, let there be another aspect of the grasper; nevertheless...
Since an object that is being cognized simultaneously is necessarily [cognized] together with the cognition, by what characteristic could its distinctness from that [cognition] be established? (388)

[409,xi] For there is a simultaneous perception of the object, such as blue, together with the cognition; it is not separate from the cognition. Therefore, how can the object be something other than that perception? It must be that the perception itself is of such a nature, for it has been established that it is impossible to distinguish them. If it is argued that a manifestation of difference occurs, [409,xii]
And this differentiation would be seen by erroneous cognitions, just as the non-dual moon appears as two;

that is to say, just as the perception of two moons is a perception of difference within a single moon located in one place, so it is with respect to the self of consciousness. [Objection: But surely, even in the case of a single object, the perception of difference is logical because of the diversity of the forms (*ākāra*) of consciousness. However, how could this be the case with respect to the self? For at that very time, it cannot be otherwise. Indeed, how could its own nature be apprehended by that very same form of another? For that would entail the consequence of its own non-apprehension.
[409,xiv] This is not correct. Because:
If it is impossible to cognize the intrinsic nature in any other way,
then it is even more impossible to cognize the extrinsic nature.

If it is impossible to perceive the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) otherwise, and the extrinsic nature (*pararūpa*) cannot even be perceived as the intrinsic nature, then it follows that the extrinsic nature, like the intrinsic nature, is simply impossible to perceive. Therefore, this is the meaning: when self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) occurs, difference cannot be perceived within the intrinsic nature. However, if consciousness were a single, variegated form (*citrākāra*), it could be perceived through self-awareness, for otherwise it would be untenable. Consequently, even in the case of seeing two moons, if there were no unity, it could not be perceived, because it is impossible to perceive it either by itself or by another; this has already been established. Therefore, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a later time, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which postulates a duality of forms, is not a perception (*pratyakṣa*). This very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "And difference [is perceived] by erroneous cognitions" (*bhedaś ca bhrāntavijñānaiḥ*). That which is intended as two moons is actually non-dual (*advaya*), because it is contained within a single cognition. If this is so, then one must also admit that blue and yellow, when seen together, constitute a single variegated form, since that variegated form of the nature of awareness is unitary even in those cases. If, however, a distinction between them is desired, then it must be accepted in this way.
There is no restriction of simultaneous cognition for two distinct things, such as blue and yellow. (389)

This alone is the cause of distinction, namely, the state of having different fates (*bhinnayogakṣematā*). However, because the appearance of two moons lacks this state of having different fates, it is indeed one.

[Objection: But how can there be unity given the superimposition of contradictory properties? For this very thing is what is called "difference," namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties; and here, contradiction is characterized by the state of mutual exclusion.
[Response: This is not so.
That kind of contradiction exists only between permanence and its opposite;
there is no contradiction between the two when they enter into the process of cognition. (PVA 1042)

[410, vii] Precisely because they enter into a single cognition, there is no contradiction between the two. That very fact—that it is called "inseparable"—is its nature. And it is not contradicted by that very same thing. Therefore, it is said through conceptual construction that it has only a single form, based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He shows that, in ultimate reality, that very absence of positive and negative concomitance does not exist.
[410, viii]
There is no object whatsoever that is not perceived, nor is there the perception of a non-object;
since both are observed as being perceived, there is no distinction between them. (390)
Because there is neither positive nor negative concomitance, the cognition of blue is indeed one, since it is not observed to exist apart from the other; for instance:
An object is not observed to be non-cognized, nor is cognition [observed] without an object;
because they are never dissociated, there is therefore the absolute cognition of the object.
One who knows distinctions desires a distinction for the sake of its specific application.
If that [difference] does not exist, then what indeed is the distinctness between difference and non-difference?

(PVA 1044) Therefore, in this case, the opponent must establish "difference" as a mere name; there is no harm whatsoever to the [proponent's] position. If there is no distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted therein, what is the use of such a difference?

[410,xiii] How then is it that when one says, "Bring the blue," the bringing of yellow is not performed? At that time, because that yellow does not appear at all, it is not brought. However, the blue which is inseparable from it is indeed what was intended. And that which is established within cognition is distinct; it cannot be led otherwise. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the conventional usage of difference is merely non-real (*atāttvika*) based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Therefore, it is unavoidable that an object appearing at the same time as its cognition is non-different from that cognition.

Because they share an identical state of security and well-being (*yogakṣema*), the oneness of the object with the cognition is unavoidable; for it cannot be averted. Thus, cognition possesses a form (*sākāra*).

[Objection: If that is so, then only cognition is perceived, not the object. If that [object] were also perceived, there would be the experience of two forms—the blue and so forth; and if that too were to appear at the time of the cognition, the object would again not be seen. Thus, by necessitating further forms, there would be an infinite regress and a logical inconsistency.
[Response: Here is the rebuttal.
Inference based on the distinction between causes would occur. // 391 //

For one who has perceived a cognition possessing a blue form, a cause corresponding to that [form] is inferred on the grounds that there must be some cause for it; however, this [cause] is not directly an object of perception, due to the fault of contradiction mentioned previously. If it is asked, "How can there even be an inference of something that is absolutely unperceived? he says:
Because of the absence of sensory cognitions, even though other causes are present.

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭam anumānam*) proceeds solely by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). For instance: even when the eye, light, and attention are present, visual consciousness (*akṣavijñāna*) bearing the form of a pillar does not arise in a place intended to be empty of a pillar, whereas elsewhere it arises instantaneously. From this it is known that there must be some other object (*vastu*) present here; because of its absence, there is an absence [of the cognition] elsewhere. That such an object is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), being external and known as devoid of the conditions for perception (*darśanopādhi*). [Objection: How then can that be the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? [Reply: Because the form of that [object] is the object of direct perception, there is no other way [to account for it]; thus, it is called an "object" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). If this is so, then the object of knowledge is indeed the external object itself, and not mere consciousness (*samvedana-mātra*). He shows that this is not the established position (*sthita-pakṣa*) here.
If one were not to state a restriction regarding the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), [verse 392].

[411, viii] Should another object be postulated as the producer of the distinction in mental aspects, or is it simply some particularity of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)? In this regard, the postulation of an object that is entirely unobserved is not sound, precisely because such a postulation occurs only when there is no other possible recourse. However, when this mental aspect is established solely through the power of previously observed perceptions, then the postulation of an external object is redundant. Furthermore, postulation follows what has been observed and not otherwise; for it is impossible to postulate what has never been observed. Indeed, postulations are seen to follow observation; therefore, it is impossible to postulate otherwise.

[411,ix] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is permanent or impermanent; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is permanent or impermanent. He does not perceive that form is pleasant or painful; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is pleasant or painful. He does not perceive that form is self or non-self; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is self or non-self. He does not perceive that form is calm or not calm; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is calm or not calm. He does not perceive that form is empty or not empty; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is empty or not empty. He does not perceive that form is with signs or signless; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is with signs or signless. He does not perceive that form is wishful or wishless; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is wishful or wishless. Why is this? Because form is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither calm nor not calm, neither empty nor not empty, neither with signs nor signless, and neither wishful nor wishless. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent, neither pleasant nor painful, neither self nor non-self, neither calm nor not calm, neither empty nor not empty, neither with signs nor signless, and neither wishful nor wishless. Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive these dharmas in this way, he practices the perfection of wisdom. The Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom should train as follows: 'I shall not abandon all sentient beings. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates such a thought, he should train in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives that 'I shall abandon all sentient beings,' he is not training in the perfection of wisdom. But surely, even an external object is indeed observed to be the producer of a form, just as the state of having a globular shape does not exist without a tree. [Objection: Even in that case, by whom is it seen that the tree itself is the producer? [Reply: No, because for that very person, it is not an object of cognition. [Objection: It is seen by another person. [Reply: This has already been examined; it is seen by that very same person. [Objection: If it is seen later by him, how do you know it existed previously? [Objection: Because of its being seen later. [Reply: If it is indeed perceived later, let it come into existence only later; for that perception does not operate with respect to the prior time. Furthermore, that perception belongs only to the form of the cognition, not to the object. Therefore, the determination that "the object exists there" based on later perception is merely a conclusion. Since "later" is not a final point, there is no actual apprehension. Thus, since the object is not seen and its dependence on mental impressions (*vāsanā*) has already been established, one must conclude—through the process of subtle analysis—that the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) alone is the cause of the restriction. However, if someone is not thus proficient, they may maintain the existence of an external object of knowledge through the inference of a distinction in causes.
[411,x] But surely, in the absence of external objects, how can there be the relation of cause and effect, as well as the relation of the signified and the signifier? For instance:
For those who understand, the relation of cause and effect could exist even without external objects;
yet, because there would be no fixed rule for those [cognitions], there would be neither effect nor cause.
(PVA 411, xiii) 1045
For instance:
[411,xiv] Because it appears yellow after appearing blue, it is like the appearance of blue.
In this way, how can there be a state of mutual causality between cause and effect?

When a cognition appearing as yellow occurs immediately after a cognition appearing as blue, since there is no yellow apart from that appearance of yellow, the cause of that [yellow cognition] is only the appearance of blue, not the yellow object itself. Nor is there any fixed rule in that regard; for from an appearance of yellow, an appearance of blue could likewise arise. To have mutual causality would contradict reason. How indeed can there be mutual causality between cause and effect? If external objects exist, however, the blue object itself is the cause in that case, while the appearance of yellow is merely the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). And the immediately preceding condition, being differentiated by the distinctness of its objective auxiliary (*arthasahakārin*), does not attain identity; thus, there would be no lack of fixed rule. Alternatively, the function of the immediately preceding condition lies in the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatā*); whereas regarding the form (*ākāra*), it belongs to the blue object and so forth. Since there is a fixed rule in that regard, there is no fault. If the nature of consciousness were to arise from something other than the nature of consciousness, or if that form were to arise from something other than the blue object, then there would be a lack of fixed rule.

[412,ii] But is it not the case that even from a white object, such as a conch, a yellow form is perceived, and even from something small, a large form is perceived? Therefore, in this case as well, there is simply no fixed rule.
This is not so; for:
[412,iv] Because it is produced by a deluded continuum, this is inconsistent in that case.
But in the case of the negation of non-erroneousness, there is no other alternative than restriction.

(PVA 412,v) Since that which is an incongruous perception arising from error is simply not authoritative, there is no deviation [of the reason] by means of it. Likewise, the production of a sprout from a seed is accepted, and not the reverse.

For the Vijñānavādins, however, there is no seed or the like other than the appearance of a seed and so forth; therefore, there is no fixed rule that from the appearance of a seed comes a sprout, and from that [sprout] comes the appearance of a seed. And thus, conventional practice would be abolished. Furthermore, the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*jñāpyajñāpakabhāva*) is utterly cast aside. It is established that "there is fire because of smoke," and that which is beyond perception is the object of inference (*anumeya*). Now, neither external fire nor the appearance of fire is anything other than immediate (*aparokṣa*), since both consist of the nature of cognition. Nor is the appearance of another’s [fire] being established there, because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). If it is argued that it is only one's own future appearance that is inferred, we say no, because there is no fixed rule. Therefore, the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*) alone is more sound.
To this, it is said:
[412, viii]
The production of a sprout from a seed, the establishment of fire through smoke—such is the status of the causal and the indicative, even when it relies upon external objects. (393)

If it is argued that those [objects] also, appearing with such forms and having such indeterminate connections, are merely conceptualized in dependence upon cognitions, then what contradiction is there? (394)

[412,x] In this context, the purpose is fulfilled by the appearance alone, not by the object itself. For that which does not appear, even if it exists, is no different from the non-existent. To explain: existence is defined as perception. Thus:
Even in the absence of an external object, a manifestation is not defective;
however, without manifestation, the external would always remain merely external.

It has been established that a manifestation occurs even without an external object; and an external object does not exist apart from its manifestation, because it is never perceived independently of that manifestation. Therefore, what contradiction is there in the causal relationship where the manifestation of a sprout arises from the manifestation of a seed? In that case, the manifestation of the sprout should not occur by itself. For if it were to manifest alone in the absence of the manifestation of the seed, it would follow that it is causeless. However, for the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), there is no charge of causelessness, because the seed exists even while it is being clearly manifested. To explain:
Even when the external object does not appear, its externality is not lost;
however, for one who knows, when there is no appearance at all, it simply does not exist. (PVA 1049)

[413,i] Now, if there exists therein the appearance of another, then it is not causeless. Yet, this is not so because of the absence of restriction; nor does the arising of a dream-appearance proceed from the appearance of another. That too is the same, because:
If this object does not appear at all to anyone,
what proof is there for its existence, by virtue of which a sprout could have it as its cause?

For that which is devoid of description (nirupākhya) is characterized by the absence of any designation of causal capacity (*sāmarthya*). If it is argued that it exists because it is perceived later, the answer has already been stated.
If it is argued that its existence is known through its effect, then its existence is understood only once the relationship of cause and effect has been established.
If that existence were already established, there could be a causal relationship;

however, because of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), there is simply no establishment. This [superimposition] is also observed precisely due to the superimposition of identity upon the object.

But surely, who prevents superimposition (*āropa*) even in the case of consciousness? Since consciousness itself is non-existent, how can there be superimposition? This is the same for the external object as well; the external object is also said to exist only because of superimposition. Thus, even the appearance exists indeed from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). For the existence of the external object existing at the time of inference is nothing other than its superimposition. And so, if something were present here [in the fire], then the fire would be seen. And likewise, if something were present here, the appearance would certainly occur. If you say that the appearance is one thing and the object is another, this is the same [as our position]: that the object is another. Even in that case, their identity is not ultimate. Just as in the case of two people with ophthalmia seeing two moons, the conventional usage occurs within consciousness and elsewhere. Therefore, even in the Vijñānavāda (Idealist) doctrine, if the relation of cause and effect is established by relying on cognitions through the connection with a determinate appearance of that form, what contradiction is there? But in the Bāhyārthavāda (Realist) doctrine, contradiction has been demonstrated due to the lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore:
[413,vii] If the external object were eternal, it would be perceived only later. If it were perceived previously, then everything would be perceived in all its forms. (PVA 1052)
If external fire and so forth were eternal, their cognition would have already occurred in a single form; for what purpose, then, would one proceed by means of inference?

Now, if its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not apprehended through inference, how then can there be a cognition of its existence? The apprehension of it through another form (*pararūpeṇa*) is equally applicable to the nature of consciousness itself. The conceptualization of something else proceeds by unifying the perceived object with the mental construction (*vikalpa*); it thus superimposes that [conceptual form] upon it. What is the use of this superimposed [form]? Otherwise, in the absence of that [superimposition], the object would subsequently appear as something interrupted. How could there be the existence of something interrupted without that [unification]? If it is argued that the purpose is served by the conceptualization of non-interruption, then the mental impression (*vāsanā*) will exist in the interval. Even so, there is still only interruption for the mental impression, because it lacks that [objective] form. If it is argued that the same must be accepted regarding the object, then it possesses that form; for what is seen cannot be cognized as identical to what is unseen. It is merely a case of superimposition alone. This is the same even for the proponents of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*).
[413,x] But surely, how can that [continuity] remain uninterrupted by a latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of a heterogeneous consciousness situated in between?
Just as when there is the emergence of something heterogeneous from the application of lac-dye, the world considers there to be no interruption of the lac-fruit, so it is here. (PVA 1053)
In the interval, there occurs the arising of a collection of heterogeneous cognitions.
Precisely because it follows from that very latent impression (*vāsanā*), there will be no interruption.

Likewise, in the world, it is designated that the application of lac-dye to the seeds, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and so forth—which fall within the interval—bestows a specific potency inferable from the final fruit, and thus produces [the result] without interruption. Similarly, let the preceding cognition of fire also be designated or determined as producing its effect without interruption, because it imparts its own potency into the succeeding cognition of fire—even while passing through heterogeneous intervening cognitions—as if it were mounted upon them. Therefore, that very preceding cognition produces the cognition of fire, not the cognition of smoke. In this regard, just as the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins) postulate that "there was previously fire" based on the subsequent cognition of fire, so too the proponents of consciousness-only (vijñānavādins) postulate that "there was a latent impression (vāsanā). There is no difference between these two positions. From the cognition of smoke, too, a latent impression of smoke is postulated, and the causality of the latent impression has been established; however, the status of an external object as a cause is not logically tenable. And this has already been demonstrated.
[414,ii] Smoke might be something not produced by fire; thus, there would be no cognition of the cause from its effect.
Or, even if it were a cause, how could there be a certain cognition [of that specific cause]? 395.

[414,iii] If the appearance arises solely from the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of smoke, then that [appearance] itself is the smoke; it is that very thing which constitutes the relationship of cause and effect. For in that case, smoke would not arise from fire, because it would be bound exclusively to its own latent impression. Alternatively, if the appearance of fire is also a cause of the appearance of smoke—by virtue of being conducive to the awakening of that [smoke's] latent impression—then in that case, smoke too would be a cause of fire. And if there is such mutual causality, how can there be any certain determination [of the direction of causation], given the possibility of deviation?
To this it is replied:
Even in that case, the cognition appearing as smoke possesses a latent impression (vāsanā) potent for awakening.
One should understand that it is only the cognition appearing like fire that is being conveyed, not the actual fire itself.

[414, vi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Non-Origination of All Dharmas. Ānanda, you should learn it thus. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the non-arising of all dharmas? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, ignorance is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Formations are the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Consciousness is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Name-and-form is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. The six sense bases are the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Contact is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Feeling is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Craving is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Grasping is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Becoming is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Birth is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Old age and death are the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Thus, Ānanda, ignorance is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; formations are the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; consciousness is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; name-and-form is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; the six sense bases are the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; contact is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; feeling is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; craving is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; grasping is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; becoming is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; birth is the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas; old age and death are the cause and condition for the non-arising of all dharmas. Therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Non-Origination of All Dharmas. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many kinds of non-arising are there? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are two kinds of non-arising. What are the two? They are the non-arising of the conditioned and the non-arising of the unconditioned. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are three kinds of non-arising. What are the three? They are the non-arising of the past, the non-arising of the future, and the non-arising of the present. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are four kinds of non-arising. What are the four? They are the non-arising of form, the non-arising of feeling, the non-arising of perception, and the non-arising of volitional formations. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are five kinds of non-arising. What are the five? They are the non-arising of eye-consciousness, the non-arising of ear-consciousness, the non-arising of nose-consciousness, the non-arising of tongue-consciousness, and the non-arising of body-consciousness. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are six kinds of non-arising. What are the six? They are the non-arising of the aggregate of form, the non-arising of the aggregate of feeling, the non-arising of the aggregate of perception, the non-arising of the aggregate of volitional formations, and the non-arising of the aggregate of consciousness. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are seven kinds of non-arising. What are the seven? They are the non-arising of the element of earth, the non-arising of the element of water, the non-arising of the element of fire, the non-arising of the element of wind, the non-arising of the element of space, the non-arising of the element of consciousness, and the non-arising of the element of ignorance. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are eight kinds of non-arising. What are the eight? They are the non-arising of the eye-base, the non-arising of the form-base, the non-arising of the ear-base, the non-arising of the sound-base, the non-arising of the nose-base, the non-arising of the odor-base, the non-arising of the tongue-base, and the non-arising of the taste-base. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are nine kinds of non-arising. What are the nine? They are the non-arising of the body-base, the non-arising of the tangible-base, the non-arising of the mind-base, the non-arising of the mental-object-base, the non-arising of the realm of desire, the non-arising of the realm of form, the non-arising of the formless realm, the non-arising of the realm of sentient beings, and the non-arising of the realm of insentient things. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are ten kinds of non-arising. What are the ten? They are the non-arising of the realm of hell, the non-arising of the realm of animals, the non-arising of the realm of hungry ghosts, the non-arising of the realm of humans, the non-arising of the realm of gods, the non-arising of the realm of the four great kings, the non-arising of the realm of the thirty-three gods, the non-arising of the realm of Yāma, the non-arising of the realm of Tuṣita, and the non-arising of the realm of Nirmāṇarati. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are eleven kinds of non-arising. What are the eleven? They are the non-arising of the realm of Paranirmitavaśavartin, the non-arising of the realm of Brahmakāyika, the non-arising of the realm of Brahmapurohita, the non-arising of the realm of Mahābrahmā, the non-arising of the realm of Parīttābha, the non-arising of the realm of Apramāṇābha, the non-arising of the realm of Ābhāsvara, the non-arising of the realm of Parīttaśubha, the non-arising of the realm of Apramāṇaśubha, the non-arising of the realm of Śubhakṛtsna, and the non-arising of the realm of Anabhraka. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are twelve kinds of non-arising. What are the twelve? They are the non-arising of the realm of Puṇyaprasava, the non-arising of the realm of Bṛhatphala, the non-arising of the realm of Avṛha, the non-arising of the realm of Atapa, the non-arising of the realm of Sudṛśa, the non-arising of the realm of Sudarśana, the non-arising of the realm of Akaniṣṭha, the non-arising of the realm of Ākāśānantyāyatana, the non-arising of the realm of Vijñānānantyāyatana, the non-arising of the realm of Ākiṃcanyāyatana, the non-arising of the realm of Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana, and the non-arising of the realm of the cessation of perception and feeling. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are thirteen kinds of non-arising. What are the thirteen? They are the non-arising of the realm of the Stream-enterer, the non-arising of the realm of the Once-returner, the non-arising of the realm of the Non-returner, the non-arising of the realm of the Arhat, the non-arising of the realm of the Pratyekabuddha, the non-arising of the realm of the Bodhisattva, the non-arising of the realm of the Tathāgata, the non-arising of the realm of the Dharma, the non-arising of the realm of the Saṅgha, the non-arising of the realm of the precepts, the non-arising of the realm of concentration, the non-arising of the realm of wisdom, and the non-arising of the realm of liberation. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are fourteen kinds of non-arising. What are the fourteen? They are the non-arising of the realm of the emptiness of internal phenomena, the non-arising of the realm of the emptiness of external phenomena, the non-arising of the realm of the emptiness of internal and external phenomena, the non-arising of the realm of the emptiness of emptiness, the non-arising of the

For cognition appearing as smoke is bound by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire; therefore, that impression is inferred from it. Since that impression is on the verge of being awakened, it produces the appearance of fire; thus, through the attainment of the appearance of the fire, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example, for those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), fire is inferred, and there is either the appearance of fire or another fire, and from that, the attainment of fire dependent upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*). In the same way, the appearance of smoke and the future appearance of fire are dependent upon the latent impression. If it is argued that the two fires—the one perceived and the other—must be identical, we say no, because there is a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such identity. If you claim that their identity arises solely from the power of the latent impression, we reply that it has already been established that, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is the latent impression alone that is one, not the actual object. Furthermore, even regarding an external object, it is not the fire itself that is inferred, but rather the future appearance [of fire], because the purposes of living beings consist in that [appearance]. For no one has any need for a fire that does not appear. And if the object to be inferred is necessarily accompanied by an appearance, let it be the future appearance itself; what is the use of inferring the fire? If it is asked how there can be an inference of something that is yet to be (*bhāvin*), we reply: precisely because it is observed to be so.

[414, vii] Since it has been seen that "it is exactly thus," this is not observed to be illogical; however, regarding an external object, there is neither correspondence nor the possibility of perception. (PVA 1055)
[414, viii] Everything is entirely consistent when it is inferred by means of a future manifestation itself. But in the case of external objects, even a dream is not possible. For instance:
Likewise, the cognition of a future object is well-ascertained through inference; however, it has been demonstrated that there is no cognition of a present object. (PVA 1056) [414,x]

Otherwise, no one would engage in activity with respect to a future object. If, however, one engages by determining the identity between the present and the future, then this is simply a cognition of the future object and not a cognition of the present; [and it is] that cognition which is "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭā*). For the truth of a cognition is inferred through its attainment (*prāpti*); therefore, because the present form is not attained and the future is the opposite, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has the future as its very object. Although the present state exists, it is non-existent in that regard. Even perception (*pratyakṣa*) is a means of valid cognition only with respect to the future; and so it has been demonstrated.

[414,xi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to speak of the Tathāgata as being ‘in this world,’ that would be a wrong view; if one were to speak of the Tathāgata as being ‘not in this world,’ that would also be a wrong view. If one were to speak of the Tathāgata as being ‘both in this world and not in this world,’ that would also be a wrong view; if one were to speak of the Tathāgata as being ‘neither in this world nor not in this world,’ that would also be a wrong view. Thus it was said. And so forth, as in the Sūtra. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to say that the Tathāgata exists after death, that would be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, that would also be a wrong view. Thus it was said. And so forth, as in the Sūtra. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to say that the Tathāgata exists before birth, that would be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata does not exist before birth, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist before birth, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist before birth, that would also be a wrong view. Thus it was said. And so forth, as in the Sūtra. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to say that the Tathāgata exists after death, that would be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death, that would also be a wrong view. Thus it was said. And so forth, as in the Sūtra. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to say that the Tathāgata exists before birth, that would be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata does not exist before birth, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist before birth, that would also be a wrong view; if one were to say that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist before birth, that would also be a wrong view. Thus it was said. And so forth, as in the Sūtra. Thus it was said. And so forth, as in the Sūtra.
