Therefore, what was stated—that this object is future and does not exist at the time of cognition—is refuted. Since [the cognition] does not occur without the future object, perception arising from that sensory contact is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, this [objection] is also answered: "It is not a cause [of valid knowledge], because it is the apprehension of something presently existing. Therefore, since perception and inference have the future as their object, and because they conform to the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [future object], they possess the status of valid knowledge. In the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), everything has only its own nature (*svarūpa*) as its object; in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), however, it has the external object as its object. And since that future object is the object of attainment, it alone possesses the status of being an "object" (*artha*) because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). If conventional usage is accepted, then it follows that the object must indeed be the present one; and since that object is only the present, why is it asserted that [perception] has the future as its object?
To this, it is said:
This conventional discourse is threefold, according to the distinctions of the unlearned and so forth;
based upon it, all this appears as if it were logical.

For those who are untrained, linguistic convention consists of perception whose object is a present thing; for the trained, it has a future object; and for the highly trained, it has as its object mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*) alone. Thus, if the status of having an object in the present is established with respect to ordinary people who are untrained, we are exactly in the same position. Therefore, the cognition appearing as smoke leads only to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire. And that impression, being perceived as identical with a future appearance, is the motivator toward an appearance of that form; thus, that very future appearance is what is understood, just like a future fire in the view of those who maintain external objects. Consequently, in ultimate reality, the object is nothing but appearance itself.
[415,iv] But surely, if even subsequently there is a mistaken appearance, there can be no desire for that object.

In this world, there is a desire for an object only when it is a real thing; however, there is no desire for what merely appears, for no worldly person seeks after something like the pleasure experienced in a dream.
That is incorrect; for:
[415, viii] If, having attained the firmness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it were not subject to reconnection (*pratisandhi*)...
That would be a dream-like pleasure; what harm is there in that for you?

Where there is such a lack of dissolution precisely due to a particularity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that is not merely dream-happiness. Even for the Vijñānavādins, the distinction between dream and non-dream certainly exists due to a particularity of latent impressions, just as within a dream itself there is the distinction between being awake and otherwise. Or let it be a specific kind of dream; even in that case, there will be desire for it—what loss is this to you, O unrefined ones? But for those who desire liberation—the supreme jewels adorning the crest of the wise—it is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) that all happiness is simply undesirable. Thus, since there is no engagement [with it], attachment is established as something already proven. To explain: [The verse follows: *svapne dṛṣṭamivātyantavismṛtaṃ jāgrati smṛtam / sukhaṃ me nābhimantavyaṃ tadvad bālajanair api // tasmān na kiṃcid duḥkhena sukhena ca phalaṃ mama / iti niścayavān yogī na sukhaduḥkhābhibhūyate //* In the waking state, one remembers what was seen in a dream and completely forgotten; even so, one should not cherish the thought "this happiness is mine. This applies even to ordinary people. Therefore, the yogin who possesses the certainty, "There is no fruit for me whatsoever through either suffering or happiness," is not overcome by pleasure or pain.*/[End of verse] For instance: *na hi svapne 'pi saṃsārasukhaṃ kaścid abhīpsati / mohād eva hi tatrāpi sukhabuddhiḥ pravartate // tasmāt sarvasukheṣv eva nāstikyam upapadyate / tadabhāvāc ca saṃsāre pravṛttir naiva yujyate //* Indeed, no one desires the happiness of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) even in a dream; for it is only through delusion (*moha*) that the notion of happiness arises therein. Therefore, the doctrine of universal nihilism regarding all happiness is logically consistent. And because of its absence, engagement in cyclic existence is not at all tenable.*/[End of verse] Thus it is said: *duḥkhābhāvo na caiva syāt sukhābhāvād ṛte kvacit / tasmāt sarvasukheṣv eva nāstikyam upapadyate //* And nowhere can the absence of suffering exist without the absence of happiness. Those who desire liberation and possess patience do not seek the pleasures of saṃsāra; therefore, their livelihood is based on dharma for the sake of establishing their turning away from those [pleasures]. (PVA 1060)

[415,xi] For those discerning persons who have directed their gaze toward liberation and who regard all means of accomplishing the Dharma for the sake of worldly happiness as nothing more than the play of children, there is an engagement with the Dharma in order to turn away from the mockery of worldly conventions. Therefore, valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely conventional and has only the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) as its object. If, then, the appearance of fire and so forth is strictly bound to latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and that [appearance] is bound specifically to a predisposition of its own kind, then from the appearance of smoke, only that [smoke’s] predisposition should be inferred; how, then, can there be a comprehension of the predisposition for fire? To this [it is replied]:

Indeed, the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) which operate as the manifestation of a particular form are the cause for the manifestation of that very form, and not for the manifestation of anything else. (PVA 1061) [415,
xiii]

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fire does not produce the appearance of smoke, because that appearance is produced solely by the latent impression of smoke itself. Therefore, one thing that is produced by another cannot lead to the cognition of something else that is not its producer.
To this, it is replied:

[415,xv] It is precisely the mental continuum, containing within it the latencies suitable for that [cognition], which manifests the cognition appearing as smoke; therefore, smoke [is known] from fire. || 397 ||

[415,xvi] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Thus it was said. What is the meaning of this? Here, “physical food” refers to edible food that is substantial. “Contact” is the conjunction of the three—eye, visible form, and visual consciousness—and so forth, up to the conjunction of mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness. “Mental volition” is the intention directed toward the three realms of existence. “Consciousness” is the sixfold consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness. Among these, physical food sustains beings who have already been born in the desire realm. Contact sustains beings who have already been born in the form realm. Mental volition sustains beings who have already been born in the formless realm. Consciousness sustains beings who are seeking a new existence. Why is this? Because when one has not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, one is reborn there; when one has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm, one is reborn there; when one has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm, one is reborn there; and when one has not yet abandoned craving for existence, one enters the womb. The entire manifold of saṃsāra arises from the mind alone. Therefore, the appearance of fire arises from a continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*) supported by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) capable of generating the appearance of fire. And that same continuum produces the appearance of smoke through the embellishment of another moment of consciousness that awakens the latent impression of smoke. Thus, the latent impression of smoke is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the appearance of smoke, with the latent impression of fire acting as its auxiliary cause (*sahakāri*). For the future appearance of fire as well, the latent impression of fire is the material cause, while the appearance of smoke is the auxiliary cause because it acts as the awakener; and the latent impression of smoke is also an auxiliary cause. Consequently, because they depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*), the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) between fire and its effect, smoke, is perfectly logical.

[416,i] But surely, if the status of being a signifier (*gamaka*) depends on dependence upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then the relationship of signified and signifier (*gamyagamakabhāva*) would exist only between two things that are simultaneous; there could be no cognition of what is future, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is not so;
for it has been established that the state of being an object of cognition applies to everything that is yet to come.
Is fire also apprehended from smoke at that very moment?

(PVA 1062) [416, iv] Only that which is to be (bhāvin) possesses the status of being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For if it were understood from smoke that "fire exists right now," and not that "it will exist later," then there would be no valid cognition at all; for there is no need for that fire existing at that [future] time. If it is argued that there is indeed doubt regarding what is to be, how can it be a valid cognition? A valid cognition is so called because it reveals the object. It is not the case that an object must be revealed by a valid cognition to the cognizer only at a different time.

[416,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the eye as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive form as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the earth element as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive ignorance as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the conditioned as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the past as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the future or the present as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the world of desire as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the world of form or the formless world as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the once-returner, non-returner, or arhat as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the Tathāgata as having an intrinsic nature. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as having an intrinsic nature.”

[Objection: But surely, even if that [object] is perceived, it does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*); thus, it is merely a non-entity (*anartha*). [Response: Because a future causal function is possible, this too performs a causal function by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), since the effect is metaphorically attributed to the cause. [Objection: If that is so, then for the Vijñānavādins as well, there is indeed the state of being accessible through a latent impression (*vāsanā*) at that time. If you ask, "What is the point of that, given the absence of the performance of a causal function?"—this is the same for the external object as well. Since it performs a causal function by means of a future object, it too is a performer of a causal function; this is equally true for the latent impression. Even the object, at that time, is accessible solely through the latent impression. If it is accessed by another [means], then the latent impression is likewise accessed by another. For it is not the case that, regarding the latent impression, there is no comprehension for another person through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, the inference is the same for both the proponent of external objects and the proponent of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Consequently, representation-only alone is logical.

[(kha) Duality based on dependence on another: How then is it that the Teacher has stated that cognition possesses a dual form even with respect to external objects? Is it not rather logical that this [dual form] belongs to cognition alone?
To this, it is said:
[416, viii]
This is the consensus of the learned; however, it is accepted by resorting to external objects.
Its dual nature is established through the rule of simultaneous cognition. (398)

[416,ix] The possession of two forms is described from the perspective of others who accept external objects; however, for the wise, there is only consciousness (*vijñāna*). For it has been established that a restriction of cognition is not logical between two distinct things. Furthermore, if consciousness were formless and its form were something else entirely, then at times the form of the apprehender would be perceived as separate. Yet, when perceiving yellow, that very same form is perceived as distinct from the blue. If it is argued that "that very same blue [appears] with the form of pleasure, and that very same [blue] with the form of pain," this is not so. [416,x]
That very same form of the apprehender which was previously seen as yellow and so forth is indeed this very cognition; is this then perception or inference? (PVA 416, xi) 1063.

It is not, first of all, perception (*pratyakṣa*), because perception does not operate with respect to the relation of prior and posterior. In the absence of that [perception], there is no inference (*anumāna*); thus, priority and posteriority are not objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How then is there inference elsewhere, such as in the case of fire, given that perception is incapable of grasping positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? It is not so, because inference has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. Inference intends a single object of a single reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*); for instance, having superimposed a unity upon those residing in the kitchen and other locations by means of another individual, it is proven that "this very same fire" exists. But [in reality] there is no ultimate unity at all. Likewise here too, having accepted the non-difference of the continuum (*santāna*)—thinking "this very same form of the grasper and this very same blue exist even today, distinct from that"—the difference between the grasped and the grasper is proven, or rather, the difference between the nature of consciousness and the form of blue. Therefore, there is no difference in the real entity (*vastu*), but rather in the continuum which exists as a conceptual construct (*prajñaptisat*) by way of a universal. However, with respect to the ultimately real particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is indeed the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*). Thus, non-difference alone is the ultimate truth. Furthermore, if consciousness were formless (*nirākāra*), then it would always be pure and never possess forms such as sharp, dull, or turbid; yet it does occur otherwise. For instance:
[(ga) The twofold nature of consciousness: Cognition, according to the differences of the sense faculties, possesses qualities such as being sharp, dull, or blurred.
Even while bearing a distinction in its appearance regarding the object, it is seen as one. || 399 ||
[417,ii] How can there be a multiplicity of forms within a single object? For this reason:

Because the object has an undifferentiated nature, the mind would have to be of a single form. If it were argued that all [cognitions] are of that same object because of the object itself, then in that case, there would be no subjectivity (āmata) belonging to it. // 400 //

[417,iv] If consciousness were formless (*nirākāra*), then only the object would be the apprehended (*grāhya*). Furthermore, it appears as having only a single form; therefore, it appears as that very single form. Consequently, there would be no distinction in the appearance. This establishes that there is no multiplicity of forms in the object.

But even if there is the assumption of the form of the object, how can there be a single form when there is multiplicity of forms? Therefore, the fault of multiplicity of forms remains exactly as it was. It is not a fault, because:
[417, vi] For that which arises based on the object and imitates its form, [the cognition assumes a single form].
It may have a distinction from others even in some respect. (401)

vii] Because it would follow that there is the arising of that form [in the cognition], the possession of that form could arise from something other than the object, just as the form of the moon arises through the power of cataracts and so forth. [417, viii] Thus, there would be a dual form.
For in this way, although a son resembles his father by depending upon him, he nevertheless maintains a distinction from his father in certain respects for some reason. (402)
For a son, though born resembling his father, does not fail to take on even the features of his mother; thus he demonstrates difference precisely through the distinction of the sense faculties.
Those with weak vision perceive a circular halo around lamps and other light sources, appearing like the eye of a peacock's feather, radiant with blue and red hues. (403)

Those whose visual power is impaired by darkness perceive a lamp as radiant, surrounded by a halo, and differentiated by distinct forms such as blue and so forth. Now, if that very form of the lamp were real in that manner,
then—
If that [cognition] were external in form, what would be the objection regarding one with clear vision?
Even one with clear vision would perceive it; or rather, he too would indeed have clear vision and not have impaired faculties. For:
And seeing what is real, how could one who perceives it have impaired faculties? (404)

[417,xv] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, are called ‘true sons of the Śākya. What are these four? They are: one who is a trainee (śaikṣa), one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa), one who has entered the stream (srotāpanna), and one who has attained parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin). They are: one who is a trainee, one who is beyond training, one who has entered the stream, and one who has attained parinirvāṇa through the body (kāyasākṣin). Thus it was said. What is the meaning of this? Thus it was said. What is the meaning of this? Vision is said to be impaired because of the perception of what is non-existent (*asat*). If one were to assume impairment even in the case of perceiving what is existent (*sat*), then those who perceive pillars and other such things correctly would also have to be considered as having impaired vision. For it is not the case that an impairment of the power of vision is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its own nature; therefore, it must be assumed on the basis of inference. And just as a capacity is inferred from the observation of its effect, so too is an impairment of that capacity inferred from the impairment of its effect. Now, the effect is vision, and that vision is either the perception of the existent or something else. Even if the perception of the existent occurs, there could be no "non-impairment" by virtue of such an assumption; rather, one who has impaired faculties would see even an existing object as being otherwise. This being the case:

[417,xvi] When his eye, which is beyond the reach of the senses, has been purified of cataracts and clearly perceives an object visible to other eyes, how could that same eye then fail to perceive it clearly? 405

For how could one who perceives even that which is otherwise visible perceive another visible object indistinctly? Such a thing is not observed. Indeed, it is observed that he who perceives a subtle object otherwise visible perceives that other visible object more clearly; since this is not the case, it is logical that he is not a perceiver of that [subtle object].
But surely, it is contradictory to say that what is non-existent is seen.
If that which is being seen is non-existent, how can there be existence for that which is non-existent?
Apart from error (*dṛṣṭi*), there is no other basis for what is real or unreal.

(PVA 1064) [418, iv] If it is established that "what is seen is unreal," it follows that even "the real" does not exist, because there is no distinction [between them]. And nothing that is actually perceived can be called "impossible."
That is incorrect.
In whatever form something is perceived, it is apprehended in that very form;
otherwise, how could that which is being seen be understood in any other way? (1065) (PVA) [418,vii]

It is not tenable that what is perceived as following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of sensory organ modifications, such as *timira* (visual impairment), has its birth produced by other causes and is not permeated by the nature of cognition (*saṃvedana*). Furthermore, the very point to be proven is simply the conformity to the modifications of *timira* and so forth. Nevertheless, if one accepts its externality, it is a mere assertion. For instance: [418, viii] "Other than light, the sense organs, and mental attention, nothing else is perceived."
Therefore, power is the cause; how could that which is not other than it, being a non-cause, be the object? (406)

[418,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a dharma called ‘bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive a dharma called ‘perfection of wisdom. He does not perceive a dharma called ‘all-knowledge,’ nor does he perceive a dharma called ‘the dharmas of a bodhisattva. Because he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell upon them. Since he does not dwell upon them, he trains in the perfection of wisdom. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva.”

The power of the lamp itself is perceived as distinct from its light and so forth, but not that of its circle [of light]. Therefore, because another [the circle] lacks the status of being a cause, it does not possess the status of being an object (*viṣayatā*). It has been established that what is not a cause is not an object. It is not logical to say that an object is such merely by virtue of appearing (*pratibhāsanāt*), because even an erroneous appearance is possible. If it is asked, "How can that which appears in its own form be an error?", [we reply: if that which appears in its own form were not an object, then self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would not be an object either. If it is argued that self-awareness occurs through appearing elsewhere, how is it logical for that which appears in its own form to appear elsewhere? For if it were to appear in that [other place], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding that [other place] as well. If it appears in its own form, then just like that [self-awareness], since the other also appears in its own form, it is simply self-awareness. If they appeared to one another, then even blue and other [colors] would appear to one another, and thus they would be nothing but awareness. Since blue and the rest are included within awareness, they are of the very nature of awareness; therefore, an object is a cause of that nature whose capacity is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, the determination of capacity through positive and negative concomitance does not apply to the eye of a peacock's tail-feather (*mayūracandraka*); therefore, it does not have the status of an object. This is because it is impossible to establish it as distinct from the form residing in awareness. As for pillars and the like, which are perceived while awake, their distinction is established because they are seen by another cognition and because their effect—such as burning—is observed. If it is argued that here too, perception occurs due to a common visual disorder (*timiropaplava*), we say no, because those [disorders] are also common [to all]. For the burning of a patch of ground caused by fire perceived through delusion is not observed as an effect. Therefore, both [the fire and the burning] are erroneous. If it is argued that the fire is actually non-burning, no, because it is not perceived as such. Perception of something as it is not is precisely error. If it is argued that "error" is relative to worldly convention (*loka-vyavahāra*), then "being an object" (*arthatva*) is also relative to worldly convention. Since everything is such by virtue of appearing in its own form, a distinction [between object and non-object] is not logical. Therefore, the principle is: "An object is that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*); another is not. If it is asked, "Why is not everything an object?", we ask, "Why is not everything admitted to be awareness? And if everything is awareness, then since the entirety is simply self-awareness, how can there be "objectivity"? If it is argued that awareness is imperceptible (*parokṣa*), no, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this. If it is asked, "How then is there self-awareness?", no, because it is observed. If it is argued that it is seen being experienced by another, what is the proof for this? If you ask, "What about for you?", [we reply: for you, there is simply the non-awareness of the other.

If it is asked: "In the absence of an illuminator, how can there be illumination of that which is not itself luminous, as in the case of a jar? We reply: No, because of its very nature of luminosity (*prakāśatā*).

Because it lacks established existence, just like a lamp. If you ask, "How is this so for a jar?"—because it exists in a state of causal capacity (*samartha-kāraṇa*). From what source is it known that color exists there? Because its touch and other qualities are perceived through a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), and by others such as nocturnal prowlers (*niśācara*). But in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), this is not the case; this is precisely our intended position. Therefore, like a lamp, everything is self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) alone, appearing as a form seen by one with cataracts. Furthermore, if that [jar] possessed causal capacity, it would follow that a single part of it could be seen even without a lamp, just as in the case of a multicolored cloth. To explain: [419,ii]

If that very [object] is the cause of cognition, why does it depend upon a lamp? If it is argued that a portion of an extended form is perceived even without another portion, and that the cause is exactly like that, we say no; for blue and other colors are perceived only in dependence on other forms. Thus, the causality of both is postulated.
Since it exists even with only a lamp, neither of the two is the cause. 407.

[419,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does not perceive the bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving as real; he does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the first dhyāna as real, nor does he perceive the second, third, or fourth dhyāna as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, or the emptiness of essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real; if he does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real; if he does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real; if he does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real; if he does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real; if he does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real; if he does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real; if he does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real; if he does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real; if he does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; if he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; if he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; if he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; if he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as real; if he does not perceive the bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving as real; if he does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real; if he does not perceive the first dhyāna as real, nor does he perceive the second, third, or fourth dhyāna as real; if he does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, or the emptiness of essential nature as real; if he does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real; if he does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of the paths or the knowledge of all aspects as real—then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does

Even when that place is covered, [the perception] occurs because the lamp alone remains present; thus, that perception does not arise from both causes. If it is argued that it is impossible to cover that [lamp], because otherwise it would not arise, then its arising occurs at that very moment, and therefore it does not have a non-luminous nature. It is inconsistent to say that "perception operates there, and therefore there is no self-awareness," because perception, being simultaneous, lacks any causal operation upon it. However, if its operation upon that form is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then it would follow that the object itself is produced by the lamp, like light. Or, just as a lamp arises with its own light from its own cause, so too the eye arises endowed with a form manifesting before it; thus there is no fault. If it is argued that light is indeed distinct from the lamp, let there be such distinction. But it follows that light is not something to be illuminated by the lamp, just like the lamp itself. Therefore, since there is a lack of evidence, there is no other cognition here distinct from the eye and the form. Rather, those two [eye and form] themselves, being established in self-awareness, constitute the cognition; thus, one must postulate another cause for such a cognition, and so the cognition is proven to be dual-aspected. Furthermore, if the object itself existing in front were possessed of a form and were the very thing grasped by cognition, then the object would be grasped in its own nature.
It is not logical for there to be a distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest based on differences such as distance and proximity;
if it is argued that this distinction arises from a difference in illumination, then that would apply equally to the cases of its being covered and uncovered.
Vision and non-vision are equal.

Indeed, an object (*artha*), existing without transgressing the limits of the range of perception, would appear by its very own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) due to its acquisition of a fixed nature through the abandonment of other natures brought about by the succession of its own causes. How could there be a difference in its manifestation even when situated at distant or near locations, such that it would follow that it possesses the nature of being both manifest (*vyakta*) and otherwise? Yet, such a difference is observed; therefore, it is not the external object itself that appears by way of assuming a formative nature (*ākāravat*). For when a fixed and complete form is manifested, there can be no manifestation of difference, as that would entail a difference in the form itself. That form which appears before one is indeed the object, because the definition of an object is precisely that. Therefore, if there were a difference in that [manifested form], there would be an undifferentiated difference in the object itself. And if the object were different, there would be no designation of it as "manifest" and so forth. When another thing is being manifested, there is nothing else called "unmanifest. Its very nature is that [form], and that is indeed manifest.
If that very thing is its own nature, how can it be the nature of another?
If it is because of being perceived as having that form, then how could there be such perception when there is a difference in form? (PVA 1066)
If there is cognition [of objects] as non-different, let there indeed be a difference in the cognition itself;
however, if the nature of the object to be grasped is non-different, how can a difference in it be maintained?

Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that there is a distinction between the manifest and the non-manifest due to the distinction between near and far, or due to the distinction between the light and the object perceived, because this does not transcend the conceptual alternatives of appearing with its own nature or otherwise. Even if there is a difference in the light, if it appears by way of its own nature, how could it not appear clearly? And if it does so appear, why would it not be clear? Thus, this argument amounts to nothing. For when there is a difference in the light, there is another factor involved therein.

But how can the object be grasped in an unmanifest form and so forth? If it is argued that the perception is dull due to the intervention of a distant location, then even for you, it should not be seen at all because of that very same intervention. Alternatively, if it is intervened by that distance, then it should be seen quite clearly; so whence comes this distinction?
There is some subtle part of it.
And if a distinction [between the two] is seen because of the dimness of the light, [then... 409.
[420,iii] For it is only the subtle part that is obstructed by distance, not the gross form; however, the subtle part, being obstructed by distance, is simply not seen at all.

Now, surely this whole (avayavin) exists as a single entity by virtue of its magnitude; therefore, since it is entirely perceived, how can there be an indistinct apprehension? If, on the other hand, it is not a single entity, then there could be no cognition at all of "the entirety" or "subtlety. Or, if such a cognition were to occur, it would have to grasp the forms of the atoms as being perfectly distinct. He demonstrates this very point:
"If the external object were a single entity, how could there be a distinction between its being seen and its being unseen?"
If it were divided into multiple atoms, how could there be a distinction between the visible and the invisible? (410)

[420, vi] But surely, even for a single composite whole (*avayavin*), because it is joined with subtle parts, when it is perceived while devoid of those [gross parts], its form is indistinct; otherwise, there would be a change in its nature.
That is incorrect; for:
[420, viii] Without blue or yellow, what object could be apprehended that is said to be indistinct?
When one thing is not apprehended, the apprehension of another's own nature is clear.
(PVA 1068) [420,ix] But if there were multiplicity, then upon the apprehension of one, there would be non-apprehension of the others, and thus it would be indistinct.

That too is incorrect, because the same [objection] applies there as well. When the object is being apprehended, what else could that [cognition] be which is perfectly clear? If it is the nature of the object, then even when something else is not being apprehended, it is that very same thing; so how could there be a lack of clarity? If, on the other hand, it arises from that [object], then in that case it is not the object itself; so how can there be an apprehension of the object? If it is argued that even then, while it exists in that manner, it is the very form of the real entity (*vastu*), then if it possesses the nature of the real entity, it should be seen by another in exactly the same way. If it is not seen by another, then it has been established that it is merely a cognition, because it is unique (not common) to the individual. To explain: a person who possesses cognition thinks, "My cognition has arisen with a distorted form. Thus, the cognition is designated as such only through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Because one sees the object as distorted, the cognition is also designated as being of that same nature, just as a person is designated as a "staff" due to his connection with a staff.
That too is incorrect, because:
My eye is opened wide by that same encounter with the vision;
let that designation [of "seeing"] be applied simply because its effect is observed.
There is no other effect of seeing than this, for there is no persistence [of the object] through that [act of seeing]. (PVA 1069)
Likewise, if it were [the case that] even the blue [object] were to be sorrowed over merely through conjunction, [then consider:
"Whose is this vision of mine? For it is never admitted by you.
Therefore, the lack of clarity in perception is established by the common consensus of all the world.
For it is not said that the certainty of all people is erroneous without cause.
For an effort that establishes unerring worldly practice cannot be conceived otherwise; therefore, a distinction in cognition is logically justified by the appearance of the object itself.
If the distinction in cognition is due to a difference in clarity and dullness of appearance, [then...]
When one thing is distinct, how can there be an appearance of that which is non-distinct through the distinction [of the other]? (411)

Another says: "The difference in cognition regarding even a single object arises solely from the distinction between the dullness and intensity of external light, and not from an intrinsic difference in the nature of the cognition itself; therefore, that form does not belong to the mind. This is untenable, because:
If there were an appearance of an object endowed with light,
then when it appears conjoined with another thing, there would be no dimness of manifestation.

For when there is the appearance of forms of light mutually excluded from one another, it is precisely those two that appear in such a way; thus, there is no appearance of an indistinct form. Indeed, when one thing possesses the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), another distinct thing does not thereby become that [same] thing. If it is argued, "It certainly does, just like the appearance of an object screened by cloth dyed with safflower," we say: No, for the same [objection] applies there as well. By manifesting through its own nature, there is the appearance of redness. If one accepts that it appears in that way because that very [redness] is its form, then since that too has that very form due to the dimness of the light, everything would appear in that same way; how then could there be a difference in cognition? Therefore, even when there is a difference in light, there is no appearance of difference. And furthermore:
[421,v] Even if that light is faint, why does it not manifest here? Because of the light's subtlety; this [subtlety] exists elsewhere as well, though not in such a degree. // 412 //

If light is obscured by dust at a more distant location, then its form is perceived dimly; likewise, the location itself is perceived dimly there, because it is possible for that location too to be screened by dust. Indeed, it is not the case that the pervasive wind being stirred up here does not exist. Even though it exists, the dust is not a cause of obscuration due to its extreme thinness. At a more distant location, however, the dust is not more abundant simply because it does not fall in the intervening space; this is the very "logic of the cow and the rabbit. Light, too, is indeed more abundant there. But near at hand, just as the dust is thin, so too is the light; what is the point of saying this?
And when it is very near, that light would be clearly manifest and perfectly distinct.

If there is a clear manifestation due to the thinness of the film (*rajas*) when the light is not dim, then at an even closer proximity, it would become extremely clear because the film is thinnest; yet, if you argue that this is not so because of the incapacity of the sense organ in that case, it has already been stated that total non-perception would follow as a consequence.
Even in that situation, if another form were to arise by relying on unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), [it would still be untenable]. (413)
Because they would mutually obstruct one another, their luminosity would consequently be impaired.

If one were to rely on an insentient object whose connection [to light] is unperceived, then a different form would arise there, and by that, the light would be obstructed or covered; thus, that other [object] would not be seen. This being the case, everyone would see only that one [object] and nothing else, because the light is obstructed for them. Yet both are seen when near; therefore, there is no such obstruction at all, because it stands behind that [object]. It is not the case that only one part is seen. For the form situated behind an object located in a near place is not perceived as indistinct by someone standing in a distant place. If you say this is an illusion, how could an illusion be possible for those who perceive the true nature of objects? There is indeed an illusion regarding location, just as the sun is seen as conjoined with the tops of trees.
If that object were non-existent in that place, it might still be seen there; but why is it not associated with perception even at that time when it is non-existent? 1073 (PVA)

If there were a perception of that which does not exist at that time, then for one who perceives all objects, everything would be seen; yet that is not observed. If all this is asserted on the grounds of an unseen connection, [it is untenable].
From that, the arising of the vision of everything is seen even by another.
As it has been said: "When something is stated by you for the sake of refuting the views of others, then the other person also [sees] all of this of yours. (PVA 421, xv) 1075.

It may be said that you yourself are subject to this fault: it appears that you have only refutation, not justification, because you have not perceived the capacity [of the reason] in such a manner. Just as there is the warding off of what exists due to non-perception, so too is there the presentation of what does not exist. Therefore, it is only a non-existent refutation that appears to you; even if it were existent, it would not be a justification, and the same would apply to the assembly of judges. Thus, no one at all would be a valid disputant.
In whatever manner an object is perceived, it should be understood exactly as such;
it should be understood that there is no [cognition] following behind it that is not obscured by indistinctness.

If there were an obstruction behind something, then because it would be hidden by the obstruction standing in front, everyone would see only that single obstruction as having an indistinct form. However, if that [obstruction] were not itself obstructed, then even one situated at a great distance would simultaneously see both [the object and the obstruction], characterized respectively as distinct and indistinct; thus it follows that he would see that very thing all at once. To this he says: "In that case, only one would be seen; if it were unobstructed, [both would be seen] simultaneously. (414)
One would perceive a form that is both distinct and indistinct.
Now, it might be argued: "Only one thing is perceived, because the perception of another is prevented by the unseen. To this, it is said: if that were so...
[422,vii] Or,
when there is a negation by means of what is unperceived, it is singular.
[422,viii]
The ellipsis of the sentence is "it is not seen. That is incorrect: how can that by which neither benefit nor harm exists produce an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)? (415)

[422,x] For this so-called "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), characterized as merit and demerit (*dharmādharmalakṣaṇa*), is understood through the sudden occurrence of gain and loss, and not through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*). If it is argued that its description is due to the fact that even in the absence of anything other than [visible] objects, what is seen from a distance or indistinctly is produced by the "seen," then this too is accomplished. If it is asked how, the answer has already been given: everything, whether a refutation or a defense, would exist in reality. Even though you have stated it well, you do not understand it because of the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭavaśāt*).
Therefore, consciousness, arising according to its causes by depending upon objects, assumes various appearances; all other [theories] are the fallacious conclusions of those with poor intellects.
[422,xii] Furthermore: (gha) there is no manifestation of that which is non-momentary.

[422,xiii] Because of their momentariness, the preceding moments of cognition, sound, and lamps— whether they be direct perceptions or otherwise— are destroyed by the time they have produced [their effects]. // 417 //
How can there be the manifestation of non-existent things through cognition?

For that which is not present cannot be seen in its own form. Furthermore, if it exists as a cause, it must exist prior to the cognition; yet if it exists prior to it, it does not exist at the time of the cognition due to its momentariness. Alternatively, if it exists only when it is being perceived, then the apprehension occurs without it being a cause; or else, causality itself would consist in their being simultaneous.
That is incorrect; for that which does not provide assistance to cognition [is not its cause].
[422,xvii]
If it were something that does not assist another,
then upon the manifestation of one thing, every object would be manifested.
That which is simultaneous cannot be a cause, because it is not perceived as such; furthermore, if there were the apprehension of what is unconnected, then everything would be apprehended.
If there is a restriction [of the cause] because of that [restriction of the effect]. (418)

[423,iii] It is not the case that everything is grasped, because the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) are restricted by their respective causes. Such a grasper is determined by the eye such that it grasps only a specific object; or the grasped is grasped only by that specific [organ]. Or else, both are restricted—this is the opponent's view. That is incorrect, because:
This conceptualization also does not exist in cognition.

There is no grasping of a specific [object] by means of this conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). For the restriction of causes for entities lies in their own nature (*svarūpa*) and in their causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇa*). First, it does not lie in their own nature. If there were a restriction of own-nature, then the very own-nature of those two would appear as such due to its cause; consequently, it would follow that the appearance of the own-nature itself depends on its preceding cause and not on each other, and thus there would be no mutual relationship of grasped and grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*), because they arise simultaneously. Indeed, it is logical that those two are the grasped and the grasper only insofar as they depend on that [cause] upon which their status as grasped and grasper depends. Furthermore, there is no status of grasped and grasper other than the cognized own-nature itself. How then is there the cognition: "I am the grasper, this is my grasped object"? It is not so; since no other relation appears, this is merely a conceptual construction dependent on beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*). And so it has been said: "It appears as if possessing an activity. Therefore, because the own-nature is restricted by its own cause, there is no relationship of grasped and grasper. Now, suppose the restriction of the cause lies in the production of an effect. Even then, if a specific effect-nature is produced by those two, how could there be a relationship of grasped and grasper? There would only be a state of cooperation (*sahakāribhāva*). And that much does not constitute a relationship of grasped and grasper. Therefore, the relationship of grasped and grasper does not arise from the cause. Alternatively, this conceptual construction does not even apply to cognition. When one cognition is the grasped object of another cognition—whether that other is perceptual or otherwise—is there simultaneity of the two cognitions? Or does the arising of the grasped and grasper come from a cause? Simultaneity of the two is not admitted. If there were simultaneity, then by that same logic, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions, each requiring another simultaneous one. Furthermore, the object (*artha*) would also have to be grasped at that time, which is not admitted. Nor does an object that was initially non-existent become a grasped object later, because that would entail the consequence that its form is never apprehended. If it is argued that the form of the grasped object exists even before, then it follows that it must be grasped even before. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the fault? It is not so, because it would follow that the grasper also exists before. Moreover, if its arising is due to the causal complex of the eye and so forth, then the cognition itself would be the form of the grasped object, and not the object. Even if it were an object, the form of the grasper would likewise exist. If it is argued that this is not the case because the object exists prior to the grasper and the grasper is otherwise, we have already stated that its prior non-existence is not apprehended. Furthermore, if one allows for conceptual construction, it would entail the possibility of every kind of construction. How then is there the construction of an object? This has been explained as being in reference to the view of others (the Sautrāntikas). For this very reason, he says:
Cognition, however, manifests the object;
it may be said that it reveals that [object], even in its absence, because it is produced by it. (419)

Because it appears with that form, there may be the designation that "an object, though non-existent, appears. When an object is established as being perceived by another person and also cognized by oneself through inference, it is logical that upon the arising of a cognition bearing its form, that object has been apprehended. However, in the absence of such an object, the established position is that a mistaken cognition has arisen. But, in the ultimate sense, no inference exists at all.

All inference proceeds based on perception. If perception were to depend upon inference, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). As long as inference is not established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), perception cannot become a valid means of knowledge regarding external objects. Furthermore, if perception lacks validity, inference—being dependent upon it—would likewise fail; otherwise, it would result in a "blind tradition" (*andhaparamparā*). Therefore, in ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), only the self-nature (*svarūpa*) of cognition is cognized, not the object. Nevertheless, this is stated while provisionally accepting [the common view]. For everything is not established according to ultimate reality alone. Thus, when an object exists beforehand, that aspect (*ākāra*) in which the consciousness arises is the apprehended (*grāhya*).
Furthermore,
another object does not produce a cognition because it arises simultaneously and thus provides no assistance.

The object-essence, having arisen from its own cause exactly as it was just described, cannot be the apprehended object of cognition because it provides no assistance to that cognition, since it does not produce a cognition bearing its own form. Therefore:
How could that which is manifest, without imparting its own form to cognition, be [the object]? (420)

[424,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, do you see that dharma by which one might perceive the Tathāgata? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, I do not see that dharma by which one might perceive the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, do you see even that dharma which is designated as 'a bodhisattva'? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, I do not see even that dharma which is designated as 'a bodhisattva. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, do you see even that dharma which is designated as 'an Arhat'? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, I do not see even that dharma which is designated as 'an Arhat. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, since you do not see that dharma, nor perceive it, do you therefore apprehend anything at all? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, I do not apprehend anything at all. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because you do not apprehend any dharma whatsoever, nor perceive it, that you have been anointed by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones with the prediction of supreme, perfect enlightenment. Subhūti, it is because you do not apprehend even that dharma which is designated as 'an Arhat,' nor perceive it, that you have been so predicted. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a woman or a man were to fill this billionfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; and if another person were to hear this teaching of the Dharma and, having heard it, would not reject it—then, compared to the former, the latter would generate a far greater accumulation of merit, an immeasurable and incalculable accumulation of merit. Why is that? Subhūti, this very perfection of wisdom is the great vehicle of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, study it, and correctly practice it according to the teaching, they would be protected, guarded, and shielded by the deities of the earth, the deities of the four great kings, the deities of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma deities, the Tuṣita deities, the Nirmāṇarati deities, the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities, the deities of Brahmā’s retinue, the deities of the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, the deities of the Bṛhatphala heaven, the deities of the Avṛha heaven, the deities of the Atapa heaven, the deities of the Sudṛśa heaven, the deities of the Sudarśana heaven, the deities of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the deities of the Cāturmahārājika heaven, the deities of the Sāhasra-cūḍika world-system, the deities of the Dvisāhasra-madhyama world-system, and the deities of the Trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra world-system. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill this billionfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; and if another person were to hear this perfection of wisdom and, having heard it, would not reject it—then, compared to the former, the latter would generate a far greater accumulation of merit, an immeasurable and incalculable accumulation of merit. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones have fully awakened to supreme, perfect enlightenment by means of this very perfection of wisdom.
