The nature of an object that is imperceptible exists as the generator of a cognition bearing its form; since its own essence is not known by itself, it is logical that its apprehension occurs solely through the awareness of the cognition bearing that form. By this, its "manifestness" [is established]. However, if it were to appear by its own essence, then—due to the capacity of its own cause—it would not be simultaneous with the cognition, for nothing else [could affect] it at that time; thus, its apprehension would be merely the exclusion of others. Let it be so for non-existent things like cognitions and the like, which, being unapprehended by their own essence at the time of cognition, lead to the conceptualization of a cognition bearing their form due to their causal efficacy. But as for a stable object such as a diamond or a stone, how could the apprehension of its own essence be untenable?
[424,v] That too is trivial, because:
Even objects such as diamonds and crystals, being stable and independent of other causes, would by themselves produce all cognitions of the world simultaneously. (421)

[424, vii] For that which is eternal and stable is said not to pervade the divisions of time (*kālakalā*). And if its very nature were such, then by the cognition that fully appropriates the totality of those forms, it would be grasped as having a limit; thus, being completed at the very moment of a single cognition, it could not be eternal. That which is completed at that very moment cannot be called "eternal. Furthermore, by seeing all the divisions of time simultaneously, there would be no extension of time; summer and other seasons would exist all at once. This same fault applies even if the cognition is unitary. [424, viii]

[Objection: But how can there be a simultaneous apprehension of temporal parts (*kālakalā*) that occur sequentially? If there is no such apprehension, then this [entity] would not be pervaded by time; how, then, could it be eternal? Therefore, if it were a single entity, it would have to be apprehended all at once in that very same way. Alternatively, if there is a sequence in the production of successive cognitions due to dependence on other causes, [we reply: that too is incorrect, because of its independence. For something produced from its own cause in a single form does not depend on anything else for its existence. If it is argued that a subsequent state of being perceived occurs later, which is the object only at that later time, then in that case, it is not eternal. Thus he says:

Those [auxiliaries] come into being for it sequentially through the assistance of cooperating causes; they say that there is a difference at every moment, but the fault in this case is the same as before.

[424,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is established as a bodhisattva. He does not perceive a dharma called 'perfection of wisdom,' nor does he perceive a dharma called 'all-knowledge. Since he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them. Because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Not becoming attached, he does not tremble; being without fear, he has transcended all error and attained the ultimate nirvāṇa. All those who practice the perfection of wisdom in this manner shall attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is established as a bodhisattva? How does he not perceive a dharma called 'perfection of wisdom,' nor a dharma called 'all-knowledge'? How is it that because he does not perceive them, he does not apprehend them; and because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them; and because he does not become attached, he does not tremble; being without fear, he has transcended all error and attained the ultimate nirvāṇa? The Blessed One said to Subhūti: "It is thus, Subhūti. A bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever that is established as a bodhisattva. He does not perceive a dharma called 'perfection of wisdom,' nor does he perceive a dharma called 'all-knowledge. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of form is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the emptiness of form is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of form; the emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of consciousness. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Tathāgata is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Tathāgata is empty of the intrinsic nature of a Tathāgata; the emptiness of the Tathāgata is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of a Tathāgata. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Dharma is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Dharma is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Dharma; the emptiness of the Dharma is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Dharma. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Dharma-nature is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Dharma-nature is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Dharma-nature; the emptiness of the Dharma-nature is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Dharma-nature. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Suchness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, Suchness is empty of the intrinsic nature of Suchness; the emptiness of Suchness is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of Suchness. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Reality-limit is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Reality-limit is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Reality-limit; the emptiness of the Reality-limit is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Reality-limit. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Unborn is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Unborn is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Unborn; the emptiness of the Unborn is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Unborn. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-arising is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-arising is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Non-arising; the emptiness of the Non-arising is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Non-arising. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-existence is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-existence is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Non-existence; the emptiness of the Non-existence is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Non-existence. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-essentiality is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-essentiality is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Non-essentiality; the emptiness of the Non-essentiality is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Non-essentiality. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-perception is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Non-perception; the emptiness of the Non-perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Non-perception. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-duality is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-duality is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Non-duality; the emptiness of the Non-duality is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Non-duality. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-manifestation is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Non-manifestation is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Non-manifestation; the emptiness of the Non-manifestation is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Non-manifestation. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Unconditioned is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Unconditioned is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Unconditioned; the emptiness of the Unconditioned is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Unconditioned. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Ultimate Truth is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bodhisattva. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Ultimate Truth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the Ultimate Truth; the emptiness of the Ultimate Truth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the emptiness of the Ultimate Truth. This emptiness is neither a bodhisattva nor a non-bod

If those cognitions occur sequentially by way of the assistance provided by the auxiliary causes such as the eye and so forth, then, given that the cognitions occur sequentially, their perceptibility must also occur sequentially. For perceptibility does not exist apart from cognition, since that would entail the absurd consequence of the object being self-cognizing. Furthermore, perceptibility, which exists simultaneously with the cognition, cannot possess a prior or posterior form, because the cognition itself lacks such a nature. Therefore, just like the cognition, there is a difference at every moment. This [perceptibility] is either dependent on causes existing within its own preceding continuum or otherwise; consequently, the same fault mentioned previously applies here as well. Alternatively, if the application of the causes such as the eye and so forth were uninterrupted and constituted a single [continuous] process, then, due to that lack of interruption, perceptibility would likewise be uninterrupted; thus, there would be permanence for things such as diamonds and stones.
This is not so.
In the case of diamonds, sapphires, and the like, there is no cognition of them at all without an interruption;
by what means, then, can this non-interruption be apprehended?

Even when there is no interruption, it has been stated that there would be the consequence of cognition persisting until the very limit of its termination. Therefore, this is exactly the same even in the case of diamonds, stones, and so forth. Consequently, since it is impossible for non-existent causes such as sound and the like to be perceived, it is established that consciousness possesses the form of the object. This has also been demonstrated by the Master: "And because of memory at a later time; for this [memory] does not occur with respect to what was not experienced."
Thus it is said:
And thus, the dual nature of memory is established.
<(3) Consideration of Self-Cognition> <(ka) Cognition with the Form of the Object>

[425, vi] Furthermore, it might be argued that the meaning of the text is that [cognition] has a dual nature by way of being both the object of cognition (*samvedya*) and the cognizer (*samvedaka*), and not by way of having the form of the object (*viṣayākāra*). That is incorrect.
"But the two-fold nature [of cognition] arises from the distinction between the cognition of an object and the cognition of that [cognition];
this is the subject under discussion.

And therein, the fact that [cognition] possesses the form of the object (*viṣayākāratā*) is what is intended to be established, following the introductory question: "How, moreover, is it known that cognition has two forms? In that regard, cognition indeed has a dual appearance: the appearance of itself and the appearance of the object. Among these, there is great concern specifically regarding its status as an object. For: "No one disputes that [the object] is of the same nature as the cognition."
Its status as having the nature of an object is unestablished; yet that too is established through conventional consensus.
But is it not the case that there is indeed a dispute even regarding self-awareness?

This is not so. It is stated thus with the intention of referring to mere awareness (*saṃvedana*) alone; however, it is indeed correct that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) remains to be proven. And so it is said:
"And its being self-cognizable shall be established later."

Therefore, the point here is this: the dispute concerns whether cognition has a nature distinct from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). However, the dispute regarding its having the form of an object (*arthākāratā*) arises because that [object-form] is not established. Furthermore, that very possession of the object's form is established through the distinct recollection of that [form], based on correct memory.

[Objection: But even if cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), memory is indeed possible as something possessing differentiation (*vibhāgavat*). Therefore, how can the object be established on the basis of a non-conclusive reason?
[Reply: This is not so, because:
In this context, memory is intended as that which possesses mutual differentiation; since such memory does not exist without a clear distinction, its status as a logical reason is stated. (PVA 1079)

When this [reality], which is undivided and not experienced as distinct by its own objects of cognition, is [conceptualized] as "it is thus" or "it is certainly not thus," that [cognition] would not be non-differentiating. (424)
Nor does mere experience distinguish any difference;
for a cognition that lacks clarity regarding the distinction cannot be discerning, just as in the case of [the perception of] twins and the like. (425)

[426,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is called ‘a bodhisattva. Since he does not perceive that dharma, he does not apprehend it. Because he does not apprehend it, he does not dwell with a mind fixed upon form, nor does he dwell with a mind fixed upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not dwell with a mind fixed upon the eye, nor with a mind fixed upon the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. He does not dwell with a mind fixed upon forms, nor with a mind fixed upon sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. He does not dwell with a mind fixed upon the element of earth, nor with a mind fixed upon the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness. He does not dwell with a mind fixed upon the realm of desire, nor with a mind fixed upon the realm of form, nor with a mind fixed upon the formless realm. He does not dwell with a mind fixed upon the conditioned, nor with a mind fixed upon the unconditioned. He does not dwell with a mind fixed upon the past, nor with a mind fixed upon the future, nor with a mind fixed upon the present. Why is that? Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend it. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he does not dwell with a mind fixed upon any dharma. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not perceive any dharma, nor apprehend it? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the perfection of patience, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the perfection of vigor, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the perfection of meditation, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of the external, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal and external, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the great emptiness, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of the ultimate, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the conditioned emptiness, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the unconditioned emptiness, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the absolute emptiness, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of nature, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of all dharmas, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of self-characteristics, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of non-existence, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of existence, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of non-attainment, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the emptiness of non-reliance, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the four analytical knowledges, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the thirty-two marks of a great man, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eighty minor marks, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the fruit of a non-returner, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the fruit of arhatship, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the state of a bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend it. He does not perceive the state of a Tathāgata, nor does he apprehend it. Why is that? Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend it. Since he does not perceive or apprehend any dharma, he does not perceive or apprehend a dharma that would constitute a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive or apprehend a dharma that would constitute a Tathāgata.”

If that cognition does not arise as a distinct, clear blue form differentiated by the force of passion, then it would not be remembered with discrimination. If it is argued that some difference is necessarily present due to a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and therefore memory possesses differentiation for that very reason, that is incorrect. For a distinction that is merely inferred from the power of the causal complex is not the basis of memory, because there is no clear differentiation [in the experience itself]. Nor does memory discriminate solely on the basis of an unclear difference, as seen in the case of twins and the like. If it is argued that the object is also remembered because it was experienced therein, and since that [experience] is non-deviant, then even though the [cognition] itself is undifferentiated, it becomes the object of memory as something differentiated precisely through that [object's] difference. Even in the case of twins, when they possess distinct attributes such as sticks and so forth, there certainly occurs the perception of a distinction. Just as experience is postulated by the force of the object, so too is it [postulated] from what is being remembered; therefore, the conventional usage "memory of cognition" arises.
[426,ii] That is incorrect.
In the absence of the form of the object, how could there be recollection of that object?
For that form of a past object is not perceived [now].
Indeed, if that [object] were present, how could it be called recollection?
If that form belongs to the recollection, does it arise from consciousness or not?
(PVA 426, vi) It is logical that a recollection arising from an experience possessing a specific form takes on that same form. For instance:
If memory were to arise from the object itself, it would occur everywhere without distinction;
even when objects are at a distance, one would perceive them through the arising of memory. (PVA 1082)
Furthermore, relying upon experience, that very experience is our reason;
for even in the absence of an external object, the arising of memory is possible due to experience.

If cognition were not possessed of a form (*sākāra*), how could memory possess that form? To explain: even by one who is highly disciplined in yoga, when consciousness is apprehended as an object by a recollective cognition, it is not apprehended as something distinct from its form. Whatever is made an object through a particular mental inclination (*adhimukti*), it must be understood as being exactly so. Therefore, it is established that memory possesses a dual nature; thus, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is also logical. And so says the Master (*Ācārya*): "Or rather, there is self-awareness. And he says: [426,x] "By means of proving the twofold nature [of cognition], self-awareness is for the most part established."
Because at that time, there is the perception of the manifestation which constitutes its own essential nature. || 426 ||
[426,xi] But surely, when the dual nature is being established by everyone, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not already established; why then is it said "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*)?

This is not so. When the proof of duality is established primarily, the establishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanatā*) follows as a secondary consequence; for when the manifestation that constitutes its own nature is perceived at that time, there is no perception of it other than through self-awareness.

Now, it might be argued that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the apprehender of the self, and therefore that very same thing is both the apprehended and the apprehender. Yet, there is no example whatsoever for such a nature, by which its establishment could be achieved. If it is claimed that the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator is like that of a lamp and so forth, we say no. Since lamps and the like do not depend on another illuminator, they lack the status of being something illuminated; how then can they serve as an example for the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator? However, when those [lamps] are themselves objects of apprehension, then the sense organ becomes their apprehender.
Furthermore, for both cognition and the sense-faculties, self-awareness is not established as certain.
Therefore, that which is called "self-awareness" does not exist at all.
But is it not the case that you yourselves maintain that the self is both the nature of the grasper and the grasped?
That too is incorrect; for:
[426,xviii] Even in that case, the nature of the grasped and the grasper can be established through a distinction of properties (*dharma*).
The state of being the apprehended object exists in the form of a substance, while the state of being the apprehending subject exists otherwise.

It is logical that the status of being the apprehender belongs to the self-nature (*ātmatva*) which is uncommon to other substances, whereas the status of being the apprehended object belongs to the nature of being a substance (*dravyatva*), which is common [to all].

[427,i] But for you, all of this is inconsistent. Furthermore, an example does not function as such merely by virtue of being established for the opponent, because it lacks the status of a means for one's own realization.
This is incorrect:
for, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the state of apprehended object and apprehending subject does not exist at all.

Form is not dependent on another, because it is excluded from being other than itself. (PVA 1086) For that in which the illuminating nature of another is not perceived is designated as "illuminating by itself," because it is excluded from being illuminated by another. And just as in the case of a lamp or similar objects appearing [to consciousness], there is no illuminating power belonging to another—this has already been demonstrated—it is for this very reason that the lamp serves as an example.
Even when the eye is active, an object is not perceived in darkness;
through the proximity of a lamp, that object becomes manifest because of it. (PVA 1087)
Lamps and the like are not thus; therefore, they are illuminators of themselves.
Nor is the sense organ the grasper therein, because [the lamp] is manifested by its own nature.
(1088) (PVA) Furthermore, these [mental states] such as pleasure and the like do not arise from the cognition of another.

If pleasure and the like were apprehended by the self, they would become external. (1089) (PVA) Due to the presence of inherence, that very [apprehension] would be self-cognition; however, it has been established that inherence is not a means of valid cognition. (1090) (PVA)

[427,ix] But surely, if self-awareness is admitted for form and so forth—which are considered to be objects of apprehension—there would arise the cognition "I am form" and so on, just as there is [the cognition] regarding the self. Likewise, there would be [the cognition] "I am pleasure.
This is not so;
for why is it that the cognition "I am fair" or "I am dark" is not observed?
Nevertheless, there is indeed the state of being an object of apprehension for form and the rest, which inhere in the body.
(PVA 1091) For form and the rest, as inhere in the body, are apprehended by the cognition "I"; yet, according to your own view, they are not self-cognizing.
[427,xiii] But surely, "I am form" is not perceived; therefore, it lacks the status of being an object of apprehension, yet this does not mean it lacks self-awareness.
That too is incorrect;
for even in the absence of that [object], the perceived [cognition] is not bound to its form.
White and other such qualities are not established as being distinct from the nature of form (*rūpatva*).

(PVA 1092) [427,xvi] If this notion of "I" were not directed toward the apprehended object, it would not occur with respect to white color and the like; yet the thought "I am form" does not occur. Therefore, the notion of "I" is neither based on the state of being an apprehended object, nor is it in contradiction with the state of being an apprehended object. Now, if it is argued that the notion "I am white" arises through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) due to its connection with the self, because one perceives a distinction in saying "my form," [we reply:]

[427,xvii] But surely, because there is no difference [between the self and the body], the cognition "I am fair" does not occur; however, the cognition "my form" does occur—what is the basis for this? Therefore, this cognition is indeed without a basis. Consequently, since the term "I" is excluded [from the sense organs], it is not established that color and the other [sensory objects] lack self-awareness (*asvasamvedanatā*). Nor is the expression "I am fair" a figurative usage (*upacaritavṛtti*), because there is no other primary [usage] to which it could refer. Furthermore, there is no objective referent (*ālambana*) whatsoever for the cognition "my face" and so forth, such as [the phrase] "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputraka*), where the form of a distinction is the object of perception. For instance:
The word *śilāputraka* is seen to denote a stone;
yet, that very same word is further observed to denote a body. (PVA 1093)
In that way, the body has become the denoted object of the word "mine";
however, no other [object] is perceived for words such as "form" and so forth.

Even when thoroughly investigated, no further objective basis for the notion "I" is perceived other than the form and so forth belonging to the body. Therefore, the cognition "my face" is merely a relation to the body, arising through a specific construction of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). If, then, the notion "I" occurs with respect to the form and so forth of the body because they are self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*), then it would likewise occur with respect to walls and such things, such that one might think "I am the wall. Just as the wall's being "in front" is relative to the body, so too the body's being "in front" would be relative to the wall. But this does not happen. Therefore, walls and such things are not self-cognized.
To this, it is said:
Just as there is no sense of "I" with respect to a wall and the like even though they possess self-cognition,
so too there is no sense of "I" with respect to a wall and the like even though they possess self-cognition.
Or, just as a wall and the like lack a body due to the absence of the attachment of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
In that same way, the abandonment of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arises precisely from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that are determinate.

Just as there is a mutual distinction between a wall and a body due to the power of their respective specific latent impressions (*vāsanā*), so too is there the state of being either the object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃkāra*) or other than it. Therefore, because it is impossible for [consciousness] to be the object of the operation of another perceiver, it possesses self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanatā*). And there is an illustrative example for this: that which has no external presiding agent is perceived as independent. Since there is no presiding agent whatsoever for walls and the like in the case of consciousness, consciousness is independent; thus, the state of self-awareness is established. As for the eye, its status as a perceiver does not arise from its being an object of perception as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever between a producer (*kāraka*) and a manifester (*vyañjaka*); this will be demonstrated later. Therefore, in relation to something distinct, the absence of a manifester is simply the presence of a producer. It is logical that the state of being manifested belongs to itself alone, because it is seen in that very way and remembered in that very way—this is the principle. Moreover:
Because it is associated with impermanence, the sense of "I" does not arise in a wall; its connection with the body, however, is due to a constant, continuous association. (PVA 1097)

Therefore, the constant association with the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) is the cause; thus, there is no such notion of "I" with respect to walls and the like—this is the distinction. Furthermore, self-awareness does not arise from the notion of "I," because that which is known independently of anything else remains as it is. Now, if it is argued that its awareness occurs by way of the form of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*):
That too is incorrect,
because the form of that [object] is not perceived apart from the eye and the other [senses].
And all of those are asserted by the proponents of external objects to have the nature of an apprehended form.
Furthermore, there is no perception of pleasure and so forth apart from that [consciousness];
therefore, because their connection is independent, everything is self-cognized.

[428,x] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, there is not. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme and perfect enlightenment? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, there is not even the slightest dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme and perfect enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because of this very reason that the Tathāgata calls this 'the perfection of wisdom,' for there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to. Therefore, Subhūti, this is called 'the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone were to say, 'The Tathāgata has fully awakened to some dharma,' one should know that such a person speaks falsely and slanders me; they speak falsely because they misrepresent the Dharma and the Vinaya. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme and perfect enlightenment. Indeed, nothing else is perceived apart from the body and the forms of the elements (*bhūta-rūpa*) and so forth, which could serve as the grasper (*grāhaka*). Even pleasure and the like are not perceived as distinct from the body; and even when they are perceived, they do not function as graspers, because they terminate in their own nature alone (*svarūpa-mātra-paryavasānāt*). Furthermore, if there were a difference in the state of being an object (*grāhyatā*) within pleasure and the like, there would necessarily be a difference [in their nature]. If it is argued that "there is indeed a difference because they appear as having different forms (*virūpa*) due to the difference in desire (*abhilāṣa*) and so forth," we reply: no, for if they appear with a difference of form, they lack the nature of an external object (*artharūpatā*). Indeed, it is not logical for a single thing to possess mutually contradictory forms. Nor should it be said that "there is no contradiction in relation to the grasper," because such a relative dependence (*apekṣā*) is impossible. For a thing does not become something other than itself merely by depending on another grasper; otherwise, it would follow that the grasper is its cause. Therefore, if it is claimed that the nature of being "different in form" and so forth is manifested only while already existing, then if it exists and is manifested, how could it later be sublated by reflection? This argument is trivial. Alternatively, if all of this [pleasure, etc. presented here is only the object (*grāhya*), then the cognition (*buddhi*) which is the grasper must be another [entity] known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). It is in relation to that [grasper] that it is not self-cognizing (*asvasamvedana*). Consequently, even at a later time, it is recognized as being of that very same nature through memory.
That too is incorrect.

The world does not at all understand that this [cognition] knows another form as its object; rather, it perceives either the clarity of that form through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) or through direct cognition (*pratīti*). (PVA 1100) [428, xiii]

Indeed, people engaged in worldly affairs do not perceive through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) a cognition possessing a form distinct from color, pleasure, and so forth, such that they think, "I have a cognition. For the world, there merely revolves above [the mind] a web of conceptual constructions (*vikalpajāla*) consisting of a cognition with a specific form that appears to be distinct from the manifested form of the object. Now, it is only the embodied self of an entity, established by the restriction of place and so on, that manifests a specific form; but cognition is not of such a nature. Since its nature consists solely in the illumination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it does not manifest a specific form in the way that color and other qualities do.
That too is incorrect.
If there were a state of being a grasper even for those whose forms are not manifested, why would a rabbit's horn not also be a grasper?
If it is argued that this is because such things are not perceived in that way, then the same applies to cognition as well; it too is not perceived.
Furthermore, one who knows another self does not think, "I possess cognition," with respect to form and so forth.

It is precisely the particularity of form (*rūpa*) and so forth that, entering into the illuminator, is designated as such by taking up a distinction among the properties that constitute its very nature. For form and the rest are common to both the imperceptible and the perceptible; however, the state of being manifest (*prakāśamānatā*), as a specific quality of form, is excluded even from form of the same class. Thus, due to this difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is a difference in properties (*dharma*). Consequently, the designation "the cognition of form" and so forth functions through a process of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, since no other cognition is perceived at the time of immediate experience or at the time of recollection, it is established that self-awareness (*svavedana*) exists in the form of the aspects of form and so forth—this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
By this, the following is also refuted:
If the apprehended object and the apprehending subject were one, then from the cognition of one,
there would necessarily be the cognition of the other, or else the opposite.

It follows that by the cognition of one, there is also the cognition of another, and by the non-cognition of another, there is also the non-cognition of yet another. For indeed, the nature of form and so forth, as well as the nature of luminosity, are certainly cognized; of this there is no doubt. As for what was also said—that they remember only the grasper because of the recollection, "Something was seen by me"—[that is not the case].

That is incorrect because, in that case, there is doubt even regarding the specific [object] as the grasper; however, there is no doubt regarding the universal as the grasped. Furthermore, when people say "mine," they demonstrate a connection with the body. And for that body as well, its nature is simply self-luminosity and not otherwise. This has already been stated. Nevertheless, there is the intention of the opponent: [429,ix]
This is true: cognition is not something other than form and the rest;
nevertheless, its self-awareness is not a non-apprehension because it is apprehended by another means.
That is incorrect; for:
[429,xi] Since cognition has a form other than that [of the object], how can there be an experience of what has ceased within the consciousness?
She does not know her own form; thus, the experience of the wise is sublated.

[429,xii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Furthermore, monks, I declare that the cessation of craving is the relinquishing of these nutriments, their abandonment, their exhaustion, their fading away, and their cessation. And what, monks, is the cessation of craving? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment. This, monks, is called the relinquishing of the nutriments, the abandonment of the nutriments, the exhaustion of the nutriments, the fading away of the nutriments, and the cessation of the nutriments. And what, monks, is the path leading to the cessation of the nutriments? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the path leading to the cessation of the nutriments. Thus, monks, when one understands the nutriment, the origin of the nutriment, the cessation of the nutriment, and the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment, one is said to understand suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering. And what, monks, is the nutriment? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the nutriment. And what, monks, is the origin of the nutriment? It is the arising of that very craving; this, monks, is called the origin of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the cessation of the nutriment? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, and its non-attachment; this, monks, is called the cessation of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view... right concentration. This, monks, is called the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. If it is claimed that the [first] cognition is known by another subsequent cognition—occurring at a later time—which lacks the form of that [object] and takes the form of an *arthāpatti* (presumption) or the like, then the preceding perception would have already ceased. For it is accepted that it is momentary and does not persist until the time of another cognition. Therefore, since the prior experience has ceased at the time of the other perception, how can there be an experience [of it]? Because its own nature (*svarūpa*) is not perceived and the object lacks its own nature, every experience would utterly vanish. Indeed, that which lacks its own nature cannot be experienced; for the experience of one's own nature constitutes experience in all cases. And since the prior experience, being non-existent [at that later time], lacks its own nature, there is no experience of it. It is neither desired nor stated that the prior [experience] is experienced by the subsequent experience through its own nature. This is because [the subsequent cognition] is devoid of the form of the object; or, even if it possessed the form of the object, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would not be admitted, as this would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), as will be demonstrated.

Moreover: that cognition is experienced by another is not correct; for: [429,xiv] Cognitive awareness is not perceived by another, because it is self-cognizing. Furthermore, if it were perceived by another, there would be an infinite regress. And if that other were also perceived by yet another, there would be no certainty regarding the existence of the first cognition. Therefore, this is untenable. Moreover, since the nature of cognition is luminosity, it is established that it is self-cognizing. Thus, it is not perceived by another. Consequently, the claim that "cognition is experienced by another" is not valid. This is because: [429,xiv] Cognitive awareness is not perceived by another, because it is self-cognizing. Moreover, since the nature of cognition is luminosity,
And that cognition appears as being directed outward, manifesting as the appearance of an object;
whereas the cognition that apprehends the intellect is always inwardly directed toward the Self.

[429,xv] If there were another cognition that apprehends a cognition, then it would have to appear as directed toward the external, like the cognition of form and so forth; for one thing cannot be perceived as not being external when it is apprehended by another. Yet cognition always appears as internal. Alternatively, its status as internal is determined by its belonging to the self.
Even by the mere recollection of the Buddha, there would be grasping and an internal radiance.

When even by means of recollection one’s own cognition is apprehended, it still would not appear as something external. If it is argued that it appears thus due to a difference in time, then why is it not accepted here as well that it appears thus due to a difference in its own nature? Furthermore, it is impossible to determine that something which does not appear as having a distinct form is other than the apprehending subject. Therefore, it is logical that a cognition being experienced as internal is of the very nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If it is argued that it is experienced thus because of occupying the same location, no; for even things occupying the same location are grasped precisely through their difference in nature. Moreover, the non-distinction resulting from contact has already been refuted. Consequently, the principle is this: for one who holds that a cognition is apprehended by another cognition, that [second] cognition must indeed be external. Furthermore:
That which appears as an object to someone, he knows that [appearance], but not the [external] thing itself.

For when a certain object appears within cognition, one does not truly know that cognition as it appears in its object, because there is no awareness of the appearance of the object as being identical with its own nature (*svarūpa*). Indeed, if the experience of the form of the object occurred through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then that object would also be experienced in reality; this alone constitutes the apprehension of the object (*arthāvagraha*), just like the grasping of the general form of a tree or the like. But if self-awareness is denied, everything becomes inconsistent.
If you hold the view: "What other awareness could possibly exist? [The object is known] because of its conformity [to the cognition]" (v. 426).
If cognition arises in that form, then that alone is the perception of the object;
in the absence of the perception of that form, there would be no perception of the object.

Let it be that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not something other [than cognition]. For in its absence, that [cognition] does not fail to exist; indeed, in the absence of self-awareness, blue is not non-blue, and likewise, cognition is not non-cognition. If cognition were known by another, it would not be self-awareness. Furthermore, the state of having the form of an object (*artharūpatā*) is the definition of self-knowing, not self-awareness; for otherwise, it would follow that even the Self (*ātman*) is a cognition. Therefore, established within itself and bearing that form, it is indeed cognition even without self-awareness. If, then, even without self-awareness, it [the cognition] arises from the mere form of a prior object or otherwise, then— [430, viii]
Consciousness is attained through mutual similarity among all things that are alike.

[430,ix] For if there is no self-awareness (*asvasamvedana*), only the mere possession of that form remains. At that time, there would be no distinction at all between the object and the cognition, since if cognition consists merely in having that form, the object too would possess it. Therefore, the object—being of the nature of something other [than itself]—would be nothing but cognition, because it possesses the defining characteristic of cognition. If it is argued that this is not so because of its "object-ness" (*arthatva*), then what is this "object-ness"? If it is "non-cognition-ness," then even if the object exists as non-cognition, neither [cognition nor object] is established for either one. Therefore, self-awareness alone is the principle; otherwise, it would simply be the state of being cognition. Furthermore, if it is argued that [the object is distinct] because it is established in the self, whether by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) or otherwise, [this is untenable].
[430,x] That too is incorrect.

Even though the self and its properties possess the nature of being cognitions, since effort and the rest share a mutual similarity with cognition, they would consequently attain the status of cognition; how then could their location in the self be distinguished?

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that effort and the other mental factors would also be perceived as having a mutual similarity of form. Or by what means could their existence within the self be determined? Certainly not by another cognition.

But surely, the very nature of cognition (*buddhitva*) is not ascertained; how then can it be said [to be grasped] "by another cognition"? If both cognitions reside in the self (*ātman*), how can there be a mutual apprehension of them? For, being in the same location, there would be no distinction between them. If a distinction is perceived, then a distinction must also be perceived in the self; thus these three would be entirely separate. Indeed, if the self is not perceived, its being the locus [of the cognitions] cannot be perceived. And if the self is not perceived, how can it be perceived by a cognition through the form of that cognition? For even forms and so forth, when perceived by a cognition, are not objects [of that cognition] by virtue of residing in the self. If you argue that this is because they do not reside in the self, we reply: since the self is all-pervading (*vyāpin*), how could they not reside in it? If you say it is because they do not have an inherence relation (*asamavāya*) with it, then why is there no inherence? If you say it is because they are not perceived therein, then cognition itself is certainly not perceived in the self, since the self is never perceived apart from it. But surely this perception exists as an action (*kriyā*); there must necessarily be an agent for it, for there is no action without an agent.

[431,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer conceive the notion that he is a stream-enterer? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the fruit of once-returning conceive the notion that he has attained the fruit of once-returning? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the fruit of non-returning conceive the notion that he has attained the fruit of non-returning? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained arhatship conceive the notion that he has attained arhatship? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has entered the bodhisattva path conceive the notion that he has entered the bodhisattva path? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the stage of irreversibility conceive the notion that he has attained the stage of irreversibility? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the stage of the prediction conceive the notion that he has attained the stage of the prediction? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the stage of the crown of the head conceive the notion that he has attained the stage of the crown of the head? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the stage of the dharma-king conceive the notion that he has attained the stage of the dharma-king? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who has attained the stage of the Tathāgata conceive the notion that he has attained the stage of the Tathāgata? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because they do not conceive such notions that these noble sons and noble daughters are called ‘stream-enterers,’ ‘once-returners,’ ‘non-returners,’ ‘arhats,’ ‘bodhisattvas,’ ‘irreversible ones,’ ‘those who have received the prediction,’ ‘those who have reached the crown of the head,’ ‘dharma-kings,’ and ‘Tathāgatas. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata, when he was with the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, was predicted as: ‘You, young man, shall in a future time become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Śākyamuni’? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is no dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata, when he was with the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, was predicted as: ‘You, young man, shall in a future time become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, named Śākyamuni. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, or by means of which he teaches the Dharma? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, nor is there any dharma by which he teaches the Dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, nor any dharma by which he teaches the Dharma, that the Tathāgata is called a ‘Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of physical marks? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the possession of physical marks. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to say that the Tathāgata can be seen by means of the possession of physical marks, would he be speaking correctly? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. He would not be speaking correctly. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has spoken of the possession of physical marks as the absence of possession of physical marks; therefore, it is called the ‘possession of physical marks. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift, would that person on the basis of that produce much merit? Subhūti replied: “Very much, Blessed One. Very much, Sugata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, I declare to you, I proclaim to you: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up this perfection of wisdom, bear it in mind, recite it, study it, and teach it extensively to others, that person on the basis of that would produce even more immeasurable and incalculable merit. Why is that? Subhūti, all the dharmas of the Buddhas, the dharmas of the Pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the Śrāvakas, and the dharmas of the bodhisattvas—all these arise from this very perfection of wisdom. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man? Subhūti replied: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has spoken of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man as the absence of marks; therefore, they are called the ‘thirty-two marks of a Great Man. If it is argued that the very [causes] from which this [cognition] arises—namely the eye and so forth—are themselves the agent, because they possess the nature of instruments (*karaṇa*), then what is the use of postulating another agent? For these [senses] would not lack the status of instruments without another agent. Furthermore, if the body itself were the agent, what need is there for another? In that case, cognition (*buddhi*) residing within the body is perceived as having an inward-directed manifestation; for this very reason, the cognition of another is not perceived [in such a way]. If that were so, then certain parts of the body itself would possess the nature of cognition; consequently, if there were no self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cognition would be identical to [the perception of] color-form (*rūpa*) and other objects. Thus, it would follow that all similar things would have mutual awareness of one another. Therefore, through self-awareness and the like, there is the exclusion of other forms.
If it is argued that cognition possesses a form because it knows that [object];

Not every cognition that possesses similarity to its object is the apprehension of that object; rather, it is the similarity residing within the cognition, provided that it is a cognition, which constitutes the apprehension of the object. It is not mere apprehension, nor is it mere similarity. For if there were mere apprehension, there would be only apprehension itself and not the apprehension of an object; and if there were mere similarity, it would follow that objects themselves would mutually apprehend one another.
This is incorrect, because:
Now, it is not of the same nature as cognition. (430)

[431, vii] If having a similar form (*sarūpatā*) is the defining characteristic of cognition, then the object as well, being of a similar form, would result in being cognition; to this, the reply is "it is consciousness" (*buddhi*). On that point, it has already been stated: if they were to cognize one another, it would follow that they too possess the nature of consciousness. As for the one who said that "cognition" follows [from similarity], he has already admitted that they also possess the nature of consciousness. In that case, how can the cognition of those [objects] be the answer? Because there is no distinction. For: [431, viii]
"Apprehension" (*samvedana*) and "cognition" (*buddhi*) do not have different designata;
therefore, only a further distinction must be stated, and that cannot be anything other than similarity (*sārūpya*).

[431,x] But surely, it is observed that objects of similar form do not apprehend one another, and cognition (*buddhi*) is of an apprehending nature. If this is so, then cognition, being of an apprehending nature, would not be unobservable. If it were merely by similarity to the state of being an apprehender that color-form (*rūpa*) and the like were also considered apprehenders, then the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that they too are cognitions. If you say it is because they are not apprehenders, [we reply]: once the status of being an apprehender is established, the non-apprehending nature of one thing and the opposite of that for another can only be established; however, that very status of being an apprehender is not established at all. [431,xi]

Now, [the opponent claims] that the apprehender (*grāhaka*) is distinct from form (*rūpa*) and so forth. But how can that which is similar in nature to form and the rest, and is not self-cognizing (*asvasamvedana*), be distinct from form and the rest? Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its postulation. If it is argued that the object cannot otherwise be an apprehended thing (*grāhya*), [we reply: since it exists exactly as it is perceived, what is the use of anything else? Therefore, the distinction is simply self-cognition (*svarūpasamvedana*). This being the case, that very quality by which it is excluded from objects such as form—that is itself the nature of cognition (*buddhitva*); thus, the nature of cognition does not consist in similarity (*sārūpya*). When the nature of cognition is characterized by self-cognition, that which is similarity is merely the characteristic of cognition; the nature of cognition is not characterized by similarity. For what purpose, then, is similarity accepted as the validity (*prāmāṇya*) [of cognition]? Similarity is accepted as the cause for the determination of a specific cognition produced by that [object]. Therefore, what is called "similarity" exists only when the nature of cognition is present; it is merely a particular feature of the nature of cognition, which is characterized by self-cognition. There is no other similarity apart from that. [Objection: In that case, it follows that the nature of cognition is also merely a particular feature of similarity and nothing beyond that. [Reply: This is true. Nevertheless, for the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), similarity is necessarily bound to self-cognition, whereas self-cognition does not arise from mere similarity. Moreover:
That self-experience of it is not caused by similarity of form.

For sameness of form (*sārūpya*) is not the cause of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If its own nature is directly apprehended without dependence on another, what is the use here of sameness of form? If it were known through similarity with something else, then one could distinguish whether "this is known" or "otherwise it is not"; but this is not the case. For there is the maxim: "Who indeed would build a dam when the water has already flowed away? Nor should it be asked, "What is the use of sameness of form now? Because:
"It would be the basis for the establishment of the relationship between action and object in the world. (431)

[432,iv] Its nature as the cognition of a distinct object is established by this [similarity]; it does not occur otherwise than through similarity (*sārūpya*). It is accepted for the sake of the specific determination of action and object—that there is a cognition of a blue object and not of a yellow one. For those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), blue and so forth are external; they are therefore established as self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) because of the presence of similarity. Otherwise, in the world, there would be no establishment of the externality of blue and other such objects. Because: [432,v]

Due to the cognitive distortion of superimposing that form which is its own intrinsic nature, there is the designation of "experienced" for blue and so forth; it is not due to the experience of another entity. (432)

That which is the blue and so forth, constituting the very nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), is projected by means of a cognitive distortion (*vipalava*)—carried along by the stream of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)—upon external blue and so forth; this is what is called the "experience" of blue and so forth. However, an object such as blue that exists as something other than that [self-cognition] is not, in any way, within the range of experience. Rather, the experience of that [external object] is merely the experience whose nature is self-cognition, used figuratively (*upacāra*). For:
Even in the case of the cognition of another, when an object of that same form is perceived as something else,
the conventional usage "this has been known by me" proceeds.

For in common worldly usage, it is well known that "this is experienced by another who possesses the characteristic of height"; it is for this very reason that he says "in the world. But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is only self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
If cognition itself possesses the form of blue and so forth, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could there be for an external object?
If cognitions do not have forms such as blue and so forth, how can that [object] be their experience? (433)

If consciousness itself, having the form of blue (*nīlākāra*), is what illuminates its own nature, then by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would an external object be known? For perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not apply there, as it terminates solely in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Nor does a blue [object] appear beyond that [consciousness], because two forms of blue are not perceived. Now, if that [blue] were the form of the object, then consciousness would be known either by another form or as unknown. If it is unknown, how could it be the experience of that [object]? How can it be consistent to say "the experience of this [object] is known" when it is not known in its own nature? If it is known, even so, whether it is being experienced simultaneously or otherwise, how could it be the experience of something else? Since its own form is what is revealed by these two, how can there be a mutual relationship of the experienced and the experiencer? If, however, the blue and so forth are imperceptible (*parokṣa*), then their designation would arise from the experience of their form, and thus the conventional usage "this was known by me" would be possible. But if there were direct perception of both, then the experience would be mutually bound; in that case, there would be no proof whatsoever. Therefore, it is better to hold simply this: that what is not itself cognized is made known by another that is cognized.

[432,xi] Is it not the case that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not merely the nature of consciousness itself, but rather [consciousness] existing when there is similarity (*sārūpya*)? No; for consciousness is not established by mere similarity alone. If you say it is [established] when there is self-awareness, then if this is so, let there simply be the nature of self-awareness—what is the use of similarity? If it is argued: "If there were no similarity, would it not still be consciousness?"—then what is the point of similarity now? If it occurs even without similarity, then let it be so; however, it is said that "cognition [occurs] through similarity," because that [similarity] also exists. [432,xii]
This is not so; for:
[432, xiii] When the nature of cognition is not based on similarity of form,
If it is established that this [cognition] is self-evident, for what purpose is it brought forward? || 434 ||
Its very own nature is that by which it possesses the character of cognition.

Furthermore, its own nature [is known] by itself alone. Therefore, what connection could there be between cognition and similarity [to an object], if that [cognition] were not of the nature of that [object]? Would the state of being self-cognizing, once it has arisen, ever depart? Consequently, its nature is established as being from itself alone; what need is there for another? If it is argued that [in this case] there would be no cognition of the object, this too is not tenable. Even if it were to cognize its own form as having a form similar to something else, let it cognize that very thing. How, then, could the object be cognized by it? Thus, what relevance is brought forward regarding the object? It is measured [by us] as "the cognition of the object. For the object does not enter into self-cognition such that it would thereby become cognized; therefore, there is no such thing as "the cognition of an object. Moreover, if cognition were based on similarity, then a great calamity would follow, because: [The verse continues: If the cognition of blue and the like were dependent upon similarity, then even a yellow object would be perceived as blue. Furthermore, since all cognitions are similar to one another in being of the nature of consciousness, they would all perceive everything. And if the cognition of an object were based on similarity, then the cognition of a jar would also perceive a cloth, because both are equally similar to their respective cognitions. Or, if it is held that the cognition of a jar does not perceive a cloth because of a lack of similarity, then how is it that the cognition of blue perceives blue? [For] the cognition of blue is not similar to blue in the same way that the cognition of a jar is not similar to a cloth. If it is argued that the cognition of blue is indeed similar to blue, then why is the cognition of a jar not also similar to blue? If it is argued that the cognition of blue is similar to blue because it possesses the specific characteristic of blue, then that very characteristic must be admitted to exist within the cognition itself. Therefore, the cognition of blue is established as being of the nature of blue by itself alone. What is the use of postulating similarity?
