For if there were identity in every respect, cognition would become non-cognition; if there were similarity in only some respect, then everything would be the cognition of everything. (435)

[433,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to supreme perfect enlightenment? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that dharma which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as supreme perfect enlightenment—that dharma is neither real nor unreal. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Can one apprehend even a hair’s tip of a dharma that is called ‘a bodhisattva’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; one cannot. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a dharma exist that is called ‘an arhat’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; such a dharma does not exist. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a dharma exist that is called ‘one who has entered the stream’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; such a dharma does not exist. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a dharma exist that is called ‘once-returner,’ or ‘non-returner,’ or ‘arhat’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; such dharmas do not exist. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a dharma exist that is called ‘the Dharma-body’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; such a dharma does not exist. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a dharma exist that is called ‘emptiness,’ or ‘signlessness,’ or ‘wishlessness,’ or ‘the unconditioned,’ or ‘the unproduced,’ or ‘the unmanifested,’ or ‘the non-dual,’ or ‘the absence of conceptual proliferation’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; such dharmas do not exist. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a dharma exist that is called ‘Nirvāṇa’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; such a dharma does not exist. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to them as they truly are. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this very perfection of wisdom, thinking: ‘I shall fully awaken to all dharmas as being like a dream, like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflection, like a city of the gandharvas, and like a transformation. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of wisdom. [433,v]

For identity in every respect (*sarvātmanā sārūpya*) would only occur when all differences have vanished. In that case, this [cognition] would be nothing other than the object itself, like another object's manifestation. How then could it be cognition? For it could not possess identity in every respect while having the additional property of being cognition. If, on the other hand, there is difference even with respect to some part, then everything would be the cognition of everything, because no object would be excluded from being similar to something in at least one respect. If you argue that there is no cognition through similarity with anything else except by abandoning the form of awareness (*bodhākāratā*), then it follows that there would be cognition of all cognitions. If you say, "Only that from which [the cognition] arises is what is cognized," then even if it does arise from that, why is it not cognized? It is cognized because of the cognition of its own form, not because of its arising from it. Furthermore, there is no mutual relationship of producer and produced between twins. And yet, when one is perceived, there is the conventional usage of perceiving the other as well. If the perception of something consists in its arising from [an object] and its possessing a similar form, then:
Just as the experience of blue and so forth is considered to be due to its having the nature of blue and so forth,
so too, because it has the nature of experience, experience should be uniform even when [the objects] are different.

Because it is identical with the cognition through its nature as that which makes [the object] known, it is also identical with the blue and so forth through its nature as the blue and so forth; therefore, just like the cognition of the blue and so forth, there is also the cognition of the experience itself. Now, if it is argued that the blue and so forth must exist as the condition (*upadhāyaka*) for the experience of the blue and so forth, then it must likewise be postulated that the experience itself cannot exist without being conditioned by something else.
That too is incorrect, because:
viii] There is no postulation of an optical defect for the appearances of hair and so forth.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of an external adjunct is not logical.

For one who perceives the appearance of hair due to ophthalmia (*taimirika*), there is no concern with the conceptualization of an actual hair-pillow. If it is argued that in that case, a hair was previously seen [as the basis for the concept], then this same method should be postulated in all instances. Just as the conceptualization of "blue" arises from the perception of a blue form because it belongs to that class, so too could it occur even without an external pillow. Furthermore, regarding the conceptualization of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), there is an absence of grasping a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) because the object is always to be inferred. Moreover, since a prior perception is seen to be the producer [of the cognition], and since the perception of an object does not occur in every case—given that dispute is possible everywhere—what could be the "imposer" (*upadhāyaka*) of the object-form upon the immediately preceding [cognition]? It is not so; for it has been demonstrated more than once that even a remote agent, such as lac-dye (*lākṣārasa*), is observed to act as an imposition. Or, it might be argued as follows:

If it is argued that there is no fault because the determination of that [object] is meaningful insofar as it is not an experience of what has already been experienced, this is not so, for this [determination] does not exist with respect to the object either at all times.
[433,xi] If the worldly determination that "the experience has been experienced" is a cognition corresponding to reality, then from that determination [434,i]...

It should be understood that this experience of an object arises from seeing the cause of seeing, and not from the experience itself; for if it were indeed from the experience, such a certainty would certainly occur.
To this, it is replied:
A cause does not produce its effect at all times merely by virtue of being a cause;
rather, having encountered auxiliary conditions, the cause becomes an agent. (PVA 1109)
He demonstrates that very point:
This [ascertainment] does not exist with respect to the object either at all times.

For an ascertainment regarding the object does not occur in every case, since it is observed that [the object] sometimes appears [without being ascertained]. Alternatively, this ascertainment never exists with respect to the object, because only the aspect (*ākāra*) which consists in the nature of experience (*anubhava*) is the object of ascertainment. If it is argued that it is so by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), we say no, because such a conceptualization of metaphorical designation is untenable.
The nature of an object is not perceived anywhere by anyone in its primary sense;
in the absence of that, from what could the conceptualization of metaphorical usage arise? (PVA 1110)

Therefore, the determination that "this is the object" relies on the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) and is not produced by experience alone. Even in a dream, there is no perception of an actual object, yet the determination that "it is an object" still occurs. Consequently, since such a determination may be absent even when there is experience of an object, and may be present even when it is absent, the determination lacks certainty. How, then, can reality be established?
Or why would there not be experience when existence, which is the basis for being, is present?

For in every experience, there is a basis for that experience; nevertheless, why is it that there is no certainty? If you say, "It does not arise in some cases due to a deficiency of auxiliary causes," then the determination of an experience cannot be based on certainty. To say that [certainty] is absent even when the experience has occurred is nonsensical. The determination of an experience, however, occurs through its having that [object's] form; thus, the experience of an entity is not sublated. For the absence of certainty—caused by the absence of other factors—is not capable of establishing the absence of experience. One may understand that other factors simply do not exist, but not that the experience itself is absent.
Moreover, this which appears when something white or the like is being perceived— // 438 //

The clear cognition of men, which consists in the manifestation of white and so forth—is that [cognition] of a nature other than the manifestation of white and so forth, or is it of its own nature? (439)

[434, xiii] For the mere existence of an object is not itself the perception of that object; necessarily, the perception of an object must be something more than the object itself. If that "more" were external to what appears, it too would be of the nature of an object; how then could it be the perception of the object? Therefore, it must exist as that which appears. And as for that clear cognition which shines forth when white or other such things are being seen—that which you consider to be the manifestation of the white and so on—would it be distinct from or identical to that manifestation?
If the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) does not manifest its own form, how can it manifest a white object?

For nothing is manifested by that which is itself unmanifested. Therefore, that very form which has been made manifest and is cognized is itself the manifestation; any other [manifestation] would be imperceptible, like the eye and other sense organs. That [other manifestation] is not the manifestation, nor is it perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as distinct from the eye and so forth, since the desired result is established by the eye and other organs alone.

[434,xvi] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. What is edible food? It is of two kinds: physical and mental. What is physical edible food? It consists of boiled rice, cooked grain, porridge, meat, fish, dried meat, dried fish, milk, curd, butter, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, sugar-cane juice, sugarcane, salt, ginger, potherbs, garlic, and various other types of food that are chewed, swallowed, eaten, tasted, or consumed. This is called physical edible food. What is mental edible food? It is the perception of food, the thought of food, the intention of food, the aspiration for food, the desire for food, the longing for food, and the inclination toward food. This is called mental edible food. What is contact as nutriment? It is the contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called contact as nutriment. What is mental volition as nutriment? It is the volition of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called mental volition as nutriment. What is consciousness as nutriment? It is the consciousness of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called consciousness as nutriment. Furthermore, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have maintained themselves by means of these four nutriments, they all did so by means of these very four. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will maintain themselves by means of these four nutriments, they all will do so by means of these very four. Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present maintain themselves by means of these four nutriments, they all do so by means of these very four. Monks, I too, having known this as it really is through direct knowledge, declare that these four nutriments are the cause, the source, the origin, and the condition for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. Monks, if one were to say: "I shall abandon these four nutriments and maintain myself by means of some other nutriment," that would be impossible. Why is that? Because, monks, apart from these four nutriments, no other nutriment exists for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall abandon attachment to these four nutriments and cultivate revulsion toward them. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, if one were to say: "I shall abandon attachment to these four nutriments and cultivate revulsion toward them, and yet I shall not realize the unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life," that would be impossible. Why is that? Because, monks, for one who has abandoned attachment to these four nutriments and cultivated revulsion toward them, it is impossible that the unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom should not be realized in this very life. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "Having abandoned attachment to these four nutriments and cultivated revulsion toward them, we shall realize the unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. Furthermore, monks, if one were to say: "I shall abandon attachment to these four nutriments and cultivate revulsion toward them, and having done so, I shall realize the unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, and yet I shall not dwell having fully understood the arising and passing away of these four nutriments, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them," that would be impossible. Why is that? Because, monks, for one who has abandoned attachment to these four nutriments and cultivated revulsion toward them, and who dwells having fully understood their arising and passing away, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, it is impossible that the unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom should not be realized in this very life. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "Having abandoned attachment to these four nutriments and cultivated revulsion toward them, and having realized the unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, we shall dwell having fully understood the arising and passing away of these four nutriments, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. If it is argued that this very manifestation is imperceptible and not anything else, [we reply: even if a manifestation has arisen that is indeed imperceptible, let that alone have arisen; how then is the object illuminated? For upon the arising of this [manifestation], nothing at all happens to the other [the object]. If it is argued that "this [manifestation] belongs to the object," then what kind of relation is there with the object? If it is argued that "it perceives the object," [we ask: surely perception itself is not perceived; how then can it be said that "it perceives"? If it is argued that the object possesses the status of being an object (karmabhāva), then what is this so-called "object-status"? If it is perceived as something additional to the mere object, then for that [status] there must be another perception, and for that, yet another—thus, from the status of being an object, that [status] is perceived, and from that again the status of being an object; there is no escape from infinite regress. Therefore:
Knowledge is manifestation; since that manifestation is not manifest, the entire world is unmanifest.

[435,iii] For it is not the case that an object arises merely as something luminous in form, like a lamp; rather, its manifestation consists in the nature of cognition. And if that [manifestation] were not itself perceptible, how could the object be manifest? If you say it is manifest by its own nature, then it would follow that everything is manifest. If you say it is manifest through its own particularity (*svaviśeṣāt*), then another cognition is useless. If you say its manifestation occurs in that very same way [as the object], by what is this [manifestation] cognized? If you say by another manifestation, no; because: [435,iv] [The verse follows: "If it were perceived by another manifestation, there would be an infinite regress, and so on. (See verse 1230)
Because even when one manifestation is manifested by another manifestation, the same fault would follow;

for that too would not be perceived as a distinct manifestation, and thus it would be the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the prior manifestation that is manifested. Furthermore, since the manifestation of that too would not be perceived by yet another, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the succession of manifestations. Therefore, when its own nature is perceived, it is perceived precisely as being endowed with manifestation. Otherwise, there would be no cognition that "this has been manifested. For:
And how can one distinguish, by means of that perception, an object whose relationship [to the word] is unknown? (441)

[435, vii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his deep observation of the five aggregates, beheld that they were all empty and thereby delivered all beings from suffering and distress. Thus, O Śāriputra, all phenomena are empty of self and what belongs to a self; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and even no non-attainment. Therefore, O Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; transcending all perverted views and illusions, he reaches ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Chapter on the Heart of Prajñāpāramitā, the thirty-sixth. Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling in Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "If, O Śāriputra, a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should observe that all phenomena are empty of self and what belongs to a self. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: "O World-Honored One, why is it that all phenomena are empty of self and what belongs to a self? The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, O Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and even no non-attainment. Therefore, O Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; transcending all perverted views and illusions, he reaches ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Chapter on the Heart of Prajñāpāramitā, the thirty-sixth. In the expression "the object is seen" (*dṛṣṭo ’rthaḥ*), it is understood that "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) functions as a qualifier. And there can be no apprehension of a qualified object when its qualifier is not apprehended. [Objection: But in the case of "it is a cow" (*gaur iti*), is the "cowness" (*gotva*) perceived as something distinct from the apprehension of the qualifier? [Reply: No, because cowness consists in the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*). Nor is it accepted by you that the cognition itself consists in the exclusion of non-cognition. If that were so, it would follow that the object is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, you maintain that cognition is distinct [from the object]; and if that [cognition] is not itself cognized, how could it be the basis for the linguistic usage "it is cognized"? [Objection: How then do you yourself employ the linguistic usage "it is cognized" when the distinct cognition is not cognized? For even you do not admit that both the cognition and the object distinct from it are being cognized. And in this regard: * *dṛṣṭo ’rtha iti dṛṣṭiviśeṣaṇatā pratīyate |* In the expression "the object is seen," it is understood that "seen" functions as a qualifier of the object. * *na ca viśeṣaṇāgrahaṇe viśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭaviśeṣyagrahaḥ |* And there can be no apprehension of a qualified object when its qualifier is not apprehended. * *nanu gauriti viśeṣaṇagrahaṇādeva kiṃ gotvamaparaṃ dṛśyate |* [Objection: But in the case of "it is a cow," is the "cowness" perceived as something distinct from the apprehension of the qualifier? * *na | gotvasyāgovyāvṛttirūpatvāt |* [Reply: No, because cowness consists in the exclusion of non-cows. * *na ca pratītirapratītivyāvṛttirūpā bhavateṣyate |* Nor is it accepted by you that the cognition itself consists in the exclusion of non-cognition. * *tathā satyarthasya svasaṃvedanatvaprasaṅgaḥ |* If that were so, it would follow that the object is self-cognizing. * *vyatiriktā ca bhavatā pratītiriṣyate |* Furthermore, you maintain that cognition is distinct [from the object]. * *sā cāpratipannā kathaṃ pratīte iti vyavahāranibandhanam |* And if that [cognition] is not itself cognized, how could it be the basis for the linguistic usage "it is cognized"? * *kathaṃ tarhi vyatiriktapratītyapratītau pratīta iti bhavato ’pi vyavahāraḥ |* [Objection: How then do you yourself employ the linguistic usage "it is cognized" when the distinct cognition is not cognized? * *nahi bhavatāpi pratītirarthaśca tadvyatiriktaḥ pratīyate ityabhyupagamyate |* For even you do not admit that both the cognition and the object distinct from it are being cognized. * *atra ca |* And in this regard:
Because when two things move as one, there is the perception of the second.

At the time of the cognition of the object, there is no cognition of the perception, nor at the time of the cognition of the perception is there a cognition of the object; how, then, could there be a cognition of their qualified relationship? Therefore, it is not logical to ask, "How is this so?
[435,x] It is only when two things are seen in conjunction that there can be the certain conviction, "This has been seen. // 442 //

For even the certainty that "it has been seen" is indeed a certainty regarding a composite [object]; therefore, according to your own view, this [certainty] must arise from an experience of exactly that nature, for there is no other logical principle than yours. For us, however, the mind—driven by the wind of powerful latent impressions (vāsanā)—causes the yellow leaves of certainty to fall from elsewhere, like the shadow of a tree of objects; thus, the determination of reality arises from mere certainty alone. Consequently, there is no cognition of an object, nor is it the case that "this is not the object. Therefore, the logical conclusion is that your position is untenable. Now:

If it is argued that when a cognition possessing a certain form is perceived by another mind, the term "seen" applies to it, then its self-awareness is established through its similarity to itself. (443)

[435, xiii] It might be argued: "The determination that 'the object has been seen' does not arise from the cognition of the object as having a nature similar to itself; rather, it arises from the cognition of that very object without [any prior] cognition [of its similarity]. Just as in the case of 'the man with a staff,' when a person joined with a staff is apprehended through a cognition of that [person] which is distinct from [the staff], there is a determination. The intention [of the opponent] is that the grasping of objects existing as qualifier and qualified is never observed in self-cognition. This, however, results in a refutation of your own position. For instance: [436, i]
The relationship of qualifier and qualified does not exist between the two in an ultimate sense;
rather, at some time, something may be considered as the qualified and so forth for someone.

Indeed, the relationship between qualifier and qualified is not ultimately real, because at times even the qualified is perceived as the qualifier. Therefore, it is simply cognition that is perceived in such a manner; and since that [cognition] is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), self-awareness is established. For: When there is similarity (*sārūpya*) with this [object], the awareness of its own form is established. But the object existing in that [perceived] way does not exist at all. If cognition were not self-cognized, it would follow that only the object—existing as the qualifier and the qualified—is perceived. [436,iii]
Now, how can one who knows his own form know the form of another?

If it does not know its own form, then it must know only the form of another. And since there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) between them, how can there be a cognition of it as being qualified by that? Now, if it is argued that the perception of that form has arisen, but there is no self-cognition (*svarūpasamvedana*) of it; and that when it is subsequently perceived by another through that very form, it is called "seen"—[we reply: but if the particularity of non-perception is first grasped, how can there subsequently be a cognition of its being a qualifier by means of another? Or, if it is said that it is cognized later, and therefore this fault does not apply—[we respond: [436, iv–v] If it does not know its own form, then it knows only the form of another. Since there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified between them, how can there be a cognition of it as being qualified by that? Now, if it is argued that the perception of that form has arisen, but there is no self-cognition; and that when it is subsequently perceived by another through that very form, it is called "seen"—but if the particularity of non-perception is first grasped, how can there subsequently be a cognition of its being a qualifier by means of another? Or, if it is said that it is cognized later, and therefore this fault does not apply—[we respond:]...
That is incorrect; for:
[436, vi] When that form is experienced, it is subsequently [cognized] by another consciousness.
Let that [cognition] possess only that form [of the object], but not the state of being qualified by the object of cognition.

(PVA 1112) For at the time of its own apprehension, the object of cognition is known as being indistinguishable from the perception itself. However, at a subsequent time, when there is a cognition of that form [of the object], let it simply possess that form; but it does not follow that there is a cognition of it as qualified by itself through that [form].
If what was previously known in one way is perceived otherwise at another time,
then it is not understood what truthfulness belongs to in this case. (PVA 1113)
[436,ix] Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even though there was initially no perception of the qualifier, what contradiction is there in perceiving it later? That too is incorrect, because:
If there is no perception of the qualifier and the qualified as being non-joined, then the state of being qualifier and qualified is not perceived at all.
For it is not possible to understand the relationship of qualifier and qualified based solely on the perception of two distinct entities at all times. Moreover:
"And the designation of 'feeling' [as being identical to the object] due to similarity has already been established. (444)

[436,xiii] For the cognition of that [object] does not arise merely from the emergence of similarity; it is impossible for another to cognize it by thinking, "This is similar [to my own experience]. To explain:

If the apprehension of similarity occurs only between two things that have already been seen, then how could one determine the similarity of this [object] with that [other object] through perception, since one has not previously seen it? (445)
For one who does not even accept similarity [between object and cognition], there is no perception of both;
thus, the discussion regarding whether the object is known as "the object" or as "cognition" has come to an end.

[436,xvi] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four ways of entering the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*). What four? There is one who enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, and departs from it with full awareness. There is one who enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, but departs from it without full awareness. There is one who enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein without full awareness, but departs from it with full awareness. And there is one who enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein without full awareness, and departs from it without full awareness. These, monks, are the four ways of entering the womb. [437,i] Regarding this, what kind of person enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, and departs from it with full awareness? Here, a certain person is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Awakened One; he enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, and departs from it with full awareness. This is called the first way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, what kind of person enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, but departs from it without full awareness? Here, a certain person is a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakravartin*); he enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, but departs from it without full awareness. This is called the second way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, what kind of person enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein without full awareness, but departs from it with full awareness? Here, a certain person is a Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*) who possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; he enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein without full awareness, but departs from it with full awareness. This is called the third way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, what kind of person enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein without full awareness, and departs from it without full awareness? For in the perception of a mere [form], there is no cognition of similarity; this is because cognition occurs in the form "this is similar to that. Furthermore, since past and future perceptions of objects do not occur simultaneously, such a cognition does not arise. Even if one were to superimpose [the object] upon that [cognition], it would be only the knowledge itself, not the cognition of the object. Moreover, if that [knowledge] were also not self-cognizing (*asvasamvedana*), the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has already been stated. As for one who does not even accept similarity (*sārūpya*), for him the object is not cognized, because the superimposition of it [upon the cognition] is impossible. Subsequently, when the perception is cognized in a form distinct from the object, it cannot be superimposed as being of that [object's] nature, because its having that nature is not admitted. And if it is cognized by way of its own nature, it is simply another entity; thus, the question "What is the object? What is known? By what? becomes moot, and one must remain silent. If, however, [the object] is indeed seen...

[437,ii] But surely pillars and the like are perceived as objective entities; for indeed, there is no such thing as the impossible when something is actually seen. To this, the answer has already been given: if it is seen in its own form, then it is seen as such; therefore, if that which appears when white and other colors are being perceived were itself another form, then clearly the white and other colors would not exist.
Now, if that [cognition] were to manifest its own nature by itself, then when it is not manifesting, the object would remain unmanifested. (447)

If that manifestation is indeed its own nature (*svarūpa*), then it shines by itself, because there is no other illuminator. On the other hand, if it does not shine by way of its own nature, then while that form remains unmanifested, the object would remain unmanifested; for an object is not said to be manifest when its manifested form is not manifested. In this case, the object is indeed remote (*parokṣa*). This very manifestation of the clear form of the apprehended [object] occurs when cognition is remote; thus, that which is being manifested is itself remote, and consequently, the clear form being manifested is simply unmanifested. This being so, the object would be entirely remote, just like in the case of inferential cognition (*anumāna-jñāna*). Even in inference, remoteness consists precisely in the remoteness of the clear manifestation. If even in that inferential cognition an unclear form were not manifested, then there too there would be no comprehension of the object. Therefore, it is established that if there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), there is no perception of any object whatsoever; thus, consciousness is self-cognizing.

By this very [argument], those who maintain the position that the self is the knower— and who assert that cognition is imperceptible because all objects are not seen by it— have also had their answer refuted.
Thus:
"The same reasoning applies here if there is no awareness of one's own parts."
Cognition would be the knower of neither the object nor of itself.

(PVA 1115) It is not the knower of the object because the appearance [of the object] is imperceptible (*parokṣa*), nor of itself because its existence is not admitted. Furthermore, pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so forth arise as being self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*); and since they are of the very nature of awareness (*bodha*), how can the imperceptibility of cognition—which is contradicted by direct perception—be an object of acceptance? If, on the other hand, it is claimed that they are not of the nature of cognition, that is incorrect.
Due to differences in their basis, object, and practice, they function differently; those cognitions are indeed nothing but pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth. [449]

[437,x] First, there is a difference in the basis (*āśrayabheda*): pleasure produced by the eye and other faculties is indeed mutually distinct, as are its objects such as visible forms (*rūpa*). Likewise, through habituation (*abhyāsa*), even when the objects of the eye and other faculties are the same, there is a degree of intensity, such as being more vivid and so forth. Furthermore, it is consciousness alone that is produced from the objective support (*ālambana*) and other factors, not the object itself. If the object were also to arise solely from the causal complex of consciousness (*vijñānasāmagrī*), then one would be offering a funeral libation to it. Consequently, if one were to admit that these [objects] are imperceptible (*parokṣa*), there would be a contradiction with direct perception (*adhyakṣabādhana*). For: [437,xi]
[The objects] are directly perceived, and nothing else distinct from them is discerned.

It has been stated more than once that when the cognition of the grasper is not discerned as something other, its very state of being directly perceived is called self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Now, if it is accepted that these [cognitions] are known by another cognition, then in that case:
If that cognition were known by another means, then even another person could experience it. (450)

For by means of another consciousness, even the pleasure and so forth residing in the continuum of another are experienced. Therefore, even when there is the experience of another's pleasure and so forth—

There would be [the distinction of] being happy and so forth. For when there is cognition through another as an object of apprehension, there is no difference whatsoever between one's own happiness and that of another. If it is argued that there is "happiness-ness" in the cognition of one's own happiness, we say no; for even that which belongs to another consists of a nature of delight. Fire belonging to another is not non-burning, nor is sandalwood belonging to another non-delightful. Or rather:
[438,ii] Just as sandalwood delights the mind of one who possesses self-awareness, so too does it delight another.
What is the true nature of that which belongs to another? It is simply of the nature of fire.
O mindless one, what talk can there be of the arising of happiness as one's own in that case?
Let it be conceived in exactly the same way regarding the experience of another's happiness.

When that which belongs to me has not arisen, why is there no happiness for it? If you argue that its state of being happy is due to its own happiness, that is not so, because there is no distinction from its own nature.
If there is awareness of that form [of pleasure] despite its distance, what indeed constitutes distance?
If it were not so, then due to the absence of contact, there would be no self-cognition in the case of contact.
For contact in its entirety is characterized by self-cognition;
if there were contact only in part, that [self-cognition] would not exist, as it would be a cognition of something else.

If there were a penetration (*anupraveśa*) of pleasure and so forth into the self and the body in their entirety, then either self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) or the self and the body themselves would be attained. Penetration occurs either directly or otherwise within that which is cognized. For one who cognizes [the object] in its entirety, self-awareness alone is attained, because such is the very definition of cognition. Even if another's pleasure were to penetrate [one's own awareness], it would necessarily be self-awareness; otherwise, the cognition of that [other's pleasure] would be impossible. Now, if it is argued that even without penetration, the cognition of pleasure does not occur because of non-distinction (*avibhāga*), we reply: since distinction is possible, what is this distinction? It is not the case that the cognition of pleasure arises from that [object] or manifests as its appearance in an arbitrary manner. However, in the case of cognizing another's pleasure, [the cognition] does not arise directly from that other's pleasure, but rather arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*); it does not arise from the object itself, for it is a cognition of another's pleasure through inference. Furthermore, self-awareness consists in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the manifestation of that [pleasure's] form. This is the distinction. Here, [the opponent] says:
If a cognition knows [an object] either by being produced from it or by having its appearance,
then for any other [cognition] that takes that as its objective support, these two [conditions] necessarily exist as well. (451)

[438,ix] Furthermore, even another person who takes another's happiness as an object perceives its very nature; therefore, since it is admitted that [the cognition] has that [nature] as its manifestation, it is established [as being of the same kind]. Consequently, the observation of the mark (*liṅga*) is identical to that of the eye and other [senses]; thus, in reality, it follows that it is produced from that very [object], and so there is no distinction between the two cases.
If, however, it does not arise, then that cognition which appears as that [object] would follow as being without an object; and yet, the universal cannot exist if it is not apprehended. (452)
It is said that it is not apprehended, yet that entity is not anything at all.

This admission does not rely on the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this alone is the ultimate truth: cognition is observed to arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*), neither from an object nor as a manifestation of that object. If this is so, then since the characteristic of an object is absent, another's pleasure and so forth are not objects; thus, this [cognition] manifesting the experience of another's pleasure does not manifest as having the form of an object, but rather manifests as a universal (*sāmānya*). If it is argued that this is because inference has the universal as its object, we say no. It has been established that there is no apprehension of a universal when the particular (*vyakti*) is not apprehended, and because the universal is devoid of the form of the particular and its syllables. If it is then argued that cognition likewise lacks that form, and therefore this [cognition] would not have the form of cognition itself—
That is incorrect.
For it is not considered impossible that cognitions should possess an affection for their objective support;
the knower of the world holds that cognition takes on the form of that [object] through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, he says:
[438,xvi] "Consequently, this appearance of the object is not other than that cognition. (453)
When one has attained the realization of the nature of consciousness through direct perception;

The fact that the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is perceptible and self-cognized when it has the nature of cognition is well-established. Even if inference [is admitted] regarding the nature of another’s pleasure, in the case of its aspect being otherwise, there is only self-cognition. If it is argued that even that [inference] is the very form of another’s pleasure, we say no, because it is not cognized by the other person. How can something contradicted by another’s cognition be the form of that [other]? For there is no possibility of obstruction (*vyavadhāna*) and so forth for it. And how could pleasure be one's own if it were obstructed? If it is argued that it is because it is cognized as being related to that [other], we say no, because there is no perception of such a relationship by the other person.
Saying that there exists a form unknown to others,
he stands at the top, following the sequence of the steps of the king’s command. (PVA 1122)

[439,iii] Even another person, while investigating, does not determine that "your experience is of such a nature," because their cognition is: "This is my own perception; this is not his perception. Now, even if another person were to understand that very same form, even so, he would not be an enjoyer of pleasure, for the enjoyment of pleasure occurs through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not through inference (*anumāna*). To this it is replied:

If it is argued that [the mind] grasps them again [but] not through direct perception, then from what source does this distinction arise between two [mental states] that are equally capable? || 454 ||

[439,v] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound Prajñāpāramitā, beholds that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivers all beings from suffering and distress. Thus, Ānanda, one should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great compassionate one who bestows fearlessness upon all beings. If there are those who, during the present age of the five defilements, hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall all be delivered from suffering. If one were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems with seven kinds of precious jewels and offer them as a gift to all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, it would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a koṭīth part, a hundred koṭīs part, a thousand koṭīs part, a hundred-thousand koṭīs part, or even a number of kalpas equal to the sands of the Ganges River; it would not equal a fraction, a portion, a calculation, or a comparison. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to provide protection for those who take refuge in him. If there are those who seek sons, they shall obtain sons, handsome, virtuous, and endowed with wisdom; if they seek daughters, they shall obtain daughters, virtuous and intelligent. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are those who are bound in shackles, fetters, or stocks, or who face the threat of execution, if they single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall all be released from their bonds. If there are those who are adrift on the great ocean, beset by waves, wind, and water-demons, or threatened by fish, crocodiles, and other sea-monsters, if they single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately find safety and reach the shore. If there are those who travel through mountain passes and wildernesses, beset by robbers and bandits, if they single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately find safety and pass through without harm. For these reasons, Ānanda, one should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great compassionate one who bestows fearlessness upon all beings. If there are those who, during the present age of the five defilements, hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall all be delivered from suffering. Therefore, Ānanda, you should uphold this Dharma-door of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. For it has been established that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is indeed the direct realization of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, this very distinction between two things of identical form is not tenable. If it is argued that the distinction arises from a difference in causes, then the distinction must reside in the intrinsic nature itself; for if the distinction is admitted to exist even without a cause, then why not simply accept that the distinction resides in the intrinsic nature? Indeed, it is logical that the distinction belongs to the intrinsic nature. Since the direct realization of the intrinsic nature belongs to both [cognitions], a difference in causes is not tenable. If, however, such a difference is observed, then a difference in intrinsic nature must also be accepted. Consequently, the identity of form between the two is not tenable. Alternatively, if it is claimed that there is a specific distinction in the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatā*) due to a difference in causes, we reply: no, because even when there is a specific distinction in the nature of consciousness, that which possesses a clear form remains a perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If it is argued that the restriction of cognition arises from the connection with an unseen single object and so forth, then no one else would ever perceive it; furthermore, the distinction between cognitions has already been refuted.

[439, vii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern region, beheld five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who had fallen into the five states of ruin. Having seen them, he approached them and addressed them thus: "Sisters, you have fallen into the five states of ruin; how will you escape from this suffering? They replied: "Venerable sir, we do not know how to escape from this suffering. He said: "Sisters, if you wish to escape from this suffering, you must first abandon the five hindrances. What are these five? They are: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These are called the five hindrances. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness. What are these four? They are: mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of feelings, mindfulness of the mind, and mindfulness of phenomena. These are called the four foundations of mindfulness. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the four right efforts. What are these four? They are: the effort to prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, the effort to abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, the effort to bring about the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the effort to maintain and perfect wholesome states that have already arisen. These are called the four right efforts. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the four bases of psychic power. What are these four? They are: the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy accompanied by effort, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by effort, and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by effort. These are called the four bases of psychic power. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the five faculties. What are these five? They are: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These are called the five faculties. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the five powers. What are these five? They are: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These are called the five powers. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment. What are these seven? They are: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity. These are called the seven factors of enlightenment. Furthermore, sisters, you must cultivate the noble eightfold path. What is the noble eightfold path? It is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called the noble eightfold path. Sisters, if you practice in this way, you will be able to escape from this suffering. When they heard this teaching, those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained the fruit of stream-entry. Thereafter, they traveled through various villages, towns, cities, kingdoms, and palaces, preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Avalokiteśvara, who dwells in the southern region. He possesses great supernatural power and great spiritual might. If there are sentient beings who take refuge in him, they shall all be liberated from suffering. Bhikṣus, if there are sentient beings who are bound by the five fetters of the lower realm, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, they shall all be liberated from that place of suffering. Bhikṣus, if there are women who, when giving birth, suffer greatly and their lives are in danger, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, they shall immediately give birth to a healthy child and their own bodies shall be free from suffering. Bhikṣus, if there are those who travel on the great ocean in ships seeking treasures, and if a sudden windstorm arises and they fear for their lives, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, they shall immediately be delivered from that perilous place. Bhikṣus, if there are those who are imprisoned in dungeons, shackled with cangues and manacles, or subjected to various forms of corporal punishment, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, they shall immediately be released from their bonds. Bhikṣus, if there are those who are surrounded by bandits and robbers, intending to kill them, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, those bandits and robbers shall immediately develop thoughts of compassion and refrain from harming them. Bhikṣus, if there are those who are afflicted by various diseases—whether caused by wind, heat, or phlegm, or by a combination of these, or by external causes—if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, those various diseases shall immediately be extinguished. Bhikṣus, if there are those who are pursued by kings, officials, or creditors, or who are terrified of being beaten, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, they shall immediately be delivered from that fear. Bhikṣus, if there are those who dwell in mountain forests, or in remote wildernesses, or in places frequented by yakṣas and rākṣasas, and who are afraid of tigers, wolves, lions, and other such beasts, if they hear the name of the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon his name, they shall immediately be delivered from that fear.
