Now, it might be argued that even when there is no difference in form (*ākāra*), the restriction of being perceptual or otherwise is due to the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), as well as from the connection with the sense organs (*akṣa*) and from inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*). For instance, one’s own pleasure is inherent in one’s own self, whereas another’s is not; therefore, by feeling another’s pleasure, one does not become happy. If, even in the absence of a difference in form, the restriction characterized by perceptibility and non-perceptibility is possible through direct realization, then it follows that even within perceptibility itself, there would be a restriction of perceptibility and non-perceptibility. This being the case, what is the use of postulating differences in objects and so forth? It is simply the connection with the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors that causes a thing to be thus or otherwise—for example, that pleasure itself becomes pain and so on. Therefore, a real distinction is not logical. If it is argued that this too is due to a difference in the unseen, then let it be so; let self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and the difference in form also be likewise [due to the unseen]. For that very reason, one person should not perceive anything at all that is different [from themselves]. Even in the case of having the same object, the difference in consciousness has already been refuted. Furthermore, the eye and other senses are also postulated only because of a clear difference [in their respective capacities]. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues here.]
First there is the perception of clarity, from which follows the establishment of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"I have not seen this through direct perception; this was observed indistinctly. (PVA 1123)

[439,ix] It is precisely by means of clarity (*vaiśadya*) that the world, at the outset, apprehends through its cognition and understands it to be perception (*pratyakṣatā*). For this reason: even when the eye and other causes are present, if one does not perceive the clarity of the manifestation, there is this uniform consensus among people: "I have seen something quite indistinct; this is not a perceptual cognition. One might say that perception consists in being produced from an object and a sense-faculty, provided there is clarity. To illustrate: [439,x]
Because it is clear, there is correct apprehension by the sense-faculty when there is proximity;
however, because this pair does not exist, the attainment of that pair cannot occur in any way whatsoever.

Indeed, that alone is accepted by the world as the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) which is apprehended through its proximity and clarity; and there can be no cognition of proximity without the sense faculty. Therefore, due to the deficiency of that factor [the sense faculty], it would follow that [the object] is not directly perceived.
This is incorrect, because:
Proximity and its opposite are not the causes for perception and its opposite;
otherwise, that which is seen from afar by vultures would not be perceptible. (PVA 1125)

For instance: suppose there is one person who sees from afar, and another who does not. Does it follow that their respective cognitions are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and its opposite? Or rather, it might be argued that for that [first person], that very object is called "clear" and "not distant."
The determination of whether something is distant or near depends solely upon the power of vision.
If it is argued that "whatever one is capable of seeing clearly is indeed near to that person," then if this were so:
If it is said that everything clearly perceived is "near," then its absence would be "far"; however, the sense faculty is not the cause of this [distinction]. (PVA 1126)

Therefore, it is logically established that there can be no distinction between what is direct perception and what is otherwise regarding sensory consciousness and mental consciousness, both of which possess an equally clear manifestation. In every respect, even when experiencing another's happiness, one would become happy through direct realization; and if there were no direct realization, then due to its having a form, it would simply be self-awareness.
(kha) The Absence of Affliction in Yogins.

And for those yogins who perceive the pleasure and so forth of another through direct perception, they too would become afflicted, since their experience would be identical to that [of the other]. (456)

[440,x] For those logicians (*lokāyatamīmāṃsakas*) and practitioners of yoga (*yogins*), such as Kaṇāda and others, who maintain that these [yogins] necessarily perceive the pleasure and so forth of others through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), those yogins would likewise be possessed of passion (*rāga*) and other afflictions. The rest of the elaboration has already been provided and will not be repeated here. Now:
If it is argued that suffering does not arise for them because of the absence of the contact between objects and the senses, which is the source of that [suffering];

[440,xiii] Now, only that person for whom pleasure and so forth arise upon the contact of the sense-faculties and their objects deserves the designation "one who possesses pleasure" and so on. And since for the yogin there is no arising of pleasure and so forth from contact with objects such as women, he does not possess that status. For his pleasure and so forth are those produced by the sense-faculties and their objects.
That too is incorrect; for: [440,xv] "Indeed, there is no arising of suffering. (457)
It is not a non-perception of suffering, but rather the arising of the cognition of suffering;
for that which is unperceived as suffering and so forth cannot be the cause of affliction or benefit. (458)
Because:
[440,xviii]

For instance, why does the pleasure arising from the mutual contact of the organs of touch between a man and a woman not produce a common experience of horripilation and so forth? In that case, there would have to be a common cognition of consciousness. Therefore, when there is awareness, there is happiness.

Not otherwise. Nor would there be an equality of pleasure for both simply because the arising [of pleasure] or the contact with the eyes and so forth is not absent, if there were no self-awareness (*asvasamvedana*). If it is argued that "there is no cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of that [pleasure] in that [person]," we say: No. Cultivation has its operation solely in the arising of pleasure, and since that pleasure has arisen, the two would have an identical experience. If you ask, "How then is this distinction [between the two] possible? he says: "When pain, manifesting by its own nature, is itself suffering..."
The cognition that has that as its object does not, at that very time, entail such a consequence. // 459 //

[441,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thus delivered all beings from suffering and distress. Subhūti, if a good man or good woman wishes to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* as practiced by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they should perceive that all five aggregates are empty and thereby deliver themselves from all suffering and distress. Subhūti, if a good man or good woman, during the final fifty years of this Dharma-ending age, should hear this *prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and be able to accept, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, one should know that such a person has been protected, sustained, and shielded by the Buddhas of the ten directions. Subhūti, if a good man or good woman were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift to all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; and if another person were to hear this *prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and be able to accept, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, the latter would generate far more merit than the former. Why is this? Subhūti, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can extinguish all suffering. It is true and not false; therefore, one should know the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra as it is spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, Māra and his host will be unable to find an opportunity to harm them. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, the Buddhas of the ten directions protect and sustain them. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot surpass them. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner, they will quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, Subhūti, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can extinguish all suffering. It is true and not false; therefore, one should know the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra as it is spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. [442,i] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha told Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* by perceiving that form is empty, feeling is empty, perception is empty, formations are empty, and consciousness is empty. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should perceive that form is neither increasing nor decreasing, and likewise, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither increasing nor decreasing. Why is this? Subhūti, because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and likewise, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should perceive that form is neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing; and likewise, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Why is this? Subhūti, because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and likewise, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. Furthermore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should perceive that within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; no realm of the eye up to no realm of the mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had an attainment, they would not be called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Therefore, Subhūti, one should know that because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, they are called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should perceive that all dharmas are marked by emptiness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness of all dharmas, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects; no realm of the eye up to no realm of the mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had an attainment, they would not be called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Therefore, Subhūti, one should know that because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, they are called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should perceive that all dharmas are marked by emptiness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness of all dharmas, there is no Bodhisattva, no *prajñāpāramitā*, and no practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had an attainment, they would not be called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Therefore, Subhūti, one should know that because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, they are called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should perceive that all dharmas are marked by emptiness—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness of all dharmas, there is no Bodhisattva, no *prajñāpāramitā*, and no practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment. If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva had an attainment, they would not be called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Therefore, Subhūti, one should know that because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, they are called a 'Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. [442,ii] At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, how do they attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? The Buddha told Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through non-attainment. Why is this? Subhūti, because what is called 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi' is itself unattainable. Therefore, it is called 'Anuttara-s

He whose self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is pleasure is one who possesses pleasure. However, for a yogi whose [awareness] consists merely in taking another’s pleasure and so forth as an object by means of a different awareness, that yogi does not possess passion and the like. Therefore, those yogis are not afflicted by that [other's] suffering and so forth. If it is asked: "How is it that there is affliction in the experience of fire and such?"—[the answer is: because that [self-awareness of the object as suffering] is absent for yogis. If it is asked: "How then does it occur for others?"—[the answer is: No, because external objects and the like are perceived in exactly that way [as they are]. But that which constitutes pleasure and so forth through one's own self-awareness is not produced by another; therefore, all those who know [pleasure] do not have identical experiences.

[441,iv] Therefore, since all cognition is distinct [from its object], its apprehension consists in the similarity to the object, which is the objective support; its own nature is the self-evident experience. || 460 ||

[441,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a buddha? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the perfection of giving as a dharma, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a dharma, nor does he perceive them as a non-dharma. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as a dharma, nor does he perceive it as a non-dharma; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainability, or the emptiness of essential nature as a dharma, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. He does not perceive the ten powers of a tathāgata as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas; he does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, or the great compassion of a tathāgata as dharmas, nor does he perceive them as non-dharmas. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a buddha, become one who has trained? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic, in that way he becomes one who has trained. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive form, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the eye, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive forms, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the eye-consciousness element, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness elements, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the eye-contact element, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact elements, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the earth-element, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the water-, fire-, air-, space-, or consciousness-elements, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive ignorance, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive formations, nor perceive their mark, nor perceive their characteristic; when he does not perceive consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship, nor perceive their marks, nor perceive their characteristics; when he does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic; when he does not perceive the state of a tathāgata, nor perceive its mark, nor perceive its characteristic—in that way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a buddha, becomes one who has trained. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to. Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then Māra, the Evil One, would have been able to obstruct him. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore Māra, the Evil One, was unable to obstruct him. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to grasping and clinging. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to grasping or clinging. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be something to be known by the Tathāgata. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not something to be known by the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to conceptualization and discrimination. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to conceptualization or discrimination. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be something to be attained or realized. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not something to be attained or realized. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to increase or decrease. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to increase or decrease. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to coming or going. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to coming or going. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to arising or ceasing. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to arising or ceasing. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to defilement or purification. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to defilement or purification. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to past, future, or present. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to past, future, or present. Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, then that dharma would be subject to birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair. But because there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, therefore that dharma is not subject to birth, old age, sickness

The object of cognition (*ālambana*) is that which is capable of imparting its form to the consciousness. However, the nature of the self (*ātmarūpa*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and thus it constitutes the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of pleasure; it does not do so merely through the imposition of that form. If it is asked, "What is the difference between the two?"—there is none from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between the pleasure and its form. It is only because one considers oneself to be grasped by it that one determines, "I am suffering. But since the yogi is not like that, he does not experience pleasure in that way. Therefore, consciousness is indeed self-cognizing; otherwise, the differentiation of pleasure and so forth would be impossible.

[441, vi] But surely wisdom (*prajñā*) and the other [faculties] also arise solely from a particular cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Nor is there any distinctness in them from the object that appears [to them], yet that object does not have the nature of wisdom and so forth, because cultivation does not operate with respect to it; for in that case, the object is not something produced by cultivation. Therefore, wisdom, which is distinct from the object, is not endowed with an aspect (*sākārā*).

[Objection: But surely wisdom (*prajñā*) and the other [faculties] do not have consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their intrinsic nature; therefore, even when they lack that form, consciousness would still not be formless. [Response: That is incorrect.
Wisdom is the discernment of reality (*tattva-pravicaya*); how could it exist if reality were not apprehended? [441, viii]

If that wisdom (*prajñā*), even when grasping an object, is without aspect (*nirākārā*), then for this very reason, consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well—when it grasps an object—should likewise be without aspect. If you say, "Let that too be without aspect," this is not correct, because: *arthagrahe 'pyanākārā sā cedvijñānamapyataḥ* ॥ 1127 ॥ (PVA) [441,ix] If that [wisdom], even while grasping a specific object, is without aspect, then why is consciousness, which also grasps an object, not without aspect? If you say, "Let that too be without aspect," this is not so, since:
What is called *prajñā* is the instantaneous manifestation of a pure object;
likewise, inference is not [so called], because it is impossible for anything else to possess the nature of *prajñā*. (PVA 1128)

[441,xi] And that [cognition] is indeed endowed with an aspect (*sākāra*); this has already been established and will be further demonstrated. Moreover, if self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not admitted for consciousness, then there would never be any apprehension of it, and thus there would be a total absence of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). Thus he says:

Moreover, in the absence of direct perception, the cognition of the intellect would have to occur through a logical mark (liṅga). And that [mark] would have to be either the sense organ, the object, the cognition itself, or the preceding mental attention (manaskāra). || 461 ||
In this causal complex [of the sense-organ, object, attention, etc.], there is no other related factor;
for no capacity is observed therein, and the sense-organ is not [the cause] due to its deviation. (462)

[442,i] The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound by both ends; the person who is bound at one end and free at the other; the person who is free at one end and bound at the other; and the person who is free from both ends. And how, monks, is one a person bound by both ends? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, and he does not attain the deliverance of mind that is temporary and devoid of sensual lust, which belongs to this very life. He also performs actions that lead to states of misery, to hell, and to rebirth in the animal realm. This person, monks, is called 'bound by both ends. And how, monks, is one a person bound at one end and free at the other? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, and he does not attain the deliverance of mind that is temporary and devoid of sensual lust, which belongs to this very life. However, he does not perform actions that lead to states of misery, to hell, or to rebirth in the animal realm. This person, monks, is called 'bound at one end and free at the other. And how, monks, is one a person free at one end and bound at the other? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind detached from sensual lust, and he attains the deliverance of mind that is temporary and devoid of sensual lust, which belongs to this very life. However, he performs actions that lead to states of misery, to hell, and to rebirth in the animal realm. This person, monks, is called 'free at one end and bound at the other. And how, monks, is one a person free from both ends? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind detached from sensual lust, and he attains the deliverance of mind that is temporary and devoid of sensual lust, which belongs to this very life. Furthermore, he does not perform actions that lead to states of misery, to hell, or to rebirth in the animal realm. This person, monks, is called 'free from both ends. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, friends! "Venerable friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: "Friends, the Blessed One has taught these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound by both ends... [as above] ...This person, friends, is called 'free from both ends. Now, friends, it occurred to me: 'It would be well if I were to explain in detail the meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One. Friends, the meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One is to be understood in this way. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Having said this, the Teacher and the community of monks were pleased.

In the absence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*) operates upon an object that is beyond the senses. That inferential mark (*liṅga*) is precisely the sense organ and so forth, up to mental attention (*manaskāra*), because nothing else possesses the requisite relationship (*sambandhitā*). Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also functions only through the observation of a related entity, since it cannot otherwise be established; thus, it does not apply here. Among these, first of all, the sense organ is not [the mark] due to its variability (*vyabhicāra*). For an inferential mark must be non-deviant, and the sense organ is not such, as it is accepted as being a cause [only when functioning], whereas the capacity of something whose effect has not yet been seen is not certain. The same applies to the object (*artha*); for it, too, there is variability just like the sense organ.
Likewise, the object, the intellect, and mental attention— these and knowledge itself are not established.

Because it is not established, it lacks the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*); for that [mental attention] is yet to be proven. Mental attention, however, is simply that preceding cognition. And since it is not established at the time of the [subsequent] arising, how could it be established at any other time? For:
"That which is unestablished cannot function as a logical mark."

[442,v] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this is the first great miracle of the Tathāgata. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the village of Nādikā and say to the lay follower Citta, the son of Gahapati: ‘Citta, the Tathāgata has arrived at Nādikā and is staying at the Brick House. “Very well, Blessed One,” replied the venerable Ānanda to the Blessed One. Having received his instruction, he took up his bowl and outer robe and entered Nādikā for alms. Having finished his alms round in Nādikā, he returned from the village with his meal. He then approached the venerable Cunda the smith and said to him: “Cunda, the Tathāgata has arrived at Nādikā and is staying at the Brick House. When the venerable Cunda the smith heard that the Blessed One had arrived at Nādikā and was staying at the Brick House, he went to the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, he prostrated himself at his feet and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the venerable Cunda the smith with a discourse on the Dharma. Then the venerable Cunda the smith, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with that discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One keeping his right side toward him, and departed. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and outer robe, entered Nādikā for alms. Having finished his alms round in Nādikā, he returned from the village with his meal. He then went to the Brick House, where he washed his feet; having entered the Brick House, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, I shall teach you the seven conditions for the non-decline of a community of disciples. Listen, and pay close attention; I shall speak. “Yes, Bhante,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then said: “Monks, what are the seven conditions for the non-decline of a community of disciples? Here, monks, the community of disciples dwells in harmony, with mutual affection, without quarreling, like milk and water mixed, viewing one another with eyes of love. They all train together in the training taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is the first condition for the non-decline of a community of disciples. Furthermore, monks, the community of disciples dwells in harmony... [as above] ...viewing one another with eyes of love. And they all practice the higher morality, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom as taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is the second condition for the non-decline of a community of disciples. Furthermore, monks, the community of disciples dwells in harmony... [as above] ...viewing one another with eyes of love. And they all practice the four foundations of mindfulness as taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is the third condition for the non-decline of a community of disciples. Furthermore, monks, the community of disciples dwells in harmony... [as above] ...viewing one another with eyes of love. And they all practice the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path as taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is the seventh condition for the non-decline of a community of disciples. These, monks, are the seven conditions for the non-decline of a community of disciples. For there must be a well-established mark (*liṅga*); otherwise, if everything were a mark, then everything would be established for everyone. Furthermore, the object is indeed manifest and established by perception; otherwise, even the conventional usage that "something exists" would not occur, and the world would be blind and mute. Nor is the manifestation of an object due to the mere existence of the object, because that would entail the manifestation of everything, leading to the absurd consequence that everyone would be omniscient. Therefore, that from which the object’s manifestation arises is cognition (*buddhi*). For this very reason he said: "For no one perceives cognition when the object is unknown; but when it is known, one understands it through inference."

Furthermore, in the absence of direct perception, the cognition of the intellect would have to proceed from a logical mark (*liṅga*). That [mark] could be either the sense organ, the object, the preceding cognition, or even the mental operation (*manaskāra*). (PVA 1129)
To this,
the following reply is given:
If it is held that the manifestation of the object [is what constitutes its cognition], || 461 ||

The mark (liṅga); surely that itself is knowledge, for by it the object is described as manifested. For if the manifestation were not experienced, there would be no certainty regarding its being manifested. (464)

[442,xi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the six supernormal knowledges, he is called a ‘bhikṣu who has completed his task. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for a bhikṣu to abandon the five lower fetters and attain the six supernormal knowledges? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is because a bhikṣu has cultivated the four foundations of mindfulness that he abandons the five lower fetters and attains the six supernormal knowledges. The venerable Ānanda asked: “Blessed One, how does a bhikṣu cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness so as to abandon the five lower fetters and attain the six supernormal knowledges? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, here a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is by cultivating these four foundations of mindfulness, Ānanda, that a bhikṣu abandons the five lower fetters and attains the six supernormal knowledges.”

If the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*), or if the object is manifested, then in either case there is no purpose in the experience of the manifestation itself. This is because the experience of the manifested object is preceded by the experience of the manifestation; at one time the manifestation is inferred independently, and at another time it serves as a qualifier. In every case, there must be an experience through perception (*pratyakṣa*). If the experience were through inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, since that manifestation of the object is perceptual, the cognition (*buddhi*) itself is also perceptual. Therefore, if the object were indirect (*parokṣa*) due to the manifestation being indirect, the object would necessarily remain indirect; thus, it could not be a logical mark. Now, if the object appearing as an objective datum (*karman*)—which is synonymous with "the state of being graspable" (*grāhyatā*)—is the logical mark, this is not so, for the state of being an object does not exist without an action (*kriyā*). And cognition is the action. As it has been said:
That [cognition], being connected with an external object, is perceived through direct perception.
To this it is replied:
For the status of being an object (*karmatā*) exists only when a specific change (*viśeṣa*) is produced by an action, and never otherwise.
If it is argued that the distinction is produced by action, then one would infer only the action itself.

(PVA 442, xvi) If that which is called "objectness" (*karmatā*) is indeed a distinction produced by action, then let only the action be inferred; there would be no inference of a mental action (*buddhikriyā*). Nor is there any other action apart from the nature of the object-entity (*padārtha*). For instance:
[442,xvii] Action is said to reside either in the object or in the agent; it is certainly not something else.
That which resides in the agent is not other than the agent, and that which resides in the object does not exist apart from the object. (PVA 1131)

Therefore, perception is not distinct from the object being perceived, nor is it something else. Alternatively, the object alone is cognized as the apprehended (grāhya), while cognition is [cognized] only as the apprehender (grāhaka). For such is the common experience: "The object has been grasped by me through cognition."
That too is incorrect:
"In that case, the intellect (buddhi) possesses the nature of an instrument, whereas the apprehension [of the object] occurs subsequent to it."
Let that very thing be the supreme cognition; why is anything else postulated?
If perception were [to grasp] the ultimate reality, then a dual nature would be apprehended.
[443,v] Or, perhaps, some particularity of the object itself is intended as its manifestation.
At that time, it is produced by action;
for an object that possesses neither arising nor decay, there is no distinction whatsoever.

[443, viii] For it is not admitted that an object being apprehended by cognition possesses origination; rather, the apprehending cognition merely presents what is already established. Just as there is the mere act of apprehension by the cognition that "it exists," so too the object does not become qualified at the very moment it is being apprehended. If it were apprehended in a different form, there would be error; and if it were apprehended in its own true form, there would follow the consequence of apprehending its prior and subsequent states.
Just as lamps and the like do not exist at the same time as jars and the like, so too is the ignorance that conceals them similar; the same objection applies there as well.

If an object is manifested by a lamp exactly as it already exists, then that lamp must also be of a nature that pervades all moments of time; otherwise, it would be a mere illusion. Alternatively, if at the time of perception the object arises in a different manner, then, if that is accepted, the consequence follows that every cognition is subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

[443,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? Here, monks, one person is like a blue lotus; another person is like a red lotus; another person is like a white lotus; and another person is like a jasmine flower. And how, monks, is a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, some person dwells with a mind that is sometimes constricted and sometimes expanded, and he does not attain the cessation of perception and feeling. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus. And how, monks, is a person like a red lotus? Here, monks, some person dwells with a mind that is sometimes constricted and sometimes expanded, and he attains the cessation of perception and feeling, and having emerged from that cessation of perception and feeling, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This, monks, is called a person like a red lotus. And how, monks, is a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, some person dwells with a mind that is sometimes constricted and sometimes expanded, and he attains the cessation of perception and feeling, and having emerged from that cessation of perception and feeling, he dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus. And how, monks, is a person like a jasmine flower? Here, monks, some person dwells with a mind that is sometimes constricted and sometimes expanded, and he attains the cessation of perception and feeling, and having emerged from that cessation of perception and feeling, he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space. This, monks, is called a person like a jasmine flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said: “Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after saying: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world... “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling after saying this, what was the underlying intention of the Blessed One? “Friend Sāriputta, it was because the Blessed One saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna seated at the foot of a tree, his mind constricted and expanded, and he did not attain the cessation of perception and feeling. Seeing him, the Blessed One thought: ‘This Venerable Mahāmoggallāna dwells with a mind that is sometimes constricted and sometimes expanded, yet he does not attain the cessation of perception and feeling. It would be well if I were to teach him the Dhamma in such a way that he might dwell with a mind that is sometimes constricted and sometimes expanded, and might attain the cessation of perception and feeling. It was with this underlying intention that the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling after saying: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world... “But, friend Ānanda, why did the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in such a way? “Friend Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is one who delights in the higher mind (adhicitta), and the Blessed One knows: ‘The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is one who delights in the higher mind. Therefore, friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in such a way. “But, friend Ānanda, why did the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in such a way? “Friend Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is one who delights in the higher mind, and the Blessed One knows: ‘The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is one who delights in the higher mind.
