Therefore, friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One taught the Dhamma to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in such a way. “But, friend Ān

If this [cognition] arises as something entirely distinct from the nature of awareness (*avabodha*), then it is simply self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), being momentary due to its simultaneity with the cognition; so what is the point of postulating an external object? But surely it has been established that the intellect is perceived as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the object as the grasped (*grāhya*). True, it has been so established, provided the object were of a different nature [from the cognition]. However, when the object arises in precisely that same form [as the cognition], then one who says that "that very thing" arises in such a way—how can he speak of the object’s "otherness" as the grasped? Furthermore, the designation "I have grasped this by means of my intellect" establishes nothing more than the mere arising [of the cognition] in dependence [on something else]. Thus he said: "All relations between things are established for people only through the force of specific utility, as if they were distinct from the slight difference in the relation of cause and effect, for the sake of indicating a particular state. But the reality of a thing is not established by the designation alone, since that [designation] is possible otherwise as well. For instance:
This object existed previously as well, by virtue of its own causal nature; therefore, this perception of it has now arisen with respect to that very thing. (PVA 1134)
This object is not established through either perception or inference;
therefore, this worldly convention is merely a succession of conventional truths.
Moreover, if it is the specific property of the object itself that constitutes its being apprehended,
then that property must be either known or unknown; for only if it is known can it serve as a logical mark (liṅga).
If cognition is not itself determined, how can it be known that "this has been cognized"?

If the determination [of an object] as "known" is of that very same nature [as the object itself], then a further cognition is useless; let it be said that it is merely a particularity of that [object]. (PVA 1136)
How can that [cognition] be an indicator, even if it is not delimited by its own state of being known? (466)
One who cognizes "the object is known" understands [it] as cognition;
one who cognizes "it is the object" is the knower of its being that object.
Through the cognition of that form, there is the establishment of the objects' possessing that same form. (PVA 1137)

"In the cognition of a white object, what other whiteness could there be for that object?"—this has already been stated. Now, if the seeing were something else entirely, then there would be no determination that "it has been seen. Thus he says:
That which is unseen is seen by another, and that which is seen is never unseen anywhere.

If the vision of what is unseen is distinct from the vision of what is seen, how can there be a determination of the form of what has been seen? Otherwise, even when something is seen by another, there would be the conventional usage of "seen" and the thought "this was seen by him," just as one thinks "it was seen by me. This occurs because, from the mere seeing of the object, there is a vision of a specific feature of that object; since that specific feature is invariably present even when the object is seen by another, one might think, "this was seen by another. Now, if it is argued that this very [object] is not that specific feature, and therefore, because one does not see the specific feature seen by another but only sees the vision seen by oneself, the cognition arises as "seen by myself"—that too is incorrect. Why? Because: [The verse follows: *na cāstyanyo viśeṣo'smin dṛṣṭe'rthe yena gamyate | dṛṣṭamityeva nānyena dṛṣṭenāstyatra darśanam ||* And there is no other specific feature in this seen object by which it could be understood as "seen"; for there is no separate act of seeing here apart from the fact that it is simply "seen," nor is there a seeing by another. [The commentary continues: This is also untrue. Since: *viśeṣo vā tathābhūto na dṛṣṭo'nyatra tena ca | na dṛṣṭamiti gamyeta svadṛṣṭe'nyadṛgāgame ||* Or, if such a specific feature were not seen elsewhere, then upon the arrival of another's vision regarding what was seen by oneself, one would not be able to understand it as "seen by another. *svadṛṣṭe'nyadṛgāptau ca syāt svadṛṣṭamiti smṛtiḥ | yadi nāmānyadṛṣṭatvaṃ svadṛṣṭatvaṃ ca gamyate ||* Furthermore, if the state of being seen by another and the state of being seen by oneself were indeed cognized, then upon encountering another's vision regarding what was seen by oneself, the memory "this was seen by me" would arise. *smṛtimātraṃ tadā syācca na tu dṛṣṭamidaṃ mayā | tasmānnaivāsti dṛṣṭatvaṃ pūrvadṛṣṭe'nyadarśane ||* In that case, there would be merely a memory, and not the cognition "this was seen by me. Therefore, there is no such thing as "having been seen" in what was previously seen by another. *athānyadṛṣṭamapyetad dṛṣṭamityeva jāyate | pratītistadviśeṣasya darśanāditi cenmatam ||* Now, if it is thought that even though it was seen by another, the cognition "this was seen" arises because of the perception of a specific feature; *tadapyayuktamanyasya dṛṣṭe'pyanyasya darśane | dṛṣṭamityeva na jñānaṃ viśeṣasyāpravedanāt ||* That too is illogical; for even when one person sees what was seen by another, there is no cognition of "it was seen" [by me], because the specific feature [of the other's experience] is not known. *viśeṣasyāparijñāne kuta etad viniścayaḥ | mayaitaddṛṣṭamityevaṃ nānyeneti ca niścayaḥ ||* If the specific feature is not fully known, how can there be the certainty "this was seen by me," and the certainty "it was not seen by another"? *viśeṣaparijñāne ca sarvathā pariniścaye | svadṛṣṭamiti vijñānaṃ jāyate nānyadarśane ||* And if the specific feature were fully known and completely determined, the cognition "this was seen by me" would arise, but not in the case of seeing what was seen by another. *athānyadṛṣṭamapyetad dṛṣṭamityeva budhyate | tadānyadṛṣṭamapyetat svadṛṣṭamiti gṛhyate ||* Now, if even what was seen by another is understood as "this was seen," then even what was seen by another would be grasped as "seen by me. *tasmānnaivāsti dṛṣṭatvaṃ pūrvadṛṣṭe'nyadarśane | viśeṣasyāparijñānānna ca dṛṣṭamiti smṛtiḥ ||* Therefore, there is no such thing as "having been seen" in what was previously seen by another; and due to the lack of knowledge of the specific feature, there is no memory of "it was seen. *smṛtimātraṃ tadā syācca na tu dṛṣṭamidaṃ mayā | tasmānnaivāsti dṛṣṭatvaṃ pūrvadṛṣṭe'nyadarśane ||* In that case, there would be merely a memory, and not the cognition "this was seen by me. Therefore, there is no such thing as "having been seen" in what was previously seen by another. *athānyadṛṣṭamapyetad dṛṣṭamityeva budhyate | tadānyadṛṣṭamapyetat svadṛṣṭamiti gṛhyate ||* Now, if even what was seen by another is understood as "this was seen," then even what was seen by another would be grasped as "seen by me. *tasmānnaivāsti dṛṣṭatvaṃ pūrvadṛṣṭe'nyadarśane | viśeṣasyāparijñānānna ca dṛṣṭamiti smṛtiḥ ||* Therefore, there is no such thing as "having been seen" in what was previously seen by another; and due to the lack of knowledge of the specific feature, there is no memory of "it was seen. *smṛtimātraṃ tadā syācca na tu dṛṣṭamidaṃ mayā | tasmānnaivāsti dṛṣṭatvaṃ pūrvadṛṣṭe'nyadarśane ||* In that case, there would be merely a memory, and not the cognition "this was seen by me. Therefore, there is no such thing as "having been seen" in what was previously seen by another. *athānyadṛṣṭamapyetad dṛṣṭamityeva budhyate | tadānyadṛṣṭamapyetat svadṛṣṭamiti gṛhyate ||* Now, if even what was seen by another is understood as "this was seen," then even what was seen by another would be grasped as "seen by me. *tasmānnaivāsti dṛṣṭatvaṃ pūrvadṛṣṭe'nyadarśane | viśeṣasyāparijñānānna ca dṛṣṭamiti smṛtiḥ ||* Therefore, there is no such thing as "having been seen" in what was previously seen by another
Since that distinction exists even when another has seen it, there would be comprehension through one's own cognition.

[444,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-observability, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature as real. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as real, nor does he perceive the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as real. He does not perceive the four meditative concentrations as real, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten spheres of totality, the eight bases of mastery, the three gateways to liberation, the six supernormal knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha as real. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the state of a fully enlightened buddha as real. He does not perceive the level of a śrāvaka as real, nor does he perceive the level of a pratyekabuddha or the level of a buddha as real. He does not perceive the dharma of a śrāvaka as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of a pratyekabuddha or the dharma of a buddha as real. He does not perceive the dharma of a bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of a tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the dharma of the past as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of the future or the present as real. He does not perceive the dharma of the world of desire as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of the world of form or the formless world as real. He does not perceive the dharma of the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the dharma of saṃsāra as real, nor does he perceive the dharma of nirvāṇa as real. For what reason? Subhūti, because all those dharmas are non-existent and cannot be apprehended; they are empty, signless, wishless, and beyond conceptualization. Because they are thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real."

Even though there are many particularities (*viśeṣa*), since they lack self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), they too must be seen by something else; consequently, there would be a cognition of both self and other. Therefore, it must be self-aware, by virtue of being "seen. Now, if that [self-awareness] is also seen by another cognition, then in that case too there is "being seen," leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, if "being seen" is one and the same, then even when that particularity is seen by another, it would still be nothing but the cognition of oneself. When the "being seen" of another object is perceived by another person through its existence, then—even in the absence of self-seeing—there would be a cognition of oneself because the "being seen" by another is observed. For there is no distinction in that "being seen" with respect to self or other. If it is argued that "being seen" exists for oneself as well, and therefore there is a cognition of oneself, this is not so, because there is no difference between what is seen by oneself and what is seen by another. Self-seeing is known only upon the perception of a connection to one's own seeing. But if that is not perceived, how can it be said that "this was seen by me"? Therefore, even if something is seen by oneself, if there is a perception of it being "seen by another," there would be a cognition of oneself. Now, if it is argued that there is no fault in the possibility of a cognition of oneself for the very person who perceives the "being seen," we reply: there is indeed no loss here. Yet, even if there were no loss, there is still a loss insofar as the reality of things is not thus. To explain:
For how could it be known whether "this is unperceived by me" or "by another"?
Indeed, in that case, no one can prevent dependence upon another. (1139) (PVA)
But if self-awareness exists, this [objection] would be refuted;
for it is a rash assertion to claim that self-awareness is an object of awareness for something else.
This very self-awareness is what is called "manifestation" when it does not have anything else as its object.
Therefore, the inference of cognition does not depend upon its own attributes.
What is higher than one's own duty (svadharma), which consists solely of wealth and merit, is one's own intellect (svadhiya).
That which is the cause of cognition is directly perceived;

For the inference of one’s own cognition must be based on something that resides within that cognition. Indeed, a property common to both [the subject and the object], such as the nature of the object and so forth, can only establish what is to be inferred in a manner common to both. Therefore, there must be a property of the self (*ātman*) that serves as the inferential indicator of the self’s cognition. And there is no other property of the self apart from cognition itself; if cognition alone were the property of the self, then being imperceptible, how could it serve as an inferential indicator? Now, if it is argued that pleasure and so forth arise from the same causal complex as cognition, and that cognition is inferred by means of them because they are properties of the self—here he replies:
[444, xiii] "Arising from a common cause..."
Whence could there be a distinction in that cognition, since it is both erring and born of something else? (470)

[444,xiv] If it has been established that everything such as pleasure (*sukha*) produced by the totality of objects, sense faculties, and so forth, is of the very nature of cognition (*saṃvedana*), then, when pleasure arises with respect to a perceived object, the inference of one's own cognition from that [pleasure]—even that pleasure does not belong to another; how then could it be? How is it possible for another to cognize the pleasure of another?
For if there were no self-awareness, how could this distinction exist?
Indeed, even from fear and other such states, horripilation certainly arises.

If pleasure and the like exist as self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), it is logical that they are not perceived when they belong to another; otherwise, who could prevent them from belonging to another? If you argue, "They cause horripilation in me, therefore they belong to me alone," from where does this [certainty] come? For it is not the case that another's wife does not produce pleasure. Indeed, it is the nature of pleasure itself, when being experienced, that produces horripilation and the like—whether in relation to oneself or otherwise. What is the use of this [distinction]? If it is established that horripilation and the like are produced by one's own pleasure, then there is the cognition of its belonging to oneself; and if there is the cognition of its belonging to oneself, then [the pleasure] produces it—this is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Furthermore, that which either conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the intellect, or conforms to the causes of that [intellect], would be the inferent of the intellect. In that regard:
Apart from the five objects such as form, the sense faculties, and the act of apprehension, no other effect of that [cognition] is perceived. (471)
The sense organs and so forth arise from the same causal complex as the cognition, or else the subsequent cognition [arises from them].

In that regard, among the five objects, not even one of the two [types of] imperceptible [causes] is observed; for that which arises from the perception of form would otherwise be impossible in its distinct occurrence. (472)

[445, vi] Both the sense faculty and the apprehension are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Among the five objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, not even one is observed to be of such a nature that it arises from the seeing of form. For form and the other objects do not arise from the seeing of form, because they are produced from other causes. If they were indeed produced from the seeing of form, then they would no longer be those very objects. To explain:
The perception of forms of all objects is possible for everyone;
yet it would differ for each individual, since the object itself arises from that [perception].

Just as the perception of form differs for each individual, so too do form and the other objects; for if both were perceived in their entirety, then there would be a definitive determination of their specific distinctions.
The cognition that is illuminated in various ways is present in every living being.
However, if there is a perception for each individual self, then in the case of self-awareness, it is simply cognition itself.

[445,xi] What is the aggregate of feeling? It is the threefold feeling: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Furthermore, it is the six classes of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact. This is called the aggregate of feeling. What is the aggregate of perception? It is the perception that perceives blue, the perception that perceives yellow, the perception that perceives red, the perception that perceives white, the perception that perceives long, the perception that perceives short, the perception that perceives square, the perception that perceives round, the perception that perceives high, the perception that perceives low, the perception that perceives level, the perception that perceives female, the perception that perceives male, the perception that perceives neuter, the perception that perceives self, the perception that perceives sentient beings, the perception that perceives life, the perception that perceives person, the perception that perceives human, the perception that perceives Deva, the perception that perceives Māra, the perception that perceives Brahmā, the perception that perceives the world, the perception that perceives the formless, the perception that perceives the conditioned, the perception that perceives the unconditioned, the perception that perceives the past, the perception that perceives the future, the perception that perceives the present, the perception that perceives the internal, the perception that perceives the external, the perception that perceives both the internal and the external, the perception that perceives the field of forms, the perception that perceives the field of sounds, the perception that perceives the field of odors, the perception that perceives the field of tastes, the perception that perceives the field of tangibles, and the perception that perceives the field of mental phenomena. This is called the aggregate of perception. What is the aggregate of formations? It refers to all mental factors associated with the mind. Furthermore, it consists of fifty-two formations. What are the fifty-two? They are: contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity, faith, diligence, shame, dread, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, right view, wrong view, right thought, wrong thought, right speech, wrong speech, right action, wrong action, right livelihood, wrong livelihood, right effort, wrong effort, right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness, right concentration, wrong concentration, restlessness, lack of shame, lack of dread, greed, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, concealment, vexation, envy, parsimony, deceit, guile, stubbornness, harmfulness, pride, excessive pride, pride beyond pride, conceit, arrogance, haughtiness, negligence, torpor, agitation, lack of faith, indolence, forgetfulness, distraction, and lack of discernment. These are called the aggregate of formations. What is the aggregate of consciousness? It is the six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called the aggregate of consciousness. What is the element of earth? It is the solidity within the internal body. What is the internal solidity? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is solid, hard, and firm—such as hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs, large intestines, small intestines, stomach, excrement, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is solid, hard, and firm. This is called the internal earth element. What is the external earth element? Whatever is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is solid, hard, and firm—such as stones, pebbles, gravel, sand, rock, iron, copper, silver, gold, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystal, coral, amber, red pearl, emerald, sapphire, or whatever else is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is solid, hard, and firm. This is called the external earth element. What is the water element? It is the liquidity within the internal body. What is the internal water element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is liquid, watery, and moist—such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is liquid, watery, and moist. This is called the internal water element. What is the external water element? Whatever is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is liquid, watery, and moist—such as rivers, streams, ponds, lakes, wells, springs, pools, oceans, rainwater, dew, frost, snow, hail, or whatever else is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is liquid, watery, and moist. This is called the external water element. What is the fire element? It is the heat within the internal body. What is the internal fire element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is heat, hot, and heating—such as that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, that by which one is feverish, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is heat, hot, and heating. This is called the internal fire element. What is the external fire element? Whatever is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is heat, hot, and heating—such as forest fires, lightning, or whatever else is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is heat, hot, and heating. This is called the external fire element. What is the wind element? It is the motion within the internal body. What is the internal wind element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is wind, windy, and moving—such as upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds in the limbs, in-breath, out-breath, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is wind, windy, and moving. This is called the internal wind element. What is the external wind element? Whatever is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is wind, windy, and moving—such as east winds, west winds, north winds, south winds, whirlwinds, winds from the four quarters, winds from the intermediate directions, winds from above, winds from below, winds that blow, or whatever else is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is wind, windy, and moving. This is called the external wind element. What is the space element? It is the voidness within the internal body. What is the internal space element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is void, empty, and hollow—such as the apertures of the ears, the nostrils, the mouth, the throat, the esophagus, the stomach, the rectum, or whatever else is internal, belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is void, empty, and hollow. This is called the internal space element. What is the external space element? Whatever is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is void, empty, and hollow—such as the openings of windows, doors, or whatever else is external, not belonging to oneself, and derived from the four great elements, which is void, empty, and hollow. This is called the external space element. What is the consciousness element? It is the six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called the consciousness element. What is the ignorance element? It is the ignorance regarding suffering, the ignorance regarding the origin of suffering, the ignorance regarding the cessation of suffering, and the ignorance regarding the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called the ignorance element. What is the formation element? It is the three types of formations: meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and immovable formations. This is called the formation element. What is the consciousness element? It is the six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called the consciousness element. What is the name-and-form element? Name refers to the four aggregates; form refers to the four great elements and the matter derived from the four great elements. This is called the name-and-form element. What is the six sense-bases element? It is the six internal sense-bases: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base. This is called the six sense-bases element. What is the contact element? It is the six

If all forms and other objects, each possessing a distinct nature for every individual living being, were perceived by everyone, then there would be a simultaneous perception of multiple forms and so forth; yet such is not the case. Therefore, this position is first of all untenable. If, on the other hand, only that form and so forth which produces its own vision is perceived, then, because it is not experienced by another, its status as an object (*arthatā*) would be lost once self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is admitted. If, however, it is perceived by another, then it must possess some specific quality produced by that [other] for the sake of being perceived by him. That [quality] too would have to be perceived by another, and that by yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, to claim that a mark (*liṅga*) is something unperceived—either through self-cognition or non-self-cognition—is sheer audacity. Indeed, that which is unperceived cannot function as a mark. Consequently, the assertion that "cognition is apprehended through inference" is incorrect, due to the absence of the defining characteristics of a mark. Let it be granted, then, that there is the cognition of an object or something else; even so, [the conclusion remains flawed].

[445,xii] To claim that a logical mark (*liṅga*) is "unperceived" in this way is an extreme act of audacity; for even when a logical mark exists, one does not see it together with that [conclusion]. || 473 ||
For how can a sign that is itself perceived reveal that which has not been seen?

[445,xiv] The inference of fire, which has already been perceived, is made through its own product, such as smoke, and not otherwise. Indeed, it is not the case that smoke has ever been seen to be the inferential indicator of a fire perceived previously.
Therefore, it is precisely from this indicative mark that its prior established existence is described.
That too would require another example to be established; thus, there is an infinite regress.

For inference does not reject the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). If it did, then inference itself would not exist, just like perception. If you claim that perception has another definition, then that same [definition] applies equally to this [inference] as well. Therefore, that inference which establishes the example would require another example, and that one another, leading to what is called the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if you argue that its establishment is through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), no one has such a cognition. For no one has the cognition: "The object itself would not be possible if there were no cognition. If you say, "The cognized object would not arise if there were no cognition," then what is this so-called "cognized-ness"? If it is being made an object by a cognition, then surely, while cognition is itself not yet cognized, that very state of being made an object by cognition must be examined. If you say it is "being present before one" (*purovarttitā*), then how could even "being present before one" establish cognition if it is itself uncognized? If it is cognized, then there must be another "being present before one" in that case as well, and thus the aforementioned infinite regress occurs. Therefore, neither "being present before one" nor anything else serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for establishing the fourfold types of cognition.
Thus, the establishment of the object is through cognition; it is by no means from the object that cognition is established. (475)

If that [cognition] is not established, the object itself remains unestablished. If the establishment of the object depends upon cognition, then everyone would be an omniscient seer. If cognition perceives itself as being actively engaged with an object, then the object may be said to be "apprehended"; otherwise, nothing would be cognized. Or else, everything would be cognized by itself [without dependence on cognition]. Therefore, the establishment of cognition does not arise from the object, because that would entail the faults previously mentioned.
And having perceived direct perception as a cognition, and its subsequent activity, expression, and so forth, [one infers the existence of the object]. (476)
Furthermore, there would be no inference of another's mind, because the relationship [of that mind] is not perceived in oneself.

[446, vii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates are empty and thus delivered all suffering beings from peril. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness and emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete. Within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, no object of mind; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origination, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; transcending all perverted thoughts, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Chapter 25: The Profound. [447, i] At that time, the Buddha spoke to the Venerable Subhūti: "If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he should rely on this teaching. Then the Venerable Subhūti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* rely on this teaching? The Buddha told Subhūti: "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* should observe that all phenomena are empty, and he should not give rise to a mind of attachment. Why? Subhūti, all phenomena are characterized by non-attachment. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes that all phenomena are empty, he will not give rise to a mind of attachment. Why? Subhūti, because all phenomena are empty, one cannot apprehend their characteristics. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions will protect him. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, Māra and his host will be unable to find an opportunity to harm him. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not fall into the stages of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born among the long-lived gods. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the eight difficult conditions. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the borderlands where the Dharma is not heard. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born with defective faculties. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born with dull faculties. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born as a woman. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born as a hermaphrodite or a neuter. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of the Form Realm or the Formless Realm. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of the Desire Realm. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings, nor in the heavens of the Thirty-three, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, the Nirmāṇarati, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of Brahmā’s Retinue, Brahmā’s Ministers, or the Great Brahmā. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of Light, Limited Light, Infinite Light, Pervasive Light, or the Heaven of Ultimate Purity. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of Minor Virtue, Infinite Virtue, or Vast Virtue. Why? Because a Bodhisūtta Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, he will not be born in the heavens of Minor Purity, Infinite Purity, or Vast Purity. Why? Because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already attained mastery over birth and death. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in

If, through perception, there were some way of cognizing the self along with cognition and its connection [to that object], then, by seeing a mark (liṅga) connected to them, one could infer cognition in another person as well; otherwise, it would not be logical. If you say that the inference is "the object was seen by another," then from what source is the cognition of what was seen by oneself? If you say it is from inference alone, then for that too there must be another example, leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā). If you say it is cognized by perception itself, [we ask]: perception cognizes an object such as blue and so forth; how then is there the state of being "seen" (dṛṣṭatva)? If you say it also cognizes its own connection [to the object], then the state of being "seen" is simply this connection to oneself. If that is cognized, then the self must be established through self-cognition (svasaṃvedana). If that [self] were cognized by another, there would be an infinite regress, because in that case too the state of being "seen" would likewise be an object of cognition. Thus, the object is seen, the cognition is seen, the cognition-of-cognition is seen, and so on. And when one cognizes the cognition, at that time the state of being "seen" is no longer present, for then the cognition itself would become the visible object. Therefore, only the mere object is cognized; there is no such thing as a "state of being seen. Consequently, there is no basis for the arising of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). Moreover:
For that [cognition] is not perception, such that the object could serve as its logical mark (*liṅga*). Indeed, memory itself is not perception. Therefore:
Because the object and its indicative mark are not established for the cognition of the mind. (477)

"How is it that inference [is a means of cognition]?"—this is the supplementary question. Now, if in that case too it is the object itself, such as the universal (*jāti*) and so forth, that appears, then [you have] inference. To this, the answer has already been given: since that is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could the object appear? If it is argued that "while appearing, it is seen to be either real or unreal; at most, there is only a dispute [regarding its status]," then what is this so-called "unreality"? It is non-correspondence (*visaṃvāditā*). No, for there is no non-correspondence with respect to that form. Therefore, it must necessarily exist as something real in that form. If it is argued that "it is unreal because of the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'unreal'," then what is this "conventional usage"? If it is a valid means of cognition, then how can that which is apprehended by a valid means of cognition be unreal? If it is apprehended precisely as unreal, then no, for unreality is not perceived apart from that very form. The claim that "only the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is perceived, and not the performance of a purpose for another" is also not tenable; for if that were so, it would follow that it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*). If it is argued that "it is cognized by another," no, because memory (*smaraṇa*) is attached to the state of having been seen, and since this [object] lacks that prior form, there is no perception of it. If it is further argued that "this [memory] also takes that as its object," then it is not memory. Self-cognition, however, is perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus it is logical [to say] that such is the case here. For indeed, the conventional usage is: "This is my perception of the object in this way. Unreality is simply the perception devoid of an object of cognition (*prameya*). It is not a state of being "non-worldly" (*alaukika*) and so forth, because there is no such conventional usage. Moreover, [the object is known] through another cognition, through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), or by some other means.
Or how could cognition be manifested for you by another cognition?
For how could cognitions be illuminators of one another? Because:
[447, iv] How could there be that relationship of the manifested and the manifestor between two things whose nature is non-luminous? (478)

For it is not logical that two things which are non-luminous by nature should stand in the relation of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifester (*vyañjaka*), whether through mutual interaction or otherwise. Indeed, it is by means of luminosity— such as the light of a lamp— that non-luminous objects like cloth and the like are made manifest, and not otherwise.

How is there the manifestation of an object? Through its transfer into the light. For when it is transferred into the light itself, that object is manifested—just as, for example, a jar or similar thing is manifested when it has been transferred into the light of a lamp and so forth.
And that luminosity, being of that very nature, manifests by itself alone.
In that case, just as the form of a jar is one thing and that of its radiance is another, so too the form of consciousness is one thing and the forms of visible objects and so forth are another.
This is incorrect;
for even so, this [consciousness] exists just like an external lamp.
For in the absence of cognition, there can be no understanding of the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator.

(PVA 447, xii) Even if it were the case that the object and the cognition occurring at different times are related in such a way, nevertheless, like a lamp, it must exist as a self-luminous nature of consciousness. Or else, just like that [lamp], it would have to be graspable by another cognition.
That is incorrect.
If its cognition were by means of a consciousness distinct from itself,
then this consciousness would also possess externality precisely because it shares that same nature [of being cognized by another].
(1145) Or, if it lacks externality, why should it not possess self-cognition?

Even that [light] is not illuminated by a light distinct from itself. If it is accepted in that way, then cognition is self-cognizing within cognition.
Otherwise, the object, possessing identical properties, would also be established as being [self-cognizing] together with the intellect.

[447,xix] If, because of the transition of cognition into a manifest cognition, the cognized cognition is self-manifesting by means of that cognition, then cognition would be otherwise. If cognition were manifested by something other than itself, then, due to their identical nature as phenomena and by virtue of having the same form, the object too would become a manifester of the cognition.
Thus, our own intellect, being of the nature of light, shines forth by itself;
another object shines forth as light only through the transfer of its form into this [intellect]. (481)

In the same way, the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator exists between form (*rūpa*) and cognition (*buddhi*); that is to say, one is self-illuminating, while the other arises in the form of that [self-illuminating one].
(g) The illumination of the object occurs by way of the nature of consciousness.

[448,i] But surely, let it be that cognition is self-luminous, while another [cognition] is the object of illumination because similarity is possible—just as one is said to "grasp" the form of the father. To this he says:

For even when there is similarity, another cognition is not considered to be manifested by that [first cognition], because it is self-manifesting; rather, the object is manifested in the form of that [cognition]. (482)

For that which is not manifest cannot be made manifest by another, just as light itself cannot be so made. This is because they share only a common property; even for that which is not manifest, there is no manifestation in the ultimate sense. How, then, is an object manifested? An object is manifested by means of its own form—that is, by the form of the manifesting cognition—and it is not manifested by something else. Furthermore, since both cognitions possess the quality of self-manifestation equally, there can be no relationship of the manifested and the manifestor between them.
Just as in the case of two lamps, or a lamp and a jar, the conventional usage based upon them is extended through the relationship of the manifested and the manifestor. // 483 //
For even though the production of similarity between two lamps is possible, there exists no relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator between them.

In that case, how is it with the lamp and the jar? The jar arises from the causal complex of the lamp in a form identical to that [lamp]; therefore, it too is illuminated as being self-luminous, and not otherwise. Thus, such conventional usage is established through the analytical extraction based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), but it is not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Enough of this digression.
[448, vii] It is certain that vision does not occur by means of the object and the sense faculty alone.
Therefore, for that [cause] from which this [cognition arises], the perception of another [object] must also be stated. (484)

[448, viii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be learned by you. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. This concludes the Discourse on the Lion’s Roar, the eighth. The Ninth Discourse: The Discourse on the Great Lion’s Roar. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was seated not far from the Blessed One, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the Venerable Ānanda sitting nearby, with his body drooping, his mind weary, and his senses dull. Seeing this, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, why do you sit with such a drooping body, a weary mind, and dull senses? “Friend Moggallāna, I am exhausted from traveling through the villages, towns, and marketplaces; therefore, my body is drooping, my mind is weary, and my senses are dull. “Friend Ānanda, it is good for you to attend to the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, which is profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only to the wise. You should listen attentively and bear it well in mind; I shall speak. “Yes, friend,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. If the determination that "it has been seen" were to arise from the mere presence of the object and the sense faculty alone, then everything would be determined as "seen. Or rather, it would be determined that "only what is seen is seen. If you say, "It is determined that only what is seen is seen," then what is this so-called "the seen"? It is that in which seeing has arisen. And what is this "seeing"? That very thing which was questioned; namely, that wherein the eye and so forth are directed. How is it understood that the eye is directed? Even there, how is the conventional usage of "having been seen" established? Thus, there is an infinite regress. Alternatively, if the determination arises merely from the occurrence of seeing, it is not because of a determination based on having experienced [the object]. Nor does a determination that "it is not experienced" arise from mere experience alone. For indeed, when whiteness is not experienced, there is no determination that "it is white. Therefore, since a determination follows upon experience, it is logical that the determination must be by means of an experience that has become the very locus of that determination.
<(4) Proof of Self-Cognition> <(ka) Self-cognition through Recollection> [448,ix]
The existence of memory is also established for one who knows the self, because cognition is perceived by something other than itself;
otherwise, there would be no apprehension of long [vowels] and so forth, since multiple moments do not persist. (485)
Self-awareness is established not only from the specific nature of cognition regarding its object, but also from memory.

[Objection: Surely, memory establishes only that there was an experience, not self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Memory is indeed appropriate even if the cognition were known by something else. [Reply: That is not a valid answer. If cognition were known by another, there would be no apprehension of length and so forth, because many moments do not persist simultaneously.

[449,i] As was previously established, when two short vowels are employed in immediate succession, because they do not persist, that which is non-persistent is not perceived as a unity with that which is persistent. Consequently, there would be no apprehension of long or protracted measures (*mātrā*) at all. If each individual measure were not apprehended, there could be no apprehension of a "long" vowel or the like; nor is a composite whole (*samudāya*) perceived. If it is argued that perception occurs through the synthesis of the preceding and succeeding moments, we say no, because that synthesis itself must have a perceived object as its domain.

Is it not the case that the object characterized as "long" and so forth is indeed perceived? It is not perceived; rather, the object characterized as "long" and so forth is not perceived. Therefore, just as in the case of two short vowels, that [designation] is perceived in respect to two morae (*mātrā*), but there is no other distinct "long" vowel.

Now, one might object: even for one who holds that cognition is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), how can there be the apprehension of length and so forth? [The answer is: the determination of the perception of length occurs when there is the experience of a single cognition possessing that form. But then, even for the proponent of non-self-cognition (*asvasaṃvedanavādin*), there is indeed the experience of a single cognition possessing that form; it is simply by means of another cognition. And there is no difference between these two states, for: "The object of cognition is cognized by another [cognition], because it is an object of cognition, like something external to the object of cognition."
"Then cognition itself, being an object of knowledge, would also be known by another [cognition].
(PVA 449,v) This is incorrect, because even so, the following would occur:

That which is manifested is manifested by something else, because it is a manifested object, like the entity of a jar. Consequently, it now follows that even the lamp itself must be illuminated by something other than itself. (PVA 1148)

And something has already been said on this point: if a preceding cognition were perceived by a subsequent cognition, then, because that [subsequent] cognition would not perceive the form of the former, and because the object would likewise be absent at that time, there would be no perception at all; thus it has been established that experience would be lost for one who seeks it. Now, it might be argued that there is no instability [of the mind] regarding the *mātrās*, and therefore there is no failure to grasp long vowels and the like.
[This leads to the refutation of the *sphoṭa*:]
That too is incorrect, because:
If the mind were to apprehend [the phonemes] simultaneously while they remain in a non-sequential state, then a long vowel would be perceived as lacking sequence.

For a thing that remains fixed does not become "long" when perceived through a lack of sequence; rather, the designation "long" is established based on its being perceived through a temporal succession. Furthermore, there is indeed a sequence among the constituent *mātrās*, for the cognition of "long" and so forth does not occur at the final stage alone. At that time, the sequence being perceived is not otherwise than what was present in the preceding cognitions. Or, perhaps, this single cognition itself grasps both the prior and posterior parts.
That too is incorrect. For instance:
[449,xiii]
How can that which possesses sequence be without sequence? // 486 //
The parts of the phoneme (*varṇabhāga*) would assist [the cognition] without being joined to one another.

For the preceding and succeeding parts of the phoneme are unconnected due to their lack of simultaneous duration; how then could they assist a single cognition? Indeed, cognition is the grasping of an object, and when the object differs, the cognition must also differ; thus, there is no single cognition. How, then, can there be a perception of sequence? As it has been said: "Indeed not."
[449,xvi] And because of the simultaneous apprehension [of objects], there would be no cognition of a sequence, just as in the case of the sequence of the destruction [of things]. // 487 //

[449,xvii] Someone perceives a cognition when an object is unknown; however, once it is known, one understands it through inference. Just as this [cognition] is postulated in accordance with the knowledge of the object, so too is it [postulated] in respect to that which possesses its distinctions. For instance, people in the world designate: "Now, my cognition has arisen. Furthermore, this very essence of the object, such as length and so forth, is perceived. Indeed, a single entity such as length first arises. Consequently, since there is the apprehension of only a single length, the cognition of length is also singular. [450,ii]
That too is untrue; for:
[450,iii] The sound, increasing from its previous state, would become the final one.

[450,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these three things, he is called a 'Bodhisattva'. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva does not perceive a Bodhisattva, how then does he course in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-coursing. Subhūti, this is the coursing of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva courses in this manner, he is said to course in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva courses in this manner, how does he become one who has set out for full enlightenment? How does he train in the training of a Bodhisattva? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sets out for full enlightenment when he does not perceive a being, nor a soul, nor a person, nor a life-principle, nor a life-sustainer, nor a spirit, nor a human, nor a man, nor a doer, nor a feeler, nor a knower, nor a seer. Subhūti, when he trains in this way, he trains in the training of a Bodhisattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a being, how does he perfect the perfection of giving? How does he perfect the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perfects the perfection of giving by way of non-apprehension. He perfects the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom by way of non-apprehension. Subhūti, when he trains in this way, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva becomes one who has set out for full enlightenment and trains in the training of a Bodhisattva."

If this phoneme were a single entity, it would have been apprehended by the very first cognition, and thus there would be no delay. Furthermore, if the initial portion were not heard, a long vowel or the like would still be perceived by the final cognition alone. On the other hand, if the perception of "long" and so forth occurs through the successive perception of each subsequent portion, then there could be no such thing as a single "long" vowel. If you argue that the preceding portion persists while the subsequent portion is being perceived, then it follows that the sound is increasing in magnitude, since the preceding part continues to exist while the succeeding part arises. And if the cognition "this is long" occurs only at the final stage, then the apprehension would be non-sequential; thus, it could not be said to be "sequential. If you claim that sequence exists in relation to the preceding [parts], we say no, because the cognitions of the preceding and succeeding parts are distinct from one another. Alternatively, if you hold that the cognition produced at the outset remains as a single unit, [then the aforementioned difficulties persist].
That too is incorrect.
And the cognitions themselves do not have that as their locus, because they are established in an object higher than that. // 488 //

For a sound that has not been accumulated does not remain for the duration of the time it takes to accumulate; if it were so, there would be another accumulation, leading to the same infinite regress. Now, even if the object does not persist, if the sound itself remains, then likewise:
In that case, it would not perish by itself, nor would it subsequently undergo any change.

(450, ix) If cognition, whose nature is the apprehension of that [sound], were to persist even without the apprehension of the object, it would never perish; thus, there would be an excessive duration. Alternatively, if the absence of the apprehension of the object occurs when the object is absent, then it would not be a grasper of a long [sound], because only a portion of it has been apprehended. Or, if it is argued that a single phonetic entity (*varṇātmā*) arises simultaneously and persists for a period of time—that too is incorrect.
This same fault applies even if the phonemes are established as arising simultaneously and without succession. [450,x] 483.
[450,xi] If it were to remain for some time after having arisen all at once, it would have to persist forever, because there is no difference in its state later on either. Furthermore:
Because it arises from a single effort, subsequent efforts would be useless.
By that very same effort by which the first form was produced, the subsequent part would also be produced, since it is not distinct from it; therefore, the latter effort is indeed redundant.
Even if there were manifestation, this same fault would attach to the phonemes. [450,xiv] 490.

[450,xv] Since everything would be manifested by a single effort, a subsequent effort would be purposeless; therefore, long constituent parts are not grasped by a single cognition. It must be admitted that their grasping occurs through multiple cognitions.
And at that time:
[450,xvii] When it is apprehended by multiple [cognitions], that final cognition is what is experienced.
Furthermore, that [cognition] would not grasp [the object] as long; consequently, there would be no memory of a cognition of length.

When the parts of a long object are not apprehended by a single cognition, then the final cognition is experienced by another subsequent cognition. And that [final cognition] does not itself grasp the length; therefore, how could there be a memory of the cognition of length? There is no memory of what has not been experienced. Yet, the final cognition is experienced by another cognition, whereas the preceding cognitions are not experienced because they are intervened by [the intervening cognitions]. Furthermore, the final cognition is not occupied with the grasping of length.

Consequently, even the recollection of a long [series of cognitions] would not occur. Suppose it were argued that because each individual cognition is apprehended by subsequent cognitions, all of them are remembered, and thus there is a recollection of the long series of cognitions.
That too is incorrect, because:
If each cognition were perceived separately, there would be no appearance of continuity in the hearing of the sound, and the synthesis [of the parts into a whole] has already been refuted. (492)

[451,iv] Because the cognitions apprehending the parts of sound are separated by the cognitions that apprehend the [individual] sounds, there could be no perception of them as uninterrupted. For it is not possible to perceive what is interrupted as being uninterrupted. If it is argued that this perception occurs through a synthesis [of the moments], he says in response:

And the objection regarding the formation [of the word] has been refuted by the passage beginning with, "In other cases as well, that [simultaneity] is the same, or there is the simultaneous hearing of its two phonemes," and so forth.
Furthermore:
Even for one who hears [the sounds] as discrete, if there were an illusion of non-interruption, then there would also be an illusion of non-interruption when two short vowels are pronounced. (493)

[451, viii] There is no uninterrupted utterance of two short vowels; because of the interruption, there is an absence of a single cognition. If, however, that same interruption applies even to the *mātrās* (prosodic units), then there is nevertheless the conceit of non-interruption. In that case, since this same principle applies equally to the utterance of two short vowels, why is it not perceived?

And in this case, there is not even the perception of a separation; rather, there is indeed a separation. It is not an illusion—this alone is the tenable position. Furthermore: when the visual perception is interrupted, there is the superimposition of what is uninterrupted by the sense organ.
Not from the sense organ, because it would follow that all cognitions of the senses are false. (494)

If this cognition of non-interruption is indeed an error, it must be either produced by the senses (*akṣaja*) or mental (*mānasa*). If it were produced by the senses, then all sensory cognitions would be false. For instance:
For even the final phoneme, whose duration is equal to the blink of an eye, comes to an end through its successive connection with multiple atoms. (495)
The time of a single atom’s displacement is considered the shortest duration, a moment (kṣaṇa);
and since cognition is momentary, it perceives the phonemes in succession. (496)

Thus, regarding colors, forms, and so forth, every cognition—even one that appears as interrupted by another [cognition]—would have a false object, because it would appear without interruption [to itself]. (497)

[451,xv] For the comprehension of all phonemes occurs sequentially; cognition is momentary because it grasps phonemes in a form consisting of a continuous succession of distinct [moments]. Form and the other [sensory objects] are also born in a sequence. Therefore, even in that case, if a sense faculty were to produce a deluded cognition—like a whirling firebrand—there would be no delusion anywhere. If, on the other hand, it is a mental error, then there is another fault. To explain: [451,xvi]
And that which is the synthesis of entities elsewhere due to a sensory illusion—a memory confused by the non-perception of distinctions—that is conceptual construction (vikalpaka). (498)
How could that which is associated with verbal discourse possess a clear manifestation?
For it is untrue to claim that a mental distortion, by exceeding the limit of clarity while still occurring, becomes clear.

Furthermore, consciousness is held to have a clear form, such as the form of color and so forth. How, then, is it logical to claim that this is a mental error? For it has been stated that clarity is impossible for that which is associated with verbal discourse (*jalpa*), and that there is no manifestation of a clear object for that which is bound up with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Likewise:
It has been analyzed that there is no application of words to objects perceivable by the senses. (499)
[452,v] Now then.

If conceptual construction were to join together the object and its cognition—which are appearing continuously—even for one who perceives them as interrupted by the senses, [it would be impossible]. (500)
"In the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), how can it be that [the cognition] is interrupted when there is a logical consistency?

[452, viii] That which appears as uninterrupted should not be conceptualized as interrupted. Indeed, perception does not admit of a conceptualization otherwise; rather, it is proper to conceive of the non-existence of the conceptualization itself, because it is subverted by perception. Therefore, this [position] is untenable. Now, if one maintains that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) does not exist and accepts the awareness of a subsequent cognition (*buddhyantara*), and since two cognitions cannot occur simultaneously, then the perception would be interrupted by the intervention of that other cognition. To this, he replies:
If it is argued that this is due to the restriction of the capacities of cognitions, from what is that [restriction] held to arise? (501)

And if it is argued that this is because cognitions are observed simultaneously, then this very point is what must be investigated: [452,x] For if there is a restriction of capacity among cognitions, then their non-simultaneity follows; but from where is that very restriction of capacity to be ascertained? If it is argued that the restriction of capacity is due to the non-observation of simultaneous cognitions, then such observation would be intermittent, for even non-observation is possible in that case. If it is claimed that non-observation is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) there, then how can non-observation of simultaneity be a valid means of knowledge either?
Is that very same non-apprehension, which does not establish the absence of the arising of a discrete cognition, capable of establishing simultaneity? (PVA 1149)

In this regard, it must be investigated whether the simultaneous arising of conditions results from an uninterrupted perception, or whether an interrupted perception is to be postulated because they are not perceived simultaneously.

But surely, the non-perception of cognitions simultaneously does indeed exist; for even in the case of eternal things, the perception of their past and future forms is not found to occur simultaneously, since they are perceived only in succession. Furthermore, you yourself have a scriptural authority (āgama) to this effect: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two minds, one prior and one posterior, should arise simultaneously.
That too is incorrect.
There would be a restriction of their capacity with respect to that which is of the same class. [452,xv] 502.
For instance, conceptual constructions (vikalpas) are correctly perceived as occurring in a sequence.

Indeed, the restriction of the capacity of cognitions (*buddhi*) is with respect to the production of a cognition of the same kind, not in a general sense. Visual and other sensory cognitions do not produce only visual and other sensory cognitions of the same kind, nor do they produce everything. In that case, if they were to produce a duality consisting of the grasped and the grasper which are of different kinds, what contradiction would there be?

< (5) Refutation of Recognition > [453,i] Now, it may be argued that even conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), which has a clear manifestation, is accepted by others as a perceptual cognition called recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Let it be so; however, it is not actually so. For instance:
By this, [it is refuted] that which [asserts] the conceptualization of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) regarding an object present before one’s eyes. (503)
He who imagines that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) possesses a clear manifestation (*spaṣṭāvabhāsā*) and is thus perceptual (*pratyakṣa*) is also refuted.

[453,iii] Since sensory cognition lacks the capacity to grasp prior and subsequent forms, and since he maintains that what possesses a clear manifestation is perception even when it is a conceptual construction, he too is refuted. For instance: conceptual construction does not possess a clear manifestation; how then could it be perception? Even if it possessed a clear manifestation, it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its fallibility (*vyabhicāra*). To illustrate:
Because even in cases such as a tuft of hair, a pebble, or a lamp, there is a clear manifestation. (504)

How could a perceptual cognition be such even when a difference is well-known? Because perception is sublated in that case, it lacks the status of perception. By what is it sublated? By an interruption. Here too, there certainly exists an interruption characterized by the non-appearance of the preceding and succeeding forms.
Therefore, the determination of oneness regarding phonemes and the like does not arise from recognition. (505)
Therefore, because of the absence of validity, as for whoever says:
[453, viii]
Even when there is a difference in duration, the identity of phonemes is recognized through recognition;
therefore, by what means could there be a non-apprehension of long vowels and the like?

Even his statement is merely a word, for it has been established that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, recognition is not a perception produced by the senses (*akṣaja*). For instance:
[453,x] Without the recollection of a previous experience and the superimposition of its properties, [recognition does not occur].
The cognition "this is that very same [thing]" does not exist; how then could it arise from what is produced by the senses? (506)
