There can be no recollection without a prior experience, and there can be no recognition in the form "this is that very same thing" without recollection. For recognition consists in grasping the identity with what was previously experienced regarding that which is now being experienced. And without recollection, there can be no grasping of the former state. Furthermore, an object that is the content of recollection cannot be within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); otherwise, everything previously experienced would be directly perceived—so what then would be the use of the operation of the sense organs? If it is argued that since what was seen before might have died or perished, the operation of the sense organs is required now [to confirm its existence], then let the operation of the sense organs apply to that very [previous] object; why go to that place? If it is said that the sense organ is not capable [of perceiving it] without its being in a suitable location, then there would be no recognition here of something seen in another location, for a form connected to another location does not abide in a suitable location. If it is replied that the same single entity is connected to both locations, and therefore that very [other] location is the suitable one, and thus this fault does not arise—then why is it not perceived in that way even without recollection? It is not perceived because the connection [between the two states] has disappeared. If so, how could there be the thought "this is that very same thing" even in recollection? There is no fault, for there is recollection even of that which has passed away. Thus, recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that when the connection has ceased, the thing is no longer the "connected" entity, then in the absence of its connection to the previous place and time, it would possess only its present form; thus, there would be a difference between the earlier and later states. Therefore, the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not a perception of difference.

[453,xii] Is it not the case that this very point must be investigated: by what means is that cognition itself established? For mere cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); otherwise, why...

By means of insisting on the proof of perceptibility: if permanence were asserted even when a connection with prior time and so forth is not perceived, then all things whatsoever would be permanent, including those that possess an origin.
Even if they are perceived by way of their present form, they would still be permanent.
If it arises at that very moment, why is it not eternal?

(1151) [PVA 454, iii] Even if its prior state has not arisen, nevertheless it certainly exists. The objection—"How can that which has not arisen exist? How can that which has perished exist?"—is equally applicable. Furthermore, there is no difference between antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). This is the distinction: that which has been destroyed is remembered; whereas that which did not previously exist is cognized through inference based on possibility (*sambhava*), being cognized as something yet to be (*bhāvitayā*), but not as something prior.

[454,iv] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be learned by you. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful how this Dharma-discourse, which is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand, has been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that it is easy to understand. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not surprising that this Dharma-discourse, which is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to understand, has been taught by me in such a way that it is easy to understand. For, Ānanda, there are other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than this one, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “What are those other Dharma-discourses, Blessed One, that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than this one, yet have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four noble truths that I have taught in such a way that they are easy to understand. What are the four? They are: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These, Ānanda, are the other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than this one, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One, how these four noble truths have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not surprising that these four noble truths have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. For, Ānanda, there are other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four noble truths, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “What are those other Dharma-discourses, Blessed One, that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four noble truths, yet have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these twelve links of dependent origination that I have taught in such a way that they are easy to understand. What are the twelve? They are: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-and-death. These, Ānanda, are the other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four noble truths, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One, how these twelve links of dependent origination have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not surprising that these twelve links of dependent origination have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. For, Ānanda, there are other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these twelve links of dependent origination, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “What are those other Dharma-discourses, Blessed One, that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these twelve links of dependent origination, yet have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four nutriments that I have taught in such a way that they are easy to understand. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second nutriment; mental volition as the third nutriment; and consciousness as the fourth nutriment. These, Ānanda, are the other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these twelve links of dependent origination, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One, how these four nutriments have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not surprising that these four nutriments have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. For, Ānanda, there are other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four nutriments, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “What are those other Dharma-discourses, Blessed One, that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four nutriments, yet have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four stations of consciousness that I have taught in such a way that they are easy to understand. What are the four? They are: form is the station of consciousness, and consciousness dwells supported by form; feeling is the station of consciousness, and consciousness dwells supported by feeling; perception is the station of consciousness, and consciousness dwells supported by perception; volitional formations are the station of consciousness, and consciousness dwells supported by volitional formations. These, Ānanda, are the other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four nutriments, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One, how these four stations of consciousness have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not surprising that these four stations of consciousness have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. For, Ānanda, there are other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four stations of consciousness, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “What are those other Dharma-discourses, Blessed One, that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four stations of consciousness, yet have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four perversions of perception, four perversions of mind, and four perversions of view that I have taught in such a way that they are easy to understand. What are the four? They are: to perceive the impermanent as permanent, to perceive the painful as pleasant, to perceive the non-self as self, and to perceive the impure as pure. These, Ānanda, are the other Dharma-discourses that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four stations of consciousness, yet they have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One, how these four perversions of perception, four perversions of mind, and four perversions of view have been taught by the Blessed One in such a way that they are easy to understand. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is not surprising that these four perversions of perception, four perversions of mind, and four perversions of view have been taught by me in such a way that they are easy to understand. The venerable Ānanda said: “What are those other Dharma-discourses, Blessed One, that are even more profound, more difficult to see, and more difficult to understand than these four perversions of perception, four perversions of

[Objection: Is it not the case that because [the object] is perceived as "to-be-become" (*bhāvita*), there will be a future perception? Thus, the meaning is that at that time [the object] does not exist, but will exist later. [Reply: Here too, it is perceived as having been [existent], such that "perception occurred"; thus, it does not exist now. [Objection: Let it be so; but how can it exist even now? [Reply: Because it is perceived even now, it exists now. [Objection: Then how can it be said to exist in the interval? For it is seen only now. Indeed, what was previously non-existent is not perceived now. [Reply: In that case, this is neither perception nor inference, because no connection [of the object] with its prior existence has been grasped. [Objection: If it is argued that the connection is grasped through uninterrupted perception... [Reply: No, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for uninterrupted perception. For there is no means of valid cognition other than the memory "my perception was uninterrupted. [Objection: This very thing is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). [Reply: No, because its status as a means of valid cognition must be examined. [Objection: It is a means of valid cognition because it is non-contradictory (*avisamvāda*). [Reply: No, because there is an absence of non-contradiction regarding permanence. Therefore, this non-contradiction pertains merely to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); and by such an entity, such an efficient action is produced, but not by that same [entity] [as before]. This is because there is a lack of proof. Otherwise, if it were connected to causal efficiency at all times, that very [efficiency] would have been experienced then. [Objection: Because the efficient action was absent [then]. [Reply: How then is there no difference between that which is connected to efficient action and its opposite? [Objection: Because the efficient action is experienced later in that very same [object]. [Reply: This is not tenable, because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). For in that case too, another non-contradiction of efficient action would have to be admitted, and in that case yet another, so there would be no finality. Therefore, it is established that recognition is indeed not a means of valid cognition.

Therefore, because the perception of the *mātrā* is intervened by [other moments], there is an absence of contiguity (*nairantarya*), and consequently, there is no perception of long vowels and the like.
Now, if it is claimed that cognitions arise simultaneously, that too is untenable; for:
And the simultaneous occurrence of the object, the cognition, and the awareness [of that cognition] is not accepted.
The appearance [of the object] is perceived as distinct from both the external object and the cognition of that object. (507)

Because of the statement [in the Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.16]: "The non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is the mark of the mind. Furthermore, neither a cognition manifesting an object nor an object alone is perceived as appearing. Rather, it is the external appearance of blue and so forth that is perceived by virtue of having a self-cognized nature; nothing else is present there either. The failure to distinguish between the two [the cognition and the object] is due to their having the same form as the object, just as in the case of pleasure and its awareness.
That too is incorrect, because:
For there is no cognition appearing as an object, nor is there merely an external object alone.
Because it would follow that there is no differentiation in that which is grasped by a cognition of a single form. (508)

[454,xi] If pleasure and so forth, as well as cognition, possess a single form, then there is indeed non-difference even in that case. There is no difference without the appearance of difference. It is logical that there is merely the self-awareness of pleasure, and likewise for blue and so forth. Therefore, since there is no other awareness in this world apart from pleasure, blue, and so on, it is correct to conclude that blue and so forth are self-aware, just like pleasure.
Now, even if a cognition characterized by a perfectly distinct difference is not perceived here, nevertheless it certainly exists; for instance, light is restricted to form and so forth.
That too is incorrect; for as follows:
If two cognitions of objects are not perceived as distinct by means of a clearly discernible difference, how can they later be remembered separately? (509)

[455,iv] Even as for light, if there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends its distinction from this [object], it does not exist separately at all. For a distinction could only be considered through perception if there were a discernment of difference; but such is not the case. Therefore, there is no perception of light separate from blue. However, sometimes light is perceived alone, or form is perceived by some. Consequently, just as there is form alone, light alone, and form together with light, so too there would have to be consciousness alone, the object alone, and the object together with its perception. Thus, there would be a twofold appearance. [455,v]
Even if experience arises sequentially, this fault of the objection regarding the multiplicity of appearances for the object and the mind remains difficult to remove. (510)

Just as the fault that the simultaneous admission of cognition entails the consequence of two appearances—an object and its representation—is difficult to avoid, so it is also with respect to succession. For instance:
First there is the cognition of the object, and from that follows the cognition of the absence of the object;
for a pure cognition [of itself] alone could not be the cognition of an object. (511)

For the experience of an object, when being experienced by another cognition, must be experienced precisely as having the nature of an experience of that object. In that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the object appearing twice. Otherwise, how could another cognition experience that experience of the object? Therefore, even at a later time, there ought to be an appearance of the object; yet this is not so. For instance:
For instance, the form of blue and so forth is perceived as one, and the cognition is perceived as one; however, within the cognition appearing as blue, no further cognition is perceived. (512)

Here it is investigated: Is the fault only in the position of simultaneous cognition (*yugapajjñāna*), or also in the position of successive cognition (*kramajñāna*)? If [the fault applies] to simultaneity, then that is settled; for two things—the blue form and the cognition—are not perceived simultaneously. And this has already been established. Now, if [it is argued they occur] successively, even then it is not mere cognition that is subsequently observed, because remembrance perceives [the object] precisely as accompanied by the blue. Therefore, this is not a fault. It is not a fault. This is its meaning: the blue form is one thing, and the cognition is another; and the cognition is one thing, and the blue form is another. However, in the cognition appearing as blue, we do not perceive another cognition distinct from the object. Or rather, we experience the blue form as one thing and the cognition in the form of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth as another; yet we do not perceive another grasper in the cognition of pleasure and so forth, nor yet another in that [second], and thus there would be no experience of an infinite series of forms and cognitions.
[455,xi] Now he returns to the subject at hand.

There would be an experience by means of another cognition, and in that case too, memory is observed; by what, then, is that [second] cognition known? If it were by yet another, then this [same problem would follow]. (513)
Who produces this continuous chain (*mālā*) of those who possess knowledge?

[455,xiv] If one cognition is experienced by another cognition, how is that [second cognition] to be known? Since memory is observed even in that case, it must therefore be known by yet another cognition; thus, in that instance as well, memory alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And in that case, what cause would produce this continuous chain of cognitions and their respective experiences?
If that very same prior cognition were to persist, there would be no transition to another object.
[456,iii] Since each preceding cognition alone would be apprehended by each succeeding one, and not an object such as blue, there would be no apprehension of that [object] at all. For:

Without having apprehended that preceding cognition—which has attained the status of being an object, is proximate, and is the producer—how could a subsequent cognition apprehend another [object]? (515)

[456,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of giving. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift, and he does not perceive that gift as a gift, nor does he perceive himself as the giver, nor does he perceive the recipient. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of giving. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of morality? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, neither perceives that morality as morality, nor perceives himself as the one possessing morality, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of morality. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of patience? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that patience as patience, nor perceives himself as the one possessing patience, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of patience. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that vigor as vigor, nor perceives himself as the one possessing vigor, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of vigor. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of meditation? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that meditation as meditation, nor perceives himself as the one possessing meditation, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of meditation. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that wisdom as wisdom, nor perceives himself as the one possessing wisdom, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill all the dharmas of a Buddha? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive those dharmas of a Buddha as dharmas of a Buddha, nor perceives himself as one who has attained them, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills all the dharmas of a Buddha. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive those marks of a great man as marks of a great man, nor perceives himself as one who possesses them, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the thirty-two marks of a great man. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the eighty minor marks? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive those minor marks as minor marks, nor perceives himself as one who possesses them, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the eighty minor marks. The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive those unique qualities of a Buddha as unique qualities of a Buddha, nor perceives himself as one who possesses them, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that dharma of omniscience as a dharma of omniscience, nor perceives himself as one who has attained it, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the dharma of omniscience. The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that dharma of the knowledge of all modes as a dharma of the knowledge of all modes, nor perceives himself as one who has attained it, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the dharma of the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the dharma of the Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that dharma of the Tathāgata as a dharma of the Tathāgata, nor perceives himself as one who has attained it, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the dharma of the Tathāgata. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the dharma of the Arhat? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that dharma of the Arhat as a dharma of the Arhat, nor perceives himself as one who has attained it, nor perceives the field of merit. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the dharma of the Arhat. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the dharma of the Pratyekabuddha? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bod

If cognition, being of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), were to grasp an external object, then—since it would grasp an object that is in immediate proximity—there would be a shifting of the object of perception. However, when one cognition is grasped by another cognition, how could the subsequent cognition, without first grasping that [preceding] cognition which has attained the status of being an object (*grāhyalakṣaṇaprāpta*), grasp something such as blue? For there is no capacity for grasping another thing while bypassing what is proximate and connected to oneself as an object. If it is argued that the external object is present and acts as an obstacle [to the grasping of the preceding cognition], and thus there is a shifting to another object; [we reply: ...
That is incorrect, because:
And since that [cognition] is fixed in its own nature for the production of knowledge within itself, who indeed could obstruct it—an internal factor—by means of an external one? (516)
For even an external object, though present nearby, is not capable of obstructing that [cognition];
otherwise, no one would experience cognition while an object is in its proximity. (517)
And in that case, there would be no recollection. Or, it might occur when there is an absence of obstacles.
That is untrue; for:
[456,xi] And there is no state whatsoever in which an object is present to the cognition.
Since even the Smṛti has its roots destroyed, it is clearly held that [the Veda] is also destroyed. (518)
[456,xii] Only the object would be remembered, not that it was experienced. Or, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the experienced object might lead one to infer its own experience.
[456,xiii]

That too is incorrect. When the experience of an object has arisen as a continuous stream, there is no need for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) either. If presumptive testimony is to be remembered, then another presumptive testimony would be required, leading to that very same infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, it is an experienced experience that is remembered, and not otherwise. Consequently, due to the contradiction regarding the function of the object, there would be neither experience nor memory. Nor does the experience of an object arise from mere existence. From what, then, is that [experience] to be known? If it were from a further connection with a sense faculty, there would be an infinite regress.
This is especially so for conceptualizations of the past and so forth, for which the presence of an object does not exist.
Due to the absence of a cause for movement, the contemplation of objects would perish.

[456,xv] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound Prajñāpāramitā practice, beheld that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivered all those who suffer. Thus spoke the Blessed One. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One as follows: “O Blessed One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā? The Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, he should first observe the five aggregates as being empty of self and what belongs to self. Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. What is form is emptiness; what is emptiness is form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise. Therefore, Ānanda, one should know that all phenomena are empty of characteristics. They have no birth and no death; they are neither defiled nor pure; they neither increase nor decrease. Within emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness. There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no eye-element up to and including no mind-consciousness-element. There is no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path. There is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the state of non-attainment, thereby crossing over the suffering of old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, Ānanda, one should know that the profound Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. At that time, the Blessed One having thus spoken, the Venerable Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, and all those present, including the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had taught. Thus ends the Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Since there is no connection with the sense organs regarding conceptualizations of the past and so forth, how can there be a determination of their having been experienced? Consequently, there would be no reflection upon objects. There would be an infinite regress of reflection upon reflection. Alternatively, if in those cases too the object itself were to exist in a different manner (i.e., as past or future), then it would necessarily always be an obstructer [of cognition]. And in that case, there could never be a transition [to another object], because it would be rendered ineffective by that very [past object]. For in sensory perception, only an object present [at that moment] acts as an obstructer; therefore, sometimes there might be an interruption of the continuity of cognitions and their feelings, and sometimes otherwise. But in the stream of reflection, even an object that is remote acts as an obstructer at all times, because it remains its object.

In that case, if only the object were perceived and not the cognition, there would be no recollection of the cognition. If, on the other hand, it does not cause a contradiction, then, such being the case, the very perception of the continuum of thought and non-thought and so forth—which constitutes the thinking of the object—would surely perish. Furthermore, it might be argued: "There is a certain potency which produces cognition within itself; when that potency wanes and arises gradually, there may be a transition to another object."
That too is incorrect, because:
[457,iii] Due to the gradual exhaustion of the capacity for producing cognition within itself...
If there is a transition to another object, how can that very same cognition of the [previous] object exist? (520)

If the preceding cognition, being devoid of capacity, lacks the power to apprehend a subsequent cognition, then that object-cognition too would not be intended as possessing the quality of transitioning to another object. Therefore:
Upon the exhaustion of the capacity of the preceding cognition,
there is no transition to another object; for this reason:
For cognition does not exist without a preceding cognition.
What is the reason?
Because when cognition is impaired by attachment to another object, the arising of [another] cognition does not occur. (521)
[The storehouse consciousness] (ālayavijñāna) [457,x]

If, however, the preceding cognition were not the cause, then another cognition would arise even when there is a deficiency due to attachment to a different object. For the deficiency or non-deficiency of that which is not a cause cannot produce either an obstruction or its opposite. Therefore, the preceding cognition is indeed the cause. Since it would be incapable [of producing an effect], the cognition of the object would likewise not occur; thus, there would be an absolute absence of transition to other objects. [Objection: Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*—for one who holds that the *ālayavijñāna* is the producer of all evolving cognitions (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it does not have the status of being the cause of a preceding cognition, because the evolving cognitions arise from that very *ālayavijñāna* simultaneously. Therefore, for us as well, it is not the cause [of the subsequent cognition]. However, if the preceding evolving cognition were the cause, then the effect would follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [preceding cognition]; thus, the *ālayavijñāna* would not possess the status of being the cause. To this, it is replied:

[457,xi] Even when there is the simultaneous arising of a dissimilar [state], no other [state] can arise from the ālayavijñāna because its capacity has been impaired by a single, more powerful mind. 522.

[457,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. Furthermore, monks, when one seeks the nutriment of physical food, one seeks the root of suffering; when one seeks the nutriment of contact, one seeks the root of suffering; when one seeks the nutriment of mental volition, one seeks the root of suffering; when one seeks the nutriment of consciousness, one seeks the root of suffering. When one seeks the root of suffering, one seeks birth; when one seeks birth, one seeks old age; when one seeks old age, one seeks death; when one seeks death, one seeks sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, monks, this entire mass of suffering comes to be. Furthermore, monks, when one does not seek the nutriment of physical food, one does not seek the root of suffering; when one does not seek the nutriment of contact... when one does not seek the nutriment of mental volition... when one does not seek the nutriment of consciousness, one does not seek the root of suffering. When one does not seek the root of suffering, one does not seek birth; when one does not seek birth, one does not seek old age; when one does not seek old age, one does not seek death; when one does not seek death, one does not seek sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, monks, this entire mass of suffering ceases. Furthermore, monks, I shall teach you the nutriment, the origin of the nutriment, the cessation of the nutriment, and the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then said: “What, monks, is the nutriment? It is these four nutriments: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. This, monks, is called the nutriment. And what, monks, is the origin of the nutriment? It is craving, which gives rise to further existence, is bound up with delight and lust, and finds pleasure here and there. This, monks, is called the origin of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the cessation of the nutriment? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, which gives rise to further existence, is bound up with delight and lust, and finds pleasure here and there—its relinquishment, its abandonment, its release, and its non-adherence. This, monks, is called the cessation of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. [458,i] Furthermore, monks, I shall teach you the nutriment, the origin of the nutriment, the cessation of the nutriment, the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment, and the fruit of the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then said: “What, monks, is the nutriment? It is these four nutriments: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. This, monks, is called the nutriment. And what, monks, is the origin of the nutriment? It is craving, which gives rise to further existence, is bound up with delight and lust, and finds pleasure here and there. This, monks, is called the origin of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the cessation of the nutriment? This, monks, is called the cessation of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment? This, monks, is called the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. And what, monks, is the fruit of the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment? It is the cessation of birth, the cessation of old age, the cessation of death, the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. This, monks, is called the fruit of the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. This applies even for one who holds that the *ālayavijñāna* is the cause. For, even when at some time several heterogeneous cognitions arise simultaneously, there can be no further production from anything other than the *ālayavijñāna*. This is because [the subsequent cognition] is rendered defective by a preceding, more powerful active cognition (*pravṛttijñāna*) which has impaired its capacity through attachment to another object; therefore, in that case as well, it is that very [preceding cognition] which serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). If it is argued: "In that case, since the arising or non-arising of a cognition results precisely from that [preceding cognition] being defective or not, what is the use of the *ālayavijñāna*?"—let this inquiry into the *ālayavijñāna* rest. Or, if it is postulated as the substratum of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is no fault. However, if the causality of the preceding cognition is not accepted, then when...
Otherwise, one would not expect the subsequent state of the mind to be equal to the preceding mental activity.

For if a preceding mental state were to require another subsequent mind as its cause, it would have to depend upon something equal to itself; however, this is impossible because that which is not a cause cannot be depended upon. Therefore, since it is indeed dependent, it is logical to conclude that it is necessarily a cause.
Furthermore:
The sequential arising of mental cognitions must also be established as being dependent [on causes]. (523)

For the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the cause is indeed nothing other than its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). If it were without a cause, it would arise simultaneously [with all other things] due to being causeless. Therefore, since the subsequent consciousness has the preceding consciousness as its very cause, if the power of the preceding consciousness were absent, nothing at all would come to be.

If, because the mind is unitary, another [cognition] does not arise when it is attached to one [object] due to its inability to go elsewhere, then other cognitions would never arise at all, since they arise simultaneously [with the first]. (524)
[458,v] If that mind were a single entity, then because it moves to one place and does not move elsewhere, the preceding consciousness would be entirely without cause.

That too is incorrect; for even that is merely a cognition preceded by the mind (*manas*), and nothing else established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, it is established by the non-arising of cognitions simultaneously, and that [non-arising] occurs precisely because the previous cognition is rendered defective by its own attachment. Furthermore, simultaneous arising is sometimes observed. And if they were functioning equally, there would always be the arrival of another [cognition], since they would be identical.
But for one who holds that the non-arising of another cognition is caused by the unity of the mind, there would be non-arising at all times— both during its equal functioning and at other times.
But for us, there is arising when the conditions are equal and non-arising at other times; thus, nothing is contradicted.
[458,x] Now, one might ask: "How can there be succession without the mind? It has been established that this is due to the deficiency of the consciousnesses.
Furthermore, for those [cognitions] arising from the mere conjunction of the self and the mind, birth would occur simultaneously. (525)

For in that case, there is no movement toward another object from which a sequence could arise; it has been established that the cognitions of pleasure and so forth consist merely in the conjunction of the self and the mind.
Now, because the mind is a single entity, there would be only a single cognitive activity. That is incorrect, because:
If the action were one and the same, then how could a single lamp be seen by many?

Just as a single lamp produces multiple perceptions, so too does the mind. Thus, it is the same here: [the objection applies] both by virtue of multiple perceivers and by virtue of multiple objects of apprehension. Furthermore, the mind cannot be the cause [of cognition], because the restriction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) belongs to consciousness alone; were the mind to possess such a nature, it would follow that it is eternal.
[458,xvii] Even sequentially, it would not be capable [of producing cognitions], since there would be no distinction [in its state] even later on. (526)

[458,xviii] For there can be no conferring of a distinction upon that which is eternal, because a distinction could only arise through the application of practice toward a change in its very nature. Since:
Then there would be a distinction within its own self; if it were something else, what would happen to that [self]?
Even if there were a relation with that [other], it could not possess a single uniform nature.
By this, the body and the person have been discussed; if [the self is held to be] due to conditioning...
Whence comes that restriction? If it is from the subsequent cognition, let that be accepted. (527)

By this, the body and the person have been discussed. As for the one who thinks that because the body and the person are one, there is only a single action—that too is refuted by this very point: "Is a lamp a seer of many things?"

Even in the case of succession, there is no capacity [in the body or soul], because there is no distinction [between one moment and the next]. If, however, there is a distinction, then consciousness itself, endowed with a superior capacity, must be the cause of that succession; thus, the assumption that the body and the person (puruṣa) are the causes is futile. "If it is argued that the restriction [of succession] is due to a latent impression (saṃskāra), from what does that [impression] arise? If it arises from cognition, let it be as we agree. The latent impression is indeed already established; therefore, there is no [external] restriction. If it is argued that it arises later, from what does it come? A latent impression is born of cognition and is the cause of cognition; thus, the latent impression belongs to cognition alone. If this is so, this is exactly what we agree upon: the restriction [of succession] comes from the previous cognition itself, since there is no other proof for anything else. Indeed, apart from cognition, there is no such thing as a latent impression. Furthermore, it might be argued: "The mere production of another cognition occurs, but not its being apprehended (grāhyatā). Therefore, although the preceding cognition is the producer, because it is not apprehended, there is a transition to another object."
That is untrue, because:
There is no other state of being apprehended than the act of producing [cognition]; production is the defining characteristic of the apprehended.
For when an object is apprehended, the very fact of generating cognition is the defining characteristic of its being apprehended.
Because:
There is no light that is ungraspable; nor [can it exist] in that which is partless due to its subtlety and so forth. 528.

Light does not produce consciousness in any way because it is ungraspable; for everything that is grasped is seen to possess parts. Now, light, because it has constituent parts, might be a producer by means of its "other-side" and so forth, yet it is not itself grasped. This is because consciousness, which lacks parts, cannot have parts. Light, however, possesses parts, and thus it is logically consistent for it to be so.
There would be a loss of the capacity for being apprehended, but not of that which has the nature of producing another;
this is incorrect, because:
Indeed, in the case of the characteristic of being apprehended, there is no production of something other than that which is apprehended. (529)

For otherwise, form and the other [sensory objects] could not be directly beneficial to cognition. Indeed, it is through a mediated succession that even an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) can be beneficial to cognition by virtue of its being an object of apprehension; but not otherwise in a direct manner. Thus, cognition is beneficial only as that which generates [itself] and as that which is itself an object of apprehension.
Apart from the characteristic of being an object of apprehension, what other determination of its existence could there be for it? (530)
"Since that [capacity] exists even for the intellect, it too is established in reality"—
this is an intermediate verse.
Therefore, cognition is not ungraspable; for:
The perception of the object of apprehension and its appropriation constitutes the characteristic of the apprehended for the mind. (531)

[459,xvii] The Blessed One said: "O monks, there are these four kinds of persons existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a white lotus flower, and the person who is like a red lotus flower. What, O monks, is the person who is like a lotus flower? Here, O monks, a certain person dwells having entered the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, born of detachment, filled with joy and bliss, and which the noble ones describe as "peaceful and sublime. Having emerged from that attainment, he teaches the Dharma to others. He himself does not practice the cultivation of that state, nor does he encourage others to cultivate it; rather, he merely praises its virtues. This, O monks, is called the person who is like a lotus flower. What, O monks, is the person who is like a blue lotus flower? Here, O monks, a certain person dwells having entered the second dhyāna, which is free from vitarka and vicāra, inwardly serene, focused on a single point, free from vitarka and vicāra, born of concentration, filled with joy and bliss, and which the noble ones describe as "peaceful and sublime. Having emerged from that attainment, he teaches the Dharma to others. He himself practices the cultivation of that state, but does not encourage others to cultivate it; rather, he merely praises its virtues. This, O monks, is called the person who is like a blue lotus flower. What, O monks, is the person who is like a white lotus flower? Here, O monks, a certain person dwells having entered the third dhyāna, which is free from joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and clearly conscious, experiencing bliss with the body, and which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss," and which is the third dhyāna. Having emerged from that attainment, he teaches the Dharma to others. He himself practices the cultivation of that state and also encourages others to cultivate it; however, he does not praise its virtues. This, O monks, is called the person who is like a white lotus flower. What, O monks, is the person who is like a red lotus flower? Here, O monks, a certain person dwells having entered the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is purified through the earlier abandonment of pleasure and pain, and the earlier disappearance of elation and dejection, and which is described by the noble ones as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the purity of mindfulness through equanimity. Having emerged from that attainment, he teaches the Dharma to others. He himself practices the cultivation of that state and also encourages others to cultivate it, and he further praises its virtues. This, O monks, is called the person who is like a red lotus flower. These, O monks, are the four kinds of persons existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after teaching this Dharma discourse on the four kinds of persons. Friends, let us go to the Blessed One and inquire about the meaning of what was said. "Yes, friend," those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with a large assembly of monks, approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after teaching this Dharma discourse on the four kinds of persons. Venerable sir, what is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One? "Ānanda, when I taught the Dharma discourse on the four kinds of persons and then rose from my seat and entered my dwelling, I did so thinking: 'If I were to teach this Dharma discourse again, it would lead to weariness for both myself and others. Therefore, Ānanda, I shall now explain to you the meaning of what was said in that Dharma discourse on the four kinds of persons. Listen closely and attend well; I shall speak. "Yes, venerable sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, regarding the person who is like a lotus flower, he is so called because, just as a lotus flower grows in the mud and water but remains unsullied by them, so too this person, though born in the world, remains unsullied by worldly things. Regarding the person who is like a blue lotus flower, he is so called because, just as a blue lotus flower is beautiful and fragrant, so too this person is beautiful in appearance and possesses the fragrance of virtue. Regarding the person who is like a white lotus flower, he is so called because, just as a white lotus flower is pure and stainless, so too this person is pure in conduct and free from defilement. Regarding the person who is like a red lotus flower, he is so called because, just as a red lotus flower is radiant and draws the gaze of all, so too this person is radiant in wisdom and inspires the devotion of all beings. Thus, Ānanda, the meaning of what was said in the Dharma discourse on the four kinds of persons has been explained to you. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Ānanda and those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.

For the state of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatā*) consists in the mind’s capacity to grasp and its status as the material cause (*upādāna*) for consciousness; and this state of being an object is simply the nature of being experienced (*saṃvedanatā*), with no other quality such as subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*) involved. Thus, it is not the case that [the self] is unapprehendable. If the state of being an object were merely the status of being a material cause, then that status of being a material cause would belong only to one’s own cognition; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of experiencing the cognitions of others as well. The non-apprehension of another's mind, however, is due to its not being a material cause. Furthermore, the non-apprehension of form (*rūpa*) is due to its being distant or subtle, because the sense organ is not the material cause for the apprehending consciousness. Such is the distinction between objects. If, however, cognition itself were unapprehendable, then it too would not be an object of apprehension, just like the eye and other senses. But since cognition is known through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*), there is consequently memory of it.
That is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that [the entity] exists at all times, which is impossible.
When one quickly enumerates pillars, pots, and so forth,
because the conceptual proliferation is too vast, there is no arising of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) from that.

For one who does not deliberate quickly, there is no emergence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Furthermore, even if presumptive testimony were operative there, it would not be so, because no such operation is perceived. Nor is the existence of presumptive testimony cognized by those engaged in worldly practice.
This [cognition] would arise either from the object, or from the knower of the object, or from both.
(1154) First of all, it cannot be from the object; for not every cognition follows immediately from an object.
Nor does the cognition of the object proceed by way of the thought "this is mine" regarding the knower of the object. (1155)
From both [of these], the movement and non-movement are indeed established;
therefore, because it is self-cognized, the status of self-awareness is secured.
If cognition is understood through the object itself, then only the cognition would be understood, not self-cognition. Or, if it is from the cognition of the object...
[460, viii]

But surely, that very cognition of the object is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). How then can there be presumptive testimony from that very [cognition], given the fault of mutual dependence? For presumptive testimony is the postulation of an unperceived object because a perceived object would otherwise be inexplicable. And since the cognition of the object is not itself perceived, how can there be presumptive testimony? Nor is there perception of both [the object and its cognition] for this very reason; indeed, the perception of one is not the perception of both. Therefore, cognition is simply self-cognizing, as it cannot be established otherwise. Consequently, it is accepted that it is known by another subsequent cognition whose nature is perceptual. In that case, if all preceding cognitions were grasped, there would be no transition to another object. If the cognition of the object is due to the [subsequent cognition] being its material cause (*upādāna*), and the cognition of color and so forth is due to their subtlety and other qualities, then how could yogis have the cognition of another's mind or the subtle form and so forth? This is not a fault, because: [The verse follows: *paracittasūkṣmādyālambanaṃ jñānaṃ yoginām / dṛṣṭaṃ yadi kathaṃ tatra paracittādivedanam // yadi nāsti kathaṃ tatra paracittādivedanam / tasmāt sarvam idaṃ jñānaṃ svasaṃvedanam iṣyate //* If the cognition of yogis directed toward another’s mind, the subtle, and so forth, were [itself] perceived, how could there be the cognition of another’s mind and so forth therein? If it does not exist [therein], how could there be the cognition of another’s mind and so forth? Therefore, all this cognition is held to be self-cognizing.)* This is the meaning. Furthermore, if the cognition of the object were dependent on another cognition, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, if the cognition of the object were not self-cognizing, then even the final cognition at the end of a series would not be established, and thus the entire sequence would remain unproven. Thus, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is established. Furthermore, if cognition were not self-cognizing, then memory would be impossible, for memory arises from the impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by a prior experience. Since the prior experience is not remembered, the impression cannot be produced; and without an impression, memory is impossible. Therefore, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is established. Moreover, if cognition were not self-cognizing, then the cognition of another’s mind would be impossible, for the mind of another is not an object of the senses. Therefore, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is established. Furthermore, if cognition were not self-cognizing, then the cognition of the Buddha would be impossible, for the Buddha’s cognition is said to be omniscient. Since he does not perceive external objects, his cognition must be self-cognizing. Therefore, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is established. Thus, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is proven by these various arguments. Therefore, the view that cognition is self-cognizing is the correct one. Thus ends the discussion of the self-cognizing nature of cognition. [The verse continues: *svasaṃvedanatābhāve jñānasyārthasya saṃvidaḥ / smṛtir na syād anubhave tasyāḥ pūrvaṃ nirākṛteḥ // paracittajñatā na syād anyathā tasya vedane / sarvajñatāpi na syāt tadviṣayāparavedanāt //* If cognition lacked self-cognizing nature, there would be no memory of the cognition of an object, because its prior experience would have been negated. There would be no knowledge of another’s mind if that [mind] were not experienced [by oneself]. Omniscience would also not exist, because that which is the object [of omniscience] would not be experienced [by the knower]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, if cognition were not self-cognizing, then the cognition of the Buddha would be impossible, for the Buddha’s cognition is said to be omniscient. Since he does not perceive external objects, his cognition must be self-cognizing. Therefore, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is established. Thus, the self-cognizing nature of cognition is proven by these various arguments. Therefore, the view that cognition is self-cognizing is the correct one. Thus ends the discussion of the self-cognizing nature of cognition. [The verse concludes: *tasmāt svasaṃvedanaṃ jñānam iṣyate / tataś ca na doṣo 'yaṃ paracittādivedane // yadi nāma paracittādivedanaṃ na syāt, tathāpi na doṣaḥ / yataḥ / paracittajñatā na syād anyathā tasya vedane / sarvajñatāpi na syāt tadviṣayāparavedanāt //* If the cognition of another’s mind and so forth were not [self-cognizing], then there would be no knowledge of another’s mind. Thus, for those of impure intellect, there is this consideration regarding the definition of the apprehended object in relation to form and so forth, as well as the mind; however, the way of the yogins is inconceivable. (530)

[460,x] Indeed, how it is that yogins perceive things distant, subtle, and so forth, as well as the minds of others, is not even considered at this point. This definition of the "graspable" (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*) has been stated by us with reference to those of limited vision. As for the lords of yogins whose mental continua are completely purified—how could they be described? Let this matter rest; enough of such deliberation. And how this is so has already been reflected upon in part. Now, if one's own cognition were grasped, why would it follow that everything would be grasped? It is understood that it is not grasped simply because the mind moves to other objects. But even that is not logical, because:

In that regard, by becoming subtle and so forth, the object of apprehension would reach a state of non-apprehensibility. What has arisen subsequently in the cognition of form and so on that was not present before? (533)

Indeed, its state of being subtle, distant, and so forth was not something that did not exist previously. Even if there is no specific difference [in the object], if there is nevertheless a distinction in its apprehension, then that [distinction] would not have a cause, and thus it could not possess such a division.

Therefore, when there is the grasping of one's own cognition, that very state of being the immediate cause of the mind is itself the state of being the object; hence, there is no apprehension of anything other than that. (534)
Thus is the intermediate verse:
<The Discourse on the Causal Complex>.

[460,xv] Is it not the case that being a cause itself constitutes being an object of apprehension? This is not tenable, because entities possess multiple potencies. Therefore, the potency of being an object of apprehension is one thing, which ceases at the time of shifting to another object; and the potency for mere production is another, by the power of which the arising of a subsequent cognition has the entity as its object.

The possession of multiple powers by entities is determined precisely because they produce multiple effects; otherwise, there would be no production of multiple effects. Yet that too is trivial, because:
even in the absence of multiple powers, an entity does not fail to produce multiple effects.
"It is said that it is by its very nature;

This nature (*prakṛti*) of entities whose birth is dependent upon causes deserves to be questioned: "How is this so? For those that attain their arising from their own causes according to specific determination, who is the prohibitor of that? Otherwise, [if one asks] "From where does such a power (*śakti*) come?", there is no escape from questioning. If it is said to be from its own cause, then let the conclusion be reached through this very nature; what is the use of postulating another entity? [Objection: But surely the world’s understanding is that this power is dependent upon its own cause. [Reply: This understanding exists, but it is not an understanding of a power as a distinct [entity]. It is an understanding based merely on the superimposition of a distinction between properties that constitute the very nature [of the thing]. If it is asked how this is so: because even in the case of a power, we observe the cognition of another power. To illustrate:

If it is argued that a thing is the cause for the production of an effect because of its connection with a capacity (*śakti*), then why is it not further analyzed: from what does the capacity itself derive its capacity? 1157 (PVA)
Therefore, capacity is merely a mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because it is established through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
But surely, how can diverse entities arise from a single source without the existence of capacities? It is logical that they arise when there is a diversity of capacities. To this, he says:
"If it does not arise from the one, then it is not from the many. (535)
No single effect arises from a single cause; rather, an effect is produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
It has been stated that a single [effect] may belong to two complexes, and thus it is produced by many [causes]. (536)

For when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, there is generally the production of effects; however, some [effects] arise from one [cause], while others arise from many, and many [effects] may arise from one. Whatever kind of causal complex belongs to a thing, from that alone it becomes either one or many. This is the general rule for the manifold world (*prapañca*). To explain: an effect, whether one or many, arises from its own cause in such a way that it produces either a single or multiple effects. A difference in potentialities (*śakti*) is not required anywhere. Even potentialities are merely parts of the assistance provided by that [cause]; they are designated as "its" because they participate in its efficacy. Otherwise, potentialities would not exist at all; for if they were distinct entities, they would appear as separate things. And if they were separate entities, it would follow that they would be perceived as such. Alternatively, there is nothing at all that is a single entity producing multiple effects from a single [cause]; rather, it is the arising of multiple effects from the causal complex itself. How then is it said that "the many arise from the one"? It is so designated because a single [cause], being included within two different complexes, produces a single effect. For example, a single lamp is the producer of multiple visual perceptions, because it is conjoined with the various immediate causal complexes (*samanantara-sāmagrī*) of multiple persons. Just as a single thing may possess multiple powers, so too may it possess multiple effects; therefore, the state of having multiple effects does not necessarily imply the possession of multiple powers. If this is so, then just as one [thing] has multiple effects, a single cognition (*buddhi*) will likewise produce both a cognition of its own object and a cognition of another's object. In that case, sometimes the cognition would have its own object as its domain and sometimes another's object, resulting in a transition between objects. It cannot be that it produces both always, because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. If you say that it indeed produces them, that is not so, because: [at that time...]
If a subsequent cognition were to grasp both the object and the preceding cognition, then,
because it would manifest both the prior and subsequent objects, there would be a single mind at the very beginning and end. (537)
Two expressions would not be desired, whether appearing in sequence or non-sequentially;
for both the self and its cognition would appear twice each, because of their simultaneous manifestation. (538)

[462,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without marks, nor does he perceive that marklessness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is unproduced, nor does he perceive that non-production is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unproduced, nor does he perceive that non-production is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is unceased, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are unceased, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is pure, nor does he perceive that purity is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are pure, nor does he perceive that purity is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without increase, nor does he perceive that non-increase is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without increase, nor does he perceive that non-increase is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without decrease, nor does he perceive that non-decrease is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without decrease, nor does he perceive that non-decrease is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is without attainment, nor does he perceive that non-attainment is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without attainment, nor does he perceive that non-attainment is consciousness. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. Thus spoke the Blessed One. The Buddha said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, he does not abide in the perfection of giving, nor does he abide in the perfection of morality, nor does he abide in the perfection of patience, nor does he abide in the perfection of vigor, nor does he abide in the perfection of meditation, nor does he abide in the perfection of wisdom; he does not abide in the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he abide in the fruit of a once-returner, nor does he abide in the fruit of a non-returner, nor does he abide in the fruit of arhatship, nor does he abide in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood, nor does he abide in all-knowledge. Why is that? Alternatively, if the two [cognitions]—the preceding cognition that grasps [itself] and the cognition that grasps objects such as form—are both produced, then because the preceding cognition and the subsequent object both appear, the two linguistic expressions (abhilāpa-dvaya) that are perceived sequentially would appear simultaneously. For a cognition does not appear without having the nature of grasping an object, since that is its very essence. And when there is the appearance of grasping an object, the object itself appears; thus, the two linguistic expressions of the preceding and succeeding moments would appear together. Likewise, a single thing would appear twice, because of the appearance of the object’s own nature and the appearance of the cognition thereof. First, the object itself appears, and subsequently, when the cognition of it appears, there is the appearance of two. If it is argued that the cognition is not apprehended immediately after the appearance of the object, [we reply: cognition is not apprehended by perception, whether by itself or by another. If it appears even through presumptive proof (arthāpatti), then the same logical consequence follows, namely, that there is the appearance of both the self and the knower of that [self]. If it is argued that presumptive proof occurs at a later time, [we reply: no one experiences presumptive proof during the time of the sequential grasping of multiple objects in a continuous stream.
This is not so.
If it is argued that comprehension occurs through capacity, then it would either occur at all times or not at all; consequently,
when there is cognition through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there would indeed be a manifestation [of the object] a hundredfold.
Now, when one synthesizes one's own cognitions, then there arises an implication (arthāpatti) at a later time.
Even then, nothing was perceived at that [earlier] time from which [the implication] could arise.
[The opponent argues: "Since it has passed away, it is by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that [the cognition] is established.

(PVA 1159) [462, viii] How can there be the occurrence of presumptive testimony from a past perception of an object? If it is argued that presumptive testimony arises even from what is being remembered at another time, then the understanding derived from presumptive testimony belongs to the memory itself, not to the original experience. In that case as well, there would be a twofold appearance of verbal expression and a threefold appearance. If it is argued that what has not been experienced is not remembered, and therefore the experience is understood [through memory], that is not so.
When memory functions in the form "this was experienced by me," the occurrence of the notion "I had a cognition" is impossible through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). (PVA 1160)

[462,x] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be learned by you. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar’? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the Dharma, the lion’s roar of the Vinaya, the lion’s roar of the non-retrogression of the bodhisattvas, and the lion’s roar of the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Moreover, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the destruction of all Māras, the lion’s roar of the subduing of all adversaries, the lion’s roar of the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, and the lion’s roar of the establishment of the lineage of the Three Jewels, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Also, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the transcendence of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair, and because it roars the lion’s roar of the attainment of the state of peace and nirvāṇa, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the realization of the Four Noble Truths, the lion’s roar of the cultivation of the Eightfold Noble Path, the lion’s roar of the abandonment of the five lower fetters, and the lion’s roar of the attainment of the fruit of arhatship, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Moreover, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the purification of the six sense-bases, the lion’s roar of the mastery over the six supernormal powers, the lion’s roar of the fulfillment of the six perfections, and the lion’s roar of the attainment of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Also, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the non-attachment to the three realms, the lion’s roar of the non-abiding in saṃsāra, the lion’s roar of the non-clinging to nirvāṇa, and the lion’s roar of the great compassion for all sentient beings, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it roars the lion’s roar of the unshakability by all worldly dharmas, the lion’s roar of the invincibility by all heterodox teachers, the lion’s roar of the fearlessness in the four grounds of self-confidence, and the lion’s roar of
