Ānanda, because it roars

When one thinks, "I remember a previous experience," it is memory itself that first arises in the mind. At that time, there is no prior *arthāpatti* (presumption), nor is there any subsequent one; so how could memory be possible? Even when there is a memory of an object, there would still be an inference of both the memory and the experience; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the forms of the memory, the experience, and the object appearing simultaneously. And if that were so, there would be the consequence of perceiving the clear form of the object even at the time of memory. If, on the other hand, there is the perception of two indistinct forms, that too has never been observed, so it is not a solution. If you say that for someone who desires something, there is then an *arthāpatti*: "Because I remember, therefore it was experienced," or "Because there is memory, therefore there was experience"—then in that case, the verbal formulation would simply be: "Because there was experience, therefore there was experience. Likewise, "Because there is memory, therefore there is memory" is a great feat of logical ingenuity! Or, desire arises toward what has been experienced. But since an experience has never been experienced [by another cognition], how could an *arthāpatti* arise through desire? Therefore, the perception of a cognition by another cognition is simply non-existent.

If the final [moment of consciousness] is not experienced during the transition to another object, then it would follow that none of them are experienced, just like the experience of another person. (539)

For at the time of transitioning to another object, if the final cognition of the stream of consciousness were [the same as] the preceding cognitions prior to that transition to another object, then all experience would be like the experience of another. This is because an unexperienced experience lacks the status of being experienced, just like the experience of another. Consequently, due to the non-experience of the final [cognition], there is a non-experience of those preceding it, extending even to the first one. Just as in the case of another's experience, where there is no experience by another because that experience was not experienced by anyone else, so too in the case of what is experienced by oneself—since the nature of that object remains the same even in relation to another—how can there be experience?

[463,ii] But surely, just as the experience of another is established because one does not experience it oneself, so too should one's own experience be established because the other does not experience it.

That is incorrect. Let it be established if there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to do so. However, just as what has been experienced by another cannot be established as being either one's own perception or that of another, so too even that which is claimed to be one's own perception cannot be established as belonging either to oneself or to another.
[463, iv] But surely an object is cognized in its own form; how then can it be non-perceptual? For when one thing is not being cognized, it is not the case that another thing remains uncognized.

[463,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive forms, or eye-consciousness, or contact at the eye, or feeling born of contact at the eye as real. He does not perceive the ear as real, nor does he perceive sounds, or ear-consciousness, or contact at the ear, or feeling born of contact at the ear as real. He does not perceive the nose as real, nor does he perceive odors, or nose-consciousness, or contact at the nose, or feeling born of contact at the nose as real. He does not perceive the tongue as real, nor does he perceive tastes, or tongue-consciousness, or contact at the tongue, or feeling born of contact at the tongue as real. He does not perceive the body as real, nor does he perceive tangibles, or body-consciousness, or contact at the body, or feeling born of contact at the body as real. He does not perceive the mind as real, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, or mind-consciousness, or contact at the mind, or feeling born of contact at the mind as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or Arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of Buddhahood as real. Why is this so? Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Since they are empty of intrinsic nature, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they do not arise; because they do not arise, they do not cease. Because they do not arise and do not cease, they are neither defiled nor purified. Because they are neither defiled nor purified, they are neither increased nor diminished. Because they are neither increased nor diminished, they are equal to Nirvāṇa. Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to train in the equality of all dharmas should practice the perfection of wisdom."

[If it is argued that] truth is perceived [by another], let it be perceived by itself. That which is perceived by the self must also be perceived by itself; therefore, there is only self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). If it is argued that the self is perceived as an agent, no; for there is no self apart from the body. If it is the body that is the agent, no; because the body is also an object [of action]. This is because self-awareness does not exist for the body and such things. Or, if there were self-awareness, there would be no dispute at all. If it is argued that there is no awareness of cognition (*buddhi*), then since the self is self-aware, its experience of objects is sufficient in itself, and thus cognition would be useless. Therefore, he says:
If what is experienced by oneself is direct perception, yet not experienced by others, from where is that self-experience established by which it is so asserted? (540)

[463,vii] From what source is it known that there is an experience of a self? If it were experienced by another, from what source would it follow that this is not another's self? If it is experienced through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), then the establishment of self-cognition itself follows; thus, there is no dispute on this point. Therefore, if there were no self-cognition, it would follow that nothing at all could be experienced.
[463,viii]

[Objection: But surely, even when something has not been experienced by the eye and so forth, there occurs the conventional usage that "it was experienced by the eye and so forth. Why, then, is it not accepted that the same applies to self-cognition (*ātmasamvedana*), even though it is not experienced?
[Response: To this it is said:
For one who desires the manifestation of a manifestation, there would be the non-establishment of the cause of manifestation;
yet if this world were manifest even when manifestation itself is unestablished, then everything would be manifest. (541)

For the eyes and other sense organs are the causes of manifestation; even if they themselves are unmanifest, there is no lack of manifestation for the object, because the manifestation of the object is its being manifested. As for the designation "our eye," how is it that it is called "our eye" simply because it generates our cognition? The "ours" of the cognition, however, exists only through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Furthermore, if that very cognition were not self-cognized, nothing would be apprehended as being connected to oneself. Thus, if manifestation occurred merely by way of the object's own nature, the entire world would become manifest—an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
[Objection: But surely, where a manifestation (*vyakti*) has arisen, that is "manifest" (*vyakta*); how then could there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? [Response:
If something were manifest merely by the arising of a manifestation, then everything would be so.
However, this manifestation [of an object] cannot exist without a relationship [to a cognition].
(1161) Therefore, everything would have to be manifest by its own nature alone.
Or else, let it be said that the object, being of that very same nature [as the cognition], is self-cognized. (1162)
[463,xv] Thus ends the second chapter, on Direct Perception, in the *Pramāṇavārttikālaṃkāra*. 2.

[467,i] <1. The Purpose of Specifying "Seen by Oneself">

Inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is stated immediately after inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), because inference for others is preceded by inference for oneself. In this context, inference for others is the communication of an object perceived by oneself. "Perceived by oneself" (*svadṛṣṭa*) means that which has been perceived by the proponent and the opponent—the communicator and the one to be communicated; it also includes the members of the assembly (*prāśnika*), since they too have the authority [to judge]. The removal of misconception, however, is established by implication alone. By means of this, the object perceived by oneself is communicated to another. And that [communication] consists of the nature of bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*). Among these, the object perceived by oneself is the probans (*liṅga*) in its essential form.

[467,ii] But how is it that the logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses three characteristics? Because it is possible to communicate all objects by means of grasping an object perceived by oneself. Therefore, it follows that inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*) is the illumination of the entirety of the inferable (*anumeya*), which is by nature beyond the senses, for the sake of another.
To this it is replied:
Apart from the three-fold mark (liṅga), there is no manifestation of anything else.
It is impossible for anyone other than that [self-awareness] to realize it; thus, there is no illumination by another.

For that [object] is said to be "manifested" (*prakāśita*) wherein there is the agreement (*saṃpratipatti*) of another. Therefore, the prefix *pra-* denotes excellence (*prakarṣa*). And the agreement of another occurs regarding what is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If the object of inference (*anumeya*) were also already established by a means of valid cognition, then there would be no dispute at all. However, since the understanding of the object of inference—which has become the locus of dispute—occurs through the medium of manifesting the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), the statement is not useless. Consequently, because inference arises from it, that [statement] is also metaphorically called "inference" (*anumāna*). If, because it produces an inference, a statement were considered "inference," then because it produces direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), direct perception too would be "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*). This is not tenable.

Just as the arising of inference occurs when there is the recollection of a previously grasped relationship based on a statement, so too does the arising of perception never occur in that manner. (PVA 2)
When there is recollection of the three-fold mark, there is necessarily the arising of inference;
however, in the case of a statement regarding an object merely known to oneself, there is no perception.
(PVA 467, viii)
A direct perception of another does not arise from mere words.
[467,ix] But surely, one observes the arising of a perception in the case of "Look, the deer is running! No; for even there, it is immediately followed by inference. To explain:
When there is an orientation toward that object, one is enjoined with the words "you see"; this has been established by implication through my own cognition. (PVA 4)

“O gazelle-eyed one, appear before me!”—this is an injunctive statement. And appearing before me is just as it is for me, so too for you. Thus, remembering that the operation of the causes lies in such an appearance, one acts; this is indeed inference. Therefore, having observed the possibility of perception through that inference, one acts. In this case, then, it is an inference based on probability (*sambhavānumāna*) that operates upon the object of perception, being a reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*). A reason of effect (*kāryahetu*) is not directly revealed by the speech. For instance: [467,xii]
By the statement "there is fire here because of smoke," it is made manifest;
however, the mere connection [of smoke with fire] is manifested by direct perception.

Consequently, the statement in the *Pramāṇasamuccayavṛtti* that "inference for others consists of the three-fold statement of the mark" would be contradicted. This is not tenable; because all speech is for the purpose of recollection, therefore, in that context, it is designated as a means of valid cognition (*pramā*).
"But when [an object] is perceived through direct perception, the word is always useless. This has already been stated.
For the wise, indeed, only the reason itself is to be stated.

Likewise, it should also be understood that the connection (*pratibandha*) alone is [the basis for certainty]. Alternatively, even in that case, one must indeed rely on the statement of another, "This is smoke," in order to eliminate error. For it is said: "Through my own ascertainment, this smoke has come to be recognized here."
Why is it that even here you are awakened by another from this very delusion?
(7) [PVA 468, vii]

This is the meaning of the statement: it is not the case that an object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is communicated to another by means of speech; rather, that [speech] is indeed inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), because it is the cause thereof. This smoke must be viewed as nothing other than what was previously observed as smoke; it does not become something else. By implication, this is what is being said, because it possesses that characteristic. Therefore, it is only the operation of inference that is communicated by the word. The function of speech never pertains to direct perception. However, due to extreme familiarity, it appears otherwise to people, and thus the elaboration of inference is not [explicitly] formulated. Consequently, speech is capable of being accepted only as the cause of inference. Thus, speech is itself an inference based on essential identity (*svabhāvānumāna*); it is not an inference based on causality (*kāraṇānumāna*), as in the case of "this is smoke," because speech is an inference based on essential identity.

That is incorrect. For even in an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), when smoke is perceived as the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*), there is still no elimination of error in the interim, because the person discerning it lacks the nature-reason. To this, he says:
What contradiction could there possibly be here? For the cause of an effect is not lost;
even when there is an intervention, it does not forfeit its status as the cause of that effect.
(PVA 468, x)

If it is intended merely to state that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) certainly exists in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), then what is the use of demonstrating this mediation? However, in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the effect-reason is simply not possible, because the function of the statement "smoke" and so forth operates directly as a nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Therefore, inference for others does not exist by means of inference.
This is not so.
The author of the treatise has stated that inference for the sake of others exists based on what is possible; even if that were not the case elsewhere, what harm would there be? (PVA 9)

Alternatively, where there is no error, in that case, in *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself), the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is indeed immediate. Since the same principle applies to *parārthānumāna* (inference for others) as well, inference arises directly from words. If it is asked, "What is the use of speech if there is no error?", the answer is that there is no fault, because speech serves to demonstrate the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Furthermore, it was stated just now that the statement of the three-fold characteristic of the logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) occurs according to the circumstances. Moreover: [468,xiv]
Inference is not the authority for speech because it is inseparable from it;
this much alone is intended, but not that every word is so.
(PVA 468, xv)

As for the one who says: "How can there be validity only for perception and inference? Since speech is also a cause for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), worldly transaction is not complete without speech.
To this it is replied:
Without perception, inference, and verbal testimony, there is no worldly activity whatsoever; yet, what kind of validity can these possess? (PVA 11)

Even after recollecting an object previously perceived, why does one not act without [the aid of] perception and so forth? Is memory, then, also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Or is it indeed not a means of valid cognition at all? It is the same in the case of verbal testimony (*vacana*): it is not a means of valid cognition regarding its object in that way. However, where there is a means of valid cognition, it is only as a cause of inference and not otherwise. Only this much is intended here; it is not that every word is a cause of every inference. Verbal testimony is indeed a form of inference, but not an independent means of valid cognition. A demonstration that [all] words are inference is useless. Therefore, verbal testimony is simply the communication of a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*).

[469,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. This is called the ‘perfection of wisdom’ of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive form, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the eye, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive forms, nor their arising, nor their cessation; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive eye-consciousness, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive eye-contact, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the realm of form, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the formless realm, nor its arising, nor its cessation. He does not perceive ignorance, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of the essential nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of absolute non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of other-nature, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness, nor their arising, nor their cessation; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor their arising, nor their cessation; he does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the state of a Stream-enterer, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the state of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat, nor their arising, nor their cessation. He does not perceive the state of a Pratyekabuddha, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the state of a Bodhisattva, nor its arising, nor its cessation; he does not perceive the state of a Tathāgata, nor its arising, nor its cessation. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom, how then does he course in the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the perfection of wisdom? How does he fulfill the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-coursing. He trains in the perfection of wisdom by way of non-training. He fulfills the perfection of wisdom by way of non-fulfillment. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form is neither bound nor liberated; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. The eye is neither bound nor liberated; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are neither bound nor liberated. Forms are neither bound nor liberated; sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are neither bound nor liberated. Eye-consciousness is neither bound nor liberated; ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Eye-contact is neither bound nor liberated; ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are neither bound nor liberated. The feeling born of eye-contact is neither bound nor liberated; the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are neither bound nor liberated. The element of earth is neither bound nor liberated; the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. The realm of desire is neither bound nor liberated; the realm of form and the formless realm are neither bound nor liberated. Ignorance is neither bound nor liberated; volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death are neither bound nor liberated. The perfection of giving is neither bound nor liberated; the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom are neither bound nor liberated. The emptiness of the internal is neither bound nor liberated; the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of the essential nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of absolute non-existence, the emptiness of self-nature, and the emptiness of other-nature are neither bound nor liberated. The four foundations of mindfulness are neither bound nor liberated; the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are neither bound nor liberated. The ten powers of a Tathāgata are neither bound nor liberated; the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata are neither bound nor liberated. The state of a Stream-enterer is neither bound nor liberated; the states of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, and an Arhat are neither bound nor liberated. The state of a Pratyekabuddha is neither bound nor liberated; the state of a Bodhisattva and the state of a Tathāgata are neither bound nor liberated. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva courses in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the perfection of wisdom, and fulfills the perfection of wisdom.”

How, then, is the Vedic word a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? In that case too, its status as a means of valid cognition arises solely from its stating objects that are established by perception and inference, as in the statement "there are twelve months" and so forth. In other instances, however, it lacks validity, just like the speech of a human being. If it is argued that its validity stems precisely from its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), we say no, because it does not inspire confidence. For confidence does not arise from mere words alone. If the Veda were like perception, why would everyone not have confidence in it? Yet even from an inference such as that of momentariness, not everyone has confidence. If you say this is due to delusion (*bhrānti*), then there is delusion here as well; in the case of inference, that delusion is removed by another inference of the same class that serves as a basis for confidence. But in the case of the Veda, it is not removed by another word of the same class—thus, these two cases are not equal.
The validity of inference consists in its being connected with a positive concomitance (*anvaya*);
however, it was previously examined that no such positive concomitance is observed in the case of the Veda. (PVA 12)

Alternatively, this is the meaning: inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists solely of a statement that expresses a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*); it is not the Vedic word. This is because the Vedic word lacks those three characteristics. For in its case, neither a concomitance (*anvaya*) with truth is observed, nor is there the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). To explain: since it is non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), it is devoid of truth; and as for the concomitance with existence, there is no such concomitance. If it is argued that there is a concomitance in the form "there are twelve months," we reply: [469,vii] Here it is said:
It is not certain that the sentence concerning the *agnihotra* and other such rites possesses the status of a Veda;
for it is possible that this too was composed by some person.

Perhaps this was interpolated by someone among the non-human (apauruṣeya) [Vedic texts]; moreover, it is heard in some other recensional branch (śākhāntara) that they were composed. If it is argued that such usage occurs because there is a memory [of their authorship], no; for it lacks credibility, and because it would lead to the same consequence in other cases as well. Since all of this has already been established previously, it will not be elaborated upon here; let it rest.

If the term "seen by oneself" (*svadṛṣṭa*) refers only to the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*), then it should simply be stated that "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*) is the communication of the three-featured mark. What is the purpose of including the mention of "an object seen by oneself"? It is not for any other reason; for as follows:
since it is the other person who is to be convinced, even if [the object] was not seen by oneself, it must be seen by others.
Some say that what is perceived is the means of proof; the statement regarding the perception of the self is for the purpose of refuting that. (1)

In inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), there is no concern with one's own realization, because it is the other person alone who is to be convinced. If that logical mark (*liṅga*) is established for the other person, then the other person certainly realizes it. It should not be asked: "How can the other person possess realization without the proponent’s own realization?
[469, xi–xii]
Even when the proponent has attained understanding, another does not necessarily attain it.
If that [understanding] occurs without his own realization, let that [realization] alone suffice; what is the use of another here?
(PVA 469, xiii)

One does not understand that this is the proponent’s own apprehension in this case; rather, it is understood through his own conviction that "I have apprehended it exactly thus. Whether he has made it known after having ascertained it for himself or otherwise—what is the use of this investigation involving such an excessive proliferation? Therefore, even if something is not apprehended by oneself, it is accepted as a logical mark (*liṅga*) for others because of the [proponent's] intention. This is for the purpose of refuting that intention.

[The phrase] "one's own observed" (svadṛṣṭa) [is used]. If it were simply "observed by oneself," then because it would exclude what is observed by others, it would result in a redundant meaning. No; for its purpose is to establish what has been observed by both. This is its definition as it stands. And by this, disagreement (*vipratipatti*) is also refuted. Therefore, it should not be [understood as] "for that very purpose"; rather, it is logical that the purpose for which this undertaking is begun is precisely what is expressed by the word. For it is impossible to say of something that one has not perceived oneself that another has perceived it. [470,ii] [In inference, scripture is not a means of valid cognition.]

[Objection: Let it be that [the reason] is recognized by the opponent; however, the thorough knowledge that "it has been understood by the opponent" is not useful, because the purpose is fulfilled for the opponent through his own recognition alone. How then can there be the presentation of something unknown to oneself? If it is by virtue of what is established for the opponent, then it follows that "it is established for the opponent"—but how can this be so if it is not recognized by oneself? For one with limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*) does not directly perceive the cognition of another. Even inference depends upon one's own recognition; therefore, what is determined to be recognized by the opponent is also recognized by oneself. Alternatively, if it is understood by the opponent through scripture (*āgama*), then it is indeed recognized by oneself as well. However, because the proponent does not accept that scripture, it is designated as "not recognized by oneself. Therefore, even that which is recognized by the opponent through scripture, but not by oneself, is still a means of proof (*sādhana*). To this, it is replied:

[470,iii] The authority of speech is not accepted regarding the domain of inference, because it consists of the acceptance of what has already been examined; for inference does not operate in this regard. || 2 ||

[470,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, there are four kinds of persons who, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti asked: “What are those four? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a certain person, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, does not train in the perfection of giving; he does not train in the perfection of ethical discipline; he does not train in the perfection of patience; he does not train in the perfection of vigor; he does not train in the perfection of meditative concentration; and he does not train in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is the first kind of person who, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. “Furthermore, Subhūti, here a certain person, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, does not train in the emptiness of the internal; he does not train in the emptiness of the external; he does not train in the emptiness of the internal and external; he does not train in the emptiness of emptiness; he does not train in the great emptiness; he does not train in the emptiness of the ultimate; he does not train in the conditioned emptiness; he does not train in the unconditioned emptiness; he does not train in the infinite emptiness; he does not train in the emptiness of dispersion; he does not train in the essential nature emptiness; he does not train in the emptiness of all phenomena; he does not train in the emptiness of own-marks; he does not train in the emptiness of non-existence; he does not train in the emptiness of existence; he does not train in the emptiness of non-attainment; and he does not train in the emptiness of nature. Subhūti, this is the second kind of person who, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. “Furthermore, Subhūti, here a certain person, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, does not train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he does not train in the four bases of psychic power; he does not train in the five faculties; he does not train in the five powers; he does not train in the seven factors of enlightenment; and he does not train in the noble eightfold path. Subhūti, this is the third kind of person who, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. “Furthermore, Subhūti, here a certain person, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, does not train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata; he does not train in the four grounds of self-confidence; he does not train in the four analytical knowledges; he does not train in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; and he does not train in the great compassion of a Tathāgata. Subhūti, this is the fourth kind of person who, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, what is the reason why these four kinds of persons, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because they do not train in the perfection of wisdom, and because they lack skillful means. Therefore, these four kinds of persons, having set out upon the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, will not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.”

Is that scripture a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is a valid means of knowledge, then [the property] must be established for both parties, just as with something perceived by another valid means of knowledge. If it is not a valid means of knowledge, then it is not established for anyone at all. [The opponent might think: "Because of the opponent's own acceptance, it is established for him alone. This is not so. Scripture is a valid means of knowledge only regarding the domain of inference, because one accepts what has been examined. It is not a valid means of knowledge regarding the domain of perception or inference. If it were a valid means of knowledge in all cases, what would be the use of inference, since the object would be established by mere words? For example, the Sāṃkhya’s intended position—well-known to others—is that pleasure and so forth are insentient (*acetana*) because they arise or because they are impermanent, like color-form (*rūpa*) and so on. However, the Sāṃkhya himself does not accept that they possess arising or impermanence. In that case, if establishment occurs through the validity of the word, then the Sāṃkhya’s own word is indeed a valid means of knowledge; thus, the insentiency of intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure, and so forth would be established from that very source—what is the use of inference? Alternatively, if the Buddhist statement establishing impermanence and so forth is the means, then by that, the sentiency of intellect and so forth is established; therefore, the establishment of the opposite [insentiency] does not occur through inference, making inference entirely useless.
[470,v] Now, if the opposite of that [non-existence] were established through the validity of inference as well, then it would not be a means of valid cognition; thus he says:

Since the proponent states the means of proof (sādhana) for the sake of refuting [the opponent's position] by means of scripture, that [scripture] is not a valid authority (*apramāṇa*) for him at that time; therefore, everything [the opponent relies upon] remains unestablished (*asiddha*) for him. (3)

[470, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "It was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking birth. It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain in detail the meaning of this statement which was spoken in brief. At the very moment one begins to establish the opposite [thesis] by means of inference, that statement [of the opponent] is indeed no longer a valid authority (*apramāṇa*), because it cannot withstand critical examination and because its acceptance has become weakened. For when the status of a scripture as a valid authority is established through acceptance, if that acceptance becomes lax, its authority likewise becomes so. Consequently, due to the weakening of the reason well-known to them, there is also a weakening of the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*). Indeed, that which is entirely dependent upon something does not fail to follow it, for if it did, the consequence would be that it was not dependent upon it at all. If it is argued that the reason is not established as a valid authority because it lacks sentience (*acetanatva*), we say no; for if one were to see a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in one instance, it would lead to the consequence of a lack of confidence in all cases.

[471,i] Now, if that portion of the statement is consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃvādī*), then that reason would possess establishment for both disputants. Alternatively, even if it is established by valid cognition, because the Sāṃkhya is ignorant of the functioning of valid cognition, it remains established for the opponent alone.
That too is incorrect; for in this way, that Sāṃkhya would merely be exposing his own private parts. Even so, what is the fault?
For he has been convinced by that very mark which is established for himself.
It is not the case that one is ignorant only in some instances; rather, one must be considered ignorant regarding everything.

(PVA 471, iv) For it is not the case that because one is unable to prove a particular reason, one is likewise unable to prove the probandum. First of all, for that person, the probandum is already established by their own cognition, since the existence of the reason is established for themselves. If, on the other hand, the proponent is bold enough to claim that this [reason] can be refuted, [then the following applies].
That too is incorrect. For once a reason (*hetu*) is established, it establishes the probandum (*sādhya*); what need is there for anything else? To explain:

To that extent, this [person] is already well-known; but what benefit is gained by our establishing it? What rule is there that says, "Every activity must be performed by me alone"? (16) (PVA) [471,vii]

"Is this a royal decree that the reason (*hetu*) must also be established by me alone, just as the probandum (*sādhya*) is? For it is not possible to establish [the reason] for one who is not omniscient. Now, if it is argued that the proof is stated out of a desire to produce certainty in others just as one has certainty oneself—this is incorrect according to the *Nyāya*.
[471, viii] That too is not correct. To explain why:
The purpose here for another is merely the production of certainty;
therefore, the qualification "as in one's own certainty" is useless. (PVA 17)

For the other party’s interest lies in the mere certainty itself, and not in some further qualification that serves no purpose therein; indeed, a discerning person does not accept a qualification that is useless.
To this it is replied:
He who does not understand another's intention through discernment—

"How could he have the thought, 'I have understood by means of this'? (PVA 471, xiii) If he himself does not realize, "This person has not been deceived by me; rather, he has simply reached an understanding," how can there be comprehension? Furthermore, it might be argued: "What if there is merely an understanding for the other party? To that extent, the statement of the proponent has fulfilled its purpose; what fault is there in this? In that case, the following reply would also apply:
Even if what I have said to you is nonsensical, you have been awakened by my conviction; what further purpose could there be in this for you? (PVA 471.xiv)

[471,xv] The Blessed One said: “O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, O monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. But how is this to be understood? Is it that the four nutriments are the cause for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence? Or is it that the four nutriments are themselves the beings who have already come to be, and those seeking a new existence? If the former, then the statement that the four nutriments are the cause for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence, would be correct. If the latter, then the statement that the four nutriments are themselves the beings who have already come to be, and those seeking a new existence, would be correct. How is this to be understood? It is to be understood according to the following reasoning: edible food, coarse or subtle, is the nutriment for beings who have already come to be and for those seeking a new existence; contact is the nutriment for beings who have already come to be and for those seeking a new existence; mental volition is the nutriment for beings who have already come to be and for those seeking a new existence; and consciousness is the nutriment for beings who have already come to be and for those seeking a new existence. Therefore, it is established that the four nutriments are the cause for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. And this is the meaning of what was said by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, O monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. But how is this to be understood? Is it that the four nutriments are the cause for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence? Or is it that the four nutriments are themselves the beings who have already come to be, and those seeking a new existence? If the former, then the statement that the four nutriments are the cause for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence, would be correct. When someone, having elaborately set forth some semblance of a proof (*sādhanābhāsa*), says, "I have demonstrated this to you," what answer should then be given? If it is argued that a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) should be stated there, we say no; for by means of a refutation, the opponent's understanding (*pratipatti*) must be obstructed. But then the proponent would give this reply: "What business do you have with my understanding? If he were to say, "This is a non-understanding (*apratipatti*) because it is not established as valid cognition (*pramā*)," then in that case, a refutation should not be presented to the other party. One should simply say, "This is my own non-understanding. However, a refutation must indeed be stated in order to show that this is not a mere non-understanding, but one supported by reasoning. If that is so, then:
If the opponent is to state a refutation accompanied by reasoning,
then the proponent must also state a proof accompanied by reasoning. (PVA 20)

[471,xvii] The Blessed One said: “The Tathāgata has taught that there are two kinds of dependent origination: one concerning phenomena (*dharma*) and one concerning time (*adhvan*). What is the dependent origination concerning phenomena? It is as follows: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; conditioned by birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. This is called the dependent origination concerning phenomena. What is the dependent origination concerning time? It is as follows: there are three periods of time—past, future, and present. Therein, the past dependent origination is as follows: in the past, ignorance existed; the formative forces existed; consciousness existed; name-and-form existed; the six sense bases existed; contact existed; feeling existed; craving existed; grasping existed; becoming existed; birth existed; and old age and death existed. The future dependent origination is as follows: in the future, conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; and conditioned by birth, old age and death exist. The present dependent origination is as follows: in the present, conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; and conditioned by birth, old age and death exist. This is called the dependent origination concerning time. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “I shall teach you, monks, the dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena. What is dependent origination? It is as follows: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; conditioned by birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. This is called dependent origination. What are the dependently arisen phenomena? They are: old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair. These are called the dependently arisen phenomena. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “I shall teach you, monks, the dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena. What is dependent origination? It is as follows: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say: conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces; conditioned by the formative forces is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; conditioned by birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. This is called dependent origination. What are the dependently arisen phenomena? They are: the five aggregates of clinging. These are called the dependently arisen phenomena. Thus it was said. Furthermore, the Blessed One said: “I shall teach you, monks, the dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena. What is dependent origination? It is as follows: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises.
