The opponent must state with supporting reasons: "Just as there is no such understanding for me in this case, so it is for you. Likewise, the proponent must also provide a proof with supporting reasons; otherwise, the doubt might not be dispelled that "just as there is no understanding for me here, perhaps there is none for the other person either. Indeed, one who acts for the sake of others does not find satisfaction without relying on what is established for the sake of others. Nor do scholars engage in treatises or their subject matter merely out of a desire for victory, since those works are intended for the realization of reality (*tattva*). Therefore, only when one has understood it for oneself does it occur: "This has been understood by him," whereas to say something is understood by another without having understood it oneself is nothing but a false statement.

[472,i] However, if the opponent does not accept it, the proponent would not be one who establishes [the point]. For who would desire their own defeat? But when one has cognized [the point] for oneself, even if the opponent does not accept it through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the opponent’s state of being a speaker of falsehood is nonetheless cognized.

Now, even if one has understood for oneself, how can it be known that the other has understood? If the understanding belongs to the opponent, the judges will understand it. If the proponent does not understand what has been understood by the judges, then he lacks the necessary causal conditions (*sāmagrī*); it is not a fault of the speaker. Just as when milk is described to a blind man, there is no loss of the status of being an instructor.
The eye should not be given by any proponent to the opponent.

(PVA 472, iv) If, when it is stated that "milk is white," the opponent does not understand it due to a defect in his own eyesight—being blind—this is the fault of the opponent alone. How could this be a fault of the proponent? The statement of the proponent has fulfilled its purpose once it has been understood by the judges (*prāśnika*). Even so, it might be argued:
[472,v] For those who act for the sake of others, whose minds are drawn by compassion,
how could it be appropriate that they be subject to refutation merely because of the position of an opponent? (PVA)

For those who act for the sake of others, mere self-satisfaction is not what they desire; rather, their intended purpose is the removal of the delusions of others. In that context, where is the commitment of one who has girded his loins to instruct the opponent, yet finds satisfaction merely in instructing the judges? Where is the beginning of the effort to instruct the opponent, and where is its conclusion by merely instructing the judges? Furthermore:
If an arbiter, being prejudiced by partiality for one side, should engage in dispute,
then once again another arbiter must be sought from among the disputants. When such a transition to another arbiter occurs, [the same applies] to the arbiter who acts as the respondent.
Consequently, there would be an infinite regress; of whom, then, would the proponent be the communicator?
(24) Now, suppose the assembly of judges is also partial toward the proponent;
even so, due to that bias, their status as judges is not at all clear. (25)
To this, it is said:
Is this one who acts for the sake of others likewise [active] even toward the unworthy?
Having disregarded [their lack of worth], he does not fail in his capacity, for he is not by nature devoid of compassion.
Even one possessed of compassion is capable of accomplishing the welfare of those who are worthy.
[472,xiii]

For there is no contradiction in the power [of a statement] being directed toward an unfit [person], nor is there a lack of compassion; for it is not the case that such a person is perceived as being devoid of compassion. However, if the members of the assembly (*prāśnika*) were to be partial, they would themselves become the opponents, and thus one would necessarily have to rely on another assembly. Furthermore, it is not the case that everyone disputes, because there is a lack of motive or because of mutual dependence. If, moreover, those very members were to act as proponent and opponent to one another, then all worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed; yet this is not observed. Therefore, the conclusion of the debate consists precisely in the awakening of the members of the assembly. Moreover, it is indeed a lack of mercy that the defeat of others occurs through the imposition of non-comprehension and so forth. Consequently, having communicated one's own realization to the members of the assembly and others, one should appropriate the power of demonstration for oneself. Therefore, it is established neither by one’s own scripture (*āgama*) nor by the scripture of another.

[472,xiv] But surely, when that scripture is also accepted by the opponent as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then he himself must indeed understand it through the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) established therein. For it is impossible for one whose position is sublated to accept it in such a manner. Therefore, he says:
If [the scripture] is established for someone who possesses that scripture, then whose is it, and what is its source?
How can that scripture be established when it is being sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? 4.

[472,xvi] If it is not accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not admitted by the opponent, then whose scripture (*āgama*) would it be? If, even in the absence of such admission, it were to possess the status of a scripture for the Sāṃkhya as well, then it would be established for both parties. On the other hand, if because of non-admission it does not have this status, then it is not a scripture for anyone at all.

It is not established for anyone. Furthermore, this scripture (*āgama*) cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge; thus, it would be a fallacious scripture (*āgamābhāsa*). If one understands through a fallacious means of knowledge, that person is indeed deluded; therefore, such [scripture] does not remove the delusion of another, and thus one would not be a true debater (*vādī*). How could the other person not be deluded if they do not recognize the fallacious nature of the means of knowledge? And yet, they are not unaware of it. For instance:
how could there be an acceptance of something contradictory to that very [scripture] by means of that same [scripture]?
If one accepts something other than that, then that member of the syllogism which constitutes the exclusion [of the reason from the heterologue] lacks authoritative status. (5)

[473,iii] At the very moment that he accepts something contradictory to that [scripture], he simultaneously realizes the unreliability of that scripture as well, because the acceptance of a contradiction is inseparable from it. If it is argued that this is not a fault because of his ignorance, we say no; for it has been stated that in a state of ignorance, there is no capacity for communication. If it is claimed that the proponent’s task is accomplished because the opponent was led away after being deluded, we say no, for that would entail the undesirable consequence of even administering poison [being considered a valid means]. If it is argued that being a debater consists in deluding through eloquence, we say no, because eloquence consists in the clear communication of a thoroughly purified subject matter. For instance:
The knowers of reality maintain that eloquence is the illumination of a thing— devoid of error— by means of both its concise and detailed forms. (PVA 27)

If it is argued that one who desires victory must somehow or other remove the opponent, we say no; for by removing him in any manner whatsoever, one merely becomes an object of ridicule. If, then, the opponent is deluded even by a statement of a perfectly pure fact, how can one be called a speaker? Because the purpose is fulfilled simply by convincing the judges. It is not the case that the sun fails to illuminate because a blind man does not see it. For instance: [473, vi] The opponent is indeed to be removed by the proponent who desires victory, but not by any means whatsoever. This is because by removing him in any way, one becomes a target of derision. If, then, the opponent is confused even by a statement concerning a completely pure object, how can he be considered a respondent? Because the task is accomplished by establishing the matter before the judges. It is not the case that the sun lacks the power of illumination because a blind person does not perceive it. To explain:

The fault would belong to the speaker if he failed to communicate; for even a competent person does not understand a meaning that is of a different nature from his own unless it is expressed through speech.

If he has no faith even in the opponent’s status as a respondent despite such clear statements, then it is only proper for him to enter the school of a teacher who recites the *siddhamātrikā*. Furthermore, it might be argued that such a formal presentation of proof is not intended for the learned alone, but is presented for an unlearned opponent, since the latter too would offer nothing but irrelevant refutations. For indeed, with every price, there is a corresponding wrapping of the package. Thus, this results in the fable of the leather-worker: "This beggar drank wine from my bowl; I, however, must make him drink urine. Moreover:
The Sāṃkhya does not himself perceive insentience because of its permanence;
therefore, for the Sāṃkhya’s own cognition, there would have to be another means of valid cognition. (29) (PVA)

[473,ix] It is not logical to understand a matter to be proven for oneself through a means of proof established only for another. Therefore, one must possess a means of proof established for oneself that accomplishes that purpose. If you say, "That indeed exists," then it follows:
Why then has that means of proof not been stated, from which one's own cognition arises?

Why is that very thing—the cause for one's own conviction—not presented as the proof? What is the use of this other effort, like chewing on empty space? For when a reason with a perfectly clear nature is available, an effort involving arduous conceptualization is not appropriate. [The Sāṃkhya might argue: "That is established for me through scripture; therefore, I do not present a proof based on my own cognition."

[473,xii] But surely that scripture is a proof for the opponent as well? No; because it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the opponent. How can there be understanding even for oneself from what is not a means of valid cognition? Because it is a means of valid cognition for him [the proponent]. If it were a means of valid cognition, why would it not be so for everyone? Because of the absence of acceptance (*abhyupagama*). How, then, does the Sāṃkhya have acceptance of it? Because it has been examined by him. If that were the case, it would also be so for the opponent. Why? [474,ii]
By whatever reasoning scripture is to be accepted, why is that same reasoning not also what accepts it? (6)

[474,iii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these three things, he is called a 'Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm. He does not perceive the conditioned, nor does he perceive the unconditioned. He does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive the present. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he is called a 'Bodhisattva. [475,i] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom; and if he does not perceive form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and if he does not perceive the eye, nor forms, nor the ear, nor sounds, nor the nose, nor odors, nor the tongue, nor tastes, nor the body, nor tangibles, nor the mind, nor mental phenomena; and if he does not perceive the element of earth, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; and if he does not perceive the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm; and if he does not perceive the conditioned, nor the unconditioned; and if he does not perceive the past, nor the future, nor the present—then, Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom as a sign, nor does he apprehend the perfection of wisdom as a basis. He does not apprehend form as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis. He does not apprehend feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the eye as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend forms as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the ear as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend sounds as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the nose as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend odors as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the tongue as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend tastes as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the body as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend tangibles as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the mind as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend mental phenomena as a sign, nor does he apprehend them as a basis. He does not apprehend the element of earth as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as signs, nor does he apprehend them as bases. He does not apprehend the realm of desire as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend the realm of form as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend the formless realm as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis. He does not apprehend the conditioned as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend the unconditioned as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis. He does not apprehend the past as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend the future as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis; he does not apprehend the present as a sign, nor does he apprehend it as a basis. Subhūti, because he does not apprehend these things as signs or as bases, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. [475,ii] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not apprehend a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom; and if he does not apprehend form, nor feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; and if he does not apprehend the eye, nor forms, nor the ear, nor sounds, nor the nose, nor odors, nor the tongue, nor tastes, nor the body, nor tangibles, nor the mind, nor mental phenomena; and if he does not apprehend the element of earth, nor the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; and if he does not apprehend the realm of desire, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm; and if he does not apprehend the conditioned, nor the unconditioned; and if he does not apprehend the past, nor the future, nor the present—then, Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, give gifts? How does he guard morality? How does he perfect patience? How does he exert vigor? How does he enter into meditative concentration? How does he cultivate wisdom? How does he fulfill the perfection of giving? How does he fulfill the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom? How does he fulfill the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he fulfill the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? How does he fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he fulfill the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift while not apprehending that gift, nor the donor, nor the recipient. He guards morality while not apprehending that morality, nor the one who guards it, nor the field of merit. He perfects patience while not apprehending that patience, nor the one who perfects it, nor the object toward which patience is perfected. He exerts vigor while not apprehending that vigor, nor the one who exerts it, nor the field for which vigor is exerted. He enters into meditative concentration while not apprehending that meditative concentration, nor the one who enters it, nor the object through which meditative concentration is entered. He cultivates wisdom while not apprehending that wisdom, nor the one who cultivates it, nor the object by means of which wisdom is cultivated. Subhūti, in this way a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fulfills the perfection of giving. He fulfills the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom in the same manner. He fulfills the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in the same manner. He fulfills the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path in the same manner. He fulfills the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion in the same manner. He fulfills the knowledge of all modes in the same manner. [476,i] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not apprehend a Bodhisattva, nor the perfection of wisdom, nor one who courses in the perfection of wisdom;

Just as the *āgama* of the Sāṃkhya, when examined through reasoning (*yukti*), is accepted by them as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why would this same reasoning not also be valid for the Buddhist? If you argue that it is not accepted by him, then how could he accept the reasoning that "because they are impermanent, [the elements] are insentient"? It is equally true that whatever is established by logic must necessarily be accepted even regarding the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*). Thus, when a proof established for both parties is possible, why would one undertake the effort of presenting another proof for oneself? This object is accessible to yogis; therefore, the opponent should be convinced by whatever means of proof is appropriate.

[474,iv] But surely, since this is accessible to yogis, the opponent is likewise capable of asserting it regarding his own probandum. Nor can it be maintained that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a yogi. For instance:
Those means by which, for one who is [previously] ordinary, there previously occurred comprehension and direct perception;
those same means are sufficient for this person’s knowledge of the capacity of objects. (7)

[474, vi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as consciousness. He does not perceive the eye as the eye, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as the mind. He does not perceive forms as forms, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as mental phenomena. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as mind-consciousness. He does not perceive eye-contact as eye-contact, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as mind-contact. He does not perceive the feeling arisen from eye-contact as the feeling arisen from eye-contact, nor does he perceive the feeling arisen from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as the feeling arisen from mind-contact. He does not perceive the element of earth as the element of earth, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire as the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as the formless realm. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as conditioned phenomena, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as unconditioned phenomena. He does not perceive the past as the past, nor does he perceive the future or the present as the present. He does not perceive all phenomena as all phenomena. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, these phenomena are empty of their own intrinsic nature; they are not apprehended, and they cannot be apprehended.”

Indeed, no yogi exists who is established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because there is a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a thing; this was already demonstrated previously when it was stated that "even if [the yogi] were impermanent, there would be no valid cognition. Therefore, one who is initially an ordinary person subsequently attains the state of a yogi through the practice of means, not by means of some self-existent perfection. And so: those means by which the understanding of the method for achieving that [state] occurs—through the practice of that method, the capacity of the senses arises; and that very perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists in the understanding of that object, has been described. Alternatively, the means for such an understanding has been explained. Those means for achieving it are capable precisely of making known the power (*sāmarthya*) or capacity of the sense-organ, which serves as the means for the object. If one accepts the object as understood by such a yogi, then what is the point of putting forward proofs for something non-existent? Just as the proof for the existence of a yogi has been stated by the Buddhists (*saugata*), it is equally reasonable for others to state it as well. If, however, even by way of the possibility of a yogi, that proof cannot be accepted, then silence is the only appropriate course here. For:
And for those things whose sequence is interrupted and which are not even within the scope of generality,
there is no consideration whatsoever regarding the probandum or the probans. (8)

[474, viii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as a real entity, nor does he perceive the bodhisattva as a real entity, nor does he perceive the one who courses in the perfection of wisdom as a real entity. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as a real entity, nor the bodhisattva as a real entity, nor the one who courses in the perfection of wisdom as a real entity? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because form is non-apprehensible; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-apprehensible; because the eye is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the mind; because forms are non-apprehensible, and so on up to mental phenomena; because eye-consciousness is non-apprehensible, and so on up to mind-consciousness; because eye-contact is non-apprehensible, and so on up to mind-contact; because feeling born of eye-contact is non-apprehensible, and so on up to feeling born of mind-contact; because the element of earth is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the element of consciousness; because the realm of desire is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; because the conditioned is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the unconditioned; because the stream-enterer is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the arhat; because the pratyekabuddha is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the Tathāgata; because the perfection of giving is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the perfection of wisdom; because the first dhyāna is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna; because the friendliness is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the equanimity; because the emptiness of emptiness is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the emptiness of the non-existence of self-nature; because the recollection of the Buddha is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the recollection of the deities; because the power of a Buddha is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha; because the fruit of a stream-enterer is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the fruit of arhatship; because the fruit of a pratyekabuddha is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an all-knowing one; because the path of a bodhisattva is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the path of an all-knowing one; because the knowledge of all aspects is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one—Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as a real entity, nor the bodhisattva as a real entity, nor the one who courses in the perfection of wisdom as a real entity. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if form is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, then how can there be the designation of a bodhisattva? How can there be the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is precisely because form is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the bodhisattva is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the one who courses in the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if form is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, then how can there be the designation of a bodhisattva? How can there be the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because form is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the bodhisattva is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the one who courses in the perfection of wisdom is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘bodhisattva’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘perfection of wisdom’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘one who courses in the perfection of wisdom’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘form’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘feeling,’ ‘perception,’ ‘mental formations,’ and ‘consciousness’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘eye’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘forms’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘eye-consciousness’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘eye-contact’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti, it is because the name ‘feeling born of eye-contact’ is non-apprehensible, and so on up to the state of an omniscient one is non-apprehensible, that there is the designation of a bodhisattva, and the designation of a bod

For when an object can be followed by a means of proof—either by way of a generality (*sāmānya*) or by way of a particularized generality (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*)—then an investigation into the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) may be undertaken. In that case, the investigation is conducted by way of a generality: "First, it is possible for us that such a person is a yogi; therefore, it is also possible that he has perceived this object," or else, "Only this specific object is possible," which is an investigation by way of a particularization. However, regarding those things which cannot be made into objects even by way of a generality because they are entirely beyond comprehension, there can be no investigation whatsoever concerning the locus of the probandum and the probans. Let alone any investigation into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); even if this object were accessible solely through scripture (*āgama*), one who introduces a means of valid cognition into such a matter merely reveals his own wretched ignorance regarding the domain of the means of valid cognition.

[474,ix] Now, as long as that person is not proficient, he does not recognize it as a fallacy of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*). Therefore, from his perspective, it is indeed a proof (*sādhana*). But when he realizes, "This is not a proof," then it will no longer be a proof; what fault is there in this?
That too is untenable,
because: "If the determination of what is real and what is unreal were based on the power of men's intentions," [475,i]
The reason and its fallacious counterpart are both excluded from that [inference], because it relies upon a real entity (vastu). // 9 //

[475,ii] For if it were merely a matter of a person’s intention, then even what is not a reason would possess the status of a reason, and even what is not a reason would possess the status of a reason; thus, the distinction between a reason and its fallacy would not be real. Or, if such a distinction did exist, it would set aside the intentions of persons. Therefore, a means of proof accepted by another is not valid. Furthermore, from an unexamined scripture, there arises only a mere cognition, not a certainty regarding the object. Nor is an object established by mere cognition alone. Why? [475,iii]
An existing object depends upon cognition, whereas a non-existent one cannot be established by cognition.
Even for that which exists, its mode of apprehension is similar [to that of a non-existent thing] if it lacks connection with the actual reality. (10)

[475,iv] Only that which exists is a means of establishing another; that which does not exist cannot be established. If it were established from what is non-existent, it would follow that it is causeless. If it is argued that there is knowledge regarding the non-existent, and therefore its establishment occurs, then how can that knowledge belong to something that is non-existent? If it is argued that the knowledge itself is the direct means of establishment, we say no, because it would follow that [the object] is perceptible. Therefore, there is no establishment of a non-existent thing through knowledge. [475,v]

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is indeed comprehension even from mere cognition, in whatever way it may be, through an object that has been superimposed? [Response: No. In the case of a superimposition that possesses a real basis (*savastuka*), comprehension occurs precisely by means of that real entity. If, however, this comprehension were to occur without a real inferential mark (*liṅga*), then it would be a mere semblance of comprehension, because it arises from a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
There is no true comprehension of fire from the perception of smoke where there is no smoke.
Even a reversed logical mark (*samāropa*) is not a means of proving the probandum.

(PVA 475, vii) Furthermore, this has been established in the *Svārthānumāna-pariccheda*: only the three types of logical marks (*liṅga*) are the means of proving an object, and nothing else. Therefore:

The logical mark (liṅga) is either an essential nature (svabhāva), an effect (kārya), or simply the non-perception of the perceptible; it is established as being connected with the thing in reality. Why then is that [connection] not established for oneself? 11.

[475,ix] If the nature of the probandum (*sādhyasvabhāva*) is established in reality because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what is not established for the Sāṃkhya himself? For the establishment by valid cognition is common to both parties, since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is shared. If, on the other hand, there is no valid cognition, then:
It is also improper to go elsewhere by means of another.

For just as the Sāṃkhya presents [the argument], "Since the reason, such as impermanence, is established for you, therefore accept it," so too does the opponent [argue]: "This is established for you by means of a proof that is itself established; just as you have understanding from that, so too will another discerning person. Otherwise, the Sāṃkhya would not even be acting with deliberation. Indeed, the notion that "I alone am clever, but the other is not" is not the perception of a conscious being. Therefore, among the learned, the employment of a proof based merely on the opponent's own admission is not appropriate. How then is it that the earlier masters and yourself sought to establish the probandum through reasons established for the opponent?
That is incorrect, because:
[475,xiii]
In a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) based on the constructs of others, because of the connection between two [terms], the negation of one serves to negate the other. (12)

That is a *prasaṅgasādhana* (reductio ad absurdum); however, the ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhya*) does not arise from it. For the ascertainment of the probandum does not occur merely through the acceptance by another. What, then, is its purpose? It is for the sake of establishing the absence of one thing when the other is necessarily present; for [the probandum] would not [be established] in the absence of the probandum.

The possibility of proof: this is a *prasanga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum). Because there is an absence of any other nature that would be delimited by association with a single individual restricted to a particular place, time, or state, a single entity that subsists in many cannot be conjoined with another thing possessing a specific place and so forth. Likewise, because of non-difference, if one part were colored, the whole would be colored, and so on. This is because such a nature is contradictory to conjunction with different places and so forth. **(1) Refutation of Time:** [476,ii]

[Objection: Surely, even a single entity, by virtue of its pervasiveness, may be connected with multiple locations and so forth; what contradiction is there? [Reply: No, because a connection with multiple times cannot be perceived. Indeed, pervasion across prior and subsequent times is not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because the state of being prior and subsequent is an object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). That which has past perception belongs to the prior time, and that which has future perception belongs to the subsequent time. Furthermore, there is no other "time" apart from the objects perceived at those respective times.

[Objection: But surely, since time does not exist, how can there be the conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior"? Likewise, since direction does not exist [as a separate entity], how can this be? Furthermore, even if time did exist, how could there be the conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior"? For it is not the case that something is the object of the convention "prior" and so forth simply by being connected with time; otherwise, it would follow that this applies even to the present. [Reply: It is because of the difference in time. To explain:
that which is connected with a prior time and so forth is what receives the designation "prior" and so on.
Its state of being prior or posterior also arises from its own essential nature alone, and not from anything else.

That which exists at a prior time is "prior," and likewise, that which exists at a subsequent time is "subsequent," and so forth. If it is asked how time itself can be "prior," [the answer is that] time's status as prior and so on exists by its very nature; the same applies to space.
vi] This is untrue, because:
For how could eternality and omnipresence possess priority and so forth?
If it is argued that this is because they coexist with such properties, then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence.
(PVA 476, viii)

For since the concomitants, such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, possess priority and the like, it follows that even space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*), though all-pervasive, likewise possess those properties; what contradiction is there? Indeed, nothing whatsoever is not designated by means of its concomitant, just as in the expression "the beds cry out. Likewise here, there is the designation "that time has passed. However, in this case, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) pursues you with great speed.
As for the priority of the concomitants, it arises from their association with prior time.
And the priority and so forth of time [is established] through the separation from that which co-exists with it.
(32) (PVA) If one [of the two] is not previously established, how can there be the existence of the other?
In the case of simultaneous existence, there could be no "priority" produced by one relative to the other. (33) (PVA)

As long as time does not possess priority and so forth, its concomitants likewise do not; thus, that which you intend to prove remains unestablished. Now, if both [the entity and time] share an identical lack of priority and so forth, then since two things existing at the same time cannot be perceived as having a mutual operation, there can be no state of being produced by one another. Therefore, that nature arises from its own causes, and this absence of priority and so forth belongs to the entities themselves; thus, the conceptualization of "time" is useless. For instance: that object which is past is called "prior"; that which is future is "subsequent"; and that which exists is "present."
But surely, since time does not exist, how can this very point be established? And even if time did exist, how could it be so? This too has already been demonstrated, so it is no answer. Furthermore:
"Because of the existence and non-existence of the cause, the effect is both existent and non-existent. [476, xiii]
Is the determination of priority and posteriority also a conceptualization of the unperceived?

(PVA 34) For the existence of priority, posteriority, and mediacy occurs through simultaneous determination; and that [determination] occurs through the presence or absence of a cause. That cause, too, exists or is absent only due to its own cause. Thus, it is not reasonable to postulate an unperceived entity.
[477,i] Now, if it is maintained that time—which is without beginning or end—is the cause for the discernment of forms such as "slow" or "quick," that too is insignificant. Why?
How can there be cognitions of "quick" and so forth from time, which is without beginning or end?
If it is maintained that time is the object of apprehension for cognitions such as "long" and "quick," [how could it be so]?

If these cognitions grasp the very nature of time, then let that [time] itself be grasped as being without beginning or end and as all-pervasive, since it is impossible to grasp such a thing through another means such as "long duration" and so forth.
Whatever form is actually grasped, that alone is logically consistent with the object.
The existence of entities is not accepted in any other manner [than that described].
(PVA 36) Since forms such as "slow" and "quick" are mutually distinct, this [same problem] would also apply to time; how then could it be all-pervasive and unitary? (PVA 37)
Through the discernment of its status as "this object is of long duration," the various distinctions such as "long" and "not long" follow the nature of time.
(PVA 477, vii)

For terms such as "slow" (*ciram*) and "quick" (*kṣipram*) are perceived through conformity with the nature of time, not through entry into the nature of a [discrete] object; thus, there is an all-pervasive establishment of time. To explain: whatever is perceived as conforming to something else is a possessor of that [quality], just as a brindled cow (*śāvaleya*), being perceived in the form of a cow, is a possessor of that [cowness]. The same logical status applies to time as well. If this is so, then regarding the distinctions of "slow," "quick," and so forth, which follow the nature of time—
If "time-ness" (*kālatva*) is a universal (*sāmānya*), then time itself is not established.
(PVA) [477,ix] If "time-ness" is a universal, then time is not proven to exist.

[477,x] For time is held to be among the categories of substantial entities (*dravyapadārtha*), and not a universal (*sāmānya*), because that [universal] is a distinct category. Nor is time perceived as something distinct from the forms of "long duration" and so forth. The term "time" (*kāla*) is merely a designation applied by someone for the sake of brevity to those very [phenomena].
Even these [terms] such as "long" (*cira*) and so forth are certainly not distinct from action;
for, as in the expression "done for a long time," they enter into the form of the action itself.
(PVA 477, xii)

For since it is perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the action— as in "it lasts for a long time" (*ciraṃ karoti*)— in reality, terms such as "long" (*cira*) and so forth merely conform to the form of the action.
[477, xiii] <The Refutation of Action>
Nor is action distinct from the categories of object and agent; for instance:
"Devadatta acts"—here, the act is not something other than the agency.
That which is cognized by means of valid cognition is so because of the cognition of its unity.

(PVA 477, xv) For indeed, in the case of the statement "the mat-maker makes the mat," no action (*kriyā*) is perceived through direct perception as something distinct from the specific agent and object of the mat-making. Since it is absent there, it is likewise absent through inference; thus, action is simply non-existent. To explain:
When something is being divided, there is no division other than that [act of dividing]; there is no other possibility for sublation.
Due to the difference in beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it is only the cognitions themselves that are differentiated. (PVA 42)

[477,xvii] For, having constructed a distinction through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the ordinary person—whose mental continuum is supported by beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*) and whose adherence to the reality of entities has been loosened—perceives a distinction even when there is no distinction; thus, this determination of a distinction in action is merely a cognitive error (*viparyāsa*). Why is this so?
[477,xviii]

If the action were not non-different from Devadatta, then another [person] would also be connected with that action; thus, it is conceptually distinguished as "the action is different" because of its connection with another. (43) [PVA 477, xix]

And this has already been established previously. Furthermore, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are not accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are accessible only through mental cognition produced by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Now, it may be argued that this so-called "action" (*kriyā*) is non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*), and therefore it is not perceived through direct perception. Even if it were indeed non-substantial, there would still be no connection with logical marks (*liṅga*) and the like. However, if it were distinct from the category of real entities (*padārtha*), there would be a contradiction regarding its perceptibility. Therefore, "slow," "quick," and so forth are merely specific instances of imagined action; they are not ontologically real.
"How is it so? and so forth is meaningful. For instance:
How could these [terms] "how," "thus," and "so" be distinct from the objects they denote?
They would be so only if the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of their exclusion (*vyatireka*) were their establishers.

If whatever conceptual construction arises were to have that very object as its form, such that the referent of that term (*padārtha*)—the object of conceptualization—is ultimately real, then what would become of such entities as time and so forth? For they are not accepted as being based upon those [conceptual constructions], nor are they perceived [as such]. If, on the other hand, they are merely specific actions, then the same applies to "long" and so forth; thus, the effort expended in postulating time and the like is futile.
Therefore, because there is no apprehension of objects existing at prior or subsequent times by means of perception, an all-pervading entity (*vyāpin*) is simply not grasped by direct perception.

**(3) Refutation of the Universal:** Now, suppose it is thought that even if the pervasion by time (*kālavyāpti*) is not apprehended, the apprehension of pervasion by space (*deśavyāpti*) is not contradictory. This is not so; for in that case as well, nothing such as a universal (*sāmānya*) is perceived apart from its substratum (*tadādhāra*). This is because a nature of such a kind is contradictory with connection to different locations and so forth. For that which has not entered into one place cannot exist in another at that same time; otherwise, due to the absence of distinction, there would be entry into all places simultaneously, resulting in a single lump (*ekapiṇḍatā*). Indeed, if it does not enter into the substrata of those [other things], it cannot enter into what has already entered them.
[478, vii] Now, if the cognition "these two are the same" arises from that, then the universal would be both different and non-different [from its instances]. To this it is replied:
[478, viii]
If cognitions possess a common form, how can there be a commonality of objects?
For if one thing possesses commonality with something else, another thing cannot thereby become identical to it.
(45) If the object itself were to possess a common form, it would have to be perceived as distinct [from the cognition].
How can that which is not perceived among objects be postulated with respect to those very objects?

"What is the meaning of the statement that 'cognition possessing a conforming form arises'? For a word does not establish the reality of an object merely by its being understood in some way or another without its meaning having been examined. And examination consists in [the cognition] having an identical form, because there are two possible modes for a word's object: either through identity of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or through identity with the form of the object. Since no other mode is possible, if it were identity of intrinsic nature, it would be the intrinsic nature itself and not the object; thus, the universal (*sāmānya*) would be the object as that which possesses the identical form. Yet that form of cognition is nothing but the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*); it is not a universal, because it is absent in other cognitions and because it does not reside in the object."

[478,xi] Now, if it is argued that the very form of the object is common [to both], and thus the cognition has that form—this too is untrue, because it would entail the appearance of two forms. If it is claimed that those two forms indeed appear, we say: no, because:
In this matter, the statement is not based on conviction due to partiality toward one's own view;
rather, the meaning is established for everyone because *dhvani* functions everywhere.
Therefore, the notion that "the cognition has a uniform form" is a confusion for those of steady intellect; hence, there is no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*).

[Objection: If it is argued that the state of having a uniform form consists in possessing a dewlap and so forth, and that this universal—characterized as non-different from those [individuals]—is joined with other individuals restricted by place and time, then there is no fault. [Reply: This is incorrect, because:
Even the universal form (*ākṛti*) does not possess unity, because it is not apprehended as such by perception.
If it were a single entity, then upon a single cognition of it, there would be the apprehension of all individual instances (*vyakti*). (PVA 48)

[479,ii] Because the form (*ākṛti*) is one, even when that single form is apprehended, there would follow the undesirable consequence of grasping all things possessing that form. Now, if it is argued that the form itself is indeed apprehended, but the apprehension of the possessor of the form is impossible because they are distinct—indeed, it is not possible to apprehend what is distinct; rather, something else is apprehended precisely because of identity (*tādātmya*).
That too is incorrect;
for identity is indeed [constituted by] having that as one's nature, but it is not called "identity" [in the sense of being a separate entity].
If there were identity through a succession of forms, non-difference alone would result.

(PVA 479, v) Identity with that form means that one form possesses the nature of another form. Since that other form is identical in essence with the possessor of the form, the grasping of that which possesses the form is the grasping of its identical essence. If that which is non-different from the possessor of the form were not grasped, then even when one form is grasped, the other form would not be grasped; for non-difference is not the basis for grasping, since the possessor of the form is not being grasped.

[479, vi] Now, if it were the case that because of that difference, it is simply another configuration (*ākṛti*), then, by the same logic, because there is no difference in configuration, there should likewise be no other thing possessing that configuration (*ākṛtimat*).

By this, the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya is refuted. For it is not the case that because [a form] has perished in one instance, it has perished everywhere; another individual [of that class] is indeed perceived. Indeed, an individual is not non-different from the universal simply because the universal is undivided, just as [individuals belonging to] different universals are distinct.

[479, viii] Now, if it is argued that there is only a difference between individuals possessing the universal due to differences such as blackness and so forth, and not a difference in the universal itself—that is incorrect.
If this [universal] were distinct from blackness and so forth, how could it be differentiated by their difference?
If its differentiation is due to association with them, why would that not also apply to the generic form (*ākṛti*)? (PVA 50)

If blackness and so forth are something entirely other than that which possesses the form (ākṛtimat), how can there be a distinction [in the substance] based on the distinction between them? For one thing that is distinct does not cause another distinct thing to be distinct. If it is argued that it causes it to be distinct by way of being its cause, we say no; because there is an absence of causality. For qualities alone are not the cause of a substance, since they arise with a single shared destiny (ekayogakṣema) with it. Or, if they were a cause, then from that [quality] another distinct [substance] would arise, and for that too there would have to be another distinct differentiator through conjunction. Furthermore, a cause itself is not a conjoined entity; otherwise, fire would also be a conjoined entity of smoke. If you argue that this is not so because it is never observed, then we reply: since causality is not observed even in the case of a conjoined entity, causality should not be postulated.
[479,xi] If there were difference even within the position of non-difference, then the generic form (*ākṛti*) would also be divided.
For that which is non-different from what is different is indeed different; otherwise, there could be no such thing as difference. (PVA 51)

[479,xiii] It was said: “Physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle. To what extent is it called “gross” and to what extent is it called “subtle”? That which is edible, chewed, swallowed, and consumed by mouthfuls is called “gross”; that which is not so is called “subtle. Blackness and so forth are non-different from that which possesses form; yet that which is non-different from what is different [from the former] is itself different—thus there is a difference from that which possesses form. But then, by virtue of its non-difference from that [blackness], it follows that even the form must be different. Furthermore, the form does not differ from that which possesses form; consequently, being non-different from what is different [from blackness], it would be different from another thing possessing form and from the form itself. If it is argued that the form is indeed non-different, this is not so; for there can be no connection between the form, which is subordinate, and the quality of blackness and so forth, because qualities do not co-inhere (*asamavāya*) with one another. It is a tenet that qualities co-inhere only in that which possesses qualities. This is not tenable.
[479, xiii] This is appropriate to say when there is a distinction; for when there is no distinction, there is no differentiation.
Indeed, the thought "this is here" and "this is not that" arises only when things are distinct. (PVA 52)
"In that case, let there be difference; this would be like a child's plaything, since one abandons the position of difference and resorts to another position.
(PVA 479, xv)
In that case as well, because the defect is seen again through recourse to the previous [position], therefore neither the universal nor the configuration constitutes a defining characteristic.

By this, the definition of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is also refuted. For if there were a continuity (*anvaya*) [of the *pradhāna*], then because all its states would be apprehended, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient, since those states are not essentially different from the nature of the *pradhāna*.
Now, [the opponent might argue: "In ultimate reality, everything indeed appears, but it is an error that it does not appear; this is the delusion. This too is incorrect, because:
Is there a non-appearance of everything, or is the delusion [of non-appearance] despite its appearance?
There is no valid means of cognition here at all; it is merely a conceptual construction.
That which exists in its causal form as the potentiality of all things—that is the Pradhāna, from which the emergence of the entire world proceeds.
If that very universal, by virtue of its pervasiveness and permanence, were to remain as such,
then each individual manifestation would appear distinct from the others due to their mutual differences.
(PVA 480, v)
This is contradictory here, namely what is said:
"The exceedingly great form of the qualities does not come within the range of vision."
But that which has come within the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion.
vii] For:
viii] Since that which is postulated by way of its effect is indeed insubstantial,
its cause must also be insubstantial, because only that which possesses such a nature can arise from it. (PVA 58)
Now, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is being abandoned;
for that object which is not perceived is precisely what is non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*).

Therefore, even that which is characterized as the "Primal Matter" (pradhāna) is not a universal (sāmānya). [480,xi] Furthermore, it might be argued: although it is not perceived as a universal pervading individuals distinguished by differences in time—since perception does not function with respect to prior and posterior states—it is indeed perceived as pervading individuals situated in different locations at the same time.
That too is incorrect, because:
[480,xiii]

When there is no apprehension of the pervasion between distinct times, states of existence, and individual manifestations, there is no utility for a universal; for empirical practice does not proceed in that manner.
(PVA 480, xiv)

Regarding the injunction "one should sacrifice a white goat," because the individual instance being sacrificed is recognized as "this is that very same [type]" through the continuity of the genus (*jāti*) with what was previously perceived, a universal (*sāmānya*) is postulated by those seeking such linguistic usage for the purpose of that sacrifice. However, there is no utility for such usage in the case of two things perceived simultaneously, since both are cognized as belonging to that same genus by means of following the previous [perception]. Furthermore, neither in the case of the prior and posterior [moments] nor in the case of two simultaneous ones is any universal observed apart from the distinct and non-distinct forms of the preceding and succeeding individuals. Likewise, in the case of two simultaneous [individuals], [the universal would be nothing more than] the form of the two clear [individuals]. How then does the cognition "these two are similar" arise? This cognition is the same even for those occurring at prior and subsequent times; for instance: [The text continues: "Just as the cognition 'this is that' arises regarding a single object seen before and now, so too does the cognition 'this is that' arise regarding two objects seen at different times. Thus, the notion of similarity is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on the exclusion of dissimilar things (*anyāpoha*), and not a perception of a real universal. Therefore, the universal is not established as a real entity. Consequently, the inference of the self (*ātman*) based on the notion of a universal is also refuted. Thus, the self is not proven by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Hence, it is established that the self is non-existent. Therefore, the statement "I know myself" is merely a conventional expression (*vyavahāra*) based on the continuity of the stream of consciousness (*vijñānasaṃtāna*), and not a designation of a real, permanent self. This concludes the refutation of the self. Now, the refutation of the person (*pudgala*) follows. Just as the self is not established by any means of valid cognition, so too is the person not established. For the person is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor can it be inferred, as there is no logical mark (*liṅga*) for its existence. Nor can it be known through scripture (*āgama*), for the scriptures of the various schools contradict one another. Therefore, the person is also non-existent. Thus, all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of a self and devoid of a person; they are empty (*śūnya*), signless (*animitta*), and wishless (*apranihita*). One who understands this is liberated. This is the teaching of the Blessed One. Thus ends the chapter on the refutation of the self. Now begins the chapter on the refutation of the person. Herein, the author first states the opponent's position: "Some say: 'The person exists as a real entity, because it is the basis for the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*'). To this, the author replies: "If the person were a real entity, it would have to be either identical to or different from the aggregates. It cannot be identical, because the aggregates are impermanent while the person is held to be permanent. Nor can it be different, because it is never perceived apart from the aggregates. Therefore, the person is merely a conceptual construction and has no real existence. Thus is the refutation of the person. Now, the refutation of the external objects (*bāhyārtha*) follows. Some say: "External objects exist, because their cognition occurs. To this, the author replies: "If external objects existed, they would have to be either atoms (*paramāṇu*) or composites (*saṃghāta*). They cannot be atoms, because atoms are imperceptible. Nor can they be composites, because a composite is not distinct from the atoms. Therefore, external objects do not exist. Thus is the refutation of external objects. Now, the refutation of the Yogācāra position follows. Some say: "Consciousness alone exists, because everything is of the nature of mind. To this, the author replies: "If consciousness alone existed, then the distinction between subject and object would be impossible. Since we perceive the duality of grasper and grasped, consciousness alone does not exist. Thus is the refutation of the Yogācāra position. Now, the refutation of the Madhyamaka position follows. Some say: "All phenomena are empty, because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). To this, the author replies: "If all phenomena were empty, then even emptiness itself would be empty. Since emptiness is not empty, phenomena are not entirely empty. Thus is the refutation of the Madhyamaka position. Now, the conclusion follows: "Therefore, all these views are mere conceptual constructions. The ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is beyond words and thought. One who realizes this is liberated.
