In that regard, there is no common form observed by means of direct perception.
The sense organ does not perceive even simultaneous individuals;

the word "of the whole" (*sāmānyasya*) is the ellipsis to be supplied. A distinct commonality (*samānākāratā*) is not perceived among simultaneous individuals in the same way it is between preceding and succeeding individuals. This is merely a conceptual construction (*pratyaya*), because that which is being perceived is not seen [as distinct]. Indeed, a cognition devoid of a perceived form does not cognize anything at all.
The cognition has a similar form; it arises without an objective basis.
Because it does not manifest as that which is apprehended, like the preceding and succeeding particulars.

(PVA 61) Whatever cognition has a uniform appearance is entirely without an external object (*nirālambana*), because its apprehended object does not manifest therein. For example, just as a cognition intended to have as its object a universal (*sāmānya*) residing in distinct individuals at different times lacks a manifesting form of a universal, so too a cognition whose object is a universal residing in individuals at the same time [lacks such a manifesting form]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
[480,xxi] Now, how could that causal condition arise if there were no similarity, since everything would otherwise be of a different character? That too is trivial.
If this cognition were to arise only in some particular instance, then there would be a restriction [of its occurrence] to mere causes; but how could there be such a movement toward a universal?

Since a restriction cannot be without a cause, it is the cause alone that deserves to be postulated. But what follows for the universal (*sāmānya*)? Or rather, let the universal be merely the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*); there is no harm in this. And it has been established that this [exclusion] is formless (*arūpa*). Furthermore:
The superimposed form arises from the awakening of the seeds of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
Is it not sufficient for that much alone? Is another universal (*jāti*) not useless?

(PVA 481, iv) Even by means of a universal whose true nature is not investigated, mere conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is indeed accomplished; why then is further effort expended regarding something else?
If birth is ultimately real for the purpose of establishing dharma and adharma,
by what means of valid cognition could its status as a means of accomplishing dharma be measured?

For the fact that a universal (*jāti*) is the means for accomplishing religious duties (*dharma*) and so forth cannot be understood through its own nature alone, even if it is well-known, because it is not perceived as distinct from other universals due to its lack of differentiation. Nor can a universal that is not thus established be useful for the purpose at hand; therefore, the apprehension of a universal is entirely useless.

Alternatively, it is precisely those individuals characterized by such specific conditions that serve as the means for accomplishing dharma and so forth; this is what constitutes the universal (*sāmānya*).
Now, if the universal were not eternal and all-pervading, then the cognition of a uniform form would likewise not be pervasive. That is incorrect.
It is understood that its cause is some kind of causal condition (*pratyaya*).
Because the form of the object of cognition exists, there is the conceptual construction of the object of cognition. (PVA 65)

Nor is there an experience of an object of cognition (*prameya*) that possesses a common form; this has been established previously. Therefore, because it is not experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the universal (*sāmānya*) simply does not exist. Even in the case of a form that is being perceived, it is not a universal because it is not experienced as being shared with anything else.

But surely, because a universal resides in a single individual, the substratum (dharmin) is absent; thus, for you, since the substratum is unestablished, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatā).
This is not correct.
This is a *prasaṅga* proof; therefore, there is no fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
If it were so, then this [proof] would also not exist, because both [the subject and the property] are accepted [by the opponent]. (PVA 66)
If it were thus restricted to a single individual, then there would be no connection with another [individual] possessing a different location; nor could both [properties] exist [in one thing].

[Objection: But if its connection with another were not restricted to a single individual, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established; for it does not reside in one individual alone, since it pervades all individuals. A universal is not intended to reside in only one individual. [Response: This is not a fault. For if it were common [to many], its pervasive cognition would remain unimpaired.
For that form cannot be apprehended by another form without error.
(PVA 481, xvii)

If a universal were pervasive, it would have to be apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being pervasive at the very moment of perception; for indeed, a means of valid cognition cannot be one that apprehends its object erroneously. Furthermore, if pervasiveness were perceived, there would necessarily be the perception of all individual instances (*vyakti*), because the property of being pervasive is not perceived unless the pervaded [instances] are apprehended. Yet it is not so perceived; therefore, it does not exist in that manner. Consequently, the universal itself does not exist, which is the negation of both properties [pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness]. If this were the established position, the fault of the unestablished locus (*dharmyasiddhi*) would arise; however, this [argument] is merely intended to demonstrate mutual contradiction. We are not capable of accepting such a thing, because no other such entity is observed. Moreover, inference does not function without an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

[481,xviii] Now, a universal (*sāmānya*), being apprehended through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), is indeed distinct from all other categories of entities; therefore, its contradiction should not be pointed out by way of its opposition to the properties of other things. For it is not logical for the property of one thing to belong to another. Indeed, the properties of material objects (*mūrta*) cannot be applied to a universal that is immaterial (*amūrta*). This is not so, because:
Even though it is formless and lacks specific qualities, others do not accept that [space] is all-pervasive;
likewise, let it be understood that the universal also would consequently be non-pervasive.

Furthermore, even those ultimate particularities (*viśeṣas*) which are conjoined with formless [substances] are restricted to their respective substrates and are not pervasive. Likewise, a universal (*sāmānya*) also cannot transcend the state of being non-pervasive while remaining formless.

If it is argued that a particular, despite being formless, is nonetheless non-pervasive precisely because of its nature as such, then this distinction is not caused by the essence of being "form" or "other than form. If it is asked, "In that case, let the very relationship of universal and particular be the basis for pervasiveness and its opposite; what is the fault?"—we reply: that is simply unproven (*asiddha*).
[482,v] But surely the universal (*sāmānya*) is already established by you as well, since it is taken up as the subject (*dharmin*). This is not so; for:
If there is no apprehension of the foremost [part], how can it be said that there is an apprehension of the universal?
If its apprehension occurs by way of its own nature, then how can there be similarity?
"It is apprehended" is the completion of the sentence. For a universal, when apprehended in its own form, would be apprehended either as pervasive or otherwise.
If it were apprehended as pervasive, perception would not have such a limited scope.
When its application is directed toward a universal that pervades all individual instances, [it functions as a means of valid cognition].

Now, if the individuals are not apprehended, then how can the universal, when being apprehended as associated with a single individual, be apprehended as all-pervasive? If it is qualified by one individual, then, like that individual, it would be a particular and not a universal. If, on the other hand, by another way of speaking, its qualification by other individuals is also apprehended, then how can there be the cognition that "this is that very same universal"? It has already been examined that the cognition "this is that very same" is not perceptual. Therefore, since its nature as a universal is unestablished, how can it serve as a proof for its pervasiveness? Thus: [482,x]

Because it is formless, the proof of its omnipresence cannot be established through its status as a universal (*sāmānya*); nor is there any perception of it by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, it is devoid of universality.

If the universal (*sāmānya*) is unestablished, how can you prove that it pervades the objects of the universal? For a property (*dharma*) can be established only when the universal is taken as the locus (*dharmin*), and not otherwise.
[482,xiii]

This is not correct. Why? Because this has already been stated: this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), but it is not a primary (*maula*) reason (*hetu*). If you accept that a universal (*sāmānya*) is all-pervasive (*vyāpin*), then it must be apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the acceptance [of such a thing] is based upon a means of valid cognition, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*). And how could it be logical to accept that it is all-pervasive when it is perceived as being devoid of any other nature, being delimited by a single individual (*ekavyakti*) restricted by place and time? Furthermore, since perception grasps multiple objects, whether [the universal] is perceived as distinct from them or otherwise, an acceptance of something not being perceived is not logical. If it is argued that "it is the form (*ākṛti*) itself that is perceived as the universal," we say no. This is because a form lacks pervasiveness. If it were perceived as pervasive, there would have to be a perception of all individuals; and in that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all individuals distinguished by place and time. Moreover, if the form is established as residing in a single individual, then the lack of pervasiveness is proven, and the objection regarding the non-establishment of the locus (*dharmyasiddhi*) is likewise avoided. How then is this a *prasaṅga-sādhana*? It is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* because the opponent accepts that the form alone is the universal, whereas another [proponent] holds it to be something else. Thus, it functions as a reductio.

Alternatively, the meaning of the reductio (*prasaṅga*) is that because [the universal] is all-pervasive, its perception could not be restricted to a single individual instance. The reversal of this constitutes the original reason (*maula-hetu*). The reductio serves solely to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) for the original reason. Others, however, hold that "because of absence" (*virahāt*) is the original reason, while the reductio is merely a derivative of it. This presentation is made in this way in order to demonstrate the basis of the original reason. And "because of absence" is the reason.

It is of the nature of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). And that is indeed established even in the case of a universal being non-existent; for when the reason is non-existent, a real entity as the locus (*dharmin*) is not admitted.
Furthermore, because of its absence, the understanding of it [the universal] arises even from the statement "it is not there."
That is simply non-existent.
If the universal were the locus of properties (dharmin), then the proof of its non-pervasiveness would be possible.
But when the reason consists of mere absence, what could be established by whom, and where?

If mere absence were the reason, then since it would have no connection with anything else, how could there be a proof of the probandum? If, on the other hand, it is the absence of connection with another individual instance, even then it must be determined whose absence it is. Therefore, by the rule stated by the opponent, there must be a universal present in the mind. And a reason is not capable of proving the probandum without the application of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*).

Now, if the universal characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is established for the Buddhists, then that is precisely what the opponent desires; for even he intends to refute that which is accepted by the other party. Moreover, a universal characterized as the exclusion of others is indeed intended to be all-pervasive. For it is said: "Even through exclusion there is similarity.
There is indeed a real entity, but it does not persist [as a single entity], because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of [the word] being applied to everything. (PVA 73)
viii] Now, even though the universal does not exist, the reason characterized by its absence certainly exists.

That too is incorrect, because that which does not exist cannot function as a reason (*hetu*). If it is argued that there is indeed a logical connection (*yoga*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is non-existent, we say no. Only when a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) exists can the absence of one thing lead to the cognition of the absence of another. And that connection is grasped through positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therefore, by the force of that [connection], one merely demonstrates the absence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), showing that "wherever the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is absent, there the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is absent. That [mere demonstration] is not the fundamental reason (*maulo hetuḥ*).

Now, even the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakatānupalabdhi*) is employed to establish the absence of a specific object. If that were the case, then according to the principle "there is no *śiṃśapā* here," there must be another locus (*dharmin*) established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that here too a locus common to both existence and non-existence is employed, that too is incorrect; for there is nothing else that is common to both existence and non-existence. If it is claimed that the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpapratibhāsa*) itself is the common property of both, then in that case:
When its non-apprehension is the means of proving that there is no appropriation of entities therein, [it is established].

To say that the reason is something entirely different is trivial. Therefore, there is no fundamental reason (*maulo hetu*) here, because the subject (*dharmin*), which is the universal (*sāmānya*), is not established.

In the position that form and the other [sensory objects] themselves constitute the universal, this is not a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*), because their non-pervasive nature is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, the reason must be established for both parties; it cannot belong to one party alone, namely the opponent.

<3. The Purpose of Including the Term “artha”> [483,xv] Now, one might object: if that which is established for both parties is indeed the *artha* (the real object), what is the purpose of including the term *artha*? This is not so; for:
Just as for both [parties], it is established merely through conceptual construction;
for these conceptual constructions are certainly not names that arise without a fixed connection. (PVA 74)

Therefore, even though [the property] is established for both [proponent and opponent], it is not a valid reason because properties such as "being either the subject or a similar instance" lack the status of being a real entity (*artha*).

The inclusion of the word "object" (artha) is for the purpose of establishing that those things whose nature is superimposed by the conceptualization of words are not logical reasons (liṅga), because [the reason] is established from the object itself, not from the object as [conceptualized]. (13)

The inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*), which qualifies the inclusion of "what has been seen by oneself," is for the purpose of demonstrating that things whose nature is constructed merely through conceptualization (*kalpanā*) are not valid reasons (*hetu*), because it is only the object itself that can function as a means of cognition (*gamaka*).

Is it not the case that a reason characterized as unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is precisely what fails to convey an unproven object? If this [reason] possesses the three-fold form (*trairūpya*), how can it be a non-reason? If, on the other hand, it lacks the three-fold form, then its exclusion follows from the very definition of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*); what then is the purpose of including the word "object" (*artha*)? For inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is indeed the communication of a mark possessing the three-fold form. [Response: No. Even in inference for oneself, the three-fold form—though superimposed by conceptual construction—is indeed attained as the defining characteristic of a reason. How then could there be an exclusion of it? In that case, the inclusion of the word "object" should not be made here at all, since the necessity for it would apply only to inference for oneself.

To this it is replied: Since it is stated that "it should be for others just as it is for one's own certainty," there is no fault in performing it here, even though it will take effect there. If it is asked why it is not performed right there, we reply: what contradiction is there in performing it either there or here? Furthermore, there is a specific purpose in doing so. To explain: [484,iv]
No one would postulate a cause produced by conceptual construction for their own sake;
would anyone ever deceive themselves regarding what they desire?

Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) here is intended to convey that the effort of a great-souled person should be directed primarily toward the welfare of others, and that this very objective requires the greatest exertion. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), a reason (*hetu*) based on conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance:
Because conceptualization and scripture follow merely the whim of their author...
And because things undergo change, [reasons] produced by them are fallacious. (14)

Indeed, there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the object to be proven (*sādhya*) for that which is superimposed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because it proceeds solely from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). If this is so, then [the reason] would not be a logical reason (*hetu*) precisely because of the lack of connection. No; for the connection is implied by that very fact. There is no direct demonstration of the connection; rather, the object is apprehended through it. For being a member of the subject class (*pakṣa*) or the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is not fixed in one place for both the eternal and the non-eternal, since whichever thing is made the subject shifts accordingly in each instance. Nor is such an establishment of a real entity (*vastusiddhi*) achieved, because another property is being proved according to a different intention (*vivakṣā*).
<2. Examination of the Thesis> <1. The Statement of the Reason and the Thesis is Not a Means of Proof> <(1) The Statement of the Reason is Not a Means of Proof>

[484, viii] But surely the thesis (*pakṣa*) is precisely that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), since anything else in relation to it is a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). In that case, the property called "being either the thesis or a similar instance" is excluded from its opposite (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, why is this not a logical reason (*hetu*)? For a property restricted to the thesis and the similar instances cannot deviate from what is to be proven.
That is incorrect because:
[484,x] There is no restriction anywhere regarding the existence of the subject (*pakṣa*) or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
The mere permanence of the subject [of the thesis] is not [the reason], because it is possible for another [property] as well.

If this meaning is: "Because it is either the subject (*pakṣa*) or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)," or "Because it possesses a property that is invariably concomitant with the generality of the impermanence of sound and the jar," then that property is precisely characterized as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), etc., since the invariably concomitant similarity is expressed by the word "either" (*anyatara*). It is not, however, the case that the non-deviating property is precisely characterized as being produced, etc. And this being so, the reason (*hetu*) is the actual object itself, not something imagined. Alternatively, it is because it is intended [to be understood] as being other than that which has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*).

That is incorrect. Even if one intends to designate it as the subject (*pakṣa*) by virtue of its being impermanent, impermanence is not thereby established; for if it were intended as permanent, that very intention would have already ceased. And if its status as the subject were established through actual impermanence, then what was already proven would simply be restated. Therefore, an imagined property (*dharma*) cannot serve as the means of proof (*sādhana*).

And that established object is the means of proof (*sādhana*). Since the logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses precisely three forms, the communication of the three-formed mark is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). Consequently, it is demonstrated that those who maintain that even the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) is a means of proof are speaking incorrectly; for that [statement] is not established as a means of proof. Indeed, a means of proof must establish what is to be proven (*sādhya*); the thing to be proven itself cannot [be established] by the means of proof. If it is argued that the verbal expression is the means of proof, we say no. This is because the verbal expression is not directly a means of proof, as it lacks an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) with the thing to be proven. There is no invariable connection between the verbal expression and its object. Therefore: [485, iv]
Since the understanding of the object follows from the object itself, there is no capacity in the statement of the thesis and the reason regarding that object;
therefore, these two do not possess an inherent status as means of proof.

[485,v] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is as if there were a great mountain of rock, solid and unbroken, extending for one hundred yojanas, rising up from the great ocean. A man might come along carrying a single arrow, and thinking, ‘I shall split this great mountain of rock with this single arrow,’ he would strike it. What do you think, Ānanda? Would that man be able to split that great mountain of rock with that single arrow? “Certainly not, Blessed One. “Ānanda, it is even more difficult than that for a person who has committed the five heinous crimes to be reborn in the human world after passing away from hell. But, Ānanda, it is even more difficult than that for a person who has committed the five heinous crimes to attain the fruit of stream-entry after passing away from hell. It is even more difficult than that to attain the fruit of once-returning; it is even more difficult than that to attain the fruit of non-returning; it is even more difficult than that to attain arhatship; it is even more difficult than that to become a pratyekabuddha. But, Ānanda, it is even more difficult than all these for a person who has committed the five heinous crimes to become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, after passing away from hell. “Blessed One, it is wonderful! Sugata, it is marvelous! How difficult it is for a person who has committed the five heinous crimes to become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, after passing away from hell! “Indeed, Ānanda, it is difficult for a person who has committed the five heinous crimes to become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, after passing away from hell. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, those who have committed the five heinous crimes are obstructed by their own karma; they are obstructed by the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of afflictions, and the obstruction of maturation. Therefore, Ānanda, those who have committed the five heinous crimes are obstructed by their own karma and cannot escape from it. However, Ānanda, even though a person who has committed the five heinous crimes is obstructed by their own karma, if they hear the Dharma taught by a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, they may give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, how should we regard such a person? “Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained the fruit of stream-entry. “Blessed One, what is the reason for this? “Ānanda, because that person has heard the Dharma taught by a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, they will no longer fall into the states of misery, nor will they be born among the gods of the Long-lived Heavens, nor will they be born in the border regions among foolish people, nor will they be born into families of outcasts or hunters, nor will they be born into families of butchers, nor will they be born into families of liquor-sellers, nor will they be born into families of those who follow false views. They will not be born in such places. Therefore, Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained the fruit of stream-entry. “Blessed One, it is wonderful! Sugata, it is marvelous! How profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! How well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, how profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! It is wonderful, Ānanda, how well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, how should we regard such a person? “Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained the fruit of once-returning. “Blessed One, what is the reason for this? “Ānanda, because that person has heard the Dharma taught by a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, they will not be born again in the hells, nor will they be born among animals, nor will they be born in the realm of Yama. Having abandoned these three miserable states, they will be born among humans or gods. Therefore, Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained the fruit of once-returning. “Blessed One, it is wonderful! Sugata, it is marvelous! How profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! How well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, how profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! It is wonderful, Ānanda, how well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, how should we regard such a person? “Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained the fruit of non-returning. “Blessed One, what is the reason for this? “Ānanda, because that person has heard the Dharma taught by a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, they will not be born again in the realm of desire. Having abandoned the realm of desire, they will be born in the form realm or the formless realm. Therefore, Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained the fruit of non-returning. “Blessed One, it is wonderful! Sugata, it is marvelous! How profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! How well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, how profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! It is wonderful, Ānanda, how well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, how should we regard such a person? “Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained arhatship. “Blessed One, what is the reason for this? “Ānanda, because that person has heard the Dharma taught by a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, they will abandon all afflictions and realize nirvāṇa. Therefore, Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already attained arhatship. “Blessed One, it is wonderful! Sugata, it is marvelous! How profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! How well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is wonderful, Ānanda, how profound is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! It is wonderful, Ānanda, how well-expounded is the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata! For even those who have committed the five heinous crimes, upon hearing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, can give rise to the thought of enlightenment and eventually reach the goal of supreme perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, how should we regard such a person? “Ānanda, you should regard such a person as having already become a pratyekabuddha.”

"Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—here, it is *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced), which possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*), that alone brings about the understanding of impermanence, because it is never found to deviate from it. Neither the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) nor the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) does so. Otherwise, the proof of the probandum would occur even in the case of "Sound is permanent because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), for here too there exists the statement of a reason and a thesis. If you argue that this is not a reason because its meaning lacks a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the probandum, then it follows that the understanding of the object arises from the object itself through its necessary connection, and not from the verbal expression; for speech can exist even in the absence of the object. And since the statement of the reason is not the means of proof, the non-proof-status of the statement of the thesis is established without even being mentioned. Now, if it is argued that the statement of the probandum is the means of proof because it communicates the meaning of the probandum, we say no; for this would entail the uselessness of the reason. If it is argued that the mere proposition (*pratijñā*) is not the means of proof, and thus the reason is employed, then how can that which is not a means of proof become one? If you say it becomes a means of proof when combined [with the reason], how can something useless bring about such a combination? No one desires a combination with what is useless. Therefore, the verbal expression is not the means of proof.
Moreover:
(2) The statement of the thesis is not a means of proof.
That statement of the thesis is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for communicating the speaker’s intention; however, because it gives rise to doubt, it is not a direct proof (*sādhana*). 16.

For it is not the case that the cause of doubt itself is the reason (*hetu*) in that context. Moreover, its status as a cause of doubt arises from its lack of necessary connection (*apratibaddhatva*) with the object. Otherwise, the formulation of the reason would be purposeless. If that is so, then just as the statement does not establish the probandum (*sādhya*), the meaning of the proof (*sādhana*) likewise cannot be understood from it; for even there, there is no necessary connection. Or, if there were a connection, what connection would there be for the probandum itself? What is the nature of that connection?

This is true. Even for the sake of establishing a proof (*sādhana*), speech does not itself bring about realization. In that regard, it serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only in communicating the intended meaning; therefore, it is not the direct proof. Although it is a means of valid cognition regarding the proof, it is only by means of speech that the [actual] means of valid cognition is implied. If it is argued, "Then let the means of valid cognition also be implied regarding the probandum (*sādhya*)," we say: no. Because at that very moment, the means of valid cognition already exists there. For it is the previously occurred means of valid cognition that is implied.

Because there is the possibility of forgetting [the thesis] in that case due to verbal expression. But when [the object] is present, perception alone is the means of valid cognition; what need is there for a verbal statement there? For in the case of an object perceived directly, instruction from another is not more authoritative. This is because a verbal statement is not a direct means of proof (*sādhana*). [Objection: Then the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) is an indirect means of proof, just as [the statement] of the proof (*sādhana*) is. [Reply: This too is incorrect. Since it merely expresses the probandum (*sādhya*) itself, it is not even indirectly [a means of proof].
The statement of a reason, even if it is itself incapable [of proving the conclusion], is indicative for one who is capable. (17)

Just as the statement of the proof (*sādhana*) is a proof, so too would the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) be a proof, if it were an indicator of that which is capable and established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But how can the indication of what is unestablished be a proof? For that which is itself incapable does not become capable by depending on something else that is incapable. To illustrate:
A falling object never becomes stable by depending on another falling object;
likewise, that which is unestablished is not established by that very same unestablished thing.

Since the thesis is stated by the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*) as something not yet established, how can the statement of the subject be a means of proof (*sādhana*)? However, the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*), although itself incapable, is called a means of proof because it expresses that which is capable. This is because it expresses the reason as being necessarily connected to the object to be proven.
Speech is said to be the means of proof, but that means of proof does not exist by itself.

Therefore, as for what was said—that inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is a contradiction—it is refuted as follows: with respect to the person being persuaded (*pratipādya*), it is indeed "for oneself" (*svārtha*); but with respect to the persuader (*pratipādaka*), it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). That [objection] is rejected because inference is spoken of metaphorically (*upacāra*) as the cause of that [inference], not in its own right. Consequently, the claim that it is "for oneself" from the perspective of the opponent (*prativādin*) is merely the talk of one who says whatever comes to mind. For him, only the three-featured logical mark (*liṅga*) is "for oneself" because it is the means of persuasion, not the verbal expression; for the object is not understood from the words alone. If it is argued that the verbal expression is indeed a means of persuasion because it assists through recollection (*smaraṇa*), we say no. This is because the verbal expression merely prescribes a mere eulogy (*arthavāda*) of the object. Therefore, even from the perspective of both parties, the verbal expression is nothing but a restatement. Its status as "for others" (*parārthatā*) is relative to the persuader, yet there is no benefit whatsoever to the persuader by means of it. However, it is considered "inference" in the sense of being the cause of inference, specifically from the perspective of the person being persuaded.

[486, viii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound by all fetters; the person who is freed from the five lower fetters but has not yet abandoned the desire for existence; the person who has abandoned the five lower fetters and has also abandoned the desire for existence; and the person who has abandoned the five lower fetters and has also abandoned the desire for existence, and who, having realized the state of non-returning, will attain parinirvāṇa there itself without returning from that world. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Among these four kinds of persons, monks, which one do you consider the most excellent? When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, among these four kinds of persons, the person who has abandoned the five lower fetters and has also abandoned the desire for existence, and who, having realized the state of non-returning, will attain parinirvāṇa there itself without returning from that world—this one, Blessed One, I consider the most excellent. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, it is well said! It is well said, Ānanda! Among these four kinds of persons, Ānanda, the person who has abandoned the five lower fetters and has also abandoned the desire for existence, and who, having realized the state of non-returning, will attain parinirvāṇa there itself without returning from that world—this one, Ānanda, I consider the most excellent. Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, why among these four kinds of persons, the person who has abandoned the five lower fetters and has also abandoned the desire for existence, and who, having realized the state of non-returning, will attain parinirvāṇa there itself without returning from that world—this one, Blessed One, is considered the most excellent? But surely, it follows that [inference] is for the sake of another (*parārtha*) in relation to the object, and inference [itself] in relation to something else. How is this so? Is it not the case that a quality itself is superimposed as a defect? For precisely that reason, it is not an inference for that proponent; rather, it is for the sake of another (*parārtha*) for the person being addressed. Otherwise, it would also be for one's own sake (*svārtha*), since he himself also effects the purpose by means of it. Furthermore, the purpose for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) has been stated: because there is no other way for the word to establish the object. Now, is the word a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not even a valid means of knowledge in the case of recollection (*smaraṇa*)? If it is a valid means of knowledge, why is it not [directly] toward the object? If it is not a valid means of knowledge, how can recollection arise from it? Precisely for that reason it is otherwise. Therefore, it would indeed be a valid means of knowledge and not recollection. And in the case of recollection, that [word] is its producer (*kāraka*), not its indicator (*jñāpaka*); such is the nature of a valid means of knowledge. How then can it be recollection from that? Because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the object. For smoke is connected to fire, and thus it produces recollection. If the word were also connected in that way, it would likewise produce recollection.
For instance: whatever is a memory exists by virtue of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*);
just as there is a memory of the invisible dark essence from [the perception of] smoke. (PVA 79)

That is incorrect. The connection is that it is not mere recollection because it is bound [to its object]; yet recollection will also occur because it is unbound. What contradiction is there between these two? For instance:
Why does recollection not arise even from mental attention toward an object that has been seen?
For it generally arises from some object that is associated with it.
Furthermore, recollection that possesses a determinate form arises only from what is connected [to the object], and not from anything else.

That is not correct. Because certainty arises precisely from reflecting upon a previously operative means of valid cognition, and not from the mere utterance of the word. Furthermore, since the word is a cause of recollection, it is not a *pramāṇa*, just as the act of recollecting is not a *pramāṇa*. Just as a lamp is not a *pramāṇa* for things already seen, so too the word is not a *pramāṇa* for what has already been ascertained by another means. [487,ii] This very point is accepted here regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): that it is not [established] by itself. Even if this matter were established, there would be no harm whatsoever to us, because [it does not affect our position]. (PVA 81)

[487,iii] For with respect to an object (*artha*), speech is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, when it concerns the means of valid cognition itself, there is no loss whatsoever [in its being called] a means of valid cognition. Nor is the means of valid cognition established by speech, because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). In that case, there is merely recollection (*smaraṇa*). Certainty, however, arises from self-awareness alone. Why then [rely] on speech alone? For recollection is indeed seen to occur even from mere mental attention (*ābhoga*). If it is argued: "When [recollection] does not arise from attention, then speech is the means of valid cognition," this is not correct. Because: [487,iv]
Even a false recollection regarding an object is seen to arise from speech;
no distinction in the speech itself is observed by way of being true or false.
(82) [According to the *Pramāṇavārttika-alaṃkāra*] the observation of the object would then be an inference, and that would be only for one's own sake (*svārtha*).
Even from mere mental application (*ābhoga*), false modes of recollection arise.

Therefore, the determination of the nature of a prior means of valid cognition occurs only through intense reflection based on some logical mark (*liṅga*); thus, verbal testimony is not a means of valid cognition in itself. Even when there is mental application toward an object by means of a means of valid cognition, inference alone is the means of valid cognition regarding an imperceptible object; it is through that [inference] that verbal testimony functions.

[487, vii] But surely, since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehended the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has now passed away, how can there be a determination of that connection? [One might argue: "This is now merely a memory, and memory is not a means of valid cognition. [We reply: It is indeed a means of valid cognition, because it is produced by that [prior] means of valid cognition. And therefore: [487, viii]

Memory arises from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); why is it not [itself] considered valid by way of metaphorical designation? However, that which arises from what is not a means of valid cognition is accepted as being invalid (*apramāṇa*).

Now, one might argue that this recollection arises from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus memory itself is the basis here as well. But then, how can the certainty arise that even that memory is purified by another memory?
If it is claimed that this memory is firm, why is such firmness not considered false?

"If it is not false because of the attainment of the object, then that is simply the presence of what is already established. (PVA 85) To this it is replied: This has indeed been stated at the outset: "The cognition of its own nature is intrinsic; its validity is through worldly practice" (*Pravṛttiviniścaya* 1.4). And it is observed that worldly practice is characterized solely by the attainment of the object, and no other useful practice is found.

[487,xii] But surely, some recollection is firm by its very nature; therefore, the certainty that "this is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) arises from that [recollection] itself, and not from linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). [487,xiii] If this is argued:
That is incorrect; for:
[487,xiv] That firmness exists solely through repeated practice, by virtue of relying upon attainment.
What has been practiced in one place does not produce firmness in another.

(86) (PVA) [487,xv] If this conventional practice, characterized by the attainment of an object, did not exist as something practiced, how could there be the firmness necessary for attainment? That what is practiced in one place produces firmness in another would result in the total destruction of worldly convention. Therefore, since this much is the extent of the cognitive range of those in cyclic existence, conventional valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārikapramāṇa*) remains unshaken; thus, there is no fault. Consequently, it is established that speech is inference because it is the cause of inference.

[487,xvii]
With the desire to produce in others a certainty equivalent to one's own certainty,

there is the exclusion of anything else [than the three characteristics], namely the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the connection (*sambandha*), and the probandum (*sādhya*).
This is not so; for:
[488,ii] Because it has the meaning of the reason as its object, the statement of that [reason's] incapacity is said [to be a fallacy].
As it has been said: "But for us...
In that context, the statement of the object to be inferred (anumeya) is considered to have the meaning of the reason (hetu) as its objective domain.

For us, however, the statement of the example (*udāharaṇa*) functions as the object of the reason (*hetu*), not as the actual proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, because its status as a direct proof is rejected, it is said that the statement of that [example] lacks the capacity to establish the probandum (*sādhya*). How, then, can there be an acceptance of the statement of the probandum as being connected to the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the relation (*sambandha*)? This is not what is meant by "the property of the subject, the relation, and the statement of the probandum. Rather, the "statement of the probandum" is that which is conjoined with the "statement of the relation"; thus, it is the "statement of the probandum in connection with the relation. The statement of the probandum—such as "whatever is produced is impermanent"—is contained within the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and is not in the form of a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). For the pervasiveness of the probandum over the means of proof must necessarily be demonstrated. Consequently, only two members [of the syllogism] need to be shown. Since the other two forms [of the reason] are implied by the relation itself, the reason possesses the three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Therefore, the conclusion such as "sound is impermanent" should not be stated at the beginning or at the end; for the probandum is established from the mere presence of the two forms alone.
If it is argued that this [statement] also possesses efficacy because it prompts the utterance of the reason (hetu), [we reply: 18.
For one who desires to know due to doubt regarding that [reason], there would be reliance on further arguments;
and since this would be the same even when a counter-example is admitted, there would be an infinite regress. (19)

Now, it might be argued: "If the statement of the reason (*hetu*) does not proceed because it would be like the falling of a blindfolded mallet—meaning it would be irrelevant—in the absence of the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*), then that [statement of the thesis] is indeed a means of proof (*sādhana*) because the statement of the reason proceeds from it. This is not so. For if this were the case, doubt, desire to know, the context, the understanding of that [context], and the wish [to prove] would also attain the status of being means of proof, and the speech would consequently have ten members (*daśāvayavatā*). [One would have to say: "This is what is doubted by you; this is what you desire to know; this is precisely what has been introduced by you; this is what I have understood; here is my wish"—thus, one who fashions such a "beauty of the beard" (*kūrcaśobhā*) would have to employ a ten-membered syllogism. Furthermore, the means of proof would proceed even when the counter-position (*vipakṣa*) is admitted; consequently, that counter-position would also result in being a means of proof along with it. [Reply: Now, the mere ascertainment of the probandum (*sādhyaniścaya*) occurs even without the presentation of doubt and so forth. Therefore, since those [elements] serve only as verbal elaboration (*śabdaprapañca*) and do not contribute to the comprehension of the meaning, doubt and the rest are abandoned, because the restatement (*anuvāda*) of them is ineffective. If this is so, then the statement of the thesis (*pratijñāvacana*) is also merely a restatement for the proponent, and it lacks internal necessity (*antaraṅgatā*).
[488,ix] However, the internal capacity is established in the three forms;
therein, the application of mindfulness is established precisely in that speech. 20.

[488,x] Precisely from the three-fold mark (*trirūpa*), that object—the probandum (*sādhya*)—is understood in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). For in inference for oneself, the probandum does not appear first; rather, the reason must be determined by him. Therefore, just as in one's own ascertainment, there is no initial mention of the probandum. If it is argued that the mention of the forms [of the reason] comes later, even then there is no such mention, just as in inference for oneself. This applies to the other person (*para*) as well. [489,i]

When a cognition arises from that which possesses the three characteristics (trirūpa), what distinction is there between that [cognition] and inference for oneself (svārthānumāna)? Therefore, the proposition (pratijñā) and the conclusion (nigamana) are certainly not to be stated. Nor should the application (upanaya) be stated, because its purpose is to demonstrate the observed capacity [of the reason]. And there is no capacity other than the mere existence [of the reason] in that [subject]; and that mere existence is already understood in the case of the word [as the subject] simply by virtue of its being a property of the subject (pakṣadharma).

Now, it might be argued: "The thesis (pratijñā) is scripture (āgama); the reason (hetu) is inference (anumāna); the example (dṛṣṭānta) is perception (pratyakṣa); the application (upanaya) is analogy (upamāna); and the conclusion (nigamana) is intended to demonstrate the domain of the operation of all means of valid cognition. This is incorrect, because:
If establishment is through inference, what is the use of other means of valid cognition here?
If establishment is not through inference, what is the use of other means of valid cognition here? (PVA 88)

[489,v] If that object is understood through the power of the cause alone, what is the use of the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? What can we do about this, since the entire collection of causal factors (*kārakagrāma*) is certainly not dependent solely on the cause? If it were so, one would be subject to the following objection: "Why does this become such? This is true if it were indeed so; however, a thesis (*pratijñā*) is certainly not a means of valid cognition, because it has been established that doubt arises from it. [(kha) Refutation of the Application (*upanaya*) and Comparison (*upamāna*):]

[489, vi] Analogy is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, without analogy—in the form "and this is likewise"—there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the reason (*hetu*). This is not so; for:
This very property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is demonstrated by means of comparison (*upamāna*);
and thus it is shown that "sound is produced" (kṛtaka).
(PVA 89) [489, viii]

For if the connection [between the reason and the property to be proven] were grasped only in a general sense, how could there be the establishment of [the reason] as residing in a particular subject (*viśeṣādhāratā*)—such as impermanence and so forth? It is precisely through the establishment of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and the like as residing in a particular subject that this very "residing in a particular subject" is established. Thus, by means of the establishment through comparison (*upamāna*) that "this is such-and-such," it is demonstrated by way of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmitā*) that "this resides in something. If it is argued that comparison (*upamāna*) would consequently be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for it is included within inference (*anumāna*). The proof of the specific relation, namely "this is a *gavaya* because of its similarity to a cow," does not differ from the domain of verbal testimony (*śabda*) or comparison; rather, inference alone is the means of valid cognition in that case. Even those who advocate for comparison do not accept inference as something separate. If it is argued that similarity is its object by virtue of "being produced," we say no; for there is no existence of similarity apart from the two instances of being produced. There is no similarity of "being a staff-bearer" apart from the two instances of being the bearer of a staff.
If similarity does not exist here, how can there be a cognition of exclusion?
It follows that one must postulate another cause for the notion "this is similar. (PVA 90)
That is incorrect.
If the cause is inferred from the effect on the basis of a perceived connection, then by that same logic, the perception of the cause itself would also have to be attained. (91) (PVA) [489,xii]
Moreover:
[489, xiii] If similarity exists here, why does it not appear?

If it is argued that [the object] exists because of its subtlety, then how can reality be postulated regarding something unperceived? (92) Even in conceptual construction, nothing appears apart from the nature of an entity. That there should be a determination of something distinct from its own appearance is truly marvelous! (93)

Resemblance, which possesses the limbs of beginningless latent impressions and consists of a nature superimposed by conceptual construction, does not exist as "That art thou" under critical examination;
nevertheless, worldly transaction is established through this connection with real entities. (PVA 94)
Whence comes causal efficiency, and why is it not observed to arise from that which is merely similar?
xvii] If you say it is due to an internal distinction, why is that distinction not observed there as well?

Indeed, it is not from what is merely considered similar that the attainment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) occurs, such that similarity would be the cause of that causal efficiency; for even from buffaloes and the like, the causal efficiency of milk and so forth is obtained. If you argue that there exists an internal distinction (*avāntarabheda*) therein, and therefore the causal efficiency produced by dissimilar things is dissimilar and not the very same, then this being the case, there is likewise an internal distinction among cows themselves. Consequently, there would be no causal efficiency corresponding to their mutual similarity, and thus there would be no correspondence (*saṃvāda*). Furthermore, since a distinct cognition arises, it follows that there must also be a distinctness in the other object.

If it is argued that [the cognition "that"] arises merely from the absence of dissimilarity (*sādṛśyābhāva*), then it follows that similarity (*sādṛśya*) itself is merely the absence of dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇyābhāva*). If you say that similarity is indeed the absence of dissimilarity, we ask: how can a positive entity (*bhāva*) be an absence (*abhāva*)? Or, why not consider the absence of dissimilarity to be similarity? Furthermore, dissimilarity is well-established for both parties in the debate. [Objection: No, because the conventional usage of "similarity" is fully accounted for by the mere absence of that [dissimilarity], the postulation of a further "similarity" is useless. Therefore, comparison (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [(g) Refutation of the Proposition (Scriptural Authority)—] [490, iv]

Now, if it is argued that the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is established by scripture (*āgama*), and thus the thesis is stated as scripture—even so, what is the purpose of the thesis? For instance:
"If this matter is already established from scripture alone, what is the use of a thesis?"

If this object is not established by scripture, what is the use of a thesis? (96) Why is it not established by means of a non-scriptural authority? Merely stating a thesis does not prove that something is the meaning of scripture. (97)
Moreover, even if comprehension is established through mere proposition and reason due to extreme familiarity with the practice, the word of the proposition still serves a purpose there.
Even then, since the five-membered [syllogism] has been practiced, why [use] the speech?
At that time, even that thesis does not exist, because one perceives it as having the nature of the five [factors].

[99] (PVA) [490,ix] How then was this stated: "But for us, that which is the presentation of the thesis is not for the sake of being a means of proof (*sādhana*), but rather for the sake of being the object of the meaning of the reason (*hetu*)"? He says this very thing:
[490,x] For if the object were not made known, the operation of the reason would be impossible.
If it is thought that its capacity [to prove] arises solely from the making known of the object, [then... 21.

[490,xi] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thus delivered all beings from suffering and distress. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no field of visual contact up to no field of mental contact; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; likewise, no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all error and inverted views, he attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequalled mantra, which relieves all suffering and is truly real, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. [491,i] Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, along with the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught. The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* is here completed. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. If one were to say "it is impermanent" based merely on the reason "because it is produced," it would not be known for what the property of impermanence is being proved. Therefore, the thesis-statement (*pratijñā*) "that sound is impermanent" must be employed. Now, this [thesis] may or may not be employed as the object of the reason; in any case, if this external arrangement is not disclosed, the operation of the reason is impossible because there is no object. Thus, the object must necessarily be disclosed. Consequently, prior to the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), the thesis must necessarily exist, because otherwise the means of proof (*sādhana*) would lack its status as a means of proof. If it is argued that this is merely the presentation of the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), we reply: in such a description, the thesis is the subject (*pakṣa*) which is the fruit of the means of valid cognition; therefore, this is not a solution, as it is merely a change of name. This logic is like saying, "He called a stake a wheel. Therefore, its capacity is established precisely through the disclosure of the object. It has been stated in this regard: "There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even doubt and the like would be means of proof."
[490,xii] This non-perception of the object is expressed as being preceded by pervasion;
otherwise, it would be established in a different way. Thus, both of these [alternatives] are untenable. (PVA)

[490,xiii] It is now considered here whether the object (*viṣaya*) is to be illustrated by means of a proposition (*pratijñā*), or rather when the reason (*hetu*) is indicated by the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*).
What follows from this?
Even without this [logical reason], there is pervasion: "Sound is produced; it is of such a nature."
Even when it is stated that "all things are impermanent," the cognition of their destruction follows by implication.

[491,ii] When the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is demonstrated through a universal application—namely, that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), which is pervaded by that [impermanence], is shown therein. Since it is thus understood that sound is indeed of such a nature, i.e., impermanent, what is the purpose of the proposition (*pratijñā*) for the sake of indicating the subject (*viṣaya*), given that the subject is established in quite another way? [Objection: But how can there be the ascertainment of a contradictory reason (*viruddhahetu*) without the proposition? [Response: This is not a fault. [491,iii]
The opponent must be one who thoroughly understands the contradictory;
why then make an effort for one's own destruction by making such a proposition?

If the thesis-statement (*pratijñā*) is not employed, how is it known by the opponent that this reason (*hetu*) is contradictory? To whom does this question apply? If you say it applies to the proponent (*vādin*), that is not correct. It would simply be a stroke of good fortune for the opponent if he did not know what assistance ought to be rendered by me to him. When the author of the treatise has stated that the application [of the reason] must be preceded by pervasion (*vyāpti*), the proponent is greatly assisted by the fact that a contradictory reason becomes impossible; thus, there is no fault even on the part of the author of the treatise. For he did not compose the treatise for the purpose of killing the proponent. If you argue that the opponent must certainly be assisted, then what is the hostility toward others? This is merely trivial. For example: "Sound is eternal because it is produced; whatever is produced is non-eternal. Here, the charge of a contradictory reason is made. At that time, no one who is not insane would, having already asserted eternity as the thesis, then demonstrate a pervasion with non-eternity. If, however, he were to demonstrate a pervasion with eternity, then the recognition of contradiction follows precisely from the reversal of the pervasion. Furthermore, the designation "contradictory" is relative to that which employs the thesis-statement. And this occurs at the point where one says, "Sound is eternal because it is produced. Otherwise, a syllogistic statement that lacks the thesis-statement—acting like the fall of an unseen mallet—would cause distress. Therefore, the thesis-statement is employed, since the thesis serves to announce the subject matter of the discussion (*prakaraṇa*).

To this it is replied: Even the statement of a thesis (*pratijñā*) is like an unseen mallet without an introductory context (*prastāva*). If it is argued that the context was provided by the opponent, then the word "thesis" is superfluous; enough of this digression.
[2. The thesis is not a member of the proof.]

[491, vi] But would there not be a deficiency in the proof (*sādhana*) without the proposition (*pratijñā*) as a member? Thus it has been said: "That which lacks even one of the members, such as the proposition and so forth, is deficient.
For if it were established that the thesis is a member of the proof, then its deficiency would follow;
however, the status of the thesis as a member of the proof has already been refuted.
A proof that lacks a member of the proof is deficient. Furthermore, the thesis is not a member of the proof; for:
[491,ix] Even when the thesis is not stated, there is no obstruction to its establishment.
The deficiency is stated by the non-mention of even one of the three forms [of the probans]. 23.

[491,x] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. It should be understood as such. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great vehicle of the śrāvakas, the great vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the great vehicle of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle that leads to the transcendence of all suffering, the great vehicle that leads to the transcendence of all conditioned phenomena, the great vehicle that leads to the transcendence of all afflictions, and the great vehicle that leads to the transcendence of all views—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Moreover, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle that brings about the realization of the emptiness of all dharmas, the great vehicle that brings about the realization of the signlessness of all dharmas, the great vehicle that brings about the realization of the wishlessness of all dharmas, and the great vehicle that brings about the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Finally, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle that leads to the attainment of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. The venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One’s words, was delighted and remembered them well. For that which is unrelated to it cannot be a part of it; nor can it be deficient because of it. Even if there were a deficiency consisting of something useless, since the useless is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*), there would be no deficiency at all. If, on the other hand, it is argued that it is not deficient even in the absence of the useless, then by the same logic, the case of the proposition (*pratijñā*) term would be identical whether it exists or does not exist, and thus the objection is invalid. Furthermore, if the proposition is accepted as being established only when there is a proof, then the definition of the proposition—"the statement of the probandum" (*sādhyānirdeśaḥ pratijñā*)—would be over-extensive (*ativyāpin*). Since the probandum is also a "proof" (*sādhana*) insofar as it is unestablished, the statement of an unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*) would also become a proposition. For one who holds that the proposition is not established by a proof, the definition of the proposition—"the statement of the probandum"—would result in the fallacy of a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) being a proposition, because the statement of the probandum that is not itself a proof would still be a proposition.
Therefore:
Or, by stating the proposition (*pratijñā*) as the thing to be proven, he is not subject to faults;
for since the context is restricted to the means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no possibility of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). (24)

Indeed, that which is not a proof (*sādhana*) does not become a proof; therefore, because it is a proof, there is no such contingency there. This is because a pseudo-reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is what is under discussion by virtue of being a proof, and because it lacks the status of being a statement of the probandum (*sādhya*). Since it lacks the definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*), the statement of a pseudo-proof is not a thesis.

But surely, the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*), not the statement of the proof (*sādhana*). Why then would there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) would also be a proposition? To this it is replied: Regarding the phrase "the statement of the probandum," if "statement of the probandum" means a statement *as* something to be proven, then a fallacious proof cannot be a proposition, because it is not stated as something to be proven. However, the object to be stated would remain unstated. If it is not understood that the statement is "as something to be proven," it is not known what is being stated.

[492, vii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, monks, physical food as gross nutriment sustains beings who have already come to be, and assists those seeking birth. Contact as the second sustains beings who have already come to be, and assists those seeking birth. Mental volition as the third sustains beings who have already come to be, and assists those seeking birth. Consciousness as the fourth sustains beings who have already come to be, and assists those seeking birth. Monks, if physical food as gross nutriment were non-existent in the world, would beings come to be or continue to exist? "No, Blessed One. "Therefore, monks, it is because physical food as gross nutriment exists that beings come to be and continue to exist. Monks, if contact as the second were non-existent in the world... [and so on for the other two]. Monks, if consciousness as the fourth were non-existent in the world, would beings come to be or continue to exist? "No, Blessed One. "Therefore, monks, it is because consciousness as the fourth exists that beings come to be and continue to exist. Thus, monks, these four nutriments sustain beings who have already come to be and assist those seeking birth. Furthermore, monks, these four nutriments have craving as their source, craving as their origin, craving as their cause, and craving as their condition. And what, monks, is the source of this craving? It has feeling as its source, feeling as its origin, feeling as its cause, and feeling as its condition. And what, monks, is the source of this feeling? It has contact as its source, contact as its origin, contact as its cause, and contact as its condition. And what, monks, is the source of this contact? It has the six sense bases as its source, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its cause, and the six sense bases as its condition. And what, monks, is the source of these six sense bases? It has name-and-form as its source, name-and-form as its origin, name-and-form as its cause, and name-and-form as its condition. And what, monks, is the source of this name-and-form? It has consciousness as its source, consciousness as its origin, consciousness as its cause, and consciousness as its condition. And what, monks, is the source of this consciousness? It has formations as its source, formations as its origin, formations as its cause, and formations as its condition. And what, monks, is the source of these formations? They have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their cause, and ignorance as their condition. Thus, monks, this entire mass of suffering originates from this single source. Furthermore, monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering," and "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—then, monks, one abandons ignorance and gives rise to true knowledge. With the abandonment of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, the formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering," and "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—then, monks, one abandons ignorance and gives rise to true knowledge. With the abandonment of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, right view arises; with the arising of right view, right resolve arises; with the arising of right resolve, right speech arises; with the arising of right speech, right action arises; with the arising of right action, right livelihood arises; with the arising of right livelihood, right effort arises; with the arising of right effort, right mindfulness arises; with the arising of right mindfulness, right concentration arises. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, monks, when one sees with right wisdom as it really is: "This is suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering," and "This is the cessation of suffering," and "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—then, monks, one abandons ignorance and gives rise to true knowledge. With the abandonment of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, the fetter of ignorance is abandoned. With the abandonment of the fetter of ignorance, the underlying tendency toward ignorance is abandoned. With the abandonment of the underlying tendency toward ignorance, one is no longer bound by the five lower fetters. Being no longer bound by the five lower fetters, one attains final knowledge in this very life. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
