Now, as for the definition of that which deserves to be the *sādhana* (means of proof): even then, how is it defined? Because no specific mode is specified; for there is no distinction made as to whether it is by way of being a *sādhana* or by way of being a *sādhya* (that which is to be proven). Consequently, even a fallacious *sādhana* (*sādhanābhāsa*) would possess the status of a *pratijñā* (thesis). Furthermore, it must be stated how it is defined both as a *sādhana* and as a *sādhya*. Definition by means of a word in the ablative case or any case other than the nominative constitutes [the definition] as a *sādhana*; definition by the nominative case constitutes it as a *sādhya*. Why is this so? Because such is the established usage of words. If this were the case, the definition of a *pratijñā* as "the definition of the thesis is the statement of the *sādhya*" need not be formulated. For in common worldly usage, the meaning of the word is well-established as being precisely the statement of something as a *sādhya*. We shall explain later that the definition of the *pakṣa* (subject) is intended to exclude misconceptions. Therefore, since the definition "the *pratijñā* is simply the statement of the *sādhya*" is redundant, the consequence follows that even a fallacious *sādhana* would be a *pratijñā*.

[492, viii] But surely, even on your own position, the statement of the probandum is indeed the thesis (*pratijñā*); so why is it not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)? [492, ix] This has already been answered: it is because that which is the statement of the probandum is not itself a means of proof (*asādhana*).
But surely, it might sometimes even be a means of proof (*sādhana*); what, then, is the reason for removing this doubt? We reply: it is precisely its being of a different class (*vijātīyatva*).
To explain: [492,x] Thus, indeed:
Even a statement made without qualification brings about doubt regarding that which belongs to a single class;
otherwise, it would follow that every statement of a probandum would constitute a thesis (*pratijñā*). (25)

[492,xii] First, this person, who is eager for objections, must be challenged as follows: If it is said, "A pot is being made," then the statement of the probandum (*sādhyanirdeśa*) would follow as being the thesis (*pratijñā*). However, since the context concerns the reason (*hetu*) as that which makes known, the statement of the probandum is a thesis only insofar as it depends upon that [reason]. If this is so, then it is established that a statement of the probandum that does not constitute a means of proof is not a thesis; thus, a fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) is not a thesis.
[492,xiii]

If it is argued that because it is stated as an established fact (*siddha*), it serves as a means of proof (*sādhana*) for the opponent as well, then how can the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) at this point be inseparable from the means of proof? (26)

[492,xiv] But would not the opponent also say this: "The statement of the probandum (*sādhya*) which functions as a means of proof (*sādhana*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*). However, that which is a fallacy of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*) is not a means of proof because it is unestablished (*asiddha*); and since it is not a means of proof, it is not a thesis, for a thesis is a means of proof. If a fallacy of proof is not a means of proof due to being unestablished, then how can a thesis—whose object is itself unestablished—be a means of proof? Is it not precisely by virtue of being unestablished that the thesis possesses the status of a means of proof? If [493,i]...

It would be successful [in its function], yet it would not even constitute the presentation of the object [of proof]. If this were so, then even a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) would be an unprevented means of proof (*sādhana*) by virtue of being a thesis (*pratijñā*). If it is argued: "Let it be a means of proof by virtue of being a thesis; what fault is there in this? [The response is: There would be no fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*). If it is argued: "A thesis designated as a fallacious reason is not a means of proof for a thesis that has the nature of something to be proven (*sādhya*); therefore, it is indeed a fault," [we reply: If it is a means of proof, how is it not a means of proof? If it is a means of proof with respect to its own purpose (*svārtha*), [we say] no, because it is a means of proof only when accompanied by the actual object. Nor is that [thesis] itself the means of proof for itself; rather, it is merely a verbal赘疣 (*śabda-gaḍu*, useless verbal proliferation) that serves as the means of proof, since in all cases it is the denoted object (*abhidheya*) that is the means of proof. However, regarding the communication of one's intention, its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) has already been stated.

[493,ii] Now, if the meaning itself were the proof (*sādhana*), then every thesis (*pratijñā*) would be capable of conveying an external object; consequently, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) would occur from that alone. Therefore, since neither direct nor indirect proof arises from it, the thesis is not the proof.

Another, however, says: "The thesis (*pratijñā*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*), because it is stated as being accompanied by fallacies (*sābhāsatva*); for one observes that being accompanied by fallacies occurs together with being a means of proof. The proponent of the refutation (*dūṣaṇavādin*) says: "There is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to perception (*pratyakṣa*. The response is: "There is no fault, because [the definition] is qualified by the nature of being speech (*vacanātmakatva*). If it is argued that there is still inconclusiveness due to refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), the response is: "[It is valid] provided that it is not a refutation (*adūṣaṇatve sati*)."
All of this is incorrect. To explain why:
The mockery regarding the neglect of [objections] such as "the statement with fallacies" (sābhāsokti) and so forth is incoherent;
for it has been indicated that this is not a valid principle (nyāya). // 27 //

[493, vii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Furthermore, monks, I have taught that the cessation of craving is the cessation of these four nutriments. And what, monks, is the cessation of craving? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving—its relinquishing, its abandoning, its release, its non-attachment, and its non-arising. This, monks, is called the cessation of craving, which is the cessation of these four nutriments. And what, monks, is the path leading to the cessation of craving? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the path leading to the cessation of craving, which is the cessation of these four nutriments. Thus, monks, I have taught the nutriment, I have taught the origin of the nutriment, I have taught the cessation of the nutriment, and I have taught the way leading to the cessation of the nutriment. Therefore, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past declared the cessation of the four nutriments, all of them spoke of the cessation of craving, which is the cessation of these four nutriments. And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will declare the cessation of the four nutriments, all of them will speak of the cessation of craving, which is the cessation of these four nutriments. And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the present declare the cessation of the four nutriments, all of them speak of the cessation of craving, which is the cessation of these four nutriments. Why is that? Because this is the only way, monks, for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the destruction of suffering and grief, for the attainment of the true path, and for the realization of Nirvana. [493, viii] Monks, suppose there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and a man would come along with a sharp axe, desiring its heartwood. He would cut down the great tree at its root and would carry it away on his shoulder. Having carried it away on his shoulder, he would cut it into logs. Having cut it into logs, he would carry them away on his shoulder. Having carried them away on his shoulder, he would split them into pieces. Having split them into pieces, he would carry them away on his shoulder. Having carried them away on his shoulder, he would split them into splinters. Indeed, the probans (*hetu*) does not possess the capacity to indicate [the presence of the probandum] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) merely by its non-perception there. Nor is there a single way to avoid [this objection], for it is avoided in some way or another by means of a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) that is incompatible with the dissimilar instance. This has already been stated previously: when the objection was raised that "studying is preceded by another study" based on the example of the study of the *Bhārata*, the avoidance was stated by qualifying it with "Vedic [study]. But what is the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) in the Veda? If it is impossible to study it otherwise, then there is no avoidance at all; for a qualification that is not incompatible with the dissimilar instance is not capable of excluding the probans from it. Otherwise, who would not be able to say: "provided that there is multiplicity"? Therefore, this introduction and avoidance, etc., are incorrect; the refutation remains as before regarding the thesis and its status as a proof (*sādhana*).

<3. The Purpose of Formulating the Definition of the Thesis> [493, viii] If, then, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is not strictly necessary, for what purpose is there a definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*)? Since the object to be proven (*sādhyārtha*) is understood through the power of the reason (*hetu*), it becomes the thesis regardless; what is the use of this investigation? It will be exactly as it is understood.
[493,ix] This is true.
Even though the statement of the probandum (sādhya) is already implied by its meaning, the definition is provided for the sake of avoiding confusion;
that [definition] consists of four characteristics, which are stated by the proponent himself through words involving case-endings (rūpa) and indeclinables (nipāta). (28)
The inclusion of the proponent's own admissions consists of what is unestablished, what does not constitute a means of proof, and what has been stated as the meaning of the argument.

Indeed, every characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) must be elucidated in its entirety for the sake of destroying delusion, and so too must the [entire] word (*vacas*). In this regard, even great scholars possess significant disagreements concerning what is the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya*) and its contrary; and if these are not resolved, they lead one onto a path that spreads great calamity. Indeed, an unrefuted collection of faults does not lead to welfare. For instance: regarding the argument "the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another," some say that "being for the sake of another" alone is the probandum, even though it is not actually so; others say that "being for the sake of the self" is not the probandum even though it is; and those who assert the authority of scripture (*śāstra-prāmāṇya-vādin*) say that something is the probandum even though it is already established by scripture. Furthermore, there is disagreement that even what is indicated as a means of proof (*sādhana*) would fall under the category of the thesis (*pakṣa*) by the definition "the statement of the probandum is the proposition" (*pratijñā*). Even if [the proponent] does not accept it, it is still the probandum; therefore, in order to exclude that, the restriction of its own nature (*svarūpa-nipāta*) is intended by the words themselves: "unestablished" (*asiddha*), "not a means of proof" (*asādhana*), "stated by the sense" (*arthokta*), and "acceptance by the speaker" (*vādibhyupagama*). It should be understood that only the unestablished is the probandum, and the same applies to the other terms. Thus, by this restriction, the exclusion of the opposites of these should be understood. [Regarding the logic here: If this matter is already established from scripture itself, which is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why then is it established again by another means of knowledge? If you say, "Scripture is not a means of knowledge for another person, therefore it is for his sake," then how is it a means of knowledge for oneself? If you say, "Because of one's own acceptance (*abhyupagama*)," then the opponent must also be made to accept it. Likewise, if that is the probandum, why is it indicated as a means of proof? If that which is stated by the sense is not the probandum, then there would be no understanding of the meaning of the sentence at all, and elsewhere there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*), since the meaning of a word is determined through context, capacity, and the proximity of other words. Furthermore, one who does not know the context does not comprehend the intended meaning; so what connection can there be with him on the path of linguistic convention? And thus, the meaning uttered by a wandering mendicant might even be grasped by a beast—what excellence of capability is there in that? Therefore, he said: *(The following verse is implied by the commentary)* "Unestablished, not a means of proof, stated by the sense, and accepted by the speaker; this is to be known as the fourfold restriction of the probandum. Thus, the text concludes.
Even if not explicitly stated, that which is pervaded by the proponent's intention is considered to be the probandum, just like the self for its own sake. (29)

[494,iii] The Discourse on the Three Jewels Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are three jewels. What are the three? They are the jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dharma, and the jewel of the Saṃgha. These are called the three jewels. Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: “World-Honored One, what are the qualities of the Buddha-jewel? What are the qualities of the Dharma-jewel? And what are the qualities of the Saṃgha-jewel? The Blessed One told Ānanda: “Listen attentively and bear it well in mind; I shall explain it to you. Ānanda replied: “Yes, World-Honored One,” and listened to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, the Buddha-jewel has thirty-two qualities. What are the thirty-two? First, the Tathāgata is worthy of offerings. Second, he is perfectly enlightened. Third, he has attained true knowledge and conduct. Fourth, he has practiced the holy life. Fifth, he has well understood this world. Sixth, he has well understood the world beyond. Seventh, he has well understood all realms of existence, both divine and human. Eighth, he has well understood all states of being, whether high or low. Ninth, he has well understood all destinies, whether good or bad. Tenth, he has well understood all paths leading to their respective destinations. Eleventh, he has well understood all meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments. Twelfth, he has well understood all the afflictions and their outflows. Thirteenth, he has well understood all the defilements and their outflows. Fourteenth, he has well understood all the fetters and their outflows. Fifteenth, he has well understood all the bonds and their outflows. Sixteenth, he has well understood all the obscurations and their outflows. Seventeenth, he has well understood all the hindrances and their outflows. Eighteenth, he has well understood all the coverings and their outflows. Nineteenth, he has well understood all the veils and their outflows. Twentieth, he has well understood all the obscurations and their outflows. Twenty-first, he has well understood all the entanglements and their outflows. Twenty-second, he has well understood all the attachments and their outflows. Twenty-third, he has well understood all the cravings and their outflows. Twenty-fourth, he has well understood all the thirsts and their outflows. Twenty-fifth, he has well understood all the desires and their outflows. Twenty-sixth, he has well understood all the clingings and their outflows. Twenty-seventh, he has well understood all the grasping and their outflows. Twenty-eighth, he has well understood all the obsessions and their outflows. Twenty-ninth, he has well understood all the delusions and their outflows. Thirtieth, he has well understood all the ignorances and their outflows. Thirty-first, he has well understood all the latent tendencies and their outflows. Thirty-second, he has well understood all the underlying tendencies and their outflows. These, Ānanda, are the thirty-two qualities of the Buddha-jewel. “Furthermore, Ānanda, the Dharma-jewel has thirty-two qualities. What are the thirty-two? First, the Dharma is well-expounded. Second, it is visible in this very life. Third, it is immediate. Fourth, it is timeless. Fifth, it is inviting inspection. Sixth, it is onward-leading. Seventh, it is to be personally realized by the wise. Eighth, it is not dependent on another. Ninth, it is not subject to change. Tenth, it is not subject to decay. Eleventh, it is not subject to destruction. Twelfth, it is not subject to exhaustion. Thirteenth, it is not subject to loss. Fourteenth, it is not subject to diminution. If that "other" is the self, it is established by means of the example. But if it is merely the establishment of another [entity], then it is not the proof of the subject at hand, or it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). What fault, then, does the opponent have in saying this? If, on the other hand, the inclusion of the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is for the purpose of demonstrating that even what is not explicitly stated is the probandum (*sādhya*) when it is pervaded by the proponent's intention; and likewise, for the purpose of excluding what is not intended, since a statement has the function of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*); and since there is nothing such as "unintended," because everything is intended by someone in some way; therefore, the inclusion of the word "intended" is for the purpose of establishing that it is intended by the proponent (*vādin*). In that case, the meaning of "himself" (*svayam*) is indeed obtained. Even if something is intended by the authors of treatises (*śāstrakāra*), if it is intended by him [the proponent], it is simply intended; thus, there is no exclusion of that. If it is argued that there is an exclusion when it is not intended, no; for it is excluded by the very inclusion of the word "intended. Just as it is established by the inclusion of the word "intended" that what is intended by the opponent or the judges is not the probandum, so too is there an exclusion of what is intended by the authors of treatises from that very same [term]. Since the inclusion of the word "himself" excludes everything intended by others, why did the Teacher state only the purpose of the treatise? He shows that "himself" indicates an acceptance independent of the treatise.
[495,ii] Here is the rebuttal:

In order to prevent the possibility of doubt regarding the exclusion of all other desired [meanings], he himself stated this in his commentary; and this [exegesis] was composed for that very purpose. (30)

Although by the very mention of "intended" (*iṣṭa*), all other intended [propositions] are excluded from the perspective of the proponent, nevertheless, a doubt may still arise regarding that which is intended by the author of the treatise as being the probandum (*sādhya*). For some might hold the view that what is intended by the author of the treatise must necessarily be accepted by the proponent as well; otherwise, a reason (*hetu*) that contradicts the treatise would not be a means of valid cognition (*gamaka*). Therefore, the term "himself" (*svayaṃ*) is included in order to eliminate this ground for doubt. For this very reason, the exclusion of the treatise is stated to be the sole purpose of the inclusion of "himself," since this explicit mention of "himself" was made for the sake of excluding what is intended in the treatises. The exclusion of other intended [propositions], however, is established effortlessly. Thus, this is precisely the purpose of the inclusion of "intended": that the probandum is pervaded by intention even if it is not explicitly stated. Consequently, in the case of the phrase "for the sake of others" (*parārthāḥ*), the probandum intended by the inclusion of "intended" is the state of being for the sake of others who are not [already] assembled.

**(2) The Purpose of Using the Term "viśeṣa"** [495,v] Now, one might object: that *viśeṣa* (distinction) of the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is not the probandum (*sādhya*); for if it were the probandum, how could it be a "distinction"? There is no identity between the probandum and its distinction. And as the Teacher has stated: "For [the reason is] contradictory because it proves the opposite of the specific property," and so forth. To this, he says:
The distinction between the property and the property-bearer is stated to be due to their mutual dependence on that [distinguishing mark].

That very same thing, when made the object of a desire, is stated as the specific property to be proven (*sādhya*) with respect to another; thus it is said that "the *sādhya* has already been stated. The "other" is one of delicate intellect. For instance:
"The eyes and so forth are for the sake of another."

The self is not established in the example; therefore, its being the object [of the inference] is not established. If you say that it is not the probandum (*sādhya*), then let that specific property belong to it for you. (PVA 103)

[We reply: It is not out of a desire to avoid [the charge of contradiction] from the perspective of the opponent; for if the opponent were refuted by that much alone, who would undertake the effort of establishing their own position? [The opponent asks: "How then can something be the probandum even if it has not been stated? [We reply: Only what is stated is the probandum, otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Since there is no difference in the fact that everything else is unstated, everything would then be the probandum. Furthermore, it is not possible to demonstrate everything in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). And if that were so, because it would prove the opposite [of what is intended], nothing at all would be a valid reason (*hetu*). To this, he says:
Even if the desire [to prove] is not explicitly stated, its understanding would arise from the context. (31)
For the fault of "lack of positive concomitance" (ananvaya) in the example has been stated as follows:
if that [self] were another, it would be unestablished; thus, in that case, it would result in the subversion of what is intended. (32)

Even though this very point was indeed stated by him, nevertheless, the meaning here should be understood in light of the context; for certainly, not every statement is capable of conveying its meaning independently of the context.
Therefore, having investigated the intended meaning according to the noble standard, those who dwell in the world proceed to determine the meaning of the sentence. (98) (PVA) [496,iii]

This indeed is the established position of all wise people: that here, the eyes and so forth are for the sake of another. The meaning of the sentence is that they are for the sake of the self (*ātman*). Consequently, there is also a lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) with respect to that [self], because the example is itself the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*). This has been shown by the Teacher (*Ācārya*) as well: "If it were both self and other, it would be unestablished (*asiddha*). It should be understood that this means it is not established by way of an example. Therefore, since the opposite of what he desires is established, this [reason] is a "destroyer of what is desired" (*iṣṭavighātakṛt*).
[Objection: But how is it known that at that time the subject under discussion (*prākaraṇika*)—the self—is indeed the thing to be proven? To this, he says:
If that which was not presented as a proof (sādhana) in the debate is not established,
what is there to be proven? Otherwise, it would either result in an undesirable consequence or be utterly futile.

[496, vi] If that very thing about which there is dispute is not what is being proven—since the state of being for one's own sake is already established in relation to the self—then even the proof of something else is irrelevant, and thus nothing at all is proven. Furthermore, depending on the proof of either of the two positions, it would be undesirable because it proves the opposite; or, if that position is abandoned, the proof is futile, since it results in proving what is already established.

Now, even if the self is not the probandum (*sādhya*), it is established when the means of proof (*sādhana*) is established, because it possesses the mere quality of being "other. Furthermore, the opponent should not raise the fault of lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) regarding a subject that is not the probandum; for faults such as lack of concomitance depend upon the status of something being the probandum.
[496, viii]

This is not the case. Why? Because if, while one thing is being proven, something else that is not to be proven were also established, then everything would be established in that way. For without a gradation of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), how could one thing be established and another not? If by the proving of one thing another were established, then the opposite of what is intended would also be established. And in that case, every reason (*hetu*) would be contradictory (*viruddha*) and every example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because no collection of mutually contradictory properties could ever be concomitant (*anvaya*) in any single instance. If it is argued: "Only that which is intended is established, and nothing else, because it is what is desired," we say: No. It is impossible to divide the operation of a reason based on mere desire. Furthermore, since the opponent may also intend the opposite, the establishment of both opposites would be unavoidable, as there is no distinction in desire itself. Nor is there any specific logical connection (*pratibandha*) such that the proof would belong only to the proponent and not to the opponent. If it is argued: "There is the fault of the non-concomitance of the intended property," [we reply]: If this were so, no contradictory reason that subverts what is intended would exist. This is because, according to what has been said, non-concomitance exists everywhere. A reason is contradictory precisely because it proves the opposite of the property to be proven when there is non-concomitance with what was stated. However, a "contradictory reason regarding a specific property" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) is so called only in relation to what was *not* stated, because it establishes the contrary of that.

In the arguments involving a second entity, there is the fallacy of the non-sequential (*niranvaya*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*). By this, the probandum (*sādhya*) has been stated; or else, it is accepted in its general form. (34)
Since there is no other object [to be perceived], that very [consciousness] is not established when the body is not attained;
for those who prattle such empty nonsense, this is merely the product of their dull-wittedness. (35)

<(1) Refutation of the Cārvāka Doctrine> [496,xi] By this very same reasoning, the fault of the lack of positive concomitance (*niranvaya-doṣa*) or the contradiction (*viruddhatā*) has been demonstrated in the formulations for proving a second entity. For example: "A jar is accompanied by a second entity, either a jar or a person characterized as a body possessing distinct consciousness, because it is unproduced."

[497,i] The Cārvākas say: "Like a wall. The person (*puruṣa*) is the body characterized by manifest consciousness; there is no other self (*ātman*) or such entity that migrates to another world. In this regard, since it is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they state the reason that inference alone is the means of proof. The intention is that a person of such a nature cannot be established [by perception], because it is not established in an example through "seizing by the horns" (i.e., specific identification). Therefore, one establishes in a general sense that [the subject] is accompanied by something else. These are the means that accomplish what is to be proven. [497,ii]
To this it is replied: Whether it be a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*), that which is [the object of cognition] should here be established as the probandum (*sādhya*).

"There must be a definitive certainty that [the reason] is to be established by the intended probandum"—this is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*). For instance, the previous logical argument applies here: either the person is not included within the word itself, or there is no connection with respect to him. Furthermore, if it were merely established [by the reason], but not established as the probandum, then too an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur; this has already been demonstrated.

[497,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either a bodhisattva or the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive those dharmas, he does not apprehend them; and because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. He does not think, ‘I am a bodhisattva,’ nor does he think, ‘This is the perfection of wisdom. Because he does not conceive such notions, he is not attached to the thought, ‘I am a bodhisattva practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is called the non-attachment of a bodhisattva mahāsattva to the perfection of wisdom.”

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no implication of a specific [instance] here? [Reply: That is incorrect. Because, if the body is unestablished, there is an absence of individuals; how then could there be a universal (*sāmānya*)? For there is no universal in the absence of individual cows. Even upon the destruction of an individual, the universal does not perish because it is eternal; it simply does not become an object of conventional usage due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). If it is argued that it becomes so when an individual is possible, [we reply: No, because in this case there is no possibility [of such an individual]. For a person of such a nature is not possible without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or rather, just as a universal is not an object of conventional usage in the absence of an individual, so too is the universal of "either one" (*anyatara-sāmānya*). If it is argued that its establishment comes from a means of valid cognition, [we reply: No, because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If inference (*anumāna*) exists as a means of valid cognition, then the universal exists; and if the universal exists, then inference exists. For that which is unestablished cannot have the form of a universal. Therefore, just as "being either one" (*anyataratva*) is not a valid reason, so too is the probandum (*sādhya*) non-existent. To explain: regarding the reason "because it is either the subject (*pakṣa*) or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)," the property of being the subject itself is what is expressed by the word "either one" (*anyatara*), since there is no contradiction between the two in the word. Because the word "either one" has conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as its domain, there is no implication of the other when a restricted property is present. And without such an implication, there is no introduction of the other through the hearing of the word "either one. Therefore, this [reasoning] is invalid.

Furthermore, if it were not the case that a person of such a nature is being established here, then one would simply have said, "The pot is accompanied by either a person or a pot. For [the reason "not being a lotus"] applies to both [the wall and the person] because of its connection with the class of pots (*ghaṭajāti*) as the material cause (*upādāna*); since it cannot logically coexist with itself, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the person alone is what is to be proven. How is it that the mention of only one [of the two] serves to establish its opposite? It is not so, because the mention of one is for the purpose of establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). There is no positive concomitance of the wall with the person. If it is asked: "But if there is concomitance with another, how is the proof of the other—the person—established? If you say "by implication," then whose implication is this? Is it the implication of the reason (*hetu*) or of the statement (*vacana*)? First, it is not the implication of the reason, for "not being a lotus" is not invariably connected (*pratibaddha*) with "having a person as a companion," because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To explain: even the proof that "a pot has as its companion either a person belonging to another world or a pot" would [otherwise] follow. If it is argued: "Let it be that in another intended sense (*vivakṣā*), there is also a proof of the other," we say no. For it has already been demonstrated that there can be no status of being a reason based on mere intention.

[498,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Non-arising of All Phenomena. Ānanda, you should learn it by heart in this way. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the non-arising of all phenomena? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, the non-arising of form is the non-arising of all phenomena; the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is the non-arising of all phenomena. Furthermore, Ānanda, the non-arising of the eye is the non-arising of all phenomena; the non-arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is the non-arising of all phenomena. The non-arising of forms is the non-arising of all phenomena; the non-arising of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects is the non-arising of all phenomena. The non-arising of eye-consciousness is the non-arising of all phenomena; the non-arising of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness is the non-arising of all phenomena. The non-arising of contact is the non-arising of all phenomena; the non-arising of feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death is the non-arising of all phenomena. Thus, Ānanda, the non-arising of all phenomena is the non-arising of suffering. At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the non-arising of form? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, form is empty of self and of what belongs to a self; its nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of self and of what belongs to a self; their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, Ānanda, one should understand the non-arising of form. The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the non-arising of the eye? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, the eye is empty of self and of what belongs to a self; its nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty of self and of what belongs to a self; their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, Ānanda, one should understand the non-arising of the eye. The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the non-arising of form? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, forms are empty of self and of what belongs to a self; their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are empty of self and of what belongs to a self; their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, Ānanda, one should understand the non-arising of form. The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the non-arising of eye-consciousness? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, eye-consciousness is empty of self and of what belongs to a self; its nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty of self and of what belongs to a self; their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, Ānanda, one should understand the non-arising of eye-consciousness. The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the non-arising of contact? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, contact is empty of self and of what belongs to a self; its nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death are empty of self and of what belongs to a self; their nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, Ānanda, one should understand the non-arising of contact. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the non-arising of suffering? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, suffering is empty of self and of what belongs to a self; its nature is non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, Ānanda, one should understand the non-arising of suffering. When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the venerable Ānanda said to him: “Blessed One, this Dharma-discourse is profound, exceedingly profound. Blessed One, who would believe this teaching? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, those who have practiced the holy life under past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones will believe this teaching. Furthermore, Ānanda, those who have cultivated the roots of goodness, purified their conduct, and perfected their wisdom will believe this teaching. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is the ultimate truth, the finality, and the exhaustion of the outflows. At that time, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and said: “Blessed One, may the Tathāgata out of compassion for future generations explain further the meaning of this Dharma-discourse. The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, listen well and attend closely. I shall explain it to you. “Very well, Blessed One,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then spoke: “Ānanda, the non-arising of all phenomena is the gate of liberation. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, when one realizes the non-arising of form, one transcends attachment to form; when one realizes the non-arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one transcends attachment to consciousness. When one realizes the non-arising of the eye, one transcends attachment to the eye; when one realizes the non-arising of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, one transcends attachment to the mind. When one realizes the non-arising of forms, one transcends attachment to forms; when one realizes the non-arising of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, one transcends attachment to mental objects. When one realizes the non-arising of eye-consciousness, one transcends attachment to eye-consciousness; when one realizes the non-arising of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness, one transcends attachment to mind-consciousness. When one realizes the non-arising of contact, one transcends attachment to contact; when one realizes the non-arising of feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death, one transcends attachment to aging-and-death. Thus, Ānanda, the non-arising of all phenomena is the gate of liberation. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse? How should I remember it? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Non-arising of All Phenomena. Ānanda, you should remember it by this name. Having spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Now, [it may be argued that] this [inference] is observed as distinct [from perception] by virtue of the power of the statement. However, meanings are not established by the power of the statement alone, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) therein. To illustrate: when such statements as "The fat man does not eat during the day" are possible, eating at night is not necessarily implied, since even a false statement is possible. If such a person were established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like a jar, then a statement prompted by a speaker’s intention rooted in a *pramāṇa* would constitute an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), because the illumination of an object perceived by oneself is what constitutes an inference for others. If it is argued that [the object] is established by this very *pramāṇa*, we say no; for this involves the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). It has been demonstrated that if the *pramāṇa* exists, there is the proof (*sādhana*), and if the proof exists, the *pramāṇa* exists.

**(2) Examination of Impermanence** [498, ii] But surely, even if destruction (*nāśa*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the same logic applies. To explain: is the impermanence to be proven that which resides in sound, or that which resides in a jar? If it is that which resides in sound, then a jar is not a similar instance (*sapakṣa*); if it is that which resides in a jar, then sound is not such [an instance]. Thus, there is a contradiction. The same applies to "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Now, if this is called "balancing the alternative" (*vikalpasama*), because a distinction is stated despite the common property (*sādharmya*), then it is "balancing the alternative. If that is so, it is the same in the case of the "person" (*puruṣa*) as well.
[498,iii] Here is the rebuttal:
If it is argued that destruction is the same even when conceptualized through the distinction between sound and a jar, [we reply:
no, because the sound is established by means of its destruction which is already proven. (36)
Likewise, if there were a separate entity [of impermanence], then even a jar would possess it;

yet, just as a person is not established because he is not brought about by the power of the statement, so too impermanence is not established—thus this is not the case. Just as "being one or the other of the subject or the similar instance" [is not established], so too "being produced" [is not established]. For in the case of a jar, impermanence—which exists between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—is not established as its own nature (*svabhāva*). Even if that [impermanence] were established, it would be something else entirely. Therefore, how could sound be impermanent? Indeed, that very same impermanence cannot exist in sound; at best, it could only be something similar to it.

How can similarity be established when there is no possibility of concomitance with anything else? If that were the case, then even a person would possess such establishment; thus, the subsequent [proof] would be useless. (PVA 101)
That is incorrect.
Similarity can only exist in the case of difference; otherwise, how could there be a state of becoming otherwise?
For if there were identity, there would be no similarity, because similarity depends upon a counter-correlate.

For instance: whatever kind of impermanence is characterized by prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence after destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) in a jar, that very same kind exists in sound as well, because prior non-existence and so forth are possible in the case of sound. Indeed, there is no dispute that phonemes perish as soon as they are uttered. Thus, if the jar, as the subject (*dharmin*), were to possess that [impermanence] due to its similarity to a wall, then this proof would be valid. However, there is no similarity between the wall as the subject and the jar regarding the property of being accompanied by a person.

[Objection: But even here, if it is the case that while the universal of impermanence (*anityatā-sāmānya*) is expressed by the words, the intended meaning (*aidaṃparyārtha*) is actually the particular (*viśeṣa*) residing in the sound itself, and there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with that [particular], how can its establishment be achieved? [Response:
To this we reply:
[498,xiii] Impermanence is distinguished by sound; if it were not so, it would not exclude non-connection. // 37 //
For exclusion is of two kinds: that of dissociation and that of non-connection.
When exclusion is intended to preclude non-connection, there is no occurrence of a lack of positive concomitance (ananvaya). // 38 //

Even if it is the case that the qualified impermanence does not follow [the reason], the following [reason] will be qualified. For it is the aggregate (*samudāya*) that is to be proven. If that were already established beforehand, what would be the purpose of the proof? Therefore, when impermanence is established through a reason that follows [the subject] alone, the word reveals its own nature as both an aggregate and something qualified.

Now, if there were concomitance (*anvaya*) with the mere [property], how could a specific impermanence be established? If there were concomitance with something else, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one thing is being proved by means of another. And in that case, every reason (*hetu*) would be contradictory and every example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of the property to be proved (*sādhyavikala*). If it is argued that this fault applies only when there is concomitance with the aforementioned property and not otherwise, we say no; for there is no difference in their status as properties to be proved (*sādhya*). If there were no such fault, there would be no subversion of anyone’s desired position, and thus everyone could prove whatever they intended. [The opponent replies: No, because the qualification is made by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). For a qualification is of two kinds: by excluding non-connection and by excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). It is not the case that one says, "Sound alone is impermanent"; rather, one says "sound also [is impermanent]," because of the similarity of impermanence. However, this is not possible in the proof of a person (*puruṣa*). For the state of having a second (*sadvitīyatva*) is not the same for a wall and a jar. If it is argued that the state of having a second is the same insofar as it is "one or the other," we say no, because even that is absent. For a similarity based on "having a second" occurs only if there is an absence of restriction (*niyama*). But here there is indeed a restriction: the wall has a second only in the form of a jar, whereas the jar has a second only in the form of a person of that kind; such is the intention of the opponent.

[499,iii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. It should be learned, Ānanda, by those sons and daughters of good family who desire to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great vehicle of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle that carries out the crossing over of all sentient beings, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Moreover, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle that brings about the attainment of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Also, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle that leads to the realization of the state of omniscience, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Thus, Ānanda, because it is the great vehicle, the supreme vehicle, the foremost vehicle, the best vehicle, the most excellent vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle, the peerless vehicle, the incomparable vehicle, the unequalled vehicle, and the vehicle that transcends all others, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Exposition of the Great Vehicle. “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse should be learned, retained, recited, and fully mastered by those sons and daughters of good family who wish to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well has this Dharma-discourse been spoken by the Blessed One! This Dharma-discourse, Blessed One, will be a source of light for those sons and daughters of good family who have set their minds on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. The Blessed One said: “So it is, Ānanda. So it is, Ānanda. This Dharma-discourse will indeed be a source of light for those sons and daughters of good family who have set their minds on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. The Venerable Ānanda, having heard the Blessed One’s words, was delighted and remembered them well.
