But surely, even when there is a restriction (*pratiniyama*), the expression "one of the two" (*anyatara*) is indeed employed. Therefore, how can there be an absence of "one-ness" by necessity? Consequently, there is no contradiction between optionality (*vikalpa*) and a single restriction. For instance: in the case of the statement, "One of Devadatta or Yajñadatta should be fed," the act of eating is restricted to one person alone by necessity. Likewise here, there is a restriction to the person as being accompanied by a second entity. This restriction is not one brought about by the power of the words; rather, the possibility of such a restriction occurs by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim (*kākatālīya-nyāya*). And that [restriction] is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, in this case, when it is stated that "the person or the jar is accompanied by a second," the restriction to the person is not established by direct perception. For the act of eating is restricted to a single individual due to the capacity of the thing itself, not due to the capacity of the words, since the servant proceeds to act according to his own preference, whether for the eater or the giver. If he were told, "If you do not feed him, then you yourself shall not eat," the lack of restriction would remain unsettled. If it is argued that here too the restriction is brought about by the capacity of the means of proof (*sādhana*), we say no; for it has already been demonstrated that this is possible even in the opposite case. By this, the following point is also refuted.
[499,iv] There is no following after a particular; [499,v] in the case of a universal, there is the proving of what is already established.

If what is being proved is impermanence in its general sense (*sāmānya*), then because that is already established in certain cases such as lightning and the like, it would be a case of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*). If, on the other hand, what is being proved is impermanence as qualified by sound (*śabda-viśiṣṭam anityatvam*), then because that does not exist in a jar, there would be an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya-abhāva*). For it is the generality itself that is being proved in sound, since it is not yet established there. Thus he says:
**(3) Refutation of the Generality** [499, vi]
That which is to be proven is indeed the universal, and it is not the proving of what is already established;
and that [universal] as qualified by the subject is not subject to the fault of being "without a logical connection" (niranvaya).

[499,vii] If impermanence were to be proven independently of a specific substratum, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). However, since it is the universal (*sāmānya*) that is being proven in relation to sound, there is no such fallacy of proving the already established.
[499,viii]

Is it not a contradiction to say that a universal is established in a word? For the very fact of being qualified by the word is its particularity. If it is a universal, how can it be a particular? And if it is a particular, how can it be a universal?
This is not so.

When the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been established in a general sense, its restriction to a particular [subject] occurs through the connection with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), by way of grasping the relationship. (PVA 103)

[500,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. He does not perceive form as real, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor forms, nor eye-consciousness, nor contact at the eye, nor sensation born of contact at the eye. He does not perceive the ear as real, nor sounds, nor ear-consciousness, nor contact at the ear, nor sensation born of contact at the ear. He does not perceive the nose as real, nor odors, nor nose-consciousness, nor contact at the nose, nor sensation born of contact at the nose. He does not perceive the tongue as real, nor tastes, nor tongue-consciousness, nor contact at the tongue, nor sensation born of contact at the tongue. He does not perceive the body as real, nor tangibles, nor body-consciousness, nor contact at the body, nor sensation born of contact at the body. He does not perceive the mind as real, nor mental phenomena, nor mind-consciousness, nor contact at the mind, nor sensation born of contact at the mind. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor the element of water, nor the element of fire, nor the element of wind, nor the element of space, nor the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor unconditioned phenomena. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor the fruit of a once-returner, nor the fruit of a non-returner, nor arhatship. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Why is that? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, what is the distinction, what is the difference, and what is the specific characteristic between a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, and a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha? The Blessed One said: “Śāriputra, it is precisely because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature that there is no distinction, no difference, and no specific characteristic to be found among them. However, Śāriputra, although all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet through the power of skillful means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the six perfections, matures beings, purifies the buddha-field, and finally attains unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

For when a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is demonstrated by means of something qualified by its verbal expression, the qualification by that verbal expression is not established [as an inherent property]. Even when a positive concomitance is shown by the bare object itself, the qualification by that [verbal expression] is nonetheless established, because it is intended as a unity based on similarity. Indeed, one who wishes to demonstrate "just like that" must show that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire. Once that [smoke] is established as being thus pervaded by fire, wherever it is brought forward, it generates the cognition of fire in that very place, because the relationship has been grasped in precisely that manner. For the fire produces smoke in its own location; since the relationship is perceived through the movement from one location to another, [the smoke] brings about the cognition of fire in that same location.

[500,iii] But if there is a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) in general, how can there be a cognition of the particular (*viśeṣa*)? There is no fault in this cognition because the universal does not exist apart from the particular. Indeed, the establishment of anyone’s practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is not possible through a cognition that lacks the specific determination of place, time, and state. And since this has already been established previously in the investigation of validity (*prāmāṇya*), it need not be repeated here. Therefore, because the universal is proven as qualified by its locus (*dharmin*), there is neither the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) nor the fallacy of lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).

[Objection: Surely the generality must be cognized together with the probandum (*sādhya*), and the probandum will be cognized through the power of inference. Yet, that [probandum] is not established by mere external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*). For pervasion is not demonstrated in this way: "Whatever is produced is impermanent," while depending on all [individual instances]. Therefore: If there is no establishment of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), and if the pervasion is external, then the establishment of the probandum would never occur. If its establishment were to occur through a pervasion with something else, then everything would be established for everyone; such a consequence would follow. That too is trivial. For it is as follows:

This has been stated: since pervasion is perceived through the coexistence with the subject (*dharmin*), whatever place may be such [as possessing the reason], that very place is inseparable from the probandum (*sādhya*). (PVA 104)

[500, vii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a white lotus flower, and the person who is like a red lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Just as, monks, a lotus flower born in water and grown in water rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Just as, monks, a blue lotus flower born in water and grown in water remains submerged at the surface of the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Just as, monks, a white lotus flower born in water and grown in water rises up above the water and remains untouched by the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a red lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Just as, monks, a red lotus flower born in water and grown in water rises up above the water and remains untouched by the water; even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. This, monks, is called a person like a red lotus flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

"This place possesses fire because it possesses smoke, like a kitchen area. It is said that [the probandum] was already grasped previously through the power of such a cognition. Otherwise, if the nature to be proven were also already grasped, what would be the point of inference? For when smoke was perceived before, this very smoke was also perceived, and thus the perception of fire [would have occurred]. Moreover, that which is non-existent and yet to come cannot be perceived. Therefore, it is merely said, "it is perceived," by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) alone, simply because a cognition of that form is possible. How could there be no discrepancy (*visamvāda*) if grasping by way of mere convention were considered grasping in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*)? There is no discrepancy because that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) pertains precisely to that which performs the causal function (*arthakriyā*) of such a kind.

[500, viii] But how is that very rule to be apprehended? Precisely from this conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). It has been established that through conventional practice everything is known as being consistent, but not in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, when the connection (*pratibandha*) is apprehended in a general sense, since that [connection] does not exist without its particulars, there is the cognition of the particular. All conventional practice is exactly like this.
By this, the property and the subject as qualified by [the other] are refuted; for one who rejects them does not establish [the probandum] in the subject itself in such a manner. (40)

[500,x] Regarding the proposition (*pratijñā*) "sound is impermanent," if "impermanent sound" is the probandum (*sādhya*), it follows that what is to be proven is impermanence as qualified by sound; or else, it is sound as qualified by impermanence. Consequently, because this would prove the opposite of that [intended object], it would be contradictory (*viruddha*). Thus, one who says that this reason (*hetu*) proves impermanence in sound, yet likewise proves the absence of impermanence as qualified by sound—and is therefore contradictory—is also refuted by this statement defining the intended probandum. For it is not the case that "the soundness of impermanent sound" is being proven; rather, it is mere impermanence [that is established].

[This is] because of its establishment [as such]. If it is asked, "How is there an establishment of the aggregate (*samudāya*) when only impermanence is being established?", we say: No, because the aggregate is established in that very same way. This is because the aggregate is established together with the subject (*dharmin*). For no other aggregate of sound’s impermanence is to be established in the sound as the subject. Therefore, even if that [aggregate] is refuted, there is no fault; for the fault would lie in the refutation of mere impermanence. If it is asked, "How is there a reversal of the aggregate?"—because when one of the two is absent, the aggregate is refuted. There can be no possibility of an aggregate if only one remains. Therefore, only the property (*dharma*) alone is to be established in the subject. This is because the aggregate is established in that very same way: since the attainment of the aggregate occurs when a second element is established in one [locus]. If so, how is there a distinction between the refutation of the property, the subject, and their aggregate? It is because they are refuted by means of those [respective elements]. For an aggregate is designated by that means through which the aggregate is refuted. In ultimate reality, it is simply the refutation of the aggregate. If you say that the refutation of the aggregate consists in [the propositions] "Sound is impermanent" or "Sound possesses the impermanence of sound," this is not so, because such a thesis (*pratijñā*) is impossible. However, in the thesis "Sound is impermanent," there is no cognition of an establishment of an aggregate in another subject. Therefore, since an establishment of the aggregate is otherwise impossible, the refutation of the aggregate occurs precisely through the refutation of the subject and so forth taken individually.

But this is not so in the case of sound, because the property of being an impermanent sound is what is being negated. Thus, since it is the un-intended [property] that is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no fault in negating what is unintended.

For a denial of the whole is not contradictory with respect to the subject; since the means of proof is applied here to that which is undesired, the property to be proven (sādhya) here is the property alone. (41)
[501,iv] — Thus is the summary. <5.
The Fruit of Including the Word "Self">

[501,v] If, then, the inclusion of the word "intended" (*iṣṭa*) is intended to demonstrate that there is no fault even when excluding a probandum that is not intended, then just as there is no fault when the permanence residing in the sound itself is sublated in the subject (*dharmin*), so too there would be no fault whatsoever when the impermanence qualified by being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) is sublated.
This is true. Nevertheless, the inclusion of the word "itself" (*svayam*) is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions. For it is said:
[501,vii] Even though various properties may be established for a single subject (*dharmin*) in a treatise, ...
"The goal would be desired by oneself alone"—thus the scripture (śruti) has been cited of its own accord. (42)

[501, viii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: edible food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "It was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already been born and for the support of those seeking birth. It would be good, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain in detail the meaning of these words spoken in brief. The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, when a noble disciple understands nutriment, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation, he is called a noble disciple who has understood the Dharma, who has seen the Dharma, who has reached this Dhamma, who has arrived at this Dhamma, who has crossed over doubt, who has transcended uncertainty, who has attained fearlessness, and who dwells having relied upon the Teacher's instruction. And how, Ānanda, does a noble disciple understand nutriment? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple understands nutriment as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is nutriment'; he understands the origin of nutriment as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is the origin of nutriment'; he understands the cessation of nutriment as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is the cessation of nutriment'; he understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment as it really is with correct wisdom: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment. Thus, Ānanda, a noble disciple understands nutriment. And how, Ānanda, does a noble disciple understand the origin of nutriment? Here, Ānanda, craving is the origin of nutriment; thus a noble disciple understands the origin of nutriment. And how, Ānanda, does a noble disciple understand the cessation of nutriment? Here, Ānanda, the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, which is accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there—that is the cessation of nutriment; thus a noble disciple understands the cessation of nutriment. And how, Ānanda, does a noble disciple understand the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? Here, Ānanda, it is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; thus a noble disciple understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment. Thus, Ānanda, a noble disciple understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment. In this way, Ānanda, a noble disciple understands nutriment, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. When a noble disciple understands nutriment, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation in this manner, he is called a noble disciple who has understood the Dharma, who has seen the Dharma, who has reached this Dhamma, who has arrived at this Dhamma, who has crossed over doubt, who has transcended uncertainty, who has attained fearlessness, and who dwells having relied upon the Teacher's instruction."

Some maintain that what is established by the treatise (*śāstra*) must indeed be the probandum (*sādhya*), and that if it is contradicted, there is a fault in both the reason (*hetu*) and the proposition (*pratijñā*). For instance, in the *Nyāyabhāṣya*: "The scripture (*āgama*) is the proposition (*pratijñā*). The *Nyāyavārttika* explains: "It is called 'scripture' because it points out the meaning of the scripture, and not otherwise. Otherwise, since scripture is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while the proposition is a means for establishing doubt, how could they be one? That very meaning of the scripture, when pointed out to another, is the meaning of the proposition. Therefore, scripture is the proposition; if its meaning is contradicted, there is a fault in the reason, because it contradicts the meaning of the treatise. Furthermore, a reason that contradicts the treatise does not prove the probandum, and it is a fault in the proposition as well. For example, let impermanence (*anityatva*) be the probandum, which is possible through co-inherence (*ekārthasamavāya*) with the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*). Just as the quality of being a property of space is established there by some other reason or by the treatise, such impermanence is the meaning of the proposition. If that [impermanence] is refuted by that [treatise], it is a fault in the proposition. To illustrate:
[1] Momentary and without a substratum:
if it perishes immediately after a moment, its nature as a quality of space is futile.
Even if there is destruction after some time, it would still be in vain for it to have the nature of being a quality of space.

If that which is of the nature of sound perishes immediately after its moment because it lacks a cause for further existence, what is the use of its being a quality of space? For a substratum is indeed the cause of stability, and there is no stability for a momentary thing; its existence for even a single moment arises solely from its own causes. Alternatively, if it were to endure for a period of time having arisen from its own causes, then it would continue to exist by the power of those very causes—so what is the use of a substratum? If you argue that its endurance over time is due to the power of the substratum, then surely it will persist simply because it is indestructible; what need is there for a substratum? Furthermore, sound possesses no weight such that its falling would be possible without a substratum. Nor does space possess the nature of supporting things; indeed, heavy objects are not supported by space.
Because of its heaviness, there is no capacity for the sky to support that which is falling; those things that are light do not fall at all—what, then, could a supporter do for them? (PVA 106)
Carried away by the wind, that sound falls; let it be supported by that [wind].
For that whose support in space is not obstructive would surely meet with destruction.
Indeed, its very nature is such that it perishes only in dependence upon something else.

"As long as there is no destroyer, there is no movement from its place to another. (PVA 108) Thus, the certainty is that its staying occurs even without a substratum; for it does not stay for a single moment, nor does it stay for any other duration of time. (PVA 109)
Even for eternal things, having a basis is not at all purposeless;
this is true, yet such a nature is always innate. (PVA 110) [502,x]
Nor can there be the notion that "this [subject] is not to be questioned," for that reason.

Therefore, since the impermanent nature of the entity is not its locus, the [reason] that establishes impermanence is a subverter of the property of being a locus; thus, there is a fault of the reason and a fault of the thesis.
[2] "Qualities have no substratum.
To this it is replied:
[502, xiii] Precisely because one has accepted the treatise, everything is included;
therefore, if there were a contradiction therein, even a single instance would constitute a fault for both the reason and the thesis. || 43 ||

If the destruction of sound is what is to be proven, then the reason would be contradictory because the quality of smell as a property of earth remains unimpaired; if it is argued that this is not so because [the reason] does not apply to the subject, then that same [objection] applies elsewhere as well.

[502,xv] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchants being pursued by the bandits and, by means of his miraculous power, manifested himself as five hundred yakṣas. Having done so, he stood before each of the five hundred merchants. Then the bandits, seeing those five hundred yakṣas standing before the five hundred merchants, became terrified and fled. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having liberated those five hundred merchants from the hands of the bandits, spoke these verses: “O you who have come here seeking wealth, Do not fear this perilous place. I am Avalokiteśvara; I shall protect you all. Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara led those five hundred merchants out of the great ocean and established them safely on dry land. Then, having liberated those five hundred merchants from the great ocean, he returned once more to Mount Potalaka. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, do you see how the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara has brought those five hundred merchants out of the great ocean and established them safely on dry land? The Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One: “Yes, Blessed One, I see it. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if there are sentient beings in the world who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, invoke him with a single thought, then by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s vow, they shall all be delivered from suffering. Therefore, Ānanda, one should always invoke the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is called ‘Avalokiteśvara’? If it is argued that a fault occurs in the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) whenever there is a contradiction with a treatise (*śāstra*), simply because the treatise has been accepted, then this would apply just as in the case of contradicting the quality of sound being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), even when one overturns the fact that odor is a property of earth (*pṛthivīguṇatva*). Consequently, just as impermanence is the probandum (*sādhya*) because its connection with the quality of being a property of space—as enumerated in that [treatise]—is possible, so too is the status of being taught by the treatise connected to the property of being a property of earth as intended for another subject (odor) by the author of that treatise. Therefore, if that [status] is contradicted, it would indeed be a fault in the proposition, since the connection with that treatise would be untenable. One should not say, "How can this be, since odor is not introduced as the topic (*aprakaraṇāpanna*)? For the quality of being a property of space is likewise not introduced as the topic; thus, there is no distinction between the two cases.
[502,xvi] Now, if the subject (dharmin) under discussion here were that very one [intended by the opponent], there would be a contradiction with the meaning of the treatise.

[Objection: Why is the subject (*dharmin*) not also [included] when it occurs in another treatise, since it is accepted as the subject matter of that treatise? [Response: Even if this subject is indeed the topic at hand here, it is so only as the locus for those specific properties (*dharma*). Or, by virtue of the treatise, it may also be the locus for other properties. If that is the case, then the fault is the same: namely, that there would also be the inclusion of properties belonging to another subject mentioned in that same single treatise. Furthermore, it might be argued: "The subject is the locus for those [specific] properties, and thus even other properties are included within the side of the thesis (*sādhyapakṣa*), because they are likewise intended by the proponent. To this he says:
Alternatively, one might state that [the property] is intended by the proponent through the means of proof consisting of the subject, its properties, and so forth. (45)

[503,iv] Even the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) is indeed accepted by the proponent, because it is a property of the subject (*dharmin*) that has been taken up as the locus of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), just like impermanence. Likewise, [it is accepted] because it is a specific instance of a part of the collection of the probandum, and so forth. Thus he says: "The mere fact that something is not a specific instance of a part of the collection of the probandum does not constitute the intended [subject] of the context. For instance, [503,v]
Through certain arguments, this desire may arise and is understood by them;
yet that "this is your will" is asserted by force—this is clearly the work of a Lord. (46)

The mere fact of being a specific instance of a portion of the aggregate to be proven does not motivate desire. Or, if it did motivate it, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-cessation of both the desire for proof and the activity of the means of proof. Now, if the view is that it is because it is not desired as a specific instance of a portion of the aggregate to be proven, then in that case, that very "desirability" is the probandum (*sādhya*) and that very thing is the means of proof (*sādhana*); thus, the means of proof is nothing other than the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). Therefore, desire occurs only where there is a context; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, desire proceeds only toward that which is the locus of dispute, and not toward the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*).

But surely desire arises from context, and context is its cause. Therefore, how can the effect be established by the cause? If it is argued that a cause which is unobstructed makes known the effect—then how is this to be understood? It is understood through the observation of the speech, which is its effect. In that case, the comprehension comes from the effect, namely the speech, and not from the context; so why is it said that it is understood by those very factors [context, etc.]? To this it is replied: [503, viii] Here it is said:
The capacity [of the speaker] is to be understood from the statement itself; therefore, comprehension arises from that.
Because of the restriction of intention, comprehension is said to arise from the context. (PVA 111)

[503,x] From a statement, there is only the comprehension of a mere intention (*icchā-mātra*); and since context (*prakaraṇa*) is merely a cause for that intention, it is not a definitive indicator. Therefore, it is said by those [logicians] that the context, whose capacity is restricted by the statement, is what indicates the specific determination of the intention. However, there is no logical principle here to establish that "this is the only intention" even in the absence of a context. Consequently:
When one speaks [of a reason] ending with an effect or a mark [other than essential identity], it is sublated by deviation;
but when an unrelated meaning is sublated, what harm is done to the other? (47)

[503,xii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Thus it was said. But how many nutriments are there in total? There are four nutriments. Which four? Physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Among these, which nutriment is intended by the Blessed One when he says, “There is this one nutriment that sustains beings who have already come to be and supports those seeking a new existence”? It is this: consciousness. Why is that? Because it is the root of rebirth. For consciousness is the root of rebirth. How so? Consciousness is the seed of rebirth. Contact is the field. Craving is the moisture. Ignorance is the covering. Thus, with consciousness as the seed, and with contact as the field, craving as the moisture, and ignorance as the covering, beings proceed toward renewed existence. Therefore, consciousness is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the seed of rebirth. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the sixfold consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the mind-consciousness. Why is that? Because it is the basis for the other five. For the five sense-faculties are dependent upon the mind-consciousness. Therefore, the mind-consciousness is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the arising of future existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness associated with the roots of merit, demerit, and the imperturbable. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness associated with the root of merit. Why is that? Because it leads to the cessation of suffering. For the consciousness associated with the root of merit leads to the cessation of suffering. Therefore, the consciousness associated with the root of merit is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that has already arisen and is present. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that has already arisen and is present. Why is that? Because it sustains beings who have already come to be. For the consciousness that has already arisen and is present sustains beings who have already come to be. Therefore, the consciousness that has already arisen and is present is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is yet to arise in the future. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is yet to arise in the future. Why is that? Because it supports those seeking a new existence. For the consciousness that is yet to arise in the future supports those seeking a new existence. Therefore, the consciousness that is yet to arise in the future is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the production of future existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the cause of future existence. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the cause of future existence. Why is that? Because it produces future existence. For the consciousness that is the cause of future existence produces future existence. Therefore, the consciousness that is the cause of future existence is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the condition for the aggregates. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the condition for the aggregates. Why is that? Because it maintains the aggregates. For the consciousness that is the condition for the aggregates maintains the aggregates. Therefore, the consciousness that is the condition for the aggregates is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the seed of the aggregates. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the seed of the aggregates. Why is that? Because it supports the aggregates. For the consciousness that is the seed of the aggregates supports the aggregates. Therefore, the consciousness that is the seed of the aggregates is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the production of future existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the root of the cycle of existence. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the root of the cycle of existence. Why is that? Because it produces the cycle of existence. For the consciousness that is the root of the cycle of existence produces the cycle of existence. Therefore, the consciousness that is the root of the cycle of existence is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the continuity of birth. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the continuity of birth. Why is that? Because it maintains the continuity of birth. For the consciousness that is the continuity of birth maintains the continuity of birth. Therefore, the consciousness that is the continuity of birth is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the cause of clinging. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the cause of clinging. Why is that? Because it supports clinging. For the consciousness that is the cause of clinging supports clinging. Therefore, the consciousness that is the cause of clinging is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the production of future existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the basis of the formations. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the basis of the formations. Why is that? Because it produces the formations. For the consciousness that is the basis of the formations produces the formations. Therefore, the consciousness that is the basis of the formations is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the support of the faculties. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the support of the faculties. Why is that? Because it maintains the faculties. For the consciousness that is the support of the faculties maintains the faculties. Therefore, the consciousness that is the support of the faculties is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the condition for the arising of the aggregates. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the condition for the arising of the aggregates. Why is that? Because it supports the arising of the aggregates. For the consciousness that is the condition for the arising of the aggregates supports the arising of the aggregates. Therefore, the consciousness that is the condition for the arising of the aggregates is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the production of future existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the cause of the continuity of existence. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the cause of the continuity of existence. Why is that? Because it produces the continuity of existence. For the consciousness that is the cause of the continuity of existence produces the continuity of existence. Therefore, the consciousness that is the cause of the continuity of existence is the nutriment intended by the Blessed One. Furthermore, it is said: “Consciousness is the nutriment for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Thus it was said. But what is that consciousness? It is the consciousness that is the root of the world. Among these, which consciousness is intended? It is the consciousness that is the root of the world. Why is that? Because it maintains the world. For the consciousness that

For either the effect or the cause is the indicator of a desire (*icchā*). Context (*prakaraṇa*) is a cause, but it does not indicate the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), because that [quality] is absent therein. Speech is an effect, yet even that is not [the indicator] of the quality of being a property of space. Nevertheless, you say, "This is your desire. By stating a desire whose logical mark (*liṅga*) is not an effect, you are sublated by the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For [qualities such as] being a specific part of the collection of the probandum (*sādhyasamudāyaikadeśaviśeṣatva*) and so forth are not the effect of a desire. Nor is [the desire] the cause with unobstructed capacity (*apratibaddhasāmarthya*). And when there is a sublation of the inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatva*), the probandum would be absent due to the absence of its pervader (*vyāpaka*); thus there would be a fault in the probandum or the probans. But since the quality of being a property of space is not inseparable [from the probandum], when that which is not inseparable is sublated, what harm is done to the probandum, which is something other than that?
<3. An Examination of the Invalidity of Verbal Testimony> <1. Contradiction with Scripture is Weak in the Case of Inference> [504,i]

[Objection: Surely debate proceeds only by accepting a treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, for one established within their own treatise, there is necessarily a fault if that [treatise's] meaning is subverted. [Response: No, because this has already been answered. It was stated that even when the quality of being an earth-attribute (*pṛthivīguṇatva*) is overturned in the case of odor, it is not a fault. And it has been said: "Inference does not depend upon scripture regarding its own object-domain."
By that, it is established as well-established; at that time, no other scripture is observed.

For inference, in relying upon the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) within its own domain, depends upon scripture (*śāstra*), because it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) just like perception (*pratyakṣa*). Whatever is perceived, does that depend entirely upon scripture? Likewise, must inference also depend upon scripture? Thus, our perception (such as ours) necessarily depends upon scripture; therefore, by virtue of being sublated by scripture, it is nothing but an error (*bhrānti*). Indeed, the word of those with divine vision is not sublated by our perception, nor does the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) sublate the vision of another.

This is true. If the author of all [scriptures] were one possessed of divine vision, then such a statement would indeed be appropriate. However, even if some being were such, our certainty that "he is thus" does not clarify this matter. For, due to the mutual contradiction among their words, those who compose the scriptures are nowhere perceived to be omniscient. Even if they were not omniscient, it does not follow that you yourself are exempt from error. In that case, the contradiction with all the scriptures must be avoided; yet that is simply impossible. Therefore, no inference could possibly arise.

[504,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive form as unreal; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the door of mindfulness on the body as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the door of mindfulness on feelings, the door of mindfulness on the mind, or the door of mindfulness on dharmas as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the right exertions as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal; he does not perceive the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the beginningless emptiness, the nature-emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of characteristics, the non-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of what has no attainment, the emptiness of self-nature, or the emptiness of other-nature as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal; he does not perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the state of a bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal; he does not perceive the state of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive it as unreal. For this reason, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, then how does he train in the six perfections? How does he train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata? How does he train in the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, arhatship, the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, and the state of a Tathāgata? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he trains in the six perfections. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Tathāgata. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he trains in the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, arhatship, the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, and the state of a Tathāgata. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he trains in the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, then how does he generate the thought of awakening? How does he practice the six perfections? How does he enter the first stage, and so on up to the tenth stage? How does he enter the path of seeing? How does he enter the path of meditation? How does he enter the path of no-more-learning? How does he enter the stage of a pratyekabuddha? How does he enter the stage of a bodhisattva? How does he enter the stage of a Tathāgata? How does he enter the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he generates the thought of awakening. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he practices the six perfections. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he enters the first stage, and so on up to the tenth stage. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he enters the path of seeing, the path of meditation, the path of no-more-learning, the stage of a pratyekabuddha, the stage of a bodhisattva, and the stage of a Tathāgata. It is because he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, that he enters the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal, then how does he purify the buddha-fields? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he attain the dhāraṇīs? How does he attain the samādhis? How does he attain the unhindered liberation? How does he attain the unhindered knowledge of the Dharma? How does he attain the unhindered knowledge of eloquence? How does he attain the unhindered knowledge of meaning? How does he

Now, one might argue that only the removal of contradictions with one's own accepted scripture (*svāgama*) regarding the subject matter of the treatise should be performed. If that is the case, then even that acceptance must be made after critical examination (*parīkṣā*). At the time of examination, inference (*anumāna*) is not an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because the contradiction with scripture has not yet been removed. If it is argued: "At that time, there is no acceptance of the scripture at all; so what is the point of removing [the contradiction]? [Response: In that case, it is established that the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed perfectly established by that [inference]. For that which is established does not subsequently become unestablished. If it is argued: "It is precisely unestablished because of the acceptance of a scripture that contradicts it. [Response: Then that itself is the removal of the contradiction with the entire scripture. If it is argued: "It occurs only in relation to what has been accepted, and not otherwise. [Response: Why then is there no acceptance [of the scripture] everywhere? If it is argued: "Only that which is capable of withstanding examination is [to be accepted]. [Response: In that case, the very examination is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that same [examination] is being sublated by that [scripture]. This is a way of raising a weapon for one's own destruction. Therefore, because it contradicts the means of valid cognition, the scripture itself is not relied upon at that time; consequently, it cannot be a sublater [of the inference].
If, then, the treatise is not to be relied upon, it follows that the very abandonment of one's position has occurred.

If it is argued that there would then be an abandonment of the debate, that is not so, because it is not due to a lack of means; for this [reasoning] is the very means for the acceptance, and even then, it remains a constituent part of it. (49)

For there can be no debate without relying on a treatise (*śāstra*), since one does not accept it at that time. Acceptance is itself the means for examination. If something were accepted without being examined, then even if it existed, it would be irrelevant because it would be sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, a treatise that cannot withstand examination cannot serve as a sublater at that time. When, then, is a treatise accepted as a constituent part of the proof?
To this it is replied:
[505,i] Thus, when the two objects have been purified, there is the mastery of the treatise.
For that would indeed be the time for one desiring to act; at that time, there would be sublation by the scripture. (50)

[505,ii] Thus, when both types of objects—the perceptible and the imperceptible—have been purified through inference and direct perception, if one is not yet satisfied by that much alone, then it would be the time for the acceptance of the treatise (*śāstra*), provided there is a desire to adopt it. At that very moment, sublation occurs by means of the treatise.
For:
[505,iv] Because reflection that contradicts it is impossible regarding those things established by it.
Upon transitioning to the third stage, it is proper to undertake the study of the scriptures. || 51 ||

[505,v] For when an object is under investigation, it is not proper to deliberate upon a matter established by that treatise in a way that contradicts the position accepted within that very treatise. To explain:
If that treatise has already been thoroughly examined by means of a formal thesis, how can it be said to require further examination?
If it is not yet examined, then its examination must be performed; but if it has already been examined, then no further examination is necessary. (PVA 112)

Therefore, having examined it through perception and inference, one accepts a treatise as a means for transitioning to a third position regarding that which is not the object of those two; thus, a treatise does not subvert what is the object of inference.
Furthermore, it might be argued that for one who accepts a treatise without critical investigation, that treatise would constitute a sublation, and thus there would be a flaw in the thesis.
This is not so; for:
In that case as well, only the sublation of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) when it is connected [to the subject] is to be avoided;
not the sublation of other [properties], because that would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). (52)

[505,xii] If it is argued that simply because a treatise has been accepted, any contradiction of its contents must be avoided, then there would be a fault even when one contradicts the quality of earth as being odor. Therefore, it is established that only the contradiction of that which is connected with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) must be avoided, not the contradiction of other unrelated things.
[505,xiii]

But surely, even without accepting a treatise (*śāstra*), one could be a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) in debate; for one who does not rely on a treatise is a nihilist (*nāstika*). [Objection: But what is nihilism for one who accepts what is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Likewise, it is for one who does not accept what is sublated by valid cognition. It is only in the third case—that one who does not accept a treatise—that one is a nihilist. What, then, is the use of a treatise in any situation other than that third case? For instance: By whom was this rule established that in all investigations a treatise must be accepted?
Now that [the proof] has been rendered invalid by these non-tenets, fire cannot be apprehended by means of smoke.

[505,xv] If the operation of all means of valid cognition were dependent solely upon the acceptance of a philosophical tenet (*siddhānta*), then even in the world, fire would not be cognized from smoke by cowherds and others.
Furthermore, it might be argued that "only that matter which is useful for the next world is preceded by the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*), and no other.
This is incorrect.
[505,xviii] If, when a treatise has not been accepted, one’s ascertainment of it arises from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what use is that treatise as a precursor? (113) (PVA)

[505,xix] If it is not accepted, one suspects sublation by the treatise (*śāstra*); but if it is accepted, sublation by the treatise is known. Therefore, that [proposition] is simply not established. For there is no existence of what is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) merely because of a lack of desire [to accept it]. At that time, however, the treatise is abandoned.

If it is asked, "How can that which belongs to the self be worthy of abandonment? [the answer is]: No, because there is no connection. Its belonging to the self is due to its possessing qualities. For instance:
<(1) The scripture is a remedy for a harmful grasp>.
Alas, by whom have these treacherous demons of dogmatic tenets been bestowed upon a person born empty and unable to discern virtue from fault? (54)

[506,iii] If a tenet (siddhānta) cannot be abandoned even when contradicted by reasoning, then it is not a tenet at all; for under the guise of a tenet, it is a harmful obsession that cannot be released from once it has taken hold of the foolish.
Because of its connection and because it is co-nascent, it cannot be abandoned;
for how could that conjunction be co-nascent for a being who is born empty?
(PVA 506, v)
Furthermore, how can there be a discernment of merits and defects for one who abandons the means of valid cognition?
Therefore, inference is not preceded by the acceptance of a treatise.

[506, vii] But is it not the case that an inference which contradicts a treatise (śāstra) cannot be determinative? Therefore, the contradiction with the treatise must be avoided by means of an illustrative example (nidarśana) that is concordant with it.
[506, viii]
That is incorrect; for:
[506, ix] If the entire treatise were contained within the proof and the illustrative example in one place...
"One should demonstrate the means of accomplishment"—this is the supramundane state. || 55 ||

Indeed, a contradiction with the scriptures (*śāstra*) is simply impossible to avoid, because the scriptures themselves contradict one another; thus, they must all either be authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or non-authoritative. If they are authoritative, there can be no resolution of their mutual contradictions, precisely because they are contradictory to each other. Nor can they be non-authoritative, for since contradiction exists at all times among the words of all people, an infinite number of contradictions could never be resolved. And yet, you claim that such a means of proof (*sādhana*) exists—this path is utterly beyond the world!

Now, if only that which is a property of the subject (*dharmidharma*) is sublated even when it has been stated, what assurance is there? For it is impossible for a sublater (*bādhaka*) to be a prover (*sādhaka*). This too is not tenable; for in that case, no proof whatsoever would exist. For one who proves in this manner must necessarily sublate the other.
Furthermore:
When a property is unrelated, what is it that is not established by its non-establishment? Why would the reason stated to prove it be considered defective when it is established therein? // 56 //

For if the sublation of a property that is unrelated [to the subject] were to be avoided, then it would not be a logical reason (*hetu*) at all. And if one thing is sublated, why should another not be established? Indeed, even a single instance of smoke is observed to establish both the presence and absence of fire and cold touch respectively. If it is argued that the proof is [only valid] when there is no contradiction, then the same contradiction applies equally to the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*).

Now, let it be granted that this reason is the means of establishing both existence and non-existence; however, how can there be for the person being instructed an understanding of a meaning that contradicts the treatise? Therefore, conformity with the meaning of the treatise must also be demonstrated in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For indeed, if its properties (*taddharma*) are not introduced, there is no understanding of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the reason.
This is not so, because:
Without even introducing the properties of the subject into the example, people infer from smoke and the like, which are merely words, the fire of consciousness and so forth. (57)

[507,iii] Let alone for the moment the case of a property well-known from scripture (*śāstra*) which lacks a [logical] connection; even regarding some property of that subject (*dharmin*), when it is introduced by means of an example, this world understands [the presence of] the fire of consciousness and so forth from a reason such as speech or smoke. For it is not the case that another property [of that subject] is sublated, such that there would be a failure to establish the fire.
And it is not the case that the person to be convinced does not understand; moreover, even against the will of the person to be convinced,
the object— by proving its own nature or its cause through non-deviation— [establishes itself].
Even when some [proposition] is sublated by a formal argument, it does not cease to exist by virtue of its own nature. // 58 //

Indeed, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, which depends upon its own causes, does not turn away from them according to human desire. Furthermore, the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) is the basis for establishing what is to be proven (*sādhya*); since that [non-deviation] exists, why would it not be a means of proof?

Now, let it be granted that he is a prover; but how does that person who is to be convinced (the respondent) come to understand? To this he says: "And another, while apprehending its intrinsic nature, [apprehends] that which is inseparable from the desired [consequences]."
How could that [reason] not be established by the reasons which are the very objects to be proven? (59)

For a cause that has set out to produce an effect can be prevented from doing so by another thing, because its capacity is unimpeded; however, an indicator, which generates cognition through the force of a necessary connection, cannot be prevented by that very same thing once its three aspects have been apprehended.
For a person being burned by fire would surely disregard the pain of burning even without a desire for it, if there were no certainty regarding the cause. (115) [507,xi] (PVA)

For one who perceives its non-deviation would not fail to perceive that [object], because the perception of a qualified object is inseparable from the perception of the qualifier. Everything exists, but one might act in a manner inconsistent with the proponent's position.
To this, it is said:

xiii] Even if the reason has been stated— or even if it has not— what does it matter to the proponent here if it is contradictory? For it does not become a subverter of the treatise merely through a defect in its statement.

[507,xiv] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. (The Sūtra on the Four Nutriments) [508,i] Furthermore, it is said: “Monks, there are these four nutriments. What is the meaning of this? It is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four aggregates. How so? Physical food nourishes the aggregate of form; contact nourishes the aggregate of feeling; mental volition nourishes the aggregate of formations; and consciousness nourishes the aggregate of consciousness. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four modes of existence. How so? Physical food nourishes the desire realm; contact nourishes the form realm; mental volition nourishes the formless realm; and consciousness nourishes rebirth in all three realms. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four types of birth. How so? Physical food nourishes birth from a womb; contact nourishes birth from moisture; mental volition nourishes miraculous birth; and consciousness nourishes birth from an egg. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four types of nutriment. How so? Physical food nourishes physical food itself; contact nourishes contact; mental volition nourishes mental volition; and consciousness nourishes consciousness. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four types of craving. How so? Physical food nourishes craving for form; contact nourishes craving for touch; mental volition nourishes craving for existence; and consciousness nourishes craving for consciousness. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four types of clinging. How so? Physical food nourishes clinging to sense-pleasures; contact nourishes clinging to views; mental volition nourishes clinging to precepts and vows; and consciousness nourishes clinging to a self-theory. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four types of grasping. How so? Physical food nourishes grasping for sense-pleasures; contact nourishes grasping for views; mental volition nourishes grasping for precepts and vows; and consciousness nourishes grasping for a self-theory. Alternatively, it is said that there are four nutriments because they nourish the four types of becoming. How so? Physical food nourishes the becoming of sense-pleasures; contact nourishes the becoming of form; mental volition nourishes the becoming of formlessness; and consciousness nourishes the becoming of non-perception. For it is the merits and defects of the *vacana* (the verbal expression) that are relevant in an inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*), not those of the object (*artha*). [The opponent might argue: "No collection of defects whatsoever was committed by the speaker here. [Reply: "If you say, 'The treatise (*śāstra*) has been contradicted,' we say no; for the reason (*hetu*) itself, even if unstated, is the contradictor of the treatise. [The opponent asks: 'Why did he employ such a reason? [Reply: 'Because no other is possible. For there exists no proof for impermanence that does not contradict [qualities] such as being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*). [The opponent asks: 'Why does he not simply remain silent? [Reply: No; because the failure to state a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) is all the more a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Indeed, the opponent must necessarily be made to understand. Therefore, in this case, there is no fault on the part of the proponent."

If it is argued that there is a fault because of the statement of a sublation, and if he were not to state it, why would he not sublate? Since he does nothing improper, by what means is he at fault? (61)
This is an intermediate verse.

If that is the case, then there is no fault even in stating a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Since the fallacious reason is itself of such a nature, why would it be a fault for the proponent? For this too is not rendered defective by the very fault stated [by the opponent], but is defective by its own inherent fault.
[508,ii] Whether the reason has been stated or unstated, if it is unestablished (*asiddha*), what is the fault here for the proponent?
"It is not the case that because of a defect in its statement, that [reason] would be unestablished or contradictory.
This is incorrect. (PVA 116) [508, iii]

In other fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), one would be censured for stating something useless because they fail to establish their own intended point; but this is not the case here, because that very point is established.

[508,v] In this context, when a proof must be stated for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*), there is a fault in stating that which does not prove it, because such a statement is purposeless. For while the topic at hand concerns purposeful statements, a purposeless statement is indeed useless. However, in this case, there is no fault regarding the establishment of the probandum; rather, the fault lies precisely in non-statement. If it is argued that here too there is a fault in not stating the quality of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), we say no. Since a proving factor is also possible, it would be logical for non-statement to be a fault only in the case of a probandum desired by the proponent. But in this case, there is no possibility of a factor that contradicts the quality of being a quality of space as established by the treatise. Therefore, non-statement is not a fault.
[508, vi] But if the reason contradicts the meaning of the treatise, how could it establish even impermanence? For it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by that very fact. To this it is replied:
If something is not logical in some treatise, it is refuted; yet one may state that another thing is logical—such is the established practice of royal courts. (63)

[508, viii] There is no contradiction with the meaning of the entire treatise, because that [fault] exists only in certain parts of a treatise. Since a proof is valid or invalid based on the presence or absence of a logical connection (*sambandha*), what contradiction could there be here? To negate what is unreasonable while also negating what is reasonable is merely a royal decree.
Moreover:
Having treated all undesirable consequences as equivalent, it is impossible to state a proof.
By that [reasoning], this entire framework of the means of proof and the object to be proven would be destroyed everywhere.
