No proof can be stated that is not in conflict with all [accepted] facts; rather, it is required only that there be a connection with the specific probandum under discussion, because otherwise it would be impossible [to prove anything]. If it is argued that one must ensure non-contradiction with the meaning of the treatise (*śāstra*), we say no, for since there is no distinction [between them], this would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to accept everything else as well. If, on the other hand, one maintains that contradiction with the treatise must also be avoided, then in that case there would be no proof at all, and the relationship between the probandum and the proof would collapse everywhere. If it is asked, "Why then was the treatise accepted?"—this very point is what ought to be established here as our intended position: one should not initially accept a treatise. Once it has been accepted, if it is found to contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is better to abandon it later. However, according to the opinion of others, the acceptance of a treatise constitutes a formal proposition (*pratijñā*). Therefore, having accepted a treatise, one must not contradict it, because the operation of the rules of debate proceeds only when there is an accepted tenet (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*).

[508,xii] If, then, there is no fault in the reason even when the property of being a quality of space is sublated, how can the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) be a fault of the proof? In that case too, the fault arises from the contradiction with a fact established by another means of proof; here too, the fault is precisely the contradiction with a fact established by the treatise (*śāstra*).
[508,xiii]
This is not correct; for:
[508,xiv] Since two contradictory [properties] cannot coexist in a single substratum, let there be sublation.
In this case, there is likewise a state of contradiction with that which is invariably opposed. (65)

[509,i] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. He does not perceive form as real, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. He does not perceive giving as real, nor morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor the state of a tathāgata, arhat, perfectly enlightened one as real. He does not perceive the perfection of generosity as real, nor the perfection of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainment, or the emptiness of non-reliance as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a tathāgata as real, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, or the great compassion of a tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the thirty-two marks of a great man as real, nor the eighty minor marks as real. He does not perceive the path of a śrāvaka as real, nor the path of a pratyekabuddha or the path of a bodhisattva as real. He does not perceive the level of a śrāvaka as real, nor the level of a pratyekabuddha or the level of a bodhisattva as real. He does not perceive the level of a tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the dharma-element as real, nor the sphere of space as real. He does not perceive the dharma-realm as real, nor the limit of reality as real. He does not perceive the past as real, nor the future or the present as real. He does not perceive the world-system of desire as real, nor the world-system of form or the world-system of formlessness as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive saṃsāra as real, nor nirvāṇa as real. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are without marks, unproduced, unceased, originally quiescent, and by nature parinirvāṇic. Since they are thus, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real."

In this case, for two [reasons] that are "non-deviant with respect to contradictory [conclusions]" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), the fact that both are non-deviant with respect to their mutually contradictory objects is indeed equal in strength for both, because both rely upon scripture (*āgama*). However, inference (*anumāna*) which functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala*) and scripture are not of such a nature. Therefore, there is no mutual sublation between those two, as in the case of the *viruddhāvyabhicārin*. Nor is there proof for both, because two contradictory [properties] cannot coexist in a single locus (*dharmin*). Furthermore, since scripture lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in comparison to a contradictory inference, its object is simply sublated; it is not a sublater like the *viruddhāvyabhicārin*. Moreover, the validity of scripture that is not supported by the force of a means of valid cognition is strictly refuted. Consequently, the position that introduces the category of the *viruddhāvyabhicārin* is not tenable.

[509,ii] Furthermore, if it is argued: "How can there be sublation by inference of a treatise (śāstra) promulgated by one who perceives supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*)? Consequently, even that inference would be invalid because it is obstructed by it. Therefore, since they possess equal strength, there is a fault here just as in the case of a 'non-erroneous contradiction' (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
That is incorrect; for:
[509,iv] If there were a sublation by scripture regarding a contradictory inference, [then it would be so].
All means of valid cognition have perished; only scripture remains.

If all inference (*anumāna*) were sublated by scripture (*śāstra*), then the meaning of scripture could not be established for another person through inference; how, then, could scripture serve as a formal proposition (*pratijñā*)? For there is no inference or any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is not sublated by scripture. This is because inferences such as [the proof of] impermanence or permanence are sublated by various other scriptures. Even [the inference] "fire exists" and so forth is sublated by the scripture on emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If you argue that [scripture on emptiness] is not a valid means of cognition, [we ask]: how can that which is not a valid means of cognition be a sublater of inference? If you say, "Not every [inference] sublated by inference is invalid," [we reply]: But is it not your own position that precisely that inference is invalid when sublated by scripture? Therefore, it is not logical for you to abandon your own position. If you say, "It is only that which has been examined as a valid means of cognition that constitutes sublation," [then we respond:]...

[509, vi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as existing. Subhūti, because he does not perceive any dharma, he does not become attached to any dharma; and because he is not attached to any dharma, he transcends all dharmas. Subhūti, this is called the 'perfection of wisdom' of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by practicing the perfection of wisdom, transcends all dharmas? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive giving as real, nor does he perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship as real. He does not perceive the state of a Pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma as real, he does not become attached to any dharma; and because he is not attached to any dharma, he transcends all dharmas. Subhūti, this is called the 'perfection of wisdom' of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva."

But surely, inference alone is the means of examination; therefore, how can an examination sublated by that [inference] be a cause for the authority of a treatise? Indeed, what is impossible therein cannot establish its possibility. Therefore, inference alone—preceded by perception—is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it has a firm foundation. A treatise sublated by such [inference] is not a valid means of knowledge at all, and thus it is not a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*). Consequently, there is no fault here as in the case of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). Since the proof establishes impermanence together with the absence of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatvābhāva*), it is simply a valid proof and not faulty. The "non-erroneous contradictory," however, is not a reason at all, because it is impossible for both permanence and its absence (impermanence) to be established in a single locus. But since there is no contradiction between the absence of being a quality of space and impermanence, how could there be a fault in establishing them together in a single subject (*dharmin*)?

Even if there is no relationship of sublated and sublator between those two, if invalidation were to occur despite the lack of connection due to the failure of the meaning of the scripture, then everything would invalidate everything. (66)
[509, viii] Also in the case of odor, because of the overturning of the notion that it is a quality of earth; by another [reason], and by that aforementioned reason.
If it is argued that there is a connection [of the reason] with that very [subject] because of sublation therein, that is not so;
for one must examine the merits and defects of every reason with respect to its own probandum. (67)

[509,x] Even if that quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) were indeed present in that subject (*dharmin*), such a connection would still not establish what is to be proven (*sādhya*), because it is irrelevant; furthermore, irrelevance is not a fault of sublation (*bādhana*). This is because the consideration of a fault for any reason (*hetu*) is intended only with respect to its own specific probandum.

If there is a fault characterized by the subversion of the treatise (*śāstrapīḍā*) when one obstructs another unrelated [property], even while not obstructing that which is to be proven (*svasādhyānuparodhe*), then he says—demonstrating that the same fault-causing subversion applies equally to any other property in any other subject by means of any other reason:
"The connection [of the reason] with the probandum consists in its being inseparable (*nāntarīyakatā*); such a connection is not observed here. [510,i]
In this world, the fault of contradicting the scriptures is the same whether it is committed by oneself or by another.

[510,ii] For one must avoid establishing the absence of a pervading property (*vyāpaka*) that is the probandum (*sādhya*). This is because when that which is invariably concomitant with the probandum and the probans is sublated, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is also necessarily excluded in its absence. However, the state of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*) is not invariably concomitant with the probandum; therefore, even in its absence, there is no contradiction of the probandum. Furthermore, [510,iii]

If everything seen in the treatise were to be proven simply because of the acceptance of that treatise, it would follow that the reason and the example are already established by the thesis itself. (69)

The commentator on the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* states: "Because one accepts a treatise (*śāstra*), everything seen in that treatise becomes the object of proof (*sādhya*). Otherwise, the acceptance of the treatise would be purposeless; for if its subject matter were not to be proven, the acceptance of the treatise would be of no use anywhere, nor would it deserve such acceptance. There is nothing [established] by means of an independent proof (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, having accepted the treatise, its subject matter must be proven. Consequently, if there is a contradiction with it, there is indeed a fault. [510,v]

To this it is replied: there would be the status of a *pratijñā* (thesis) for both an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*) and an unestablished example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because these two also sometimes constitute the subject matter of a treatise (*śāstrārtha*). If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", [the answer is: the entire [treatise] would then result in being merely a *pratijñā*, and consequently, faults such as being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) and so forth could not be stated.

[Objection: Should it not be stated that only that which is not the subject matter of a treatise (*śāstra*) is the [valid] reason (*hetu*), since in that case defects such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) would find scope? [Reply: No, because even that [subject matter of a treatise] is accepted by one’s own mouth [when it is put forward]. Or, if it is argued that what is accepted by one’s own mouth is not a thesis (*pratijñā*), then what is accepted by another’s mouth is certainly not one either—such as in the case of the Vaiśeṣika and others. Furthermore, according to the definition "the statement of the probandum is the thesis," the statement of an unestablished means of proof (*sādhana*) would also become a thesis. Even if the subject matter of a treatise is not explicitly stated, it might not be a thesis; however, if it is explicitly stated, it certainly is. For it has been said in the *Bhāṣya*: "Scriptural authority (*āgama*) is the thesis. But it is not the case that whatever is a thesis is scriptural authority. [Objection: Is it not the case that scriptural authority is simply the thesis? [Reply: No, because scriptural authority is the thesis by virtue of its being the statement of the meaning of scripture, not by its own essential nature. Therefore, according to the rule "the statement of the probandum is the thesis," the unestablished reason and so forth would also be theses, because they too are the meaning of scripture.

[510,vii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration with joined palms; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are these four? They are: a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry; a person who has attained the fruit of once-returning; a person who has attained the fruit of non-returning; and a person who has attained arhatship. These, Ānanda, are the four persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration with joined palms; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This was said by the Blessed One, and having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One further said this: “The stream-enterer, the once-returner, The non-returner, and the arhat— These four persons in the world Are the unsurpassed field of merit. What are these four? These, Ānanda, are the four persons who are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, and worthy of veneration with joined palms; they are the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is true. The entire meaning of a treatise (*śāstra*) is indeed that which is to be established (*sādhya*). Nevertheless, in the *Nyāyamukha* treatise, that which is stated as a means of proof (*sādhana*) does not possess the status of a thesis (*pratijñā*), because it is not intended as something to be established. For in that work, the subject (*pakṣa*) is defined as "that which is intended by oneself as the thing to be established and is not contradicted by opposing meanings. Furthermore, that which is designated as a means of proof cannot be the "most desired object" (*īpsitatama*), nor can it be the "object" (*karman*) in the sense of being the thing to be established. That which is intended as a means of proof is not the object; for example, in the expression "he eats rice with milk," the milk [is the instrument, not the object]. This is because the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* uses the restrictive phrase "not merely in its own form" (*na svarūpeṇaiva*). And for the Naiyāyika, the definition of a thesis is "the statement of the thing to be established" (*sādhyānirdeśaḥ pratijñā*); since the emphasis is on the state of being the thing to be established (*sādhyatva*), the restriction implies it must be intended precisely as such, and thus the statement of a means of proof is not the thesis. To this, it is replied: [The text continues with the response.]
If it is argued that because the two [the thesis and the reason] have been stated as means of proof, the status of the probandum does not belong to the former; we reply:
the status of being the probandum, which is established by logic, is not revoked merely by a statement. (70)

If this is the principle that "one accepts the treatise," then how can there be a reversal by means of a statement of what is established by that very principle? For a statement that indicates a principle does not contradict the principle itself. Alternatively, even a principle indicated by a statement is indeed a proof, since it is the non-probandum that has been specified as the probans.
This is not so;
for if that were the case, these two would constitute a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
"Because of the acceptance of a treatise, this statement regarding what is desired and so forth is likewise [unestablished].

(PVA 511.iv) If, by means of logic, the fact that the probans is not the "probandum" is established because it consists of the statement of what is desired and so forth, then by the phrase "because of the acceptance of a treatise," its status as the "probandum" would likewise be established. This being the case, since these two establish mutually contradictory meanings in a single instance, they would both produce doubt. And thus, since "because of the acceptance of a treatise" is not a valid proof, how can there be the status of being a "probandum" even for that which is accepted as not being a probans because it is seen in the treatise?

[511,v] Now, the argument that "it is because of the acceptance of the treatise" is not logical. If that were the case, then what is desired by the proponent would be the probandum (*sādhya*), and not something intended as a means of proof (*sādhana*). To this, he says:

If a property not intended by the proponent is unprovable, then any other unintended property would likewise be unprovable; in that case, how could the sublation of an unprovable [property] constitute a contradiction? (71)

[2] Refutation of the claim that sound is a quality of space: Even the status of being a quality of space is not desired by the proponent; therefore, it is not the probandum (*sādhya*). For what discerning person would abandon the subject at hand and pursue something irrelevant as their primary objective?

[511, viii] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four modes of practice. What four? The mode of practice that is pleasant with a result that is pleasant; the mode of practice that is painful with a result that is pleasant; the mode of practice that is pleasant with a result that is painful; and the mode of practice that is painful with a result that is painful. These, monks, are the four modes of practice. The venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause and what is the condition for the mode of practice that is pleasant with a pleasant result? “Ānanda, it is because of the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness that the mode of practice that is pleasant with a pleasant result comes to be. “What, venerable sir, is the cause and what is the condition for the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness? “It is, Ānanda, because of the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment that the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness comes to be. “What, venerable sir, is the cause and what is the condition for the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment? “It is, Ānanda, because of the cultivation of the noble eightfold path that the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment comes to be. “What, venerable sir, is the cause and what is the condition for the cultivation of the noble eightfold path? “It is, Ānanda, because of the cultivation of right view that the cultivation of the noble eightfold path comes to be. “What, venerable sir, is the cause and what is the condition for the cultivation of right view? “It is, Ānanda, because of the cultivation of association with superior persons, because of hearing the true Dhamma, and because of careful attention that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘It is because of the cultivation of association with superior persons, because of hearing the true Dhamma, and because of careful attention that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is because of the cultivation of association with superior persons, because of hearing the true Dhamma, and because of careful attention that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one cultivate association with superior persons so that the cultivation of right view comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple associates with a person who is accomplished in faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one cultivates association with superior persons so that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one hear the true Dhamma so that the cultivation of right view comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple hears the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, and which reveals the perfectly complete and pure holy life. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one hears the true Dhamma so that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one attend carefully so that the cultivation of right view comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple attends carefully to the nature of arising, attends carefully to the nature of passing away, and attends carefully to the nature of both arising and passing away. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one attends carefully so that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one cultivate right view so that the cultivation of the noble eightfold path comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses right view, which is imbued with the thought of renunciation, free from the thought of sensual lust, and directed toward Nibbāna. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one cultivates right view so that the cultivation of the noble eightfold path comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one cultivate the noble eightfold path so that the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment; he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena... the factor of enlightenment that is energy... the factor of enlightenment that is rapture... the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility... the factor of enlightenment that is concentration... the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one cultivates the noble eightfold path so that the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment so that the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment; he cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of phenomena... energy... rapture... tranquility... concentration... equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, resulting in relinquishment. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment so that the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness so that the mode of practice that is pleasant with a pleasant result comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings... mind as mind... phenomena as phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness so that the mode of practice that is pleasant with a pleasant result comes to be. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘It is because of the cultivation of association with superior persons, because of hearing the true Dhamma, and because of careful attention that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is because of the cultivation of association with superior persons, because of hearing the true Dhamma, and because of careful attention that the cultivation of right view comes to be. “Venerable sir, how does one cultivate association with superior persons so that the cultivation of right view comes to be? “Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple associates with a person who is accomplished in faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. [Objection: Surely, having accepted a treatise (*śāstra*), one must necessarily be faulted for contradicting its meaning by means of a reason stated by oneself. [Reply: No. This has been established that there is no fault, because one is proving what is desired by the opponent while also establishing it for oneself. Now, as for the contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): if sound were not a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatā*), it would be heard only at the very place of its production. But if it were a quality of space, then due to its connection with that [space], it would be heard elsewhere as well. This is not so; for it is perceived only where it is produced, just like color (*rūpa*). [Objection: Why is it not perceived by someone standing at a distance? [Reply: In that case, color too would result in being a quality of space. Furthermore, is that space one or many? If it were one, then its quality would be heard even from a thousand *yojanas* away. If it were many, then [the sound] would be heard only at the location of the speaker. Therefore, there is no perception whatsoever of sound being a quality of space.

[511,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered all suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete. Within emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touchable object, and no mental phenomenon; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origination, no cessation, and no path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. Since there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted dreams, one ultimately rests in *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the unequaled mantra; it is able to remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* should be proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, as well as the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and faithfully upheld what the Buddha had taught. [Objection: Surely, without being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), existence itself would be impossible. For an entity that possesses stability must necessarily have a substratum. In that regard, the four great elements—earth and the rest—are the substrata for color, touch, taste, and smell; but for sound, it is space, because it is impossible for it not to have a substratum. [Response: Then earth and the others would also have space as their substratum for that very same reason. [Reply: No, because they lack the status of being qualities (*guṇatva*). That very absence of being a quality is established by the fact of having a substratum. Furthermore, if sound were a quality because it has a substratum, and earth and the others are not qualities because they are themselves the substrata of qualities, then that [status of being a non-quality] is not established as long as a substratum—space—is possible. For color and the like, as well as earth and the like, could be dependent on space. This is because earth and the like, as well as color and the like, do not possess *inherence* (*asamavāyin*) in space. Indeed, color and the like are inherent in earth. What is this so-called "inherence"? If you say it is "subsisting in a state of unified blending" (*ekalolībhāva*), then sound cannot be a quality of space, because it is not perceived in a state of unified blending with it. And if you argue that smell is dependent on earth because it is perceived in space, and therefore sound is dependent on that [space] and that alone is its location; [we reply: then cotton and the like would also be dependent on space because they are perceived there and are supported by it. If you say that their subsistence is due to their own lightness (*laghutva*), then the same would apply to sound, and thus it would not be a quality of space. Or, if you say that while earth is the location of cotton and the like, their subsistence in space is not caused by space because they are held there by the wind, and the same applies to sound, then it is not a quality of space. To explain further: ... [The argument continues regarding the nature of inherence and the relationship between substrata and qualities. ... Therefore, sound is not a quality of space. Thus: * **Inherence** is not a real relation, as it lacks the characteristics of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*). * **Space** is not the substratum of sound, as it is intangible and lacks the capacity to support. * **Sound** is not a quality of space, as it is not perceived as unified with it, nor does it share its location in the way color does with earth. Thus, the claim that sound is a quality of space is untenable. Instead, sound arises from the contact of the vocal organs and air, and its perception depends on the auditory faculty and the presence of air. Space, being all-pervasive and devoid of resistance, cannot serve as a substratum for sound in the manner of earth for color. Therefore, sound is not a quality of space.
A sound impelled by the wind is not heard elsewhere;
the wind itself is its substrate—what need is there for this postulation of something else? (PVA 119)
For just as cotton and the like, being supported by the wind, do not possess the quality of the wind, so it is with sound as well.
Just as cotton is propelled through the sky by the wind,
does a knower of sound ever perceive sound as moving against the wind?

Now, sound cannot be impelled by the wind at all, because of the absence of conjunction with that quality; however, there is no contradiction in the case of cotton-wool, since it belongs to the category of earth (*pṛthivī*). Otherwise, even shadow, sunlight, and so forth would be impelled. How could there be such impelling of that, since impelling occurs only of a substance (*dravya*) which is its substratum?
Or, if it were impelled by the wind through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), [then...]
This conception is also not tenable regarding sound; for how could there be an impelling of space? (121) Even if space were impelled, it would then not be inactive;
moreover, since it is all-pervading, its impulsion is extremely difficult to establish. (122)
Moreover:
If it is claimed that there is an impelling by means of a conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*),
why is there not [impelling] by means of inherence (*samavāya*) for that which is inherent in the air?

Let sound possess the quality of air itself, since it travels to another location by means of that [air]. If it is argued that air has only touch as its quality, we reply: there is no rule that a substance must have only one quality; for according to the established tenets of others, earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch, and so forth. Furthermore, the propulsion of a quality—namely, smell—by air is observed. If it is argued that even in that case, the propulsion occurs only because of the inherence [of smell] in the earth which is conjoined [with air], we say: no, because when that [smell] is perceived, the earth is not perceived. Therefore, what contradiction is there in air propelling that which has arisen from it in isolation? If it is argued that this is because a quality is devoid of action (*niṣkriyatva*), then that very state of being devoid of action is not established in the case of isolated propulsion. If it is argued that even the possession of action is unestablished in the case of joint propulsion, we say: no, because joint propulsion is unestablished. If it is asked how a quality can possess action, this is merely another fault of yours.
If, in some treatise, qualities and so forth are denied because they are considered illogical, yet are accepted here despite being logical, then this is merely a royal decree. (PVA 124)
Furthermore, there is no such thing as "impulsion" for things that perish in their own place;
nor is there any so-called "activity" for a perishing entity.
What purpose, then, would there be in the production of a similar moment in another location? (PVA 125)
Is sound not considered by others to have movement like the waves of water?
(PVA) Furthermore:
[512,xv] One who possesses qualities is not perceived as distinct from the qualities themselves;
what else is perceived apart from touch and the other [sensory objects]? (PVA 127)

[512,xvi] And if odor is drawn along with the earth by means of the wind through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), then sound, too, is simply a quality of earth and the other elements; therefore, let it be drawn along with earth and the others—what is the use of postulating space?
<(3) Refutation of Space as an Element>

Furthermore, let it be granted that earth and the other elements are so designated by virtue of their functions such as supporting; but how is space (ākāśa) so designated? If it is argued that space is also such because it provides room (avakāśa), what is this so-called "providing room"? It is the non-obstruction of persistence. Earth and the others obstruct one another's persistence in a given location; therefore, there must be some other great element (mahābhūta) that grants the possibility of such persistence, and that is space.
That too is trivial. For instance:
"If there is the persistence of another element, there is no obstruction to its own persistence."

Even in the absence of one another, there is no contradiction, because they remain established [as distinct]. (128) (PVA) When one great element is absent, another great element remains; let space be defined as the mere absence of other great elements. (129) (PVA)

[513, iv] But if space does not exist, where would another great element, such as wind, reside? And if there were no other great element, where would space itself reside? Thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is argued that space has the nature of being without a support while serving as the support for others, then wind likewise must have the nature of being without a support while serving as the support for others; therefore, the postulation of a distinct entity is not tenable. Moreover: [513, v]
How is it that space is not the support for a clod of earth as it falls nowhere?
And how can there be a movement of space when the air possesses motion? (130) [PVA] If you say that space is the cause of the non-obstruction of the air's movement, this is no answer.
For the absence of an obstruction to a state of transition is indeed that which is devoid of an obstructing factor.
(PVA) [513,vii] Now then.
Space is pervasive and eternal, yet it is supported by something else; how can that be?
Therefore, its lack of a support is established, while for others it is merely a supporter. (132) (PVA)
This same state of being pervasive and formless applies to the self as well;
why then is its status as a substratum not postulated with respect to something else?
(133) For one who has no such self, what function could there be for space?
Let the function of space, which pervades the directions, be performed by those [directions] themselves.
xii) If there is mutual pervasion, why would there not be oneness among those things that pervade?

[513, xiii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation; they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna). This is the first kind of person who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation; he is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has attained the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin). This is the second kind of person who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation; he is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin). This is the third kind of person who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation; he is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “Furthermore, Ānanda, a certain person is one who has attained arhatship (arhat). This is the fourth kind of person who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation; he is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dharma and Vinaya, are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation; they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”

But surely, the conventional usage "space is light" does not apply to the self and so forth; how then can there be identity? [Objection: If one follows conventional usage, then the conceptualization of objects must be exactly in accordance with that usage. Space is simply a cavity (*chidra*); and when there is an absence of anything that creates a cavity, the conventional usage of it as "space" occurs. But when something exists that creates a non-cavity, where has that space gone? For it is not said that space moves to the side or elsewhere. And in the absence of that [non-cavity], where has the space gone—to that very spot or elsewhere? If it is destroyed, then its permanence is lost. If you say, "Let it remain right there," then it is contradictory to say "space is a non-cavity. For otherwise, that object could not even exist. Now, what is this "existence"? Is it being supported, or is it being unimpeded? If it is being supported, that is incorrect; for jars and the like are not supported by space, but rather by the earth. If it is being unimpeded, that too is false, because: [The verse follows: "Since [the world] is pervaded by space, nothing whatsoever is obstructed anywhere. Therefore, how can space be unimpeded? (PV 1.6) For space is all-pervasive; thus, nothing is obstructed anywhere by space. Consequently, how can space itself be unimpeded? [513,xiv] An impairment occurs for something because of the absence of that [cause]; it does not come from space. Clearly, to claim otherwise would be like chewing on the sky. (PVA)
Therefore, space is said to be the absence of the four elements;
there is no valid cognition for its existence in any other great element, nor is there any conventional usage [of it as such]. (PVA 136) <Refutation of Direction>
By this, space (*dik*) is also explained. Even for that, there is no such thing as providing room or the like, because it is all-pervasive. To explain:
[513,xvii]
The cognition of "west" and so forth arises through pervasiveness, not from anything else;
there is no other mode of movement for it, as that would entail the consequence of its non-existence.
(PVA 137) [513, xviii]

If space (*diś*) is all-pervasive, then that very same [space] would be "east" for one person; how then could it be "west" for another situated elsewhere? If, on the other hand, it possesses both natures simultaneously, then there would follow the consequence of having cognitions of both [natures] at once.

[513, xix] Now, if it is argued that some particular state of space is manifested due to the absence of a specific manifestor (*vyañjaka*), then why is it not the case that the nature of a father, son, and so forth—which is a single essence—is also manifested as "father-ness" in dependence upon "son-ness"?
That too is unreal because:
Since the manifestation of a fixed direction arises from something other than itself,
for that very reason the states of entities exist, just like "prior-ness" and so forth.

Since the status of a spatial direction as "eastern" and so forth is established only in relation to persons situated in preceding and succeeding locations, why is it not accepted that this [distinction] belongs to the entities themselves? Because persons and others are situated in an eastern location, that location is "eastern" in relation to another location; and that [other location] is likewise [defined] in relation to the sun and so forth. What need is there for the postulation of a separate "direction"? It is argued that the direction is manifested by the sun, and by that [manifestation], the sun's status as "eastern" and so forth is established. This, however, is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Since worldly practice is well-established by that much alone, what is the use of the laborious effort of postulating further dependencies?

[514,iv] But surely, even without dependence [on other things], this [notion of "straight"] occurs through conventional usage; therefore, direction (*dik*) is indeed a distinct category of entity (*padārtha*).
That too is untrue; for:
"Even in that case, there is the perception of 'straight' due to a difference in perspective."

Through extreme habituation, there is subsequently such a process even without another [cause]. (PVA 514, vii) For indeed, the worldly convention is observed as "this is straight for you. Therefore, due to extreme habituation, there is subsequently a following of that [straightness] even without dependence [on a further cause]. Why is this so? Because the cognition of the relationship between cause and effect occurs elsewhere as well through the conformity with the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of those two. For instance:
[514, viii] When situated in the midst of the ocean, men experience confusion;
however, by observing the planets and the constellations, they determine the divisions of the directions. (PVA 140)
Direction is not perceived as something other than the mere connection with the stars and so forth; for if its own nature does not manifest, how can it be designated? (PVA 514, x) 141.
For instance, the notion "this is the eastern direction" resides solely within the mind as a coincidence with the rising of the sun.

[514,xi] Now, even when the sun is seen in another location, for those whose minds are carried away by a confusion regarding the directions, that very same direction previously perceived appears as the east, and not by virtue of the sun's rising. For indeed, even the rising of the sun may appear as if it were occurring in dependence upon the western direction.
To this,
it is replied:
[514,xiii]

That very direction in which the setting [of the sun] is observed by one whose mind is unconfused and free from attachment is well-practiced; it is there that the village, garden, and so forth are perceived. (142) (PVA) [514,xiv]

That very garden, village, and so forth, which was previously perceived continuously as being characterized by directions such as "north" in relation to the rising of the sun and other markers—that very same direction, though it does not follow the subsequent rising of the sun due to the force of habituation to that [previous perception], is nonetheless designated as such through the attachment of a firm latent impression (*vāsanā*). Therefore:
"For those whose minds are brought face-to-face with the attachment of beginningless latent impressions... [514,xv]

Due to the absence of any object of cognition, these are merely cognitions alone. (PVA 143) Indeed, even one whose mind is utterly exhausted by the effort of intense concentration does not determine the intrinsic nature of the directions and so forth. It is simply because the world has not determined their nature that, lacking any reflective awareness and with a mind led by the maxim of "following what has gone before," it conducts itself in such a manner; what can we do about this?
[514,xvii] But if [the world] were real because it is beginningless, then this [conceptual construction] would also lack reality.
Why then is the conceptual construction of Īśvara and so forth not also [beginningless]? (PVA) 144.
Therefore, this established status of directions and so forth is a non-existent convention;
it is merely a matter of worldly usage derived from the study of treatises.
(PVA) Even if treatises were beginningless, it does not follow that all of them are true.
Due to their mutual contradiction, there exists a relationship between the sublated and the sublator.

(PVA 515, iii) Therefore, the elders established the conventional designations such as "prior" and "subsequent" for things themselves, in mutual dependence upon one another, for the sake of linguistic usage. Alternatively, because mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are beginningless, the very previous usage has reached a state of awakening and is thus employed in such a manner.
< (5) Refutation of Time > [515,iv]

And that very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), when designated through its distinctions, receives the names of "time" and so forth. For instance, the determination of Devadatta and others as belonging to the past, present, or future arises from such cognitions as "he was," "he is," or "he will be. Furthermore, from [the cognition] "that time existed," it follows that time itself must exist within another time, which leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if one were to argue that time is prior by its own nature and not in dependence upon another time—and that the same applies to space—then the designation "the eastern direction" would likewise be due to a distinction in the properties constituting its intrinsic nature. If this is the case, then objects such as trees would also possess priority by themselves, rather than depending on their priority relative to another time or other factors. Alternatively, if one argues that time and the like do not possess priority intrinsically, but rather in dependence upon the objects associated with them—for example:
With regard to those kings who have passed away long ago, time is established as "long past" in relation to that very connection with them. (PVA 147)
To this, it is said: [515,
viii]
If the pastness of time were due to its connection with a past entity, then that entity’s pastness would depend upon that very time;
[thus], because of mutual dependence, neither of the two could be established. (148) (PVA)
If their pastness were due to simultaneity, there would be an infinite regress.

Two things that arise simultaneously cannot be causes for one another. If it is argued that they [become past] through something else, then for that too [the same question applies], resulting in an infinite regress. (PVA 149–150)

[515,xi] Furthermore: If sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), touch a quality of air (*vāyu*), form a quality of fire (*tejas*), taste a quality of water (*ap*), and smell a quality of earth (*pṛthivī*), then it must certainly be stated what the quality of time (*kāla*) is—namely, "ka" (the letter *ka*). The same applies to the self (*ātman*) and so forth. If [you argue that] largeness and so on belong to time, then they would also belong to the self and other categories. Therefore, some specific [quality] belonging to each must be stated. Alternatively, if you claim that the restriction and permission regarding things arise from their causes through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), then those [restrictions] also arise from their own causes; thus, there is an infinite series of temporal causes. Moreover: [515,xii] Time is not perceived by the senses, like the self and so forth. Nor is it established by inference, because its relationship with anything else is unestablished. If it were established by verbal testimony (*āgama*), then since the scriptures are diverse, there would be an infinite variety of times. Furthermore, if time were eternal, it would be either one or many. If it were one, how could there be the distinction between past, present, and future? If it were many, then the distinctions of past, present, and future would be established even without time, as they would exist within the various moments themselves. Therefore, time is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā-mātra*) based on the succession of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Thus, it is said: "Time is not something distinct from the conditioned phenomena themselves; it is merely a designation for the continuity of conditioned states. Thus ends the section on time.

If the power of the eternal and all-pervading [Self] consists in obstruction and permission, then that same power would apply to the self as well; otherwise, there would be no difference between it and what is not desired. (PVA 151) [515,xiv]
For instance: time, space, the self, and ether—these are similar in their being eternal and so forth. Therefore:
[515,xv] "Because they share the same location and time, and because they are devoid of activity..."
"How can one who knows the difference between things say, 'This was done by this person, not by another'?

(PVA 152) [515, xvi] Therefore, the doctrine of [space as a substance], such as space and so forth, is simply non-existent. Consequently, the claim that sound is a quality of space is not supported by any means of valid cognition. Furthermore:
[515,xvii] Since sound originates from space and air, why has it not been stated that this is a quality of air?
Because its audition occurs in space alone, it is therefore established as a quality of the ether (*vyoman*). // 153 // (PVA)
A flame and the like, when situated in space, are not perceived; therefore, it is not said that they possess the quality of being its [space's] attribute.
To claim that there is another substratum for it is incorrect, for in the case of sound as well, the drum and so forth would be distinct from it.

If that which is perceived as being located in something were to possess the qualities of that thing, then why would flame and the like not be qualities of space? Since it has other supports such as walls and wood, when it is perceived as being located in those, it is not a quality of space.

That is incorrect. If it were located in both [the source and the perceiver], let it possess the qualities of both. Why then would drums, conchs, and the like not be the substratum (*āśraya*) of sound as well? If you argue that this is because [sound] is heard in another location, then this is equally true for light and other such phenomena. If you argue that it is perceived even when its substratum—such as a gem—is present, then this is equally true for the sound of substances being boiled. Therefore, sound does not have space (*ākāśa*) as its quality. Furthermore, its perception while residing therein is just like light residing therein. Nor can space act as a support (*sthāpaka*), because it is non-obstructive (*apratigha*). Space is formless (*arūpi*), invisible (*anidarśana*), and non-obstructive. It is only when light exists that space is known; since space is designated only where there is light, space is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptimad*). Therefore, the claim that "sound is a quality of space" is not well-stated. Consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in refuting the view that sound is a quality of space.

The word "itself" (*svayam*) is indeed for the purpose of excluding that which is intended by the authors of the treatises as a probandum simply because it has been accepted in the treatise; it has no other purpose. For:
Those who perform actions preceded by reflection do not act out of mere desire;
for wise men, acting after deliberation is the first step.
If, however, one acts without prior reflection, then his desire alone is the cause.

(156) Thereafter, the second and even the third will be the same.

If it is argued that this very principle—that a treatise (*śāstra*) should be accepted according to one's own desire—is stated by [the author's] own words, then this too must be accepted by you according to your own desire, just as before. In that case, the Nyāya perspective—"Having examined [it], what is logical should be accepted; mere desire is no refuge here"—is appropriate, as it opposes the operation of arbitrary desire. Therefore, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is something seen in a treatise, accepting it arbitrarily is indeed improper. If that were so, then even when establishing a desired object for oneself, if there were no sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*), no one would proceed [to act] while abandoning the meaning of the treatise. And if there is no sublation, one proceeds by one's own desire anyway. What, then, is the use of the term "arbitrary acceptance" (*svayaṃgrahaṇa*)?
ii] The rebuttal.

In this regard, he himself established the scriptural authority for the various conflicting views regarding perception, demonstrating that [the opponent's position] would entail the loss of what is accepted, the impossibility of proof, and infinite regress. (75)

[517,iii] For the purpose of refuting misconceptions, the entire treatise is relevant; therefore, here too, that which is seen in the treatise is the probandum (*sādhya*). If one asks by what logic this refutation of misconceptions occurs: it is by demonstrating the loss of what is intended, the fact that something is not the probandum, and the consequence of infinite regress. For there is no loss of what is intended when there is a sublation of what is seen in the treatise, because the two are not invariably concomitant (*anāntarīyaka*). Furthermore, even if they were invariably concomitant, proving that would lead to an infinite regress—this logic is shown by the inclusion of the word "himself" (*svayaṃ*).
Therefore, this is incorrect:
[517,v] "The subject (dharmin), by excluding the distinctions imposed by convention..."
Another [teacher] himself proclaimed a scriptural passage (śruti) for the purpose of grasping that which is already well-known. (76)

The term "himself" (*svayam*) is used so that there may be the inclusion of a subject (*dharmin*) which is established by itself—excluding those subjects whose distinction, characterized as being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), is formulated by a treatise (*śāstra*) rather than being established by the author of the treatise. For this reason, it follows by implication that only that subject which is established by itself and not established by another is a valid subject, and no other.
That is incorrect; for,
viii] by the very commencement of this investigation, the locus is established as proven.
Since there is no dispute regarding categories whose distinctions are merely imagined according to one's own whim. (77)

[517,ix] For an investigation (*vicāra*)—being conducted with respect to some subject (*dharmin*) in the form of "permanent," "impermanent," and so forth—is carried out upon that which already possesses an established nature. However, whatever nature it is that must be proven, let that very thing first be investigated; for when the subject is unestablished, a proof is impossible.

Now, the nature of sound is indeed established. In that case, that very thing should be taken as the subject (*dharmin*); what is the use of taking an unestablished qualification? If it is argued that this is for the purpose of proving impermanence for one who asserts [sound] to be exactly so, that is incorrect; because:
[517,xii] Because the listener has no intention regarding that [subject], and because it is therefore not established for him,
the statement of a probandum endowed with the quality of space is futile. (PVA 158)

[517,xiii] For those who act with deliberation, there is no engagement in speech that is devoid of purpose. To begin with, the qualification "not being a quality of space" is not intended by the opponents as a property of impermanence; nor can something unintended be established merely by a thesis statement. For if that were so, it would follow that "sound is impermanent because it is produced, since it is not a quality of space," or any other desired object whatsoever would be established. If, on the other hand, this is precisely what is pleasing to the proponent, then who could prevent such a person—devoid of discernment and driven by mere whim—from asserting whatever he likes?

Therefore, this is incorrect. Alternatively, he asserts that the subject (*dharmin*) is not something to be proven (*asādhyatā*) because it is already established by authoritative testimony (*siddhādeśena*).
By the very statement "it is to be designated by its own nature alone," that which pertains to it [is established]. 78.
Because:
[517,xvii]
For if a statement were possible in the form of something already established, then the rule that "it must be stated precisely as something yet to be proven" would be fruitful. (79)

[518,i] Now, it might be explained in this way: the subject (*dharmin*) is not to be proven in its own nature, because of the statement that "it is already established by itself. Otherwise, what purpose would the qualification "by itself" serve? For instance, the statement is not for the sake of merely establishing the existence of the subject, since that is already well-known from the very context of the inquiry. Therefore, it is already established and not something to be proven; the word "by itself" is intended to negate its status as a probandum (*sādhya*). Thus, it has been stated that the status of being a probandum does not belong to the subject.
That too is incorrect, because:
There is no discerning person who would attempt to prove what is already established;
for how could one, having already accepted that [fact], cause it to become something yet to be proven?

In that case, the statement "by its very nature" (*svarūpeṇaiva*) is redundant; for it is precisely because the subject under investigation is unestablished that it must be proven. Indeed, that which is unestablished does not become a locus of dispute. Thus:
"Because the reason is stated regarding what is doubtful, the reason has no basis when [the subject] is excluded. (PV 4.18)
Likewise for investigation; likewise for that which is already established.

To this it is replied: For the mention of "its own nature" (*svarūpa*) is not for the purpose of excluding what is already established, because its purpose is to exclude that which is unestablished but has been indicated as a means of proof. Therefore, by the phrase "by its very nature," only the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) itself is shown to be fruitful.

Otherwise, both [the subject and the property] would have to be presented separately. Why, then, was it stated that [the subject is presented] in the form of something already established (*siddha*)? It should be explained as follows: [it is presented] in an established form when the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished; likewise, the property (*dharma*) is presented in the form of the means of proof (*sādhana*). Furthermore, that presentation of the locus in its established form may be of the mere locus itself, such as "the self is the inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*); or it may be as a qualification of the locus, such as "sound is an impermanent quality of space" (*ākāśaguṇaḥ śabdo ’nityaḥ*). Now, in a case where there is a qualification of the locus, since the statement is "sound is an impermanent quality of space," how is it understood that impermanence [is the property to be proven] and not the being-a-quality-of-space? Is it that whatever sound is impermanent is a quality of space, or that whatever is a quality of space is impermanent? This too must be understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*). And although "sound" is common to many things, it has been demonstrated accordingly. How, then, in the case of "sound is audible" (*śrāvaṇaḥ śabdaḥ*), is the object of exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) for the apprehension of the essential nature shown? For if it were intended for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), that would be incorrect.

This is true. Nevertheless, it was stated on the assumption that what is intended for one purpose may also serve another purpose. Furthermore, even if it were to establish the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no fault because the apprehension of its own nature (*svarūpa*) functions as a differentiator. How could there be the attainment of that which has been refuted? For a dispute is observed regarding that point; we shall demonstrate this later.
And it has been described that inference has a universal as its object;
even so, nothing here is contradicted by the [proponent's] position, even if it has not been explicitly stated. (80)

[518,xii] It has been established by the Ācārya that inference has the universal (sāmānya) as its object. Neither the subject (dharmin) nor anything else distinct from it that is being proved is a universal. Therefore, even if the mention of the word "itself" (svayaṃ) does not exclude the subject from being the object of proof, there is nonetheless no fault, because it is excluded precisely by virtue of being a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
[518,xiii]
Moreover:
If one were to make the subject itself the probandum, what would follow? Why is that not possible?
Why? Because of the absence of a logical reason and a positive concomitance, is this not indeed a fault in those two? (81)
If it is claimed that a defect is not considered a defect of the thesis (pakṣa) because it depends upon subsequent members [of the proof],
then by that same logic, defects such as those of the reason (hetu) and so forth would also follow as being defects of the thesis.

Because the thesis is sublated by all [the means of valid cognition], therefore only those [reasons] which possess that [sublation] as their mark are considered defects of the thesis, and no others, just like contradictions with perception and so forth. (83)
[519,iii] But is it not so?

The definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is: that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*), and which is not refuted by contradictory meanings. In this regard, what fault would there be if one were to make the locus (*dharmin*) itself the probandum? Now, it may be argued that the locus cannot be proven because a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not something to be proven. For if the existence of the locus were the probandum, it would entail the proof of the particular characteristic; however, this is impossible because the reason (*hetu*) lacks a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the specific instance. If it is then argued that the capacity of the reason lies precisely in that [locus], since it lacks an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then it is not logical to say, "the fault belongs to the one, while the fault belongs to the other.

Now, this [fault] is indeed a fault of the thesis (*pakṣa*) as well, because it renders the thesis unestablished. If that were the case, then every fault of the reason (*hetu*) would become a fault of the thesis, since by means of that [reason’s] fault, the thesis itself becomes unestablished. Alternatively, one might argue: "In a case where another proving reason is possible for the thesis—such as in the case of 'Sound is impermanent'—there the fault lies with the reason, as in [the argument] 'because it is visible' (*cākṣuṣatvāt*), and so forth. For in such cases, there is no fault of the thesis being unfit for proof, since it is established by another reason. However, where not even a single reason is possible, that is a fault of the thesis. Indeed, one's intended meaning (*svābhiprāya*) must be demonstrated through the statement of the thesis. If that [meaning] is impossible due to sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhā*), it is likewise impossible in the case of being a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇatva*). Therefore, it is logical that this is strictly a fault of the thesis. This is the reasoning.
To this, it is said:
Is this impossibility of the thesis due to its dependence on the reason? Or is it inherent in the thesis itself? Both of these [alternatives] are untenable.
If that defect arises from the connection with the reason, then the defect belongs to the reason alone.
But this fault does not apply to our own position, because it is established through direct perception.

If the state of being an Arhat were not established by its very nature, it would not be established even through perception. If it is argued that it is not established through inference, then that fault belongs to inference itself. Therefore, even if the subject (*dharmin*) is already established, if it were made the object of proof (*sādhya*), there too the fault would lie solely with the reason (*hetu*), because the reason lacks positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in that case. Furthermore, the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) applies when [the subject] is established by inference; that is indeed a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*). However, regarding a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) established by perception, the fault lies with the reason due to the absence of positive concomitance. But in the case where the self (*ātman*) itself is established by perception, the fault of the thesis—characterized as proving what is already established—applies to both [the reason and the thesis].

Therefore, a thesis that is established for oneself through inference is [valid] with respect to another; however, one established through scripture is not a thesis at all, just like one established through direct perception.

[Objection: But surely, since the *svalakṣaṇa* (particular) is not established by perception, it cannot be the subject (*pakṣa*) due to a fault in the reason (*hetudoṣa*). However, if it is established by scripture (*āgama*), how can a universal (*sāmānya*) be the object of scripture? And since there is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by way of the universal, how can this be a fault of the subject? [Reply: Has it not just been stated that this is a fault of the subject because of a fault in the reason? [Objection: Then why is it not simply [a fault] because of its being restricted to that alone (*tanmātrabhāvitva*)? [Reply: In this case, there is indeed such restriction to that alone. For instance: [519,xii] "If this is established by scripture, what is the purpose of a reason?"
But if it is already established by scripture, how can it be said to be established by scripture?
xiii) Or, perhaps, although it is not established for another, it is established for oneself through one's own scripture.
[519,xiv] That too is incorrect. Because:
If the authority of scripture is established even for the opponent, then it is established for both. If, however, the scripture lacks authority, then it is unestablished for both.
Therefore, the subject (pakṣa) is indeed established for oneself by means of inference.

[Objection: But surely fire, even though established by perception, is not [considered] a *pakṣa* (the subject of inference) for another person? [Reply: No, because it is not a *pakṣa* in that specific form. For it is a *pakṣa* in its general form, not in its particular form. However, in its own specific nature (*svarūpa*), it is not established by perception. Therefore, it is established that there is no inference at all regarding what is already established by perception. [Objection: If this is so, this is like the proverb of "putting out a splinter with a hammer" (*gaḍupraveśe akṣinirgama*). If there is no inference regarding what is established by perception, then it is all the more so when it is not so established, because inference is preceded by perception. Likewise, since there is no perception regarding the object of inference either, how can a *pakṣa* be sublated by perception? Furthermore, "sublation" (*bādhana*) does not mean the destruction of the object, but rather the making known that it does not exist. In that regard, whatever negation there may be, it is all due to non-perception; thus, sublation by non-perception is itself sublation by inference. And so it has been said: "Because of the contradiction in [perception] having non-existence as its object."

[520,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form; he does not perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. He does not perceive that the eye is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the eye; he does not perceive that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the mind. He does not perceive that forms are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is forms; he does not perceive that sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty, nor does he perceve that emptiness is mental phenomena. He does not perceive that eye-consciousness is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is eye-consciousness; he does not perceive that ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is mind-consciousness. He does not perceive that eye-contact is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is eye-contact; he does not perceive that ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is mind-contact. He does not perceive that feeling born of eye-contact is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is feeling born of eye-contact; he does not perceive that feelings born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is feeling born of mind-contact. He does not perceive that earth-element is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is earth-element; he does not perceive that water-element, fire-element, wind-element, space-element, and consciousness-element are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the consciousness-element. He does not perceive that ignorance is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is ignorance; he does not perceive that volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is old age and death. He does not perceive that suffering is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is suffering; he does not perceive that origination, cessation, and the path are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the path. He does not perceive that the fruit of a Stream-enterer is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the fruit of a Stream-enterer; he does not perceive that the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, and an Arhat are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the fruit of an Arhat. He does not perceive that the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha; he does not perceive that the state of an All-Knowing One is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is the state of an All-Knowing One. Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive these dharmas as empty, nor does he perceive emptiness as those dharmas. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With one voice, the venerable Subhūti and the assembly of monks and bodhisattvas, along with the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had said.
