To this it is replied: Regarding what was stated—that inference is preceded by perception—it is not the case that [inference] is preceded by perception with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object; rather, where the probandum (*sādhya*) is a universal such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*), and there is no perception whose object is that particular (*vyakti*), there inference does not operate. This is because inference is preceded by a perception that has operated upon that particular. If, however, perception were to function with respect to the universal, what would be the use of inference there? That very particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), when being established by inference, would assume the form of a universal. Indeed, the particular itself is the universal when it is not perceived in its specific detail. Thus, the meaning is this: inference operates upon the object of perception; yet that which is apprehended by inference is not perception itself. Therefore, [the statement] "that fire is indeed perceived through perception in the kitchen and so forth"—meaning "the thesis (*pakṣa*) is sublated by perception"—carries this very sense, because perception has already operated upon the manifestation of the opposite of that [probandum]. Furthermore, where there is no particular, that universal is simply impossible, since a universal is manifested by a particular. Moreover, it will be demonstrated that in the case of the thesis "sound is not audible," the thesis is precisely the negation of the particular. And in the refutation of a negation, the refutation must be understood as occurring by means of that very object which is being negated, because any other [object] would not be contradictory to it.

[520,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive forms as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive eye-contact as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the earth element as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive ignorance as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as existent, nor does he perceive them as non-existent. He does not perceive the conditioned as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the unconditioned as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the world as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent; he does not perceive the transcendence of the world as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as existent, nor does he perceive him as non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the once-returner as existent, nor does he perceive him as non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of once-returning as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the non-returner as existent, nor does he perceive him as non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of non-returning as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the arhat as existent, nor does he perceive him as non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of arhatship as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as existent, nor does he perceive him as non-existent; he does not perceive the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as existent, nor does he perceive him as non-existent; he does not perceive the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata as existent, nor does he perceive it as non-existent. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, then how does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of morality? How does he train in the perfection of patience? How does he train in the perfection of vigor? How does he train in the perfection of meditation? How does he train in the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How does he train in the dharmas of a once-returner? How does he train in the dharmas of a non-returner? How does he train in the dharmas of an arhat? Now, how can perception be refuted by inference? [It cannot,] because that [perception] has as its object the domain of inference and words. For this very reason, it is refuted as being "refuting" [only] when it expresses a [logical] connection (*sambandha*). Alternatively, there is no fault because of the identification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object as one. Therefore, there is no fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) consisting in the fact that an established subject (*dharmin*) is treated as something to be proven; for in that case, the fault belongs solely to the reason (*hetu*). Nor is a fault that arises through a fault of the reason a fault of the thesis, because such a fault is excluded by the definition of the reason itself. Furthermore, what has been excluded by the definition of the reason need not be excluded by the definition of the thesis as well, because that would be redundant and because it is not within its scope.

Setting aside that which is sublated by the characteristics of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is stated for the purpose of avoiding under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*vyatireka*). (84)

[520,v] Having set aside the fault already refuted by the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is stated in order to avoid other faults. For the entire definition is intended to avoid the faults of under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*vyatireka*). Nor would a definition suffer from under-extension or over-extension simply because it fails to avoid a fault that has already been avoided by another definition. Let this much alone be the definition; what is the use of anything else? Since that for which another definition was made has already been avoided by the other, the inclusion of "itself" (*svayaṃ*) is redundant. By what, then, are those faults of under-extension and over-extension refuted?
To this we reply:
The mention of the term "itself" (svayam) precludes the possibility of a fallacy consisting in a deviation [from the intended meaning].
The mention of the word "intended" (iṣṭa), when not excluded by the co-occurrence [of the reason], prevents the fallacy of over-extension (avyāpti). (85)

[521,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend form as form, nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as consciousness. He does not apprehend the eye as the eye, nor does he apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as the mind. He does not apprehend forms as forms, nor does he apprehend sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as mental phenomena. He does not apprehend the eye-consciousness as eye-consciousness, nor does he apprehend ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as mind-consciousness. He does not apprehend eye-contact as eye-contact, nor does he apprehend ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as mind-contact. He does not apprehend the feeling arisen from eye-contact as the feeling arisen from eye-contact, nor does he apprehend the feeling arisen from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as the feeling arisen from mind-contact. He does not apprehend the earth element as the earth element, nor does he apprehend the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as the consciousness element. He does not apprehend ignorance as ignorance, nor does he apprehend volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as aging-and-death. He does not apprehend the conditioned as conditioned, nor does he apprehend the unconditioned as unconditioned. He does not apprehend the past as past, nor does he apprehend the future as future or the present as present. He does not apprehend the stream-enterer as a stream-enterer, nor does he apprehend the once-returner as a once-returner, the non-returner as a non-returner, or the arhat as an arhat. He does not apprehend the pratyekabuddha as a pratyekabuddha, nor does he apprehend the Tathāgata as a Tathāgata. He does not apprehend the perfection of giving as the perfection of giving, nor does he apprehend the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as the perfection of wisdom. He does not apprehend the emptiness of the internal as the emptiness of the internal, nor does he apprehend the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of the infinite, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of entities, the emptiness of non-entities, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-entities as the emptiness of the nature of non-entities. He does not apprehend the ten powers of a Tathāgata as the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he apprehend the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as the great compassion of a Tathāgata. He does not apprehend the buddha-fields as buddha-fields, nor does he apprehend the dharmas of a buddha as the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend anything that he courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom become one who has set out for a long time? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the one who sets out, nor does he apprehend the one who has set out for a long time, nor does he apprehend the one who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who has set out for a long time. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom become one who has practiced for a long time? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the one who has practiced for a long time, nor does he apprehend the one who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who has practiced for a long time. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom become one who has been predicted by the Tathāgatas? It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who has been predicted by the Tathāgatas. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom become one who is irreversible? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend irreversibility, nor does he apprehend the irreversible bodhisattva. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who is irreversible. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the secondary marks, nor does he apprehend the one endowed with the secondary marks. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who is endowed with the secondary marks. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom become one who is endowed with the dharma of the voice of Brahmā? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the voice of Brahmā, nor does he apprehend the one endowed with the voice of Brahmā. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom becomes one who is endowed with the dharma of the voice of Brahmā. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom become one who is endowed with the dharma of the lion’s roar? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend the perfection of wisdom, nor does he apprehend the bodhisattva, nor does he apprehend the lion’s roar, nor does he apprehend the one endowed with the lion’s roar. It is in this way, Subhū

Is the definition complete with just this much? What is the use of anything else? If the word *svayam* (himself) were not used, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even what is desired by the author of a treatise (*śāstrakāra*) would become the probandum (*sādhya*). If the particle [the negative *na*] were not employed, there would be the [undesirable consequence] of an unestablished (*asiddha*) [reason] being indicated as a means of proof (*sādhana*). If the phrase *svarūpeṇa* (in its own form) were not used, there would be the [undesirable consequence] of an established subject (*dharmin*) [being the probandum]. But there is no other fault; therefore, the inclusion of the word *svayam* is for that purpose. It is useless, because it does not serve to avoid any fault. [Objection: For what purpose, then, is the inclusion of the term *anirākṛta* (unrefuted)? [Response: Even if someone were to make something refuted the probandum, a fault in the reason (*hetudoṣa*) will still occur therein. If you say, "Because it is refuted by that very [fault]," we say no. The sense is that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is sublated along with the "unrefuted" [condition]. Indeed, without the word "unrefuted," the negative concomitance cannot be sublated. [Objection: If you say, "Because that fault is sublated by the definition of the reason itself," we say no. That [fault] pertains only to the thesis (*pakṣa*), so there is no fault. That belongs to the reason. If even what is desired is not a thesis when it is refuted, then for what purpose is the word *iṣṭa* (desired) included? He says: "The mention of *iṣṭa* excludes non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). For it is not only the refuted that is intended to be pervaded (*vyāpta*), since there is also the possibility of non-refuted things being objects of pervasion. Alternatively, from the statement "the mention of *iṣṭa* excludes non-pervasion," it follows that it has the sense of pervasion; therefore, even the refuted would be pervaded. To this he says: "Along with the unrefuted. If the word "refuted" were not used, there would be pervasion even of that [refuted thing] due to the inclusion of the word *iṣṭa*. Since the word *anirākṛta* is used together [with *iṣṭa*], how could such a possibility arise? Therefore, if even an object seen in a treatise (*śāstra*) is to be the probandum, then this much alone—the definition devoid of the word *svayam*—is sufficient; what is the use of anything else? In that regard:

The definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*) is the acceptance of what is to be proven (*sādhya*). Among those [cases], there is no status as a thesis: in the case of the refuted, because of sublation (*bādhana*); in the remaining cases, because they do not fall under the definition. (86)

[521,iii] This is the true meaning here: the thesis (*pakṣa*) is the acceptance of that which is to be proven. If it were merely the acceptance [of something], then even those things such as the "refuted" (*nirākṛta*) would possess the status of a thesis, because they too involve acceptance. To exclude that, [the definition specifies] "that which is not refuted," because the refuted is sublated. Furthermore, regarding the "remaining"—such as the "established" (*siddha*) and so forth—the definition simply does not apply; thus, the definition applies only to what is intended (*iṣṭa*), and not to anything else. [521,iv]

This is incorrect. What is to be accomplished by this, and what is to be established here? If you mean that it is for the purpose of establishing what is to be established (*vidheya*), that is not so, because the thing to be established has already been established previously.

Furthermore, the claim that "the summary refers back to the acceptance of the proponent's position, which was stated for the sake of proving what was unestablished" is also not sound. For if the meaning of "here" is simply the presentation of that very point, what is the purpose of a summary?

[(The Definition of a Vārttika)—] Others, however, say: this is indeed the work of the author of the Vārttika himself regarding the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*). For it is said: "The definition of a vārttika consists of pointing out the inconsistency of the sūtras, the refutation thereof, and the statement of a specific qualification (*viśeṣābhidhāna*). This [present passage] is that very statement of a specific qualification.

That too is incorrect; for by the phrase "acceptance of the probandum," the inclusion of both that which is intended as a means of proof and that which is merely intended by the author of a treatise remains unavoidable.

Now, it is explained as being "in the state of being the probandum" (*sādhyatvena*). And there is no desire for something to be the probandum when it is desired as the means of proof (*sādhanatvena*).

That too is incorrect. For even as something to be proven (*sādhya*), that [reason] is indeed intended [by the proponent]. Now, if it is restricted such that "only as something to be proven" is accepted, then this [definition] would serve to exclude what is accepted as a means of proof (*sādhana*). In that case, even if not explicitly stated, something would become a *sādhya* merely by being intended. Furthermore, if "acceptance as something to be proven" were the very definition of a thesis (*pakṣa*), then even that which is accepted as a means of proof would possess the status of a thesis if it were accepted as something to be proven. For at that time, there is no impossibility of both occurring; nor is this a rule for a single designation [that applies only to the opponent], since it would also apply to what is intended by the author of the treatise, because that too is accepted. Finally, if it is argued that "acceptance" belongs only to the proponent due to proximity, [we reply:]...

That too is incorrect, because even that which is desired by the authors of the treatises is accepted by the proponent. Furthermore, why is it not accepted that [the pervasion] is due to logical necessity (*nyāya*)? Moreover, a proximity created by the intellect exists even in what is desired by the authors of the treatises. And even when the non-conclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the proximity has been refuted, there is still the consequence of accepting the probandum (*sādhya*).

[Objection: "But surely, when [the thesis] has been refuted by means of sublation (*bādhana*), there is no acceptance of the probandum (*sādhya*); therefore, it does not deserve to be a 'probandum' (i.e., a subject for proof). [Reply: That too is incorrect.

For if that were so, even the definition "The statement of the probandum is the proposition (*pratijñā*)" would be faultless. Furthermore, how could one who follows such a definition be a knower of the distinction between what is worthy and what is unworthy? Therefore, this [objection] is invalid. In that case, this is the definition of the "position" (*pakṣa*) according to the *Nyāyamukha*.
The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended as the probandum (*sādhyatvena iṣṭaḥ*), and is not refuted by contradictory meanings (*viruddhārthānirākṛta*).

For it is said here as follows: If [the opponent argues that] the particle *svayam* (itself) is a sublater (*bādhikā*) because it is not distinct from the form of a verbal noun (*ākhyā*), then how can there be a sublation of the distinction? To this he says: “The acceptance of the probandum” (*sādhyābhyupagama*), and so forth. Even in that case, since the sublated [element] is excluded by way of sublation, there is no fault regarding the remaining [elements], as they function according to their definition. The suffix *-niṣṭhā* (past participle), which denotes past time, does not apply to that which is being desired as a probandum (*sādhyatayā*). Therefore, its exclusion is established; thus, there is no fault. If this is so, then since even here the word *iṣṭa* (desired) implies that something presented as a means of proof (*sādhana*) is being excluded, the mention of the particle (*nipāta*) is redundant.
This is true.

Although the restriction [of the meaning] is already understood through the very expression of the desired [term], it is stated [here] to exclude other times, because of its connection with a word ending in a kṛtya suffix. || 87 ||

The phrase "desired by oneself" would serve to exclude what is desired at another time, were it not for the connection with the principal element ending in the suffix *kṛtya*; however, that connection does indeed exist. Therefore:
"Even that which has been made the object of a desire at another time would possess the status of being a *pakṣa* (the subject of inquiry).
Therefore, the mention of the particle *eva* in the *Nyāyamukha* must be made for the purpose of excluding such cases. To this, it is replied:

In this context, since the goal is not sought through the absence of a member, it is rather within the very member that is intended that the unestablished reason (*asiddhahetu*) and so forth are negated by that [negation]. (88)

[522,xii] Here, in this *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the thesis (*pakṣa*) to be indicated is that which has the suffix *-kṛtya* as its final member. Of what nature is it? It is "intended" (*iṣṭa*). Consequently, there is an adherence to another time. For example: "Devadatta, having arrived, is to be seen. Therefore, the restriction is for the purpose of excluding what is intended at other times.
[522,xiii]

In this context, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) following the verb *iṣ* (to desire) denotes something that is not a subordinate factor (*anaṅga*) with respect to the word expressing the desired object (*īpsita-pada*). However, in the case of the word expressing the desired object itself, it is indeed a subordinate factor (*aṅga*).

This is a case of distributive connection (*vyasta-sambandha*). That is to say, it should be explained as follows: in the word expressing the desired object, it is the primary factor (*pradhāna*), whereas here [in the case of the *niṣṭhā*], it is strictly a subordinate factor (*aṅga*).

Alternatively, in this *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the particle (*nipāta*) is not an essential factor for establishing the past tense. However, in the *Nyāyamukha*, it is indeed not an essential factor in the word "desired" (*īpsita*). By that certainty, unestablished reasons (*asiddhahetu*) and the like are excluded; therefore, the particle is not mentioned there. Consequently, the subject (*dharmin*) does not possess the status of being the probandum (*sādhya*). The inclusion of the word "himself" (*svayaṃ*) is for the purpose of exclusion, nor is it for the sake of allowing one's own preference to operate within the treatises, according to the reasoning stated previously.

Furthermore, because it is non-expressive, it is illogical for that [object] to be desired by itself through its own nature; thus, the status of being the probandum belongs to what is intended by him, regardless of the entire treatise. (89)

[523,ii] Wherever it may be in a treatise (*śāstra*), that which is to be praised must be established by oneself; and because the term "by oneself" (*svayam*) is not merely redundant—since the subject (*dharmin*) is indeed already established by oneself—it is improper [to claim otherwise]. Therefore, "that which is desired is not [established] by another commentator, but by oneself (*ātmanā*). Consequently, "without depending on the entire treatise, that which is intended [by the proponent] is the probandum (*sādhya*).

Therefore, even when that which is desired is sublated by something undesirable with which it is conjoined, the thesis and the reason are not defective, because the probandum itself remains unsublated. (90)

Therefore, even when there is a sublation of that which is conjoined with what is intended by the author of the treatise, since the sublation occurs by overstepping the mere probandum (*sādhya*) in the proof, there is no fault in the thesis (*pakṣa*) or the reason (*hetu*). Otherwise, even if there were a fault, it would merely be the pointing out of a non-fault.

But surely, if there is a contradiction with what is intended by the author of the treatise, what is the point of proving that? For it would result in a loss of one's scholarly confidence (*prauḍhatā*). To this it has been said: "If anything at all... and so forth. Furthermore:
when total ruin has occurred, it is better to have achieved something.
When a jar has fallen into a well, it is not necessary to throw down the rope.

The phrases "itself," "the form of a particle," and "not distinct from a verbal designation" are intended as refutations [of certain views]. This has been explained by the expression "together with what is not excluded.
<3. The Purpose of Including the Term "Not Excluded">
Therein, he explains that remaining term "not excluded" (*anirākṛta*).
And that acceptance which is not refuted by the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is what is intended;
what is the logic here?
Because a reason is stated regarding what is doubted.

When the opposite [of the probandum] is established by a single means of valid cognition, there is no basis for the reason—that is, for the means of valid cognition—due to the absence of that [probandum]. Thus it is said: [523,xiv] "The excluded [opposite] is the non-basis of the reason. (91)

[523,xv] But if there is a proving reason (*hetu*), why is it not the thesis (*pakṣa*)? If, on the other hand, it is not, then that fault will belong to the reason itself; what is the point of stating that [the thesis] is "unrefuted" (*anirākṛta*)?

This is true; nevertheless, since [the thesis] must be refuted first by way of a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) itself, independent of any faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), this is indeed a fault of the thesis, because it exists solely as such. For when something is refuted by perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*), no one requires a means of proof (*sādhana*). If that were the case, there would be no confidence at all; thus, what confidence could there be even in a proving [reason]? Therefore, the object of the reason is that which is doubtful. And here, the mere absence of proving or subverting means of knowledge is indicated by doubt; it is not the actual presence of doubt itself. Even one whose doubt is not manifest understands fire from a single inference. Alternatively, the status of being an object of the reason belongs to that wherein a doubt can be produced, but not to that which is ascertained through its own nature or its opposite by means of proving or subverting [means].

[4. Fourfold Sublation] [524,i] If the status of being an object for the statement of a reason belongs to that which is not sublated by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then sublation is indeed only twofold. How then did the Teacher demonstrate its fourfold nature?
To this, it is said:
That sublation (bādhā) has been stated to be fourfold through the division of inference (*anumāna*).

[524, iv] It has been shown that sublation by inference alone is threefold, and sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) is the fourth. The demonstration of these four types of sublation does not invalidate the twofold classification of sublation. If that were so, then sublation by scriptural authority (*āgamaprasiddhi*) would also be merely a form of inferential evidence (*liṅga*); otherwise, it would not constitute a distinct variety of inference.
<1. Scriptural contradiction is irrelevant> [524,v] This is so, because:
In that regard, the means consists of the member of effect (kāryāṅga), the member of essential nature (svabhāvāṅga), and the established order of the world (jagatsthiti). || 92 ||

[524, vii] Authoritative testimony (āptavacana) consists of that which resembles an effect (kāryapratirūpaka), that which resembles an essential nature (svabhāvapratirūpaka), and established convention (prasiddhi). Why is this not a primary logical mark (liṅga)? He says:
[524, viii]
One who speaks with words endowed by the certainty of reality regarding what is considered not to obstruct the self is an *āpta* (reliable authority);
thus has he been described everywhere as both his own word and the scripture. (93)

[524,ix] Indeed, there is no authoritative person (*āpta*) established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another person, because it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to know someone who is entirely free from mental defects; and because he cannot be ascertained through inference due to the confusion of worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, an "authoritative person" is accepted as such only out of necessity, but in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), he does not exist. This statement together with his own words has been made to demonstrate their equality. For:

Just as speech does not proceed when one lacks authority regarding oneself, so too there can be no inquiry into an object perceived through scripture if that scripture is not accepted as authoritative. (94)

[524,xi] If one does not accept that the self is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it follows that no speech whatsoever should be uttered—just as when one says, "Everything I say is false. If your position is that everything must indeed be spoken falsely, then the meaning of what has been said here is not to be understood from my words; nor is anything at all to be done on the basis of my words. If that is so, why have we troubled ourselves? For even without speaking, this matter would be established. Furthermore, whatever has been studied by those whose intellects are shaken by poor wit—that too is utterly shaken.
Just as when one says, "I speak everything falsely," this very statement is not itself negated; for if that were declared false, the matter under discussion would not be established. (65)
Thus [524,
xiii],
because:

[524,xiv] Even if there were a negation of the three times, this statement would still not be coherent; for if the statement lacks authority, its very manifestation would lead to its own subversion. (165) (PVA)

If one were to argue in this way, then everything stated would be false, for it would be illogical due to self-contradiction and so forth; by uttering these words, you yourself [are contradicting your own position].

Since he has attained the status of an authority (*pramāṇa*) and is thus accepted as such, how can his lack of authority be established? If you say it is due to regret, even so there is still a contradiction. It would have been better simply not to speak at all; why this exertion? If you say it was done without due reflection, is that not itself the very fault? Thorough reflection is precisely what constitutes right reasoning (*nyāya*). Alternatively, if you say, "I am saying this to negate [the authority] of those who are present or those yet to come," then even so, what is the point of this statement? But regarding those who will exist in the future, there is no listener at all; for what purpose is the speech? If you argue that there is no fault because it is like the talk of wandering minstrels (*cāraṇa*), we say no, because this is the context of a formal debate (*vāda*). For the purpose of a debate is indeed the determination of the reality of the matter.

Therefore, this is incorrect. Likewise, regarding an object established by a treatise, if one does not accept it, the same applies to the investigation; thus, there is indeed parity between the treatise and one's own words.
For when that [subject] serves as the basis for the discussion, the treatise acts as a sublater;
in order to state this point, its mention together with its own words is for the sake of observing their equality. (95)

[525,iv] If there is no acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*), how can there be an investigation into its meaning? If an investigation cannot proceed without a treatise because the very subject (*dharmin*) would be non-existent, then it must be established that a treatise is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) and not otherwise; for it is the view of others that a treatise possesses a capacity exceeding one's own words, even without being explicitly mentioned. It would be exactly so.
In this regard, he has also shown a corresponding example:
for in the absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), the words of the scriptures would be untenable. (96)

For this very reason, in order to demonstrate their equivalence, he provides a similar example: because when valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is rejected, there is an absence of both treatises (*śāstra*) and verbal statements. If valid cognition is negated, even a treatise would not be a valid authority for you; thus, what could be accepted? There would be nothing but mutual contradiction.
In the case of contradiction with one's own words, the example is clear in the scripture: "The dharma that brings happiness after death [is not taught by me]. (97)

[525, viii] But surely, since there *are* means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can this be a contradiction with the treatise? For a subject (*dharmin*) does not arise from the treatise alone. However, if there were no means of valid cognition whatsoever, how could the subject and so forth be established? Thus, it would be a contradiction with one's own words.

Now, if some established fact is admitted, then that very means by which it is established would itself be its authority (*pramāṇa*), because the establishment of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs only through an authority. For it must be stated that nothing whatsoever is known in the absence of an authority. Therefore, this is not a contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*). If one were to speak while having accepted the treatise, saying "it would indeed be so," there would be no fault. But how is it to be known that the treatise has been accepted? [525,x]

This is true. For this very reason, this is not a clear example of contradiction with scripture (*śāstra*); rather, it is merely a demonstration of the general direction. The author of the *Vārttika* stated clearly: "Dharma is that which bestows unhappiness after death. In such a case, scripture must necessarily be accepted. Therefore, in the face of contradiction with scripture, this alone is the clear example; thus, there is here a mutual contradiction, just as in the case of one's own words.

In that case, wherever a subject (*dharmin*) is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*) therein would indeed be subverting, because it is itself a means of valid cognition. However, when the subject is one established by a treatise, the acceptance of that [treatise] would be subverting precisely because of its own restriction.
To this, he says:

[525,xiii] Even for a teacher, when stating a contradictory [reason] regarding a real entity that does not serve as the basis [for the thesis], there can be neither sublation nor obstruction, because the two are of equal status. 98.

[526,i] For there is no distinction between a treatise and one's own statement, even for a single one, other than the authority conferred by their acceptance. Therefore, because both possess equal power, there is merely a mutual contradiction between them, not a relationship of sublation and sublated.
Just as it is in one's own words, so too at that time [the word] consists of its own statement;
whichever of those two possesses the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) shall be the sublater of the other. (99)
Otherwise, how could a thesis or an inference—whether it be devoid of logical justification or equal in status to its object—subvert that very object? (100)
The validity of scriptures has already been refuted;
therefore, this fault is intended [only] in the case of those who accept [the authority of such scriptures] while subjecting them to investigation. (101)
these are the intermediate verses.

Therefore, although it is not external to inference, this means [of cognition] has been treated separately in order to demonstrate the distinction of its object, because it serves as a sublation. (102)

Precisely for this reason, because it is accepted as a sublation (*bādhana*), scripture (*āgama*), although not external to inference, is treated separately from inference. This is for the purpose of demonstrating a difference in their objects: inference is indeed a sublater, whereas scripture is an obstructer (*pratibandhaka*). And that [scripture] is an obstructer only when it is accepted, not otherwise.

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension, or the separate treatment would be purposeless; for if difference were a mere matter of words, there would be a contradiction even with one's own statement. (103)

If, however, one were to treat one’s own statement and the statement in a treatise as distinct from inference even in the absence of a specific purpose, it would be useless and would merely indicate the speaker’s lack of skill. In that case, how could there be a separate treatment of "contradiction by one's own statement" (*svavacanavirodha*) and "contradiction by what was previously accepted" (*pūrvābhyupagamavirodha*) within the *Nyāyamukha*? If those who speak contradictory meanings are sublated by their own words—as in the case of "everything spoken is false"—or by what was previously accepted—as in the case of an Ulūkyan (Vaiśeṣika) attempting to prove that sound is impermanent—then, since there is no difference in the underlying object (*viṣaya*), a separate illustration is indeed pointless.

[526,x] It is true that there is indeed no difference; nevertheless, since the latter [statement] subverts what was established by the former, there is a contradiction with one's own tenet (*abhyupagamavirodha*). Furthermore, because that very same statement subverts its own meaning, there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
[The opponent claims: "A treatise (*śāstra*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is accepted [as such]."
Therefore, because of that acceptance, the treatise is an authoritative means of knowledge regarding all things.
If it is argued that there is indeed a subverting proof (bādhaka); [526, xiii] if so—
If he does not accept that subverting proof, what else could there be? 104.
There would be a contradiction with one's own words, as well as a lack of distinction between contradiction with one's own words and contradiction with a treatise.

For if he did not desire it, how could that [treatise] be a sublater? Or if it were a sublater even when he desires it—[this is impossible], for the desire of one who is not an authority does not produce authority. What is gained by stating what was previously accepted in a different way later on? If it is done, [then there is a contradiction].

There is a contradiction; it is indeed a contradiction with one’s own words. If, then, a contradiction with one’s own words is admitted, it follows that there is no difference between a contradiction with one’s own words and a contradiction with a treatise (śāstra), and thus no distinction from sublation by a treatise.
And its status as a means of valid cognition, established by human desire, is fully accomplished. 105.

If the authority of a treatise (*śāstra*) is established by human intention, then that same [authority] is fully present in one's own words as well; therefore, there is no distinction between one's own words and the treatise. Now, if it is argued that the treatise is authoritative because it has been accepted for the sake of establishing its own subject matter, whereas one's own words are for the sake of another, and thus [the former] is not at all [authoritative], then indeed, in the case of what is for the sake of another, there is no great effort [to establish its authority].
That is incorrect; for: [527,v] If it were examined, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be the sublater (*bādhaka*) therein.
If no investigation has been undertaken, one's own word is not distinguished [from mere assertion].

(PVA 166) [527, vi] If that which is accepted has been investigated, then it is established by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object; thus, there is indeed a contradiction by valid cognition. On the other hand, if it has not been investigated, it is merely a verbal statement; therefore, there is no distinction between one's own word and scripture (*āgama*).
[(kha) A treatise is useless regarding matters that are established beyond perception.
Therefore, there is no harm even in abandoning a treatise with respect to matters that are already well-established.
When objects are beyond the senses and there is no acceptance of scripture, no inquiry whatsoever proceeds. (106)

[527, viii] The Blessed One said: “O monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the assistance of those seeking birth. What are the four? They are: physical food as gross nutriment; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, O monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the assistance of those seeking birth. What, O monks, is physical food as gross nutriment? It is the edible food that is coarse or subtle, whether it be masticated or drunk. This, O monks, is called physical food as gross nutriment. What, O monks, is contact as nutriment? Whatever contact there is, whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, this, O monks, is called contact as nutriment. What, O monks, is mental volition as nutriment? Whatever mental volition there is directed toward the realm of form, the realm of formlessness, or toward liberation, this, O monks, is called mental volition as nutriment. What, O monks, is consciousness as nutriment? Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—this, O monks, is called consciousness as nutriment. These, O monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the assistance of those seeking birth. Furthermore, O monks, when one has seen with right wisdom the origin of the nutriment of physical food as it really is, then one’s craving for physical food ceases. When one has seen with right wisdom the origin of the nutriment of contact as it really is, then one’s craving for contact ceases. When one has seen with right wisdom the origin of the nutriment of mental volition as it really is, then one’s craving for mental volition ceases. When one has seen with right wisdom the origin of the nutriment of consciousness as it really is, then one’s craving for consciousness ceases. And when craving has ceased, grasping ceases; when grasping has ceased, becoming ceases; when becoming has ceased, birth ceases; when birth has ceased, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, O monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Since there is no obstruction to inquiry regarding a subject (*dharmin*) established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no harm whatsoever even for one who abandons a treatise (*śāstra*); there is only a contradiction with one's own commitment (*abhyupagama*). Because it contradicts what has been accepted, this [contradiction] is not a clear case of contradiction with a treatise. However, when the subject is established by a treatise, since it is impossible to abandon that treatise, that very [subject] is the clear object of contradiction with a treatise. For if the scripture (*āgama*) is not accepted, no inquiry can even arise therein. If that is so, then by establishing that treatise, one establishes the subject; therefore, it subverts [the thesis]. But how then does that treatise, being itself without authority (*apramāṇaka*), establish the subject? [It does so] because it is accepted as authoritative. In that case, it is one's own acceptance alone that confers authority and establishes the subject. And that same [acceptance] is what opposes the other property (*dharmāntara*); thus, contradiction with a treatise does not differ from self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*).
[527,ix] Furthermore, the investigation here consists primarily in pointing out contradictions, as follows:
"Passion and the like are the root of unrighteousness, yet bathing is the purification of unrighteousness. (107)
And thus it has been said:
A mind that is corrupt within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
even if washed a hundred times, it remains as impure as a vessel that once held liquor.
(PVA 527, xii)
Furthermore, it is said:
"At Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Vilvakī, and the Blue Mountain."
Having bathed at the Kaṇakhala tīrtha, one shall not be born again.
(PVA) [527,xiv] It is illogical for this to be contradicted by common renown.
If, then, nothing at all is sublated and there is merely a contradiction, for what purpose is there the "contradiction with the acceptance of that"? To this he says:
[A treatise] which is not sublated by the reasoning established by itself, nor by its own words—
Whether [the object] is perceived or unperceived, the thought "that is to be grasped" arises. (108)

A treatise that is not contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or one’s own words must be accepted regarding both the seen and the unseen; otherwise, if it were accepted otherwise, one would be acting without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakārī*). That which is refuted by what is commonly recognized (*prasiddhinirākṛta*) is also not a [valid] thesis (*pakṣa*). In this context, “common recognition” is a mark of essential nature (*svabhāvaliṅga*), but it is not the word of a reliable person (*āptavacana*). For that [word] does not function in that way without such an actual state of affairs; how then could it be accepted as such? For in that case, the connection (*pratibandha*) is established by mere acceptance and is not established by valid cognition; thus, it is not a primary effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). If, however, the connection even for common recognition is real, then it is indeed a primary essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*). If [the connection] is established by acceptance, then—just like the word of a reliable person—it is merely a contradiction of that acceptance. So how can this be a separate form of sublation (*bādhā*)? Or rather, this is simply the sublation by a reliable person, since he will say: "The reliable person here is one whose speech is unimpaired. And in the phrase "by perception, object, inference, reliable person, and what is commonly recognized," the word "commonly recognized" (*prasiddha*) is connected with each term individually. Therefore, there are only three types of sublation.
[528,iii] That is incorrect.

Because of the statement, "That sublation is said to be fourfold through the division of inference," and because the Master [Dignāga] also demonstrated the fourfold nature by providing separate examples in the passage beginning with "yatrāpi... (even where...), it would not be established [otherwise].
To this, it is replied:

This first [argument] contradicts the entire world; furthermore, this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) has been formulated by oneself either in the form of an essential nature (*svabhāva*) or as an effect (*kārya*). (169) (PVA)
[528, vii] Sublation by what is established for all the world is "sublation by what is established" (prasiddhibādhā). Sublation by what is established only for oneself is the other kind.
[528, viii]

Alternatively, this is intended to demonstrate two types of *prasaṅga*-proofs: one in the form of a *svabhāva-hetu* (essential reason) and one in the form of a *kārya-hetu* (effect-reason). For indeed, only two things must be performed by a proponent: a primary proof and a *prasaṅga*-proof; there is no other mode of the proponent’s statements—this is for the sake of showing that.
Or else:

Since the meanings of words must always be understood by those engaged in worldly convention (*vyavahārin*), and not according to the tenets of the treatises (*śāstra*), it is for this reason— because of their non-difference— that there is no separate treatment of them. (PVA 170)
[528,xii] Even though it is not primary, the contradiction with common consensus must necessarily be accepted on the basis of the treatise; therefore, it is treated separately.
[528,xiii]

Now, since there is no difference whatsoever between a treatise and one’s own statement, the sublation by one’s own statement is indeed the same as sublation by the treatise. Therefore, by one who intends to establish something else and who initiates a dispute regarding a subject (*dharmin*) well-known in the treatise, the validity of both one’s own statement and the statements of the treatise must necessarily be admitted. So how can it be that such admission is not mandatory?

Even then, it is non-existent, because it is stated by way of the opponent’s own admission. For when engaging in debate, the opponents—the disputants—must necessarily accept a treatise (*śāstra*). Even in a dispute regarding the properties of another subject (*dharmin*), this is stated in order to establish that point; therefore, the treatise must necessarily be accepted. Alternatively, the separate mention of the "treatise" is for the purpose of excluding the intended object from the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); for in that case, there is no sublation of the intended meaning, such as the statement, "A woman is both a mother and a barren woman. Therefore:
The distinction of the object is intended here as being external or otherwise;
the division is based on the contradiction [of the former] by what is established in the treatise, and thus there is a difference. (PVA 171)

Furthermore, monks, one enters the womb with full awareness, remains therein with full awareness, but departs from the womb without full awareness. This, monks, is the second way of entering the womb. Furthermore, monks, one enters the womb without full awareness, remains therein without full awareness, but departs from the womb with full awareness. Furthermore, monks, one enters the womb without full awareness, remains therein without full awareness, and departs from the womb without full awareness. This, monks, is the fourth way of entering the womb. These, monks, are the four ways of entering the womb. Among these, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is one who enters the womb with full awareness, remains therein with full awareness, and departs from the womb with full awareness. Why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), is one who attains parinirvāṇa in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin*). Why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who attains parinirvāṇa in this very life. Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who goes upstream to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of nothingness. Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of infinite consciousness. Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of infinite space. Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*). Why is that? Because, monks, the Tathāgata has long cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Therefore, monks, the Tathāgata, having abandoned the five lower fetters, is one who dwells in the realm of the cessation of perception and feeling. Thus spoke the Blessed One. The incidental discussion is concluded; the main subject is now commenced. What is this so-called "notoriety" (*prasiddhi*)? If it refers to worldly notoriety, whether taken in its entirety or by way of a partial pervasion, then even [qualities] such as permanence would be universally renowned throughout the world; consequently, if one were to subvert them through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be a subversion of worldly notoriety, as well as of other things that contradict valid cognition. Nor is there any other meaning denoted by the word "notoriety," such as [the claim that] "a human skull is impure" and so forth. If, on the other hand, it is argued that it is improper to subvert what is recited in the scriptures, then there would likewise be a fault in subverting [doctrines] such as the permanent self (*ātman*).
[529,ii] To this it is replied:
Established renown (*prasiddhi*) is the state of being denotable by a desired word, provided it is unshakable.
For established renown is indeed linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*); it is so called because it arises from that [usage].

*Prasiddhi* is preeminent accomplishment (*prakṛṣṭā siddhiḥ*). Being denotable by a desired term arising from that [accomplishment] constitutes the nature of preeminent accomplishment; however, qualities such as permanence (*nityatva*) and so forth actually fluctuate. It is impossible for a treatise (*śāstra*) to render such things stable, for that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be subverted by a treatise.
Because it is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its status as a valid cognition is revoked.

(PVA 173) However, there is no such displacement of the inferential cognition regarding the fact that something is denotable by the word "intended" (*iṣṭaśabdābhidheyatva*), because there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) of that inference. This will be demonstrated accordingly. For, since being denotable by an intended word conforms to human desire, there is no application of an inferential sublater with respect to objects.
[(gha) The definition of a reliable authority:
For this very reason, he says: [529, vii]

Since it is not prohibited with respect to objects and follows the will of persons, the person here whose speech is unimpaired is one for whom the status of being denotable by desired words is accepted. (109)

[529,ix] For that which is denotable by a desired word is a universal form, such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which is conceptually constructed. It is impossible to negate it. Indeed, that which is constructed by mere intention cannot be excluded from the satisfaction of the conceptualized object. Certainly, what is well-known cannot be negated. And thus it is said: "(2) The relationship between word and object is conventional (*sāṃketika*)."

[529,x] But surely, only that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can serve as a sublater. To this it is replied: self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself is the means of valid cognition; for by that, the state of being denotable (*vācyatva*)—characterized by the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) with respect to the word—is established. If this is so, then since denotability is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) is indeed sublated by perception. If it is argued that only the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established by perception, and not some other relationship of the denoted and the denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*), we say no. The relationship of the denoted and the denoter consists in nothing more than that very [causal relationship]. How then can there be an acceptance of it otherwise? [529,xi]
To this it is replied:
Here, the state of being denotable (*vācyatva*) exists as a universal (*sāmānya*), established through its future and past states.
Therefore, since its manifestation is pervasive, how could there be a cognition of it through direct perception? (PVA) [529,
xiii] (Refutation of the Universal)
It is only because of the existence of such conventional usage that,
due to beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), it is perceived as "existing.

And so it will be said: "That too is accepted as participating in conventional usage. For the universal, characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is intended as the denotable object of the desired word. And that [universal] cannot be negated, because a corresponding cognition arises due to the specific restriction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*). And that mental impression, awakened by the restriction of convention established by mere desire, invariably establishes the universal. To illustrate: the nature of being a Brahmin and so forth is unmanifest; it is made determinate through a particular instance by means of desire.
By means of a word whose function is based on convention (*saṃketavṛtti*), there is the exclusion of others [from its referent].

(PVA 174) Indeed, universals such as "twice-born-ness" (*dvijatva*) cannot be manifested by an individual (*vyakti*) because they do not possess a fixed color or shape. Therefore, these [universals] attain manifestation solely through the power of a convention restricted to a particular individual, which is characterized by usage restricted to that individual.

[530,iii] Is it not the case that no convention has been established here at present, since there exists a denoted-denoter relationship established by beginningless intrinsic nature? No; for instruction itself constitutes the convention. Furthermore, the reason why one is a Brahmin or not a Brahmin is this very point. As for the claim that his status is caused by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit), that is what remains to be proven here; otherwise, what would distinguish these castes from those such as the Caṇḍālas? By this, the universal of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth is also refuted. For them too, there is no distinction from the universals of donkeys and the like. If it is argued that they are distinguished by being perceived [as such], [530,iv]...
The purpose here is merely the capacity for carrying loads, yielding milk, and so forth;
therefore, being characterized by that [capacity] is not at all inconsistent in this context.

Likewise, for universals such as "cow" and the like, the very definition is that they are the objects of a single word. Therefore, a universal is nothing other than an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus, because its existence is attained merely through conventional renown (*prasiddhi*), that property is born of linguistic usage. It is expressed by the word "renown.
Thus it has been said: "The property born of that linguistic usage is what is denoted by the word 'renown'."
vii] This dharma is not expressed solely by the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) characterized as being established for the proponent; rather, [530,
viii]...
Those [objects] measured by perception and other means are indicated through the superimposition of the term "means of valid cognition" (māna). 110.

Even objects established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) serve as subverters (*bādhaka*) of another object known as a "pseudo-thesis" (*pakṣābhāsa*). Therefore, since the property of being denotable by the word "intended" (*iṣṭaśabdābhidheyatva*) cannot be negated in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, the negation is subverted by that very fact. For it is well known that no sane person would negate a designation—such as "physician" (*vaidya*) and so on—which has been established by applying a word for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). He says this very thing:

Because those things which arise based on that [consciousness] proceed according to one's will and do not exclude [other possibilities], the entire universe is by its very nature suitable for both what has been done and what has not been done. (111)

[530,xi] By its very nature, the universe is fit for the various conventional usages that arise based upon it—such as "cowness" and so forth—whether those usages have been produced or not, and whether they are about to be explained by oneself or not; for the universe is everywhere non-opposing. Non-opposition itself is fitness (*yogyatā*). Therefore:
Whether it be future or past, that which conforms to the mere object is sublated by one who opposes it through its fitness for verbal expression.

[530, xiii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, illuminated and observed how all phenomena are empty, and thus delivered those suffering beings. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. Among them were the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the venerable Revata, the venerable Ānanda, and others such as these—five hundred bhikṣus in total. There were also many bodhisattvas mahāsattvas present, including the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Gaganagañja, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajramati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya, and others such as these—immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. Furthermore, there were gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as kings, ministers, elders, householders, and brahmins, who had all come to the place where the Buddha was staying. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, for what reason does the Tathāgata smile? It is not without cause or condition that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, manifest a smile. Having said this, he further addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, what kind of merit will they obtain? Having said this, the venerable Śāriputra remained silent. At that time, the venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts of the venerable Śāriputra, addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying: “Venerable Śāriputra, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this *prajñāpāramitā* being taught, they will obtain immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless merit. Why is this so?
