Indeed, neither potentiality (*bhāvinī*) nor actualized capacity (*bhūtā*) can be negated by a prohibition in the case of a word such as "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice" with respect to the eating of dog-meat and the like. This is because [the capacity] conforms to the mere object (*arthamātrānurodhitvāt*). In that context, capacity is simply the non-opposition (*apratikūlatā*) toward that object. For no object whatsoever—whether perceived or understood through instruction—is seen to be opposed to the act of eating. The word "mere" (*mātra*) is intended to include all things without distinction, just as in the expression "Feed the Brāhmaṇas alone," one desires merely the act of feeding and does not intend to restrict it to a specific subset. And since this capacity conforms to the mere object, there is no logical justification for a prohibition in that regard.

Therefore, the negator is sublated by that very same capacity [of cognition]. For the negatability of capacity is not established by perception; at most, inference might apply, but it will be demonstrated that such inference is impossible due to the absence of an example.

"But surely the Teacher has said that [the object] is not [negated] by what is well-known through verbal testimony. [To this we reply: There is no sublation by way of fitness (*yogyatā*). For fitness does not consist in being denotable by the intended word, nor is there such established usage (*prasiddhatā*). Indeed, fitness is the cause of established usage, but it is not established usage itself.
To this, it is said:
By the very power of its suitability, sound is in fact produced from the jar;
therefore, even if that [jar] is not perceived, its establishment [as the cause] follows from that [sound]. (113)

[531,v] This is precisely the Master’s intention as well: that it is *yogyatā* (fitness) alone that is established by the expression “well-known through linguistic usage,” and not an already accomplished denotability (*vācyatā*). And this *yogyatā* conforms merely to [the speaker’s] intention; it is a lack of incompatibility with respect to the convention (*saṃketa*).
For the operation of a word occurs everywhere toward an object by mere intention;
how then could a word that operates only upon that [intention] apply to anything at all?
(PVA 176) Indeed, an object does not cause its designator to operate by virtue of its own nature.
Non-contrariety with respect to a convention is designated as "fitness" (yogyatā). (177) (PVA) That which is a creation by means of desire is precisely the conformity to the mere object.
How could there be a desire for a convention if there were no expectation even regarding the mere object? (178) (PVA)

When the negation of the denotability of the word "wheel" is applied to a jar, it is intended that the proof rests upon conventional usage (*prasiddhi*); this is the method [to be followed]. (179) (PVA) [531,x]
— These are the intermediate verses.
[531,xi] Now, [one might ask]: "Non-opposition is fitness; how can that be future or past? To this it is replied:
[531,xii] Since the object has become existent, its capacity is likewise of that same nature;
for no so-called "capacity" is observed to be distinct from the essential nature [of the object] itself. (PVA 180)

In this regard, whatever object is intended to be expressed by a particular word is fit to be expressed by that word; for example, by the word "tree," there is no contradiction whatsoever for anyone anywhere.
[Objection: But surely the example itself is not established, since a refutation is possible even in that case.

[Reply: This is not so. Once the conventional usage of the relationship between the signified and the signifier has been set in motion, what is there to be refuted? For people are seen to engage in it through the comprehension of its object. Indeed, this very thing is the relationship between the signified and the signifier. And thus it has been said:
When a certain meaning is understood upon the utterance of a word, that is said to be the meaning of that word; this is not the definition for one who holds a different view. (PVA 181)
If this is so, then the meaning of the thesis is already contradicted by direct perception; what is the use of contradicting it by means of common consensus?
To this it is replied: not only this much is to be established here, but furthermore:
All words are considered to be denotative of something in some place or at some time;
for by this reasoning, perception does not operate here [in such matters].

This has already been stated: even when the status of being denotable by the word "moon" is denied of a jar, there is still a contradiction with established convention (*prasiddhi*). Now, if it is argued that "this does not appear to me as being denotable by this word," that would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, it is argued that it does not appear to another person, or not at this particular time, or that [the object] is not suitable [for such a designation], then this [objection] is invalid, because [linguistic usage] occurs merely through the will [of the speaker]. Why is it not possible [that a different relation exists]? For in other places, times, or among other people, the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is seen to be otherwise; so how can there be a fixed restriction? By this principle, everything is accepted as being denotable by every [word], and thus there is no fault.
The meaning of the statement "one should eat dog-meat," which is prohibited because it contradicts common experience, is sublated by its lack of semantic fitness (*yogyatva*). (PVA 183)
If it is argued that "this flesh and so forth now appears as such an object," then there would be a contradiction with direct perception; otherwise, how could this be? (184) (PVA) [532,iii]

For there is no sublation by perception here; there is only sublation by common cognition. And that too occurs solely by virtue of convention through fitness. Or rather, such fitness exists even in the case of dog-meat and the like.
[Sublation by the Veda] (532.iv)

[Objection: Is it not the case that this lack of restriction applies only to those worldly words which are dependent upon convention? As for those Vedic words, however, whose connection with their objects is natural (*svābhāvika*), how could there be a lack of restriction? Furthermore, convention is established for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*) only within the domain of perceptible objects; since there is no means of cognition regarding that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), how is one capable of establishing a convention for it? Since cognition would rely solely on scripture (*āgama*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Nor is it logical for one who follows that scripture to establish a convention otherwise. [Reply: To this it is said:
[532, vi] But surely, by whom was this Veda established as possessing its inherent meaning?
An ignorant person might establish a convention there, or a wise person out of hatred, compassion, and so forth. (PVA 185)

Just as a convention regarding fire and so forth being used for burning and so forth is established by one person according to his own will, so too is it established even for dogs and other such things. It is not proven that this meaning is inherent (*svābhāvika*), because its determination is made in accordance with worldly usage. And in the world:
[532, viii]
The perception of objects as manifold due to differences in place, time, and so forth,
does not constitute a certainty regarding an object that pervades those places, times, and so on.

In that regard, sometimes an ignorant person alone might establish a convention or provide an instruction concerning place, time, and so forth. If there were merely a succession of such instructions, it would be a "blind tradition. Therefore, a convention established otherwise is for the purpose of setting aside those who are inclined toward that [ignorant view]. Alternatively, there is no contradiction, as it may be one who perceives supersensible objects who establishes it, having avoided any prior apprehension of the object that could lead to error. Or else: even here, perception does not occur at all upon the occasion of conceptual determination.
From the word "moon," there is no cognition of the lunar mansion without an inference.

It is not logical for the cognition of an object from a word to be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As the proponent of the Veda says: "The cognition of an object from the words of the Veda is indeed direct perception. If it is argued that this cognition is direct perception because its nature is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then his established tenet (*samaya*) is contradicted; or else, [it is not direct perception] because it has another cognition as its objective support, since it is established that "cognition is not [itself] directly perceived. Or, if you accept [that it is direct perception], then one might say that the cognition of fire from smoke is also direct perception. If it is argued that it would be so because it lacks the form of inference—even for one who cognizes fire from a single instance of smoke—then [we reply]: in that case, there was a prior recollection (*anusandhāna*) here as well at the time of the convention (*saṃketa*). Otherwise, even for one who follows an explanation, the explanation itself is the convention. If it is argued that the explanation is not [the convention] because the convention is merely something created by one's own will, then this fault does not apply.

This is not so. It has already been demonstrated that an interpretation may be formulated otherwise than through hatred and the like. If it is argued that the explanation is established through the elision of phonemes (*varṇalopa*), etymological derivation (*nirukta*), and so forth due to its being Vedic (*chāndasa*), and that it is an interpretation based on the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*); [we reply: it is likewise [untenable].
If it were arrived at through a succession of explanations, it would be a "succession of the blind.
Therefore, it possesses neither direct perception nor inference as its means of establishment, since there is no absence of defects.
(PVA 532, xiv)

Therefore, even in the case of "the moon is *śaśin*," there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*) here either. And so it has been stated: "For words and logical marks (*liṅga*) convey their own objects only by depending on the observation or non-observation and the recollection of the presence or absence of that [object]. In this context, one who says "that which is the moon is *śaśin* because it possesses a hare (*sattva*)" does not say that such a cognition does not exist at all. For if that were the case, there would be a contradiction with cognition (*pratītibādhā*). Even if cognition is indeed direct perception, it may still be false, like the cognition of two moons. Thus, a contradiction with cognition is demonstrated for that [position].
Because it arises from the recollection of preceding [perceptions], its status as inference is established;
therefore, this sublation by inference is accepted by the authors of the treatises.
Since the cognition of the relationship occurs at the time of convention,
it follows that the stability of the world is a factor of essential nature (*svabhāvāṅga*); thus it is established.

[533,v] But surely this is an inference; how then can it be a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*)? For the cognition produced from a word, aided by previous perception, is of the nature of an inference and serves as a sublater. Yet a word is not the essential identity of the object.
If the relationship between word and object were indeed that of cause and effect, then cognition from a word would be an inference; such being the case, it would be a form of inferential knowledge.

Cognition [of the object] arises from inference; thus, there is a dependence upon a relationship (*sambandha*). And that relationship between the word and the object is one of material cause and its effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhāva*). Furthermore, in the ultimate sense, the word is produced solely by the activity of the palate and other vocal organs, not by the object to be expressed. Therefore, here the relationship of cause and effect is established through intention (*icchā*), like a hand gesture (*hastamudrā*) and so forth, and not otherwise. For a causal relationship imagined through intention is not real, like the connection between a rope and a peg. Nor is such a cognition necessarily inevitable. Consequently, this [inference] is not primary. How then is it a reason based on essential identity (*svabhāva-hetu*)? That object which serves as the material cause and is manifested through convention (*saṃketa*) is made to be such by intention. In the ultimate sense, it possesses the nature of a cause, because it exists even in the absence of the desire to express that specific object—whether there is a desire to express something else or no desire at all. Moreover, that without which something else exists cannot be the cause of the latter. Therefore: [The verse: "Because it is produced by the activity of the palate and so forth, and because it is intended, it is a reason based on essential identity. [The commentary: It is produced by the activity of the palate and so forth, and it is also produced by the intention to speak. Therefore, it is a reason based on essential identity. It is not a reason based on non-perception (*anupalabdhi-hetu*), because it is not a negation. Nor is it a reason based on effect (*kārya-hetu*), because there is no necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the object. Thus, it is a reason based on essential identity. Alternatively, it may be considered a reason based on non-perception: since the object is not perceived when the word is present, the word is the means of negating the object. However, this is not the case, because the object is indeed perceived. Therefore, it is not a reason based on non-perception either. Consequently, it must be a reason based on essential identity. Since it is an effect, it is a reason based on effect. This is the meaning. Alternatively, it is a reason based on essential identity: the object is the material cause of the word. Why? Because it is produced by the activity of the palate and so forth, and because it is intended. It is produced by the activity of the palate and so forth, and it is also produced by the intention to speak. Therefore, it is an effect of the object. Since it is an effect, it is a reason based on effect
Its status as the denotable is established merely by its being intended as the basis of appropriation (*upādāna*).
When its nature has reached the state of being constituted solely by that [conceptualization], it becomes expressible.

Denotability is merely the establishment [of a thing] by way of being a material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) precisely by way of being a material cause is what constitutes established reality (*prasiddhi*). Since it is established through conventional usage, the status of being a material cause is also established. Consequently, the fact that something is inexpressible is not contradicted when it appears as a material cause. For if something does not appear as the effect of a material cause for another thing, it is at most inexpressible; because that thing would not appear from the word. If that object were not to appear as the cognition of the effect of a material cause even when there is a desire [to speak], it would be inexpressible.

[Objection: But surely it does not appear at all, for there is no status as a material cause (*upādānatā*) for an external object; this has already been stated, since [the cognition] exists even in the absence of that [object]. [Reply: No, because it appears when there is a desire [to speak]. For when, upon seeing an object, there is an application [of words] through the desire to express it due to extreme habituation, why then does its status as a material cause not appear? Alternatively, if it is said thus because the external object does not appear to the cognizer, then inference also would not have an external object as its domain, precisely because it does not appear therein. Or, if it is said thus regarding the real thing (*vastu*) itself by means of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then the same applies to its being denotable (*vācyatva*). As for the attainment of the external object, it occurs at all times; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the cognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor, even if it were a valid means of knowledge, would there be an absence of the relationship between denoter and denoted (*vācyavācakabhāva*), because the relationship between denoter and denoted is established precisely in such a manner. Therefore:
Whatever object exists as a substratum by virtue of being a material cause must necessarily be denotable;
and that status as a material cause cannot be obstructed by mere desire. (PVA 192)
Every object that is the domain of such conventional renown is said to be denotable.
Therefore, because its operation depends upon the speaker's intention, there is no restriction regarding *dhvani*.
(PVA 533, xiv)
— This is the summary.
[533,xv] Therefore, it is precisely the teacher’s capacity that is intended by the term "renowned" (prasiddha).
If it is asked why this is so, it is said in response:
By that [argument], uniqueness is not established in the case of the word;
for that [uniqueness] would not exist if it were not accepted that everything is denotable due to its fitness.
He says this very thing:
otherwise, there would be no uniqueness for the subverting reason here.

[534,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; there is no such dharma by which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti replied: "As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata’s body made of real flesh? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata’s body is not made of real flesh. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata’s body is a Body of Dharma (dharmakāya). The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of physical marks? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the possession of physical marks. Why is that? Because the possession of physical marks spoken of by the Blessed One is itself not a possession of physical marks; therefore it is called the 'possession of physical marks. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-system with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti replied: "Yes, Blessed One; yes, Sugata; that person would produce much merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is that merit a substantial thing? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; that merit is not a substantial thing. Why is that? Because the Blessed One has said that merit is non-merit; therefore it is called 'merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the possession of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Why is that? Because the possession of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man spoken of by the Blessed One is itself not a possession of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; therefore it is called the 'possession of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If a woman or man were to grind as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā into fine powder and divide them so that each grain of dust represents one world-system, and if they were to go through all those world-systems, dropping a single grain of dust at each, until all the world-systems were exhausted, would those world-systems be numerous? Subhūti replied: "Yes, Blessed One; yes, Sugata; those world-systems would be very numerous. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill all those world-systems with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti replied: "Yes, Blessed One; yes, Sugata; that person would produce much merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is that merit a substantial thing? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; that merit is not a substantial thing. Why is that? Because the Blessed One has said that merit is non-merit; therefore it is called 'merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to teach and explain this perfection of wisdom even to a single sentient being, would that person on account of that produce much merit? Subhūti replied: "Yes, Blessed One; yes, Sugata; that person would produce much merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is that merit a substantial thing? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; that merit is not a substantial thing. Why is that? Because the Blessed One has said that merit is non-merit; therefore it is called 'merit. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma by which he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma by which he has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma that he has taught? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma that he has taught. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma that has come from somewhere or gone anywhere? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma that has come from somewhere or gone anywhere. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata perceive any dharma that is established in the world? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma that is established in the world. Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One; the Tathāgata does not perceive any dharma that is not established in the world. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? If the Teacher’s intention were not toward [the property of] fitness (*yogyatā*), how could the inference that serves as a sublater (*bādhaka*) be an "uncommon" reason (*asādhāraṇahetu*)? This is because [the reason] "existence" (*sattva*) is established in things such as pots, which are not denotable by the word "moon. For when [fitness] is the [intended] object, everything would indeed be its denotation; however, it is not established in anything that is not the moon. And the Teacher said: "Even where there is an absence of inference due to being uncommon, that is not a [valid] subject (*pakṣa*) when it is set aside by a contradictory meaning established through verbal convention (*śabdaprasiddha*). In whatever domain an opposing inference is uncommon, for that very reason there is an absence [of that inference]. In the absence [of that inference], the verbal-convention-based inference is the sublater; that is not a [valid] subject. He spoke thus to demonstrate the impossibility of negating this, or rather, to establish certainty through a counter-means of valid cognition (*pratipramāṇa*). For there can be no negation without a means of valid cognition, nor can there be uncertainty when a determinative [means of knowledge] exists. And in this case:

The latter is conjoined with the former, and the former is conjoined with the latter; when the existence of both the subsequent and the prior meanings is present, this pair is fully operative. (195) (PVA)

[534, vii] When, first of all, the primacy belongs to the preceding member—which is well-known through verbal testimony—and it functions as a qualifier, then there is certainty in the absence of a counter-proof (*pratipramāṇa*). But when the subsequent member functions as the qualifier and the preceding member has primacy, then its negation is impossible.
[534, viii]

Now, even if inference is indeed unique [to its object], how can it be impossible to negate? For inference alone is not the only means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since perception (*pratyakṣa*) also exists.
To this, the following is the rebuttal:
The negation of that [non-existence] must proceed from inference, because the word does not function with respect to the sensory object. (114)
[534,xi] But is it not so?
That form which is well-known through verbal testimony is, for that reason, perception; it is not inference.
Is the statement regarding "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatva) not then rendered useless?

No; because the sense-faculties do not operate upon the object of a word. For the object of a word cannot be directly perceived. Even if the "fitness" (yogyatā) determined as being the object of a word appears when the object established by verbal cognition functions in practical activity (*vyavahāra*), nevertheless, one should not act upon it [as if it were that object]; thus, there is a negation of its fitness. Or, [it refers to] the connection with the word of that which is appearing. And such a connection is not within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The word appears in auditory consciousness, whereas its object appears in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) or in visual consciousness. Furthermore, there is no mutual confusion of the objects of these two.

But surely, since fire and smoke also appear in the cognition of their own objects, how can this [distinction] hold? The same applies to odor and the bearer of odor, and so forth. Let this fault apply there as well; nevertheless, that [point] remains unestablished. For those [objects] are grasped by sensory cognition, and thus there is no fault. In this case, however, it is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone that grasps the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cognition, not its denotative capacity. Furthermore, a pervasive relation does not appear in perception. Nor is verbal usage consistent with reality. Therefore, it is not within the scope of perception, because perception has only real entities (*vastu*) as its object. Consequently, this [relation] is exclusively within the scope of inference.

For when existence (*sattva*), which pervades all things, is made the unique [reason] in a given case, what need is there to speak of anything else that does not so pervade—that wretched thing? Indeed, one who is capable of refuting a powerful opponent does not tolerate another [weaker] alternative for that purpose. It is for this very reason that he taught the thesis (*pakṣa*) together with its logical reason (*hetu*): "The rabbit-marked one (*śaśin*) is not the moon (*acandra*), because it exists (*sattvāt*). Otherwise, in the context of introducing fallacious theses (*pakṣābhāsa*), what occasion would there be for stating a reason? Otherwise, one would also have to state a reason for such claims as "sound is inaudible" or "a pot is eternal. If you argue that a reason is impossible in a case where the subject is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādhita*), then the same would apply here; thus, your objection is trivial.
[535,iii] But has it not already been stated that he showed this [reason] to be impossible to refute? For the same consequence would apply even in the case of the term "inaudible" (aśrāvaṇa).
To this it is replied:
This is indeed established by verbal testimony; it is not said to be a primary means of valid cognition.
"Therefore, there is no absence of a counter-argument; thus, here there is faultlessness.

(PVA) [535, vi] In this case, a subverting argument is possible, but not in the case of perception and inference. Therefore, it will be stated that by refuting [the former] here, the absence of a counter-argument for inference has been declared.
[535,vii] How, then, is there an impossibility of an antidote? For not everything is expressible.
[535,viii]
Thus he says:
[535,ix] Words depend upon convention, and that convention depends solely upon desire.
"There is no non-establishment of those things established by words"—this is the statement regarding what is established through verbal testimony. (116)

[535,x] Every verbal form is indeed well-established, because it exists merely as a word whose convention is set in motion by mere intention (*icchāmātra*). For there is no place where a word cannot be applied. It is for this very purpose that the statement "by what is established through verbal usage" (*śābdaprasiddhena*) and so forth was made. Otherwise, it would have been impossible to demonstrate its lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇatā*); this has already been stated.

But surely, if there is an absence of inference, then what is established by verbal testimony is uncontradicted; yet if there is no contradiction, there is an absence of inference—thus there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Nor can the fact that something proceeds from mere whim be established by itself.

The validity of existence established through verbal testimony is intrinsic. (PVA 198) For the absence of a counter-argument, which is established by verbal testimony, does not depend on mere wishful thinking nor is it disregarded because of anything else; this is because its strength is intrinsic. Furthermore, a negation that is itself unimpeded is not a means of proof by virtue of being intrinsic.

[Objection: But surely existence (*sattva*) is perceived as being inexpressible (*avācya*). Therefore, because it is pervaded by inexpressibility, why does [the word] not constitute a negation? [Reply: No, for it has been stated that what is set in motion by mere whim cannot be negated. However, if existence is inexpressible, how can it be expressed by the very word "existence"? Therefore, because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), the fact that [the object] is established by verbal convention (*śābdaprasiddha*)—which is not sublated—is indeed a sublation [of the contrary]. If, however, there were a suspicion of sublation even toward that which is itself sublated, then the relationship of the sublated and the sublator would never exist anywhere, and the world would become a state of non-comprehension. Therefore, it is only that which is established by verbal convention that constitutes the sublation, not its opposite. And thus:

[535,xv] Thus, in cases where [the object] is to be established by inference, [the author] demonstrates the absence of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin); for inference proceeds from such cognition. 117.

By the expression "established by verbal convention" (*śābdaprasiddha*), he shows that it is not [refuted] by a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*). Just as this inference is without a counter-argument, so too is any other. Even that [other inference], because it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) when a counter-argument is possible, would not be subverting, exactly like [the inference] established by verbal convention. Therefore, since that too is non-common (*asādhāraṇa*) to the counter-argument, it serves as its proof. For example: "There is fire here, because there is smoke"; versus "There is no fire here, because there is existence," [which is] like a place devoid of fire.

[Objection: "But surely, since denotative power is set in motion by mere intention (*icchāmātra*), even a jar could possess the nature of the moon; thus, there is no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*). In this case, a place that is not fire certainly exists. [Response: This is not so.
In the case of a sublation by what is established through verbal convention (*śābdaprasiddha*), there would be the fault of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatā*).
In this case as well, why would there not be a sublation of the [proponent's] reason by means of the effect of the entity?
For when fire has been established in a particular location by inference, why is it not accepted as the prover of the negation of that very fire? (200) (PVA)
The suspicion of sublation by a contrary factor has already been refuted.
Therefore, in every case of valid cognition, no counter-entity exists.

Therefore, there is no possibility of a "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) in inference based on the power of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta*). Otherwise, if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) could be sublated, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases. If it is argued that there is confidence where no such [sublation] is observed, we say no; for mere non-perception is not a means of valid cognition. Even if sublation were possible, it could not be suspected because it has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). By this, the intention to express a singular number is refuted; for that [singular term] also indicates either mere non-perception or a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). If it indicates mere non-perception, then since that is not a means of valid cognition, it amounts to nothing. If, however, it indicates a necessary connection, then there is no possibility of a non-deviating contradiction, because another [reason] possessing a necessary connection cannot exist there, since one thing cannot simultaneously have both existence and non-existence. Therefore, in inference proceeding by the force of real entities, there is an absence of the non-deviating contradictory.

[536,vii] Now, if it is argued that by the statement "there is an absence of inference due to its being over-exclusive" (asādhāraṇatva), one indicates the absence of the "non-deviant contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārin), then why is this not stated specifically regarding inference itself? For even in a case where there is an absence of inference due to over-exclusiveness, the subject (pakṣa) is set aside by a contradictory object established through either an effect-reason (kāryahetu) or an essential-nature reason (svabhāvahetu). The same should be said for perception as well.
[536,viii]
This is nothing at all; for by this very [argument], perception and inference have already been explained.

As for one who says: "A real entity does not exist as an object of perception, because it is a cognition, like the cognition of hair, mosquitoes, and so forth, by one suffering from ophthalmia," the following is the reply to him:
The negation of non-existence is effected by means of an entity whose necessary connection is established; for if there were existence, the entity would indeed be present everywhere. (PVA 202)

[536,xi] If it is argued that when a condition is devoid of an impediment, the object is either doubtful or otherwise, then what has already been established would be proven. Alternatively, if it were the opposite, then since the object exists everywhere, the counter-position would lack a common locus (asādhāraṇatā).

Now, it may be argued that neither inference nor anything else can subvert perception, because it is directly perceived. And how can that which is directly seen be established as non-existent? For it is impossible for both the seeing and the non-seeing of the very same thing to occur at the same time. [Objection: But surely the proof of non-existence is by means of another reason (*hetvantara*), not by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*). [Reply: This is not correct, because: *pratyakṣe ’pi yathā deśe smaryamāṇe ca cetasā | viśiṣṭarūpābhāvasya gamakatvam na duṣyati ||* Even when a place is perceived and remembered by the mind, the capacity of the absence of a specific form to indicate [non-existence] is not impaired. *na hy anyopalabdhyānyasyābhāvaḥ sidhyati |* *abhāvo hi viśiṣṭasya rūpasyānupalambhanam ||* For the non-existence of one thing is not established by the apprehension of another; rather, non-existence is simply the non-apprehension of a specific form. *anyathārthasya nāstitvaṃ gamyate ’nupalambhataḥ |* *upalambhasya nāstitvam anyenety anavasthitiḥ ||* Otherwise, the non-existence of an object is understood through non-apprehension, while the non-existence of that apprehension itself would have to be understood by something else, leading to an infinite regress. *anupalambhātmakatve ’pi pratyakṣasyāsti ced gatiḥ |* *sābhyupāyasya nānyasyeti bhedaḥ kiṃkṛto ’nayoh ||* If it is granted that perception, though consisting of non-apprehension, has this cognitive function, but it does not belong to any other [means of knowledge], then what is the basis for this distinction between these two? *anumānānumeyavyavahāro buddhyārūḍhena rūpeṇa |* *bāhyārthāśrayo ’pi san ||* The conventional practice of inference and the inferred, although based on external objects, occurs by means of forms mounted upon the intellect. *na khalu kaścit pratyakṣeṇa padārthasvabhāvo dṛṣṭo yaḥ punar dṛśyate |* *tasmād dṛṣṭasya darśanam anupalabdhir eva ||* Indeed, no nature of an object is ever seen by perception such that it could be seen again; therefore, the seeing of what was already seen is nothing but non-apprehension. *ato ’nupalabdher eva sarvatra pratiṣedhasiddhiḥ |* *saiva ca viśiṣṭābhāvapratipattihetur iti sthitam ||* Thus, the establishment of negation in all cases proceeds from non-apprehension alone; and it is established that this very [non-apprehension] is the cause for the cognition of a specific absence.
[536,xiv] There is no sublation of any cognition whatsoever by means of what has been directly perceived;
for if that were the case, then every cognition would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) without distinction. (PVA 203)

[537,i] For even in the case of an erroneous cognition that directly perceives the form of hair and so forth, there is no sublation; therefore, validity does not follow from mere direct perception alone.

By this, the state of being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*) is also refuted. For uncontradictedness, unlike direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), is not by its very nature over-pervasive (*ativyāpin*). If it is argued that "it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when there is non-contradiction and it is uncontradicted," this follows the maxim: "Having obtained the *harītakī* fruit, the deity causes purging. If non-contradiction exists, what is the use of non-contradiction? There is no fault through non-contradiction alone. Furthermore, that non-contradiction does not reside in that which is appearing. And that which is to be understood is not appearing, because it is connected to the appearing form. And since that form of connection is the same in inference as well, the possibility of a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) applies to both equally, or rather, it does not apply anywhere at all; thus, it is the same. Therefore, even perception is not a means of valid cognition by virtue of being a direct realization.
For this very reason, he says:
Since there is no cognition in the absence of the object, even in the case of perception, its status as a means of valid cognition is established;
and since that which possesses a nature necessarily connected to it is the cause of that cognition, both cases are equal.
For indeed, the basis for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely the absence of obstruction (*pratibandha*).

Now, one might ask: why was it not stated that there is an absence of inference (*anumāna*) in that very case of perception (*pratyakṣa*) in order to demonstrate its lack of a counter-position (*apratipakṣatva*), if this were the intended purpose? Because there is no purpose in deviating from the established sequence.
This is not correct, because:
[537, viii]
The validity of that which is not established by verbal testimony is free from contradiction;
it is for the purpose of declaring this that the refutation of counter-measures has been stated here.

If, in that case, the removal of obstructing means of knowledge is said to apply to perception or inference, then the efficacy of inference based on what is established through verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*) would remain unobstructed and unestablished. Consequently, there would be a bypassing of what was first encountered. Furthermore:
even in an inference that is not firmly established, where there is no counter-inference (*apratyanumānatā*), [the same would follow].

In that case, this mature inference has already been refuted from afar. For where even an immature verbal inference (*śābda*), being unopposed, serves as the cause for rendering [the subject] unique (*asādhāraṇīkaraṇa*), there a more mature one is established without effort precisely by virtue of being unopposed.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that everything is indeed fit for being denoted by the word 'desired' (*iṣṭa*), according to the principle that fitness (*yogyatā*) is simply the absence of opposition (*aprātikūlya*)? In this regard, the inference would proceed solely by the force of the real object (*vastubala*), because it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [Reply: No, because there is likewise an absence of favorability (*ānukūlya*). Just as its opposition is not perceived, so too is its favorability [not perceived] either through direct perception or from any other source. Therefore, how could this [inference] proceed by the force of the real object? In this context, the purpose to be established here is this very point: if, in an inference based on what is well-known through verbal convention (*śābdaprasiddha*), a property derived merely from desire (*icchāmātra*) is not contradicted by a real entity, then how could that [property] be derived from the force of an essential connection (*pratibandha*)? This alone is the objective to be demonstrated here.
[537,xiii] But is it not so?
One who is dependent solely upon mere desire is certainly not obstructed,
because that [desire] is always present and is constantly realized.
However, that which arises through the power of real entities might not exist anywhere at all.

For there is no necessity of causes with respect to their effects. (208) Therefore, there might be a suspicion of sublation regarding a means of valid cognition that pertains to a real entity; thus, it is only in that case that this refutation of sublation is appropriate. (209)
The reasoning and the refutation that were stated regarding the *daṇḍāyūpa* do not apply here; for there is no sequence of transgression following the first transgression.
(PVA 210) [537, xviii]
To this it is replied:
inference occurs because the relationship [between the reason and the probandum] is established through mere conventional usage regarding the operation upon non-entities.
How can there be any deliberation regarding a matter that is not sublated [by valid cognition], yet where the sublation of another [position] will occur?
(211) (PVA) One who understands the object in this way does not lack conformity with the principles of logic;
for since the application [of a rule] is dependent upon one's own desire, even the abandonment [of a position] is seen to occur when that [desire] is abandoned. (212) (PVA)
Even the renunciation of that which is desired and brought about by pleasure is, for him, merely a formality;
yet in reality, it is not so, for the mountain cannot be shaken.
(213) Thus, if this entire collection of practices following wrong paths were entirely free from doubt, then this would indeed be the conduct of the supreme sages, and not mere ignorance.
How could there be a perception of evils here for those nihilists whose eyes are impaired, since they do not perceive things in their manifest state?
(PVA 214) Therefore, it is correct that the demonstration of the absence of sublation applies to this very case.
Alternatively, it is stated that for the speaker, there is an absence of inference regarding the relationship between the designation (*saṃjñā*) and the designated object (*saṃjñin*).
But how can there be a cognition with a different object from that [perception] by means of inference? (118)

[538,xi] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive contact as real, nor does he perceive feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not perceive form as real, nor perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real? How does he not perceive the eye as real, nor perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real? How does he not perceive forms as real, nor perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real? How does he not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real? How does he not perceive contact as real, nor perceive feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real? The Blessed One said to Subhūti: “It is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real; it is because feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of perception, mental formations are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental formations, and consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. It is because the eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye, the ear is empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear, the nose is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose, the tongue is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue, the body is empty of the intrinsic nature of the body, and the mind is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. It is because forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms, sounds are empty of the intrinsic nature of sounds, odors are empty of the intrinsic nature of odors, tastes are empty of the intrinsic nature of tastes, tangibles are empty of the intrinsic nature of tangibles, and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental phenomena that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. It is because eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-consciousness that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. It is because contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of contact, feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, craving is empty of the intrinsic nature of craving, grasping is empty of the intrinsic nature of grasping, becoming is empty of the intrinsic nature of becoming, birth is empty of the intrinsic nature of birth, and aging-and-death are empty of the intrinsic nature of aging-and-death that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and if feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, then what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom? What is the perfection of wisdom that the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices? Who is it that will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? Who is it that will turn the wheel of Dharma? Who is it that will lead the assembly of disciples? The Blessed One said to Subhūti: “It is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, that there is no bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom, no perfection of wisdom that the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices, no one who will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, no one who will turn the wheel of Dharma, and no one who will lead the assembly of disciples. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, and it is because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, turns the wheel of Dharma, and leads the assembly of disciples. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature, then what dharma does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? What dharma does he fully awaken to? What dharma does he teach? What dharma does he lead? The Blessed One said to Subhūti: “It is because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, and it is because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that he fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, teaches the Dharma, and leads the assembly of disciples. Regarding the passage beginning with *yatrāpi* (even where): the connection is that even where there is no inferential proof (*anumāna*) because of its uncommonness (*asādhāraṇatva*), [the word] is established. For an inference based on the fact of being denotable by the word "moon" does not arise through the power of the thing itself (*vastubalabhāvin*). If, then, there is no proving inference, [one might ask] how the non-existence of the opposite is established. [The answer is: when the non-existence is established through verbal convention (*śābdaprasiddha*), it cannot be set aside by a contradictory [inference]. By this negation of inference, it is demonstrated that this is not an inference arising from the power of the thing itself. If, however, this too were an inference, then the negation of inference would be excluded by its contradiction; yet its status as an inference is certainly not denied, because of the statement: "The stability of the world is a factor of its own nature" (*svabhāvāṅga*). For in this case, only what is established by verbal convention is the signifier, not an inference proceeding by the power of the thing itself. Indeed, the state of being denoted cannot be apprehended here through perception, because in that [perception] only the thing-in-itself appears. Furthermore, it might be argued that since perception is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), only the thing-in-itself appears and not the relationship between the denoter and the denoted. But in that case, the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would likewise not appear at all. Just as the relationship of cause and effect [is not perceived], so too is the relationship of denoter and denoted.

[538,xii] This is true. Nevertheless, the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) has all things as its domain, whereas the relation of signifier and signified (*vācakabhāva*) does not. For instance:
[538,xiii]
This relationship between the signified and the signifier varies across different places, times, and persons;
therefore, it certainly cannot constitute a causal relationship.

For although the relation of cause and effect is established by the means of valid cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), nevertheless, due to its being well-known throughout the entire world, it appears as if it were directly perceived. To illustrate:
"Previously, I observed that smoke has fire as its cause."
Otherwise, how could the cognition "this is that very same thing" be subject to sublation?
(PVA 538, xvi)

If it is argued: "Even if it was not previously conceptualized by me, it was nonetheless seen by me; therefore, perception has resulted in being conceptual," we say: No. This is because there is the recognition that "it was seen by me at that time precisely while not conceptualizing, prior to the conceptualization. Nor is a conceptualization occurring at a later time the basis for the conceptual nature of a perception that occurred earlier, because there is no connection between the two. But if it is asked: "Since a conceptualization occurring at a later time lacks an object [of that earlier perception], how can the non-conceptual nature of that [perception] be established by it? Or: "How can the non-conceptual nature be established by a perception whose object is past? We reply: No, because there is no contradiction in a past object being the domain of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). For instance, the non-perception characterized by the cessation of the perceiver’s direct perception—whether of the past or the present—is what establishes the linguistic convention of non-existence. It is in this very way that all worldly convention functions. Otherwise, if convention were impossible, it would follow that no one could either remain or establish themselves in the world.
Therefore:
When the cognizer possesses unimpaired memory-impressions regarding the negation of what was previously perceived and what is currently being perceived,
then he proceeds to employ the linguistic convention of non-existence. (PVA 217)
This matter is established for the entire world without dispute.
(PVA 539, v.
218) However, no one has the realization that "the relationship between the signifier and the signified has been apprehended by me through direct perception. For instance:

The word and its object are grasped as the signifier and the signified through perception alone; it does not occur without instruction, yet that instruction is not observed to exist independently of those two. (219) (PVA)

Indeed, no one could ever have the cognition that "this is the signified and this is the signifier" based merely on the perception of the word and its object in the absence of instruction. Furthermore, even regarding instruction, if someone were to state it otherwise, one would certainly reject it; otherwise, there would be no possibility of alternative interpretations. For the relationship between cause and effect cannot be led to any other [conclusion].

But surely the Vaiśeṣikas declare that “the act of naming is perception. For instance, when one perceives an object and hears the words, “This is Yajñadatta,” at the time of the convention, one understands it precisely through perception. Indeed, at the time of establishing a convention, when people see before them an object that has been made the focus of the desire to apply a name such as Devadatta or the like, and when the form of the word such as “Yajñadatta” enters the range of their hearing, then there arises for the agent of the linguistic usage the certain cognition: “This is its name. Nor is it the case that what is grasped by a perceptual cognition of a different class cannot be determined as being related [to it]. For instance:
Recollection and experience would not be definitively established otherwise; they are mutually connected, yet they exist as being of different kinds. (220) (PVA)
The relationship between a name and the named object is not perceptible.
This is incorrect, because:
[539,xii] If the connection between the name and the named were established by direct perception, [then it would be real].
Otherwise, there would be no change in its nature even when another time is taken into account.

(PVA 219) [539, xiii] If the relationship between a name and the named were established by the means of valid cognition that is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could it be otherwise in a different place, time, or person? For what is grasped by direct perception—such as blue or any other objective relation—does not become otherwise. Yet, this cognition of the relationship between a name and the named is seen to follow from instruction. To explain:
[539,xiv] Thus, for the time being, he clearly says, "This is the name of this"; however, he does not know with perfect clarity that "this is the name itself of this. (PVA) 220.1//1//
At another time, this [mind] will surely do something else entirely.
By whom indeed can its ever-shifting desires be restrained?
(221) This very same situation applies to me as well; there is no warding off of desire anywhere.
That [result] can never be achieved by anyone through anything, even by Brahmā himself.

[Objection: "Surely, according to the principle that 'one should give a name that is internal, situated within, not augmented, followed by three generations, and established among non-kinsmen,' how is it that desire is not restricted? [Reply: No. If there are many individuals possessing those characteristics, how can there be such restriction? Furthermore, this too is merely an instruction (*upadeśa*). Nor is it observed that an instruction being transgressed is invalid. Therefore, the act of naming is not a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, since the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācaka-bhāva*) is not like the relationship between cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa-bhāva*), that which is well-known through verbal testimony (*śābdaprasiddha*) is not an inference functioning by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta*).

Therefore, it has been indicated that because [the cognition] conforms to the existence or non-existence of things through inference, its occurrence is distinct from those [objects], and thus it is called "dependent on them" (tadicchāya). // 119 //

This inference, which is established through verbal convention, proceeds solely from mere desire; it does not arise from the power of real entities, and therefore it does not lead to the cognition of a real entity.
Just as this meaning of words such as *agnihotra* has been established according to convention,
so too may another meaning, such as "dog-meat" and so forth, be imagined at will.

If there were a restriction regarding the intrinsic natures of entities based on the conceptual construction of one's own desires, then there would be no such construction due to the contradiction with what is unobserved (*adṛṣṭa*); for when one constructs something for another purpose, there is no establishment of the unobserved.
Indeed, the attainment of a desired result never occurs through mere conceptual construction.
Otherwise, by mere name, everyone could establish everything.
(PVA 540, vi) This is true; we too have made such a claim. However, you alone are the one who possesses the great power to set in motion this course toward a path of futility. For instance:
If a succession were examined for the sake of determining the object, that very succession of instruction would be nothing but a blind succession of useless things. (225) (PVA)
If there were perceivers of this object who see what is beyond the senses,
then there would be an appearance of those who are mutually contradictory.
For no other person who perceives supersensible objects has been found to be as harsh toward you.

Therefore, this object too must have been merely imagined by someone. And since conviction does not arise from that alone, another [perceiver] must also be postulated. If it is asked, "How can one who knows for himself imagine that he does not know it?", [we reply: He himself will know it; what is the use of your worrying? If it is argued, "He might deceive me even without my investigating him, therefore I worry," then let go of your hope for mere instruction.

[540,xi] If it is argued that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) occurs through the following of roots (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), then surely even that meaning of the root and suffix is established only through instruction; therefore, that too must be supported solely by the observation of usage (*prayoga*). If it is further argued that usage itself would not function as a property (*dharma*) if it were to rely on a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayaṇa*) within a succession of relationships between roots, suffixes, and their meanings, this has already been addressed. Moreover, the claim that "dharma arises in such a way" is also merely an instruction; thus, this argument is trivial.

But surely, "The moon is *śaśin* because it exists, like a well-known object of denotation. Therefore, how can this inference be one that proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubala*)? To this it has been said, and furthermore:
[540, xiii] Not accepting the moon's status as *śaśin*, what cognition does he desire?
Thus, that [reason] which lacks a corroborative instance is considered to be "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) with respect to that [subject]. (120)

Because [the opponent] who rejects all cognition provides no example, it has been stated that there is an absence of inference due to its being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatva*). For it is well known that he, while refusing to accept the reality of the moon—which is renowned throughout the entire world as being denoted by the word "moon"—also refuses to accept any other cognition. Therefore, for him, an inference such as "it exists" (*sattvāt*) and so forth lacks an example; and in that case, it has already been stated that all logical reasons (*hetu*) are uncommon. Consequently, what is the meaning of the argument "The moon is not the moon because it exists"? It means: "The moon is not the moon because of the reason 'existence'. By this, one cannot establish its being the moon. If one asks, "By what then is it established?"—and how can that [argument] be a subverter?—the intention is that it is not a subverter, since it arises from the power of linguistic convention (*śābdaprasiddha*) rather than from the power of real entities (*vastubalabhāvin*).
[540,xv] But surely, since the moon is a single entity, it is not a common locus; how then can this inference be intended as "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) with respect to one who denies all cognition?
This is nothing of the sort;
for it is not said with reference to the mere absence of an example.
Because it is a defining characteristic, and because there would be a contradiction if one were to say that a non-tree is a dhātrī fruit. (121)

[541,ii] Regarding the argument "A *śiṃśapā* is not a tree because it exists," there is no rebuttal on the grounds that "the tree is one," for a definition does not function by intending to refer to a single specific example.

Now, what is this logic? A definition does not function by aiming at a single example; for that example is certainly not something that need not be established. If, on the other hand, the definition must be formulated by including other examples as well—since such is the labor of a definer of definitions accomplished through the treatise—then there would be no hardship for the learner. Yet, where no other example exists, is it observed that the definition fails to apply? For instance, in the case of *akuṭilikā* and so forth; likewise:
[541, iv] "Meru, Mandara, Maināka, Kailāśa, Uśīra, and the rest."
Since each individual form exists [as such], there is not even a single instance that could be cited as an exception.
To this, it is replied:

For a definition must be formulated such that it is free from under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*); otherwise, according to the opponent's statement, this [definition] would be under-extended. (PVA 232)

For instance: even in the case of "The chest is a *śiṃśapā* because it is an existent," one must state that there is sublation by cognition (*pratītibādhā*). How could that [sublation] follow from the logic propounded by the opponent? For a tree is not a single thing, since there is also the existence of *plakṣa* trees and others. If it is argued that inference exists precisely because of commonality, and therefore there will be sublation, to this he says:
[541, viii]
In this case as well, since [the word] is seen in the world to apply to camphor, silver, and so forth by convention, what can be called its "uncommon" nature? (122)

The designation by the word "moon" (*candra*) is indeed observed in the case of camphor and other such things. Therefore, how can there be oneness of the moon? Furthermore, words that function solely by convention do not fail to apply anywhere. Consequently, even in this case, there is simply a sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*). Thus, it follows that what is called "sublation by cognition" (*pratīti-bādha*) does not exist at all.

Now, as for the fact that silver and so forth are denoted by the word "moon," this is not established through common usage; rather, it is merely imagined in some arbitrary way by proponents of olfactory logic and the like, and is not based on the actual nature of things.
This is incorrect.
If that [reason] were to be established for him in some respect, it would be established by the force of real entities (*vastubala*).
For if one accepts what is established by cognition (*pratīti*), there would be no way to prevent it even in the case of a non-existent moon. (123)

[541,xiii] This is the meaning: if [the property] is not established in an ultimate sense in camphor and so forth, yet is imagined by those very proponents of the "logic of fragrance" (gandhayukti) and others, then how can the moon—which is established as a real entity—be an example of sublation by what is commonly recognized (prasiddhibādha)?

If it is argued that because it is established by cognition itself, it is therefore a sublation by cognition (*pratītibādha*), then upon accepting what is established by cognition, there would be no way to prevent it even in the case of the moon; for in the case of camphor and the like, cognition indeed occurs. Therefore, this is simply a sublation by inference (*anumānabādhana*) and not a sublation by cognition. If it is further argued that in the case of camphor and the like, one acts because of a cause such as refreshing coolness, and thus that is not a valid example, then it is a common [fallacy].
To this, it is said:
When that entity is established, it cannot be denied even in the case of the moon; if that entity is absent, there is no fault even if one denies its presence in the moon. (124)

[542,iii] If the application of the word "moon" to camphor and the like is based on a specific cause (*nimitta*), then since that same cause exists in the [actual] moon as well, its application there is indeed unavoidable. If, however, it is excluded from the moon due to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—just as it is excluded from camphor—then there is no fault even in excluding it from the moon. That a thing connected to a real entity (*vastu*) comes into being through the absence of that entity is not an unestablished principle.
Therefore, objects are capable of being associated with properties produced by sounds whose conventions are not fixed to a specific thing, because there is no restriction upon one's will. (125)

[542,v] For those phenomena that arise merely through conventions fixed upon non-existent things, all entities are suitable; therefore, if their suitability is subverted, there is a fault characterized by the subversion of cognition.

Even for words such as *ḍavittha* and the like, there must be some causal ground consisting of a general or particular form, rather than being based on mere conventional renown alone. [Response: This is incorrect. There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that a word, having taken up a causal ground for its application, applies to that which possesses such a ground. [542, viii] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is bound in both ways, the person who is bound by the lower fetters, the person who is bound by the higher fetters, and the person who is liberated in both ways. What, monks, is the person who is bound in both ways? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual desire, accompanied by sensual desire; he is not free from sensual desire, not free from lust for sensual desire, not free from craving for sensual desire, not free from thirst for sensual desire, not free from fever for sensual desire, and not free from passion for sensual desire. He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, accompanied by ill will; he is not free from ill will, not free from lust for ill will, not free from craving for ill will, not free from thirst for ill will, not free from fever for ill will, and not free from passion for ill will. He dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, accompanied by sloth and torpor; he is not free from sloth and torpor, not free from lust for sloth and torpor, not free from craving for sloth and torpor, not free from thirst for sloth and torpor, not free from fever for sloth and torpor, and not free from passion for sloth and torpor. He dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, accompanied by restlessness and remorse; he is not free from restlessness and remorse, not free from lust for restlessness and remorse, not free from craving for restlessness and remorse, not free from thirst for restlessness and remorse, not free from fever for restlessness and remorse, and not free from passion for restlessness and remorse. He dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, accompanied by doubt; he is not free from doubt, not free from lust for doubt, not free from craving for doubt, not free from thirst for doubt, not free from fever for doubt, and not free from passion for doubt. This, monks, is called the person who is bound in both ways. What, monks, is the person who is bound by the lower fetters? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual desire... But he has abandoned the five lower fetters. This, monks, is called the person who is bound by the lower fetters. What, monks, is the person who is bound by the higher fetters? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters, but he dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual desire...
