If that [term] were established in some respect by the force of the thing itself, then it would be established as having a cause; this is the completion of the sentence. For if one accepts establishment through mere non-cognition, there is no restriction even in the case of a rabbit [on the moon]. If one accepts that the meaning of a word is established by mere cognition, there is no restriction even in the case of what is not a rabbit. Indeed, the relationship between the denoted and the denoter, when occurring anywhere at all, cannot admit of a fixed restriction, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such a restriction. In that regard, just as it occurs with respect to a cause even without a cause, so too does it occur with respect to that which possesses a cause. For even with respect to a cause, there is no occurrence otherwise than by the power of desire.

Now, if it functions there by its very nature (*svabhāva*), then who can prevent that same nature from functioning elsewhere as well? If you say that it functions only toward the universal (*jāti*) and so forth because it has a connection with them in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), how is this to be known? A word is observed to function according to mere intention; how could it otherwise function toward something else? It is designated as "functioning" because it is observed to function [in that way]; but no, for it is possible for it to function even through mere intention. Indeed, we perceive no difference between that which functions through mere intention and anything else. If you argue that there is non-perception due to intention, this very perception occurs even when the intention is past. For non-perception does not invalidate every instance of intention; it invalidates only that specific instance which is present and proximate, not all. Therefore, if someone—even the Buddha long ago—had such an intention regarding this, what is contradictory in the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of people today based on his teaching? Consequently, since it functions even toward that which possesses a cause (the particular), what is the point of postulating a useless cause (the universal)?

[542,x] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive a dharma that is full enlightenment, nor does he perceive a dharma that is one who fully awakens to full enlightenment. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if there is no dharma that is a Bodhisattva, nor a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor a dharma that is full enlightenment, nor a dharma that is one who fully awakens to full enlightenment, then, Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the six perfections? How does he train in the thirty-seven dharmas conducive to enlightenment? How does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How does he train in the eighteen unique dharmas of a Buddha? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique dharmas of a Buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive a dharma that is full enlightenment, nor does he perceive a dharma that is one who fully awakens to full enlightenment. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, trains in the six perfections; he trains in the thirty-seven dharmas conducive to enlightenment; he trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; he trains in the eighteen unique dharmas of a Buddha; he trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique dharmas of a Buddha. It is because he does not perceive any of these dharmas that he is called a ‘Bodhisattva. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a dharma that is a Bodhisattva, nor a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom, nor a dharma that is full enlightenment, nor a dharma that is one who fully awakens to full enlightenment, then, Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generate the thought of awakening? How does he enter into the first stage? How does he enter into the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages? How does he enter into the stage of the Irreversible Bodhisattva? How does he enter into the stage of the Tathāgata? How does he enter into the knowledge of all aspects? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening through the non-apprehension of a thought. He enters into the first stage through the non-apprehension of a stage. He enters into the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages through the non-apprehension of those stages. He enters into the stage of the Irreversible Bodhisattva through the non-apprehension of that stage. He enters into the stage of the Tathāgata through the non-apprehension of that stage. He enters into the knowledge of all aspects through the non-apprehension of that knowledge. It is in this way, Subhūti, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, trains in the six perfections, and so forth, up to the knowledge of all aspects.”

Another, however, says: [The word] does not first operate upon the cause (*nimitta*) and subsequently upon that which possesses the cause (*nimittavat*), because such a sequential operation is never observed. If it is argued that [the word] is seen to apply to a cause in some instances—as in "the state of being a cow" (*gotva*) with respect to the object "cow"—this is not so, because that [word] is a different word. For its status as a denoter depends on where it is employed; the establishment of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator for all [words] follows from the force of usage. Indeed, when one constructs positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), a word ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) functions only with respect to a substance (*dravya*). This is because, in the absence of the abstract suffix, it functions as a substance. Now, if an abstract suffix is attached to something functioning as a substance, how can it have the status of denoting the mere cause? But when...

At that time, when it functions as a mere sign (*nimitta*), it is logical that the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) reveals that very same object. For, without the abstract suffix, the distinction between the two words "cow"—one denoting the substance (*dravya*) and the other denoting the state of being (*bhāva*)—is not perceived with clarity; therefore, the distinction arises from the abstract suffix.

This is not so. For it is not the case that every suffix is merely *svārthika* (denoting its own meaning). In that case, when a suffix is applied to that which functions as a substance (*dravya*), the cognition of the cause—which serves as its qualifier—occurs; thus, there is nothing contradictory here. Furthermore, the distinction between the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*). It is from usage that we perceive only wholes (*samudāya*) as expressive. The division into base, suffix, and so forth, is merely devised in some way or another for the sake of instructing beginners, since otherwise it would be impossible to instruct a beginner through the medium of words. Therefore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that [a word] applies to the possessor of a cause by taking up the cause itself.

Another says: A word functions only with respect to a causal basis (nimitta), but that basis, while not being explicitly denoted, serves as a delimiter; for it is impossible [for it to be denoted], because it is the cause of that [denotation].
This is incorrect, because:
If that were established in some respect, it would be established by the force of real entities.
If one accepts what is established by conventional cognition (*pratīti*), then there is no obstruction even in the case of the moon [as a subject].

(PVA 233) If that [exclusion] were established in some basis (*nimitta*), then it would be established by the force of real entities (*vastubala*). But how can a word that does not indicate a basis cause one to engage with what is excluded by it? If there is an understanding of that exclusion, then since that too has ascended into the intellect, how could it be denotable? Even for that which possesses a basis, the understanding from a word is said to be "denotability" (*vācyatva*); that [denotability] is equally present in the basis as well.

[543, viii] Now, it is substance (*dravya*) itself that is primarily established; whereas qualities (*guṇa*), such as sweetness and so forth, even if not explicitly expressed, are not to be considered the primary denotation, because they are understood through necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatayā*).
The principle of primary and subordinate status is not inseparable from the speaker’s intention;
rather, that toward which an activity is directed is what possesses the connection with primacy.

In this regard, sometimes sweetness alone is primary, and sometimes the substance itself; such is the worldly convention. And it is by virtue of this worldly convention that the relationship between the signifier and the signified is established. For instance: "If you desire sweetness, then always eat molasses."
If the purpose is the absence of disease, then consume honey for that end.
(PVA 543, xii)

When someone of a greedy disposition is a consumer, the instruction regarding molasses (*guḍa*) serves to establish its sweetness. But when, due to a particular efficacy, one prescribes honey and so forth for the sake of alleviating phlegm (*śleṣman*), then it primarily indicates the substance alone; therefore, only two things are perceived. The distinction between primary and subordinate status depends on whether, at a certain time, in a certain way, or for a certain person. In that regard, since there is no other cause for the non-perception of these two, only what is conventionally established remains.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the crow is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) or a sign (*nimitta*), and not itself the denotation (*vācyatā*) of the word. For example, in the expression "Which is Devadatta’s house? The one where the crow is," the crow is not the referent of the word "house. Just as it is not the denotation, so too, even in its absence, it is simply Devadatta’s house; therefore, the crow is not what is to be adopted [as the primary object]. Likewise, when the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth are used to indicate humanity and the like, the crow does not serve as an indicator of the improper (the non-Brāhmaṇa), because the crow is impermanent. Indeed, a person acting with foresight takes another sign—such as a temple or the like—which is indicated by the crow, as the actual basis for their activity. Otherwise, there would be no practical linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

[543,xiv] The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a heap of filth; the person who is like a jewel casket; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. And what, monks, is the person who is like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, a wealthy kṣatriya family, a wealthy brahmin family, or a wealthy householder family, possessing great wealth and many possessions, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and granaries, abundant wealth and grain. He is handsome, attractive, graceful, endowed with supreme beauty of complexion, possessing a complete set of limbs and faculties, and free from physical defects. Yet he is unlearned, ignorant, dull-witted, slow to understand, and lacking in wisdom. He does not know what is beneficial and what is harmful, nor does he know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is base and what is sublime, or what leads to the welfare and happiness of both this life and the next. This, monks, is called the person who is like a heap of filth. And what, monks, is the person who is like a jewel casket? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family... [as above] ...and is endowed with supreme beauty of complexion. He is learned, wise, intelligent, quick to understand, and possessed of wisdom. He knows what is beneficial and what is harmful, and he knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is base and what is sublime, and what leads to the welfare and happiness of both this life and the next. This, monks, is called the person who is like a jewel casket. And what, monks, is the person who is like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family... [as above] ...and is endowed with supreme beauty of complexion. He is learned, wise, intelligent, quick to understand, and possessed of wisdom. He knows what is beneficial and what is harmful, and he knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is base and what is sublime, and what leads to the welfare and happiness of both this life and the next. But while he lives the holy life under the Teacher or under a disciple of the Teacher, he attains only the lower distinction—that is, the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning—and does not attain the higher distinction—that is, arhatship. This, monks, is called the person who is like a blue lotus. And what, monks, is the person who is like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family... [as above] ...and is endowed with supreme beauty of complexion. He is learned, wise, intelligent, quick to understand, and possessed of wisdom. He knows what is beneficial and what is harmful, and he knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is base and what is sublime, and what leads to the welfare and happiness of both this life and the next. He lives the holy life under the Teacher or under a disciple of the Teacher, and he attains the higher distinction—that is, arhatship. This, monks, is called the person who is like a white lotus. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. How, then, is the crow—which is itself inexpressible—an indicator? Because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is for this very reason designated by the word "crow" itself. However, the causes [of denotation] such as the universal (*jāti*) and so forth are not established as being expressed by other words in that same way. Therefore, even that which is inexpressible can be a delimiter (*vyavacchedaka*) when it is presented separately. But that which is understood from that very word is indeed expressible (*vācya*), because that which is introduced into the intellect by a word is designated as "expressible. If it is argued that there is only cognition (*pratīti*) of it from the word, but no "expressibility," [we reply: since expressibility is not excluded in the case of the moon (*śaśin*) when its existence is established through cognition, then [expressibility] would likewise be absent in the case of the indicator (*nimitta*) as well as the indicated (*nimittavat*). Therefore, if expressibility is based solely on cognition, it is the same in the case of the indicator as well.

[544,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while traveling through the southern region, beheld five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were afflicted with leprosy. Seeing them, he felt great compassion and addressed them as follows: "Sisters, you have committed many unwholesome deeds; therefore, you have been born with such a foul body. Listen now to what I say. Having spoken thus, he recited these verses: "Those who commit evil deeds, And do not perform wholesome deeds, Will surely experience suffering In this world and the next. If one does not abandon evil deeds, One will not attain happiness. Therefore, having abandoned all evil deeds, One should practice only what is wholesome. By abandoning evil deeds, One attains happiness in this world; Having abandoned evil deeds, One will not experience suffering. The wise person, seeing this, Should always practice wholesome deeds. By practicing wholesome deeds, One will not experience suffering. Therefore, sisters, you should now Abandon all evil deeds; By abandoning evil deeds, You shall attain happiness. Now, one might object: "Even if a vessel is perceived when one says, 'Let oil be given,' it cannot be denoted by the word 'oil' [as a secondary indicator]. This is because that [vessel] is not always perceived; furthermore, even if the vessel is brought by oneself, there can be no desire to give oil [into it]. Therefore, for that which is not being denoted and is not conveyed by another word, there is no possibility of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). For something can only be indicated by what has already been indicated; if indication were possible by what is not indicated, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued: "First there is indication as a secondary marker, and then, through extreme habituation, that word comes to function as referring exclusively to that excluded object even without the perception of its cause at that time," then in that case, the word *agnihotra* and so forth should also apply to dog-meat, since its cause (fire) occurs there just as it does in a crow. Otherwise, why would the word 'cow' not apply to actual cows? If you say, "Because it is well-known (*prasiddha*) in that context," we ask: how is it known that there is no cognition of [the word 'cow'] even with respect to dog-meat in other times and places? Therefore, the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is indeed unrestricted, as it depends on the power of conventions fashioned by will. Thus, there is no damage to the Veda's faultlessness even if it is non-human (*apauruṣeya*), because suitability (*yogyatā*) is not precluded in any case.
The inference whose object is the capacity known as "cognition" (pratīti) sublates that capacity which is produced by the negation of conventions and which obstructs it. (126)
"The restriction of words to their meanings follows convention; it was stated here [in the previous verse] that this is not so. By this, the denial of these [words] is contradicted. (127)

[544,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of wisdom as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the bodhisattva as a substantial entity. He does not perceive form as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as substantial entities. He does not perceive the eye as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as substantial entities. He does not perceive forms as substantial entities, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as substantial entities. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as substantial entities. He does not perceive eye-contact as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as substantial entities. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the sensations born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as substantial entities. He does not perceive the element of earth as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as substantial entities. He does not perceive the realm of desire as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as substantial entities. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as substantial entities, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as substantial entities. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as substantial entities, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, or the eight liberations as substantial entities. He does not perceive the nine successive meditative attainments as substantial entities, nor does he perceive the ten spheres of totality as substantial entities. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as substantial entities, nor does he perceive the four truths of the noble ones as substantial entities. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the beginningless and endless emptiness, the essential emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-attainment as substantial entities. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as substantial entities, nor does he perceive the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion as substantial entities. He does not perceive the knowledge of all modes as a substantial entity, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all aspects as a substantial entity. Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive these things as substantial entities that he is called a ‘bodhisattva.’”

For one who asserts that dog-meat and the like is not the meaning of words such as *agnihotra*, inference regarding their semantic fitness acts as a counter-argument. This is because there is no restriction on the denotation of words that function solely through convention; what kind of restriction could there be that they must have only a single denotation? In this regard, he who says that the postulation of eating dog-meat is contradicted by common experience (*pratītibādhita*) is questioned: even this [claim] is contradicted by experience if the Veda is considered human in origin. For there is the experience: "They made *ṛc*s out of the word *ṛk*," and "They made *sāmans* out of the word *sāman*. If it is argued that the verb *karoti* (to make) refers to recollection and not to actual production—since it is seen used in the sense of refinement, as in "make a back" or "make feet"—[we reply: no, for in these cases, the cognition arises precisely because otherwise it would be impossible. If it is further imagined that its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) would otherwise be untenable, then it would follow that all scriptures (*āgama*) are non-human in origin, since the grounds for that same imagination exist for them all. It is for this very reason that the Buddhist [says]: [the Veda is not a valid means of knowledge].
One who denies the conventional meaning or the ultimate meaning of words based on indicative scripture should not be addressed by a proponent of the Veda. (128)

If one were to say that there is no such thing as a word based on a specific cause (*naimittikī śruti*), there would be no fault in that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Even if one were to reply that it is not so because of the force of a relationship (*sambandhabalena*), that person should not be addressed at all. However, it is precisely the Mīmāṃsaka and others who claim that even a conventional (*sāṃketika*) word does not exist who are being spoken to here. Therefore, it is improper to refute what is well-established by common consensus (*prasiddhi*).
Therefore, in order to demonstrate the difference in their objects, even cognition—which is not external to inference—is treated separately, just as before. (129)

Just as a treatise and one’s own words, when accepted as the basis for the context of discussion, constitute a sublation, but not otherwise—because they sublate the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā) asserted—and because there is no sublation of a contrary [position] in every respect due to both being of equal status; so too, perception (*pratīti*) does not sublate an ultimate reality, but rather sublates a denial established merely by conventional perception. This is the ultimate point.

Demonstrating the purpose for explaining the two types of proof separately, he states that these two—reasoning and scripture—are accompanied by their respective grounds, whereas inference and perception are not subject to sublation [by those same means]. (130)

[545,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered all suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form. What is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touch, no object of mind; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains ultimate *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which pacifies all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* should be proclaimed: *Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.* [546,i] Then the Blessed One spoke these verses: "O Śāriputra, all phenomena are empty of self-nature; they are neither born nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, knowing them to be empty, one is liberated from all suffering. [546,ii] At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Buddha, "Blessed One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way: they should not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the word 'Bodhisattva,' nor the *prajñāpāramitā,' nor the word 'prajñāpāramitā,' nor even the word 'practice. Why is this? Śāriputra, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive anything, they are called a 'Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives form as form, they do not practice the *prajñāpāramitā. If they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as consciousness, they do not practice the *prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Śāriputra, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives form as form, they are attached to form; if they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as consciousness, they are attached to consciousness. Because they are attached to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they are attached to the five aggregates. Because they are attached to the five aggregates, they are attached to the six sense bases. Because they are attached to the six sense bases, they are attached to the eighteen elements. Because they are attached to the eighteen elements, they are attached to dependent origination. Because they are attached to dependent origination, they are attached to the view of a self. Because they are attached to the view of a self, they are attached to the view of a sentient being, the view of a living soul, and the view of a person. Because they are attached to these views, they fall into the two extremes. Because they fall into the two extremes, they do not transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair; they cannot escape the suffering of birth and death. Therefore, Śāriputra, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not perceive form as form, nor should they perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as consciousness. Why is this? Śāriputra, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive form as form, nor perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as consciousness, they do not perceive the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the eighteen elements, or dependent origination. Because they do not perceive these things, they do not fall into the two extremes. Because they do not fall into the two extremes, they transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair; they can escape the suffering of birth and death. Therefore, Śāriputra, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way. [547,i] Then the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Buddha, "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, what dharma do they attain? The Buddha said to Śāriputra, "If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* in this way, they do not attain any dharma. Why is this? Śāriputra, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains any dharma, they would not be called a 'Bodhisattva. Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment. [547,ii] Then the Venerable Subhūti asked the Buddha, "Blessed One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, how can they be called a 'Bodhisattva'? The Buddha said to Subhūti, "Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, they are indeed called a 'Bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has no attainment, they are called a 'Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives a Bodhisattva, they do not practice the *prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives a Bodhisattva, they are attached to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a living soul, and the view of a person. Because they are attached to these views, they are attached to the five aggregates. Because they are attached to the five aggregates, they are attached to the six sense bases. Because they are attached to the six sense bases, they are attached to the eighteen elements. Because they are attached to the eighteen elements, they are attached to dependent origination. Because they are attached to dependent origination, they are attached to the view of a self. Because they are attached to the view of a self, they are attached to the view of a sentient being, the view of a living soul, and the view of a person. Because they are attached to these views, they fall into the two extremes. Because they fall into the two extremes, they do not transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair; they cannot escape the suffering of birth and death. Therefore, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor the word 'Bodhisattva,' nor the *prajñāpāramitā,' nor the word 'prajñāpāramitā,' nor even the word 'practice. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive anything, they are called a 'Bodhisattva. In this regard, the Teacher has stated: "A thesis (*pakṣa*) is that which is intended by [the proponent] himself as something to be indicated by its own nature alone, and is not contradicted—provided it is not [contradicted] by what is established through perception, inference, or scripture. For example: 'Sound is inaudible,' or 'A pot is eternal. It is not [a valid thesis] by mere assertion, such as the proposition: 'There are no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for objects of cognition (*prameya*). Even in a case where, due to the lack of a common locus (*asādhāraṇatva*), there is an absence of inference, if [the thesis] is sublated by a contradictory object established through scripture, it is not a [valid] thesis. Regarding sublation by inference and perception, he spoke of sublation by what is established through scripture as being "with a reason" (*sahetuka*), namely: "by mere assertion" and "by what is established through scripture. Otherwise, if the Teacher had not intended to demonstrate the distinction between their respective domains, he would not have stated that these two [types of sublation] are "with a reason. Therefore, this is precisely the intention of the preeminent one among all proponents of logic (*nyāyavādin*), the Supreme Lord of Logic (*nyāyaparameśvara*).
Indeed, eloquent persons whose minds are intent on discerning the primary purpose and whose speech is nourished by other relevant purposes do not exist. For instance:

The Teacher is not the sun; he is not surpassed by others, nor is he a novel sun. He is the one who destroys the dense, spreading darkness dwelling within the Vindhyas, and whose mass of rays trembles as it continuously strikes the exceedingly high mountain of sunrise. (PVA 236)
[One who is] rendered fruitless in their undertakings by the hand of the sun’s rays as they set;
therefore, a distinction of objects alone is appropriate here. The remainder has already been explained.
[5. Refutation by Perception] In that case as well, there is this refutation by perception: because sound possesses a manifold nature.
Whatever form appears in the scripture of that which is well-known [in common usage], [that alone is its nature]. 131.
Non-duality [is established] because no birth of cognition is observed that has a variegated appearance.

The same must also be said regarding sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*). Even if it was not stated by the Teacher because it is already understood, it should still not be stated [in that context]. The statement "sound is inaudible" is not a negation of the relation; rather, what is it? It is the form that appears in hearing, which is non-dual, because a variegated cognition is never experienced. For there is no appearance of universals, relations, and so forth, that accompanies the appearance of the word. And how can that which does not appear be perceived? Furthermore, if it is not perceived, how can there be sublation by perception? This will be demonstrated later. Therefore, the fault characterized as sublation by perception occurs only when one negates a form that actually appears.
The statement of its meaning is for that very purpose; its refutation occurs when it is sublated by direct perception. (132)
It was for that very purpose that it was stated by the Teacher.

"By that which is established through perception, inference, and authoritative testimony, [the object] is excluded. This inclusion of the word "object" (*artha*) is because that very form is the object; for universals (*jāti*) and so forth are not objects, since they lack the capacity to appear in perception.
< 4. Examination of Universals > [546,ii]
But where there is no appearance, that is not perception; therefore, its rejection is not contradicted by perception.
He says this very thing:
<1. Universality has exclusion as its characteristic> [546,iv] That very form is the object there; the remainder has exclusion as its characteristic.
Since a universal has the nature of a non-entity, it is therefore not within the range of the senses.

Because the non-perceptibility of general properties (sāmānyadharma) is thereby established, it was demonstrated by the mention of "audibility" that there is no sublation even when [the property] is rejected. (134)

Only that object which appears in the form of something manifesting before one is the real thing (*artha*). However, universals (*sāmānya*), relations (*sambandha*), and so forth, are merely conceptual constructs (*parikalpita*) based on the exclusion of things from such forms; they do not possess the nature of a real object. This is because one perceives only the distinctness from the forms of heterogeneous classes, and because no other universal ever appears as a second form. But [one might object]:
This so-called "distinctness" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) belongs only to members of the same class (*sajātīya*) in relation to one another.
How, then, can there be a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) between those of different classes and those of the same class?
Just as, for example, the exclusion of non-cows from cows is observed only in relation to something other [than a cow].
Just as from cows and horses, and from other things distinct from both cow and horse, [a universal is not established];
therefore, by mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), their causal efficiency (*kārya*) is not established.
For a real entity (*vastu*) as a universal is established through its specific differentiation. (239–240) (PVA)
It brings about non-confusion in the conventional usage of those who seek it;
for there is no possibility of confusion in that which is perceived in its own essential form. (241) [Refutation of the Universal]
This is incorrect, because:
[546,xiii]
If [an entity] were ever perceived by way of its own nature as a universal and so forth,
then for that which is perceived by way of its own nature, no confusion could possibly occur. (242) Even if its own nature does not appear, if non-confusion were possible...
Let it be understood that there is no confusion among those [universals] whose capacities and forms have been observed.
(243) For a universal, which is manifested by an individual, does not manifest its own form without the individual being perceived;
since there is no distinction [in the manifestation], how can there be linguistic usage based upon it? (244)

[546,xvii] As long as there is no non-confusion among individuals—whether of the same or different classes—the universal is not cognized through that non-confusion. And as long as the universal is not cognized through non-confusion, there is no cognition of the non-confusion of individuals; thus, because of this mutual dependence, there is simply no cognition of the universal.
[546,xviii]

Now, if it is argued that the universal alone is apprehended first, on the grounds that there can be no cognition of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) when its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) has not been grasped—this is incorrect. For even a universal is sometimes itself the qualified object, due to their mutual relationship as qualifier and qualified. Furthermore, if the universal were always the qualifier, why would there be no cognition of it even when the individual (*vyakti*) is in doubt? A thing is a qualifier only if it is a differentiator; and a thing is a differentiator only if it is capable of removing doubt. To illustrate:
The nature of an object that exists by way of its own essence never ceases;
however, that which lacks an inherent form is brought to cessation by fate alone. (245) (PVA)
Even with a thousand qualifiers, there is no exclusion of the former;
therefore, because of the determination of the individual, there is the ascertainment of the universal.
The determination "this is that cow" proceeds from the mere discernment of its form;
for the similarity between the universal and the individuals is indeed their similarity.
Therefore, because of the distinction between configuration and capacity, a universal is purposeless.

If the specific configuration [of parts] such as the hump and so forth, or the capacity for carrying loads and so forth, is the cause for the determination of a universal (*sāmānya*), then that very thing is the universal, and it is indeed non-different from those [individuals]. If there is internal difference [among individuals], how can that be a universal? And for the proponent of the universal, how can there be an individual? If you say it is because they are indeed distinct, why is it not the case with white horses (*karka*) and the like? If you say it is because they lack the capacity [for the function], then since these [white horses] are equally distinct, how could they possess that capacity in relation to one another? If you say the answer must be given in terms of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things, no; this is merely a futile stretching out of the legs—a last resort. Otherwise, even without a universal, the mere configuration and color would suffice to establish the conventional usage of non-confusion; thus, one should not have asked, "How [is there non-confusion] without a universal? For in this matter, the rebuttal that "the answer must be given in terms of the intrinsic natures of things" has been devoured by crows. There is no confusion regarding the configuration of the hump and so forth, because it is never seen elsewhere. However, where there is confusion of configuration and so forth—as among Brahmins and others—there the refuge is merely the convention of the people (*viṭasamaya*), which is nothing more than the conduct of the virtuous, like that of drunkards and the like. Therefore, even going as far as possible, the cause is simply the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*); any other [universal] posited through a division of universals is useless. Furthermore:
The determination of demerit and merit, such as the killing of a Brahmin or the giving of gifts, arises from the scripture alone; therefore, the investigation into authority is useless. (PVA 248)

This has been stated. Here, there is no contradiction even if one rejects general properties (sāmānyadharma) such as the capacity to produce merit or demerit; [the rejection] does not result from that [rejection]. This is made clear by the term "audible" (śrāvaṇa). Since these [general properties] do not appear in sensory cognition, there is no sublation by inference either. If it is to be established that there is a fault in subverting its form therein, why was it not simply stated that "the specific characteristic of sound (śabdasvalakṣaṇa) does not exist"? It is because it was stated by means of a word ending in a secondary suffix (taddhita), which serves as the cause for a relation. However, by speaking in this way, what is intended here is precisely the negation of the relation. And since that [relation] is only accessible through the comprehension of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), how can this be cited as an example of sublation by perception? There is no fault, because even by this word, the intended object is indeed expressed through the force of the speaker's intention (vivakṣā). If it is asked, "Why is it not expressed by a denotative word (vācaka)?"—no, because:
Because its nature is in every way inexpressible, and because it is established by relying upon that [inexpressibility],
the object of the senses is said to be [established] as "audible" through the force of that [inexpressibility]. (135)

[547,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma as real. He does not perceive form as real, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor forms, or eye-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the ear as real, nor sounds, or ear-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the nose as real, nor odors, or nose-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the tongue as real, nor tastes, or tongue-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the body as real, nor tangibles, or body-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the mind as real, nor mental phenomena, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor the elements of water, fire, air, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the faculty of faith as real, nor the faculties of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the power of faith as real, nor the powers of vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the limb of awakening of mindfulness as real, nor the limbs of awakening of investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, tranquility, concentration, or equanimity as real. He does not perceive the path of the bodhisattva as real, nor the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor the fruit of buddhahood as real. He does not perceive the stage of dry wisdom as real, nor the stage of heat, the stage of summits, the stage of patience, or the stage of supreme mundane dharmas as real. He does not perceive the stage of the śrāvaka as real, nor the stage of the pratyekabuddha as real, nor the stage of the bodhisattva as real, nor the stage of the Tathāgata as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, or the emptiness of the essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion as real. He does not perceive the knowledge of all modes as real. Subhūti, it is because he does not perceive any dharma as real that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom."

Even the word "specific individuality" (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not denotative of a specific individuality, because all words have universals (*sāmānya*) as their object. If it is argued that the word "specific individuality," although functioning through a universal, indicates the specific individuality by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), then in that case, the word "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*) would also denote the specific individuality itself—the form characterized by being graspable by the auditory faculty—because that is the very definition of a specific individuality. Indeed, there is no other well-known universal [that could serve as its referent], and there is certainly a purpose [in using this term]: namely, the demonstration that it is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because one relies upon, or takes recourse in, its subverting power through the establishment of [the specific individuality] by means of valid cognition; for it is by its force alone that subversion occurs. For an object established by a means of valid cognition subverts another object not established by a means of valid cognition. Indeed, when it is perceived as contradictory, it brings about the awareness of the non-existence of the other. Subverting power consists precisely in the demonstration of that non-existence; it is not a [real] relationship between the subverted and the subverter. Therefore, this is a means of valid cognition: "The specific individuality of sound is established by this means of valid cognition. For a demonstration that includes its supporting factors (*saparikara*) leads to a clear understanding; this is the purpose. Regarding contradiction with inference, consider the claim: "A pot is eternal. This is the acceptance of eternality by the Sāṃkhya, who perceives only the manifestation of existing things but has not discerned their true nature. That [position] is subverted by inference.
If this were the case, causes would possess no efficacy whatsoever; therefore, an investigation into the nature of causality would be in vain. (249) (PVA)

[548,iii] Indeed, the search for that which is considered a cause would be in vain without the existence of causality itself, because there would be nothing whatsoever to be produced by it. If it is argued that "manifestation (*vyakti*) is produced," [we reply: surely manifestation is also the very nature of the object; and since the object is eternal, manifestation too must be eternal, and thus would be perpetually present—so nothing at all remains to be produced. Furthermore, if manifestation is produced and is not distinct from the object, then it must be different from the object due to the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). If, on the other hand, there is no difference, then it follows that the object itself is a product (*kāryatā*). [548,iv]
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition that establishes the existence of a jar or the like within the lump of clay;
since it exists there by virtue of being an effect, what further action could there be for an effect that already exists?
Manifestation cannot occur without existence, yet if manifestation were possible [without existence], [the effect would be eternal].

If you think that manifestation [occurs] from everything, as in the case of a lamp and so forth, (PVA 251) why is it not accepted that production occurs from everything, as in the case of a potter and so forth? Furthermore, even when a lump of clay is brought in piece by piece, it is observed elsewhere [that the jar is produced]. (PVA 252)
If that [object] exists there despite being unperceived, then it would also exist in the case of a donkey’s horn.
If it is not perceived later, then it must have been perceived later.

If the jar is perceived later, let it exist only then, like its manifestation (*vyakti*). But how can there be existence prior to that? If you argue that manifestation is otherwise not possible, let this be another fault; however, one cannot say that it exists while remaining unperceived.

But surely, non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension; therefore, since apprehension itself does not exist, how can there be the absence of an entity? If this were so, the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn would not be established. Consequently, the reason “because that which is non-existent cannot be produced” would be invalid. As a result, even one who seeks a rabbit’s horn would have to take up its material cause. For it is said: “That exists there; by that, its apprehension occurs through its being the cause of that.”
If that which has come into being without the production of that [effect] is considered non-existent,
then [the cause] is understood to possess the power to produce it simply by virtue of its existence; otherwise, if it were perceived in another way, its existence would not be understood.
Now, since it is understood that whatever has arisen exists therein,
how can that which was unknown prior to its arising be understood by means of that [arising]?
(PVA 256) For arising is not established in such a way through a connection with existence.
And just as an effect arises from a cause, it would likewise arise from its existence [as a cause].

For it is established that whatever effect is preceded by something, that effect belongs to that [cause]; how then could an effect preceded by the existence of that [cause] belong to anything other than that very cause? (PVA 257–258)
If, as in the other case, all effects arise from power alone, then power would indeed possess power; and how could this be if there were no distinction?
(259) Furthermore, if the universal (*jāti*) arises from the manifesting power (*vyakti-śakti*), is the manifestation itself something other than that power?
If the universal is non-existent, it would be unproduced; if it exists, how can it be produced?
(260) Furthermore, that cognition which is the manifestation also exists [prior to the object]; therefore, it too cannot be something produced.
Now, if manifestation is consciousness, what kind of production could there be for that which is unproduced? (261)
Therefore, the view that the causal factors produce the individual manifestation is not supported by valid cognition.
However, regarding a jar situated in deep darkness, the knower of inference possesses valid cognition [for its existence].
But as for the lump of clay and so forth, the knower of valid cognition finds no such proof for the jar and other effects.

Therefore, everything is indeed impermanent because it is produced, just like individual instances. Consequently, how could this position of permanence not be sublated by inference regarding its own subject (*svadharmin*), through that which is established by perception, by inference, by authoritative testimony, or by what is commonly recognized?
vii] If this is so, then for what purpose is the mention of "its own subject" (*svadharmin*)? To explain:
It is a reasonable view that a thesis contradicted by valid cognition is not [to be accepted].
However, whether [that contradiction occurs] in another [context] or in that very subject (*dharmin*), what relevance does this have here? 265 (PVA)

[549,ix] For that which is sublated in the case of another's property does not become unsublated. Since it is impossible to establish what is sublated in every respect, it is not a valid subject (*apakṣa*) because it lacks the status of being an object for the logical reason; such is the rule.
To this it is replied:
In all cases, that property which the proponent desires as his own probandum—
There would be sublation of the subject (dharmin) insofar as it possesses that property, but not by means of another property.

[549,xii] Although that property may exist in every possible subject according to one's own or another's doctrine, nevertheless, if there should be a sublation when the subject qualified by that very property which the proponent himself intends to prove is sublated, then it is a fault; but it is not a fault when a subject qualified by some other property is sublated. This is the purpose of the expression "one's own subject" (*svadharmin*).
[549,xiii]
Otherwise, what obstruction would there be to this [inference] if it were sublated in another locus?
This is the principle here: when a locus possessing that property is sublated, there is sublation; there is no harm when one possessing a different property is [sublated].
Since the meaning has already been understood through this definition, the mention of "its own subject" (*svadharmin*) is not repeated here. (137)

In order to establish that there is sublation of the subject (*dharmin*) as well when there is sublation [of the property], it is because the contradiction of the substratum entails the contradiction of what is dependent upon it. (138)

[549,xvii] It is established by the very definition that [the subject] must be stated in its own form as "itself. Furthermore, it is the proponent's own intended subject (*dharmin*) precisely as endowed with its own properties (*svadharma*). This being the case, when only that [intended subject] is subverted in a manner consistent with that [intended property], there is no possibility of a fault arising from the subversion of anything else.
[549,xviii]

This is not so; for even when there is a sublation of the locus (*dharmin*), it must be so that through the contradiction of its substratum, the non-existence of its property (*dharma*) also follows. Otherwise, by the very statement that "such a property is the probandum" (*sādhya*), [the sublation of the locus would entail the sublation of the property].
Therefore, one should consider that very statement as being consistent with one's own duty. 139.

"A phenomenon of such a kind" means qualified by the subject under discussion (*prakṛtadharmin*). A fault would occur only in the sublation of that very [property], and the sublation of the subject itself is not considered to be faulty.
Indeed, this too is established by implication; yet some have fallen into error even when there is a negation of the mere locus (dharmin) alone. (140)
If there is a sublation of that property— whether it occurs by way of the subject (*dharmin*) or directly— in every case, the sublation of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is faulty,
as in the case of "space and so forth are non-existent."
This is true; nevertheless, this is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions. For instance, some maintain that there is indeed a fault even when only the locus (*dharmin*) is sublated.

When it is stated that "just as space and so forth do not possess a prior form that can be produced by others, because they are not causes for sound and so forth simultaneously," the opponent replies: (141)
In the same way, even if the subject (*dharmin*) such as space (*vyoman*) and so forth is non-existent by its own nature, there is no sublation whatsoever of the intended probandum (*sādhya*). (142)

The proponent says: Through other auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), the nature of sound and so forth does not become something previously non-existent, because the effect—sound and the like—is not produced all at once. If its nature were not produced [by auxiliaries], it would produce its own effect, such as sound, simultaneously.

Here the opponent says: Now, if this [reason] establishes the non-existence of the unproduced and non-previously-existent nature of space and so forth, it likewise establishes the non-existence of the reality of the subjects (dharmin) such as space. It is not only the sublation of the subject that is faulty. For there is no fault for the proponent in this case; for he intends to prove precisely that space and so forth are not real entities. Therefore, when the subject—space—is a non-entity, there is no fault in [the argument]: "Space and so forth, which are unproduced and non-previously-existent, do not exist, because they are not causes even once. Since the proof and the probandum are established with respect to a subject determined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pariniṣṭhita*), the real entity is not his [subject]. Thus, even if there is a sublation of that [real] subject alone, there is no fault; this is what is meant by the expression "one's own subject" (*svadharmin*). For when a subject belonging to another [system] is sublated, that property (*dharma*) is not thereby unestablished. Consequently, since there is no contradiction in the establishment of the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), there is no fault.

Alternatively, it does not possess a previously non-existent form that is newly produced, because it would otherwise lack a cause at once. This is the meaning: space is impermanent; in this regard, the opponent [claims] that space is permanent, which constitutes a contradiction of the subject (*dharmin*). Even if it were thus contradicted, space will still remain the subject as something impermanent. For the opposite of the probandum must necessarily be refuted by the reason. Since a permanent subject does not have the form of the property to be proven under discussion, what fault could there be in its being so refuted? Only if that property were established through such a refutation would there indeed be a fault.
For likewise, space is impermanent because a change in tone is possible;
for indeed, an affliction by phlegm and so forth is possible for the constriction of the throat.
(PVA 550, viii) 266.

For when the throat-cavity (*galabila*) is impaired, a change in the voice occurs; thus, the non-stability and impermanence of apertures is observed through their contraction, expansion, and so forth. Now, if it is argued that there is indeed a distinct entity [of space] there, yet that very [space] does not appear as expansive and so on as before—[if you say] "because it is obstructed"—then how can there be obstruction for something eternal? This is trivial. Furthermore, the whole (*avayavin*) such as a cloth has not arisen at all; there is merely the movement of other threads within the thread [itself]. If it is asked why they do not become separate upon pulling, [we reply: why would the body not become separate from the throat-cavity upon pulling it? This is trivial. Therefore, this is the definitive position: space is either impermanent or a non-entity, according to the Buddhist view. Alternatively, the established position is that space is merely light and so forth conjoined with resistant objects, while space as a distinct entity unassociated with other things is impermanent. Thus, the property-possessor (*dharmin*) being of such a nature is proven as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in subverting a different property-possessor. For:
For when both members of the probandum are to be established, any sublation of the locus that obstructs the property to be proven is what is described here as "sublation" (bādhā). || 143 ||

[551,i] Even though the subject (*dharmin*) is indeed a component of the composite probandum (*sādhyasamudāya*), nevertheless, when that subject is sublated and the property under discussion (*prakṛtadharma*) is thereby obstructed, it is in that case that there is a fault. This is what is expressed by the term "one's own subject" (*svadharmin*); it does not refer to the sublation of a subject imagined by another that is unrelated to it. For:
In the same way, since it is the property-possessor (*dharmin*) as qualified [by the property] that is the object of proof here, the property-possessor in its isolation is not [the object].

For a property-possessor is already established in its own nature; otherwise, if the property-possessor were unestablished, there would be no utility in proving the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Therefore, what is intended to be proven is that [property-possessor] as being so qualified, not [it] in its own nature. Consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in the sublation of the [property-possessor] in its isolation.

[551,iv] But surely, if a substratum is intended in its capacity as such by means of a certain form, there is no fault in the restriction [of the negation] to the sublation of that very form. This is because space is not intended here either as a real entity (*vasturūpa*) or as something eternal (*nityarūpa*). Moreover:
If the subject were to possess a nature other than its similarity with the probandum,
or if the reason were otherwise, who are we— mere investigators of reality— to deny that?

Indeed, nothing that proceeds by the force of real entities can be negated by anyone intent on investigating the nature of things, because one who relies on valid cognition must follow what is established by valid cognition.
If this were so, there would be a contradiction here: [the claim that] "that which lacks the capacity to produce another [effect]... (144)
Because sound and the rest are not causes [of pleasure and so forth] simultaneously, pleasure and the rest are [unreal], as before.

[551,ix] For the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is held to be the cause of manifest entities such as sound; therefore, because it is not the cause [of them] all at once, pleasure and the rest would be non-entities (*avastu*). Since the permanence of the nature of the *pradhāna* is thus sublated, they must indeed be non-entities.
That is incorrect, because:
In this case, there would be a contradictory reason if the [probans] were of one-sided necessity (aikāntika). || 145 ||
Because there is no contradiction between gradual action and impermanence,
and because there is doubt regarding their exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa), this variety [of inference] is accepted as being "like the remainder" (śeṣavat).

[551, xiii] Here, the reason for sequential action is the negation of non-sequential action. And since there is no contradiction between sequential action and impermanence, the absence of impermanence does not entail the absence of that [sequential action]. How, then, could there be a sublation of the locus (*dharmin*)? And through the sublation of that, there would be a sublation of the property (*dharma*). Therefore, the mention of "one's own locus" is made. <2. Refutation of the Essential Nature of the Locus>

Since the property (*dharma*) intended by oneself is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), it has been indicated that its locus (*āśraya*) alone— not something unrelated to it nor one based on another— is what is to be sublated. (147)

[551,xv] For there is no subversion of the probandum intended by the proponent merely by subverting the locus (*dharmin*) alone, nor by subverting a locus that serves as the substratum for something other than that [probandum]. Therefore, a fault occurs only when there is a subversion of a property (*dharma*) that is useful for the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*). Consequently:
It is stated that by the direct scriptural statement (svayaṃśruti) of the attributes of one thing, there is either sublation or non-sublation [of the attributes] of another;
likewise, it is stated that by the subject (dharmin) itself, there is [sublation or non-sublation] of another subject as well. 148.

For this very reason, he says: "Indeed, when a subject (dharmin) is qualified by a property (dharma), if it is not sublated therein by something established through perception, inference, or scripture that is contradictory to the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), then that is a valid thesis (pakṣa); otherwise, it is a fallacy (tadābhāsa). This is precisely the meaning previously stated. <5. Faults of the Thesis>

[1. Fallacies of the Thesis Independent of the Reason] [552,i] But is there not another set of fallacious theses (*pakṣābhāsa*), namely: that whose qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is unestablished, that whose both [qualificand and qualifier] are unestablished, and that whose qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished? For example: "The self (*ātman*) is omnipresent" is one whose qualificand is unestablished; "Sound is perishable" with respect to a Sāṃkhya is one whose qualifier is unestablished; "The self is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*)" is one whose both are unestablished. So why are these not mentioned?
[552,ii] This is not correct, because:
This is not a valid fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), because it resides in a subsequent member [of the syllogism];
for its status as a fault of the thesis is established merely by the presentation of the thesis itself.

Regarding the statement "where [the subject] is the all-pervading self" (*vibhurātmā*): if someone were to make the "all-pervading self" the probandum (*sādhya*), what would be the fault in the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*)? If it is argued that it is because the reason (*hetu*) lacks a locus due to the non-existence of the subject (*dharmyabhāva*), then the fault belongs to the reason, not to the probandum, since the reason follows the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [probandum]. Likewise, in the case of "sound is perishable" (*vināśī śabdaḥ*), where is the qualifier unestablished (*asiddha*)? If it is unestablished in sound, then this is not a fault [of the thesis]. For if it is established by that very [subject], otherwise what would be the meaning of being a "probandum"? If it is called "unestablished" because its opposite is established, then even if a fool establishes the opposite, there is still no fault in the thesis merely on that account. If the opposite is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the thesis is simply sublated by that valid cognition; thus, that fault is characterized by contradiction with authority (*mānaviruddhatā*), and is not a separate fault. If it is established by an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then the fault is that the example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavikala*); thus, that fault belongs to the example itself, not to the thesis. However, in the case of one for whom both [the subject and the predicate] are unestablished, the fault is twofold; yet all these are actually faults of the reason alone. If it is argued that the thesis-fault arises precisely from the reason-fault because the thesis is in no way established, then all faults of the reason and so forth would become thesis-faults. There is no such thing as a reason-fault that does not obstruct the thesis. For: [The verse: "Because the reason is the instrument for establishing the thesis, therefore the faults of the reason are indeed the faults of the thesis. [The commentary: Since the reason is the means for establishing the thesis, the faults of the reason are indeed the faults of the thesis. Just as when a person is struck by a sword, the pain is felt by the person, not by the sword. But this is not a distinct category of fault; rather, it is a designation based on the fact that the reason-fault prevents the establishment of the thesis. Thus, the faults of the reason are themselves the faults of the thesis. This is because the reason is the instrument for the establishment of the thesis. Therefore, the faults of the reason are designated as faults of the thesis. It is not that there is a separate fault of the thesis apart from the reason-fault. For if there were a separate fault of the thesis, then even a correct reason would have to be considered faulty, which is absurd.
