[552,v] By every defect of the proof, it is the thesis itself that is obstructed;
nevertheless, the status of being a "defect of the thesis" belongs only to that which is designated as a mere proposition (*pratijñā*). 149.

[552, vi] A flaw in that thesis does not arise merely from the fact of its being obstructed; for otherwise, it would follow that even a flaw in the proof would constitute a flaw in the thesis. If it is argued that although it obstructs the thesis, the flaw in the proof is not a flaw in the thesis because there is no such principle here, then we reply: since it occurs at a time and in a form distinct from the thesis—transcending both the nature of the thesis and its proper occasion—it is not a flaw of the thesis, but rather a flaw of the reason (*hetu*), such as lack of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).

That too is incorrect, because non-concomitance (*ananvaya*) is the same [in both cases]. For non-concomitance is a lack of connection, and since that [lack of connection] resides in both [the subject and the property], it applies to both as well. Now, it might be argued: "The fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) consists in the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*), which depends upon the probandum (*sādhya*), not upon the means of proof (*sādhana*). However, dependence upon the means of proof is indeed a fault of the means of proof. To this it has been said: If both [the locus and the property] were to establish each other mutually, how could that be a fault of the thesis? Nor is there such a rule: that once the locus (*dharmin*) is established, one must prove only the connection with the probandum, on the grounds of the statement that "[the locus] is to be indicated by its own nature alone. How then was it stated that "since the means of proof is impossible when the locus is unestablished"? The intention is that, due to the unestablished nature of the locus, the reason (*hetu*) itself is impossible there. Therefore, even a collection of properties where the locus is unestablished is indeed the thesis (*pakṣa*). Consequently, the fault regarding the thesis is independent of the reason. From that:

The fault that depends upon subsequent members of the argument is what is connected by the word "thereby" (tena); therefore, it is said that defects such as an unestablished locus (*asiddhāśraya*) and so forth are not defects of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*). // 150 //
This has been stated.
If it is claimed that no fault resides in the thesis because it depends upon subsequent members [of the proof],
then by the same logic, faults such as those of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth would also follow as faults of the thesis.

Because the thesis is sublated by all [of these], therefore only those [reasons] that adhere to the mere [thesis] are considered defects of the thesis, and no others, just like contradictions with perception and so forth. (PVA 270)
Therefore, it is a logical principle that there is no fault in the thesis (pakṣadoṣa) such as an unestablished locus (asiddhāśraya) and so forth.

Now, one might object: "The inference 'sound is eternal because it is inaudible' is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is presented as a positive formulation that contradicts the nature of the property (*dharma*), just like the statement 'the moon is not the moon. It is not a case of sublation regarding the subject (*dharmin*), its properties (*dharma*), or the specific nature of the subject; nor is the example (*udāharaṇa*) unintelligible when not explicitly shown. Therefore, we do not understand what the reason for this is. To this, it is replied:
[553,vii] Of the subject, its properties, and their specific qualities, as well as the essential nature of the subject itself...
By this very [definition], the defects consisting of contradictions and the deficiency of essential members have been demonstrated. // 151 //

By this very example, which is intended to demonstrate the refutation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of phenomena (*dharma*), the sublation of all specific intrinsic natures has been shown. If it is asked, "How can one thing be demonstrated by another?", the answer is: because there is no distinction in their being the objects of proof (*sādhya*). In that regard, it is not possible to present an example for every individual instance, nor is there any purpose in presenting them; for by the presentation of a single example, that property (*dharma*) is easily understood. Indeed, an example is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). <2. Refutation of the Whole (*avayavinirāsa*)>

[553,ix] But how can a particular (*viśeṣa*) be a property (*dharma*) of both the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and that [other] property? It is not so; its status as a particular is relative to what was previously stated. Otherwise, the probandum (*sādhya*) would be that very thing, and the means of proof (*sādhana*) would be futile.
In this regard, a mere direction for an illustration is stated so that the meaning may be seen:
there is another object, characterized by substance and endowed with conjunction, which possesses visibility. (152)

A thesis concerning that which is invisible and undifferentiated is purposeless. [553,xii] These are the examples: "The whole is not other than its parts, because no difference in weight is perceived"; "The parts are not other than the whole, because it would follow that they are imperceptible"; "Substance does not exist, because it would follow that qualities and substances would themselves be substances. The last one among these refutes the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*). The first two examples refute the specific characteristics of the subject and the predicate (*dharma*) respectively.
Whatever is distinct from a certain form is perceived as such;
however, if that form is not perceived, the distinction is not established. (PVA 271)

[553,xiv] For that which is not perceived as distinct cannot be directly perceived as distinct. It is perceived as non-distinct, yet it is accepted as being distinct; therefore, this is a contradiction.
<3. Refutation of Substance, Quality, and Universal>
[553,xv] But if the parts are not distinct [from the whole], then perceptibility is unimpeded; where the whole is perceived, its parts are likewise of that same nature. (PVA) 272

[554,i] Otherwise, if the parts were distinct [from the whole], yet the whole were perceptible while the parts were not, there would be no distinction at all. Alternatively, the parts cannot be other than the whole, because that would entail the non-perceptibility of the whole. For if they were distinct, then when those parts are imperceptible, it would follow that the whole is also imperceptible; indeed, it is not logical for a whole to be perceptible while its parts are imperceptible, just as in the case of the first [postulated] whole.

Now, if it is held that only a gross composite (*sthūlavayavin*) is perceptible and nothing else, it has already been demonstrated that "grossness" in a single entity is a contradiction. Therefore, it is established that the composite is merely a collection of parts; there is no other [composite] distinct from them, nor are the parts anything other than that [collection].

Likewise, the phrase "there is no substance" is to be connected with the phrase "distinct from qualities. This is because it would follow that qualities and substances would themselves be either substances or non-substances. The meaning is that either the quality would possess substantiality, or the substance would possess the nature of a quality. For if there were indeed a distinction [between them], then by virtue of their mutual exclusion, the principle would be that form—when established by existence—is perceivable as a substance, and the same would apply to qualities. Consequently, since the two would exist through mutual exclusion, how could there be a discernment such that "one is a quality and the other is a substance"? And even if they did not exclude one another, how could there be a discernment? Now, if the thought is that the discernment consists in "the quality having the nature of a quality" and "the substance having the nature of a substance," [that too is untenable].
That too is incorrect.
Apart from its own essential nature, "quality-ness" (guṇatva) and so forth do not exist.
And if quality-ness were something distinct, existence (sattā) would also have to exist therein.
Consequently, that [quality] would be no different from a substance; thus, the aforementioned undesirable consequence remains unavoidable.
In the case of existence, the substance would be entirely present in both its difference and its non-difference [from its properties].

If substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and its opposite were established through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), then the distinction between them would not be proven; this point is already established. However, if there were a difference [between them], one might suspect a distinction based on the reasoning that "it is a substance because of its connection with substance-ness" and "it is a quality because of its connection with quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). But even that is not correct. Since they exist in mutual exclusion, like color (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), how can there be substance-ness and its opposite? If you say it is due to the connection with quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and so forth, we say no. Quality-ness is manifested by a particular quality (*guṇavyakti*) and not otherwise. Both quality-ness and substance-ness consist merely in a common form. Their distinction is simply their being manifested by particulars of a different genus (*vijātīya*). Furthermore, being manifested by a particular of a different genus means being superimposed by a different genus; thus, there is the fault of circular reasoning (*itaretarāśraya*).

Now, if it is argued that universals (*jāti*) possess their own distinctness from themselves and from one another, even in that case, the cause of their differentiation is precisely their being superposed upon different particulars (*vijātyadhyāsitatva*). If they were differentiated by their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), then individuals (*vyakti*) would also be so; thus, a further universal would be redundant. [The opponent might argue: "Because it is the basis for the cognition of a common form, such as 'quality' (*guṇa*). [We reply: If this is so regarding "the quality-ness of quality" (*guṇatva*), then what is the use of this useless internal tumor (*antargaḍu*) of a universal? For the fact that a universal is the basis for a cognition of a common form is well-established through its own specific function alone. And thus, there is no difference whatsoever between substance (*dravya*) and non-substance (*adravya*) in terms of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, if substances exist, there is indeed no distinction between substance and non-substance. However, if they do not exist, a distinction does arise; this is logical. [Thus we conclude: "Substance is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*); qualities are other than that. This is an illustration by way of refuting the distinction between the intrinsic natures of both. For example: "Every sentence has a false object."
[554,ix] "All speech has an unreal object"— in this case,
when one intends to refute the specific nature of that speech and its unreality, there is a fault in the refutation. (PVA 275)

When it is intended to refute "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and "being false" (*anṛtatva*) in a general sense, there is a refutation of the essential nature of both. However, when the property of the subject (*dharmin*), namely the sentence, is its impermanence (*anityatva*), and [the property to be negated] is the state of having a false referent (*anṛtābhidheyatva*), then there is a refutation of both specific attributes. This is because of the refutation of every particular sentence and of the state of having a false referent. For the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of speech arises from its capacity as an utterance; therefore, by that [capacity], there is a refutation of the absence of being a sentence and of having a false referent. Furthermore, in this context, some specific property of the subject, such as impermanence and so forth, is to be understood. For if impermanence...

[555,i] Accepting the authority of the speaker is indeed rendered useless and not established. If there were eternality, the speaker would perform no action whatsoever; thus, the speaker would be entirely purposeless, and therefore this is a contradiction of one's own words.
If the sentence were eternal, it would follow that its speaker is rendered useless;
if it assists by means of a non-sentential form, it would follow that it is already established prior to its appearance.

For one who does not assist the very nature of the sentence, there can be no status as an assistant to the sentence. If the assistance were not produced by that [sentence], it would contribute nothing to it; thus, one who provides no assistance would not be required by the sentence. Yet, he is indeed required. Therefore, its impermanence must be established. Consequently, by way of refuting its specific characteristics, this is stated to be a fallacious thesis (*pakṣābhāsa*). In this regard, the author of the *Vārttika* provides merely an indication of the examples. By this direction, for the purpose of understanding the explanation of the remaining examples, it is not merely the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from its parts that is being proven; rather, it is [proven] through its possession of the definition of a substance—namely, "substance is that which possesses action, possesses qualities, and is an inherent cause"—and likewise through its state of being perceived as such.

[555,v] However, if merely the otherness of the whole (*avayavin*) is being proven, then that is already established as being merely conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*). Since the parts are ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) while the whole is conventionally real, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) when mere otherness is the probandum. <4. Absence of gravity and downward motion>

For the whole (avayavin) is indeed accepted as the effect, which is impossible among [the parts] that are unperceived. And if another [entity] that is indistinguishable [from it] were being proven, that would be the proving of what is already established. 153.

[555, vii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from suffering. Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "If there be any good man or woman who seeks to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should observe that all five aggregates are empty in nature and thereby deliver themselves from all suffering and distress. The venerable Śāriputra then said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "How should a son of good family who practices the profound Prajñāpāramitā observe that all five aggregates are empty? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied: "O Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, O Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained, a Bodhisattva relies on the Prajñāpāramitā and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the unequalled mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, as well as the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and faithfully practiced it. The form of an erroneous cognition is indeed established merely as being distinct from parts, atoms, and so forth; if one were to prove that very [form], there would necessarily be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Furthermore, it is observed that for things situated in close proximity to one another and not too far away—such as a mass of hair—there arises a cognition of a single, dense form. Therefore, the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) distinct from the form of cognition cannot be established by that alone. Consequently, what must be proven in that case is precisely its possession of the defining characteristics of a substance (*dravya*). In that regard, weight is its quality (*guṇa*) and downward motion is its action (*kriyā*); and since it is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of these two, once the possession of these characteristics is established, the distinction of the whole from the form of cognition is proven. And thus:
If this were a depression of the scale, then there would be heaviness and downward motion. [555, viii] 154.

[555,ix] For if there were necessarily a downward motion induced by gravity, there would also be a bending of the end of the scale being pulled down by it; yet this does not occur. Since it possesses more parts than that [downward-moving portion], he says that it is not endowed with the characteristics of a substance.
Therefore, being devoid of quality and action, it is not an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).
This is the conclusion: since it is the inherent cause of those two—quality and action—it does not function as such in their absence.
For that very reason, it is not perceptible, because neither its effect nor its form is perceived. (155)

[555,xiii] Visibility (*dṛśyatva*) does not belong to it at all. For its manifestation occurs in two ways: figuratively (*upacārataḥ*) and primarily (*mukhyataḥ*). It is not, first of all, figurative, because its effects, such as weight (*gaurava*) and so forth, are not observed. Nor is it figurative in the sense of being the form of consciousness (*vijñānākāra*), because no form is perceived apart from the parts (*avayava*), since nothing additional is seen.

Because another particular [quality], which necessarily arises as the sublation of that [other], possesses the definition of a substance by virtue of its dependence on the mere difference from what was stated, it is the probandum (*sādhya*) due to its necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatvena*). Otherwise, mere otherness would not be the probandum. For instance:
When weight and downward motion are abandoned, there remains only its appearance;
and this appearance is not difficult to establish, even though it is not distinct from consciousness. (277) (PVA)

Even for those whose visual faculty has its power of perception distorted by *timira* (ophthalmia), things such as hair, gadflies, mosquitoes, and flies—which are categorized among the objects of false conviction—appear as if they were perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Yet, it is not the case that these things do not exist simply because they appear in that way. Regarding this:
Because a series of substances, down to the most subtle, is capable of being weighed, like a mass of rays of light. 156.
Another said: "There is no motion of gravity belonging to a distinct substance.

Because the weight of another substance situated in the midst of many substances cannot be perceived—due to the lack of a corresponding change in the measurement on the scale when there is a series of substances beginning with subtle dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)—there is no apprehension of a specific deviation in the scale’s depression. For even though, upon the conjunction of two lumps of gold, a further composite whole (*avayavin*) arises possessing qualities and actions, the series of intermediate substances starting from the dyads still exists therein. Consequently, the weight falling within that interval is not perceived, just like the weight added by a hundred locusts landing in the middle of a load of cotton. Yet, it is not the case that its weight and downward motion do not exist simply because they are unperceived; therefore, the claim that it is devoid of qualities and actions is unproven.
That is incorrect, because:
[556, viii]
If gravity is not perceived, how can there be its excessive motion?
For this very [perception] is the basis for the expectation of its cognition; how then could it be its effect?

Apart from a specific downward motion due to gravity, only a mere appearance is established. Nor does that which is thus established involve the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*). Furthermore:
[556,x] When it is joined to a heap of dust either sequentially or all at once... (157)
There would be a difference in weight when it is weighed separately and together.

For when a heap of dust is joined gradually, there is a great weight because of the presence of many parts possessing gravity; but when joined all at once, there is only a single composite whole, and thus no great weight. Therefore, a difference [in weight] follows [as a consequence]. Yet, no such difference is perceived; rather, it is observed only when a collection of many particles falls. Consequently, that [example of the dust heap] is not a valid illustration.

[556, xiii] Now, if the preceding whole (avayavin) is destroyed, there remains only a single whole at the end; thus, in the absence of multiple wholes, it is exactly the same whether the heap of dust is joined in succession or otherwise. Therefore, there is no fault. If that were the case, it would not be logical to say that "the substance is weighed by the scale" (*mālātolya*). Furthermore, it is not logical for the final [particle] to be characterized by the inference of weight (*gaurava*).

Alternatively, as long as the weight of the two constituent parts remains when they are separated, the weight of the whole composed of them remains exactly the same; therefore, no difference in the depression of the scale occurs. If that were the case, then since the production of a whole follows the destruction of all its parts, it would follow that atoms themselves are destroyed, which contradicts the established tenet that atoms are eternal.

Now, if it is argued that while there is destruction [of objects], there is no disjunction of atoms because they lack parts (*anavayavatvāt*), we say: no, for such partlessness is untenable. For those things possessing form (*mūrtimat*) must necessarily have spatial divisions of front and back. Therefore, it is not logical to claim that there is no destruction of the composite whole (*avayavin*).
Alternatively, it might be thought: "Let there be the destruction of atoms; this causes us no harm. If that is so, then:
[556,xvii] It is not logical that there should be an equality of number between the māṣaka and the others in their gradual sequence. 158.

[557,i] There would be no "five-māṣaka" aggregate because the parts—the individual *māṣaka* components—of the whole (*avayavin*) have perished; there would only be "one gold [piece]," and so forth. For it is when multiple weights are possible that numbers such as "five" can occur. But since the whole is a single entity, there is only the number one, due to the oneness of the whole.

Now, even if weight (*gaurava*) is a single entity, if such a designation [of it as distinct] occurs, then number (*saṃkhyā*) is not ultimately real. Therefore, when the constituent parts (*avayava*) are not destroyed, the number residing in them is established based on the similarity [of weight] in units such as *māṣaka* and so forth. Consequently, since composite wholes (*avayavin*) arise sequentially when multiple substances are present, there is a necessary distinction in weight. Alternatively, if [the difference were not perceived], then from a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) onwards, each subsequent [weight] would not be perceived at all, just as a single [unit] is unperceived, because there would be no distinction among all of them.
This is not so.
Even if a single part (*aṃśu*) is imperceptible, it does not follow that the collection of those parts is also imperceptible; therefore, this [argument of yours] is not tenable.

For it is not the case that when this [single part] is not perceived, its aggregate is also not perceived; because even when a single part is not perceived due to its lightness, the weight of the load is still perceived. Furthermore, a collection of parts constitutes what is designated as a "load of cotton.
Moreover, from a mustard seed up to a great heap, there is a progressive increase in magnitude.
If heaviness is not perceived at all in the series of effects, [then how could it exist in the cause]? 159.
The weight [of the body] up to a mustard seed is not insignificant;
it is the cause of the wound and the loss of color, because the heaviness of the effect is not perceived. (160)

[557,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld the sufferings of those beings and, by means of his compassionate power, liberated them all from their suffering. Then, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one understand the practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara? The Blessed One replied to the venerable Śāriputra: “If, Śāriputra, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should hear that the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara has been proclaimed, and if they should keep it in mind, then, Śāriputra, at that time, if they should fall into a great fire, they will be delivered from that great fire by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. If they should fall into great waters, they will not die therein; by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will stand upon dry land. If, Śāriputra, a multitude of yakṣas and rākṣasas should seize someone, and if that person should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, those yakṣas and rākṣasas will not be able to harm them. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there should be five hundred merchants traveling on the great ocean, and if a kāla-makara fish should appear and threaten to swallow the ship, and if among those merchants there should be one who calls upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, that kāla-makara fish will lose its grip and the ship will safely reach the shore. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One further said this to the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if a woman or a man should desire to have a son or a daughter, and if they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, a son or a daughter will be born to them, endowed with beauty, nobility, and wisdom, and free from all defects. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One further said this to the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if a woman or a man should wish to offer incense, flowers, necklaces, perfumes, ointments, powders, garments, or parasols to the Tathāgatas, and if they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will obtain all these offerings. Śāriputra, if a woman or a man should wish to give alms to the Tathāgatas, and if they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will obtain the merit of giving alms to as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One further said this to the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if a woman or a man should wish to see the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and if they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will see those Tathāgatas. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One further said this to the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if a woman or a man should wish to hear the Dharma from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and if they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then, Śāriputra, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they will hear the Dharma from those Tathāgatas. Thus spoke the Blessed One. A mustard seed (*sarṣapa*) consists of four parts of a *raktikā*. From that mustard seed onwards, up to a great mass, one does not perceive an increasing weight resulting from a continuous series of successive effects. However, prior to the mustard seed, weight—characterized by decrease—is even more imperceptible in each preceding stage; this being established, the logical conclusion is clear: since the weight of the effect is not perceived, it is the cause alone that is weighed, according to the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Weight is perceived only as something useful for distinguishing specific weights, and nothing else. For, when the weight of each subsequent effect is not perceived, that weight belongs to its cause; if that [effect] is what is weighed, then its cause is weighed, and that cause’s cause as well, and so on until the atoms (*paramāṇu*) are reached as the ultimate causes, because they have no further constituent parts. Thus it is.
When the destruction of the ultimate parts occurs, heaviness likewise belongs to those two;
yet we perceive that very same [heaviness] again when those two are further destroyed. (280) (PVA)
From that, we know the existence of weight in atoms through inference;
therefore, a substance that possesses the defining characteristics of a substance does not dissolve away.

Moreover, even if the weight of the parts is not perceived, it is the weight itself that is observed in them; the whole, however, is not visible. Its existence is established solely through the observation of its effects.
And all of that is non-existent, because:
And that object is not seen like a portion [of a whole], nor is its effect observed; for, just as with the non-descent of weight, all scales fail to perceive it. (161)

The absence of excess or deficiency in a māṣaka and so forth is merely an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa), just as when one does not perceive through one's own sense organ [the difference between] greater and greater degrees of color-form and so on. (162)
How can that which is not apprehended through either perception or inference be understood to exist?

[Objection: But surely, even if gravity is involved, since motion can occur by other means as well, how can it be said that [the whole] does not exist? [Response: No, because other properties such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth are likewise not perceived. A whole (*avayavin*) such as a *māṣaka* coin is nothing more than its constituent parts (*avayava*). [Question: If that is so, then why did the Teacher state the restriction [that the whole exists] on the grounds that the specific depression of the scale is not apprehended otherwise? [Response: No, for that depression is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Even when stated alone, it indicates the existence of the substance (*dravya*). [Question: How is it to be understood that everything else is not perceived? [Response: What is there to be known here? It is simply that color and the rest are not cognized in greater or lesser degrees by the eye and other senses according to their respective capacities. For even if a whole were possible, there is no perception of any distinction between color, taste, and so forth, and the parts. Therefore, just like qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*), the whole is simply non-existent as a perceptible entity; thus, this is a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) by way of contradicting a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*). And this thesis is contradicted by one's own tenets (*abhyupagama*), one's own words (*svavacana*), inference (*anumāna*), and common experience (*pratīti*).
[558,iv] However,
because there is the possibility of contradiction by one's own words and so forth,
another example may also be understood through the direction already stated. || 163 ||

[558,v] As in the case of the sublation of form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Therefore, other examples demonstrated by the Master (*ācārya*) illustrating the logic of the refutation of the whole (*avayavin*) should also be understood; and that has already been shown above. <5. Faults in the Naiyāyika’s definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*)>
[The inclusion of the term] “*sādhya*” is redundant.

[Objection: But surely the definition of the thesis (*pakṣa*) according to the Naiyāyikas is that “the statement of the *sādhya* is the thesis (*pratijñā*)”; what is the fault in this? [Response: It would follow that even an unestablished reason (*hetu*) or example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would possess that status.

[558,vii] But surely, that which is being proven is the "probandum" (*sādhya*). Since the unestablished reason (*hetu*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) will themselves be proven later, how can there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they too would be the thesis (*pratijñā*)?
[558,viii]
This is true, provided that it could be understood as a statement of a present probandum (*sādhya*). However,
because verbal suffixes (*kṛtya*) have the three times as their object, it does not possess such a nature.
Likewise, even when that [fault] is attributed to another, it remains a fault for the one who is being proven [guilty]. (164)

For all verbal suffixes denoting action (*kṛtyapratyaya*) have the three times as their domain. Therefore, even the state of being a future goal (*bhāvisādhyatva*) would constitute a thesis (*pratijñā*). How can there be the futurity of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*)? Because at that time it is designated as not having that nature [of being already established]. Even though it is a *sādhya*, at that time it is designated as a means of proof (*sādhana*). Consequently, at that time it is not a *sādhya*. And that which is unestablished cannot be a means of proof with respect to the *sādhya*. Therefore, its status as a means of proof occurs subsequently; thus, its designation as a thesis consists precisely in its being a *sādhya* at a later time.

[Objection: But surely, just as the word "sādhya" (to be proven) does not convey the sense of being "proven" with respect to the factors of action—as in the expression "the jar is being made"—so too, even that which is designated as a "means of proof" (*sādhana*) will not cause it to be understood as such. How, then, could there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that an unestablished means of proof constitutes a thesis (*pratijñā*)?
[Response:
This is true, provided that the context of making something understood were not the governing factor here.
But in the context of making something understood, [the word "probandum"] includes everything that has not been established;
therefore, the term "probandum" does not depend upon a specific qualification intended by the proponent. (165)

In the context of communication (*pratyāyana*), the term "probandum" (*sādhya*)—which subsumes all other things to be proven—is employed in relation to the factors of action (*kāraka*) that are to be excluded. Therefore, it is not capable of excluding other [types of] probanda. However, the exclusion of what is to be produced by a causal factor (*kāraka-sādhya*) follows from the context of the indicator-reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*). Furthermore, nothing exists with a cause and yet is not produced; for if it were so, it would follow that everything could exist everywhere. Nor is there any basis for the rule that only that which is designated as "not being a means of proof" (*asādhana*) constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*) as a probandum. Consequently, the word "probandum" is not capable of relying upon a specific intended [meaning]. As for the exclusion of what is to be produced by a causal factor, this arises from the context of communication; thus, there is no parity between the two cases.
Therefore, he has provided examples of reasons and illustrations that are unestablished and doubtful;
otherwise, even in the case of things like a hare's horn, which are entirely unestablished, they would be subject to proof. (166)
And thus, it follows that there would be a doctrine of reasons and examples that are unestablished.

"Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot"—this is directed against the Sāṃkhya. Or: "because it is visible, like space. If, however, there were no regard for the context (*prakaraṇa*), then for one who establishes a definition by mere opposition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things such as a hare's horn could be subject to being proven.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even here, regarding the rule "the statement of the probandum is the thesis" (*sādhyanirdeśaḥ pratijñā*), the status of being a thesis does not belong to every [probandum] simply because of its capacity to be communicated; rather, it belongs to that which is the *sādhya*. This is because the gerundive suffix (*kṛtyapratyaya*) is prescribed in the sense of the object (*karman*). And according to Pāṇini’s rule, "the object is that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*), the object is specifically that in which there is excellence (*prakarṣa*). Now, that which is indicated as a means of proof (*sādhana*) is not "most desired" because it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*). Otherwise, in the expression "he eats rice with milk" (*payasaudanaṃ bhuṅkte*), milk—which is intended as the instrument—would not have the status of an object, even though it is being consumed by the act of eating. Likewise, [only] what is already desired is the object, not what is merely about to be desired. Moreover, since the five members of the syllogism are under discussion as the objects of definition, the definition of the thesis is established by excluding the scope of the definitions of the other members. Thus, it is understood that "the statement of the probandum that is not itself a means of proof is the thesis. Furthermore, since the fourfold system of "axioms" (*siddhānta*)—namely, the universal axiom (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*), the specific axiom (*pratitantra-siddhānta*), the contextual axiom (*adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*), and the accepted axiom (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*)—is introduced at the outset of the *Nyāyasūtra*, and the definition is formulated therein, it is understood that the statement of the probandum is the thesis characterized as an accepted axiom (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*). Therefore, there is no fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
All of this is incorrect, because:
[559, viii]
Furthermore, since everything is in some way unestablished, [the arguments] regarding the introduction and refutation of the distinctions between action and so forth are not tenable. (167)
It is incorrect to say that the thesis is a member [of the proof] because its own nature is not yet established;
for those [members] are characterized by acceptance (upagama) in the same way as the tenet (siddhānta). || 168 ||

Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the Tathāgata’s appearance and non-appearance in the world? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, it is because sentient beings have long been afflicted by the three poisons, the four inverted views, the five hindrances, the six sense bases, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold wrong path, the nine fetters, and the ten unwholesome paths of action, yet they do not practice the three kinds of wholesome conduct, the four foundations of mindfulness, the five faculties, the six perfections, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten wholesome paths of action, that the Tathāgata appears in the world. It is because sentient beings have long practiced the three kinds of wholesome conduct, the four foundations of mindfulness, the five faculties, the six perfections, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten wholesome paths of action, yet they are not afflicted by the

Indeed, a tenet (*siddhānta*) does not function to exclude [the use of] unestablished reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), because everything that is unestablished is accepted [as a tenet]. For that which is seen in a treatise and accepted is precisely what constitutes an "accepted tenet" (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*). And even when such a thing is accepted as a reason, its status as something to be proven (*sādhya*) necessarily follows, for that which is unestablished cannot serve as a reason. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that verbal suffixes denoting action (*kṛtyapratyaya*) have the three times as their object; the word "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*) is likewise a cognition whose object pertains to the three times, since the mention of "action" is intended as an illustration. Consequently, the status of being a tenet would apply equally to everything, and therefore the objection regarding the introduction of a tenet is not a valid refutation.

[560,i] Now, while the definitions of both the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the object to be proven (*sādhya*) are under discussion, the statement that "the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the indication of the *sādhya* to the exclusion of the definition of the *sādhana*" implies that the proposition is indeed the *sādhya* itself, and not the indication of the *sādhana*.

That too is incorrect. Because all the definitions of the members [of a syllogism] are unestablished, and because the meaning [of those definitions] is unestablished prior to the statement of their definitions; consequently, the rule that "the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*)" would imply the statement of *everything* that is a probandum. Furthermore, it would follow that what is excluded from that [proposition] possesses the status of a means of proof (*sādhana*), or else that what is excluded from being a means of proof possesses the status of a proposition as the statement of a probandum—who is capable of making such a distinction? If it is argued that there is simply doubt [regarding this], we say no, because an answer to this will be stated later.

But surely, in the term *sādhya*, the kṛtya suffix denotes the object (*karman*). And an object is that which is most desired by the agent; however, for that which is intended as a means by virtue of being an instrument of accomplishment, there is no state of being "most desired. So how can it possess the status of being the "probandum" (*sādhya*)?

That is not so; for since the means itself is desired as the most sought-after object by virtue of being the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), no superlative suffix (*atiśaya-pratyaya*) is accepted there. This is because some accept a split in the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*), while others have rejected the superlative suffix altogether. Furthermore, neither the past-participle suffix nor the singular number would be mandatory there, since one intends to say "two mats" (*kaṭau*) or "many mats" (*kaṭān*). Moreover, this is indeed a case of an "accepted tenet" (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*). Therefore, the claim that "the statement of the goal to be accomplished is the thesis" (*sādhyanirdeśaḥ pratijñā*) is incorrect. And in this context, the subject (*dharmin*), the property (*dharma*), or the aggregate (*samudāya*) may be the thing to be proved.
In that case, the reason (hetu) which possesses similarity with the property to be proven (sādhya) in respect to the subject (dharmin) would be meaningless.

If *dharma* (the property) were the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), then the definition of the thesis (*pratijñā*) as "the statement of that [property]" would result in the [thesis] being non-eternal. Likewise, it would contradict the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which is: "An example is that which, through similarity with the thing to be proven, possesses the property of that [probandum]. For the property of impermanence, which is the *dharma* to be proven, does not possess properties such as "being produced" (*autpattimatva*) belonging to a jar or the like, by virtue of which it could "possess the property of that. Furthermore, since the substratum (*dharmin*) is already established, the definition of the reason (*hetu*)—"that which proves the thing to be proven"—is not applicable. If both [the property and the substratum] were to be proven, the fault would reside in both positions.

[560,vii] Is it not the case that the collection (*samudāya*) is what is to be proven? [560,viii] No; for the collection is not established, nor does the property of being subject to origination (*utpattimattva*) belong to it.
To this it is replied:
Even though the composite whole is the probandum, there is mutual qualification [of its parts].
Then that which is to be proven is unestablished, as are the characteristics of the reason and the example. (169)

[560,x] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a basis for form; he does not perceive a basis for feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive a basis for the eye; he does not perceive a basis for the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. He does not perceive a basis for forms; he does not perceive a basis for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. He does not perceive a basis for eye-consciousness; he does not perceive a basis for ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness. He does not perceive a basis for contact; he does not perceive a basis for feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death. He does not perceive a basis for the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a basis for any dharma whatsoever."

The definition of the reason (*hetu*) is: "The reason is that which establishes the probandum through similarity with the example. The definition of the example (*udāharaṇa*) is: "An example is that which, through its similarity to the probandum, possesses the property of that [probandum]. This would be inconsistent if the "probandum" were the aggregate (*samudāya*). For, since the aggregate does not exist apart from its constituent parts (*samudāyin*), those two [the subject and the property] alone would be the probandum. Furthermore, there is no similarity between the example and the property of the subject as qualified by the property to be proven—such as "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*) and so forth. Since the reason is unestablished for the opponent regarding such a subject, the definition of the reason is not tenable. Nor is there any similarity between the example, such as a jar, and the subject as qualified by impermanence; thus, the definition of the example is not tenable. Consequently, the definitions of the reason and the example are not established. Because the aggregate is impossible, the word "probandum" must refer to the subject (*dharmin*), according to the principle that words applied to aggregates also apply to their individual components.
That too is incorrect.

If it is claimed that the word "probandum" (sādhya) refers to the locus (dharmin) because [the property] cannot exist [therein], then enough with the treatise; let people proceed according to what is appropriate in common worldly usage. (170)

For what purpose would there be a formal definition at that time? Just as one might explain a poorly formulated definition otherwise because the meaning is impossible, so too will one falsely imagine the essential nature of the reason (*hetu*) and other members. Just as that [reason] is understood, so too the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the treatise (*śāstra*) would be rendered useless.

But is it not the case that you yourselves also accept, by way of metaphorical usage, that the word "pakṣa" (the subject) refers to the locus (dharmin), since you maintain that "the reason is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) pervaded by a part of it"? And thus, the subject (pakṣa) is the locus (dharmin), because the term for the whole is metaphorically applied to its part. Here too, the same fault remains.
This is not so; for:
When the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific qualities are sought to be known possesses the nature of the "thesis" (*pakṣa*),
and its property (*dharma*) serves as the reason (*hetu*), how can there be figurative usage (*upacāra*) in this case?

For it is precisely that subject (*dharmin*) which possesses the specific property (*viśeṣa*) characterized as the probandum (*sādhya*) sought to be known that is the "thesis" (*pakṣa*); thus, there is the apprehension of the primary thesis itself. Since the reason (*hetu*) is a property (*dharma*) of that [subject], there is no fault. [561, viii] But surely, if the aggregate (*samudāya*) is unestablished, how can it be established that it has a property? This too is not tenable, because:

If it is argued that [the subject] is established as a collection, how could that be the thesis (*pakṣa*)? For the status of being a thesis belongs only to the locus (*dharmin*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is doubtful. (PVA 283)

For when the aggregate (*samudāya*) is already established, it cannot be the subject (*pakṣa*) because its specific nature is not what is sought to be known. Thus it has been said: "In that context, the subject is that which is intended by oneself as something to be proven. If it is already established, how can it be intended as something to be proven? Therefore, what is the meaning of "the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*)? It means the property of the locus (*dharmin*) whose property (*sādhyadharma*) is doubted. In that case, if the aggregate is not established, how could its being a property of that [locus] be established? How then was it stated that [the term is applied] through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the whole to its part?
To this it is replied:
[561,xii] The employment of metaphorical designation is for the purpose of resolving the objection.
If it is stated as "the property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*), there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the definition.

[PVA 561, xiii] For in this regard, they raise the objection: "The term 'property of the subject' (*pakṣadharma*) is not correct. Indeed, at the time of determining the nature of the reason (*hetu*), the subject (*pakṣa*) does not yet exist. Having perceived the reason in the mere subject—such as a location—and having recalled the pervasion (*vyāpti*), one subsequently forms the cognition of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), such as permanence. But prior to that cognition, since that [proven property] is absent, only the mere subject remains known; if it is argued that the property to be proven is merely suspected, we say: no.
Because there is no necessity.

[Objection: Surely a logical reason operates when there is doubt; how then can there be a restriction? [Response: No, because it is only that which is established or rejected that one wishes to refute. A reason operates only with respect to what is certain or what has been refuted, because of the absence of purpose and because of incapacity. Therefore, one should simply state that [the reason] is a property of the subject (*dharmidharma*). [561,xvi]

To this it is replied: If one were to say simply "the property of the subject" (*dharmidharma*), then even the property of the subject in an example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmidharma*) would function as a logical reason (*hetu*); for instance, "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) would also become a reason. Therefore, the term "subject" (*pakṣa*) is included so that the subject which constitutes the *pakṣa* itself may be understood. To the question, "How can the subject alone be the *pakṣa*? he says: "Because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part. Although at the time of grasping the reason the whole does not yet exist as a mental construct, nevertheless, it will come to be later.

But surely, how can that which will exist later be present in the first [moment]? Precisely for this reason, it is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*); otherwise, it would be primary (*mukhya*). Metaphorical designation is a superimposition by means of the intellect. If it is asked, "How can there be an intellectual cognition regarding that which is not present?", is there poverty even in one's daydreams? For it is not the case that the expression "weave the cloth-thread" (*śāṭaka-sūtra*) is not observed. For in that case, if it were a cloth, it should not be woven; if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth. To say "it is a cloth and it is to be woven" is a contradiction. In that context, the speaker’s intention is: "That which will become a cloth is what is to be woven. If it is asked, "What is the purpose here?"—there is a purpose. If one simply said "the thread" (*sūtra*), there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including cloth, garments, and so forth. Therefore, such a statement is made precisely for the sake of excluding others. Likewise, in this case as well, the property of that which will be the subject (*pakṣa*)—wherein the proof of the probandum (*sādhya*) is to occur—is its property; thus, there is no unwanted consequence of including the property of the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). Therefore, the meaning is: "the property of the subject whose probandum-property is suspected. How then is it that "a part of that" (*tadaṃśa*) is "its property" (*taddharma*) by virtue of the speaker’s intention? It is not "a part of that" because the word *pakṣa* does not denote the whole collection—this is the statement [of the definition].
[562,ii] That is incorrect.
How indeed can a fault belonging to another be attributed to someone else?

This is the fault of the wicked commentator alone. Indeed, when one person eats a *karkaṭikā* fruit, another’s nose is not cut off. The "subject" (*pakṣa*) is the aggregate of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*). In that context, if it were stated in a general sense that [the reason] is "pervaded by a part of that," then the locus (*dharmin*) would also be a "part of that," and thus the definition [of the reason as being] "pervaded by the property to be proven" would fail to apply. Therefore, he says: "A part of that (*tadaṃśa*) is its property (*taddharma*). Although the word "part" (*aṃśa*) can denote a generality, here only the property is understood as the "part," due to the intention of the speaker; for it is not established that the property of the subject is pervaded by any other locus. The meaning of "not merely a part of that" (*na tadekadeśamātram*) is not "merely a portion. This is because the word "subject" (*pakṣa*) does not denote an aggregate. For by the word "subject," the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by the doubtful property to be proven is expressed. Thus, the word "subject" does not denote an aggregate. The cognition of the aggregate-meaning occurs only by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). Since it is a "part" (*aṃśa*) of that locus, by implication it is the property itself; for that [locus] cannot be its own property.

[562,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. Why is that? Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty; they are neither real nor unreal. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that all dharmas are empty? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, they are neither real nor unreal. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, generate the thought of awakening? How does he train in the six perfections? How does he enter the stages? How does he fulfill the factors of enlightenment? How does he purify the buddha-fields? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he turn the wheel of Dharma? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, yet by means of skillful means, a bodhisattva mahāsattva generates the thought of awakening. He trains in the six perfections without apprehending them. He enters the stages without apprehending them. He fulfills the factors of enlightenment without apprehending them. He purifies the buddha-fields without apprehending them. He matures sentient beings without apprehending them. He turns the wheel of Dharma without apprehending it. Why is that? Subhūti, because emptiness does not conflict with emptiness. Emptiness does not produce any dharma, nor does it cause any dharma to cease. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal.”

If, however, by the word *pakṣa* (the subject) a whole is meant—one whose parts possess an equal degree of primacy—then [the statement] "pervaded by a part thereof" could also mean "pervaded by a part characterized as the locus (*dharmin*)"; and this is undesirable. Therefore, it is explained in this way: for that reason, we have not anywhere imagined the word "other" (*anya*) elsewhere because of impossibility. Moreover, this is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "admission of the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*). To fail to refute a fault in one's own position while pricking at a fault in the opponent's position is "admission of the opponent's position. Alternatively, we have a purpose: the adoption of a locus suitable for metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). To say "let it not be so" is not a fit use of metaphor. Furthermore, when a primary sense is possible, the assumption of a metaphorical sense is improper. Moreover, regarding the definition "the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the statement of the probandum (*sādhya*"), there must be either an initial restriction (*pūrvāvadhāraṇa*) or a subsequent restriction (*parāvadhāraṇa*). [The former would mean: the statement of the probandum alone is the proposition, not the statement of the means of proof (*sādhana*). Or [the latter would mean: the statement of the probandum is only the proposition, and not otherwise. In that regard:

The restriction placed on the first [member] would be useless, whereas in the other case it would be undesirable. If the restriction were placed on the first [member], it would be redundant; for the status of being a *pratijñā* (thesis), which applies to the statement of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), would be sublated by the specific rules defining those two, since the general rule (*utsarga*) operates only after setting aside its domain of exception (*apavāda*). However, if the restriction were placed on the latter [member], it would follow that even the statements of the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason, and the example would be *pratijñās*, which is undesirable.

Now, if it is restricted that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement of only that which is yet to be proven (*sādhya*) and not that which is already established (*siddha*), what is the fault? For there is no implication of the latter by means of the proof (*sādhana*) and so forth.
To this, the following is said:
By the force of the exposition of the proof, it is considered that the state of being the probandum (sādhya) resides in its object.

For every means of proof (*sādhana*) is employed for the purpose of proving what is not yet established; once it is established, what is the use of a means of proof? By the very power of explaining the definition of a means of proof, it follows that the state of being the probandum (*sādhya*) resides only in an unestablished object. Since there is no possibility of it applying to what is already established, there is no need for a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) to exclude that case. Furthermore, because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the definitions of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, the status of being a means of proof is not even to be suspected in such a case. (171)

[563,v] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* by Vasubandhu, Chapter 5: Exposition of the Faculties (*Indriyanirdeśa*). Homage to the Buddha. Now, having explained the aggregates, elements, and bases, we shall explain the faculties. Among these, the faculty of mind (*manas*) has already been explained; however, the remaining faculties have not yet been explained. Therefore, they will now be explained. What are the faculties? They are twenty-two. Which are these twenty-two? They are: the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the faculty of mind, the faculty of female, the faculty of male, the life-faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental pleasure, the faculty of mental displeasure, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). These are the twenty-two faculties. Among these, the first five are the faculties of the sense organs (*indriya*). The sixth is the faculty of mind. The next two are the female and male faculties. The one following those is the life-faculty. The next five are the faculties of sensation. The next eight are the faculties beginning with faith. The last three are the faculties of the noble ones (*ārya*). Why are these called faculties? Because they exercise sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over their respective objects. Among them, the five beginning with the eye are faculties because they exercise sovereignty over the apprehension of their own specific objects. The faculty of mind exercises sovereignty over the apprehension of all objects. The female and male faculties exercise sovereignty over the differentiation of the continuum of existence into female and male. The life-faculty exercises sovereignty over the maintenance of the continuum of existence. The five faculties of sensation exercise sovereignty over the experience of the results of karma. The eight faculties beginning with faith exercise sovereignty over the purification of the mundane and supramundane paths. The three faculties of the noble ones exercise sovereignty over the attainment of the state of an Arhat. Thus, because they exercise sovereignty, they are called faculties. However, some say that the faculties are so called because they exercise sovereignty in the production of their own effects. But this is not correct, for in that case, the sense organs and the objects would also be faculties, since they too contribute to the production of their effects. Furthermore, the mind and its concomitants would also be faculties, as they produce their own subsequent moments. Therefore, it is because they exercise sovereignty in their respective domains that they are called faculties. Among these, the first eleven are common to both the mundane and the supramundane. The last three are exclusively supramundane. Among the faculties of sensation, the faculty of equanimity is common to both the pleasant and unpleasant states, while the others are distinct. The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" belongs to those on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). The faculty of "perfect knowledge" belongs to those on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). The faculty of "one who has known" belongs to those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship. Why are there exactly twenty-two faculties? Because they serve as the basis for the continuity of existence, the distinction of existence, the experience of the results of karma, and the purification of existence. The faculties of the sense organs and the mind serve as the basis for the continuity of existence. The female and male faculties serve as the basis for the distinction of existence. The five faculties of sensation serve as the basis for the experience of the results of karma. The faculties of faith and so forth serve as the basis for the purification of existence. Since these purposes are fulfilled by twenty-two, there are no more than that number. Nor are there fewer, because the purpose of the faculties is not accomplished otherwise. Thus, the faculties are established as twenty-two. Now, among these, how many are material? How many are immaterial? Eleven are material: the five sense organs, the three faculties of sensation (excluding the mental faculty), and the two sexual faculties. The rest are immaterial. How many are visible? Only one is visible: the eye-faculty. How many are resistant? Ten are resistant: the five sense organs and the five objects of the senses. The rest are non-resistant. How many are internal? Seven are internal: the six faculties of the sense organs and the faculty of mind. The rest are external. How many are appropriated? Eight are appropriated: the five sense organs, the female and male faculties, and the life-faculty. The rest are not appropriated. How many are derived from the primary elements? All material faculties are derived from the primary elements. How many are not derived? The immaterial ones are not derived. How many are past? How many are future? How many are present? All are of the three times. How many are wholesome? How many are unwholesome? How many are neutral? Twenty-one are either wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; the faculty of "one who has known" is exclusively wholesome. How many are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)? How many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)? Nineteen are associated with outflows; the last three are without outflows. How many are conditioned? All are conditioned. How many are unconditioned? None. How many are included within the truths? Twenty-one are included within the truth of suffering and the truth of origination; the last three are included within the truth of cessation and the truth of the path. How many are not included? None. How many are to be abandoned by seeing? How many are to be abandoned by cultivation? How many are not to be abandoned? Nineteen are to be abandoned by cultivation; the last three are not to be abandoned. How many are of the desire realm? How many are of the form realm? How many are of the formless realm? Seventeen are of the desire realm; the five beginning with the eye and the five objects of the senses are of the form realm; the life-faculty and the four faculties of sensation (excluding the mental faculty) are of both realms; the last three are of neither realm. How many are of the three realms? All are of the three realms. How many are included within the aggregates? All are included within the five aggregates. How many are included within the bases? All are included within the twelve bases. How many are included within the elements? All are included within the eighteen elements. How many are faculties? All are faculties. How many are not faculties? The objects of the senses and the unconditioned are not faculties. How many are faculties of grasping? The faculties of pleasure, pain, mental pleasure, mental displeasure, and equanimity are faculties of grasping. How many are not faculties of grasping? The rest are not. How many are faculties of bondage? The faculties of pleasure, pain, mental pleasure, mental displeasure, and equanimity are faculties of bondage. How many are not faculties of bondage? The rest are not. How many are faculties of liberation? The last three are faculties of liberation. How many are not faculties of liberation? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the noble ones? The last three are faculties of the noble ones. How many are not faculties of the noble ones? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the worldlings? The first nineteen are faculties of the worldlings. How many are not faculties of the worldlings? The last three are not. How many are faculties of the learner (*śaikṣa*)? The last two are faculties of the learner. How many are not faculties of the learner? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*)? The last one is a faculty of the non-learner. How many are not faculties of the non-learner? The rest are not. How many are faculties of both? The faculty of "perfect knowledge" is a faculty of both. How many are not faculties of both? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the fruit? The last three are faculties of the fruit. How many are not faculties of the fruit? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the cause? The first nineteen are faculties of the cause. How many are not faculties of the cause? The last three are not. How many are faculties of the effect? The last three are faculties of the effect. How many are not faculties of the effect? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the path? The last three are faculties of the path. How many are not faculties of the path? The rest are not. How many are faculties of the mundane? The first nineteen are faculties of the mundane. How many are not faculties of the mundane?
