It might be argued as follows: the restriction “the statement of that which is to be proven (sādhya) alone is the thesis” is intended to exclude cases where something already established is stated as a means of proof (sādhana), by taking into account the function of the words [of the definition]. For it is not the case that there is no capacity for proof in such instances. To this, he replies: because of the pervasion (vyāpti) by the definitions of the reason (hetu) and so forth, what is stated as a means of proof cannot be suspected [of being the thesis]. Just as, with respect to the function of the words, there is a rejection of what is unestablished (asiddha) when it is stated as a means of proof—on the grounds that it must be stated as something to be proven (sādhya)—so too, by the definition of the reason and so forth, such as “the reason is that which proves the probandum through similarity to the example,” the reason is indeed that which proves the probandum by way of its nature as a means of proof. Likewise, it can be explained that the example itself is likewise [a means of proof]. Thus, there is pervasion by the definitions of the reason and so forth.
<6. The Fault in the Definition of the Proposition> [563,
vi] By that [definition], when the restriction is placed on the former [element], there is the statement of the definition of the proposition (*pratijñā*).
That statement, whose fruit is the pervasion, is useless; therefore, it is understood through implication.

[563, vii] If the restriction were applied to the first term, it would be redundant; therefore, by the method of elimination, the restriction applies to the latter term, and its fruit is pervasion (*vyāpti*). For instance, [the definition] "the statement of the probandum is the thesis alone" (*sādhyanirdeśaḥ pratijñaiva*)—even if there were pervasion through another characteristic, the sentence would still have the fruit of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), meaning that the statement of the probandum, even when stated as a means of proof (*sādhana*), is indeed the thesis and nothing other than the thesis. Otherwise, it would be redundant.
[563, viii]
But is it not stated by [the opponent] himself:

"In that case, the fallacy of citing an unestablished example or reason follows"? When the opponent offers a rebuttal by means of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the definitions of reasons and so forth, the rebuttal is that [the reason] was previously unestablished in its essential nature, and likewise [the objection] beginning with "because everything is unestablished. This too is not a fault.
[563,x] Thus, by this very [reasoning], a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) has been established through mutual contradiction; however, it does not establish what is desired by oneself. (PVA 285)

[563,xi] This is merely a demonstration of mutual contradiction; however, the probandum is not established by this reason, because the intention is solely the refutation of the opponent’s position. Therefore, this is simply a restriction regarding the subsequent term. Thus, through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), whatever non-status as a thesis (*apratijñātva*) there may be is entirely negated: "It is indeed a thesis, not a non-thesis. Consequently, even that non-status as a thesis which exists in the capacity of a means of proof (*sādhana*) is also excluded. [563,xii]
The definition of a thesis (*pratijñā*) has already been refuted. Now, he speaks in order to refute the definition of a fallacious thesis (*pratijñābhāsa*):
"It is incorrect to say that a defect of the thesis occurs when there is a contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the thesis."
For that very thing has been stated as an example by those unskilled in the method of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
As the opponent says: "The so-called contradiction between the thesis and the reason is a fault of the thesis; for example: 'Sound is eternal...'"

[564,i] "Because everything is impermanent. The proposition (*pratijñā*) is "Sound is eternal," and the reason (*hetu*) is "because everything is impermanent. If everything is impermanent, how can sound be eternal? For without sound, there would be no "everything-ness. Alternatively, if sound is also impermanent, how can it be said that "sound is eternal"?
To this he replies: This is not a fault of the proposition (*pratijñā*), because:
[564,iii] "Contradiction, lack of connection with what is intended, non-assistance, and co-existence."
In this way, all defects of the members [of an argument] would become defects of the proposition (pratijñā). ॥ 173 ॥

[564,iv] When there is a contradiction, the so-called "contradiction between the proposition and the reason" is a defect of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*). That contradiction consists in a lack of connection with what is intended (*iṣṭāsambandha*). Furthermore, that lack of connection with what is intended is either non-utility (*anupakāraka*) or coexistence (*sahāvasthiti*). If, first of all, the reason does not assist that object because it is defective and contradicts the probandum (*sādhya*), then it would follow as a consequence that all defects of the constituent members [of the syllogism] would be defects of the proposition.

No defect of the members of the proof, such as the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, is contradictory by virtue of the contradiction characterized by failing to assist the probandum (*sādhya*). Consequently, it would follow that every defect of the logical mark (*liṅga*) would be a defect of the proposition (*pratijñā*), yet this is not the case. For it has been established that: "A defect of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) does not depend upon anything else."

If a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) were to exist even in relation to something else, then there would be no such thing as a fault of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*) at all. Since it would be included within the faults of the thesis by virtue of contradicting the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*), there would be no separate mention of the faults of the proof. For what person of unclouded intellect would speak of something separately when it is already included within another? Therefore, a fault of the thesis of this kind does not exist at all. Now, if contradiction (*virodha*) has the nature of co-inexistence (*sahāsthiti*), then:
And there is the "unestablished due to impossibility in what is intended" (*iṣṭāsambhavyasiddha*).

If a reason is impossible in the intended subject (*pakṣa*), then it is unestablished; thus it would be refuted by its very lack of establishment, not by contradiction with the thesis. If, on the other hand, the refutation of what was proposed by that [reason] were to occur, then the fault of the thesis would be one refuted by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which it is established; thus, there would be no such thing as "contradiction. Furthermore:
That very [position] has already been refuted. 174.
If one were to proclaim that impermanence and its cause reside in sound itself in this manner:
"If one were to proclaim that impermanence and its cause reside in sound itself in this manner."
To whatever extent.
[564,xiii]
Apart from the narration of examples, what further observation of the meaning is there here? || 175 ||

This explanation is not for the sake of the reason (*hetu*), but rather for the sake of the example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). [The argument is: "Sound is eternal, because everything is impermanent. In this case as well, it should have been stated thus: "Because everything is impermanent. However, it was expressed in this way due to a lack of training. And so it has been said: [564,xv]
For that has indeed been stated as an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) by those who are poorly trained;
we see no purpose other than the mere mention of an example here.

If it is asked why this is so, it is because this would only be a valid reason if the word itself were to establish impermanence; however, this is not tenable. Why? [This is discussed in the section on] <7. The Examination of Universals>.

Having designated a distinction as distinct, if one then follows after the universal, what is the result of that following after the universal? Is it not the case that there is neither pervasion by it nor any fruit in such following? (176)

[565,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the truth of suffering as real, nor does he perceive the truths of origin, cessation, or the path as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or Arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of Buddhahood as real. Subhūti, it is because he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom. Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom train? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who wishes to train in the perfection of wisdom should train in this way: ‘Just as all dharmas are ultimately empty, so should I train. Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in this way, he does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. He does not perceive a self, a being, a soul, or a person as real. He does not perceive form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact, that which arises from ear-contact, that which arises from nose-contact, that which arises from tongue-contact, that which arises from body-contact, or that which arises from mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the truth of suffering, the truth of origin, the truth of cessation, or the truth of the path as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer, the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or the fruit of Arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood or the fruit of Buddhahood as real. Subhūti, it is by training in this way that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom.”

For all applications [of rules] are understood through adherence to the logic of verbal expression (*śābdanyāya*). And this verbal logic consists of injunction (*vidhi*), prohibition (*niṣedha*), and restriction (*niyama*). Furthermore, an injunction may be either subverting (*bādhaka*) or subverted (*bādhya*); the same applies to a restriction. In that regard, the relationship of subverter and subverted exists between a general injunction and a specific injunction. In such cases, sometimes the first is the subverted and sometimes it is the subverter. However, the established rule is that in every instance, the specific is the subverter and the general injunction is the subverted; for it is observed that linguistic usage proceeds in this very manner. In this context, regarding the statement "the word is eternal," there is an injunction of the specific property of eternality with respect to the specific subject "word. Conversely, there is an injunction of non-eternality with respect to the general locus (the substratum). Thus, the relationship of subverter and subverted is logical. This is just as when it is said, "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya": the general act of giving curd is subverted by the specific injunction of giving buttermilk. As the principle goes: "The general rule (*utsarga*) applies only after setting aside the scope of the exception (*apavāda*). Therefore, the pervasion of that specific [rule] occurs through the operation of the general rule. Moreover, this result does not arise from the power of the [specific] statement itself, because the statement [of the general rule] has its own scope of application (*sāvakāśatva*).

If this were the intended meaning, then one should say: "Sound is eternal because it is impermanent. If you argue that there might be a convergence of two qualifiers—each having its own unfulfilled purpose—upon a single object, and that such being the case, a contradiction would arise due to sheer stupidity, we reply: no such possibility exists. For it is not possible for a person to be so stupid as to first establish eternity in that very same thing and then, at that very same time, establish impermanence. Furthermore, one who lacks even the basic understanding of the meaning of sentences has no entitlement to engage in debate.

Now, an example of the contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) must be conceived in some way. If someone were to say this, then one might claim: "Because there is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason, it is a fault called 'contradiction of the proposition' (*pratijñāvirodha*). This is indeed accepted. The formal argument (*prayoga*), however, would be: "Sound is eternal, because it is non-eternal. For in this way, by necessity, non-eternality would belong to sound alone. Consequently, there is a contradiction in the negation of eternality. Therefore, he says:
"There may be a negation [of eternality] only by means of what is established as sound; therefore, he speaks [thus]. [565,v]

The Teacher says: There might be a refutation of the meaning of the proposition here by means of a reason, if sound were something that persists. Only through the persistence of sound could there be a refutation; however, because two contradictory things cannot coexist, this demonstration elsewhere is not a refutation at all. This is merely the presentation of an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) does not exist now, he says: [565,vii]

Where the variability of the counter-example to the probandum is described by means of the fifth case-ending, there the example is considered the reason, while the application is derived from the introductory statement. (287) (PVA) [565,
viii]
If it is asked how it is understood that "whatever is impermanent is all [included], and sound is not [all]," he says:
"By stating [the reason] in a subject that is contradictory [to the thesis], one asserts the difference of the audible. (177)

Furthermore, that [exclusion] is not tenable for universals because their differentiation is not rejected. By demonstrating impermanence—which is the opposite of permanence—in a domain other than sound, one is indeed asserting the distinctness (*anyatā*) of sound. Since everything is pervaded by impermanence, and sound is impermanent, it follows that it is "other" than that [everything]; thus, this reason would result in sound being non-universal (*asarvatva*). He states that such distinctness is an unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*), because sound itself is universal.
And that [existence] is not tenable for universals, because they do not exclude difference.
For a universal cannot acquire its own nature without excluding particularity, because particulars themselves are restricted to the domain of excluding their own internal subdivisions.
Furthermore, it might be argued that by the word "all" a collection (*samudāya*) is expressed, and a single word is not a part of a collection.

That is incorrect. For if one were to exclude each [part] individually in this manner, nothing would be "all. It is observed that in the statement "a tree is not merely a *śiṃśapā*," there is a rejection of the distinction [between them]. That too is incorrect.
Just as in a certain context it is said, "A tree is indeed a *śiṃśapā*. (178)
A negation that applies to all hearing would not [occur] merely by that much; for such a negation of all distinctions is impossible unless they are non-identical with that [negation]. (179)

[566, vii] Now, if it is argued that "all" is merely the word itself according to the speaker’s intention, then, in that case, the term "non-all-word" would be a synonym for "word," and there would be the fallacy of the unestablished nature of a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthekadeśāsiddhatā*), just as in the argument: "Sound is impermanent because it is a sound," and so forth.
[566, viii]

Now, is it not the case that the sound-ness (*dhvanitva*) of sound is unestablished? For nothing is possible in the absence of its own nature (*svarūpa*). It is not unestablished by virtue of being the subject (*dharmin*) in its own nature; rather, it is called "unestablished" because it is unestablished as a reason (*hetu*). For the state of being a reason exists only when there is a distinction [between the reason and the subject], and not otherwise. Why? Because a distinction between the object to be known (*jñāpya*) and the knower (*jñāpaka*) is necessarily required. Indeed, a sound is not made known by a sound, because the object to be known would itself be unestablished. Nor is an unestablished thing proven by means of what is unestablished. Furthermore, if the sound were already established, it still could not be proven; for that which is already established is not proven by means of what is established.

[566,ix] But surely, the identity of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is not accepted. However, what contradiction is there in the non-difference between the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the probans? There is indeed a contradiction. For if one says, "It is impermanent because of being sound," the entire aggregate (*samudāya*) would not be the probandum.

[Objection: But surely, by implication, it is sound itself that is impermanent; thus, there is no contradiction regarding its being a collection [of properties]. For when one says "it is impermanent because of its being sound," impermanence is not understood to apply elsewhere, nor is it understood as something isolated. Indeed, smoke does not fail to possess fire simply because of its being smoke. In that case, there is a distinction through the relation of universal and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*). Here too, if it were formulated as "this is permanent because of its being sound, like the word 'cow'," then it would indeed be a valid reason. However, in the present case—"all sound is impermanent because of its being sound"—there is no such relation of universal and particular.

Now, is it not the case that if "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is the subject (*dharmin*), its status as a probans (*sādhana*) is contradictory? If there is an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), how could it not be a probans? On the other hand, if such a concomitance does not exist, then it is simply inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, the fault called "unestablished" (*asiddha*) does not apply; for it is inconclusive due to being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). Consequently, when a property belonging to the subject functions as a reason, the fault is precisely its inconclusiveness, not its unestablishedness. [566,xii]

Furthermore, if the connection with being further specified is not established, it is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*). For there is nothing distinct that remains to be further demonstrated. In that case, one must state either "sound is eternal because it is sound" or "it is non-eternal because it is sound.
[566,xiii] But is it not both? This is not so.
When it is stated that "sound is impermanent," another reason is required;
to exclude that [requirement], the phrase "because it possesses the nature of sound" is stated once again. (PVA 288)
In the argument "sound is perishable because it possesses the nature of sound," once other substrata have been excluded,
the application of the word "sound" (śabda) again accords with its functional capacity.

If it were said that "it is impermanent because of its being sound," there would be a dependence upon another property (*dharma*). And in the case of "sound is impermanent," there would be a dependence upon another reason (*hetu*). To exclude those [objections], both are employed; thus, there is no fault.
To this, it is replied:
If the capacity of the property of being a sound (śabdatva) renders other reasons redundant,
then if it lacks such capacity, what is the point of that repetition? (290) (PVA)
Therefore, in a subsequent statement, since that which was intended to be expressed is not present here, the fault is simply its lack of establishment (*asiddhatā*).

"Why is the fault of *ananvaya* (lack of positive concomitance) not mentioned here? Let it be that this fault also applies in the case of unrestricted debate (*aniyatakathā*) by way of conjunction; however, in restricted debate (*niyatakathā*), it is not appropriate because there is no defeat of one who has already been defeated, and because one must attend to the point of censure (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*). Therefore, the subject (*dharmin*) is indeed unfit for proving its own property (*svadharma*). If it were capable [of proving itself], it would follow that there is no dispute, and thus the reason (*hetu*) would be redundant. Therefore:
Because of the distinction between the object to be made known (*jñāpya*) and the means of making it known (*jñāpaka*), the subject (*dharmin*) which is to become the reason [cannot prove itself].
Since the status of being an indicator is unestablished, there is a lack of establishment of the locus (dharmin) in its own proof. (180)

For a distinction between the indicator (*jñāpaka*) and the indicated (*jñāpya*) is observed; in the absence of that [distinction], the status of being a reason (*hetutva*) is unestablished. Indeed, a lamp, while illuminating by its very nature of luminosity, is not capable of accomplishing its own causal function if that form [of luminosity] is not perceived. And it is only when there is a distinction that the indicator effects the making known of the indicated. Yet here, there is no distinction from the nature of the subject (*dharmin*). Therefore, because the status of being an indicator is unestablished, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*). If it is argued that the unestablished status of being an indicator follows also from the unestablished nature of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), we say no. If a distinction existed, there would be an inquiry into positive concomitance; but here, since there is no distinction at all, what role does an inquiry into positive concomitance have when the fault is already present by that much alone? Consequently, the subject is unestablished for its own proof.

[567, viii] But surely lamps and the like are indeed established in their own proof. True; they are established, but it is an unequal comparison to say that they establish what is imperceptible by being themselves perceptible. For there is no dispute regarding the intrinsic nature when a lamp is seen. Here, however, even when a sound is heard, there is indeed a dispute regarding its impermanence. If there were no dispute, then [impermanence] would be established by perception just like the nature of sound itself.

If it is argued that the fault is equal everywhere because the distinction between property and property-bearer is unestablished in all entities, [we reply] no, because there is a distinction by way of conventional reality (saṃvṛti). 181.

[Objection: But surely, producedness (*kṛtakatva*) and being sound (*śabdatva*) are also established by perception just like the lamp. [Response: If it is argued that there is no relationship of probandum and probans because they are distinct due to the conceptualization of different properties (*dharma*), this is the same for the lamp as well. For even there, the conceptual distinction exists in the form "the nature (*svarūpa*) of the lamp. [Reply: No, because the distinction exists conventionally (*saṃvṛti*). Just as there is a conceptualization of a distinction in the phrase "the nature of the lamp," it is not so in the case of the means of proof (*sādhana*). The designation "lamp" applies to its state of having activity (*vyāpāra*) or lacking activity; however, "nature" refers merely to the nature itself. In that regard, it is the nature because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*), and causal function arises from the nature. The lamp, however, is the locus of properties (*dharmin*). But for that which lacks activity, there is no such thing as a "nature" at all. It is not tenable to say that there is a lack of activity simply because the intended causal function is absent, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is any purpose achieved by speaking in this way. If you claim it is a conceptualization of difference, then it is not so, because that [distinction] is established even through the relation of universal and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). Therefore, the locus of properties is not the means of proving the nature, because there is no difference [between them]. However, in the case of producedness, impermanence, and sound, there is indeed a difference created by their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). To explain: *Note: The original text contains a complex debate regarding the ontological status of the lamp (the *dharmin*) versus its nature (*svarūpa*), and the role of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in establishing the relationship between the property (*dharma*) and the subject.*
When a single objective entity is itself directly perceived, what other unperceived part could there be that would need to be examined by means of valid cognitions? (291) (PVA)
For that single nature of the object has been directly realized by perception; what else remains of it to be examined?

If it is asked: "Is it not the case that only the substratum (*dharmin*) is established by perception, while impermanence and so forth are not? What then is the property (*dharma*)? [We reply: No, because it is one with impermanence. For that which is called "impermanence" is not something other than that [substratum].
For if impermanence were distinct from it, how could there be a cognition of the substratum, sound?
Otherwise, if it were not so, these two would be non-existent.
iii] If the apprehension [of an object] as pervading another time is due to its being eternal, [then...]
Even by a thousand other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no apprehension of impermanence in that same way;
for how could there be [such apprehension] through another means of valid cognition regarding what has already been cognized by perception? (PVA 293)

[568,v] There would be a total rejection [of all other means of knowledge]. Every other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has perception (*pratyakṣa*) as its foundation. For those who share the nature of crabs are indeed princes who are devoured by their own progenitors; they are not cognitions that function as means of valid cognition. And perception is the primary means of valid cognition among all means of valid cognition. So then, is Great Time (*mahākāla*) himself being devoured by *ḍākinīs*? [568,vi]

Now, neither permanence nor impermanence is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By that [perception], only the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of every entity is measured; whether it be permanence or impermanence, these depend upon subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: But how can impermanence—which is the very essence (*svabhāva*)—be said not to be apprehended? For permanence is the state of pervading extended divisions of time, and impermanence is the opposite of that.
In that case, the apprehension of permanence occurs when the pervasiveness of the entity is apprehended;
if that is not apprehended, then the perception of impermanence is attained. (PVA 294)

If it is argued: "Precisely when the persistence of entities through another time is not perceived, at that very moment the perception of impermanence is perfectly clear; it is simply that this persistence is not perceived, but not impermanence itself," [we ask]: what indeed is this so-called "impermanence"? It is merely another name for that very [persistence] acting as a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Does that [impermanence] exist at that same time, or later? If you say it exists at that same time, why is it not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? How can that which is not being perceived be identical with its nature? For that which is perceived as identical is indeed identical in nature; whereas that which is perceived as related must necessarily be distinct. But if you argue that while it is not being perceived, it is nevertheless perceived later as being related to that [entity], [we reply: ...
When that which meets the conditions for apprehension is not cognized by perception, how can it be said to exist? Otherwise, there is no other way to understand its non-existence. (295) (PVA)

Where there is no perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility, only that [object] is established as non-existent; there is no other way to prove non-existence. And so it has been said:

"For those who state that [the absence of the reason] is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it follows by the very fact of the matter from the opposite [of the probandum]. Now, if this were an error, then there would be no fault even if [the reason] is not perceived.
[But] if an error were to occur in every apprehension of the locus (*dharmin*)," [568, xiii]
For if there is no means of valid cognition for the subject (*dharmin*), how can inference be a means of valid cognition?

(296) How could a reason whose connection with the subject is unestablished attain validity? When neither perception nor inference would be a means of valid cognition, (297) [how could inference exist?]

Then there would be the establishment of the object of cognition, and thus [the world would be] mere representation (vijñaptimātraka), when through direct perception there is no grasping of future or past forms.
At that time, since the connection with the subject of the thesis (dharmin) is established through direct perception, [the proof is complete]. (PVA 298)
The establishment of an object, whether future or past, occurs through inference from a logical reason; thus,
the proof of an object other than that which is directly perceived is well-founded.

[568,xviii] But if it is maintained that the future and the past forms of matter (*rūpa*) are one and the same, then inference would be redundant because [the object] is already established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If there were the presence of error, there would be a total annihilation that sweeps everything away, and thus nothing at all would exist. Therefore, whether impermanence or permanence, it is indeed established by direct perception. Now, if it is argued that it is not established by direct perception because it is a property (*dharma*), [we reply]: only the substratum (*dharmī*) is established by direct perception; otherwise, there would be no inference. For the establishment of all properties occurs through direct perception itself. [569,i]
That is incorrect, because:
[569,ii] For when a property (dharma) is established through direct perception, the locus (dharmin) is thereby established.
Even perception is not a means of proving a mere locus devoid of properties (dharmin).

Indeed, nowhere is a locus established as such when stripped of its properties, because it is necessarily grasped by way of its being a sound or its being an object. Therefore, just as there is a grasping of "sound-ness" and so forth, there is likewise a grasping of "eternality" and so forth; in that regard, there is no difference whatsoever.
[569,iv] But surely, if there is no perception of some deviant property, what fault is there in this? For example, in the case of a post and a person.

For indeed, it is possible to perceive mere verticality without [the specific qualities of] being a post or being a person; however, there can be no cognition of an object without [the perception of] its distinctness from others. (301) (PVA) [569, vi]

For it is not possible to apprehend [an object] while abandoning its pervasive nature; that very nature is its form, and if that is not apprehended, then it is simply not apprehended at all. [569, vii] But surely, even when length is not apprehended as "length," it is still seen? No, because in that case only the parts are seen, and that length does not belong to them. Rather, that length belongs to the whole (avayavin), and that [whole] is to be known through inference; for instance:
When one part moves, it is understood that the whole moves;
because of that, this oneness is established through inference. (PVA 302)

[569,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of all perfections. Subhūti asked: “For what reason, Blessed One, is this perfection of wisdom the perfection of all perfections? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, because within this perfection of wisdom all the perfections are contained; therefore, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of all perfections. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how many perfections are contained within this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom—Subhūti, these six perfections are contained within this perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does the perfection of giving become contained within this perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives a gift while not apprehending that gift, not apprehending the recipient, and not apprehending himself as the giver. Thus, Subhūti, the perfection of giving becomes contained within this perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does the perfection of morality become contained within this perfection of wisdom? When one part is being pulled, it is perceived that the entire collection of parts is being pulled along with it; thus, they are considered "one" with the other. However, this is not an inference. It is only the mutual connection that is inferred in such a way, not oneness. Nor is that [oneness] the object of inference. For if perception does not operate, it cannot become the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, it is not logical for that very same thing to be both seen and unseen. Therefore, whether it pervades time or is non-pervasive, it is grasped by perception alone; it is not the object of inference. In this regard, if a thing is not an object of perception in a certain form, then that is not its form. Indeed, yellow and so forth are not apprehended as objects through perception in the form of blue. That which is grasped as not pervading another moment of time must be understood as being exactly like that. Otherwise, if all the clusters of temporal divisions were combined at once, everything would be completed at that very moment, and the consequence would follow that all purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) to be performed throughout all time would occur simultaneously. If it is argued that this is because the future and past temporal divisions are not grasped, then since their pervasion is also not grasped when they are not grasped, it follows that only its connection to that specific moment is grasped. And thus, like lightning and the like, it is simply impermanent.

[569,x] Is it not the case that impermanence consists in the destruction of lightning and such things, and not merely in their connection with a particular moment? If it is asked how there can be destruction in the absence of any destroyer, and if it is argued that destruction occurs simply through the impact of clouds, then why is it not accepted here as well that there is an impact from homogeneous or heterogeneous causes? Therefore, even in the case of lightning, destruction is simply its non-perception at a subsequent time; and since this applies to all entities, it is impossible to apprehend their permanence.
(1) Memory is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[569,xi] But surely, even when jars and other objects are perceived at a later time, how can it be said that they were not perceived [previously]? No; because that very [time] was not perceived. Indeed, even the prior time is not perceived. Furthermore, what is this existence or non-existence of that time? Certainly, no time—whether a moment, a day, a month, or the like—is established by the means of direct perception as something distinct from entities such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. There is no cognition of a "month" on the first day, nor is there a cognition of a "day" and so forth during the first watch of the night. This is because, at that time, neither the preceding nor the succeeding [unit of time] is perceived. [570,i]

If it is argued that time, such as a day and so forth, will be established through recollection, we say no; for recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, recollection does not establish a previously unknown object.
Recollection is preceded by perception and does not have an unperceived object as its domain.

Furthermore, time such as a month is not apprehended through direct perception (pratyakṣa). If it is argued that time consists in the aggregation [of moments], it has already been established that there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the apprehension of such an aggregation. (PVA 303–304)
If it is thought that there is no lack of proof because [the existence of many perceivers] is established by multiple witnesses,
is this establishment by multiple witnesses capable of being proven by anyone?
(PVA 305) It has already been demonstrated that recollection is not a means of valid cognition.
That which arises from memory is conventional, but it is not ultimate.
(PVA 306) And since time is conventional, its pervasion is clearly conventional as well.
Therefore, let it be understood that impermanence is the very nature of existence. (PVA 307)
If this difference were indeed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), how could it be conventional (*sāṃvṛta*)?
A conventionality without a basis is neither the probandum (*sādhya*) nor the means of proof (*sādhana*).
It is precisely because a relation is possible that the status of the probandum and the means of proof is established.
"For there can be no probans and probandum in the absence of the existence of a relationship.
To this, it is replied:

Conceptual construction takes as its object that which is excluded from others on one side and is manifold, yet presents it in a single form; by means of this, the distinction between the subject (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*) is established. (PVA 310)
The exclusion of all entities from things of their own class and from others is apprehended by perceptual cognition; concomitance, however, exists only through conceptual construction.
(PVA 311) If it is argued that perception is determinate because it follows the operation of the sense faculties...
Even if there were coexistence, there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) perceived as prior and posterior.

For one who first perceives only a single [instance] in that concomitance, it does not appear [as a universal], because it would follow that all individual instances must appear [simultaneously]. (PVA 312–313)

If it is established that the manifestation [of the universal] does not appear because of its distance and so forth, then, when the individual is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of the universal that pervades it. (PVA 314) [570,xv]
If it is argued that the apprehension of another individual occurs in that same manner due to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) from the apprehension of a previous individual, this is not so; for:
The cause of the recollection of an impression is the apprehension of that very object which produced it.
How can there be cognition of another object from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of grasping an individual entity?

For the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the apprehension of an individual is the cause of the memory-cognition of that very same [individual], not of the perception of a previously unperceived object, nor of the perception of a previously perceived object, nor of the memory of something never before seen. Furthermore, since the universal (*sāmānya*) is a distinct entity from the individuals, how could there even be a memory of it when it has never been seen? Nor do we perceive any other form—apart from the nature of the manifestation as clear or otherwise—by virtue of seeing and remembering previous and subsequent objects. For in the act of seeing, there is no cognition of another form apart from the two clearly manifest forms; indeed, only the two individuals appear therein. If it is argued that they appear because of the occurrence of a cognition of a common form, that is untrue.
It has been stated that the appearance is to be established by means of inference.
But is the appearance of a wall and so forth established by means of inference? (PVA 316)

[570,xix] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is bound in both ways; the person who is bound by the fetter of desire but liberated from the fetter of views; the person who is bound by the fetter of views but liberated from the fetter of desire; and the person who is liberated in both ways. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

If the prior appearance has been forgotten, then inference—or some other effort—might be employed for its recollection; but it cannot be [employed] at the very time of the appearance itself. For it is not the case that the appearance of a wall or the like is established by inference, nor are the walls themselves. Indeed, there is no worldly consensus that "because there is an appearance in the form of a wall, therefore the wall exists or appears. Rather, [one says] "it exists" or "it appears" because one perceives it in its own nature, which is distinct from the nature of another. Furthermore, there is no manifestation of a universal (*sāmānya*) through a nature that is distinct from the manifest form (*vyakti*). We certainly do not perceive the universal as having a different color or configuration (*saṃsthāna*). If it is argued that the nature of the universal is indeed external to color and configuration, then the universal does not exist at all, because nothing external to color and configuration exists externally. If it is argued that its nature is simply pervasiveness (*vyāpitā*), then that which is dissimilar to color and configuration is simply dissimilar. Pervasiveness does not possess color and configuration. If it is argued that pervasiveness belongs to the color and configuration themselves, then if pervasiveness were perceived as pervasiveness itself, it would be perceived even at a later time. If it is argued that it is indeed perceived at a later time, we say no; for there is no difference between the existence and non-existence of the individual (*vyakti*). Even when the previous particularity has perished, it is perceived in exactly the same way. Nor is there non-destruction of the former; if it is asked how there can be destruction since it is perceived there, we reply: if it has perished, why is it not perceived previously by another, or by you? If it is argued that this is because pervasiveness is absent, we say: that form is indeed perceived; it is merely the pervasion of space that is not perceived due to concealment (*tirodhāna*). What is this concealment? It is the state of being invisible. How can that which is visible have the nature of being invisible? If it is argued that in another location it has the nature of being visible, but that the object (*padārtha*) has passed away, we have already determined that there is no object apart from the nature of being visible. Moreover, if the visibility in another location were destroyed, then pervasiveness itself would be destroyed. And thus, the universal would not be eternal. Consequently, it follows that the universal is nothing but the form of the individual, because a uniform aspect distinct from the individual is a mere cognition and lacks reality. If it is asked, "How then is there the cognition 'these are similar'?", there is no fault, as it is due to similarity produced by color, configuration, and action—simply because they are similar, like the similarity of *rāṣṭrakūṭa* coins and the like.

[571,ii] Furthermore, as for one who says: "A universal (*sāmānya*) is the basis for a cognition of a common form," [we reply: that common cognition will arise either from the performance of a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*), or from being produced by a single cause; it is not produced by a common form, as in the case of the commonality of "Brahmin" and so forth. [For] even without a universal such as the caste of "Brahmin" and so on, there is the determination of merit and demerit.

[571,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and the ship’s captain, who were being swept away by the waves of the great ocean; seeing them thus, he resolved to deliver them all from their suffering. Then, by means of his supernatural power, he transformed himself into a great white elephant and descended into the great ocean. Having reached the place where the merchants were, he raised his trunk and rescued them all, bringing them safely to the shore. Thereupon, the merchants, having escaped from the peril of the great ocean, were filled with joy and, bowing their heads at the feet of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, praised him with these verses: “O Great Compassionate One, you have delivered us from this great danger. We have been saved from the waves of the great ocean, which were like mountains of fire. Homage to you, O Lord of the World, who possesses the ten powers! Homage to you, O Great Hero, who is skilled in saving beings! Having offered these praises, they circumambulated the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara three times and departed. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having liberated those five hundred merchants and the ship’s captain from the great ocean, returned to the city of Rājagṛha. There, he entered the assembly of the Śākya clan and sat upon the lion throne. Having seated himself, he addressed the Śākyas: “O sons of the Śākyas, you must always keep in mind the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because if there are those who are bound in prison, whether for murder, theft, or other crimes, and who call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, their bonds shall all be severed. At that time, the Śākyas, hearing the words of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, were filled with great joy and faith. They bowed their heads at his feet and departed. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, through his great compassion, delivers sentient beings from all fears and calamities. This is called the third chapter, “The Deliverance from the Great Ocean.”

[Objection: But how can there be a determination of merit and demerit without the castes such as the Brāhmaṇa? And even if the caste exists, how [is it determined]? For a caste is not killed, nor does it drink liquor. Furthermore, the determination of merit and demerit does not exist through any means of valid cognition other than scripture (āgama). How then could that very scripture establish it? For it is not possible to establish the injunction "a Brāhmaṇa must not be killed" without [the concept of] a caste, because it is impossible to apply it to every individual instance. [Reply: There is no fault, for [the application occurs] through instruction (upadeśa) or through the perception of a common form (samānarūpaparāmarśa). And this perception of a common form arises precisely from the instruction of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā). Apart from that, no other means of valid cognition is established here. Moreover:
The cognition of similarity possesses a nature distinct from the individual instances; otherwise, it should be understood as such, for otherwise it would be the behavior of a blind man. (PVA 317)
The cognition of a self distinct from its specific attributes does not possess established validity;
otherwise, if such a cognition were to exist, the existence of the object of knowledge would not be real.

If the uniform cognition is associated with a form distinct from the individual entities, that [form] is not established as such; how, then, could there be an establishment of a universal (*sāmānya*) from it? If, on the other hand, it were merely a cognition, then a universal is not established, for a specific object is not established by a mere cognition. Whatever form a cognition has, only that is established from it; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that the universal is both different and non-different [from the individuals], no, because of mutual contradiction.
For instance: "If it is non-different from what is different, how can it possess difference?"
If there is the appearance of difference, how can there be non-difference for this [entity] again?
(319) (PVA) If difference is admitted by anyone [in some respect], then that very thing would indeed be a universal;
however, its non-otherness would not exist because of absolute difference. (320) (PVA)
If it is claimed that there is no difference [of the whole] from its parts, then that [whole] would be neither different nor non-different [from them].
But if it were non-different from those very [parts], then that [whole] would again become a thousandfold.
Consequently, when it is extracted from those [parts], it would not exist at all, having reached its destruction.
If it were both different and non-different, it would follow that it is both visible and invisible. (322) It would be a great marvel if one thing were both seen and unseen;
for an entity is established as either existent or non-existent by virtue of its being visible or invisible. (323) (PVA)
[571,xii] For it is thus:
[571,xiii]
For in this way, even that which has died attains immortality;
therefore, let it be understood that the universal has a merely imagined nature.
Consequently, the distinction between property and property-bearer arises through the difference in their exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).
Wherever that [universal] does not exist, there is precisely the state of being a part of the meaning of the thesis. (325) [572] (3) The universal is conventionally real.
In investigations into the ultimate truth, since such things are not established as they appear, identity and difference are negated with respect to conventional entities. (182)

Conventionally, the universal is indeed distinct from the individual, as it is discerned through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And that [universal] consists precisely of the form of color and so forth. For instance:
If [the universal] were not established as distinct from the individual, it would not exist in other individuals;
thus, the establishment of difference [is required].
It is logical that what is excluded and what is inclusive cannot be non-different.
Therefore, the distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is unestablished through conceptual construction.
However, there is no apprehension of such a distinction by the senses; thus, it does not exist in reality.
For that which is established through direct perception possesses ultimate reality.
Where inference proceeds preceded by perception, there occurs the cultivation of that which has the form of a means of proof as established by conventional reality.
However, in terms of ultimate reality, neither identity nor difference exists for it, as these would require valid cognition [to establish them]. (PVA 329)

If the difference exists merely through conceptual construction, then in reality there is the nature of the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, let it be understood that the individual itself is established by perception;
furthermore, the proof of the individual through inference is preceded by perception. (PVA 330–331)
Therefore, however, if the universal were established as not cognizing difference,
then it could not subsist in particulars, because particulars are infinite.

For instance: if the universal (*sāmānya*) were perceived, then, since the particular (*bheda*) would not be mentioned, its occurrence [in relation to particulars] would necessarily be through difference. No one acts toward that which has not been determined. Now, if it is argued that the apprehension of the universal is preceded by the perception of the individual, and thus the apprehension of their relation occurs—namely, that "wherever there is a universal, there must be an individual"—then its occurrence is indeed in difference. But how can this be for one who perceives that very difference? Consequently, it follows that the cognition of the individual arises from the universal through inference. And so, the cognition of the individual would be by means of an inference based on an inference; thus, there would again be a cognition of a universal in that case as well. From that universal too, there would be another cognition of the universal of the individual, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, one perceives the individual at the end, then since there is no distinction [between the first and last moments], one should have perceived it at the very beginning; what is the use of this exhausting succession? Furthermore, if the individual were perceived, all purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) would be established [immediately], and thus one would never even begin to act. Therefore, it is logical that the universal is merely a mental construction and not external.

[572,xi] But surely, even if there is a cognition of the form of the intellect (*buddhi*), how can there be an operation upon the external object? Precisely because the relationship of cause and effect is observed in this very way. In that case, for us as well, the operation upon the individual (*vyakti*) will follow from the cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*), since the relationship of cause and effect is equally present here too. This leads to the absurd conclusion that "having reached the *harītakī* fruit, the deity causes one to purge. If it is simply the relationship of cause and effect, what is the use of an internal, useless universal (*antar-ḍarbha*)?
Therefore: [572,
xiii] Let it be understood that every universal is conventionally real.
For if there were no existence of a commonality of things (*vastusāmānya*), there would be neither engagement nor desistance.

(PVA 333) One who accepts a universal (*sāmānya*) must necessarily accept the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*), because otherwise there would be no purposeful activity. If the individual is cognized, let it be from that very mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke and so forth; what is the use of a universal? Even if it is through a universal, its cognition arises precisely from that which serves as the mark.
[572,xv] Now,

if there is no connection with another individual instance for the individual instance that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*), whereas such a connection exists for the universal because it is all-pervasive, then the universal must be accepted.
This is incorrect;
for even though the universal is all-pervasive, it is perceived in exactly that same way.
How could it be maintained, in reality, that one individual instance indicates another?

Even though the universal (*sāmānya*) is all-pervasive, if its pervaded form—which exists at the time of inference—is not apprehended, how could it be grasped as the "pervader" (*vyāpaka*)? Furthermore, if there were cognition [of the pervader] despite the relationship [between the two] being unapprehended, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because one would then have to cognize other instances of universals as well. If it is argued that [the pervaded] is not related to that [other instance], then there would still be cognition even for one whose relationship has not been apprehended. Moreover, it was previously established how this [cognition] is to be known. Furthermore, if the cognition of an individual occurs through the universal, and since the universal is also cognized from a word, why would there not be an attainment of the individual [from the word]? If you say that this cognition is unreal, then all cognition of the universal would be unreal; what, then, is the use of a universal?

[573,iv] But surely the universal exists everywhere; it is only because the individual instances are not perceived that there is no correspondence [with reality]. Since only individual instances possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), and since they cannot be cognized without a universal, the universal is postulated. As for the non-perception of the individuals, however, it is due to the absence of a sign (*liṅga*) connected to them.

But surely, even from a logical mark (*liṅga*), only the universal (*sāmānya*) is to be cognized. If, in that case, there is a cognition of the individual (*vyakti*), why does it not occur everywhere? [Opponent: Only the universal is made known by the word. [Proponent: Then it follows that the individual is also cognized through the logical mark; and if so, the aforementioned fault remains. Alternatively, it might be argued: "The universal, being distinct [from the individual], is faulty; for if it possessed both forms, there would be no fault. That too is incorrect.
[573, vii] Is the fault of [the cognition being] manifest not possible even in this case?
For even from that, there is no comprehension of the individual through the universal, because it does not touch the individual. (PVA) 335

[573,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a basis in form, nor does he perceive a basis in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor does he perceive a basis in the eye, nor in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; nor does he perceive a basis in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; nor does he perceive a basis in eye-consciousness, nor in ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness; nor does he perceive a basis in eye-contact, nor in ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact; nor does he perceive a basis in feeling born of eye-contact, nor in feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact; nor does he perceive a basis in the element of earth, nor in the elements of water, fire, air, space, or consciousness; nor does he perceive a basis in the realm of desire, nor in the realm of form, nor in the formless realm; nor does he perceive a basis in the conditioned, nor in the unconditioned; nor does he perceive a basis in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, become one who trains in the dharmas of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, does not perceive any dharma as a basis, nor apprehends any dharma, nor conceptualizes any dharma, nor discriminates any dharma, in that way he becomes one who trains in the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all those dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable; they are neither produced nor ceased, neither defiled nor purified, neither increased nor diminished. Subhūti, it is because they are thus empty that those dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable. Subhūti, it is for this reason that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, becomes one who trains in the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, become one who trains in the dharmas of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, yet a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through skillful means, enters into the knowledge of the modes of all dharmas, and having entered therein, he attains the realization of the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, becomes one who trains in the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable, what is the distinction, what is the difference, between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and a Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, there is no distinction, there is no difference, between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and a Tathāgata, except for the fact that the bodhisattva mahāsattva has not yet fully realized the dharmas of a Tathāgata, whereas the Tathāgata has fully realized them. Subhūti, it is in this way that there is no distinction, there is no difference, between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and a Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if there is no distinction and no difference between a bodhisattva mahāsattva and a Tathāgata, why is it that the bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain parinirvāṇa in the midst of the dharmas of a Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva has great compassion for all beings that he does not attain parinirvāṇa in the midst of the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva were to attain parinirvāṇa in the midst of the dharmas of a Tathāgata, he would not be called a ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva,’ nor would he be called a ‘Tathāgata. Subhūti, it is because he does not abandon all beings that a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain parinirvāṇa in the midst of the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, becomes one who trains in the dharmas of a Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain parinirvāṇa in the midst of the dharmas of a Tathāgata, how does he attain parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains parinirvāṇa by means of the parinirvāṇa of all dharmas. Subhūti, all dharmas are by nature parinirvāṇa; therefore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains parinirvāṇa by means of the parinirvāṇa of all dharmas. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains parinirvāṇa. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are by nature parinirvāṇa, for what purpose does a bodhisattva mahāsattva set out on the path? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are by nature parinirvāṇa, yet sentient beings do not know, do not see, and do not realize this nature of parinirvāṇa. For the sake of these sentient beings, a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out on the path, thinking: ‘I shall cause these sentient beings to know, to see, and to realize this nature of parinirvāṇa. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva sets out on the path. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are by nature parinirvāṇa, how can there be the designation of ‘sentient beings’? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, the designation ‘sentient beings’ is merely a conventional expression; it is not a real entity, nor is it a non-entity. Subhūti, all dharmas are beyond conceptualization and beyond discrimination; they are like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflected image, like a magical creation. Subhūti, it is in this way that the designation ‘sentient beings’ is merely a conventional expression. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage, like an echo, like a reflected image, like a magical creation, then what is the distinction, what is the difference, between an illusion and a Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, there is no distinction, there is no difference, between an illusion and a Tathāgata. Subhūti, an illusion is empty of intrinsic nature, and a Tathāgata is empty of intrinsic nature. Subhū

For if a universal (*sāmānya*) is held to be either distinct from or non-distinct from the individual (*vyakti*), then cognizers cannot avoid two possible courses: either there is a cognition of the individual or there is not. If there is a cognition [of it], why does one act when such a cognition of everything is impossible? If there is no cognition, how can there be action? If it is argued that one acts even toward what is not cognized by treating it as if it were cognized, then it is contradictory to say that "the very same thing is both apprehended and unapprehended in that same form," because affirmation and negation cannot both obtain their own nature in a single instance. If it is argued that this is precisely the difference between synonyms (*paryāya*): that by one synonym it is cognized as distinct, while by another it is not—then how can there be action for the sake of that which is not cognized? If it is argued that it is a synonym of that very thing, then if it is unapprehended, how can there be the cognition that "it belongs to that very thing"? And if it is already cognized, one still does not act; thus the same fault remains. Therefore, the characteristic of the subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*) exists only as conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisat*). In that case, the same would apply to the argument: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses sound-ness (*śabdatva*). Why would the fallacy of being "a part of the thesis" (*apratijñārthaikadeśatva*) not apply to one for whom the universal is distinct [from the individual]? Because the connection with that universal is expressed by the word "subject" itself. [Objection: In this case too, since the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is being expressed, the fallacy will not occur.
The connection with a universal is either the exclusion from others or the cognition of that [universal];
the connection with a universal does not occur at all without the cognition of it. (PVA 336)
The cognition of that [positive] form has already been refuted;
therefore, it is only exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) that is understood here from the word.

If it is your position that the connection with a universal is understood from the word as the particulars themselves, then how can that [connection] be understood when the individuals are not understood? For he alone who has food is the one who suffers from a broken vessel. Furthermore, it has already been determined previously that the intrinsic nature of particulars is not fit to be expressed. Therefore, the established conclusion is that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) alone is the meaning of a word.

But surely, how can even exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) be cognized without the cognition of the excluded entity? If it is cognized, what is the use of exclusion? If you argue that the conceptualization of exclusion is due to its being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapatti*), then why not simply accept a universal (*sāmānya*)? [Opponent: One accepts [an entity] in accordance with its cognition; this is not the case for a universal. [Reply: But is there not the worldly cognition, "Do I perceive exclusion? [Opponent: No, because one perceives distinctness (*vilakṣaṇatva*). [Reply: This is not a fault, for it is indeed a cognition. To explain: [The verse continues: Just as the cognition of a universal arises from the perception of similarity, so too does the cognition of exclusion arise from the perception of difference. Just as one who has seen a cow remembers it when seeing another similar animal, so too, having perceived a certain object, one remembers it when perceiving another dissimilar object. Therefore, the cognition of exclusion is established by the very fact of perceiving difference. Thus, there is no need to postulate a universal. Furthermore, since the cognition of a universal is also based on the perception of similarity, and since that perception is nothing other than the cognition of similarity itself, there is no separate universal. Consequently, the universal is merely a mental construct (*vikalpa*) arising from the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) produced by repeated experience. Therefore, the universal is not a real entity. Moreover, since the universal is not perceived apart from the individuals, and since it is not perceived in the intervals between them, it is like a sky-flower. Thus, the universal is not established. Furthermore, if the universal were a single entity, it would be perceived in all its loci simultaneously; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, the universal is not a real thing. Consequently, exclusion alone is the means of differentiation. Thus, the universal is not required. Therefore, the universal is not a real entity. Hence, the universal is not established. Therefore, the universal is not a real thing. Consequently, the universal is not established. Thus, the universal is not a real entity. [574,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, air, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as real. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as real, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, or the nine successive meditative attainments as real. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as real, nor does he perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of both internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the ultimate emptiness, the conditioned emptiness, the unconditioned emptiness, the infinite emptiness, the beginningless and endless emptiness, the emptiness of dispersion, the essential nature emptiness, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainment, or the emptiness of nature as real. He does not perceive the recollection of the Buddha as real, nor does he perceive the recollection of the Dharma, the recollection of the Saṅgha, the recollection of virtue, the recollection of generosity, or the recollection of deities as real. He does not perceive the recollection of peace as real, nor does he perceive the recollection of death as real. He does not perceive the absence of covetousness and malice as real, nor does he perceive the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in the impermanent, the perception of non-self in suffering, or the perception of renunciation as real. He does not perceive the perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of distaste for the entire world, or the perception of the cessation of all formations as real. He does not perceive the perception of the unattractiveness of all conditioned things as real, nor does he perceive the perception of the state beyond sorrow as real. He does not perceive the knowledge of suffering as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, or the knowledge of the path as real. He does not perceive the knowledge of exhaustion as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of non-arising as real. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of buddhahood as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the skillful means of a bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the ten stages of a bodhisattva as real. He does not perceive the dharma-body as real, nor does he perceive the marks and secondary characteristics as real. He does not perceive the attainment of the dharanis as real, nor does he perceive the attainment of the samādhis as real. He does not perceive the turning of the wheel of dharma as real, nor does he perceive the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata as real. Why is this so? Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are non-existent and cannot be apprehended; they are empty, signless, wishless, and without attainment.
