For one must necessarily have a cognition [of an object] through a form that is distinct from what is of a different class; otherwise, one would not act by avoiding what is undesired. If it is argued that its distinction from the undesired follows simply from the universal-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), [we reply: how can there be such a state in something that is not itself such, even when it is conjoined with another property? If it is argued that "this is so perceived because of its conjunction with that," then for something that is not that [itself], which is not perceived in its own nature while conjoined with another, perception is simply not logical. If the comprehension of its being distinct occurs through its own nature, then the conjunction with a universal is useless. That very difference would not be discerned if the universal did not exist. If it is asked, "From where then does the discernment of the difference between universals come?"—the answer is: it is established through conjunction with another universal. If it were discerned through its own nature alone, then the same consequence would apply to individuals as well; thus, the universal is useless. Furthermore, when there is a cognition of the difference between two things, how could it be [due to a universal], since a universal does not reside in only one of them? Therefore, the difference of these individuals must necessarily be cognized by this [means]; and since that difference from what is of a different class belongs to all of them, that alone is the universal.
[574,v] But surely, without a universal (*jāti*), how can that very distinction between similar and dissimilar things exist? For instance:

If there were a mutual difference between individuals, the universal would not be mutually distinct. There would indeed be a difference between individuals, yet for that [universal], there is no such cognition.

If difference were based on the individual instance (*vyakti*), then just as there is a difference between a *śāvaleya* and a *bāhuleya* from a *karka*, there would likewise be a difference between a *karka* and a *śāvaleya* from a *bāhuleya*; consequently, it would follow that even those two belong to the same class. Since no one perceives everything, by what means could a perceiver of all things establish a distinction when making a convention (*saṃketa*) manifest?
This [objection] is neither logical nor illogical, because:
Even if a universal were to exist, the fault that has been refuted would not apply;
for it is held that a universal is manifested by its individual instances, and not by way of its own intrinsic nature. (PVA 340)
Because its manifestation is not observed in places devoid of individuals and the like, manifestation itself must be accepted as the [defining characteristic];
yet that manifestation is not seen in all cases.
Therefore, even in that case, the pervasion by the act of establishing a convention is not established.
[574, xiii]

Even a universal (*sāmānya*) must be indicated before a convention can be established or employed; yet a universal cannot be indicated without [the perception of] individuals (*vyakti*). For only upon seeing all the individuals would a convention become unconfused through the perception of a fixed universal. Even then, since it is only the individuals that are seen, the universal is indeed useless. For instance, by seeing a single individual, how could this convention "this is a cow" result in the cognition of a specific universal? Indeed, no one perceives a distinction among universals such as "animal-ness" (*paśutva*) and so forth. If it is argued that "cow-ness" (*gotva*) is the object of the convention here, then there is no way to distinguish what that cow-ness is. If one says, "It is that which is manifested by such-and-such individuals," then the individuals possess this state [of being manifestors], which results in the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the indication of the universal depends on the unity of the individuals, and the unity of the individuals depends on the indication of the specific universal. If it is argued that the distinction is made by the very words "cow, cow," we say no; for the universal "cow" is indicated precisely by its non-occurrence in white horses (*karka*) and the like. If it is argued that there is a cognition [of the form] "this is the very same cow-ness," then [we reply]: how can a cognition whose object (prameya) has not been manifested manifest that object? For we do not perceive any object in this [cognition] apart from color and shape. If it is argued that this very [color and shape] is the universal (*sāmānya*) because it is recurring, [we say] no; for recurrence is impossible. Indeed, color does not have a nature that recurs in other individuals. If it did, it would follow that its recurrence would be perceived even upon seeing a single individual; and thus there would be a perception of all individuals at once. If it is argued that the universal is not perceived in that way because it is manifested by the individuals, then it would never be perceived at all. If it is argued that it is perceived as much as the individuals are seen, [we say] no; for the universal does not consist merely in that [perception]. If that were so, the universals would be nothing but the individuals themselves, and there would be no other universal. If the response is that the universal is simply the production of such a non-differentiated cognition, then the universal would be nothing but the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*). The universal of many things is indeed the exclusion of what is other than them. For it is impossible to point out a universal other than the mere exclusion of heterogeneous things; and even heterogeneity is simply the exclusion of what is other than that. Just as one thing is distinct from that, so too are others; there is no other illustration. Furthermore, it is impossible to point out a universal as "this is that" because it lacks differentiation. To say "there is no illustration because of its non-differentiation" is no answer, as it would entail the non-existence [of the universal]. For it is impossible to establish a universal by setting aside the individuals, as that would entail the absence of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). [The opponent might say: "The same applies to the negation of the universal. [We reply: This is not correct, because linguistic convention is possible even when based on the exclusion of others, as in the case of non-action (*akarma*) or non-substance (*adravya*). Even among universals, their mutual exclusion alone is the cause of linguistic convention.
[575,ii] Now, if it is argued that the connection with individuals is the cause for the conventional usage of distinctions between universals, even so, there remains a fault. For:
If it is not distinct by its own nature, how can it be distinguished from another?
It is through the connection with whiteness that the distinction "the other is white" is perceived.

Indeed, the difference of one thing does not reside in another. If it is argued that it does indeed reside there because of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between the individual and the universal, then the non-difference of the universal would be inherent in the individual, and thus the individuals themselves would be non-different. Consequently, due to the connection with every universal, even a cow would be a horse and so forth. Furthermore, the universal of the cow, which is "cowness," and the essential nature of the individuals—whether of the same or different classes—are not mutually distinct from one another. Therefore, how could individuals be the differentiators of the universal?

Now, if it is argued that individuals are distinct from others of a different class by their very nature, then let that very distinction itself be the universal; what is the use of another? Even if a universal is admitted, it is that same distinction between individuals that differentiates one universal from other universals. In that case, this particular universal would be established as a given fact. Alternatively, if the universal is distinct from other universals by its own nature, then the distinction among the possessors of the universal arises through connection with it—just as whiteness is white in itself, while a cloth is so through its connection with it. This too is not tenable, because: [575, vii]
A white color-form is never perceived anywhere in its isolation;
therefore, how can its own whiteness be established?

Since white and so forth always reside within the substance and are never perceived as separate from it, how could anyone understand that they are themselves of the nature of that substance? Why is it not accepted that their purity derives from the substance itself?
[The Refutation of Substance] (4) [575, ix]

Now, if whiteness is the very nature of that substance, then what is the nature of that substance itself? That same fault remains. If it is argued that it is perceived simply as "substance," even the cognition "substance" does not involve contact with color and shape (*varṇa-saṃsthāna*). And since color and shape are indeed qualities (*guṇa*), how can another substance, being of such a nature, be the object of perception? Furthermore, shape (*saṃsthāna*) does not admit of being distinct from color and so forth; it is color itself that appears in the form of roundness and the like.

[576,ii] But surely substance also appears [in cognition]. For instance, even by means of tactile cognition, there is an appearance of identity in the form, "This is that very same jar. Furthermore, recognition does not occur with respect to a mere quality; otherwise, one would have [the cognition] "this is color" or "this is touch. Nor is it logical for color to be apprehended by the sense of touch. Therefore, recognition is logically possible only with respect to a substance. Consequently, whatever is apprehended by a cognition whose object is distinct from another is distinct from that other, just as a cloth is distinct from a jar. And since a substance is apprehended by a cognition whose object is distinct [from qualities], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). [576,iii]
To this it is replied:
There is no observation of recognition with respect to an object that is distinct from form and the other [sensory qualities].
For there is no object of a prior cognition for one who does not remember it.

(PVA 344) First of all, there is no appearance of a jar or the like in the visual perception; nor is there such an appearance in the tactile cognition at first. For initially, only the mere parts appear, and that appears in exactly the same way even in the absence of other parts. But that is not the jar, because a jar is the whole (avayavin) that pervades the parts distributed across all spatial directions. Nor is the jar merely color (rūpa), because the term is applied to the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of color, and because at that time there is an absence of recognition (pratyabhijñāna).
vi] Alternatively, it may be thought that the apprehension of the whole occurs when there is the appearance of various other parts, qualities, and so forth.
That also does not exist, because: [576,
viii] At that time, it is possible to apprehend only another part [of the object].
There is no possibility of perceiving the configuration or the whole;
likewise, there arises a recollection even when another quality has perished.
Let the understanding derived from inference proceed [only] when preceded by perception.

[576,x] When there is perception of other qualities and parts in a jar and the like, yet there is no perception of those other qualities and parts [at the same time], how can there be [perception of] the wholes? A jar is not merely that much [i.e., its perceived parts].
<(5) Refutation of Recognition>

[576,xi] Now, if the cognition of a composite whole such as a jar arises from recognition aided by memory, then when the qualities of that composite are mentally abstracted away, the question "What is the jar there? would also arise. However, their non-separation exists because they depend upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Yet, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends this non-separation, since they are perceived as mutually exclusive. Furthermore, non-separation is to be grasped through the cognitions of memory and recognition; nor can a collection attain validity if memory and recognition individually lack validity. [576,xii]

[Objection: Is it not observed that those who are individually incapable of carrying a palanquin possess a different kind of capacity when [acting together]? [Reply: No. In that case, their nature—which is produced by such prior causes—is itself the capacity for generating the effect; it is not something distinct. But here, what is the effect of memory and recognition? If you say it is the cognition of a composite whole (*avayavin*), no; because there is no cognition of anything other than those [parts]. Or, if another cognition arises in the form of a certainty (*niścaya*), that is incorrect. A certainty that is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) is simply not a certainty at all. Indeed, a certainty that is not a valid means of knowledge would render the valid means of knowledge useless.

[576,xiii] Now, if at that time another part is ascertained through inference, then the cognition of the whole arises from the perception of identity based on recognition; for there is no identity of one part with another part, nor of one quality with another.

That too is incorrect, because inference is preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Whatever has been apprehended by perception exactly as it is, that very same thing must be cognized by inference in that very same way. Therefore, since the thing is cognized by perception as being non-distinct from its unity, its cognition through inference must also be of that very same thing. And thus:
[577, ii] Unity [is established] through recognition; otherwise, in the case of an object seen [previously], [there would be no such unity].
How could it proceed directly onto the path of what is to be known by means of perception?

For that which has been perceived otherwise by direct perception cannot be perceived otherwise even by a thousand acts of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). If it is argued that recognition itself is indeed direct perception, we say no; for it operates within the domain of inference (*anumāna*), and that inference has multiple objects. If it is asked how recognition can be a cause for conventional usage, we reply: simply by virtue of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and its status as a means of valid cognition is through its being an inference. If [the opponent argues], "In that case, it is by inference alone that that unity is established, and from that, the reality of the whole (*avayavin*) is proven—thus our position is established," we say no; for an ultimate unity is not being proven. That unity therein is based on its performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and thus it is not ultimate. Nor is there a rule that a purposeful action must be performed by that very [single entity] alone, since the act of burning is observed even by other fires. If it is asked, "In the absence of a primary [unity], how can there be a figurative unity? we reply: this is merely a succession of figurative designations arising from beginningless mental predispositions (*vāsanā*); thus there is no fault.

Alternatively, first, primary oneness is stated in perception; subsequently, through superimposition upon that, it is figuratively attributed based on the performance of purposeful action. (348) (PVA)

[577,v] Therefore, because the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*) are conceptually abstracted (*apoddhāra-parikalpanāt*), their identity or difference exists only in that sense, not in reality. In truth, there is no distinction; rather, the distinction is produced by the conceptual abstraction of the intellect. Furthermore, this abstraction arises neither from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor even from inference preceded by it, but has come down through a succession of inferences produced by beginningless predispositions (*anādi-vāsanā*). Thus, it is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). If it is asked, "In that case, since identity and difference do exist, why are they denied?", the answer is: No. [577,vi]

In investigations of ultimate reality, identity and difference are denied of things that exist only conventionally, because such things are not established as being truly existent. (349) (PVA) [577,vii]

Thus it has been said. For there is no non-difference in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); rather, difference exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*). This is the view of the Digambara Jains. However, both are ultimately real.
Therefore, he says:

This establishment of the conventional usage of the means of inference and the object to be inferred is constructed by relying upon a distinction that is thoroughly established through cognition. (183)

[577,x] This might be the case: if there is no difference, how can there be the conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) of inference and the object of inference? [The answer is: because of the existence of a difference derived through abstraction (*āpoddhārika*). It relies upon a conventional difference. For a conventional difference is not something that is not relied upon; yet, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is non-difference. Thus, by means of conventional difference alone, there is no contradiction. And since there is no conventional practice in the ultimate sense, there is a purpose served by both. Therefore, when—[577,xi]
In cognitions that are established upon their respective particularities, the discerning person perceives both the property and the properties; conventional usage is based upon that.

Otherwise, there would be no conventional usage of inference and the like. Thus it has been said: "This entire conventional usage of inference and the object of inference proceeds by way of the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) as they are mounted upon the intellect. Therefore, the distinction based on the difference of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) is the very refuge for [establishing] distinction.
In this context, that very [cognition], when brought forward in formal debate and devoid of the notion of difference, is the probandum;
yet, when it is led to the status of a means of proof, it is thereby shown to be unestablished. (185)

[578,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a buddha as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are non-existent, how can a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, give a gift? How can he guard morality? How can he perfect patience? How can he exert vigor? How can he enter into meditative concentration? How can he cultivate wisdom? How can he fulfill the perfection of generosity? How can he fulfill the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom? How can he fulfill the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How can he fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How can he fulfill the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and great compassion? How can he fulfill the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said to Subhūti: “It is thus, Subhūti. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he gives a gift without apprehending anything. He guards morality without apprehending anything. He perfects patience without apprehending anything. He exerts vigor without apprehending anything. He enters into meditative concentration without apprehending anything. He cultivates wisdom without apprehending anything. He fulfills the perfection of generosity without apprehending anything. He fulfills the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom without apprehending anything. He fulfills the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without apprehending anything. He fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path without apprehending anything. He fulfills the ten powers of a tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and great compassion without apprehending anything. He fulfills the knowledge of all modes without apprehending anything. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he gives a gift without apprehending anything, and so on, up to fulfilling the knowledge of all modes without apprehending anything.”

Exclusions (vyāvṛtti) do not differ according to the differences of the things excluded, because that [exclusion] is unitary; rather, they differ according to the difference of that from which something is excluded. In this context, by the exclusion of "non-sound," "sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); by the exclusion of "the unproduced," however, "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is the property (*dharma*). This is because they differ in being common and uncommon [respectively]. But such is not the case for "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) and "non-sound-ness. Therefore, how could there be an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) when there is no difference? Or, let it be, but it would merely be a synonym (*paryāya*). If it is argued that the difference exists simply because it is expressed by an abstract suffix, we say no, because of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). An abstract suffix arises from a word ending in the genitive case; and the genitive relation arises from the abstract suffix expressing a difference. Furthermore, a name must be based on the object (*artha*), not the object on the basis of the word. Such indeed is the nature of that object. For we take words as our authority (*śabdapramāṇaka*); whatever words declare is our authority. And when that same object is presented by another word, it is indeed different. If that were so, it would follow that there is no synonymy. Therefore, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because of sound-ness" (*śabdatvāt*), that very same "sound"—which lacks the cognition of any internal difference—is taken as the probans (*sādhana*) while serving as the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*); thus, it is unestablished (*asiddha*). Moreover, if impermanence follows from "sound-ness," then since "sound-ness" is already understood as being simply "sound," why is it stated again? If it is argued that the repetition is for the sake of emphasizing the property (*dharma*), we say no, because there is no further result. Even if the subject (*dharmin*) is emphasized, the reason remains valid—as in: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced. However, the logical practice of inference does not proceed according to the analogy of a lamp (where the light reveals the object). Thus, this is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "repetition" (*punarukta*). It is established that if one intends to express a difference, the reason is simply unestablished.
[578,ii] Because of the distinction between properties, there is a relationship of mutual dependence (aṅgāṅgitā) between the particular and the universal;
for example: "Sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, due to its being produced by effort. || 186 ||

[578,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those sentient beings suffering such various miseries and, moved by great compassion, addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall keep it in mind, then, Blessed One, how will those sons or daughters of good family be liberated from such various miseries? The Blessed One said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall keep it in mind, then, son of good family, when they are bound in shackles, stocks, or fetters, they shall be released from those shackles, stocks, and fetters. Son of good family, if there should be a great conflagration, those sons or daughters of good family who keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind shall be delivered from that great conflagration. Son of good family, if there should be a great flood, those sons or daughters of good family who keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind shall not die therein, nor shall they be swept away by the water. Son of good family, if there should be robbers or enemies, those sons or daughters of good family who keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind shall be delivered from those robbers and enemies. Son of good family, if one were to travel along a perilous path, one should keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind; then, son of good family, one shall be delivered from those dangers on the perilous path. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the World-Honored One further addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with these verses: “Son of good family, if you wish to deliver all sentient beings, And wish to quickly attain the supreme enlightenment, Then you should always keep in mind the name of Avalokiteśvara, The Great Compassionate One, the Lord of the World. If one is bound in shackles, stocks, or fetters, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; Instantly, one shall be released from those bonds, As if emerging from a dream. If one encounters a great conflagration, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; The fire shall be extinguished as if by rain, Without fear of being burned. If one encounters a great flood, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; One shall not perish in the water, Nor be swept away by the current. If one encounters robbers or enemies, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; They shall be unable to harm one, As if protected by a powerful king. If one travels along a perilous path, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; One shall safely reach the destination, Without fear of any danger. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having spoken these verses, addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, how should they dwell in the practice of the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? The Blessed One said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should view the five aggregates as being like a dream. And what are those five? Namely, form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Son of good family, if a son or daughter of good family views these five aggregates as being like a dream, then this is called practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, son of good family, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he perceives that form is empty, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise empty. Therefore, son of good family, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or objects of mind; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and even no non-attainment. Therefore, son of good family, because there is nothing to attain, the Bodhisattvas rely on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwell in the heart of non-obstruction, thereby attaining the ultimate Nirvāṇa in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, together with the entire assembly, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. [578,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those sentient beings suffering such various miseries and, moved by great compassion, addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall keep it in mind, then, Blessed One, how will those sons or daughters of good family be liberated from such various miseries? The Blessed One said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “If there are sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall keep it in mind, then, son of good family, when they are bound in shackles, stocks, or fetters, they shall be released from those shackles, stocks, and fetters. Son of good family, if there should be a great conflagration, those sons or daughters of good family who keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind shall be delivered from that great conflagration. Son of good family, if there should be a great flood, those sons or daughters of good family who keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind shall not die therein, nor shall they be swept away by the water. Son of good family, if there should be robbers or enemies, those sons or daughters of good family who keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind shall be delivered from those robbers and enemies. Son of good family, if one were to travel along a perilous path, one should keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind; then, son of good family, one shall be delivered from those dangers on the perilous path. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the World-Honored One further addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with these verses: “Son of good family, if you wish to deliver all sentient beings, And wish to quickly attain the supreme enlightenment, Then you should always keep in mind the name of Avalokiteśvara, The Great Compassionate One, the Lord of the World. If one is bound in shackles, stocks, or fetters, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; Instantly, one shall be released from those bonds, As if emerging from a dream. If one encounters a great conflagration, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; The fire shall be extinguished as if by rain, Without fear of being burned. If one encounters a great flood, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; One shall not perish in the water, Nor be swept away by the current. If one encounters robbers or enemies, One should call upon the name of Avalokiteśvara; They shall

Since this fault arises when there is no difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) due to their having non-different exclusions (*abhinnavyāvṛttikatayā*), therefore, because of the difference in exclusion between particularity (*bheda*) and generality (*sāmānya*), the relationship of "member and possessor of the member" (*aṅgāṅgitā*) in the form of probandum and probans is not contradicted. For a fault that occurs in the case of non-difference cannot exist when there is difference; indeed, the fault of deafness does not apply to one who possesses hearing. Therefore, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately after effort," there is no fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*). For "following immediately after effort" residing in sound is the property-bearer (*dharmin*), while [the same quality] residing in non-sound is the reason (*hetu*); thus, the distinction between probandum and probans is established. Indeed, "following immediately after effort" residing in sound differs even from another instance of "following immediately after effort"; however, when intended in its general form, it does not differ from another instance of that [same quality], but rather [differs] precisely from "not following immediately after effort. Consequently, there is indeed a difference based on pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) and non-pervasiveness (*avyāpitva*), just as in the case of "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapātvayoḥ*). For that which is non-pervasive does not become pervasive. Thus, the qualifier "sound" is the non-pervasive property-bearer, while the reason—residing in both that and what is not that—is distinguished by its pervasiveness. [Objection: "In that case, since there is an absence of pervasiveness, there is no difference for 'sound-ness' (*śabdatva*); thus, this results in the very fault of lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*). Therefore, regarding the reason 'because of sound-ness,' the fault of lack of concomitance is clearly manifest, and not the fault of being unestablished. [Response: Even in the case of being unestablished, the cause is precisely the lack of concomitance; thus, that very fault is rightly considered the manifest one.
This is not so, because:

This lack of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not a fault; this is what is expressed by the statement "it does not exist. Nevertheless, the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) is indeed clearly present here.

Indeed, the absence of non-establishment (*asiddhatā*) does not follow from the absence of difference. Therefore, while non-establishment exists, to point out another's fault by assuming that [non-establishment] does not conform to logic. For it has been stated that when a reason (*hetu*) is present, it is the object of inquiry regarding its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth. Consequently, we consider it correct that the fault of non-establishment in the case of the absence of difference is simply the fault of [failing to establish] difference itself. Therefore:
"Even though it is a constituent part of the thesis (*pakṣāṅga*), there is no non-establishment because it is not sublated (*abādhatvāt*) in the case of a different substratum (*bhinnadharmiṇi*)."
Just as a horse does not possess horns because it lacks the nature of having horns, so too this lump [of clay] does not possess horns. (187)

Even if "having horns" (*viṣāṇitva*) is a qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) for the purpose of excluding other objects, it does not contradict its status as a logical reason (*hetu*). For a reason that is connected with the probandum (*sādhya*) and is perceived as such is the establisher of the probandum. And that connection is not contradicted even when it serves as a member of the probandum. Therefore, the reason itself, though a qualification of the subject in a different locus, remains a reason even when it functions as a member of the probandum at the time of inference.
Alternatively, it is not by perceiving the cessation that its status as an auxiliary to the time of the probandum is established.

Indeed, a qualifier is not necessarily an auxiliary only when it exists at the same time as the qualified object; rather, it may serve as such even after having ceased, provided it was perceived previously—just as in the case: "Which of Devadatta’s houses is it where a crow caws? Even though the crow has now departed from that house which served as Devadatta’s residence, it still serves to identify that very house at a later time.

[579, iv] But how can that which is non-existent be an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*)? Because the cognition that results from it—the cognition established in its specific particularity—is possible. Therefore, the indicator does not incur the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*) by virtue of being a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*). If, then, because of the distinction between the universal and the particular within a distinct substratum (*dharmī*), there is no fault of the indicator being a part of the proposition’s meaning, it follows that the same fault would apply even to "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) and so forth, as well as to "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), since these possess an identical pervasion (*vyāpti*).

This is not correct. Because of the distinction in properties (*dharmabheda*), it is not tenable that the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is a specific instance of the root *yat* (to strive). [579, vi] 188.

[579,vii] It is not only [the reason] such as "because of having horns" and so forth; even a specific property (*viśeṣa*) that is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), such as "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) and so forth, does not [function as a valid reason], precisely because of the difference in properties (*dharmabheda*).
[579,viii]

[Objection: But surely, since sound-ness (*śabdatva*) arises precisely from the exclusion of what is non-sound, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) must arise from that alone. As it has been said: "Sound is characterized by being apprehended by the auditory organ. Therefore, how can there be a difference in properties (*dharmabheda*) when there is no difference in the exclusions (*vyāvṛttibheda*)?
[Reply: That is incorrect, because:
For if there were mutual inclusion, the distinction between phenomena would not be tenable;
indeed, distinctness consists in the presence or absence of a connection with a different object. (PVA 351)

Audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is the exclusion from that which is unrelated to the connection with auditory cognition; whereas sound-ness (*śabdatva*) is the exclusion from what is not a generality of sound. Although there is no such thing as "verbal" (i.e., being expressed by words) that is not audible, nevertheless, due to the absence of the necessary causal complex (*sāmagrī*), even something that is not audible might exist in relation to another person. However, that which is not a sound does not exist even in relation to another person. Thus, there is no exclusion from non-audibility; sound-ness would therefore be identical to audibility, and not to sound-ness, because the latter is common to both the audible and the non-audible.

By this, [the following] statement of the Teacher is addressed: "Is it not seen that the state of being for the sake of another belongs to composite things because they are composites? Conditioned things are impermanent because they are conditioned"? Here, the reason is a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*). It is not the case here that all composites or all conditioned things constitute the meaning of the thesis; rather, it is the eye and so forth [that are intended], and a part of that [is the reason]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of an example. Furthermore, [if one were to argue that] "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) would be an uncommon [reason], it could indeed be so. For it is appropriate that the uncommon property of the meaning of the thesis—namely, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*)—be uncommon. But there is no other "sound-ness" belonging to sound [other than its nature as sound]; thus, the fault of the reason is precisely its being unestablished (*asiddha*). As it has been said: "The definition of the thesis has been stated."
<6 Investigation of the Reason> <1. Definition of the Reason> [579,xiii]
The definition of the reason (*hetu*) is stated: therein,
the reason and its fallacies are for the most part properties of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
Therefore, its detailed exposition is presented first, based on the meaning of the [three] reasons and so forth:

The property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is of two kinds—present in the similar class (sapakṣa) and absent from it; furthermore, it is of three kinds according to whether it is present, absent, or both present and absent in each of the dissimilar classes (asapakṣa). (352–353)

[580,iii] But surely, only the definition of a valid reason (*hetu*)—such as "that which exists is of the same class"—and the definition of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) should be stated. For what purpose is this detailed exposition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? A valid reason or a fallacious reason is, for the most part, indeed a property of the subject; therefore, the initial presentation of its divisions is for the sake of clearly explaining the definitions of the valid reason and the fallacious reason through their distinction. When that is so, it is easily explained and grasped that "this property of the subject is a valid reason," "this is contradictory (*viruddha*)," and "this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For this very reason, he says: [580,iv]

In order to facilitate easy comprehension through the various classifications of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the summary of the meaning of the types of reasons is stated in the aphorisms (*sūtra*). (189)

The summary that is stated by way of the classification of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is for the sake of easy comprehension of the very meaning of the section on logical reasons (*hetuprakaraṇa*). The meaning of the section on logical reasons is the instruction on the definitions of the valid reason (*hetu*) and the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*); its "meaning" is the state of being a valid reason or a fallacious reason. For this very reason, it was said [to be placed] "before the fallacious reasons. Both the valid reason and the fallacious reason constitute "fallacious reasons" (*hetvābhāsa*). And because of proximity, "fallacious" refers specifically to the fallacious reason and not to mere appearance.

But is it not the case that a property (*dharma*) being presented merely as a property of a subject (*dharmin*) is the means of proof (*sādhana*), and not by way of being a property of the thesis-subject (*pakṣadharman*)? For in the statement, "There is smoke here in this region, in the forest thicket, etc.," it is shown merely in respect of the subject alone. Nor is the mere subject the thesis-subject (*pakṣa*), because the subject itself is already established; for it is stated that "the subject qualified by a property is what is to be inferred. This is precisely that point.

Because the meaning of the whole is what is to be proven, the status of being the "probandum" is metaphorically attributed to the property alone or even to the subject, since they are merely parts of that whole, even though [the subject] is not primary. (PVA 354)

The aggregate that is the object of the causal operation is the probandum (*sādhya*). However, that is not the subject (*pakṣa*), because it is already established. Therefore, the subject is that locus (*dharmin*) which possesses an unestablished property (*asiddha-sādhyadharma*) as its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). How can an unestablished qualification be [applied]? It is by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). [Objection: "There is no metaphorical designation because there is no purpose. In this way, the exclusion of [qualities such as] being visible to the eye (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth is achieved.

Because the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is the meaning of the whole, it is metaphorically designated as "to be proven" even when applied to the property alone or to the subject (*dharmin*), which is not primary, since they are both parts of that whole. (PVA 355)
For the subject (*dharmin*) alone, when not used figuratively, is not the thesis (*pakṣa*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*) is what is to be inferred (*anumeya*), and that no metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is possible there? [Response: No, because the intention there is that it is not [the subject] as qualified by a property that is sought to be known (*jijñāsita*). Furthermore, the term *anumeya* has the sense of "that which deserves inference" (*anumānam arhati*). And that which deserves inference, as well as that whose particularity is sought to be known—in these cases, the probandum (*sādhya*) is merely metaphorical because it is unestablished (*asiddha*). Therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is indeed of a metaphorical meaning; that is to say, it is the subject (*dharmin*) alone as qualified by the metaphorical constituent of the probandum.

[581,ii] But might it not also be the case that the property (*dharma*) is qualified by the subject (*dharmin*) as it has been metaphorically designated? The mention of the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is for the purpose of grasping the "subject of the thesis" (*sādhyadharmin*). That which is the property of the subject of the thesis is alone the reason (*hetu*), and not the contradictory (*viruddha*) or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The property of that subject is the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*).

But surely, in this relationship of qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*), because the qualifier functions as an exclusionary factor (*vyavacchedaka*), there would be a lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇatā*) for every [reason], since it would exclude other subjects (*dharmin*). For a qualifier is not non-exclusionary. And how could "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*)—which is qualified by sound and thus identical with sound—ever apply to cloth or other things? It might perhaps do so if there were a difference [between them]. Yet, a difference between the subject and its properties is not admitted. Nor is there a qualifier other than the cause of that which is distinct. If that were the case, every reason would be merely a "reason based on effect" (*kāryahetu*). Therefore, if there is a qualifier, there is a lack of commonality; but if there is no qualifier, there is the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the absence of being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).
This is not so; for:
The particle used in the sense of exclusion (vyatirecaka) excludes non-connection [of the property] with others, connection [with them], and absolute non-connection [with them]. (190)

[581, vi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is a victim of others but not a victim of self; the person who is a victim of self but not a victim of others; the person who is a victim of both others and self; and the person who is neither a victim of others nor a victim of self. Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of others but not a victim of self? Here, Ānanda, someone is one who has committed many evil and unwholesome deeds, yet he does not conceal them. Because he does not conceal them, he does not experience remorse. Because he does not experience remorse, his mind is not troubled. Because his mind is not troubled, he attains concentration. Having attained concentration, he sees with wisdom as it really is. Seeing with wisdom as it really is, he becomes disenchanted. Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Thus, Ānanda, this person is a victim of others but not a victim of self. “Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of self but not a victim of others? Here, Ānanda, someone is one who has committed many evil and unwholesome deeds, and he conceals them. Because he conceals them, he experiences remorse. Because he experiences remorse, his mind is troubled. Because his mind is troubled, he does not attain concentration. Not having attained concentration, he does not see with wisdom as it really is. Not seeing with wisdom as it really is, he does not become disenchanted. Because he is not disenchanted, he does not become dispassionate. Because he is not dispassionate, he is not liberated. Thus, Ānanda, this person is a victim of self but not a victim of others. “Ānanda, what kind of person is a victim of both others and self? Here, Ānanda, someone is one who has committed many evil and unwholesome deeds, and he conceals them. Because he conceals them, he experiences remorse. Because he experiences remorse, his mind is troubled. Because his mind is troubled, he does not attain concentration. Not having attained concentration, he does not see with wisdom as it really is. Not seeing with wisdom as it really is, he does not become disenchanted. Because he is not disenchanted, he does not become dispassionate. Because he is not dispassionate, he is not liberated. Thus, Ānanda, this person is a victim of both others and self. “Ānanda, what kind of person is neither a victim of others nor a victim of self? Here, Ānanda, someone is one who has not committed many evil and unwholesome deeds, and he does not conceal them. Because he does not conceal them, he does not experience remorse. Because he does not experience remorse, his mind is not troubled. Because his mind is not troubled, he attains concentration. Having attained concentration, he sees with wisdom as it really is. Seeing with wisdom as it really is, he becomes disenchanted. Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Thus, Ānanda, this person is neither a victim of others nor a victim of self. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

If the relationship between the excluded (*vyavacchedya*) and the excluder (*vyavacchedaka*) were of only one kind, this fault would arise. However, it is observed to be of many kinds; its divisions are such that in some cases it excludes non-connection (*ayoga*), in some cases connection with others (*anyayoga*), and in some cases absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*). For the exclusion must be established by means of a particle (*nipāta*) that performs the differentiation (*vyatirecaka*), not by the exclusion of connection with another. Its meaning consists solely of a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) by way of necessity, and there is no fault in such a restriction. [Objection: How can there be this distinction if the expression is of a single form, given the absence of any difference in the object? [Response: It is not that there is a difference in the object of the isolated term itself, but rather due to the difference in its correlates (*saṃsargin*). As for the difference in the correlates:
vii] It is uttered together with the qualifier, the qualified, and the action.

"Even when it is not employed by intention, this meaning of it is understood. (191)

The connection [of the words] is according to their respective order: that which is uttered together with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) excludes non-connection (*ayoga*); that which is [uttered] with a qualificand (*viśeṣya*) excludes connection with another (*anyayoga*); and that which is [uttered] with a verb (*kriyā*) excludes absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*). Thus, it is the very words such as the qualifier and so forth that convey the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). The particles (*nipāta*), however, are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), because they serve to clarify that very [restriction]. For instance, in the sentence "Bring water with a jar" (*ghaṭenodakam ānaya*), if there were no expectation of a specific instrument (*kāraṇaviśeṣa*), the employment of the specific instrument would be useless. The same applies to the object (*karman*) and so forth; thus, the restriction is conveyed by the words "jar" and so on themselves. And since these [words] are distinct, there is a difference in meaning.

[581,xi] But surely, because they are distinct, a distinction in their objects must follow; yet we perceive both the common and the uncommon. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and by means of conceptual abstraction (*apoddhāra-parikalpanā*), it is only that which is expressed by the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa-nipāta*). No, this is not so, because it would follow that there would be no cognition when that particle is not employed. For how can something be the object of another when it is cognized even without it? How then can there be a single denotation for words that express distinctions? Moreover, exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) alone is not the denotation of words. [581,xii]
This is not the case, because that [word] denotes a real entity (vastu), whereas exclusion (vyavaccheda) is of the nature of a non-entity (abhāva). [581,xiii]
A statement has exclusion as its fruit, as for example: "Caitra is an archer," or "Pārtha is an archer," or "The lotus is blue. (192)

[582,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, nor does he perceive one who causes to act; he does not perceive a doer, nor does he perceive one who causes to do; he does not perceive a feeler, nor does he perceive one who causes to feel. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive one who perceives form; he does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive one who perceives feeling; he does not perceive perception, nor does he perceive one who perceives perception; he does not perceive formations, nor does he perceive one who perceives formations; he does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive one who perceives the eye; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive one who perceives the ear; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive one who perceives the nose; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive one who perceives the tongue; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive one who perceives the body; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive one who perceives the mind. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives the eye-consciousness; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives the ear-consciousness; he does not perceive the nose-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives the nose-consciousness; he does not perceive the tongue-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives the tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive the body-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives the body-consciousness; he does not perceive the mind-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives the mind-consciousness. He does not perceive contact, nor does he perceive one who perceives contact; he does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive one who perceives feeling; he does not perceive craving, nor does he perceive one who perceives craving; he does not perceive grasping, nor does he perceive one who perceives grasping; he does not perceive existence, nor does he perceive one who perceives existence; he does not perceive birth, nor does he perceive one who perceives birth; he does not perceive old age and death, nor does he perceive one who perceives old age and death. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, nor does he perceive one who causes to act; how is it that he does not perceive a doer, nor does he perceive one who causes to do; how is it that he does not perceive a feeler, nor does he perceive one who causes to feel? How is it that he does not perceive form, nor does he perceive one who perceives form; how is it that he does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive one who perceives feeling; how is it that he does not perceive perception, nor does he perceive one who perceives perception; how is it that he does not perceive formations, nor does he perceive one who perceives formations; how is it that he does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives consciousness? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, nor does he perceive one who causes to act; he does not perceive a doer, nor does he perceive one who causes to do; he does not perceive a feeler, nor does he perceive one who causes to feel. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive one who perceives the eye; he does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive one who perceives the ear; he does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive one who perceives the nose; he does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive one who perceives the tongue; he does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive one who perceives the body; he does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive one who perceives the mind. He does not perceive forms, nor does he perceive one who perceives forms; he does not perceive sounds, nor does he perceive one who perceives sounds; he does not perceive odors, nor does he perceive one who perceives odors; he does not perceive tastes, nor does he perceive one who perceives tastes; he does not perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive one who perceives tangibles; he does not perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive one who perceives mental phenomena. He does not perceive eye-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives eye-consciousness; he does not perceive ear-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives ear-consciousness; he does not perceive nose-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives nose-consciousness; he does not perceive tongue-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives tongue-consciousness; he does not perceive body-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives body-consciousness; he does not perceive mind-consciousness, nor does he perceive one who perceives mind-consciousness. He does not perceive contact, nor does he perceive one who perceives contact; he does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive one who perceives feeling; he does not perceive craving, nor does he perceive one who perceives craving; he does not perceive grasping, nor does he perceive one who perceives grasping; he does not perceive existence, nor does he perceive one who perceives existence; he does not perceive birth, nor does he perceive one who perceives birth; he does not perceive old age and death, nor does he perceive one who perceives old age and death. Why is this? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are ungraspable and cannot be apprehended. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if all

A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words whose meanings are mutually connected. Here, however, it is the word that completes the sentence which is designated by the term "sentence," because it alone has the function of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), and because there exists no other sentence [beyond it]. Whatever is the result of a sentence, that alone is its object of demonstration; that is the "meaning" (*artha*). Furthermore, there is no exclusion other than the thing being excluded. Therefore, since the cognition of the excluded object occurs, the excluded [object] itself is also cognized through its differentiation from others; thus, exclusion alone is what is demonstrated.

[582,iii] Now, while the positive entity (*vastu*) is being established, its exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), which is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) and is to be established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is implied; and that very implication is made manifest by the particle *eva* and so forth.
That too is incorrect; for:
How could one thing be implied when another is being denoted, without a positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
Furthermore, even if there were no connection, the over-extension [of the consequence] in the case of an implication would remain unprevented.

For if non-exclusion (*avyatireka*) were to imply exclusion (*vyatireka*) due to identity (*tādātmya*), then even in the case of exclusion, it would be implied by way of a relation. If this is argued, we say no. Because if the object were perceived as excluded from another through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving it as non-excluded. Therefore, even if exclusion is perceived through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely non-apprehension (*abhāva*), its perception would still occur precisely as something unrelated to that [object]. For it is not possible to perceive a relation of exclusion with that which is non-exclusive. Now, if it is argued that the object arises together with exclusion itself because they depend on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), [then the same applies] to non-exclusion as well.
< (1) Examination of Non-existence > [582, viii] That is incorrect, because:

Because that [universal] follows along with that entity even when it is distinct [from it], it cannot itself undergo differentiation when there is the existence of something different; for that which is non-differentiated does not admit of differentiation. (PVA 357)

[582,xi] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a noble disciple has abandoned five factors and possesses five factors, he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, one who is firmly established, and one who has attained the right path leading to full enlightenment. What are the five factors that he has abandoned? They are: (1) personality-belief (*sakkāyaditthi*), (2) doubt (*vicikicchā*), (3) attachment to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), (4) sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), and (5) ill will (*vyāpāda*). And what are the five factors that he possesses? They are: (1) the factor of noble virtue (*ariyasīlakkhandha*), (2) the factor of noble concentration (*ariyasamādhikkhandha*), (3) the factor of noble wisdom (*ariyapaññākkhandha*), (4) the factor of noble liberation (*ariyavimuttikkhandha*), and (5) the factor of noble knowledge and vision of liberation (*ariyavimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha*). Ānanda, when a noble disciple has abandoned these five factors and possesses these five factors, he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, one who is firmly established, and one who has attained the right path leading to full enlightenment.
