[582,xvii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a noble disciple has abandoned thirteen factors and possesses thirteen factors, he

There is no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) in the case of "this is the horn of that [horn]," because both are perceived as existing simultaneously through mutual exclusion; thus, there would only be a conjunction (*samuccaya*), not a relation of qualifier and qualified. If it is argued that their simultaneity is due to mutual assistance, [we reply: no, because the relation of locus and located (*ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva*) is the basis for the relation of qualifier and qualified. If it is argued that the relation of locus and located exists because the object is perceived in the midst of its absence (*vyatireka*), then in that case there is no perception of a [real] relation. For one thing is not designated as belonging to another simply because it is situated in the middle of it. Indeed, light is not designated as belonging to a jar, nor is darkness so designated. Nor is something situated in the middle of a jar designated as "the jar of the jar. Furthermore, staying in the midst of an absence is inevitable; for without an absence, there can be no existence of cloth or other things, otherwise they would have to be all-pervading (*vyāpin*). [Objection: Even in the midst of an absence, there can be no stay without another absence, for the same reason—that it would otherwise be all-pervading. [Reply: No, for this object would remain in the midst of the absence by its very nature. Whatever stay occurs in the midst of something does not happen without an absence distinct from the locus, just like the stay in the midst of a cloth. And the stay in the midst of an absence is also a stay.

[583,i] This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). The abiding in the midst of non-existence occurs by its very own nature, because non-existence has that as its essential nature. For it is not the case that lacquer requires a further uniter when it is joined to wood; rather, it exists in that manner by itself.
This is incorrect, because:
[583,iii] If lac were to acquire its connection with wood by its own inherent nature, it would never be separated from it.
Non-existence, by its own nature, is incapable of performing the functions of pervading or occupying a middle space.
(358) (PVA) If that entity were non-pervasive, then non-existence would be purposeless.
Even if non-existence were pervasive, how could another thing exist within it? (359) (PVA)

[583, vii] It is not by its mere intrinsic nature that it is non-pervasive; for if it were pervasive, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the middle state. If you say, "We accept that [entities] are indeed non-pervasive," then what is the use of "absence" (abhāva) now? For absence is accepted so that there may be no confusion among things; yet since that [non-pervasiveness] is already established by the very fact that the entities themselves are non-pervasive, the utility of postulating "absence" is unavoidable as being redundant. How could there be a contradiction in something being pervasive either through absence or through its own cause accompanied by absence? [583, viii]
That too is incorrect:
"If non-existence were to make an entity that is not pervasive into something pervasive..."
There would first be a confusion of this [entity]; how then could there be its alteration?

(360) (PVA) Indeed, it is not possible to establish that something is both the pervader and the pervaded. For if it were pervasive at first, there would be a confusion of entities. Or perhaps it was not pervasive at all initially. In that case, its very nature is such, since it is perceived as being otherwise. Or perhaps it is neither pervasive nor non-pervasive by its own nature; it is pervasive through the application of pervasion, and non-pervasive through the absence of that [application]. And so he said:
Whether they are "diverse" due to external adjuncts or "non-different," this conceptual proliferation regarding the nature of entities is observed only when they are combined. (PVA 361)
That too is incorrect, because:
Otherwise, if there were for it a cognition that excludes duality, then, because of its connection with something else, it would be understood as partaking of two entities. (362) (PVA) [583,xv]
Otherwise, however, it would be as follows:
that entity, those two others, and likewise another beyond them.
They are perceived in their own nature, independent of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
(363) (PVA) If there were a perception of them as mixed with those [adjuncts], it would be nothing but an error.
Likewise, there would be an absence of real entities, which would establish the existence of ignorance (avidyā). (364) (PVA)

Furthermore, since that which possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is itself divided by those very adjuncts, the postulation of further adjuncts is redundant. It is divided by the adjuncts themselves; there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that it is divided from another possessor of adjuncts through an adjunct. And if it is divided by its own nature alone, then that same state of being divided remains even when there is a dependence on another possessor of adjuncts. If it is argued that the state of being divided is something entirely different depending on each case, we reply that there is no utility in such multiple states of being divided.
Since it is distinct from all things by virtue of its own nature and its exclusion from them,
what purpose is served here by postulating another distinction?

Now, if one were to conceive of difference based on the cognition "it is different from this" and "it is different from that," then indeed, what is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be dismissed as useless or made an object of rejection. If that is so, then because of the perception that even a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is different, another difference must be admitted; and because there would be a difference from that as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of differences. Consequently, the absence of difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*) would necessarily follow.
[584,i] "Let this fault be welcome; surely this is precisely our position. This is not so.

For even if difference does not exist in its own nature, it cannot exist through the nature of another; since its "otherness" would itself lack difference, how could that otherness come to be? (366) (PVA)

For that which is not differentiated by its own nature cannot be differentiated by the nature of another; in the absence of difference, the otherness of that [other] is lost. Indeed, if there is no differentiation from its own nature, the "other" does not exist at all. Since that [other] is absent, how can there be a difference from it?
Now, it might be argued that the differentiator, being distinct by its own nature, will differentiate the substratum even though the latter is non-different from it.
That too is incorrect, because:
If its difference from another were by way of its own nature, then even for one moving far away, it would be impossible to draw near. (367) (PVA)

[584, vii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to take all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees found in Jambudvīpa and reduce them to a single pile of wood, and then, with a single stroke of the sword, reduce that entire mass to ashes; and if one were to take another mass of grass, shrubs, herbs, and trees from Jambudvīpa and likewise reduce it to a single pile of wood, and with a second stroke of the sword reduce that too to ashes; and if one were to continue in this manner until all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees of Jambudvīpa had been reduced to a single great heap of wood and entirely consumed by fire—compared to that, Ānanda, the merit arising from the gift of a single meal to a single person who has entered the stream would be far more abundant.”

When one differentiator is itself differentiated by its own nature from another, then for that which is other than it, the clusters of *kiṃśuka* flowers—adorned as ear-ornaments—are as if dyed by fate. It is impossible for something to be both different and non-different [from itself]. Indeed, a difference does not become a difference unless it differentiates the other. Therefore, when there is a difference in the nature of one thing, the same applies to the difference and the possessor of difference; thus, there is no difference from another. Consequently, the nature itself, by virtue of having an essence that excludes connection with others, is the difference; therefore, identity (*tādātmya*) is the very essence of the meaning of difference. Thus, difference alone is the sentence-meaning. That alone must be expressed as the primary intention (*tātparya*), otherwise even the expression of word-meanings would not occur, because a confused entity cannot function as a word-meaning. For a real thing (*vastu*) is that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*). And a causal function is not possible in a state of universal connection. Furthermore, that difference from other word-meanings is cognizable through perception by way of its own nature; when a convention is established therein, that very [difference] is what is cognized by the word. Thus, exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) alone is the denotable object of a word. For it is not possible to denote what is excluded as being non-excluded.

**(2) Refutation of the Universal** [584, viii] Now, is that exclusion inherent in the individual's own nature (*svarūpa*)? In that case, if the individual nature itself is not denoted, how can there be a denotation of an exclusion that is non-different from it? Or, if the exclusion were distinct [from the individual], then, because it would follow through its own manifestations, it would simply be the universal (*jāti*) presented by another means. Thus, since it is the recurring form (*anugata-rūpa*) alone that must be established, and not the exclusion, how can a sentence have exclusion as its result?
This does not exist, because:
For that very thing is called a "jar" because it is excluded from others, and not by virtue of its connection with a universal; for it is precisely through being excluded that there is distinctness.

This has already been established: that which is not itself excluded cannot become excluded through connection with another. For if it were connected with a universal (*sāmānya*), it would simply be a universal. Alternatively, it would not exist at all; for it is not logical for that which is non-uniform to possess uniformity even through connection with another.
If it is uniform by its very nature, then the postulation of a universal is redundant.

〈a〉 Even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), there is no identity with it. (PVA 369) [584, xiv] Even if something were to possess a universal, it would not be the universal itself. This is because it appears in its own specific form. For it is appropriate to say "possessing a universal" when there is an appearance of difference; however, when there is an appearance of non-difference, one simply says "the universal. If there were no apprehension of difference, it would have to be called either "the universal" or "the particular. Now, suppose there is an appearance both through difference and through non-difference.
That is incorrect, because:
If it appears as distinct, then by that it would be like a particular;
if it appears without distinction, then by that it would be a universal.

For it is not logical for a single entity to possess two natures, both distinct and non-distinct. It is not the case that the universal is distinct from the individual by that very same nature and non-distinct by that very same nature; rather, the established position is that it is distinct by one nature and non-distinct by another nature. That is true and otherwise. Why? Because:
Furthermore, a universal cannot possess two forms due to their mutual distinction;
in that case, there would be two entities, and the universal would be something other [than them]. (PVA 371)
Because of the difference between the universal and its form, it follows that it must be an individual;
yet, because of the difference between its forms, it is not tenable for it to be both an individual and a universal.

If it is argued that the universal has two forms—one distinct from something and another non-distinct—then, because those two are mutually distinct, they would possess the nature of individual particulars (*vyakti*). For there is no such thing as an individual apart from its own distinct intrinsic nature. If it is argued that it is an individual because of its connection with "individuality" (*vyaktitva*), then surely "individuality" is itself a universal; thus, by connection with that, there would be sameness.
If its manifestation were non-different from it, pervasiveness would not follow as a consequence.
Furthermore, in the postulation of two forms, the same undesirable consequences as before would arise.
Therefore, the very nature of individuals is their distinctness; consequently, that universal is [defined] by way of individuality.

Now, due to the connection with a universal, there is another universal therein; therefore, that pair is not a universal, because it does not possess a universal. For a universal is not merely that which possesses a universal. Consequently, the cognition "this is common" arises with respect to the two forms of the universal. That [cognition] does not apply to the individual (vyakti), for it is not connected to a universal, since it is established by means of distinct universal-forms.

Now, if it is argued that although particularity (*bheda*) and generality (*sāmānya*) are distinct, they are differentiated in one respect and non-differentiated in another, then in the case of their difference as well, a further generality would arise. If that were so, there would be a state of individuality (*vyaktitā*) for both the generality and the form of the generality; consequently, there would be no equality with the previous generality, because of the lack of connection with that generality due to the intervention of another generality. Thus, not even a single thing would have a connection with generality, and there would be a lack of equality.
Therefore, this cognition, though appearing uniform, is devoid of a real object.

For those who maintain that universals exist, there can be no finality [to the process of cognition]. Everything remains unmanifest as the object of comprehension; even at the point of finality, it is only the manifest that is so. For those who do not accept a universal, a universal cannot possibly exist there [in the final stage], nor could it have existed previously. If the final [particular] were identical [to the universal], then because of its non-difference from that, the preceding one would also be identical; thus, the cognition of a universal would have a real objective basis (sālambanā). But this is not the case, so this argument is trivial. Likewise, regarding particulars: if a particular difference exists that pervades all particulars, then, even though distinct things are mutually differentiated, their connection with that [pervasive difference] would not sublate their non-difference; consequently, everything would become entirely non-different. If you argue that there is a difference between the universal and its possessors (the particulars), we say: no.
If there is no difference from the individual, there can be no universal; rather, it would be the individual itself.
And since that individual is not inherently distinct [from others], the consequence follows that there is non-duality. (PVA 375)
Therefore, exclusion alone is the universal.

But surely, exclusion is non-distinct from the object; just as it is from what is of a different class, so too is it from what is considered to be of the same class. Therefore, how can that exclusion be cognized as being distinguished from only those of a different class? This is true, provided that every cognition were to grasp the thing’s own nature in its entirety.
Being undivided, it cannot be split by division in any way whatsoever. (376) (PVA) But when, however:
Even from mere error, there is attainment, which is the worldly course of conventional usage.
At that time, that which arises from a distinct connection is consumed as if it were distinct. (377) (PVA)

[586,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive 'Bodhisattva' as a designation. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive 'perfection of wisdom' as a designation. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive 'form' as a designation. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he perceive 'consciousness' as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend the sign of a Bodhisattva, nor the sign of a perfection of wisdom, nor the signs of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. It is because he does not apprehend these signs that he is called a 'Bodhisattva. Furthermore, Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the sign of the perfection of wisdom, nor the sign of the perfection of giving, nor the signs of the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom. He does not perceive the sign of the emptiness of the internal, nor the sign of the emptiness of the external, nor the sign of the emptiness of the internal and external, nor the sign of the emptiness of emptiness, nor the sign of the great emptiness, nor the sign of the emptiness of the ultimate, nor the sign of the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, nor the sign of the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, nor the sign of absolute emptiness, nor the sign of the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, nor the sign of the emptiness of non-dispersal, nor the sign of the emptiness of nature, nor the sign of the emptiness of all dharmas, nor the sign of the emptiness of own-marks, nor the sign of the emptiness of non-existence, nor the sign of the emptiness of existence, nor the sign of the emptiness of non-duality, nor the sign of the emptiness of non-observation. It is because he does not apprehend these signs that he is called a 'Bodhisattva.'"

For indeed, even though a distinction exists, it cannot be apprehended by one situated at a very great distance from a post, because only its configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is perceived there. Yet, a mere configuration devoid of specific qualities is impossible. However, since that [configuration] does not appear due to the great distance, a mere appearance arises identically everywhere; thus, that which is distinct from the individual instance (*vyakti*) is precisely the universal (*sāmānya*). Through the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object, that very [universal] is non-different according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), yet it is different [from the individual]. This difference is not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Why then does the difference not exist ultimately? Because in the conceptual construction of unification, neither of the two appears. Let it be, then, that the difference is ultimate, since only the universal appears. And that which appears as distinct is indeed distinct.
That too is incorrect, because:
That would be a universal because of the appearance of a form that is not conjoined with individuals;
for a universal is not like the form of an individual alone.
Now, it might be argued that even a single entity is a universal (*sāmānya*) because of its connection with commonality; but that too is incorrect.
For the commonality of universals exists only through their connection with distinct [particular] universals.
But thereafter, it is the individual itself that is clearly manifest as the universal.

In that case, the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely an erroneous cognition, because it is common to those individuals. If that were so, then there would be neither cognition nor activity directed toward the individual. For it is not logical that there should be cognition of an individual or activity toward one based on the cognition of the nature of an erroneous mental state, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If you argue that activity occurs through error, we say no; for there is no other non-erroneous [cognition] to serve as a basis. Or, even in that case, it would be merely the cognition of its own nature, and not the cognition of the individual. Therefore, if one accepts a succession of ever-further errors, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), resulting in no cognition at all. Thus, this [position] is trivial. If, then, there is no connection with a universal—neither as something distinct from it, nor as having both forms, nor as being of the nature of error—and furthermore, there is no cognition of the individual, what then is the means (*upāya*) by which objects are cognized through words and logical marks?
Since its result is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), it is by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) the means (*upāya*).
What other principle could there be for the comprehension of an object from a word? (PVA 380)

[586,xi] But surely, the establishment of a real entity occurs through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), yet no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is found that apprehends the cognition of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
To this it is replied:
Because its occurrence is perceived as being distinct from anything other than that.
Why is it not determined that a statement has exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its result?

(PVA 381) For it is observed that those engaged in conventional practice proceed by means of the exclusion of what is other than that [object]. Nor does one proceed on the basis of non-cognition; therefore, the cognition of exclusion is inferred. For that [object] is cognized as being unassociated with others, both by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). In that regard, in the case of direct perception, the object of cognition is the exclusion itself, which is inherent in the very nature of the thing. However, conceptual constructions do not have real entities as their objects. Therefore, the object of words and conceptual constructions is exclusively the exclusion alone.
[586,xv] But surely, when an entity is apprehended, how can its exclusion be apprehended part by part?
On this point, the following is said:
There exists a real entity which is the object of exclusion (*vyatireka*) and the domain of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
But what person rich in wisdom would postulate another distinction based on whether [the universal] is real or unreal?

(382) (PVA) Let there be for you only that much which is reached through the connection with non-exclusion (*avyatireka*). If the purpose is served by means of a general [universal], what benefit is there in its particularity? (383) (PVA)

To the extent that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) cannot be understood without a thing (*vastu*), only that much is capable of fulfilling the purpose of those engaged in conventional discourse (*vyavahārin*). Furthermore, it is not possible to understand exclusion as being necessarily connected with a real entity (*sadvastu*), because its cognition is observed even through connection with what is unreal (*asat*). Therefore, a statement has exclusion alone as its object, since the thing itself is unreal in that context.
But surely, if there is existence of the real entity (*vastu*), then there is also the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of it; if there is no such exclusion, how can that which is merged within it be real?
To this it is said:
[587, viii] Even though this is being perceived, why is it considered unreal?
If it is unreal because of contradiction, then how can difference be considered real? (PVA 384)

[587,ix] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not even the slightest thing that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not even the slightest thing that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because there is not even the slightest thing that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that the Tathāgata is called ‘Tathāgata. Subhūti, if there were even the slightest thing that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to as a dharma, he would not be called ‘Tathāgata,’ but rather ‘Dharmanirmita’ (One Fabricated by Dharmas). Subhūti said: “Blessed One, it is wonderful! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well has the Blessed One spoken this teaching! For, Blessed One, those who will hear this teaching and believe it will be endowed with roots of merit planted under many Buddhas. The Blessed One said: “So it is, Subhūti. Those who will hear this teaching and believe it will be endowed with roots of merit planted under many Buddhas. Furthermore, Subhūti, if someone were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and if another person were to hear this teaching and, having heard it, believe it, the latter would generate a greater mass of merit than the former. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas is inconceivable, and the one who teaches it is inconceivable, and the one who hears it is inconceivable, and the one who believes it is inconceivable. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how is it that the Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas is inconceivable, and how is it that the one who teaches it is inconceivable, and how is it that the one who hears it is inconceivable, and how is it that the one who believes it is inconceivable? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because that Dharma cannot be conceived by means of thought or mental consciousness, and it cannot be known by means of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Subhūti, it is because that Dharma is neither form, nor sound, nor smell, nor taste, nor touchable object, nor mental phenomenon; it is not past, nor future, nor present; it is neither produced nor ceased; it is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither increased nor decreased. Subhūti, it is because that Dharma is thus inconceivable that it is called ‘inconceivable. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take up, bear in mind, recite, and master this Sūtra, and were to teach it extensively to others, they would be reviled by gods, humans, and asuras. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, Mara, the Evil One, will exert great effort to cause obstacles for such a person. The Blessed One said: “So it is, Subhūti. Mara, the Evil One, will exert great effort to cause obstacles for such a person. However, Subhūti, if that son of good family or daughter of good family relies on the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the Saṅgha, and if they dwell in friendliness toward all beings, then Mara, the Evil One, will be unable to find an opportunity to create an obstacle. Furthermore, Subhūti, if that son of good family or daughter of good family dwells in the dwelling of emptiness, dwells in the dwelling of signlessness, and dwells in the dwelling of wishlessness, then Mara, the Evil One, will be unable to find an opportunity to create an obstacle. Furthermore, Subhūti, if that son of good family or daughter of good family dwells in the dwelling of the four foundations of mindfulness, dwells in the dwelling of the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, then Mara, the Evil One, will be unable to find an opportunity to create an obstacle. Furthermore, Subhūti, if that son of good family or daughter of good family dwells in the dwelling of the four immeasurables, dwells in the dwelling of the four formless attainments, dwells in the dwelling of the eight liberations, dwells in the dwelling of the nine successive meditative attainments, dwells in the dwelling of the ten spheres of totality, dwells in the dwelling of the three gateways to liberation, dwells in the dwelling of the six supernormal knowledges, dwells in the dwelling of the four analytical knowledges, dwells in the dwelling of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and dwells in the dwelling of the great compassion, then Mara, the Evil One, will be unable to find an opportunity to create an obstacle. Furthermore, Subhūti, if that son of good family or daughter of good family, when teaching this Sūtra, does not perceive a self, does not perceive a being, a soul, a person, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a human, or a man; if they do not perceive form, nor sensation, perception, formations, or consciousness; if they do not perceive the eye, nor the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; if they do not perceive form, nor sound, smell, taste, touchable objects, or mental phenomena; if they do not perceive the realm of eye-consciousness, nor the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness; if they do not perceive the realm of ignorance, nor the realms of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or old age and death; if they do not perceive the attainment of the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor the fruits of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat; if they do not perceive the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood, nor the fruit of Buddhahood—then, Subhūti, it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family is teaching this Sūtra while relying on the power of the Buddha, the power of the Dharma, and the power of the Saṅgha. Subhūti, it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family is teaching this Sūtra while dwelling in friendliness toward all beings. Subhūti, it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family is teaching this Sūtra while dwelling in the dwelling of emptiness, the dwelling of signlessness, and the dwelling of wishlessness. Subhūti, it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family is teaching this Sūtra while dwelling in the dwelling of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. Subhūti, it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family is teaching this Sūtra while dwelling in the dwelling of the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative attainments, the ten spheres of totality, the three gateways to liberation, the six supernormal knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion. Subhūti, it should be known that such a son of good family or daughter of good family is teaching this Sūtra while not perceiving a self, a being, a soul, a person, a life-force, a nourisher, a spirit, a human, or a man; while not perceiving form, sensation, perception, formations, or consciousness; while not perceiving the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; while not perceiving form, sound, smell, taste, touchable objects, or mental phenomena; while not perceiving the realm of eye-consciousness, nor the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-consciousness; while not perceiving the realm of ignorance, nor the realms of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense-bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or old age and death; while not perceiving the attainment of the fruit of a Stream-enterer, nor the fruits

First, the proponent of non-exclusion (*avyavacchedavādin*) must be questioned: What is this so-called "unreality" (*asatyatva*) of the object of cognition? If it exists in the very form in which it is cognized, how can it be unreal? If, on the other hand, it is unreal in a form not being cognized, then everything is unreal, and thus [your position] is itself unreal. Thus, the opponent’s position is like the milk of a donkey—it is utterly non-existent. Now, suppose you argue that it is unreal because it lacks the nature of being attainable (*prāpyarūpatā*) due to contradiction, and not because of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Even if it possesses intrinsic reality, for one who seeks the nature of attainment, its absence renders it unreal; unreality is simply a contrary cognition (*viparyayapratīti*), since it consists in grasping that which is not of the nature of attainment as being of the nature of attainment. And there is no unreality other than a contrary cognition. If this is the case, then it follows that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is real, because [it is established by the negation of what is contrary].
[587,x] That which is excluded from others is what is attained by those engaged in practical activity (*vyavahārin*).
In that case, any further distinction between the exclusion of a real entity and the exclusion of a non-entity is useless. (PVA 385)
[587,xi] If that which is attained is what has come to be real, then the reality of exclusion follows from its attainment.

[Objection: But surely, what is apprehended by that [cognition] is the exclusion of a non-existent entity, yet that [exclusion] is not attained, because it is the exclusion of an existent entity that is attained. And since there is no non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) when one thing is cognized and another is attained, how can there be the reality of the exclusion? [Reply: What kind of misplaced inquiry is this from one who is obsessed with what is misplaced? First of all, a distinction is indeed attained; by that much alone, the person engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahārin*) is satisfied. Furthermore, those engaged in worldly practice, being satisfied with what they have attained, are not capable of determining further distinctions [between entities], such that through the determination of a distinction between exclusions, they would encounter the experience of discrepancy. Therefore, this "non-discrepancy" is spoken of out of regard for the satisfaction of people engaged in worldly practice. It is not a reality in the sense of non-discrepancy when there is an investigation into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This has been stated: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its object the exclusion [of others] only in a conventional sense," according to the statement [in the *Pramāṇavārttika*]: "Validity is [established] by way of worldly practice" (PV 1.7). If a means of valid cognition were to be cognized by another means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it were cognized without a means of valid cognition, then the same would apply to the object of cognition (*prameya*); thus, the comprehension of the object of cognition would not be dependent upon the means of valid cognition. Therefore, it was said:

Validity is apprehended through conventional usage, but not in reality. If validity were established by another means of cognition, it would lead to an infinite regress; thus it has been stated. (PVA 386)
Because even there, further investigation is required.

If conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has already been pointed out. If [the object] is understood from what is not a means of valid cognition, that same [regress] will apply to the object of cognition (*prameya*) as well.
Thus, the definition of a means of valid cognition becomes useless, since everything is established [by such means].
"To say 'without a means of valid cognition' is not tenable.

(PVA 388) Therefore, non-contradiction in all cases is based merely upon worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), without investigating the subtle reality, and not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For it is thus:
"On this side is the bank; on that side is a tiger. By what means can there be an escape for a living being?
For consistency is not possible in either case, whether there is difference or non-difference.

If the object to be attained were different from that which is being cognized, how could there be an absence of contradiction—that is, non-contradiction—when one has attained something else? If, on the other hand, it were non-different in its entirety, then since that [object] would already have been apprehended at that very moment, for what purpose would one act? Or what would one attain from it? Thus, there would be no contradiction; this is the logic of "the tiger is here, and the bank is there. Therefore: A sentence has exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its result; it never has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object.
Even when the particle *eva* is not employed, that which is understood from these [words] remains;
let this matter rest for now. Is such a thing observed anywhere? Indeed it is observed: "Pārtha is the archer," "Caitra is the archer," and "the lotus is blue."

[588,v] When qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), qualificands (*viśeṣya*), and actions (*kriyā*) are employed, there is a distinction: when the qualifier is emphasized, there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*); when the qualificand is emphasized, there is the exclusion of connection with another (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*); and when the action is emphasized, there is the exclusion of absolute impossibility (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). [588,vi] But how can there be an emphasis on a specific restriction when [the word] is not employed? It is due to the context, the speaker's intention, and other such factors.

Now, one might object: just as in the case of "Pārtha alone is the archer," where the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) occurring in proximity to the qualificand excludes other qualificands, so too, when in proximity to a qualifier, it should exclude other qualifiers. Consequently, in the statement "Caitra is indeed an archer," there would follow the exclusion of all other qualities. But this is not tenable; nor is there any distinction between the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).
This is true.

Even in those cases, the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*) is understood regarding the objects, due to established convention, logical capacity, and the following of the speaker’s intention in the expression. (193)

[588,x] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be learned by you. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar’? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, because it roars like a lion regarding the four kinds of fearlessness, therefore this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. What are the four? Here, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans: ‘I am perfectly awakened. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘With respect to those things that have been fully known by the Tathāgata, there exists some dharma not yet fully known,’ I see no ground for that. And since I see no such ground, therein I abide with confidence, and I roar the lion’s roar in the assembly and turn the wheel of Brahmā, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, god, Māra, or Brahmā in the world. This, Ānanda, is the first kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans: ‘I have exhausted all outflows. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘In the Tathāgata, there exist outflows that have not been exhausted,’ I see no ground for that. And since I see no such ground, therein I abide with confidence, and I roar the lion’s roar in the assembly and turn the wheel of Brahmā, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, god, Māra, or Brahmā in the world. This, Ānanda, is the second kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans: ‘Whatever I have declared as obstacles to the noble life, those things are indeed obstacles. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘Those things declared as obstacles by the Tathāgata are not actually obstacles to the noble life; even while practicing them, one may still realize the supreme goal of the holy life,’ I see no ground for that. And since I see no such ground, therein I abide with confidence, and I roar the lion’s roar in the assembly and turn the wheel of Brahmā, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, god, Māra, or Brahmā in the world. This, Ānanda, is the third kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans: ‘I teach the path leading to the cessation of suffering. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘That path taught by the Tathāgata does not lead to the cessation of suffering; by following it, one cannot realize the supreme goal of the holy life,’ I see no ground for that. And since I see no such ground, therein I abide with confidence, and I roar the lion’s roar in the assembly and turn the wheel of Brahmā, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, god, Māra, or Brahmā in the world. This, Ānanda, is the fourth kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Because he roars like a lion regarding these four kinds of fearlessness, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar.’”

In that regard, if in a context of doubt as to whether this person is an archer or not, the statement "Caitra is an archer" is employed, then it effects the exclusion of that very doubt; thus, only the state of being a non-archer is excluded. Otherwise, one who speaks without providing a refinement for the listener would not be a speaker [in the proper sense]. Therefore, only the exclusion of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is understood, and nothing else. Likewise, even in that case of a sentence expressing the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), if a specific counter-correlate is under discussion—such as, "Of Pārtha and Rādheya, which one is the wielder of the bow?"—then Karna alone is excluded. The statement "Pārtha alone is the archer" does not exclude Rāma and others. Similarly, regarding the exclusion of connection (*yogavyavaccheda*), if it is being considered whether he possesses other qualities as well, then there is indeed an exclusion of all other qualities except for those that are infallible (infallible qualities). [The meaning is: "Caitra is an archer only, not a scholar, and so forth. Even in the investigation of Pārtha, if the context of doubt is whether there is anyone else in the world who is an archer, then there is an exclusion of all other possible subjects, because everything is then introduced as a potential counter-correlate.

By excluding its non-connection [with the subject], it qualifies the property-bearer (dharmin) and the property (dharma); thus, because the property is qualified by that [exclusion], it does not incur the fault of being without a basis (*niranvaya*). (194)

When it is established that a certain property (*dharma*) is connected with something else, it is precisely its non-connection [with the subject] that is suspected. Therefore, by demonstrating that connection, there is an exclusion of others; thus, there is no fault of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For this very reason, it is well known that "this is indeed a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*); otherwise, this would be non-existent. This is because non-connection is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), whereas connection with another is its opposite. Furthermore, this meaning is understood through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*).

For when a connection with something else has already been established, a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) does not apply to that very thing, because it would be contradictory. Indeed, only that which is doubtful is either excluded or affirmed; not that which is already established or prohibited. And the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) conforms to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). The word, too, functions in exactly this same way. For the speaker’s intention is not one thing while the capacity of the word to convey meaning is another. It has already been demonstrated that sounds (*dhvani*) are not inherently expressive by their own nature, like a lamp.
<2. Types of Reasons> [589,ii]

[Objection: But surely, even with the qualification "only Pārtha is the archer," the restriction excludes only connection with another (*anyayoga*) and not non-connection (*ayoga*); thus, there is a contradiction with the subject at hand. [Reply:
There is no contradiction, because:
[589,iv] Although Pārtha’s status as a qualifier is presented by the word, it does not exist for him in an ultimate sense. (PVA) 391

[589,v] The Bodhisattva, having attained the stage of non-retrogression, dwells in the certainty of the Mahāyāna; he is no longer subject to falling back from the path to enlightenment. He possesses the power of great compassion and the skillful means of wisdom, and thus he acts for the benefit of sentient beings without interruption. His conduct is in accordance with the Dharma, and his mind is free from the stains of affliction. He has transcended the realms of both gods and humans, and abides in the state of a true son of the Buddha. This is called the fifth stage of the Bodhisattva, known as the "Difficult-to-Conquer" (Sudurjaya).

In this context, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is said to be a property (*dharma*) that is dependent [on the qualified] by virtue of its subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*). Pārtha (Arjuna), however, is the qualified (*viśeṣya*) because he is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the quality of being an archer. For the actual principle (*vastava nyāya*) is one thing, while the linguistic principle (*śabdanaya*) is another. And here, since the property of the real object is grasped through the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no fault at all. Here, the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), which consists in exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), is understood through perception and inference by way of distinction; thus, there is no fault of non-comprehension. For, by means of the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), when a qualifier belongs to one thing, the non-existence of that [quality] in another would follow; and there is no difference regarding the particle (*nipāta*) connected to the qualifier and the qualified, such as the sense of restriction. If "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) were a property of the subject (*pakṣa*) alone, then everything else would be unproduced, and other locations would not possess smoke. This would contradict both perception and inference. For smoke is perceived elsewhere through perception, and [the absence of the reason in the contrary] is known through inference from such reasons as "being differentiated by the diversity of cognitions. Or, having perceived "being produced" through perception, there is the comprehension—either through worldly convention or through the definition of inference—of the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) of the particle expressing restriction (such as *eva*) associated with the qualifier and so forth, or of its meaning, namely the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and so on. So what could be otherwise in that case? This is the explanation of the meaning of the compound *pakṣadharma*. Since the meaning of a compound sentence is understood through distinctions—as a difference (*bheda*), a conjunction (*saṃsarga*), or both difference and conjunction—it is established. [An opponent asks: "Let it be that it is a property of the subject; why has the Teacher specified it as ninefold? [The author replies: He says: "It is for the purpose of demonstrating the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the valid reason (*samyaghetu*) that exactly that many [types] must be specified; there is no need for nine."
For the sake of establishing essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*), there are two types of reasons for each; their contraries are likewise two.
Because of dispute regarding particularity (*bheda*) and generality (*sāmānya*), the remaining [reasons] are those that establish exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). (195)

Physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Monks, what is the nutriment for craving? It is ignorance. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It is unwise attention. [589, ix] 11. The Discourse on the Four Noble Truths. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks! "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, these four noble truths should be fully understood by those who have gone forth. What are the four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not obtaining what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to further existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, releasing it, and detaching from it. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. Monks, what is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. [589, x] 12. The Discourse on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness. Thus have I heard. When, monks, you have developed the foundation of mindfulness, supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and resulting in relinquishment, you will soon realize the ultimate goal of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. But how, monks, is the foundation of mindfulness developed so that it is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and results in relinquishment? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is how the foundation of mindfulness is developed so that it is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and results in relinquishment. [589, xi] 13. The ninefold enumeration is given because all nine types are indeed applicable. Only two [types] are specified because they function as reasons (*hetu*) due to the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*) respectively, whereas others do not. Another two are specified because they constitute a contradiction (*viruddha*) when used to prove the opposite of those two. Another two are specified to exclude the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), which some others have claimed to be conclusive based merely on observation and non-observation. As for the remaining three, their specification is intended to demonstrate the predominance of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); the meaning demonstrated is that a reason is a means of cognition by way of exclusion, and therefore, through inference, only exclusion is what is to be proven.
<1. The nine types of property of the subject> [589, viii]:
Among these, those are the nine types of property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

The objects of cognition (*prameya*), the produced (*kṛtaka*), the impermanent (*anitya*), the produced (*kṛta*), the audible (*śrāvaṇa*), that which arises from effort (*yatnajā*), the impermanent (*anitya*), that which does not arise from effort (*ayonijā*), and touch (*sparśa*)— these nine are the examples for proving impermanence and so forth. (PVA 392)

[590,i] But surely, since "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "occurring immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) are one and the same, how can there be multiplicity even when they recur? How then can there be the status of being a reason (*hetutā*) and the status of being contradictory (*viruddhatā*)? And how can there be novelty (*navatva*), for that very same thing recurring cannot be the basis for a difference in number?
To this it is replied: Because—
[590,iii] The middle triad and the eternal ones arise from the effort toward the eternal and the non-eternal.
And [the properties of being] effortless, non-eternal, and eternal are established by means such as "being an object of cognition" (prameyatva). Therefore, everything is logically consistent.

[590,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the world of desire as real, nor does he perceive the world of form or the formless world as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real; he does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as real; he does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as real; he does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as real; he does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does not perceive the bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the state of a bodhisattva as real. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata as real. Why is that? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, then what dharma does the bodhisattva mahāsattva take hold of when he practices the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, the bodhisattva mahāsattva takes hold of no dharma whatsoever when he practices the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if the bodhisattva mahāsattva takes hold of no dharma whatsoever when he practices the perfection of wisdom, how does he train in the perfection of giving, how does he train in the perfection of morality, how does he train in the perfection of patience, how does he train in the perfection of vigor, how does he train in the perfection of meditation, and how does he train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a gift as real, nor does he perceive a giver as real, nor does he perceive a recipient as real. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of giving. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive morality as real, nor does he perceive one who observes morality as real, nor does he perceive one who breaks morality as real. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of morality. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive patience as real, nor does he perceive one who is patient as real, nor does he perceive one who is angry as real. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of patience. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive vigor as real, nor does he perceive one who exerts vigor as real, nor does he perceive one who is indolent as real. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of vigor. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive meditation as real, nor does he perceive one who is concentrated as real, nor does he perceive one who is distracted as real. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of meditation. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive wisdom as real, nor does he perceive one who is wise as real, nor does he perceive one who is ignorant as real. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s training in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, enter the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of heat, the stage of summits, the stage of patience, the stage of the worldly supreme dharmas, the stage of the dharmas of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, or the stage of the bodhisattva? How does he fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks? How does he fulfill the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion? How does he turn the wheel of Dharma? How does he establish sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship? How does he establish them in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood? How does he establish them in the path of the bodhisattva? How does he establish them in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature that the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, enters the stage of dry wisdom, the stage of heat, the stage of summits, the stage of patience, the stage of the worldly supreme dharmas, the stage of the śrāvaka, the stage of the pratyekabuddha, and the stage of the bodhisattva. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he fulfills the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor marks. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he fulfills the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he turns the wheel of Dharma. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he establishes sentient beings in the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he establishes them in the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he establishes them in the path of the bodhisattva. It is because they are empty of intrinsic nature that he establishes them in the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, then what is the distinction between the dharmas of the śrāvaka, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharmas of the Buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, yet the dharmas of the śrāvaka do not realize the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha, nor do the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha realize the dharmas of the Buddha. Why is that? Subhūti, because the dharmas of the śrāvaka, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharmas of the Buddha are each established according to their own characteristics. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if the dharmas of the śrāvaka, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha, and the dharmas of the Buddha are each established according to their own characteristics, then how does the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, transcend the dharmas of the śrāvaka and the dharmas of the pratyekabuddha and enter the irreversible stage?
