Indeed, what is called a "probans" (*sādhana*) has no essence in itself; it acquires the status of being a probans only in relation to that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). And since the object to be proven is characterized by differentiation, it is not at all tenable to say that a single [probans] is both a valid reason and a contradictory one. Therefore, there are two types of reasons: "it is impermanent because it is produced" is a probans of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*); and "because it follows immediately upon effort" is a probans of effect (*kāryahetu*). How is it known that "producedness" is a probans of essential nature and "following immediately upon effort" is a probans of effect? Why does the reverse not occur? Because they possess their respective defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and because the other defining characteristic is absent, the reverse does not occur.
For there is no pervasion of the object to be known by anything other than its own nature when it is a cause;
because deviation is possible, the result of the two modes of occurrence follows from that. (196)

[590, vii] The Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the three gates of liberation. What are they? They are as follows: first, the gate of emptiness; second, the gate of signlessness; and third, the gate of wishlessness. What is the gate of emptiness? It refers to the emptiness of internal phenomena, the emptiness of external phenomena, the emptiness of both internal and external phenomena, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-attainment, and the emptiness of non-dispersal. This is called the gate of emptiness. What is the gate of signlessness? It refers to the absence of signs in form, the absence of signs in sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the absence of signs in the eye, the absence of signs in the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the absence of signs in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; the absence of signs in the eye-consciousness, and so on up to the absence of signs in the mind-consciousness; the absence of signs in the contact of the eye, and so on up to the absence of signs in the contact of the mind; the absence of signs in the feeling born of eye-contact, and so on up to the absence of signs in the feeling born of mind-contact; the absence of signs in the earth element, and so on up to the absence of signs in the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements; the absence of signs in ignorance, and so on up to the absence of signs in old age and death; the absence of signs in the realm of desire, the absence of signs in the realm of form, and the absence of signs in the formless realm; the absence of signs in the conditioned, the absence of signs in the unconditioned, and the absence of signs in all phenomena. This is called the gate of signlessness. What is the gate of wishlessness? It refers to the absence of wishing for birth in the desire realm, the absence of wishing for birth in the form realm, and the absence of wishing for birth in the formless realm; the absence of wishing for the conditioned, the absence of wishing for the unconditioned, and the absence of wishing for all phenomena. This is called the gate of wishlessness. These three gates of liberation are the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva, by means of these three gates of liberation, is able to enter the stage of non-retrogression, and because he is able to mature sentient beings and purify the Buddha-field. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, by means of these three gates of liberation, is able to transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and enter the stage of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, by means of these three gates of liberation, is able to sever all afflictions and secondary afflictions, and attain the unobstructed wisdom of a Buddha. Therefore, these three gates of liberation are the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. What is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the four foundations of mindfulness? What are they? They are as follows: first, mindfulness of the body; second, mindfulness of sensation; third, mindfulness of the mind; and fourth, mindfulness of phenomena. What is mindfulness of the body? It refers to the Bodhisattva contemplating the body as impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and selfless; contemplating the body as arising from causes and conditions, like a phantom or an illusion, without substance or essence, and ultimately having no place of abiding. This is called mindfulness of the body. What is mindfulness of sensation? It refers to the Bodhisattva contemplating all sensations—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as being empty, without self, and without owner; contemplating that all sensations arise from the conjunction of the three factors and have no fixed nature, and that they are ultimately extinguished and do not abide. This is called mindfulness of sensation. What is mindfulness of the mind? It refers to the Bodhisattva contemplating the mind as having no color, no shape, no location, and no dwelling place; contemplating that the mind is like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection, and like a magical creation, ultimately ungraspable. This is called mindfulness of the mind. What is mindfulness of phenomena? It refers to the Bodhisattva contemplating all phenomena as being empty of inherent nature, without marks, and ultimately quiescent; contemplating that all phenomena are like space, without coming or going, without birth or extinction, and without increase or decrease. This is called mindfulness of phenomena. These four foundations of mindfulness are the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva, by means of these four foundations of mindfulness, is able to observe the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena without attachment, and thereby attain the unobstructed wisdom of a Buddha. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, by means of these four foundations of mindfulness, is able to sever the bonds of craving and views, and enter the path of the Bodhisattva. Therefore, these four foundations of mindfulness are the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. What is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the four right efforts? What are they? They are as follows: first, the right effort to prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising; second, the right effort to abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen; third, the right effort to produce unarisen wholesome states; and fourth, the right effort to maintain and increase wholesome states that have already arisen. What is the right effort to prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising? It refers to the Bodhisattva generating the will, exerting vigor, applying the mind, and striving with diligence to prevent unarisen covetousness, malice, sloth, restlessness, doubt, and other such evil and unwholesome states from arising. This is called the right effort to prevent unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising. What is the right effort to abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen? It refers to the Bodhisattva generating the will, exerting vigor, applying the mind, and striving with diligence to abandon covetousness, malice, sloth, restlessness, doubt, and other such evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen. This is called the right effort to abandon evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen. What is the right effort to produce unarisen wholesome states? It refers to the Bodhisattva generating the will, exerting vigor, applying the mind, and striving with diligence to produce unarisen faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and other such wholesome states. This is called the right effort to produce unarisen wholesome states. What is the right effort to maintain and increase wholesome states that have already arisen? It refers to the Bodhisattva generating the will, exerting vigor, applying the mind, and striving with diligence to maintain and increase the wholesome states of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and so forth, that have already arisen, so that they do not decline but continue to grow and expand. This is called the right effort to maintain and increase wholesome states that have already arisen. These four right efforts are the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva, by means of these four right efforts, is able to eliminate all evil and unwholesome states and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and thereby attain the supreme, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha. Therefore, these four right efforts are the Bodhisattva’s skillful means. What is the Bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding the four bases of psychic power? What are they? They are as follows: first, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort; second, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of vigor accompanied by effort; third, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by effort; and fourth, the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by effort. What is the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort? It refers to the Bodhisattva, relying on the desire-faculty, generating the will, exerting vigor, applying the mind, and striving with diligence, and through the power of concentration, attaining various supernormal powers, such as multiplying one body into many bodies, or manifesting various forms according to one's will. This is called the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort. What is the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of vigor accompanied by effort? It refers to the Bodhisattva, relying on the vigor-faculty, generating the will, exerting vigor, applying the mind, and striving with diligence, and through the power of concentration, attaining various supernormal powers, such as traveling to distant lands in a moment, or emitting light to illuminate the world. This is called the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of vigor accompanied by effort. What is the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied

Because "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) possesses an equal pervasion (*samānavyāptikatva*). Nor is an effect (*kārya*) necessarily of equal pervasion, because an effect may deviate from its cause; causes do not necessarily possess that [effect]. Therefore, every effect falls into two categories: that which occurs in both ways and that which is invariably concomitant with effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*). Consequently, this is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*). For not all things that are impermanent (*anitya*) initiate the effect of cognition immediately following effort. Thus, that [impermanence] exists in two ways within the similar class (*sapakṣa*). However, for those who initiate the effect of cognition through another cause, all impermanent things are invariably so. Therefore, because of its pervasiveness, even the cognition that is an effect is in reality a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) is said to be nothing but perception (*upalambha*). And existence is not defined merely by the cognition that follows effort, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that other things are non-existent. Thus, cognition—its distinctions being constructed through the presence or absence of positive and negative concomitance—ascends to the pinnacle of the category of effects. Therefore, that cognition, when designated by the term "invariably following effort," is a reason based on an effect.

[590, viii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. It should be learned by you. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar’? The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, because it roars like a lion regarding the four kinds of fearlessness, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. What are the four? Here, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, including gods and humans: ‘I am a Tathāgata; I have attained perfect enlightenment. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘O ascetic, these dharmas have not been fully realized by you through direct knowledge,’ I see no ground for that. And seeing no ground for it, I abide in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity, and I roar the lion’s roar and turn the wheel of Brahmā that cannot be turned back by any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in the world. This, Ānanda, is the first kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims: ‘I have exhausted all outflows; there is no further existence. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘O ascetic, these outflows have not been exhausted by you,’ I see no ground for that. And seeing no ground for it, I abide in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity, and I roar the lion’s roar and turn the wheel of Brahmā that cannot be turned back by any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in the world. This, Ānanda, is the second kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims: ‘These are the obstacles; if one practices them, they will obstruct the path to supreme enlightenment. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘O ascetic, these things do not act as obstacles when practiced,’ I see no ground for that. And seeing no ground for it, I abide in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity, and I roar the lion’s roar and turn the wheel of Brahmā that cannot be turned back by any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in the world. This, Ānanda, is the third kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Ānanda, a Tathāgata claims: ‘I teach the path leading to the cessation of suffering; if one practices it, it leads to the complete cessation of suffering. If anyone should challenge me, saying: ‘O ascetic, even if one practices this path, it does not lead to the complete cessation of suffering,’ I see no ground for that. And seeing no ground for it, I abide in security, fearlessness, and intrepidity, and I roar the lion’s roar and turn the wheel of Brahmā that cannot be turned back by any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in the world. This, Ānanda, is the fourth kind of fearlessness of a Tathāgata. Because he roars thus like a lion regarding these four kinds of fearlessness, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Blessed One. Indeed, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Therefore, Ānanda, learn this Dharma-discourse as ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Very well, Blessed One,” replied the Venerable Ānanda to the Blessed One. He then learned this Dharma-discourse as ‘The Lion’s Roar. At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was seated in that very assembly. Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful how well this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Blessed One. Indeed, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. The Blessed One said: “Kāśyapa, because it roars like a lion regarding the four kinds of analytical knowledge, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. What are the four? Here, Kāśyapa, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible; this is the first analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the maturation of the results of karmic actions performed in the past, present, and future; this is the second analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the various inclinations and dispositions of beings; this is the third analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the faculties of other beings and other individuals, whether they are dull or sharp, superior or inferior, and so forth; this is the fourth analytical knowledge of a Tathāgata. Because he roars like a lion regarding these four kinds of analytical knowledge, Kāśyapa, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Blessed One. Indeed, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. The Blessed One said: “Therefore, Kāśyapa, learn this Dharma-discourse as ‘The Lion’s Roar. “Very well, Blessed One,” replied the Venerable Mahākāśyapa to the Blessed One. He then learned this Dharma-discourse as ‘The Lion’s Roar. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was seated in that very assembly. Then the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated himself at the feet of the Blessed One, and said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful how well this Dharma-discourse has been spoken by the Blessed One. Indeed, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. The Blessed One said: “Śāriputra, because it roars like a lion regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Lion’s Roar. What are the eighteen? Here, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata is subject to no error; this is the first unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no rough speech; this is the second unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no loss of mindfulness; this is the third unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no non-equanimity of mind; this is the fourth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no lack of discernment regarding the objects of meditation; this is the fifth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no lack of exertion; this is the sixth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no lack of desire to act; this is the seventh unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no loss of wisdom; this is the eighth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no loss of liberation; this is the ninth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata has no loss of the knowledge and vision of liberation; this is the tenth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata’s bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; this is the eleventh unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata’s verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; this is the twelfth unique quality of a Buddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Tathāgata’s mental actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom; this is

How, then, is it understood that knowledge produced by a further effort is an impermanent effect? To this, he says: "Because there is a multiplicity of effects produced by effort, [the objection] is *kāryasama* (balancing the effect). Manifestation (*vyakti*) is also an effect of effort, as is the case with non-manifestation; for example, the effort of bringing a lamp near does not establish the production of a jar, whereas the effort of rotating the wheel and so forth does. Since both cases are observed, how can there be a single conclusion? Thus the author of the *Bhāṣya* says: "If we shall establish sound as eternal, then sound is manifested; otherwise, it is produced. Nor do we understand that "sound is produced" merely because of the conventional usage of the verb "to do," since the root *kṛ* (to do) is used in the sense of application, as in "make my feet" or "make my back. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the reason for the eternity of sound. Therefore, sound being eternal, its manifestation—just like a jar—is from a lamp.

That which has its establishment through valid cognition at both that time and other times is manifestation (*upalambha*); moreover, manifestation is nothing other than the act of manifesting. (394) (PVA)
Likewise, the perception of something previously existing from some source does not constitute being an effect; for that which exists prior [to its perception] was not an effect at that time.
To this it is replied:
Knowledge immediately following effort does not necessarily belong to that which already exists.
Because it is in every respect useless for the words of that [Veda] and its repetitions and phonemes. (197)

Just as a jar that comes into being immediately after an effort is the product of that effort and not something manifested by the potter’s effort—otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the entire collection of causal factors being rendered useless; for if everything were already present in everything, nothing would need to be striven for by anyone, and the world would be devoid of activity. A restriction is established by the causal factors, otherwise there would be a state of disorder. What, then, is this so-called "restriction"? Because:
There exists no such thing as a "restriction" that functions by excluding others;
therefore, there can be no exclusion [of a cause] even by means of hundreds of reasons.
Furthermore, how could there be a transition to non-existence for that which has been excluded?
Furthermore, that arising in a destination belongs to something that does not [yet] exist.

(397) Moreover, there is indeed a restriction for every proponent of the theory that the effect exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*); therefore, for them as well, the production of something non-existent is nowhere logical. (398)

Furthermore, if the manifestation of this [entity] while it exists in a state of differentiation is being prescribed, and if that manifestation were itself something to be produced, then there would be a twofold conceptualization:
[the question arises] if it is non-existent, action is impossible; and even if it were existent, how could it be a cause?
Existence and non-existence do not both belong to a single thing in connection with the mind.
(400) Even if it were an existent, that [existence] would always already be there; what, then, has been done by the causal factors (*kāraka*)?
Since the capacity for action belongs to non-existence, the status of being a causal factor is futile. (401)

Therefore, a jar produced by a potter and other such causes, which comes into being immediately after an effort, is not something manifested (*vyaṅgya*). [Objection: Just as that very same jar, though perceived at a later time, is manifested by a lamp, so too will sound be manifested by an effort. [Reply: No, because the jar exists prior to its perception through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); whereas for sound, there is an absence of any means of valid cognition prior to the effort. [Objection: If it exists, then its existence prior [to the effort] is established here as well by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). [Reply: No. [This is the refutation of recognition.]
The cognition of recognition has been refuted hundreds of times; for what has been discarded does not return, nor does the dead come back to life.

Furthermore: What does recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) establish? Does it establish the existence of what has been known, or that which exists between two known moments? If it establishes what has been known, then since that was already established by the previous cognition and subsequently dealt with by memory, what is the utility of recognition there? Recognition establishes that "it exists even now," whereas memory establishes it only at that [past] time, as in the case of remembering what was seen.
[591,xiv] That is incorrect, because:

If recognition proceeds from the existence of memory, then that recognition regarding an object of memory is indeed not produced by the sense organs. Nor is any other cognition admitted apart from sensory perception and memory. (PVA 402)
Therefore, because it lacks the quality of being born from the senses, recollection is not a valid means of cognition (*apramāṇatā*).

For the senses do not function toward an object that is being remembered; otherwise, even places such as Kānyakubja would become objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*), and it would follow that even the dead would be objects of direct perception.

Now, if the operation of the sense organ occurs toward that which is being seen, what is the use of recognition even when the object is being seen? If it is argued that the purpose is the cognition of identity with that which is being remembered:
That is incorrect.
Since recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), how can there be identity of its object?
For if the property (*dharma*) is unreal, the unreality of the substratum (*dharmin*) is evident.
(404) (PVA) The connection with a previous time is not established by memory;
rather, the mere appearance of form occurs even without recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). (405) (PVA)

[592,iii] For that which is merely a white or yellow appearance is not an appearance of permanence, because it exists even at its first appearance. Now, if it is argued that even there, permanence—characterized by persistence over time—is indeed manifested; for there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that negates it.
They say that perception is an affirmer, not a negator of an object,
if the sense organ were to grasp an object as pervading a duration of time.

If there were a grasping that relies upon all moments of time until the limit of death, then the reliance on a previous time would occur through recollection and not through direct perception. Therefore, because recollection is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), the identity of the object perceived therein is unreal. Since the subject (*dharmin*) is unreal, the property (*dharma*) is also unreal. Now, [if one objects]:
If the present is real and the prior state is established as unreal,
then their identity would certainly be characterized by both reality and unreality. (PVA 407)
[592, viii] If two things possess both reality and unreality, then their unity must also be characterized by both reality and unreality, and not by unreality alone. That too is trivial, because:
If its status as true or false were determined by the nature of the substratum—
such that it is true by virtue of being present and false by virtue of not being present— [then the following would apply].

Since the present form is real, its unity is also real because it persists as the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*). However, the unity being remembered is consequently unreal for that very reason; thus, the unity of a real entity is not established.
[592,xi] If the unity of each individual were indeed real, why would there not be a corresponding cognition?
Why is there a contradiction within one's own statement regarding the self itself?
(409) (PVA) Now, this recognition is observed to occur when [an object] is seen as distinct;
therefore, it is determined that when it is seen as non-distinct, [the object] becomes [identical]. (410) (PVA)

Therefore, this cognition of recognition, by excluding what is different, establishes itself upon what is non-different. An entity consists of nothing more than being either different or non-different. Thus, by turning away from the different, it establishes non-difference; otherwise, it would not exist at all.
Indeed, it is not possible to exclude [the object] from everything; therefore, that [objection] is false. For:
Even though there is a difference, there is another specific quality [in the object] by which [the cognition] is excluded.
It is better to assume a specific quality of that very same thing than to postulate a different object altogether.

It is better to postulate that this [recognition] is merely a specific kind of difference arising from the mere emergence of the cognition of recognition, rather than [postulating] identity, which is of a different genus from difference; for this emergence of recognition is unobserved in cases such as young *darbha* grass that has been cut and grown again, where there occurs a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of an identical form. Therefore, it is more logical to postulate the same [difference] elsewhere as well. In those cases, the state of being cut is perceived persisting in the interval; thus, there is no postulation of identity despite the difference. But here [in the case of the hair], it is not so; indeed, the introduction of the example of the mass of hair is inconsistent. This has truly become a clumsy attempt by one who is falling to clutch at *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass. For instance: [The verse follows: "Even though the hair is different, the notion of non-difference arises due to the similarity of form; likewise, even though the *darbha* grass is different, the notion of non-difference arises due to the similarity of form. This is not so. For in the case of the hair, the difference is directly perceived through the senses, whereas in the case of the *darbha* grass, the difference is not perceived. Furthermore, the notion of identity regarding the hair is sublated by the perception of the difference between the past and present states, while in the case of the *darbha* grass, there is no such sublation. Moreover, the notion of identity regarding the hair is produced by a defect (the appearance of similar new hair), whereas in the case of the *darbha* grass, there is no such defect. Thus, the two cases are not equal. Therefore, the claim that recognition proves identity is refuted. It is merely a desperate grasp at a straw by one who is falling. Thus it is said: "Like a blind man led by another blind man, like a boat tossed upon the ocean, like a fire-fighter entering a burning house, this [recognition] leads only to ruin. Thus ends the section on Recognition.
What is called "cutting" is a severance, a non-reconnection with what follows;
and since that occurs through the prior abandonment [of the preceding], how could cognition be connected? (PVA 412)
And the view that is not compounded is equal to both the illustrative example and its counterpart.

Furthermore, even when there is fragmentation, the deceased maintains recognition; yet that evil-minded one strikes himself with his own self. When the previous form has perished, there can be no identity with that which has perished.
In this way, both diversity and unity have been established as existing.
Furthermore:
That which has perished is never an object for the senses; therefore, it must operate within the domain of memory alone.
Since the validity of memory has already been refuted previously, permanence can only be accepted on the basis of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). 414 (PVA)

Therefore, even if memory, in its apprehension of an object, were not to establish the object as it exists at the present moment, it nevertheless apprehends the object as it existed then; thus, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that past state is indeed established.
How could the firm determination of identity with that [past object] be anything other than a means of valid cognition? (415) (PVA)
Even if a firm conviction has arisen in virtuous people, it might be overturned; thus, contradiction is inherent.

(416) (PVA) Even if one’s mind is encouraged by a conviction based on an unshakable certainty, if one were to overturn that very certainty, then there would be one thing in his speech and another in his mind.
This is the very essence of consciousness for the proponents of *pratyabhijñā* (recognition):
those who have ascended too high fall down even instantaneously. (PVA 417)
For one who has ascended to a very precarious and distant height, a fall is imminent;
for a lamp, inclining toward extinction, perishes after having shone intensely for a long time.
For instance: If memory has as its object an experienced thing, how can there be [the claim that it is directed toward] what has perished?
If it has as its object an experienced thing, how can it be memory? (419) (PVA) [593,xvi]

If memory has as its object an entity that has been previously experienced by its very nature, then there would be no recollection of the past, for the past was not apprehended through perception. If, on the other hand, it is something unapprehended that is determined by memory, then in that case it is not memory; for memory must have as its object something previously known. Even so, it is not recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), since recognition is held to have as its object an entity previously seen through perception; otherwise, it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that "that very same thing which is past is called 'previously' [seen]," that too is mutually contradictory.
That which is past cannot be grasped; that which is being grasped is not thus [past].
In its remembered form, that which is past is not a real entity.
Furthermore, because of the firmness of the ascertainment, its validity is established.
"Even so, recognition would likewise be useless as a connection with the senses.

(PVA 421) [593, xix] If firmness of certainty were a valid means of knowledge even without a connection to the senses, then this is merely the intolerance of that wicked person who is incapable of investigation; for it is thus:
Cognition is accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of the existence of non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*).
However, this non-discrepancy pertains to the present [object], not to that which has already perished. (PVA 422)
If that unity did not exist, how could there be causal efficiency? It is not [absent].

Even by another [cause], the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is indeed accomplished. However, the unity [of that cause]—characterized by the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what does not produce that specific causal efficiency—is accepted as merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). For designations and conceptual constructions such as "one" are properly established solely through the capacity for that object. Indeed, discerning people do not rely upon designations or certainties whose objects are devoid of causal efficiency. Therefore, unity, as the performance of that causal efficiency, is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Consequently, inference is not based on that form as its logical mark (*liṅga*). As for the multiplicity of form, it arises from its connection with other imagined properties. Thus, recognition is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding actual unity. If this is so, why is there no recognition in the case of jars and the like—which are intent upon performing their respective causal efficiencies—in the form of "this is that very jar" or "this is similar to that"? [The answer follows:]...
Recognition is indeed a condition (*pratyaya*). Moreover, it is as follows: "This very same jar has been brought here," or "This is that very same cold water. For instance:
When it is said, "Bring another," one brings that other individual;
then there arises the certain cognition: "That very same thing has been brought again.

When a pot, a small jar, or another such object distinct from a [specific] pot is intended to be brought, and when it is said, "Bring another," if what is brought is a different individual instance of that same pot, there is the observation of the conventional usage: "This very same pot has been brought.
Because this usage is so deeply rooted and due to the attachment of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is no realization that this is merely a figurative application of the term.
Therefore, the determination of the oneness of a sound does not arise from recognition; rather, such an illusion occurs because the capacity for communication remains the same. (PVA 424)
If [the object] were other [than the cognition], how could trust be directed toward something else? For no one trusts anything regarding that which is not known.
(425) Even if there were identity, there would be no trust, because deviation is observed.
Likewise, someone may place their trust in another who is similar to that person.

ix) Just as trust is placed in such a person’s son and so forth by relying on an unfailing expectation based on similar mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too is it placed in the continuum (*saṃtāna*) that has that [person] as its material cause (*upādāna*).

<3. Refutation of the Permanence of the Self> [594,x] Now, how can there be a desire to give in return if there is momentariness? Furthermore, it is even more impossible if there is identity. To explain:
The practice of giving that is joined with fear or shame belongs to one for whom fear and shame are predominant; but what is the cause of that fear and shame? (PVA 427)
[594,xii] Now, by virtue of its proximity to that, there is the movement of this self which has been seized by it.
[594,xiii]
Even when there is no grasping of that [object], there is the grasping of it; this is an error even regarding its own self.
(428) Even in the case of a continuum of moments, that very same error occurs; why then is this not the cause for such conventional usage?
It is not so even in the case of permanence, because another cause arises from which subsequent [notions] also become causes for such conceit. (429)

[594,xvi] The Bodhisattva, having heard this teaching on the Dharma, was filled with joy, and having paid homage at the feet of the Blessed One, he departed. Then, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, this Bodhisattva has attained the stage of non-retrogression; he shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha by the name of *Vimalaprabhāsa*. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. This concludes the *Vimalaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the sixteenth discourse. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are four kinds of persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. What are these four? They are: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha; the Pratyekabuddha; the Śrāvaka who has entered the stream; and the person who dwells in the fruit of the once-returner. These, bhikṣus, are the four persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many... [The text continues with the detailed exposition of these four types of individuals. ...“Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall become like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, the venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat shortly after the Blessed One had left, approached the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and said: “Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Blessed One has arisen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking these words. Venerable one, it would be well if you were to recite the *Sūtra of the Four Persons* before the community of monks. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied: “Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One has indeed taught the *Sūtra of the Four Persons*. However, I am now old, aged, advanced in years, and my life is near its end. My faculties are dull and my memory is failing. Therefore, I am unable to recite the *Sūtra of the Four Persons* before the community of monks. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is fitting that you should teach the Dharma to others. It is fitting that you should instruct others. It is fitting that you should encourage others. It is fitting that you should cause others to enter the path. It is fitting that you should cause others to attain the fruit. It is fitting that you should cause others to realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied: “Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One has entrusted me with the teaching of the Dharma. The Blessed One has said: ‘Kāśyapa, you must teach the Dharma to others; you must instruct others; you must encourage others; you must cause others to enter the path; you must cause others to attain the fruit; you must cause others to realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. The Venerable Ānanda said: “Venerable Mahākāśyapa, if the Blessed One has entrusted you with the teaching of the Dharma, then please recite the *Sūtra of the Four Persons* before the community of monks. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa consented, saying: “So be it,” and then addressed the community of monks: “Listen, O monks. I shall recite the *Sūtra of the Four Persons* as I have heard it from the Blessed One. [The text continues with the full recitation of the Sūtra. ...“Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall become like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha. Thus spoke the Venerable Mahākāśyapa. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in what the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had said. This concludes the *Sūtra of the Four Persons*, the seventeenth discourse. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, in the Kalandakanivāpa, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are four kinds of persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. What are these four? They are: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha; the Pratyekabuddha; the Śrāvaka who has entered the stream; and the person who dwells in the fruit of the once-returner. These, bhikṣus, are the four persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many... Then, the venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat shortly after the Blessed One had left, approached the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and said: “Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Blessed One has arisen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking these words. Venerable one, it would be well if you were to recite the *Sūtra of the Four Persons* before the community of monks. The Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied: “Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One has indeed taught the *Sūtra of the Four Persons*. However, I am now old, aged, advanced in years, and my life is near its end. My faculties are dull and my memory is failing. Therefore, I am unable to recite the *Sūtra of the Four Persons* before the community of monks. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, there are four kinds of persons who appear in the world for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. What are these

Even for one who accepts the self as eternal, there is no logical justification for the conceit [of suffering] produced by the relation of cause and effect. For the self does not deviate from its single nature throughout the sequence of before and after. Consequently, since transformations such as fear and shame are impossible for it, how could there be fear arising from fear? If it is argued that fear arises in it, and that it becomes afraid through connection with that [fear], [we reply: its own nature is not characterized by fear, so there is no actual affliction for it; it is merely a matter of the relation of cause and effect. Such a relation is simply the basis for conventional usage. And affliction does not become an affliction merely through conventional usage. If it is argued: "Even though [the pain] is distinct from the son's pain, he is indeed afflicted because of the connection [between them]," we say: No. He is afflicted because there is another, internal pain belonging to himself. Otherwise, he would also be afflicted by an enemy's pain, for even in that case, there certainly exists a connection characterized by the relationship between the victim and the victimizer.

[594,xvii] Even if a son were an enemy, there would be no harm caused by the suffering inflicted upon him. Therefore, suffering exists in the form of being afflicted oneself, and not from the act of afflicting another. (PVA) 430.
Therefore, since it is merely momentary, it does not differ from a continuum;
thus, this entire conventional usage regarding a "self" is of that same nature.

For it is merely by way of a continuum that the conventional usage "this is that very same thing" occurs in its entirety. Therefore, sound is not eternal; how then could there be its manifestation immediately following effort? Rather, its production alone is the object of valid cognition, because it possesses the characteristics of being produced.
Due to the difference in the cognition [of it], the status of being an effect belongs to the sound, not to the manifesting noise (*dhvani*).
Objects such as jars are not differentiated by the differences in their illuminators, such as lamps.

Indeed, the manifested object is not differentiated by the smallness or greatness of the manifestor. Yet, it is observed that a blue lotus manifested by a lamp appears red; one manifested by moonlight appears yellow or white; and a face manifested by a sword, though fair, appears dark, and so forth.
That too is incorrect, because:
If entities possess a nature other than that of their manifestor, then because it produces that other nature, the manifestor would be a producer (kāraka). (433) (PVA) [595, vi]

For by means of a manifestor that causes the loss of its true form, a nature contrary to its own essence must be revealed. But how can that which is non-existent as its [the object's] form be revealed? Otherwise, even things such as a hare’s horn would be revealed. If it is argued that even that is indeed revealed through a distorted manifestation (*viparītākhyāti*), the answer to this has already been given.
Now, if it is argued that this is an error and therefore this fault does not apply—
That is incorrect, because:
If that which causes error is the manifestor, how can it be a manifestor?
For only by making something manifest can one clearly be a manifestor.
Otherwise, even things such as cataracts would possess the nature of a manifestor.
For even for them, there is no further refutation because [the sound] causes an illusion.

(435) Now, if even in the case of an illusion another form of that [sound] is apprehended, then by that [reasoning], it is held by the wise that effort and so forth are the manifestors of this sound. (436)

<4. Refutation of the Sphoṭa> [595,xiv] Even if there is indeed a distinction in the word (*śabda*) due to its conjunction with sounds (*dhvani*), such as smallness, greatness, and so forth, this is produced solely by error and not in reality. Even in the case of error, another reality of the word does indeed manifest, namely that which consists of the *sphoṭa*. To this, too, it is replied:
[595,xv] If a form distinct from the erroneous form exists for the word, it would appear as something different; otherwise, there is no understanding of its being erroneous. (PVA 437)
For that which appears as non-different from what is different cannot be understood as "different"; otherwise, it would simply be non-different.
(438) Even in the case of error, if error itself were [itself] erroneous, then error would utterly vanish.
When there is the cognition of error or non-error, it is recognized as "this is an error.

For it is not logical that there should be no manifestation of the true nature of sound as distinct from the form appearing in error, provided that such a true nature exists. If it is argued that "the distinction does not appear because of error," then since the distinction would also be another true nature of sound distinct from the erroneous form, one would have to posit yet another error for its manifestation as distinct, and then another distinction of that form; thus, due to this infinite regress, there would be no comprehension at all of the true nature of sound. Furthermore, even in the case of error, it is not that the true nature of sound alone remains while the error does not exist; rather, if that [true nature] were what manifested, then what we call "error" would not exist at all.
Therefore, when there is the manifestation of reality, no such thing as error exists; for it is established that error is defined as the total abandonment of all objects of cognition. (PVA 440)

[596,iii] But surely, there exists a causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) characterized by the comprehension of an object produced by the mere sound; however, there is no difference in the cognition of the object caused by [features such as] magnitude and so forth. Therefore, because it performs causal efficacy, the *sphoṭa* alone is real, while the other is unreal, due to the opposite being the case.
That too is untrue; for:
The capacity of a word to produce an object is not held to be its causal efficacy toward that object.
However, from the cultivation of convention (*saṃketa*), there arises the manifestation of that object.
The knower of words is considered the cause of the awakening of the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*);
though it is a producer [of the cognition] through a traditional succession, it is not held to be a differentiator.
The difference [in the effect] arises from the difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), not from the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*).
Even in that case, because it is an auxiliary cause, sound is not considered to be the differentiator.

The cognition of an object arises solely from the convergence of similar latencies (*sabhāgavāsanā*); it emerges in the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) bearing the aspect of that object. Sound, however, is merely an auxiliary factor therein. Since it produces [the cognition] indirectly by way of awakening the latencies, it lacks the capacity to differentiate [the object]. But for sound, there is a direct causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), namely the production of a cognition of it; and this [cognition] is indeed differentiated according to whether [the sound] is distant or near, through its being clear or indistinct, and through its being accompanied by agitation or lack of agitation.

How then could difference not be that which performs a causal function for its own sake? Thus, difference is indeed a real entity (*vastu*), not a mere illusion. Furthermore, if sound were eternal, cognition would not necessarily arise immediately following effort. Why does it not convey its meaning even prior [to being uttered]? If you argue that it does not convey it because it lacks the capacity to convey it when it has not been heard—[596,x]

[Objection: But surely, that which was heard at the time of the convention persists even now; therefore, there should be cognition [of it immediately]. There should not be a lack of cognition prior to the subsequent effort. If you say, "No, because of the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) at that time," [we reply: for a manifestor produces a manifestation that is simultaneous [with itself]. This is incorrect, because:
Just as that which manifests something simultaneous would be a manifester, so too would the manifester of the manifested be a manifester by means of its entire self. 444 (PVA)
If it were to persist for a period of time and be manifested by that [cause],
then how could there be a requirement for a manifestor of it at another time?

Indeed, that which does not manifest an object in its non-erroneous form cannot be a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). Furthermore, when an object whose nature persists through time is manifested, nothing at all is produced by the manifestor at a later time. If there were a dependence on a manifestor for what is already unmanifested, then there would have to be another manifestor for that, and yet another for that, such that manifestation itself would never occur; thus, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would be unavoidable. As for the argument that there is no perception prior to the subsequent cognition, that too is incorrect. For it is illogical that a thing existing prior to an effort should necessarily lack cognition regarding its nature immediately after that effort. Indeed, it is not tenable that the very same nature which was previously perceived should be unperceived while that same object is being perceived. Moreover, the preceding effort would be entirely useless for that [nature], because the object would already be manifested in its entirety by something else. If you argue that the manifestor manifests only the nature associated with its own time, is this not simply the exclusion of one thing by another? If the cognitions of the earlier and later moments are one and the same, then even a difference in effort cannot produce a distinction. If they are many, then the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) must also differ from the time of the cognition.
[596,xvii] Furthermore, when there is an absence of obstruction, perception occurs; for even that which exists may not be perceived due to being screened by an obstruction.
[596,xviii]
Even though a mat exists, it is not seen when separated by a wall;
yet, when that [obstruction] is removed by another, it becomes an object of perception once again.
This is established through direct perception and determined by valid cognition.

Even in the case of sound, the absence of an obscuration is brought about by effort. (PVA 447) Even when [the cause] exists, there is non-perception due to the presence of an obscuration; conversely, there is perception when that [obscuration] is absent. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the failure of perception is caused by the presence of an obscuration. It is not the case, however, that the sound itself ceases to exist or undergoes some other transformation when there is an obscuration, because it is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to remain in its very same state.
[597,ii] This is the statement of another who has not reflected upon what precedes and what follows; for:
In that case as well, cognition occurs precisely through the arising of recognition by means of unaltered [mental states].
But if there is no perception, how can there be cognition through direct perception?
For it is the cessation of perception that establishes the absence of that form.
"The apprehension of another [moment] is not regarded here as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
(449) If the proof for that [continuity] were based on recognition even in the interim, then recognition would be an inference and not preceded by perception. (450) (PVA)
For if it were not preceded by perception, there would be a blind tradition;
for that inference as well, such a thing is unestablished.

For when something is not perceived because it is obstructed by a veil, there is no perception of it as unaltered through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) at that very time. If it is argued that there is perception later on when it is free from the veil, then its existence at that [earlier] time must either be its non-alteration, or the intermediate state is cognized as being beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). And thus, there is inference (*anumāna*), because: "It is unaltered now; therefore, it was so before. Since this conforms to the definition of inference, [one might object]: "In that case, since there is an absence of direct perception, how can that inference be preceded by direct perception? In all cases, the relation between prior and posterior is established solely by the means of valid cognition that is recognition. If it were preceded by inference, then that inference would also have to come from another inference, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and a "succession of the blind. If it is argued that another person perceives it directly and thus it is "preceded by direct perception," there too there is no direct perception; for one person does not have the cognition "this was perceived directly by another" simply because another has perceived it. If it is argued that the other person will say, "No, [I did perceive it]," that is not so, because speech lacks intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya*). Furthermore, another person is not even capable of establishing his own truthfulness, such that he could say, "What was perceived by him is exactly what was perceived by me. For what is being perceived cannot be perceived as mixed with another's perception in the form "this is that very same thing. Consequently, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), since the identity is established only through their mutual statements.

[597, viii] Now, if it is argued that there is cognition through inference because one observes a transformation of the earth, and that by means of this [inference] that very same thing is apprehended—then in that case, only its being of such a nature is established, not its identity; thus, this is not logical.

Inference does not indeed have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; for it is not the case that by means of smoke, that very same fire is established. If [you argue that] there is oneness between pleasure and so forth and the self due to a common conventional usage based on the occurrence of horripilation and the like, why [is this not the case]? If [it is argued that] there is no oneness because pleasure and so forth are perceived as mutually excluded, then, given that even those two being perceived are perceived unmixed with each other by themselves and others, their difference alone is logical. Even their occupying the same location is indeed perceived through the absence of a perception [of them as distinct]. For location is nothing other than the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity itself. Therefore, the claim that "there is perception [of things] despite the existence of an obstruction" is not established.

< (5) The commencement of the treatise for the sake of subtle investigation—> [597,x] Now, there is indeed a cognition: "That very thing which has been apprehended by another has been apprehended by me. Nor is there any sublation [of this]. Nor should a sublation be brought forward here through subtle investigation; for:
For whoever, out of delusion, might imagine a subverting factor even where none exists, that person, being characterized by doubt in all worldly transactions, shall come to ruin. (452) (PVA)
For nothing at all deserves to be established when it is being scrutinized with subtle analysis.
That is incorrect; for,
by negating subtle atoms, there is a negation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For those who possess subtle discernment (*sūkṣmekṣika*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than this is accepted.

(PVA 598, i) If it were held that subtle discernment—which contradicts worldly convention—should not be introduced, then one would have to act independently of the means of valid cognition; and in that case, the undertaking of a treatise (*śāstra*) would be useless. For the function of a treatise is not for the sake of promoting the conventions of those with coarse intellects. This is because it is universally admitted that "a treatise is that which turns back delusion."
If there is an obstacle to its being determined, it cannot be warded off;
for a thunderbolt falling upon one's head is not turned back by a mere leaf. (PVA 454)
Furthermore, worldly convention (*saṃsāravyavahāra*) should not be abolished by a wise person;
for what harm is there in conventional practice being conducted according to how it is observed?

The conventional practice consisting of the relationship between cause and effect continues uninterrupted for those engaged in worldly activity solely through a blind tradition. For this very reason, its cessation through the analysis of phenomena is the goal of those intent upon the path to *nirvāṇa*.
Indeed, cyclic existence is not perceived as something ultimate, because it is merely conventional.

And when one thus abides in reality alone, which is indeed Nirvāṇa, there is no distinction between reality and unreality; this is the ultimate truth. One should consider that what is called "unreality" is simply reality itself when left unexamined. (PVA 456–457)

Indeed, when reality (*tattva*) is investigated, everything becomes non-dual; however, through the investigation of what is not that, that very same [reality] takes the form of the manifold world (*prapañca*), which is unreality (*atattva*)—namely, *saṃsāra*. Therefore, it follows as a desired consequence that the cessation of *saṃsāra* occurs precisely through such investigation. For how could worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) not be sublated so long as there is the vision of the reality of one's conduct? Thus, what has occurred is exactly what was intended; this indeed is the conventional practice of learned people. In that regard, for the sake of gradually removing ignorance, the impermanence of that in which the world is deluded is first established. Therefore, whenever anything is perceived, it is because it is grasped as being delimited by preceding and succeeding moments. One must understand that "in whatever way something is perceived, it is exactly so"; otherwise, there would be no stability whatsoever in the determination of objects.

[598, viii] Here, an opponent says: Even if the preceding and succeeding forms, being non-present at the time of perceiving the middle, are not apprehended by direct perception because they have reached the condition of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*), nevertheless, their non-existence does not follow from mere non-apprehension. At another time, they do reach the condition of apprehension, and at that time, they are indeed apprehended. For instance:
Wherever something possesses the conditions for perception, it is perceived there;
for a jar that is such [as to be perceptible] in one place is not perceived elsewhere.
Likewise:
when there is the state of being perceivable, then there is the perception of that.
Its suchness does not exist at other times, nor is it perceived at other times;
for that too is not subject to observation.
If that form were a single entity, how could its being real or unreal occur? But if it were manifold, then it would be perceived later; thus, [the opponent's position] is untenable. (PVA 460)

[598,xiv] There is no other entity called "time" by virtue of whose absence there would be a non-perception of form situated therein when that form is absent. Rather, that very same form, being perceived through its prior and posterior states, receives the designation "time. For instance, one says, "This time is occurring for us," yet the state of being afflicted by cold is not something other than the "cold season.
If that entity were one, then time would also be one;
because of the absence of such time, there would consequently be no non-perception of it.

While that [time] exists, the non-existence of time is not established. Or, if it were something else, since time itself is eternal, it would indeed be perceived even previously in its form as prior, posterior, and so forth. If, on the other hand, moments, instants (*lava*), and so on are parts of time, then it follows that time is merely momentary. If it is argued that the universal called "timeness" (*kālatva*) is eternal, we say no; for time is a substantial entity (*dravya-padārtha*), and thus even then, because the state of being prior and posterior is perceived, there would be perception at all times. If it is argued that there is no perception because the parts of time are not perceived, this too is incorrect. Why? [599,ii]
Since there is no perception of anything else, how can there be non-perception of that which has been seen?
How could oneness with that which is unperceived be understood by anyone?
By this, the conditioning by means of past co-occurring entities has been refuted.

Furthermore, it is not logical for "temporality" (*kālatva*) to be manifested by preceding and succeeding moments. Therefore, if a sound is perceived immediately after an effort, it would also have to be perceived in its previously established form; and if it were perceived by a subsequent [effort] as well, this would be an absolute certainty. Consequently, since that previous and subsequent form would be perceived at that very same time, there would be no other nature [to it], and thus it must be momentary. Moreover, because that moment of a jar or similar object is perceived in its entirety, an obscuration is illogical, as it would be ineffective. Now, if the effort assists the sense organ, even then, since the perception occurs in its entirety, the perception of the previous form [would occur simultaneously]; thus, the assistance to the sense organ does not produce the perception of a restricted form. Therefore, the claim that it is necessarily perceived only in its subsequent form is untenable. Yet, it is observed to be perceived only immediately [after the effort]. Thus, its duration is merely that much, and there is no assistance to the sense organ in the case of a permanent entity. For instance:
[599,v] Even from the perspective of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is because that very thing is perceived as being thus;
for one who has no impression regarding something, there is no perception of it therein. (PVA 463)
That which does not exist cannot be apprehended as permanent; since existence is nothing but apprehension, there is no permanence distinct from apprehension. (PVA 464) [599,vii]
Indeed, permanence cannot be apprehended as anything else.

[599, viii] Now, even if it is not apprehended, how can there be an absence of impermanence? Non-apprehension itself is the mark of the non-existence of that which possesses the conditions for being apprehended. And its nature is not such that it lacks the conditions for being apprehended.

For this very reason, existence is nothing other than perception; in the absence of that, how could there be existence? Thus, permanence is impossible. However, in the view that [the word] is assisted by sounds, that itself constitutes impermanence. For this very reason:

Since it is impossible for that which is independent [of causes] to produce an effect at a specific time, such knowledge—which has an occasional result—is established as its logical mark (liṅga). || 198 ||

[599,xi] If that sound or whatever else were to persist through another time, it would be perceived in exactly that same way at all times; there could not be an occasional perception as its effect. For it does not possess an occasional nature, nor can it be perceived otherwise than in its own form. Now, if this [occasional perception] is an error, then indeed one who perceives only what is near is not capable of perceiving a pervasive form. And even when there is such incapacity, the object of apprehension does not become something else; moreover, even an error is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its non-contradiction (*avisamvāda*). [599,xii]

[Objection: Surely, error is sublated by a non-erroneous perception; at that time, it can be determined to be an error. [Response: No, because it is set aside by the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which establishes a nature that pervades both time and space.
This [objection] is incorrect.
The capacity of recognition has already been rejected in this context;
it has been established that its sublation occurs by means of perception itself. (PVA 465)

[599,xv] Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not a valid means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Direct perception is that which grasps an object whose form is non-pervasive (*avyāpin*), because it arises from the operation of the sense faculties and because it possesses non-deceptiveness (*avisamvāda*). Therefore, it has already been established that recognition is sublated by direct perception itself. Furthermore:
If there were apprehension by parts even when there is pervasion of the object,
then every object would be one and the same, since its apprehension occurs part by part.

If it is possible that even a single entity, by being related to various forms, times, and places, is perceived otherwise [than it truly is], then the entire object would be one, because everything is recognized as "an object, an object. If it is argued that if there were unity, distinctions such as those between a jar and other things would not exist, then it follows equally that for sound as well, distinctions such as smallness and greatness, or the distinction between acute (*udātta*) and other accents, would not exist. If it is claimed that despite the difference in acute accents and so forth, sound is treated as a single entity because of the conventional usage "this is sound," then why is there not the same conventional usage "this is an object, an object" despite the difference between jars and other things? If it is argued that both unity and plurality may coexist, then it follows that unity itself must be unreal. For instance:

When oneness is apprehended through the power of recognition, both oneness and multiplicity would result; however, that [recognition] has been rendered invalid as a means of valid cognition. (PVA 467)
For when recognition is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then oneness— which is established by recognition— is unreal; thus, difference alone remains as the reality.
Therefore, there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere that apprehends a non-different thing as having a differentiated form;

however, when an entity is indeed differentiated, the establishment of its non-difference arises only from conceptual construction (*vikalpaka*), and thus that [conceptualization] is not a valid means of cognition.

For if difference were non-existent, then that non-difference would be merely constructed by the imagination, established solely through the means of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*). But if difference is unreal, of what would this non-difference be the property? Nor can there be any practical activity (*vyavahāra*) based on mere non-difference alone. Therefore, there must be a substratum (*dharmin*) characterized by difference, of which non-difference is the attribute (*dharma*). For if the substratum is unreal, its non-difference cannot be real either. Indeed, when a rabbit’s horn is unreal, its sharpness is not real. [Objection: But if difference is also absent, of what could it be perceived, given that the substratum of non-difference does not exist? That very relation by which there is a connection with another is called "exclusion" (*bheda*). Otherwise, if there were a connection with something else, exclusion itself would dissolve. (PVA 469)
Non-difference, however, occurs through the negation of difference, because it has the nature of a property (*dharma*), like a universal property (*sāmānyadharma*). Therefore:
Since it is impossible for that which is independent of anything else to produce an effect at one time and not at another,
such knowledge— which has occasional results— is established as its logical mark (*liṅga*).

If there were no other nature of the entity (*padārtha*) that is non-interrupted in its own-being at all times, then cognition would likewise always be its effect. That occasional non-production of the effect, which consists in its interruption, would not exist. For when that very nature is being apprehended, it cannot be an apprehension dependent on another; otherwise, there would follow the consequence that even that [other-dependent nature] would not be apprehended. Therefore, such a cognition is of an interrupted form; it is established that this interrupted form is the result of that very [entity] which is occasional. From that effect, the perception of impermanence follows. [The Result of Indicating the Effect-Reason and the Essential-Nature Reason] (6) [600,xii]

[Objection: Is it not improper to state that two reasons have been specified by means of two examples for the sake of establishing both essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*)? For this very reason—that "being immediately subsequent to an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*)—can be shown to be both an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and an essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Indeed, among proponents of this view, there is a single consensus here that this is an essential-nature reason. Furthermore, it has just now been established that cognition is the mark (*liṅga*) of an effect-reason. Therefore, since both are indicated by a single system (*tantra*), the separate mention of "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is redundant. [Reply: This is true; nevertheless...

By this very [method], even though it is well-established, the separate treatment of the essential nature (svabhāva) together with the effect is intended so that one should not think that everything is of such a kind. (199)

[601,i] For when it is mentioned together with its effect, such is the nature of every essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) due to its association with that [effect]. There might be the suspicion that even an essential reason could exist as one that subsists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*); therefore, in order to exclude that, there is another type of essential reason which pervades the entire similar instances. This is why "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is mentioned separately.
Now, in this regard: that which exists in the similar class, and is absent in both ways from its absence;
"A reason that is contrary to this is the contradictory (*viruddha*); another is the uncertain (*aniścita*).
For what purpose is this separate statement? To this it is replied:
The statement of the reason is made for the sake of comprehension, even though the meaning has already been established through inference.
This is merely to explain the classification; the defining characteristic, however, does not differ.

[601,vii] For by stating them separately, that very point becomes clear. In this regard, that which exists in the similar class (*sajātīya*) and is of two kinds [in the dissimilar class]. For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced and because it follows immediately upon effort. Otherwise, if the two were not demonstrated, only the definition "and of two kinds" would be possible; whereas the definition "it exists only in the similar class" would be impossible as a definition due to the absence of any illustrative instance (*udāharaṇa*).
[601,viii]
Now, it might be argued that there is no need for concern that all cases would be subsumed simply by its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

This is true; nevertheless, this detailed exposition of examples is for the sake of providing a clear understanding of that very definition of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). Indeed, that which constitutes the definition in inference for oneself is precisely what is intended here.

[601,x] But then, would it not follow that three things must be shown: the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) of that kind, and the pervasion of the similar class (*sapakṣavyāpin*)? And in that case, the demonstration would become impossible.
This is not a valid objection; for:
"Therefore, by means of that effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*) itself, which resides in a single part, [is established]."
It has been explained. [601,xiv]
Therefore, an illustrative example that corresponds [to the definition] must be provided with effort for the sake of clarifying its origin. 201.
