Since the detailed classification is intended for the sake of thorough understanding, it is by this very same effect-reason (*kāryaliṅga*) that the Master has demonstrated that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) also possesses a partial aspect. For this very reason, the example is similar. Otherwise, why would he not have cited "there is fire here because of smoke" as a perfectly clear example of an effect-reason? Why instead provide the example of "arising immediately after effort" as an effect-reason to be established with such exertion? Therefore, a similar example was stated for the arising of a manifestation from effort, which is characterized as both an effect and an essential nature. For cognition also occurs immediately after effort; thus, since it is also an essential nature, the example is similar.
[601,xvi] But surely, it is the very nature [of the sound] that follows immediately after effort, and not another nature, because cognition has no object that lacks a cause.
[601,xvii]

This is not correct, because it was stated from the perspective of the opponent. For those who maintain the eternity of sound (*śabda*) maintain that cognition itself arises immediately after effort; it is with reference to them that this is said: the object also possesses the status of being a cause, since that which is not a cause cannot be an object. Therefore, that cognition which you desire to arise immediately after effort must be produced by the sound as well, through the imparting of its own form (*ākāra*). Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the entirety of the sound's form as it exists in both preceding and succeeding moments, because it is impossible to perceive it otherwise. It has already been established that perception does not occur in fragments.

<3. Connection with Memory> [602,i] Furthermore, it might be argued that the nature of the object as both future and past, pervading the entire collection of temporal divisions, is indeed apprehended; otherwise, how could there be recollection upon later perception, such as: "This is that very thing which was seen by me at that time"? For instance:
"This was seen even then" does not function [as a cognition] with respect to what has not been grasped;
for it is by means of memory that the fact of having been previously experienced is established. (472) (PVA)
That too is indeed a faulty objection, because:
Perception does not know, "I shall exist" or "it is being perceived";
however, memory knows this; this is truly most wonderful.
(PVA 602,v)

For where there is no operation of perception—which has the nature of grasping—there the operation belongs only to the recollection that follows it; this is indeed a great skill in discerning the true nature of things. Indeed, a future form cannot be grasped because of doubt; it might perhaps not even come to be. Now, if the thought is: "If it will exist, it has already been grasped by me," and one thinks, "I shall later make it the object of my recollection as something grasped," then how can that too be said to have been grasped?
For even if an object were grasped, how could one act toward it in this regard?

If that which is both doubted and apprehended were mutually contradictory, then if it were to exist, it would necessarily be apprehended; thus, the operation of apprehension would be immense. For a cognition that exists must be either of the nature of apprehension or otherwise; there is no other possibility, because they are mutually exclusive by virtue of being defined as the exclusion of one another.

If there were apprehension [of the future], then, just as in the case of the present, there would be no doubt, because of its non-difference [from the present]. And at that time, the object being apprehended would be just like the present, because it is not different from the nature of the future and the present. If it is argued that it is "future" due to its connection with a future time, then the states of being present and so forth do not belong to things by way of their own nature; rather, they are merely the coexistence with objects that are future, present, or past, since there is no other time. Or, if such a time exists, it too would be a functional entity (*padārtha*) acting as a cooperative cause. This being the case, when its future form is apprehended, the future nature itself is apprehended, and thus there would be no doubt. If it is argued that "being future" or "having been" consists in being accompanied by impermanent entities, we say no. For it is impossible to apprehend something in such a state; how then could there be the recollection, "This very thing was apprehended by me"? Nor is it correct to say that the nature [of the object] was indeed apprehended even if the accompaniment was not apprehended. Indeed, it is your own view that the nature [of an object] is neither "past" nor "future. Therefore, since it is apprehended by a cognition of the present, let it be apprehended as simply present.
Just as there is a cognition of blueness through a cognition appearing as blue,
so too there is a cognition of presentness even when there is an appearance of the present. (PVA 476)
[602,xi] Now, if it has not been grasped, how can there be recollection? But surely this same consequence applies even to that which has been grasped. For instance:
When [an object] is being perceived, there is no memory, for that [memory] occurs immediately after the perception.
Since the perception has passed away and its form no longer exists, that is not memory.
[Objection: Now, since memory has arisen, how does it know of its own prior state?
How can that which is non-existent and formless possess the form [of an object] for memory?
(478) It is an extreme audacity to claim that memory, though not possessing that form, knows it.
Even if the self were ignorant [at that time], it would nonetheless have known its own prior state. (479)
For its capacity for apprehension is also applicable to recollection;
thus, both apprehension and recollection are distinct from the self at the outset.
Perception and recollection do not exist in that manner for it (the self), because it does not have that nature.

[603,i] If there were no distinction between perception and recollection, then for that which lacks such a nature, there could be no status as perceiver or rememberer, since this would entail the same for the body as well. If it is argued that this is not the case because of its impermanence, then it would follow for space and so forth as well. If it is thought that these two [perception and recollection] do not inhere in those [space, etc. because they lack inherence there—[then the same applies to the self].
That too is equivalent to non-existence, because:
Through investigation, there would be a connection with grasping and memory even for space and so forth; the same objection applies there as well.

"Since recollection would otherwise be inexplicable, a rememberer is postulated; for this is not logical without someone existing at both the prior and subsequent times. And if that is so, let this [recollection] belong to space and the like themselves—what is the point of the effort to postulate a separate entity? In the same way, inherence (*samavāya*) should also be subjected to such an objection. Alternatively, the permanence of recollection and the rest should be accepted. If it is argued that this [permanence] resides in the self, then the very same [conclusion] follows.
And having remembered, how could it be known where there is non-apprehension and doubt?
Since recollection does not exist at that time, how can there be an understanding of its prior existence?

Therefore, the claim that this is not established by perception is trivial. Consequently, in the case of an eternal entity, it is impossible for there to be a perception following effort through the mediation of prior recollection. Thus, it is established that sound is impermanent because its form is perceived as neither previously nor subsequently existing.

As for what was stated—that cognition as a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not follow immediately after effort—that can be refuted otherwise: even if it is indeed immediately following its own intrinsic nature, it is nonetheless possible for it to also follow immediately after effort. For in this case, overly subtle scrutiny is not purposeful. Therefore, by this very example, both members of the pair—the two types of logical marks consisting of the effect (*kārya*) and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—are demonstrated.

Now, why have only the examples of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the intrinsic-nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) been presented separately, and not other varieties as well? To this, the resolution is as follows:

That whose existence is inseparable from effort, or that which is one's own self and non-distinct [from it], would be non-deviant from that [cause]; therefore, there is a distinction between these two meanings. (202)

That whose existence follows immediately upon another is itself the cause of that other, because of the absence of deviation; for nothing distinct from it can be non-deviant unless it possesses the nature of an effect.

But is it not the case that a reason is a reason precisely because of its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and not because it is an effect? For even ash is an effect of fire, yet it does not have non-deviation [from fire]. Likewise, water, by being a conjoined thing, indicates its container even without being its effect.
[603, xiii]

This is incorrect because it is not said that [the mark] is an indicator solely by virtue of being an effect; rather, it is an indicator precisely as an effect. A distinct thing does not indicate [its cause] except through its state as an effect. For example, ash, which is the effect of fire, indicates exactly that kind of fire—even if it has passed away or is located in another place. Therefore, the status of being an indicator is conditioned by the state of being an effect, by which it is distinguished from other particulars. Indeed, even in this case, the relationship between cause and effect is of this very nature. If, however, [the indicator were defined merely by] the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), then the substratum (*ādhāra*) would also be an indicator of the superstratum (*ādheya*). If it is argued that the substratum exists even without the superstratum and therefore is not an indicator, whereas the superstratum—such as water—does not exist without its substratum and is therefore an indicator, then it follows that only the effect is the indicator. For that without which something does not come into being is the effect of that thing. Now, the existence of the superstratum does not occur without the substratum; thus, it is an effect. But it is not the existence itself that is the effect, nor is it the water. In that case, it is the existence alone that is the indicator, not the water; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

[604,i] Now, if it is argued that it is the water itself as qualified by its stability that causes the inference, why not say that it is the stability itself as qualified by the water that causes the inference? This latter view alone is logical, because it is that [stability] alone which possesses the capacity to cause inference through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and there is no other water apart from the stability.

Now, one might object: "Even this falling water is indeed water; that water is not something other than water, for it is simply water. Furthermore, it has been established that there is no such thing as a universal 'water-ness' (jalatva). Or, even if such a universal existed, it would not be the indicator [of the cause]. It is the individual instance alone that is the indicator, and since that instance is an effect, nothing other than the effect can possess the status of an indicator.

Now, if it is held that there is only one single individual (*vyakti*), that too is incorrect; for it would entail the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that "that very thing remains" and "that very thing becomes otherwise. If it is argued that there is no fault even if it exists in such a way through successive stages (*paryāyeṇa*), then, since there is no cognition of identity between the prior and the subsequent states, how can there be a single individual? Indeed, a cognition does not establish identity with another when it is not being cognized along with it; it is not a case of both cognition and non-cognition [simultaneously]. For it is impossible to establish the existence of a thing through non-cognition. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has already been refuted. Therefore, in all cases, when examined, the fact of being an effect (*kāryatā*) alone is the basis for being a means of proof (*gamakatve nibandhana*).

By that very form in which water, ashes, and other such things possess the property of being produced, they also possess the capacity to signify [their cause]; thus, since this is established, there is no comprehension [of the cause] from anything else. (PVA 483)

Or rather, that which is the very nature (*ātman*) of something is its differentiator. Whatever is the nature of a thing is the indicator (*gamaka*) of that thing; for example, the *śiṃśapā* tree, being the very nature of a tree, is the indicator of "treeness."

[Objection: Is it not the case that just as the *śiṃśapā* has the tree as its essence, so too the tree has the *śiṃśapā* as its very essence? For a tree exists even apart from the *śiṃśapā*, such as the *palāśa* and other species; but the *śiṃśapā* does not exist thus [apart from the tree]. Therefore, it is the *śiṃśapā* alone, as that which possesses inseparability, which serves as the indicator (*gamaka*). Identity (*tādātmya*) would be the sole basis for the capacity to indicate [the probandum] in the case of identity-reasoning.

For its lack of a cause cannot be established through positive and negative concomitance.
This is incorrect.
It has already been stated that identity (tādātmya) does not exist anywhere without causal origination (tadutpatti).
Because they possess the quality of being indicative and non-deviant, they are based upon that [essential nature].

If it is asked, "How can there be an indicator in the absence of restriction? [the answer is: because the basis for being an indicator exists precisely through non-restriction. For it is thus: if something follows upon another, that basis is possible; otherwise, the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that anything could be anything. If it is argued that the same applies to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), that is not so, because: [605,x] [The verse continues: "Conjunction is not a cause, nor is it an effect; therefore, it is not an indicator. (PV 1.34) Conjunction is not a cause, because it does not exist prior to its effect. Nor is it an effect, because it does not exist after its cause. Therefore, since it is neither a cause nor an effect, it cannot be an indicator. Furthermore, conjunction is not an indicator because it is not restricted to a single object. If it were restricted, it would be a cause or an effect. Since it is not restricted, it is not an indicator. If it is argued that even though it is not restricted, it is still an indicator because it is perceived together with the object, that is not so, because that perception is itself dependent on other causes. Thus, conjunction is not an indicator. The same logic applies to inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, the capacity to indicate is established solely through non-restriction. This is the meaning. [605,xii] That which is conjoined (*saṃyogin*) is not the locus (*ādhāra*) for that which is contained (*ādheya*), because conjunction is symmetrical. That which is inherent (*samavāyin*)—namely, the categories of universal (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*)—is likewise not the locus for that which is contained. This is because the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), known as the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), is impossible here. Similarly, even when a universal is perceived in isolation, it does not lead to the cognition of its possessor (*jātimat*) once the individual instance (*vyakti*) has perished; this is precisely because the causal relationship is impossible.

Now, one might think that the effect makes known the substratum because the relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is possible therein. If that were so, then it is simply the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) that is the indicator. If you say, "It is indeed inseparable connection," that too is incorrect. For inseparable connection is nothing other than the relation of cause and effect. Therefore, he says:
"But when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), that alone is the means of comprehension. [605,xiv]
For invariable concomitance is indeed a necessary restriction; that which is non-restricted is not a means of proof. (204)

[605,xv] Furthermore, it has been established that this restriction consists precisely in the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between one thing and another, because otherwise there would be no capacity for logical proof (*gamakatva*). It has also been explained that two reasons and two counter-reasons were specified for the sake of establishing essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*).
<(1) Explanation of the statement "From dispute, there is difference and generality":>

[605,xvi] Now he explains that "particularity (*bheda*) is the universal (*sāmānya*) because of dispute": particularity is the uncommon [reason], which is exclusively negative (*ekāntavyatirekin*); the universal is exclusively positive (*ekāntānvayin*). The opponent asserts that even these two, though non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum]. To that, the Teacher demonstrates the true state of affairs with the words beginning, "In that case, that which is present... [and so forth], thereby showing their lack of indicative power. [605,xvii]

Is it not the case that, apart from being exclusive (*aikāntika*), it is only logical that [the reason] lacks probative force? True; however, this would be so if exclusion (*vyatireka*) were established from one extreme alone, but that is not established, because there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself.
To explain: exclusivity is said to be the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the exclusion.
And that [inference] does not apply to things that are unconnected; for that very reason, the establishment of positive concomitance (anvaya) occurs. // 205 //

[606,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from their suffering. Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "If there be any sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should perceive that all five aggregates are empty in nature and thereby deliver themselves from all suffering and distress. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "How should a son of good family or a daughter of good family perceive that the five aggregates are empty in nature? The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara replied to the venerable Śāriputra: "Form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: these are all empty. Then, at that time, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: "Excellent, excellent! O Noble One, it is as you have said. Because all dharmas are empty in nature, there is no birth and no death; because all dharmas are empty in nature, there is no defilement and no purity; because all dharmas are empty in nature, there is no decrease and no increase. Therefore, O Noble One, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives that the five aggregates are empty in nature, he transcends all views of perverted existence, he overcomes birth and death, and he attains the ultimate Nirvāṇa. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha: "O World-Honored One, how should one understand the meaning of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s name? The Buddha told the venerable Śāriputra: "If there be any sons of good family or daughters of good family who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and, with single-minded devotion, call upon his name, then all difficulties shall be immediately dispelled. For this reason, Śāriputra, one should know the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had taught, were filled with joy and received it with faith. Thus ends the second chapter, "The Practice of Avalokiteśvara," in the *Bhadrapāla-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in twenty-five thousand lines. How can breath and the like be established as being excluded from that which is selfless? This would be possible only if there were an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) with the state of possessing a self. And that [concomitance] is not possible among things that lack a necessary connection, because it is impossible to apprehend the exclusion from all heterogeneous instances (vipakṣa) by means of its own positive form. Indeed, there is no perception of every single heterogeneous instance by which one could cognize, "It is not here; it is not there. However, it is possible by way of positive concomitance (anvaya). For, the apprehension of necessity is the apprehension of the necessary connection (pratibandha), and that is the operation of the means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa). Therefore, through the apprehension of necessity, the exclusion of others is implied; otherwise, there would be no apprehension of a necessary form at all. Even when another exists, that thing does not exist; and when that exists, it is indeed absent.
Even when others are absent, it is absent; therefore, there is no understanding of its being an effect thereof. (PVA 493)

For when, even in the presence of another thing, the existence of the sandalwood scent is absent, yet its existence occurs when that [sandalwood] is present, then it is established that the sandalwood scent is its effect; otherwise, it is not. This is the determination. And since that [determination] does not exist without negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), negative concomitance also is established as being of the same nature as that [effect].
But surely, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as a pervasive relation is not established, because it does not mean that "from this [cause], its arising occurs everywhere. This is not so;
for the understanding of that [concomitance] is achieved by the mere fact that "its arising is from this alone."

And that non-arising from another is understood at that very moment. For it is not the case that "it occurs only from this and not elsewhere" that constitutes the basis for its being a prover; rather, it is the fact that "it arises from this alone and not from another. And such a cognition certainly exists. For those who perceive its prior non-arising from another, there is an immediate realization of its absence when that other is absent.

[606, viii] Now, even if it were the case that this [entity] does not arise from anything else due to some specific difference, it would still follow that it is not necessarily so; for it is not the case that everything is identical simply because it is "other. Therefore, the negative concomitance—that its absence follows upon the absence of the other—is not certain, since even something invisible might still be possible.
This is incorrect, because:
[606,x] This reason would belong to you alone; this favor would be yours alone.
If you have no desire even for your own favor, alas, then you are in every way exactly as described;
thus, this reason is a prover of your very nature because it cannot exist otherwise.

[606,xii] If this which has been established is not accepted, then let another course be sought; yet since no such course is possible, you are, as it were, a carpenter fashioning a stake for your own execution. Moreover:
[606,xiii]
In the absence of that [cause], how could this non-existence of it occur instantaneously?
It would not occur immediately if there were another cause as well.

Because the complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present without deficiency, that [effect] indeed occurs; but in its absence, it does not occur immediately. Thus, even though [the effect] is impermanent, it is possible for a *piśāca* (demon) or the like to be the cause. If you accept that even such a thing approaches and departs immediately, then that *piśāca* is actually subdued by fire, and thus fire alone possesses the status of the cause. If [the effect] were to arise from something else as well, then—due to the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the correspondence would be merely accidental, and the search for means by those who act with foresight would not invariably bear fruit. For us, however, the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), there is no such thing as a causal relationship in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*). Therefore, when one accepts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the state of positive concomitance is perfectly clear. For:
For it is only when identity with the self or the status of being a reason is established that negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established;
therefore, regarding a specific [property], there is neither negative concomitance nor positive concomitance (anvaya).

[607,ii] For that which does not possess the nature of another cannot necessarily be absent when that other is absent. Indeed, what lacks a necessary connection (*apratibandha*) cannot exclude another by its own cessation, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And thus: "This living body is not soulless, because [otherwise] there would follow the consequence of lacking breath and so forth"—this is the reason (*hetu*). For when that which is not connected [to another] is absent, there is no absence of that which is connected to it. Nor is that which possesses a connection non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Furthermore, there is no relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) without the connections of identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*). If it is asked: "Why does it not occur through some other mode?"—the answer is: "No, because no other mode is possible. Even that mode, once established, is the means of proving what is intended. But since this is not the case, for that which is intended as being characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is neither negative concomitance nor positive concomitance (*anvaya*); thus, due to the absence of both, the reason "because it possesses breath and so forth" is simply non-probative regarding the fact that "the living body possesses a soul."

How then, given the absence of both [the positive and negative concomitances], did the Teacher state this as a negative-only (vyatirekin) inference? It would be intended by him as well to say exactly this.
This is not a fault, because:
"The negative concomitance (vyatireka) is established by taking mere non-perception alone."
Therefore, it has been stated that what is inconclusive cannot otherwise be a means of cognition. (207)

[607, vii] By relying on a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that is established merely through the non-perception [of the reason] in the opponent’s view, the Teacher has presented this as a "negative-only" (*vyatirekin*) argument; however, it is not one where the negative concomitance is certain. Otherwise, if a certain negative concomitance were possible, it would be a probative indicator (*gamaka*). In that case, the Teacher would not have included it among the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) reasons. Therefore, the Teacher did not intend for there to be a certain negative concomitance here. < (2) Refutation of the Permanence of the Self > The teacher has demonstrated this as a "negative-only" (vyatirekin) argument by relying on a negative concomitance (vyatireka) that is established merely through the non-perception [of the reason] in the opponent's view; however, it is not one where the negative concomitance is certain. Therefore, the teacher did not intend for there to be a certain negative concomitance here. < (2) Refutation of the Permanence of the Self > The teacher has demonstrated this as a "negative-only" (vyatirekin) argument by relying on a negative concomitance (vyatireka) that is established merely through the non-perception [of the reason] in the opponent's view; however, it is not one where the negative concomitance is certain. In that case, the teacher would not have included it among the "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) reasons. [607, viii] But surely, the absence of breath and so forth pervades selflessness, and since that absence does not exist in a living body, by the rule of the exclusion of the pervader, there is the exclusion of the pervaded—namely, selflessness—in the living body; how then is the self not established?
Because there is no proof;
for the absence of breath and so forth pervades selflessness, and thus [the reason] does not exclude it.
If the vital breaths and so forth were to cease from the self, that too would not be the case. // 208 //

[607,xi] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, illuminated and observed how all five aggregates are empty, and thus delivered all suffering beings. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Bhagavat, why is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva called ‘Avalokiteśvara’? The Buddha said to the venerable Śāriputra: “If, Śāriputra, there be any sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, they should perceive that all phenomena are marked by emptiness, and thus deliver all suffering beings. Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he illuminates and observes that the five aggregates are all empty, and thereby delivers all suffering beings. Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. What is form is emptiness; what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Therefore, Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete. Within emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon; no realm of the eye up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the heart of non-attachment, having no hindrance in his mind. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, the unequaled mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Bhagavat, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā*? The Buddha said to the venerable Śāriputra: “A son of good family or a daughter of good family should perceive that all phenomena are marked by emptiness—neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete—and that within emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or phenomenon; no realm of the eye up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells in the heart of non-attachment, having no hindrance in his mind. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, Śāriputra, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should perceive that all phenomena are marked by emptiness—neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete—and dwell in the heart of non-attachment, having no hindrance in their minds. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear. Having transcended all inverted dreams, they attain *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, Śāriputra, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should practice the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in this manner. When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, including the gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, rejoiced and practiced it with faith. Thus ends the *Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom*, translated by Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang. 1. *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (The Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom) 2. If the pervasion between the two counter-examples were established, then the cessation of "non-breathing" and so forth in a living body would entail the cessation of "selflessness," and thus the self would be established even without positive concomitance (*anvaya*). However, that very pervasion between the two counter-examples cannot be established without reaching the subject (*pakṣa*). If there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the self, its status as a negator is not established at all. Furthermore, for that which is not a negator, its own cessation is not established as being pervaded by the cessation of the thing to be negated. Therefore, since the non-cessation of the non-pervader does not follow from the absence of the cessation of the non-pervaded, the self is not proven.
Because it is illogical for one thing to cease through the cessation of another;
if it were of the same nature as that or produced from that, then this would not be the case when that very nature is perceived. // 209 //

If cessation were to occur even in the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that "it is of the same nature as that" or "produced from that": if the self (*ātman*) is meant—whereby this entire world, such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is indeed the self—or if it is produced from the self because the self is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).
This is not a valid rebuttal, because: when this self is apprehended,
its perception, its cognition, and its movement are established.

If it were established that the self is perceived because another thing possesses its characteristics, then that other thing would also be proven to have that same nature. However, since the self itself is not perceived, how can the reason "because it possesses its characteristics" be established? Furthermore, inherence (*samavāya*) is based on the cognition "here [in this]," and it does not exist because the self is not perceived. As for the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), it is established through perception and non-perception; it is not something imperceptible. Therefore, how could there be the nature of that [self] or its production in relation to the self? Thus, [the reason] is unestablished.
And for that which is absolutely beyond the reach of perception, seeing and not-seeing are not established. (210)
And there is no selflessness in things such as jars, because:
If it were absolutely imperceptible, its non-existence would follow from the fact that it is not perceived.
If there is no possibility of the self being non-existent, how can there be a cognition of its pervasion? (PVA 497)

For you, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) establish the status of being a cause or a pervader (*vyāpaka*) only for that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*). Since there is no perception of a self (*ātman*), how can it possess the nature of being a cause or a pervader? And in its absence, it is not established that vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth have that as their essence or are produced from it. Furthermore:
[608, ix] How can one say "it is not" in the case of a jar and such, when its form has never been seen elsewhere?
How can there be pervasion by exclusion for that which has no known distinction? // 211 //

For when something is perceived in one place or at one time, it is understood that it does not exist here or now; such is the cognition regarding the entire world. But as for that which has never been an object of cognition, how can there be any mental representation that "it does not exist here"?
For conceptual constructions do not arise in anyone with respect to anything that has not been perceived;
however, if the negation of identity were indeed dependent upon everything [perceived], [then it would be established].

For a conceptual construction (*vitarka*) indeed proceeds regarding something seen in one place, even when it is not being perceived elsewhere, wondering "does it exist or not? But how can there be certainty that it does not? If at most this is merely a negation of identity—that "this self does not exist"—it is certainly not a certainty that "the self does not exist in a jar or other such things. This is all the more so in the case of its alleged omnipresence. If there were certainty that "the self does not exist" because of the perception of something devoid of it, [that would be the case].
Since this [inference] does not apply to a living being in the case of a jar and so forth, let it be so.

Just as a jar or similar object, being perceived as distinct [from the self], is understood to be devoid of a self, so too should the living body be [understood]. For that [living body] is not perceived as distinct from that [self] either. Therefore, because there is no perception [of the self as distinct], one cannot conclude the non-existence of the self in jars and the like. Consequently, since its distinction [from the subject] is unknown, how can there be for the self a pervasion by the exclusion [of the reason] (i.e., the absence of breath, etc.)? For when the exclusion of X is pervaded by the exclusion of Y, then the exclusion of X is pervaded by Y. Now, it is not known that the exclusion of the self is established as being pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth; therefore, how can the exclusion of the absence of breath and so forth be established as being pervaded by the self, such that the existence of the self could be proven from the exclusion of the absence of breath and so forth? Thus, there is no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka) here.

[608,xvi] But surely, just as it is perceived that vital functions (*prāṇa*) and so forth do not exist in a jar and the like, why is it that there is no such perception that "the self does not exist"? This is an unequal comparison, because:
Furthermore, the existence or non-existence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth is understood through their being observed in certain cases,
not from mere non-perception alone.
Likewise, if the self were perceived, its existence or non-existence would be understood. (213)

[609,iv] Since the conditions for perception are met, the absence of breath and so forth is cognized in a living body. But if this is so, it follows that there is a misconception regarding the self. Furthermore, let it be granted that jars and the like are devoid of a self; nevertheless, the self is not established by the mere non-cessation of the absence of breath and so forth.

Objection: If the self (*ātman*) did not exist in the living body, then breath and so forth would also be impossible; for it is observed in the case of jars and the like that the absence of a self is what causes the cessation of breath and so forth. Response: No, because it is the absence of something else that acts as the cause of cessation. To explain: it is by the absence of a certain cause that breath is not observed in a jar.
Even in the case of the body, if this [consciousness] were not present, its arising in conjunction with the body would be illogical. // 213 //

Intellect, effort, and so forth are likewise entirely absent in a jar and the like. Therefore, what indeed is your reason for dispelling the doubt as to whether the cessation of breath and so on is due to the absence of those [mental factors] or rather due to the absence of the self? In this regard, if that very cause—such as intellect—by whose absence breath and so on are not observed in a jar were not present in the body, then the consequence would be the absence of breath and so on. But since intellect and the rest are not absent [in the living body], how can there be the consequence of the cessation of breath and so on?

Now, there is a similarity in terms of selflessness (*nairātmya*) between living bodies and things such as jars; even if there is a dissimilarity caused by the presence or absence of cognition and so forth, nevertheless, because of their lack of a self, the living body—like a jar and the like—is devoid of breath and so forth. Or, conversely, it possesses a self by virtue of having the property of not being devoid of breath and so forth.
To this, it is said:
If reality is perceived even when things are distinct, on account of some similarity, [then what need is there for inference?]
Then:
[609,xii] Since jars and other things are objects of cognition, why is their possession of a self not cognized? (214)
For even in this case, it is not that there is no similarity whatsoever.
If invalidity were indeed the basis for all desired [cognitions], then who would be capable of establishing the distinction between existence and non-existence without it? (215)

[609,xv] Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exist by virtue of desire; rather, it is where valid cognition is possible that there is the desire of a discerning person. Even that which is undesired does not contradict what is brought forth by valid cognition. For it is logical that valid cognition exists independently, without dependence on desire. Otherwise, if valid cognition were dependent on desire rather than being independent, there would be no determination of existence and non-existence. [If one were to argue: "The presentation of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the object of the proponent’s desire, is abandoned according to the desire of the opponent"—in this way, there would be no non-confusion in the determination of existence and non-existence.

We shall, therefore, demonstrate that those [factors] such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth would likewise be absent due to the absence of a self (*ātman*). Consequently, what was stated—that the cessation of breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth does not occur when cognition and the rest exist—is incorrect. It is not incorrect; for it is precisely other [factors] that act as the motivators (*pravarttaka*) in that case. If the self were determined to be the motivator of cognition and the rest, it would be logical that, upon ceasing, it causes them to cease. But this is not so, because:
[610,i] Respiration, the winking of the eyes, and so forth, arise from that; they are produced by memory, desire, and effort.
From the objects, the senses, and the mental modifications, those [cognitions] arise from their own respective classes.

Mutually dependent upon one another and partaking in positive and negative concomitance, the nature of the self is limited to this much; any further conceptualization leads to an infinite regress. (217)

In some cases, there is memory, desire, and effort regarding what is undesirable or otherwise; from these, vital functions such as breathing and blinking proceed. If it is asked, "From what do memory and the others arise?"—they arise from cognitions dependent upon objects and sense-faculties, originating from their own respective classes. This is because the object depends on its own preceding object, and likewise, the cognition depends on the mutual influence of the sense-faculty and the object. Since this personal existence is bound to this collection of causes and conditions, what is the use of any other superfluous factor?

Is it not the case that memory, whose nature consists in the synthesis of what precedes and what follows, cannot exist without a self? For instance, he alone who saw [an object] is the rememberer; for what was seen by one cannot be the object of another’s memory. But even this is merely a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); how can proof be established from this alone? Memory is not observed to occur when there is identity, because the identity between the earlier and later moments is not apprehended through perception, and because memory itself lacks the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even if what was perceived by another is not remembered [by him], it will nevertheless be remembered with specific distinctions. It is not the case that everyone is identical simply because they are "another. He has arisen from his own causes as such that he alone is the cause of the memory and no other, due to the restriction of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Memory does not occur simply because of a self; rather, it occurs due to the state of the continuum (*saṃtāna*) arising from proficiency and repeated practice. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of memory occurring at all times.
[610,v] But is it not said that memory occurs only when there is a self? For if memory occurs only when there is a self, then memory would be absent in the case of another self.
This also is not correct, because: [610,
vii] Due to being modified by its modifications, according to positive and negative concomitance.
This is the relationship of cause and effect; otherwise, there would be no established order.
Memory follows the sequence of positive and negative concomitance with the practice of previous experience and changes in accordance with its modifications; therefore, the self is not the cause.

[610,ix] Now, if it does not exist without an eternal and all-pervading entity, then it would follow that time and so forth are also causes, since there is no distinction [between them]. Or, if it does not exist without an experiencer and a rememberer:
This is incorrect.
For it is by means of memory and experience that there exists one who remembers and one who experiences.
The existence of that [self] is postulated in space; how is it understood that it does not exist?

(PVA 501) [610,xii] For it is by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for memory and experience that some rememberer and experiencer is postulated, but one who is distinct from space and so forth is not. Thus, let it be postulated that there is some single entity; yet it is not different in nature from space and so forth, because there is no distinction in terms of being pervasive, eternal, formless (*amūrta*), and so on. Now, the self perceived as the agent in the sense of "I" is not merely formlessness.

[610,xiii] But surely, in the cognition "I," it is only the body that appears, as in "I am Devadatta, a descendant of Garga, dark-complexioned. If it is argued that the body is impermanent, we say no; for it is the states of the body that are impermanent, but the one who abides in those states is not different in the next world and so forth.

This very hypothesis is preferable: it is not that a distinct entity is perceived as the substratum of the body, for recollection and so forth are understood to be based on something incorporeal. Now, if an eternal cognizer is established, what is the use of further deliberation as to whether the body is different or not?
That too is incorrect.
Since there is no perception of anything other than the collection of states, for this very reason, the establishment of our position— that the body is such a collection— is unassailable. (502) (PVA)
Moreover:
In that which is eternal and unchangeable, how can there be recollection and experience?
If the rememberer is that very same [eternal] nature, why would he be a knower of objects? (503) If it undergoes change through pleasure and so forth, its eternity is not tenable.

For one who is unchanging in the face of pleasure and so forth, the state of being "pleased" and so on is not tenable. (504) (PVA) Since recollection is the fruit of experience, why [should it not belong to the self]?
Or, because of the cognition "I," it is not merely a matter of cause and effect. (505) (PVA)
For in this way, every person understands their own agency, thinking: "I recognize, by means of memory, that object which was previously seen and determined as 'I'.
That is incorrect;
for it is not by the mere arising of a self that one thinks, "I remember what was seen previously."
Every means of valid cognition is a cognition; thus, it is consistent with reality.

If cognition were valid merely by virtue of having the self as its cause, then every cognition would be valid; consequently, everything would be established for everyone, which is a great inconsistency. Therefore, only that cognition which arises from an unimpaired basis is valid. This being the case, since a cognition produced by the eye and other [senses] does not discern a synthesis (*anusaṃhita*), how could the unity of the preceding and succeeding [moments] be real? By means of what memory would its capacity for synthesis exist, so that the statement [that it] "possesses truth" might attain validity? For the self does not perceive itself or anything else as synthesized without a cognition that has become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the thought "I remember" is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, everything is indeed consistent only with respect to the conventional self. Moreover:
[611,xii] That [reason, "because it is audible"] is similar to that [fallacy], because of the deviation [of the reason] in the case of breath and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no deviation for that [reason] even when there is a negative concomitance (vyatireka), how [can this be]? 218.
[Objection: Surely it is said that its disjunction [from the object] occurs only from that which is impossible to accomplish. [Response:
Since the absence of persistence in the case of the possible follows as a matter of course, this same [principle] applies equally elsewhere as well. (219)

[611,xiv] There is no distinction between audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) and [the reason] such as "being a vital breath" (*prāṇatva*), because the mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is identical in both cases. Therefore, what logic is there to say that one is deviant while the other is not?

Is it not the case that the exclusion (*vyatireka*) is not identical because the objects differ? For audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is excluded from both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), whereas the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are excluded only from that which is not the probandum (*asādhya*). [Objection: But by stating that audibility is excluded even from the similar instances, the absence of its concomitance with the similar instances (*sapakṣānugama*) is being demonstrated. That [absence] is exactly the same for the vital breath and so forth; for since those [vital breaths] do not abide in the similar instances, what use is there in mentioning their presence or absence in the similar instances? To explain: when one says "exclusion only from that which is not the probandum," it is the existence [of the reason] in the probandum (*sādhyastiti*) that is expressed.
For this very reason, it has been stated that by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), there is the perception of two through one.

[611,xvii] Restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) by necessity establishes the opposite of that which is being restricted; otherwise, if exclusion were from the non-probandum alone, it would also apply to the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and thus that restriction would be purposeless. For this very reason, you yourselves have established through implication (*arthāpatti*) that the observation of two things is made from this statement such that there is exclusion from the non-probandum alone.
Such non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) is not established in the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For how could that non-deviation—which is characterized by a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and pervaded by positive concomitance—exist in the absence of the pervader’s (*vyāpaka*) positive concomitance? Alternatively, it might be argued that there is simply a separation from the non-probandum (*asādhya*) itself; however, this is not cognized without the cognition of positive concomitance. Indeed, it is impossible to observe all instances of the heterologue (*vipakṣa*); yet, it is possible through the gateway of positive concomitance.
Because it is bound to the self, it turns away from other things;
if it does not turn away from those other than that, how can it be bound to it?
[612,iv] Now, if the existence of the probandum does not exist, then non-existence is obtained; how then can there be non-deviation from that which is non-probandum? Because:
And what other kind of negation of a negation could there be than through affirmation? // 221 //

The restriction that "that which is indeed non-provable does not exist" negates non-existence with respect to the provable. By negating the negation—namely, that "it does not exist only in what is non-provable, but it is not non-existent in what is provable"—one would instead establish an affirmation. Now, [612, vii]...

The cessation of what is non-existent cannot be achieved; therefore, [cessation] does not occur in the case of the unachievable. [Objection: Is it not the case that "it is not" is itself the cessation? [Reply: What do you consider to be the cessation of a non-existent thing? (222)

[612, viii] The Blessed One said: "The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the one who knows the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and the future limit (*aparānta*). Why is that? Because he has fully understood the nature of all phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata is the one who knows the past limit and the future limit because he has fully understood the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Now, because there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for the reason "because of being a vital breath" (*prāṇādi*), there can be no exclusion from it. For it is not possible to exclude something that is non-existent, since it cannot function as an ablative (*apādāna*). Furthermore, there is no such thing as "non-existence" from which an exclusion could be perceived. If there is no exclusion of the non-existent, how can there be an exclusion of exclusion? If you say that this too does not exist, then [we ask]: if the negation of the exclusion of exclusion occurs, how can there be an exclusion of the exclusion of the exclusion of the non-existent? Because of this infinite regress, there would be no comprehension. Moreover, "negation" (*pratiṣedha*) and "exclusion" (*nivṛtti*) have the same meaning. That very thing which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the exclusion of exclusion is itself the ablative (*apādāna*) of the exclusion.

[612,xiv] The non-existence of what is unreal is not a negation; rather, it is an affirmation characterized by the existence of a real entity. That exists even for what is unreal. But non-existence, even if it conforms to reason, does not exist in the case of non-existence, nor does its opposite exist in the case of its contrary. What is this other than the behavior of the blind? For: [612,xv]
Affirmation and negation exist through mutual exclusion;
since there is no other mode of being, it is illogical to say that both are absent.

Since non-existence (*asattva*) is necessarily concomitant with the absence of an entity, that very absence is also designated as "cessation" (*nivṛtti*). For there is nothing non-existent therein that has not ceased. Nor is that which is non-existent there a locus, because it is impossible for it to possess the nature of a substratum. It is not the case that mere non-existence of existence is what constitutes non-existence there. If it is argued that even that [non-existence] does not exist, we say no; for since existence and non-existence are of the nature of mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), how could both be negated? Indeed, existence acquires its identity through the necessary exclusion of non-existence. Since existence would not occur in the absence of non-existence, existence is necessarily concomitant with the cessation of that [non-existence]. Otherwise, if it were not present even when existence has ceased, it simply would not exist at all. To illustrate:
If an entity is not perceived when there is non-existence,
then an entity is indeed perceived only when non-existence does not exist at all. (PVA 511)
That too is not a negation, because it is non-perception due to the non-existence [of the object].
Since both are non-existent, the existence of the absence is not precluded.

Although both existence (*bhāva*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) are equally non-existent, nevertheless, the non-existence of existence is indeed unavoidable. For the non-existence of existence occurs when something does not exist as existence; likewise, the non-existence of non-existence would occur when it does not exist as non-existence. When existence is not apprehended, that very thing is cognized as non-existence. Therefore, negation, while being in operation, is established by perception through the characteristic of the apprehension of what is distinct from it, by way of exclusion from affirmation (*vidhi*). Consequently, by the very functioning of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when one state is otherwise, the establishment of the other state occurs; there is no possibility of a third alternative. Whatever is excluded there by perception is entirely other than what is grasped by the perception that apprehends the form of existence. In that regard, whatever is not determined by that [perception] in its own form, its non-existence in that form is precisely what is meant, not a different category. Even when non-existence is being determined, that which is not determined in such a way is simply existence; how then could there be a third alternative? Let there be the absence of a third alternative; however, whether that [object] is existence or non-existence cannot be determined with respect to a locus in the case of non-existence, because that [locus] itself is not determined. Indeed, that which is non-existent cannot be determined.
That is incorrect, because:
If there is no activity of the reason with respect to that [object], why is its cessation desired? Even that [cessation] is not a negation; what kind of cessation is being negated here? (224)

[613, vi] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who dwells in suffering and practices for the sake of suffering; the person who dwells in suffering but practices for the sake of happiness; the person who dwells in happiness but practices for the sake of suffering; and the person who dwells in happiness and practices for the sake of happiness. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One: 'There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Regarding this, Blessed One, how should one understand the person who dwells in suffering and practices for the sake of suffering? The Blessed One said: "In this case, Ānanda, a certain person is born into a low family—a family of outcastes, bamboo-workers, hunters, cartwrights, or sweepers—poor, with little food and drink, where livelihood is difficult to obtain, and where they must endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and blows from sticks and clods. Furthermore, he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with limbs that are deformed, eyes that are squinting, a hunched back, a potbelly, and a crooked neck; he is short in stature, weak, and sickly. He is afflicted by many diseases: he suffers from chronic ailments of the head, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the tongue, the teeth, the throat, the chest, the belly, the back, the sides, the hands, the feet, or the whole body. He is constantly tormented by hunger and thirst. This, Ānanda, is called the person who dwells in suffering and practices for the sake of suffering. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this person does not gain wealth through right effort, nor does he gain it through wrong effort; he does not gain it through right conduct, nor does he gain it through wrong conduct; he does not gain it through right livelihood, nor does he gain it through wrong livelihood. Thus, Ānanda, this person dwells in suffering and practices for the sake of suffering. The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding the person who dwells in suffering but practices for the sake of happiness, how should he be understood? The Blessed One said: "In this case, Ānanda, a certain person is born into a low family... [as above] ...and is afflicted by many diseases. However, he possesses faith, is virtuous, and is endowed with wisdom. He gains wealth through right effort, not through wrong effort; he gains it through right conduct, not through wrong conduct; he gains it through right livelihood, not through wrong livelihood. Thus, Ānanda, this person dwells in suffering but practices for the sake of happiness. The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding the person who dwells in happiness but practices for the sake of suffering, how should he be understood? The Blessed One said: "In this case, Ānanda, a certain person is born into a high family—a family of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, or householders—wealthy, with abundant food and drink, where livelihood is easy to obtain, and where they do not endure cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or blows from sticks and clods. Furthermore, he is handsome, beautiful, and attractive, with limbs that are well-proportioned, clear eyes, an upright back, a slender waist, and a straight neck; he is tall in stature, strong, and healthy. He is free from many diseases. However, he does not gain wealth through right effort, nor does he gain it through wrong effort; he does not gain it through right conduct, nor does he gain it through wrong conduct; he does not gain it through right livelihood, nor does he gain it through wrong livelihood. Thus, Ānanda, this person dwells in happiness but practices for the sake of suffering. The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Regarding the person who dwells in happiness and practices for the sake of happiness, how should he be understood? The Blessed One said: "In this case, Ānanda, a certain person is born into a high family... [as above] ...and is free from many diseases. He gains wealth through right effort, not through wrong effort; he gains it through right conduct, not through wrong conduct; he gains it through right livelihood, not through wrong livelihood. Thus, Ānanda, this person dwells in happiness and practices for the sake of happiness. The venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One: 'There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. The Blessed One said: "Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, the monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [613, vi]

Let us first question you: if there is no exclusion from that non-existent similar class (*sapakṣa*), what kind of occurrence (*vṛtti*) could there be? For there is no other possibility. In this way, exclusion would not be of the nature of non-existence. If it were an existence, it would have the form of occurrence. If you say that it [existence] also does not exist, then exclusion has not been excluded; for by this very fact, it would be established. Exclusion is a negation; therefore, what is being negated? Indeed, it is not logical that the very thing which has been established should be negated. Therefore, exclusion is simply the negation of occurrence; thus, there is no negation of that [exclusion].
vii] Now, if it is argued that there is no cognition of it as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or as an ablative (*apādāna*), and therefore there is no cessation from it;
[613, viii]
To this it is replied:
Apart from affirmation and negation, there is no other verbal [cognition].
And since that conventional usage does not apply to non-existent things, one arrives at the state of being mute in this matter.

[613,x] If someone were to challenge you thus: "Is it not the case that 'vitality' (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not observed in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*)? Therefore, being excluded from them, it is an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason; how then can it be non-probative? If that were so, then even 'inaudibility' (*aśrāvaṇatva*) would be probative. To this, one must reply: "In the absence of a similar instance, there is no exclusion by necessity; otherwise, silence would follow here. [613,xi]

Moreover, let it be exactly so. For it is not possible for there to be any determination [of non-existence] by itself; while speech may be prevented, cognition (*buddhi*) cannot. It must necessarily be understood in some way or another. Furthermore, if non-existence could not be cognized either as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or as an ablative (*apādāna*), then all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) would be abolished at all times. For: "There is no negation of existing things, nor does it apply to non-existent things."
By this principle, the meaning of the negative particle [nañ] has reached dissolution in the world. (226)
The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is simply non-existence; therefore, if that non-existence is not itself delimited, how can it be employed? For:
The signifier is employed by the Buddhist for the sake of the signified;
since that [signified] is not perceived, this pair of non-existents is impossible.

If mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*) were made the object [of negation], the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be entirely useless, because a negative particle cannot be employed when its object has not been determined. Or, if it were employed, there would be no purpose for it. Now, if that whose non-existence [is asserted] must be made the object, then how can there be the non-existence of that very thing which is being perceived? If it is argued that it is perceived in one way and its non-existence is [asserted] in another way—for instance, that things which actually exist are denied by virtue of their connection with a certain place and so forth—[we reply:
To this, it is said:
If it is argued that there is a negation of place and time, then that which exists as it is cannot be negated;
nor can that which does not exist as it is be negated. (227)

[614,iv] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, nor does he perceive that emptiness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is the markless, nor does he perceive that the markless is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the markless, nor does he perceive that the markless is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are wishless, nor does he perceive that wishlessness is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-arising, nor does he perceive that non-arising is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-cessation, nor does he perceive that non-cessation is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-defiled, nor does he perceive that non-defilement is consciousness. He does not perceive that form is non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purity is form; nor does he perceive that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-purified, nor does he perceive that non-purity is consciousness. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Why is this? Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from form, nor is it conjoined with or disjoined from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. It is not conjoined with nor disjoined from the past, nor is it conjoined with or disjoined from the future, nor is it conjoined with or disjoined from the present. Why is this? Because, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is unconditioned, and because all dharmas are also unconditioned. Therefore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is neither conjoined with nor disjoined from all dharmas. This is called the perfection of wisdom of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who dwells in the dwelling of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he cannot be crushed by any Māra or by any followers of Māra. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he quickly attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will not fall into the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, but will quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will not be reborn in the eight unfavorable conditions, nor will he be born among the long-lived gods, nor will he be born in border regions where there is no Dharma, nor will he be born as one who is deaf or mute, nor will he be born as one who holds wrong views, nor will he be born at a time when a Tathāgata has not appeared in the world. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born in the presence of Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, and will never be separated from them. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born in Jambudvīpa, or in Pūrvavideha, or in Aparagoyānī, or in Uttarakuru, and wherever he is born, he will always be born in a place where there is no lack of the Buddha-Dharma. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born in a noble family, whether that of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or householders, and wherever he is born, he will always be born in a noble family. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a complete set of sense faculties, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a complete set of sense faculties. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a male body, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a male body. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue of male attendants, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue of male attendants. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not mixed with women, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not mixed with women. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to retrogression, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to retrogression. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the three evil realms, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the three evil realms. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the five hindrances, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the five hindrances. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the four perversions, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the four perversions. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the eight worldly dharmas, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the eight worldly dharmas. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the ten unwholesome paths of action, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the ten unwholesome paths of action. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the five heinous crimes, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the five heinous crimes. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the four grave offenses, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the four grave offenses. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the two vehicles, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the two vehicles. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the three poisons, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the three poisons. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this dwelling, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the eight difficulties, and wherever he is born, he will always be born with a retinue that is not subject to the eight difficulties.
