Now, it is not even possible to negate that "it does not exist here in this form. To explain: if that form, that time, and that place exist, how can they be negated? On the other hand, if they do not exist, there is no possibility of making them an object of cognition, because non-existence cannot be determined. If, however, it is made an object of cognition, then it must also exist as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth; otherwise, it would be impossible to make it an object of cognition. For the determination [of an object] necessarily occurs through its status as a causal factor (*kāraka*), since otherwise it would be impossible. In the case of the statement "it does not exist in this place," if the state of being a locus is made an object of cognition, how can there be non-existence? If there is non-existence, then there is no making it an object of cognition.

[614,v] Now, if even that which is being negated is not negated, then in that case, since there is indeed a withdrawal from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) even by means of its attribution to the similar instance, how could there be no exclusion from the similar instance? Consequently, the conventional practice of affirmation and negation cannot possibly have an external basis. Therefore, there would be a total cessation of conventional discourse.

[Objection: But surely the linguistic practice of affirmation (*vidhi*) is possible; therefore, there is no annihilation of linguistic practice. [Reply: No, because there is no affirmation of that which has already been made an object of cognition. If, in the case of "the jar exists," its apprehension as existent is itself the affirmation, then what further purpose is served by the act of affirming "it exists"? On the other hand, if it is apprehended as non-existent, then due to contradiction, it is impossible to affirm "the non-existent exists. If it is determined as existent, then affirmation therein is redundant.
When there is a determination by way of non-existence, a positive injunction therein is purposeless. (PVA 514) [614.viii] [The Establishment of Affirmation and Negation]
Because it is delimited by non-existence, no further positive injunction is possible.
Therefore, relying upon the referent of a word, which serves as the basis for both existence and non-existence— [614, ix]
All injunctions and prohibitions are held to have no external substratum whatsoever. (228)

[614,x] For the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇārtha*) is one thing, and the object of a word (*śabdārtha*) is another. The object of a word rests upon both existence and non-existence, but the object of valid cognition does not rest upon existence and non-existence in that way. Indeed, the object of valid cognition cannot be otherwise, because it is apprehended in a determinate form.
The cognition produced from a word is the same whether the object has perished or not;
therefore, since it relies upon both existence and non-existence, the referent of a word is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) in that way.

Therefore, when an object is examined by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), it is the basis for affirmation and negation; this is because conceptual cognitions lack any necessary connection with the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*). Furthermore, not everything that is non-conceptual is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it functions in an affirmative form, it is not a valid means of knowledge, and thus negation is employed to demonstrate its invalidity. Conversely, if it functions in a negative form, it is an affirmation. [614,xiii]

Now, if this cognition is indeed erroneous, then it manifests itself precisely as such [erroneous], because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is non-erroneous. For it is impossible to show one's own nature otherwise, since that would entail the loss of its very nature. If there were an appearance of another form, then that [other form] would be its nature, and in that case too it would be the same, leading to an infinite regress. Furthermore, when the nature [of a thing] exists, its being the material cause of existence is negated. And how could that subject (*dharmin*), having been apprehended in its own form, be common to both affirmation and negation, such that it might be connected with them?
To this, it is said:

That subject (dharmin) is perceived as being connected with those two [the universal and the particular] even in their absence; because verbal usage occurs [regarding it], it too is accepted as participating in conventional discourse. (229)

[615,iv] Indeed, this conventional usage does not have as its basis the external or internal intrinsic nature; rather, it has as its basis words and their referents. Nor is there a cognition of an external or internal intrinsic nature from a word.

[Objection: But since there is nothing else apart from that [exclusion], upon what basis does the linguistic practice of affirmation and negation rest? [Reply: We say it rests upon the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). [Question: What is this so-called "exclusion of others"? [Answer: It is that which is cognized from the word.

Is it not the case that this very point is being stated? What is it that is perceived? Nothing at all. Nevertheless, this linguistic convention carries on from beginningless delusion; for the subject characterized by word and object appears as connected with affirmation and negation, even though such an external or internal entity does not exist when subjected to critical inquiry. And thus it has been said: "Its form is nothing whatsoever."

[Objection: Surely, its form as something superimposed with an external nature does indeed exist. [Reply: No, because there is nothing else apart from cognition and the object of cognition. [Objection: It is an erroneous form. [Reply: If that too is perceived in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), how can it be erroneous? On the other hand, if it is not an object of perception, how can it be determined that it exists when it is not being perceived? [Objection: Its erroneous nature is known later. [Reply: In that case, it was not initially perceived in its own nature; how then could it be the object of the determination "it exists"? If it were perceived through another form, then that other perception would be erroneous, and that one would require yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

[615, viii] The Blessed One said: "Bhikṣus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower in the mud; the person who is like a blue lotus flower in the mud; the person who is like a white lotus flower in the mud; and the person who is like a red lotus flower in the mud. And how, bhikṣus, is one a person like a lotus flower in the mud? Here, bhikṣus, a certain person is born into a low family—a family of outcastes, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or waste-removers—and is poor, destitute, and lacking in livelihood. He is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he has a hunchbacked back, a crooked body, a squint eye, a flat nose, or is leprous, with scabs, or afflicted by skin disease. He is short-lived, often ill, and weak. He is dull-witted, slow in understanding, and possesses little wisdom. Yet, having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he attains the destruction of the taints in this very life and dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are taintless, supramundane, and free from clinging. This, bhikṣus, is called a person who is like a lotus flower in the mud. And how, bhikṣus, is one a person who is like a blue lotus flower in the mud? Here, bhikṣus, a certain person is born into a low family... [as above] ...and possesses little wisdom. Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he attains the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path; he attains the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. This, bhikṣus, is called a person who is like a blue lotus flower in the mud. And how, bhikṣus, is one a person who is like a white lotus flower in the mud? Here, bhikṣus, a certain person is born into a high family—a family of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, or householders—possessing great wealth and abundant property. He is handsome, attractive, and fair to behold; he is long-lived, healthy, and strong. He is wise, quick in understanding, and possesses great wisdom. Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he attains the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. This, bhikṣus, is called a person who is like a white lotus flower in the mud. And how, bhikṣus, is one a person who is like a red lotus flower in the mud? Here, bhikṣus, a certain person is born into a high family... [as above] ...and possesses great wisdom. Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, he teaches the Dharma to others, establishes them in the Dharma, and leads them to the attainment of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship. This, bhikṣus, is called a person who is like a red lotus flower in the mud. These, bhikṣus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."

Now, even though that [exclusion] is real, it is called "erroneous" because there is no certainty regarding its reality. What is its reality? It is the non-contact with [external] objects. [Objection: But surely that is its very nature; how can it be unreal? For remaining in its own nature is not itself unreality. [Objection: If it is unreal because it produces a certainty [of something else], then the certainty itself must be unreal. [Reply: No, for that [certainty] is produced by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the certainty itself. [Objection: In that case, the erroneousness belongs to the certainty. [Reply: This too is not tenable, because that [certainty] also abides in its own form. Therefore, the referent of a word is indeed formless (*arūpa*). How, then, is there the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "it exists"? It is conventionally expressed as "it exists" due to the operation of words. For from the conventional usage characterized by the application of words, one understands "it exists," and this is what is communicated under the name "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), consisting in the exclusion of the apprehension of universals and so forth. If, however, it were said that "nothing at all exists," then others would be terrified. For this very reason he says: "That too is accepted as participating in conventional usage. Otherwise, the opponent might object that there would be a total cessation of conventional usage.
For it is thus:
The exclusion of other things by means of a word occurs solely through the relationship of cause and effect among those things that are not mutually perceived.

When it is said, "Bring fire," one proceeds while avoiding what is not fire. Even though one understands the fire through the word, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises is a self-awareness that does not touch the actual object; from that comes the conceptual construction of activity; from that comes the experience of the nature of the movement; and from that comes the worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) of whether there is attainment or otherwise. Indeed, there is no such thing as a relationship between the denoted and the denoter;
otherwise, there would be [an impossibility] in the affirmation and negation of things.
The affirmation of the universal nature and the negation of the particular nature of a single dharma. // 230 //

Because they are not non-distinct, just as there is a plurality of affirmations and negations regarding distinct [objects], there is no coexistence of affirmation and negation within a single substratum. (231)

[616,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing the practice of the Dharma and, having beheld them, addressed the Bhagavat: “Bhagavat, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs are practicing the practice of the Dharma; may the Bhagavat grant them the prophecy of their future enlightenment. The Bhagavat said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara: “Avalokiteśvara, it is well that you have requested this from me. Listen attentively, and I shall explain to you how these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs will attain parinirvāṇa. Avalokiteśvara, in the future, after an incalculable number of aeons, when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, there will appear in the world a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. At that time, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs will become śrāvakas of that Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Having become śrāvakas, they will all attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, at that time, in that era, there will be a king named Śubhavimukta, a righteous ruler, a wheel-turning monarch, possessing the seven treasures, a conqueror of the four quarters, one who has established the stability of the land, a king of dharma who rules by dharma. He will have eighty-four thousand cities, with the city of Rājagṛha as the foremost. His queen will be named Yaśovatī, his crown prince will be named Śūradatta, and he will have eighty-four thousand ministers. At that time, the king Śubhavimukta will hear the name of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Having heard it, he will take up the five precepts and, together with his retinue, will go to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni to pay homage and make offerings. Having paid homage and made offerings, he will plant roots of merit. After his life has ended, he will be reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. There, he will see Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and will hear the Dharma from him. Having heard the Dharma, he will plant further roots of merit. After his life there has ended, he will descend to Jambudvīpa and become the Tathāgata Maitreya, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. At that time, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs will become the śrāvikās of the Tathāgata Maitreya. Having become śrāvikās, they will all attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of the Tathāgata Maitreya. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, at that time, in that era, there will be a king named Brahmadatta, a righteous ruler, a wheel-turning monarch, possessing the seven treasures, a conqueror of the four quarters, one who has established the stability of the land, a king of dharma who rules by dharma. He will have eighty-four thousand cities, with the city of Kapilavastu as the foremost. His queen will be named Brahmadattā, his crown prince will be named Brahmadatta, and he will have eighty-four thousand ministers. At that time, the king Brahmadatta will hear the name of the Tathāgata Maitreya. Having heard it, he will take up the five precepts and, together with his retinue, will go to the Tathāgata Maitreya to pay homage and make offerings. Having paid homage and made offerings, he will plant roots of merit. After his life has ended, he will be reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. There, he will see Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and will hear the Dharma from him. Having heard the Dharma, he will plant further roots of merit. After his life there has ended, he will descend to Jambudvīpa and become the Tathāgata Śikhin, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. At that time, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs will become the śrāvikās of the Tathāgata Śikhin. Having become śrāvikās, they will all attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of the Tathāgata Śikhin. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, at that time, in that era, there will be a king named Puṣya, a righteous ruler, a wheel-turning monarch, possessing the seven treasures, a conqueror of the four quarters, one who has established the stability of the land, a king of dharma who rules by dharma. He will have eighty-four thousand cities, with the city of Bandhumatī as the foremost. His queen will be named Puṣyavatī, his crown prince will be named Puṣyadatta, and he will have eighty-four thousand ministers. At that time, the king Puṣya will hear the name of the Tathāgata Śikhin. Having heard it, he will take up the five precepts and, together with his retinue, will go to the Tathāgata Śikhin to pay homage and make offerings. Having paid homage and made offerings, he will plant roots of merit. After his life has ended, he will be reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. There, he will see Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and will hear the Dharma from him. Having heard the Dharma, he will plant further roots of merit. After his life there has ended, he will descend to Jambudvīpa and become the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. At that time, these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs will become the śrāvikās of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū. Having become śrāvikās, they will all attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū. Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara, at that time, in that era, there will be a king named Kṛkin, a righteous ruler, a wheel-turning monarch, possessing the seven treasures, a conqueror of the four quarters, one who has established the stability of the land, a king of dharma who rules by dharma. He will have eighty-four thousand cities, with the city of Varanasi as the foremost. His queen will be named Kṛkī, his crown prince will be named Kṛkidatta, and he will have eighty-four thousand ministers. At that time, the king Kṛkin will hear the name of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū. Having heard it, he will take up the five precepts and, together with his retinue, will go to the Tathāgata Viśvabhū to pay homage and make offerings. Having paid homage and made offerings, he will plant roots of merit. After his life has ended, he will be reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. There, he will see Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and will hear the Dharma from him. Having heard the Dharma, he will plant further roots of merit. After his life there has ended, he will descend to Jambudvīpa and become the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Ś

If there were no difference between the subject (*dharmī*) and its properties (*dharmas*), then upon the affirmation or negation of a single property, there would follow the affirmation or negation of all properties. For when that [property] is affirmed, it is not possible for its own nature (*tadātman*) to remain unaffirmed; otherwise, it would follow that even that [nature] is not affirmed. The same applies to negation. Indeed, when a cow is affirmed or negated, because there is no difference [between the cow and its nature], there could be no absence of the state of being a "broken-horned one" (*khaṇḍatā*). For it is not logical that when something is conveyed by a word, its own nature remains unconveyed. That [nature] is indeed conveyed; it is simply not apprehended due to error. In that case, everything would be unapprehended, which results in the collapse of cognition. Nor can it be maintained that "some things are apprehended and some are not," because there is no such distinction. Such a thing occurs only when a distinction exists, and not otherwise. For existence (*sattā*) is said to be nothing other than perception (*upalambha*). Since there is a distinction [in perception], there is a distinction in existence itself. Therefore, how could it be that of the very same thing, some part is apprehended while another is not?

This is trivial. Surely, even when momentariness is not ascertained, blue is ascertained; and there is no such thing as what is perceived being impossible. No, for there too there is a contradiction. To explain: [616,v] This is trivial. Surely, even when momentariness is not ascertained, blue is ascertained; and there is no such thing as what is perceived being impossible. No, for there too there is a contradiction. To explain: [616,v]
If, by necessity, that cognition of blueness is devoid of the establishment of a momentary duration,
then the proof of the momentariness of entities by others is not established by perception, nor is it sublated by others.

If that which is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sublated by another means of valid cognition, then there would be an infinite regress, as that [sublating cognition] too would require another; thus, there would be a total lack of confidence. Now, even if the ascertainment of blue does not apply to momentariness, nevertheless, momentariness is not sublated by it, nor is the ascertainment of blue sublated by the proof of momentariness, because both operate through conjunction (*samuccaya*). For there are three types of logical relations: conjunction, alternative (*vikalpa*), and sublation (*bādhana*). Conjunction is, for example, "this is blue and it is a lotus," due to the conjunction of two properties. Alternative is, for example, "is it a post or a person? because the two cannot exist in one place simultaneously. Sublation is, for example, "it is a snake, [but actually] a rope," because the state of being a snake is impossible [in the case of a rope]. Therefore, what fault is there in the conjunction of blueness and non-momentariness?
To this, it is said:
How can there be a synthesis here by way of the characteristic of sublation?
Nowhere is it possible for that which is sublated to be synthesized with its sublator.

For if the ascertainment of blueness were to occur to the exclusion of momentariness, then momentariness would indeed be sublated, because its form is apprehended as being distinct from that [blueness]. Indeed, the demonstration of a distinct form is itself the sublation. [616,xi] But is it not the case that sublation occurs here by means of the absence of something through the instrument of non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*), and that perception is not the sublater of anything?
This is not tenable, because:
[616,xiii]
This ascertainment is indeed not the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it is its result;
rather, the apprehension of that [object] as distinct from it is the means of valid cognition, and from that, ascertainment arises.

Indeed, this ascertainment (*niścaya*) is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It follows the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), and there is no possibility of its being otherwise. Even if, for some reason, it does not arise despite the emergence of a cognition of a distinct [object], nevertheless, its negation occurs precisely by virtue of its [perceptual] capacity. We shall demonstrate this further on. In that regard, if blue is ascertained by excluding momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), then momentariness is sublated by that very [ascertainment]; how then could it be established by another [means]? Or, if it has already been established even by that [ascertainment], it is nonetheless clarified by the other [means].
To this, it is said:

If that [cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can there be a lack of clarity regarding its preceding movement? It is a contradiction to say that the object has been established and proven, yet it has not been made clear.
How indeed could this lack of clarity exist even when there is certainty?
In this case, there is clarity; in the other, certainty is not consistent with reason.
Therefore, it should be understood that either the former [cognition] is erroneous or the latter.
For two cognitions that are mutually contradictory cannot have the same object.

Therefore, when one [thing] is established, there is the establishment of everything that is not distinct from it; thus, the introduction of another word or another conceptual construction is redundant. Now, if it is argued that diverse limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are the objects of diverse words and conceptual constructions, then this objection does not apply.
That is incorrect. For there is no coexistence within a single substratum of that which is affirmed and that which is negated when they are distinct.

If there is a difference [between the two] due to their mutual dependence, then those objects (*artha*) would be entirely distinct, and the substratum (*dharmin*) would not be anything other than them. In that case, how could there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)? For instance, in the expression "blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), when a quality (*guṇa*) and a substance (*dravya*) are being expressed, there is no further common substratum for the two; thus, there is no coreferentiality. Nor is there a cognition of the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatā*), because they express separate meanings, like a jar and a cloth. Now, if it is argued that "blue" is not [expressed] alone—[that is, it is always expressed with a substance]—then, in that case, the cognition of the substance occurs through the very cognition of the blue form, since there is no cognition of [the components] in parts. Or, if it is [the universal and the quality], even so, there is no cognition of coreferentiality because there is no other word denoting a common substratum. Or, if it is argued that the substance itself is cognized as "blue," and not merely blueness—then, since two things are denoted by one word and likewise by the other, how can there be coreferentiality or the relation of qualifier and qualified when four or three things are being denoted? Indeed, things of distinct forms denoted by one or several words do not partake in coreferentiality. Alternatively, if it is argued that "blue" and so forth cannot be cognized in isolation, and therefore—as opposed to a cognition of distinct things—there is no lack of coreferentiality; and that these "blues" and so forth necessarily imply a genus (*jāti*), while the genus and so forth necessarily imply a quality (*guṇa*), and thus another word is employed to establish this necessity—[we reply: this is not so. Even if the blue and so forth were not cognized in isolation, they would still be distinct from the genus and so forth. Furthermore, since the genus and so forth are not restricted to a specific quality, and the quality and so forth are not restricted to a specific genus, the application of another word would be for the sake of establishing restriction. But if they are already restricted by their own nature, what is the purpose of another word? Moreover, if the blue and so forth were restricted to the genus, and the genus and so forth were restricted to the quality, then the application of another word would be redundant. And if the blue and so forth were restricted to the genus, and the genus and so forth were restricted to the quality, then the application of another word would be useless. Therefore, the application of another word is for the sake of expressing a different meaning. Thus, the relation of qualifier and qualified is established based on the cognition of a different object. That is incorrect.
If the distinctness of blue and so forth from direct perception is not understood,
how else could that same object be cognized by means of a word?

If an extracted [quality] such as blue does not appear in perception, then it should likewise appear from a word as well, because the apprehension of the relationship [between the word and its referent] occurs in that very [quality]. If it is argued that there is no such cognition because [the object] is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), how can that which is being cognized be beyond the senses? If you say it is because of non-proximity (*asannihitatva*), we say no; for verbal cognition functions even with respect to what is not proximate. If you argue that this is because of the absence of sensory activity (*akṣavyāpāra*), we say no; the sense organ itself is not the cause of cognition. If it is the manifestation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [that is the cause], then what is the difference between the sensory and the non-sensory [means of cognition]? Furthermore, where there is proximity, how could there be a different mode of cognition? The mere absence of sensory activity does not remove anything [from the object]; if you say it removes clarity (*spaṣṭatā*), then even if there is an absence of clarity, the blue must still be manifested as inherent in a specific substance. How else could it be cognized? And in that case, there would be no need for the employment of another word. Alternatively, if [you claim that] qualities like blue do not reside in a fixed substance, then in that case, even "blue" would be understood from the word "blue" as being non-fixed, and "lotus" would also be understood from it, since it too denotes that [same quality].

Furthermore, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because it is impossible for two terms whose denotations are not fixed to convey a single object. Nor is it tenable to claim that such a cognition arises solely from mutual exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
How could there be a mutual exclusion of that which is already apprehended?
For it is in the act of exclusion itself that "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) becomes the denotable object.

If that which is undetermined—such as what is conveyed by the word "blue" and so forth—is not capable of being restricted by another [word], then it cannot be overturned by anything else, for what is apprehended through perception cannot be set aside by another [means of knowledge], as that would entail the consequence of [the former] being erroneous. [Objection: Then perhaps doubt is removed by another word. For that which is apprehended through a conjunction (*samuccaya*) cannot be removed. But when there is an alternative (*vikalpa*)—such as "Is it a blue lotus, or something else?"—then the removal of that alternative is logically established by another word. [Response: That too is incorrect, because: *The cognition of an object is produced by the word itself; how could it be otherwise? For if it were not produced by that [word], how could it be determined by another?* (PV 1.45) The very cognition of the object is brought about by the word itself; how could it be otherwise? For if the cognition of the object were not produced by that [word], how could it be determined by another [word]? It is impossible for one thing to be determined by another when it has not been produced by that [first thing]. Therefore, since the cognition of the object is produced by the word itself, it is not possible for it to be removed by another word. Furthermore, even if it were produced by another [word], it would still not be removed by yet another, because it is impossible for a cognition already produced to be negated. Thus, the aforementioned [position] is untenable. Moreover, if the word were to produce a cognition of the object, it would follow that it produces a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*), because it is observed that the cognition of the object is always associated with a universal. And since it is impossible for a single entity to possess both a universal and a particular, it follows that the word does not produce a cognition of the object. Consequently, the word does not denote the object. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, if the word were to denote the object, it would follow that it denotes the particular (*viśeṣa*), because the object is invariably concomitant with the particular. And since it is impossible for a single entity to possess both a universal and a particular, it follows that the word does not denote the object. Therefore, the word does not denote the object. For if even a conceptual construction were a real object understood through that word,
from what could its cessation arise upon the encounter with another word? (PVA 525)

If that object itself is unreal and is merely the domain of conceptual construction, how can it be made otherwise by anything else? For both [the cognition and the subsequent one] would possess the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, if it has been presented by that [first cognition] as having a doubtful nature, then this state of being doubtful is precisely what is to be removed by firm conviction. Therefore, its removal by another [cognition] is logical; for it is not the case that something which is of such a nature is simultaneously not of such a nature.
That too is incorrect;
for by that very word, the state of being capable of being negated is established.
Then, what will be the function of the subsequent word?

(526) [PVA 618, ix] But surely, it has been established that exclusion is brought about by the preceding cognition through restriction; however, there is a utility for the subsequent restriction as well.
That too is incorrect, because:
How could that lack of restriction, which has been established by the force of valid cognition, be otherwise? It is settled that it cannot be overturned even by another means of knowledge.

Therefore, neither the former nor the latter is authoritative, because it lacks probative power; for the latter, too, is of that same nature. When only a generality is stated, the latter is redundant.
[The generality is merely conceptualized.

Now, it might be argued that inference is indeed the sublater [of the claim that fire is not hot]. This is not so; for that [inference] too is sublated by perception. One does not grasp specific qualifiers such as "intense flames" through inference; therefore, even in that case, there is only doubt. If it is argued that there is doubt regarding the universal (*sāmānya*), we say no; because the cognition of the universal is itself of the nature of doubt. For the cognition of the universal is the cognition of an indefinite particular. Indeed, a universal cannot possess a fixed form. To explain:
"A universal exists wherever there is an individual, but not as a specific individual of this kind."

Therefore, all cognition of a universal is an error. (PVA 528) [618, xvi] In that case, what is the use of anything else being non-erroneous? For even when a universal is cognized, it does not bring about a cognition restricted to a specific individual. Consequently, the cognition of the universal is erroneous. If it is argued that while the cognition is erroneous regarding the individual, it is not so regarding the universal, that is incorrect.
If that [cognition] is subsumed within the individual, then what use is there for a universal?
A universal has no utility anywhere, such as in tasks like carrying loads or milking. (PVA 529)
If that which is the purpose for which this undertaking was begun is itself subverted by that very undertaking, [then it is futile].

But surely, without the apprehension of a universal, that very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) whose object is the particular would not be possible. But surely, even when the universal is ascertained, that same universal must be ascertained; how then could there be doubt regarding another? It is not logical for there to be doubt about one thing when another has been ascertained, for if everything were ascertained, it would follow that there is doubt about everything. Or perhaps it might be argued: only a possible object can be the domain of doubt, not any other. For instance: whatever is observed to be possible in a certain place is what may be subject to deviation in that place.

Upon seeing that [common property], doubt arises regarding that very [object]. (PVA 530) For doubt is not possible regarding what is impossible or what is non-deviant. When a common property is perceived, doubt occurs regarding that which is possible therein; for instance, when "cowness" is ascertained in a *śābaleya* cow, there is doubt regarding "horseness" in a *karka* horse, and thus there is no over-extension.
This is incorrect, because:
Since there is no cognition of anything else here beyond the mere cognition of a doubtful form such as "variegated" (*śavaleya*), how can there be a conceptualization of a universal?

"Is this a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow) or a *bāhuleya* (a black cow)? Only the sound of its bellowing is heard; we cannot ascertain the specific distinction such as being a *śābaleya* and so forth. Thus, people perceive only a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the form of a *śābaleya* and the like; in the same way, other conceptualizations of universals (*sāmānya*) are to be understood.
Alternatively:

Because cognition possesses a universal aspect that adheres to beginningless habitual tendencies, it is similar to conceptual construction; thus, there is no conceptualization of an object that is truly equal [to that aspect]. (PVA 532)

Therefore, the linguistic practice of affirmation and negation does not have an external substratum as its basis, because such things as co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible. Now, it may be argued that only the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) themselves are cognized by words and conceptual constructions, while the cognition of the possessor of those adjuncts occurs through "indication of what is indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇa*). If that is so, then the various adjuncts function as logical marks (*liṅga*); consequently, once the substance has been ascertained by means of that mark, there can be no doubt. Thus, what is the point of communicating further adjuncts? It might be replied: the substance is not known in its specific nature; for that purpose, other adjuncts are presented.
That is incorrect.
[619,xi] If that object were cognized by means of a single attribute in its own essential nature, [then it would be cognized in its entirety].

What else can the cognition of another qualification do? (533) Or, if that [entity] is perceived otherwise when one qualification is present, the association with another qualification is incapable of producing anything further. (534)

[619,xiii] Now, if it is held that only the mere connection with another attribute (*upādhyantara*) is what is conveyed by another word, and not the specific property (*viśeṣa*) itself; then, if it is conveyed in its isolation, how can there be the establishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? For causal efficiency cannot indeed be enjoined by the mere attribute alone. If it is argued that there is a cognition of the possessor of the attribute (*upādhimat*) by means of that [attribute], we say no, because it has already been conveyed by the previous attribute itself. If it is argued that the previous attribute conveys [the object] as being devoid of any other attribute, then this was stated by you yourself: "It cannot be [conveyed] by anything other than that. [619,xiv]

Now, if it is argued that although that [entity] is established as being otherwise by one limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) through a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could it be established as otherwise even by a thousand other limiting adjuncts? For what has been established by one valid cognition cannot be established otherwise by another valid cognition. Indeed, because it exists as inseparable from all its limiting adjuncts due to the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), how could it be cognized otherwise? Or, if it were so presented, since that very form belongs to it, how could it be established otherwise by another? Alternatively, if it is not the case that it is established otherwise by another, but rather there is merely a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) from elsewhere—whereas the exclusion of the other is certain because of impossibility—for it is impossible for something to be both endowed with those properties and endowed with properties other than them.
[619,xv] That is untrue, because:
If the attainment of other animals has been established by means of valid cognition,
it cannot be overturned even by a thousand superimpositions.
Alternatively, if others have not attained that object through valid cognition, [then it remains unestablished for them].
What is there here to be negated by another qualification? Indeed, nothing at all.

Therefore, by means of a non-erroneous cognition, the entire object of cognition is apprehended, just as in the case of the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, the demonstration of adventitious attributes (*upādhi*) is useless. If, however, the attributes were distinct and the possessor of attributes were distinct from them, then by the mere demonstration of the attributes—due to the definition being "indicated by what is not indicated" (*alakṣitalakṣaṇa*)—there would be no synthesis within a single substratum (*dharmin*). Alternatively, if even when the attributes are demonstrated, the possessors of the attributes [are apprehended], then, since there is a cognition through one attribute, all attributes would be grasped; for it is not the case that such a grasp does not occur through perception. Now, if it is argued that even by perception, sometimes only the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is grasped from a distance, whereas at close proximity the color (*varṇa*) is directly perceived; [we reply: this is not so.
That too is untenable.

If there were a perception of mere color and shape without a substance, then a substance would never be perceived, and it would follow that it is not a real entity. (537) (PVA) Now, if it is argued that shape cannot be apprehended without a substance...
Since even color is not a non-substantial entity, how then could it be a further substance?
(538) (PVA) Therefore, there is no co-referentiality.
If it is asked, "How is that so for you as well?", he says:
[620, viii]
With reference to a single subject (dharmin) which is the locus of various properties, [the sentence] prescribes one [property] while remaining indifferent toward the others that possess it. (232)
Just as the intellect, when there is a negation, constructs a conventional usage that has no real object—a usage that is both distinct from that [negated thing] and dependent upon other things. (233)
Having resorted to that very [conceptualization] which relies on a distinction of objects while remaining non-conceptual,
they do not invalidate the worldly object produced by beginningless latent predispositions.

[620,xi] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as a basis for apprehension; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the eye as a basis for apprehension, nor does he perceive forms, nor the eye-consciousness, nor the contact of the eye, nor the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the ear, nor sounds, nor the ear-consciousness, nor the contact of the ear, nor the feeling born of the contact of the ear as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the nose, nor odors, nor the nose-consciousness, nor the contact of the nose, nor the feeling born of the contact of the nose as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the tongue, nor tastes, nor the tongue-consciousness, nor the contact of the tongue, nor the feeling born of the contact of the tongue as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the body, nor tangibles, nor the body-consciousness, nor the contact of the body, nor the feeling born of the contact of the body as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the mind, nor mental phenomena, nor the mind-consciousness, nor the contact of the mind, nor the feeling born of the contact of the mind as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the element of earth as a basis for apprehension, nor the element of water, nor the element of fire, nor the element of wind, nor the element of space, nor the element of consciousness as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the realm of desire as a basis for apprehension, nor the realm of form, nor the formless realm as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the conditioned as a basis for apprehension, nor the unconditioned as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive the past as a basis for apprehension, nor the future, nor the present as a basis for apprehension. He does not perceive all dharmas as a basis for apprehension. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature."

Indeed, this conventional usage of ours, which concerns co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the like, is not ultimate; for it proceeds by relying on the meaning of words as something that does not exist as a real entity. To explain: the word "sound" is established as a subject (*dharmin*) in dependence upon the exclusion of non-sound (*aśabdavyāvṛtti*); and that sound is accepted as eternally persistent on the strength of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Furthermore, it is not excluded from being produced (*kṛtakatā*). Therefore, even though impermanence appears [to cognition], because its opposite conventional usage has been removed, it is established as if unperceived and as if non-existent. Consequently, when another convention is set in motion by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves impermanence, the object of the contrary convention is removed. At that time, it is understood that what was previously established and enjoined as existing is now [negated]. Thus, that subject—the referent of the word "sound"—is apprehended as having an essence that partakes of those properties. Upon negation, that [essence] is displaced; and when it is apprehended as distinct from that, it is perceived as depending on the properties contrary to it. Cognitions alone possess affirmation and negation; reality itself does not deviate from its such-like form. For instance, "I apprehended it exactly thus before"—that very same apprehension, being perceptual, is brought into the scope of conventional usage as such. But therein, nothing at all is enjoined or negated by successive conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

**(1) The meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha):** [620,xii] Indeed, conceptual constructions do not touch upon the form of a past cognition, because that [past cognition] does not exist at that time. For this very reason, the meaning of words and conceptual constructions is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), since it merely excludes error. But what then happens when there is no occurrence of error? For instance, immediately after perception, there is the conceptual construction "this is a jar," or the cognition of fire from smoke without any [prior] intervention. In those cases, how can the meaning of a word be the exclusion of others?
[621,i] This, too, is not well-founded. For instance:
Fire, which was previously the object of non-activity, has now been made the object of activity;
thus, even in that case, the state of being an object of non-activity is removed.

For instance: the ascertainment of fire says, "This fire is the object of my activity; why do you remain indifferent toward it? The purpose of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is merely to remove that state of indifference. For in that case, the fire is not perceived in its own form, nor is there a perception of it as something else. Furthermore, the cognition [of the word] is not a conceptualization of a real entity occurring subsequent to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because blue is not apprehended as the object of the word due to the absence of both prior and posterior forms. Indeed, the thought "this is that" is not a conceptual construction at all, because it is a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). If momentariness were not apprehended by it, then it would not be a perception; nor would it be a perception of the present. It has been explained, and will be further explained, that the very apprehension [of the object] is the apprehension of its momentariness. Therefore, linguistic conventions such as the relation between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are based upon the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For when the object of linguistic convention is a distinction between things, everything is logically consistent. Since that [object] itself is excluded from everything else, there is no exclusion other than that; thus, the unification of a single object would not occur through any other means. How then is there the expression "the impermanence of sound," where the case-ending is based on a distinction? It is like the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputraka*)."
[621,iv] But surely, since exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are non-different, how can there be distinction? For the exclusions of a real entity do not themselves differ.
This is not a fault;
for while they are differentiated conventionally, that differentiation does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Therefore, based on the nature of difference and non-difference between word and object, (PVA 540):
from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is never any difference; however, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), they possess both forms. For instance:

An object that bears its own fruit and one that does not bear its own fruit are distinct from each other; yet they appear as a single unity through various disturbances, as if their accumulation and depletion were being led along by those very factors.
Even one who does not possess that [quality] is brought [to mind] through some connection;
for those [cognitions] also rely on a distinction in perception, and therefore they are not aware of their own distortion. (236)

[621,x] Now, if this conventional usage is based merely upon latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) by way of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), why is it not considered non-contradictory by worldly people and not abandoned? Indeed, no one abandons a conventional usage that is non-contradictory. This has already been stated: “One should not conceptualize that [object] as being exactly thus,” and so forth. But how is this so? For even one who is utterly deluded does not remain without considering the sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

To this it is replied: Non-conceptualization follows from non-contradiction. For when non-contradiction is established, it is not appropriate for a person engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahārin*) to engage in further subtle investigation. Indeed, one who seeks non-contradiction is capable of conceptualizing only for the sake of attaining it.
Of what use, then, would an investigation into difference or non-difference be for such a person? [621,xii]
Causal efficacy does not arise from a distinct entity, as it does not occur from molasses [when one expects sugar].
(541) The emergence of causal efficacy occurs through the mere exclusion of what is other than that, which is what is actually obtained.

The differentiation of phenomena (*dharmabheda*), however, is imagined through the forms of cognition based on beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), which are restricted by their own effects and their opposites. Because it is connected to real entities, it is non-deceptive. In that regard, when investigating the difference in appearances, a person who has attained his desired result does not pay further heed. Even one intent on investigating the true nature of reality, when seeking its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), follows nothing but worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*).
As it has been said:
Established on the worldly path through the conventions of "form" and "designation," the ignorant and the wise are alike in their cognition and verbal expression. (543) (PVA)

Therefore, that subject (*dharmin*) is brought before the view—from some connection with conventional usage—by means of the disturbances characterized by conceptualization, which are based on distinctions of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), as if by accumulations and aggregations. It is brought within the path of vision from the characteristic of identity or origination to the characteristic of attainment. Consequently, those practitioners have fully understood the delusion. Therefore, exclusion from the non-existent dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) or from the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is not contradictory.
(2) Refutation of the Permanence of the Self:

Furthermore, when the selflessness of jars and so forth is established, the pervasion (vyāpti) between the absence of breath and the like is established, but not otherwise. Nor is it established that a self does not exist in jars and so forth.
Furthermore, because it functions to establish existence, that which is non-existent would be doubtful;
moreover, its non-existence is not tenable, since it is accepted on the basis of [your own] lack of valid cognition. (237)

For since the self is doubted in the living body, how could it be free from doubt in a jar or similar object? Indeed, that which is doubted cannot be made an object of cognition by a probans such as breath or anything else. And therefore:

Even though there is no exclusion from non-existent things, its exclusion from the similar class (sapakṣa) is doubtful; and its exclusion from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is doubtful because of doubt regarding that [non-existence]. // 238 //

[622,vii] When there is doubt regarding the self, only jars and the like would constitute the similar instances (sapakṣa). Therefore, the exclusion from the similar instances is doubtful. Consequently, how can this be a negative-only (vyatirekin) reason?
[622,viii]

But surely, according to the Buddhist admission, jars and other things are indeed devoid of a self (*nirātman*). If that is so, then by the principle that "all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self," there would likewise be no self even in the living body. If you argue that the Buddhist admission is simply without proof, then in that case, jars and other things would also not be devoid of a self due to that same admission; thus, the very same fault remains. For:
When a restriction is established in one instance, the exclusion [of its opposite] is necessarily established.
Even when the two categories have been seen as real, there may still be doubt regarding those things that have not been seen. (239)

Even when there is non-perception, if things are not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perceptibility (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), there is only doubt. For no one is capable of proving non-existence based on mere non-perception alone. Furthermore, although the absence of a self (*ātman*) in jars and the like is established, even so, vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not capable of proving the self. This is because their exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) is not established, since their presence there is also possible.

[Objection: But how can that which is excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa) exist in that very same place? For it is not logical that one and the same thing be both devoid of self and possess vital breaths and so forth; indeed, this "half-old-woman" approach is inadmissible, as a restriction to a single nature is alone appropriate.
[Response: This is not so, because:

There are objects that, although not pervading their individual instances, belong to a genus; there is no certainty observed in some cases, as with the property of being scratchable by iron applying to all earthen things. (240)
If no contradiction is observed in the case of existence, who could dispel doubt?

[623,i] For it is not the case that everything is identical simply because it is "selfless" (nirātman), such that by virtue of being selfless, the living body would be devoid of breath and so forth. Rather, some things are selfless yet possess breath and so on, while others are otherwise. Just as some things composed of earth are scratchable by iron while others are not; for instance: Thus it is said:
If a contradiction is not observed even when [the two properties] exist together, who could dispel doubt?

Indeed, it is not the case that the exclusion of breath and so forth from selflessness is established through a lack of proven contradiction with selflessness. For selflessness is not contradicted by breath and so forth—either through their non-coexistence or by any other definition of contradiction—such that it would exclude them. Now, if it is argued that even in the absence of direct contradiction, there is contradiction through a mediated succession, and thus breath and so forth are the excluders of selflessness—that is incorrect, because:
In some cases, due to restriction, what else could it be? And that [restriction] exists because of its being of the nature of that effect. (241)

[623, vi] If breath and the other [vital functions] were restricted to the self, there would be an indirect contradiction with selflessness (*nairātmya*), because that which is pervaded is also contradicted by the contradiction of its pervader. However, there is no such restriction of breath and the rest to the self, because a restriction is impossible without identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from it (*tadutpatti*). Otherwise, restriction would be unaccountable. Furthermore, it is not established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that breath and the rest are either effects of the self or identical in nature to the self.
Therefore, its exclusion even from selflessness is doubtful for him.

"Even from selflessness" means because there is no necessary connection with a self. Its exclusion is doubtful; for that which is not connected to something does not necessarily turn away from its opposite.
[623,ix] Let it be so; nevertheless, the self is not established by means of non-selfhood. ॥ 242 ॥

By this [reasoning], he does not accept the non-existence of that which possesses exclusion as being an existent thing, just as he does not accept [the existence of] breath and so forth in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) even though there is no exclusion [of them from it]. (243)
If a reason lacks exclusion from the similar class (sapakṣa), then it is a reason that possesses positive concomitance (anvayin).
If it lacks positive concomitance and lacks exclusion [from the dissimilar class], then "that which is not selfless is not possessed of a self. (244)

Just as there is no presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) even when the absence of the similar class is non-existent, so too, even in the absence of selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is no self in the living body.

[Objection: Is this not an uneven presentation? For in the case of the similar class (*sapakṣa*), even though there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there is no positive presence (*bhāva*) because that [reason] does not exist there; for a positive presence is impossible when something is non-existent. In the living body, however, because that [reason] exists, there is necessarily a positive presence despite the absence of negative concomitance, since the other category (the dissimilar class) is absent. [Reply: This is true. The desired conclusion is not established merely by an uneven presentation. If there is no absence in the similar class, then that very presence has not been excluded. But when absence is excluded, there is necessarily presence; for presence is simply the exclusion of absence.

[623,xv] If it is argued that this is not so because of the absence of similar instances (*sapakṣa*), we say no, for such an absence is untenable. For if there were breath and so forth, how could there be an absence of similar instances? Just as when there is no similar instance, there is no reversal [of the reason] even though there is an exclusion of non-breathing and so forth, so too in the case of a living body, there would be no reversal even though there is an exclusion of selflessness (*anātmatva*). Now, if it is argued that there is no reversal because the living body exists, whereas in the case of the similar instance there is none because it is non-existent—since a positive entity cannot possibly exist in what is non-existent—[we reply: no.

In that case, it follows that non-existence itself has not been excluded. For there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence; thus, while existence is excluded, there is no contradiction with non-existence, and so it is not excluded. Just as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is non-existent, so too is it in that case. Indeed, there is no contradiction between non-existence and non-existence.

Now, if that non-existence also does not exist therein, then even though there is the exclusion of selflessness (*nairātmya*) from the living body, there would still be no exclusion of selflessness. This is because, just as in the case of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), even if there is both presence and absence, there is no absence [of the reason], since it exists there—if this is your argument, it is not so. Why? Because:
How indeed can that which is errant with respect to another sentient being be restricted?
Otherwise, how could that which is errant due to its own defect be [restrained] by another? (PVA 544)

[624,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is nothing whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One; there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because of this very reason that the Tathāgata is called ‘Tathāgata. Subhūti, if there were a dharma that the Tathāgata had fully awakened to, he would not be called ‘Tathāgata. Why is that? Subhūti, the term ‘Tathāgata’ is a mere designation.
