For how could that which is itself variable be non-variable with respect to another entity, or otherwise? Furthermore, if something that is non-existent is neither existent nor non-existent when [something] is existent, why is it not accepted that even what is non-existent is neither existent nor non-existent in relation to the existent? Just as a non-existent thing lacks the status of being a locus (*ādhāra*), so too it lacks the status of being a located object (*ādheya*); thus, this [objection] is trivial. Moreover, this has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, selflessness (*nairātmya*) is not merely the absence of existence, but rather the absence of a self characterized by specific attributes. And the absence of such a self is not established simply by the non-perception of specific attributes. Indeed, absences do not differ from one another; for they differ only when there is a difference in the positive entities (*bhāva*) of which they are the absences. In the absence of a restriction regarding positive entities, how could there be a distinction among their absences? Nor is a self perceived as having specific attributes, such that its absence could be established through the contrary of that perception. Therefore, in the case of the absence of selfhood, there is merely the cessation of an absence, but no establishment of a self. Consequently:
If a reason lacks exclusion from the similar class (*sapakṣa*), then that reason is one possessing positive concomitance (*anvayin*);
if it lacks positive concomitance, it does not possess exclusion, as in the case: "That which is not selfless is not possessed of a self. (PVA 545)
Furthermore, there is the summary verse [624, viii]:
That whose own nature is established as being invariably concomitant with its activities is, for that reason, the very thing that causes cessation; and it is also the instigator of activity. (245)

[624,x] That very smoke whose nature is invariably concomitant with fire, as established in its occurrences and operations, is the producer of fire; it [is the producer] when it itself is present, and not otherwise. Furthermore, in its occurrence, that very fire is the producer of the smoke and so forth; such indeed is the path of those who follow valid cognition.
And that invariable concomitance (nāntarīyakatā) depends upon a means of proof;
for the perception [of the effect when the cause is present] and the non-perception [of the effect when the cause is absent] constitute, indeed, the causal relation. (246)
Indeed, the demonstration of invariable concomitance through observation and non-observation does not establish itself without the proof of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

[Objection: But surely, for two distinct things, the proof of the necessary concomitance (*anāntarīyakatā*) of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not achieved by perception and non-perception (*dṛṣṭyadṛṣṭī*). [Response: No, because it is precisely those two—perception and non-perception—that constitute the causal relation. For there is no causal relation other than positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), nor are there positive and negative concomitances other than perception and non-perception. However, for one who holds that: "Of a separate entity (*arthāntara*), there is no necessary absence when that [other thing] is absent; thus, [the causal relation] is not understood. [This is the view of the opponent.]

[624,xv] It is not a proof for another entity because it lacks invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*). Even if that [entity] exists, there is no necessary rule that another must be absent; thus, there is no comprehension of its absence when the other is absent, because it lacks pervasiveness (*vyāpakatā*). And that which is not pervasive, when it ceases, cannot cause another to cease. Furthermore, the self is not established as pervasive; how then could it be the cause of the cessation of breath and so forth? For this reason: [625,i]
Because their non-existence is impossible, they must exist eternally in the absence [of those conditions]. || 247 ||

[625,ii] For the self does not itself cease to exist across different places and times, because it possesses the nature of being eternal and all-pervading. Therefore, the claim that vital functions such as breath would be absent due to its absence is unproven.
[The diversity of forms arises from the differentiation of the powers of the causal complex.]

[625,iii] Now, if the self were the cause of the vital breaths and so forth merely by virtue of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, it would not require negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Would this not imply that every causal relationship everywhere is of such a nature?
That too is incorrect, because:
[625,v] Since the various distinctions of effects and intrinsic natures arise from their causes.
Without those [causes], how could that produced form arise from anything else? (249)

If the causal relationship were established by mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone, then it would follow that the effect could exist even in the absence of those [causes]. Consequently, since the effect would arise from something else even without them, how could it possess a nature produced by those [specific causes]? If you argue that it will indeed arise from something else, we say no; for from something else, that specific nature would not exist.
If it were not of that nature, it would simply not exist; for:
[625, viii] Indeed, the manifold nature of things arises from the diversity of the potencies of their causal complexes.
If that [difference] were not a differentiator, this world would have attained a single form.

[625,ix] But how is it known that difference arises from a difference in the causal complex? Difference is indeed perceived; whether this is due to a difference in causes or otherwise is a separate matter of inquiry.
That is incorrect; for:
[625,xi] The self is postulated as unperceived on the basis of its necessary connection with breath and so forth.
Without a necessary rule, how could there be an obstruction for that?

(PVA 546) Just as the self is all-pervading and eternal, and a cause by mere concomitance, so too are space and the other elements. Therefore, since the movement of space and so forth would be like that of the self, the intended object is not established.

[625, xiii] Now, if the vital breaths and so forth do not exist without a self as their impeller, then the self is inferred to be like one who inflates a bellows, or like one who moves the eyeball by means of the sense organs, or like a spectator looking through a window by means of vision. [625, xiv]
That too is incorrect, because:
[625,xv] For that which is inactive and all-pervading cannot possibly be a motivator, as there is no proof for it.
Since perception does not occur without the instruments of action, the self is not established [as a distinct entity].

For one who blows a bellows is an agent and an impeller; likewise, [the self] would not be so because of its non-pervasiveness. How, then, could it be an impeller? Indeed, for that which is of a pervasive form, being an impeller is not logically tenable. If it were an impeller, there would have to be another impeller for it as well, leading to an infinite regress. Furthermore, a person situated behind a window-lattice is endowed with the instruments such as the eyes and so forth, but the self is not of such a nature; how then could it be a spectator? If one argues that it too possesses instruments, then the same logic of the "window-lattice" applies there as well, resulting in nothing but an infinite regress.

Moreover: the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in the case of fire and so forth is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). How could that be otherwise here? If it were [established] there too by positive concomitance alone, then it would follow that [the effect] could arise from something else even without those [causes]. Alternatively, negative concomitance is also possible. And thus, for that which arises without them—even from something else such as the head of Indra—how could it have fire as its cause? If you say it is produced by both, no; since it arises from something other than those, neither of the two is the cause. Therefore, for that which arises from something else, there can be neither the status of being an effect of that [fire] nor the status of being an effect of something else; thus, the very notion of a causal relationship would be lost. This being the case, since the difference or non-difference of effects depends on the difference or non-difference of causes, those two [properties] would not exist due to the absence of that [causal relationship]. If you ask, "How can this [causal relationship] be rejected when it is actually perceived?"—no, for perception itself is impossible if a causal relationship is impossible.

For blue is indeed perceived from the cognition of blue when there is a restriction in that perception; otherwise, it is not perceived at all. Thus, the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognition is established. (PVA 548)

If there were a fixed rule that such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces only erroneous or non-erroneous cognitions, then there would be a definite restriction regarding the objects of cognition (*prameya*). Otherwise, if it were merely a random appearance, it would follow that all worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*) would be destroyed.
Now, if it is argued that the appearance itself is differentiated from others and is an object of cognition through the means of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
that too is untrue.
The worldly convention of the world is not established by mere appearance alone; for when there is the manifestation of that much, what further purpose remains to be accomplished? (PVA 549)

For the worldly convention of discerning persons is that an entity capable of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is to be accepted, while another is otherwise. That which is a mere appearance, existing as such for only a single moment, is neither to be rejected nor accepted. Likewise, since it is mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*) and non-dual, there is neither difference nor non-difference. Furthermore, that relation of cause and effect is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Since the self (*ātman*) is not the cause of anything, there can be no inference of it from anything whatsoever. Therefore: [626, ix]
For the manifold nature of things arises from the diversity of the capacities of their causal complexes;
if that [diversity] were non-differentiating, this world would necessarily be of a single form.
(PVA 626, x)

"Just as [the claim that] it is of a single form means it is neither to be abandoned nor acquired, being a mere appearance and non-dual; yet, since there is also a fiery nature in the head of Śakra, which is distinct from that [non-dual nature], fire will arise from that [distinct nature] as well. To this, he says:
"If there were both the state of being differentiated and the state of being non-differentiated, the nature of being non-distinct would be contradicted."
If a single entity were to possess manifold forms, then there would be two forms: fire and that which is other.

Since the distinction between categories is characterized by a difference in form, fire alone is the producer of smoke; thus, there is no deviation in the case of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). Indeed, within that nature of fire, there is nothing else such as the head of Śakra. As for that form by which it would be distinct, that [form] is simply not its producer; so how could there be any suspicion of deviation?
If that which is the non-production of one thing were the very nature of another, then how could that [nature] possibly belong to it if it were not its own non-production? (251)
Therefore, the natures of cause and effect are mutually determined.
Consequently, when that [cause] is perceived, it is understood even from the effect, just as in the case of one's own perception.
[626,xv] But is it not so?
How can one [effect] arise from many, as in the case of the moisture from milk and water?
Since moisture arises from the power of fluidity, that power is indeed one and the same in both. (253)
Is its nature different or non-different? And how could there be fluidity if it were different?
For it is said that [the cognition] is non-different because the cognition, which has that form, is non-different. (254)

Indeed, milk and water do not possess an identical nature because they are excluded from other hard forms; their oneness is due to this exclusion. The same applies to the effect, which is moistening (*vikleda*). For even moistening is not ultimately identical; rather, it is designated as such through the exclusion of what is other than it. Thus, there is no logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Similarly, even though there is difference, fire is the basis for the cognition "fire"; by whichever aspect it possesses smoke, by that very aspect it is so apprehended. (255)

Because smoke arises from a causal factor that is fire itself, yet depends on other conditions, it is non-deviant with respect to that [fire]; likewise, an effect is similarly [non-deviant] with respect to another [cause]. (255)

"In the same way" means just like milk and water; even though there is a difference due to the exclusion of what is other than that fluidity, it is like being the basis for the cognition of a substance (*dravya*). Likewise, difference is also the basis for the cognition of fire precisely through the exclusion of what is other than that. By whichever aspect—that is, by being the cause of the cognition of fire—it is by that very aspect that there is comprehension. This is because in other cases there is deviation from the substance. Since smoke does not arise without being a constituent part of the cognition of fire, there is no deviation from that. For instance: [627,vii] It is as follows:

Since fire resides in that which possesses smoke, fuel, transformation, and parts, if this smoke were not accompanied by fire, it would not be smoke; and if it is smoke, then it must possess fire. (257)

Smoke and the transformation of fuel are merely parts of those two; fire is not something other than them. Therefore, if that [fire] characterized by heat and so forth were the head of Śakra or the like, then it would not be smoke, but rather chaff and such.

Why is this so? For that which is not perceived cannot be subject to a restrictive rule such as "it does not occur otherwise. Well then, blue also does not occur otherwise at another time. Why is this? If it is argued that "if that were the case, it would simply not be blue," this is the same [as our point]. It would mean "it would simply not be smoke. Why is this? This applies equally elsewhere as well. [Objection: But blue and the like are defined by their own nature (*svarūpa*); they do not exist when their own nature is absent. Smoke and the like, however, are defined by being produced; even there, it is the very nature [of the cause] that serves as the definition. Therefore, these two cases are not the same.
To this, it is said:
The status of a thing as a real entity does not depend merely on the appearance of its own form in reality;
for the appearance of a form is the same for those who possess erroneous knowledge and those who possess its opposite.

For the manifestation of mere intrinsic forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth is the same for both erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions; thus, no real entity is established. The distinction between cause and effect, however, is produced by conceptual construction. Enough of this digression. If it is asked, "How is there an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) in the case of the essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*)?", it is said in response: [627,xv] To this it is replied:
The state of being inseparable (nāntarīyakatā) should be understood according to its respective cause,
as was previously stated regarding the nature of destruction and the property of being produced. (258)

It has already been established that destruction is necessarily concomitant with the mere entity; therefore, there is no need for a re-chewing of what has already been chewed. Consequently, the causal relation is defined solely by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); since this does not exist between the self and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, they are not indicators [of the self].
This entire intention belongs to the Teacher as well. If one asks, "Why is this so? [it is because:
"All this logic regarding the non-causality of a negative concomitant (vyatirekin)..."
It is to be inferred from the statement that it is "audible," made for the sake of demonstrating parity. (259)

[628,iv] It should be understood that this entire logical principle is also intended by the Teacher (*ācārya*), since he demonstrated that the reason "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*)— which is a purely negative (*vyatirekin*) reason— is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for the purpose of explaining the similarity between all such negative reasons and their examples.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that the purely negative (vyatirekin) reason is not a valid logical mark (*hetu*). This is because every purely negative reason is dissimilar to the case of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), and because that [audibility] is inconclusive due to its being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). To explain:
the exclusion from both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is not real.
It is called "negative-only" (vyatirekin) merely because its presence is possible through observation alone.

Apart from the two groups—the eternal and the non-eternal, and the selfless and the possessing-a-self—there is no other group. This is because the mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence is ontologically real; otherwise, the world would be incoherent and devoid of all conventional discourse. Nor is there anything that could belong to neither category. If audibility were not excluded from both the eternal and the non-eternal, then it would simply not exist at all, as it would lack a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). If it is argued that sound itself is the locus, we say no; the same fault applies to "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) as well. That too would not exist, since it is likewise excluded from everything. For instance: [628, viii]
When there is doubt regarding the permanence or impermanence of sound, the adducing of a reason is intended to resolve it.
If that reason is deficient on both counts, how can there be doubt between those two?

For it is not the case that doubt regarding those two [permanence and impermanence] could arise concerning something already ascertained as being excluded from them. If that is so, then audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) is not the cause of doubt, since doubt arises from sound-ness (*śabdatva*) alone.
[628,x] But surely, if there is doubt because of sound-ness, why should there not be another factor besides it that also possesses the status of being a cause of doubt?

[628,xi] But surely, that which has been observed in one place, when observed elsewhere, would give rise to suspicion regarding it; and it is precisely this that is called being a cause of doubt. Why then is audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) not a cause of doubt?
This is not so; for:
[628, xiii] Since, when something is perceived, it is established by way of affirmation, whereas here [in the case of non-perception], there is negation in the face of doubt.
When there is doubt regarding existence and non-existence, what is the point of adopting one's own position?

(PVA 554) For where there is doubt regarding a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, that doubt occurs through the door of perception in an affirmative manner; whereas in the case of the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), it occurs through negation. What, then, is the difference between these two?

[628,xv] But surely, since audibility is not observed in either the eternal or the non-eternal, it is logical that it should be a cause for non-comprehension of those two; for it is observed precisely as a door to non-comprehension.
This is not correct; for:
[628,xvii] When the exclusion of one thing occurs necessarily from its counter-positive...
For when there is a contradiction between two things that cannot coexist through their modes of being, there is no exclusion of both;
indeed, it is not possible for both mutually contradictory things to be excluded from a single locus, nor can neutrality be maintained here.

[629,i] But surely, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both [existence and non-existence] in one place, the doubt arises precisely from that lack of evidence, not from the reason of "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*). At most, that [reason] is simply a cause for non-comprehension. If that is so, then even in the case of a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), the doubt arises only from the lack of a means of valid cognition, not from the reason itself. That [common inconclusive reason] is indeed a cause of doubt by way of being observed; audibility, too, is similar, as it is a cause of doubt by way of not being observed.
Furthermore, if there is doubt, then the removal of that doubt does not follow from it; thus, it is called a cause of doubt. Since audibility is exactly like this, this [argument] is trivial.
Moreover:
The state of being an object of cognition is observed in both; why does it not produce certainty in both?
For when there is the conjunction of seeing both, there would be [certainty] for both as well. (PVA 556)

For whatever is seen in a certain place must produce a cognition of that very thing; how then could there be a reliance on a second part, namely that "it does not exist"? Now, it is not logical for two mutually contradictory things to exist in one and the same place. If this is so, then the doubt resides in the subject itself (*pakṣa*) and is not mediated by the subject. Even when there is perception, the doubt is mediated by the doubt regarding the subject; that is the same even when there is no perception of either side.

But surely, doubt is produced by exclusion from one side alone, because there is certainty through its being excluded from both sides. For that which is excluded from two groups—other than which no third possibility exists—is the cause for non-cognition in that very form. And thus this has been called a "negative-only" (*vyatirekin*) reason even by the Teacher. As he said: "That uncommon property of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) which encompasses all [instances] through whatever differentiation is the cause of doubt; because it encompasses those possessing that [property], and because of its exclusion from one side alone, how can this be a cause of doubt merely from exclusion? [629, vii]
This is not so.
For it has been stated that the ascertainment of a thing arises from its exclusion by two [alternatives].

Otherwise, if that [non-existence] were present elsewhere, there would be a certainty of non-existence for both as well. (557) (PVA) Furthermore, how can that which excludes [one thing] from that very place cause doubt?
Since it is other than those two, the exclusion of that [absence] does not establish a negation for both. (558) (PVA)

For how could that which is excluded from something else not establish its exclusion? Now, it might be argued that it is a cause for non-comprehension precisely because it establishes the exclusion of both.
This is not so; for:
[629, xiii] Every reason possesses the status of a reason in establishing a specific exclusion.
It is established that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is proven by means of words and logical marks (*liṅga*).

(PVA 559) [629,xiv] It is true that a reason (*hetu*) only establishes the exclusion of others; however, it does so by implying the affirmation of something else. In this case, however, nothing else is implied, because both [the positive and the negative] have ceased. But through "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), there is an implication of impermanence by way of the exclusion of permanence.
This is true. [629,xvi]
Nothing other than the constant exclusion [of others] is prescribed as impermanence;
for by the very exclusion of what is other, the purpose of inference is accomplished.

Inference fulfills its purpose merely by excluding the superimposition of permanence upon that which is impermanent; for when one of the two alternatives—permanence or impermanence—is excluded, the other is established by itself. If it is argued that even this [exclusion] might not occur at some point, we say no, because it is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*). [Objection: How so in the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*)? [Reply: Let that be for now. However, if both [alternatives] were excluded by the property of being inaudible (*śrāvaṇatva*), then the establishment of their opposite would be established by perception, and thus [the reason] would indeed be a valid reason (*hetu*). [Objection: But if it is established by another reason that proves only one of those two, then it is not a [valid] reason. [Reply: No. When something is established by perception, how could there be another [reason]?

[630,i] The Blessed One said this: "Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who have entered the stream and are not subject to falling back. What are these four? They are: one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry through the path of seeing; one who has attained it through the path of cultivation; one who has attained it through the path of no-more-learning; and one who has attained it through the path of the non-returner. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons who have entered the stream and are not subject to falling back. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having understood that the Blessed One had risen and entered his dwelling, addressed the monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen and entered his dwelling after saying: 'Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons who have entered the stream and are not subject to falling back... When this was said, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita asked the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, what is the distinction, what is the difference between one who has entered the stream through the path of seeing and one who has entered the stream through the path of cultivation? "Friend Koṭṭhita, the person who has entered the stream through the path of seeing has abandoned the three fetters: identity view, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals. The person who has entered the stream through the path of cultivation has, in addition to those, attenuated sensual desire and ill will. This, friend, is the distinction, this is the difference between one who has entered the stream through the path of seeing and one who has entered the stream through the path of cultivation. "What is the distinction, friend, between one who has entered the stream through the path of cultivation and one who has entered the stream through the path of no-more-learning? "Friend, the person who has entered the stream through the path of cultivation has abandoned the five lower fetters. The person who has entered the stream through the path of no-more-learning has abandoned all defilements without remainder. This, friend, is the distinction... "What is the distinction, friend, between one who has entered the stream through the path of no-more-learning and one who has entered the stream through the path of the non-returner? "Friend, the person who has entered the stream through the path of no-more-learning has realized the fruit of arhatship. The person who has entered the stream through the path of the non-returner has abandoned the five lower fetters and will attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. This, friend, is the distinction, this is the difference between one who has entered the stream through the path of no-more-learning and one who has entered the stream through the path of the non-returner. When this was said, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, friend Ānanda! Well said, friend Ānanda! It is wonderful how well this matter has been explained by the Venerable Ānanda. Now we understand the distinction, the difference between these four kinds of persons who have entered the stream and are not subject to falling back. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Delighted, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Ānanda. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks! "Venerable sir," they replied. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons who have entered the stream and are not subject to falling back. What are the four? Here, monks, a certain person has entered the stream through the path of seeing; another has entered the stream through the path of cultivation; another has entered the stream through the path of no-more-learning; and another has entered the stream through the path of the non-returner. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons who have entered the stream and are not subject to falling back. [The rest of the discourse follows the same structure as above. Thus have I heard. The reason must be either a negator or an affirmer. Now, perception does not perform negation; therefore, the affirmation or negation of one thing by another is not established through "audibility" (śrāvaṇatva). If there were an exclusion of both, how could there be affirmation by another? Otherwise, if there were affirmation by yet another in that case as well, how could even that other have the status of a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa)? Thus, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases. Furthermore, perception is not a non-negator; for if it were so, it would not be an affirmer either. Affirmation is the presentation of a real entity (vastu), and a real entity is not presented without the negation of what is other than it. Why is this so? [Because...]
That entity would either be unmixed with anything else or mixed with another.
If it were mixed with another, it would not be an entity from the perspective of conventional usage. (561) (PVA)
Likewise, even from another, the negation cannot possibly arise.

On this point, it is investigated: Is a thing, by its own nature, excluded from others or not? If it is excluded, is it so apprehended by perception or not? If it is apprehended, how can there be a non-denial of the other? For that very exclusion of the other is precisely what constitutes its appearing as a distinct form through the avoidance of the other; otherwise, because cognition would be confused, there would be no practical activity (*vyavahāra*), and thus the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be fruitless. If it is argued that the practical activity of excluding one thing by another is accomplished by a different means of valid cognition, that too is incorrect. Why? Because:
If that which is cognized by perception were sublated by another [means of knowledge],
then, given the invalidity of perception, the other [means of knowledge] would also be invalid. (PVA 563)

[630, vii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those suffering beings and, by means of his compassionate power, caused them all to attain liberation from suffering. Thereupon, he addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "If there be any good sons or good daughters who wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should thus observe: 'All five aggregates are empty of self and what belongs to self. When one observes in this way, the mind is neither perverted nor disturbed; and because there is no perverted or disturbed mind, fear arises not. Having transcended all error and delusion, one ultimately attains Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying upon the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra, which can remove all suffering and is true and not false. If perception were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), what confidence could there be in anything else? If [the opponent claims that] the mixing with another object is itself the other [means of knowledge], then even by a hundred other means of knowledge there can be no negation; for it is impossible to alter the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [of a thing]. If [it is argued that] the negation is based on the fact that [the object] is unmixed in some respect, then that form in which there is mixing must also have been grasped by perception itself. Otherwise, if it were grasped differently, how could there be the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the object? [If it is argued: "The understanding of exclusion occurs through the cognition of another [person]," [we reply: if it is cognized differently by another, then—as has already been established—there would be a lack of confidence in all cases.
As soon as one has entered from a camel into the womb, there arises another perception within the interior of the womb; because this is directly perceived, it sublates the previous one. (PVA 564)

[630,ix] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal. He does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive form as unreal; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive forms as unreal; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the eye-consciousness as unreal; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as unreal; he does not perceive the feelings born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the earth element as unreal; he does not perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive ignorance as unreal; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real, nor does he perceive them as unreal. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the conditioned as unreal; he does not perceive the unconditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as unreal. He does not perceive the world as real, nor does he perceive the world as unreal; he does not perceive the transcendence of the world as real, nor does he perceive the transcendence of the world as unreal. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the stream-enterer as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry as unreal. He does not perceive the once-returner as real, nor does he perceive the once-returner as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of once-returning as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of once-returning as unreal. He does not perceive the non-returner as real, nor does he perceive the non-returner as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of non-returning as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of non-returning as unreal. He does not perceive the arhat as real, nor does he perceive the arhat as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of arhatship as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of arhatship as unreal. He does not perceive the pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the pratyekabuddha as unreal; he does not perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood as unreal. He does not perceive the Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the Tathāgata as unreal; he does not perceive the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as real, nor does he perceive the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as unreal. Subhūti, this is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Subhūti and those monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas praised what the Blessed One had spoken. For at the first entry into the inner chamber, the first perception is indeed not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); therefore, it is sublated by that [subsequent cognition], but it is not itself a valid means of knowledge. Consequently, if the apprehension of the word as excluded from both [categories] were established by perception, then there would be no doubt regarding the other [category], nor otherwise, such as through its audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*). Therefore, because audibility is not excluded [from either category], there is doubt. Thus, every [reason] is a negative-only (*vyatirekin*) one. However, the Teacher [Dignāga] propounded the negative-only reason by taking recourse to mere non-perception (*adarśanamātra*). How then is the statement "because of exclusion from one side" (*ekāntavyāvṛtteḥ*) to be understood? It does not mean "because of exclusion with absolute certainty" (*ekāntena niścaye vyāvṛtteḥ*), but rather "because of the exclusion of absolute certainty" (*ekāntasya niścayasya vyāvṛtteḥ*). For there is no certainty regarding this [word's existence] in the eternal or the non-eternal, whether by its presence or its absence. Therefore, in the ultimate sense, there is indeed no exclusion; hence, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). Thus, for now, the phrase "distinction from dispute" (*vivādād bheda*) has been explained.

[630,x] Now, generality (*sāmānya*) is explained. Just as that which is exclusively excluded (*ekāntavyāvṛtta*) is a negative (*vyatirekin*) indicator, so too is that which is exclusively concomitant (*ekāntānvayin*). For instance:
Sound is impermanent because it is an object of cognition, just like a jar and other such things;
since this reason is excluded from non-existent things such as space, it is a positive concomitant (*anvayin*).

For space has neither existence nor non-existence, because it is non-existent. Therefore, a reason that possesses an invariable positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is indeed a means of cognition (*gamaka*).
This is not so.
[630,xiv] For even if this [non-existence] is not possible on the side of the non-existence of space,
nevertheless its status as an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is not in any way negated. (PVA 566)

[631,i] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding those beings, through his great compassion, liberates them from those fivefold bonds of existence. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a person possessed of faith hears that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such power and virtue, and if they call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, then all their perils shall immediately be extinguished. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit. If there were someone who, for the sake of others, were to fill as many world-systems as there are sands in the Ganges River with the seven precious jewels and offer them as a gift to the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; and if there were another who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, were to bear it in mind for even a single moment—Śāriputra, the latter would generate far more merit than the former. Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness upon those who are afraid. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be any women who, during their lives, desire to be born as men, they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara; by the power of that Bodhisattva’s vow, they shall immediately be transformed into men and shall never again fall back into the female form. Śāriputra, if there be any women who, at the end of their lives, desire to be born in the presence of the Buddha Amitāyus in the world-realm of Sukhāvatī, they should call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara; by the power of that Bodhisattva’s vow, they shall immediately be born there. Śāriputra, if there be any women who, throughout their lives, practice the ten wholesome paths of action, and if they call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara at the time of death, they shall not fall into the three evil realms, but shall immediately be born among gods and humans. Śāriputra, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the bodhisattva path, they should take the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as their teacher and serve him. Why is this? Because, Śāriputra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great compassionate master who can grant fearlessness to all living beings.
