Even non-existent things possess, in some sense, the status of being objects of cognition (*prameyatā*); otherwise, there could be no linguistic or practical activity (*vyavahāra*) through affirmation and negation. For existence alone cannot be the object of such activity. Indeed, the natures of entities are established in mutual exclusion; they are the domain of linguistic activity, for otherwise, due to the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), they would be non-entities. Furthermore, if there were no distinction between self and other for those seeking causal efficiency, who would engage in activity, where, or for what purpose? Everything would become nothing but non-existent. For one who does not cognize the opponent’s position as non-existent is unable to establish their own position. Moreover, space must necessarily be cognized as the mere absence of obstructive objects; otherwise, it would follow that one could not even move from one place to another. Therefore, by establishing existent entities according to their specific determinations, non-existence itself is established as an object of cognition. It is called an "object of cognition" (*prameya*) because it is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For a means of valid cognition does not have only a real entity as its object; since the definition of a means of valid cognition is "ascertainment," it is precisely the act of ascertainment that constitutes the means of valid cognition, provided it is not sublated regarding its own object by another [cognition]. Thus, because it is ascertainable by a cognition that establishes non-contradiction in practical activity, non-existence is indeed an object of cognition. Consequently, the reason "because it is an object of cognition" does not have an unerring positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Therefore, due to its being common to both [the similar and dissimilar instances], it is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Now, if "being an object of cognition" is said to mean only being ascertainable by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then, since perception arises from a real entity, "being an object of cognition" would be nothing but the capacity for causal efficiency. From this, it follows that the capacity for causal efficiency alone is the indicator (*gamaka*). And since that [capacity] is possible even for a non-entity through the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) [of others], how can it be a reason with positive concomitance (*anvayin*)? It has already been demonstrated that even for a non-existent thing, there is exclusion.

By this, properties such as being an entity (*vastutva*) and so forth are also explained. Therefore, the logical reason (*hetu*) characterized by effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*) is exclusively one that possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
But surely, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) has also been established as a third type of reason, by such statements as: "In all cases, however, negation is established through non-apprehension.

Now, this [passage] might be intended as a demonstration of the divisions of reasons that have real entities (*vastu*) as their objects. If that were so, then the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of non-apprehension would have to be demonstrated; yet it has already been established that there is no mode of connection other than identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).
To this, it is said:
The absence of the pervader and the cause leads to the cognition of the absence of the pervaded and the effect;
there is no other means for establishing such an absence.

For what is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is not some independent object of linguistic convention; rather, it is simply the very thing intended [to be absent]. And that thing, while being doubted, cannot be established as "not existing" by virtue of its being beyond perception (*parokṣa*). For its non-perception alone is not the means of cognition (*gamika*) regarding its absence, because [the object] meets the conditions for non-perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*). However, its absence is established in this way: if its cause does not exist. And in that case, since that very [necessary connection] has been shown to be twofold—namely, the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) and the relation of causality (*tadutpatti*)—non-perception is indeed a proof based on a proven necessary connection (*siddhapratibandhika*).
< 5. Anupalabdhicintā >
[1. Non-apprehension is a separate reason.
Why is no example provided? Because it has indeed already been provided.

Because the exclusion of the object is described precisely through the exclusion of the nature of the cause, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is stated as a "proven example" (*siddhodāharaṇa*); it is not, however, [treated] separately. // 260 //

The example for non-perception is indeed included within the "appropriated" (upātta) category and is not separate from it. What is the reason? Because by the very exclusion of the cause and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), the exclusion of the object—that is, the effect—and the intrinsic nature itself—is stated.
This has been explained:
for only when the existence of a self or its status as a cause is established can there be negative concomitance (vyatireka).

The non-apprehension of the nature [of a thing], such as "it is established," has also already been indicated, because it is precisely through the non-apprehension of the cause and the nature that a thing is excluded. And so it has been said: "By one who speaks by means of valid cognitions," and so forth. How is it established that "having reached the conditions for apprehension" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*) is a qualification?
To this it is replied:
Even in that case, because vital breath and so forth do not exclude the possibility of an imperceptible person.
By explaining that it is the cause of doubt, it is indicated that this [non-apprehension] pertains to an object of perception. 261.

Another has said: "If the absence of breath and so forth in a jar and such things results from the absence of the self, then if the self were excluded even from a living body, breath and the other signs would also be excluded."

On this point, the Teacher has established that in the case of a jar or similar objects, the self (*ātman*) is indeed existent and visible; it is not established as invisible merely because of non-perception, due to its connection with the body. Therefore, it has been indicated that non-perception is a means of cognition only regarding an object that is perceptible.
[Objection: But if exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is what is being proven, then every logical reason (*hetu*) is nothing but non-perception; so how can there be a triad of reasons?
This is not a fault, because:
By means of this method (naya), a negation that does not acknowledge any portion of the entity is established;
however, regarding the entity itself, through the first two [methods], there is an exclusion (paryudāsa) by way of affirmation.

[632,xii] Even regarding a real entity (*vastu*), it is not a partial exclusion (*paryudāsa*) that is being proven; rather, a negation (*niṣedha*) is being proven with respect to the non-existence of an entity that has not been accepted. However, by means of the two previously mentioned reasons—essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*)—it is established through the mode of partial exclusion. Therefore, even though the nature of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is the same, there is indeed a distinction due to the difference in their objects (*viṣaya*).
[632,xiii]
Now, one might ask: what is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature? He says:
"In that regard, existence consists in being perceived; there is nothing other than perception. [632,xiv]
For non-existence is not something other than non-apprehension; rather, it is non-apprehension itself.

Is it not the case that non-apprehension is the absence of cognition? Non-apprehension is the absence of existence. But since the absence of existence is non-existence itself, how can there be identity between these two? And just as there is a distinction between cognition and the object of cognition, so too there is a distinction between their absences. Indeed, cognition itself is not the existence of an object, for the object exists even in the absence of its cognition. For instance: [632,xvii] "The existence of objects, even when imperceptible, is apprehended through inference."
Is the nature of fire not inferred by the observation of smoke?

(568) [PVA 632, xviii] Furthermore, in that case as well, existence is not merely the apprehension through inference. For there is a deviation [in the argument] regarding existence even in the absence of inference. The non-occurrence of inference does not indicate non-existence, because inference does indeed occur with respect to the past and the future.
[632,xix] This is not well-founded.
For non-existence is not established by the non-perception of other things that are themselves unperceivable.

For the conventional designation of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) is established through the non-perception of that which has met the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*); yet, there is no existence (*sattā*) of these [objects] other than their perception. For it is a contradiction to say: "It is capable of being perceived, yet it is not perceived. Therefore, the existence of an object that meets the conditions for perceptibility is nothing but its perception itself. To explain: if perception is the state of being perceived, then it is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the object. Or, if perception is called the act of perceiving as residing in the agent (*kartṛsthatā*), even then the existence of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility is necessarily attained by that [perception]. And since there is no difference [between them], there is no cognition of distinction, because distinction is understood only through difference (*vyatireka*). Because it is never absent from it, perception is called existence. Furthermore, the perception of objects does not arise from a perception that is separate [from the object] and simultaneous with it; rather, it arises precisely from the perception characterized by the state of being perceived, which has entered into that [object]. Therefore, perception itself is existence. Consequently, he will state that non-existence is simply the non-perception of that [perception]. For in reality, there is no mutual distinction between absences (*abhāva*). Distinction exists only when there is a difference in the qualifiers of the positive entity (*bhāva*), such as "the absence of a cloth" or "the absence of a cart. Nor does a positive entity attain its true nature (*tattva*) without a qualifier. Now, if the qualifier that constitutes the positive entity is one and the same for both existence and non-existence, then their absences must also be identical. And in reality, even if there is a difference in the thing to be negated, there is no [distinction] in the absence itself.
[633,iii] But surely, if non-apprehension is simply non-existence, then there would be no disagreement at all. This is true; for:
Thus, this illustration of the "inexplicable" (anupākhyā) is considered to be for the purpose of making known that which is beyond cognition.

[633,v] One is characterized by the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). This is for the sake of the understanding of the ignorant person who, being devoid of thorough knowledge, does not comprehend the non-difference between the absence of cognition and the absence of the object of cognition; or for the Sāṃkhya who is utterly deluded and holds the dogmatic view that "everything exists everywhere. What, then, is established there?

In that case, because the object does not exist, the subject is negated; just as one might doubt the term "cognition" [if it lacks an object], or as something is not called "fire" because it does not burn. (264)

For the existence of an object is the basis for both cognition and verbal designation, as well as for doubt regarding them. In the absence of that object, cognition, verbal designation, and doubt necessarily cease, because there is the presence of its opposite. For example, there is no fire because of the absence of burning; for while there may be doubt about whether something is fire in other cases where burning exists, when that burning is absent, since its opposite is present, how could such doubt arise? Since there is no state of being non-fire other than the absence of burning, and just as there is no state of being non-fire other than the absence of burning.

Likewise, the non-existence of other things is established through their non-apprehension; for words denoting those [objects] are proven to be based upon them, because they exist when those [objects] exist. (265)

Indeed, non-existence is not something other than the very nature of non-perception among those things that have reached the conditions for perceptibility. Therefore, when that [non-existence] is established, its identity with that [non-perception] is necessarily established.
[Objection: Surely, non-existence is established by non-apprehension; how then can there be identity between the probandum and the probans?
[Response:
That too is incorrect.
[633,xii] This very point is not established here, nor is it unestablished due to being unestablished;
it does not attain establishment here at all, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and therefore that [reason] is not [a valid one]. (PVA 569)

[633, xiii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the five supernormal powers, he is called a ‘bhikṣu who has reached the ultimate goal,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has performed his task,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has laid down the burden,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has lived the holy life,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has accomplished what was to be done,’ and a ‘bhikṣu who has cast off the bonds of existence. What are those five? They are: the supernormal power consisting of the various bases of mastery; the supernormal power consisting of the various kinds of divine hearing; the supernormal power consisting of the knowledge of the minds of others; the supernormal power consisting of the recollection of past lives; and the supernormal power consisting of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows. These are the five supernormal powers. What are the five lower fetters? They are: self-identity view, doubt, attachment to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will. These are the five lower fetters. What are the four higher fetters? They are: lust for form, lust for the formless, pride, and ignorance. These are the four higher fetters. What are the four analytical knowledges? They are: the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence. These are the four analytical knowledges. What are the four foundations of mindfulness? They are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. These are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four right endeavors? They are: the right endeavor to prevent the arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, the right endeavor to abandon arisen evil and unwholesome states, the right endeavor to bring about the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the right endeavor to maintain and perfect arisen wholesome states. These are the four right endeavors. What are the four bases of psychic power? They are: the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort of will, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy accompanied by effort of will, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by effort of will, and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by effort of will. These are the four bases of psychic power. What are the four meditative absorptions? They are: the first meditative absorption, the second meditative absorption, the third meditative absorption, and the fourth meditative absorption. These are the four meditative absorptions. What are the four immeasurables? They are: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. These are the four immeasurables. What are the four formless attainments? They are: the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are the four formless attainments. What are the four fruits of the ascetic life? They are: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. These are the four fruits of the ascetic life. What are the four noble truths? They are: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These are the four noble truths. What are the four analytical insights? They are: the analytical insight into the conventional, the analytical insight into the ultimate, the analytical insight into the definitive, and the analytical insight into the provisional. These are the four analytical insights. What are the four reliances? They are: reliance on the teaching, not on the person; reliance on the meaning, not on the letter; reliance on wisdom, not on consciousness; and reliance on the definitive sutras, not on the provisional sutras. These are the four reliances. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One further said this: “The bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters, And has attained the five supernormal powers, Is called one who has reached the ultimate goal, One who has performed his task, One who has laid down the burden, One who has lived the holy life, One who has accomplished what was to be done, And one who has cast off the bonds of existence. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower fetters and attained the six supernormal powers, he is called a ‘bhikṣu who has reached the ultimate goal,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has performed his task,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has laid down the burden,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has lived the holy life,’ a ‘bhikṣu who has accomplished what was to be done,’ and a ‘bhikṣu who has cast off the bonds of existence. What are those six? They are: the supernormal power consisting of the various bases of mastery; the supernormal power consisting of the various kinds of divine hearing; the supernormal power consisting of the knowledge of the minds of others; the supernormal power consisting of the recollection of past lives; the supernormal power consisting of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows; and the supernormal power consisting of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. These are the six supernormal powers. What are the five lower fetters? They are: self-identity view, doubt, attachment to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will. These are the five lower fetters. What are the four higher fetters? They are: lust for form, lust for the formless, pride, and ignorance. These are the four higher fetters. What are the four analytical knowledges? They are: the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence. These are the four analytical knowledges. What are the four foundations of mindfulness? They are: the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. These are the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four right endeavors? They are: the right endeavor to prevent the arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states, the right endeavor to abandon arisen evil and unwholesome states, the right endeavor to bring about the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the right endeavor to maintain and perfect arisen wholesome states. These are the four right endeavors. What are the four bases of psychic power? They are: the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of desire accompanied by effort of will, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy accompanied by effort of will, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind accompanied by effort of will, and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by effort of will. These are the four bases of psychic power. What are the four meditative absorptions? They are: the first meditative absorption, the second meditative absorption, the third meditative absorption, and the fourth meditative absorption. These are the four meditative absorptions. What are the four immeasurables? They are: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. These are the four immeasurables. What are the four formless attainments? They are: the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These are the four formless attainments. What are the four fruits of the ascetic life? They are: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. These are the four fruits of the ascetic life. What are the four noble truths? They are: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These are the four noble truths. What are the four analytical insights? They are: the analytical insight into the conventional, the analytical insight into the ultimate, the analytical insight into the definitive, and the analytical insight into the provisional. These are the four analytical insights. What are the four reliances? They are: reliance on the teaching, not on the person; reliance on the meaning, not on the letter; reliance on wisdom, not on consciousness; and reliance on the definitive sutras, not on the provisional sutras. These are the four reliances. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One further said this: “The bhikṣu who has abandoned the five lower fetters, And has attained the six supernormal powers, Is called one who has reached the ultimate goal, One who has performed his task, One who has laid down the burden, One who has lived the holy life, One who has accomplished what was to be done, And one who has cast off the bonds of existence. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a bhikṣu has abandoned the five lower

As for the claim that there must be a distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), that very relationship of probandum and probans is not established here. How, then, can there be an establishment of such a distinction? Indeed, that which is unestablished cannot be established by means of something else that is itself unestablished; as long as the relationship of probandum and probans is not established for the opponent, so long is there no establishment of the distinction. And as long as there is no establishment of the distinction, so long is there no relationship of probandum and probans. For the relationship of probandum and probans exists only when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*); and for non-perception (*anupalambha*) and non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no other connection than identity (*tādātmya*). Indeed, a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) does not exist between those two.
[634,i] But surely non-apprehension is produced by absence; for it is precisely when someone removes a jar or the like that non-apprehension occurs.

This is true: if non-existence were known by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through non-perception, then its necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that [object] would not be established merely through non-apprehension. Otherwise, by what means could the spread of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) be averted?
When the connection is established by a means of valid cognition, then non-apprehension functions as a means of valid cognition.
The connection of non-perception with being a means of valid cognition is established [by this].
(PVA 570) Because of mutual dependence, not even one of these two is established; for this very reason, a reciprocal causal relationship is not proven. (PVA 571)

Therefore, non-existence is not established from non-perception alone, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). However, when there is a connection of identity (*tādātmya*), that very non-perception is what establishes the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that "it is non-existent."
For this conventional usage is established: that [an object] is non-existent when it is not perceived despite being perceptible.
Once that [non-existence] is established, the cognition and the verbal expression regarding its being an effect of that [perception] are also established without doubt. (266)

[634, vii] But surely, even in establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), there is no example at all. For the entirety of conventional usage must be established by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone. In that case, if another example were to be established, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, conventional usage is itself an effect of non-apprehension; therefore, it is improper to establish an effect from its cause. Causes do not necessarily possess their effects. [634, viii]
That is incorrect, because:

This conventional usage [of non-existence] is indeed established based on the non-perception of what is perceptible. Since its basis is restricted to that alone, the fitness for the conventional usage of non-existence is of the very nature of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because this fitness is not distinct from it. As for the conventional usage itself, a conscious being must necessarily engage in it by virtue of seeing that [non-existence]. One who possesses consciousness is necessarily such [a being] when remembering the conventional usage of non-existence as having that [non-perception] as its sole basis. Even if one does not actually initiate physical or verbal activity, let them not do so; for the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists in establishing the cognition of the object, not in establishing physical or other forms of activity. Therefore:
For when the object is actually present, if another person, out of delusion, does not state it here, he is merely reminded of the convention by means of its similarity with what is established. (267)
Thus is the summary.

Just as the relationship of cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception, for it is the terms "effect" and so forth that are conceptually constructed for the sake of conventional discourse regarding those two. (268)

Indeed, causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) does not exist apart from the distinction between perception and non-perception. The meaning of "this is its effect" is precisely this: that it does not occur without this [cause]. If, however, it were distinct from this, then it would certainly occur even in the absence of that; such being the case, any further connection (*pratibandha*) would be useless.

Now, if it were not the case that [the effect] does not occur in the absence of that [cause], then that very [absence] would be the relationship; thus, the other [positive relationship] would be redundant.
[634, xv] But surely, when a relationship exists, it is established that [the effect] does not occur in its absence and occurs when it is present.
If it is maintained that when a relation exists, the effect arises upon the existence of that [cause],
then one must consider whether the relation of the preceding [cause] persists even in the absence of that [effect]. (PVA 572)
For a relation necessarily resides in two things; how could it exist if only one were present?
If fitness (*yogyatā*) were the relation [between] a cause and the arising of its effect, then it would be logical that the existence of the effect proceeds from the cause alone. (573) (PVA)
For a cause is of such a nature as to arise from its own causes.

(PVA 574) Furthermore, no causal relationship other than that established by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) appears even to those who perceive supersensible objects. Therefore, the conventional usage of the causal relationship is to be established through positive and negative concomitance.

[635,iii] How then is it that the difference between words does not exist without a difference between objects? For the sake of conventional usage regarding those very two—perception and non-perception—the terms "effect" and so forth are applied with brevity. Therefore:
The successful accomplishment of an effect from its cause occurs through its inclusion within its own nature;
thus, this illustration has been shown separately by means of explaining the various types of reasons.

For a capable cause is in reality nothing other than the very nature of the effect. Therefore, non-perception is simply a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Consequently, it is not presented as a separate category.

[Objection: But how can the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) be included within the reason of essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) without a relation of identity (*tādātmyapratibandha*)? For just as there is no mutual difference between two existents, so too there is no non-difference; indeed, identity is not possible for that which lacks a self-nature (*nirātman*), for a rabbit’s horn is certainly not of the nature of a donkey’s horn. [Response: To this, it is replied: Non-perception has as its very essence a nature that is the opposite of the object to be negated. For instance:
From the experience of perceiving one thing, there arises the conceptualizing cognition that "I do not perceive this" or "I do perceive this. (270)

[635,ix] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition for the Tathāgata’s teaching that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, unarisen, unceasing, and quiescent from the beginning? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, it is because sentient beings have long been attached to the signs of self, person, being, and life; they are attached to the signs of permanence, impermanence, suffering, pleasure, purity, impurity, existence, non-existence, oneness, otherness, both, and neither; they are attached to the signs of coming and going; they are attached to the signs of birth, abiding, and cessation; they are attached to the signs of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; they are attached to the signs of the twelve links of dependent origination; they are attached to the signs of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; they are attached to the signs of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they are attached to the signs of the three gates of liberation; they are attached to the signs of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative concentration, and the ten spheres of totality; they are attached to the signs of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; they are attached to the signs of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion; they are attached to the signs of the dharmas of a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha; they are attached to the signs of the dharmas of a bodhisattva; they are attached to the signs of the dharmas of a tathāgata; they are attached to the signs of the dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned; they are attached to the signs of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. For this reason, Maitreya, the Tathāgata teaches that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, unarisen, unceasing, and quiescent from the beginning. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, unarisen, unceasing, and quiescent from the beginning, then why does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma by means of causes and conditions? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative concentration, and the ten spheres of totality? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a bodhisattva? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a tathāgata? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned? Why does he teach the Dharma by means of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa? The Buddha told Maitreya: “Maitreya, although all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, unarisen, unceasing, and quiescent from the beginning, yet there are sentient beings who, having long been attached to the signs of self, person, being, and life; attached to the signs of permanence, impermanence, suffering, pleasure, purity, impurity, existence, non-existence, oneness, otherness, both, and neither; attached to the signs of coming and going; attached to the signs of birth, abiding, and cessation; attached to the signs of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields; attached to the signs of the twelve links of dependent origination; attached to the signs of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; attached to the signs of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; attached to the signs of the three gates of liberation; attached to the signs of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative concentration, and the ten spheres of totality; attached to the signs of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; attached to the signs of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion; attached to the signs of the dharmas of a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha; attached to the signs of the dharmas of a bodhisattva; attached to the signs of the dharmas of a tathāgata; attached to the signs of the dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned; and attached to the signs of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa—for their sake, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of causes and conditions. He teaches the Dharma by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. He teaches the Dharma by means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative concentration, and the ten spheres of totality. He teaches the Dharma by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. He teaches the Dharma by means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a bodhisattva. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a tathāgata. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Maitreya, it is like a skilled physician who, seeing that his children have ingested poison, prescribes various medicines according to their specific ailments to eliminate the poison. Although the medicines differ, the elimination of the poison is one. In the same way, Maitreya, although all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unconditioned, unborn, unarisen, unceasing, and quiescent from the beginning, yet for the sake of sentient beings who are attached to various signs, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of causes and conditions. He teaches the Dharma by means of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. He teaches the Dharma by means of the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eight liberations, the nine successive stages of meditative concentration, and the ten spheres of totality. He teaches the Dharma by means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. He teaches the Dharma by means of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, and the great compassion. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a bodhisattva. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of a tathāgata. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned. He teaches the Dharma by means of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Maitreya, this is called the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma

Indeed, an absence that is a mere void is not more capable of being the object of investigation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor does that [absence], even when established, possess any established nature in its own right alone. It is only through the eyes of those who investigate the intermixture of real entities (*vastu*) that it is accepted as such. In this regard, if [an entity] is excluded from other entities, places, times, and states by its very nature, what is the use of postulating another "absence"? On the other hand, if it is not excluded by its nature, then too another "absence" is useless. That it is useless in one case and incapable in the other has already been demonstrated previously. Therefore, it is designated as the "absence of a jar" and so forth by means of a distinction in its own-nature (*svabhāva*), which consists precisely in its being devoid of the existence of another. For, the perception of a single object whose nature is distinct from the nature of the intended object—when the experience of that [perception] occurs through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—gives rise to a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in the form of the thought "I do not perceive this," which revolves within memory. In that context, the experience of the location itself is the non-perception of the other. Since the meaning here is simply "I do not perceive this by way of another's nature," its non-perception is by way of that nature; thus, "this does not exist" in that form.

[635,x] But surely, since there is nothing here that could harm it, its non-existence in this form is what is to be proven; so how can there be a statement of the contrapositive? This is true, provided that no other meaning were included here. However, that is indeed included. For instance:
Whether it be the region as distinct from that form, or the pot as distinct from this [region],
no difference whatsoever appears to the wise in this case.

If this [object] were not distinct from that form, then even this [cognition] would not be distinct from it; since the meaning is perfectly clear, what delusion could there be for another? Therefore, its very distinction from that is its non-existence here. And because the cognition "I do not perceive that" arises precisely from seeing a place distinct from that, and the cognition "I perceive it as having a form other than that," non-perception is in fact perception itself, due to the identity between non-perception and perception in that regard.

[Objection: Let this non-apprehension be [established] for another cognition; but how can it be so for another object of cognition? [Response: There is no fault, because it has been demonstrated that there is no difference between cognition and its object. Alternatively, the word *vā* has the sense of *iva* (just as). Just as apprehension (*upalambha*) is determined as such because it is the object of the conceptual construction "I apprehend," so too is non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) determined through the judgment "I do not apprehend.

If this is argued, we say no. For if there is no cognition of the non-distinct, there is no capacity for the cognition of non-existence, because that which has been apprehended by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) cannot be made otherwise. And this has already been established, so it is not stated here. To explain:
indeed, without memory, there is no possibility for the means of valid cognition regarding non-existence.
Since there is no recollection of a counter-positive without a specific experience [of it], [it is argued:

"But surely, the establishment of the distinction between entities arises precisely from the possibility of their non-existence; therefore, how can there be non-confusion without non-existence? [576] (PVA) [636,v]
This is not so; for:
The distinction between objects is understood from the cognition of that which is itself distinguished;
and for this [cognition], the self-awareness of its own such state is the cause of the awareness of difference. (271)

If a specific sensation were not distinct and isolated from other sensations, there would be no cognition of the particularity of the object of experience. Furthermore, if that specific form of sensation were not experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then its distinctness would likewise not be apprehended. It could only be apprehended through the awareness of its absence.

For the arising of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding non-existence does not occur without the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Nor is there a recollection of the counter-positive in the absence of a specific cognition [of it]. If it is argued that there was previously a specific experience of it, then since that [experience] exists as well, non-existence would be entirely redundant. If it is argued that by means of non-existence itself that very linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence is established, then what is the use of establishing one thing by means of another when it is already established? In the case of establishing linguistic usage, that very non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) has the nature of a "reason based on essential identity" (*svabhāvahetu*). Therefore, the conceptual construction of difference arises precisely from the state of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as distinct from others; and that very difference is the non-existence of anything other than it.
Therefore, the distinction between cognitions is established by themselves, and from those [cognitions], the distinction between their objects is established.
Otherwise, due to infinite regress, the distinction of anything whatsoever would not be established. (272)

The exclusion of others from cognition is established solely through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); from that, too, the [exclusion] of the object [is established]. Thus, the conventional usage of self-awareness is complete. However, if difference were not established through perception alone, but rather through the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), then, because of infinite regress, there would be no comprehension.
For instance:
xiii] If the conceptualization of difference is based on the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (abhāva),...

That non-existence (*abhāva*) too cannot be introduced by another [means of knowledge] through the non-existence of something else. (577) [PVA] That [non-existence] would require yet another, and that another yet another; thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*), and no practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) would be possible. For if a distinction (*bheda*) not previously apprehended is perceived by the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence, then that non-existence can only function when there is a recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). And such recollection as a counter-correlate occurs only when the distinction has already been grasped through perception. Therefore, non-existence is useless, since even now, as before, the grasping of the distinction occurs through perception alone.
[636,xv] Now, even so, since there is no difference without non-existence (abhāva), non-existence is not purposeless. That being the case, there too [another...

The entry into the cognition of non-existence must be brought about by the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Since that recollection itself requires another recollection, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even granting this for the sake of argument, it is not possible for that which is being perceived now to be recollected at that time as a counter-positive, such that, upon the entry into the cognition of non-existence at that time, there could be a grasping of its difference from this [present object]; thus, the entry into the cognition of non-existence is impossible. Therefore, in the view of others, there is simply no apprehension of difference. Because difference is the experience of a specific form, there is no exclusion of one thing by another other than this.
Therefore, because there is the perception of that which is qualified by it, there is also the non-perception of that [qualifier]. (273)

[637,iii] The very experience of a specific form is the proof for the non-existence of anything else; however, without the experience of that specific form, the establishment of the non-existence of another thing therein is not possible.

[Objection: Surely, because there is an experience of a qualified form, its existence as such is established. How then could it be non-existent therein? For it is not the case that what exists in another place or time is absent therein, since it has reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatvāt*).
[Reply:
That is incorrect, because:
In the experience of a specific form, how can there be the exclusion of others?
For if there were no exclusion of others, that very specific form would not be established. (PVA 578)

For if there were no experience of a qualified form (*viśiṣṭarūpa*), there would be no experience of the object at all. If the qualified form of a jar or other thing is apprehended, what is the use of the cognition of another’s absence? Nor can there be an experience of a qualified form even through the cognition of a thousand absences, without the cognition of the specific nature (*svarūpa*) [of that form]. Indeed, the cognition of the specific nature must necessarily be admitted. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that another entity cannot be cognized in its own nature. Therefore, the very experience of a qualified form is the proof for the absence of another. Non-apprehension (*anupalambhana*) of that [other] is likewise simply the apprehension of something else as qualified.
Therefore, this non-apprehension, being itself known through direct perception, establishes the absence of that [object], because it functions solely with respect to its own presence. (274)

It is established that non-existence is simply the perception of that specific form; thus, the identity between non-existence and non-perception, as well as its establishment through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is proven. Therefore, there is no fault regarding the lack of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) due to being unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, that non-perception is indeed a capable logical reason (*hetu*), acting as the motivator for the conventional usage of non-existence precisely by occurring in relation to itself alone. Otherwise, if non-perception were the absence of experience and non-existence were the absence of an entity, then because of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it would be unestablished; thus he says: [637,x] If non-perception were the absence of experience and non-existence were the absence of an entity, then because of infinite regress, it would be unestablished. Thus he says: [637,x]
Otherwise, the non-existence of an object is understood through its non-perception;
the non-existence of that perception would be known by another [perception], leading to an infinite regress. (275)

Just as the non-existence of an object is established through non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), so too non-apprehension itself is of the nature of the non-apprehension of apprehension. If its non-existence were established by another non-apprehension, and that [non-existence] by yet another, there would be no liberation from infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, if the non-existence of the object is proven by the absence of apprehension because apprehension is the means of proof for it, then since the existence of apprehension does not require another means of proof, its non-existence likewise does not require another means of proof.
This is incorrect;
for it is logically sound that the apprehension [of cognition] is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
To claim that the cognition of its absence occurs through itself is an extreme rashness.
For if there were self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), this [absence] would indeed exist;
if absence were established by perception, it would be due to the cognition of something else.
[637,xv] Now, if non-existence is established by perception other than that [of the object], then it follows that it must also apply to the cognition of a real entity.

Now, since the object has not reached the conditions for perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāptatvāt*), it is not established through the direct perception of another; for its nature is other than cognition. Since consciousness is consciousness, it lacks any other form; thus, the absence [of the object] is established by the direct perception of that other [consciousness]. And so: "I do not perceive this"—here, by means of the first person, one negates only the act of perceiving, not the object itself, saying "this does not exist. Therefore, this non-perception is understood through one's own direct perception as being characterized solely by the absence of cognition.
[638,iii] That is incorrect.
How can the non-existence of one thing be understood through the perception of another?
If it were so by virtue of being distinct from that [other], why would it not be a case of non-perception?

Indeed, the proof of the non-existence of another cognition does not occur through the perception of that other cognition without the exclusion of the former. And it is precisely because of the perception of what is excluded from it that there is the non-perception of it. Therefore, how could the absence of the perception of anything other than that be established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Now, if one argues that the qualification "having reached the conditions for perceptibility" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is unnecessary because there is no deviation [from the rule], then, in that case, the qualification would be superfluous; however, its status as a non-perception (*anupalabdhitā*) does not thereby disappear. Consequently, whatever negation there may be, all of it arises from non-perception; thus, non-existence characterized as a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) is established by direct perception. And that very same thing, in relation to something else, is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalambha*). Furthermore, as for this use of the first person in the expression "I do not perceive," it arises from the context of non-perception characterized as the relative negation of cognition, and not for the purpose of excluding the existence of the object itself. Since the two are inseparable, this very [non-perception] is also the non-existence of the entity. For when existence and perception are one and the same, then the exclusion of the entity is also established by direct perception; it cannot occur in parts.

[638,vii] But is it not the case that non-existence is established through the non-perception of the pervader? For instance: the existence of something that has reached the conditions for perception is pervaded by perception; therefore, from the absence of that [perception], the non-existence of the object possessing that nature is established.
[638,viii]
This is true:
this non-perception of intrinsic nature (svabhāvānupalambha) does not establish non-existence.
In every case, it would be thus: one would know the absence of that [object] through direct perception.

If the non-existence of that which meets the conditions for perception is established by direct perception through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), then its absence would be established by direct perception everywhere; there would thus be no such thing as "non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Furthermore, if this non-perception of the pervader establishes absence for one who is not confused, then for one who is confused, let that very same [non-perception] be made an object of cognition through memory—what is the use of postulating another kind of non-perception? Or, if the non-perception of the essential nature applies to the confused person, it will likewise apply to the unconfused person, just as in the case of the cognition of smoke; indeed, the threefold classification does not disappear in that case. Moreover:
[638,xi] Here, there is no distinction between the pervaded and the pervader from the perspective of ultimate reality,
because it was previously established that existence is nothing other than apprehension. (PVA 583)
