For the proponent of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) maintains that the existence of a perceptible object is necessarily pervaded by its apprehension. This [principle] is exactly the same even in the doctrine of the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Indeed, when there is identity (*tādātmya*), the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) does not fail to exist. Thus, it has been established that apprehension itself is existence. Since the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is not distinct from the pervasion [of its cause], it is not different from its own essential nature; therefore, the non-apprehension of that [effect] is said to be nothing other than the non-apprehension of essential nature. How then could one who, being utterly deluded, explains the non-apprehension of an effect as being included within the non-apprehension of essential nature, fail to explain the non-apprehension of cognition as the non-apprehension of essential nature? Therefore, the existence of one thing is simply the non-existence of another, and the apprehension of one thing is simply the non-apprehension of another. And that is precisely the non-apprehension of essential nature.
[2. Non-perception of the perceptible as a subverter of existence.

But even so, is it not the case that the non-perception of a pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi) is impossible? True; however, it is precisely our position that all [types of non-perception] are included within the non-perception of essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi), and thus they are already subsumed. There is no loss for us whatsoever. How, then, is there a distinction?
Due to the difference between the pervaded and the pervader, and because of the occurrence of increase and decrease,
there is a distinction between "tree" and "śiṃśapā," as well as through their being distant or near. (PVA 584)

[639,iii] Tree-ness is inclusive, whereas *śiṃśapā*-ness is exclusive. At a distance, there is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to the pervaded (*vyāpya*); however, in close proximity, there is the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). This is the distinction between these two. But regarding existence that has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) and its perception, since they stand in a mutual relationship of pervaded and pervader, no distinction can be conceived. Therefore, it is established that it is simply the non-perception of the essential nature; thus, non-perception is included within the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For this very reason: [639,iv]
Because certainty is impossible regarding that which is unperceived, its existence elsewhere is precluded;
just as, in the absence of a logical mark (liṅga), conceptual construction and the like cannot be established among other beings. (276)
Therefore:
For this [reason], which has non-determination as its result, is not capable of establishing exclusion;
rather, the first [type of reason] is employed for the establishment [of the probandum] through determination alone. (277)

This non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) does not establish the absence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because such certainty is impossible in cases such as distant locations. For, with respect to that which is invisible, this is not a "non-apprehension of what has reached the conditions for perception" (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānupalabdhi*). However, the former type [of non-apprehension] functions to ascertain the total exclusion of the reason from the counter-example. This includes the types described as the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) and the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which operate through the very exclusion of the reason’s own nature (*svabhāva*). Even in those cases, it is established as a proof by accepting them as *prasaṅga* arguments.

Is it not the case that "contradiction" (*virodha*) is indeed another type of logical mark (*liṅga*), as in: "There is no cold touch here because of fire"? How then is it stated under the definition of a sub-division? Because it is included within non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) itself;
for, in its own formal applications, either its own nature is employed.
Or it consists in the sublation of the object, because [the cognition] exists when [the object] exists and does not exist when [the object] is absent. (278)

For the contradictory reason (*virodhī hetuḥ*) is merely a subdivision of that very non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), just like its other subdivisions. Otherwise, the opponent would have to provide separate definitions for the contradictory, the effect of the contradictory, the pervader of the contradictory, and so forth. However, when this is understood as a manifold subdivision of that very [non-apprehension], then there is no such fault. For instance, either the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is employed—such as "non-apprehension of the self-nature, the cause, the pervader, or the effect"—or it is the form of sublation (*bādhana*) of what is not being negated, as in: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire. Just as non-apprehension establishes absence, so too does the apprehension of a contradictory, whether directly or indirectly. Why? Because contradiction is that which causes cessation. How is contradiction established? The understanding of contradiction arises from the absence of things like cold, whose causes are unimpaired, when fire is present. For contradiction is characterized by apprehension and non-apprehension. Therefore, through the perception of the contradictory, the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is established. In that case, the non-apprehension of fire situated at a distance—which has reached the conditions for apprehension—is established by inference; thus, it is not the case that the apprehension of a contradictory is something other than the non-apprehension of the self-nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Indeed, that very sensation of heat is the absence of the sensation of cold, and because it is devoid of that, it is also the sensation of neither-hot-nor-cold. Consequently, the non-apprehension of one thing is simply the apprehension of the other. Likewise, the apprehension of a contradictory effect is also a non-apprehension of the self-nature established by the inference of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). In the former case—the apprehension of the contradictory—the inference proceeds on the basis of dependence upon a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Or, because their mutual distinction is established, like permanence and destruction.

Contradiction is characterized by the state of mutual exclusion, as in the case of the eternal and the non-eternal. For the negation of identity is established through contradiction characterized by the state of mutual exclusion; for example: "This place is not possessed of a jar, because it is perceived in the absence of that jar. In all cases, it is precisely the perception of the opposite that establishes non-existence directly.
Or, [non-existence is established] through sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of dependence and permanence. (279)

Just as there is contradiction (*virodha*) when things mutually exclude one another, so too is there contradiction when they are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of dependence and necessary existence. To explain: "dependence" and "independence" are mutually contradictory; likewise, "necessary existence" and its opposite are contradictory. Furthermore, even in the absence of mutual exclusion between dependence and necessary existence, there is a contradiction characterized by sublation by valid cognition; this constitutes another form of contradiction. To explain further: [640,v]
A contradictory state arises from that which is dependent; this applies even to the permanent and the impermanent.
In the ultimate sense, contradiction consists in mutual exclusion.

If this is so, then it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the contradictory, and there is no such thing as a "contradiction with a means of valid cognition" distinct from that.

This is true; nevertheless, this was stated because there is a contradiction by implication through a nature pervaded by the contradictory. What is the purpose of this? It is for the sake of showing that even the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory is a prover of negation. For instance, the following formal argument (*prayoga*) is observed: "The destruction of an entity, even one that has come into being, is not necessarily certain, because it depends upon other causes."
Yet another says:
When the perception of that which is pervaded by a contradictory effect is employed, it is because the reason consisting of the nature of the effect is already included therein.
Thus, all [reasons] are one with non-perception; they are not distinct from it.
Therefore, even though it is threefold, it is merely a differentiation of that very same non-apprehension;
non-apprehension alone is the single reason for both effect and essential nature.

Because it is a differentiation of that [very thing]. Indeed, a differentiation of that does not differ from it; for there is no difference between a brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*) and its "cowness" (*gotva*). In this context, the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is the perception of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*), and the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is likewise the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), because it establishes the absence of non-fire and non-eternality.
This is incorrect:
if a reason is postulated in accordance with its necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
The essential nature and the effect [are established] through identity and through origination from that, respectively.

When there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with fire by way of impermanence, the reason is contradicted by that which is contradictory to the pervader; thus, the conceptualization of its non-perception as a positive entity occurs. In that case, it is impossible to abandon the direct conceptualization of the reason and resort to an indirect one. When fire is apprehended through its effect, there is the cessation of cold, which is contradictory to it, but smoke does not have a direct operation toward the cessation of cold itself. Therefore, the conceptualization of causality through a mediated sequence is "inference of an inferred" (*anumitānumāna*). Nor is this reason anything other than the three [factors] when two or three are expressed by a single word. [640,xvi]
For an object does not exist in some cases by virtue of the word;
otherwise, the distinction between mere usage would have to be considered imaginary.
(PVA 589) [640, xviii]

"There is no sensation of cold here because of smoke. The inference of fire from smoke is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). The proof of the absence of the sensation of cold by means of fire is the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*). The proof of the conventional usage of the absence of cold by means of the non-perception of cold is the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). Therefore, among these indirect reasons, inference based on what has been inferred (*anumitānumāna*) is simply another form of inference. And there is no [need for] a single term to express all three.

There would be both identity and the state of being a different cause; this is a compound of application (*prayoga-samāsa*), not a compound of form (*rūpa-samāsa*). Therefore, it is incorrect to say that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the reason in every case.

Now, if it is argued that all non-apprehension is the reason for establishing exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), no; because the reasons differ precisely due to the difference in their objects. And so it has been said:
By this [inference], a negation is established that does not admit any part of a real entity;
however, regarding a real entity as well, there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by way of affirmation through the two previous [types of inference]. (PVA 590)
Thus ends [section] 8: An Investigation into the Intrinsic Nature of Entities.

Now, if it is thought that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone is the means of establishing exclusion from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then why is it not simply stated that perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself is self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? Therefore, this [position] is incorrect. Consequently, the distinction [between types of non-apprehension] arises solely from the difference in their formal application (*prayoga*): [it is] the apprehension of what is pervaded by the contradictory [of the probandum]. Because destruction is dependent [on causes], it does not have a necessary occurrence. For:
[641,vii] How can there be a restriction when that which arises from another cause is present?
[641,viii]
Since that other cause as well depends upon its own cause, there is no certainty; and since this applies to yet another as well, there is no certainty regarding the existence of the effect.
Now, if it is argued that the very cause of an entity—such as a potter—is also the cause of its destruction, thereby establishing a certainty, to this it is replied:
If existence arises from an existent cause, what is the use of these exhausting efforts involving a succession of causes?
For it is thus:
If that cause, having produced another destruction, were the destroyer of that [entity], what would happen if it were to produce that very same perishable entity? (281)

[641,xiii] If its very cause, having produced destruction, is itself the destroyer of that [entity], then let it produce only that which is perishable; what is the use of this indirect succession? If it is argued that here the answer must be stated in terms of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, [we reply]: otherwise, because it is the intrinsic nature of things, this is not so. For instance:
When he exists as one whose self is already perfected, who could be a benefactor to him?
And since no benefactor to his self exists, whom could he possibly require? (282)

[641,xv] If a cause of destruction that assists the self is not possible for that which exists as an established intrinsic nature, then it must exist by means of an intrinsic nature other than the established one—that is, by means of an unestablished intrinsic nature. And in that case, it is not the cause of its destruction.

Now, suppose it is the creator of even a particularity that is already established. In that case, would that particularity be something already established or something other than that? If it were already established, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) as before would follow. If, on the other hand, it is something other than that [established thing], then since it is impossible to produce its own nature once it is established, it would not be an auxiliary to it at all; what, then, would it be to it? The meaning is: nothing at all. Or rather, if it has already been produced, it is not something to be produced again. [641,xvii]

Furthermore, that entity must either persist through a period of time due to its own cause or not. If the former position is held, then it would persist through all divisions of time and be the producer of every effect.

If [the object] has already perished, then what can the destroyer do? (591) (PVA) Indeed, when the water has already flowed away, what is the use of building a dam? For a dam is for the purpose of obstructing water; a dam that does not obstruct the water is merely a laborious effort, for it is just a dam in name. (592) (PVA)

[642,iii] Now, if it does not apprehend the object in that manner, then how could a cause of destruction function when its own object has not been determined? If it is argued that it functions by determining a future entity, we say no. For if the nature of the entity is already established, what utility would there be for a cause of destruction? If it is argued that its utility lies in the potsherd, which is of a contradictory nature, then surely that too is merely a remover. In that case as well, the same previous logical consequence (prasaṅga) applies. Moreover, by mere mutual exclusion, one thing would not be a remover of the other. [642,iv]

Now, if one argues that the cause of destruction, characterized by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), brings about the non-existence of an established entity by means of its persistence over time—that is, it effects the absence of that which persists for a duration—[we reply: emptiness being produced as something that persists over time is not contradictory to that entity, and thus it cannot be its remover, just as water is not the remover of its container. If it is argued that even water is indeed the remover of a jar when it is attached to it, we say no; for in that case, the persistence over time is not established. [Objection:
But surely it is precisely by means of inference that what is established as persisting over time is removed. [Reply: That is incorrect.
That which is not established by inference cannot be excluded as being that very thing; nor can it be excluded on the grounds that another is non-existent. (593) (PVA)

[642, vii] Just as perception, inference too is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since that [object] is established, it is certainly real; how then could it be non-existent? For if it were non-existent, the cognition of it would be unreal, and thus neither perception nor inference would exist. In the absence of these two, there is no establishment of existence; so whose division [of existence and non-existence] would there be? If you say, "The division belongs to that which is being conceived," then this is a mere trifle, for this is simply a repeated mental construction (*abhyāsa*) based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and not a definitive determination of a real entity.
[642, viii]

Now, the cause of destruction brings about a change in that very thing, characterized by shards and so forth. To this it is replied: Is this change in the jar and such desired to occur in the jar itself, or rather in the substance of clay?
Since the state of being otherwise (*anyathātva*) is established in the case of a jar and so forth, how could that not be an existent entity?

(594) [PVA 642,x] If that state of being otherwise exists in the form of the jar, then that very thing is the substratum (*ādhāra*) of the state of being otherwise; in that case, since the jar was perceived in its own form, how could it be otherwise? On the other hand, if the jar is not perceived, of what would this state of being otherwise be the property? It is designated as "the state of being otherwise belonging to that jar" because it is preceded by the jar.

[642,xi] But surely, if destruction exists, then that [destruction] would be preceded by another destruction, which would itself be a change of state, leading to an infinite regress. Or, if it is a change of state of the clay-substance, then that [substance] is not yet destroyed; how then can there be a destruction characterized as a change of state for it? In that case too, there is no destruction of the prior clay-substance because it is then non-existent, nor is there [destruction] of the subsequent one because it has come into being. But surely this same fault applies to your position as well. For at the time of the effect, the cause does not exist; how then can that be its effect? This is not so, because: [642,xii]
A cause must necessarily exist prior [to its effect]; it is not a cause if it is simultaneous [with it].
To claim that destruction is simultaneous with the entity is an incorrect response.

For it is not logically tenable that existence occurs at one time and destruction at another; rather, it is reasonable that when there is existence, at that very moment there is destruction, such that [the entity] is destroyed. However, it is not logical for non-existence to occur in relation to non-existence, because there is no further death for one who is already dead. It is indeed logical to speak of an "effect" even regarding one who is dead, since that is a different state of being (*bhāvāntara*). But non-existence is the very emptiness of that [entity], because it is perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "that does not exist. The lack of coreferentiality, however, in the expression "the destruction of the object," occurs by virtue of the treatment of a term as if it were a proper name (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), just as in the case of "the body of Śilāputraka. But there is no such coreferentiality as in "fire is smoke."

[642,xiv] But even here, there is no co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). For the preceding form, which is being remembered, is perceived as having perished; and there can be no such co-referentiality with the destruction that occurs at a subsequent time.
That too is incorrect; for if this were the case, there would be a great contradiction. To explain:
in reality, there is no destruction of the form that is being remembered.
Then, to claim that there is the destruction of the visible form would be a rash assertion.

"Annihilation" (vināśa) is said to be non-existence (nāstitva). Now, there is no non-existence in the state of being present; rather, it is only in the state of not being present that something is "non-existent. Therefore, for one who asserts that non-existence is a distinct entity, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) [between "existence" and "non-existence"]. Consequently, non-existence is not other than existence. From this follows their coreferentiality. For that which arises at a later time is precisely the non-existence of the prior entity that possessed its exclusion. And its perception is the non-perception of another form of apprehension. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that if there were an apprehension of that which is conjoined with a subsequent [moment]—which has the nature of a direct perception (pratyakṣa) grasping a present object and its grasper—there would follow the undesirable consequence of apprehending the entire causal series. Therefore, the cognition of that which is not conjoined with anything else occurs from its mere arising; thus, destruction is independent of anything else.
[643,iii] But is it not the case that its very nature (*svabhāva*) is such that it perishes by depending [on something else]? How then can it be independent? To this it is replied:
If an entity were all-pervasive, what else would it depend upon?
On the other hand, if its existence were not all-pervasive, then dependence on another would be futile.
Thus it has been said. For this very reason, he says:
"And how could an independent entity ever be otherwise than what it is?"
Just as that very [cause] which is not subject to delay is what brings about the destruction of what has arisen. (283)

[643, vii] How could that which has already been perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being in a state of disintegration ever be otherwise at any time? Just as, for example, that very same thing [is perceived] by a proponent of permanence (*nityavādin*) in its state of perishing.
[643, viii]
If it is argued that "even for a single moment, there is no existence of one thing in another if it is independent," [then]:

if a thing were independent regarding its destruction such that it did not depend on anything else even for a single moment, then one thing would not exist as a thing of another, even for a moment. To explain:
That which is causeless must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because it does not depend on anything else.
Thus it has been said. Likewise, how could destruction, which occurs immediately after the moment of the entity's existence, be of the same nature as that entity?
And if it were not of that nature, there could be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Therefore, this too is merely clutching at straws.
For that entity is of such a nature; how could there be an entity in the absence of non-existence? // 284 //

[643,xiv] The Blessed One said: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a jasmine flower, and the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree. What, monks, is the person who is like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion... with a mind full of sympathetic joy... with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, likewise toward a second, likewise toward a third, and likewise toward a fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind full of equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Just as a lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and remains unsullied by the water, even so, monks, this person is called "one who is like a lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains submerged at its base and does not rise above the water, even so, monks, this person is called "one who is like a blue lotus flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity. Just as a jasmine flower, though born on a branch and grown on a branch, falls when it has reached maturity, even so, monks, this person is called "one who is like a jasmine flower. What, monks, is the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [as before] ...with a mind full of equanimity. Just as a sandalwood tree, though surrounded by thorny trees, yet emits a sweet fragrance, even so, monks, this person is called "one who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What do you think, monks? Which of these four persons would you consider the most excellent? [The monks replied: "Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their resort. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it. [The Blessed One said: "Then listen, monks, and attend closely; I shall speak. "Yes, venerable sir," the monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree is the most excellent among these four persons. Why is that? Because, monks, the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent among these four persons. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall become like the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree. This is how you should train yourselves. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. [643,xiv] The Discourse on the Four Persons is concluded. The First Fifty Chapters is concluded. The First Division is concluded. Destruction is simply the entity itself when it is no longer conjoined with subsequent entities; how could that [destruction] exist in the absence of the entity? For it is not logical that something should both be identical to that entity and yet exist when that entity is absent. If this is so, then since destruction exists, how can the thing be destroyed while destruction exists? Even if destruction is distinct [from the entity], since the essential nature [of the entity] has not fallen away, how can there be destruction? If you argue that the very falling away [of the nature] occurs even when destruction is distinct, let it be so; nevertheless, since that [falling away] is the object of cognition precisely as something distinct, the entity should still be perceived in its original state. This is precisely what constitutes the "distinctness" of a distinct thing: namely, that it does not destroy the other's form. Any objection regarding obstruction based on contradiction is already refuted, because contradiction is not established in the absence of destruction. Therefore:

Those things which exist independently of anything else are necessarily existent when those [causes] are present; for, provided there is no obstruction, the causal complex is certain to perform its effect. (285)

For example, just as the final causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), being free from the possibility of obstruction, does not depend on anything else for the production of its own result and is thus determined to produce it; so too, an entity (*bhāva*) in regard to its destruction (*vināśa*) is independent. Because it is independent regarding destruction, an entity is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Since destruction would not be necessarily manifest if it were dependent, [the opponent might argue: "But surely, because it possesses origination (*utpattimat*), it must possess destruction. This is not so, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). For without a necessary connection, a reason (*hetu*) is not a prover of that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).
Even if destruction were causeless, the proof of the probandum would still hold through identity;
however, it is not logical for the probandum to have causality, because it occurs subsequently.

It is not logical for destruction, which occurs later, to be the cause of that which possesses origination and exists prior to it. Furthermore, an effect does not necessarily follow from its cause; therefore, destruction cannot be a cause by virtue of being an effect. [Objection:

But how is it established that destruction is causeless through identity (*tādātmya*)? Or rather, how can destruction have a cause, given that it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with a hammer and the like? For that very conformity is the characteristic of an effect. To this, it is replied:
If destruction were the non-existence of an entity consisting in the failure to connect with a subsequent moment,
then since that [non-existence] was already observed previously, how could it be caused by a cause of destruction? (PVA 599)

For how can that which is observed even in the absence of something else have that as its cause? It has already been established that a thing is not a cause merely by virtue of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Just as there is a cognition of a jar that is no longer joined with anything else when it exists in the state of shards and so forth upon the presence of a destroyer, so too is there a cognition of it immediately after its arising. For it is demonstrated that even previously, no joining with another form is perceived; otherwise, it would follow that such joining would be perceived up until the point of death. Furthermore, in this case as well, non-joining itself is what constitutes destruction. If it is argued that non-joining is produced by destruction itself, that is incorrect, because: [644, viii]
Because it lacks capacity and because it is purposeless, that action does not occur through destruction alone;
for destruction is not capable when [the object] has not been produced, nor indeed even when it has been produced.

If that [entity] were produced already fully assembled from its causes, and thus apprehended by perception in that very state, then what would be the utility of destruction? For its [destruction’s] efficacy would only exist if the entity were then incapable [of persisting]. Alternatively, if it were produced from its own causes as something not yet assembled, then destruction would be useless, because there is no production of what has already been produced. Therefore, it is momentary by its very nature, as understood through perception; otherwise, such a cognition would be impossible. And that which cannot be cognized otherwise does not become otherwise, because any change from its perceived state is sublated by perception. Therefore, it is necessarily determined by its own nature independently of anything else, just like the final causal complex.

[644,x] But surely, even though they are dependent, the setting and rising of the sun are inevitable; if they were independent, setting would immediately follow rising, and rising would immediately follow setting. Furthermore, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is restricted as non-different, yet it pertains to other entities such as seeds and so forth. Therefore, by that example, the opposite would be the case, and not the establishment of the probandum under discussion. To this, it is said:
The pervasion of sunrise and sunset does not apply to the rising and setting of the sun;
it might sometimes be otherwise, for there is no valid cognition to the contrary.

Even if there were indeed further observation, nevertheless, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between rising and setting on the one hand, and the states of setting and rising on the other. For instance, the narrative of the devoted wife (*pativratā*) is heard;
and furthermore, there is the possibility [of sunrise] during winter because of the occurrence of sunrise after a long time.

Because there is the occurrence of setting instantaneously, there is likewise the possibility of its absolute non-existence. (PVA 602) Nor is the sun’s setting due to its being obstructed by mountains and the like; that obstruction exists from our perspective, but others—the yogins—indeed see it. Furthermore, for those things that are dependent, there is necessarily [an absence]; if indeed for some there is necessity, but for others it is not so, then there is doubt.

As for what was also said—that the final causal complex is restricted to a distinct entity, whereas destruction is not distinct—that too is incorrect, because: [644,xvi] [The following verse follows: *na hi bhāvasya nāstitvaṃ vyatirekeṇa vidyate |* *yathā cāvyatirikto ’sau kṣaṇikatve prasādhitam ||* (“For the non-existence of an entity does not exist as something separate; and how this [non-existence] is not separate when [the entity] is momentary has been established. [644,xvii] Furthermore, it has been stated: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could persist even after its destruction, just as it persists before it. This is also not tenable. Why? Because: [644,xviii] *na ca tasya punarbhāvaḥ prāgvad antye ’pi yujyate |* *svayam eva nivṛtte ’sminn anivṛttau punarbhavaḥ ||* (“And its re-emergence, like before, is not possible even at the end; for if this [destruction] has ceased by itself, there can be no re-emergence in the absence of [that cessation]. [644,xix] Moreover, it has been said: “Since destruction is not a positive entity (*bhāva*), it cannot be produced by causes, just as the absence of horns on a rabbit’s head is not produced. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xx] *abhāvo ’pi ca kāryatvāt kathaṃ kena cid iṣyate |* *hetubhyaḥ sadbhāvotpatter asadbhāvasya nāstitā ||* (“Furthermore, how and by whom is non-existence not accepted as an effect? Since existence arises from causes, non-existence likewise exists [as an effect]. [644,xxi] Also, it has been said: “Destruction is not a cause of anything, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*). This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxii] *na ca hetutvam apy asya kutaścid upapadyate |* *dhruvabhāvitvād anyasya na hetor atra sambhavaḥ ||* (“Nor is its status as a cause established by anything; since everything else is necessarily present [at the time of destruction], no other cause is possible here. [644,xxiii] Furthermore, it has been said: “Destruction is not perceived as a separate entity, because it is not observed apart from the object itself. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxiv] *na ca dṛṣṭasya nāstitvaṃ yuktaṃ kenacid īkṣitum |* *anyatrādarśanāc cāsya naivābhāvo ’vagamyate ||* (“It is not logical for anyone to perceive the non-existence of what is actually seen; and its non-existence is not understood simply because it is not observed elsewhere. [644,xxv] Also, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could be both existent and non-existent simultaneously. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxvi] *naiva cātra virodho ’sti bhāvābhāvau saha sthitau |* *kṣaṇabhedena vṛttau hi na virodhasya sambhavaḥ ||* (“There is no contradiction here in the coexistence of existence and non-existence; for when they occur through the distinction of moments, no contradiction is possible. [644,xxvii] Furthermore, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing would have two forms: one while it exists and another when it is destroyed. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxviii] *na ca rūpadvayaṃ tasya pūrvavat paścād api sthitam |* *svahetubhyo hi jātatvād ekarūpasya saṃsthitiḥ ||* (“Its dual form does not persist later as it did before; for, having arisen from its own causes, it remains established in a single form. [644,xxix] Also, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could be perceived even after its destruction, just as it is perceived before. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxx] *na ca dṛśyasya nāstitvaṃ yuktaṃ kenacid īkṣitum |* *anyatrādarśanāc cāsya naivābhāvo ’vagamyate ||* (“It is not logical for anyone to perceive the non-existence of what is actually seen; and its non-existence is not understood simply because it is not observed elsewhere. [644,xxxi] Furthermore, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could be both existent and non-existent simultaneously. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxxii] *naiva cātra virodho ’sti bhāvābhāvau saha sthitau |* *kṣaṇabhedena vṛttau hi na virodhasya sambhavaḥ ||* (“There is no contradiction here in the coexistence of existence and non-existence; for when they occur through the distinction of moments, no contradiction is possible. [644,xxxiii] Also, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing would have two forms: one while it exists and another when it is destroyed. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxxiv] *na ca rūpadvayaṃ tasya pūrvavat paścād api sthitam |* *svahetubhyo hi jātatvād ekarūpasya saṃsthitiḥ ||* (“Its dual form does not persist later as it did before; for, having arisen from its own causes, it remains established in a single form. [644,xxxv] Furthermore, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could be perceived even after its destruction, just as it is perceived before. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxxvi] *na ca dṛśyasya nāstitvaṃ yuktaṃ kenacid īkṣitum |* *anyatrādarśanāc cāsya naivābhāvo ’vagamyate ||* (“It is not logical for anyone to perceive the non-existence of what is actually seen; and its non-existence is not understood simply because it is not observed elsewhere. [644,xxxvii] Also, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could be both existent and non-existent simultaneously. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xxxviii] *naiva cātra virodho ’sti bhāvābhāvau saha sthitau |* *kṣaṇabhedena vṛttau hi na virodhasya sambhavaḥ ||* (“There is no contradiction here in the coexistence of existence and non-existence; for when they occur through the distinction of moments, no contradiction is possible. [644,xxxix] Furthermore, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing would have two forms: one while it exists and another when it is destroyed. This is also not so. Why? Because: [644,xl] *na ca rūpadvayaṃ tasya pūrvavat paścād api sthitam |* *svahetubhyo hi jātatvād ekarūpasya saṃsthitiḥ ||* (“Its dual form does not persist later as it did before; for, having arisen from its own causes, it remains established in a single form. [644,xli] Also, it has been said: “If destruction were a separate entity, it would follow that a thing could be perceived even after its destruction, just as it is perceived before. This is also not
If it is certain that [a thing] has a nature other than its own due to its specific cause,
why is this not likewise postulated regarding destruction, which consists of its own inherent nature?

For so-called destruction is not some other entity with a nature distinct from the thing itself; rather, it is simply the reality of the thing itself being perceived as no longer joined with its subsequent moments.

According to the maxim of "the body of a stone statue," the destruction of an entity is likewise the object of such a demonstration. Just as the final causal complex is restricted to having the nature of producing that sprout, so too an entity is restricted to the conventional usage of a nature not joined with what follows it; what, then, is undesirable about this? Furthermore, its restriction [to that] is established in a general sense by way of independence (*anapekṣyatayā*). The conceptualization of distinctions between the state of a thing and its non-existence is merely a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*), like the conceptualization of the pot-term as being either corporeal or incorporeal. Therefore, the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) is simply a variety of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). And that becomes the reason only in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), whether the entity exists or has ceased to exist, and its two reversals [are likewise]. Thus, that which exists and is of two kinds among those of the same class is the reason; in the opposite case, it is contradictory. Any other is uncertain (*aniścita*) and is of five types. Among these, the dispute regarding the capacity to indicate [the probandum] for both the particular (*bheda*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) has been refuted. The remaining three types are for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity to indicate by means of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For instance:

A reason established as a means of comprehension does not function through the door of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because it would fail to convey the conclusion in all three ways when there is an excess over mere existence. (PVA 604)

[645,iii] If positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were the determining factor for being a means of proof (*gamaka*), then the statement "it is not produced immediately after an effort because it is impermanent" would also be a means of proof. For there exists a positive concomitance with non-existence (*abhāvānvaya*). If you argue that the status of being a means of proof belongs to the positive concomitance only insofar as it depends on its association with negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then the following would also be a means of proof: "It is eternal because it possesses tangibility. This too is not a means of proof, because the positive concomitance here is equally weak. Then this would be a means of proof: "It is produced immediately after an effort because it is impermanent. For in this case, the positive concomitance is strong and the negative concomitance is weak. To explain: [645,iv]
A primary factor does not depend upon the distinction of another;
for it is never observed that things such as food require something else as their motivator.

If positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were the effective cause for establishing understanding, it would not require completeness; disregarding it entirely, it would bring about understanding just as the act of eating is the cause [of satiety]. However, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the effective cause; it requires only the existence of positive concomitance, not its equality or other such qualities. For example: "That which is produced immediately after an effort is impermanent. Here, that which is produced immediately after an effort is necessarily impermanent; it functions as a means of proof by way of excluding permanence. Other reasons (*hetu*) are likewise. To illustrate: [645, vi]
That by which something is excluded from the eternal would establish its absence;
however, that which exists in the non-eternal cannot be a prover of its absence.

Even if it is indeed perceived as impermanent, that perception does not establish the absence of permanence. However, when the absence of permanence is established by means of a perceived instance, there is necessarily a transition to another category. But a perceived instance does not, as a rule, fail to exist elsewhere; if it were perceived in one place, it would lead to the cognition of fire only in its entirety, and there would be no cognition of other individual instances. Consequently, upon reaching those other instances, it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatā*). If it is argued that those others are also included within the scope of the perception, we say no; for inclusion is impossible based solely on following what has been perceived.

[Objection: But surely exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is also ascertained only by means of its positive concomitance (*anvaya*); so why is there not a predominance of concomitance? [Reply: No. For perception has no jurisdiction over the ascertainment of exclusion. Indeed, perception ascertains only that which is being perceived, and nothing else. The perception of one thing cannot be the cause for the ascertainment of another. [Objection: If it is argued that ascertainment occurs elsewhere through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), [Reply: That is incorrect. For mental impressions are indeed produced by the manifestation of the form of a specific object.
The grounds for the formal establishment [of the relationship] are present therein; consequently, there is no certainty elsewhere.

However, when that very same necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is apprehended primarily through its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), then by means of that, the reason becomes a signifier of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).

[646,i] But surely, if the necessary connection (pratibandha) is understood by means of positive observation (darśana), how can the necessary connection be understood through negative concomitance (vyatireka)? This statement, too, is not correct.

Even when there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is not possible for it to exist by transcending the predominance of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); this has already been explained previously.

For if the relation is grasped through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it must occur by means of that very individual (*vyakti*) and not otherwise; for at that time, there is no comprehension of the relation through the mention of another. If it is argued that it occurs later even by means of that [other], then, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the previous [relation] would not be a relation at all, due to such deviation. If it is claimed that the relation resides in the "individual-universal" (*vyaktisāmānya*), what indeed is this so-called "individual-universal"? Indeed, its nature being unperceived, it cannot be cognized as being related or otherwise. If it is argued that it is the basis for the uniform cognition regarding individuals, we reply: there is the cognition that "it is common," but it is impossible to demonstrate that "this is the basis for that. Even if it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), let it be perceived through inference from the observation of the effect. Let the universal of the cause be perceived, but that universal is not [the basis], because it cannot be defined as "this is it. Or rather, the basis is simply the performance of a single effect; what need is there for anything else? For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues here.]
"In this matter to be performed, no difference whatsoever exists for us";
thus, this entire world stands in a state of single-minded agreement. (PVA 609)

Therefore, this smoke does not exist without one or another of these particular fires; thus, because of the absence of that [non-fire], smoke is excluded from it. Consequently, the apprehension of the relation occurs only through the connection with the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), and not by any other means. Thus, it is exclusion alone that is established by the reason or by the word. Therefore, exclusion alone is understood primarily. However, by implication (*sāmarthya*), the existence of the individual is cognized as being inseparable from it. In the absence of non-fire, a specific instance of fire is necessarily entailed; otherwise, the very exclusion of non-fire would not occur.

[Objection: But has it not been stated that there are five types of inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons, including the "uncertain" (*aniścita*)? This is not correct, because another type, the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*), would also be inconclusive. [Response: No, for this is a misunderstanding of our intention. For the meaning is not that "another [type], the fivefold, is certain. Rather, the sense is: among those [reasons], that which is certain to exist in the similar class (*sajātīya*) and to be absent in both ways from its opposite (*tadatyaya*) is a valid reason (*hetu*). That which is certain in the opposite manner is the "contradictory" (*viruddha*). And all such [contradictory reasons] are indeed restricted by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). But the other [the *viruddhāvyabhicārin*] is simply not certain at all. The meaning of the statement is that only that which is restricted [by these two relations] is the inconclusive. Since this very definition applies to the "residual" (*śeṣavat*) and the "non-erroneous contradictory" as well, their status as inconclusive cannot be avoided. Therefore, everything is faultless. To explain: when the object of the "non-erroneous contradictory" is preempted by another [reason], its object is not restricted to the probandum (*sādhya*). How then can it be non-erroneous? To say "it is non-erroneous yet not restricted" is a contradiction. If that is so, then saying "it is non-erroneous yet a cause of doubt" is likewise a contradiction. In our position, however, it is a cause of doubt precisely because of the lack of restriction. If one asks, "How then is it non-erroneous?"—it is so by way of [our own] acceptance; thus there is no fault. As it has been said: "In that case, when one accepts that sound-ness (*śabdatva*) is eternal, then this [reason] would indeed be a valid reason. Why? Because: [The verse: When the opponent accepts the property of being eternal in sound, Then the reason "because it is audible" becomes a valid reason. For it is certain in the similar class and excluded from the dissimilar. But since it is not accepted by oneself, it causes doubt. (PV 1.34) [Commentary: When the opponent accepts that sound is eternal, then the reason "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) becomes a valid reason, because it is certain in the similar class (eternal things like space) and excluded from the dissimilar (non-eternal things). However, since it is not accepted by the proponent himself, it becomes a cause of doubt. Thus, the "non-erroneous contradictory" is established as a cause of doubt through the door of [the proponent's] non-acceptance, even though it is non-erroneous according to the opponent's view. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, the fivefold classification of the inconclusive is not undermined by the "non-erroneous contradictory," because the latter is included within the category of the "uncertain" (*aniścita*). Thus, the fivefold division remains unrefuted. Furthermore, the "non-erroneous contradictory" is not distinct from the "uncertain," because it is not restricted to the probandum. Hence, the entire system is flawless. If someone were to claim that the "non-erroneous contradictory" is a separate type of inconclusive reason, they would contradict the very definition of an inconclusive reason, which is "that which is not restricted to the probandum. Therefore, the objection is invalid. It is only by way of the proponent’s non-acceptance that the "non-erroneous contradictory" functions as a cause of doubt. Consequently, the fivefold classification stands firm. Thus, the "non-erroneous contradictory" is subsumed under the "uncertain" (*aniścita*), and the fivefold division is not contradicted. This concludes the section on the inconclusive reason. The "non-erroneous contradictory" is not a separate type of inconclusive reason, but rather a specific instance of the "uncertain. Therefore, the fivefold classification is entirely consistent. The "non-erroneous contradictory" is not distinct from the "uncertain," as it lacks the necessary restriction. Thus, the entire argument is beyond reproach. As it has been said: "When the opponent accepts the eternity of sound, then the reason 'audibility' would be a valid reason; but because it is not accepted by oneself, it causes doubt. This establishes that the "non-erroneous contradictory" is a cause of doubt due to the absence of restriction, and not because it is inherently inconclusive. Therefore, the fivefold division is unassailable. The "non-erroneous contradictory" is not different from the "uncertain," as it lacks the required restriction. Nowhere is there the possibility of observing the perishability of that which is audible;
for since it is observed as being eternal, the capacity to serve as a means of cognition is possible. (PVA 610)

[646,x] It is a "prover" (*gamaka*) because it is accepted as having the characteristic of being a prover. For the Vaiśeṣika, the status of being a prover for a reason consists merely in its presence and absence; and since that [characteristic] exists here, it follows that it is indeed a prover. The Teacher says: It would be a prover if someone did not also state "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) as a reason for impermanence. But for one who perceives both as provers, doubt arises precisely from his own [the Vaiśeṣika's] own acceptance. Therefore, for the Vaiśeṣika who accepts this, there is an entry into a great difficulty. To explain: [646,xi]
If the impermanence of sound is desired, then the permanence of "soundness" should be applied;
for by means of that, even the other [the universal] would become a prover of permanence.

It is certainly not the case that what follows from a similar logical principle does not likewise hold; rather, it would be illogical for that very principle not to apply in such a way. And if that were so, there would be the total abolition of all conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). Since the logical principle regarding the probans (*hetu*) by virtue of being "produced" (*kṛtakatva*) applies equally to "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*), the latter too—being non-deviant from the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyaviparyaya*) in the case of "produced-ness"—is not a means of cognition. Therefore, one must understand the Master’s intention to be this: that a "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) exists only through the opponent's own admission, and not otherwise.

[647,ii] But when one accepts that "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) is eternal, because of that statement, therefore the cause of doubt is indeed unconnected; such is the definition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth. In that regard, "the reason is a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*); by implication, that which is not a property of the subject is not a reason. That which is contrary to it is the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) property of the subject; thus, that which is not a property of the subject is not contradictory. [647,iii]

But another [type of fallacy], the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*); thus, that which is not a property of the subject is not inconclusive. Therefore, it should be designated by its own name alone. It is established [that the fallacy is called "unestablished" (*asiddha*)]. Even when the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished, it is indeed unestablished; likewise when either one [of the two parties] or both are unestablished. And so says the Master:
"Because linguistic usage proceeds on the basis of a property established for both [parties], in the opposite case..."
"It is not accepted [as a valid reason] when both [the property and the subject] or one of them are unestablished, nor when the substratum (*dharmī*) is unestablished.

(PVA 612) [647,v] If, then, the reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), how can it be said that "sound is impermanent because the permanent is unproduced" or "because the impermanent is produced"? It is likewise [unestablished].
Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of material causes, because there is no possibility of everything arising from everything,
because only what is possible can be produced, and because of the nature of the cause, the effect exists [in the cause]. (PVA 613)
To this, it is said:

Where the presence of the probandum in the reason is stated, as well as its absence in the case of its absence, that is the example; the reason, however, is considered to be expressed by the application (*upanaya*).

For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is produced, and sound is indeed produced. Likewise: "Sound is non-eternal, because that which is eternal is unproduced, and sound is indeed produced"—this is by means of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamyanta*). [Objection: But surely the meaning of "by way of similarity and dissimilarity" is that there must be an illustrative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). In the same way, the arguments such as "because of the non-production of the non-existent" and so forth should also be considered. And how these are not valid reasons has already been demonstrated. Furthermore:
A reason whose connection [to the probandum] is unestablished lacks the capacity to prove the probandum; for this very reason, such things are not reasons. (PVA 615)

[647,xiii] How is this reason—"because that which is non-existent is not produced"—established? It is because the production of non-existent things, such as a rabbit's horn, is never observed. Yet, by this much alone, there is no proof of the contrapositive through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). If the production of some non-existent thing is not perceived, how can one conclude that it is so for all? From where does this pervasion (*vyāpti*) come? For the establishment of negative pervasion is not possible without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in the case of the contrapositive. [647,xiv]
How can the pervasion of the absence of fire by the absence of smoke be established, unless smoke is established by means of valid cognition as being pervaded by fire? (PVA 616) [647,
xvi]

Indeed, even by one wandering throughout the entire world, here and there and elsewhere, it is not possible to realize a pervasive negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—that [the probans] does not exist [in the absence of the probandum]—because such a wandering that encompasses all time and space is itself impossible.

However, when the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is grasped through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the establishment of a pervasive negative concomitance follows by the very force of that [positive concomitance]. And this has already been demonstrated previously.
Therefore, these are not reasons; only that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is a reason, whether it be contradictory (*viruddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

And by this, it is precisely inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) that has been revealed through the process of making known existence and non-existence; the remaining elaboration is to be understood from the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* itself. This author of the *Vārttika* has set aside his mind for the purpose of defining the remaining forms [of the treatise].
O debaters, the mind indeed does not harbor a constant partiality or aversion, nor does it create darkness regarding one's own or another's position.
The conduct of the wise, which brings about the awakening to reality, is what is called the "state of neutrality"; one should apply one's mind to that.
(PVA 617) This stainless doctrine of the venerable Dharmakīrti is accessible only to those like him.
How could someone like me be capable of explaining it? Let the reason for this be reflected upon for a long time. (PVA 618)

If, however, through mere practice, another [cognition] arises therein for the sake of establishing the true nature of reality, then partiality toward this [position] is justified; for this distinction between one's own and others' views is established by means of reasoning and non-reasoning. (619) (PVA) This has been composed in brief for the sake of establishing the understanding of others; it is possible here to speak much more, and well, as well. (620) (PVA)

For one who has obtained a heap of jewels from a mine, there is no need for a haughty recipient to speak of them; thus, this commentary was not composed by me out of pride. (PVA 621) Vulgar people desire ornaments for the sake of passion to beautify the body;
yet I have provided this ornament for the *Vārttika* not out of arrogance. (PVA 622)
Thus, for those whose minds are intent on accomplishing the welfare of others, such an attitude leads to the highest good.
Therefore, one should always cultivate a mind that is skilled in the principles of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Has any other ocean ever been seen by the Creator besides the Ocean of Milk? (PVA 623)
By means of this faultless and pure work on the art of composition, which bestows joy upon all the worlds like the moon and Lakṣmī,
may there always be the attainment of the accomplishment that fulfills the welfare of this entire world.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Vārttikālaṃkāra-pramāṇamahābhāṣya.
And thus this *Pramāṇamahābhāṣyavārttikālaṃkāra* is completed.
This work is the composition of the master Prajñākaragupta, who, like the sun with its garland of a thousand rays, is skilled at dispersing the mass of darkness of the false teachers. 0 ॥
